experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In 1995, the Mir space station had been in operation for almost a decade. This presented a unique opportunity to quantify the air pollutants that had accumulated within the spacecraft over a long time period. Russian toxicologists and analytical chemists measured air pollutants periodically inside the Mir using AK-1 (Tenax) sorbent traps. However, their ground-based gas chromatography methods of quantifying pollutants were designed to quantify only a portion of the pollutants suspected to be present in Mir. Interest in the Mir atmosphere was heightened by reports that benzene was present in quantities averaging above 1 mg/m3 during the Mir 10 mission (the U.S. standard for safe levels of atmospheric benzene is 0.2 mg/m3).

The objective of the Toxicological Assessment of Air Contaminants experiment was to assess whether the Mir atmosphere met the U.S. toxicological standards for air quality. This objective was accomplished by obtaining valid samples of the Mir atmosphere during the Mir 17 - 20 missions, analyzing those samples in a ground-based laboratory, and applying toxicological assessment methods for mixtures to the analytical results. In addition to this general assessment of Mir air, spatial variations would be measured from various points within the Mir space station. A well-designed spacecraft should contain few "dead volumes" where air movement is low and pollutants can accumulate. Since the crew's duties require them to work in all Mir modules, it is important to know whether their exposure to pollutants depends on their specific location within the Mir. Temporal variations in the atmosphere were also quantified so that future sampling protocols could be designed to detect important variations in pollutant concentrations. A final objective was to compare three methods of air sampling according to the pollutant concentrations found in samples taken simultaneously during the Mir 19 mission.

APPROACH:
During Mir 17, air samples were collected using the solid sorbent air sampler (SSAS), which consisted of seven samples tubes containing 500 mg of Tenax sorbent each. This sorbent trapped contaminants found in the atmosphere for analysis on Earth. Seven samples were collected on seven different days during the mission with sampling times from 23.0 to 24.3 hours in length per tube. Upon return to the Johnson Space Center (JSC) laboratory, the SSAS tubes were thermally desorbed at 210 degrees Celsius into proofed (verified clean), 4-inch SUMMA-treated canisters. The canisters were filled with clean, humidified air to 14.7 psia. Samples were then analyzed in duplicate using gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) methods to identify and quantify compounds found on board the space station.

During Mir 18, 19 and 20, air samples were collected using the SSAS, grab sample canisters (GSC), Russian AK-1 sorbent system (Mir 19 and 20 only) and formaldehyde badges. Grab sample canisters and formaldehyde badges were added to supplement data during these missions, because the SSAS was not able to quantitatively trap highly volatile contaminants, such as carbon monoxide and formaldehyde.

Instantaneous air samples were taken using the GSCs. Grab samples were collected at the central control post, and periodically during Mir 19 at the core module post N1. Late in the Mir 18 mission, five grab samples were taken in a 30 minute time span from attached modules to assess spatial variations. GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography for highly volatile compounds such as carbon monoxide, hydrogen and methane, and by GC/MS to identify and quantify approximately 80 targeted compounds and an unknown number of non-targeted compounds. The quality of gas chromatography data was assured by the analysis of blanks, generation of calibration curves and data tracking with control charts. Calibration curves up to 440 ppb (parts per billion) were performed on the GC/MS for all target compounds. GC/MS facilitates the identification and quantification of many more contaminants than gas chromatography alone.

Two instantaneous Institute of Biomedical Problems (IBMP) AK-1 system samples were acquired during Mir 19 from the core module, presumably by using a calibrated bellow pump to aspirate 500 ml of air through a tube that had been inserted into the pump inlet. The tube remained sealed before and after sampling.

Time integrated air samples were taken by the solid sorbent air sampler (SSAS) over 24-hour periods by electronic pulsing of a diaphragm pump which drew air through a sorbent tube. One sorbent tube was used per sampling session, and the SSAS device was off most of the flight. Start and stop times were recorded on the instrument by a crewmember. SSAS sample analysis was similar to GSC sample analysis. The air flow through each SSAS tube was measured before and after flight to determine the volume of spacecraft air sampled during the sampling period on orbit. SSAS tubes were also cleaned and proofed before flight. After flight, selected tubes were sent to Johnson Space Center (JSC) where they were heated to 200 degrees Celsius and desorbed into canisters by passing ultra-pure nitrogen at 10.1 ml/min for 20 minutes through the tubes. The canister pressure was measured and the analyses were completed by following the GC/MS method for canisters.

Formaldehyde badges were used to measure the amount of atmospheric formaldehyde. After removing the face covering, the badges were attached to the cosmonaut's uniform with velcro. The badge was worn while the cosmonauts were active for periods of 11.5 to 13.2 hours (by a Mir 18 crewmember on nine days separated by 1 to 2 weeks) and for 11.9 to 13.0 hours (by a Mir 19 crewmember on four days separated by 1 to 2 months). A single T-value above the acceptance level of 1.0 does not suggest poor air quality when all other values were well below 1.0. The sample was paired with one taken 2 minutes earlier and the earlier sample was similar except that it showed significantly less acrolein, furan and carbon monoxide. All three contaminants are known to be associated with pyrolysis of organic materials.

Two anomalies occurred during Mir 19. The three earliest GSCs were returned from Mir via the Soyuz, which landed in Russia. Considerable delay occurred in getting these samples out of Russia and delivered to Houston. The second problem encountered was that the earliest GSC used for sampling in the dining area was lost due to a valve leak, which was discovered during in-processing in the JSC Toxicology Laboratory.

The flows had been reduced to approximately 1/3 their preflight values. Although the samples were paired for the purposes of comparison, even a few minutes difference in sample times could result in some variation in the atmosphere sampled. The most likely possibility seems to be that the seals on the ends of the AK-1 tubes may have leaked, permitting air contaminants from Mir and other locations to concentrate on the sorbent during transport and storage. The Russians have noted this sort of difficulty in the past. Well-controlled, ground-based testing with thoroughly characterized atmospheres is the best way to compare the GSC, SSAS and AK-1 air sampling methods.

In conclusion, data indicates that the Mir air quality meets U.S. standards for spacecraft; however, reference data from the formaldehyde badges indicates that sources of formaldehyde may need to be identified and controlled. The concentrations of most air contaminants were relatively stable during the missions; however, some activities resulted in spikes in pollutant concentrations on this stable background. experiment_title: Human-System Performance Verification
experiment_description:
Human-in-the-loop (HITL) tests play a critical role in the development and certification of space systems. An important aspect of planning a HITL test is determining the appropriate sample size needed for the test. While NASA requirements often specify number of participants required for verification, several recent major spaceflight programs have approached NASA with a request to use fewer subjects to certify their spacecraft, and NASA management has agreed. However, the NASA Human Health and Performance Subject Matter Expert community is concerned about this trend. The proposed study seeks to provide spacecraft verification-relevant data to NASA to better inform decisions about sample size minimums.
This project had the following specific aims: 1. Understand what sample size rules-of-thumb are available in the literature, and how they may or may not apply to spaceflight HITL verifications. 2. Perform knowledge elicitation with relevant internal and external experts on sample size for the verification outcomes selected for the lab study. 3. Identify/develop high-fidelity NASA-representative systems for the study. • Partner with the Rapid Prototyping Laboratory to replicate recently completed Orion display verification tests 4. Investigate how sample size impacts data characteristics for selected verification outcomes, systems, and tasks.

Approach

The investigators performed a systematic study to compare the impact that varying samples sizes have on selected HITL verification outcomes with NASA-representative systems. The research team also worked with a Biostatistician to perform a complementary modeling analysis. This study was composed of five groups with a total of 52. Crew-like participants were recruited from the NASA Test Subject Facility. Additionally, the US Space Force, US Air Force, and US Navy Test Pilot Schools may be used to recruit participants. During the first session demographics were collected, and measures of stress were be taken during pre- and post-test. The investigators consulted with the Behavioral Medicine (BMED) Discipline Scientist for recommendations. Participants completed standard verification outcome measures, like the Bedford Workload scale and the NASA Modified System Usability Scale (NMSUS), at the end of each assignment. The quantity of mistakes, task completion duration, and achievement were also recorded. A modeling analysis was conducted to assess how sample size can affect the probability of a particular result based on the laboratory study data to provide more information regarding the number of participants questioned utilizing an alternative approach.
The projected duration of the project was 12 months.

Results

Results consist of analyzed data that vary in sample sizes (n = 3, n = 5, n = 10, n = 15, n = 32) to see how verification decisions may change. Data was analyzed using boostrap sampling analysis as well as with simulations.

experiment_title: Content and Representation of Information Needed to Support Time-Constrained Problem Solving
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA’s mission-operations paradigm, which originated with Project Mercury in 1958, has relied on near-complete real-time dependence on support of ground teams to manage the combined state of the mission, vehicle, and crew and serve as the safety net for crewed spaceflight. This approach relies on the availability of many engineers and operators with access to large, distributed datasets, computing power, and the deep expertise required to interpret the information in front of them and make decisions. This paradigm, which has changed very little over the past 60 years, will be challenged by increasingly long-duration missions as crewed spaceflight explores beyond low Earth orbit. The greater distances these missions involve will reduce opportunities for resupply, rescue, and evacuation, and will increase the lag time between communications, effectively prohibiting real-time operational and medical support to the crew.
As a result of the increased distance and time delays between communication with the ground, the burden of integrating information, problem-solving, and decision-making increasingly falls on the crew. The purpose of this work was to assess the content and representation of information needed to support time-constrained problem-solving and decision-making during procedure execution and anomaly resolution by the crew under conditions of reduced and/or intermittent communication with the supporting ground team.
The specific aims for this investigation include:
(1) Investigate the construction and manipulation of the mental models of expert problem solvers in time-constrained contexts. These experts will include former ISS MCC flight controllers, flight directors, operations support officers, and MER back-room engineers. Also included, will be those from other safety-critical industries, such as nuclear power plant operators, etc.
(2) Evaluate processes with which expert problem solvers organize and integrate information. Tailor or modify these processes for crew who are more likely generalists rather than the specialists.
(3) Assess integrated data sets and systems and dashboard information approaches that are used to support decision making within spaceflight and other relevant sectors. These examinations will be made within the context of existing research on information used in problem solving.
(4) Classify historical life-cycle spaceflight vehicle systems data (e.g., ISS) into types of problem-solving information (i.e., declarative, procedural, schematic, and strategic). Use this classification as a guide for future vehicle data.
(5) Determine necessary countermeasure development and testing to support time-constrained, crew-reliant problem-solving and decision-making during procedure execution and anomaly resolution.

APPROACH:
During this 12-month study, the investigators produced an annotated literature search to identify common themes and features of problem-solving models used in time-constrained contexts such as those experienced by ground teams supporting flight operations. The investigators combined the results of the literature search with lessons obtained from interviews with expert problem-solvers (e.g., former ISS MCC flight controllers, flight directors, operations support officers, MER back-room engineers, and experts from other, related safety critical industries such as nuclear power plants). This information was leveraged to identify and evaluate the processes expert problem-solvers use to organize and integrate information. The investigators then proposed modifications to these processes that could improve performance of the crew, who are more likely to be generalists instead of specialists in the domains where problem-solving actions are required for the success of the mission.
Human Systems Integrated Architecture (HSIA) was also evaluated during this study. The investigators assessed dashboard information approaches and integrated datasets and systems that are used to support decision-making within spaceflight and other sectors. Further, historical life-cycle spaceflight vehicle systems data (e.g., ISS) were classified into types of problem-solving information categories in order to better inform future vehicle design.

RESULTS:
This investigation sought to address the need for on-board, intelligent systems that will support crew health and performance on long-duration spaceflight missions outside of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and establish the thresholds that would define how these systems should be implemented both in-mission and at landing. The primary deliverable for this study was a literature review. No new data were generated for this study.

experiment_title: Omics and Biochemical Markers of Cardiovascular and Bone Health: Relationship with Bedrest and Standard Physiological Measures
parameter_html:
Sclerostin
Ventricular volume
MicroRNAs (miRNA)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Ade, CarlCo-Investigator: Bembe, Debra
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The long-range goal of this research was to identify and characterize the omics and biochemical mechanisms that underlie the changes in cardiovascular and musculoskeletal function following prolonged space flight. It is well established that microgravity elicits central and peripheral decrements within the cardiovascular system. Traditional cardiovascular measurements have demonstrated significant decreases in left ventricular volume and mass within only a few weeks of exposure. Similarly, human and animal models suggest that microgravity exposure significantly alters vasomotor reactivity to various physiologic stressors. However, despite the recognition that cardiovascular function is decreased with prolonged microgravity exposure, the mechanistic underpinnings of these changes are not completely understood. In addition to changes within the cardiovascular system, significant decreases in bone health occur with prolonged microgravity. These changes are mediated, in part, due to general deconditioning and muscular/mechanical unloading that occurs with microgravity. As such, the average monthly rate of loss in areal bone mineral density can reach 1.0-1.5% when measured over a 14 month period. Given the significant and time-dependent changes in cardiovascular function and bone health associated with microgravity exposure, a continued evaluation of these systems is required, particularly within the genomic and biochemical sciences.

APPROACH:
Eleven participants (five women, six men) completed a 30 day head down bed rest (HDBR) period at the :envihab bed rest facility located at the institute for Aerospace Medicine in Cologne Germany. The bed rest consisted of three phases: (1) baseline control experiments pre bed rest; (2) a 30 day period of -6° head-down tilt bed rest without countermeasures with an ambient CO2 of 0.5% consistent with the average levels on the International Space Station; and (3) post bed rest experiments. Blood sampling for complete blood count and c-miRNA analysis was performed on BDC-3 and immediately upon completion of the bed rest period (R+0). All blood samples were obtained following an overnight fast with no exercise eight hours prior.

RESULTS:
This work found significant alterations in cardiovascular-health related c-miRNAs following 30 days sedentary HDBR. Importantly, several of these c-miRNAs were significantly correlated with changes in stroke volume, cardiac output, and maximal aerobic exercise capacity. The investigators speculate that miRNA may play an epigenetic effect on modulating the cardiovascular responses associated with prolonged microgravity exposure. Future work will need to confirm these results in a larger bed rest cohort and in the true space flight environment. In addition, serum levels of miRNAs associated with bone and muscle function (miRNA-21, -100, -125b, -126) were analyzed using qPCR. Sclerostin and TRAP5b concentrations were assayed using commercial ELISA kits. TRAP 5b (p=0.001) and sclerostin (p=0.05) significantly increased post bed rest. miRNA-21 was significantly upregulated (p = 0.019) from pre to post bed rest. miRNA-125b showed a trend (p = 0.11) for upregulation with 10 participants showing increased expression and 1 showing decreased expression post bed rest.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Neurons and astrocytes form an interconnected network; a syncytium in which an alteration in one cellular component inevitably affects the other. Disturbances in neuron-astrocyte interactions appear to be at the center of several neurological disorders such as cerebral ischemia and neurodegeneration. A significant portion of neuroglial coupling is mediated via glutamate uptake and metabolism, and involves the recycling of substrates between neurons and astrocytes (e.g. glutamate-glutamine shuttle and lactate shuttle). Thus, metabolic and functional cooperativity between astrocytes and neurons is dependent on glutamate. Preliminary data suggested that astrocytes and neurons have reciprocal functional responses to irradiation and very different recovery kinetics.

The objective of this investigation was to better understand the mechanistic changes occurring in the astrocytes-neuron couple following exposure to radiation. It was hypothesized that ionizing radiation disrupts the metabolic coupling between neurons and astrocytes by altering glutamate transport and metabolism. It was proposed to investigate the mechanism for this uncoupling by measuring alterations in glutamate uptake and metabolism, and to determine how abnormal glutamate uptake affects intercellular signaling following irradiation. NTera2/D1 cells, which can be induced to differentiate into mature neurons and astrocytes, would be utilized first. Then findings would be confirmed using primary astrocytes and neurons. These differentiated cell types would be used to investigate the mechanism of neurometabolic uncoupling following acute exposure to 290 MeV carbon and 1 GeV iron ions.

Specific aims of this investigation were to:

  1. Measure glutamate transport and metabolism in human astrocytes and neuronal cultures following acute exposure to 290 MeV carbon and 1GeV iron ions delivered as single fractions of 0, 10, 50 and 200 cGy. Also explore the physical and soluble dependency of homeostatic cooperativity between astrocytes and neurons.
  2. Measure the endogenous and temporal changes in expression of antioxidants and reactive oxygen species in astrocytes and neurons using the same radiation conditions described in aim 1.
  3. Examine alterations in inter-astrocytic and neuronal communication after exposure to ionizing radiation by analyzing essential elements of physical coupling and calcium signaling.
APPROACH:
Both cultured and primary human astrocytes and neurons were exposed to gamma rays and protons as well as 290 MeV carbon and 1 GeV iron ions. Harvest points were at 3 hours, 2 days, and 7 days post irradiation. Proton, carbon, and iron samples were stored frozen. In addition to conducting experiments with the isolated astrocytes and neurons, sets of astrocytes and neurons mixed at a 10 to 1 ratio and allowed to establish for 4 days prior to exposure to radiation were also studied.

The glutamate transport and metabolism response of the astrocytes and neurons was measured. Standard assays were used to determine endogenous and irradiated antioxidant status of cultures of isolated neurons and astrocytes

RESULTS:
Collectively, the glutamate data from the carbon and iron exposures showed similar results as the gamma ray experiments with the astrocytes having decreased glutamate uptake and the neurons having an increase in glutamate uptake. For gamma rays the response of the astrocytes was only significant at 3hrs post exposure, by the 2 day time point the cells returned to normal with respect to their glutamate uptake. The neurons which normally do not take up glutamate show a radiation induced increase that stays elevated throughout the 7 day time point, the last harvest point in these experiments. The results of the sustained glutamate uptake in the neurons showed some dose dependence with higher doses persisting through the 7 day point post irradiation. The difference with respect to high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation was that the duration of the change in the astrocytes persisted longer, with depressed glutamate uptake through the 2 day time point. The neurons response to LET was reduced magnitude of the increased glutamate uptake. In general the magnitude of the signal was inversely proportional to the LET.

The results for glutamate function and apoptosis following gamma rays, protons, carbon, and iron ions were muted with respect to the same measurement taken from the isolated cell types. The oxidant/antioxidant levels measured for gamma rays were also muted in the mixed cultures.

The LET effect on radiation-induced changes in glutamate uptake lead to the possibility that the change may be due to fluence differences which decreases as the LET increases. The other possibility is the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) which also decrease as the LET increases.

The first measurements done in attempt to explain changes in function were to measure the levels of the transporters expressed on the respective cell types. The changes in glutamate uptake were not due to an overt change in the levels of the transporter’ protein levels as western blots and quantitative immunocytochemistry confirmed that the transporters did fluctuate with time but not with dose of radiation. The change in function was also not fully attributed to reactive oxygen species as the levels were mimicked using paraquat to stimulate super oxide levels and only a very slight change in the glutamate uptake was seen. To rule out ROS as a suspect in the radiation-induced changes in glutamate uptake measured in these experiments, significant investigation of oxidant/antioxidant activity following exposure to gamma radiation was undertaken. A complete set of oxidant/antioxidant studies have been conducted following carbon and iron exposure and the samples stored frozen.

experiment_title: Effects of Space Travel on Mammalian Gravity Receptors
experiment_description:
Objectives:
Previous research indicates that vestibular gravity sensors (maculas) are functionally specialized structures. There are two main interacting circuits: type I macular sensory hair cells are part of the highly channeled (or direct) circuit; type II macular hair cells sense, distribute and modify information flowing through the system as part of the distributed modifying (or local) circuit. Based on their participation in local circuits, it was predicted that type II cells would show more synaptic changes in an altered gravitational environment than would type I cells.
Approach:
Synapses were recorded from four sets of 50 serial thin sections from right maculas. Two consecutive series of 50 sections were obtained from the macula of one animal in each group to determine whether results would vary between the two sites. Only those synapses with an electron opaque central ribbon and a halo of vesicles were counted. Photographic mosaics were made of every seventh section for locating and numbering cell profiles accurately, and to ensure that no synapses were counted twice. More than 6,000 synapses in over 1,000 utricular macular hair cells were analyzed.
Results:
Increased numbers of hair cells in R+0 flight animals support the thesis that the local circuit is the more dynamic and would exhibit more change. Spaceflight appears to retune vestibular gravity sensors so that they can function in microgravity. The observed increments in pairs and groups of synaptic ribbons may increase the efficacy of the synaptic site in microgravity, i.e., the addition of synaptic ribbons at a site increases the probability of release of transmitter substance, making the hairs more sensitive. If post flight stress was a factor, it acted selectively on neural elements of the local circuitry, which did not differ at R+ ML. This is in contrast to findings at R + 0, when both receptor hair cell types were affected.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space travel is inherently dangerous for humans due to the large amounts of radiation present beyond Earth's atmosphere. The danger is even greater during times of extreme solar flare activity and during long duration crewed missions such as those proposed for Mars or other planets. High doses of radiation can kill cells and damage tissue, leading to cancer, cataracts, and even injury to the central nervous system.

In an effort to learn more about how to protect crewmembers from the effects of radiation, monitoring devices have flown on several Space Shuttle missions and the Russian space station Mir. These measurements yielded valuable information, but were limited to radiation doses on the external part of the body.

The Bonner Ball Neutron Detector (BBND) measures neutron radiation. Neutrons are uncharged atomic particles that have the ability to penetrate living tissues. Neutrons, especially those with energies exceeding 1MeV, are a major cause of astronaut exposure mainly because of their high radiation quality factor. Neutron radiation can affect the blood-forming marrow in the bones of human beings and other animals. By operating the Bonner Ball in space, neutron radiation information can be collected and used for the development of safety measures to protect crewmembers during long duration space flights.

APPROACH:
The BBND hardware was launched on March 8, 2001 by STS-102 and was placed aboard the US Laboratory Module of the International Space Station (ISS) on March 18, 2001. The BBND continuously collected neutron radiation data from the inside of the ISS for over eight months, from March 23 through November 14, 2001, corresponding to the maximum solar-activity period. Useful data was acquired for 219 days 4 hours and 36 minutes with a temporal resolution of 1 minute. On August 9, 2001, the BBND hardware was relocated from the starboard side to the deck in the US Laboratory. BBND operations performed on-orbit consisted of daily hardware clock checks, weekly status checks with calibrations, and weekly neutron radiation data downlinks. The BBND experiment did not have data collection measurements pre- or postflight.

RESULTS:
During the Increment 2 mission, crewmembers were unable to perform the weekly data downlink of the on-orbit recordings due to unforeseen hardware problems. However, a plan was developed late in the increment to return the first two Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) drives filled with data to Earth. The data was returned to Earth by STS-104 and STS-108, and was forwarded to the investigator for analysis.

The investigator compared the neutron energy spectrum averaged for the entire investigation period to the results of a previous investigation on STS-89 in 1998. The neutron flux obtained during the ISS investigation was consistently lower than that in the previous investigation (shield thickness for the ISS and the STS-89 are not known). Galactic cosmic rays were the major cause of secondary neutrons measured inside the ISS by the BBND, and were inversely correlated with the 11-year solar activity.

The investigator also examined the variation of the dose-equivalent rate observed throughout the investigation period. The average dose-equivalent rate was calculated at 3.9 micro Sievert (Sv)/hour. The highest rate was 96 micro Sv/hour and appeared in the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) region. The characteristics of the distribution of the dose-equivalent rate averaged for the entire investigation period are a result of the geomagnetic rigidity cut off for galactic cosmic rays at the ISS orbital altitude, except in the SAA region where trapped protons caused a high rate.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Impaired musculoskeletal function has been reported in astronauts upon their return to Earth. This effect may not be caused only by muscle atrophy; other factors related to neuromuscular control or contractile force of individual muscle fibers may contribute to the decrease in muscle strength as well. Previous measurements of maximal voluntary muscle strength provided important information on overall muscle function, but did not reflect muscle endurance capacity. The aim of this experiment is to investigate changes in fatigue of muscles over time by testing the quadriceps femoris muscle.

It was hypothesized that isometric, concentric and eccentric quadriceps strengths decrease during maximal effort following 17 days of space flight, which will be reflected in a decrease in maximal electromyographic (EMG) activity. It was also hypothesized that space flight would increase muscle fatigue, which should be noted as a greater increase in EMG activity over time during a sustained submaximal isometric action for a given force.

The specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To study the effects of space flight on musculoskeletal functions by measuring maximal force and power output during voluntary leg press exercise.
2. To determine changes in the cross-sectional area (CSA) of thigh muscles.
3. To determine changes in the muscle activation pattern of the quadriceps femoris.

APPROACH:
An ergometer was specially designed for measurement of muscle activity. The ergometer uses the inertia of a fly-wheel to provide resistance during both shortening (concentric) and lengthening (eccentric) muscle actions. The test protocol incorporated strength measurements of isometric, concentric and eccentric muscle actions, assessing strength and velocity of different types of muscle actions. In addition, EMG activity from the knee extensor group was measured during maximal isometric action. The EMG data will provide information on stimulation of the muscles by the nervous system.

In a collaborative effort with experiment E029, the CSA of the knee extensor muscle group was measured before and after space flight by using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). All measurements were taken before and after the 17-day space flight.

RESULTS:
Lower-limb FWE exercise can produce forces and thus muscular stress comparable to what is typical of advanced resistance training using free weights. FWE also offers greater training stimuli during eccentric relative to concentric muscle actions, as evidenced by force and electromyographic (EMG) measurements. Muscle use of specific muscle groups, as assessed by the exercise-induced contrast shift of magnetic resonance images, is similar during lower-limb FWE and the barbell squat. Unlike free-weight exercise, FWE allows for maximal voluntary effort in each repetition of an exercise bout. Likewise, FWE exercise, not unassisted free-weight exercise, produces eccentric "overload." Collectively, the inherent features of this resistive exercise device and the results of the physiological suggest that resistance exercise using FWE could be used as an effective exercise counter-measure in space. The flywheel principle can be employed to any exercise configuration and designed into a compact device allowing for exercises stressing those muscles and bone structures, which are thought to be most affected by long-duration space flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study was to utilize a systematic approach toward evaluation of current data, identify gaps in knowledge, develop confidence levels, identify risks, and determine acceptable and unacceptable risks. The study used quantitative microbial risk assessment approaches that have been applied to great success in the food and potable water industries. The application of these methods to the latest data sets obtained in space travel allowed the most appropriate data sets to be assessed for health assessment.

APPROACH:
The objective of this study was to develop and apply the quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) framework at the International Space Station (ISS). Specifically, QMRA was used to translate ISS microbial water monitoring data to flight crew health impact in order to direct water monitoring practices and inform health risk reduction strategies. QMRA is a four-step paradigm – including (1) hazard identification; (2) dose-response assessment; (3) exposure assessment; and, (4) risk characterization – that is used to evaluate human health risks resulting from environmental exposure to pathogens. For this project, the framework was reviewed and modified for its applicability to address flight crew health risks associated with exposure to potable water at the ISS. The research plan was divided into four (4) phases. Phase 1 involved the initial evaluation of the QMRA process with the objective of identifying critical areas where QMRA can be effectively applied to the space flight scenario as well as areas where data are needed. Potable water monitoring data for microorganisms were reviewed and potential waterborne pathogens at the ISS were identified and characterized.

Phase 2 specifically addressed the dose-response step of the QMRA process. Using microbial water monitoring data obtained at the ISS, dose-response relationships that represent the flight crew (host) and microorganism (potential pathogen) interaction were developed. This Phase of the project identified Pseudomonas as an appropriate model microorganism to address potable water quality at the ISS. Pseudomonas was chosen as a microbe of interest because of its occurrence in ISS water, the availability of dose-response data derived from human volunteer studies and published in the peer-reviewed literature, and its association with a wide range of human health effects. Pseudomonas offers unique challenges because it is ubiquitous in the environment, is an opportunistic pathogen, is resistant to different types of disinfectants, is capable of forming biofilms, and has the ability to grow in unusual environments. In addition, in some ways Pseudomonas is representative of several members of the heterotrophic plate count (HPC) bacteria, which are routinely detected in ISS potable water. Furthermore, Pseudomonas is transmitted through water through a variety of different exposure routes, which is a necessary consideration when addressing flight crew exposures to water at the ISS.

Phase 3 focused on the exposure assessment aspect of the QMRA. Several pertinent questions related to exposure were initially identified and included: (1) What factors affect the occurrence of pathogenic microbes at ISS?; (2) What factors affect the likelihood of flight crew exposure to waterborne microbes at ISS?; (3) What factors affect the extent of flight crew exposure to waterborne microbes at ISS?; (4) In what ways are flight crew exposed to waterborne microbes at the ISS?; (5) How important are certain exposure factors to flight crew health risks?; and, (6) How do estimated risks associated with ISS potable water compare to health risks in terrestrial water environments? Previous QMRAs involving the terrestrial water environment have shown that it is the exposure assessment step that contributes the greatest source of variability and uncertainty in the QMRA. Typically, exposure-related input parameters are either unknown or they represent a wide-range of plausible values. This Phase identified key aspects of the ISS environment that introduce different challenges related to exposure, which can subsequently impact health risks.

Phase 4 integrated all of the information learned from the first three Phases to complete a risk characterization of flight crew exposure to identified hazards in ISS potable water. The approach was both qualitative and quantitative, with the overall objective to predict flight crew health outcomes from exposure to water at the ISS. Infection risk ranges estimated in Phase 3 for Pseudomonas, Salmonella, and E. coli were evaluated for practical implications.

RESULTS:
Results for this experiment will be available once the investigators have published their findings.

experiment_title: Microfluidic Device-Based Capture and Concentration of Microbial Contaminants in Recycled Water
parameter_html:
Echovirus
Escherichia coli
MS-2 virus

Salmonella species
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pillai, Suresh
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As the duration of space mission’s increase, recycling of metabolic and hygienic wastes becomes a necessity. Thus, the microbiological quality of recycled water is of critical importance to astronaut health and environmental quality during such missions. Accidental or catastrophic failures of the recycling process can introduce opportunistic organisms, pathogens, and organisms that cause biofouling of water distribution lines. It is critically important that water quality monitoring systems are able to capture, concentrate, and detect these contaminants effectively and efficiently. An efficient microbial capture and concentration device is needed for concentrating the sample prior to detection. The overall objective of this project was to design, fabricate, test, and optimize a prototype microfluidic device that can capture and concentrate microbial contaminants based on electrostatic trapping and electrophoretic motion principles. The microfluidic device was designed to concentrate microbial contaminants from 120L/day of recycled water on a continuous basis. The salient feature of the device is that the final concentrated volume will be 1 mL which will facilitate integration with any current or future contaminant detection technologies. In this pilot study proposal, investigators proposed to demonstrate bacterial capture and concentration by the microfluidic device and detection by culture and PCR-based detection and characterization. This interdisciplinary project involving engineering and microbiology delineated the design and performance characteristics of the microfluidic device. In addition to the benefits to NASA, the proposed technology has value in terrestrial and homeland security applications as well.

APPROACH:
Reclaimed and bottled water samples at pH values ranging from 5.2-6.5 were seeded with bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, and Pseudomonas) and viruses (MS-2 and Echovirus). Negative control and capture experiments were performed simultaneously using two identical devices. Culture based methods were utilized to characterize the capture efficiency as a function of the species type, time, flow rate, and applied electric field.

RESULTS:
Funding from the NASA Phase 1 Pilot Study project was used to design and demonstrate the applicability of a microfluidic device-based capture and concentration of microbial contaminants in recycled water. During the initial phases of this project investigators developed a basic understanding of the electrophoretic mobilities of selected bacteria under conditions that were realistic within recycled and drinking water distribution systems. Electrophoretic mobility and zeta potential measurements of bacterial cells in municipal drinking water can lead to enhanced understanding of bacterial surface interactions and adhesion to surfaces in realistic environmental conditions. During the second half of this project a large number of laboratory experiments were performed to design, fabricate, and test the efficacy of a microfluidic-device based microbial capture system. These studies have led to the development of a microfluidic device based on electrophoretic transport and electrostatic trapping of charged particles for continuous capture and concentration of pathogens from water. Reclaimed and bottled water samples at pH values ranging from 5.2–6.5 were seeded with bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas) and viruses (MS-2 and Echovirus) and used in device testing. Both culture based methods and real-time PCR analysis were utilized to characterize the capture efficiency as a function of time, flow-rate, and applied electric field. Based on differences between the capture and negative control data, capture efficiencies of 90% to 99% were achieved for E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas, and MS-2, while the capture efficiency for Echovirus was around 75%. Overall, the device exhibits 16.67 fold sample volume reduction within an hour at 6 mL/hr. This results in a concentration factor of 15 at 90% capture efficiency. Scaling of the device to sample 5 L/hour can be achieved by stacking 835 identical micro-channels. The device can thus function either as a filtration unit or as a sample concentrator to enable the application of real-time detection sensor technologies. The ability to continuously sample water without chemical additives facilitates the use of this device for NASA applications within enclosed environments. The successful completion of this project constitutes the first step in the development of a continuous, microbial capture and concentration system from large volumes of potable water. A key driving force in the device design was to achieve reduced mass, and reduce power and volume requirements.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous studies have shown that long-duration exposure to microgravity causes bone loss. In the absence of gravity, bone mass decreases in the load-bearing regions of the skeleton. This space condition mimics osteoporosis, a medical condition characterized by brittle bones. By learning more about the process of bone mineral loss and recovery, researchers hope to be able to implement effective countermeasures in space, and develop more effective treatments for those who suffer from bone disorders on earth.

In the absence of effective countermeasures, crewmembers will lose significant amounts of bone mineral, manifested as a decrease in bone mineral density assessed by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA). Bone loss will show significant intra and inter-subject variability. Recovery of bone may take several months or more, and may be incomplete in some individuals. The degree and rate of bone recovery will depend in part on the amount of bone lost during flight, as well as on postflight muscular fitness.

Space flight without appropriate or effective countermeasures will also cause significant loss in muscle mass and strength, similar to losses experienced during horizontal 1-g bed rest. These muscle losses will be manifested as degraded performance or as decrements from preflight strength tests. Readaptation to the 1-g environment will result in rapid recovery of muscle mass and strength. Recovery will be complete by 6 months after return from microgravity.

Changes in the metabolism of bone can be assessed indirectly by measuring serum and urinary markers of bone metabolism and bone related hormones. This investigation measured the space flight induced losses in bone mineral density and lean body mass of long-duration crewmembers and will determine the rate and extent of recovery after returning to earth. The objectives of this study were to:

  1. Determine the regional losses in bone mineral density and lean body mass of the crewmembers of each of the four Phase 1B Shuttle-Mir flights
  2. Determine the regional rate and extent of recovery of the bone mineral and lean tissue in the same crewmembers
  3. Determine the muscle strength of the lower extremities and back before and after flight and relate this data to the bone loss during flight and to the degree and rate of bone recovery postflight
  4. Determine the levels of serum and urinary markers of bone metabolism before and after flight.

APPROACH:
To measure bone density, DEXA scans were obtained pre- and postflight using a Hologic QDR 2000 whole body densitometer (United States) or QDR 1000W densitometer (Russia). Bone mineral density data were obtained from scans of the whole body, lumbar spine, proximal femur (hip) and calcaneus (heel). Whole body and regional measurements of lean tissue mass (LTM) were obtained from the whole body scans.

Strength testing was performed pre- and postflight using a LIDO isokinetic dynamometer. Peak torque was measured for muscle groups in the legs and back. Testing time points were the same as for DEXA scans.

Urine markers included total calcium, pyridinium cross-links, n-telopeptide, hydroxyproline, and creatinine. Serum markers included total and ionized calcium, pH, calcitonin, PTH, osteocalcin, total and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D. Testing time points were 30 and 7 days before launch, the day of landing, and 7, 14 and 180 days after landing.

PRELIMINARY RESULTS:
Preliminary DEXA findings on the seven crewmembers whose data have been analyzed to date (including six astronauts and one cosmonaut) indicate that the regional bone changes are similar to those documented in the 18 cosmonauts studied previously, both in terms of degree and in terms of "between-subject" and "within-subject" heterogeneity. Muscle strength results will be correlated with the bone density results during the 3-year recovery period. Recovery DEXA data are too limited to report at this time; these results and corresponding muscle strength changes will be reported at a later date. There are no preliminary bone marker findings at this time.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Roma, PeterCo-Investigator: Hursh, Steven
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overarching goal of this study was to generate experimentally-derived insights on how crew composition and trait-like cooperative motivation predict task cohesion, social cohesion, and biopsychosocial adaptation in long-term work groups through systematic ground-based research and development of a simple, rapid, and objective behavioral assay of implicit propensity toward cooperation, productivity, and fairness.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Investigate effects of group composition on voluntary cooperation.
  2. Investigate effects of crew composition on performance, task cohesion, social cohesion, and psychosocial adaptation in long-term work groups.
  3. Develop next-generation Task Performance Task (TPT) software.
  4. Extended long-term research of group cohesion, team performance, and biopsychosocial adaptation to several space analog environments; the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility, NASA's Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) laboratory, and the investigator's laboratory using Planetary Exploration Simulation (PES).

APPROACH:
Investigators conducted ground-based experiments to systematically investigate the effects of group composition (gender and personality) on voluntary cooperative propensity in three-person teams. They also assessed the predictive validity of pre-mission TPT "social personality profiles" and the effects of group composition on performance, task cohesion, social cohesion, and biopsychosocial adaptation in mixed-gender "crews" participating in a long-term simulated space exploration task. In addition, investigators also developed next-generation software to advance the technology beyond their current prototype used for proof-of-concept/validation research into a broadly applicable tool with cross-platform networking and connectivity, enhanced usability/human factors features, extensive parameter manipulation/flexibility to maximize sensitivity, and integrated data collection and processing capabilities.

RESULTS:
Results indicate that the TPT/COHESION objective social behavioral assay approach is sensitive to team composition factors and temporal dynamics in both laboratory and field settings. Laboratory experiments reveal a potential risk of decreased cooperation and reduced cooperative resilience in majority female teams and teams with whose members are all high in conscientiousness. The TPT/COHESION tool quantifies "individual differences" in social behavioral processes over time at both the person and team levels, which correlate with subjective ratings of team cohesion. A single pre-mission TPT/COHESION session can predict several objective in-mission team performance outcomes.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Shuttle astronauts receive medical evaluations 10 and 3 days before launch, on the day of landing, and 3 days after landing. These medical evaluations are performed for three purposes: 1) identification of occult disease before flight, 2) surveillance of health impacts, and 3) collection of normative data on biomedical parameters for use in flight operations. A wide variety of lab analytes (blood and urine chemistry, hematology, immunology, and endocrinology) are assayed during each evaluation.

APPROACH:
Laboratory data collected three days before launch and on landing day were analyzed with regard to statistical significance and clinical relevance of the differences. The paired t-test was used to compare differences between preflight and postflight mean values. The results were presented at the 1997 Aerospace Medicine Annual Meeting.

The severity of space motion sickness had been reported to decrease with successive flights. First flight experiences influence behavior and use of countermeasures such as in-flight exercise, fluid loading, and G-suit use. Because of the possible influence of previous flight experience on response to subsequent flight, only first time flight experience was analyzed.

RESULTS:
Nearly all lab parameters showed predictable changes following shuttle flights. More than half of the approximately 90 analytes were statistically significant at the 0.05 percent level. These data demonstrate the importance of examining data for clinical relevance when a statistically significant result is reported. Although the t-tests were statistically significant at the 0.05 percent level, all lab parameters remained within normal ranges. For example, the normal range for serum glucose is 78 to 110 mg/dl. The group mean glucose value at L-3 (3 days before launch) was 92 mg/dl. The group mean glucose value at R+0 (landing day) was 101. Both of these group mean values are well within normal ranges. The difference between the group means is 8.7 mg/dl, that is, the R+0 group mean is 8.7 units greater than the L-3 mean value. Although this difference is significant at the 0.05 percent level (exact P value = 0.0001 percent), it is not clinically important. There is no health impact from this small temporary increase in serum glucose.

There are many factors that may influence postflight lab parameters. In-flight factors include space motion sickness, fluid shifts, neurovestibular and cardiovascular changes associated with weightlessness, diet, medications usage, in-flight illness or injury, fatigue, circadian dissynchrony, exposure to environmental toxins, and mission duration. Factors encountered during reentry include exposure to G-forces following prolonged weightlessness, heat stress caused by the suits worn, and fluid loading. Postflight factors include varying time lag between landing and collection, crew activities scheduled in the postflight period, and consumption of fluids and food after landing, but before sample collection.

Many of the differences between preflight and postflight lab parameters can be explained by physiologic stress, hemoconcentration, and relative hypovolemia, which are experienced in the short-term by space participants. An important confounding factor is that the preflight serum samples were collected following a 12 to 14 hour fast. Postflight serum samples were collected after a meal (breakfast) and fluid loading and possibly food intake between landing and blood draw.

In conclusion, the differences between preflight and postflight measurements can be attributed to any of the factors described above. However, the differences appear to be too small to be clinically significant. Future analyses will examine the recovery curve between R+0 and R+3 because crew members typically return to duty and return to flight status after R+3.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Meck, JaniceCo-Investigator: Charles, John
experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Hypovolemia may be one cause of the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a decrease in body fluid. These effects are also produced by head-down tilt bed rest. Fludrocortisone (Florinef) is a drug that increases plasma volume by causing the kidneys to retain sodium. It has shown some ability to restore plasma volume and orthostatic tolerance after bed rest. However, the absorption of a drug may be altered in microgravity, and a dosage regimen that is effective on the ground may not be effective in space. The objective of this study was to test the use of fludrocortisone during space flight to expand plasma volume and improve postflight orthostatic tolerance, comparing three dosage regimens.

APPROACH:
There were 25 male astronauts who were randomized into 2 groups: placebo (n = 18) and fludrocortisone (n = 7), and participated in stand tests 10 days before launch and 2-4 hours after landing. Three regimens of fludrocortisone were used: (1) 0.2 mg twice daily (B.I.D.) for the last 5 days of flight,(2) 0.1 mg twice a day for the last 5 days of flight, or (3) a single dose of 0.3 mg taken 7 hours before landing. Supine blood volume, supine and standing heart rate and arterial pressure, as well as plasma catecholamines were measured before and after flight.

RESULTS:
Only limited conclusions could be made because participation in the protocols was incomplete, and were also limited by subjective evaluation of the medication. The first two protocols (five-day regimens) were not well-tolerated by the crew, being found to cause unacceptable side effects such as congestion, head fullness, and headache. The third regimen (single-dose) did not restore plasma volume and did not seem to improve orthostatic tolerance on landing day.

None of the protocols restored blood volume. The percent change in plasma and red blood cell volumes from preflight to postflight was not significantly different in the fludrocortisone vs. non-fludrocortisone group. Fludrocortisone subjects did not have greater orthostatic tolerance than control subjects on landing day.

On landing day, 2 of 18 in the placebo group and 1 of 7 in the fludrocortisone group became presyncopal (chi2 = 0.015, p = 0.90). Plasma volumes were significantly decreased after flight in the placebo group, but not in the fludrocortisone group. During postflight stand tests, standing plasma norepinephrine was significantly less in the fludrocortisone group compared with the placebo group.

The conclusion therefore, was that treatment with a single dose of fludrocortisone results in protection of plasma volume but no protection of orthostatic tolerance. Fludrocortisone was, therefore, not recommended as a countermeasure for spaceflight-induced orthostatic intolerance.

experiment_title: High Capacity Thermally Regenerated Supported Amines for CO2 Capture
parameter_html:
Ethyleneamine E-100
Tetraethylenepentamine (TEPAN)
Triethylenetetramine (TETA)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Helble, Joseph
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Zeolite sorbents are presently used for CO2 removal on long-term human-occupied space missions. These sorbents are regenerable, but the regeneration process is energy intensive. The focus of this project is therefore to investigate novel supported amine sorbents that can be regenerated at much lower temperatures and with lower energy than presently required by zeolites. These sorbents will be prepared by immobilizing amines on polymeric supports, chemically modifying the amines to maximize CO2 capture capacity, and demonstrating the efficacy of a temperature swing process as the regeneration step. The temperature swing process has the potential to provide a major reduction in the energy required for sorbent regeneration, an important benefit in space environments. Supported amines also have the potential to reduce the energy costs associated with the pumped liquid systems envisioned for terrestrial flue gas CO2 removal If successful, this project is ultimately expected to lead to the development of commercial systems for high capacity reduced cost CO2 removal, suitable for both enclosed habitats and terrestrial applications. Develop low cost CO2 sorbents that require reduced energy consumption for thermal regeneration.

The focus of this project is to investigate novel supported amine sorbents that can be regenerated at much lower temperatures and with lower energy than presently required by zeolites. The proposed use of a temperature swing regeneration process has the potential to provide a major reduction in the energy required for sorbent regeneration, an important benefit in space environments. Supported amines also have the potential to reduce the energy costs associated with the pumped liquid systems envisioned for terrestrial flue gas CO2 removal If successful, this project is thus expected to lead to the development of commercial systems for high capacity reduced cost CO2 removal, suitable for both enclosed habitats and terrestrial applications.

APPROACH:
An experimental system was designed and constructed for testing the supported amines for CO2 cyclic capacity under temperature swing conditions. In a temperature swing system, the bed is heated to a specific desorption temperature and pressure is reduced by exposure to vacuum conditions to desorb the CO2. The system used in this study consisted of two absorbing beds filled as a packed bed reactor with supported amine material. The beds absorbed and desorbed CO2 cyclically and sequentially. Usually 15-20 cycles were completed before the beds desorbed as much as they absorbed and reached a steady state of operation. Steady state efficiency was calculated for varying conditions of the system and statistically analyzed for the importance of variables considered.

Three amines were tested for cyclic CO2 capacity under TSA as part of this project: triethylenetetramine (TETA), tetraethylenepentamine (TEPAN), and ethyleneamine (E-100). TEPAN and E-100 have been modified by reaction with acrylonitrile to form secondary amines from primary amines. These three liquid amines were chosen for their low vapor pressure and high secondary amine content. A low vapor pressure minimizes amine losses at high temperatures and low system pressures experienced in the TSA process. The high amine content is a requirement because amines reversibly react with CO2 and are responsible for the capture of CO2 in the TSA system. The high amine content allows more CO2 to be captured per mass of amine.

RESULTS:
TETA was found to have too high a vapor pressure at the required desorption conditions and amine losses were substantial. TEPAN and E-100, on the other hand, had such low vapor pressures that amine losses were undetected. A fractional factorial statistical experiment was conducted on the TEPAN and E-100 amines in order to determine the importance of seven variables to the system. These included cycle time (15-20 min), CO2 inlet concentration (6-9mmHg), absorption temperature (25-30 degrees C), residence time of the gas through the bed (1.7-3sec), inlet dew point (0-25 degrees C), desorption temperature (50-60 degree C) and desorption pressure (26-93mmHg). Important variables to the TEPAN molecule were found to be the inlet concentration of CO2 (12% importance), the absorption temperature (6%), desorption temperature (19%), and desorption pressure (61%). For the E-100 molecule, only desorption pressure was important to the system.

A full factorial experiment expanded on the relationship between desorption temperature and pressure for the E-100 molecule in an extended range. Desorption temperature was varied between 40, 50, and 60 degree C and desorption pressure was expanded to include 26, 51, and 93mmHg. Over this range, desorption temperature was the most significant to the results, contributing 61% of the importance to the system while desorption pressure contributed 33%.

Three new amines were also considered as possible alternatives to TEPAN and E-100. These included N,N’-bis(2-hydroxyethyl)-ethylenediamine (BED), an acrylonitrile modified 1-(2-aminoethyl)piperazine (AEP), and cyclam. The same experimental setup described above was used to examine total CO2 capacity and compare these to the original TEPAN supported amine. The results indicate that there was no change in total capacity with the addition of BED or cyclam. With AEP, there was a decrease of less than half capacity of the original material. No cyclic testing was conducted on any of the three amines.

PMMA, TEPAN and modified E-100 were tested at temperatures of 100-200 degree C for thermal stability in a gas chromatograph / mass spectrometer (GC/MS). Decomposition of PMMA begins at 150 degrees C and increases in extent at 200 degrees C. Acrylonitrile begins to appear at 150 degree C. The loss of acrylonitrile may hinder the capture ability of CO2 if the beads are left at these temperatures for extended periods. At 200 degrees C, the decomposition of the amines becomes excessive. Because the proposed operation temperature is 60 degrees C, however, thermal decomposition of PMMA, TEPAN, or modified E-100 should not be a concern.

In summary, supported amines utilized under temperature swing conditions have been demonstrated to be a viable alternative to the current zeolite sorbent system of CO2 capture.
