OBJECTIVES:
Zeolite sorbents are presently used for CO2 removal on long-term human-occupied space missions. These sorbents are regenerable, but the regeneration process is energy intensive. The focus of this project is therefore to investigate novel supported amine sorbents that can be regenerated at much lower temperatures and with lower energy than presently required by zeolites. These sorbents will be prepared by immobilizing amines on polymeric supports, chemically modifying the amines to maximize CO2 capture capacity, and demonstrating the efficacy of a temperature swing process as the regeneration step. The temperature swing process has the potential to provide a major reduction in the energy required for sorbent regeneration, an important benefit in space environments. Supported amines also have the potential to reduce the energy costs associated with the pumped liquid systems envisioned for terrestrial flue gas CO2 removal If successful, this project is ultimately expected to lead to the development of commercial systems for high capacity reduced cost CO2 removal, suitable for both enclosed habitats and terrestrial applications. Develop low cost CO2 sorbents that require reduced energy consumption for thermal regeneration.

The focus of this project is to investigate novel supported amine sorbents that can be regenerated at much lower temperatures and with lower energy than presently required by zeolites. The proposed use of a temperature swing regeneration process has the potential to provide a major reduction in the energy required for sorbent regeneration, an important benefit in space environments. Supported amines also have the potential to reduce the energy costs associated with the pumped liquid systems envisioned for terrestrial flue gas CO2 removal If successful, this project is thus expected to lead to the development of commercial systems for high capacity reduced cost CO2 removal, suitable for both enclosed habitats and terrestrial applications.

APPROACH:
An experimental system was designed and constructed for testing the supported amines for CO2 cyclic capacity under temperature swing conditions. In a temperature swing system, the bed is heated to a specific desorption temperature and pressure is reduced by exposure to vacuum conditions to desorb the CO2. The system used in this study consisted of two absorbing beds filled as a packed bed reactor with supported amine material. The beds absorbed and desorbed CO2 cyclically and sequentially. Usually 15-20 cycles were completed before the beds desorbed as much as they absorbed and reached a steady state of operation. Steady state efficiency was calculated for varying conditions of the system and statistically analyzed for the importance of variables considered.

Three amines were tested for cyclic CO2 capacity under TSA as part of this project: triethylenetetramine (TETA), tetraethylenepentamine (TEPAN), and ethyleneamine (E-100). TEPAN and E-100 have been modified by reaction with acrylonitrile to form secondary amines from primary amines. These three liquid amines were chosen for their low vapor pressure and high secondary amine content. A low vapor pressure minimizes amine losses at high temperatures and low system pressures experienced in the TSA process. The high amine content is a requirement because amines reversibly react with CO2 and are responsible for the capture of CO2 in the TSA system. The high amine content allows more CO2 to be captured per mass of amine.

RESULTS:
TETA was found to have too high a vapor pressure at the required desorption conditions and amine losses were substantial. TEPAN and E-100, on the other hand, had such low vapor pressures that amine losses were undetected. A fractional factorial statistical experiment was conducted on the TEPAN and E-100 amines in order to determine the importance of seven variables to the system. These included cycle time (15-20 min), CO2 inlet concentration (6-9mmHg), absorption temperature (25-30 degrees C), residence time of the gas through the bed (1.7-3sec), inlet dew point (0-25 degrees C), desorption temperature (50-60 degree C) and desorption pressure (26-93mmHg). Important variables to the TEPAN molecule were found to be the inlet concentration of CO2 (12% importance), the absorption temperature (6%), desorption temperature (19%), and desorption pressure (61%). For the E-100 molecule, only desorption pressure was important to the system.

A full factorial experiment expanded on the relationship between desorption temperature and pressure for the E-100 molecule in an extended range. Desorption temperature was varied between 40, 50, and 60 degree C and desorption pressure was expanded to include 26, 51, and 93mmHg. Over this range, desorption temperature was the most significant to the results, contributing 61% of the importance to the system while desorption pressure contributed 33%.

Three new amines were also considered as possible alternatives to TEPAN and E-100. These included N,N’-bis(2-hydroxyethyl)-ethylenediamine (BED), an acrylonitrile modified 1-(2-aminoethyl)piperazine (AEP), and cyclam. The same experimental setup described above was used to examine total CO2 capacity and compare these to the original TEPAN supported amine. The results indicate that there was no change in total capacity with the addition of BED or cyclam. With AEP, there was a decrease of less than half capacity of the original material. No cyclic testing was conducted on any of the three amines.

PMMA, TEPAN and modified E-100 were tested at temperatures of 100-200 degree C for thermal stability in a gas chromatograph / mass spectrometer (GC/MS). Decomposition of PMMA begins at 150 degrees C and increases in extent at 200 degrees C. Acrylonitrile begins to appear at 150 degree C. The loss of acrylonitrile may hinder the capture ability of CO2 if the beads are left at these temperatures for extended periods. At 200 degrees C, the decomposition of the amines becomes excessive. Because the proposed operation temperature is 60 degrees C, however, thermal decomposition of PMMA, TEPAN, or modified E-100 should not be a concern.

In summary, supported amines utilized under temperature swing conditions have been demonstrated to be a viable alternative to the current zeolite sorbent system of CO2 capture. Supported amines offer comparatively low desorption temperatures and energy requirements, high capacity for CO2, and high tolerance of humidity. In addition, this study has shown that increasing the thermal energy can significantly reduce the vacuum pump requirements of the desorption step. Lastly, the amines have been shown to be thermally stable at the 60 degrees C system condition.

experiment_title: Acoustic Noise During the Phase III Chamber Test
parameter_html:
Sound intensity, decibels
Sound intensity, decibels perceived
Sound intensity, frequencies perceived
investigators: Principal Investigator: Foley, TicoCo-Investigator: Feeback, Daniel
image_name: Sound Level Meter and Frequency Analyzer
Sound Measurements Taken in the Chamber
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP), four test subjects participated in the 91-day experiment. As part of the acoustic study, they measured sound decibels in different life support areas of the test chamber. The LMLSTP enclosed test chamber was divided into three levels. The first level contained general living quarters with a dining/work table, communications, test and video equipment. The first level also contained a kitchen, bathroom and laundry facilities. The second level contained the mechanical equipment for air revitalization, storage and stationary bicycle. This level was the noisiest, and due to the location of the stairs, the subjects had to pass through this level while traveling between the first and third levels. The third level contained primary living quarters with bedrooms, partial bath and entertainment equipment. This level was the quietest. The goal of the acoustic noise study was to monitor and describe the noise environment of the 20-foot chamber during its extended 91-day operation. Noise levels were measured at multiple locations and subjects performed hearing threshold tests called audiograms at various frequencies before and after the chamber experience. The hearing threshold is the softest sound a person is able to hear. It is not clear what level of hearing threshold shift is cause for concern, but it is certain that larger changes in threshold are more serious. Monitoring acoustic noise in the chamber enabled recommendations to be formulated for hearing protection, if necessary. These measurements also established a baseline measure of the noise environment for comparison with other Earth-bound analog test facilities.

In acoustic studies, noise is defined as undesirable sounds in the air in the hearing range of approximately 20 to 20,000 Hz. A certain level of noise can be tolerated over an eight-hour workday without long-term hearing detriment, but this same noise level may not be acceptable if it is continuous over a 24-hour period, such as in the closed environment of a space vehicle. During periods of loud noise, the blood vessels in the ear involuntarily constrict and reduce blood flow to protect the hair cells responsible for hearing. Outer hair cells respond to low intensity sound and become continuously stimulated or "saturated", by loud noise. The inner hair cells remain functional because they respond only to high intensity sounds. A temporary hearing threshold shift may thus occur due to chronic noise. An upward shift of hearing threshold can become permanent, since the outer hair cells that respond to low intensity sound would not have a chance to recover their normal function and would eventually die. Government regulations developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) set the maximum background noise level that an individual may be exposed to during an eight-hour day at 90 dB. Exposure to levels over 85 dB requires routine monitoring for hearing loss and the institution of hearing conservation programs. The EPA suggests that an eight-hour average noise level over 75 dB presents a reasonable risk for hearing loss.

APPROACH:
LMLSTP test subjects collected sound level measurements in various locations throughout the chamber module starting with entry day ceremonies, continuing regularly during the 91-day operation and ending with the welcome home celebrations. In total, 283 sample measurements of acoustic noise were collected from the chamber during the experiment.

Noise levels were measured using an audio dosimeter and a more accurate sound level meter to obtain an A-weighted overall sound pressure level measurement at each location. The A-weighting represents the ear sensitivity by combining all frequencies together and averaging them to give a decibel value. Sample measurement locations were determined using two methods. In one method, each subject was asked to subjectively identify the noise sources and noisier locations in the chamber. Following discussion, the subjects jointly decided upon 25 locations to measure noise, including quiet locations that served as controls. The other method of determining measurement locations was the use of predetermined, geographically-spaced areas on each chamber level. Four different heights above the floor were monitored based on locations where a hypothetical fiftieth-percentile person's ear would be located during various activities. Measurements were taken at 10 cm above the surface of the floor to represent a person lying down, at 75 cm above the floor to represent a person sitting on the floor, at 120 cm above the floor to monitor a person sitting in a chair, and at 150 cm above the floor to represent a person standing. The locations were spaced at 30-degree increments about 60 cm from the wall, space permitting, and at the center axis of each level. Locations where the subjects were likely to spend more time were also chosen, such as a computer workstation, bed, stove, table, exercise machine, etc. A measurement was taken within 60 to 100 cm of the middle of any large area not already measured by other methods. Since this was a screening procedure, most data were rounded off to the nearest unit.

Noise loudness is measured using sound level meters. Total noise exposure over a period of time is measured with a noise dosimeter. To determine how acoustic noise levels varied throughout a typical 24-hour day for each subject, an Ametek Audio Dosimeter (Model MK-3) was used in the dosimeter mode. An average was determined each minute as loudness equivalent (Leq 1 min) of a 24-hr period. This method produced 1440 samples each day. Data was downloaded to a desktop computer and graphed as noise level versus time, creating a histogram for each selected noise level interval.

Each test subject wore the dosimeter over two 24-hour periods. Additionally, one subject wore the dosimeter for approximately one hour before, and one hour after, entering the chamber on the first day and an hour before and after exiting the chamber on the last day. On each of three other days, the dosimeter was placed in a central location in a bedroom, left among equipment on the second level, and attached to the ceiling in the middle of the first level. The exact days that the subjects wore the dosimeter, and the exact days and locations that the dosimeter was placed in a room were up to the subjects' discretion.

Investigators wanted to know whether or not the noise levels inside the chamber would affect the threshold hearing levels of the subjects over the course of the 91-day stay in chamber. Hearing tests, called pure-tone air conduction audiometry, were conducted under standard conditions at the health clinic at NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in a sound-insulated booth. A microprocessor-controlled audiometer presented pure tone stimuli to the subject and recorded his or her responses. The subject wore a headset through which the sounds were transmitted to each ear. When the subject heard a sound, he or she pushed a button, and the monitoring computer recorded the response. The computer presented sounds at predetermined frequencies and at incremental amplitudes, getting softer until there was no subject response, and then louder until there was a response, to double-check the person's threshold. Each ear was tested independently starting with frequencies of 1000 cycles per second (Hz). This first measurement at 1000 Hz was a training run. Then, the test was conducted at frequencies of 500 Hz, 1000 Hz, 2000 Hz, 3000 Hz, 4000 Hz, 6000 Hz and 8000 Hz for a total of seven data collection sessions and 42 audiogram measurements per subject.

In an audiometry test, the hearing level is quantified based on what the normal ear detects, and a score of zero indicates normal hearing. Scores above zero indicate hearing loss. A 100 dB hearing loss at any frequency is nearly equivalent to complete deafness at that particular frequency tested. The four chamber test subjects were each given three audiograms. The first, conducted at the time of medical examination for eligibility, established a baseline measure. The second audiogram was performed within two hours after the subject left the chamber to determine whether there was any shift in hearing threshold after 91 days in the chamber. The third audiogram occurred between six and fourteen weeks after chamber egress to determine whether the hearing threshold had returned to baseline. It was expected that there would be a hearing threshold shift on egress day, but that no permanent shift would occur.

RESULTS:
On the first chamber level, the acoustic noise from 105 measurements averaged 63.2 dB(A). The noisiest general area was the airlock, which averaged 63.7 dB(A), and where major noise contributors included exercise machines and ventilation fans. The only measurements that equaled or exceeded 70 dB(A) were from intermittent noise sources. The television was the loudest measured equipment noise source (average 75.2 dB(A)).

The second level was much noisier, and the subjects reportedly avoided the area. The average noise level over 94 measurements was 74.6 dB(A). Only two of the samples were measured at less than 70 dB(A). Twelve measurements were in excess of 80 dB(A).

On the third level, which was quieter than the others, noise levels were similar to those in a typical single-family residence. The average noise level over 84 measurements was 51.5 dB(A). Measurements in the immediate proximity of the beds averaged 42.4 dB(A). The noisiest area on the third level was in the hallway, averaging 59.8 dB(A), especially near the ladder that led to the noisier second level.

Data from the dosimeter attached to a subject for a 24-hour period was consistent with that obtained by the sound level meter. It was possible to discern where the subject was in the chamber by analyzing the readings from the dosimeter. The first level's background noise was measured in the mid-60 dB(A) range, with an occasional spike attributed to human voices during conversation. Periods of time where noise measured above 70 dB(A) represented transitions through, or short visits to, the louder second level. Rest or quiet work on the third level could be assumed from the periods of time that measured 60 dB(A). When the subjects exited the chamber at egress, the dosimeters measured above 90 dB(A) during the first 10 minutes and above 80 dB(A) for most of the first hour.

Audiogram measurements of the subjects on the pre-test ranged from 0 to 50 dB. A measure of 0 indicates that the threshold of hearing is the same as that for an average person without hearing loss, while larger numbers indicate hearing loss. Shifts of 5 dB or less are not considered problematic because they are within the range of expected test errors. On egress-day, audiogram measurements were 0 to 50 dB. Post-test measurements were 0 to 45 dB. For two subjects, all measurements were at or below 20 db; for another subject, all were at or below 25 dB. The final subject gave readings at or below 10 dB in one ear, while the other ear measured hearing loss in the 45 to 50 dB range for all three-test administrations. Audiometry data graphs indicate no clear distinction among pre-test, egress day and post-test audiometry measurements.

A modified sign test was performed on the data as an indication of the overall tendency of the measured hearing threshold. Arithmetic differences between the egress day and pre-test measures were obtained for each data pair. There was no significant difference between the two measurements for hearing loss or improvement. However, a similar comparison showed that the hearing threshold measured at the post-test was better than either the pre-test or egress day tests. Yet, of the 56 comparisons among the pre-test, egress day and post-test, there were five for which the egress day measurements suggested hearing threshold loss that did not return to pre-test baseline level.

Some interesting factors may explain the audiogram results. Upon egress, cheering crowds generated more noise than that found in the living areas of the chamber. This can be observed from the dosimeter readings. The loud celebration noise may have confounded the results of the egress day measures that were taken within two hours after egress. Another confounding factor may have been the subjects' environment during the pre-test baseline measures. During this timeframe, the subjects were involved in the development, assembly and testing of the mechanical equipment for the chamber. All pre-test hearing measurements were taken during the afternoon, after at least a half-day of work in a noisy environment. The subjects were also involved in the operation and maintenance of this equipment during the 91 days of the chamber test. About a week after egress day, the subjects took vacations, and the equipment was turned off. So the post-test measures were obtained after the subjects had been in a different noise environment, and under different stress conditions that were not monitored.

After the first data were analyzed and reported to the subjects in the chamber, steps were taken to reduce the noise. Noise insulation barriers were constructed and redundant equipment was turned off. Schedules were changed so that the noisiest equipment was not operated when the subjects were in that area. The results of this study will be used to provide motivation to reduce the noise levels of the air and water revitalization equipment. A continuing benefit for habitation study crews is an increased understanding and awareness of the noise levels in a closed environment.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity-Induced Weightlessness on Aurelia Ephyra Differentiation and Statolith Synthesis
experiment_description:
Objectives:
Aurelia polyps and ephyrae were exposed to microgravity for nine days as part of the SLS-1 mission. This experiment was to study the effects of microgravity on: the development of ephyrae from polyps; the development of the graviceptors (rhopalia) of ephyrae; the formation or demineralization of statoliths of rhopalia; and the swimming/pulsing behavior of ephyrae.
Approach:
Polyps were induced to strobilate at 28°C, using iodine or thyroxine, at forty-eight (L-48h) and twenty-four (L-24h) hours before launch, and eight hours after lift-off (L+8h). Some ephyrae that formed in space were fixed in space on mission day eight, while others were fixed postflight. Postflight, light, and electron scanning microscope examinations were performed.
Results:
The number of ephyrae formed per polyp were slightly higher in the L+8h groups as compared to those induced at L-24h and L-48h. On Earth, iodine is used by jellyfish to synthesize jellyfish-thyroxine (Jf-T4), which is necessary for ephyra production. Since iodine-treated polyps gave rise to ephyrae in space it appears that jellyfish are able to synthesize Jf-T4 in space. The two groups of polyps not given the inducer still formed ephyrae in space presumably due to enhanced Jf-T4 synthesis, utilization, or accumulation. Morphologically, ephyrae which developed in space were very similar to those that developed on Earth. Quantitation of arm numbers revealed that there were no significant differences between space and Earth-developed ephyrae. Pulsing abnormalities, however, were found in greater numbers (18.3%) than in Earth-developed controls (2.9%). These abnormalities suggest abnormal development of the graviceptors, the neuromuscular system, or a defect in the integration between systems in these microgravity-sensitive animals.

__description:
Objectives:
Aurelia polyps and ephyrae were exposed to microgravity for nine days as part of the SLS-1 mission. This experiment was to study the effects of microgravity on: the development of ephyrae from polyps; the development of the graviceptors (rhopalia) of ephyrae; the formation or demineralization of statoliths of rhopalia; and the swimming/pulsing behavior of ephyrae.
Approach:
Polyps were induced to strobilate at 28°C, using iodine or thyroxine, at forty-eight (L-48h) and twenty-four (L-24h) hours before launch, and eight hours after lift-off (L+8h). Some ephyrae that formed in space were fixed in space on mission day eight, while others were fixed postflight. Postflight, light, and electron scanning microscope examinations were performed.
Results:
The number of ephyrae formed per polyp were slightly higher in the L+8h groups as compared to those induced at L-24h and L-48h. On Earth, iodine is used by jellyfish to synthesize jellyfish-thyroxine (Jf-T4), which is necessary for ephyra production. Since iodine-treated polyps gave rise to ephyrae in space it appears that jellyfish are able to synthesize Jf-T4 in space. The two groups of polyps not given the inducer still formed ephyrae in space presumably due to enhanced Jf-T4 synthesis, utilization, or accumulation. Morphologically, ephyrae which developed in space were very similar to those that developed on Earth. Quantitation of arm numbers revealed that there were no significant differences between space and Earth-developed ephyrae. Pulsing abnormalities, however, were found in greater numbers (18.3%) than in Earth-developed controls (2.9%). These abnormalities suggest abnormal development of the graviceptors, the neuromuscular system, or a defect in the integration between systems in these microgravity-sensitive animals.

experiment_title: Electron Microscopy, Light Microscopy, and Protease Activity of Rat Hindlimb Muscles
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This spaceflight study examined the degree of atrophy for muscles used primarily to oppose gravity with those not weightbearing and investigated the cellular and chemical basis for atrophy. Another objective was to characterize the degeneration of neuromuscular junctions. Understanding how structural and chemical changes in muscle are induced by the stress of launch, low-gravity, re-entry, and readaptation to Earth's gravity will help define how several factors contribute to muscle weakening, and effective counter measures can be developed to overcome atrophy during spaceflight.
APPROACH:
A total of 1490 muscles were analyzed by light and electron microscopy for evidence of shrinkage or death of muscle cells, break down of muscle fibers, or degeneration of motor nerves. The chemical basis for atrophy was investigated by immunostaining for ubiquitin proteins that catalyze the breakdown of proteins. Cross sectional areas of muscle fiber types in the slow and mixed (fast and slow) fiber regions of the adductor longus and the central portion of soleus were measured by computer-assisted digitizing morphometry of fibers in myofibrillar ATPase reacted sections.
RESULTS:
Space flight induced significant atrophy (fiber shrinkage) and increased expression of fast muscle characteristics (fast myosin) in the slow fibers. The slowly adapting myosin change most likely occurred inflight. Adductor longus muscles showed increased susceptibility to pathological damage upon resumption of weight bearing activity at 1G. Postflight damage included thrombosis of the microcirculation, interstitial and cellular edema, muscle fiber fragmentation, sarcomere disruptions, activation of phagocytic cells, and elevated ubiquitin conjugation suggestive of increased protein breakdown. Accelerated aging-like involution of neuromuscular junctions was significantly more prominent in rats housed in flight cages inflight and during DFPT, indicating caging-induced effects. The soleus also atrophied but showed less pathology than the adductor longus which appeared related to greater resumption of loaded contractile activity postflight by the adductor longus.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Lang, ThomasCo-Investigator: Keyak, JoyceCo-Investigator: LeBlanc, AdrianCo-Investigator: Majumdar, Sharmila
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Three-dimensional quantitative computed tomography (CT) was used to assess the biomechanics of the proximal femur where significant differences in the patterns of cortical and trabecular bone loss have been found in a group of astronauts. This research will provide insight into the physiological response of proximal femoral bone tissue to space flight and may result in a more sensitive method for tracking the efficacy of countermeasures aimed at preserving skeletal strength.

The overall objective of the task was to determine the extent to which hip strength is lost during space flight and whether it is recovered as the skeleton readapts to Earth gravity. The most important aspect of this task is the use of finite element analysis to analyze bone strength with respect to loads exerted by the hip in falls. The second objective was to combine the finite element analysis of the hip with inter-subject registration techniques so that it will be possible to visualize the overall response of the proximal femur at the organ level to changes in loading. The idea is to use the technique to identify regions of the hip that may be at highest risk for failure due to abnormal loading in falls or during excursion activities. The third objective was to develop an approach for assessing muscles that are of key importance for protecting hip bone strength. If these muscles are identified, then it would be possible to reduce the time burden and injury risk associated with exercise programs by finding activities that are more efficient for protecting bone strength.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study is embedded in the Results section below.

RESULTS:
Finite element analyses
The investigators installed finite element software developed by Dr Joyce Keyak in the laboratory at UCSF. The software, which creates biomechanical models of the hip from CT scans to estimate the whole bone strength of the proximal femur in loading conditions simulating normal ambulation and a fall to the side, has been applied to pre-flight, postflight, and a subset of one year scans from the astronauts of increment 2-8. Finite element modeling of pre- and postflight scans and one year are complete for 16 subjects, and 5 one-year scans are available for data reduction as they are computing FEM-specific corrections for a scanner change that took place during the study.

After obtaining institutional review board approval and informed consent, pre- and post-flight CT scans were obtained of the hips of astronauts who participated in long-duration International Space Station (ISS) missions. Mission length ranged from 4.3 to 6.5 months. Demographic data cannot be provided due to HIPAA regulations. A four-sample calcium hydroxyapatite (CHA) calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) was placed under the subjects’ hips during scanning and used to calibrate the CT scan data in terms of CHA concentration.

From the CT scan data, a finite element (FE) model of each subject’s left proximal femur was generated using methods described previously. These models employed patient-specific geometries and material properties. Ash density (rho ash, g/cm3) of each element was computed from the calibrated CT scan data (rho QCT, g/cm3), rho ash=0.0633 + 0.887 rho QCT. Mechanical properties were calculated from as densities. These properties were calibrated to result in accurate predictions of FFE.4 The models were analyzed under loading simulating single-limb stance2, and impact from a fall onto the greater trochanter. For stance loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 20 degrees to the shaft axis, within the coronal plane. For fall loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 60 degrees to the shaft axis and 25 degrres to the coronal plane, as the opposing surface of the greater trochanter was restrained in the opposite direction. FE-computed hip strength (FFE) in each loading condition was determined. A paired t-test was used to evaluate differences between pre- and post-flight values of FFE.

RESULTS: For stance loading, the average proximal femoral strength decreased significantly (p<0.001) from 13,200 N (SD=2300 N) pre-flight to 11,200 N (SD=2400 N) post-flight . The average rate of loss of hip strength for stance loading was 2.6 percent/mo (SD=1.4 percent). For fall loading, average hip strength decreased significantly (p=0.003) from 2,580 N (SD=560 N) pre-flight to 2,280 N (SD=590 N) post-flight . The average rate of strength loss for fall loading was 1.9 percent/mo (SD=1.4 percent). The preliminary one year FEM data show that for 4/5 subjects, strength is recovered in the stance loading condition, but for 4/5 subjects strength is not recovered in the fall loading condition.

DISCUSSION: This study has shown that astronauts exposed to microgravity for 4.3 to 6.5 months lose hip strength at an average rate of 2.6 percent/mo under single-limb stance loading and 1.9 percent/mo under fall loading. Previous DXA measurements of astronauts returning from the ISS indicated that aBMD decreased by 1.4 percent/mo in the neck and 1.5 percent/mo in the total femur.1 Thus, estimates of bone strength loss that are based on DXA aBMD alone will understate the reduction in hip strength. The recovery data available thus far seem to be consistent with the investigators finding in their 2006 bone recovery paper that shows that the recovery of bone mass and areal density is nearly complete at one year, but that volumetric bone density, particularly the density of trabecular bone does not recover. This seems to be driven by periosteal expansion, which increases bone volume and mass, while the recovery of volumetric bone density lags. The larger bone may be optimized for the loads incurred in normal usage but may still be at risk for fracture in pathologic conditions such as falls. Thus, recovery of bone mass may not be sufficient to gauge the recovery of bone after space flight.

Intersubject registration
The investigators obtained the Montreal Neurological Institute Animal intersubject image registration program, installed it in their laboratory, and have applied it to successfully co-register CT scans of the hip from 16 subjects with pre- and postflight image data. They have carried out voxel by voxel statistical comparisons of those models for the pre- and postflight time points, and have demonstrated a focal pattern of accelerated bone loss in the compressive trabecular band in the femoral head region.

Quantitation of muscle cross-sectional area and attenuation coefficient from Hip CT scans
Acquisition of volumetric CT scans of the hip: Analysis of proximal femoral musculature was carried out using volumetric CT scans optimized to analyze the density and structure of the proximal femur. In these studies, the patient lied supine on the imaging table, and an anteroposterior scoutview was acquired which spans the iliac crest to the mid-thigh. The operator then defined a helical scan volume between the superior limit of the left femoral head and an inferior limit 3-5 mm inferior to the lesser trochanter. The muscle analyses was carried out on images obtained with 120/80 kVp, 150 mAs, 3 mm or 1-mm section thickness (pitch=1), 48 cm field of view, reconstructed with a soft tissue filter. Images in all studies were obtained with a QCT calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) positioned below the patient’s hips.

Analysis of images for muscle cross-sectional area and mean attenuation coefficient: Based on previous studies of gait, balance and muscle function, the investigators have selected four groups of muscles to quantify which are well-visualized within the field of view of the proximal femur QCT scan: these include the hip extensors (gluteus maximus), hip abductors (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and piriformis), hip adductors (adductor magnus, adductor brevis, adductor longus, quadratus femoris, quadratus externus, pectineus) and hip flexors (rectus femoris and sartorius). These groups are easily distinguishable on almost all of the cross-sections in the field of view in CT scans of the proximal femur. Because the cross-sectional areas of these muscle groups vary differently as a function of slice location within the QCT scans, they developed a method to select individual cross-sections on which to quantify the areas and mean attenuation coefficients of these muscle groups. This involved two steps. First investigators examined annotated optical and CT images in the Visible Human data set to determine the locations in the CT scan field of view where the muscle groups are of maximal size and are optimally distinguished from the surrounding tissue, and second they developed a protocol for employing boney landmarks to calculate the locations of these cross-sections relative to the hip anatomy, so that the muscle measurements could be compared between individuals and reproduced within an individual over time. To select the slice location, a mid-coronal reformation of the image is employed to display the proximal femoral anatomy. The user marks the slice position of the superior aspect of the femoral head and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter to generate a metric by which the individual muscle cross-sections can be reliably located. SH is the slice position corresponding to the superior aspect of the left femoral head. D is the distance between SH and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter, which defines the inferior limit of the proximal femoral analysis. The cross-sections are chosen as the slice numbers corresponding to the nearest integer to the calculations. Thus three cross-sections are selected for display, one for the extensors, one for the abductors, and a third cross-section containing the adductors and flexors. Each slice is then displayed in an image window, and the user draws the boundary around the fasceal plane of the corresponding muscle group. Once the drawings have been completed, the program processes each cross-section according to the following steps:
1) The program finds the water equivalent cell of the calibration phantom. Based on the mean and standard deviation of the HU in the water equivalent cell, the program calculates HU intervals to be used for calculations of muscle and fat areas within defined tissue boundaries.
2) The program generates the outer body contour by performing a region growing operation, searching for the skin-air boundary on each section from a user-placed seed point inside one of the muscle groups. Following that, the program performs a region growing, starting from the same seed point, finding the cortical bone/muscle boundary. The region within the bone boundary is then excluded from subsequent soft tissue calculations.
3) The program then starts at the body contour, and grows inward, searching for the fat/muscle boundary. This provides mask of lean tissue.

Findings:
Astronaut study: Investigators have applied this methodology to pre- and post-flight scans of their astronaut data, including 16 subjects with pre- and postflight QCT scans. Comparison of pre- and post-flight scans showed 1-5 percent losses in total lean area and in the areas of the flexor, abductor, adductor and extensor muscle groups, with only a 5 percent loss in the adductor area being statistically significant (p=0.02) Small losses may reflect effect of inflight and postflight exercise protocols and the acquisition of CT data over 2-4 weeks post-return, allowing for some recovery of muscle area.

Hip fracture study: To test the hypothesis that hip muscle size and attenuation are associated with hip fracture, investigators compared CT scans of the contralateral hip in 45 women (mean age 74.71±5.94) imaged within 48 hours of their hip fractures to 66 age-matched control subjects (mean age 70.70±4.66). A volumetric CT scan encompassing the proximal part of the femur was analyzed for total percentage of fat tissue in the in the CT field of view and for the CSA and lean tissue Hounsfield Unit (HU) values of the hip extensor, abductor, adductor and flexor muscles. The CT scan was also analyzed to compute areal bone mineral density (aBMD) of the hip bone. Logistic regression analyses were employed to determine differences between fracture subjects and controls in body composition measures after adjustment for age, height, and BMI. Receiver-operator curve (ROC) analyses were employed to determine if combinations of aBMD and body composition were better discriminators of hip fracture than aBMD alone.

Investigators found that subjects with hip fractures were on average 5 years older (p<0.001) had 8 percent lower BMI (p<0.05), 8 percent lower percentage fat (p<0.0001) and roughly 20 percent lower extensor and adductor CSA values than controls (p<0.0001). Despite having lower total adiposity, they had higher muscle adiposity as indicated by lower lean tissue attenuation in all four muscle groups, with statistically significant differences in the adductor, abductor and flexor groups. After adjustment for age and BMI, the fracture subjects had lower total percent fat, smaller extensor and adductor CSA values, and greater adipose infiltration (lower attenuation) in the adductor (0.001 (less than) p (less than) 0.05). ROC analyses showed that models combining percent fat, muscle CSA and muscle attenuation values with aBMD had higher AUC values than models containing only aBMD (0.97 vs 0.88, p<0.001). The investigators conclude that reduced total adiposity and increased hip muscle adiposity appear to be independent correlates of hip fracture, and combination of skeletal and body composition variables appears to enhance diagnostic efficacy compared to skeletal variables alone.

The most important aspect of this task is the use of finite element analysis to analyze bone strength with respect to loads exerted by the hip in falls. The second objective was to combine the finite element analysis of the hip with inter-subject registration techniques so that it will be possible to visualize the overall response of the proximal femur at the organ level to changes in loading. The idea is to use the technique to identify regions of the hip that may be at highest risk for failure due to abnormal loading in falls or during excursion activities. The third objective was to develop an approach for assessing muscles that are of key importance for protecting hip bone strength. If these muscles are identified, then it would be possible to reduce the time burden and injury risk associated with exercise programs by finding activities that are more efficient for protecting bone strength.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study is embedded in the Results section below.

RESULTS:
Finite element analyses
The investigators installed finite element software developed by Dr Joyce Keyak in the laboratory at UCSF. The software, which creates biomechanical models of the hip from CT scans to estimate the whole bone strength of the proximal femur in loading conditions simulating normal ambulation and a fall to the side, has been applied to pre-flight, postflight, and a subset of one year scans from the astronauts of increment 2-8. Finite element modeling of pre- and postflight scans and one year are complete for 16 subjects, and 5 one-year scans are available for data reduction as they are computing FEM-specific corrections for a scanner change that took place during the study.

After obtaining institutional review board approval and informed consent, pre- and post-flight CT scans were obtained of the hips of astronauts who participated in long-duration International Space Station (ISS) missions. Mission length ranged from 4.3 to 6.5 months. Demographic data cannot be provided due to HIPAA regulations. A four-sample calcium hydroxyapatite (CHA) calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) was placed under the subjects’ hips during scanning and used to calibrate the CT scan data in terms of CHA concentration.

From the CT scan data, a finite element (FE) model of each subject’s left proximal femur was generated using methods described previously. These models employed patient-specific geometries and material properties. Ash density (rho ash, g/cm3) of each element was computed from the calibrated CT scan data (rho QCT, g/cm3), rho ash=0.0633 + 0.887 rho QCT. Mechanical properties were calculated from as densities. These properties were calibrated to result in accurate predictions of FFE.4 The models were analyzed under loading simulating single-limb stance2, and impact from a fall onto the greater trochanter. For stance loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 20 degrees to the shaft axis, within the coronal plane. For fall loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 60 degrees to the shaft axis and 25 degrres to the coronal plane, as the opposing surface of the greater trochanter was restrained in the opposite direction. FE-computed hip strength (FFE) in each loading condition was determined. A paired t-test was used to evaluate differences between pre- and post-flight values of FFE.

RESULTS: For stance loading, the average proximal femoral strength decreased significantly (p<0.001) from 13,200 N (SD=2300 N) pre-flight to 11,200 N (SD=2400 N) post-flight . The average rate of loss of hip strength for stance loading was 2.6 percent/mo (SD=1.4 percent). For fall loading, average hip strength decreased significantly (p=0.003) from 2,580 N (SD=560 N) pre-flight to 2,280 N (SD=590 N) post-flight . The average rate of strength loss for fall loading was 1.9 percent/mo (SD=1.4 percent). The preliminary one year FEM data show that for 4/5 subjects, strength is recovered in the stance loading condition, but for 4/5 subjects strength is not recovered in the fall loading condition.

DISCUSSION: This study has shown that astronauts exposed to microgravity for 4.3 to 6.5 months lose hip strength at an average rate of 2.6 percent/mo under single-limb stance loading and 1.9 percent/mo under fall loading. Previous DXA measurements of astronauts returning from the ISS indicated that aBMD decreased by 1.4 percent/mo in the neck and 1.5 percent/mo in the total femur.1 Thus, estimates of bone strength loss that are based on DXA aBMD alone will understate the reduction in hip strength. The recovery data available thus far seem to be consistent with the investigators finding in their 2006 bone recovery paper that shows that the recovery of bone mass and areal density is nearly complete at one year, but that volumetric bone density, particularly the density of trabecular bone does not recover. This seems to be driven by periosteal expansion, which increases bone volume and mass, while the recovery of volumetric bone density lags. The larger bone may be optimized for the loads incurred in normal usage but may still be at risk for fracture in pathologic conditions such as falls. Thus, recovery of bone mass may not be sufficient to gauge the recovery of bone after space flight.

Intersubject registration
The investigators obtained the Montreal Neurological Institute Animal intersubject image registration program, installed it in their laboratory, and have applied it to successfully co-register CT scans of the hip from 16 subjects with pre- and postflight image data. They have carried out voxel by voxel statistical comparisons of those models for the pre- and postflight time points, and have demonstrated a focal pattern of accelerated bone loss in the compressive trabecular band in the femoral head region.

Quantitation of muscle cross-sectional area and attenuation coefficient from Hip CT scans
Acquisition of volumetric CT scans of the hip: Analysis of proximal femoral musculature was carried out using volumetric CT scans optimized to analyze the density and structure of the proximal femur. In these studies, the patient lied supine on the imaging table, and an anteroposterior scoutview was acquired which spans the iliac crest to the mid-thigh. The operator then defined a helical scan volume between the superior limit of the left femoral head and an inferior limit 3-5 mm inferior to the lesser trochanter. The muscle analyses was carried out on images obtained with 120/80 kVp, 150 mAs, 3 mm or 1-mm section thickness (pitch=1), 48 cm field of view, reconstructed with a soft tissue filter. Images in all studies were obtained with a QCT calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) positioned below the patient’s hips.

Analysis of images for muscle cross-sectional area and mean attenuation coefficient: Based on previous studies of gait, balance and muscle function, the investigators have selected four groups of muscles to quantify which are well-visualized within the field of view of the proximal femur QCT scan: these include the hip extensors (gluteus maximus), hip abductors (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and piriformis), hip adductors (adductor magnus, adductor brevis, adductor longus, quadratus femoris, quadratus externus, pectineus) and hip flexors (rectus femoris and sartorius). These groups are easily distinguishable on almost all of the cross-sections in the field of view in CT scans of the proximal femur. Because the cross-sectional areas of these muscle groups vary differently as a function of slice location within the QCT scans, they developed a method to select individual cross-sections on which to quantify the areas and mean attenuation coefficients of these muscle groups. This involved two steps. First investigators examined annotated optical and CT images in the Visible Human data set to determine the locations in the CT scan field of view where the muscle groups are of maximal size and are optimally distinguished from the surrounding tissue, and second they developed a protocol for employing boney landmarks to calculate the locations of these cross-sections relative to the hip anatomy, so that the muscle measurements could be compared between individuals and reproduced within an individual over time. To select the slice location, a mid-coronal reformation of the image is employed to display the proximal femoral anatomy. The user marks the slice position of the superior aspect of the femoral head and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter to generate a metric by which the individual muscle cross-sections can be reliably located. SH is the slice position corresponding to the superior aspect of the left femoral head. D is the distance between SH and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter, which defines the inferior limit of the proximal femoral analysis. The cross-sections are chosen as the slice numbers corresponding to the nearest integer to the calculations. Thus three cross-sections are selected for display, one for the extensors, one for the abductors, and a third cross-section containing the adductors and flexors. Each slice is then displayed in an image window, and the user draws the boundary around the fasceal plane of the corresponding muscle group. Once the drawings have been completed, the program processes each cross-section according to the following steps:
1) The program finds the water equivalent cell of the calibration phantom. Based on the mean and standard deviation of the HU in the water equivalent cell, the program calculates HU intervals to be used for calculations of muscle and fat areas within defined tissue boundaries.
2) The program generates the outer body contour by performing a region growing operation, searching for the skin-air boundary on each section from a user-placed seed point inside one of the muscle groups. Following that, the program performs a region growing, starting from the same seed point, finding the cortical bone/muscle boundary. The region within the bone boundary is then excluded from subsequent soft tissue calculations.
3) The program then starts at the body contour, and grows inward, searching for the fat/muscle boundary. This provides mask of lean tissue.

Findings:
Astronaut study: Investigators have applied this methodology to pre- and post-flight scans of their astronaut data, including 16 subjects with pre- and postflight QCT scans. Comparison of pre- and post-flight scans showed 1-5 percent losses in total lean area and in the areas of the flexor, abductor, adductor and extensor muscle groups, with only a 5 percent loss in the adductor area being statistically significant (p=0.02) Small losses may reflect effect of inflight and postflight exercise protocols and the acquisition of CT data over 2-4 weeks post-return, allowing for some recovery of muscle area.

Hip fracture study: To test the hypothesis that hip muscle size and attenuation are associated with hip fracture, investigators compared CT scans of the contralateral hip in 45 women (mean age 74.71±5.94) imaged within 48 hours of their hip fractures to 66 age-matched control subjects (mean age 70.70±4.66). A volumetric CT scan encompassing the proximal part of the femur was analyzed for total percentage of fat tissue in the in the CT field of view and for the CSA and lean tissue Hounsfield Unit (HU) values of the hip extensor, abductor, adductor and flexor muscles. The CT scan was also analyzed to compute areal bone mineral density (aBMD) of the hip bone. Logistic regression analyses were employed to determine differences between fracture subjects and controls in body composition measures after adjustment for age, height, and BMI. Receiver-operator curve (ROC) analyses were employed to determine if combinations of aBMD and body composition were better discriminators of hip fracture than aBMD alone.

Investigators found that subjects with hip fractures were on average 5 years older (p<0.001) had 8 percent lower BMI (p<0.05), 8 percent lower percentage fat (p<0.0001) and roughly 20 percent lower extensor and adductor CSA values than controls (p<0.0001). Despite having lower total adiposity, they had higher muscle adiposity as indicated by lower lean tissue attenuation in all four muscle groups, with statistically significant differences in the adductor, abductor and flexor groups. After adjustment for age and BMI, the fracture subjects had lower total percent fat, smaller extensor and adductor CSA values, and greater adipose infiltration (lower attenuation) in the adductor (0.001 (less than) p (less than) 0.05). ROC analyses showed that models combining percent fat, muscle CSA and muscle attenuation values with aBMD had higher AUC values than models containing only aBMD (0.97 vs 0.88, p<0.001). The investigators conclude that reduced total adiposity and increased hip muscle adiposity appear to be independent correlates of hip fracture, and combination of skeletal and body composition variables appears to enhance diagnostic efficacy compared to skeletal variables alone.

experiment_title: Packaged Food Mass Reduction Technology Development
parameter_html:
Beverage shelf life
Food, shelf life
investigators: Principal Investigator: Leong, MonicaCo-Investigator: Cooper, Maya
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Advanced Food Technology (AFT) project seeks to define a safe, palatable, and nutritious food system to support long-duration space missions beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO). Balancing resources such as water, food preparation time, stowage volume, launch mass, and power requirements is central to defining a functioning food system solution for these missions. Prior AFT work has addressed the need to decrease the mass of the food system, and has recommended means such as reducing the moisture of the food system, increasing the nutrient density of the food system, and streamlining food packaging systems to accomplish this. Building on these recommendations, the objective of this project was to identify technologies required to formulate meal replacement options that would decrease the mass and volume of the food system, as well as decrease the crew time associated with meal preparation. As commercially available meal replacement products are not adequate for NASA needs, this project proceeded by formulating new products that meet the unique requirements of spaceflight beyond LEO. The development of meal replacement options for the packaged space food system were achieved by:
1. Aligning previous studies on nutrition and mass savings to compile the nutritional requirements and consumption guidelines for meal replacement beverages and bars.
2. Developing meal replacement bar(s) meeting nutrition, sensory, and shelf life requirements for space food systems.
3. Developing meal replacement beverage(s) meeting nutrition, sensory, and shelf life requirements for space food systems.
4. Assessing the meal replacement system and creating an implementation plan for the meal replacement options.

APPROACH:
Some accommodations have been made in the product development design to ensure that the project is completed within budget and on schedule. The recipe development of the bars and beverages were baselined from existing commercial bars and beverages rather than starting from new formulas even though significant changes are likely required to meet nutritional needs. Researchers leveraged flavor concepts from existing commercial bar and beverage products. Accelerated shelf life testing was done to assess stability as the project duration is shorter than the desired shelf life. While the ideal sensory evaluation would be a repeated exposure test to ensure acceptability levels were sustained over multiple experiences, the product amounts and the availability of panelists required a one-time sensory evaluation for each product. Upon the completion of this study, an assessment of representative formulated meal replacement options will be provided to stakeholders, in order to offer an understanding of meal replacement technology and associated mass savings.

RESULTS:
The task work began by meal replacement bar and beverage prototypes being developed to meet macronutrient requirements for breakfast and lunch meals, based on current consumption guidelines. Additional food categories were identified as having low nutrient density and commercial food products and new formulations were proposed as replacements. Accelerated shelf life testing was conducted for all products to determine acceptability and general stability. Bars were confirmed to have a 48 to 72 week shelf life while beverages and most category replacements remained stable for 96 weeks. A variety of menus implementing these substitutions in the ISS Standard Menu were proposed and estimated mass savings ranged from 11%-25%, and packaging savings of 16% - 18% when one meal was replaced each day.

experiment_title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Psychological Stress Measures
parameter_html:
Positive affect negative affect scale (PANAS), negative score
Positive affect negative affect scale (PANAS), positive score
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pierson, Duane
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prolonged exposure to reduced gravity, physiological stress or other factors associated with space flight may result in immune system dysregulation. Latent herpesvirus reactivation, a measurable result of dysregulated immunity, has been detected in crewmembers during and immediately following space missions.

In the investigator's previous studies of astronauts, investigators found altered peripheral leukocyte distribution, altered cytokine production profiles, elevated levels of latent viral reactivation and elevated levels of cortisol during or immediately following long and short duration space flight. In addition, significant increases in stress hormones (i.e., cortisol, catecholamines) were found after landing. Notably, investigators found increased shedding of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV), two medically important herpesviruses, during space flight along with evidence of decreased cellular immunity. These increases in stress hormones directly correlated with CMV and EBV reactivation. Thus, latent herpesvirus reactivation in these astronauts may have resulted from both direct (i.e., stress hormones) and indirect (i.e., decreased immune function) mechanisms stemming from launch and landing acceleration. These results underscore the need to determine the causes underlying immune suppression in space in order to develop countermeasures.

APPROACH:
A panel of assays was designed to monitor immune system dysregulation, viral reactivation, and physiological stress has been developed and validated at the Johnson Space Center (JSC). These assays will be applied to a future ISS/Shuttle Supplemental Medical Objective (SMO). This assay panel is also appropriate to monitor the status and function of the immune system, viral reactivation, and physiological stress during ground-based analog studies. These assays were included on all several bed rest campaigns for the purpose of monitoring the immune status of the participants. While bed rest is not the most appropriate model for space flight-associated immune dysregulation, it is possible that the various countermeasures proposed for evaluation during bed rest may affect immune function. For this reason, the immune function of the participants was monitored. Along with physiological stress, psychological stress will also be monitored for the bed rest studies.

The measurement of psychological stress was done using two standard questionnaires, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS). Each subject was asked to complete both questionnaires prior to all saliva sample collections.

RESULTS:
This experiment was performed during Bed Rest Campaigns 3A, 3B, 3C, and 5A. In general, subjects did not display altered peripheral leukocyte subsets, constitutive immune activation, altered T cell function, or significant latent viral reactivation (EBV, VZV). Levels of constitutively activated T cells (CD8+/CD69+) and virus-specific T cells (CMV and EBV) decreased during the study. Cortisol levels (plasma and saliva) did not vary significantly during 90-day bed rest.

No significant difference was found in the Positive Assay score, the negative scores, or Perceived Stress Scores in the subjects during bed rest as compared to the pre-bed rest values.

Conclusions: These data demonstrate the absence of significant immune system alteration and physiological stress during 90-day bed rest, and establish control data against which future studies (including countermeasures) may be compared.

experiment_title: Effects of Simulated Microgravity on the Anesthetic Properties of Propofol
parameter_html:
Cognitive function
Neurocognitive function
Propofol metabolites changes in clearance
Propofol metabolites half-life and pattern
Propofol metabolites mean residence time
Propofol metabolites volume of distribution
Propofol pharmacokinetics
Bispectral index (BIS) score
Complete blood count (CBC)
Propofol, plasma
investigators: Principal Investigator: Seubert, Christoph
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Despite careful health screening by NASA, astronauts adapted to microgravity are likely to require the administration of anesthesia for a variety of surgical conditions not only in the highly autonomous environments of space habitation or Mars-type missions but also for immediate surgical care after evacuation from low orbital missions. Little-to-no information is available regarding the most appropriate anesthetic technique in microgravity. Physiologic adaptation to weightlessness (e.g., changes in blood and plasma volume, fraction of cardiac output directed to brain, autonomic nervous system activity) can be expected to markedly alter the in vivo behavior and characteristics of anesthetics/hypnotics. Such an altered/increased effect may underlie the anesthetic complications encountered in the two rhesus monkeys aboard Bion 11 that were anesthetized for minor surgery on post-flight day one. On the other hand, data from medication use during space flight indicates normal efficacy of bezodiazepines and even a decrease in the self-reported incidence of sedation caused by promethazine. Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) is probably the ideal cost-effective method of rendering subjects insensitive to pain during surgery under microgravity conditions. Unlike volatile agents, which require vaporization and waste gas scavenging, TIVA is a light, compact and self-contained (closed) system that interfaces the patient. It consists of a small programmable syringe pump, which holds a syringe containing an intravenous (IV) anesthetic, which in turn, is attached to tubing that allows drug to be directly infused from the syringe into the vein of a patient. Among the TIVA agents in use today, propofol (2, 6-diisopropylphenol) is the best single suitable agent for use in space. Propofol has several key properties that make it a desirable anesthetic in a space environment: 1) rapid induction of and emergence from anesthesia, 2) ability to adjust the dose to achieve anesthetic states ranging from conscious sedation to general anesthesia 3) lack of drug accumulation in the body, even during long procedures, 4) significant anti-emetic properties, and 5) a simple and reliable means for assessing the depth of anesthesia/hypnosis, the bispectral index (BIS), derived from the electrical activity of the brain

The hypotheses for this study are: !(1) Adaptation to microgravity increases the hypnotic/anesthetic effect of propofol by changing its pharmacokinetics (PK), but not pharmacodynamics (PD). (2) Adaptation to microgravity does not change the recovery of cognitive function after propofol anesthesia.

This study will determine the effect of microgravity on the following characteristics of propofol anesthesia: 1) onset and offset kinetics, 2) dosing requirements for sedation and anesthesia, 3) PK/PD/metabolism, and 4) recovery of neuro-cognitive function in the postoperative period 5) occurrence of delayed postoperative cognitive dysfunction.

APPROACH:
Twenty volunteers were enrolled to receive propofol anesthesia, ten volunteers for each of the two groups.

RESULTS:
Of the 20 volunteers in the propofol groups, 18 completed the study without complications. Two anesthetics in Group II were stopped, one because of persistent coughing – likely a residual from a respiratory tract infection - and one because of regurgitation without aspiration – most likely caused by inadequate anesthesia. Independent review of all anesthetics by a panel of 4 anesthesiologists as part of Data Safety Monitoring oversight did agree with the investigators that no unexpected novel safety concerns were raised by the study anesthetics. Antiorthostatic bed rest led to hemoconcentration and typical mild symptoms of back pain or a sensation of fullness of the head/ headache.

For both propofol groups the anesthetic effect of propofol was similar in normal gravity and simulated microgravity. The clinical assessment by the modified observer’s assessment of alertness/sedation scale was corroborated by BIS monitoring. As intended, subjects in group II underwent clinically equivalent anesthetics in normo- and simulated microgravity. Consistent with the expected hemoconcentration, but unexpected from the clinical course, these anesthetics resulted in propofol plasma concentrations for up to 60 minutes after the anesthetic that were higher in simulated microgravity than in normogravity (p<0.05, repeated measures ANOVA). While propofol impaired aspects of cognitive function early after the anesthetic, the recovery was the same for normal and simulated microgravity. There was no evidence of delayed postoperative cognitive dysfunction.

The results suggest only a minor impact of the adaptation to weightlessness on the pharmacodynamic/pharmacokinetic profile of propofol. There are important limitations to the study. First, adaptation to microgravity was only brief, i.e. simulated by 48 hours of antiorthostatic bed rest. While this duration is sufficient to cause the changes in blood volume and blood flow characteristic of microgravity, and thereby simulates microgravity-induced changes in distribution and elimination of drugs, it falls short of reproducing the clinical scenario of anesthesia care after a medical evacuation from ISS or autonomous care on a long-term mission. Second, anesthesia was studied in the absence of surgery and surgical disease. Both alter the neuro-humeral milieu and may profoundly influence the patient’s response to an anesthetic.

Antiorthostatic bed rest led to hemoconcentration and typical mild symptoms of back pain or a sensation of fullness of the head/ headache.

For both propofol groups the anesthetic effect of propofol was similar in normal gravity and simulated microgravity. The clinical assessment by the modified observer’s assessment of alertness/sedation scale was corroborated by BIS monitoring. As intended, subjects in group II underwent clinically equivalent anesthetics in normo- and simulated microgravity. Consistent with the expected hemoconcentration, but unexpected from the clinical course, these anesthetics resulted in propofol plasma concentrations for up to 60 minutes after the anesthetic that were higher in simulated microgravity than in normogravity (p<0.05, repeated measures ANOVA). While propofol impaired aspects of cognitive function early after the anesthetic, the recovery was the same for normal and simulated microgravity. There was no evidence of delayed postoperative cognitive dysfunction.

The results suggest only a minor impact of the adaptation to weightlessness on the pharmacodynamic/pharmacokinetic profile of propofol. There are important limitations to the study. First, adaptation to microgravity was only brief, i.e. simulated by 48 hours of antiorthostatic bed rest. While this duration is sufficient to cause the changes in blood volume and blood flow characteristic of microgravity, and thereby simulates microgravity-induced changes in distribution and elimination of drugs, it falls short of reproducing the clinical scenario of anesthesia care after a medical evacuation from ISS or autonomous care on a long-term mission. Second, anesthesia was studied in the absence of surgery and surgical disease. Both alter the neuro-humeral milieu and may profoundly influence the patient’s response to an anesthetic.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objectives of this research were to characterize the persistent defects in neuro-signaling and cellular damage to central nervous system (CNS) tissue after cranial exposure to space radiation and to identify the critical molecular changes associated with individual variation in persistent neurocognitive deficits, using the rat model. The investigators reported global changes in transcript expression profiles in the hippocampus and choroid plexus (CP) tissues of old animals that were exposed to 56Fe or 12C beams in their youth. They identified changes in the predicted protein expression in the CP that correlated with the magnitude of persistent neurocognitive deficit (i.e., to ~22 months of age). They conducted comparative analyses of radiation-induced changes in CP signaling and cellular architecture that are associated with neurocognitive deficits, using CNS tissue collected from animals exposed at various doses of 56Fe or 12C after they were tested for neurocognitive deficits. Furthermore, they also investigated the early onset of radiation-induced changes to hippocampal and CP signaling, CP architecture, hippocampal neurogenesis, and composition of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at ~3 months after exposure to both high and low-fluence 56Fe, and examined the association between molecular defects and neurocognitive changes within each irradiated animal.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Characterize the dose dependence of persistent signaling and cellular defects in the CP and hippocampal zones of neurogenesis of 12C- and 56Fe-exposed rats that have persistent deficits in their cognitive function and motor behavior.
  2. Characterize the time course of cellular and signaling defects in the CP of rats irradiated with 56Fe beams and determine the temporal relationship between CP defects and abnormal hippocampal neurogenesis.
  3. Determine whether irradiated animals with defective CP also produce CSF deficient in critical metabolites or proteins that are critical for adult neurogenesis, using proteomic and metabolomic approaches.

APPROACH:
This project provided NASA with an improved mechanistic understanding of the risks for impaired neurocognitive performance and individual susceptibility for neurological diseases after exposure to HZE radiation. The approach used a rat model and: (a) employed state-of-the-art ‘omics and tissue technologies to investigate CNS damage response functions in animals exposed to low-fluence HZE particles (i.e., <1 hit per cell), (b) linked the type and magnitude of molecular defects with neurocognitive performance, and (c) validated the predicted damage response functions in brain tissue. This study focused on CNS tissue damage to the hippocampus (site of spatial and performance memories) and the choroid plexus (CP, small cauliflower-like tissue in the ventricles adjacent to the hippocampus that produces cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) and maintains blood-brain homeostasis). The research distinguished between two broad categories of risk mechanisms: (1) mechanisms related to exposure dose, and (2) mechanisms of inter-individual variations in risks for neurocognitive performance, and neurological diseases (e.g., Alzheimer Disease (AD)). The working model is that neurocognitive damage after radiation involves direct cell damage to specific CNS target cells as well as indirect damage mediated by the irradiated microenvironment, such as abnormal CSF produced by an abnormal choroid plexus. The hypothesis of this study was that exposure to space-relevant doses of HZE radiation (less than one ion per cell) induces abnormal molecular signaling and cellular damage in CP and hippocampus that determine the risks and individual susceptibilities for neurocognitive deficits and neurological diseases such as AD.

RESULTS:
The investigators confirmed the radiation-sensitivity of the CP, measuring significant cellular and molecular damage to the CP after exposure to X-ray and 56Fe radiation. The experiments include young and age-matched old reference groups to provide a means to distinguish between radiation effects and normal aging. The investigators discovered long-lived molecular signaling changes in the CNS after exposure to space radiation using transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomics analyses of several brain regions (hippocampus, CP, CSF, and cortex) collected at ~3 days to ~21 months after whole body HZE or X-ray exposures (10-200cGy), usually for rats also tested on one or more psychometric assay. Expression profiling and bioinformatics identified a significant Huntington’s disease subnetwork and significant associations with neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and various neurological diseases and neurocognitive dysfunctions.

The investigators demonstrated that cranial exposure of young adult rats to heavy particle ionizing radiation (HZE, 56Fe, and 12C) causes neurocognitive deficits that persist to very old age, that the magnitude of the deficits are variable across animals and was associated with molecular and cellular damage to the CP and hippocampus. At ~2 years after exposures, there were histological changes of the CP including occluded endothelial vessels, increases in the frequency of amyloid deposits throughout the CNS, and decreased epithelial expression of proteins that normally prevent amyloid fibril formation in CNS. In support of observation, the investigators found increased frequencies of amyloid plaques in exposed animals but noted that the increase in plaque frequency was delayed 4-9 months after exposure. These findings suggest that space radiation may increase the risks for Alzheimer-related pathologies in the brain, long after the exposure. The investigators also confirmed the hypothesis that radiation exposure damaged the ability of the CP to produce normal cerebral spinal fluid. Animals exposed to 10 and 100cGy 56Fe showed changes in many proteins associated with various neurological diseases, psychological disorders, neuronal cell death and survival. They also discovered molecular signaling changes that are associated with inter-individual variation in behavioral responses to HZE radiation, related to memory deficits and increased anxiety in rats.

In summary, this research in a rat model identified persistent histological and molecular defects in the various CNS tissues (CP, CSF, and hippocampus) that are different from normal aging and are associated with long-term neurocognitive dysfunction related to memory deficits, increased anxiety, and increased plaque formation long after HZE exposures.

No data sets are available. A final report was archived.
