experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to the microgravity conditions of space flight causes astronauts to experience alterations in multiple physiological systems including sensorimotor disturbances, cardiovascular deconditioning, and loss of muscle mass and strength. Some or all of these changes might affect the ability of crewmembers to perform critical mission tasks immediately after landing on a planetary surface. The goals of the Functional Task Test (FTT) study were to determine the effects of space flight on functional tests that are representative of critical exploration mission tasks and to identify the key physiological factors that contribute to decrements in performance.

The FTT was comprised of seven functional tests and a corresponding set of interdisciplinary physiological measures targeting the sensorimotor, cardiovascular and muscular adaptations associated with exposure to space flight. The set of functional tasks making up the FTT included the: 1) Seat Egress and Walk Test, 2) Ladder Climb Test, 3) Recovery from Fall/Stand Test, 4) Rock Translation Test, 5) Jump Down Test, 6) Torque Generation Test, and 7) Construction Activity Board Test. Corresponding physiological measures include assessments of vestibular function, dynamic visual acuity, fine motor control, postural and locomotor stability, plasma volume, orthostatic intolerance, upper and lower body muscle strength, power, fatigue, control, and neuromuscular drive.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the effects of short and long-duration space flight on functional performance.
  2. Compare the rate of recovery in functional performance between short and long-duration space flight.
  3. Determine how postflight changes in sensorimotor, cardiovascular, and muscle physiology impact functional performance.

APPROACH:
The FTT was comprised of seven functional tests and a corresponding set of interdisciplinary physiological measures targeting the sensorimotor, cardiovascular and muscular adaptations associated with exposure to space flight. Both Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers as well as bed rest subjects participated in this study. Space flight data were collected in three sessions before flight, on landing day (Shuttle only), and on days 1, 6, and 30 after landing. Bed rest subjects were tested three times before bed rest, immediately upon getting up after 70 days of 6° head-down bed rest, as well as 1, 6, and 12 days during the subsequent re-ambulation period. The bed rest analog allowed investigators to isolate the impact of body unloading without other space flight environmental factors on both functional tasks and on the underlying physiological factors that lead to decrements in performance, and then to compare those results with the results obtained in the space flight study.

RESULTS:
Results demonstrate that for Space Shuttle, ISS, and bed rest (control and exercise) subjects, functional tasks requiring a greater demand for dynamic control of postural equilibrium (i.e., fall recovery, seat egress/obstacle avoidance during walking, object translation, jump down) showed the greatest decrement in performance. Functional tests with reduced requirements for postural stability such as hatch opening, ladder climb, manual manipulation of objects, and tool use showed little reduction in performance. These changes in functional performance were paralleled by similar decrements in sensorimotor tests designed to specifically assess postural equilibrium and dynamic gait control.

The muscle function data showed reductions in lower body muscle performance metrics in both space flight groups and bed rest subjects who did not exercise. Bed rest subjects who performed an integrated high intensity interval-type resistance and aerobic training program while in bed showed significantly improved lower body muscle performance compared to bed rest controls and space flight subjects. However, resistive and aerobic exercise alone was not sufficient to mitigate decrements in functional tasks that require dynamic postural stability and mobility and point to the need for the addition of balance training to current in-flight countermeasures.

Bed rest subjects experienced similar deficits both in functional tests with balance challenges and in sensorimotor tests designed to evaluate postural and gait control as space flight subjects indicating that body support unloading experienced during space flight plays a central role in postflight alteration of functional task performance. Additionally, ISS crewmembers who walked on the treadmill with higher pull-down loads had enhanced postflight performance on tests requiring mobility. Taken together the bed rest and in-flight exercise training data point to the importance of providing increased body loading during in-flight treadmill and lower body resistive exercise.

Both space flight and bed rest data indicate that an elevated heart rate was required to maintain arterial blood pressure during performance of multiple functional tasks. Space flight data indicated that restoration of plasma volume alone did not prevent the elevated heart rate experienced while prone or standing during postflight testing. These data indicate that additional countermeasures are necessary to maintain central blood volume, prevent or reverse changes in peripheral vasoconstriction, and minimize the need for elevations in heart rate during various functional tasks.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biostereometrics is the science of measuring, and describing in mathematical terms, the three-dimensional form of biological objects. Exposure to weightlessness results in a dramatic change in the patterns of muscular activity in the human body insofar as they control posture and are responsible for locomotion. These changes in muscular activity might be expected to result in changes in the bulk of particular muscle groups, and in the overall energy consumption of the body, which, unless accompanied by a compensating change in food intake, would cause a change in body fat. Biostereometric analysis of the Skylab crewmembers enabled changes in muscle bulk to be measured, and by examining those areas of the body containing fat deposits enabled general conclusions to be drawn about changes in each Skylab crewmember's body fat.

APPROACH:
The biostereometric measurements of the Skylab crewmen were made using four-camera stereophotogrammetry, during the immediate preflight and postflight periods of Skylab 2, 3, and 4. The subjects were weighed within a few minutes of taking the photographs. Each subject was instructed to stand between two control stands, which provided dimensional information in the three orthogonal axes. Two cameras in front, and two cameras behind then simultaneously photographed the subject. The subject was nude except for an athletic supporter, and a skullcap to press his hair down. To minimize variations in chest volume, photographs were taken in maximal forced exhalation. Between each pair of cameras was a strobe-projector, which through a focusing lens projects a pattern of lines onto the subject's skin, making it easier to visualize during the subsequent plotting process. The stereophotgrammetry cameras were modified to accept fine-grain glass plates, for dimensional stability of the image. Duplicate sets of plates were exposed to insure against breakage or camera malfunction. The equipment was portable, and photographs were taken at Johnson Space Center (JSC), Kennedy Space Center (KSC), and on the recovery ships. After development the plates were analyzed on a stereoplotter, which derived the three-dimensional coordinates of thousands of points on the body surface, punching them on IBM cards for subsequent computer analysis. The computer program derived area, shape, and perimeter of between 80 to 100 sections of different parts of the body, the volume of any segment of the body, and of the body as a whole.

RESULTS:
Measurements of leg circumference derived from stereometric analysis were compared to tape measure circumferences obtained on the same day. A pattern typical of all comparisons made between the two methods, resulted in the stereometric techniques exceeding the tape measurements by 10 to 20 millimeters. There are two probable causes for this difference. Firstly, the stereoscopic photographs were made with the subject standing, whereas the tape measurements were made with the subject supine; the leg volume standing would exceed that supine by the volume of blood and interstitial fluid brought into the leg under the influence of gravity. Secondly, stereometric analysis, being a noncontact method, did not involve the compression of tissues, however small, which resulted from the use of a tape measure. The 10 to 20 millimeter discrepancy between the methods represents a difference in limb volume of 250 to 500 milliliters, which is entirely reasonable for the increased volume of blood and tissue fluid in the leg after transferring from the supine to the standing position.

Next, a comparison was made between the mean preflight weight and volume of the nine Skylab crewmembers and the first postflight determination. Density for all measurements was within the range 0.98 to 1.04 g/cm2. This is less than the normal range of density (1.02 to 1.10 g/cm2) derived from hydrostatic weighing or gas displacement, because the volume figure includes the residual lung volume, the volume of air enmeshed in the hair, and the volume of those areas which cannot be visualized by the cameras (axillae and perineum). These additional volumes should be reasonably reproducible from one measurement to another on the same subject, except for the hair volume, which is probably the largest single source of error. It is unrealistic to calculate the density of the tissue lost during the course of the flight, as small errors in the volume determination would lead to impossible values for tissue density. Two of the Skylab 4 crewmembers showed little or no weight change, although a redistribution of body volume did occur. Generally speaking, the changes in weight and total body volume were of similar magnitude, and the apparent changes in density were probably not significant.

Differences between the mean preflight and first postflight measurements of regional and total body volume, and body weight were also analyzed. It was difficult to reproduce the "cutoff" plane between the arms and the trunk; because of this the arm volumes were subjected to considerable random variation. There was no statistically significant difference in mean arm volume between preflight and postflight measurements. However, the mean losses of volume of 1.2 liters in the head and trunk, and 1.3 liters in the legs, were significantly different from zero (P<0.005). The mean preflight volume of the head and trunk was 45.8 liters, and that of the legs was 18.9 liters, so that the postflight change in volume was proportionately much greater in the legs.

The head and trunk segments of the body contain the extensively fatty areas of the buttocks and abdomen. It is probable that the volume changes seen in this body segment are due more to changes in fat than to changes in muscle, whereas the legs contain much more muscle than fat, except in the grossly obese, and are more sensitive to changes in muscle bulk. Both regions of the body would be affected by changes in body fluid.

A typical plot of the cross sectional areas of the body shows differences between preflight and postflight measurements in the regions of the head, shoulder, and arms were slight, and resulted from differences in posture. Marked loss of volume is seen in the abdomen, buttocks, and calves, and a less striking loss in the thighs. The abdominal area showed a flattening of the abdomen, and the gluteal region a reduction in volume of the buttocks, both probably resulting predominantly from loss of fat. All crewmen lost volume from the abdomen, although the loss from this area was much greater in those who showed significant weight loss. The striking reduction in leg volume immediately postflight was investigated in more detail on the Skylab 4 mission, in an attempt to elucidate how much of it resulted from partial muscle atrophy, due to relative disuse of the legs in the weightless environment, and how much represented a purely temporary dehydration. The absolute loss of volume from the thigh and calf was of similar magnitude, although the much smaller dimensions of the calf resulted in a much greater proportional loss and a greater change in cross sectional area.

The differences between the volume of thigh and calf postflight in the Skylab 4 crewmen and the mean preflight value was analyzed. On recovery day there was a deficit in the lower limbs of nearly 1000 milliliters, which had reduced by about a third by the following day, and had diminished to around 300 milliliters 3 days later. Both calf and thigh volume had returned to preflight values by the measurement made 30 days following recovery. It is clear that at least part of the deficient volume must represent missing fluid, which is replaced within a day or two of recovery, but there is probably also a reduction in bulk of the tissues of the leg. If, as seems probable, this loss of tissue represents partial atrophy of the leg muscles due to relative disuse in zero-gravity, it would probably be restored fairly rapidly on return to Earth, so that the 300 milliliters deficit measured on day 4 postflight may be an under estimate of the total leg muscle lost during the flight.

The mean loss of leg volume on recovery day was 1.68 liters for the Skylab 2 crew, and 1.12 liters for the Skylab 4 crew. The mean loss on day 1 postflight was 1.06 liters for the Skylab 3 crew, and 0.77 liters for the Skylab 4 crew. While it is not possible directly to compare the Skylab 2 and Skylab 3 crews, there does appear to be a decrease in the loss of leg volume on succeeding missions. __description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biostereometrics is the science of measuring, and describing in mathematical terms, the three-dimensional form of biological objects. Exposure to weightlessness results in a dramatic change in the patterns of muscular activity in the human body insofar as they control posture and are responsible for locomotion. These changes in muscular activity might be expected to result in changes in the bulk of particular muscle groups, and in the overall energy consumption of the body, which, unless accompanied by a compensating change in food intake, would cause a change in body fat. Biostereometric analysis of the Skylab crewmembers enabled changes in muscle bulk to be measured, and by examining those areas of the body containing fat deposits enabled general conclusions to be drawn about changes in each Skylab crewmember's body fat.

APPROACH:
The biostereometric measurements of the Skylab crewmen were made using four-camera stereophotogrammetry, during the immediate preflight and postflight periods of Skylab 2, 3, and 4. The subjects were weighed within a few minutes of taking the photographs. Each subject was instructed to stand between two control stands, which provided dimensional information in the three orthogonal axes. Two cameras in front, and two cameras behind then simultaneously photographed the subject. The subject was nude except for an athletic supporter, and a skullcap to press his hair down. To minimize variations in chest volume, photographs were taken in maximal forced exhalation. Between each pair of cameras was a strobe-projector, which through a focusing lens projects a pattern of lines onto the subject's skin, making it easier to visualize during the subsequent plotting process. The stereophotgrammetry cameras were modified to accept fine-grain glass plates, for dimensional stability of the image. Duplicate sets of plates were exposed to insure against breakage or camera malfunction. The equipment was portable, and photographs were taken at Johnson Space Center (JSC), Kennedy Space Center (KSC), and on the recovery ships. After development the plates were analyzed on a stereoplotter, which derived the three-dimensional coordinates of thousands of points on the body surface, punching them on IBM cards for subsequent computer analysis. The computer program derived area, shape, and perimeter of between 80 to 100 sections of different parts of the body, the volume of any segment of the body, and of the body as a whole.

RESULTS:
Measurements of leg circumference derived from stereometric analysis were compared to tape measure circumferences obtained on the same day. A pattern typical of all comparisons made between the two methods, resulted in the stereometric techniques exceeding the tape measurements by 10 to 20 millimeters. There are two probable causes for this difference. Firstly, the stereoscopic photographs were made with the subject standing, whereas the tape measurements were made with the subject supine; the leg volume standing would exceed that supine by the volume of blood and interstitial fluid brought into the leg under the influence of gravity. Secondly, stereometric analysis, being a noncontact method, did not involve the compression of tissues, however small, which resulted from the use of a tape measure. The 10 to 20 millimeter discrepancy between the methods represents a difference in limb volume of 250 to 500 milliliters, which is entirely reasonable for the increased volume of blood and tissue fluid in the leg after transferring from the supine to the standing position.

Next, a comparison was made between the mean preflight weight and volume of the nine Skylab crewmembers and the first postflight determination. Density for all measurements was within the range 0.98 to 1.04 g/cm2. This is less than the normal range of density (1.02 to 1.10 g/cm2) derived from hydrostatic weighing or gas displacement, because the volume figure includes the residual lung volume, the volume of air enmeshed in the hair, and the volume of those areas which cannot be visualized by the cameras (axillae and perineum). These additional volumes should be reasonably reproducible from one measurement to another on the same subject, except for the hair volume, which is probably the largest single source of error. It is unrealistic to calculate the density of the tissue lost during the course of the flight, as small errors in the volume determination would lead to impossible values for tissue density. Two of the Skylab 4 crewmembers showed little or no weight change, although a redistribution of body volume did occur. Generally speaking, the changes in weight and total body volume were of similar magnitude, and the apparent changes in density were probably not significant.

Differences between the mean preflight and first postflight measurements of regional and total body volume, and body weight were also analyzed. It was difficult to reproduce the "cutoff" plane between the arms and the trunk; because of this the arm volumes were subjected to considerable random variation. There was no statistically significant difference in mean arm volume between preflight and postflight measurements. However, the mean losses of volume of 1.2 liters in the head and trunk, and 1.3 liters in the legs, were significantly different from zero (P<0.005). The mean preflight volume of the head and trunk was 45.8 liters, and that of the legs was 18.9 liters, so that the postflight change in volume was proportionately much greater in the legs.

The head and trunk segments of the body contain the extensively fatty areas of the buttocks and abdomen. It is probable that the volume changes seen in this body segment are due more to changes in fat than to changes in muscle, whereas the legs contain much more muscle than fat, except in the grossly obese, and are more sensitive to changes in muscle bulk. Both regions of the body would be affected by changes in body fluid.

A typical plot of the cross sectional areas of the body shows differences between preflight and postflight measurements in the regions of the head, shoulder, and arms were slight, and resulted from differences in posture. Marked loss of volume is seen in the abdomen, buttocks, and calves, and a less striking loss in the thighs. The abdominal area showed a flattening of the abdomen, and the gluteal region a reduction in volume of the buttocks, both probably resulting predominantly from loss of fat. All crewmen lost volume from the abdomen, although the loss from this area was much greater in those who showed significant weight loss. The striking reduction in leg volume immediately postflight was investigated in more detail on the Skylab 4 mission, in an attempt to elucidate how much of it resulted from partial muscle atrophy, due to relative disuse of the legs in the weightless environment, and how much represented a purely temporary dehydration. The absolute loss of volume from the thigh and calf was of similar magnitude, although the much smaller dimensions of the calf resulted in a much greater proportional loss and a greater change in cross sectional area.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Meck, JaniceCo-Investigator: Charles, JohnCo-Investigator: Whitson, Peggy
experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight causes adaptive changes in cardiovascular function, and serious disturbances of cardiac rhythm have occurred during extravehicular activities. However, previously available data about these changes have been inadequate and inconsistent and have often been recorded during experimental interventions rather than during routine activity. The objectives of this study were to collect normative data on cardiovascular changes during spaceflight and to document any occurrence of cardiac dysrhythmias.

APPROACH:
The heart rate and rhythm and the blood pressure of 12 astronauts were monitored over 24-hour periods of routine activity before, during, and after space flights of 4 to 14 days. During the study periods, Holter monitors worn by the astronauts made continuous electrocardiogram recordings, and automatic devices measured the blood pressure every 20 minutes while the astronauts were awake and every 30 minutes while they were asleep.

RESULTS:
There were several important findings in DSOs 463 and 602. First, heart rate, diastolic pressure, and their variabilities were reduced during space flight. Second, the diurnal variations of both heart rate and diastolic pressure were reduced during space flight. Third, monitoring records demonstrated that space flight did not increase dysrhythmias. These data are unique because they were obtained during normal 24-hour routines, rather than as a part of any in-flight experiment intervention. Therefore, they are important for establishing a normative data base for cardiovascular parameters during short duration space flight.

The results indicate that heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac dysrhythmias decreased during space flight when compared to preflight norms. This suggests that living in a microgravity environment did not cause a constant stress to the cardiovascular system. However, the adaptive changes that occurred in response to the microgravity environment left the astronauts ill-prepared for the cardiovascular stresses associated with return to Earth.

experiment_title: Acute Cutaneous Microvascular Flow Responses to Whole Body Tilting in Humans
parameter_html:
Cutaneous flow, calf
Cutaneous flow, neck
Body mass
Height
investigators: Principal Investigator: Watenpaugh, Donald
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
On Earth, upright posture establishes a linear gradient of blood pressure along the length of the body. The change from upright to supine body position is followed by an increase in local pressure from 100 to 200 mmHg in the feet and a decrease at the head level from 100 to 70 mmHg. Considering the combined effect of central and local controls for arteriolar tone, these mechanisms may work cooperatively in the lower body and antagonistically in the upper body, i.e. above the heart level, baroreceptor-induced changes in arteriolar tone may be negated by local myogenic factors, as suggested by cutaneous micro-vascular responses in a study by Aratow et al. that compared responses in the forehead and foot to two tilt angles. This study proposed to further document the different responses in cutaneous microvascular flow to graded postural changes in humans.

 APPROACH:
Ten healthy subjects (7 male and 3 female) ranging in age from 26 to 47 years (median 27.5), with average weight of 67 kg and height of 171 cm agreed to participate in the study. Flow meters were attached with adhesive tape to the neck and to the leg of each subject. Instrumented subjects were placed upright on a motorized tilt table against a footplate and mildly restrained with a canvas strap across the chest. After stabilization of cutaneous flows, subjects underwent the following stepwise protocol: (Each angle was maintained for 30 seconds with 10 minute transitions between angles) 90o , 54o , 30o , 12o , 0o , -6o ,   -12o , -6o , 0o , 12o , 30o , 54o , 90o . In 8 subjects, Ga/ln-in-silastic strain gauge plethysmography measured percent changes in leg and neck volumes. 

RESULTS:
Cutaneous flows (avg±SE) at the calf and neck increased significantly from standing to 12o head-up-tilt (247±55% and 161±15%). From 12o to –12o tilt, flows continued to increase at the calf to 479±91% of control, but decreased at the neck to near baseline (119±13% of control, NS). Tilting from head-up to head-down produced significant increments in mean neck volume of 3.8±0.5% above standing control and significant decrements in mean leg volume of 1.8±0.2% below control. Responses of body segment volumes to tilt were practically instantaneous, indicating that blood volume translocation accounted for most of the change. The researchers concluded that flow increases from standing to supine posture can be attributed to baroreceptor-mediated vasodilation at both sites with the added effect of increased pressure at the neck. The subsequent decrease in flow at the neck with head-down-tilt may be due to a myogenic response to increased local arteriolar pressure. The great dissimilarity of flow responses at the two sites suggests that the cutaneous microcirculation of the calf is more sensitive to gravitational stresses than that of the neck.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to determine the minimum G requirements of exposure to G forces to prevent the deconditioning effects of microgravity in a ground-based model. This consisted of evaluating the effectiveness of intermittent exposure to passive and active +1 Gz force on deconditioning manifested as orthostatic intolerance, changes in oxygen uptake, reduced plasma volume, increases in urinary volume, sodium and calcium excretion during a period of 4 days ­6o head down bed rest.

APPROACH:
Nine healthy men of average age (38±4.5) yrs were recruited to participate in a four day bed rest study with each individual tested across five treatment conditions: Each group consisted of 4 days bed rest with a daily treatment of 1) no intervention (OG) 2) 4 hours intermittent standing (S4), 3) 4 hours intermittent walking (W4), 4) 2 hours intermittent standing (S2), 5) 2 hours intermittent walking (W2). Walking was at 3 mph on a level treadmill. Recovery time in between each treatment was a minimum of one month. Measurements of body weight, tilt tolerance, peak VO2, plasma volume and urinary calcium were carried out just prior to and on the 4th bed rest day. Statistical analysis of the five treatments was done by repeated measures ANOVA with missing estimates adjusted by least squares except for measurements of heart rate and blood pressure precluded by the large amount of data.

RESULTS:
Of interest is that the responses of the physiologic variable to each treatment differed as a function of the variable measured. Orthostatic intolerance was mostly compensated for by an increase in HR. Standing for 4 hours was most effective with standing for 2 hours more effective than walking for 2 or 4 hours. Peak oxygen consumption was best preserved by walking either 2 or 4 hours and minimally maintained by standing for 4 or 2 hours. Either standing or walking for 4 hours prevented the decrease in plasma volume. Walking for either 2 or 4 hours prevented the loss of 4 days urinary calcium excretion. Absolute values for all data are printed in NASA TM 108800.

Conclusions: No single treatment was most effective across all dependent variables. Preventive effects of different treatments are specific to each system. Calcium balance responded favorably to activity whereas orthostatic tolerance and plasma volume were more dependent on the stimulus provided by the gravitational field. In most cases, differences between 2 and 4-hour exposures were small and it was surprising to find out how little exposure the human body needs to maintain normal health.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In weightlessness, major loads are removed from muscles and from a variety of proprioceptive sensors, especially force sensors. While these sensors are rapidly adapting to microgravity and nominally work at all angles in relation to the gravity vector, virtually all actions are modulated if not initiated by the cerebellum and higher centers. In weightlessness, signals from the gravity sensitive otolith organs are distorted and incongruent with semicircular canal vision and cause some crewmembers to experience space motion sickness (SMS).

There are extensive vestibular inputs to the higher centers of the central nervous system, especially the cerebellum, as well as the spinal cord. Without study one could not be sure that weightlessness would not affect movements, particularly finely coordinated movements and especially during SMS when a major sensory conflict is present. Simple operational experience has demonstrated that muscular activities were not significantly affected by weightlessness; however, it was difficult to say the same during SMS.

To document this in a more sensitive and orderly fashion, one of the simplest tests of sensorimotor function was devised for use on STS-5 and continued on STS-7. It consisted of a crewmember selecting a given spot on a chart with a scribe marking that location. Then, while looking away, the crewmember attempted to return the scribe to the same point, again marking the chart at that point. This was repeated a number of times with and without loading equivalent to weight of the segment used. No significant changes were found in normal subjects in weightlessness.

This study was refined and expanded on STS-8 by utilizing a recorder which moved a wide paper chart past a marker which was free to move transversely across the paper. In addition to measuring kinesthetic sensitivity, a visual tracking task was added by prerecording sine and triangular waves at various frequencies and amplitudes and a series of random step functions. This was used extensively on STS-8 but not during SMS. To reduce size and weight and to facilitate automatic data analysis, an electronic recording scale with a light-emitting diode (LED) tracking display was constructed to specification for Shuttle flights. It has provisions for both kinesthetic testing and eye hand tracking and was flown and used on SL-3 but not during SMS.

APPROACH:
The electronic tracking unit consisted of a 25 cm linear track 23.5 cm along which a pointer and handle was free to move. Adjacent to the track is a linear array of 50 LEDs one of which was illuminated. An internal generator sequentially drove the illuminated LED in a sequence of functions. Position of pointer and light was recorded by the FM instrumentation recorder. In the kinesthetic position mode, pointer position was recorded as the subject chose a position with eyes averted then moved the pointer away from it and attempted to find the original position for a total of ten times with shoulder rotation only. This was repeated with free use of all arm points. Eye hand tracking consisted of attempting to maintain the pointer on the lighted LED as it performed the various functions which were displayed for tracing.

Preflight testing and baseline data were nominally performed. Two subjects were requested to perform the in flight testing on FD-1 or 2 and then again one day from FD-3 to recovery. Records were obtained for each scheduled subject.

RESULTS:
There are not any summarized results for this study.

parameter_html:
Folic acid
Vitamin A
Vitamin C
Thiamine
investigators: Principal Investigator: Perchonok, Michele
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is working towards future long-duration manned space flights beyond low earth orbit. The duration of these missions may be as long as 2.5 years and will likely include a stay on a lunar or planetary surface. For these long duration missions, a shelf life of 3 to 5 years for the prepackaged transit food system is required.

Of the preservation methods currently being used at NASA for the Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) food systems, the thermostabilized items will have the longest shelf life. Currently four approved ISS thermostabilized packaged foods are undergoing accelerated shelf life testing in the Space Food Systems Laboratory (SFSL) at NASA/Johnson Space Center. The foods, bread pudding, carrot coins, tuna noodle casserole, and apricot cobbler, are being stored in controlled temperature chambers at 40 degrees F, 72 degrees F, and 95 degrees F. Analytical tests to measure color, texture, pH, and water activity will be correlated with the sensory tests to determine the changes occurring in the foods. The sensory tests will measure the difference from control (40 degrees F) as well as overall acceptability. Nutritional analysis will be completed three times during the shelf life test.

The objective of this research was to continue the shelf life determination of these four thermostabilized food items. Sensory and analytical data was collected every four months on the four food items that were stored at 40F, 72F, and 95F for approximately 3 years. The shelf life test was terminated after 3 years or whenever the product became unacceptable, if before 3 years. In addition to determining the shelf life of these foods, better understandings of the chemical and physical changes that can occur throughout their shelf life were learned.

APPROACH:
The entire nutritional profile was determined analytically for 26 new food items by a selected accredited laboratory at “zero time” after stabilization processing. The empirical data was then compared with the calculated nutrition data. While incongruities in the estimates prevented broad conclusions on vitamin stability, a detailed look at some of the food products confirmed previous study assumptions that the stabilization processing was resulting in degradation of many of the vitamins, including vitamin C, vitamin A, folic acid, and thiamin. Losses after retort processing were as high as 100% for vitamin A and vitamin C.

RESULTS:
For the fifteen food items tested during FY 2008, repeat analytical testing was conducted on the anniversary of their original stabilization processing. Vitamin A continued to diminish in the package for most products over the one year of storage. Likewise, most folic acid and thiamin levels decreased, and vitamin C levels in all products declined from original levels by 37% to 100%. This degradation is attributed to remnant oxygen in package after nitrogen flushing. The presence of oxygen, even at decreased levels, allowed oxidation reactions to progress which chemically destroyed the vitamins.

Given that the estimates highlighted the absence of nutrient dense menu items and that degradation of vitamin profiles was noted after processing and during storage, it is unlikely that vitamin levels will subsist through the necessary three year product life. Countermeasure exploration should begin parallel to this study completion. NASA must identify means for solving critical nutrition problems including, reformulation with more resilient ingredients; fortification and supplementation; and development of processing and preservation methods that have less effect on the nutritional content of the food, e.g., high pressure processing and microwave sterilization. Additionally, the process of nitrogen flushing the retort pouches should be revisited for optimization or replacement.
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.

experiment_title: Optimizing Crew Performance in Long Duration Space Exploration: Best Practices for Team Training and Cohesion Measurement
parameter_html:
Self-regulation
Stress
Team cohesion
Team performance
investigators: Principal Investigator: Salas, EduardoCo-Investigator: Fiore, StephenCo-Investigator: Smith-Jentsch, Kimberly
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project addressed questions regarding methods and technologies for training crews to maintain crew cohesion and optimal performance during exploration missions Specific aims of this project were threefold: (1) identify evidence-based guidelines/best practices for training to maximize team cohesion, and team performance; (2) design, develop, and validate evidence-based instructional strategies to mitigate performance failures from cohesion decrements among space flight crews and coordinating ground crews; and (3) design, develop, and validate an evidence-based index measuring and diagnosing cohesion over the course of a mission. These specific project aims meet NASA goals and objectives by capturing cohesion levels shown to be integral to long-duration space flight mission success as well as developing countermeasures designed to mitigate the negative impact of cohesion issues. Organized as a multi-year project, primary tasks for the first year included the development of recommendations for training crews to optimize cohesion and team performance, mitigate negative impacts of long-duration missions, and measuring crew cohesion over time. Second and third years of the project focused on applying recommendations derived from year one research by developing, implementing, and evaluating instructional strategies to maximize crew cohesion and mitigate negative psychosocial impacts of long-duration missions. Overarching project goals were to: (1) mitigate performance failures due to a lack of cohesion between space flight crews and coordinating ground crews, (2) diagnose cohesion decrements during exploration missions, and (3) provide just-in-time training to improve any noted cohesion decrements during space flight.

APPROACH:
Semistructured interviews centering on a recent complex problem were conducted with seven MCC professionals. In order to assess collaborative problem-solving processes in NASA's Mission Control Center (MCC) with those predicted by the Macrocognition in Teams Model, a coding scheme was developed to analyze the interview transcriptions.

RESULTS:
This research project was dedicated to providing valid, evidence based training recommendations for optimizing and maintaining crew cohesion and team performance during long-duration space flight (LDSF) missions. The specific objectives associated with Project PEGASUS included: (1) Identify evidence-based guidelines and best practices for training to maximize team cohesion and team performance; (2) Design, develop, and validate theoretically driven, evidence based instructional strategies to mitigate performance failures from cohesion decrements among spaceflight crews and coordinating ground crews; and (3) design, develop, and validate an evidence based toolkit for measuring and diagnosing cohesion over the course of LDSF missions.

The first phases of the project involved investigating the characteristics of the LDSF environment, by reviewing the literature of team performance in isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments. The literature review was organized by investigating three constructs—categorized as thrusts—that are considered important for effective team performance in ICE environments: (1) cohesion, (2) stress, and (3) self-regulation.

The literature review helped in the development of inquiries for the structured interviews with subject matter experts. These subject matter experts were astronauts with NASA who had previous experience with LDSF mission in the International Space Station (ISS). These interviews involved astronauts to provide insight into their experiences of these missions, including stress that they experience during task work and in the work environment, preparing crewmembers for space flight missions, and working with fellow teammates before and during the mission. Additionally, investigators gained insight about what conditions of training interventions they deemed useful for preparing the team for their space flight mission. Based on the literature review and talking with the subject matter experts,investigators concluded that Team Dimensional Training (TDT), a structured debriefing strategy that is associated with team self-correction, can help personnel in the space flight context for learning and maintaining optimal collective performance.

The conduction and conclusion of the field study investigated TDT in a Mission Control setting. This involved data collection, analysis, and interpretation of results. Findings indicate that participants rate the TDT debriefing strategy to allow for more open and participative debriefing, and also rated the TDT strategy with higher levels of learning value than the baseline debriefing condition. Additionally, findings indicate that the TDT strategy has resulted in quicker certification times for trainees in comparison to the baseline condition.

experiment_title: Synergistic Effect of Zero-g and Radiation on White Blood Cells
parameter_html:
Aberration frequency
Cell lysis
Chromosome aberrations
Radiation dose
Radiation type
Temperature
Time
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kondo, Sohei
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biological effects, such as genetic mutation, chromosome aberrations and cell lysis, were seen in both ballistic and orbital space flights that occurred before Gemini 3. In some cases, these effects were of magnitudes many times greater than would have been predicted from the expected radiation exposure received during flight. These magnitudes were thought to occur for two reasons: (1) it was thought that the components (particles) of radiation above the Earth’s atmosphere might have unexpected biological effects that could not be predicted in Earth-based laboratories and (2) it was thought that radiation and zero-g acted synergistically to produce unexpectedly large effects. This experiment was conducted to test these two possibilities.

APPROACH:
A series of human whole blood samples was irradiated during the mission with radioactive phosphorus (32P) beta-rays, with a known quantity and quality of radiation. Inflight control samples were also used, and were not irradiated with the experiment source, but just flew to encounter the normal radiation of the space flight. An identical series of blood samples was irradiated on the ground and used as a control. Increased aberrations in the inflight samples, including the control, would be evidence of an effect of some space flight parameter. Any effect not seen in the inflight control would be attributed to a synergism between radiation and some space flight parameter.

Because induction of chromosome aberrations is a non-linear function of radiation dose, a graded series of four different radiation exposures was used. Two complete sets of blood samples were flown to protect against loss of data; each sample set was from a different blood donor. In total, ten 3 ml blood samples were flown; eight were irradiated with each of the four doses, and two were not irradiated and served as the inflight controls. The simultaneous ground control experiment consisted of ten 3 ml samples drawn from the same donors at the same time as the inflight samples. As an additional control, blood samples were obtained from the flight crew before and after the flight, and short-term leukocyte cultures were prepared. Preflight, on Gemini 3, the samples were obtained as close to the mission as possible (2 days prior to launch) from both the flight and backup crews, so that the samples would remain viable. On Gemini 11, the samples were obtained 9 days prior to launch. On both flights, the leukocyte cultures were prepared and incubated at 37 degrees C, treated with colchicine, fixed and then chromosome preparations were made.

Irradiation was accomplished by identical experimental devices, one on the ground at the launch site, and the other on the righthand hatch of the Gemini 3 spacecraft. Each device contained 22 fluoroglass dosimeters. Approximately 9 hours before launch the two identical experiment devices were assembled and tested, then at 210 minutes before launch (for Gemini 3) and 150 minutes before launch (for Gemini 11), the flight unit was mounted into the spacecraft. On Gemini 3, the ground-control unit was placed inside a temperature-controlled cabinet, in which the temperature was periodically adjusted to correspond to the temperature readout from the spacecraft. The longer duration of Gemini 11 meant that the samples were in the weightless period much longer before they were irradiated. Samples were refrigerated inflight to ensure the survival of the leukocytes. Therefore, the ground control unit was placed inside a refrigerator that matched the refrigerator temperature of the inflight samples (2 to 4 degrees Celsius). Furthermore, the device provided a telemetry signal for monitoring the temperature on the ground, an improvement over the Gemini 3 mission.

Irradiation was initiated by the pilot 50 minutes and 18 seconds after launch, and continued for 20 minutes. Correspondingly, the ground unit was activated and deactivated at 52 and 72 minutes, respectively. Except for minor accelerations caused by maneuvering “burns” of the spacecraft, the flight device remained weightless for nearly 3.5 hours.

Ideally, the team wanted to use X- or gamma-rays to irradiate the blood samples, but could not for two reasons: (1) the small mass allotted to them for the experiment excluded it and (2) too much shielding would have been required to protect the flight crew. Therefore, beta-rays were chosen. Radioactive phosphorus (32P) was chosen as the radiation source for three reasons: (1)it emits only a single beta-particle, (2) the particle energy was suitable and (3) it had been used extensively in radiobiology studies to date. On Gemini 11, the amount of 32P in the device was decreased, since the samples would be subjected to increased beta-ray leakage and Bremsstrahlung radiation within the device.

After the mission, blood samples were obtained as soon as possible from the flight crew (6.5 hours after landing). By 10 hours after launch, all blood samples had been put into culture, and all cultures were fixed between 72 and 77 hours after launch. A cytogenetic analysis was made of each sample; the frequencies of chromosome aberrations were determined. Yields of both single-break and multiple-break aberrations were calculated, both for the flight samples as well as the ground samples.

Production of chromosomal aberrations is one of the best known effects of radiation, so it was selected as the parameter to measure for this study. Human leukocytes were chosen as the cell to be studied, since the cells would all be in a uniformly sensitive stage in the cell cycle and because the investigator team had extensive experience working with leukoctyes.

RESULTS:
Gemini 3 postflight analysis of the fluoroglass dosimeters in the experiment device showed that the doses, start/stop times of irradiation, and temperatures for the ground and flight units all agreed well. For Gemini 3, the flight device temperature stayed between 14 and 38 degrees Celsius, whereas the ground device stayed within a 2 to 29 degree Celsius range. For Gemini 11, the temperature of the flight device increased, starting at approximately 14 minutes after launch, to between 6 to 10 degrees Celsius and remained in that range for the first 24 hours of the mission. The device temperature decreased when the spacecraft was depressurized for the first extravehicular activity (EVA). The device operated within the normal 2 to 4 degree range until switched off simultaneously with the ground unit after approximately 65 hours inflight. The ground unit always remained within the normal temperature range. Later, it was discovered that an unusually high hatch temperature caused the inflight high refrigerator temperature. The higher temperatures did not affect the blood samples nor the results.

The dosimeters also confirmed that the radiation exposures were of the required duration. The inflight readings of the 22 dosimeters in the flight device compared well with the readings of the 22 dosimeters in the ground device. Doses were estimated for preflight and postflight by means of fluoroglass or Fricke-solution dosimetry. As a result, there was a 2 rad dose on the ground samples, with a large portion (about one-third) of that being Bremsstrahlung with a peak energy of about 65 keV. The inflight package registered somewhat higher exposures than 2 rad.

All of the blood sample cultures were successful and yielded satisfactory chromosome preparations. Very little hemolysis was noted. A total of 4600 cells were analyzed.

Results showed that the occurrence of single-break aberrations was much higher in the flight samples. There was no significant difference between the yields of multiple-break aberrations in the flight and ground control samples. The flight crew chromosome aberration analyses showed no increase in aberration frequency due to space flight. However, the small positive effect seen in the differences of single-break aberrations did stimulate further scientific interest in this topic. It appeared that some space flight factor did interact synergistically with radiation to affect the chromosome rejoining system (i.e. the cell’s ability to repair damage), thus producing the single breaks.

On Gemini 11, a parallel test was also conducted on the bread mold Neurospora crassa. Those results are reported in another experiment record in this archive.
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.

experiment_title: Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation
parameter_html:
Head movements
Otolith responses
Spatial orientation
Visual cues
investigators: Principal Investigator: Oman, CharlesCo-Investigator: Carpenter- Smith, TheodoreCo-Investigator: Howard, Ian
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation experiment was one of three sensory motor and performance experiments performed during the 1998 Neurolab mission. This experiment focused on how the balance between visual and vestibular cues shifts toward the visual system in microgravity.

Using virtual reality, this investigation was designed to study how visual scene content and symmetry influenced the astronauts perception of up and down, to determine how quickly a moving visual scene would produce the illusion of self-motion, and to explore how the direction of perceived "down" altered the ability to recognize shapes and interpret curvature from shading.

Information gained from this experiment will help investigators understand why, in the absence of gravity, astronauts become dependent on visual stimuli. This information is also of potential value to medical researchers seeking insight into inner ear impairments and other balance disorders in Earth-bound patients, as well as related rehabilitative testing and training methods for those individuals. As an added value, portable head-mounted displays similar to the one developed for use in this experiment may prove useful for patients, perhaps someday even providing visual prostheses for the vestibularly impaired.

APPROACH:
The Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation experiment was performed using NASA's Virtual Environment Generator (VEG), a head-mounted display, which allowed the subjects to view a succession of visual scenes rendered by the VEG graphic computer. The VEG also tracked the motion of the head, so scenes that were displayed appeared stable when the head moved. The astronauts participated in three types of spatial orientation experiments:
1) the Virtual Tilting Room Test (ROOM)
2) the Linear Vection Test (VECTION)
3) the Object Recognition Test (OBJECT). Tests were performed with the astronaut free-floating and, alternately, wearing a constant force spring harness that provided artificial "down" cues to the shoulders and hips. Preflight ROOM, OBJECT and VECTION tests were performed 1 year before launch in NASA's training airplane, the KC-135, and in the laboratory at 90, 89, 60 and 59 days before launch. The OBJECT test was performed on flight day 3, and the ROOM and VECTION tests were performed on flight day 4, with an additional session performed by one subject on flight day 16. Postflight, all three tests were performed on the day of landing and 1, 2, 4 and 6 days after landing.

The ROOM test allowed investigators to study the influence of visual scene symmetry, scene rotation, orientation expectation, and tactile/proprioceptive cues on perceived self-tilt. Subjects wearing the VEG head mounted display viewed the interior of a virtual room. Two presentation types were used, static and continuously rotating at constant angular velocity. The VEG joystick, also called the Subject Interface Device (SID), recorded subject responses. The subject made comments using a microphone and entered notes after testing using the IBM Thinkpad laptop computer.

When free-floating, the subject's body was not in contact with the Spacelab; loose cloth tethers clipped between the restraint harness, D-rings on the center aisle, and rack handrails prevented the subject from drifting. When the subject was "standing," constraint force springs connecting the harness to the floor allowed the subject to stand erect with his feet on the floor, with proprioceptive and tactile compressive loading on the trunk and lower extremities.

Several hypotheses were tested during the ROOM sessions, including:
1) Visual reorientation illusions could be created in the frontal (roll) plane using a VEG-controlled, visual stimulus. Inversion illusions could be elicited in subjects susceptible to them, because the visual cues for static self-tilt perception are usually derived from the ambiguous underlying horizontal and vertical visual symmetries in conventional room interiors
2) A subject's indication of the subjective vertical can be predicted in rooms with differing degrees of visual symmetry (dotted, walled, or furnished rooms). A subject's self-tilt report in static and rotating virtual rooms depends (in a predictable way) not only on scene symmetry, but on expectation, which is determined by internal sensory cues associated with 0-g fluid shift and saccular unloading. The latter will be manipulated using preconditioning visual and haptic stimuli
3) As subjects adapt to weightlessness, their self-orientation becomes less biased by internal sensory cues and increasingly veridical.

The VECTION test was used with and without haptic cues to determine how quickly a moving visual scene would produce the illusion of self-motion. Haptic cues are clues that allow orientation by providing input from the restraint system that, for example, forces the feet against the floor, thereby giving the feeling of standing. The VEG was programmed to present a binocular "looming vection" display to the subject in successive 30-second tests. The stimulus velocity and subject orientation were manipulated across tests. Objects in the scene moved radially on the display, simulating subject movement along a path parallel to the visual axis.

The results suggested an increasing dependence on visual and haptic cues and indicated that less weight was given to otolithic cues (probably because their response to head tilt seems initially unfamiliar in 0-g). Otolith organs physically responded equally well to linear acceleration and head tilt. Therefore, it is important to know whether otolith responses to linear acceleration were also given less weight. If so, the linear, as well as angular, component of visually induced self-motion should show changes in 0-g. If all otolith cues are discounted in 0-g, the following was hypothesized for the VECTION test: 1) the latency of linear vection onset to constant velocity visual stimulation would be shorter; and 2) vection magnitude would increase faster and with fewer dropouts than on Earth.

The OBJECT test used two types of stimuli to study the influence of perceived "down" on the visual recognition of complex figures and interpretation of shading gradients. Whether an item was determined to be concave or convex depended on how the visual system interpreted the shading. Hypotheses for the OBJECT test included:
1) For complex figure recognition and shading gradient interpretation, the critical factor would be subjective orientation of the "perceptual down," the exocentric frame of reference cognitively adopted by the subject, not gravity
2) Because subjects can voluntarily change their exocentric reference frame, the experiment should show that this change results in object recognition and concavity/convexity interpretation.

RESULTS:
Eight of 8 nominally scheduled sessions were performed early in flight. One additional session was performed on flight day 16 before a hardware failure that prevented further additional sessions. Data appear to be of good quality based on the initial evaluation. Results from this experiment are expected to add insight into how the nervous system establishes a new balance between information gathered from the eyes, inner ear, and joints. This could help in the design of the next generation spacecraft, in the testing of patients with neurological diseases, and in understanding the relative role of vision in human spatial orientation not only in space, but also in our lives on Earth.

experiment_title: Astronaut Vision Issues and One Carbon Metabolism: Expanded Polymorphism Evaluation and Evaluation in a Potential Analog Population
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Several crewmembers who have flown on long-duration missions to the International Space Station (ISS) have developed ophthalmic issues now identified as Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). The one-carbon metabolic pathway, a broad set of metabolic reactions responsible for the activation and transfer of one-carbon units for many biosynthetic processes in the body, has been identified as a possible contributor to the development of SANS. This investigation seeks to identify genetic variation in the one-carbon metabolism pathway, the effect of these polymorphisms on enzyme function, and potential relationships to SANS. Additionally, this research will investigate the utility of a clinical population that shares many similar symptoms with SANS: patients with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). This investigation will expand upon a previous study, “Risk of visual impairment and intracranial hypertension after space flight: Evaluation of the role of polymorphism of enzymes involved in one-carbon metabolism” (One_Carbon), which examined five single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and the association with a genetic predisposition for ophthalmic issues among crewmembers.

This investigation has four Specific Aims:

1) Test for SNPs of the 85 major genes associated with one-carbon metabolism (a total of 523 SNPs) in ISS crewmembers and relate these data to existing one-carbon biochemistry and metabolomic data, along with existing vision and related medical data.
2) Gather ancestry data from the crewmembers and characterize the extent to which ancestry is predictive of ophthalmic issues after long-duration space flight.
3) Evaluate the data collected in this (and the initial) one-carbon metabolism genetics studies and cardiovascular data. To this end, we will request VO2 max (pre-, in-, and post-flight), Framingham Risk Score, resting heart rate along with diastolic and systolic blood pressure (pre-, in-, and post-flight), exercise heart rate and blood pressure (both diastolic and systolic, pre-, in-, and post-flight), data obtained as part of the Vascular Compliance Study (heart rate, blood pressure, cardiac output and stroke volume), medications, diagnoses, Body Mass Index (BMI), and % body fat data from the Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) project for evaluation relative to the one-carbon genetic and biochemical data.
4) Compare one-carbon metabolism genetics, biochemistry, and ophthalmologic data from ISS crewmembers to the same measures from patients in one of four treatment groups: (1) women diagnosed with PCOS without Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), (2) women diagnosed with PCOS and IIH, (3) women diagnosed with IIH without PCOS, and (4) control participants diagnosed with neither PCOS nor IIH.

APPROACH:
This investigation will examine genetic data from a total of 79 crewmembers who have participated in missions on the ISS.
Genetic data for two crewmembers who did not participate in the previous One_Carbon study will be obtained from a fasting blood sample. A medication and supplement log will also be obtained from the participants at this time. Genetic data from the 77 crew who participated in the previous study will be obtained from archived blood samples after those crew have provided consent.
Ancestry data will be collected from all subjects via a questionnaire/survey to determine if ancestry is predictive of genetic/ophthalmic issues after long-duration space flight. Consent will also be requested for data sharing of cardiovascular, vision and eye imagery data for evaluation relative to the one-carbon genetic and biochemical data.
In the PCOS arm of this study, a total of 150 participants will provide blood samples for biochemical and SNP analysis. Ophthalmologic testing in the PCOS population will include optic nerve ocular coherence tomography, fundus photography, and ultrasound examination, cycloplegic refraction (with visual acuity), and intraocular pressure. The results of these analyses will be compared to data from an age-matched control group that is not affected by PCOS or IIH and to the ISS crew data.
Per the original PI informed consent briefing, the genetic test data will not be archived with the LSDA. If data is requested for this experiment, must obtain original PI approval and subject must be re-consented.

RESULTS:
The investigators anticipate the results of this research will help characterize the genetic mechanism that influences the development of SANS in crew during spaceflight and provide guidance for preventing and treating these eye changes in astronauts. Further, this research will expand understanding of genetic influences on the one-carbon metabolic pathway and aid in the treatment and preventing of vision and other related diseases in the broader population.

experiment_title: AR/VR and Hybrid Reality for Verification Assessments: Phase 1
experiment_description:
Objective:

NASA has a growing interest in using extended reality (XR) technologies (virtual reality, augmented reality, and hybrid reality) verification and validation activities for the Spaceflight Program. To meet NASA minimum specifications, hardware systems are required to be verified human rated. Analysis, inspection, demonstration, and testing are several methods by which verification activities can be completed. Method determination depends on the requirement type, form factors of products, and test facility availability where verification activities can take place. Verification activities can be costly, as developers must often build high-fidelity physical mockups for certain verification tests. Leveraging XR technologies in human-in-the-loop testing requires little to no hardware, construction costs, or storage facilities, which is significant in cost savings. XR allows NASA systems to be replicated by a high-fidelity virtual reality simulation which approximates the appearance, size, and functionality of a real-world experience.

The validity of verification outcomes from XR methodologies are currently unclear. The researchers for this investigation will communicate directly with NASA subject matter experts (SMEs) on using XR for activities that can help this study. The biggest concern is that verification data collected with XR technology would not be comparable to data collected in a physical mockup using traditional methods. This could result in additional risk when used for flight readiness decisions. Taking this into consideration, NASA currently limits use of XR technologies for developmental test activities only. NASA needs data and theoretical knowledge to develop guidelines for how XR technology can be applied without increasing human health and performance risk for the future. This research will help NASA understand XR technologies strengths, limitations, and gaps.

This project has the following aim:
1.           To gather and synthesize available knowledge and generate new data that will help stakeholders make informed decisions regarding the use of XR technologies for verification-related activities.

Approach:
The literature review was carried out by the project team, an overview was created of how XR technology was used for verification and related activities, such as operational testing, examining evaluations, and training. Gathered information on XR training was the start towards understanding the strengths and weaknesses of XR for different tasks. The researchers interviewed experts and stakeholders, that allowed the researchers an understanding on XR technologies success. It also helped pinpoint the strengths, weaknesses, and barriers to implementation, while giving lessons on verification. This study included a pilot study to replicate verification activities using “equivalent” virtual and physical mockups. Results of the virtual and physical mockups are compared and provide validation for XR Verification Framework. The deliverables of Phase I are used for a separate Phase II investigation. Phase II will consist of a more comprehensive study to replicate and build upon the pilot study results.
The research was conducted according to the timeline and major milestones presented below: The projected duration of the project was 12 months.
·       Literature Review – ATP + 3 months
·       Interviews – ATP + 3 months
·       Requirements Framework – ATP + 5 months
·       Pilot study protocol peer review – ATP + 5 months
·       Pilot study – ATP + 7 months
·       Research report summarizing results of the pilot test, lessons learned, – ATP + 12months.


Results:
The results from the literature review, interviews, and the pilot study generated a report that helped future developers and researchers better understand when and how XR technologies are applied and when they should be avoided in hardware system verification and validation. Results from the literature review and SME interviews produced XR Verification Decision Framework. It is the first draft for NASA to make decisions on program requirements regarding XR technologies. The framework is the foundation for identifying gaps in research. The PI team created a VR duplicate of a high-fidelity physical mockup, the Habitable Airlock. Outcomes were observed to be about the same for both mockups with two exceptions. The appropriateness of VR mockups relative to a PR mockup was evaluated, but it is both resource intensive and impractical for NASA partners. PR and VR mockup for two verification-like tasks were compared, Hand Signal Identification and Field of View. These results support the cautious conclusion from phase 1, that VR might be best suited for demonstrations.

experiment_title: Artificial Intelligence for Tracking Micro-Behaviors in Longitudinal Data and Predicting Their Effect on Well-Being and Team Performance
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE

NASA advocates psychosocial dimensions of team functioning to be critical to the success of long-distance missions. A number of factors affect team functioning, including team composition, emergent states and other moderating factors. Studies in analog environments reveal that stress and physical exhaustion account for the majority of team conflicts, with team creativity and performance on 10 intellective tasks decreasing over time. These findings suggest that team functioning during long duration missions can change in a dynamic manner and can be affected by brief, often unconscious, micro-behaviors between the team members, which are best measured via observation. Future long-distance space exploration will have a number of challenges that increase the risk of inadequate cooperation, coordination, collaboration, and psychosocial adaptation, and can lead to behavioral health and performance decrements. In this proposed research, it is hypothesized that micro-behaviors captured via audiovisual recordings, quantified via linguistic and acoustic measures, and automatically detected via artificial intelligence (AI) can provide unique insights into operationally- relevant team performance, beyond self-report team functioning measures. Micro-behaviors are small, often unconscious gestures, words and tone of voice which can influence how included (or not) the people around us feel. The most common type of micro-behaviors are micro-aggressions. Micro aggressions can have detrimental impact to well-being and team performance. Micro-affirmations reflect inclusion and caring and can counter-act the harmful effects of micro-aggressions.

This research will have three primary aims:

1. Leverage advance multimodal data analytics to detecting micro-behaviors in longitudinal team interactions.
2. Identify emotional reactivity to micro-behaviors.
3. Incorporate knowledge on micro-behaviors to predict operationally relevant team performance.




APPROACH

Previously collected peer and mission control ratings, physiological, audio and team task performance data from HERA 4 and 5 campaigns will also be analyzed. Machine learning algorithms will be leveraged to learn complex multimodal patterns of micro-behaviors. This study will deploy a mixed-methods approach to detect micro-behaviors by coding 25% of the data with human coders, this will be followed by automatic detection of micro-behaviors in the remaining a 75% data through AI algorithms. Crew interactions will be identified automatically via detection of turn-taking and speech overlap. Reliability checks will be conducted manually to address any discrepancies.

RESULTS

Results from this research contribute to a greater understanding of factors that affect team operation and performance in isolated and confined environments (ICE), and the effective management of future space crews. Particularly relevant to this project is the focus on micro-behaviors, that is small, often unconscious gestures, words and tone of voice which can influence how included (or not included) the people in the team feel. The proposed AI methods allow us to track micro-behaviors on a moment-to moment basis, thus potentially yielding a more complete picture of team dynamics.
Exploratory analysis suggests that negative micro-behaviors included increased sentences with passive voice for both the sender and the target, potentially due to the subtlety of their expression. Negative micro-behaviors also depicted fewer second-person personal pronouns (e.g., “you”) compared to turns without those behaviors. While this finding for negative micro-behaviors might initially be nonintuitive, since blaming language tends to include a large number of second-person pronouns, this result might also reflect fact that negative micro-behaviors are many times indistinct and not sharply expressed. Positive micro-behaviors had significantly higher positive affect, lower percentage of angry language, and higher percentage of language related to achievements compared to negative micro-behaviors. Acoustic turn similarity between sender and target was the highest for instances of positive micro-behaviors (i.e., indicating convergence between speakers) and the lowest for instances of negative micro-behaviors (i.e., indicating divergence between speakers).
The PI team leveraged machine learning classifiers and dialog state tracking models, combined with natural language processing techniques relying on lexicon-based methods and data-driven methods, to learn complex multimodal patterns of micro-behaviors and automatically detect positive and negative microbehaviors between team members. The experimental findings indicate that the psycholinguistic
markers extracted using the linguistic inquiry and word count (LIWC), STRESSnet dictionaries, and acoustic features can achieve an f1-score up to 55% in a three-class classification problem, which is well-above the 33% chance accuracy. The findings also suggest that modeling turns between the sender and target of micro-behaviors is significantly more effective in detecting micro-behavior than only modeling the sender’s information. Finally, the PI team demonstrate the effect of introducing context for detection purposes. __description:
OBJECTIVE

NASA advocates psychosocial dimensions of team functioning to be critical to the success of long-distance missions. A number of factors affect team functioning, including team composition, emergent states and other moderating factors. Studies in analog environments reveal that stress and physical exhaustion account for the majority of team conflicts, with team creativity and performance on 10 intellective tasks decreasing over time. These findings suggest that team functioning during long duration missions can change in a dynamic manner and can be affected by brief, often unconscious, micro-behaviors between the team members, which are best measured via observation. Future long-distance space exploration will have a number of challenges that increase the risk of inadequate cooperation, coordination, collaboration, and psychosocial adaptation, and can lead to behavioral health and performance decrements. In this proposed research, it is hypothesized that micro-behaviors captured via audiovisual recordings, quantified via linguistic and acoustic measures, and automatically detected via artificial intelligence (AI) can provide unique insights into operationally- relevant team performance, beyond self-report team functioning measures. Micro-behaviors are small, often unconscious gestures, words and tone of voice which can influence how included (or not) the people around us feel. The most common type of micro-behaviors are micro-aggressions. Micro aggressions can have detrimental impact to well-being and team performance. Micro-affirmations reflect inclusion and caring and can counter-act the harmful effects of micro-aggressions.

This research will have three primary aims:

1. Leverage advance multimodal data analytics to detecting micro-behaviors in longitudinal team interactions.
2. Identify emotional reactivity to micro-behaviors.
3. Incorporate knowledge on micro-behaviors to predict operationally relevant team performance.




APPROACH

Previously collected peer and mission control ratings, physiological, audio and team task performance data from HERA 4 and 5 campaigns will also be analyzed. Machine learning algorithms will be leveraged to learn complex multimodal patterns of micro-behaviors. This study will deploy a mixed-methods approach to detect micro-behaviors by coding 25% of the data with human coders, this will be followed by automatic detection of micro-behaviors in the remaining a 75% data through AI algorithms. Crew interactions will be identified automatically via detection of turn-taking and speech overlap. Reliability checks will be conducted manually to address any discrepancies.

Results from this research contribute to a greater understanding of factors that affect team operation and performance in isolated and confined environments (ICE), and the effective management of future space crews. Particularly relevant to this project is the focus on micro-behaviors, that is small, often unconscious gestures, words and tone of voice which can influence how included (or not included) the people in the team feel.
