experiment_title: Influence of Weightlessness on Baroreflex Function
parameter_html:
Baroreflex range
Baroreflex slope
Blood pressure
Heart rate
Orthostatic intolerance
RR interval
investigators: Principal Investigator: Meck, Janice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to weightlessness alters postflight cardiovascular responses to exercise and standing. Although these changes are probably initiated during flight, they are not known to impair cardiovascular performance in space. However, functional problems become apparent upon landing, when most astronauts have reduced exercise capacity and orthostatic intolerance. Loss of plasma volume during weightlessness may be partially responsible for orthostatic intolerance.

Orthostatic intolerance is a predictable, but a poorly understood consequence of space travel. Because arterial baroreceptors modulate abrupt pressure transients, including those provoked by standing, the hypothesis that space flight impairs baroreflex mechanisms was tested.

APPROACH:
Vagally-medicated carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex responses (provoked by neck pressure changes) in the supine position and heart rate and blood pressure in the supine and standing positions were studied in 16 U.S. astronauts (15 male and one female) before and after four to five day Space Shuttle missions. Preflight studies were performed nominally 10 and five days before launch; in practice, preflight data were collected between 13 and seven days, and again between seven and five days before launch. Postflight data were collected on landing (R+0), on R+3, and again on R+8.

The electrocardiogram, respiration (abdominal bellows connected to a strain-gauge pressure transducer), and neck chamber pressure were recorded by FM tape and strip chart recorders. The electrocardiogram and respiration were recorded during the last five minutes of a 20-minute rest period prior to any intervention. Resting vagal-cardiac activity was estimated from average R-R intervals and their standard deviations. Blood pressure was measured manually with a sphygmomanometer before barorector testing.

RESULTS:
On landing day, astronauts’ resting R-R intervals and standard deviations, and the slope, range, and position of their resting R-R intervals on the carotid transmural pressure-sinus mode response relation (operational point) were reduced relative to preflight values. Reductions of operational points (indicating reduced hypotensive buffering capacity) were related directly and significantly to reductions of postflight systolic pressure responses to standing. After landing day, baroreflex slopes and ranges were subnormal and remained so for the duration of the study (eight to 10 days). These results suggest that short-duration space flight leads to significant, functionally relevant impairment of human baroreflex mechanisms.

experiment_title: Dose Tracker Application for Monitoring Crew Medication Usage, Symptoms, and Adverse Effects during Missions
parameter_html:
Medication efficacy
Medication frequency
Medication side effects
Medication dosage
Medication usage
investigators: Principal Investigator: Wotring, VirginiaCo-Investigator: Smith, Larona
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During space flight, the body undergoes a number of physiological changes that are expected to result in altered interactions with administered medications, but it is not yet known if, or to what extent, these actually occur. The potential for therapeutically relevant alteration in either pharmacokinetics (how the body handles administered medications) or pharmacodynamics (how administered medications act upon the body) has long been a concern.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Develop an iOS application for the collection of medication usage data from crewmember participants during their missions.
  2. Employ the application to collect inflight medication usage data to elucidate whether a) data suggest in-flight pharmacokinetic changes (alterations in how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolizes or excretes a medication), b) data suggest inflight pharmacodynamic changes (alterations in how the medication interacts with target molecules and biochemical pathways), or c) unusual side effects occur during flight (frequency or quality).
  3. Use the application with the same individuals pre-flight to collect ground medication usage data as a basis for comparing medication usage and effects in the same individuals.
  4. Acquire sufficient inflight medication usage data to provide the necessary variance and effect-size information required to properly power future studies when they are needed.

APPROACH:
A handheld device-based questionnaire was used to permit fast and efficient collection of data regarding crewmembers’ medication use on a near real-time basis, eliminating the current problems associated with recall over periods of weeks. Specific questions regarding medication use were asked of each participating crewmember. The data collection process was streamlined by using a flexibly programmed computerized survey application that leverages the limited medication choices aboard, the doses available, typical dosing frequency, and side effects associated with each medication to provide an individualized short questionnaire for each medication use by the crewmember. Coded data was delivered weekly to a secure server on the ground for analysis by study investigators. Pre-flight, each participating crewmember recorded their medication usage for a duration equivalent to their on-orbit mission, so that their ground medication usage frequencies, doses, and perceptions could be compared to those recorded during flight.

This experiment was also conducted in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA), during HERA 1 Campaign, missions 2-4 to test the ease and usability of the handheld device in regards medication usage.

RESULTS:
Six crewmembers completed flight data collection and five completed ground data collection before NASA’s early study discontinuation. There were 5766 medication use entries, averaging 20.6 ± 8.4 entries per subject per flight week. Types of medications and their indications were similar to previous reports, with sleep disturbances and muscle/joint pain as primary drivers. Two subjects treated prolonged skin problems. Subjects also used the application in unanticipated ways: to note Drug Tolerance Testing or medication holiday per research protocols, and to share data with flight surgeons. Subjects also provided usability feedback on application design and implementation.

The volume of data collected (20.6 ± 8.4 entries per subject per flight week) is much greater than was collected previously (< 12 per person per entire mission), despite user criticisms regarding app usability. It seems likely that improvements in a software-based questionnaire application could result in a robust data collection tool that astronauts find more acceptable, while simultaneously providing researchers and clinicians with useful data.

experiment_title: Special Hematological Effects; Dynamic Changes in Red Cell Shape in Response to the Space-Flight Environment
parameter_html:
Hematocrit
Hemoglobin
Erythrocytes, number
Erythrocytes, shape
Potassium influx, erythrocytes
Specific gravity, erythrocytes
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kimzey, StephenCo-Investigator: Burns, Linda
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Rapid fluid shifts are known to occur in the body during transitions between the normal one-g environment of the Earth and the weightless environment of space. These shifts produce changes of unknown magnitude to the body's regulatory mechanisms. With regard to hematological changes, medical studies conducted in support of the Gemini and Apollo programs suggested possible influences of the space-flight environment on red blood cell integrity and the normal regulation of the circulating red blood cell mass. Skylab experiment M115 was specifically designed to investigate, detect, and characterize alterations in red cell shape either during or following extended exposure to the space environment.

APPROACH:
Blood samples were collected by venipuncture from the Skylab crew and from a ground-based control group of subjects during the pre-, in-, and postflight phase of each mission. All samples were obtained using the In-flight Blood Collection System (IBCS), and processed or stabilized within minutes of collection. Anticoagulants were used to collect samples for some tests. In-flight samples were collected in Na2EDTA and immediately separated by centrifugation into plasma and cellular phases by the in-flight sample processor, specially designed to operate in a weightless environment. The separated in-flight samples were frozen at -20 degrees Celsius and stored on board until postflight recovery and transfer to the ground laboratory for analysis.

In addition to measurements of standard hematologic parameters such as total red blood cell population, hemoglobin, and hematocrit, the experiment included morphological studies of red blood cells. Hemoglobin concentrations were measured during flight using a hemoglobin meter in conjunction with each in-flight blood draw. Postflight, duplicate measurements of the hemoglobin concentration measured in-flight were made using the cyanmethemoglobin method and compared to hemoglobin meter measurements. The active and passive components of potassium transport into red blood cells were determined using a ouabain inhibition, 86Rb substitution technique.

For morphological studies, the red blood cells from blood samples collected during the pre-, in-, and postflight phases of each Skylab mission were fixed in a fixative solution containing 1.0 milliliters of 0.5 percent glutaraldehyde (pH 7.4). Time in the fixative varied from 1 hour for pre- and postflight samples to 1, 2, 24, 57, and 81 days for in-flight samples (this variation had no effect on cell morphology). Following fixation, the cells were dehydrated with ethanol and then 50 percent amyl acetate/50 percent ethanol. The samples were critical point dried in a Denton critical point drying apparatus. The samples were then coated with a gold/palladium mixture and examined under a scanning electron microscope. The cells were categorized according to the cell shapes listed below:
Discocyte (disc-shaped, normal)
Leptocyte (thin, flat)
Codocyte (bell-shaped)
Stomatocyte (single concavity)
Knizocyte (pinched, triconcave)
Echinocyte (spiny)

RESULTS:
Hematology
The red blood cell count, hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit were below preflight levels in all three crewmen immediately following the Skylab 2 flights. The red cell count showed a gradual recovery by postflight days 4 to 7, but the hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration were below preflight levels during the 18-day postflight period. On Skylab missions 3 and 4, the red cell count and associated measurements were somewhat different from those on Skylab 2. The red blood cell count, hemoglobin concentration, and hematocrit were increased on recovery as compared to preflight, but began to decrease by postflight day 1, and were significantly lower than preflight values by postflight day 3. On both missions 3 and 4, these hemoconcentration-dependent parameters gradually returned to within preflight limits during the 3-week postflight period. Changes in the plasma volume were thought to be the cause for the alterations in the hemoconcentration-dependent parameters.

A consistent shift in the specific gravity profile immediately after flight toward a population of heavier cells was observed. The most dramatic changes were observed after the shorter Skylab 2 flight. On all missions the changes were transient and by postflight day 3, the population distributions of the cells were within preflight ranges. The specific gravity shift was believed to be caused by alterations in red cell membrane lipid content, cell water content, cell electrolyte concentrations, or a combination of all these factors. There were no significant changes in either the active or the passive component of potassium influx following the Skylab 2 flight. However, after Skylab 3 and 4 flights, there were significant elevations in the ouabain-sensitive, metabolism-dependent potassium influx in four of six crewmembers. The increase in potassium influx observed at recovery had returned to normal rates by postflight days 3 to 7. It was speculated that this change might be a response to transient alteration in the dynamic state of equilibrium existing across the cellular membrane with respect to electrolytes and water.

Red Cell Shape Classification
Eighty to ninety percent (80-90%) of red cells were classified as discocytes (normal shaped cells) in the preflight phase. After flight, red cells were 83% discocytes, which was not significantly different from preflight percentages. The remaining 15-20% of the nondiscoid cells present during the preflight control phase of each mission consisted primarily of leptocytes, stomatocytes, and knizocytes. During exposure of the crews to the space-flight environment, the frequency of echinocytes increased significantly, and this increase appeared to be related to the duration of each mission. The majority of the echinocytes present in these samples were of the stage I type with few progressing to stages II or III. Postflight samples indicate less than 1% of the population of cells were echinocytes, which was comparable to preflight. Therefore, a rapid reversal of echinocytes to discocytes was observed. The occurrence of echinocytes was attributed to changes in plasma, including elevations of plasma lecithin, lysolecithin, and/or free fatty acids.

The most dramatic changes were observed after the shorter Skylab 2 flight. On all missions the changes were transient and by postflight day 3, the population distributions of the cells were within preflight ranges. The specific gravity shift was believed to be caused by alterations in red cell membrane lipid content, cell water content, cell electrolyte concentrations, or a combination of all these factors. There were no significant changes in either the active or the passive component of potassium influx following the Skylab 2 flight. However, after Skylab 3 and 4 flights, there were significant elevations in the ouabain-sensitive, metabolism-dependent potassium influx in four of six crewmembers. The increase in potassium influx observed at recovery had returned to normal rates by postflight days 3 to 7. It was speculated that this change might be a response to transient alteration in the dynamic state of equilibrium existing across the cellular membrane with respect to electrolytes and water.

Red Cell Shape Classification
Eighty to ninety percent (80-90%) of red cells were classified as discocytes (normal shaped cells) in the preflight phase. After flight, red cells were 83% discocytes, which was not significantly different from preflight percentages. The remaining 15-20% of the nondiscoid cells present during the preflight control phase of each mission consisted primarily of leptocytes, stomatocytes, and knizocytes. During exposure of the crews to the space-flight environment, the frequency of echinocytes increased significantly, and this increase appeared to be related to the duration of each mission. The majority of the echinocytes present in these samples were of the stage I type with few progressing to stages II or III. Postflight samples indicate less than 1% of the population of cells were echinocytes, which was comparable to preflight. Therefore, a rapid reversal of echinocytes to discocytes was observed. The occurrence of echinocytes was attributed to changes in plasma, including elevations of plasma lecithin, lysolecithin, and/or free fatty acids.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As with the Gemini, Apollo and Skylab missions, the primary purpose of this study on the Apollo-Soyuz mission was to provide hematologic and immunologic data for the assessment of crew health preflight and postflight. A second objective was to evaluate the influence of space flight on the immunohematologic system. Supporting data and sample logistics were provided for the Cellular Immune Response and the Polymorphonuclear Leukocyte Response studies.

APPROACH:
Blood samples were collected by venipuncture from the crewmen on L-30 (30 days preflight), L-15 and L-5, R+0 (recovery day) and R+1 (1 day postflight), R+2, R+4, R+8, R+13, and R+29. In addition, identical samples were collected from the backup crewmen and three ground-based control subjects preflight and during the mission.

Radioisotope studies using chromium 51 (Cr51) and iodine 125 (I 125) to determine red cell mass and plasma volume, respectively, were conducted on L-15, R+0, and R+28.

RESULTS:
Varying degrees of hemodilution were evidenced in all three crewmen postflight. A slight reduction in red blood cell count was found postflight. Hematocrit and hemoglobin were slightly decreased at R+0 and decreased further 10-15% by R+3. These changes were the result of shifts in plasma volume inflight and postflight and are similar to those observed in previous manned space flights.

Methemoglobin increased to 4.2% at R+0 compared to 1.3 % at preflight. By R+1, it had dropped to a mean value of 2.0%. This transient rise was most likely caused by crew exposure to nitrogen tetroxide (N2O4) vapors during reentry.

There was a decrease in lymphocyte percentage postflight, but absolute lymphocyte count did not change. White blood cell count was significantly increased postflight due to increased absolute neutrophil count. The elevated neutrophil levels persisted and even showed a further increase in two of the crewmen. This continued elevation was possibly related to the resultant pulmonary damage and subsequent steroid therapy due to N2O4 exposure.

The reticulocyte counts were unchanged immediately postflight. There are no data on reticulocyte counts during the subsequent 2-week period, when the red cell mass was being replaced. However, based on previous data, only a modest response would be expected. Classification of reticulocytes, based on density of the residual intracellular ribosomal network, indicated no significant shift in the age distribution of the reticulocytes on R+0 or R+1.

Red cell mass decreases were observed immediately postflight in the two crewmembers tested. The mean decrease of 8% was less than the 10% decrease from Apollo 14-17. The change noted in one crewman was 2.5 times higher than the other crewman. By R+28, red cell mass was recovering and was decreased only 3% from preflight. Red cell survival was slightly decreased in one crewman. Plasma volume showed an 11% decrease which was greater than the mean 4.4% decrease seen in Apollo 14-17. It is possible that exposure to nitrogen tetroxide partially accounted for the greater decrease in plasma volume after this mission than in previous missions. The plasma volume of both crewmembers had returned to near preflight values by R+28. The plasma volume loss produced higher peripheral hematocrits obtained shortly after recovery (44%) than were obtained preflight (41%).

Individuals showed varied immunologic responses. No significant plasma protein abnormalities were found preflight or postflight. Total serum protein levels showed some postflight variation that was probably due to the changing plasma volume. Serum protein electrophoretic patterns were normal, except for a low albumin value on R+28.

There was a 48% elevation in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) on R+0. The distribution of LDH isoenymes did not change drastically, but there were slight elevations in the fifth band. The diagnostic significance of this small elevation in the fifth band was undetermined. Lipoprotein fractions were normal.

The most significant alteration in serum protein quantitation was a postflight elevation in the haptoglobin concentration. This change was observed frequently in crewmen returning from the earlier Apollo missions. It may have reflected an acute phase protein response, perhaps caused by tissue destruction. Because of exposure to N2O4 during recovery and subsequent lung tissue damage, it is impossible to identify the specific effects of space flight on the haptoglobin levels in this crew. The fact that the maximum values were observed 3 to 4 days after recovery is also suggestive of a response to the toxic gas rather than to weightlessness.

No changes in immunoglobins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD) were observed, with the exception of a reduction in the IgG levels in one crewman. His postflight concentration of 909 mg/100ml of serum was within the normal range but was 34% below his preflight mean.

A significant shift occurred in red cell morphology postflight. Discocytes dropped 28% and remained below the preflight mean throughout the postflight examination period. There were significantly more stomatocytes, spherocytes, and knizocytes postflight. There was also evidence of cell fragmentation and increased echinocytes. The implications of these data are not clear, but it would appear that morphology was aggravated by exposure to the space environment or N2O4.

The C-reactive protein was negative at R+0 but strongly positive on R+1. This change probably reflects the tissue destruction observed in the crew on R+1.

Iron turnover was not determined postflight. Spleen-liver ratios showed no rise in the crewmembers, but did in the controls. This is evidence against splenic trapping as the cause of the decreased red cell mass.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Sauer, RichardPrincipal Investigator: McMonigal, Kathleen
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Iodine has been used as a potable water treatment and storage bactericidal agent by NASA for over three decades beginning with the Apollo program, and was a critical factor for the achievement of human space flight. Iodine is currently used for Space Shuttle potable water microbial control and the U.S. component of the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS U.S. water system recycles water from urine and other wastewaters for human consumption and requires long-term storage. With the proposed iodine exposure levels and the crewmembers originating from many countries including regions of low iodine intake, concerns have been raised regarding the use of iodine in ISS potable water.

Iodine is a component of the two major thyroid hormones, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). These hormones regulate many key biochemical processes. Major target organs are the developing brain, muscle, heart, pituitary, and kidney. Most ingested iodine is reduced in the gut to iodide, which is absorbed almost completely. Once in circulation, iodide is removed primarily by the thyroid gland and kidney. The thyroid selectively concentrates iodide with the excess excreted into the urine. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), produced in the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, regulates the release of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland into the blood. TSH secretion from the pituitary gland increases when the levels of circulating thyroid hormones decrease. The thyroid responds to the ingestion of elevated quantities of iodine by a transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis, termed the acute Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

An investigation was undertaken during three ground-based, closed-chamber tests to examine thyroid function and hormone levels in chamber subjects who consumed potable water containing iodine. The purpose of this study was to document the thyroid functional biochemical measurements (n=12), urine iodine levels (n=8), and any clinical signs or symptoms of thyroid dysfunction in the 12 crewmembers who participated in the chamber studies.

APPROACH:

The chamber tests, in order of occurrence, were 30 days, Phase II; 60 days, Phase IIa; and 91 days, Phase III. Each chamber test had four crewmembers. Each crewmember was considered to be in good health and had normal thyroid function. In all three chamber tests, after the water recycling process was completed, 3.5 to 5.2 mg iodine/L was added to the water as the disinfectant. In Phase II (30 days) and Phase IIa (60 days), thyroid hormonal status (TSH and thyroid hormone levels) was assessed both in the pre- and postchamber period. In Phase III, the 91-day study, TSH, thyroid hormones, and urinary iodine levels were measured before and several times in chamber (first measurement at the 30-day mark). These were followed up with several more measurements in the postchamber period upon the subjects' exit from the chamber at the completion of the study. Subjects were monitored until all indices of iodine/thyroid status had returned to prechamber levels.

For the Phase III study (91 days), due to changes in TSH levels at the 30-day mark, iodine was removed from the potable water before consumption. This was accomplished by installing an iodine-removal device and a microbial filter (0.2 µm) at the point of use of the water on chamber day 35. This device removed the iodine (I2 and I-) from the drinking water but did not affect the iodine levels in the remainder of the water used, i.e., for hygiene activities. Urinary iodine levels were spot-checked to determine iodine exposure.

RESULTS:

While individual water consumption was not determined for Phases II and IIa crewmembers, analysis of diet records and the systematic evaluation of water usage indicates the crewmembers consumed from 4 to 10 mg total iodine/day. For Phase IIa (60 days), drinking water contained approximately 2 to 4 mg I/L and subjects excreted approximately 4.5 to 14 mg/day. Intake measurements were only completed twice during the study. The actual individual water iodine intakes and urinary losses were quantified for the Phase III, 91-day test. The total iodine in the water varied from approximately 3 to 8 mg/L with an average level for the first 35 days around 5 mg total iodine/L. Urinary iodine levels reflect recent iodine consumption. In all subjects, urinary iodine levels increased about 10-fold during the first 30 days of the Phase III chamber study, with iodine consumption levels ranging from 8 to 20 mg/day. Urinary excretion means for subjects ranged from 9.4 to 16.9 mg I/day. The variation in iodine intake between crewmembers was related to the individual volume of potable water consumed. Following installation of the iodine removal device at the galley sink, the total iodine levels measured less than 0.05 mg/L in the drinking water but remained in full concentration in the shower and wash water. Urinary iodine levels decreased 5- to 10-fold after cessation of the water iodine exposure but remained above baseline values. By the end of the 91-day study, 56 days after cessation of drinking water iodine, the urinary values continued to remain above baseline values in three of the four subjects. In three of the crewmembers, urine iodine levels fell to an average of 0.283 mg/24 hrs by three days after test completion.

Although mean TSH levels remained within normal range throughout the studies, there was a statistically significant increase in TSH levels in the Phase II and III studies. For the Phase II study, the values returned to baseline levels in all subjects within two weeks after the subjects exited the chamber. In the 60-day Phase IIa study, although not a statistically significant change, serum TSH in three of the four subjects had increased by the end of the study. One subject, who had a baseline TSH value close to the upper limit, had a decreased TSH value below the baseline value at the end of the chamber study. This subject had the highest iodine consumption and urinary levels of the four subjects in the Phase IIa test. At day 62 postchamber, this subject had a very high TSH level and was referred for medical evaluation by an endocrinologist. There were no other biochemical or clinical signs of thyroid disease, and the TSH returned to near baseline value several months later.

In the 91-day study, the mean serum TSH level in the four test subjects increased significantly above baseline values 30 days after entering the chamber. After the iodine was removed from the drinking water on day 35 (concentration < 0.05 mg/L), the TSH values gradually decreased but did not completely return to baseline during the subsequent 56 days in the chamber.

For one subject in the Phase III study, the TSH remained higher than the baseline value but within the normal reference range throughout the chamber study period, with no decrease in the level after removal of iodine from the drinking water. After one year, the TSH levels returned to prechamber baseline levels. All other measures of thyroid function remained within normal ranges. The consulting endocrinologist diagnosed the crewmember with iodine-induced subclinical hyperthyroidism.

During the Phase III study, urinary iodine levels remained at approximately 1 mg/day after iodine removal from drinking water at day 35, but returned to baseline levels within three days of exiting the chamber. One potential source of iodine contamination involved the methods for urine collection and measurement. A study was completed and found that this was not the cause of the persistence of urinary iodine levels above baseline. Other potential sources of iodine contamination were discussed and considered, however, no plausible explanation was identified.

The results from the three chamber tests demonstrated that the levels of iodine in the potable water system proposed for the ISS were too high. Since these studies were concluded, the Food and Nutrition Board has established an upper limit for iodine intakes from all sources as 1.1 mg/day. The subjects in the chamber studies exceeded this level and consequently, for two subjects, TSH levels were significantly changed by the end of the chamber test. Since food consumption provides about 0.25 mg/day, the requirement was set at a maximum of 0.25 mg of iodine/L in ISS water supplied by the United States. This would limit water consumption to a maximum of 3 L/day to maintain daily intake levels from all sources at less than the limit established by NASA of less than 1.0 mg/day of iodine. Consequently, there remains concern that the maximum level of 0.25 mg/L of iodine in the spacecraft water will not provide sufficient microbial control, thus increasing the risk to ISS crewmembers.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A previous study reported that the risk of developing a herniated nucleus pulposus (HNP) was higher in U.S. astronauts who had flown at least one mission, as compared with those in the NASA Astronaut Corps who had not yet flown. However, the study did not account for the cumulative effect of multiple missions. While many HNPs occurred well into astronauts’ careers or in some cases years after retirement, the higher incidence of HNPs relatively soon after completion of space missions suggests that space flight does increase the risk of HNP. To formally investigate this possibility, the investigators used a competing-risks survival model to analyze reports and dates of first HNP occurrences from 330 U.S. astronauts taking part in 745 space missions over 55 years. In this model, the outcome of interest, time from selection into the Astronaut Corps to first report of HNP is modeled as the minimum of several event times, one following each space mission plus one influenced by astronaut training and general lifestyle irrespective of participation in actual missions.

Although returning crewmembers have higher incidence of disc herniation post-flight, it is unknown if this increased incidence is related or contributes to an increased risk of injury due to dynamic loads. The aims of this study are as follows:

  1. Mine existing human space flight data on the incidence and severity of vertebral disc herniation after space flight.
  2. Analyze data (perform meta-analysis, statistics, etc.).
  3. Determine the correlation of herniation risk to flight duration and landing impact severity.

APPROACH:
This study was completed using data provided by the NASA Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) covering the period from 1959 to February 2014. OBJECTIVES:
A previous study reported that the risk of developing a herniated nucleus pulposus (HNP) was higher in U.S. astronauts who had flown at least one mission, as compared with those in the NASA Astronaut Corps who had not yet flown. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts in the space environment are at risk for a variety of health-related concerns from exposure to accelerated ions that can pass through the spacecraft hull and interact with astronauts’ cells within the body. These particles are released from the sun in solar particle events (SPE) and exist as part of the galactic cosmic ray (GCR) background radiation, although the types of ions and their energies can differ widely in SPE and GCR. A significant concern for astronaut health is an increased risk of cancer, which is linked to a variety of radiation exposures. The underlying cause of cancer, regardless of its source, is mutations in critical genes and ongoing gains, losses, and rearrangement of chromosomes. Collectively, these ongoing changes in the cell are termed genomic instability. The goal of this study was to determine how frequently different types of accelerated ions found in the GCR cause mutations and genomic instability and to describe what these changes look like. To better extrapolate the results to potential harms to astronauts from space radiation, the investigators used a mouse model for the study. This ensured that the cell types of interest found in the spleen and kidney will be exposed to accelerated ions in their normal tissue environment. A second goal of the study was to determine if mutant cells induced by space radiation exhibit signs of genomic instability, which are ongoing changes to the genome and common in many types of cancer.

APPROACH:
Investigators used an in vivo system, in which mice were exposed to a specific ion at three or more doses, because this best mimics what will happen to astronaut tissues. The mice have a genetic marker that allows mutant cells to be selected directly from cells isolated from exposed tissues. Although the mutant cells are then grown in culture to obtain material for molecular and sometimes cytogenetic analyses to determine the types of mutational events induced by exposure, mutation formation occurred in cells in the normal tissue environment within the mouse. Investigators isolated and examined mutant cells from the kidney (epithelial cells) and the spleen (blood T cells).

RESULTS:
Most work was performed with the kidney epithelial cells. In all cases, the investigators observed increased numbers of mutant cells per tissue after exposure to the ions, and in some cases (Ti and Fe ions) at doses equivalent to approximately one to two particles per cell nucleus. Simply stated, a single particle passing through a cell is the lowest possible exposure, aside from no exposure. For Fe, Ti, O, and Si ions, investigators observed a linear increase in mutations as a function of dose. The only exception was for Ti ions at the highest dose tested because no increase was observed relative to the next lower dose. For protons, no increase was observed at the lower doses tested (0.5 to 3.0 Gy), with a dramatic rise in mutations at 4 and 5 Gy. Average exposures in space for a Mars trip will be approximately 0.2 to 0.4 Gy, but could be higher if a major solar flare occurs, which would release large amounts of protons.

The mutant cells investigators selected were due to mutations that affected mouse chromosome 8. Thus, they focused molecular and cytogenetic studies on this chromosome and identified three types of radiation signature mutations, which are rare in spontaneous mutant cells isolated from unexposed mouse kidneys and relatively common in mutant cells induced by accelerated ion exposure. These are 1) large deletions in which a large piece of chromosome 8 is lost, 2) loss of portions of chromosome 8 that are not linked to loss of the target gene (discontinuous), and 3) translocations in which a portion of chromosome 8 is fused to a piece of another chromosome.

The selection assay only selected for mutational events affecting chromosome 8: To search for evidence of genomic instability, investigators also examined other chromosomes in the space radiation induced kidney cells for evidence of additional mutations. Although they found mutations affecting other chromosomes in both spontaneous mutants and mutants from the exposed kidneys, these genomic mutations were both quantitatively more frequent and qualitatively distinct in the mutant cells isolated from the irradiated kidneys. A detailed analysis of mutant cells isolated from Fe ion exposed kidneys demonstrated that these cells had very extensive genomic damage, similar to what would be expected in cancer cells. The goal for future research will be to determine if signature mutations and more extensive genomic damage will be observed in cancers induced by space radiation exposure in the kidney. If so, investigators will have identified markers that distinguish space radiation induced cancers from those that occur spontaneously, and in doing so will have established an absolute link between mutations and cancers induced by the space environment.

Investigators also examined space radiation mutagenesis in T cells from the spleen. T cells can give rise to leukemias and lymphomas, which are distinct from cancers that occur in epithelial tissues. These cells are more difficult to grow than kidney epithelial cells, so they restricted their analysis to chromosome 8. They identified radiation signature mutations (large deletions and discontinuous mutations), though unlike the kidney cells they did not observe these mutations at the highest doses tested. They believe that this absence occurred because the T cells are more sensitive to radiation exposure and high doses killed most of the mutant cells that were also induced. Interestingly, the kinetics of radiation signature mutation was similar to that reported by another group for space radiation-induced leukemias, suggesting a link between mutations and blood-derived cancers.

In sum, the investigators showed that space radiation will induce signature mutations that can be used to qualitatively and quantitatively distinguish spontaneous mutations from those induced by exposure in two distinct cell types, kidney epithelial and spleen T cells. Further, they showed that the induced mutant kidney cells had extensive mutations throughout the genome, which was surprising because mutations on chromosome 8 were the only ones required for the mutant cells to be isolated. Because of the known link between mutation and cancer, our work will be useful to estimate cancer risk in astronauts from prolonged space trips.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Vitamin D is critical for space travelers because they lack ultraviolet light exposure and have an insufficient dietary supply of vitamin D. Despite the provision of vitamin D supplements to International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers, vitamin D status is consistently lower after flight than before flight, and in several crewmembers, levels have decreased to concentrations considered clinically significant. Vitamin D has long been known to play a role in calcium metabolism, and more recently its non-calcitropic functions (functions not related to calcium metabolism, e.g., effects related to the incidence of cancer or diabetes) have been recognized. According to the results of several recent studies, functionally relevant measures indicate that the lower limit of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (a marker of vitamin D status) should be raised from the current standard of 25 nmol/L to 80 nmol/L. The mean preflight serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for U.S. ISS crewmembers to date is 63 ± 16 nmol/L, and after a four- to six-month space flight mission it typically decreases 25-30% despite a supplementation of 400 International Units per day (IU/d). The suboptimal pre- and postflight vitamin D status is an issue that needs to be addressed so NASA can better define the appropriate amount of supplemental vitamin D to serve as a countermeasure against vitamin D deficiency in crewmembers. This is very important for long-duration crewmembers, and is critical for exploration class missions.

Providing a recommendation for vitamin D supplementation to maintain serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D at optimal concentrations (±75–80 nmol/L) is important for long duration crew members on the ISS (six month flights) and is critical for exploration-class missions on the Moon or Mars that could be years in duration. Ground-based models of space flight in which subjects receive limited sunlight exposure are valuable for performing vitamin D supplementation trials. One of these models is subjects spending the winter in Antarctica, where ultraviolet B light (UVB) radiation is essentially zero during the winter months. The main objective of this study was to determine the effectiveness of three different doses of supplemental vitamin D3 in enabling subjects with no sunlight exposure to reach and maintain optimal vitamin D status (serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration of 80 nmol/L).

Specific Aims:

(1) Determine the time course and magnitude of changes in vitamin D status during winter in Antarctica, with or without vitamin D supplementation.

(2) Determine other markers of bone and calcium metabolism (such as serum calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and vitamin D-binding protein) before and after vitamin D supplementation to determine the effectiveness of supplementation.

APPROACH:
This was a five month prospective, randomized, double-blind study of vitamin D supplementation. It was conducted during winter in Antarctica at the McMurdo Station, when ultraviolet B radiation levels are essentially zero. The 55 subjects (41 men and 14 women, all white) were randomly divided into three groups for vitamin D supplementation: 2000 IU/d (n=18), 1000 IU/d (n=19), and 400 IU/d (n=18). Seven additional subjects (three men and four women) agreed to participate in the blood draws and diet logging, but they either did not want to take study supplements or were taking supplements of their own choosing. Those taking supplements of vitamin D >400 IU/d or of calcium >500 mg/d were excluded.

The study consisted of three data collection sessions, each including a seven-day diet record, an 8-hour fasting blood draw, and body weight determination. Height was recorded at the beginning of the study. Baseline data (session 1) were collected at week five of the South Polar winter (the end of March and beginning of April); session 2 was at week 18 (the end of June and beginning of July), and session 3 was at week 25 (the middle of August). During each blood collection session, two 5-mL blood tubes were filled for each subject. The tubes were centrifuged and frozen at -80 degrees Celsius until delivered to the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas for analysis.

The subjects were given two bottles, each with a known number of pills, and were instructed to take 1 pill from each bottle daily. Each bottle was labeled with a single letter code; there were 12 possible combinations (four possible combinations for each study dose) to ensure blinding of both the subjects and the on-site medical staff who conducted the study. The two bottles provided either one placebo and one 400-IU pill (the 400-IU dose group), one placebo and one 1000-IU pill (the 1000-IU dose group), or two 1000-IU pills (the 2000-IU dose group). The subjects were asked to return the bottles at the end of the study so that pill counts could be conducted to estimate compliance. Thirty-one of the 55 subjects returned the pill bottles at the end of the study.

RESULTS:
Upon receipt of the blood tubes in Houston, it was found that some tubes had inadvertently not been centrifuged before they were frozen. This affected 27-29 data points, depending on whether one or both of the tubes were affected and whether hemolysis affected the tests.

The average dietary intake of vitamin D during the study was 295 ± 224 IU/d (average for all subjects except one outlier). There were no significant differences between the supplementation groups at baseline (session 1) for any of the serum analytes measured. About five months after supplementation started (session 3), 25-hydroxyvitamin D increased to 71 ± 23 nmol/L in the 2000-IU/d group, 63 ± 25 nmol/L in the 1000-IU/d group, and 57 ± 15 nmol/L in the 400-IU/d group and decreased to 34 ± 12 nmol/L in the group not taking supplements. In both sessions 2 and 3, the serum concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D was higher in the 2000-IU/d group than in the group that did not take study supplements. When hemolyzed samples were excluded, similar results were obtained, except that 25-hydroxyvitamin D was higher in the 1000-IU/d group and in the 2000-IU/d group than in the group not taking supplements in session 3. In all groups that took study supplements, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was greater in sessions 2 and 3 than in session 1. Likewise, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D was greater in sessions 2 and 3 than in session 1, showing a significant difference between data collection sessions but not between supplementation groups. Similar results were obtained when hemolyzed samples were excluded from the analysis.

Vitamin D supplementation did not affect 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcium status (as expected); however, both 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and serum calcium increased in sessions 2 and 3 in all subjects. Bone specific alkaline phosphatase was greater in session 3 than in session 1, showing a significant effect between data collection sessions but not between supplementation groups. Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) was not significantly affected between data collection sessions or between the groups. Vitamin D-binding protein showed no significant difference between the groups.

Body weight did not change over the course of the study, but serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D status did change. When body weight was graphed against 25-hydroxyvitamin D, there was a negative correlation in both session 1 (baseline) and session 3 (after 5 months supplementation) suggesting that increased body weight is related to a decrease in circulating vitamin D.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microgravity affects cardiovascular (CV) function by decreasing circulating blood volume and central venous blood pressure and increasing stroke volume and cardiac output, potentially leading to cardiac rhythm disturbances, which have been documented during space flight On top of this, astronauts experience additional CV stress, for example, during space walks or robotic operations during Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). In addition, during any space mission, astronauts experience unusual light-dark cycles leading to some degree of chronic circadian disruption which can take the form of: (a) the whole body being at the ‘wrong time’ given the prevailing behaviors. For example, astronauts are often awake, eat, and perform activities at the time when their internal biological clocks are preparing the body for optimal physiological rest and sleep; or they may be trying to sleep during the biological day when their circadian clock normally prepares the body for activities; or (b) parts of the body can be set to suboptimal times, such ‘internal desynchrony’ when varied cells and organs are shifting to new time zones at different rates. Thus, circadian disruption may result in maladaptive physiological responses. In addition, the inevitable sleep loss that accompanies circadian disruption itself can further stress the CV system. Undoubtedly, mission requirements, such as ‘slam shifting’ before EVAs and working extended shifts during EVAs will contribute to sleep loss. The environmental conditions on the International Space Station (ISS), such as noise, and heat, also contribute to sleep loss.

Cardiac arrhythmias have been observed in astronauts and are considered a major risk endangering the success of space missions. In addition to structural changes, such arrhythmias can be triggered by numerous interacting and summating stressors such as exercise, sleep loss, working during the biological night, causing changes in cardiovascular risk markers, such as increased blood pressure, cardiac vagal withdrawal, sympathetic activation, and promotion of hemostatic mechanisms. While such responses can be vital homeostatic responses to such challenges, chronic activation of these mechanisms, or activation in individuals with underlying can be counterproductive and lead to adverse cardiovascular events, including stroke or myocardial infarction. This study had the following specific aims:

  1. The effect of circadian disruption on CV function, including the CV responses to physical and mental challenges commonly encountered during space flight.
  2. The effect of sleep loss on CV function, including the CV responses to physical and mental challenges commonly encountered during space flight.
  3. The synergetic effects of circadian disruption plus sleep loss on CV function, including the CV responses to physical and mental challenges commonly encountered during space flight.

APPROACH:
Investigators studied healthy participants throughout two 11-day ‘inpatient’ protocols that combined circadian disruption with extended sleep opportunity (sufficient sleep) or short sleep (insufficient sleep). Eight males and six females participated in the study. Each participant was studied in both the Short Sleep and Long Sleep conditions. These two protocols were called ‘forced desynchrony’ protocols because the day length was shorter than 24 hours such that the behavioral rest/activity cycle became desynchronized from the internal circadian cycle. This was achieved by scheduling participants to live on recurring 20 hour ‘days’ in dim light, allowing the endogenous circadian pacemaker to oscillate at its inherent period rather than being reset by daily exposure to the light-dark cycle. One protocol (Short Sleep) permitted sleep for five hours per 20 hour ‘day’, which is equivalent to six hours of sleep opportunity per 24 hours for an entire week. The other protocol (Long Sleep) allowed eight hours and 20 minutes sleep per 20 hour ‘day’, which is equivalent to 10 hours sleep opportunity per 24 hours for an entire week. This approach allows investigators to uniformly distribute the sleep/wake cycle across the circadian cycle to quantify the independent influences of the circadian system and behaviors and also their interacting effects.

Under these carefully controlled conditions investigators tested the hypothesis that circadian disruption combined with sleep restriction would result in unfavorable changes in CV function during behavioral challenges commonly faced by astronauts. A behavioral test battery was performed at the same time during the sleep protocol. Before each test battery, participants had been supine for at least five hours during the sleep periods in both the Long Sleep and Short Sleep conditions. Subsequently, when lights were switched from darkness to the dim light condition, participants remained in a semi-recumbent posture (upper body at 45º) for two hours. During this time participants consumed breakfast one hour after scheduled wake time. An identical behavioral test battery was repeated on each 20 hour ‘day’ and included three standardized stressors performed in the following order: (i) a mental challenge; (ii) a postural challenge; and (iii) an exercise stressor.

Astronauts experience various stressors that may result in inhibition of cell mediated immunity and increased reactivation of latent viruses. Thus, comprehensive immune assessment was performed from whole blood samples collected with heparin at the beginning of study before either protocol, and twice during each of the Short Sleep and the Long Sleep protocols. Immune function was assessed using standard techniques including peripheral leukocyte distribution by flow cytometry, T cell function, intracellular cytokine profiles, and secreted cytokine production profiles following T cell or monocyte stimulation. In addition, innate reactivation of latent Epstein Barr Virus (EBV), herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1), and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) was assessed from the DNA in liquid saliva samples taken at the beginning of study before either protocol, and every alternate day across both the short and long sleep protocols.

RESULTS:
Results show that short-term circadian disruption and sleep loss in healthy adults does not cause measurable deleterious effects on cardiovascular structure, increased susceptibility to arrhythmias, or sub-optimal cardiovascular function even during exercise and postural stresses. The duration of partial sleep loss and circadian disruption was limited to a period of 5 x 24 hour days. Thus, any physiological findings would be interpreted as acute changes across a period that is akin to a workweek. The circadian misalignment in this study was performed in continuous dim light to avoid circadian clock phase adjustment. It is conceivable that misalignment performed with exposure to bright light during the biological night may cause more internal circadian desynchrony and manifest in adverse effects.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Hoh, Joseph
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This study was to determine how microgravity affects muscle fiber type and muscle isomyosin composition. It was postulated that under zero gravity some slow fibers would convert to fast. Since stimuli to the slow-twitch antigravity muscles should be greatly reduced in low gravity, the concentration of myosin isoenzymes in these fibers should also be changed.

Approach:

Muscles were analyzed using monoclonal antibodies against myosin heavy chains. Antibodies specific to different myosin-heavy-chain types were used to identify fast and slow fibers. Mab 5-4D was specific to the slow type I fibers, and mab 5-2B was specific for type IIa and type IIx.

Results:

Soleus muscles of the flight animals showed a marked increased in the proportion of fibers expressing fast type II isomyosin. Muscle fibers tended to change from slow to fast, however, the change was not as dramatic as observed in tail-suspension studies. Slow fibers were more atrophied than fast fibers. It is likely that the conversion from slow to fast twitch fibers was not complete by the end of the flight. Changes in fiber type distribution were not detected in the extensor.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight causes adaptive changes in cardiovascular function, and many astronauts have suffered postflight orthostatic tachycardia. However, previously available data about these changes have been inadequate and inconsistent. The objective of this study was to collect normative data about the effects of space flight on the volume, mass and function of the heart, and about the orthostatic response of the cardiovascular system.

APPROACH:
The heart rate and blood pressure of 32 astronauts were recorded while they were lying supine and then standing, before and after space flights of 4 to 5 days. At the same times, echocardiograms were recorded by 2-dimensional M-mode echocardiography. The total peripheral resistance index (TPRI), left ventricular end diastolic volume index (EDVI), left ventricular end systolic volume index (ESVI), left ventricular stroke volume index (SVI), myocardial mass index and ejection fraction were calculated, and the mean velocity of circumferential shortening of the myocardial fibers was estimated.

RESULTS:
The heart rate was greater on landing day than before the flight, and the EDVI and SVI in the supine position were less. (The mean EDVI was 11% less and the mean SVI was 17% less.) The mean EDVI, ESVI and SVI in the standing position were also less on landing day, but these changes were not statistically significant. Space flight caused no significant changes in the supine ESVI, the ejection fraction, the thickness of the left ventricular wall or the mass or contractility of the heart muscle. Before the flight, the TPRI increased significantly when astronauts stood up after lying supine. This orthostatic response was reduced on landing day, so that the TPRI failed to change significantly when the astronauts stood up, while the heart rate increased. The changes resolved within 7 to 10 days of landing. These results indicated that temporary changes in cardiovascular function may be expected even after short spaceflights of only 4 to 5 days. These changes included a decrease in the left ventricular end diastolic volume and stroke volume, with a compensatory increase in heart rate, as well as loss or reduction of the normal orthostatic response that maintains the blood pressure during postural changes.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-duration space flights are associated with increased levels of psychological stress, acute and chronic exposure to space radiation, and microgravity-induced changes which are known to detrimentally impact the immune system. Studies have evaluated the magnitude of immune alterations during space flight, however, due to logistical constraints unique to the space flight environment, they have either been limited to short-duration space flight missions or to basic pre- and postflight measures. The successful implementation of exploration-class missions to Mars or other near-Earth objects requires a better understanding of the impact of long-duration space flight on the immune system in order to evaluate the risks associated with immune dysregulations. In this regard, The Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Microgravity on Salivary Markers of Innate Immunity (Salivary_Markers) and Validation of Procedures for Monitoring Crewmember Immune Function (SMO 015) were conducted in order to assess immune function relating to cells of innate and adaptive immunity, as well as salivary immune parameters during a six-month mission on the International Space Station (ISS). These studies provided important data relating to innate immunity and immune cell changes during space flight, however it remains unknown whether astronauts become immunocompromised during space flight.

The main goal of this study was to characterize acute and chronic changes in polyclonal Free Light Chains (FLC), and in Immunoglobulin (Ig) class switching, indicative of a state of chronic inflammation and overall B-cell function. Investigators also assessed if changes to these sensitive biomarkers are associated with altered risk of viral reactivation and subsequent inflammation.

APPROACH:
Using stored plasma samples collected during the two flight studies, investigators retrospectively evaluated B-cell function and humoral immunity during and following long-duration missions. Investigators analyzed archived plasma samples from two different flight studies as well as ground-based controls. The blood samples were collected from ISS crewmembers before, during, and after space flight. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to determine latent viral status, Ig, and cytokine levels were also conducted to measure other indices of immune activation and suppression.

RESULTS:
There was no effect of space flight on kappa FLC concentrations and only a marginal reduction was observed in lambda FLC levels upon return to Earth. Furthermore, IgG and IgM remained unchanged during and after space flight, when compared to pre-flight values. These results indicate that B-cell homeostasis is maintained during long-duration space flight in astronauts, advocating for potential in-flight vaccination as viable countermeasures against viral reactivation during exploration-class missions.

investigators: Principal Investigator: DeChurch, LeslieCo-Investigator: Contractor, NoshirCo-Investigator: Johnson, Jeffrey
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Among the remarkable team challenges NASA faces in long-duration space exploration (LDSE) missions is the need to maintain team shared mental models (SMMs). Maintaining team SMMs requires the ability to detect shifts in cognition that will likely occur during the mission that could lead to ineffective crew functioning and performance. Maintaining team SMMs also requires validated countermeasures for bringing team members' cognitive understanding back into alignment. Leaving low Earth orbit requires extreme teamwork. Team SMMs need to be maintained within teams operating close up (the crew), and between teams operating at an unprecedented distance (i.e., the crew and ground; 33 million miles in the case of a mission to Mars).

APPROACH:
A multidisciplinary research team leveraged expertise in psychology, industrial engineering, and anthropology to understand the emergence and outcomes of critical shifts in team cognition over long duration missions. This project utilized a novel conceptual framework of shared cognitive architecture (SCA) to understand the patterns of SMMs that dynamically link members of teams, and teams to other teams, as they go beyond low Earth orbit. Investigators used semantic analysis to identify cognitive shifts, and relational event network analysis to understand the antecedents and consequences of these shifts. Using this framework alongside an agent-based model (ABM) on LDSE analog data, investigators explored an exhaustive set of potential triggering conditions over the course of three Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) campaigns. 

The investigative team focused their data collection strategies into three distinct phases: Index of Cognitive Efficiency (ICE), leadership relations, and task and team mental modeling. The ICE Index of Cognitive Efficiency (overall score) was collected using Spaceflight Cognitive Assessment Tool for Windows (WinSCAT) which is a BHP Behavioral Medicine “surveillance” tool. For leadership relations in phase 2, the crew members completed a network survey asking about their leadership relations (i.e., “Who do you rely on for leadership?”) every five days. For phase 3, each individual’s task and team mental model was collected every day except Sundays, using the elicitation method. Crew members were asked, on a scale of 1 (totally unrelated) to 7 (very strongly related), to report their perceptions of the relationships between a list of 8 task elements, which produced 28 dyadic values for each crew member for each day.

RESULTS:
Phase 1
The research team developed a computational model that successfully predicted crew shared mental models based on personal, task, social, and situational factors. This model can be used in future mission planning and mission support. Comprehensive meta-analysis of prior research established that shared mental models are a robust predictor of team performance. Though moderators were found, the relationship between shared mental models and performance was always positive. The implication being that long distance missions should monitor and promote shared mental models among the crew, among mission support, and between the crew and mission support. Leveraging research previously conducted on Skylab missions demonstrated that crew shared mental models, and shared mental models between the crew and ground can be assessed using text analysis of unstructured text; in this case mission transcripts of spoken communication were used.

Phase 2

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Studies by NASA have shown that astronauts obtain only approximately 6 hours of sleep per day on average during space flight missions. Laboratory experiments have revealed that within a few days, such reduction of sleep can result in enhanced probability of performance failure. This vulnerability may be exposed during emergencies in space—due to equipment failure, mission timeline problems, or other stressors—involving extended mission demands and further sleep loss. However, there are substantial inter-individual differences in the magnitude of performance failure during extended wakefulness. This investigation of human vulnerability to performance failure is the first quantitative study of the biological and neurobehavioral factors that discriminate and predict these inter-individual differences.

The study consisted of repeated assessment of neurobehavioral vulnerability in a wide range of performance functions for n=21 subjects during 36 hours of laboratory-based sleep deprivation with relatively high work demands, on 3 separate occasions. These deprivations were preceded by either a week of sleep satiation (12 hours in bed per day) or a week of sleep restriction (6 hours in bed per day). This design served to address the following four specific aims: To determine the extent to which individual performance responses to extended mission demands with prolonged wakefulness reflect (1) recent sleep-wake history, and/or (2) trait-like neurobehavioral vulnerability, and/or (3) sensitization or adaptation as a consequence of previous exposure; and (4) to identify potential biological, behavioral, psychological, and/or demographic predictors of vulnerability to performance failure for future prospective evaluation and countermeasure development.

This project addressed fundamental issues about the sources and predictability of the large inter-individual differences in performance failure during sustained work involving sleep loss. The project had two broad goals: Determine the extent to which performance responses to sustained mission demands with prolonged wakefulness reflect state-like vulnerability that occurs due to variation in recent sleep-wake history, and/or stable, trait-like neurobehavioral vulnerability that occurs as a consequence of enduring biological factors, and/or evolving vulnerability due to prior exposure to sleep loss (i.e., sensitization or adaptation); Identify potential biological, behavioral, psychological, and/or demographic predictors of vulnerability to performance failure during sustained mission demands with prolonged wakefulness for subsequent prospective evaluation.

The investigation had the following four specific aims:

1. Quantify the extent to which the magnitude of performance failure during extended waking performance is dependent on variation in recent sleep-wake behavioral history. We hypothesized that a significant proportion of the variance in the performance response to 36 hours of sustained work (i.e., sleep loss) would be associated with prior sleep history. We compared performance during a 36-hour sleep deprivation period following a week of sleep satiation (12 hours time in bed per night) to performance during a 36-hour sleep deprivation period following a week of sleep restriction (6 hours time in bed per night). Numerous reports have shown that during space flight, sleep is reduced to 6 hours per day on average. By itself, this cumulative sleep loss may already lead to human error (see Figure 1). However, when it is followed by sustained mission demands with prolonged wakefulness, such performance failure may endanger both the mission and the crew. In order to effectively target countermeasures of performance failure, it is important to quantify the effect of sleep history on the vulnerability to performance deficits during extended work demands in space.
2. Quantify the extent to which the magnitude of performance failure during extended waking performance involves a trait response. We hypothesized that a significant proportion of the variance in the performance response to 36 hours of extended work involving sleep loss would be reproduced within subjects over two identical laboratory experimental sessions each preceded by a week of sleep satiation (i.e., 12 hours time in bed per night). If vulnerability to performance failure appears to be predominantly trait-dependent, then this may have consequences for astronaut selection for specific tasks in space (e.g., Extra-Vehicular Activities).
3. Quantify the effect of repeated exposure to extended waking performance demands on vulnerability to performance deficits. We hypothesized that repeated exposure to extended performance demands involving sleep loss would have a sensitizing effect, that is, performance deficits will become worse when sustained work with prolonged wakefulness is experienced repeatedly. Support for this hypothesis would indicate that adaptation to sustained mission demands cannot be practiced, and that gaining experience may not be a valid countermeasure, which may have consequences for astronaut training programs.
4. Identify predictors of vulnerability to performance failure during extended waking performance. This specific aim, which is exploratory and hypothesis generating, is addressed by entering a range of biological and behavioral variables as potential predictors into a regression equation of the individual performance deficits associated with sustained work with prolonged wakefulness (i.e., 36 hours of sleep loss with high workload in the laboratory).

APPROACH:
In this study, n=21 subjects served as their own controls through a design in which extensive neurobehavioral and physiological assessments were made during three replications of extended, 36-hour waking performance, as part of three 69-hour in-laboratory experimental sessions. The amount of sleep allowed during the week prior to each laboratory session was varied in counterbalanced order between a satiated condition (i.e., 12 hours time in bed) and a restricted condition (i.e., 6 hours time in bed). Research subjects also underwent two screening sessions and a 29-hour adaptation session in the laboratory before entering the experimental phase of the study, and a follow-up session to conclude the experiment. The study was designed with the following considerations:

1. Inter-individual differences in performance failure are exposed during extended work involving sleep loss, such as can occur under emergency circumstances in space; hence, a 36-hour sleep deprivation experiment was the paradigm of choice for this investigation.
2. Sleep history (satiated versus restricted) was carefully controlled in the week prior to the 36 hours of sleep deprivation in order to address specific aim 1. The 36-hour sleep deprivation was repeated in order to use subjects as their own controls in comparing performance failure following the satiated versus the restricted sleep conditions.
3. The 36-hour sleep deprivation following the satiated sleep condition was repeated in order to assess the stability (i.e., trait-like component) of the performance response to extended work involving sleep loss, as specified in specific aim 2, and independently of specific aim 1.
4. Counterbalancing the order of the two 36-hour sleep deprivation experiments following sleep satiation and the single 36-hour sleep deprivation experiment following the restricted sleep condition ensured that the sensitizing effect of repeated exposure to extended work involving sleep loss, as specified in specific aim 3, could be assessed independently of specific aims 1 and 2.
5. The 36 hours of sleep deprivation were conducted inside a controlled laboratory environment, so as to eliminate external sources of interference (masking) on neurobehavioral and physiological measures.

Subjects came to the laboratory for a 29-hour adaptation session. In this session, they got used to sleeping in the laboratory while being monitored polysomnographically (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG), and they practiced the neurobehavioral performance battery. Subjects began the experiment at 17:00 hours, and at 20:00 hours they practiced the performance tests, which were fully explained to them by the research staff. At 22:00 hours they went to bed for a 12-hour baseline sleep period, which was recorded polysomnographically. At 10:00 hours the next morning, directly after getting up, subjects underwent performance testing. The performance testing then occurred every 2 hours until 20:00 hours. At 22:00 hours, subjects were sent home.

After 2 weeks, subjects returned to the laboratory for their first 67-hour session with 36 hours of extended work involving sleep deprivation. The first 29 hours of this session were identical to the adaptation session. However, after the baseline sleep period, wakefulness was maintained for 36 hours (i.e., total sleep deprivation) with 1-hour performance testing every 2 hours, to simulate circumstances of extended work involving sleep loss as can occur during emergencies in space. During this period, specially trained staff kept the subjects awake when necessary, inducing mild social activity such as casual conversation. Before each performance test bout, subjects were urged to perform to their best level, and compensatory effort was encouraged. After the 36 hours of maintained wakefulness, at 22:00 hours the next day, the subjects went to bed for a 12-hour recovery sleep opportunity that was recorded polysomnographically. Subjects got up at 10:00 the next morning and were sent home at around noon.

The 67-hour laboratory session was repeated after 2 weeks, and was held a third time after another 2 weeks. Each sleep deprivation session was preceded by one week of carefully controlled sleep opportunities at home. In the two conditions of satiated prior sleep, subjects stayed in bed from 22:00 hours until 10:00 hours each day (i.e., a 12-hour sleep opportunity). However, in the condition of restricted prior sleep, the subjects’ sleep opportunities during the week preceding the laboratory session, were restricted to the period from 04:00 hours until 10:00 hours (i.e., a 6-hour sleep opportunity). This restriction was also applied to the baseline sleep in the laboratory. The 6-hour sleep restriction preceded only one of the three 67-hour laboratory sessions in a randomized, counterbalanced order. Thus, 7 of the 21 subjects encountered the prior sleep restriction before their first sleep deprivation session; for 7 subjects the second session was preceded by restricted sleep, and for the remaining 7 subjects the last session was preceded by restricted sleep. The 6-hour sleep restriction simulated the sleep duration commonly experienced by astronauts during space-flight missions.

Compliance with times in bed at home (prior to the laboratory sessions) was verified by means of a sleep-wake log and wrist actigraphy. Furthermore, subjects called a time-stamped telephone recorder each day to report their bedtimes. The conditions in the laboratory were strictly controlled in terms of ambient light (less than 50 lux) and temperature (21?C), social interactions, and performance test schedules. Meals were given at 4-hour intervals (clock times 03:00, 07:00, 11:00, 15:00, 19:00, 23:00) during wakefulness. Food was controlled in terms of calories and nutritients (proteins, fats, carbohydrates), and the amount of food subjects received during the 36 hours of extended wakefulness matched their normal 2-day calorie requirement. No caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine intake were allowed.

All in-laboratory research was performed in the General Clinical Research Center (GCRC) of the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. The GCRC has light, sound, and temperature controlled rooms within which the laboratory portions of the study were conducted. The GCRC research nursing staff provided supervision of the subjects during sleep periods, and the nurses assisted in critical portions of subject screening. In addition, subjects were provided with meals controlled for nutrients and calories through the GCRC metabolic kitchen. GCRC support of the study was at no cost to the project.

State-of-the-art equipment was used for recording of polysomnography (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG), actigraphy, core body temperature, and light exposure. In addition, a variety of neurobehavioral performance assays was administered every 2 hours of wakefulness in the laboratory, through a computerized system that was invented by the principal investigator for this specific purpose. Data reduction and analysis took place during and after each experimental session, so that quality control and tentative data analysis were possible immediately after completion of each subject’s experimental procedures.

In year 2 of the project, the study was enhanced when storage of a small sample (up to 10ml) of research subjects’ whole blood for future genetic analysis was approved by the IRBs of the University of Pennsylvania and Johnson Space Center. If in the future subjects consent to the use of their stored blood for genetic analysis, this may allow for the linking of predictors of vulnerability for the effects of extended wakefulness to genetic background information. Thus, the potential to gain scientific knowledge from the project may be enhanced significantly even after the expiration of the funding period.

RESULTS:
In summary, the results of the analyses for specific aims 1–3 contradicted the prevailing hypothesis that inter-individual differences in the response to sleep deprivation could be explained by sleep history and/or stochastic fluctuations alone. Sleep history and error variance contribute only marginally to the inter-individual differences in vulnerability to performance impairment during extended wakefulness, while the dominant determinant was stable, trait-like variability among individuals. Furthermore, it was found that repeated exposure to total sleep deprivation causes sensitization to the effects of sleep loss on sustained attention performance.

Specific aim 4, which will focus on the identification of predictors of the trait-like inter-individual differences in vulnerability to performance failure during extended wakefulness, cannot yet be addressed, because it requires the completion of all processing of a multitude of data acquired from the subjects during the study. They are not an essential outcome of the present study; rather, they will serve as preliminary data for a future study aiming to identify variables underlying the currently established trait-like inter-individual differences in vulnerability to neurobehavioral performance impairment from extended wakefulness.
