investigators: Principal Investigator: Whalen, Robert
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the first study is to investigate the differences in the bone density of the skeleton as well as the structural properties of the lower leg bones in three groups of age-matched men: soccer players, runners, and sedentary controls.

APPROACH:
Methodology used the same tools developed for a previous study in women (HR 202). Three groups of 20-30 year old men were recruited: 15 elite soccer players (S) 15 elite long distance runners (R) and 15 sedentary controls (C).

RESULTS:
Age, body weight, height and tibia length were similar in all 3 groups. Average values of age were S 21, R 24.2 and C 24.3 years; for body weight were S 79.4, R 67.5, C 75.7 Kg; for height were S 181.6, R 179.8, C 180.5 cm; and for tibial length were S 40.4, R 41.4, C 40.4 cm respectively. Area was scaled by normalized body weight while tibial structural parameters in midshaft and distal third were higher in S and R than C (S 3.03, R 3.36. C 2.68 cm2 for A, S 2.37, R 2.80, C 1.95 cm4 for Imax. S had higher whole body, spine, right hip, right leg and calcaneal BMD than C (p = 0.008, 0.041, <0.001, 0.019, <0.001 respectively). S also had higher right hip and spine BMD than R (p = 0.012 and p = 0.009, respectively). R had higher calcaneal BMD than C (p = 0.002). Forty percent of R had t-scores of the lumbar spine between –1 and –2.5, similar to C whose T-scores were either below –1 (34%) or lower than –2.5 (7%).

Structural parameters (scaled values of A, Imax, Imin, and J) of the tibia were increased in S and R, indicating increased stiffness and strength. The tibial cross-sections of S were generally more symmetric than in R, indicative of their wider variety of loading conditions compared to the repetitive loading in R. There was also a relationship between the tibia and the fibula and the relative distance between the two bones indicating the two bones work together as structural elements in the lower leg.

Conclusions: Playing soccer is associated with higher BMD of the skeleton at all sites measured while running is associated with higher BMD at directly loaded sites (calcaneus), but not at relatively unloaded sites (spine). Specific loading conditions, seen in ball sports or in running, play a pivotal role in skeletal adaptation.

experiment_title: Ultrastructure of the Brain Cortex
parameter_html:
Activity, motor, Rat, Microgravity, SLS-1 (counts)
Morphology, Pyramidal neurons, visual cortex, brain, rat, Light and electron microscopy (descriptive)
Brain ultrastructure, motor cortex
Brain ultrastructure, olfactory cortex
Brain ultrastructure, somatosensory cortex
Brain ultrastructure, visual cortex
investigators: Principal Investigator: Dyachkova, LudmillaCo-Investigator: Lowry, Oliver
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Earlier examinations of the ultrastructure of the cerebral cortex on Cosmos has suggested that the system of interneuronal contacts of the neocortex showed the highest level of adaptive changes in microgravity. This experiment was to assess spaceflight effects on the ultrastructure of nervous, glial and vascular elements of the brain cortex.

Approach:

Fragments of the motor, somatosensory and visual cortex and olfactory cortex were collected, and a layer-by-layer electron microscope examination of nervous, glial, and vascular elements of the brain cortex was conducted. While embedding in araldite, brain sections were oriented in such a way as to have all cortical layers sectioned in frontal ultrathin sections.

Results:

Results demonstrated changes in neuronal and glial cells, which pointed to an active restructuring in the cortical connections of the flight rats. Motor and sensomotory ultrastructure at R+0 suggested that synapses and stellate cells were in an excitation state, which was associated with an increased afferent flow to the cortex during the 2-3 hours after recovery. Examinations at R+9 indicated both an enhanced afferent flow, as well as an increased functional activity of large pyramidal neurons of the V layer. Changes in the visual cortex of the flight rats were similar to those in the somatosensory cortex, but less significant. Changes of the olfactory cortex suggested a slight decrease of the afferent flow and an increase of the functional activity of neurons postflight.

experiment_title: Mechanisms for Induction of Bystander Effects by High Energy Particles in Cells and Tissues

Bystander effect
Fluence

investigators: Principal Investigator: Held, Kathryn
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex and unique radiation environment composed of trapped proton and electron radiation, galactic cosmic rays (GCR; energetic protons and heavy charged ions, HZE), and solar particle events (SPE), primarily protons. Although these radiations can result in appreciable cumulative doses to astronauts during long-duration missions, the exposures occur at low fluences and fluence rates, such that particle traversals through individual cells in an astronaut’s body may be well separated in tissue location and time. Under such conditions, so-called non-targeted effects such as bystander responses may have increased significance. The radiation-induced bystander effect is the occurrence of biological responses in unirradiated cells near to or sharing medium with cells actually traversed by radiation. It is hypothesized that at the low fluences of protons and HZE particles to which astronauts are exposed in space, a significant fraction of the cellular changes may be due to bystander responses, in addition to the damages caused in cells directly traversed by ionizing particles or their associated delta rays.

The specific aims for this study are:

  1. Test the hypothesis that bystander effects occur at particle fluences so low that only 1-2 % of cells in a culture dish are traversed by an energetic proton or HZE particle.
  2. Test the hypothesis that cells that have survived an initial traversal and sent a bystander signal, can again send a signal when traversed once again by a particle or can subsequently respond as bystanders to a hit in a neighboring cell by extending low fluence work to studies using repeated exposures of cells to low fluences and mixed (actually sequential) beams of more than one particle type.
  3. Test the hypothesis that non-nuclear damage-initiated, metabolically produced reactive oxygen species (ROS) in hit cells are involved in the early steps of bystander signaling. Chemical countermeasures to reduce the bystander responses based on removal of ROS or prevention of their formation will also be studied. Previous studies have indicated that ROS are at least partially involved in transmittal of the Fe ion-induced bystander signal from hit to unirradiated cells.
  4. Test the hypothesis that radiation-induced bystander signals can be sent between differing cell types, but the characteristics of the responses depend on the cell types and the types of radiation.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
At very low iron ion (1 GeV/n) fluences, i.e., 2-50% of cells traversed by an ion, or very low proton (1 GeV) fluences, i.e., 2-200 protons/cell, there was increased damage in cells in both irradiated and bystander populations. That finding--that about 100-fold lower particle fluence is needed to produce DNA damage in irradiated or bystander populations with Fe ions than with protons of the same energy--suggests that linear energy transfer (LET) or particle track structure, including delta-rays, is a determinant of the minimum dose needed for the effect. Studies with 300 MeV/n Fe ions (higher LET) show a shift to even lower minimum particle fluence for induction of the effect, consistent with LET being important. Ongoing analysis of samples irradiated with silicon and carbon, of intermediate LET, appear to yield consistent data.

The studies with mixed cell types (fibroblasts and keratinocytes) in 2D and with the same cells in a 3D model of epithelial tissue (aim 4) have been completed. The data in monolayers show that with either X-rays or protons (low LET radiations), there is a 1.5-2-fold increase in micronuclei (MN) formation in bystander fibroblasts or keratinocytes after either cell type is irradiated, but there is no significant increase in MN in bystander fibroblasts in co-culture with irradiated keratinocytes.

In the 3D studies, the data in irradiated cells show that the fraction of fibroblasts with DNA damage when irradiated in the 3D constructs is significantly less (4-fold at the shortest time of 1 h) than in cells irradiated in 2D monolayers. With time after irradiation, the fraction of damaged cells decreases such that at 24 h it is back to background in cells in 3D, but remains elevated out to 72 h in cells in 2D. In contrast to the irradiated cells in 3D, the level of damage in the bystander portion of the 3D model is low at 1 h, but increases to a peak at 12 h after protons and a maximum at 24-48 h after Fe ion exposure. The data further show that bystander signals can travel considerable distances (mm) and that, although scavengers have no effect on DNA damage in irradiated cells in 3D, the level of DNA damage in bystander cells in 3D is reduced nearly to control, unirradiated, levels by scavenging hydrogen peroxide, superoxide and nitric oxide in the medium shared by the construct halves, findings similar to those in 2D.

In studies to assess intercellular signaling between normal fibroblasts and tumor cells, this study has shown that there is no bystander signaling with a human chrondrosarcoma cell line (HTB94) irradiated with X-rays, protons or iron ions. However, irradiated HTB94 cells can send signals to bystander fibroblasts, to elicit DNA damage, although the tumor cells do not respond to signals from the fibroblasts.

experiment_title: Salivary Cortisol Levels During the Acute Phases of Space Flight
parameter_html:
Cortisol, plasma
Cortisol, saliva
investigators: Principal Investigator: Cintron, Nitza
experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The complexity of the physiological response to weightlessness has stimulated research into identifying biochemical and endocrine parameters which might provide insight into the underlying mechanisms operative in the overall adaptation process. Available data from earlier in-flight and ground-based studies substantiate the value of performing correlative studies to evaluate and assess the neuro-endocrinologic mechanisms associated with the various conditions of space flight-induced stress. As expected, these investigations clearly indicated the central involvement of autonomic neurotransmission in the etiology of stress-related imbalances (e.g. immunosuppression, motion sickness) and pointed to the potential of correlating early changes to hormonal alterations.

Cortisol, under the direct influence of adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), is one of the key hormones associated with the control and maintenance of normal neuroendocrine processes and with the response and onset of stress-related conditions. Plasma concentrations of cortisol have been found to increase during space flight. However, no data are currently available on its changes immediately after the achievement of weightlessness. It is during these first hours of a mission that the most dramatic changes are thought to occur as part of the adaptive response to weightlessness.

The primary objectives of this investigation were to determine the feasibility under operational Shuttle conditions of collecting saliva samples for cortisol analysis and, more importantly, to examine the key facets of endocrine function (i.e. adrenal activity) during the acute and adaptive phases of space flight as derived from the resultant cortisol measurements. Information about adrenal activity and about integrated neuroendocrine function have significance in formulating the total picture of the crewmember's health status and in predicting, in conjunction with all other available metabolic data, the possible duration of man's stay in weightlessness.

APPROACH:
The general design of the overall investigation involved the serial collection of saliva samples throughout a specified 24-hour period during pre- and in-flight phases of a mission. Saliva collection activities consisted of collecting four samples throughout each 24-hour period at approximately the same times (± 1 hour) during the sleep/activity cycle. To avoid an interruption of the sleep period, the first sample was collected soon after wake-up; the second sample at wakeup plus five hours (± 1 hour); the third sample at wake-up plus 10 hours (± 1 hour); and the fourth sample, shortly before the sleep period. These operations were performed once preflight at approximately one month prior to launch and twice in flight, once early and once late in the mission. All in-flight data were compared to preflight baseline data. A total of six subjects were required for appropriate assessment and evaluation of results.

Saliva samples were obtained using the Salivary Collection Assembly which consisted of a beta cloth pouch with foam inserts to retain Sarstedt syringe tubes, each containing a dental cotton roll. The syringe barrels had a screw cap on one end and a sliding plug on the other end into which the syringe plunger screwed, so that the barrels functioned as tubes for collection of samples as well as syringes for retrieval of the samples. Squares of Teflon film which could be chewed to stimulate salivation were also stowed in the pouch. Samples were collected by placing a roll of dental cotton between the lower teeth and cheek toward the back of the mouth. The cotton roll remained in place until it was saturated or for 20 minutes whichever occurred first. The saliva samples were then stored in the designated tubes for subsequent analysis.

Samples were frozen at -70° C as soon as possible after landing. They were thawed and a plunger was inserted into each syringe. The contents of the cotton roll were squeezed into a 50-ml tube which was centrifuged with the syringe in a Beckman J-6B centrifuge. The roll was squeezed again so that as much sample as possible was transferred to the 50-ml tube. Samples were analyzed for cortisol by radioimmunoassay.

RESULTS:
For both crewmembers the sample taken late at night (2030 hours) contained the highest concentration of cortisol. The concentration had dropped by at least two-thirds by the next sampling time (0140 hours). Only one complete set of in flight samples in which cortisol could be measured was obtained. It was collected on Mission Day 6/7. The cortisol levels in these samples were almost parallel to the cortisol in the same crewman's preflight samples; each of the samples taken on MD 6/7 contained cortisol. Results show that saliva can be collected in zero gravity in quantities sufficient to measure cortisol. The noninvasive methods used in this experiment are highly advantageous for collecting samples frequently and with minimum disruption of the crewmembers' other work. The only problems encountered were insufficient saturation of the cotton rolls (possibly due to dryness of the mouth, a common side effect of anti-motion sickness drugs), and inadequate labeling of some tubes. There may also be some difficulty with collection of samples at the same time on every day of the experiment, because of other demands on the crewmembers' time.

The peak in plasma cortisol concentration generally occurs about 0700 hours, but for the two crewmembers in this study the peak occurred much earlier, not later than 2030 hours. This might be due to the strenuous preflight training schedule. There are not enough in flight data to draw any conclusions about the early effects of flight on cortisol levels in the body or on their diurnal variation, but in at least one crewmember the diurnal rhythm was the same after about a week of flight as it was preflight.

Collection of saliva samples for measurement of cortisol during space flight appears to provide a feasible approach for studying change in adrenal function during adaptation of the body to weightlessness. Specific information regarding the status of adrenal activity in the initial phases of space flight will require additional data for the appropriate assessment of changes. In this regard, the current limited data must be considered strictly as preliminary.

image_name: Solid Sorbent Air Sampler (SSAS) in Spektr Module
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts living for an extended period of time in a closed environment, such as the Mir Space Station, are continuously exposed to pollutants in respirable air. Pollutants originate from material off-gassing, human metabolism, systems and payload leaks, and utility chemicals. If pollutant concentrations reach high levels, crewmembers may experience health problems and scientific experiments could be confounded. This experiment was designed to sample the Mir Space Station air at various locations and times in order to estimate the effects of airborne pollutants on crew health. The following were objectives of this experiment:

  • Determine if Mir air meets U.S. standards for crew health during long-term exposure to trace contaminants
  • Sample air using several types of hardware to compare similarity of sampling methods
  • Sample Mir Space Station air at multiple locations simultaneously to assess spatial variations in the Mir complex
  • Measure ethylene concentrations to determine if plant growth experiments could be affected.
  • Assess the rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between shuttle and Mir.

    APPROACH:
    In-flight air sampling was performed on NASA-Mir 2-7. Instantaneous air samples were obtained using grab sample containers (GSCs), and 24 hour time-averaged air samples were obtained using solid sorbent air samplers (SSASs). Formaldehyde badges were used to measure formaldehyde concentrations throughout Mir.

    The GSCs and SSASs were tested preflight at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Toxicology Laboratory to ensure that each sampler was clean and could perform as expected. Formaldehyde badges were tested, reconfigured to fit the NASA flight configuration, and packaged for use during flight.

    During flight, GSC and SSAS samples were taken approximately every thirty days. After each sampling session, the date, time, and location were recorded. Once during each mission, a spatial variation assessment was performed by sampling multiple modules simultaneously. The formaldehyde badges were worn by the crewmembers and also placed in the individual modules.

    Upon return to Earth, the GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and a modified EPA TO-14 gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) method. The GC analysis was used to estimate ethylene concentrations. The SSAS samples were analyzed only via the GC/MS method. The filters were removed from the formaldehyde badges and extracted with formaldehyde-free water. The aqueous extracts were then analyzed for formaldehyde using a chromotropic acid-spectrophotometric method.

    RESULTS:
    The air quality on NASA-Mir 2-7 met, and exceeded, U.S. standards for human-rated spacecraft. However, the irritant group was slightly above a toxicity index of 1 during NASA-Mir 2, 6, and 7, and the carbon dioxide toxicity index was above 1 during NASA-Mir 2 and 3. The toxicity index was calculated for each toxicological group by summing the ratios of the measured concentrations to the space maximum allowable concentrations for each contaminant in a toxicological group. The high toxicity index of the irritant group was due in part to high concentrations of formaldehyde.

    As hypothesized, spatial variations of contaminants were small within the Mir complex for both SSAS and GSC samples. The variations were most likely caused by contaminants localized in the different modules. The rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between Shuttle and Mir could not be established because of too few samples. A comparison of the U.S. and Russian air sampling methods showed that the Russian AK-1 sorbent system samplers, on average, measured higher concentrations than did the U.S. samplers.

    During the course of this experiment, several opportunities arose that allowed scientists to study situations that had previously been unexamined. During NASA-Mir 4, a fire was caused by the solid fuel oxygen generator (SFOG); this presented an opportunity to study the contaminants released into the Mir atmosphere due to the fire, and also assess how well the life support system scrubs contaminants from the air. The life support system worked excellent and brought the pollutants associated with the fire back to baseline concentrations within 32 hours. During NASA-Mir 4 the investigators also had the opportunity to compare the results of the formaldehyde badges to those of the formaldehyde active sampler (FAS). Because of the difficulties involved with collecting inflight formaldehyde samples, conclusive results were not obtained. However, another opportunity arose to compare these two methods during the second phase of the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). The results of this test verified the validity of the badges when compared to other methods.

    During NASA-Mir 5, all sampling hardware was lost due to the decompression of the Spektr module. The focus of the experiment then changed to analyzing how well the humidity control system would scrub a large concentration of ethylene glycol from the air. It was hypothesized that ethylene glycol present in Mir air due to a leak would be removed quickly. However, ethylene glycol detector tubes were used to measure ethylene concentrations, and it took one month for the concentration to drop below the 180-day SMAC level. Additionally, ethylene concentrations measured by the GSCs during the other NASA-Mir missions were determined to be high enough to affect plant growth experiments.

    The final unscheduled event occurred during a low temperature catalytic oxidizer (LTCO) burn. Improper operation of the LTCO caused dangerously high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) to be released into the Mir atmosphere. The combustion products analyzer (CPA) recorded high levels of CO, but because the crew appeared to be doing well after the incident, the high levels were thought to have been caused by hydrogen interference. Because this was such a serious toxicological incident, many steps have been taken to prevent a reoccurrence. One step, which will be used on the International Space Station (ISS), is the use of a new CPA that has much less cross sensitivity to hydrogen.

experiment_title: Food Fortification Stability Study
parameter_html:
Food vitamin loss
Fortification nutrients
Food, nutrient degradation
investigators: Principal Investigator: Sirmons, TakiyahPrincipal Investigator: Cooper, MayaCo-Investigator: Douglas, Grace
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA has established the goal of traveling beyond low-Earth orbit and extending manned exploration to Mars. The length of proposed Mars missions and the lack of resupply missions increases the importance of nutritional content in the food system, which will need a five year shelf life. The purpose of this research was to assess the stability of vitamin supplementation in traditionally processed space flight foods. It is expected that commercially available fortification nutrients will remain stable through a long-duration exploration mission at sufficient levels if compatible formulation, processing, and storage temperatures are achieved.

APPROACH:
Five vitamins (vitamin E, vitamin K, pantothenic acid, folic acid, and thiamin) were blended into a vitamin premix such that the vitamin concentration per serving equaled 25% of the recommended daily intake after two years of ambient storage. Four freeze-dried foods (Scrambled Eggs, Italian Vegetables, Potatoes Au Gratin, Noodles and Chicken) and four thermostabilized foods (Curry Sauce with Vegetables, Chicken Noodle Soup, Grilled Pork Chop, Rice with Butter) were produced, with and without the vitamin premix, to assess the impact of the added fortification on color and taste and to determine the stability of supplemental vitamins in spaceflight foods.


RESULTS:

The addition of fortification to space flight foods appears to be a plausible mitigation step to inadequate nutrition concerns when considering the ease of adding vitamin premix to the formulations for provisions and the sustainability of the vitamins through the initial processing steps. Vitamin fortification with this premix did not have immediate impact to sensory and color of the food. At this stage, the caveat to introduction is the preciseness to which vitamins can be added. The total amount of vitamin premix required for the largest space production run equates to 10 - 20 grams, a tiny percentage of the formulation. As demonstrated by Italian Vegetables and Grilled Pork Chop, the homogeneity may be difficult to achieve with such small amounts so pouch-to-pouch variability, over-fortification, and under-fortification may ensue. Future analysis should reveal the extent to which this issue should be a concern.

No data sets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Novel Explorations Into the Interactions Between Light and Gravity Sensing in Plants - Seedling Growth-2
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Medina, F.Principal Investigator: Kiss, JohnCo-Investigator: Edelmann, Richard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The major goals of this project are to determine how gravity and light responses influence each other in plants and to better understand the cellular signaling mechanisms involved in plant tropisms. This proposed project builds on our previous spaceflight experiments on the ISS (TROPI-1, 2006; TROPI-2, 2010) with the EMCS using the model plant Arabidopsis. In this new proposed project, we plan to confirm and extend our discovery during the recent TROPI-2 ISS experiment of a novel red-light-based positive phototropic response in plant shoots.

Thus, the specific objectives of this proposed research are: (1) To confirm and characterize the novel red light-dependent phototropic response in flowering plants. (2) To investigate the relationship between light and gravity by measuring thresholds in fractional gravity. (3) To determine whether the red light effect on blue-light-based phototropism is a direct or indirect effect.

Seedling Growth 1: Phototropism
Seedling Growth 2: Tropisms, Auxin, and Cell Culture
Seedling Growth 3: Proliferating Cell Structure
Seedling Growth 4: Synthesis/Experiment Contingency
APPROACH:

The Seedling Growth series of experiments (1, 2, 3 and possibly 4) is supported collaboratively by NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA). The experiment will be conducted in the European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS) on the International Space Station (ISS). The EMCS is operated by ESA and is located in the Columbus Module of the ISS.

These experiments can be accomplished with telemetric science and therefore fit with the extremely limited down mass capabilities of current spaceflight opportunities. The EMCS is an automated facility and can be operated largely with telemetry. Experimental containers will be launched via Space-X, and during an experimental run, images of seedling growth responses can be downlinked to Earth. Seedlings will be returned to Earth in the GLACIER freezer.

RESULTS:

Project 2: Gene Profiling

The transcriptome of seedlings were analyzed from experiments performed on the International Space Station (ISS) to study the interacting effects of light and gravity on plant tropisms. Seeds of Arabidopsis thaliana were germinated and grown in cassettes in the European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS) for 4 days at 1g then exposed to a range of gravitational accelerations (microgravity, 0.07g, 0.13g, 0.21g, 0.39g, 0.53g, and 1g) and light treatments (blue light with or without a 1 hour pretreatment with red light). At the end of the space experiments, the cassettes containing the seedlings were frozen in the Minus Eighty Laboratory Freezer (MELFI) and returned to Earth on space shuttle STS-131. The RNA was extracted from whole seedlings and used for the transcriptome analyses. A comparison of 1g-treated-spaceflight samples with ground controls identified 230 genes that were differentially regulated at least two-fold (p < 0.01). A further comparison of all spaceflight samples with ground controls identified approximately 280 genes that were differentially regulated at least two fold (p < 0.01). Of these genes, several were involved in regulating cell polarity (i.e., auxin, calcium, lipid metabolism), cell wall development, oxygen status, and cell defense or stress. However, when the transcriptome of the all g-treated spaceflight samples were compared with microgravity samples, only approx.130 genes were identified as being differently regulated (p < 0.01). Of these, only 27 were at least 2 fold differently regulated between microgravity and 1g samples and included putatitive/pseudo/undefined genes (n=14), transposable elements (n=5), an expansin (ATEXP24; At1g21240), a cell-wall kinase (WAK3; At1g21240), a laccase-like flavonoid oxidase (TT10;At5g48100), among others. Not surprisingly, there was a difference in the % of genes represented in individual gene categories when comparing spaceflight samples with ground controls and spaceflight microgravity versus spaceflight g-treated space samples. These results emphasize the need for tissue fixation on the centrifuge for an accurate spaceflight control. These results are one of the few reports of transcriptome analyses from a space experiment with plants that had gravity treatments using an on-board centrifuge.

Additional results will be made available through Seedling Growth-3.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The deleterious effects of radiation encountered in space present a significant obstacle in space exploration. Unfortunately, due to the significant differences between space radiation and radiation encountered on Earth, the risks of cancer development following exposure to space radiation cannot be reliably predicted based solely on epidemiological data collected on Earth.

This project will study the effects of space radiation on development and/or progression of prostate cancer. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men in the United States and the second leading cause of cancer deaths. It is also the most often diagnosed type of cancer in male astronauts. However, the connection between exposure to space radiation and the development of prostate cancer is not yet known. Several lines of evidence suggest that conversion of normal prostate or prostate cancer cells into cells secreting cell growth hormones, so called neuroendocrine cells, stimulate cancer development and/or progression. Strikingly, such conversion was recently reported in prostate cells exposed to prolonged irradiation. The low doses and long exposure times used in that study are not dissimilar to the doses and exposure times encountered during space travel.

Therefore, it is postulated that space radiation could increase the risk of prostate cancer development through the transformation of prostate cells into neuroendocrine cells during space flights. Since neuroendocrine cells seem to play an important role in the development of other important and common types of solid tumors, such as breast, lung, or colon, the insight gained during this study should be also applicable to these cancers. The results obtained during the proposed studies will allow NASA to better estimate the prostate cancer health risk(s) of space exploration, as well as provide clues that will allow the development of novel preventative measures to protect astronauts.

The specific aims of this research are to:

1. Determine if dose, dose rate and the quality of space radiation have differential effects on carcinogenesis in prostate cells.

2. Determine if prolonged exposure to space radiation can induce neuroendocrine differentiation in prostate cancer cells.

3. Determine if carcinogenesis/neoplastic transformation in prostate cells exposed to space radiation is influenced by the presence of neuroendocrine cells.

APPROACH:
Two cell lines were used. RWPE-1 is a normal epithelial line and LNCaP is an androgen dependent early stage prostate cancer line. Cells in the exponential phase of growth were exposed to either to X-rays (220 kV, at the Department of Radiation Oncology, University of Virginia) or to protons (1000 MeV/n), oxygen ions (200 MeV/n) or titanium ions (1100 MeV/n), all at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY).

The effect of irradiation on cell survival was measured by clonogenic cell survival assay. In some experiments, cells were pre-treated with neurotensin (NT, 100 nM/1h) and/or SR48692 inhibitor (SR, 1µM/24h) before irradiation. The effect of irradiation on cells' ability to survive and proliferate under attachment-independent conditions was measured by soft agar (transformation) colony formation assay. Levels of protein expression and/or post-translational modifications were assessed by standard Western blotting technique. The expression of genes of interest was assessed by semi-quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) and/or quantitative RT-PCR using a Bio-Rad CFX96 quantitative PCR instrument.

RESULTS:
The data obtained in this project demonstrate that radiation dose and quality have clear differential effects not just on DNA damage and cell killing, but more importantly on the initiation of prostate carcinogenesis. While it is not possible to irradiate cells at the low fluences that would be experienced by astronauts during space exploration, the data also demonstrate that fractionated irradiations, but not a single acute exposure, induce mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition or neuroendocrine differentiation of normal prostate cells and prostate cancer cells. Further, this work defines signaling pathways and genetic alterations that effect these molecular and phenotypic changes that are involved in radiation-induced prostate cancer initiation and progression. As such, this project increases the mechanistic understanding of the fundamental biological processes involved in space radiation-induced carcinogenesis and provide NASA with important information regarding the potential increase risk of prostate cancer as a result of space radiation exposure.

Therefore, it is postulated that space radiation could increase the risk of prostate cancer development through the transformation of prostate cells into neuroendocrine cells during space flights. Since neuroendocrine cells seem to play an important role in the development of other important and common types of solid tumors, such as breast, lung, or colon, the insight gained during this study should be also applicable to these cancers. The results obtained during the proposed studies will allow NASA to better estimate the prostate cancer health risk(s) of space exploration, as well as provide clues that will allow the development of novel preventative measures to protect astronauts.

The specific aims of this research are to:

1. Determine if dose, dose rate and the quality of space radiation have differential effects on carcinogenesis in prostate cells.

2. Determine if prolonged exposure to space radiation can induce neuroendocrine differentiation in prostate cancer cells.

3. Determine if carcinogenesis/neoplastic transformation in prostate cells exposed to space radiation is influenced by the presence of neuroendocrine cells.

APPROACH:
Two cell lines were used. RWPE-1 is a normal epithelial line and LNCaP is an androgen dependent early stage prostate cancer line. Cells in the exponential phase of growth were exposed to either to X-rays (220 kV, at the Department of Radiation Oncology, University of Virginia) or to protons (1000 MeV/n), oxygen ions (200 MeV/n) or titanium ions (1100 MeV/n), all at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY).

The effect of irradiation on cell survival was measured by clonogenic cell survival assay. In some experiments, cells were pre-treated with neurotensin (NT, 100 nM/1h) and/or SR48692 inhibitor (SR, 1µM/24h) before irradiation. The effect of irradiation on cells' ability to survive and proliferate under attachment-independent conditions was measured by soft agar (transformation) colony formation assay. Levels of protein expression and/or post-translational modifications were assessed by standard Western blotting technique. The expression of genes of interest was assessed by semi-quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) and/or quantitative RT-PCR using a Bio-Rad CFX96 quantitative PCR instrument.

RESULTS:
The data obtained in this project demonstrate that radiation dose and quality have clear differential effects not just on DNA damage and cell killing, but more importantly on the initiation of prostate carcinogenesis. While it is not possible to irradiate cells at the low fluences that would be experienced by astronauts during space exploration, the data also demonstrate that fractionated irradiations, but not a single acute exposure, induce mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition or neuroendocrine differentiation of normal prostate cells and prostate cancer cells. Further, this work defines signaling pathways and genetic alterations that effect these molecular and phenotypic changes that are involved in radiation-induced prostate cancer initiation and progression. As such, this project increases the mechanistic understanding of the fundamental biological processes involved in space radiation-induced carcinogenesis and provide NASA with important information regarding the potential increase risk of prostate cancer as a result of space radiation exposure.

experiment_title: Integration of Product, Package, Process, and Environment: A Food System Optimization
parameter_html:
Food oxidation
Food preservation
Food storage
Vitamin degradation
Cell structure, fruit
investigators: Principal Investigator: Cooper, MayaCo-Investigator: Douglas, GraceCo-Investigator: Glass, JohnCo-Investigator: Leong, MonicaCo-Investigator: Nelman, Mayra
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is working to achieve manned space flights beyond low-Earth orbit within the next 25 years. Specifically, the vision includes a manned mission to Mars, which demands that astronauts survive extra-terrestrially for a minimum of three years. The space foods themselves must maintain quality for up to five years so that the food can be prepositioned on the Martian surface prior to crew arrival if necessary. This product life requirement is beyond the capability of the current stabilized food system used on the International Space Station (ISS). Thus, the food system optimization is vital for the viability of all extended duration missions.

Optimizing the food system to achieve a five-year shelf life mitigates the risk of inadequate food system during extended missions. Two causes of an inadequate food system are inadequate nutritional content within the food and inadequate acceptability of the food leading to insufficient intake. This study directly addresses those nutrition and acceptability concerns. Nutritional content and food quality, particularly as products age, are indicative of the food matrix, history, and storage environment. For example, a high availability of oxygen in a food package can be detrimental to product shelf life. The oxidative reactions that cause rancidity also lead to the degradation of vitamin C, vitamin A, folic acid, and thiamin. Likewise, a product subjected to high heat in processing may undergo nonenzymatic browning, but broad vitamin degradation should also be expected after thermal processing. By establishing the proper recipe, process, package, and storage condition, the product is better positioned to sustain nutrition and acceptability over the product life. The chances of performance decrement or illness due to insufficient nutrition or poor food intake decreases with implementation of this integrated food system.

The objective of this experiment is to optimize food product shelf life for the space food system through product recipe adjustments, application of new packiagin and processing technologies, and modified storage conditions. The aims are to:

  1. Summarize the available packaged food technologies that would offer significant barrier or antioxidant property improvements over current space packaging.
  2. Complete a risk-benefit analysis on the usage of the space environment for cold food storage.
  3. Provide recommendations as to the formulation changes, processes, packages, and environments for each space food product that would result in a five-year shelf life for that product.
  4. Identify the technology needs associated with implementing any of the aforementioned integration recommendations.

At the study conclusion, a course to shift the space food products to a five-year shelf life will be proposed. Overall system or category changes will be clearly identified, and products with little chance of meeting the five-year shelf life hurdle will be delineated for replacement or removal from long-duration menus. The required future work to deliver this postulated integration for the food system will be identified.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn't available.

RESULTS:
In this study the space food system was divided into five food category modules – thermostabilized fruits, thermostabilized vegetables, thermostabilized entrees, freeze-dried foods, and baked goods. Through hypothesis-driven experimentation alternative storage, processing, and packaging technologies were evaluated to achieve better sensory, color, texture, and nutrient quality. None of the experiments singularly resulted in five-year shelf life, but important evaluation of the technologies was achieved as indicated in the following key results. Thermostabilized fruits have significant quality issues when stored at ambient temperatures, but colder temperatures alone did not drive enough stabilization in the assessed products to reasonably achieve a five-year shelf life through storage modifications. Pressure-assisted thermostabilization (PATS) resulted in better color and texture of the fruit, but not vitamin stability, as compared to traditional retort. The greatest challenges with thermostabilized vegetables, nutrient degradation and textural softening, were not alleviated by microwave-assisted thermal stabilization (MATS) of the Carrot Coins. The MATS process did produce carrots with brighter color and better texture initially, but due to inadequate packaging barrier, improvements were not sustained over the shelf life of the product. Similarly, the MATS process did not provide a significant, sustained improvement for the evaluated entree, Sweet and Sour Pork. In the freeze-dried food module, the rehydration of freeze-dried items appeared to be most affected by the moisture content of the food. Even slight changes in moisture resulted in noticeable shifts in the amount of water absorbed. Finally, in the baked goods module the evaluation of Butter Cookies demonstrated that the initial development of off-flavors in baked goods may not be the direct result of fat reacting with residual oxygen but the rancidity and chemical activity that comes with higher moisture.

Because the five-year shelf life was not fully achieved, future research will focus on a hurdle approach, a likely stability solution for most of the foods. Cold storage has the capability to slow the chemical reactions that cause color darkening and vitamin degradation as well as slow the enzymatic reactions that lead to textural degradation. Hence, alternative processing technologies, along with colder storage, improve the probability of getting a five-year shelf life for thermostabilized space foods. Opportunities exist to alter freeze-dried product quality by optimizing process parameters and tightening end product specifications. Processing the food precisely and protecting the food against moisture ingress should result in five years of shelf life in freeze-dried items. Moisture control should be the focus area of future baked goods work. Refrigeration or freezing should be considered for baked goods as the colder temperatures slowed moisture and oxygen ingress. Encapsulated vitamins should be considered for all food items.

experiment_title: Studies of Mechanisms Underlying Orthostatic Intolerance using Ambulatory Monitoring, Baroreflex Testing, and the Valsalva Maneuver
parameter_html:
Blood pressure
Catecholamines
Neck pressure
Renin, plasma
Respiration
Valsalva pressure
Electrocardiogram (ECG)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Mikhaylov, ValeriyPrincipal Investigator: Meck, JaniceCo-Investigator: Bondar, RobertaCo-Investigator: Brown, Troy
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Over the last three decades, symptoms of altered cardiovascular function ranging from orthostatic tachycardia on landing day to serious cardiac rhythm disturbances have been associated with short duration space flight.  However, there is a lack of understanding about the effects of long duration space flight on cardiovascular function.

It was hypothesized that: (1) after flight, autonomic responses to changes in arterial pressure (supine and standing) will be compromised; (2) carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex (baroreflex) function will decrease steadily during the first four weeks of flight and then remain stable; this decrease in function will relate to postflight orthostatic intolerance; (3) blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and their variabilities will be decreased throughout the flight, and the reduced variabilities will relate to reductions in carotid baroreflex function and postflight orthostatic intolerance; (4) changes in heart rate and arterial responses during Valsalva maneuvers will reflect inflight loss of autonomic function.

The primary objective of this experiment was to assess cardiovascular function before, at regular intervals during, and after long duration space flight by performing a standard battery of tests. The second objective was to characterize the integrated responses of arterial pressure reflex control systems to standing before and after long duration space flight. The third objective was to relate inflight changes in the integrated responses of arterial pressure reflex control systems before and after long duration space flight. The last objective of this experiment was to determine the importance of changes in blood volume to postflight decrements in orthostatic tolerance.

APPROACH:
There were four functional objectives in this experiment: 24 hour ECG and Blood Pressure Monitoring, Carotid Baroreflex, Valsalva Maneuver, and Stand Test. For the 24-hour period prior to carotid baroreflex measurements, HR, BP, and cardiac rhythm disturbances were recorded during normal routines in the ground and in flight. Holter monitors recorded the electrocardiogram continuously and blood pressure monitors recorded auscultative BP automatically every 20 minutes while awake and every 30 minutes while asleep. After the flight, a Holter analysis system automatically generated reports, which included average heart rate and incidence of atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias. All reports were verified by at least one board certified cardiologist. Blood pressure results were also verified. For the carotid baroreflex, carotid barorecptors were stimulated with a stereotyped series of pressure changes applied to a neck chamber. Pressure was raised initially to about +40 mmHg, reduced to about -60 mmHg, and then raised back to +40 mmHg in 20 mmHg, R-wave triggered steps. R-R interval responses were plotted as functions of carotid distending pressure. Baroreflex responses were reduced to the following set of parameters for analysis: range of R-R interval responses, maximum slope of the stimulus-response relation, and operational point. The operational point is a measure of the amount of buffering capacity below baseline systolic pressure. The crewmembers performed two 15 second Valsalva maneuvers at 30 mmHg expired pressure after the baroreflex measurements were completed. Two minutes separated each Valsalva maneuver.  Before, during, and after each stimulus, the electrocardiogram, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and Valsalva straining pressure were recorded. Controlled frequency breathing was performed before and after each Valsalva maneuver. Valsalva responses were divided into four phases for analysis:

  • Phase I, the initial blood pressure and R-R interval rise immediately after the onset of straining
  • Phase II, the early blood pressure and R-R interval fall and partial recovery during straining
  • Phase III, the sudden and brief blood pressure and R-R interval reduction immediately after the release of straining
  • Phase IV, the blood pressure and R-R interval overshoot of recovery.

    Stand tests were performed preflight and postflight after Valsalva maneuvers were completed. For stand tests, crewmembers were instrumented for electrocardiogram, manual blood pressure, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and transcranial Doppler. An intravenous catheter was inserted into an antecubital vein. Following a 20-minute supine rest period, plasma volume was determined using carbon monoxide rebreathing. A blood sample was drawn for plasma norepinephrine and plasma epinephrine levels. Then, 2-D and M-mode echocardiography were used to determine aortic cross-sectional diameter and aortic flow was measured with continuous-wave Doppler ultrasound. Middle cerebral artery flow was measured with transcranial Doppler ultrasound. Measurements continued while subjects remained supine for six additional minutes. Crewmembers were then assisted to a standing position by three investigators. The finger with the continuous arterial pressure device was held at heart level by a system of Velcro straps. Crewmembers then remained standing without support for 10 minutes. A final blood sample was drawn at the end of the standing period. All data were recorded on digital tape and on paper.

    RESULTS:
    A number of preflight, inflight, and postflight anomalies occurred during the experiment. Data were lost due to equipment failure, subject compliance, and crew support personnel interference. Due to these various anomalies, some data collections were compromised. Nonetheless, this experiment has yielded important information about cardiac function during long duration space flight.

    Findings from this investigation are very similar to those reported from short duration space flight investigations and indicate that most autonomic cardiovascular adaptations occur within the first days of space flight, possibly the result of decreased sympathoexcitation. These changes persist for at least four months in flight. However, the occurrence of a significant event of ventricular tachycardia during the mid-portion of the flight does not preclude the possiblity that long duration space flight increases the likelihood of malignant dysrhythmias.

experiment_title: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) - 14 Project: Advanced Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Exploration Activities Study to Assess Human Performance Responses in Partial Gravity Environments

investigators: Principal Investigator: Gernhardt, MichaelCo-Investigator: Abercromby, AndrewCo-Investigator: Chappell, StevenCo-Investigator: Norcross, Jason
experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Space Exploration Vehicle (SEV) is regarded by the Exploration Systems Mission Directorate (ESMD) as an integral part of the current exploration architectures under consideration. The SEV offers numerous health and safety advantages that accrue from having a pressurized safe haven/radiation shelter in close proximity to the crew at all times during exploration operations. It also combines a comfortable shirtsleeve, sensor-augmented environment for gross translations and geological/mapping observations with the ability to rapidly place suited astronauts outside of the vehicle using suitports to take full advantage of the unique human talents of perception, judgment, and dexterity. Data from the Desert Research and Technology Studies (DRATS) 2008 field test demonstrated that this combination of features and capabilities increases the productivity of suited crew time by an average of 370% during exploration/mapping/geological operations using an SEV compared to suited crew time with an unpressurized rover.

The SEV concept is being developed through an aggressive process of designing, prototyping, and testing in close coordination with the development of other exploration systems including the extravehicular activity (EVA) suit. Different test objectives necessitate different test sites, and the objectives of the NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) 14 test required a simulated reduced-gravity environment. The ability to simulate microgravity and reduced gravity for extended durations during EVA tasks means that NEEMO missions represent a cost-effective opportunity to understand the operation and interaction of hardware and humans in these environments. The ultimate success of future exploration missions is dependent on the ability to perform EVA tasks efficiently and safely, whether those tasks represent a nominal mode of operation or a contingency capability; all systems must therefore be designed with EVA accessibility and operability as important considerations. During the 2-week NEEMO 14 mission, four crew members performed a series of EVA tasks under different simulated EVA-suit configurations and gravity levels and used full-scale mock-ups of an SEV and a cargo lander. Quantitative and qualitative data collected during NEEMO 14 will be used to directly inform ongoing hardware and operations concept development of the SEV, exploration EVA systems, and future EVA suits.

APPROACH:
Subjects were recruited from the active astronaut corps as well as through a space life sciences selection process. Through this selection, four male astronaut subjects, consisting of two active astronauts and two space life sciences investigators, participated in the mission. All subjects successfully passed a modified Air Force Class III Physical or equivalent examination. Each subject was provided verbal and written explanations of the testing protocols and the potential risks and hazards involved in the testing and signed NASA JSC Human Research documentation indicating his/her understanding and consent. All testing protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA JSC CPHS, and appropriate test readiness reviews were conducted before testing began.

Crewmembers were briefed on the objectives and methods of the study before departure for the field test site, and participated in a comprehensive training program that included review and practice of the following: 1) Study hypotheses, 2) Metrics and data collection procedures, 3) Mission rules, 4) Task procedures, 5) CG rig familiarization, 6) Mock-up familiarization, 7) Aquarius familiarization, and 8) Communications protocols. On deployment to the field test site, all crewmembers completed a brief refresher course before the start of the mission.

The SEV mock-up used in this study is based on the cabin 1B prototype that was developed as a collaborative effort among NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC), NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC), NASA Ames Research Center (ARC), and NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). The SEV mock-up also incorporated the features necessary to achieve mission objectives. A full-scale mock-up of the SEV was constructed near the Aquarius habitat to achieve the rover-based test objectives. This SEV mock-up had side-hatches that were 101.6 cm (40 in.) wide and an adjustable height from 101.6 cm (40 in.) to 152.4 cm (60 in.). The aft bulkhead of the mockup featured suitport simulators. The height of the door thresholds, suitport thresholds, and aft deck accurately simulated the expected lowest possible heights based on prototypes. The SEV interior was minimally simulated by employing fold-up benches and side-hatch doors.

The next iteration of the SEV-rover development process was the conceptual design of a Generation II (Gen II) SEV rover, which began in early fiscal year (FY) 2010. The size of the SEV side-hatches was one of the most significant drivers for the cabin geometry; and a primary driver for the hatch dimensions is the ability to transfer an incapacitated EVA crewmember into the SEV. Data regarding the adequacy of a 101.6 cm wide by 101.6 cm high (40 in. wide by 40 in. high) side-hatch for transferring an incapacitated EVA crewmember into the SEV was used by the SEV team to finalize the SEV side-hatch dimensions.

EVA interfaces, task design, suit weight and suit center of gravity (CG), and hardware accessibility and operability were quantitatively and qualitatively evaluated in simulated reduced gravity during the following EVA tasks at NEEMO 14:
1. Unloading an SEV mock-up from the deck of a cargo-lander mock-up
2. Off-loading small payloads from the deck of a cargo-lander mock-up
3. Transferring small payloads from the surface onto the deck of a cargo-lander mock-up
4. Transferring an incapacitated crewmember from the surface onto the deck of a crew-lander mock-up
5. Transferring an incapacitated crewmember from the surface into an SEV-rover mock-up via a:
6. Crewmember translation through hatchways:
7. Transferring an incapacitated crew member from the crew-lander deck into an airlock and ascent module
8. Crewmember translation into an airlock and ascent module

Each of the EVA tasks was performed a total of nine times by each of the four crewmembers to enable the combined effects of three different simulated suit weights and three different suit CG locations to be evaluated and compared. Data regarding the effects of suit weight and CG on task performance were systematically analyzed and will ensure that the implications of suit weight and CG location on EVA performance are adequately understood and considered during the development of exploration EVA suits. In addition to the EVA tasks listed above, crew members also completed a standard exploration EVA task protocol used during all EVA Physiology, Systems, and Performance (EPSP) Project tests, including previous NEEMO missions. The protocol consisted of ambulation, kneel/recover, fall/recover, shoveling, rock pick-up, and ladder climbing tasks, each of which was performed according to the EPSP protocol under each of the nine weight/CG configurations.

RESULTS:
Please refer to the document NASA TP-2011-216152. This document contains images, graphs, tables, and summarized results for each protocol of the study.

Data from the Desert Research and Technology Studies (DRATS) 2008 field test demonstrated that this combination of features and capabilities increases the productivity of suited crew time by an average of 370% during exploration/mapping/geological operations using an SEV compared to suited crew time with an unpressurized rover.

The SEV concept is being developed through an aggressive process of designing, prototyping, and testing in close coordination with the development of other exploration systems including the extravehicular activity (EVA) suit. Different test objectives necessitate different test sites, and the objectives of the NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) 14 test required a simulated reduced-gravity environment. The ability to simulate microgravity and reduced gravity for extended durations during EVA tasks means that NEEMO missions represent a cost-effective opportunity to understand the operation and interaction of hardware and humans in these environments. The ultimate success of future exploration missions is dependent on the ability to perform EVA tasks efficiently and safely, whether those tasks represent a nominal mode of operation or a contingency capability; all systems must therefore be designed with EVA accessibility and operability as important considerations. During the 2-week NEEMO 14 mission, four crew members performed a series of EVA tasks under different simulated EVA-suit configurations and gravity levels and used full-scale mock-ups of an SEV and a cargo lander. Quantitative and qualitative data collected during NEEMO 14 will be used to directly inform ongoing hardware and operations concept development of the SEV, exploration EVA systems, and future EVA suits.

APPROACH:
Subjects were recruited from the active astronaut corps as well as through a space life sciences selection process. Through this selection, four male astronaut subjects, consisting of two active astronauts and two space life sciences investigators, participated in the mission. All subjects successfully passed a modified Air Force Class III Physical or equivalent examination. Each subject was provided verbal and written explanations of the testing protocols and the potential risks and hazards involved in the testing and signed NASA JSC Human Research documentation indicating his/her understanding and consent. All testing protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA JSC CPHS, and appropriate test readiness reviews were conducted before testing began.

Crewmembers were briefed on the objectives and methods of the study before departure for the field test site, and participated in a comprehensive training program that included review and practice of the following: 1) Study hypotheses, 2) Metrics and data collection procedures, 3) Mission rules, 4) Task procedures, 5) CG rig familiarization, 6) Mock-up familiarization, 7) Aquarius familiarization, and 8) Communications protocols. On deployment to the field test site, all crewmembers completed a brief refresher course before the start of the mission.

The SEV mock-up used in this study is based on the cabin 1B prototype that was developed as a collaborative effort among NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC), NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC), NASA Ames Research Center (ARC), and NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). The SEV mock-up also incorporated the features necessary to achieve mission objectives. A full-scale mock-up of the SEV was constructed near the Aquarius habitat to achieve the rover-based test objectives. This SEV mock-up had side-hatches that were 101.6 cm (40 in.) wide and an adjustable height from 101.6 cm (40 in.) to 152.4 cm (60 in.). The aft bulkhead of the mockup featured suitport simulators. The height of the door thresholds, suitport thresholds, and aft deck accurately simulated the expected lowest possible heights based on prototypes. The SEV interior was minimally simulated by employing fold-up benches and side-hatch doors.

The next iteration of the SEV-rover development process was the conceptual design of a Generation II (Gen II) SEV rover, which began in early fiscal year (FY) 2010. The size of the SEV side-hatches was one of the most significant drivers for the cabin geometry; and a primary driver for the hatch dimensions is the ability to transfer an incapacitated EVA crewmember into the SEV. Data regarding the adequacy of a 101.6 cm wide by 101.6 cm high (40 in. wide by 40 in. high) side-hatch for transferring an incapacitated EVA crewmember into the SEV was used by the SEV team to finalize the SEV side-hatch dimensions.

EVA interfaces, task design, suit weight and suit center of gravity (CG), and hardware accessibility and operability were quantitatively and qualitatively evaluated in simulated reduced gravity during the following EVA tasks at NEEMO 14:
1. Unloading an SEV mock-up from the deck of a cargo-lander mock-up
2. Off-loading small payloads from the deck of a cargo-lander mock-up
3. Transferring small payloads from the surface onto the deck of a cargo-lander mock-up
4. Transferring an incapacitated crewmember from the surface onto the deck of a crew-lander mock-up
5. Transferring an incapacitated crewmember from the surface into an SEV-rover mock-up via a:
6. Crewmember translation through hatchways:
7. Transferring an incapacitated crew member from the crew-lander deck into an airlock and ascent module
8. Crewmember translation into an airlock and ascent module

Each of the EVA tasks was performed a total of nine times by each of the four crewmembers to enable the combined effects of three different simulated suit weights and three different suit CG locations to be evaluated and compared. Data regarding the effects of suit weight and CG on task performance were systematically analyzed and will ensure that the implications of suit weight and CG location on EVA performance are adequately understood and considered during the development of exploration EVA suits. In addition to the EVA tasks listed above, crew members also completed a standard exploration EVA task protocol used during all EVA Physiology, Systems, and Performance (EPSP) Project tests, including previous NEEMO missions. The protocol consisted of ambulation, kneel/recover, fall/recover, shoveling, rock pick-up, and ladder climbing tasks, each of which was performed according to the EPSP protocol under each of the nine weight/CG configurations.

Please refer to the document NASA TP-2011-216152. This document contains images, graphs, tables, and summarized results for each protocol of the study.

experiment_title: Use of Exercise and Partial Decompression to Reduce Oxygen Prebreathe Requirements for 4.3 PSIA Extravehicular Activity
parameter_html:
Exercise
Oxygen, prebreathe time
Decompression sickness
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pollock, Neal
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts, like divers, are exposed to changes in pressure that can lead to decompression sickness (DCS), otherwise known as "the bends." When an astronaut leaves the International Space Station (ISS) for Extravehicular Activity (EVA), the pressure of the space suit (4.3 psia) is one third of sea level pressure (14.7 psia), or equivalent to the pressure at an altitude of 30,300 feet. Astronauts breathe oxygen prior to an EVA ('prebreathe') to eliminate nitrogen from the body, thus decreasing the risk of developing decompression sickness. The prebreathe reduction program (PRP) was initiated to evaluate oxygen prebreathe protocols which combined microgravity simulation with different patterns of exercise to effectively reduce the baseline four hour oxygen prebreathe time required to control decompression stresses to acceptable levels.

APPROACH:
This study was designed to determine the safest procedure for protecting astronauts from DCS during the many spacewalks required for construction and maintenance of the ISS. Extravehicular activity is very demanding, both physically and mentally, partially due the nature of the space suit. The space suit currently in use consists of a Hard Upper Torso with flexible extremities. The resting position or maximum volume of a spacesuit is found with the arms elevated overhead in a relaxed position. Astronauts work to alter the resting position of the spacesuit in addition to the work required for the EVA. This study aimed to simulate both the effects of the space environment on the body and the effort of spacesuit/EVA activity.

RESULTS:
Completion of the first four phases of the PRP program yielded a successful two hour prebreathe protocol that combined an initial 10 minute period of heavy exercise on a cycle ergometer, followed by light intermittent exercise, followed by a final 40 minutes of resting prebreathe.

experiment_title: Comparison of Bending Stiffness in the Dominant and Non-dominant Tibias of Women
parameter_html:
Size, length; Bone
Body mass
Height
Bone stiffness
Bone strength, tibia
Muscle strength
investigators: Principal Investigator: Arnaud, Sara
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is limited information on the mechanical properties of the long bones of healthy women compared to the amount of data on the density of bone. We were interested in determining the mechanical strength of a long bone and evaluating it in reference to the strength of the muscles of the same bone. We were also interested in determining gender differences in the laterality of tibial strength since previous data in normal men revealed the left tibia was stronger than the right.

APPROACH:
Twenty women (age 44±11 yrs) were recruited from the working staff of Ames Research Center. All gave informed consent for the study and provided brief historical information on general health and physical activity. The tests for muscle strength were carried out by quantifying the forces required to extend and flex the leg with a LIDO instrument. A non-invasive test of bone strength was performed in the tibia of a relaxed recumbent subject with the probe of instrument positioned on the center of the ‘shin’ bone. The MRTA delivers a “buzz”, detects the response of the bone to a brief vibration at the same site on which the probe is centered and then analyzes the response curve by software that generates a measurement for bending stiffness or EI (E is the modulus of elasticity and I the moment of inertia) for the tibia. The instrument had been previously validated in the bones of monkeys by correlating the non-invasive measurement with three-point bending in a mechanical instrument in the same bone (0.95 was the significance of the results of the in vivo test vs. the extracted bone tested with a mechanical instrument). Gender comparisons were done on a population of 22 normal men, aged 39±7 yrs studied earlier (ref #4).

RESULTS:
In contrast to the findings in men, there was no difference in the bending stiffness of the right and left tibias (150±71 vs. 151±47Nm2). Values in women averaged 28% lower than in men, appropriate for the 24% difference in body weight (men weighed 80±10 vs. women 61±10 kg). Women were shorter than the men but had the same body mass index (BMI = wt/ht2 = 23) and tibial length. Flexion and extension of the right and left legs were also similar (83±22 vs. 84±31 in Nm for flexion and 177±38 vs. 168±51 Nm for extension) and unrelated to EI. We concluded that tibial strength is appropriate for its load carrying function in both sexes, symmetrical in women, but not in men.

experiment_title: Use of Fludrocortisone or Salt Load to Expand Plasma Volume in Ambulatory Subjects
parameter_html:
Potassium, urine
Sodium, urine
Glucose tolerance, blood
Heart function, EKG
Hematocrit
Hemoglobin
Blood pressure
Plasma volume
investigators: Principal Investigator: Vernikos, Joan
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is known that a fall in blood pressure occurs after space flight on return to Earth's gravity. This is associated with a reduced volume of plasma, an adaptation made for the weightless environment, and currently restored by the ingestion of large volumes of water and salt tablets on landing. Earlier work revealed that the synthetic corticosteroid, flurocortisone, clinically useful in patients with low blood pressure, could expand plasma volume in subjects exposed to the bed rest model for space flight. The purpose of this study was to compare the effectiveness of salt ingestion with the administration of a synthetic corticosteroid to prevent orthostatic hypotension.

APPROACH:
A previous study (HR77) had tested 4 subjects with fludrocortisone (Florinef) and 4 subjects with a saline load after 7 days of – 6o bed rest. Florineff restored plasma volume to pre-bedrest levels, but a saline load did not. The response in ambulatory subjects was opposite to this post bed rest response. This study plans to repeat the earlier study in the same subjects, reversing the protocol (giving Florinef to subjects who were treated with a saline load before and giving a saline load to subjects treated with Florinef earlier). A second group of tests was done at night to understand if the lack of effect of a salt load in some astronauts was related to a difference in the regulation of salt excretion during the evening. The saline load was 8 g NaCl, (1 g/tablet) given with 960 ml water and the dose of Florinef was 0.2 mg every 8 hrs for 3 doses.

RESULTS:
Four of 5 subjects in the saline group experienced syncope and could not complete 15 minutes of standing after bed rest, while 5 of the 6 subjects given Florinef showed no syncope. After 7 days of bed rest, the increase in heart rate was similar in Florinef and saline treated subjects (to 24 bpm) and greater than the heart rate response before bed rest (to 13 bpm, p<0.05). However the saline load failed to maintain mean arterial pressure during standing post-bedrest, while Florinef treatment did maintain blood pressure. Plasma volume decreased approximately 12% after 7 days bed rest. Following treatments, Florinef returned plasma volume to within 4% of baseline whereas saline failed to restore plasma volume. Urine volume increased during 2 hours of standing after the saline load and decreased after Florinef compared with the pre-bed rest response. Urine Na and the Na/K ratio was similar before and after bed rest following the salt load, but urine Na was decreased and the Na/K ratio reduced after bed rest following Florinef.

Conclusions: Acute treatment with Florinef appears to have distinct advantages over the administration of a saline load as a countermeasure for post-bed rest orthostatic intolerance. Florinef restored plasma volume, maintained mean arterial pressure, and reduced the renal excretion of Na and the Na/K ratio whereas a saline load did not.

experiment_title: Investigation of Microgravity Effects on Physiology, Global Gene Expression, and Biofilm Phenotypes of the Caries-Causing Bacterium Streptococcus mutans
