experiment_title: Biomedical Investigations with Laser-Polarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance
parameter_html:
Xenon
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Surface area/volume ratio
investigators: Principal Investigator: Walsworth, Ronald
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The investigators developed a laser-polarized noble gas nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) as a novel biomedical imaging tool for ground-based and eventually space-based applications. This emerging multidisciplinary technology enables high-resolution gas-space magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-e.g., of lung ventilation-as well as studies of tissue perfusion. In addition, laser-polarized noble gases (3He and 129Xe) do not require a large magnetic field for sensitive detection, opening the door to practical MRI at very low magnetic fields with a lightweight, low-power device. The investigators pursued two specific aims in this research. The first aim was to develop a low-field (< 0.01 T) instrument for noble gas MRI of humans, and the second aim was to develop functional imaging of the lung using laser-polarized 129Xe.

The investigators developed a large Helmholtz coil assembly for use in low field noble gas MRI of human lungs. The coil assembly has been used to create a magnetic field of 20 gauss with better than 100 ppm field uniformity over a 30 cm diameter volume centered between the coils. The Helmholtz coil assembly is housed inside a wire-mesh cage to provide shielding from any background electromagnetic noise. The investigators also constructed low-rf pulse/drive coils and associated electronics employing low-cost audio amplifiers with custom trigger/gate circuitry. Using this 20 gauss low-field system, they obtained high SNR signals from a laser-polarized 3He phantom, and acquired a proton NMR signal in a single acquisition. They recently began the design of signal detection coils for low field MRI of human lungs, since they are not available commercially at the audio frequencies used with low field MRI. The investigators have also begun the construction of low-noise receiver electronics for these coils.

APPROACH:
The investigators began development and testing of xenon interphase exchange NMR, a new technique designed to measure the exchange of xenon atoms between the gas and dissolved phases in porous media such as the lung. They used xenon interphase exchange NMR to determine the surface-area-to-volume ratio (S/V) of four samples of porous high-density polyethylene polymer (materials commonly used in filtering, wicking, etc.) They machined each of the four samples to fit tightly in a 0.5" glass cell that excluded free gas around the polymer core. The team performed NMR experiments on a GE Omega/CSI 4.7 T spectrometer operating at 55.3 MHz for 129Xe. They filled the samples and a similar empty cell with thermally- polarized xenon, and made NMR measurements of the sample porosity f, 129Xe partition coefficient b, and dissolved-phase 129Xe T1. For interphase exchange measurements, they evacuated the sample and admitted approximately 1 bar of laser- polarized 129Xe gas into the cell. The team performed a saturation/recovery experiment in which they selectively saturated the dissolved-phase 129Xe polarization and observed its recovery after a variable waiting time due to diffusive exchange from the gas-phase. They determined S/V by fitting this recovery of the dissolved-phase 129Xe NMR signal to an expression they derived for non-equilibrium interphase diffusion. In addition, the team performed independent measurements of S/V for each POREX sample using optical confocal microscopy, a well-established technique which requires sectioning of the sample. They found the NMR and optical measurements of S/V to be in qualitative agreement.

RESULTS:
The results with phantoms indicate the potential for MRI experiments at low field strengths in a large, open-access system, despite low-field limitations of narrow bandwidth RF coils, and gradient pulses that are not necessarily small compared to the applied field. Further system optimization and human inhalation studies are planned for the follow-on NASA grant for this project.

The coil assembly has been used to create a magnetic field of 20 gauss with better than 100 ppm field uniformity over a 30 cm diameter volume centered between the coils. The Helmholtz coil assembly is housed inside a wire-mesh cage to provide shielding from any background electromagnetic noise. The investigators also constructed low-rf pulse/drive coils and associated electronics employing low-cost audio amplifiers with custom trigger/gate circuitry. Using this 20 gauss low-field system, they obtained high SNR signals from a laser-polarized 3He phantom, and acquired a proton NMR signal in a single acquisition. They recently began the design of signal detection coils for low field MRI of human lungs, since they are not available commercially at the audio frequencies used with low field MRI. The investigators have also begun the construction of low-noise receiver electronics for these coils.

APPROACH:
The investigators began development and testing of xenon interphase exchange NMR, a new technique designed to measure the exchange of xenon atoms between the gas and dissolved phases in porous media such as the lung. They used xenon interphase exchange NMR to determine the surface-area-to-volume ratio (S/V) of four samples of porous high-density polyethylene polymer (materials commonly used in filtering, wicking, etc.) They machined each of the four samples to fit tightly in a 0.5" glass cell that excluded free gas around the polymer core. The team performed NMR experiments on a GE Omega/CSI 4.7 T spectrometer operating at 55.3 MHz for 129Xe. They filled the samples and a similar empty cell with thermally- polarized xenon, and made NMR measurements of the sample porosity f, 129Xe partition coefficient b, and dissolved-phase 129Xe T1. For interphase exchange measurements, they evacuated the sample and admitted approximately 1 bar of laser- polarized 129Xe gas into the cell. The team performed a saturation/recovery experiment in which they selectively saturated the dissolved-phase 129Xe polarization and observed its recovery after a variable waiting time due to diffusive exchange from the gas-phase. They determined S/V by fitting this recovery of the dissolved-phase 129Xe NMR signal to an expression they derived for non-equilibrium interphase diffusion. In addition, the team performed independent measurements of S/V for each POREX sample using optical confocal microscopy, a well-established technique which requires sectioning of the sample. They found the NMR and optical measurements of S/V to be in qualitative agreement.

RESULTS:
The results with phantoms indicate the potential for MRI experiments at low field strengths in a large, open-access system, despite low-field limitations of narrow bandwidth RF coils, and gradient pulses that are not necessarily small compared to the applied field. Further system optimization and human inhalation studies are planned for the follow-on NASA grant for this project.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The headward fluid shift of space flight involves the redistribution of body fluids from the legs and abdomen into the thorax and head. This fluid shift is believed to initiate the cardiovascular readaptation syndrome (CRAS) of responses to space flight factors by stimulating arterial and cardiopulmonary sensors. The physiological responses to this stimulation include the reduction of plasma volume through increased urination, decreased thirst, and perhaps even vomiting, and the resetting of cardiovascular reflexes controlling arteriolar tone, venous capacity, and vascular responsiveness to postflight orthostatic stress. A complete understanding of CRAS will require the thorough documentation of the fluid shift and its effects. This understanding can be provided in part by the use of ultrasound echocardiography to determine the dimensions of cardiac and major vascular structures and to measure their normal functioning.

Cardiac ultrasound measurements on the crew of the 84 day Skylab flight revealed a significant decrease in left ventricular volume which persisted for over a week postflight. Subsequent measurements on STS crewmembers confirmed that the loss of volume occurs during flights as short as a week or less, and may require a week or more to be completely reversed postflight. The large contribution of individual variability, due to such factors as age and physical fitness, was documented in those data. This study was proposed to continue the data collection, and to include, for the first time, measurements made while the subjects were standing upright. This additional data would have revealed the effects of space flight on the cardiovascular system's response to gravitational stress. The aim of DSO 465 was the determination of cardiovascular adaptations to space flight factors based on the echocardiographic measurement of cardiac functioning in the supine and standing positions.

APPROACH:
Cardiac images were made using an ATL/ADR 4000 S/LC real-time two-dimensional ultrasound imaging system. Images were made with the subject resting on a couch or cot in the left lateral decubitus position and during passive standing with his back flat against a wall and his feet nine inches out from the wall with his heels six inches apart. The sector-scanning end-fire transducer was positioned to acquire para-sternal long-axis, para-sternal short-axis and apical four-chamber views. A two-dimensional view was used to select appropriate scan lines for M-mode images at the aortic root for aortic and left atrial dimensions and at the level of the maximum excursion of the mitral valve for left ventricular dimensions. Ventricular dimensions were measured at end-diastole and end-systole; other dimensions were measured at end-systole. Data were collected on a tota1 of two crewmembers preflight, according to the following schedule :
Crewman A: L-38, -33, -31, -30, -13, -10 and -9 days
Crewman B: L-13, -12, -10 and -9 days

Postflight data were not collected immediately after landing on these crewmembers because a late in-flight change in landing site to NASA-Dryden Research Facility in California left inadequate time to transport the equipment and operator from the planned landing site, NASA Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Uncertainties in the crewmembers’ schedule for returning to NASA-Johnson Space Center prohibited data collection on the days after landing.

RESULTS:
The late change in landing site precluded postflight data collection. Therefore, DSO 465 produced no results. DSO 465 was supplemented by DSO 466. Please refer to DSO 466 for results.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Sams, ClarencePrincipal Investigator: Konstantinova, IrinaCo-Investigator: Giclas, PatriciaCo-Investigator: Meehan, Richard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Since the late 1960s, the immune system has been studied by United States and Russian space scientists. Depressed immune cell function has been confirmed in-flight by reduced responses to in vivo delayed-type hypersensitivity tests. Changes in cell-mediated immune function have been consistently documented. However, the effect of space flight on the humoral immune system has not been thoroughly assessed during flight. Therefore, the goal of this experiment was to test whether space flight has an adverse affect on humoral immune function similar to that observed with the cell-mediated immune system. It was expected, based on the decrease in other immune system functions, that the ability to mount an antibody response to new or recall antigens would be depressed during space flight. It was hypothesized that the specific antibody titers following immunization during flight would be significantly lower than the titers obtained from a ground-based control group. The objectives of this experiment were to (1) determine the effects of long duration space flight on baseline levels of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgD, IgE and IgM) in serum (2) assess the ability to produce appropriate antibodies in response to a specific antigenic challenge during space flight and (3) determine secretory immune function by measuring salivary IgA and lysozyme levels in response to immunization during space flight.

APPROACH:
An in-flight vaccination with specific antigens (23 pneumococcal polysaccharide antigens) was used to test the ability to mount an antibody response in vivo. These antigens produce well-characterized antibody responses in normal, healthy individuals. Blood and saliva samples were collected prior to flight and immediately before in-flight immunization to determine the baseline values of the specific pneumococcal antibodies. Vaccination took place during the late flight period. Additional saliva and serum samples were scheduled to be taken 7, 14 and 21 days after the in-flight immunization to measure the magnitude of antibody production. It should be noted that in-flight immunization was performed on two out of three subjects scheduled to receive antigen injections. In addition, the post flight sample collection schedule was significantly modified due to crewmember and medical requirements. The final post flight sample collection was delayed for two crewmembers. The result was that samples were not collected on immunization+21 days (3 weeks after immunization). Samples were collected at 4 weeks after immunization for the two crewmembers, therefore, the peak antibody response was missed. Antibodies to the immunization antigens were measured by Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) in the serum and saliva samples. The degree of response was compared to those obtained from a ground-based control group which were age- and sex-matched volunteer subjects.

RESULTS:
The three crewmembers all exhibited minor shifts in the levels of isotype specific antibodies between the preflight and in-flight pre-immunization period. In general, these variations did not appear to be highly significant, and they suggest the serum antibody levels were not altered directly by space flight. The immunized crewmembers did respond to the vaccine, indicated by the increase of antigen-specific antibody titers. However, the magnitude of response may be altered for some isotypes in some individuals. The degree of the response was not particularly robust in one crewmember. It was found that antibody titers of two of the four isotypes doubled the pre-immunization levels but did not reach 200 nanograms antibody-nitrogen/ml for one crewmember. Incidentally, a positive response is a two-fold increase over the baseline level and a post-immunization titer above 300 nanograms antibody-nitrogen/ml. However, since the data set is very small, this data may suggest a decreased response to the vaccine in this crewmember, or it could be a function of individual variability since some of the isotype levels were adequate. General immunoglobulin levels did not change significantly during or after flight in any of the crewmembers.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Nelson, GregoryCo-Investigator: Allen, AntinoCo-Investigator: Fike, JohnCo-Investigator: Komarova, NataliaCo-Investigator: Limoli, CharlesCo-Investigator: Obenaus, AndreCo-Investigator: Raber, JacobCo-Investigator: Rosi, SusannaCo-Investigator: Soltesz, IvanCo-Investigator: Spigelman, IgorCo-Investigator: Vlkolinsky, RomanCo-Investigator: Wodarz, Dominik
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Understanding the responses of the central nervous system to charged particle radiation has two main benefits – risk assessment and optimization of radiotherapy. The general population and aviation crews are exposed to charged particles during cross country and trans-oceanic air travel at high altitudes as well as to radon in their homes and workplaces. While these exposures are not as high as those of astronauts they are not insignificant. Cancer risks have traditionally been the focus of health risk estimates but the new awareness of sensitive targets in the brain such as neurogenic centers in the hippocampus raises question about the negative effects of such radiation on late neurodegenerative diseases and potential decline of cognitive abilities. This project directly addressed the cognitive and neurogenesis issues and indirectly addressed late neurodegenerative effects which share reactive oxygen chemistry with radiation as underlying mechanisms. Alzheimer’s, Huntington’s, and in particular, ALS diseases, are of interest. In the last ten years, the use of charged particles in radiation therapy has grown dramatically with proton and carbon ion treatment centers being established in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. Always limiting the effectiveness of radiotherapy is the response of normal tissue near the tumor site. The precise dose localization associated with charged particle therapy makes it ideal for tumors of the head and neck where careful avoidance of critical structures such as the optic nerve is critical. Knowledge of the dose “tolerance” of brain tissue and the reactions to relatively low doses is critical in optimizing these modalities of treatment.

APPROACH:
This study investigated responses of the mouse brain to several radiation exposure regimes corresponding to galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events. It characterized behavioral, electrophysiological, biochemical, and structural changes both in vivo and in vitro. Radiation-elicited oxidative stress mechanisms were investigated as important mediators of the biological responses in both wild type and mutant animals. In addition to characterization of normal tissue responses, the potential enhancement of three late risks by radiation exposure were explored. These were seizures, ischemic injury, and traumatic injury.

RESULTS:
The NSCOR team has demonstrated that low doses of charged particles (<=10 cGy) can elicit a number of persistent changes to the brain, especially in the hippocampus. At the structural level, these include reductions in neurogenesis correlated with microglial activation and substantial reductions in dendritic branching and spine numbers. Electrophysiological changes affect both excitatory and inhibitory neurons and include altered intrinsic membrane properties and dysregulation of excitability and synaptic plasticity. Multiple behavioral tests that measure aspects of memory and cognition show impairments in performance. Elevation of oxidative stress is seen soon after irradiation, is persistent, and is accompanied by elevated markers of inflammatory processes. The mechanistic importance of the oxidative stress is shown by the protective effects on all endpoints of elevated catalase activity in MCAT transgenic animals. Together these observations point to a broad-based undesirable reaction of brain tissue to irradiation at doses which do not cause gross pathological changes or cell death. The mechanisms are poorly understood at this time but may involve oxidative mechanisms and inflammatory process. The significance of the impairments in the rodent models to human performance are presently unknown but demonstrate that there is a basis for concern. >p>

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Pulmonary function has been studied in detail following exposure to hypoxic and hyperoxic environments at normal gravity, but few studies have dealt with normoxic environments at zero gravity. Previous space flight history has shown no major changes in pulmonary function when evaluated postflight. During the first and second Skylab missions only a functional screening test on vital capacity was performed. Due to substantial decreases in cardiac output following these two missions, a more thorough pulmonary function screening effort was undertaken for Skylab 4 and the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP). The objectives of this study were to document changes in pulmonary physiology and postflight adaptability and to determine the effect of body fluid redistribution on lung mechanics.

APPROACH:
Pulmonary function tests were performed to evaluate the mechanical properties of the lung by studying lung volumes and capacities. All three crewmen were tested in conjunction with other medical evaluations on L-45 (45 days preflight), L-30 and L-15, R+0 (day of recovery) and R+1 (1 day postflight), R+2, R+5, R+13 and R+29. The hardware was similar to the Skylab 4 pulmonary function test equipment, except the metabolic analyzer's analog computer was substituted with a PDP-8e digital computer system. This improved the system's flexibility and computational accuracy. It also allowed the volume of nitrogen washout to be computed.

RESULTS:
Due to hardware malfunction on L-45, data were not obtained, and only two data sets were used for preflight means (L-30 and L-15). The Apollo atmosphere was 258 torr oxygen, but varied from 165 torr to 200 torr during Apollo-Soyuz docking and subsequent activities.

Further complications ensued following exposure to nitrogen tetroxide fumes during reentry. Therapy was administered by breathing 100% oxygen at 760 torr for 15 to 20 minutes aboard the recovery vessel. All crewmen complained of chest tightness, retrosternal burning sensation, inability to inhale deeply and nonproductive cough. Pulmonary function tests were conducted on each crewmember on R+0, and no significant changes were observed when compared to preflight means. However, ventilatory equivalent (VA/RV) showed a 30% increase, which indicated poor ventilation during residual volume (RV) determinations. Nitrogen tetroxide exposure was anticipated to cause significant pulmonary difficulty within the first 24 to 36 hours after landing. Thus, any physiological changes associated with space flight were probably concealed by responses to nitrogen tetroxide exposure.

Twenty-four hours later, symptoms worsened for all crewmen. Because of discomfort associated with deep inspiration and breath holding, satisfactory data could not be obtained on R+1 and R+2. Blood gas analysis indicated mild respiratory alkalosis with hyperventilation and hypoxia. The only significant finding, on R+2, was a decrease in the single-breath carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (DLCOSB). These findings agreed with the observed radiograph abnormalities that revealed the presence of diffuse nodular-type infiltrates throughout both lung fields. This decrease in DLCOSB persisted until testing on R+13. R+29 data showed pulmonary function parameters, including DLCOSB and repeat blood gas determinations (breathing room air and 100% oxygen), were within normal limits.

On R+0, Crewman A showed decreased RV, total lung capacity (TLC) and forced vital capacity (FVC), which remained below preflight values on all remaining tests. This indicated that nitrogen washout at the RV position did not start during postflight determinations. FVC, TLC and maximum expiratory flow rate (MEFR) were decreased on R+29. Crewman B demonstrated increased RV, closing volume (CV), and FVC on R+0. At R+29, the CV remained increased whereas FVC was slightly reduced relative to preflight. On R+0, Crewman C showed slightly reduced maximum midexpiratory flow rate (MMFR). R+29 increases were observed in VC and FVC.

In conclusion, the weightless environment appeared to have no significant impact on either respiratory mechanics or lung structure. Although, as reported by Tripler Army Hospital, R+1 data did show nitrogen tetroxide exposure caused pulmonary difficulty, which resulted in decreased pulmonary function. Overall, no disturbing decreases or significant changes, which could be attributed to space flight, were observed when compared to preflight means.

Although, as reported by Tripler Army Hospital, R+1 data did show nitrogen tetroxide exposure caused pulmonary difficulty, which resulted in decreased pulmonary function. experiment_title: Determination of Cardiac Size From Chest Roentgenograms Following Skylab Missions

investigators: Principal Investigator: Nicogossian, ArnauldPrincipal Investigator: Hoffler, G.Co-Investigator: Gowen, RichardCo-Investigator: Johnson, Robert
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Cardiac size is a major factor in the clinical evaluation of the healthy or failing heart. Knowledge of heart size assists the interpretation of both electrocardiographic and hemodynamic information. The evaluation of changes in cardiac size has been important in the overall cardiovascular assessment of orthostatic intolerance observed among the majority of astronauts following space missions.

Decreased cardiothoracic transverse diameter ratios were reported following Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo space flights. The majority of crewmembers who exhibited postflight decreases in the cardiac silhouette size also showed a decreased orthostatic tolerance to lower body negative pressure. Similar findings were also reported by Soviet investigators following 30-day bedrest studies and in cosmonauts upon return from space missions. This paper presents further radiological data from all three Skylab manned missions and discusses the physiological factors possibly involved in the cardiac silhouette changes.

APPROACH:
Standard posterior-anterior chest films were obtained before and as soon as possible after flight on each of the Skylab astronauts following extended space flights of different durations: 28, 59, and 84 days. Systolic and diastolic exposures were triggered electronically from the electrocardiograph R-wave peak by a special device interposed with the X-ray equipment control.

Postflight chest X-rays were visually compared with the preflight films for possible changes which might have occurred in pulmonary vasculature, lung parenchyma, bony or soft tissue structures. One or two additional postflight films were taken several days following splashdown to assess trends.

Geometric analysis of the chest X-rays was utilized to quantify changes in cardiac and thoracic areas. The thoracic cage area was obtained using a modified version of the method developed by Barnhard and Loyd. Upon completion of the geometric analysis the following parameters were measured and/or computed:

  • Cardiothoracic transverse diameter ratio (C/TD)
  • Cardiothoracic area ratio (C/TA)
  • Cardiac silhouette area determined by planimetry
  • Cardiac area calculated from the product of the long and short diagonal diameters.

    All postflight data were compared to the respective preflight values using the Student's t-test and regression analysis.

    RESULTS:
    No roentgenological abnormalities were observed on either preflight or postflight films. The chest X-rays of the Skylab 3 Pilot on the day of recovery were of poor quality and not amenable to analysis; all other X-rays were of acceptable quality. Both C/TD and C/TA showed a decrease in the individual values postflight. In general there was more variability in the C/TD responses postflight, some cases in diastole showing a modest increase in the immediate postflight ratios. Comparison of the preflight and postflight cardiac silhouette area differences showed a fairly consistent decrease in the cardiac area on the day of recovery. The Skylab 3 Commander, however, showed a postflight increase in the systolic cardiac area as determined from the products of minor and major diameters (19.76 cm2) and a very slight increase in the diastolic cardiac area as measured by the planimetric method (0.30 cm2).

    The mean differences, preflight versus postflight, of the cardiac areas, measured by planimetry, and of the derived measurement (C/TA), were statistically significant (P<0.01 or P<0.05). Return to preflight values was quite variable for all crewmen, but most showed this directional trend by 4 to 5 days after splashdown. There was a significant correlation (r=-0.91) between postflight decrement in systolic heart size as measured by C/TD, and the corresponding augmentation in heart rate responses registered during lower body negative pressure stress. There was no apparent correlation between the duration of orbital stay and the postflight change in heart size.

    Previous studies have shown that a significant determinant of cardiac size is the amount of blood returned to the heart. It is quite conceivable that caudad displacement of blood and other fluids together with an absolute decrease in the circulating blood volume could account for the observed decreases in the cardiac silhouette size. At the present time there is certainly no indication that the Skylab crewmen exhibited a greater decrease in their cardiac size than that observed in the Apollo astronauts following shorter duration space missions, nor that the decrease in diastole heart size was of greater magnitude than that of the systolic phase of the cardiac cycle. A small diastolic size might more clearly delineate a deficit in blood return and chamber filling rather than loss of myocardial mass.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
VO2pk is traditionally considered the best measure for evaluation of cardiorespiratory fitness. However, literature suggests that ventilatory threshold (VT) may be a better predictor of aerobic fitness, specifically with respect to performing submaximal work over a long period of time. Determining VT in combination with VO2pk could provide valuable information regarding crewmembers’ ability to perform extravehicular activity (EVA) and lunar exploration.

VO2pk is measured by an incremental exercise cycle test whereby subjects begin at very light warm up loads and the workload is gradually increased until maximum; optimal test time is 8-15 minutes, thus requiring different incremental exercise protocols based on subject characteristics (body size, fitness, gender, etc). It is generally believed that optimal testing involves small gradual increases in workload versus fewer large steps in workload. Assessment of VT requires small gradual increases in workload, thus the investigators proposed to pilot test four different "ramp" protocols.

The primary purpose of this study was to identify a peak cycle protocol that elicits a true VO2pk and allows for the determination of VT in subjects of varying gender, body weight, and training status. In order to meet this objective a method for technicians to determine whether VO2pk was achieved and for identifying VT needed to be defined.

APPROACH:
Four different peak cycle exercise protocols were performed by subjects of varying gender, body weight, and training status. During each test, expired air was collected for metabolic gas analysis (ParvoMedics TrueOneTM) and heart rate and rhythm were measured using a 3-lead ECG. Each test was independently evaluated by three different technicians for achievement of VO2pk and VT.

Ten healthy, non-smoking males (n=5) and females (n=5), 26-48 years of age, with varied fitness levels participated in the evaluation. All test subjects successfully passed a modified Air Force Class III physical exam and gave written informed consent prior to participation in the study. This study was approved by the NASA-JSC Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS).

Subjects were asked to complete 2-4 cycle ergometer tests to peak exertion. Each protocol consisted of a three minute warm-up stage, followed by either 30 second or 60 second stages at increasing workloads until peak exertion. Selection of the protocols was based on the subject's weight. Subjects weighing less than 65 kg completed protocols A and B, and subjects weighing more than 65 kg completed protocols C and D.

Protocol A: The exercise test session included three minutes of warm-up at 0 watts followed by one minute stages, increasing 15 watts each stage until peak exertion.

Protocol B: The exercise test session included three minutes of warm-up at 0 watts followed by thirty second stages, increasing 7.5 watts each stage until peak exertion.

Protocol C: The exercise test session included three minutes of warm-up at 50 watts followed by one minute stages, increasing 25 watts each stage until peak exertion.

Protocol D: The exercise test session included three minutes of warm-up at 50 watts followed by thirty second stages, increasing 12.5 watts each stage until peak exertion.

Expired gases were collected and analyzed using a Parvomedics TrueOne™ Metabolic Cart. Expired gas fractions of oxygen (VO2) and carbon dioxide (VCO2), rate of ventilation (VE), and respiratory exchange ratio (RER) were averaged in 30 second increments during exercise. Heart rate was monitored throughout testing via ECG. Borg rating of perceived exertion (RPE) was recorded at the end of each exercise stage.

The tests were completed using Level I medical monitoring. Testing was performed in the Exercise Physiology and Countermeasures Project Laboratory (EXL). The determination of VO2pk was defined by meeting two of the following three criteria: 1) HR = 90% age predicted maximum (220-age), 2) RER = 1.1, and 3) RPE = 19.

RESULTS:
A total of 26 peak cycle tests were completed in this investigation. The criteria for achieving VO2pk were met in all tests. In general, VO2pk was higher in males than in females; however, when the male and female data were combined, VO2pk values were not different between the 30 and 60 second stage protocols.

Upon inspection of the four VT determination methods, the majority of the VT values produced by the RER and ParvoMedics V-slope method were outside the reasonable acceptable range. Therefore, VT was determined using only the technician defined V-slope and VEQ method. VEQ produced a higher VT than V-slope; however, within each method there were no significant differences in VT between the three technicians.

Taking the results together with the subject preference for 60 second stages, it is recommended that future bed rest and flight studies implement Protocol A for individuals that are less than 65 kg and demonstrate lower levels of fitness; and Protocol C for individuals that are above 65 kg and exhibit higher levels of fitness. Determination of VT can be achieved in peak cycle tests as defined by these protocols, and by implementing the data analysis methods used in this study.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Traditional muscle deconditioning is characterized by atrophy and decreases in metabolic enzymes. Previous studies have demonstrated post-flight or post-bed rest decreases in muscle tone and other alterations in neuromuscular functions. Different degrees of altered performance (strength, endurance, and coordination) appear in different muscle groups and may be related to these changes after exposure to real or simulated microgravity. Altered integrated muscle performances (walking, running, standing, etc.) have been noted after exposure to real or simulated microgravity. All changes have been reported from a series of separate flight and simulation studies on different subjects and species over "flights" of different duration using a variety of in-flight exercise countermeasures. Muscle deconditioning may be better understood by examining multiple individuals doing the same countermeasures and tests during a single space flight. The objective of this experiment was to increase the understanding of muscle deconditioning and to evaluate the effects of the inflight countermeasures on muscle performance and characteristics. Based upon previous research, the investigators evaluated the following hypotheses.

  • Muscle performance will change in a non-uniform manner during flight and will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g. These non uniform changes include:
    1. Legs, arms, back and neck muscles will decondition to different levels,
    2. Extensors muscle characteristics will have greater changes than flexors, and
    3. Different types of contractions will have disproportionate changes after flight.
  • The major mechanisms for muscle deconditioning will be atonia and changes in other muscle characteristics. These changes will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g.
  • There will be significant decreases in integrated muscle performance (treadmill and cycle exercise) during the flight which will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g.
  • The decreases in integrated muscle performance will be due to the changes in the individual muscle performance and their underlying mechanisms.

APPROACH:
Skeletal muscle characteristics and performance will be measured prior to, during and after space flight on NASA 3 crewmembers. Muscle tone will be quantified as muscle stiffness. Muscle stiffness is defined as the slope of the torque versus degree line of a concentric contraction, which immediately follows an eccentric contraction. Evoked isometric contractions (tendometria) will be used to assess the maximal force transmitted to the Achilles tendon. Single and tetanic maximal twitch forces will be recorded. The time to peak tension, one-half relaxation time, total contraction time and fatigue index also will be evaluated. The test will be performed before and after flight only.
Strength velocities characteristics will be assessed with the LIDO (LIDO Active Multi-Joint Isokinetic Dynamometer). Instruments will be adjusted for differences in body size and shapes. Subjects will be asked to contract muscles of the ankle, knee, and back on the LIDO at maximal levels against a lever arm that is moving in the same direction as the muscle contraction (concentric contraction), and in the opposite direction as the muscle contraction (eccentric). All tests will be done on the right side unless contraindicated. EMGs will be recorded on select muscle groups. This test will be performed before and after flight only.
Voluntary Isometric contractions will be assessed with the LIDO. Subjects will be asked to contract muscles of the ankle, knee, and neck on LIDO at maximal levels against a stationary lever arm. EMGs will be recorded on select muscle groups. All tests will be completed on limb that is contralateral from isokinetic strength testing.
Fatigability will be assessed a hand dynamometer (hand). Hand endurance will be assessed at current and relative strength levels. The crewmember will be asked to hold 50% of current maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) for as long as possible. The absolute endurance will be assessed with a series of contractions (3 second contraction, 2 second relaxation) at 75% of preflight MVC. The test will terminate when the target force cannot be met.
Graded Cycle Exercise was performed to evaluate integrated muscle performances. This test will be performed on a supine ergometer and consists of a 2-min warm-up (50 watts), 3 5-minute stages of steady-state exercise (100, 125, and 150 watts), followed by 25 watt/min increases until the subject reaches volitional fatigue (pre-post flight) or 85% of preflight values (inflight tests only). The test concludes with at least 1-min of cycling at 50 watts or less. EMG, aerobic economy, a-VO2, submaximal lactate production and heart rate will also be measured during this test.

RESULTS:
Initial metabolic gas analysis system (MGAS) and muscle strength data is complete. Electromyograph (EMG) data analysis is about 25% completed. Initial individual muscle strengths were close to preflight values. These values either improved or were maintained for all muscle groups except for knee extensors and flexors for 2 crewmembers. The one crewmember showed initial decreases but returned toward preflight values by the third week of recovery.
Mir22/NASA 3 crewmembers showed that the Russian countermeasures were generally effective for maintaining gross muscle function. However, integrated muscle function was slightly compromised. The Russian countermeasure program provides and excellent starting point to refine neuromuscular countermeasures for space flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bacterial growth within human habitats is not unusual and usually poses no danger to the inhabitants. However, within isolated habitats, where air ventilation and circulation may be limited and the relative humidity high, the levels of bacterial growth may increase to levels high enough to pose a health hazard to the crew.

Bacterial endotoxin is found in many bacteria, and its concentration has been used as a relative assessment of bacterial levels. However, most traditional enumeration and identification techniques require days to complete. Habitat swab samples were analyzed with an automated real-time monitor of bacterial endotoxin, called the Portable Test System (PTS). The PTS was operated by the crew during the mission. The results were then correlated with advanced microbiological analysis of the same swab samples in the laboratory following the mission. This correlation will determine if this new system can detect trends in bacterial growth that could affect crew health.

At present, there is no rapid, real-time bacterial-detection device for crew use on the International Space Station (ISS). Monitoring of bacteria onboard requires the return of swab samples for microbiological analysis on the ground. This method provides high-quality identification of bacteria onboard, but with a significant time lag between swab sampling and results. The PTS will enable the crew to obtain quick, "on-the-spot" results of bacterial levels onboard, without assistance from the ground; a factor useful for crews on long duration missions, where supply/re-supply missions may be infrequent. The crew could test key locations (such as air-conditioning vents, fluids for injection, surfaces and the water system), identify "hot-spot" areas of rapid bacterial growth at an early stage, and use cleaning procedures to prevent potential hazards to crew health.

APPROACH:
Baseline data (swabs and PTS tests) were collected by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) divers on four and three days before the mission began. The NEEMO 5 crew took daily swab samples from five different areas within the habitat: wet porch, wetsuit, living quarters, Aquarius tap water and cabin air. These samples were both analyzed during (by the crew) and after (in Johnson Space Center (JSC) laboratories) the mission. Both sets of results were compared and correlated. The crew analyzed samples for bacteria using a small, hand-held, automated device, known as the Portable Test System (PTS). The PTS specifically detects the bacteria cell membrane component lipo-polysaccharide (LPS) and provides results 10 minutes following addition of the sample. Samples (swabs and PTS tests) were also collected post-mission on R+0 before habitat power-down.

RESULTS:
The PTS was found to be a robust instrument for detection of bacterial levels during a mission situation. Sterile conditions were not required and the system was found to be user-friendly by the crew. At present, no such portable device is available on ISS to test bacterial levels, and all microbiological analysis must occur on the ground after extensive storage time and transportation in non-refrigerated conditions. NEEMO 5 proved to be a valuable opportunity to correlate results obtained with PTS in Aquarius with those obtained in the Microbiology Laboratory at JSC using culture methods. Results correlated well between the two methods and some bacterial species of potential health concern were identified using culture methods. Since NEEMO 5, the PTS cuvettes have been modified by Dr. Norm Wainwright (Marine Biology Lab, Woods Hole, MA) to allow the detection of fungi, gram–positive bacteria, and potentially dangerous bacterial species by modification of the antibodies used for detection.

1. Few species in the Aquarius habitat were found to be hazardous:

  • Wet porch: Bacterial/fungal levels consistently high, as expected
  • Wetsuit: High Bacterial levels, fungi detected on 4 days only
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that causes infections of the urinary tract and respiratory system, dermatitis and soft tissue infections was found
  • PTS data was lower and more variable
  • Possibility that following swab, bacteria could have grown within the sample tube to log phase, prior to Standard Culture testing (days/weeks later), but not before PTS testing (same day)
  • Living quarters: Similar microbial levels to office environment
  • Non-potable water: Low bacterial/fungal levels
  • Higher pre-mission levels may be due to low/absent use of faucet pre-mission
  • Air: Low bacterial/fungal levels
  • Stachybotrys, a fungus linked to indoor quality problems, was found
  • Potable water (sealed jugs): Higher than desirable bacteria/endotoxin

2. PTS performed nominally in a humid and hyperbaric environment

  • Some data errors detected, possibly due to power interruptions

3. Positive correlation (0.92) between data obtained with PTS and Standard Culture methods

  • The greatest variability was observed with wetsuit test

4. Minimum training required for crew to operate PTS

  • Crew found PTS easy to use

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMN) are phagocytic cells important in the body's defense against disease. The ultimate function of the PMN is phagocytosis and killing of microorganisms, which invade body tissues. To carry out this function, a variety of earlier steps are important. Because leukocytes pass through the blood stream, they must be able to leave the circulating blood and reach tissue spaces where potential infections occur. To do this, the leukocyte must adhere to blood vessel surfaces, migrate through tissue spaces and collect in the inflammation area, which accompanies early infection. Abnormalities in PMN function cause an increased susceptibility to infection. The objective of the Apollo Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) Polymorphonuclear Leukocyte Response experiment was to identify PMN alterations caused by microgravity that might be significant in planning future space missions of longer duration.

APPROACH:
Blood samples were obtained from the ASTP crewmembers on L-30 (30 days prior to launch), L-15, L-5, R+0 (immediately upon recovery), R+1 (1 day after recovery), R+8 and R+30. Because leukocytes are replaced in the bloodstream every few hours, samples taken at R+0 were the most important. These samples contained leukocytes formed under zero-g conditions. Three backup crewmembers were studied during the preflight period and served as a normal control population. Three other individuals aboard the recovery vessel, U.S.S. New Orleans, were studied during preflight and recovery periods. Two internal controls were tested repeatedly at the laboratory.

Tests performed included total leukocyte counts, differential counts, leukocyte adhesion, leukocyte migration and chemotaxis, phagocytosis and histochemical staining for leukocyte acid phosphatase and alkaline phosphatase.

Total white blood cell (WBC) counts and differential counts, useful as indices of host status, were measured microscopically. Leukocyte counts fluctuate with infections and stress reactions. Differential leukocyte counts were used to calculate total PMNs.

Leukocyte adhesion can be quantified in vitro and is altered with several clinical states associated with increased susceptibility to infection, such as alcohol ingestion and corticosteroid administration. To test adhesion properties, samples of heparinized blood were passed through nylon columns and the percentage of leukocytes adhering to the columns was calculated.

Leukocyte migration in a modified Boyden chamber was measured both in response to casein, a chemotactic agent, and without a chemotactic stimulus. A chemotactic index was expressed as the ratio of migration with casein compared to migration with no chemotactic agent.

PMN phagocytic capacity was measured by allowing leukocytes to form monolayers in chambered tissue culture slides and then adding heat-killed staphylococci. Phagocytic PMN percentages were determined microscopically.

Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase and acid phosphatase are histochemical tests that correlate with the amount of PMN activation. A weighted value was assigned to positive leukocytes by grading the reaction of individual cells from 0 through 4+. Cells of each reactivity degree were multiplied by the activity score, and the total value for 100 representative cells was calculated.

RESULTS:
Total WBC counts were stable and reproducible for each subject. Abnormalities included low preflight values for one crewmember (particularly on L-5) and the occurrence of elevated leukocyte counts in all three astronauts on R+1 and R+8 (when steroid administration was a factor). PMN counts were extremely reproducible among normal controls.

Leukocyte adhesion was reproducible if followed linearly, but it was influenced by high levels of steroids, aspirin ingestion, alcohol ingestion and inflammation. Two of the three astronauts had decreased leukocyte adherence on L-5. Adherence values of concurrent controls also decreased on that same day, although not to the same extent in all individuals. Control tests were stable on R+0 and R+1, making the decreases in prime crewmember PMN adherence more significant. However, because of fluctuations, serial values in the prime crew were not significantly different from the controls.

Leukocyte migration remained within the normal range. Migration was slightly decreased on R+8, but this decrease was also noted in the normal control. Because this test was performed at a temporary facility in Honolulu, comparative values obtained under the same field conditions were not available to determine whether migration was actually depressed or whether this decrease was a result of testing conditions. The chemotactic index was preserved normally in the tests performed on R+8.

Although fluctuations in PMN phagocytic capacity occurred, leukocytes retained the ability to ingest staphylococci from the prime crew cells. Increased phagocytic PMN numbers were found following recovery in the prime crew. This increase reflects the total increased leukocyte count. Leukocytes containing five or more staphylococci for the prime crew were not as markedly elevated when compared to controls. PMN phagocytic function was not impaired. In fact, because the number of circulating leukocytes was increased, the phagocytic capacity of the blood was enhanced.

Positive cell numbers for the enzyme leukocyte alkaline phosphatase paralleled total PMNs. The astronauts had elevated preflight and post-flight values. These higher values were also noted in one backup crewmember. A further weighted value was calculated by determining the mean staining characteristics of positive leukocytes. Again, the astronauts tended to have higher values than the controls, but these differences were not significant.

Total PMNs staining for the lysosomal enzyme acid phosphatase were also determined. One crewmember had low values during the preflight period, and the number decreased to 990 positive cells on L-5. All crewmembers showed a post-flight elevation in cells stained for acid phosphatase. Total leukocyte acid phosphatase scores and mean acid phosphatase scores were not significantly different from the values found in the concurrent controls.

In conclusion, the performed function studies suggest that a 9-day space mission does not impair PMN function. An increased clinical susceptibility to infection by crewmembers was not exhibited.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary goal of the Apollo Program was to land men on the moon. However, the physiological changes the astronauts experienced during the Gemini and Mercury programs raised concerns about the health and safety of future crews. One such concern was the high metabolic energy expenditure during extravehicular activity (EVA) during the Gemini missions. Another was the change in cardiopulmonary status as exhibited by decreased exercise capacity, loss of red blood cell mass, and cardiovascular deconditioning. These and other medical concerns led to establishing the following medical objectives for the Apollo Program:
  • Ensuring crew safety from a medical standpoint. This required that every effort be made to identify, eliminate, or minimize anything that posed a potential hazard to the crew.
  • Improving the probability of mission success by ensuring that sufficient medical information was available for management decisions.
  • Preventing back-contamination from the lunar surface.
  • Continuing the further understanding of the biomedical changes incident to space flight by detecting, documenting, and understanding the changes that occurred during space flight.

    There were also five additional objectives, which specifically defined the preflight medical goals of the Apollo program. They were:
    1) The discovery of latent illness during the process of selection of astronauts and preparation for missions.
    2) The implementation of the health stabilization program and other preventive measures.
    3) The determination of individual drug sensitivity to the contents of the Apollo medical kits.
    4) The collection of baseline data against which to compare postflight data for determination of space flight effects.
    5) The prevention of any situations that might delay or otherwise interfere with operational aspects of the missions.

    In-flight biotelemetry monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment were performed. Comparisons of pre- and postflight medical testing became the primary source of medical data for the Apollo program, since opportunities for in-flight medical investigations were severely restricted due to conflicts with primary operational objectives.

    APPROACH:
    Preflight Procedures: Preflight objectives of the Apollo program were addressed in the following areas:
    1) Medical screening and examinations, which consisted of physical and dental examinations, visual function test, and special studies.
    2) Health Stabilization.
    3) Drug Sensitivity Testing.
    4) Medical Training.
    5) The Astronaut Health Care Program.

    Medical Screening/ Examinations: The medical screening process consisted of:
    Medical history and review of systems
    Physical examination
    Electrocardiographic (EKG) examinations
    Treadmill exercise tolerance test
    Vectorcardiographic (VCG) study
    Phonocardiographic study
    Tilt table study
    Pulmonary function study
    Radiographic study
    Body composition study
    Laboratory examination
    Detailed examination of the sinuses, larynx and Eustachian tubes
    Vestibular studies
    Diagnostic hearing tests
    Visual fields and special eye examination
    General surgical evaluation
    Procto-sigmoidoscopy
    Dental examination
    Neurological examination
    Psychological summary
    Electroencephalographic (EEG) studies
    Centrifuge testing

    These medical tests were components of the astronaut selection process. The preflight medical examinations for Apollo crewmembers included detailed physical examinations and special studies. The special studies involved collection of baseline data for comparison with postflight findings in the areas of microbiology, immuno-hematology, clinical chemistry, and cardiopulmonary function.

    Preliminary physical examinations were conducted 30 days prior to flight (L-30) and consisted of interval history, vital signs, and a general physical examination. An interim exam was conducted on L-15 and consisted of general physical and dental examinations and monitoring of vital signs. The comprehensive examination conducted at L-5 was intended to accurately document the physical status of the crewmember at the outset of the mission.

    Cursory examinations were also conducted from L-4 to launch. The protocol consisted of recording vital signs, oral temperature, pulse, blood pressure, and weight, plus brief examination of the ears, nose, throat, heart and lungs. Other signs and systems were examined as indicated by medical histories. The final examination prior to flight involved last minute recordings of critical parameters to provide the most reliable basis that could be obtained for postflight comparisons.

    Health Stabilization - Because the flight crew could be exposed to communicable diseases prior to flight, and because illness could develop during flight, there was a need to isolate the crew for a period of time prior to launch. Though this was first thought to be infeasible, the impact of clinical illness on the preflight operations of the Apollo 9 through 13 missions elucidated the need for a health stabilization program. Thus, beginning with the Apollo 14 mission, the Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was implemented and remained in effect through the end of the program.

    Drug Sensitivity Testing - Drug sensitivity testing was performed to determine the response of flight crewmembers to each item in the medical kit to preclude allergic reactions and other undesirable side effects during flight. Each crewman was tested under controlled conditions. A physician would obtain a medical history pertinent to the experience of each crewman with each medication under test. After it had been determined that no adverse reaction had been experienced and that there was no evidence of impaired health at the time of testing, the medication was administered to the astronaut. The crewmember was then observed for an appropriate period of time following the administration of the medication and was asked about subjective responses. If positive subjective findings were reported, either a double-blind test was conducted or a replacement drug was substituted. Crewmembers were also tested for allergic reactions to electrode paste.

    Medical Training - Shortly after astronaut selection, instruction was provided in the areas of space flight physiology and therapeutics. The astronauts received 16 hours of didactic instruction provided by experts in various fields. This instruction covered these areas: cardiovascular, pulmonary, vestibular and visual systems, hematology and laboratory medicine (which addressed Mercury and Gemini findings), and the role of psychiatry in crew selection.

    The Astronaut Health Care Program - This program provided comprehensive health care to all astronauts and their families through a preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic program managed by NASA, but also supported with the aid of many civilian and military consultants. Annual physical examinations were conducted for each astronaut, regardless of his flight status. In addition, astronauts were instructed to report all illnesses and injuries for evaluation and treatment. Preventive dental care was also provided.

    Vision Testing - After Apollo 11, all crewmen except one had observed bright flashes of light while on orbit. Retinal photography was considered to determine whether the high energy particles believed to be responsible for the phenomenon produced retinal lesions. Preflight retinal photographs were taken as part of the physical exams done 30 days prior to flight and repeated three days after splashdown. Pre- and postflight retinal photographs were taken for the Apollo 15 and 16 missions only.

    In-flight Procedures: During the in-flight phase of the Apollo missions, health care was limited to long distance biotelemetry monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment with onboard drugs. Treatment was administered by the crew with direction from the ground-based flight surgeons.

    Monitoring - The Apollo astronauts each wore a biosensor harness, which provided a means of transmitting critical physiological data back to the ground. The system returned EKG, heart rate, and respiratory pattern and rate data. A two-lead EKG with synchronous phonocardiography provided an index of cardiac activity. Cardiotachometer equipment provided the means to monitor instantaneous and average heart rate information.

    The operational bioinstrumentation system was designed as an individually adjustable unit to be worn under each astronaut's flight clothing. The biobelt assembly was an electronic system that included sensors, signal conditioners, and telemetry interfaces. Data from the spacecraft biotelemetry system were displayed at consoles at the launch and mission control centers. Heart and respiration rates were displayed in digital form; electrocardiogram and impedance pneumograph data were presented on a cathode ray oscilloscope. Voice communications and real-time television observations, coupled with monitoring of the vital signs, provided the medical basis for an in-flight clinical profile of the Apollo astronauts.

    In-flight Medications - Originally, the use of medications during flight was limited to emergency situations only. With additional experience, this philosophy was altered to the extent that certain drugs were prescribed during Apollo missions when indicated.

    Postflight Procedures: Postflight physical exams involved obtaining a careful history and complete review of body systems. Laboratory studies included the following:

    1. Urine culture and sensitivity
    2. Complete blood count
    3. Urinalysis
    4. Serum electrolytes

    Characterization of viral and mycoplasma flora was initiated with Apollo 14. State of the art procedures included inoculating tissue cultures, embryonated eggs, suckling mice, and mycoplasma media with specimens obtained at various times in preflight and postflight periods.

    RESULTS:
    In general, Apollo astronauts adapted well to weightlessness. In the 7506 hours of space flight accumulated by the Apollo astronauts, no major medical problems were encountered. What was considered significant in postflight medical findings was the absence of any pathology attributable to space flight exposure. Physiological changes that did occur were reversed within a 2- to 3-day period, with the exception of the Apollo 15 crew, which required 2 weeks for complete return to preflight baselines. Cardiovascular deconditioning, reduction of red blood cell mass, and musculoskeletal deterioration were the most important physiological changes observed. All medical objectives of the Apollo program were achieved, thus providing a sound medical basis for committing man to the prolonged spaceflight exposure planned for the Skylab program.

    General Adaptation:
    The most frequently reported subjective sensation associated with initial exposure to microgravity was a feeling of fullness in the head. Of 33 astronauts, 31 reported this sensation, which was said to persist from 4 hours to 3 days. A roundness of the face, as well as engorgement of the veins of the head and neck, were also observed. This sensation was equated to standing on the head or hanging upside-down.

    Astronauts of the Apollo 7,12, 14, and 15 missions reported some soreness of the back muscles. This was relieved by exercise and hyperextension of the back. The crew typically exercised in the Command Module several times per day for periods of 15 to 30 minutes using the exercise device provided, though no in-flight exercise program was planned or implemented for the Apollo missions.

    Insomnia was also frequently reported by the astronauts. This was attributed to the shifting of the customary sleep time, altering circadian rhythm, and combating operational problems. In some cases, the use of a hypnotic facilitated restful sleep.

    The Apollo astronauts were the first of the American space crews to report any symptoms of motion sickness. Symptoms ranged from "stomach awareness" to nausea and, in some instances, vomiting. In most instances, the nausea appeared to be related to rapid body movement before adaptation to weightlessness had occurred. Symptoms subsided or were absent when crewmen moved slowly during the initial period of weightlessness. Increased susceptibility to motion sickness was thought to be the result of the relatively enhanced effect of stimulation of the acceleration-detecting nerve endings in the semicircular canals that occurs during weightlessness. The otolith, the gravity component of the inner ear, is thought to bias the input of the semicircular canals to the brain center that controls vomiting. The removal of this bias during weightlessness results in an alteration of the input to the brain from the semicircular canals. Then, in a susceptible individual, rapid head movement would result in motion sickness. Adaptation of the inner ear to weightlessness, which occurs fairly rapidly in most individuals, was hastened by appropriate head movements that produced a subthreshold stimulation of the semicircular canals. This technique was taught to all Apollo crewmen subsequent to the Apollo 9 mission. Of the crewmen who used this technique, fairly good results were achieved.

    Weight loss was a consistent postflight finding for all the crewmen with the exception of 2 of 33 Apollo astronauts. The major portion of these weight changes was attributed to loss of total body water, while the remainder was attributed to tissue mass loss.

    Crew Illness, Medications and Clinical Findings:
    Apollo 7 - Three days prior to launch, Subjects A and C experienced slight nasal stuffiness but were successfully treated and certified fit for flight. Fifteen hours after lift-off, the crew reported that Subject A had a bad head cold. Post-nasal drip did not occur and, because the secretions do not reach the lower respiratory tract, no coughing was produced. In the immediate postflight period, and for a short time thereafter, a statistically significant decrease in intraocular tension, when compared with their preflight tension, was found in all astronauts. The postflight intraocular tension reverted to preflight values at a much slower rate than expected.

Comparison of the pre- and postflight films of this crew showed no change for Subject C in the size of either the retinal veins or arteries approximately 3 hours after postflight. Subject B exhibited a significant decrease in the size of both the veins and arteries about 3.5 hours after flight; Subject A showed only a decrease in the veins 4 hours after flight. The degree of constriction of retinal vasculature in this crew was greater and persisted longer than could be accounted for by the vasoconstrictive effect of atmospheric oxygen alone.

__description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary goal of the Apollo Program was to land men on the moon. However, the physiological changes the astronauts experienced during the Gemini and Mercury programs raised concerns about the health and safety of future crews. One such concern was the high metabolic energy expenditure during extravehicular activity (EVA) during the Gemini missions. Another was the change in cardiopulmonary status as exhibited by decreased exercise capacity, loss of red blood cell mass, and cardiovascular deconditioning. These and other medical concerns led to establishing the following medical objectives for the Apollo Program:
  • Ensuring crew safety from a medical standpoint. This required that every effort be made to identify, eliminate, or minimize anything that posed a potential hazard to the crew.
  • Improving the probability of mission success by ensuring that sufficient medical information was available for management decisions.
  • Preventing back-contamination from the lunar surface.
  • Continuing the further understanding of the biomedical changes incident to space flight by detecting, documenting, and understanding the changes that occurred during space flight.

    There were also five additional objectives, which specifically defined the preflight medical goals of the Apollo program. They were:
    1) The discovery of latent illness during the process of selection of astronauts and preparation for missions.
    2) The implementation of the health stabilization program and other preventive measures.
    3) The determination of individual drug sensitivity to the contents of the Apollo medical kits.
    4) The collection of baseline data against which to compare postflight data for determination of space flight effects.
    5) The prevention of any situations that might delay or otherwise interfere with operational aspects of the missions.

    In-flight biotelemetry monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment were performed. Comparisons of pre- and postflight medical testing became the primary source of medical data for the Apollo program, since opportunities for in-flight medical investigations were severely restricted due to conflicts with primary operational objectives.

    APPROACH:
    Preflight Procedures: Preflight objectives of the Apollo program were addressed in the following areas:
    1) Medical screening and examinations, which consisted of physical and dental examinations, visual function test, and special studies.
    2) Health Stabilization.
    3) Drug Sensitivity Testing.
    4) Medical Training.
    5) The Astronaut Health Care Program.

    Medical Screening/ Examinations: The medical screening process consisted of:
    Medical history and review of systems
    Physical examination
    Electrocardiographic (EKG) examinations
    Treadmill exercise tolerance test
    Vectorcardiographic (VCG) study
    Phonocardiographic study
    Tilt table study
    Pulmonary function study
    Radiographic study
    Body composition study
    Laboratory examination
    Detailed examination of the sinuses, larynx and Eustachian tubes
    Vestibular studies
    Diagnostic hearing tests
    Visual fields and special eye examination
    General surgical evaluation
    Procto-sigmoidoscopy
    Dental examination
    Neurological examination
    Psychological summary
    Electroencephalographic (EEG) studies
    Centrifuge testing

    These medical tests were components of the astronaut selection process. The preflight medical examinations for Apollo crewmembers included detailed physical examinations and special studies. The special studies involved collection of baseline data for comparison with postflight findings in the areas of microbiology, immuno-hematology, clinical chemistry, and cardiopulmonary function.

    Preliminary physical examinations were conducted 30 days prior to flight (L-30) and consisted of interval history, vital signs, and a general physical examination. An interim exam was conducted on L-15 and consisted of general physical and dental examinations and monitoring of vital signs. The comprehensive examination conducted at L-5 was intended to accurately document the physical status of the crewmember at the outset of the mission.

    Cursory examinations were also conducted from L-4 to launch. The protocol consisted of recording vital signs, oral temperature, pulse, blood pressure, and weight, plus brief examination of the ears, nose, throat, heart and lungs. Other signs and systems were examined as indicated by medical histories. The final examination prior to flight involved last minute recordings of critical parameters to provide the most reliable basis that could be obtained for postflight comparisons.

    Health Stabilization - Because the flight crew could be exposed to communicable diseases prior to flight, and because illness could develop during flight, there was a need to isolate the crew for a period of time prior to launch. Though this was first thought to be infeasible, the impact of clinical illness on the preflight operations of the Apollo 9 through 13 missions elucidated the need for a health stabilization program. Thus, beginning with the Apollo 14 mission, the Flight Crew Health Stabilization Program was implemented and remained in effect through the end of the program.

    Drug Sensitivity Testing - Drug sensitivity testing was performed to determine the response of flight crewmembers to each item in the medical kit to preclude allergic reactions and other undesirable side effects during flight. Each crewman was tested under controlled conditions. A physician would obtain a medical history pertinent to the experience of each crewman with each medication under test. After it had been determined that no adverse reaction had been experienced and that there was no evidence of impaired health at the time of testing, the medication was administered to the astronaut. The crewmember was then observed for an appropriate period of time following the administration of the medication and was asked about subjective responses. If positive subjective findings were reported, either a double-blind test was conducted or a replacement drug was substituted. Crewmembers were also tested for allergic reactions to electrode paste.

    Medical Training - Shortly after astronaut selection, instruction was provided in the areas of space flight physiology and therapeutics. The astronauts received 16 hours of didactic instruction provided by experts in various fields. This instruction covered these areas: cardiovascular, pulmonary, vestibular and visual systems, hematology and laboratory medicine (which addressed Mercury and Gemini findings), and the role of psychiatry in crew selection.

    The Astronaut Health Care Program - This program provided comprehensive health care to all astronauts and their families through a preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic program managed by NASA, but also supported with the aid of many civilian and military consultants. Annual physical examinations were conducted for each astronaut, regardless of his flight status. In addition, astronauts were instructed to report all illnesses and injuries for evaluation and treatment. Preventive dental care was also provided.

    Vision Testing - After Apollo 11, all crewmen except one had observed bright flashes of light while on orbit. Retinal photography was considered to determine whether the high energy particles believed to be responsible for the phenomenon produced retinal lesions. Preflight retinal photographs were taken as part of the physical exams done 30 days prior to flight and repeated three days after splashdown. Pre- and postflight retinal photographs were taken for the Apollo 15 and 16 missions only.

    In-flight Procedures: During the in-flight phase of the Apollo missions, health care was limited to long distance biotelemetry monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment with onboard drugs. Treatment was administered by the crew with direction from the ground-based flight surgeons.

    Monitoring - The Apollo astronauts each wore a biosensor harness, which provided a means of transmitting critical physiological data back to the ground. The system returned EKG, heart rate, and respiratory pattern and rate data. A two-lead EKG with synchronous phonocardiography provided an index of cardiac activity. Cardiotachometer equipment provided the means to monitor instantaneous and average heart rate information.

    The operational bioinstrumentation system was designed as an individually adjustable unit to be worn under each astronaut's flight clothing. The biobelt assembly was an electronic system that included sensors, signal conditioners, and telemetry interfaces. Data from the spacecraft biotelemetry system were displayed at consoles at the launch and mission control centers. Heart and respiration rates were displayed in digital form; electrocardiogram and impedance pneumograph data were presented on a cathode ray oscilloscope. Voice communications and real-time television observations, coupled with monitoring of the vital signs, provided the medical basis for an in-flight clinical profile of the Apollo astronauts.

    In-flight Medications - Originally, the use of medications during flight was limited to emergency situations only. With additional experience, this philosophy was altered to the extent that certain drugs were prescribed during Apollo missions when indicated.

    Postflight Procedures: Postflight physical exams involved obtaining a careful history and complete review of body systems. Laboratory studies included the following:

    1. Urine culture and sensitivity
    2. Complete blood count
    3. Urinalysis
    4. Serum electrolytes

    Characterization of viral and mycoplasma flora was initiated with Apollo 14. State of the art procedures included inoculating tissue cultures, embryonated eggs, suckling mice, and mycoplasma media with specimens obtained at various times in preflight and postflight periods.

    RESULTS:
    In general, Apollo astronauts adapted well to weightlessness. In the 7506 hours of space flight accumulated by the Apollo astronauts, no major medical problems were encountered. What was considered significant in postflight medical findings was the absence of any pathology attributable to space flight exposure. Physiological changes that did occur were reversed within a 2- to 3-day period, with the exception of the Apollo 15 crew, which required 2 weeks for complete return to preflight baselines. Cardiovascular deconditioning, reduction of red blood cell mass, and musculoskeletal deterioration were the most important physiological changes observed. All medical objectives of the Apollo program were achieved, thus providing a sound medical basis for committing man to the prolonged spaceflight exposure planned for the Skylab program.

    General Adaptation:
    The most frequently reported subjective sensation associated with initial exposure to microgravity was a feeling of fullness in the head. Of 33 astronauts, 31 reported this sensation, which was said to persist from 4 hours to 3 days. A roundness of the face, as well as engorgement of the veins of the head and neck, were also observed. This sensation was equated to standing on the head or hanging upside-down.

    Astronauts of the Apollo 7,12, 14, and 15 missions reported some soreness of the back muscles. This was relieved by exercise and hyperextension of the back. The crew typically exercised in the Command Module several times per day for periods of 15 to 30 minutes using the exercise device provided, though no in-flight exercise program was planned or implemented for the Apollo missions.

    Insomnia was also frequently reported by the astronauts. This was attributed to the shifting of the customary sleep time, altering circadian rhythm, and combating operational problems. In some cases, the use of a hypnotic facilitated restful sleep.

    The Apollo astronauts were the first of the American space crews to report any symptoms of motion sickness. Symptoms ranged from "stomach awareness" to nausea and, in some instances, vomiting. In most instances, the nausea appeared to be related to rapid body movement before adaptation to weightlessness had occurred. Symptoms subsided or were absent when crewmen moved slowly during the initial period of weightlessness. Increased susceptibility to motion sickness was thought to be the result of the relatively enhanced effect of stimulation of the acceleration-detecting nerve endings in the semicircular canals that occurs during weightlessness. The removal of this bias during weightlessness results in an alteration of the input to the brain from the semicircular canals. This technique was taught to all Apollo crewmen subsequent to the Apollo 9 mission. Of the crewmen who used this technique, fairly good results were achieved.
