experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The majority of humans are infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) early in life and thereafter carry the virus in a latent form. Reactivation of latent EBV may be an important threat to crew health during extended space missions. EBV is the causative agent of infectious mononucleosis as well as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt’s lymphoma, and other B-lymphocyte lymphomas in immunosuppressed individuals. Control of replication in vivo is mediated primarily by EBV specific cytotoxic T-lymphocytes, and severe clinical symptoms have been associated with reactivation of latent viruses in patients with defective cellular immunity. Decreased cellular immune function has been reported both during and after space flight. Preliminary studies have demonstrated increased EBV shedding in saliva as well as increased antibody titers to EBV lytic proteins.

The objective of this investigation was to examine the mechanisms of space flight induced alterations in human immune function and latent virus reactivation. Specifically, this study determined the magnitude of immunosuppression as a result of space flight by: (1) analysis of stress hormones and cytokines; (2) quantitative analysis of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) replication using molecular and serological methods; and (3) determination of virus-specific T-cell immune function.

APPROACH:
The study protocol was approved in advance by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects at Johnson Space Center (JSC) and each subject provided written informed consent before participating. Eight separate samples of peripheral blood were collected from 63 astronauts; 45 flew on fourteen Space Shuttle missions and18 flew on eight ISS missions. The average length of the Shuttle missions was approximately 11 days while the average length of the ISS missions was approximately 180 days. Peripheral blood was collected 180 days before launch (L-180), L-65-44, L-10, L-2, within 4 hours after return/landing R+0, R+3, R+14-30, and R+180. Preflight blood draws were performed at the JSC, Houston, TX. Postflight blood draws for Shuttle crewmembers occurred at Kennedy Space Center (KSC), FL, or Edwards Air Force Base, CA. For ISS crewmembers, postflight blood samples were collected at KSC or Star City, Russia. Plasma was obtained after centrifugation and was stored at -70 degrees Celsius until testing. Twenty-four hour urine collections took place during the blood draws; aliquots of 24 hour pools were stored at -20 degrees Celsius until analysis.

RESULTS:
Neuroendocrine responses after short- and long-duration space flight
Adrenocortical responses for short-duration Shuttle and long-duration ISS astronauts vary. In Shuttle crewmembers, plasma cortisol was relatively unchanged until L-2, at which time a significant increase was observed. Plasma cortisol was not significantly increased postflight. There was a trend for increased urinary cortisol prior to flight; a significant increase in urinary cortisol was found at landing and returned to preflight levels by R+3. Urinary epinephrine was not increased at landing. However, a significant decrease in urinary epinephrine was found at R+3.

For ISS crewmembers, plasma cortisol was not increased at any time prior to launch but was significantly increased at landing. Urinary cortisol was not increased preflight but it was significantly increased at landing. Both plasma and urinary cortisol returned to preflight levels within 3 days of landing. Urinary epinephrine was significantly increased at landing and returned to preflight levels by R+3. For urinary norepinephrine, significant elevations were found postflight (R+3 and R+15). These elevations were resolved by R+180.

Leukocyte and lymphocyte subsets
There were significant changes in leukocyte and lymphocyte subsets both before and after short-duration shuttle flights. There were significant increases in white blood cells (WBCs) even before flight at L-2. WBCs were also increased post-landing at R+0 and R+3. Neutrophils displayed a similar pattern, increasing at L-2, nearly doubling at R+0, and remained elevated through R+3. Lymphocytes were significantly increased at L-2 but significantly decreased at R+0. Similarly, eosinophils were increased at L-2 and decreased at R+0. Monocytes were elevated preflight (L-2) and postflight (R+0) timepoints. For NK cells, there was a significant increase at L-2 but at R+0 and R+3 they were significantly decreased. B-cells were significantly increased at L-2 and R+3. Although increased at landing, this was not significant due to intrasubject variability. Total T-cells were increased at L-2 but decreased at R+0. Accordingly, both cytotoxic T-cells and helper T-cells were increased at L-2 and decreased at R+0.

For ISS crewmembers, WBCs were significantly increased at R+0 and R+3. Neutrophils were increased at R+0 and eosinophils were decreased at R+0. There were no preflight or postflight changes in lymphocytes or monocytes. For lymphocyte subsets, there were no significant changes in either NK cells or CD8+ T-cells. A significant increase in B-cells was observed at R+3. Similarly, there was a significant increase in total T-cells at R+3 which was due to a significant increase in CD4+ T-cells.

Because many prior studies have reported percent changes instead of absolute changes, the percent changes are also presented. For short-duration shuttle missions, the only significant changes in leukocyte and lymphocytes percentages occurred at landing and included: 1) increased neutrophils and B-cells; and 2) decreased eosinophils, monocytes, lymphocytes, NK cells, and CD8+ T-cells. For long-duration ISS missions, significant changes in the percentage of cell populations at landing included: 1) increased neutrophils; and 2) decreased eosinophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes at both R+0. There were no other timepoints with significant changes. No significant changes were observed in NKs, B-cells, total T-cells, CD8+ T-cells, or CD4+ T-cells at L-2 or any time post-landing.

Plasma IL-10 levels
For Shuttle crewmembers, IL-10 was significantly increased at L-2 as compared to L-180; no increase in IL-10 was observed postflight. For ISS crewmembers, three did not have detectable levels of IL-10 throughout the mission, and two of the crewmembers had large increases in circulating IL-10 at L-2 (56% and 96%); these same two subjects had even greater increases at R+3 (86% and 371%, respectively). No significant increase in IL-10 was found at L-2 or any individual post-flight timepoint as compared to L-180. However, grouped mean postflight IL-10 levels were significantly higher than mean preflight levels.

EBV antibody titers
The investigators measured anti-EBV antibodies in plasma from Shuttle and ISS crewmember samples. Anti-VCA and anti-EA titers were measured in Shuttle and ISS crewmember samples. For Shuttle crewmembers, a significant decrease was found between preflight (L-65 thru L-2) and the R+180 timepoint. This would indicate that stress-induced increases in VCA already occurred, and by the next baseline EBV reactivation had subsided. For EA, a significant increase in EA was found at L-2 through R+15 as compared to L-180 samples, indicating that lytic replication of EBV was occurring prior to and just after launch as compared to baseline samples. For ISS, no significant changes were found in VCA antibody titers. For EA, a non-significant increase was found at L-2 as compared to L-180.

EBV-specific T-cells
The investigators measured EBV-specific CD8+ T-cells in both shuttle and ISS crewmembers. There was an increase in EBV tetramer-positive cells in shuttle crewmembers at L-2 and R+0 as compared to L-180 which resolved by R+180. Similarly, there was an increase in EBV tetramer-positive cells at L-2 in ISS crewmembers. These levels resolved by R+3.

EBV T-cell function
For Shuttle crewmembers, a significant decrease in EBV functional cells was found at L-2 and R+0. Notably, levels of cortisol were elevated at these timepoints. For ISS crewmembers, the only time the percent functional EBV tetramer+ cells significantly decreased was at R+0, at which time there were also significant elevations in plasma and urinary cortisol and urinary epinephrine.

EBV DNA Levels
There was a significant increase in viral DNA in shuttle crewmembers by L-10 which increased further by L-2. As compared to L-180, no other significant changes were found. Notably, the levels of DNA were lowest at R+180; this may signal the lowest stress level as the mission has already occurred. Similarly, there was an increase in EBV DNA at L-2 in ISS crewmembers. There was also an increase in EBV DNA at R+15. However, due to the low subject number and intrasubject variation, none of these changes reached statistical significance. However, viral load was much greater in ISS crewmembers (when detectable) than in samples from ISS crewmembers. EBV DNA levels also increased after long-duration spaceflight, while they decreased after short-duration space flight. This suggested greater immunosuppression after long-duration flight, perhaps due to greater stress responses postflight.

T-cell function
For short-duration Space Shuttle crewmembers the mean percentage of both T cell subsets that could be stimulated to coexpress both activation markers was relatively consistent throughout all pre-flight assessments. Following landing day (R+0) assessments, a significant increase in the percentage of T cell subsets that could be activated to express CD69 or co-express CD69/CD25 was observed, that resolved to baseline levels by R+14. For ISS crewmembers, the mean percentage of both T cell subsets that could be stimulated to full activation (CD69+/CD25+) was also stable between both pre-flight timepoints. However, landing day assessments for the ISS crewmembers revealed a significant decrease in percentage of both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that could be stimulated to co-express CD69/CD25. The total percentage of T cell subsets expressing CD69 alone was also reduced, but not significantly different, on landing day. Thus, expression of the early activation marker CD69 was relatively unchanged, but the expression of CD25 (requiring new mRNA expression) was significantly decreased. Values for the ISS crewmembers for this assay trended to resolution at R+3 and had fully returned to baseline values by R+30.

Intracellular cytokine analysis
For the short-duration shuttle crewmembers, there was a significant decrease in the percentage of all four cytokine-producing T cell subsets at R+0 as compared to the pre-mission baseline values. All the observed R+0 intracellular cytokine alterations appeared to fully resolve by the R+14 timepoint. For ISS crewmembers, there a significant decrease in the percentage of CD4+/IL-2+ T cells at R+0 as compared to the pre-mission baseline value. In contrast to the shuttle crewmembers, there was no significant decrease in the percentage of CD8+/IL-2+, CD4+/IFNg+ or CD8+/IFNg+ T cells. There did appear to be some trends towards reduced levels of CD8+ T cells making both cytokines.

Secreted Th1/Th2 cytokine analysis
Cytokine expression data are generated as mean fluorescence intensity, and since six cytokines are assayed simultaneously, relative comparisons may be made between the cytokines. Also, since all samples were frozen and assayed simultaneously per mission, relative comparisons (per crewmember) across the data points are valid. For the shuttle crewmembers, expression of IFNg usually surpassed all other cytokines at baseline testing, yet there was a statistically significant drop in IFNg expression on R+0 that trended to resolve by R+14. Interestingly, relative expression of IFNg was lower pre-flight for the ISS (as compared to shuttle) crewmembers, but also did drop on landing day whereas other cytokines appeared unchanged. Postflight recovery data for the ISS crewmembers revealed IFNg expression that approached the Shuttle crewmembers in intensity. Expression of IL-10 among the ISS crewmembers was actually elevated at R+0, and trended downwards to baseline values by R+30.

For the shuttle crewmembers, the greatest elevation of IFNg and IL-2 expression was seen at the L-10 and R+3 data points. No other consistent pattern of altered production was observed in the shuttle crewmembers. For the ISS crewmembers, levels of IFNg and IL-2 expression were also highest at R+3. Interestingly, levels of TNFa, which were minimal at all preflight points for the ISS crewmembers, was also significantly elevated at R+3. These elevations were generally trending to resolve by R+30. Given that an IFNg:IL-10 ratio may be an indicator of Th1:Th2 balance, such a ratio was calculated using the CD3/CD28 culture data for all crewmembers. For most shuttle crewmembers, a relatively depressed ration is observed at R+0, as compared to both pre-flight baseline values and postflight recovery data. For 4 of 5 ISS crewmembers tested, a similar shift was detected, but to an even more dramatic level: R+0 IFNg:IL-10 rations were dramatically reduced compared to both preflight and post-flight recovery data. To check for inter subject and assay variability, four healthy control subjects were evaluated and relatively similar timepoints.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A number of investigators have assessed the role of vestibular-based subsystems both during and immediately following exposure to microgravity. While providing information specific to one or more sensorimotor subsystems there is little documentation of changes in the strategies used for coordination among subsystems or for those strategies supporting performance of natural, goal-directed behaviors. In particular, there may be several strategies selected for use during the process of adaptation to microgravity. These strategies may become more reliable for missions of increasing duration. Prime among these strategies are: (1) the reduced use of head movements during the early phases of the mission, (2) the reliance on either an internal coordinate system (intrinsic)or environmental coordinates (extrinsic) during different phases of space flight for spatial orientation, and (3) compensation for the changing role of proprioceptive information during flight. These strategies, we believe, can be evaluated using goal-directed head and eye coordination tasks. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to investigate the emergence or alteration of goal-oriented strategies required to maintain effective gaze when the interactive sensorimotor systems required for this function have been modified following extended exposure to the stimulus rearrangement of space flight.

APPROACH:
For baseline data collection, all subjects sat in a chair facing a visual display which consisted of miniature LED targets in the shape of a cross. The LEDs were illuminated to create either a static or moving visual pattern. The following physiological measures were taken preflight and postflight: (1) Eye movements: monitored by electrodes placed vertically above and below the right eye, horizontally over the left and right temples, with a ground behind the left ear, and (2) Head movements: measured by a tri-axial rate sensor fixed to the head.

All responses were collected on a Data Acquisition System which consisted of Macintosh computer, Data Acquisition box with Anti-aliasing filters, and custom acquisition and control software.

The following measurements constituted the experiment:

  • Predictable Target Acquisition (PTA): Used both head and eyes to acquire +/-20°, +/-30°, and +/-60° horizontal and +/-15°, +/-20° and +/-50° vertical targets in a predetermined sequence.
  • Unpredictable Target Acquisition (UTA): Used both head and eyes to acquire +/-20°, +/-30°, and +/-60° horizontal and +/-15°, +/-20° and +/-50° vertical targets in a random sequence.
  • Smooth Pursuit Tracking (SP): Moving eyes only or eyes /head together to follow a moving target. Target motion is sinusoidal using four frequencies (SP1=0.2 Hz, SP2=0.33 Hz, SP3=0.8 Hz, SP4=1.4 Hz) in both the horizontal or vertical planes, or ramp to an unpredictable displacement. NOTE: The ramp portion of smooth pursuit was never completed on any of the Mir 18/STS-71 crewmembers.
  • Head Shakes (HS): Keeping eyes on center target, oscillate head in the horizontal or vertical plane in cadence with an auditory tone at 0.2, 0.33, and 2.0 Hz. Repeat with vision occluded.
  • Memorized Head Rotations (MHR): View a sequence of target illuminations while head is stationary, then attempt to recreate the pattern by rotating the head to remembered target positions with vision occluded.

    A cruciform target arrangement was used to provide the visual stimulation for target acquisition, pursuit tracking,memorized head rotations, and sinusoidal head oscillations (as a spacecraft fixed target). experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ) was sent out in the fall of 1998 to collect nutrition data from participants in the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH). A total of 645 participants answered and returned this survey. The 116 male astronaut respondents had a mean age of 48.2 years, while the 448 male comparison participants had a slightly higher mean age of 50.8 years. The female respondents were generally younger, reporting a mean age of 39.3 and 40.5 years for astronauts (N=21) and comparison participants (N=66), respectively.

APPROACH:
To compare the LSAH participants to the U.S. general population, results of a national survey, the 1994-96 Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (CSFII), are also presented. In particular, the findings for respondents over 20 years of age (5056 males and 4816 females) are used as comparison to those of the astronaut and comparison participants.

Measurements were total kilocalories (Kcal) typically consumed by respondents of both surveys, as well as corresponding percentages of total fat, protein, and carbohydrates in their typical diets.

RESULTS:
When compared to the results of male CSFII respondents 20 years old and over, male LSAH participants reported a lower total consumption of kilocalories. The lower consumption values hold true even when compared to the CSFII respondents in the age groups closer to the mean ages of the male comparisons and astronauts (age groups 40-49 and 50-59 years of age). Female comparison participants reported a mean value similar to that reported by female CSFII respondents 20 years and older. Female astronauts, however, had a lower mean total intake than this group of CSFII respondents. Their reported value comes closer to values for those 50-59 years of age and older.

When the caloric intake is broken down into fat, protein, and carbohydrates, LSAH astronauts and comparison participants reported values similar to those reported by the CSFII respondents.

This brief summary of nutritional intake shows that in general male LSAH astronauts and comparison participants report a lower total consumption as compared to the general population, while female astronauts show a lower intake as compared to the general population. The proportions of fat, protein, and carbohydrates of astronauts and comparisons are similar to that reported in the CSFII. Therefore, the composition of LSAH participants' diet does not substantially differ from that of the general population.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) is a medical condition made up of a constellation of symptoms affecting at least 34 percent of American astronauts who have flown International Space Station (ISS) missions. SANS is defined primarily by visual acuity deficits and anatomical changes to eye structures. Exposure to head-down tilt bed rest, a well-accepted analog to induce cardiovascular adaptations similar to space flight, has not resulted in findings representative of SANS that have been observed in some astronauts participating in long-duration ISS missions. Factors other than the cephalad fluid shift observed during space flight and bed rest have been hypothesized to contribute to the development of SANS but have not been tested.

APPROACH:
This bed rest study sought to investigate two factors, age and diet, with regard to vascular compliance and ocular measures. Specifically, seven younger men and four older men participated in a 6° head-down bed rest study under standard conditions, with the exception that a higher than normal sodium intake was prescribed to match the intake of ISS astronauts. Dietary sodium intake in this study was approximately 40% higher than in previous NASA bed rest studies.

Plasma volume, vascular measures (area and diameter of head and neck vessels among other ultrasound measures), and ocular measures (intraocular pressure, optical coherence tomography, and ocular ultrasound) were collected on all subjects. Non-invasive internal jugular venous pressure was collected using ultrasound.

RESULTS:
For the majority of cardiovascular and ocular variables studied, there was no significant effect of 14 days of bed rest. The bed rest-induced decrease in plasma volume did not appear to differ from plasma volume losses that occurred during previous NASA bed rest studies using standard dietary practices. Arterial diameters and flow were not different from pre- to post-bed rest at rest during the whole body tilting protocol (-20, -10, 0, +10, +20 degrees of tilt). intraocular pressure responded to posture changes, but did not change pre- to post-bed rest. Similarly, axial length (via ultrasound) and retinal nerve fiber layer (via Optical Coherence Tomography) were not different after bed rest. In contrast, internal jugular vein area (via ultrasound) was lower after bed rest in the head-down tilt postures, suggesting a decrease in venous compliance. This effect was transient and recovered to pre-bed rest levels after three days of normal ambulation. Unfortunately, the investigators were unable to recruit a sufficient number of older subjects to test the interactions between aging and bed rest on the parameters studied. These results suggest that a high salt diet more closely matching that of astronauts during space flight does not increase the likelihood of developing signs of VIIP alone after 14 days of head-down tilt bed rest.

SANS is defined primarily by visual acuity deficits and anatomical changes to eye structures. Exposure to head-down tilt bed rest, a well-accepted analog to induce cardiovascular adaptations similar to space flight, has not resulted in findings representative of SANS that have been observed in some astronauts participating in long-duration ISS missions. Factors other than the cephalad fluid shift observed during space flight and bed rest have been hypothesized to contribute to the development of SANS but have not been tested.

APPROACH:
This bed rest study sought to investigate two factors, age and diet, with regard to vascular compliance and ocular measures. Specifically, seven younger men and four older men participated in a 6° head-down bed rest study under standard conditions, with the exception that a higher than normal sodium intake was prescribed to match the intake of ISS astronauts. Dietary sodium intake in this study was approximately 40% higher than in previous NASA bed rest studies.

Plasma volume, vascular measures (area and diameter of head and neck vessels among other ultrasound measures), and ocular measures (intraocular pressure, optical coherence tomography, and ocular ultrasound) were collected on all subjects. Non-invasive internal jugular venous pressure was collected using ultrasound.

RESULTS:
For the majority of cardiovascular and ocular variables studied, there was no significant effect of 14 days of bed rest. The bed rest-induced decrease in plasma volume did not appear to differ from plasma volume losses that occurred during previous NASA bed rest studies using standard dietary practices. Arterial diameters and flow were not different from pre- to post-bed rest at rest during the whole body tilting protocol (-20, -10, 0, +10, +20 degrees of tilt). intraocular pressure responded to posture changes, but did not change pre- to post-bed rest. Similarly, axial length (via ultrasound) and retinal nerve fiber layer (via Optical Coherence Tomography) were not different after bed rest. In contrast, internal jugular vein area (via ultrasound) was lower after bed rest in the head-down tilt postures, suggesting a decrease in venous compliance. This effect was transient and recovered to pre-bed rest levels after three days of normal ambulation. Unfortunately, the investigators were unable to recruit a sufficient number of older subjects to test the interactions between aging and bed rest on the parameters studied. These results suggest that a high salt diet more closely matching that of astronauts during space flight does not increase the likelihood of developing signs of VIIP alone after 14 days of head-down tilt bed rest.

experiment_title: (NSCORT) for Advanced Life Support at Purdue/Howard/AAMU - Solid Waste Resource Recovery
parameter_html:
Corn residue
Milled plant residue
Lignin-degrading fungi
investigators: Principal Investigator: Mitchell, Cary
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A significant fraction of waste material (plant residue, greywater and human waste) generated during space missions and on the earth, contains recoverable energy. The specific objective of the project was to optimize an approach that will demonstrate a Plant-based Anaerobic-aerobic Bioreactor Linked Operation (PABLO) that efficiently converts plant residuals and greywater into fuel grade methane (CH4), electricity, and biosolids that will be suitable for plant and fungal culture. This effort will optimize the potential for CH4 production by aerobically treating anaerobically recalcitrant waste materials - biosolids before they are used as a plant growth material. These steps will breakdown the resistant materials, freeing soluble carbon and stabilizing the materials. In a second part of the project we modified the PABLO system to a system concerned with converting human waste in to CH4 and biosolids. The Waste-ABLO (WABLO) approach is for the conversion of human waste into CH4 and biosolid residuals that are condensed but not used in the production of food.

In both the space based and Earth-based systems the starting point was waste materials. The major difference is in the space-based system we dealt primarily with dried residues that will be rewetted with greywater. In the earth-based system, the residues were wet or dry. Outputs from the system include: CH4, CO2 and solids. In this system, the residuals were treated with an aerobic process to and returned to the anaerobic system. The residuals that settle in the system were removed and land applied (earth) or used in confined growth systems (Mars).

The project was divided into three tasks:
Task 1: The objective was to use an anaerobic-aerobic bioreactor system to optimize production of methane from plant-based waste materials and for the recovery of high-quality biosolids.
Task 2: Methods for the optimization of the PABLO biosolids for use in fungal and plant cultivation were investigated. This required an evaluation of the makeup the aerobic reactor’s microbial population to maximize the formation of soluble carbon for use in the anaerobic portion of PABLO.
Task 3: The objective was to use a bioreactor system to optimize production of methane from human waste materials

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
For the first set of biological methane production (BMP) experiments, corn residue was milled and added to a phosphate buffer. Anaerobic digester sludge was used as an inoculum. Digesters were incubated at 23oC and periodically checked for gas and acid production over a period of time.

Corn residue in a phosphate buffer showed poor methane production over a 45 day time period. The maximum amount of methane produced was 0.09mLs after 32 days. Investigators also found this trend of low methane production to be true for several other crop residues that were tested. Low methane production resulted from the lignin matrix surrounding cellulose carbon sources, preventing the anaerobic bacteria from accesses these sources. Because of these findings, an efficient and simple pretreatment method should be used on crop residues to reduce the lignin content. There are several methods of pretreatment that could be employed to break down lignin including gamma-ray irradiation, alkali treatment, or aerobic composting. All of these methods would either require hauling large amounts of chemicals or supplies, or consume valuable resources such as oxygen.

Lignin degrading fungi appear to be a promising method of pretreatment for space missions. The mushroom species Pleurotus ostreatus, or Oyster mushroom, is edible, easy to grow, and is able to selectively degrade lignin, leaving the more soluble forms of carbon available for digestion by anaerobic microorganisms. This species also grows well in a high carbon dioxide environment during its longest growth stage, so oxygen consumption could be minimized with careful planning. The oyster mushroom requires a lot of water to sustain good growth; however, investigators have found that this mushroom species is able to grow well when using a mimicked hygiene graywater solution in place of regular water.

The process of growing the Oyster mushroom is quite simple. The mycelium is first grown on a grain, such as wheat or rye, to establish the fungi. Plant materials to be degraded are then pasteurized. Once cooled, the grain grown mycelium are then transferred and mixed with the pasteurized plant materials and grown under high humidity conditions. While the mycelium is being established, they grow best under a higher carbon dioxide concentration. Oyster mushrooms will begin to appear after about 18 days and grow to fruition in just 3-5 days. Graywater can be used throughout the mushroom growing process to conserve drinking water.

After one harvest of mushrooms grown on pasteurized corn residue, graywater was leached through the remaining residue and collected for methane production studies. This time, only the leached graywater and anaerobic sludge was used. No buffer was added. The digesters were incubated at 35oC. Methane production was greatly increased over digested corn residue in buffer, with a maximum production value of 8.3mLs after 35 days.

Milled plant residue alone will not produce enough methane to use a fuel source. A pretreatment method should be used to break down the lignin. The Oyster mushroom is an efficient and simple pretreatment method for degrading the lignin found in plants. This method opens up useable forms of carbon to the anaerobic bacteria and greatly increases the amount of methane produced. Using graywater throughout the methane production process will conserve valuable drinking quality water while recycling another waste material created by the crew on space missions. Degrading plant materials anaerobically is showing great promise for both long-term space missions and here on Earth.

Of the three residues tested, miscanthus produced the least amount of methane during all stages. More methane was produced after pasteurization and at the pinhead stage, but there was little difference between post-pasteurization and the pinhead stage. Corn residue produced more methane after pasteurization and after the pinhead stage, reaching a maximum methane production of 8.6mL and 8.3mL respectively. Tomato residue reached maximum methane production of all treatments at 9.5mL at the pinhead stage. Uninoculated controls were used for all treatments and consistently showed less methane production than inoculated treatments. This suggests that fungi are an effective method of pretreatment for production of methane from crop residues. Further research is needed to optimize this system. Greater methane production may be possible by extending the amount of time the bottles are incubated for. The bottles used for the experiments were small and only held a limited amount of gas. A different gas collection system should be developed so that pressure does not build up in the bottles.

experiment_title: Frames of Reference and Internal Models
parameter_html:
Ball position
Ball velocity
Hand acceleration
Marker hand position
Time shifts
Electromyogram (EMG), muscle
investigators: Principal Investigator: Berthoz, AlainCo-Investigator: Lacquaniti, FrancescoCo-Investigator: McIntyre, JosephCo-Investigator: Zago, Myrka
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
On Earth, information from the vestibular system is combined with information from gravity sensors in the joints, touch sensors in the skin, and visual information to coordinate body movements and maintain body stability. However, when space flight crews first experience weightlessness, there is an initial awkwardness in moving within the spacecraft. There is also disorientation because the signals coming from the vestibular system no longer correspond with visual and other sensory information sent to the brain.

The Frames of Reference and Internal Models investigation was designed to enhance the understanding of how the central nervous system (CNS) interprets and integrates sensory data for the production of a coordinated motor response. During the act of catching a ball on Earth, the CNS estimates the trajectory of the ball, accurately taking into account its downward acceleration due to gravity. This could involve a real-time estimation of ball acceleration based on visual information, but more likely involves the use of a priori information about the effects of gravity on free-falling objects. This in turn may involve the integration of sensory cues about the actual gravitational environment. The purpose of this investigation was to test the following hypotheses:
1. If subjects could measure the ball's acceleration, they would correctly estimate time-to-contact (TTC) in both 0-G and 1-G.
2. A first-order estimate, which assumes no acceleration, predicts TTC correctly in 0-G but overestimates the drop duration at 1-G.
3. If the brain instead uses a second-order internal model to account for gravity's accelerating effects on the ball, motor activity will be correctly timed to impact at 1-G, but the same second-order internal model applied in 0-G will underestimate the true TTC.

The scientific objective of this experiment involved a ball catching activity in which the CNS was tested to see how it adjusts for the lack of gravitational acceleration acting on the ball in weightlessness.

APPROACH:
Subjects were seated in a chair and restrained by the body restraint system (BRS). To complete the scientific objective, subjects were required to catch a ball that was projected "downward" toward the hand by a ball launcher. Muscle activity in the arm generated in anticipation of contact between the hand and the ball was measured by electromyography (EMG). Subjects wore the Kinelite headset to verify the correct position of the EMG electrodes before the session. The Kinelite headset was also used with the Kinelite Noise Generator to generate a tone to mask sounds the ball launcher made. This tone prevented the subject from using audio cues to predict when the ball would launch. Movement of the arm was measured by the Camera Illuminator Equipment (CAMILLE), and by accelerometers attached to the limb. Subjects performed 30 trials of one of three protocols. For the primary experiment protocol, random, the initial ball velocity varied randomly from trial to trial. Under these conditions, the subject adjusted motor response "on-line" on the basis of incoming visual information. For the second protocol, blocked, the initial ball velocity was constant within a given block. This tested the subject's ability to predict the ball's trajectory given prior knowledge about the initial speed. The third protocol involved repeating the experiment at a reduced height, thus reducing the viewing time below the minimum required to accurately estimate the time-to-contact on earth.

The Kinelite processing module (PM), a computerized video system, recorded and analyzed subject movements and controlled experiment performance. Then the data was transferred to the Life Sciences Laboratory equipment (LSLE) microcomputer II and subsequently transferred to the ground. Data for this investigation was collected on L-90, L-60, L-30, FD 3, FD 9, FD 15, R+0, R+1, R+5, R+9, and R+15.

RESULTS:
When these experiments were performed on the ground prior to flight, the astronaut subjects generated the peak of anticipatory biceps activity, that occurs about 40 ms prior to impact and independent of initial ball speed, as has been seen previously in other Earth-based studies. Subjects also rotated their forearm just prior to contact so as to move the hand upward to meet the ball. This upward movement was not generated by the peak of muscle activity described above, because the movement was initiated somewhat earlier than the measured EMG activity. Rather, this measurement represented two separate responses – upward movement to meet the ball and limb stiffening to stiffen the hand – both of which can tell us when the brain expects the ball to arrive. To see whether the brain uses an internal model of gravity when estimating the ball's arrival time, researchers compared the time course of these two responses between 1-G (pre- and postflight) and 0-G (inflight) conditions.

Anticipatory muscle activity occurred earlier relative to impact in 0-G compared to 1-G. This difference could not be explained by the repeated practice on this task that the astronauts had leading up to the flight because the timing returned to preflight values upon return to Earth. Nor can the shift simply be explained by the fact that subjects had more time to react in 0-G than in 1-G; dropping the ball from higher heights to increase the drop duration on Earth led to no differences in timing. One might also guess that muscle activity must start sooner during flight to overcome the fact that the muscles tend to be more relaxed in 0-G; but researchers found that supporting the forearm with an externally applied force to counteract gravity on Earth reduced the tonic activation of the biceps (as would be expected in 0-G) while causing no significant changes in timing of the anticipatory EMG peak. Thus, the timing shifts observed during flight were best explained by a failure to fully compensate for the lack of ball acceleration in 0-G.

The timing of forearm movements also changed during flight. On the ground, such movements were monotonically upward and accurately synchronized to impact, but these movements started much too early in 0-G. Unlike the simple shift observed for muscle activity onset, however, limb movements stopped or even reversed direction after the initial false start. The change from monotonic movement on Earth to the non-monotonic movements observed during flight showed that movements were not simply slower in microgravity, as was observed, or simply due to reduced muscle tone in 0-G. Instead, the evidence suggested that, once triggered, the CNS could correct the ongoing movement by updating estimates of TTC based on visual feedback.

While one might predict that catching responses would occur too early when subjects are first faced with microgravity conditions, it would be surprising if the brain was unable to adapt to this novel environment. Some evidence for adaptation exists. Although forearm movements started prematurely for all inflight tests, on flight days 9 and 15 the amplitude of the early, erroneous movement diminished and a later upward rotation developed just prior to impact. On the other hand, re-adaptation to Earth conditions occurred almost immediately. Average data from early postflight sessions (R+0, 1, 2) did not differ significantly from preflight or later postflight sessions. This indicated that subjects could rapidly retune internal models to the 1-G environment.

The key test in this experiment involved determining the magnitude of time shifts for different initial ball velocities (v0). The second-order internal model hypothesis predicted the nonlinear increases in time shifts (d) for decreasing values of v0 using reasonable, fixed values of the TTC threshold (?). These ? values were biologically plausible. Allowing for the time it takes a neural signal to travel from the brain to the periphery, threshold values of TTC used to initiate a given behavior should be somewhat greater than the lead time of the behavior itself. That is, if the brain wants to activate a muscle x ms prior to ball impact, it has to use a TTC threshold of x+y ms, where y represents the time it takes for the message to get from the brain to the muscles.

A response initiated at ?=75 ms within the brain was consistent with the arrival of the EMG peak in the muscle 40 ms prior to impact, due to neural transmission delays. Similarly, ? values of 300-400 ms were compatible with movement onset that normally occurred 200 ms prior to impact, given the time necessary to overcome limb inertia. In contrast, a first-order TTC estimate would require unreasonably long ? values (? > 1.2 seconds; i.e., longer than the total drop time of the ball in 1-G) to reproduce the time shifts observed in 0-G. Furthermore, a first-order TTC estimate cannot, with a fixed ?, predict the substantial changes of initiation time as a function of v0. Finally, had the subjects been able to directly measure the acceleration of the ball in real time, one would expect to see no time shift at all (with respect to impact) between 0-G and 1-G, irrespective of ?.

The data from these experiments were compatible with the third hypothesis; i.e., that to catch a falling ball the CNS: (1) employs a second-order estimate of TTC, (2) uses an internal model to predict gravity's effect on the ball, and (3) applies this internal model initially even in microgravity. Furthermore, it appeared that the brain gradually adapts the internal model with prolonged exposure to 0-G.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigators have demonstrated that loss of vestibular information following bilateral lesions in rats and mice decreases lower limb bone density, and that this effect may be mediated by activation of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). Based on the knowledge that reduced vestibular information, increased sympathetic activation, and bone loss are common hallmarks of long-term space missions, they hypothesized that space-induced bone loss has a vestibular and sympathetic origin, and that vestibular stimulation might increase bone density.

The main objective of this proposal is to evaluate the effect of vestibular stimulation on bone mass, with the goal of designing a new therapeutic approach to prevent bone loss in space. The project is divided into two specific aims. The first one will define the short and long-term effects of vestibular hair cell dysfunction on the vegetative system and on bone mass in mice, in order to determine whether this effect is compensated with time. Catecholamine levels, brown adipose tissue Ucp1/Gapdh expression, 3D-microcomputed tomography, and quantitative static and dynamic bone histomorphometry will be used. The second specific aim will characterize the effects of vestibular stimulation on the vegetative system and bone. Different centrifuge protocols (continuous and discontinuous, 1.5G/2G/2.5G) and galvanic vestibular stimulation will be used. Centrifugations will be performed in Dr. Makishma (UTMB, USA) and in Dr. Besnard and Prof. Denise (University of Caen, France) laboratories. Galvanic stimulation will be performed in Dr. Elefteriou's laboratory, in collaboration with Dr. Wood (Houston/UTMB, USA). All the bone analyses will be performed at Vanderbilt University (Dr. Elefteriou, Vanderbilt University). The part of the study performed in France is supported by the University of Caen Basse-Normandie and by the CNES.

The ultimate goal of this multi-disciplinary effort is to determine whether vestibular stimulation could have beneficial effects on bone mineral density and sympathetic function during extended space mission. These findings may have application on Earth as well for the treatment or prevention of low bone mass conditions.

APPROACH:
Aim1. Define the short and long-term effects of vestibular loss on the vegetative system and on bone mass in mice. Vestibular lesions (VBX) have been performed in all proposed groups for bone analyses 1, 3, and 6 months post-lesion. Group A (1 month VBX) were analyzed by uCT and histomorphometry. The second and third group of mice (3 and 6 months post lesion) were also analyzed. Lastly, we collected bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) from sham and VBX mice to assess a possible effect of VBX on osteoblast progenitor differentiation or proliferation. Cfu-ap (=osteoblast commitment) and cfu-ob (osteoblast differentiation) assays were performed using BMSCs collected 1 month post-lesion.

Aim 2. To characterize the effects of vestibular stimulation on the vegetative system and bone. a) Centrifugations. b) Galvanic vestibular stimulation. The first phase of this experiment, which consists in establishing the Hindlimb Suspension (HS) model, has been completed to confirm proper animal care and unloading-induced bone loss with our new setting.

Details of the GVS stimulation experiment: The occurrence of nystagmus with the stimulator was confirmed, using the eye tracker recording system. WT mice are currently tested for their response to daily GVS stimulation, in absence of hindlimb suspension (HS). Depending on the results of this experiment, the second phase of the proposed experiment will be performed (GVS+HS).

RESULTS:
Aim 1: Group A (1 month VBX): Significant bone loss and architectural changes were observed in the distal femoral epiphyses of VBX mice compared to sham-operated mice (both genders). Histomorphometry analyses revealed a significant reduction in the bone surfaces covered by osteoblasts in VBX mice, and increase in osteoclast number. These results validate the effect of arsenylate lesions on bone in mice, and serves as our main reference to assess the effect of time on VBX-induced bone loss.

Groups 2 & 3 (3 and 6 months post lesion): uCT analyses did not reveal significant bone changes. These results indicate that the effect of vestibular lesions on bone is transient and compensated for with time. We also collected brown adipose tissues to assess Ucp1 expression as readout of sympathetic outflow. Ucp1 expression was found upregulated in the VBX group 1 month post-lesion but not 3 and 6 months post-lesion, consistently with the bone data. These results suggest that peripheral sympathetic outflow is increased in response to VBX and contributes to VBX-induced bone loss.

No significant changes were detected in Cfu-ap and cfu-ob assays. These negative results suggest that VBX induces bone loss likely by reducing osteoblast proliferation, differentiation, or function in vivo rather than by reducing commitment to the osteoblasts lineage (in that latter case a reduction of cfu-ap colonies would have been observed). These results are in line with previous results and with a contribution of the sympathetic nervous system in VBX-induced bone loss.

Aim 2:
a) Four to five month-old het/+ (Control) and het/het mice (devoid of otoconia from birth) submitted to continuous centrifugation at 2G for 4 weeks in Dr. Besnard’s laboratory (France) did not experience any significant bone changes at the distal femur, as assessed by 3D computed microtomography (12 um resolution). Bone volume/tissue volume and tissue mineral density were indeed not significantly different between groups (n=10 per group).

b) After a set back of several months to get the centrifuge operational in Dr. T. Makishima’s laboratory, 4 month-old female WT mice have been submitted to intermittent centrifugation (2h/day) at 2G for 4 weeks. Here again, no differences were detected in term of bone volume/tissue volume and tissue mineral density between control and treated group, as assessed by 3D computed microtomography (n=10 per group).

c) Because of the negative nature of these results, this work has not been submitted for publication.

d) Galvanic vestibular stimulation

e) The Hindlimb Suspension (HS) model has been set up successfully in collaboration with Dr. D. Perrien at Vanderbilt. Following our discussions with Dr. Wood and Dr. Makishima in Galveston, we have determined the conditions of GVS stimulation that can induce nystagmus, using an eye tracker recording system. In response to GVS stimulation (0 to 300uA), eye movements in the temporal-to-nasal and upward directions were positive, and increased along with GVS current intensity, reaching a plateau at 200uA. Therefore, subsequent experiments were performed using an intensity of 200uA. Then, WT mice were tested for their response to daily GVS stimulations, in absence or presence of hindlimb suspension (HS). HS, as expected, triggered a significant bone loss in distal femurs of WT mice, as assessed by 3D computed microtomography. A decrease in all bone microarchitectural parameters was observed, as evidenced by a decrease in bone volume/tissue volume ratio (BV/TV), trabecular number (Tb.N), trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) and an increase in trabecular space (Tb.Sp). Daily GVS stimulations for 21 days in ambulatory mice did not significantly alter bone mass, although it slightly reduced body weight. Daily GVS stimulation, however, had no preventive or additional effect when applied in conjunction with HS. Mice in the HS+GVS group indeed experienced the same bone loss as observed in the HS group. Despite the negative nature of these findings, this study is the first of its kind for assessing the potential effect of GVS stimulation on skeletal homeostasis under normal and unloading conditions, and should lead to future studies based on the use of alternative GVS stimuli (duration, frequency, pulse) to prevent the deleterious effect of vestibular alterations on bone mass. The literature reports a wide combination of stimulation parameters (duration, frequency, pulse) that affect sympathetic nervous system outflow. GVS has been shown to increase muscle sympathetic nerve activity and diastolic blood pressure in humans (short 30ms trains of ten, 1ms, constant current pulses at a frequency of 333Hz / 2-4mA, every fourth heartbeat) (PMID 16308690), to decrease femoral vasoconstriction and increase brachial vascular tone in cats (30s continuous train, 0.2ms pulse width, 333Hz, 1.7 times vestibuloocular reflex threshold) (PMID 10896872) and to promote GABA release in the substantia nigra and improve locomotion in hemiparkinsonian rats (30 minutes, random frequencies <30Hz / 0.2-0.6mA) (PMID 22238601). Therefore, other modes of stimulation will have to be assessed for their potential effect on bone mass, in both normal and unloading conditions.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Basner, MathiasCo-Investigator: Dinges, DavidCo-Investigator: Gur, RubenCo-Investigator: Mollicone, DanielCo-Investigator: Mott, Christopher
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study addressed the goal of developing tools to assess crew performance in real-time and evaluate countermeasures to mitigate the effects of fatigue, circadian misalignment, and work-overload. It is responsive to the critical need to identify how a range of cognitive functions of astronauts can be affected in space flight by fatigue alone, and its interaction with other risk factors and conditions such as elevated carbon dioxide, intracranial pressure, space fog, and countermeasures. This study aimed to deliver a comprehensive, software-based, neurocognitive toolkit (Cognition). By building on state-of-the-art neuropsychological test development, the toolkit permits evaluation of a full range of cognitive functions using brief (1-5 minutes), validated procedures. The tests included, but went beyond, what is currently measured by WinSCAT and the Reaction Self Test on the International Space Station (ISS). Importantly, the toolkit permitted rapid assessment of performance in cognitive, social-emotional, and sensorimotor domains.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Development of short-duration adaptive versions of neuropsychological tests for space flight.
  2. Establish learning curves for neuropsychological tests and validate sensitivity to sleep deprivation.
  3. Cognition software development and optimization for space flight.
  4. NASA’s Johnson Space Center (JSC) field testing, astronaut learning curves, and astronaut norms for performance feedback algorithm development.
  5. Complete ISS feasibility study.

APPROACH:
The investigators completed data acquisition in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) 14-day missions (16 crew in 1-week missions, and 16 crew in 2-week missions total). They also completed data acquisition in six Hawaii Space Exploration Analog and Simulation (HI-SEAS) crewmembers in an 8-month mission. In addition, they collected Cognition data at three Antarctic research stations along with 13 control subjects at the German Space Agency to compare changes over mission-duration. Lastly, the investigators completed inflight data collection on seven astronauts. Two of them participated in the 12-month mission.

RESULTS:
The findings support the feasibility of Cognition administration in astronauts and astronaut surrogate populations, on both the Windows and iPad platform, and in space analog environments. Participant feedback provided during debriefs (N>60) provided helpful insights for current and future improvements of the battery. Cognition is currently deployed in several key studies funded by NSBRI, NASA, and European Space Agency (ESA), and it was selected as a core component in the project to develop a standardized behavioral measures toolkit (BCM) for space flight operations, demonstrating the need for and the success of the Cognition battery.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Integrated Radiation Analysis and Design Tools (IRADT) Project develops and maintains an integrated tool set that collects the current best practices, databases, and state-of-the-art methodologies to evaluate and optimize human systems such as spacecraft, spacesuits, rovers, and habitats. IRADT integrates design models and methodologies in support of evaluation/verification of design limits and design solutions to meet As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) requirements (NASA STD 3001, Vol 2). IRADT provides the radiation community access to physics and transport capabilities and research improvements. The capabilities are developed under strict version control and are independently verified and validated to the extent possible. Current customers include NASA Exploration Systems Mission Directorate's (ESMD) Directorate Integration Office studies (i.e. LAT, MAT, LSOS), Lunar Surface Systems as well as Constellation's Orion and Vehicle Integration Office, universities, industry, and Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR). IRADT is designed for utilization by future commercial customers concerned about transfer of proprietary data and results.

APPROACH:
IRADT specifically addressed the limitations associated with simplified geometry description (equivalent aluminum, three-layer transport interpolation, random orientation) and straight ahead transport. The design tools increases fidelity by incorporating common spacecraft and user specified materials in the geometry description with ray-by-ray transport to minimize the uncertainties due to range-scaling of material thicknesses and material ordering. Ray-by ray transport also establishes the basis to calculate the forward/backward neutron generation within vehicle/lunar surface geometries. The back-scattered neutron environment was calculated from the opposite sides of the vehicle for a crewmember’s specific orientation at specific tissue locations. This increases the ability to evaluate the effectiveness of shielding systems. In supporting the closure of these gaps, the Design Tool Project tools and models supported specification, implementation, verification, and monitoring of Spaceflight Human Systems Standard, Vol. 2 (NASA STD 3001, Vol. 2) radiation design and operational requirements with improved uncertainty quantification.

RESULTS:
The model can be defined one of three ways, by selecting an historic solar minimum/maximum, by entering specific dates, or by entering a fitting parameter. A comprehensive comparison of the various GCR models shown that the Matthia model was on par with the Badhwar-O'Neill 2010 model in terms of uncertainty for space radiation calculations. The Badhwar-O'Neill 2010 and 2004 models are also still available. The linear energy transfer (LET) response has been activated for all geometry and project types. It was previously only available for interpolation-based, thickness distribution jobs for free-space environments. Both the integral and differential flux/fluence versus LET is computed and the target material can be specified as either tissue or silicon.

A new atmosphere model has been added for Mars surface environments. The Mars Climate Database (MCD, http://www-mars.lmd.jussieu.fr/ ) is a database of atmospheric statistics compiled from state-of-the-art simulations of the Martian atmosphere. It is a much more refined model than MarsGRAM and takes into account the surface location (latitude and longitude), the Martian seasons (Solar longitude) and the time of day (Local solar time).

OLTARIS ( https://oltaris.nasa.gov/ ) currently has 223 active accounts. Eighty one accounts are government (including NASA, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Air Force Research Laboratory, and Federal Aviation Administration), eighty six are university professors/researchers/students, and fifty six are industry (including Boeing, Space X, Lockheed-Martin, Alliant Techsystems Inc., Northrup Grumman, and Bigelow Aerospace). There have been nearly 4000 jobs run through OLTARIS during the last reporting period and 14,500 since counting began in November 2009.

No datasets are available for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A significant hazard to astronauts going beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO) results from the presence of ionizing radiations, in particular High Energy, High Atomic Number Nuclei (HZE) Particles, such as GeV56Fe nuclei. These particles produce dense tracks of ionizations when passing through tissue and, as a result, will damage the genetic material of cells, DNA. The damage may result in cell death or the induction of mutations that could lead to cancers or germ cell (sperm or oocytes) mutations that could be transmitted to progeny.

The radiobiological effects of Low Energy Transfer (LET) radiations such as x-rays and gamma rays are well known. The carcinogenic effects of these radiations have been well documented on the survivors of the nuclear bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan. Although an increased mutation rate has not been observed in the progeny of the exposed individuals, it could be estimated by extrapolation using mouse specific locus tests (SLT). Such tests observe mutations, usually coat color mutants, in the progeny of exposed males. The tests on mice have not been carried out using HZE nuclei because the large numbers of offspring needed to detect the low frequencies of SL mutations makes these tests impossibly laborious.

  • The hazard to male astronauts from exposures to high LET cosmic rays is probably temporary sterility, but not significant mutagenic effects observable in progeny.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Research conducted during the Apollo Program showed no major changes in pulmonary function when evaluated by postflight exercise testing. Although pulmonary function has been studied in detail following exposure to hypoxic and hyperoxic environments, few studies have dealt with normoxic environments at reduced total pressure, as encountered during Skylab. The absence of a gravity vector would be expected to facilitate ventilation/perfusion relationships and result in better overall gas exchange in the weightless state.

Due to the absence in previous history of postflight pulmonary problems, and the normoxic microgravity environment of Skylab, vital capacity was initially proposed as the only functional screening. However, as a result of the magnitude of decreases in cardiac output following the first and second manned Skylab missions (Skylab 2 and 3), it was decided that more thorough pulmonary function screening was necessary for the final and longest duration Skylab mission (Skylab 4).

APPROACH:
The average composition of the spacecraft gas atmosphere during Skylab was:

  • inspired oxygen partial pressure equal to 22.6 kPa (170 mm Hg)
  • inspired nitrogen partial pressure equal to 10 kPa (75 mm Hg)
  • inspired water partial pressure equal to 1.3 kPa (10 mm Hg)
  • inspired carbon dioxide partial pressure equal to 6.7 kPa (5 mm Hg)

    The nominal composition was inspired oxygen partial pressure equal to 24.1 kPa (188 mm Hg) and inspired nitrogen partial pressure equal to 10.3 kPa (77 mm Hg), at a total pressure equal to 34.4 kPa (258 mm Hg). This atmosphere was planned to provide approximate sea level equivalent alveolar oxygen partial pressure.

    Forced vital capacity and its derivatives were measured 5 days preflight, as well as postflight on recovery day and 1 day after recovery for the Skylab 2 mission. During Skylab 3, vital capacity was measured preflight, inflight (during the last 2 weeks of the mission), and 1, 2, 4, and 5 days postflight. Comprehensive pulmonary function screening was accomplished during Skylab 4. The Skylab 4 preflight pulmonary function examinations were conducted 10 days preflight. Vital capacity was measured at 6 day intervals inflight. Complete postflight examinations were conducted on recovery day and 1, 2, and 5 days after recovery. Vital capacity measurements were continued at 11, 17, and 31 days postflight.

    Metabolic analyzers were used for all pulmonary function measurements. The Skylab 2 and 3 metabolic analyzers were designed to measure vital capacity and respiratory gas exchange. The Skylab 4 metabolic analyzer was modified to permit residual volume determination by open circuit washout of pulmonary nitrogen during oxygen breathing. A respiratory mass spectrometer monitored nitrogen partial pressure continuously at the subject interface, and an XY plotter provided continuous nitrogen partial pressure as a function of time during residual volume determinations. An analog tape recorder and strip chart were used during all Skylab 4 preflight and postflight testing to provide permanent, synchronous records of nitrogen partial pressure at the mouthpiece, tidal volume, flow rate, and nitrogen washout.

    RESULTS:
    During Skylab 2, one subject's forced expired volume in 1 second (FEV-1) was significantly reduced one day postflight (R+1). Based on the subject's normal forced vital capacity, it is possible that the decreased FEV-1 was due to less than maximal subject effort. No data were obtained postflight for one Skylab 2 subject due to orthostatic intolerance complicated by seasickness.

    During Skylab 3 one subject showed no changes in pulmonary function except for a slight increase in vital capacity 5 days post-recovery. Vital capacity of one Skylab 3 subject was slightly higher inflight but normal postflight, relative to preflight values. One Skylab 3 subject exhibited decreased vital capacity inflight but normal vital capacity postflight relative to preflight.

    Skylab 4 vital capacities were generally observed to be lower inflight relative to preflight. Vital capacity for one subject remained below preflight levels for the entire inflight period. Nitrogen washout curves for Skylab 4 crewmembers' pulmonary function tests showed no indications of trapping. All washout curves appeared to reflect the anticipated two time constants representing washout of pulmonary and total body nitrogen spaces. One subject had a pronounced vasovagal response following maximal oxygen inspiration during the first closing volume determination on recovery day, and further testing was curtailed until the next day. All other measurements on the first day following recovery, and all measurements on days 2 and 5 postflight were within normal ranges.

    Residual volume in one Skylab 4 subject was slightly increased immediately following recovery and on day 2, compared to preflight. Residual volume/total lung capacity percent indicated that these changes were probably insignificant. Ventilatory equivalents of this subject were variable and reflected the irregular respiratory pattern observed during washouts. Although vital capacity for the subject was slightly decreased on the second day following recovery relative to preflight, forced vital capacity was normal. Maximum midexpiratory flow rate (between 25 percent and 75 percent of the forced vital capacity) values for the subject were the highest ever recorded in the investigator's laboratory.

    Skylab 4 provided the first opportunity for extensive, noninvasive pulmonary function screening on astronauts before and following an extended zero-g exposure. No physiologically significant quantitative decrement in pulmonary function was shown by any crewman during examinations following this 84-day Earth-orbital mission.

    Postflight chest films for all crewmen were compared to preflight films to detect any changes in the pulmonary vessels, parenchyma, or heart size. No significant pulmonary vasculature or parenchymal changes were observed in any instance.

    Vital capacity, the only parameter measured preflight, in-flight, and postflight, showed inflight decreases approaching 10 percent in the case of one subject from Skylab 3 and all three crewmembers from Skylab 4. These decreases in vital capacity apparently resulted from one or a combination of the following factors: cephalad shift of the diaphragm in zero-g; body fluid redistribution into the thoracic cavity; or a direct result of decreased ambient pressure.

    In summary, the vital capacity changes observed inflight may be partially explained as a response to 34.5 kPa (5 psia) ambient pressure. However, the proportion of vital capacity decreases directly attributable to other factors such as body fluid shifts and a cephalad shift of the diaphragm cannot be determined from the present data. Regardless of the cause(s) of decreased inflight vital capacities, a review of postflight data shows that these changes revert to normal within 2 hours following recovery without significant impact on crew health status.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The human lung is very sensitive to gravity; consequently, on Earth there are large differences in gas flow, blood flow and gas exchange between the upper and lower portions of the lung. For example, on Earth, pulmonary blood flow (perfusion)is greater near the bottom of the lung and relatively smaller toward the top. Gas flow (ventilation) is similarly distributed, although there are still large differences in the two patterns. Scientists once believed that these differences were primarily the result of the pull of the Earth's gravity. Comprehensive studies of pulmonary function performed on the Spacelab Life Sciences-1 and -2 missions and the German D-2 Spacelab mission indicated, however, that much of the imbalance in lung ventilation and perfusion was maintained in the microgravity environment.

During the SLS-2 mission, studies of gas mixing in the small gas exchange regions of the lung (the acini) revealed that, in microgravity, these regions experienced a conformational change, which was unexpected and unexplained. Gas mixing in the acini is critical for gas exchange and often becomes compromised in people with pulmonary disease. Investigators modified the tests performed on SLS-2 to obtain further information on this fundamental process, which is essential for life.

This investigation extended studies of the human lung in four major areas:
To study lung function after the stress imposed by heavy exercise in the microgravity environment.
1. To monitor motion in the rib cage and abdomen.
2. To study the effects of microgravity on the musculoskeletal aspects of breathing during rest, during heavy exercising, and during deep breathing.
3. To measure the body's response to inhaled carbon dioxide, which may be altered by space flight.
4. To determine how gas is distributed within the lung.

A better understanding of the effects of gravity on the human pulmonary system ultimately may benefit clinical medicine on Earth. Also, a comprehension of pulmonary function in microgravity is important for long-term space flight.

APPROACH:
Data were collected before flight and throughout the mission, as well as several times during the two weeks following the mission. All seven crewmembers on board the LMS Spacelab served as test subjects.

Each subject performed a battery of pulmonary function tests before and immediately after exercise. These included measurements of cardiac output, lung water, pulmonary diffusing capacity, pulmonary ventilation, perfusion, and ventilation-perfusion ratio. Also, the metabolic rate was measured via resting oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production.

Further, the alterations in intra-acinar gas mixing in microgravity were investigated by measuring inspiratory flow rates as subjects inhaled and exhaled. In parallel, the pattern of chest wall and abdominal movements during normal ventilation, exercise ventilation, and induced hyperventilation was observed. While performing these studies, the subjects were instrumented with a respiratory inductance plethysmograph (RIP), a noninvasive device that allows continuous monitoring of the motion and expansion of the rib cage and abdomen. While the subject was not breathing through the mouthpiece, simple measurements of inspiratory and expiratory times were made.

To determine the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide during microgravity, as well as during the preflight and postflight periods, the test subjects performed a hypercapnic response test in which they rebreathed from a bag containing some CO2 in a hyperoxic gas mixture.

The ventilatory response to acute hypoxia was determined only before and after flight by a protocol that required the subjects to rebreathe a low oxygen gas mixture from a bag in which the CO2 was actively removed to maintain isocapnia in the face of increased ventilation and decreasing O2.

RESULTS:
The analysis completed to date suggests that moderate exercise in µG has no adverse consequences on the lung, although the effects of extreme exercise remain unknown. There were no changes in the ventilatory response to inhaled carbon dioxide caused by µG. However, based on measurements that were only able to be performed before and after the LMS mission, it seems likely that the ventilatory response to lowered oxygen levels in the blood (in this case caused by breathing a low oxygen mixture during a portion of the experiment) is increased in µG. Such a heightened response has the potential to disrupt sleep, and sleep is known to be of poor quality during µG.

This investigation extended studies of the human lung in four major areas:
To study lung function after the stress imposed by heavy exercise in the microgravity environment.
1. To monitor motion in the rib cage and abdomen.
2. To study the effects of microgravity on the musculoskeletal aspects of breathing during rest, during heavy exercising, and during deep breathing.
3. To measure the body's response to inhaled carbon dioxide, which may be altered by space flight.
4. To determine how gas is distributed within the lung.

A better understanding of the effects of gravity on the human pulmonary system ultimately may benefit clinical medicine on Earth. Also, a comprehension of pulmonary function in microgravity is important for long-term space flight.

APPROACH:
Data were collected before flight and throughout the mission, as well as several times during the two weeks following the mission. All seven crewmembers on board the LMS Spacelab served as test subjects.

Each subject performed a battery of pulmonary function tests before and immediately after exercise. These included measurements of cardiac output, lung water, pulmonary diffusing capacity, pulmonary ventilation, perfusion, and ventilation-perfusion ratio. Also, the metabolic rate was measured via resting oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production.

Further, the alterations in intra-acinar gas mixing in microgravity were investigated by measuring inspiratory flow rates as subjects inhaled and exhaled. In parallel, the pattern of chest wall and abdominal movements during normal ventilation, exercise ventilation, and induced hyperventilation was observed. While performing these studies, the subjects were instrumented with a respiratory inductance plethysmograph (RIP), a noninvasive device that allows continuous monitoring of the motion and expansion of the rib cage and abdomen. While the subject was not breathing through the mouthpiece, simple measurements of inspiratory and expiratory times were made.

To determine the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide during microgravity, as well as during the preflight and postflight periods, the test subjects performed a hypercapnic response test in which they rebreathed from a bag containing some CO2 in a hyperoxic gas mixture.

The ventilatory response to acute hypoxia was determined only before and after flight by a protocol that required the subjects to rebreathe a low oxygen gas mixture from a bag in which the CO2 was actively removed to maintain isocapnia in the face of increased ventilation and decreasing O2.

RESULTS:
The analysis completed to date suggests that moderate exercise in µG has no adverse consequences on the lung, although the effects of extreme exercise remain unknown. There were no changes in the ventilatory response to inhaled carbon dioxide caused by µG. However, based on measurements that were only able to be performed before and after the LMS mission, it seems likely that the ventilatory response to lowered oxygen levels in the blood (in this case caused by breathing a low oxygen mixture during a portion of the experiment) is increased in µG. Such a heightened response has the potential to disrupt sleep, and sleep is known to be of poor quality during µG.
