Software was developed to obtain segmentation of the mitral annulus using commercial three-dimensional echocardiographic review software. Another project evaluated outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a condition of excessive thickening of the heart muscle with some misalignment of the cells. Again, three-dimensional and two-dimensional techniques were compared. Another project involved volumetric changes with simulated microgravity.

In addition to four projects involving human studies, several animal studies were employed in the fourth specific aim to address the accuracy of left ventricular volume measurements and flow quantification using three-dimensional echocardiography. The projects involved aortic regurgitation, flow quantification using real-time three-dimensional color Doppler, left atrium volume quantification and non-invasive assessment of left atrium function, and quantification of left ventricular mass.

APPROACH:
Specific Aim #1 To develop the infrastructure for digital acquisition, storage, and transmission of echocardiograms, ultrasound images were evaluated using the ISS video system developed by the Human Research Facility Project at the Johnson Space Center. A design and analysis test of real-time ultrasound data transmission from the ISS evaluated the impact of reducing transmission rate on image quality. Images were tested at rates from 60 fields per second down to 1.875 fields per second.

Another project leading to the first specific aim was to develop the infrastructure to review and analyze digital echocardiographic data collected in various locations. The hypothesis that novice operators could perform diagnostic ultrasound was tested using five employees of the Cleveland Clinic Foundation who were untrained in the use of the ultrasound. Each test subject received four hours of training before attempting ultrasound examinations. All operators performed exams on normal subjects and patients with defined pathology.

Specific Aim #2 Several projects supported the second specific aim. The Haughton Mars Project Testbed involved a blinded review of echocardiographic data. A 45-minute delay in the transmission mimicked the scenario of communication from Mars. As part of the test, five pathological cases were forwarded to the Haughton Mars Project for retransmission along with normal echocardiograms. Another project was transmission of echocardiographic data across the NASA Research and Education Network (NREN). A sonographer and a cardiologist looked at cell loss and cell error ratios. For the echocardiographic image compression project, six reviewers performed blinded measurements from still frame images selected from twenty echocardiographic studies simultaneously acquired in VHS and MPEG formats.

A virtual hospital project also supported the second specific aim. A demonstration showed feasibility for high bandwidth telemedicine between remote clinics and tertiary care hospitals. One activity was real-time transmission of three-dimensional echocardiograms. Doctors received and rotated three-dimensional high-resolution color stereo medical images online at desktops and collaborated with remote colleagues for consultation, diagnosis, and treatment planning including surgical simulation. High-performance networks connected participating Virtual Collaborative Clinic sites with the application server.

Specific Aim #3 To address specific aim three, bed rest studies were conducted using fourteen days of 4 degree head-down tilt with three subsequent recovery days. Exercise echocardiographic data pre- and post-bed rest, Doppler tissue imaging, and color M-mode flow propagation were studied on five subjects. Left ventricular volumes, cardiac output, and brachial reactivity were measured to discover changes in intravascular tone. In another collaboration, combined echocardiographic indices were applied for the assessment of left ventricular filling pressures in healthy volunteers on bed rest.

Specific Aim #4 A total of eight hundred thirteen patients with a variety of heart diseases underwent three-dimensional studies to address the fourth specific aim of refining the acquisition, segmentation, display, and analysis of three-dimensional echocardiograms. In almost all subjects, the data were acquired without any geometrical assumptions. To validate real-time three-dimensional echocardiography with MRI, a total of thirty-four patients were evaluated with the three-dimensional method in the operating room or the echocardiographic laboratory. Thirteen of twenty-eight patients with heart disease and six subjects with normal left ventricular function were evaluated by three-dimensional echocardiography and MRI for left ventricular volumes and ejection fractions.

The human studies that involved volumetric changes with simulated microgravity used a tilting bed system to mimic microgravity in ten normal subjects. The stroke work of the left ventricle was evaluated as was ejection fraction and left ventricular volume.

The test of real-time transmission of ultrasound data from the ISS using the communications simulator showed that for cardiac ultrasound, optimal results were obtained at field rates of 80 or above, and rates as low as 15 per second provided useful information. For strictly diagnostic purposes, frame-rates below 7.5 fields per second were acceptable for non-moving structures. Researchers concluded that if this protocol could be used on board the ISS, then ground guidance of ultrasonic acquisition would be possible during a medical event involving crew members that do not have expert training in ultrasound.

The hypothesis that novice operators can perform diagnostic ultrasound studies was confirmed with preliminary analysis that demonstrated excellent capability for general imaging by the novice operators. The results that involved validation with MRI showed that real-time three-dimensional echocardiography was feasible in patients with heart disease and could provide a fast low-cost alternative to MRI for evaluating cardiac function. Three-dimensional techniques were also superior to two-dimensional ones when outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was evaluated. When cardiac function was studied in simulated microgravity, stroke work of the left ventricle was different from normal gravity.

The animal studies supporting the fourth specific aim showed several results. Left ventricular stroke volume and stroke work increased proportionally with the amount of aortic regurgitant volume quantitatively and reflected the additional energy consumption needed by volume overload in aortic regurgitation. Techniques were also shown to estimate the peak blood flow rate and demonstrate better understanding of blood flow phenomena and quantification. A three-dimensional technique was used to estimate left atrium volumes; although, it showed some underestimation relative to MRI. This same technique provided an excellent means to determine left ventricular mass as compared to conventional two-dimensional and other methods.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It has been sufficiently documented from Earth-based simulations of weightlessness, such as recumbency, water immersion, and from the space-flight environment itself, that orthostatic intolerance may result from relative inactivity or confinement. Potential problems of cardiovascular deconditioning were anticipated and thoroughly studied through various simulation techniques even before man first ventured into space. Cardiovascular deconditioning, or orthostatic intolerance, was consistently observed in crewmen during the early period of the Mercury and Gemini missions. With the advent of the Apollo Program, researchers were presented with new questions and uncertainties regarding this topic. The fundamental differences in the Apollo spacecraft and its operational environment, and in program goals, were expected to produce physiological responses that differed from those seen after the Gemini flights. The two-gas (oxygen and nitrogen) atmosphere and the capability to move about in the spacecraft led to speculation that returning Apollo crewmen might show little or no change in orthostatic tolerance. On the other hand, there was some concern regarding the ability of the cardiovascular system to withstand acceleration stresses associated with lunar descent and ascent (headward acceleration was imposed during lunar module descent after three to four days of weightlessness and a near 1-G force was produced by the ascent profile after a day or more of 1/6-G exposure).

The primary objective of the Apollo Flight Crew Cardiovascular Evaluations was to determine the response of the cardiovascular system to weightlessness. The results of postflight tests were expected to show differences in cardiovascular responsiveness between crewmen who walked on the moon and those who remained in weightlessness. These speculations and other unanswered questions emphasized the need to gain as much understanding as possible about the cardiovascular system and its adaptation, first to zero-G and later to 1-G. Then, as a countermeasure to orthostatic intolerance, a supplemental objective was addressed on the last two Apollo missions This objective was to evaluate the efficacy of an experimental antihypotensive garment. Though the Gemini and early Apollo missions revealed no need for such postflight support, planners of the 28- and 56-day Skylab missions envisioned the possible need for such postflight protection.

APPROACH:
The test methods used in assessing the degree of cardiovascular deconditioning or orthostatic intolerance included Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) and, when the use of LBNP was precluded by quarantine constraints, the 90 degree passive stand test. The crewmen of Apollo 7 through 9 and 15 through 17 missions underwent LBNP. As a basis for comparing the two methods, the Apollo 9 crewmen underwent both the LBNP and the stand test. The passive stand test alone was used for evaluating the orthostatic intolerance of the Apollo 10 and 11 crewmen. (The Apollo 10 through 14 missions included postflight quarantine, thus precluding the use of LBNP and the stand test was not conducted on the Apollo 12-14 missions.) Ambient temperature, oral temperature and body weight of each crewmember were recorded during each evaluation period.

Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) Protocol:
The LBNP consisted of a chamber of sufficient size to accommodate the lower body, an airtight waist seal and a regulated vacuum source. The types of physiological measurements taken during the LBNP protocol differed slightly from mission to mission. Measurements made in conjunction with the Apollo 7 through 9 missions included continuous axillary and sternal lead electrocardiograms (ECG) and indirect blood pressure taken every 30 seconds by the Korotkoff Sound techniques. Changes in calf circumference were measured by double-strand, mercury-in-Silastic strain gauges. The calf measurements were taken at the maximum girth during supine rest for the Apollo 7-11 and 15-17 missions. An assessment of total lower limb volume made on the Apollo 16 and 17 crewmembers consisted of multiple leg circumference measurements at discrete intervals from the ankle to the groin with the crew man in the supine position and the leg extended and slightly elevated.

For the Apollo 15 to 17 evaluations, the limited two-lead electrocardiogram was replaced with a modified Frank lead vectorcardiogram (VCG), and wide-band precordial heart sounds (vibrocardiogram) were recorded with a capacitance microphone system (LTV Research Center, Anaheim, Ca.). The respiration rates of the Apollo 16 and 17 crewmen were measured with a mercury strain gauge attached to the lower thorax. The carotid pulse trace was recorded for Apollo 17 crewmen. Other data considered in evaluating the test results included blood volume, exercise response, and vasoactive hormones.

Orthostatic intolerance evaluations were performed as part of major medical examinations conducted approximately 30,15, and 5 days before flight. The preflight (baseline) evaluations were compared to postflight evaluation results which were performed shortly after splashdown and at intervals of 24 hours thereafter. The number of postflight evaluations and the time at which they were performed were dictated by operational constraints and partly by the length of time required for individual crewmembers to regain their preflight status.

The supine LBNP was used with a five-minute rest control period, followed by 15-minute reduced pressure period, followed by a five-minute recovery period. The 15 minutes under reduced pressure utilized five different pressure levels:

  • 1 minute at -8 mm Hg

  • 1 minute at -16 mm Hg

  • 3 minutes at -30 mm Hg

  • 5 minutes at -40 mm Hg

  • 5 minutes at -50 mm Hg

    Passive Stand Test Protocol:
    The Passive Stand protocol consisted of a five-minute supine resting period followed by a five-minute passive stand. The subject would lean against a wall in a relaxed manner with heels spaced 15 cm (6 inches) away from the wall. The physiological measurements made during this protocol included continuous sternal and axillary lead ECGs and indirect blood pressure taken by the Korotkoff sound technique at 30-second intervals.

    Antihypotensive Garment Test:
    On the Apollo 16 and 17 missions, the experimental antihypotensive garments were tested. These garments were to be worn during postflight orthostatic evaluations to assess their antihypotensive effect. A Jobst waist-length elastic leotard was used in conjunction with the Apollo 16 mission. A garment employing the capstan principle for the application of pressure to the lower limbs was designed to be worn by the Apollo 17 subject during postflight tests.

    The Apollo 16 tests, utilizing the Jobst leotard, were performed pre- and postflight. Passive stand tests were performed 15 days before flight on the Apollo 16 subject and his backup, then repeated on the Apollo 16 subject and the ground control subjects during their respective recovery day examinations. This test followed the LBNP test and consisted of a five-minute supine rest period followed by a five-minute stand period in the manner of the earlier Apollo passive stand tests. The leotard was then put on and, after a ten-minute period of supine rest, the stand test was repeated. Blood pressure and heart-rate data were obtained using the instrumentation of the LBNP test.

    For the Apollo 17 test, the subject wore the antihypotensive garment approximately one-half hour prior to deorbit. After splashdown, while still reclining in the couch, he inflated the capstan to a pressure of 130 mm Hg and thus furnished 65 mm Hg pressure over the ankle region. This pressure was maintained until the stand test could be performed. The suit was tested by performing a stand test four hours after splashdown and before LBNP testing. Crew time constraints prevented repetition of the preflight protocol, which included tests with and without the garment, each separated by an appropriate recovery period. Therefore, the crewman spent five minutes in the supine position with the capstan garment inflated, five minutes passive standing with the capstan garment inflated, five minutes standing with the garment depressurized and four minutes standing with the garment reinflated to the original pressure of 130 mm Hg. The total duration of the continuous stand test was 15 minutes, including approximately 45 seconds for reinflation of the capstan garment. Heart rate was obtained continuously from the VCG; blood pressure was measured every 30 seconds by a Skylab automatic blood pressure measuring system.

    RESULTS:
    Physiological measurements were recorded real-time on a strip chart recorder and on frequency modulated (FM) magnetic tape. The strip chart data was used real-time for assessment of crewmember well-being and safety. In the event of manifestation of presyncopal symptoms during orthostatic stress, the protocol was terminated. Minute heart rates were derived from an analysis of ECG or VCG R-R intervals. Limb volume was computed by summing sequential, truncated, assumed-circular cones. Standard 1.8 m (6 ft) posterior-anterior chest X-rays were taken of each crewmember at his last major preflight medical examination and first postflight evaluation.

    Data Collection and Reduction:
    For each crewman evaluation, heart rate, blood pressure (systolic and diastolic), pulse pressure, and stroke volume values were averaged within each of the five minute LBNP periods and within the two five-minute passive stand periods to produce the respective mean values for each of these periods. These mean values for each crew member, during each period and by each measurement, were subsequently used as the best estimate of measurement within that period in the compilation of data tables. In the case of percentage, maximal calf volume change rather than mean values within each level of LBNP was used.

    Individual and group mean data was determined. For individual crewmembers, the mean and standard deviation of the preflight values of each measurement in each distinct protocol condition were calculated. From these values, fiducial limits of the normal range at the 95-percent confidence level were determined. Individual postflight values lying outside these limits were defined as statistically significant. It should be noted that 4 of the crewmen flew two Apollo missions each.

    Heart Rate:
    Heart rate statistics can be divided into three stressor categories: 1) during resting supine control, 2) during the highest pressure level (-50 mm Hg) of LBNP, and 3) during passive standing. Of the 24 crewmen tested, 13 (or 54%) experienced elevated resting supine heart rates on the first postflight day. By the third postflight evaluation, only 3 of 15 crewmen (20%) showed significant elevations in supine resting heart rate. With the application of -50 mm Hg pressure during LBNP, 82% (14 of 17) experienced elevated heart rates at the first postflight evaluation. One crewman experienced presyncopal symptoms during the last seconds of the -40 mm Hg pressure level and therefore was not tested at the -50 mm Hg level during the first evaluation period. Five other crewmen experienced presyncopal symptoms at the -50 mm Hg level prior to completion of the protocol.

    Immediately postflight, more crewmembers experienced a larger heart rate increase over preflight values during LBNP stress than during the rest control period, however statistically significant group differences disappeared by the third postflight evaluation. Results of the passive stand test yielded similar results with the increased heart rate immediately postflight. Eight of 9 (89%) crewmen experienced heart rates above their 95-percent preflight envelope.

    Accompanying each postflight evaluation group mean is the t-test probability that it differs for the preflight summary group mean. During the first and second evaluations, resting supine control showed significantly elevated heart rates, the reciprocal response for stroke volume and no significant change in systolic, diastolic, and pulse pressures. LBNP results at -30, -40 and -50 mm Hg levels showed elevated heart rates during the first postflight evaluation period, with a trend toward preflight values at subsequent evaluations. Reciprocal stroke volume data was again noted. Significant decreases in systolic and pulse pressures were noted during the first evaluation period of LBNP. The passive stand test results paralleled the LBNP results.

    No significant postflight calf volume changes were observed during the three conditions of reduced-pressure stress at any of the postflight evaluations. Seven of the 17 crewmen (41%) tested showed calf volume changes were significantly decreased postflight under the LBNP stress at -50 mm Hg as compared to the preflight results. The first postflight group mean weight showed a 3.4 kg (4.4%) decrease that was not regained at 90 to 160 hours after splashdown by the Apollo 15 to 17 crewmen. Also, at the first postflight evaluation, results during the resting supine control condition showed that 16 of 24 crewmen (67 %) had significantly reduced calf circumferences. Total leg volume, calculated for the Apollo 16 and 17 crewmen, showed a 1-liter decrement, though this result is not considered statistically significant.

    To determine whether heart size changes had occurred, cardiothoracic (C/T) ratios were calculated. Posterior-anterior chest X-rays were taken once before and once after flight. Twenty-four of 30 crewmen (80%) showed a highly significant decreased group mean in C/T ratios of .021 (5%). Vectorcardiographic data showed no significant clinical changes.

    Efficacy of Antihypotensive Garment:
    The Apollo 16 subject underwent orthostatic evaluations 7 hours after splashdown wearing the Jobst waist-length elastic leotard. The garment was .5 cm smaller than the one used during preflight evaluations in anticipation of decreased limb girth after flight. The leotard, although it appeared to furnish moderate protection against orthostatic hypotension, was unsuitable for the operational setting because the Apollo 16 subject was unable to put on the suit in the confined volume of the spacecraft. Consequently, any benefits the suit provided were not available until the postflight testing phase. This option proved untenable because of the problems associated with obtaining a proper fit. The decline of limb girth postflight was neither uniformly distributed nor predictable in magnitude.

    The design of the pressurized garment included features intended to overcome the difficulty of predicting change in limb girth during flight. The Apollo 17 subject was able to put on the pressurized suit while still in the spacecraft. Results showed that heart rate, while reclining with the suit inflated, was 10 beats per minute slower than during preflight testing 15 days before flight. With the garment deflated, heart rate increased and was still increasing after five minutes. Reinflating the garment, which lasted about 40 seconds, was associated with a modest reduction in heart rate and thus suggested a protective effect from the garment. Worth noting is that the Apollo 17 subject was the only one of 18 crewmen tested whose mean heart rate at the first evaluation was within the preflight envelope and who showed no decrement of performance during bicycle ergometry as compared to preflight values. Prior to deflation of the garment, the Apollo 17 subject showed an increased C/T ratio postflight as compared to the 20 Apollo crewmen who experienced continuous weightlessness.

    The Apollo 16 subject underwent orthostatic evaluations 7 hours after splashdown wearing the Jobst waist-length elastic leotard. The garment was .5 cm smaller than the one used during preflight evaluations in anticipation of decreased limb girth after flight. The leotard, although it appeared to furnish moderate protection against orthostatic hypotension, was unsuitable for the operational setting because the Apollo 16 subject was unable to put on the suit in the confined volume of the spacecraft. Consequently, any benefits the suit provided were not available until the postflight testing phase. This option proved untenable because of the problems associated with obtaining a proper fit. The decline of limb girth postflight was neither uniformly distributed nor predictable in magnitude.

    The design of the pressurized garment included features intended to overcome the difficulty of predicting change in limb girth during flight. The Apollo 17 subject was able to put on the pressurized suit while still in the spacecraft. Results showed that heart rate, while reclining with the suit inflated, was 10 beats per minute slower than during preflight testing 15 days before flight. With the garment deflated, heart rate increased and was still increasing after five minutes. Reinflating the garment, which lasted about 40 seconds, was associated with a modest reduction in heart rate and thus suggested a protective effect from the garment. Worth noting is that the Apollo 17 subject was the only one of 18 crewmen tested whose mean heart rate at the first evaluation was within the preflight envelope and who showed no decrement of performance during bicycle ergometry as compared to preflight values. experiment_title: The Influence of Rotational Cues on Human Tilt and Translation Responses
parameter_html:
Eye movements
Psychophysical translation
Psychophysical response, tilt
investigators: Principal Investigator: Zupan, LionelPrincipal Investigator: Merfeld, Daniel
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To investigate the influence of rotational cues on the neural processing of tilt and translation in humans, the investigators proposed to develop a countermeasure to adapt and/or pre-adapt astronaut canal-otolith interactions to any gravitational environment (Earth, Mars, etc.) by providing correlated sensory cues between the canals and the otoliths. The countermeasure they developed often referred to as Artificial Gravity, consisted of centrifugation combined with intermittent motion. They measured behavioral (eye movements such as vestibulo-ocular reflexes) as well as psychophysical responses (orientation estimation) during tilt alone, translation alone or combined tilt-translation motion in either a 1-G or hypergravic environment.

This study addressed the following specific aims:
1) Using psychophysics and eye movement measurements, investigate how humans utilize semicircular canal cues to help estimate the relative orientation of gravity (monitored through perceptual tilt responses) as well as the estimate of linear acceleration (monitored through translational VOR responses). Investigators proposed a ground study to measure human responses (perceptual tilt and eye movements) during combined canal-otolith stimulation on Earth, in a 1-G environment. Their goal was to provide a perceptual measure of tilt with simultaneous eye movement recording to comprehensively investigate how the human Central Nervous System distinguishes tilt from translation. Subjects were tested using protocols in which they passively a) tilt, b) translate, or c) tilt and translate simultaneously.
2) Using psychophysics and eye movement measurements, investigate how humans utilize semicircular canal cues to help estimate the relative orientation of gravity (monitored through perceptual tilt responses) as well as the estimate of linear acceleration (monitored through translational VOR responses) by measuring adaptive changes induced by exposure to a hyper-G environment. Investigators proposed to measure human perception of orientation and eye movement responses during exposure to artificial gravity. To induce adaptation, they proposed to utilize intermittent motion during centrifugation: passive roll tilt in a supine orientation will dynamically stimulate both semicircular canals and otolith organs, such that both sensory cues are correlated.

APPROACH:
Using a variable-radius roll swing motion paradigm, the investigators examined the influence of inter-aural (y-axis) and dorso-ventral, (z-axis) force modulation on perceived tilt and translation by measuring perception of horizontal translation, roll tilt, and distance from center of rotation (radius) at 0.45 and 0.8 Hz using standard magnitude estimation techniques (primarily verbal reports) in darkness.

RESULTS:
Results show that motion perception was significantly influenced by both y- and z-axis forces. During constant radius trials, subjects’ perceptions of tilt and translation were generally almost veridical. By selectively pairing radius (1.22 m and 0.38 m) and frequency (0.45 and 0.8 Hz, respectively), the y-axis acceleration could be tailored in opposition to gravity so that the combined y-axis gravitoinertial force (GIF) variation at the subject’s ears was reduced to about 0.035 m/s2 – in effect, the y-axis GIF was “nulled” below putative perceptual threshold levels. With y-axis force nulling, subjects overestimated their tilt angle and underestimated their horizontal translation and radius. For some trials a radial linear acceleration at twice the tilt frequency (0.25 m/s2 at 0.9 Hz, 0.13 m/s2 at 1.6 Hz) was simultaneously applied to reduce the z-axis force variations caused by centripetal acceleration and by changes in the z-axis component of gravity during tilt. For other trials, the phase of this radial linear acceleration was altered in order to double the magnitude of the z-axis force variations. Z-axis force nulling further increased the perceived tilt angle and further decreased perceived horizontal translation and radius relative to the y-axis nulling trials, while z-axis force doubling had the opposite effect. Subject reports were remarkably geometrically consistent; an observer model-based analysis suggests that perception was influenced by their knowledge of swing geometry.

experiment_title: Development and Use of Human 3-Dimensional Tissue Culture Models for the Study of Space Radiation Effects on the Central Nervous System
parameter_html:
Amyloid-beta 40 peptide
Cell type
Radiation dose
Tau protein
Amyloid precursor protein (APP)
Transendothelial electrical resistance
investigators: Principal Investigator: Grabham, Peter
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Human space exploration involves exposure to types of radiation not normally encountered on earth. The effect of these particles on the human central nervous system (CNS) is of particular concern since impairment of cognitive function could not only compromise missions but cause later effects on the quality of life. Studies in animals have shown that space radiation particles can have adverse effects on cognition and behavior. The effect on neurogenesis has also been documented and proposed to be a cause of cognitive loss. Information regarding the effects of space radiation on the CNS is, however, still in its infancy due to the difficulty of extrapolating data from animals and cell lines to the intact human being.

The primary objective of this investigation was to increase the understanding of the effects of space radiation on the human central nervous system with an emphasis on neurodegeneration. There were two primary goals:

  1. Develop 3-dimensional tissue models for neural tissue, achieving a more accurate representation of human neural tissue by incorporating human neuron, astrocytes, and endothelial cells into the model.
  2. Apply the 3-dimensional models to develop assays to support projected studies of the effects of space radiation on neurodegeneration.

APPROACH:
The study began with the development of the human brain tissue model. At least 3 human cell types were acquired for each of the components of the model: neurons, astrocytes and endothelial cells. This ensured the best possible model and provided back-up cells. Then, a multistep protocol was developed for the generation and differentiation of normal human neurons from stem cells. Expression of neuronal markers and degeneration markers in 3D monocultures was successfully detected. The strategy for constructing tissue models was to embed neurons and astrocytes into protein gel matrices after they had been differentiated into the respective cell type and then induce morphological or “end stage” differentiation while they were in the matrix.

Endothelial cells were added, given the right factors, and allowed to grow into the matrix and form blood vessels as in vivo during angiogenesis. Different media types and different pairings of cell types were tested. As a result, it was found that the requirement of endothelial cells was not entirely compatible with that of neurons and astrocytes. Endothelial cells, which line the vessels and are in contact with blood in vivo require serum for vessel formation. Neurons and astrocytes, normally behind the blood brain barrier (BBB), require serum-free conditions to differentiate in matrices. However, a prototype neurovascular unit using the above protocol was created by reducing the serum concentration and relying on trophic support from astrocytes for the maintenance of vessels. At this stage, it was determined that tissue models were developed enough to be incorporated into assays that assess tight junctions and provide an additional relevant endpoint.

Assay development was directed towards determination of the effects of space radiation on the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB).

Assays to determine the function of the endothelial barrier were developed. For the first assay, trans-endothelial resistance measurement was achieved by using equipment that measures electric cell-substrate impedance sensing (ECIS). Resistance monitoring of monolayers was easy and continuous. This assay is useful for determining parameters such as the time course of the effects of radiation. A second assay was developed using tissue inserts to determine the rate of labeled molecules permeation through the cell layer on the insert. This provides a direct measurement of the passage of molecules of varying sizes through the endothelial cell layer. This assay does not utilize the neurovascular unit but can still include a cell mixture of endothelial cells and astrocytes or pericytes. Endothelial cells are plated on one side of the membrane and the other cell types are plated on the other side of the membrane. Thus it represents the human blood-brain-barrier more closely than endothelial cells alone. 2 additional assays were developed for localization of the junction proteins that seal the BBB using immunolabeling of these molecules: the first examining the junction proteins in normal monolayers and the second, examining the junction proteins in the 3-D human tissue models. Further assays include endpoints more directly applied to human neuro-degenerative diseases. One such endpoint is the metabolization and localization of the protein involved in Alzheimer’s disease – the amyloid precursor protein (APP).

RESULTS:
The primary goal of this investigation has been achieved. Human 3-D tissue models have been developed sufficiently for use in novel assays to determine degenerative markers. Other assays were developed for use in future studies that address a pivotal part of the brain involved heavily in many neuro-degenerative disorders – the brain blood capillaries. Work going forward includes improving the longevity of these models and substituting neurons from stem cells for the neuroblastoma used in the prototype model.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The central nervous system (CNS) has been typically described as radiation-resistant tissue. However, there is now a sufficient body of evidence, mostly from experiments in rodents, showing that low doses of charged particle radiation (< 1 Gy) may affect some basic neuronal processes, such as synaptic excitability, neuronal firing, and propensity for epileptiform activity. In addition, it has been posited by investigators that in subjects prone to develop neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer Disease (AD), an exposure to charged-particle radiation may accelerate the onset and/or alter the progression of AD, increase amyloid plaque load, and promote neuro-inflammatory changes within their brain. While such effects have been observed with high-LET particles (e.g., 1GEv/n Iron nuclei), this hypothesis has not been fully tested with other low- and high-LET particles and protons that represent major components in space radiation spectra. Studying the impact of protons and high-LET radiation on neurodegenerative processes in mammalian CNS is a critical step for critical assessment of the space radiation CNS-risks for astronauts, and e.g. for further development of modern cranial radiotherapies using charged particle radiation.

This study had the following specific aims:


  1. To determine the temporal profile and dose-dependence of functional changes in the hippocampus after exposure to low doses of proton radiation.
  2. To correlate the functional damage in the hippocampus with radiation-accelerated amyloidosis, synaptic damage, and neuroinflammation.
  3. To compare the functional and structural effects of protons with corresponding doses (0.1-1.0 Gy) of two high-LET ions on neurodegenerative process in the hippocampus.

    4. APPROACH:
    Investigators used a murine double transgenic (TG) model of AD (the APP/PSEN1 TG mice commercially available from Jackson Laboratories) that they exposed to low- and high-LET charged-particle radiation and tested whether radiation affects the time course and severity of neurodegenerative processes in these TG mice. The functional changes were also compared to a limited cohort of wild type (WT) mice to rule out qualitative differences in response to irradiation. The combination of behavioral, electrophysiological, and histological techniques helped investigators to gather unique data on radiation effects from 150 MeV proton-, 250 MeV/n silicon-, and 600 MeV/n iron-irradiated APP/PSEN1 TG mice.

    RESULTS:
    Behavioral analyses performed in cohorts of mice irradiated with protons using water maze (WM), Barnes maze (BM), and zero maze (ZM) confirmed AD genotype-related deficits in spatial memory that were likely associated with hippocampal dysfunction. Genotype-related behavioral decrements were evident at three months post-irradiation. For example, in control (non-irradiated) APP/PSEN1 TG mice investigators observed an increased in swim distance to the target area in WM, an increased average distance moved in BM, and a reduction of time spent in the dark side of the ZM, when compared to the control (0 Gy) WT mice. Such findings indicate AD-related decrements in spatial memory (WM and BM data), but paradoxically a reduced anxiety-like behavior (ZM data) in TG mice.

    Investigators observed relatively subtle, proton- and HZE-radiation-induced behavioral effects. Significant radiation-induced effects were only observed in WT mice after exposure to 0.5 Gy protons detected in WM at six months post-irradiation. In these mice only (n=16), they observed significantly increased swim distance during the reversal learning phase of the WM test, indicating reduced cognitive flexibility. While proton radiation affected the performance of WT mice, exposures to protons and HZE-radiation did not affect the performance of APP/PSEN1 TG mice. Such results may indicate that low doses of proton and HZE radiation may not necessarily worsen the functional outcomes in mice prone to AD-like pathology, or alternatively such pathology may trump any observable behavioral radiation-induced effects. Interestingly, the TG mice irradiated with 250 MeV/n silicon particles exhibited reduced performance in WM at three months only; the decrement was reaching statistical significance at 0.1 Gy only and appeared to be transient as it could not be detected at six months post-irradiation. No significant differences were observed for either HZE species in BM and ZM. In TG mice irradiated with 600 MeV/n iron particles investigators observed a trend for improved performance in WM at six months post-irradiation at the dose of 1 Gy.

    Electrophysiological data indicate that proton radiation at doses from 0.1 to 1 Gy may impact synaptic excitability and short-term synaptic plasticity mediated by presynaptic glutamate release, but it likely does not affect long-term potentiation, the widely used cellular correlate of memory formation in the hippocampus. Investigators observed that proton radiation-induced changes in synaptic excitability are qualitatively different in TG when compared to changes observed in WT mice. In accord with their behavioral findings, the WT mice exhibit different sensitivity to radiation and, for example at 0.5 Gy, they observed increased postsynaptic excitability in CA1 neurons, whereas the TG mice exhibited opposite responses at the same radiation dose. The stimulation paradigms testing the effect of proton radiation on presynaptic glutamate release revealed that the TG mice (but not the WT mice) at nine months post-irradiation exhibited reduced paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) indicating increased glutamate release. Interestingly, in TG mice, radiation exposure to protons or HZE particles had no effect on these spontaneous oscillations.

experiment_title: Changes in Total Body Water During Space Flight
parameter_html:
Body mass
Total body water (TBW)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Leach- Huntoon, CarolynPrincipal Investigator: Inners, Lamar DanielCo-Investigator: Charles, John
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This investigation was designed to measure by means of direct in-flight assessment, the changes in total body water (TBW) occurring in humans as a consequence of several days' exposure to microgravity on the Space Shuttle. TBW measurements provide important data for several cardiovascular and fluid/electrolyte experiments making up the science payload for the dedicated life sciences missions (SLS-1 and SLS-2). According to several models, changes in TBW are predicted to parallel fluid shifts. Therefore, changes in TBW can be used as a convenient indicator of the time course of adaptation to weightlessness. Because of its ease of measurement, TBW was the method of choice to verify in flight the timing proposed for fluid compartment measurements planned for SLS-1.

APPROACH:
The subjects for this experiment were five male crewmembers of Space Shuttle missions STS-61C and STS-26. The design included no special control group or control experiment. Instead, all in-flight and postflight data were compared to preflight baseline data. Because of a delay in the launch of STS 61-C and the unavailability of some crewmembers during the immediate pre-and postflight periods, the first preflight measurements were at L-31 to L-30, while some measurements were missed entirely.

TBW was measured by the isotope dilution technique utilizing 18O-labeled water as the tracer. This method required the ingestion of a known mass of 18O water followed by sampling of representative body fluids such as urine or saliva over a period of several hours following the administration of the tracer. The measurements were initiated immediately after a sleep cycle with the crewmember in a fasted state. After the collection of background samples, the dose was consumed followed by at least 50 ml of fruit juice or galley water. The subject was allowed to consume a light breakfast 30 minutes after dose administration and was requested to abstain from caffeine containing beverages for the duration of the experiment. All food consumed during the experiment was recorded on a log sheet.

Samples of galley water were collected on FD 2 and FD 4/FD 5. The experimental design called for galley water sampling on all days on which TBW was measured because water sampled from the galley on several occasions, including ST5-51D, was found to be enriched in 18O.

Test subjects collected saliva by placing a dental cotton roll under the tongue for several minutes and then replacing the saturated cotton in the vial. It was determined in supporting studies that samples could be stored for more than a week at ambient temperature without affecting isotope content, provided they were protected from evaporation. Sample vials were replaced in the original kit and stowed in a middeck locker different from the one for used dose syringes. As mentioned above, this precaution was taken to minimize the possibility of accidental contamination of the sample vial contents. The samples were frozen at -70° C after being returned to the laboratory.

Analyses of the samples were carried out in ground-based facilities of the USDA/ARS Children's Nutrition Research Center, Department of Pediatrics, Baylor College of Medicine and Texas Children's Hospital, Houston, TX. Two methods of analysis were used because of the advance in technology between the two missions on which data were gathered.

STS-61C: Frozen samples were thawed, and approximately 0.3-0.5 g were transferred to pre-weighed 20ml VacutainerTM serum tubes using disposable plastic tuberculin syringes. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone demineralization is a biochemical process that weakens the skeletal system. Physicians have observed this degenerative process in humans during periods of inadequate calcium intake, immobilization such as bed rest, and other situations involving physical inactivity. This experiment investigated bone demineralization resulting from prolonged microgravity and immobilization associated with confinement in the Gemini and Apollo spacecrafts. The information gained about the effects of microgravity on the physiological integrity of the astronauts' bones would help researchers determine if corrective measures would be necessary during future long-duration space missions.

APPROACH:
Bone mass was measured in the primary and backup crewmembers of the Gemini 4 (4-day), Gemini 5 (8-day), Gemini 7 (14-day), Apollo 7 (10-day) and Apollo 8 (6-day) space flights using x-ray bone densitometry. In the Gemini 4 study, X-ray's were taken of the left os calcis in the lateral projection and the phalanx 5-2 of the left hand in the posterior-anterior projection. The crewmembers of Gemini 5 and Gemini 7 had the same bones examined as Gemini 4, with the addition of the left phalanx 4-2, the distal end of the left radius, and the left talus. Three exposures were taken preflight and postflight of each bone according to the following schedules:
Gemini 4: L-9 (nine days before launch), L-3, L-0 (launch day), R+0 (landing day), R+16, and R+50

Gemini 5: L-10, L-4, L-2, L-0, R+0, R+1, R+10, and R+58

Gemini 7: L-10, L-3, L-0, R+0, R+1, R+11, and R+47

Apollo 7 and Apollo 8: unknown except for L-0 and R+0

The equipment used in this experiment included standard x-ray machines, standard x-ray films, aluminum alloy calibration wedges, and a bone densitometer assembly.

The os calcis was selected as an anatomical site for evaluation because it was a large bone with a minimum of over- and underlying soft tissue and it contained a substantial amount of trabecular bone tissue. (The interchange of minerals between bone and extracellular tissue occurs more readily in newly formed trabecular bone than in older compact bone.) The phalanges were selected as anatomical sites for evaluation because they represented bone that contained a substantial amount of compact skeletal tissue. Both the os calcis and the phalanges were known to be little affected by soft tissue x-ray scatter, and they were easily accessible for x-raying. All of the sites selected were considered non-hazardous from the irradiation aspect since blood-forming marrow would not be exposed to radiation. The x-ray exposure field was strictly limited to these small areas.

The x-ray machines were standardized by three methods. The first method used an aluminum alloy wedge exposed on the film adjacent to the bone. The x-ray films were calibrated by placing an aluminum alloy reference wedge adjacent to the bone to be x-rayed. The wedge served as a means of correcting any bone scan that was traced by first correcting the trace of the wedge for deviations resulting from slight differences in film characteristics or development techniques. The alloy in the wedge was selected because it exhibited an x-ray absorption coefficient similar to that of bone. Separate calibration wedges were used for the heel bone and the little finger.

The second method used a roentgen meter immediately before making a x-ray to determine the calibrated kilovoltage that would produce identical beam qualities in each of the x-ray machines. The third method used a specially prepared phantom that was shaped like an os calcis and made of calcium hydroxyapatite in an organic matrix. The wedges were individually calibrated in terms of calcium hydroxyapatite, the major mineral component of bone. Each wedge was x-rayed on the same film with a series of known quantities of calcium hydroxyapatite encased in thin-walled Lucite containers. The values obtained from scanning certain sections of bone could also be equated in terms of the mass of calcium hydroxyapatite by means of a conversion factor. The phantom was x-rayed before and after each series of films made at any one time to detect possible technique variations. For the os calcis, milliamperes, kilovolts, and time were set to give an exposure level of 167 ± 2 milliroentgens for each x-ray made.

The x-ray film development procedures were closely controlled regarding chemicals, temperature, and timing. Densitometer control readings of all films agreed within 2 percent.

Bone mass was determined from exposed x-rays by means of a bone densitometer computer assembly. The densitometer system evaluated the x-rays in two ways. First, a single path approach known as a "conventional scan" was used. The densitometer was programmed to trace one small strip (1.3 millimeters in width) across the x-ray image between two conspicuous landmarks on the bone. Each x-ray was made with extreme care so that the image of the bone on each film could be superimposed exactly over that of the initial film. With a small steel needle, the initial film was punctured at each end of the bone image; this defined the limits of the conventional trace. The two needle picks could be identified by the densitometer, which made possible exact positioning of the film prior to scanning. The same technique was applied to the image of the calibration wedge on the same film. Before tracing the same segment on each successive film, each film was superimposed over the first film with the needle pricks made in exactly the same positions. By superimposing successive x-rays, accurate serial films could be produced for the same individual showing the density changes. The os calcis and the talus were evaluated this way. These were revealing sites for measuring bone mineral changes, since the path penetrated a highly trabecular area of bone, surrounded by a periphery of cortical bone. The conventional scan gave bone mass, in terms of wedge mass equivalency in grams.

The "parallel path" system was used to evaluate a larger section of the same bone. Without removing the x-ray film from the densitometer after making a conventional scan, a series of parallel strips 1.0 millimeter (mm) apart were made, beginning 1.0 mm above the conventional path and continuing to the lowest portion of the bone. The center of each scan was 1.0 mm from the center of the next scan, with the edges of the successive scans slightly overlapping. The total number of paths scanned was proportional to the size of the bone with its individual variations. The os calcis and phalanges were measured in this fashion.

RESULTS:
Initial results from the three missions indicated that bone mineral losses in the Gemini 7 crewmembers were significantly less than those of the Gemini 4 and Gemini 5 crewmembers. The most significant differences occurred in the os calcis between the Gemini 5 and Gemini 7 crewmembers. Bone density changes in the os calcis ranged from -15.10 and -8.90 % in the Gemini 5 subjects to -2.91 and -2.84 % in the Gemini 7 subjects. The bone mineral density changes in the Gemini 4 astronauts were -7.80 and -10.30 %. Losses in the phalanges were also less in the Gemini 7 crewmembers than those found on Gemini 4 and Gemini 5, although the differences were not as great as those changes in the os calcis.

Rapid gains in bone mass were found during the first 12 hours after recovery in all subjects. Before this study was closed, each of the six astronauts had met or exceeded his preflight bone density level in all anatomical sites that were tested. The backup crewmembers who acted as control subjects experienced only those changes in bone density found in normal healthy persons.

Several years after the close of the Gemini program, the experiment data were reevaluated using photon absorptiometry. Researchers concluded that certain factors may have been conducive to misinterpretation of bone mineral changes in the Gemini 4 and 5 astronauts. X-ray evaluations of a standard bone phantom made at the same times and on the same x-ray machines as the original films indicated that the reported mass losses in the Gemini 4 and 5 astronauts were 7 % too high. This error was attributed to a 4 % inherent absorption difference between the two calibration wedges used prior to launch and after recovery. Three percent of the error was attributable to variation in x-ray beam qualities among the x-ray machines used in the experiment.

The corrected density changes for the Gemini 4 crewmembers were -2.9 and -3.8 % instead of the -7.8 and -10.3 % values originally reported. Similarly, the corrected density changes for the Gemini 5 crewmembers -9.2 and -2.5 % instead of the originally reported values of -15.1 and -8.9 %. The modified data indicated that the observed changes in bone density pre- and postflight were so close to the overall experimental error that it was questionable whether any changes occurred at all.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment had two key objectives. The first was to compare the spectrum of tumor types that arises in a genetically diverse mouse population irradiated with HZE ions to the spectra arising in similar unirradiated or gamma-ray irradiated populations. The second objective was to identify genetic differences between individual outbred mice that make them susceptible or resistant to the induction of specific types of tumors by radiation and then to determine if the same genetic factors that control sensitivity to gamma-ray induced tumors also control sensitivity to HZE ion induced tumors.

APPROACH:
To accomplish these objectives investigators irradiated mice from an outbred, heterogeneous stock, HS/NPT, with HZE ions or gamma-rays and monitored them along with unirradiated control mice for tumor development. Tumors that arise in the mice were classified by histological examination and the tumor spectra was compared between the three groups. The investigators identified the genetic differences, known as QTL or quantitative trait loci, underlying susceptibility to HZE ion-induced and gamma-ray-induced tumorigenesis and determined their overlap by analyzing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) throughout the genomes of tumor bearing and unaffected mice for association with specific tumor types. This work addressed the solicitation's emphasis on studies of the individual basis of space radiation risk assessment including the use of genetically diverse populations of mice to represent human heterogeneity that will elucidate the spectrum of tumor types caused by HZE nuclei as well as possible differences compared to gamma-rays.

RESULTS:
Carcinogenesis
To determine whether tumors that arise following HZE ion exposure are more malignant than their counterparts arising in unirradiated or gamma-ray irradiated mice, the investigators characterized two measures of malignancy: tumor latencies (analyzed by Kaplan-Meir survival procedures) and metastatic events. As expected, tumors arising in both HZE ion and gamma-ray irradiated mice showed significantly decreased latencies. However, HZE ions did not produce tumors with decreased latencies when compared to tumors in gamma-ray irradiated mice. Pulmonary metastases were observed in cases of hepatocellular carcinoma, Harderian gland adenocarcinoma, osteosarcoma, and ovarian granulosa cell tumor. Metastases were no more frequent in irradiated animals than in controls and there was no significant difference in metastatic incidence between HZE ion irradiated mice and gamma-ray irradiated mice.

Ocular Effects
The cataract data was analyzed in conjunction with the SNP genotyping data to identify quantitative trait loci (QTL) that control susceptibility to radiogenic cataracts. The mapping phenotype was days to grade two cataract and genome wide scans were performed using the DOQTL program which was modified for use with Cox regression. Significance at 80% and 95% confidence was determined by permutation. Several QTL were identified at 95% confidence and one, on chromosome 13, was narrow enough that a strong candidate gene emerged.

Cognitive Effects
Approximately 1,850 mice were irradiated and behaviorally tested in two cohorts of 600 and 1,200 mice, respectively. Statistical analysis for behavioral and genetic analyses, the investigators detected a significant cohort effect. This might be due to the fact that urine was collected 24 hours following sham-irradiation or irradiation for NMR analysis as part of the second cohort but this additional procedure was not part of the experience of the first cohort of mice. Investigators assessed whether the NMR data was related to or could predict behavioral or cognitive outcome measures three months later but they did not detect evidence for that. They also did not detect an effect of irradiation on the NMR data. Based on the cohort effect described earlier, investigators analyzed the data separately and focused the main analysis on first cohort of about 600 mice.

The genetic data consists of approximately 77K genetic markers across the genome. Among these, about 40K markers were deemed as informative, i.e., they had a minor allele frequency above 5%. As described below, the utilization of this set of informative markers increased the robustness and reproducibility of the results. However, The investigators recognize that the low frequency alleles could also be informative in some cases and/or have a strong effect on some phenotypes.

The QTL analysis is based on more than 40 behavioral and cognitive phenotypes for radiobiological outcome measures of interest related to performance in the hippocampus-dependent contextual and hippocampus-independent cued fear conditioning tasks. This large collection of related phenotypes and genotypes required the adoption of a data reduction technique that 1) summarizes the essential features of the behavioral and cognitive measures and 2) enhances the ability to detect significant genotype-phenotype associations.

experiment_title: Use of a Molecular Marker of Learning and Memory to Assess Effects of 56Fe Irradiation on Hippocampus-dependent Cognition and Neurogenesis
parameter_html:
Arc expression
Chemokine receptor 2
Cognitive performance
Dendritic spine density
Hippocampal function
Neuronal function
Hippocampus-dependent cognition
investigators: Principal Investigator: Fike, JohnCo-Investigator: Raber, JacobCo-Investigator: Rosi, Susanna
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Particulate irradiation in the space environment may pose a significant risk to space flight crews during a mission or upon return to Earth. This may involve the central nervous system, where low radiation doses can induce cognitive or behavioral impairments. Understanding the cellular and molecular basis of cognitive injury will facilitate the establishment of risk estimates and may provide a foundation for the establishment of effective countermeasures or treatments for such injury. Using an animal model, we will determine the extent to which low doses of 56Fe irradiation affect cognitive function and will determine if such changes are associated with the alteration of a gene that is associated with learning and memory, or with the production and maturation of newly born neurons.

APPROACH:
The overall goals of this project were to determine: (1) how low doses of 56Fe ions affected behavioral performance; (2) if specific cellular (e.g. neurogenesis) and molecular factors (immediate early gene Arc) might play a role in cognition; and (3) if those endpoints were affected by inflammatory changes. The experimental methods chosen to accomplish these goals provided a means by which the effects of low radiation doses could be quantified both in terms of behavioral performance as well as specific cellular and molecular endpoints that are associated with learning and memory.

The proposed measures of behavioral performance, which were also used to induce Arc expression, involved a fear conditioning paradigm with 2 versions: one that required the hippocampus (context version) and one that did not require the hippocampus (cued version). The version that required the hippocampus consisted of two types of behavioral paradigms. The first involved no tone shock pairing (-/-) and represented the ability of an animal to recognize an environment previously encountered. Animals that recognized that environment would explore it less, a behavior that is referred to as spatial habituation learning. The second paradigm involved tone shock pairing (+/+) and represented a Pavlovian type of response; that is, animals received a mild shock the first day, and when subsequently placed in the same environment, they would freeze more if they remembered having received an adverse stimulus in that environment the day before. For each version used, thirty minutes after the end of the final testing session on day 2, tissues were collected and prepared for microscopic analyses.

RESULTS:
Investigators completed all analyses related to behavior, neurogenesis, Arc protein expression, and measures of the endogenous inflammatory cells in the brain, the microglia. These endpoints were assessed after whole body irradiation with either 0, 0.25 Gy, 0.5 Gy or 1.0 Gy of 56Fe. All animals underwent cognitive testing 3 months after irradiation using a fear conditioning training- and testing-paradigm. The three-month time point was selected because that time has been previously used to show cognitive deficits after photon or HZE irradiation, as well as changes in Arc expression. Investigators quantified the effects of whole body 56Fe irradiation (600 MeV, 0.5 or 1 Gy) on hippocampus-dependent and hippocampus-independent cognitive performance and determined if those effects were associated with changes in Arc expression in the enclosed and free blades of the dentate gyrus. Whole body 56Fe irradiation impacted contextual but not cued fear freezing and the percentage of Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In mice tested for contextual freezing, there was a correlation between Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In addition, in mice irradiated with 0.5 Gy, contextual freezing in the absence of aversive stimuli correlated with the percentage of Arc-positive cells in the enclosed blade. In mice tested for cued freezing, there was no correlation between Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In contrast, cued freezing in the presence or absence of aversive stimuli correlated with Arc-positive cells in the free blade. These data indicate that there are blade dependent effects after particulate irradiation. More studies are required to address the physiologic significance of such findings.

One of the microenvironmental factors that may influence how irradiation affects cognition is inflammation. Investigators addressed this issue by irradiating animals deficient in a specific chemokine receptor: chemokine receptor-2 (CCR2). CCR2 mediates the recruitment of infiltrating and resident microglia to sites of CNS inflammation, and is upregulated by 56Fe irradiation. CCR2 knock out (KO) and wild-type mice were used to compare effects of 56Fe radiation (600 MeV, 0, 0.25 Gy) on hippocampal function using contextual fear conditioning involving tone shock pairing during training (+/+) and exposure to the same environment without tone shock pairings (-/-). In the -/- condition, irradiation increased freezing and hippocampal Arc protein levels in WT but not CCR2 KO mice, suggesting that a lack of CCR2 was associated with a poorer outcome. In contrast, in the +/+ condition, irradiation reduced freezing but there was no genotype difference. There were no significant correlations between the number of Arc-positive cells in the dentate gyrus and freezing in either genotype but in CCR2 KO mice, there was a trend towards a negative correlation between freezing and Arc-positive cells in the enclosed and free blades. In the +/+ condition, BrdU alone and BrdU/NeuN were reduced in the free blade but not the enclosed blade of CCR2 KO. CCR2 status had no influence on total numbers of newly born activated microglia before or after irradiation, indicating that other mechanisms are involved in the genotype-dependent radiation response.

The investigators’ standard markers of neurogenesis, microglia, and the immediate early gene Arc have been shown to be good predictors of radiation response after relatively high doses of photons or heavy ions. However, in their current studies they were not particularly responsive to low dose irradiation with iron ions. Given those findings they wanted to look for other markers that might track with cognition and provide predictive value after low dose exposures. The formation of long-term memory relies on modulation of synaptic connections in response to neuronal input. This plasticity requires coordinated activity-dependent synthesis of specific mRNAs and proteins that facilitate molecular and structural changes at the synapse. Dendritic spines are bulbous membrane projections of mixed morphology, that form the postsynaptic specializations of the vast majority of excitatory synapses in the central nervous system (CNS) and their structure and density are important factors in synaptic function. Spine morphology can predict both spine stability and synaptic strength, and changes in dendritic spine density or structural reorganization of spines is thought to be important for cognitive processes such as learning and memory.

In their new study of dendritic spines, investigators irradiated young adult male C57BL6 mice with 0 or 0.5 Gy (whole body) of 56Fe ions. Within each radiation treatment group, animals were randomly assigned into cohorts that received cognitive testing using a no shock/no tone paradigm or no cognitive testing, i.e. caged controls. Half of the mice from each specific treatment group were used for the determination of dendritic spine density/morphology and the other half were used for measurement of Arc and other cellular markers. Dendritic spines were visualized using a well-established Golgi staining paradigm. In the CA1 and dentate gyrus of sham-irradiated mice, the behavioral testing enhanced the spine density as compared to behaviorally naïve mice. In contrast, behavioral testing did not affect spine density in irradiated mice. These intriguing data indicate that irradiated mice did not benefit from the environmental enrichment (i.e. behavioral testing) as sham-irradiated mice did.

Finally, investigators initiated and completed a mixed beam study to determine how the brain responds when it is confronted by two different types of irradiation. Mice either received a single whole body exposure of 1.0 Gy protons (n = 24), a single whole body dose of 0.05 Gy 56Fe (n = 24), a single whole body exposure of 1.0 Gy protons immediately before a single whole body dose of 0.5 Gy 56Fe (n = 24) or no irradiation (n =24). Two months following irradiation, all animals receives a daily i.p. injection of bromodeoxyuridine (100 mg/kg) for 7 days, and 1 month later mice were either cognitively tested for novel object recognition or acted as caged controls. Thirty minutes after the onset of the last session of the cognitive testing, animals were sacrificed and their brains bisected into the two hemispheres and then frozen. Tissues were either analyzed for cellular markers of neurogenesis, the immediate early gene Arc, or for molecular/biochemical assays for markers of inflammation/oxidative stress. No cellular, molecular, or biochemical changes were observed after either of the single doses or the combined treatment. This suggests either that the low doses used did not induce any significant alterations, or the specific endpoints chosen for study were not sensitive to minor changes induced by the relatively low doses used.

The data highlights the complexity of assessing how low doses of 56Fe affect hippocampal function. Those data suggest that even a relatively low dose of 56Fe can induce behavioral changes that involve the hippocampus, but the cellular/molecular/biochemical mechanisms responsible are still not yet known.

experiment_title: Viral Reactivation
parameter_html:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), saliva
Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1), saliva
Herpes simplex virus (HSV), saliva
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pierson, DuanePrincipal Investigator: Konstantinova, IrinaCo-Investigator: Stowe, Raymond
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Seven or more herpesviruses commonly establish infections in humans. Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex type-2 (HSV-2), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) and human herpesvirus-7 (HHV-7) are some examples of the double stranded DNA viruses that may establish a life-long latent infection in a host organism. Latent viruses are subject to intermittent reactivation. For example, replication of the reactivated herpesvirus genome may give rise to both infectious and noninfectious (defective) virus particles. Since one or more of the herpesviruses infects nearly 100% of the adult population, they are prime candidates for studying the effects of space flight on latent viral reactivation in astronauts.

Latent virus reactivation may be an important threat to crew health during extended space missions where crewmembers live and work in a closed environment for 3 months or more. Exposure to infectious agents such as bacteria, fungi, viruses and parasites can be controlled by preflight quarantine as opposed to latent virus reactivation, an infection that originates inside the host organism. The establishment of viral latency and the subsequent reactivation are not well understood, but changes in the immune system are known to increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding. Increasing scientific data indicates that the physical and psychological stressors associated with space flight cause alterations in the human immune response. Therefore, the objectives of this experiment were to evaluate the effects of long-duration habitation in space on latent virus reactivation, indicative of perturbations to the intricate host-parasite relationships. In this experiment, scientists tested the hypothesis that stressors associated with space flight will alter the host-parasite relationship in crewmembers inhabiting the Mir space station during extended stays, increasing both the incidence and the duration of herpesvirus reactivation and shedding.

APPROACH:
The approach to this experiment was to assess viral reactivation by the collection of serum and saliva samples. The original plan for sample collection included both the Mir 18 and 19 crew. The inflight and postflight sampling sessions on Mir 18 were not completed due to a cancellation of this experiment. Preflight saliva samples were obtained, but no blood samples were collected. However, contingency saliva sampling was performed on one crewmember during the flight. Preflight, inflight, and postflight saliva samples were collected from two crewmembers of the Mir 19 mission. Detection of the herpesvirus reactivation and shedding was conducted by saliva sample collection, DNA extraction from saliva, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification of herpesvirus DNA, and analysis of PCR products by gel electrophoresis.

DNA extraction from saliva
Saliva was collected and transferred to microcentrifuge tubes for extraction. DNA was extracted using a modification of the RNAzol method. Genomic/viral DNA was isolated simultaneously by adding 0.75 ml of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 6.6) RNAzol solution to 250 microliters saliva and briefly vortexing. After incubating on ice for 15 minutes, the tubes were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 12,000 x g and stored at -20 degrees Celsius overnight. The tubes were then centrifuged for 30 minutes at 16,000 x g and the supernatant removed. The DNA was then washed once with 7% ethanol and resuspended in 20 microliters DEPC-treated water. The suitability of extraction was evaluated by gel electrophoresis without nucleic acid quantitation.

PCR Amplification of Herpesvirus DNA
The oligonucleotide primers selected for this investigation amplified a highly conserved region of the DNA polymerase gene from the herpesvirus group. These primers allowed amplification of DNA to be directed to selected nucleotide fragments of the DNA polymerase genes for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV and EBV . DNA was amplified in a total volume of 25 ml or a reaction mixture consisting of 50 mM KCl, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.3), 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.01% gelatin, 5% dimethylsulfoxide, 200 micromolar deoxynucleoside triphosphates, 20 pmol of each oligonucleotide primer, 0.625 U Taq polymerase, and 2 ml purified DNA solution. The reactions were performed in an automated thermocycler. The cycle, repeated 40 times, consisted of 15 seconds of denaturation at 96 degrees Celsius, 15 seconds of annealing at 60 degrees Celsius, and 15 seconds of elongation at 72 degrees Celsius. All samples were run with simultaneous positive control and negative (reagent) control. Measures to control contamination included the use of latex gloves, aerosol-resistant pipette tips, and two separate laboratories for preamplification and postamplification procedures.

Analysis of PCR Products
Ten microliters of the reaction mixture was run on a 2% Nusieve GTG agarose gel containing 1 microgram of ethidium bromide per ml in 1x TBE buffer. The gels were then placed under UV light for visualization of the amplified products and photographed.

Results:
The cancellation of this experiment on Mir 18 resulted in a limited sample collection. Inflight and postflight samples were not collected from the Mir 18 crewmembers. Preflight samples were collected from three crewmembers and five inflight samples were collected from one crewmember as contingency samples. Therefore, the only samples analyzed were those collected from the crewmember that participated in the inflight collection. The samples collected from the other crewmembers are archived for future analysis. All of the preflight samples were negative for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. However, two of the five inflight samples were positive for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. Since these data were very limited, no conclusions were made concerning the effects of microgravity on the host-parasite relationship. However, the methodology and sample handling logistics were successful.

Two cosmonauts, both backup crewmembers for Mir 18, participated in the viral reactivation study on the Mir 19 mission. Thus, the preflight saliva specimens collected to establish baseline shedding patterns were collected prior to the Mir 18 mission. Saliva specimens were collected before, during, and after the flight. The samples were analyzed for the presence of Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV 1) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). All specimens were negative for HSV 1. Unfortunately, preflight saliva specimens were insufficient in number and frequency to establish a sound baseline for either crewmember. However, preflight shedding of EBV in the saliva was detected in over half of the total specimens. EBV DNA were detected in the saliva of crewmember A before, during, and after the flight. At least six episodes of shedding of EBV were observed during the mission. Inflight saliva specimens were collected beginning at about FD 25 and ending on FD 75. Shedding was also observed on R+14 and R+24. Crewmember B shedded EBV much less frequently during the mission than crewmember A. EBV DNA was observed in saliva from crewmember B on only two occasions during the mission. The conclusions made from this experiment were: (1) PCR methodology was capable of detecting latent viral DNA in saliva specimens collected and stored on the ground and on Mir, (2) neither crewmember appeared to be shedding HSV 1, (3) both crewmembers shed EBV before, during and after the mission, (4) shedding patterns of EBV of the two crewmembers were highly different during the inflight phase, (5) the technical feasibility of the approach was clearly demonstrated. The low number of subjects prevented any major conclusions from being drawn related to host-parasite relationships during space flight.
