Therefore, the objectives of this experiment were to evaluate the effects of long-duration habitation in space on latent virus reactivation, indicative of perturbations to the intricate host-parasite relationships. In this experiment, scientists tested the hypothesis that stressors associated with space flight will alter the host-parasite relationship in crewmembers inhabiting the Mir space station during extended stays, increasing both the incidence and the duration of herpesvirus reactivation and shedding.

APPROACH:
The approach to this experiment was to assess viral reactivation by the collection of serum and saliva samples. The original plan for sample collection included both the Mir 18 and 19 crew. The inflight and postflight sampling sessions on Mir 18 were not completed due to a cancellation of this experiment. Preflight saliva samples were obtained, but no blood samples were collected. However, contingency saliva sampling was performed on one crewmember during the flight. Preflight, inflight, and postflight saliva samples were collected from two crewmembers of the Mir 19 mission. Detection of the herpesvirus reactivation and shedding was conducted by saliva sample collection, DNA extraction from saliva, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification of herpesvirus DNA, and analysis of PCR products by gel electrophoresis.

DNA extraction from saliva
Saliva was collected and transferred to microcentrifuge tubes for extraction. DNA was extracted using a modification of the RNAzol method. Genomic/viral DNA was isolated simultaneously by adding 0.75 ml of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 6.6) RNAzol solution to 250 microliters saliva and briefly vortexing. After incubating on ice for 15 minutes, the tubes were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 12,000 x g and stored at -20 degrees Celsius overnight. The tubes were then centrifuged for 30 minutes at 16,000 x g and the supernatant removed. The DNA was then washed once with 7% ethanol and resuspended in 20 microliters DEPC-treated water. The suitability of extraction was evaluated by gel electrophoresis without nucleic acid quantitation.

PCR Amplification of Herpesvirus DNA
The oligonucleotide primers selected for this investigation amplified a highly conserved region of the DNA polymerase gene from the herpesvirus group. These primers allowed amplification of DNA to be directed to selected nucleotide fragments of the DNA polymerase genes for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV and EBV . DNA was amplified in a total volume of 25 ml or a reaction mixture consisting of 50 mM KCl, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.3), 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.01% gelatin, 5% dimethylsulfoxide, 200 micromolar deoxynucleoside triphosphates, 20 pmol of each oligonucleotide primer, 0.625 U Taq polymerase, and 2 ml purified DNA solution. The reactions were performed in an automated thermocycler. The cycle, repeated 40 times, consisted of 15 seconds of denaturation at 96 degrees Celsius, 15 seconds of annealing at 60 degrees Celsius, and 15 seconds of elongation at 72 degrees Celsius. All samples were run with simultaneous positive control and negative (reagent) control. Measures to control contamination included the use of latex gloves, aerosol-resistant pipette tips, and two separate laboratories for preamplification and postamplification procedures.

Analysis of PCR Products
Ten microliters of the reaction mixture was run on a 2% Nusieve GTG agarose gel containing 1 microgram of ethidium bromide per ml in 1x TBE buffer. The gels were then placed under UV light for visualization of the amplified products and photographed.

Results:
The cancellation of this experiment on Mir 18 resulted in a limited sample collection. Inflight and postflight samples were not collected from the Mir 18 crewmembers. Preflight samples were collected from three crewmembers and five inflight samples were collected from one crewmember as contingency samples. Therefore, the only samples analyzed were those collected from the crewmember that participated in the inflight collection. The samples collected from the other crewmembers are archived for future analysis. All of the preflight samples were negative for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. However, two of the five inflight samples were positive for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. Since these data were very limited, no conclusions were made concerning the effects of microgravity on the host-parasite relationship. However, the methodology and sample handling logistics were successful.

Two cosmonauts, both backup crewmembers for Mir 18, participated in the viral reactivation study on the Mir 19 mission. Thus, the preflight saliva specimens collected to establish baseline shedding patterns were collected prior to the Mir 18 mission. Saliva specimens were collected before, during, and after the flight. The samples were analyzed for the presence of Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV 1) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). All specimens were negative for HSV 1. Unfortunately, preflight saliva specimens were insufficient in number and frequency to establish a sound baseline for either crewmember. However, preflight shedding of EBV in the saliva was detected in over half of the total specimens. EBV DNA were detected in the saliva of crewmember A before, during, and after the flight. At least six episodes of shedding of EBV were observed during the mission. Inflight saliva specimens were collected beginning at about FD 25 and ending on FD 75. Shedding was also observed on R+14 and R+24. Crewmember B shedded EBV much less frequently during the mission than crewmember A. EBV DNA was observed in saliva from crewmember B on only two occasions during the mission. The conclusions made from this experiment were: (1) PCR methodology was capable of detecting latent viral DNA in saliva specimens collected and stored on the ground and on Mir, (2) neither crewmember appeared to be shedding HSV 1, (3) both crewmembers shed EBV before, during and after the mission, (4) shedding patterns of EBV of the two crewmembers were highly different during the inflight phase, (5) the technical feasibility of the approach was clearly demonstrated. The low number of subjects prevented any major conclusions from being drawn related to host-parasite relationships during space flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Classical Microbial Risk Assessment focuses on key components such as hazard identification and characterization, dose-response, and exposure. Thus, the determination of risk from infectious disease during long-duration missions is composed of several factors including the concentration and the characteristics of the infectious agent. Therefore, a thorough knowledge of the microorganisms on board a spacecraft is essential in mitigating infectious disease risk to the crew. While preventive measures are taken to minimize the transfer of potential pathogens to spacecraft, several medically significant organisms have been isolated from both the Mir and International Space Station (ISS). Historically, the method for isolation and identification of microorganisms from spacecraft environmental samples depended upon their growth on culture media. While extensive, culture media may still only isolate a small percentage of the viable bacteria from a consortium. Current operational monitoring care of ISS surface, air, and potable water using culture-based techniques to date has shown 1) relatively low microbial concentrations, 2) common environmental isolates, 3) several opportunistic pathogens, 4) occasional spike in microbial concentration level, often associated with unexpected moisture on surfaces, and 5) occasional fluctuation in potable water that could be associated with biofilm buildup.

The Surface, Water, and Air Biocharacterization (SWAB) Flight Experiment was designed with the general aim of developing advanced collection and analysis techniques to better understand the microbial ecology and potential health risks in spacecraft, specifically focusing on the application of molecular identification techniques. The specific aims of this experiment were:

  • Collection of preflight and in-flight surface, air and water samples using methods that would allow for long-term storage of samples
  • Extraction of DNA from environmental samples that may be used to perform molecular analyses
  • Analysis of samples using Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE)
  • Development of real-time PCR assays to detect specific molecular targets for specific medically significant organisms

    APPROACH:
    Air, surface and water samples were collected on board the ISS, approximately 48 hours before docked operations with all launch vehicles. Collection of all samples into a liquid simplified handling and enabled advanced analysis. To preserve a representative sample for microbial quantification, the samples were refrigerated after collection and destowed as soon as possible from the returning space shuttle.

    Surface samples were taken at a variety of locations, including air supply surfaces, food locker surfaces, and water dispenser surfaces. A surface sampling tube containing a Dacron swab and phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) was removed from the SWAB kit. The swab was used to swab a 25 cm squared surface area. The swab was then returned to the vial and marked with the date and location where the sample was collected using a Sharpie marker. Upon return to Earth, the swab and buffer were sonicated to facilitate microbial detachment into the liquid.

    Potable water samples were collected directly into 1 liter Teflon bags currently approved for in-flight use. ISS water sampling sites included the US Potable Water Dispenser (PWD) that distributes water for potable use. Surface samples were collected using a modified damp swab and liquid vial produced by Charm Sciences. Air samples were collected using gelatin filters incorporated into the Sartorius MD 8 Air Port System.

    Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE):
    DNA samples were analyzed for relative concentration and identity of ribosomal sequences using a combination of PCR, Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE), and 16S ribosomal analysis for identification. 16S-ribosomal DNA was extracted from the consortium and amplified using a universal primer set. This amplified mixture of various ribosomal sequences was separated using DGGE to determine the number of bacterial species present in a sample. The isolated DNA was eluted from the gels and sequenced for identification. Identification was determined by comparison of the sequences with the National Center for Biotechnology Information database.

    Real Time PCR:
    All samples except potable water were analyzed for specific fungal species using PCR primers for medically significant or indicative fungi, including Aspergillus fumigates and Stachybotrys chartarum. A relative moldiness index (RMI) multiplex technique developed by the Environmental Protection Agency was also utilized to provide a thorough fungal characterization. Samples were also analyzed for the presence of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV).

    Whole Genome Analysis:
    ISS water samples were analyzed by whole genome sequencing performed at the University of Houston Institute for Molecular Design using technology developed by Illumina, Inc.

    RESULTS:
    Preflight sampling was completed for air, surface, and water samples. In-flight sample collection was completed for a total of eight air, surface, and water sample collection sessions. In-flight hardware performed well, and the surface sampling device received positive feedback from the crew for its ease of use.

    Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis (DGGE)
    The DGGE technique was found to be less sensitive than culture-based methods. One million cells need to be present to detect a PCR band on an agarose gel. In addition, DGGE has a greater incidence of Gram-negative bacteria on surface samples when compared to culture methods. Subsequent experiments suggested that primer bias or contamination was not the cause.

    Real Time PCR
    To determine the utility of QPCR for monitoring and the potential presence of two toxigenic fungi, preflight and in flight samples were analyzed using QPCR analysis developed for the detection of Aspergillus fumigates and Stachybotrys chartarum at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. These fungi were not detected. The use of QPCR was further investigated in a collaborative effort with colleagues from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). In this study, dust from four ISS vacuum bags and two HEPA filters used from 2007 to 2009 were returned to the ground for QPCR-based molecular analysis. An environmental relative moldiness index (ERMI) multiplex technique developed by the EPA was also utilized to provide a thorough fungal characterization. The most common species measured was P. chrysogenum followed by Aureobasidium pullulans. Of the 36 species in the standard ERMI analysis, 17 were detected at some concentration. Results were comparable to what would be found in a home.

    Finally, QPCR technology was tested by analyzing 336 environmental samples (both pre- and in flight) from spacecraft surfaces (266), water (5) and air (70) for the presence of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV). These latent viruses may be carried asymptomatically by the crew and have the potential to be “reactivated” into live, infectious viruses. This reactivation has been associated with stress and suppressed immune function. Analyses revealed no CMV in any samples. VZV was detected in 6 air samples and 5 surface samples. EBV was detected in 2 air samples and 10 surface samples.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Lee, StuartCo-Investigator: Platts, StevenCo-Investigator: Soller, Babs
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reduced exercise capacity, orthostatic tolerance, and plasma volume are common observances following space flight and bed rest. The Johnson Space Center Cardiovascular Laboratory (CVL) investigated the relationship between orthostatic hypotension and plasma volume by pharmacologically inducing hypovolemia in normal subjects. The Exercise Physiology Laboratory (EXL) sought to extend this information to understanding the factors involved in decreased exercise capacity. Following orthostatic testing in normal and hypovolemic conditions, a subset of the subjects recruited performed a graded cycle exercise test to volitional fatigue to determine peak oxygen consumption (VO2pk).

The CVL was responsible for the overall administration of the project, and the EXL was responsible for the additional measurements and analyses. Specifically, the CVL recruited and instructed subjects, scheduled the testing, and was responsible for measurement of plasma/blood volume and orthostatic tolerance. The EXL was responsible for administering the test of exercise capacity using a cycle ergometer protocol similar to that used for International Space Station (ISS) and Space Shuttle (STS) astronauts. In addition to the ISS and Flight Analog Project standard measures during the cycle ergometer test, the CVL obtained echocardiographic measures of cardiac function and plasma catecholamines, and the EXL measured blood lactate concentrations and peripheral muscle metabolism by near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS).

Oxygen consumption, heart rate, rating of perceived exertion, and blood pressure were measured per standard laboratory protocols. Additionally, echocardiographic measures of stroke volume, systolic and diastolic function, blood lactate, plasma catecholamines, and peripheral muscle metabolism by NIRS was measured. Data from these testing sessions assist in understanding the factors associated with reduced exercise capacity after space flight; served as a basis of comparison for responses to similar tests after space flight and bed rest; and aided in the continued development of NIRS as a non-invasive metabolic measurement system for space flight and extravehicular activities.

The primary purpose of this study was to determine the specific effects of decreased plasma volume, independent of deconditioning, on aerobic exercise capacity (VO2pk), cardiac function, and peripheral muscle metabolism. The investigators also sought to collect pilot data regarding two pharmacological interventions that are being considered for the treatment of post-flight orthostatic hypotension that may similarly protect VO2pk. The secondary purpose of this project was to validate the use of a National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) funded sensor as a surrogate measure of oxygen consumption in an analogue of space flight and as non-invasive method to determine anaerobic threshold.

Specific Aims were:

(1) To determine whether central cardiac and peripheral skeletal indices of exercise performance are related to reduced VO2pk and anaerobic threshold in subjects whose plasma volume is reduced.

(2) To determine whether near infrared spectroscopy can be used to non-invasively, unobtrusively measure oxygen consumption during cycle ergometer exercise in normal and hypovolemic conditions.

APPROACH:
Subjects gave written informed consent prior to participation. Twelve healthy subjects (8 men and 4 women), passed a modified Air Force Class III physical examination, and volunteered to participate in this study. Subjects received written and verbal explanations of the testing procedures and provided written documentation of informed consent prior to participation. Study protocols and procedures were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects.

Following a familiarization session, subjects participated in testing in both the normovolemic and hypovolemic conditions in cross-over design. For the seven days prior to the normovolemia testing day, subjects were encouraged to drink fluids ad libitum and consume a normal diet supplemented with 2 g of sodium each day. To induce hypovolemia, subjects received a single dose of furosemide and consumed a low salt diet provided by the investigators. The order of the conditions was not randomly assigned initially due to the constraints of a companion study, but the investigators attempted to balance the order of the test conditions. Seven of the 12 subjects completed testing in the normovolemic condition first.

Hypovolemia

Subjects received a single dose of furosemide through a catheter in an antecubital vein. Blood pressure and urine output were monitored during and after the infusion until they had stabilized, typically one to two hours. Following the infusion, the catheter was removed and subjects consumed a controlled, low-sodium, caffeine-free diet for 30 hours.

The diet was developed by dieticians at Memorial Hermann Hospital General Clinical Research Center (Houston, TX), and the food was prepared by the Space Food Systems Laboratory at Johnson Space Center. The diet was limited to 600 calories and 250 mg sodium per day. Subjects were allowed to drink sodium-free bottled water ad libitum.

Plasma Volume

Plasma volume was measured using the carbon monoxide rebreathing technique, as previously described. In short, an intravenous catheter was inserted into an antecubital vein. After 20 minutes of supine rest, a 3 mL baseline blood sample was collected. Thereafter, subjects breathed 100% oxygen for two minutes using a closed breathing circuit with a two-way non-rebreathing valve. Sixty mL of carbon monoxide were then added to the system and rebreathed for 10 minutes, followed by the collections of a second blood sample.

Graded Exercise Test

Subjects reported to the laboratory in comfortable exercise clothes which allowed access to the chest for echocardiographic measures and 12-lead ECG and to the thigh for near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measurements. Subjects performed the exercise test in the upright posture to simulate orthostatic characteristics of normal gravity exercise following space flight exposure. Prior to the start of the test, subjects were instrumented with electrodes for the monitoring of 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and heart rate. Also, a small non-invasive NIRS sensor was adhered to the skin overlying the mid-point of vastus lateralis, and a catheter was inserted into the antecubital vein by a registered nurse to obtain resting, exercise, and immediate post-exercise blood samples.

During the cycle ergometer test, heart rate, metabolic rate, and NIRS were continuously measured. Stroke volume and cardiac output were measured halfway through each stage. Blood pressure, Rating of Perceive Exertion (Borg Scale, 6-20), and blood lactate were obtained near the end of each stage. Blood also was drawn from the catheter during exercise to determine plasma catecholamines, blood glucose, serum electrolytes, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and carboxy-hemoglobin at exercise stages corresponding to approximately 75% of VO2pk, estimated from RPE reported in the previous exercise stage. Based upon data previously collected in the investigator’s laboratory using the same testing protocol, the investigators estimated that the 75% VO2pk exercise stage would correspond to the exercise stage following that which a subject reported a RPE of 11 or greater. The exercise stage in which blood was drawn was determined in the first exercise test irrespective of whether the subject was normo- or hypovolemic.

RESULTS:
The primary finding of this study was that plasma volume loss to levels similar to those reported following short-duration Space Shuttle missions does not result in a decrease in VO2pk as great as that previously observed following space flight. In this study, VO2pk during a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer, using a protocol similar to that used in previous space flight investigation conducted at JSC, was eight percent lower during pharmacologically-induced hypovolemia, but this is only one half to one third that which has been reported after Space Shuttle missions. Additionally, submaximal stroke volume and cardiac output were lower during hypovolemia, as has been observed after space flight, but other symptoms of deconditioning such as elevated submaximal heart rate, respiratory exchange, and ventilation rate, were not evident.

Based upon data previously collected in the investigator’s laboratory using the same testing protocol, the investigators estimated that the 75% VO2pk exercise stage would correspond to the exercise stage following that which a subject reported a RPE of 11 or greater. The exercise stage in which blood was drawn was determined in the first exercise test irrespective of whether the subject was normo- or hypovolemic.

RESULTS:
The primary finding of this study was that plasma volume loss to levels similar to those reported following short-duration Space Shuttle missions does not result in a decrease in VO2pk as great as that previously observed following space flight. In this study, VO2pk during a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer, using a protocol similar to that used in previous space flight investigation conducted at JSC, was eight percent lower during pharmacologically-induced hypovolemia, but this is only one half to one third that which has been reported after Space Shuttle missions. Additionally, submaximal stroke volume and cardiac output were lower during hypovolemia, as has been observed after space flight, but other symptoms of deconditioning such as elevated submaximal heart rate, respiratory exchange, and ventilation rate, were not evident.

experiment_title: Fungal Pathogenesis, Tumorigenesis, and Effects on Host Immunity in Space (FIT)
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Bhattacharya, SharmilaCo-Investigator: Kimbrell, D.
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The overall goal of the FIT experiment was to gain further insight into immune system function after exposure to the space flight environment, and to study the cellular and molecular biological responses of the immune system to post-flight microbial infections.

APPRAOCH:

The payload was carried in a vented foam tray and located in a middeck locker. The FIT payload consisted of 1) ten vented FIT Fly Kits (one fly cassette containing a food tray housed in a European Space Agency (ESA) vented Type 1 Container per kit, 2) one FIT Fungus Kit (two fungus tubes (10 ml) that are housed in an ESA vented Type 1 Container, 3) one RAM Kit (one Passive Radiation Dosimeter stored in an ESA vented Type 1 Container), 4) one Hobo data logger, and 5) five Platform Kits (one Food Tray Change Out Platform carrying one filled food tray per kit).

RESULTS:

There were several observed changes in the innate immune function of Drosophila melanogaster after spaceflight. Larval phagocytosis efficiency was reduced after flight compared to ground controls. The number of actively phagocytosing hemocytes was lower in flight compared to ground, and the capacity of phagocytosing cells to internalize bacteria, was also reduced after space flight. Hemocyte counts per larva, and the size of larvae, was reduced in space-reared larvae compared to ground controls. While flight-reared adult flies inoculated post-flight with live E. coli were able to clear the bacterial infection fairly efficiently, the pattern of gene expression changes in response to infection were different between space flown adults and the analogous ground control samples.

Humoral immunity genes were downregulated in larvae after spaceflight. Several genes related to immunity were differentially expressed in space-reared adult flies and larvae as shown by microarray. Gene expression data were also matched to correlate with the observed phenotypes of reduced phagocytosis function and reduced plasmatocyte count in larvae.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Mironneau, ChantalCo-Investigator: Mironneau, J.Co-Investigator: Neuilly, G.Co-Investigator: Rakotoarisoa, L.Co-Investigator: Sayet- Colombet, L.
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The cardiovascular system adapts successfully to upper body fluid shifts by increasing heart rate, blood pressure and total peripheral vascular resistance and by decreasing venous pressure. These adaptive responses to fluid shift in spaceflight leads to a severe increase in heart rate and low blood pressure upon return to Earth. There have been few studies examining microgravity's effect on contractile properties of smooth muscles and the cellular and molecular alterations that control vascular tone. The objectives of this experiment were to look at changes in contractile response to norepinephrine of the vena cava, especially the alpha 1B adrenoreceptors and to determine the mechanism by which the adrenoreceptors are altered.

Approach:

Vena cava were removed from flight rats and cut into longitudinal strips. Specific binding to adrenoceptors was measured by incubating the strips in various concentrations of (3H) prazosin and determining radioactivity after dissolving strips in NaOH. Isometric contraction was measured in an experimental chamber using circular strips taken from the venae cavae. The maximum contractile response was determined using 30 micromolar norepinephrine. All other contractions were expressed as a percentage of maximal contraction. The inhibition of contractile response due to the binding of prazosin was also determined.

Results:

A decrease in contractile strength in response to norepinephrine was found in flight rats. (3H) prazosin binding affinity was reduced, indicating a reduction in specific affinity to alpha 1 adrenoreceptors. These data indicate that the reduction in contractile strength is due to a decrease in sensitivity of adrenoreceptors rather than a decrease in the number of adrenoreceptors. Ground control studies show a similar decrease in sensitivity through sustained activation of protein kinase C. This effect was not seen in the presence of an inhibitor of protein kinase C. This implies that desensitation of adrenoreceptors due to microgravity may be dependent on increased protein kinase C activity.

experiment_title: (NSCORT) for Advanced Life Support at Purdue/Howard/AAMU - Integrated Systems Group
parameter_html:
Decision making
Water subsystem
investigators: Principal Investigator: Mitchell, Cary
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Throughout the life of ALS NASA Specialized Center of Research and Training (NSCORT), the systems group researchers matured from learning and exploratory mode, which can be mainly characterized by proof-of-concept studies to build a viable toolbox of systems analysis methodologies suitable for ALS analysis, e.g. SimOpt (SIMulation based OPTimization), Markov Theory and Model Predictive Control, towards well-structured and coordinated efforts to improve their readiness level for repeated use in answering questions that matters to NASA and ALS community at large.

As systems group was undergoing through its voyage within ALS NSCORT, the systems group’s analysis and modeling scope has been expanded to all ALS technologies and to adopt lifecycle management view to study 15-20 year Mars Base ALS system evolution which recognizes the fact that Mars Base ALS system will not stay as it was deployed at the very first mission. Unfortunately, the plans and resources had to be revised per early termination notice as NASA was undergoing through major re-organization and re-prioritization to maximize the return on NASA’s investment in ALS NSCORT by focusing on completing the matured on going tasks and retiring the new initiatives such as, the proof-of-concept study that has been initiated in collaboration with Envision Center at Purdue University on visualizing the evolution of Mars Base and its ALS system.

A simulation was developed to assist decision-making in choosing control policies in a closed environment. This closed environment consists of a simplified representation of the water subsystem based on the documentation by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The water requirement (consumption) and generation are based on the crewmembers’ demographics, activity schedules as well as intensity of each activity. The overall goal of this project was to develop methodologies to ensure crewmembers survive while on space missions.

APPROACH:
The health of this system is the result of the intricate interaction between the crewmembers as well as the water subsystem. The primary measure of the health of the system is the “state” representation of the system. This representation is a conglomeration of various hourly assessments of different aspects of the system. These aspects include the deterministic as well as the stochastic nature of the system. Due to the potentially vast number of possible states in the entire state space, state reduction techniques as well as assessments for infeasible states are applied for state reduction. A reward system is designed for allocating reward/penalty values to system states that satisfy predetermined conditions. Due to the strong stochastic characteristics and the “memoryless” property of the system, the transition of system state can be modeled as a Markov process.

Due to the incomplete knowledge of the new system (that is not yet in existence) and its dynamics, process-control strategies need to be developed in such a way that they are comprehensive enough to manage the system given any kind of system behavior, anticipated or otherwise. However, before strategies can be developed, system states need to be captured. In order to explore the possible system states, a Controlled Random Walk (CRW) algorithm is developed to visit more system states in less amount of time, compared to traditional techniques such as the Pure Random Walk and the Round Robin Walk.

Transition probabilities are obtained through the simulation of the Markovian model. Capturing “true” state transition probabilities has been a challenge to researchers. In this research, a methodology is developed to minimize the number of data points (or simulation hours) while obtaining the transition probabilities that are closest to the system’s steady state probabilities by observing the percentage increase of states visits as well as probabilities convergence based on discrete consecutive time periods. The Kullback-Leibler Divergence distance is used as the foundation of the measurement. It is then modified in order to be used in this research study. A reference index is also defined based on this measure to study the “distance” between each probability distribution from the index. These probabilities, together with the reward values are formulated into appropriate mathematical representation and are solved by applying the Policy Iteration (PI) algorithm. The outcome from PI is an indication of the “best” policy to be applied when the system is in a given state.

RESULTS:
The simulation was done in three stages: Data Collection/State space exploration, System Evaluation with Dynamic Policy and System Evaluation with Fixed Policy. The Data Collection stage was performed through 800,000 ticks (simulation hours) of simulation time. Every set of 100,000 ticks consists of 5 sets of 20,000 ticks, each with a re-initialized starting condition. This is done to prevent the system from being “stuck” in a state or a loop of states. The proposed Controlled Random Walk technique is used during the data collection. Best policies are obtained through every set of 100,000 ticks, yielding eight sets of best policies. Every set of best policies are applied to a test system for evaluation. Results show that outcomes from applying these best policies are statistically better than using fixed policies, or using random policies.

As mentioned above, comprehensive process-control strategies are to be developed for various system states. The system might visit certain states that have not been visited before during data collection. These states will not have a corresponding “best” policy as they are “new” to the control system. In order to counter that problem, machine-learning technique is used. The See 5.0 algorithm (previously ID3) is used to generate a complete decision tree based on every set of best policies obtained from the PI. With the outcome from the See 5.0 algorithm, an action is available for use in the system given any state that the system visits. The outcomes of See 5.0 algorithm are evaluated against the outcomes from the PI using an independent test system. Results from non-parametric tests show that there is no statistical difference between the two, indicating that while policies obtained from See 5.0 perform as good as optimal policies from PI, See 5.0 also provides a complete decision tree, covering the entire state space.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Burke, ShawnCo-Investigator: Salas, EduardoCo-Investigator: Shuffler, Marissa
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The long-duration of space exploration missions and relative isolation makes it imperative that teams have the leadership capacity to address the temporal dynamics of diversity and the rifts that can occur. Leadership has been shown to be a critical component of team effectiveness and adaptation. However, leadership may be even more important within autonomous teams as it serves to create the shared behavior, affect, and cognition that allows teams to adapt and be effective within complex environments. The investigators argue that a particular form of leadership (i.e., shared or distributed leadership) is needed to produce highly functioning teams that are capable operating under varying degrees of autonomy. Shared leadership has been defined as a form of distributed leadership where the transference of leadership functions across team members occurs such that member strengths, knowledge, skills, attitudes, perspectives, and contacts are capitalized on as dictated by either internal or external demands. This study was designed to investigate the dynamic relationship between leaders and followers through the theoretical lens of shared or distributed leadership.

The aim of this research was to determine how shared leadership behaviors impact team processes and performance under long-duration and isolated contexts. Investigators were also interested in identifying the antecedents of shared leadership emergence, how shared leadership enables team autonomy, and the dynamic nature of shared leadership behaviors over the course of a team’s lifespan. Investigators used NASA's Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility and their laboratory to study these behaviors.

APPROACH:
Investigators administered a brief pre-mission survey to assess key individual difference characteristics that may impact the propensity to engage in collective leadership such as tapping personality, motivation to engage in leadership, and collective orientation. During interactions they delivered self report questionnaires after key events (i.e., autonomy changes). These included a sociometric measure of leadership and measures of teamwork, autonomy, interdependence, affect, and team effectiveness. Some of these measures were delivered after key events during the day while others were given at the end of the day after key events. Investigators recorded and analyzed the verbal output of the crew during the mission, focusing their analysis on the manifestation of leadership.

The primary focus of analog data collection was to examine team leadership in contexts whereby the team is operating within isolated, confined, and extreme environments (ICE). Analog data collection focused on the nature of team leadership over time as most of what is known regarding team leadership has occurred outside the context of space flight and similar ICE environments and has been static in nature. With regards to team leadership not only were the types of leader behavior investigated, but the degree to which these behaviors were distributed throughout the team and the relation to key team processes and outcomes were examined.

The goal of the laboratory investigation was to supplement data collection in the analog environment, where the focus was more on temporal components with respect to team leadership. Efforts with respect to this thrust were primarily geared toward data cleaning and analysis, along with the coding of a subset of the team’s communication for team leadership behaviors.

RESULTS:
During this study three thrusts were worked on that serve to examine the following research questions: 1) what leadership forms and behaviors best enable team performance in isolated, confined environments; 2) what is the role of time and contextual features in determining the type of team leadership needed; and 3) what are enablers to horizontal peer-to-peer leadership in these type of mission critical teams.

1) Longitudinal Data Collection in HERA:
Results from the HERA habitat indicated that while leadership was a mixture of hierarchical and shared, it was most often distributed through the crew, as seen in both the 14- and 30-day HERA campaigns. Most often, results indicated no single member engaging in leadership functions of a specific type such as action, transition, and interpersonal to the exclusion of other team members engaging in the specified group of leadership functions. Results also point to the functionality of sharing leadership. The sharing of transition phase leadership behaviors was significantly correlated with teamwork, cohesion, and effectiveness. Similar results were obtained with respect to the sharing of action phase leadership behaviors. Finally, the sharing of interpersonal leadership behaviors was significantly related to teamwork and cohesion.

2) Laboratory Investigation:
Results from the laboratory study tended to provide further support for what was seen in both the analog environment as well as the archival analysis. First, results suggested that team leadership behaviors were most often distributed throughout the team and not solely enacted by a single individual in the team. Second, incorporating the temporal component investigators studied how often different behaviors were performed across missions. Results indicated that over time, the variety of leadership behaviors increased as well as the density of those behaviors such as the degree to which leadership was distributed through the team or shared, with individuals, on average, having a higher density of leadership behaviors in later missions as compared to earlier missions.

Investigators also studied whether a more objective indicator, participant vocal intensity, might be an appropriate metric for recognizing the degree of shared leadership during particular team performance phases of interaction. Results indicated that the team’s vocal intensity was significantly, positively related to shared leadership. However, in the high autonomy condition, this relationship was only true for action oriented shared leadership density and not for transition leadership density. These results appear to indicate that talking more during more stressful time periods was likely to be associated with leadership behaviors. However, when autonomy was low (i.e., more structured), vocal intensity was predictive of both transition and action-oriented shared leadership. This has implications in particular in terms of the role of vocal intensity serving as a proxy for measuring leadership during high stress, action heavy performance episodes, but less so for planning phases of similar high stress teamwork contexts.

Finally, analyses were conducted to examine a set of enablers to shared leadership. Results indicated that at the individual level, motivation to lead was significantly predictive of individuals’ leadership behavior density, as perceived by their team members. This also held at the team level, where the average of team members’ motivation to lead was significantly predictive of shared leadership. However, this was only true for the sub-dimension of affective motivation to lead, implying that shared leadership in this situation may be driven by teams whose members truly enjoy taking on leadership roles. Results also suggested that personality may serve as an enabler to shared leadership.

Results demonstrated that at the team level, average extraversion and openness to experience were significant, positive predictors of shared team leadership, although agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability were not. This pattern did not significantly change across autonomy or distribution conditions. At the individual level, higher openness to experience was associated with higher individual leadership behavior density, implying that those who were more open to unknown or unfamiliar situations were more likely to step up and take on leadership responsibilities more often. Interestingly, common personality predictors of leadership were not significantly associated with individuals’ leadership behavior density ratings from their teammates, including emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness.

3) Analysis of Archival Data: A final thrust of the project was to use a bottoms-up approach to understanding team leadership in ICE. The investigators employed a mixture of historiometry and the critical incident technique to analyze archived accounts of teams operating in ICE contexts. In doing so, they focused on teams operating in the following ICE contexts – space flight, polar exploration, and long-duration, round the world, ocean sailboat racing. Using the above methodologies, 152 critical incidents pertaining to team leadership were extracted from 124 data sources consisting of blogs, autobiographies, biographies, and journals. Each critical incident was then independently coded by three subject matter experts with respect to (1) the leadership behavior represented, (2) whether the leadership behavior was enacted by a single individual or multiple individuals, (3) formality of leadership, and (4) locus of leadership. Consensus meetings were held to resolve any discrepancies.

1) Longitudinal Data Collection in HERA:
Results from the HERA habitat indicated that while leadership was a mixture of hierarchical and shared, it was most often distributed through the crew, as seen in both the 14- and 30-day HERA campaigns. Most often, results indicated no single member engaging in leadership functions of a specific type such as action, transition, and interpersonal to the exclusion of other team members engaging in the specified group of leadership functions. Results also point to the functionality of sharing leadership. The sharing of transition phase leadership behaviors was significantly correlated with teamwork, cohesion, and effectiveness. Similar results were obtained with respect to the sharing of action phase leadership behaviors. Finally, the sharing of interpersonal leadership behaviors was significantly related to teamwork and cohesion.

2) Laboratory Investigation:
Results from the laboratory study tended to provide further support for what was seen in both the analog environment as well as the archival analysis. First, results suggested that team leadership behaviors were most often distributed throughout the team and not solely enacted by a single individual in the team. Second, incorporating the temporal component investigators studied how often different behaviors were performed across missions. Results indicated that over time, the variety of leadership behaviors increased as well as the density of those behaviors such as the degree to which leadership was distributed through the team or shared, with individuals, on average, having a higher density of leadership behaviors in later missions as compared to earlier missions.

Investigators also studied whether a more objective indicator, participant vocal intensity, might be an appropriate metric for recognizing the degree of shared leadership during particular team performance phases of interaction. Results indicated that the team’s vocal intensity was significantly, positively related to shared leadership. However, in the high autonomy condition, this relationship was only true for action oriented shared leadership density and not for transition leadership density. These results appear to indicate that talking more during more stressful time periods was likely to be associated with leadership behaviors. However, when autonomy was low (i.e., more structured), vocal intensity was predictive of both transition and action-oriented shared leadership. This has implications in particular in terms of the role of vocal intensity serving as a proxy for measuring leadership during high stress, action heavy performance episodes, but less so for planning phases of similar high stress teamwork contexts.

Finally, analyses were conducted to examine a set of enablers to shared leadership. Results indicated that at the individual level, motivation to lead was significantly predictive of individuals’ leadership behavior density, as perceived by their team members. This also held at the team level, where the average of team members’ motivation to lead was significantly predictive of shared leadership. However, this was only true for the sub-dimension of affective motivation to lead, implying that shared leadership in this situation may be driven by teams whose members truly enjoy taking on leadership roles. Results also suggested that personality may serve as an enabler to shared leadership.

Results demonstrated that at the team level, average extraversion and openness to experience were significant, positive predictors of shared team leadership, although agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability were not. This pattern did not significantly change across autonomy or distribution conditions. At the individual level, higher openness to experience was associated with higher individual leadership behavior density, implying that those who were more open to unknown or unfamiliar situations were more likely to step up and take on leadership responsibilities more often. Interestingly, common personality predictors of leadership were not significantly associated with individuals’ leadership behavior density ratings from their teammates, including emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness.

3) Analysis of Archival Data: A final thrust of the project was to use a bottoms-up approach to understanding team leadership in ICE. The investigators employed a mixture of historiometry and the critical incident technique to analyze archived accounts of teams operating in ICE contexts. In doing so, they focused on teams operating in the following ICE contexts – space flight, polar exploration, and long-duration, round the world, ocean sailboat racing. Using the above methodologies, 152 critical incidents pertaining to team leadership were extracted from 124 data sources consisting of blogs, autobiographies, biographies, and journals. Each critical incident was then independently coded by three subject matter experts with respect to (1) the leadership behavior represented, (2) whether the leadership behavior was enacted by a single individual or multiple individuals, (3) formality of leadership, and (4) locus of leadership. Consensus meetings were held to resolve any discrepancies.

experiment_title: Elucidating the Relationship Between the Effects of Various Radiation Qualities and Cancer Development Processes using Novel Flow-based Assays

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Current radiation quality factors used for determining cancer risk for space radiation do not provide the accuracy needed, and there is debate as to the relevance of the experimental studies they're based upon. Therefore, one of NASA's primary goals is to improve the understanding of the carcinogenic process related to high LET exposures to better define the risk. Recently the current understanding of carcinogenesis has improved, and a number of cancer hallmarks have been identified. Some hallmarks, or surrogate cancer endpoints include genetic instability, telomere length changes, and aberrant cellular signaling. Identifying relationships between early and late cell signaling profiles, later surrogate cancer endpoints, and radiation qualities will aid in determining a better risk assessment for cancer formation. In addition, using relevant cell types, such as human epithelial cells in which the majority of cancers develop is also key. In this proposal investigators will studied critical phosphorylation signaling at early and late time points as well as surrogate cancer endpoints of telomere length changes and genomic stability as measured by centrosome amplification, at these same late times post exposure. Epithelial and fibroblast cells from the same individuals were used to better understand the etiology of cancer, and why certain cell types more easily become carcinogenic. Investigators also performed studies to understand the heterogeneous nature of high LET radiation. Energy deposition from high LET ions is dense in the track cores, resulting in closely spaced and complex damages, and delta rays originating from cores provide additional exposures similar to X-rays. Using carefully chosen charge, energy, and LETs of particles to obtain differing populations of cells hit by tracks and delta rays alone they investigated how phosphorylation profiles change.

APPROACH:
Cells were set up in flasks or chamber slides prior to irradiation, irradiated at the various doses and then fixed at multiple time points thereafter. A methanol and a combination of paraformaldehyde and methanol fixation were used depending on what was optimal for the antibody. Fixed slides were sent back to our home institution from Brookhaven in PBS to stain with the appropriate primary and secondary antibodies. Cells exposed in flasks were trypsinized and fixed at various times after exposure, and then sent back on ice in methanol. Aliquots of fixed cells were then stained for various phospho-proteins and analyzed via flow cytometry. For analysis at longer timepoints after exposure (weeks) cells were grown to confluence while at Brookhaven, then frozen down before leaving (~ 1 week post exposure). Cells were then thawed back at the home institution, and expanded to then analyze for telomere length changes and centrosome defects. Cells were stained with pericentrin antibody, then fixed with a methanol fix for flow cytometry based analysis of centrosome dysfunction, and were hybridized to a telomere probe to allow detection of telomere length changes.

RESULTS:
SUMMARY OF RESEARCH ACCOMPLISHMENTS:
Track structure studies based on phospho-kinetics in normal hTERT immortalized fibroblast cells. Normal hTERT immortalized fibroblasts were exposed to a very comprehensive range of carefully chosen high LET ions and energies, to help identify the importance of track structure in defining biological effects. Various phospho-proteins known to be activated following radiation were analyzed for phospho-kinetics including gamma H2AX, pSMC1, and pATF2. Fibroblasts were exposed in triplicate independent experiments to: Fe 300, 600, and 1000 MeV/u; Ti 300, 326, and 386 MeV/u; Si 93, 173, 300, and 1000 MeV/u at timepoints between 0.5 and 24 h. Various comparisons for early and late timepoints were made between equal LET, energy, or Z2/beta2 (roughly equivalent to the number and intensity of delta rays). These studies revealed Z2/beta2 to be a primary determinant in the phosphorylation response. In addition, residual levels of foci (24 h post exposure) correlated well with the predicted energy deposition per nucleosome. This body of work was completed and submitted to Radiation Research recently and is currently in revision (no major revisions required). Conclusions from this work include that: 1) most high LET particles induce a greater induction of gamma H2AX and higher level of residual signaling as compared to equal doses of low LET; 2) at early timepoints ATM-mediated phospho-inductions are much lower following all high LET ion exposures as compared to low LET, indicating that the ATM protein is hampered in fully activating downstream proteins following high LET irradiation as compared to low LET exposures; 3) ions with high delta-ray component (Z2/b2) appear to show a greater persistent phosphorylation signal. Phospho-protein kinetics of primary isogenic mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. To determine how phospho-kinetics may differ based on cell type and status (immortalized vs primary) we compared phosphorylation profiles of gamma H2AX, and pATF2 from primary isogenic (from same tissue biopsy) mammary fibroblasts and mammary epithelial cells. These genetically matched mammary cells where exposed to a variety of different radiation qualities: Fe 300 MeV/u, Ti 300 MeV/ u, Si93 MeV/u, cesium, and X-ray. Initial induction was assessed at 2h post exposure and the amount of residual signaling was assessed at 24 hour post exposure. We chose the 2 h timepoint as for most radiation qualities this timepoint either showed higher levels or the same levels as observed at 0.5 h. Our results indicate that gamma H2AX induction following high LET exposure is greater than following low LET exposure. For example, cells exposed to Si93 MeV/u exhibit a greater induction than following X-ray exposure. Comparing mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells, initial gamma H2AX inductions were similar for all high LET ions, although the Ti ion was uniquely higher for epithelial cells. At late times post exposure, epithelial cells revealed a much greater degree of residual gamma H2AX signal, indicative of a higher amount of unresolved damage in epithelial cells as compared to fibroblasts. This suggests that epithelial cells are more sensitive to high LET damage than fibroblast cells, since the genetic background of the lines cannot be the culprit of this difference as they are from the same individual and tissue section. A second phospho-protein that kinetics were studied in these lines post various radiation quality exposures was pATF2. ATF2 is known to have various functions within the cell however phosphorylation at this particular site (Ser490/498) has been documented to be specifically required for its role in DNA repair. As has been noted in past studies, pATF2 induction was lower than what was observed for gamma H2AX at early times, with levels saturating at about 0.5 Gy. Unexpectedly initial pATF2 induction in fibroblasts was greater than what was observed for epithelial cells for both high and low LET radiation, which is in contrast to the kinetics we observed for gamma H2AX. However, residual signaling for pATF2 was similar for both the fibroblasts and the epithelial cells. Also of interest was the fact that in general for fibroblast line pATF2 levels decreased with time; however, for epithelial cells in many cases the highest levels were observed at the latest timepoint (24h). This is very different from the findings with gamma H2AX, and suggests again that epithelial cells may have more difficulty responding to effects of high LET exposure. The difference observed between the phospho-protein results may also suggest that levels of pATF2 do not directly correlate with the level of double strand breaks (based on gamma H2AX levels), but instead might reflect others things such as perhaps the levels of oxidative stress present in cells. Similarly to the skin fibroblast study currently in revision, we had wanted to analyze data on a per cell basis on exported flow data. We are currently working with a statistician to finalize this work for publishing in next few months. High LET effects on telomere length of primary mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. To better understand the relationship between radiation exposure and carcinogenesis we analyzed how the phospho-kinetic response following various radiation quality exposures corresponded to the surrogate cancer endpoint of telomere length shortening. The Flow cytometry-based telomere length assay, or flow FISH was used to determine how various qualities of radiation affected telomere lengths of cells differentially. A dose-dependent shortening of telomeres for both mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells following high LET exposures was observed. For low LET exposures, mammary fibroblasts were fairly resistant to shortening effects even at the highest doses, whereas mammary epithelial cells exhibited a dose-dependent shortening even with low LET exposure. The Fe ion irradiations appeared to show the least difference between cell types, in particular Fe 300 MeV/u, which revealed nearly the same change in telomere length over the majority of the doses. Fe 300 MeV/u has the highest delta ray component of all the radiation qualities tested and this may be one of the major drivers in terms of effects, given both cell types failed to show a resistance to the effects. Overall mammary epithelial cells were more sensitive to the effects of radiation and showed a greater decrease in telomere shortening per dose than did fibroblast cells, consistent with the fact that they reveal a greater sensitivity to radiation induced carcinogenesis. We have also exported individual cell flow cytometry data to define how telomere lengths change on an individual cell basis. Preliminary data has revealed that fibroblasts do not show an increase in cells with short telomeres with increasing X-ray dose, yet epithelial cells did reveal an increase in cells showing short telomeres with increasing dose. This additional analysis will allow us to understand in more detail the underlying reasons for the mean changes in telomere shortening for each cell type. Given that mean lengths can change, for example to show an overall longer length, yet the underlying reason for this mean change could be more cells containing shorter telomeres were lost. A finding of an increase in telomere length upon exposure to protons has been noted in the literature, thus detailing the underlying reason for the mean change in shortening should help us to better understand cell type differences and the mechanism involved in radiation-induced telomere shortening. This work is planned to be combined with phospho-kinetic data and as noted above should be submitted in next few months.

High LET effects on centrosome amplification in primary mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. The second surrogate cancer endpoint, which investigators have studied in relationship to radiation quality, dose, and cell type, was centrosome amplifications. Again a flow-based assay was developed and used to identify increases in size or number of centrosomes as a function of dose and radiation quality, using the pericentrin antibody, which envelops the centrosome of the cell. Our preliminary study with mammary epithelial cells following levels days post X-ray exposure was performed to determine the temporal kinetics of centrosome formation and decline following radiation exposure. These studies revealed that at ~day 9 after exposure significant increases in centrosome aberrations were observed as denoted by the percent of cells showing higher pericentrin levels than the 80-90th percentile of controls. Further studies looking at dose and radiation quality effects were then initiated. We have also performed some studies to better understand how flow cytometry results may compare to the more common way of analysis, immunofluorescence and microscopic scoring of aberrant cells. These studies revealed based on Fe 1000MeV/u results, that similar results in terms of pattern of peak levels observed for both the microscopy and FACS assay were at 0.1 Gy. Why an intermediate dose may show higher levels of centrosome aberrations is uncertain; however, it may be that higher doses kill off cells with aberrant levels thus this is the dose where radiation induces damage, yet it is not enough to kill the exposed cells. Binned results for other ions and energies in assays looking at centrosome aberration frequencies were also performed. These studies revealed the greatest percentages of centrosome aberrations were obtained following Fe300 MeV/u exposures for mammary epithelial cells (far right bin for each radiation quality, showing percent of cells having pericentrin levels >80th percentile as compared to controls). Further statistical analysis was performed on individual centrosome cell data to more carefully define differences at lower doses. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K-S test) was used for these studies; it provides a nonparametric test for the equality of a continuous, one-dimensional probability distribution. It was used to investigate how different doses and radiation qualities compared in terms of the level of pericentrin fluorescence (equal to aberrant centrosomes at high levels over controls) following exposure. The K-S test quantifies a distance between the empirical distribution function of the sample and the cumulative distribution function of the control distribution. Based on KS test investigators were able to note a significant difference from control levels with all radiation qualities and at all doses for mammary epithelial cells. Results with fibroblast cells from the same tissue (mammary) have shown that fibroblasts are much more resistant to forming centrosome aberrations and that levels in general were below detection using the flow-based assay. They went on to confirm this via the microscopy method following Fe1000 MeV/u exposure, and again found no increase in centrosome aberrations over control levels using this method as well. Thus it appears similarly to the telomere shortening, mammary epithelial cells are more sensitive to the formation of centrosome aberrations following radiation exposure as compared to mammary fibroblasts from the same individual. This again points to a heightened sensitivity for epithelial cells to radiation and potentially also carcinogenesis given these endpoints have been linked to cancer and a pre-malignant state.

Conclusions: The findings of this body of work point to the importance of radiation quality and cell type in determining the effectiveness of high LET exposure. Epithelial cells for the most part appear to show a greater sensitivity to high LET exposure and of particular importance also a greater induction in the two surrogate cancer endpoints investigated, telomere length shortening and centrosome aberration frequencies. Mammary cells, both fibroblast and epithelial cells, appear to show a less robust response to radiation in terms of phosphorylation of various DNA repair proteins after exposures as compared to a skin fibroblast line (82-6). However all lines revealed a greater response to high LET as compared to low LET radiation. These studies allowed investigators to study how well early phospho-protein profiles predict a cell’s response to other endpoints more closely aligned to cancer. They determined that there was not a direct correspondence between the ion/energy that showed the highest residual level of double-strand breaks (based on persistent gamma H2AX at 24 h) and the ion/energy that showed the highest level of centrosome defects and/or telomere shortening. For example, for phospho-protein signaling at 24 h Ti300 MeV/u reveals the greatest residual levels for mammary epithelial cells, whereas for centrosome aberrations, Fe 300 MeV/u generates the greatest number of aberrant cells weeks post exposure, and Si 93 MeV/u shows the greatest effect on telomere shortening, again weeks post exposure. However, studies in skin fibroblast cells, with a more comprehensive set of energies for each ion, suggest that the ions/energies that are the most effective when compared to other energies are Ti300, Si93, and Fe300 MeV/u. Thus in each case the ion/energy showing a more dramatic response for our mammary epithelial cells when compared to other energies of the same ion are the ones in which in the skin fibroblast study revealed more effectiveness. Thus, perhaps if additional energies had been used for surrogate cancer endpoints and phospho-kinetics for the mammary cell studies we would have seen a pattern similar to what was observed with the skin fibroblast cells, whereby the ions with the lowest energy, having the greatest delta ray component, were the most effective in each case. Why different types of ions show a preference for inducing greater levels for particular endpoints is uncertain and would require further investigation.

experiment_title: Dietary Calcium Intake in LSAH Participants and U.S. General Population
parameter_html: Calcium, dietary
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Dietary calcium intake was measured to determine if Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants meet the recommendations of the National Osteoporosis Foundation for prevention of osteoporosis and promotion of bone health.

APPROACH:
The data were obtained through a Food Frequency Questionnaire sent out in the fall of 1998. A total of 651 participants responded to the questionnaire (116 male astronauts, 21 female astronauts, 448 male comparisons, and 66 female comparisons). Results of a national survey, the 1996 Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (CSFII), were used to compare the LSAH participants to the U.S. general population. investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Placing the body in a totally new force environment could produce unexpected changes in many areas of the neuromuscular system, which is known to be adaptive. Such changes are of particular concern during the Space Shuttle’s reentry into Earth’s orbit. To objectively document any effects, crewmembers measured their ability to reproduce a fixed position without visual reference by manually marking a point, moving the limb, and attempting to return to the same point. This was done pre- and postflight and early and late in the flight. Several limb segments were tested, with and without the equivalent 1g load in orbit.

Kinesthetic learning is when someone learns things from doing or being part of them. The objective of this experiment was to obtain data to determine if weightlessness results in a shift of the body's limb position.

APPROACH:
During orbit, it was desirable for each crewmember to perform these tests twice with the greatest practical time separation. A crewmember fixed himself beside the middeck lockers with foot restraints and affixed a sheet of paper to the locker. He made a designated hand, elbow, and arm motion to place the pen at a designated point on the paper he marked. Without looking, he repeated the motion several times and attempted to mark the same position. The test was repeated with a small bungee attached to the hand with a half-glove to note the effect of loading.

During reentry, the middeck mission specialist affixed a sheet of paper to his knee board and made a designated hand, elbow, and arm motion to place the pen at a designated point on the paper. Without looking, he repeated the motion several times and attempted to mark the same position. Two test periods of approximately one minute duration were desired.

RESULTS:
Preflight baselines were made with all crewmembers; however, in flight time was at a premium and it was necessary to modify the schedule to obtain the most useful data. Based on experience during the flight, this data became of less importance and was first delayed and finally eliminated. This is nice to know data and warrants collection under suitable circumstances; it may acquire additional importance when flight duration is extended.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Dorneich, MichaelCo-Investigator: Franke, WarrenCo-Investigator: Keren, NirCo-Investigator: Vardeman, Stephen
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Acute stress has the potential to significantly debilitate human performance, both physically and cognitively. For long-duration space flight, the results of such reduced cognitive performance could be life-threatening, and therefore warrants the creation of behavioral countermeasures for mitigating crew health and performance risks. Currently most emergency training focuses on performance outcomes, but new research should be centered on preventing negative performance outcomes through acute stress management techniques. Traditional training can be effective under predictable conditions, but performance can degrade rapidly if unexpected stressors are introduced. Additionally, the proposed system could serve as a preflight screening measure to help identify individuals who are more likely to perform better in high stress situations. The goal of this experiment, using Virtual Reality (VR) simulated situations, was to reduce acute stress response during space flight using an adaptive inoculation approach. Exposure was administered gradually and used a biofeedback system to respond and adapt to individual stress response in a way that promotes learning voluntary physiological control without overwhelming the subject.

Specific aims of this research included:

  1. Identifying stressors in a microgravity environment;
  2. Evaluating formal objective methods to measure baseline chronic and acute stress, in-training performance, psychological stress response, physiological stress response, and procedural errors;
  3. Developing a prototype for graduated stress training;
  4. Conducting a proof-of-concept of the training program based on NASA’s emergency protocols for the International Space Station (ISS); and
  5. Establishing guidelines for implementation of the graduated stress training.

APPROACH:

The research team and panel of experts reviewed and identified the stressors associated with emergency spaceflight situations of fire on the International Space Station (ISS) with respect to task and effect on users. Procedural information for virtual reality (VR) training was detailed, including the events likely to occur in the environment, the types of stressors encountered, NASA emergency procedures, resources to respond during the event, and the performance effects the stressors may have. Stress training requires procedural information to be included in the scenarios and conveyed to the user, so the stressors do not interfere with skill/knowledge acquisition. The stressors were categorized by manipulation type (environment or task manipulation), which indicates if a stressor may affect the task and deviate from the selected emergency procedure. From the environmental stressors, a simplified fire procedure was created based on the existing NASA ISS emergency procedures to develop adaptation and Training Module logic. The adaptations used implicit biofeedback, consisting of physiological signals exceeding a threshold “zone” and triggering a change in simulated stressors. The Training Module design was informed by past research on Stress Inoculation Training and Graduated Stress Exposure to implement a stress inoculation training strategy over five training sessions. The adaptation and training module rules taken together were used to produce a training pedagogy for use within the system.

To implement a Prototype Training System, the research team designed and implemented the system architecture for a VR-ISS with a emergency fire simulation. The VR environment was developed for the stressors and emergency procedure selected in the Training Module design. This environment was designed so that users can complete a NASA emergency fire procedure and locate the source of a fire. The procedure requires emergency equipment including a portable breathing apparatus (PBA), portable fire extinguisher (PFE), and Compound Specific Analyzer–Combustion Products (CSA-CP). Three different stressor levels were created in the simulation, involving a combination of stressors of varying intensity, including smoke density, fire alarms, and module power-outages that flickered the lights. The stressor levels were validated through objective physiological measures and subjective stress questionnaires as participants conducted the emergency procedure to locate the fire source. Results showed that the three-stressor levels implemented in a VR environment result in significantly different participant stress, workload, and distress. The adaptive nature of the VR training system required that the trainee’s stress level be measured in real-time, and a stress detection system was created with machine learning methods. Physiological signals were calculated from sensors which include electrocardiogram (ECG), respiration (RSP), electrodermal activity (EDA), and non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP). The physiological signals were streamed in real-time to apply preprocessing, high-dimensional feature extraction, feature selection, and classification using supervised machine learning approaches. Current limitations with supervised machine learning approaches propelled the development of a statistical classification method by our research team, known as Approximate Bayes (ABayes). ABayes uses kernel density probability estimates to find conditional class probabilities for three stress states: low, medium, high. The advantage of ABayes is the direct and transparent calculation of the class probabilities. ABayes was evaluated on its accuracy of predicting stress using cross-validation and hold-out on unseen data.

Three human-in-the-loop experiments were performed to test the components of the Adaptive VR turning system in isolation and as a system. The first experiment assessed the ability to manipulate a person’s stress level in a virtual environment. Specifically, an evaluation was preformed to determine the extent to which operationally relevant VR stressor levels (i.e., low, medium, high) derived from existing emergency spaceflight procedures could evoke a reliable stress response. The second experiment evaluated the ability to reliably detect the stress level of a person in VR using a combination of biophysical sensors and machine learning to correctly classify low, medium, or high stress. The third experiment was conducted to determine if the closed-loop VR training system could successfully inoculate participant’s stress over a series of training trials with graduated stress exposure. 

RESULTS:

A physiological-based stress detection system for classifying multiple levels of acute stress was developed with a novel classifier, ABayes, using a personalized time-series interval approach. The approach was evaluated against common machine learning classification systems in their ability to classify stress for two different tasks: a fire response task aboard a VR International Space Station (VR-ISS) or a computer-based (N-back) task. The current findings suggest that three levels of stress can be classified by means of the ABayes approach, providing promising accuracy when compared to past research on multi-class stress detection. Stress was accurately predicted for both the simplified lab task, N-back, and the more complex VR-ISS task. Analysis on the window sizes gave insight into which sensors/features were useful for varying time-intervals. Future work will further investigate these personalized stress detection systems with the aim of implementing real-time stress monitoring.
