experiment_title: Cellular Immune Response
parameter_html:
B-lymphocyte count, peripheral blood
Lymphocyte count
T-lymphocyte count, peripheral blood
White blood cell count
Lymphocyte responsiveness, concanavalin A
Lymphocyte responsiveness, influenza virus antigen
Lymphocyte responsiveness, phytohemagglutinin
Lymphocyte responsiveness, pokeweed mitogen
investigators: Principal Investigator: Criswell, Sue
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The functional capacity of lymphocytes (phytohemagglutinin (PHA) responsiveness only) was found to be depressed for studies conducted during Apollo missions 7 through 13 and Skylab missions 3 and 4. T-lymphocyte numbers were also suppressed in Skylab. The objective of this study was to examine the effects of space flight on the cellular immune response in Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) crewmembers.

APPROACH:
Samples of heparinized peripheral venous blood (10cc) were obtained preflight and postflight on days L-30 (30 days before liftoff), L-15, L-5, R+0 (day of recovery), R+1 (recovery +1 day), R+8 and R+13. Samples were processed within 1 to 24 hours of collection. Parameters measured for this study included: 1) white blood cell concentrations, 2) lymphocyte numbers, 3) B-lymphocyte and T-lymphocyte distributions in peripheral blood and 4) lymphocyte responsiveness to PHA, pokeweed mitogen (PWM), Concanavalin A (Con A) and influenza virus antigen. Before separation, total leukocyte counts were performed using a hemacytometer and/or a Coulter Counter. Differential counts were determined using slide preparations stained with Wright’s stain.

Lymphocytes were separated by Ficoll-Hypaque centrifugation, which uses a special liquid that provides a density gradient. Higher density blood cells are pulled far down into the liquid by centrifugal action, while the more buoyant lymphocytes remain near the center. The supernatant was removed by pipette, and the resulting mononuclear cells were washed three times in minimum essential medium (MEM).

B-lymphocyte distributions were determined by calculating the percentage of 200 mononuclear cells with surface immunoglobulins, which were detected by the immunofluorescent antibody technique. The presence of E-rosette-forming lymphocytes (T-cells) was determined using a concentration of one million lymphocytes in 0.25 ml of 0.5% sheep red blood cell (SRBC) suspension. After mixing, the tubes were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes, and then placed in ice water for 2 hours. Approximately half of the supernatant was removed, and the top cell layer was gently resuspended. Two hundred lymphocytes were counted with 3 or more adhering SRBC’s, which were used as criteria for E-rosetted lymphocytes.

Purified lymphocytes (one million cells) in MEM containing 40% fetal calf serum were placed in culture plates. The antigens were diluted in MEM (containing Pen-Strep and L-glutamine) in the following concentrations: 0.01 ml PHA/ml MEM; 0.01 and 0.05 ml PWM/ml MEM; and 25 and 50 micrograms Con A/ml MEM. These diluted antigens were placed in the appropriate wells of the tissue culture plates in 0.1 ml aliquots (in duplicate). The cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide atmosphere at 37 degrees Celsius (3 days for PHA and 5 days for Con A and PWM). On the day of harvest, samples were treated as described in the following section for influenza virus antigen cultures.

An inactivated monovalent type A influenza virus vaccine containing 1600 chick cell agglutinating units/ml of a Hong Kong strain was dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline and stored at -70 degrees Celsius until used for tests. Separated lymphocytes were added in 0.1 ml aliquots for each influenza antigen dilution, and the cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide incubator at 37 degrees Celsius for periods of either 2 or 3 days. On the day of harvest, cells were pulsed for 2 hours with 1 microcurie of methyl(tritium)-thymidine, a radioactive marker. Cells were then harvested with an automated harvester onto glass-fiber filter strips and counted in a liquid scintillation counter. Data were expressed as counts per minute (CPM)/one million lymphocytes, and the stimulation index (SI) was calculated by dividing the mean result for stimulated cultures by that for unstimulated cultures. Allantoic fluid was used separately as a control of each crewman’s reactivity to chick embryo proteins.

RESULTS:
Preflight (L-30) white blood cell (WBC) counts for ASTP and Skylab were 6640±1830 WBC/mm3 and 6013±254 WBC/ mm3, respectively. The ASTP crew had significant increases in WBC numbers noted on R+0 (11,110±4210 WBC/mm3) and R+1 (13,530±610 WBC/mm3). Individual variation in WBC values was noted among the three Skylab crewmembers at R+0 (8980±5560 WBC/mm3), which is reflected in the large standard deviation. However, all values were within clinically normal ranges (7110±2400 WBC/mm3). Less variation overall was noted for total lymphocyte values; however, values at R+0 for ASTP (1950±490 lymphocyte count/mm3) and Skylab 4 (1177±381 lymphocyte count/mm3) were decreased below their previous baseline values (ASTP L-30=2820±480 lymphocyte count/mm3 and Skylab L-30=1940±670 lymphocyte count/mm3). Fluctuations in the individual values of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and nonreactive lymphocytes of ASTP crewmembers were indicated, but values remain within one standard deviation for normal laboratory values. T-cell values ranged from 1.29 million +/- 490,000 to 2.53 million +/- 440,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=1.59 million +/- 630,000 lymphocytes/ml), B-lymphocytes from 470,000 +/- 20,000 to 710,000 +/- 40,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=510,000 +/- 300,000 lymphocytes/ml) and nonreactive lymphocytes from 120,000 +/- 120,000 to 710,000 +/- 370,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=850,000 +/- 560,000 lymphocytes/ml). In contrast, highly significant changes were noted in B and T cell distributions of the Skylab 4 crewmen.

Results from culture studies show a definite decrease in the ability of lymphocytes to react with PHA at R+0 (SI=20±15) and R+1 (SI=12±8) for all three Apollo astronauts. Baseline SI mean at L-30 was 36±4. By R+8, all were back within normal ranges (SI range=10 to 282). Crewmembers began and remained at low-level SI ranges for Con A (3 to 49) throughout the preflight and postflight periods, except for one subject, who had a strengthened Con A stimulation of 151 at splashdown. Considerable individual variation was noted in the PWM data and no consistent trend was obtained. Variation of antigen stimulation indexes may be expected, due to the rapid exchange of cells between different compartments in the body. The entire Apollo crew responded to influenza virus England strain preflight in cultures, and one of the three astronauts responded postflight to influenza virus Hong Kong strain. Total lack of reactivity may reflect influenza susceptibility.

ASTP crewmembers experienced contact with toxic gases upon splashdown. Depressions observed at R+0 were caused by either space flight or gas exposure a few hours prior to sample analysis. Similar depressions in lymphocytic responsiveness were observed in Skylab 3 and 4 data, although both of these missions were of much longer duration than ASTP. However, in comparable missions of similar lengths (i.e., the Apollo series) no changes in lymphocytic responsiveness were reported. The toxic gas exposure was severe enough to create concern for lung inflammation, which resulted in a corticosteroid treatment on R+1. Most cortisone preparations are known to cause a lymphocytic reaction. Consequently, it is likely that the increased immunosuppressions noted by cultural responses on R+1 for all mitogens and on R+8 for Con A were attributable to the steroid therapy.

On the day of harvest, samples were treated as described in the following section for influenza virus antigen cultures.

An inactivated monovalent type A influenza virus vaccine containing 1600 chick cell agglutinating units/ml of a Hong Kong strain was dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline and stored at -70 degrees Celsius until used for tests. Separated lymphocytes were added in 0.1 ml aliquots for each influenza antigen dilution, and the cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide incubator at 37 degrees Celsius for periods of either 2 or 3 days. On the day of harvest, cells were pulsed for 2 hours with 1 microcurie of methyl(tritium)-thymidine, a radioactive marker. Cells were then harvested with an automated harvester onto glass-fiber filter strips and counted in a liquid scintillation counter. Data were expressed as counts per minute (CPM)/one million lymphocytes, and the stimulation index (SI) was calculated by dividing the mean result for stimulated cultures by that for unstimulated cultures. Allantoic fluid was used separately as a control of each crewman’s reactivity to chick embryo proteins.

Preflight (L-30) white blood cell (WBC) counts for ASTP and Skylab were 6640±1830 WBC/mm3 and 6013±254 WBC/ mm3, respectively. Individual variation in WBC values was noted among the three Skylab crewmembers at R+0 (8980±5560 WBC/mm3), which is reflected in the large standard deviation. However, all values were within clinically normal ranges (7110±2400 WBC/mm3). Less variation overall was noted for total lymphocyte values; however, values at R+0 for ASTP (1950±490 lymphocyte count/mm3) and Skylab 4 (1177±381 lymphocyte count/mm3) were decreased below their previous baseline values (ASTP L-30=2820±480 lymphocyte count/mm3 and Skylab L-30=1940±670 lymphocyte count/mm3). Fluctuations in the individual values of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and nonreactive lymphocytes of ASTP crewmembers were indicated, but values remain within one standard deviation for normal laboratory values. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Currently, the deterministic space radiation transport code High charge (Z) and Energy TRaNsport (HZETRN), is the major tool used by NASA to evaluate radiation environments inside a spacecraft. Deterministic codes have been shown to be superior to Monte Carlo transport for engineering studies. However HZETRN is a one dimensional transport code. The transport of heavy ions (Z > 2) has been shown to be valid in the one dimensional approximation because the relativistic heavy ions found in the space radiation spectrum pass through materials relatively un-deflected from their initial trajectories. The cross sections required for one dimensional transport are total absorption and spectral distributions. Meson production and the associated electromagnetic cascade have not yet been incorporated into HZETRN. Phase 1 studies have shown the importance of these processes, which must be included in Phase 2. This project implemented the recommendations of several workshops by emphasizing the development of a more accurate description of neutron and light ion transport. Neutrons and light ions scatter at large angles and the one dimensional approximation is no longer valid. Therefore, the one dimensional code HZETRN must begin to include the three dimensional transport of light ions and neutrons to more accurately quantify secondary radiation environments in tissue while maintaining computational speed and efficiency. Such a three dimensional transport code in turn requires fully double differential cross sections as input.

APPROACH:
Phase II Measurements and Physics Project focused on light ion production and transport to develop space radiation transport codes capable of predicting primary and secondary spectra of space radiation environment interaction behind typical spacecraft shielding, planetary surfaces, and atmospheres with increased accuracy. Configuration managed verification and validation source codes are released to the radiation user community including Exploration, Radiation Health Officer (RHO), and Operations as well as industry partners or commercial entities. Current exploration vehicle requirements specify that HZETRN shall be utilized by the government for radiation requirement verification. Transport codes directly support verification of NASA STD 3001 Vol. 2 requirements.

RESULTS:
Active magnetic radiation shielding was re-evaluated. Many active magnetic shielding designs have been proposed in order to reduce the radiation exposure received by astronauts on long-duration, deep space missions. While these designs are promising, they pose significant engineering challenges. This work presents a survey of the major systems required for such unconfined magnetic field design, allowing the identification of key technologies for future development. Basic mass calculations are developed for each system and are used to determine the resulting galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) exposure for a generic solenoid design, using a range of magnetic field strength and thickness values, allowing some of the basic characteristics of such a design to be observed. The study focused on a solenoid shaped, active magnetic shield design; however, many of the principles discussed are applicable regardless of the exact design configuration, particularly the key technologies cited.

Shielding evaluation for solar particle events (SPEs) was studied and detailed analyses of SPEs were performed to calculate primary and secondary particle spectra behind aluminum, at various thicknesses in water. The simulations were based on Monte Carlo (MC) radiation transport codes, MCNPX and PHITS, and the space radiation analysis website called On-Line Tool for the Assessment of Radiation in Space (OLTARIS) version 3.4 (uses deterministic code, HZETRN, for transport). The study investigated the impact of SPEs spectra transporting through 10 or 20 g/cm^2 Al shield followed by 30 g/cm2 of water slab. Four historical SPE events were selected and used as input source spectra and particle differential spectra for protons, neutrons, and photons are presented. The total particle fluence as a function of depth is presented. In addition to particle flux, the dose and dose equivalent values are calculated and compared between the codes and with the other published results. Overall, the particle fluence spectra from all three codes show good agreement with the MC codes showing closer agreement compared to the OLTARIS results. The neutron particle fluence from OLTARIS is lower than the results from MC codes at lower energies (E<100MeV). Based on mean square difference analysis the results from MCNPX and PHITS agree better for fluence, dose, and dose equivalent when compared to OLTARIS results.

Elastic differential cross sections for space radiation applications were evaluated. The eikonal, partial wave (PW) Lippmann-Schwinger, and three-dimensional Lippmann-Schwinger (LS3D) methods are compared for nuclear reactions that are relevant for space radiation applications. Numerical convergence of the eikonal method is readily achieved when exact formulas of the optical potential are used for light nuclei, and the momentum-space representation of the optical potential is used for heavier nuclei. The PW solution method is known to be numerically unstable for systems that require a large number of partial waves, and, as a result, the LS3D method is employed. The effect of relativistic kinematics is studied with the PWand LS3D methods and is compared to eikonal results. It is recommended that the LS3D method be used for high-energy nucleon-nucleus reactions and nucleus-nucleus reactions at all energies because of its rapid numerical convergence and stability.

The new trapped environment AE9/AP9/SPM at low Earth orbit was evaluated. The completion of the International Space Station (ISS) in 2011 has provided the space research community an ideal proving ground for future long-duration human activities in space. Ionizing radiation measurements in the ISS form the ideal tool for the validation of radiation environmental models, nuclear transport codes, and nuclear reaction cross sections. Indeed, prior measurements on the space transportation system (STS; shuttle) provided vital information impacting both the environmental models and the nuclear transport code developments by indicating the need for an improved dynamic model of the low Earth orbit (LEO) trapped environment. Additional studies using thermo-luminescent detector (TLD), tissue equivalent proportional counter (TEPC) area monitors, and computer aided design (CAD) model of earlier ISS configurations, confirmed STS observations that, as input, computational dosimetry requires an environmental model with dynamic and directional (anisotropic) behavior, as well as an accurate six degree of freedom (DOF) definition of the vehicle attitude and orientation along the orbit of the ISS.

A new three dimensional (3D) version of the NASA transport code HZETRN was developed. The computationally efficient HZETRN code has been used in recent trade studies for lunar and Martian exploration and is currently being used in the engineering development of the next generation of space vehicles, habitats, and extra vehicular activity equipment. Code development has been based on a progression of approximations first assuming all particles are produced in the initiator direction of incidence (straight-ahead) later improved by treating neutrons produced in the backward hemisphere as moving straight-back (bi-directional). A new version (3DHZETRN) capable of transporting High charge (Z) and Energy (HZE) and light ions (including neutrons) under space-like boundary conditions with enhanced neutron and light ion propagation in transverse directions is developed. New algorithms for light ion and neutron propagation with well-defined convergence criteria in 3D objects were developed and tested against Monte Carlo simulations of 3D effects.

A deterministic (non-statistical) two dimensional (2D) computational model describing the transport of electron and photon typical of space radiation environment in various shield media was developed. The 2D formalism is cast into a code which is an extension of a previously developed one dimensional (1D) deterministic electron and photon transport code. For candidate shielding materials, using the trapped electron radiation environments at low Earth orbit (LEO), geosynchronous orbit (GEO), and Jupiter moon Europa, verification of the 2D formalism versus 1D and an existing Monte Carlo code was studied.

A GCR simulator was developed and is intended to deliver the broad spectrum of particles and energies encountered in deep space to biological targets in a controlled laboratory setting. In this work, certain aspects of simulating the GCR environment in the laboratory are discussed. Reference field specification and beam selection strategies at the NASA Space Radiation Lab (NSRL) are the main focus, but the analysis presented herein may be modified for other facilities. First, comparisons were made between direct simulation of the external, free space GCR field and simulation of the induced tissue field behind shielding. It was found that upper energy constraints at NSRL limit the ability to simulate the external, free space field directly. Second, variation in the induced tissue field associated with shielding configuration and solar activity is addressed. It was found that the observed variation is likely within the uncertainty associated with representing any GCR reference field with discrete ion beams in the laboratory, given current facility constraints. A single reference field for deep space missions is subsequently identified. Third, an approach for selecting beams at NSRL to simulate the designated reference field was developed. Drawbacks of the proposed methodology have been investigated and weighed against alternative simulation strategies.

A new Galactic Cosmic Ray Flux Model was developed. The Badhwar-O'Neill (BON) GCR model is based on GCR measurements from particle detectors. The model has mainly been used by NASA to certify microelectronic systems and the analysis of radiation health risks to astronauts in space missions. The BON14 model numerically solves the Fokker-Planck equation to account for particle transport in the heliosphere due to diffusion, convection, and adiabatic deceleration under the assumption of a spherically symmetric heliosphere. The model also incorporates an empirical time delay function to account for the lag of the solar activity to reach the boundary of the heliosphere. Using a comprehensive measurement database, it was shown that BON14 is significantly improved over the previous version, BON11.

The importance of neutrons and light ions was considered when astronauts spend considerable time in thickly shielded regions of a spacecraft. This may be relevant for space missions both in and beyond low Earth orbit. In addition to heavy ion experiments at accelerators, it is suggested that an increased emphasis on experiments with lighter ions may be useful in reducing biological uncertainties.

Estimates of extreme SPE radiation exposures on Mars were made. Estimates of effective doses and organ doses for male and female crewmembers are made for SPE proton environments comparable to several of the most significant SPEs, which occurred in the second half of the 19th century. The incident proton energy distributions for these SPEs are assumed to be similar to that of the November 1960 event, one of the most energetic of the modern space era. The crewmembers are assumed to be located at the mean surface elevation on Mars, at the lowest elevation on Mars in the Hellas Impact Basin, and on the summit of Olympus Mons, the highest surface elevation on Mars. The crewmembers were assumed to be shielded by the overlying carbon dioxide atmosphere of Mars, and locally shielded by a space suit, a surface landing spacecraft, or a surface habitat. These estimates are compared with current NASA Permissible Exposure Limits.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: A Speech-Based Artificial Intelligence System for Predicting Team Functioning Degradation in HERA Missions
experiment_description:
Objective:
NASA’s priority on the Artemis missions as a preliminary phase for Mars exploration, it is expected that long-distance space exploration will propose various challenges due to the prolonged constraint of small teams living and working together in an intense environment and the absence of real-time communication with Earth, broadening the risk of inadequate team cooperation and coordination. This proposed study aims tested the hypothesis, that a minimal set of speech-based measures, potentially different depending on the structured or unstructured nature of the focal tasks, will be indicative of team functioning degradation, and that the various parts of the mission will contribute differently to this outcome, by building a speech-based artificial intelligence system that unobtrusively predicts degradation in team functioning, including performance and cohesion, during HERA Campaign 4 (C4) and Campaign 5 (C5). The AI system conducted automated analysis of prosodic and linguistic of speech, modeled their interaction among team members, and extracted influence and turn-taking statistics among speakers, without requiring additional human coding, thus resulting in an automated method that relies on unobtrusive passive monitoring for predicting team outcomes.

The proposed research had three specific aims:
1. Pre-process audio recordings from C4/C5 HERA missions, and extract team interaction measures based on acoustic and linguistic features from these missions.
2. Design machine learning models that automatically predict degradation in team functioning using the speech measures.
3. Identify a minimal subset of speech-based measures that are effective predictors of team functioning degradation for each part of the mission and specific parts of the mission that mostly contribute to team functioning degradation.

Approach:
The PI team investigated the broad picture of team functioning throughout the whole duration of focal parts of the mission via observing structured and unstructured team interactions. Audio data were pre-processed via removing stationary and short burst noise, followed by voice activity detection and speaker identification. Speaker excerpts were transcribed via automatic speech recognition (ASR), where speaker adaptation was applied to improve ASR performance. The following acoustic and linguistic features were extracted: degree of speech periodicity (e.g., fundamental frequency-F0, jitter, shimmer); shape of the speech spectrum (e.g., cepstrum, Mel-frequency spectral coefficients); patterns of vocal intensity (e.g., loudness); grammatic features (e.g., I/you/we pronouns); and lexicon-based features capturing cognitive, affective, and social processes. Interaction measures included the degree of similarity in acoustic and linguistic features among interlocutors; the degree of connectivity of a graph, team member nodes and edges; and turn-taking measures modeling the conversation progress (e.g., alternating turns, pauses, speech overlap). Interpretable machine learning (ML) models were trained based on the interaction measures to predict self- reported team performance and coherence. Ablation studies were conducted to identify the subset of features, potentially different depending on the structured or unstructured nature of the focal tasks, and parts of the mission that are most predictive of team functioning, degradation, and feasible prediction horizon windows. Investigators used previously collected self-reports, audio, and team task performances from structured and unstructured tasks from the HERA Campaigns 4 and 5. Acoustic and linguistic measurements were used for the outputs of team functioning variables when training ML models. To better understand data and feasible system configurations, various trainings and testing occurred. Team-independent evaluation was conducted via a leave-one-team-out cross-validation, where data from 8 teams was used for training and data from the remaining team were used for testing. Team-dependent evaluation was conducted such that a subset of data from a target team was included in the training set and the remaining were in the test set. To increase the model’s robustness and generalizability investigators included data from other teams. Longitudinal data was used for multiple horizons prediction (1-5 days in advance). Once investigators aggregate the data at the day level, employ were implemented for multi-level models for hypothesis testing.

Results:
The results from this investigation allowed researchers to isolate and record only the important vocal behaviors during specific parts of the mission, instead of the entire mission. They also examined the predictive ability of speech-based interaction measures without additional sensor devices (e.g., badges for crew proximity). The reduced need for human coding will benefit future missions and crew by being both an automated, unobtrusive monitoring system for predicting team outcomes.

Team-independent evaluation was conducted via a leave-one-team-out cross-validation, where data from 8 teams was used for training and data from the remaining team were used for testing. Team-dependent evaluation was conducted such that a subset of data from a target team was included in the training set and the remaining were in the test set. To increase the model’s robustness and generalizability investigators included data from other teams. Longitudinal data was used for multiple horizons prediction (1-5 days in advance). Once investigators aggregate the data at the day level, employ were implemented for multi-level models for hypothesis testing.

Results:
The results from this investigation allowed researchers to isolate and record only the important vocal behaviors during specific parts of the mission, instead of the entire mission. They also examined the predictive ability of speech-based interaction measures without additional sensor devices (e.g., badges for crew proximity). The reduced need for human coding will benefit future missions and crew by being both an automated, unobtrusive monitoring system for predicting team outcomes.

experiment_title: Cognitive Aid Design Using Augmented Reality to Support Attention
hrr_task_title: Cognitive Aid Design Using Augmented Reality to Support Attention
experiment_description:
OBJCTIVES:
A cognitive aid is an accessory used to alleviate mental demand or to direct attention, decisions, and action towards the completion of a task. Aids improve performance by providing decision support, information, attentional guidance, and memory support to obviate human perceptual, cognitive, and communication limitations. Augmented reality (AR) cognitive aid research and applications tend to focus on the addition of visual elements to the environment, such as virtual objects, labels, highlights, or navigation arrows. Auditory augmentations are similarly additive, with sound or voice overlays triggered by interfaces, operator location, or other physical world events.

Another form of AR, diminished reality (DR), focuses on subtracting elements from the environment, both auditory and visual. This method of capturing and supporting attention works by de-emphasizing nuisance portions of the task or environment. Focusing operator attention via de-emphasis is crucial, as the human ability to ignore or inhibit responses to distracting stimuli decreases with fatigue, environmental exposure, and information overload - all scenarios likely in long-term spaceflight. With the advent of augmented reality, it is possible to de-emphasize visual and auditory elements of the task and environment. Though there are products that can de-emphasize ambient sound (e.g., “hearables”), there is no research on using de-emphasis to aid attentional focus. There is also no research on how de-emphasis should look or react to the intent of the operator, necessitating the design of new methods of human-computer interaction.

This study will investigate the design and benefit of AR in a cognitive aid for medical equipment setup via the following aims:
1. Design and create a visual and auditory de-emphasized AR user-centered prototype, and
2. Develop DR technology guidelines for future use in cognitive aids.

APPROACH:
Two experiments were conducted to understand the effects of universal and selective (context-aware) diminishment of distraction on performance, situational awareness, and subjective experience of workload in a novel assembly task. In both experiments, participants used procedural instructions to assemble a medical ventilator for use during a simulated emergency in virtual reality. In both experiments, the type of diminishment was manipulated within participants, so that each participant experienced universal attenuation of visual and auditory distraction, context-aware diminishment of the same, and a control condition with all distractions present. In the first experiment, participants experienced universal attenuation of distraction, via blurring of their peripheral vision and lowered volume for all audio. In the second experiment, attenuation was context-aware: only non-task objects were made less visible and only unimportant off-task audio was dampened.

RESULTS:
In Experiment 1, workload was perceived to be lower in the Universal DR condition compared to the control. In Experiment 2, JSC participants perceived lower workload in both DR conditions compared to control. In many studies, perceived workload changes when performance does not because participants are able to put forth the effort needed to perform even when the task is extremely difficult.. The JSC participants, with their longer work histories and experience in problem-solving for ambiguous tasks, were likely able to keep up their performance even in the control condition, though they were also sensitive to how much harder they had to work to do so.

Both graduate student and JSC participant groups were highly educated; however, the JSC participants also had work experience in science and technology. The differences in results between the experiments was the lack of performance differences by condition for the JSC participants, while those STEM graduate programs accomplished more steps in the Context-Aware condition compared to Control and had lower errors in the Universal DR condition compared to control. The same was true for situational awareness measures: diminishment harmed situational awareness for label locations and knowledge of the external concurrent emergency for the STEM graduate students, but not for those at JSC. One explanation might be the smaller sample size of JSC participants in Experiment 2, though the within-subject design meant that both experiments were adequately powered. However, even when ignoring significance, there were no trends toward performance differences in Experiment 2.

experiment_title: HCAAM VNSCOR: Responsive Multimodal Human-Automation Communication for Augmenting Human Situation Awareness in Nominal and Off-Nominal Scenarios
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES
Crew extravehicular activity (EVA) is limited on spaceflight missions. Multiple, small robotic spacecrafts with varying levels of autonomy are needed to perform tasks that might have been completed by an astronaut (e.g., an exterior surface inspection or repair). Crews on long duration exploration missions (LDEM) will have less access to ground support during task operations. As a result, they will need to process more information and communicate with autonomous robots effectively to ensure tasks are progressing safely and on schedule.
The objective of these studies are to investigate the use of virtual reality (VR) multimodal interface displays and communication pathways for improving human-robot communication, situation awareness (SA), trust, and task performance. This will lead to developing guidelines for designing human-robot system interactions that enable operational performance for crews on spaceflight missions.
 
The specific aims are to:
 
1) Develop a simulation testbed for examining communication between human-robot teams.
 
2) Develop a hardware testbed for examining communication between human-robot teams.
 
3) Evaluate human SA, trust, and task performance within a short duration and long-duration ground-based study (simulation and/or hardware) through testing various interface communication modalities and information displays.
 
4) (Option) Perform follow up studies for additional parameters of interest that could be tested using the study set up. Additional parameters include timing and persistence of information, gesture command mapping, or varying the levels of robot automation
 
5) (Option) Extend the ground-based study to a flight demonstration aboard the International Space Station (ISS)

APPROACH
 
Proposed ground testbed will simulate an LDEM inspection task. In some trials, the human subjects maneuver free-flying vehicles to obtain video imagery of the space craft exterior. In other trials the human subjects will only perform visual inspection of previously collected imagery.
 
The satellites used in the simulation study are modeled after the Synchronized Position Hold Engage Reorient Experimental Satellites (SPHERES). SPHERES are small free-floating autonomous satellites that have been used to study precision navigation and maneuvering in zero gravity experiments aboard the ISS as well as in ground-based experiments. These satellites are predecessors to the newer Astrobees satellites, which are now on the ISS.
 
For the ground-based hardware testbed, we integrate small drones to simulate the 3D positioning of a small satellite for a ground-environment. Video imagery captured by cameras on the drones will be used for automatic scene reconstruction to enhance astronaut perception of the environment. This creates a 3D model of the environment which can then by manipulated in the AR display for navigation and to obtain feedback of the surroundings.
For the simulation studies, subjects will be asked to navigate one or more semi-autonomous satellites to perform exterior inspection of a simulated “station.” Simulations will include surface anomalies that are critical and non-critical that must be discovered. Subjects will be able to control the direction of the satellites by using a joystick, computer keypad, or gesture (depending on the study phase).
 
Three visual interfaces will be examined: (1) The computer screen (CS nominal) mode provides the camera images obtained from the satellites and cameras on the station mock-up on computer monitors, (2) The computer screen exocentric mode (CS exocentric) provides an additional exocentric view on a separate computer monitor, and (3) AR environment (AR exocentric) which presents a scaled 3D model of the station mock-up to the subject built from the satellite camera images. Optional studies will include levels of automation, additional command inputs, and added environmental complexities.
 
Short-term studies will collect data over a span of two days, recording measures such as task completion time, number of anomalies detected, trust, mental workload, and SA. Long-term studies include testing within HERA campaigns, which will be 45 days long. Here additional analysis will examine how human-robot interaction strategies change with longer exposures.

RESULTS

The PI team performed 5 studies associated with this research program. The U-M Inspection Study and the HERA Inspection study used the simulation testbed for the inspection task. This simulation testbed was then extended to address additional research questions for the Docking Study. These studies addressed Aim 3. Aim 4 included 2 studies that evaluated the influence of the AR display modality on sensorimotor performance. The studies that addressed Aim 4 were the Sensorimotor Study and the Dynamic and Operational Task Study.
Both the HERA and U-M inspection studies support decreased detection accuracy using AR for this task and increase in detection accuracy during Synchronous interactions. Additional interactions with the simulation did not improve the AR outcomes to match that of the 2D display. Factors influencing the decrease in performance of AR for this task include the reduced contrast and resolution of the presented image, as well as reliability of hand interactions.
The UM docking study formalized the construct of path legibility, which presented a way to incorporate human interpretation of the motion plan into control systems, potentially supporting monitor situation awareness by influencing the monitor's takeover decision-making. The motion plan of a robotic agent is another communication pathway that can be used to convey information and support human decision making.
The UM sensorimotor study considered how holographic targets impact users’ accuracy, precision, movement time, throughput, and error rates when compared to a touchscreen device. Four distinct AR errors were discovered with varying frequencies of occurrence. The highest frequency errors were misalignments across all three axes (70.4% of errors), implying that the fingertip was not aligned in the button plane or depth axis. The second highest frequency error were misalignments in the depth axis (20.7% of errors). The tactile feedback and physical touch limits offered by the touchscreen may have supported the improved accuracy over AR where the finger was free to travel through the target.
In the UM Dynamic Operational Tasks study, the participants were able to complete both tasks in AR and meaningful measures of postural control were obtained, indicating that although different baseline performance is obtained, AR may be a useful instrumentation solution with embedded sensors to evaluate a variety of populations for postural control. The differences observed support the need for implementation- specific baselines. Participants adopted strategies similar to sensorimotor impaired crewmembers, with increased task time and reduced head and torso angular velocities. Contrastingly, participants exhibited increased head pitch angles, which is typically reduced in astronauts postflight.

experiment_title: Printed Electrochemical Sensor Strip for Quantifying Bone Density Loss in Microgravity
hrr_task_title: Printed Electrochemical Sensor Strip for Quantifying Bone Density Loss in Microgravity (Koehne)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Without the load-bearing forces of gravity experienced on earth, astronauts have an increased risk of bone-related injuries resulting from changes in bone mineral density. Microgravity disrupts the balance between bone formation and bone resorption which can lead to the development of space osteopenia/osteoporosis after extended exposure to microgravity, which can manifest in a reduction of bone density by 1 to 1.6%. Development of a sensor that monitors reliable biomarkers of bone loss is a critically important step to help mitigate this specific risk. This experiment aimed to develop a flight suitable sensor that evaluated the change in bone mass indirectly through an excreted biomarker of bone remodeling, amino-terminal collagen crosslinks (NTX). NTX, a degradation by-product of Type I collagen, is widely measured in clinical bone resorption studies and is considered a biomarker of interest when evaluating bone health.

Bone density loss is currently evaluated through the measurement of bone mineral density by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of flight crew before and after spaceflight. However, DXA only provides partial information regarding bone strength and cannot detect the early shift of bone metabolism. Several bone remodeling biomarkers have been identified and used to provide an early assessment of bone loss, when DXA data is insufficient to make a diagnosis. Moreover, the equipment necessary for DXA is bulky, heavy, and energy inefficient, making it incompatible for flight. The proposed printed bone health sensor would be more suitable for spaceflight due to its versatility, size, and ease of use. Not only is the necessary hardware more compact than DXA equipment, but the sensor is also conducive to potential in-flight manufacturing using commercially available materials for inkjet printing.

This study had the following specific aims:
  1. Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor.
  2. Print and electrochemically characterize 3-electrode device for NTX detection.
  3. Integrate sensor with urine collection device and handheld potentiostat hardware.

APPROACH:
Aim 1: Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor.
a) Develop conductive and dielectric inks
Both commercial and home-made inks were evaluated for this study. JS-B40G silver nanoparticle (AgNP) ink, XP PriElex SU-8 1.0, and 7500 Series carbon nanotube (CNT) were used without modification as inkjet conductive and dielectric inks. BQ242 carbon, FE3124 silver, and 5880 silver|silver chloride (Ag|AgCl) were used without modification. Home-made carboxylic acid functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT-COOH) ink was modified in house by refluxing commercial MWCNT-COOH in 56% nitric acid for 8 hours, sonicating by probe sonication for 3 hours, and finally resuspending in water. Home-made gold nanoparticle (AuNP) ink was synthesized using the Tukevich method and then resuspending in water. Homemade inks were evaluated by dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis to measure particle size and surface charge.

b) Develop telopeptide selective ink and conjugation reactant
Telopeptide selective inks of AuNP functionalized with NTx were prepared. A solution of 10 nM citrate capped AuNP (AuNP@citrate), 0.028% SDS in water and 0.015 mg/mL of HS-PEG-COOH was incubated overnight at room temperature. The solution was washed with DI water, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and resuspended in 25 mM MES pH 5.5 to remove excess PEG, yielding pegylated AuNP (AuNP@PEG-COOH). To 20 mL of 1 nM AuNP@PEG-COOH 250 μL of EDC (0.2M) and 500 μL of NHS (0.2M) were added. The solution was allowed to incubate for 30 minutes at room temperature, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and suspended in 10 mM phosphate buffer pH 7.4, yielding EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH. 100 μL of NTx (1 mg/mL) was added to the EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH solution and incubated overnight at room temperature. The resulting AuNP@PEG-NTx solution was centrifuged twice at 14000 xg for 30 minutes at 4°C and finally suspended in DI water as the telopeptide selective ink. The telopeptide ink was evaluated at each step of preparation, AuNP@citrate, AuNP@PEG-COOH, and AuNP@PEG-NTx, by UV-Vis, dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis (ZetaSizer Nano, Malvern PANanalytical, Westborough, MA) to measure particle size and surface charge. The AuNP@PEG-NTx will be referred to as AuNPNTx for simplicity.

c) Develop Anti-NTx conjugate
Conjugate antibody was prepared for the sensor’s competitive assay. Methylene blue-NHS was covalently bound to Anti-NTx using EDC/NHS coupling chemistry to form Anti-NTx-MB. 100 μl of antibody (0.4 mg/ml) were incubated with 10 μL of methylene blue (1 mM) for 1 hour. The labeling reaction was dialyzed using a 10 kDa molecular weight cut off dialysis membrane against PBS. The PBS was substituted with fresh PBS twice (every 2 hours) and left to dialyze overnight.

Aim 2: Print and electrochemically characterize 3-electrode device for NTx detection.
a) Print sensor
3-electrode electrochemical sensors, containing a working electrode (WE), counter electrode (CE) and reference electrode (RE), have been prepared by the following two methods: 1) precision microdispense printing by an nScrypt 3Dn-Series printer and 2) dropcast method. All sensors were print onto Kapton 500HN as the substrate material. To generate the base architecture of the electrochemical sensors, precision microdispense printing was performed. A nScrypt 3Dn-Series printer was used to laser cut 3 holes through a Kapton substrate. Next, FE3124 silver ink was microdispense printed inside the 3 holes to create a via structure and around the holes on one side of the Kapton to form the contact pads. Finally, the substrate was flipped over to expose the front side of the device. 5880 Ag|AgCl ink was microdispensed to form the RE and BQ242 ink was microdispensed to form the WE and CE. All prints were performed at the NextFlex Research Institute in San Jose, CA and delivered to the NASA ARC team for evaluation, electrochemical characterization, and further modification with 7500 Series CNT and AuNP-NTx inks.

To generate the telopeptide sensing surface, modification of the WE were performed first by a drop cast method and finally by inkjet printing. For the drop cast method, 0.5 μL of 7500 Series CNT ink was pipet on the WE surface and annealed at 125°C on a hotplate for 15 min. Finally, 1 μL of AuNP-NTx (37 nM) ink was pipet on the CNT modified WE surface and dried at 42°C for 10 min. The resulting electrochemical sensors were characterized immediately or stored in a petri dish at 4°C. For inkjet printing, the 45 layers of the 7500 Series CNT ink were deposited on the surface of the WE. The printing bed was heated to 60 °C and the print head was heated to 42°C. The CNTs were then dried at 125 °C in a convection oven at 125 °C for 15 min. The electrodes sheet was then loaded and aligned in the inkjet printer. 10 layers of the AuNP-NTx selective ink were then deposited on top of the CNT modified WE. For this deposition the print bed temperature was lowered to 40 °C and the printhead was kept at 42 °C. The resulting electrochemical sensors were characterized immediately or stored in a petri dish at 4°C.

b) Develop fluidics
Fluid delivery was accomplished using a lateral flow assay assembly. A lateral flow assay’s fluid handling components consist of various layered wicking materials that are assembled in a plastic cartridge. A sample pad consisting of bound glass fiber was placed under the sample inlet port of the top of the cartridge. A conjugation pad consisting of glass fiber and containing the dried anti-NTx conjugate was placed overlapping and underneath the sample pad. A membrane of nitrocellulose served as the fluid delivery layer and contacted the printed sensor, the conjugate pad and a waste pad consisting of high purity cotton fibers. All the layered wicking materials and the printed sensor were arranged in a clamshell configured plastic cartridge with top and bottom components that snap closed for a tight fit. The lateral flow’s fluid delivery was evaluated by assembling and running an optical assay through the assembled fluid handling layers. The conjugate pad was cut to size and saturated with 1× PBS pH 7.4, 1% BSA, 2% sucrose, 0.25% Tween 20 and dried in a convection oven at 37 °C for 2 hours. 2 μl of 70 μg/mL Anti-NTx-HRP were diluted in 18 μL of PBS and these 20 μL were pipet onto the conjugate pad and dried in a convection oven at 37 °C for 1 hour. The conjugate pads were used immediately or stored in a sealed microcentrifuge tube at room temperature. For the lateral flow fluid delivery experiment, 100 μL PBS was introduced and let flow for 10 min. It was then dried at 42 °C for 1 hour. Next, 100 μL of 3,3’5,5’-Tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) solution was placed in the sample inlet and allowed to flow for 15 minutes. Finally, the cassette was disassembled and the TMB colorimetric product was observed on the waste pad.

c) Validate sensor performance
The sensor was designed as a competitive assay. Briefly, AuNP-NTx on the WE surface served as a recognition element. If NTx is present from the specimen, it binds to the Anti-NTx-MB from the conjugate pad and thus eliminates the Anti-NTx-MB ability to bind to the NTx on the AuNP-NTx on the WE. To optimize the assay and demonstrate electrochemical readout, incubation steps were first performed without the nitrocellulose fluidics. 20 μL of Anti-NTx-MB (128 μg/mL) with various amounts of NTx specimen (0 to 100 nM) and allowed to incubate 30 minutes. The resulting mixture was incubated for 30 min on the AuNP-NTx WE surface. The sensor was washed with PBS and electrochemical measurements were performed in K4Fe(CN)6/K3Fe(CN)6 in PBS. Electrochemical measurements of cyclic voltammetry, differential pulse voltammetry and electrochemical impedance were acquired using an EmSTAT Pico Development Kit. Cyclic voltammograms were performed sweeping potentials of -0.2 to 0.6 V at 50 mV/sec. Cathodic and Anodic peak heights and peak-to-peak separation were recorded. Differential pulse voltammetry was performed from -0.2 to 0.6 V with step size of 0.005 V. Electrochemical impedance spectra were acquired from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. Resulting Nyquist plots were analyzed by NOVA software and charge transfer resistance (RCT) were recorded.

Aim 3: Integrate sensor with urine collection device and handheld potentiostat hardware.
d) Package the sensor
The printed sensor was packaged in a lateral flow cassette with lateral flow materials. The lateral flow cassette was cut to allow the electrical contact pads of the electrochemical sensor to extend outside of the lateral flow device. An EmSTAT Pico Development Kit was used as the potentiostat to drive and read the sensor. __description:
OBJECTIVES:
Without the load-bearing forces of gravity experienced on earth, astronauts have an increased risk of bone-related injuries resulting from changes in bone mineral density. Microgravity disrupts the balance between bone formation and bone resorption which can lead to the development of space osteopenia/osteoporosis after extended exposure to microgravity, which can manifest in a reduction of bone density by 1 to 1.6%. Development of a sensor that monitors reliable biomarkers of bone loss is a critically important step to help mitigate this specific risk. This experiment aimed to develop a flight suitable sensor that evaluated the change in bone mass indirectly through an excreted biomarker of bone remodeling, amino-terminal collagen crosslinks (NTX). NTX, a degradation by-product of Type I collagen, is widely measured in clinical bone resorption studies and is considered a biomarker of interest when evaluating bone health.

Bone density loss is currently evaluated through the measurement of bone mineral density by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of flight crew before and after spaceflight. However, DXA only provides partial information regarding bone strength and cannot detect the early shift of bone metabolism. Several bone remodeling biomarkers have been identified and used to provide an early assessment of bone loss, when DXA data is insufficient to make a diagnosis. Moreover, the equipment necessary for DXA is bulky, heavy, and energy inefficient, making it incompatible for flight. The proposed printed bone health sensor would be more suitable for spaceflight due to its versatility, size, and ease of use. Not only is the necessary hardware more compact than DXA equipment, but the sensor is also conducive to potential in-flight manufacturing using commercially available materials for inkjet printing.

This study had the following specific aims:
  1. Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor.
  2. Print and electrochemically characterize 3-electrode device for NTX detection.
  3. Integrate sensor with urine collection device and handheld potentiostat hardware.

APPROACH:
Aim 1: Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor.
a) Develop conductive and dielectric inks
Both commercial and home-made inks were evaluated for this study. JS-B40G silver nanoparticle (AgNP) ink, XP PriElex SU-8 1.0, and 7500 Series carbon nanotube (CNT) were used without modification as inkjet conductive and dielectric inks. BQ242 carbon, FE3124 silver, and 5880 silver|silver chloride (Ag|AgCl) were used without modification. Home-made carboxylic acid functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT-COOH) ink was modified in house by refluxing commercial MWCNT-COOH in 56% nitric acid for 8 hours, sonicating by probe sonication for 3 hours, and finally resuspending in water. Home-made gold nanoparticle (AuNP) ink was synthesized using the Tukevich method and then resuspending in water. Homemade inks were evaluated by dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis to measure particle size and surface charge.

b) Develop telopeptide selective ink and conjugation reactant
Telopeptide selective inks of AuNP functionalized with NTx were prepared. A solution of 10 nM citrate capped AuNP (AuNP@citrate), 0.028% SDS in water and 0.015 mg/mL of HS-PEG-COOH was incubated overnight at room temperature. The solution was washed with DI water, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and resuspended in 25 mM MES pH 5.5 to remove excess PEG, yielding pegylated AuNP (AuNP@PEG-COOH). To 20 mL of 1 nM AuNP@PEG-COOH 250 μL of EDC (0.2M) and 500 μL of NHS (0.2M) were added. The solution was allowed to incubate for 30 minutes at room temperature, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and suspended in 10 mM phosphate buffer pH 7.4, yielding EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH. 100 μL of NTx (1 mg/mL) was added to the EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH solution and incubated overnight at room temperature. The resulting AuNP@PEG-NTx solution was centrifuged twice at 14000 xg for 30 minutes at 4°C and finally suspended in DI water as the telopeptide selective ink. The telopeptide ink was evaluated at each step of preparation, AuNP@citrate, AuNP@PEG-COOH, and AuNP@PEG-NTx, by UV-Vis, dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis (ZetaSizer Nano, Malvern PANanalytical, Westborough, MA) to measure particle size and surface charge. The AuNP@PEG-NTx will be referred to as AuNPNTx for simplicity.

c) Develop Anti-NTx conjugate
Conjugate antibody was prepared for the sensor’s competitive assay. Methylene blue-NHS was covalently bound to Anti-NTx using EDC/NHS coupling chemistry to form Anti-NTx-MB. 100 μl of antibody (0.4 mg/ml) were incubated with 10 μL of methylene blue (1 mM) for 1 hour. The labeling reaction was dialyzed using a 10 kDa molecular weight cut off dialysis membrane against PBS. The PBS was substituted with fresh PBS twice (every 2 hours) and left to dialyze overnight.

Aim 2: Print and electrochemically characterize 3-electrode device for NTx detection.
a) Print sensor
3-electrode electrochemical sensors, containing a working electrode (WE), counter electrode (CE) and reference electrode (RE), have been prepared by the following two methods: 1) precision microdispense printing by an nScrypt 3Dn-Series printer and 2) dropcast method. All sensors were print onto Kapton 500HN as the substrate material. To generate the base architecture of the electrochemical sensors, precision microdispense printing was performed. A nScrypt 3Dn-Series printer was used to laser cut 3 holes through a Kapton substrate. Next, FE3124 silver ink was microdispense printed inside the 3 holes to create a via structure and around the holes on one side of the Kapton to form the contact pads. Finally, the substrate was flipped over to expose the front side of the device. 5880 Ag|AgCl ink was microdispensed to form the RE and BQ242 ink was microdispensed to form the WE and CE. All prints were performed at the NextFlex Research Institute in San Jose, CA and delivered to the NASA ARC team for evaluation, electrochemical characterization, and further modification with 7500 Series CNT and AuNP-NTx inks.

To generate the telopeptide sensing surface, modification of the WE were performed first by a drop cast method and finally by inkjet printing. For the drop cast method, 0.5 μL of 7500 Series CNT ink was pipet on the WE surface and annealed at 125°C on a hotplate for 15 min. Finally, 1 μL of AuNP-NTx (37 nM) ink was pipet on the CNT modified WE surface and dried at 42°C for 10 min. The resulting electrochemical sensors were characterized immediately or stored in a petri dish at 4°C. For inkjet printing, the 45 layers of the 7500 Series CNT ink were deposited on the surface of the WE. The printing bed was heated to 60 °C and the print head was heated to 42°C. The CNTs were then dried at 125 °C in a convection oven at 125 °C for 15 min. The electrodes sheet was then loaded and aligned in the inkjet printer. 10 layers of the AuNP-NTx selective ink were then deposited on top of the CNT modified WE. For this deposition the print bed temperature was lowered to 40 °C and the printhead was kept at 42 °C. The resulting electrochemical sensors were characterized immediately or stored in a petri dish at 4°C.

b) Develop fluidics
Fluid delivery was accomplished using a lateral flow assay assembly. A lateral flow assay’s fluid handling components consist of various layered wicking materials that are assembled in a plastic cartridge. A sample pad consisting of bound glass fiber was placed under the sample inlet port of the top of the cartridge. A conjugation pad consisting of glass fiber and containing the dried anti-NTx conjugate was placed overlapping and underneath the sample pad. A membrane of nitrocellulose served as the fluid delivery layer and contacted the printed sensor, the conjugate pad and a waste pad consisting of high purity cotton fibers. All the layered wicking materials and the printed sensor were arranged in a clamshell configured plastic cartridge with top and bottom components that snap closed for a tight fit. The lateral flow’s fluid delivery was evaluated by assembling and running an optical assay through the assembled fluid handling layers. The conjugate pad was cut to size and saturated with 1× PBS pH 7.4, 1% BSA, 2% sucrose, 0.25% Tween 20 and dried in a convection oven at 37 °C for 2 hours. 2 μl of 70 μg/mL Anti-NTx-HRP were diluted in 18 μL of PBS and these 20 μL were pipet onto the conjugate pad and dried in a convection oven at 37 °C for 1 hour. The conjugate pads were used immediately or stored in a sealed microcentrifuge tube at room temperature. For the lateral flow fluid delivery experiment, 100 μL PBS was introduced and let flow for 10 min. It was then dried at 42 °C for 1 hour. Next, 100 μL of 3,3’5,5’-Tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) solution was placed in the sample inlet and allowed to flow for 15 minutes. Finally, the cassette was disassembled and the TMB colorimetric product was observed on the waste pad.

c) Validate sensor performance
The sensor was designed as a competitive assay. Briefly, AuNP-NTx on the WE surface served as a recognition element. If NTx is present from the specimen, it binds to the Anti-NTx-MB from the conjugate pad and thus eliminates the Anti-NTx-MB ability to bind to the NTx on the AuNP-NTx on the WE. To optimize the assay and demonstrate electrochemical readout, incubation steps were first performed without the nitrocellulose fluidics. 20 μL of Anti-NTx-MB (128 μg/mL) with various amounts of NTx specimen (0 to 100 nM) and allowed to incubate 30 minutes. The resulting mixture was incubated for 30 min on the AuNP-NTx WE surface. The sensor was washed with PBS and electrochemical measurements were performed in K4Fe(CN)6/K3Fe(CN)6 in PBS. Electrochemical measurements of cyclic voltammetry, differential pulse voltammetry and electrochemical impedance were acquired using an EmSTAT Pico Development Kit. Cyclic voltammograms were performed sweeping potentials of -0.2 to 0.6 V at 50 mV/sec. Cathodic and Anodic peak heights and peak-to-peak separation were recorded. Differential pulse voltammetry was performed from -0.2 to 0.6 V with step size of 0.005 V. Electrochemical impedance spectra were acquired from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. Resulting Nyquist plots were analyzed by NOVA software and charge transfer resistance (RCT) were recorded.

Aim 3: Integrate sensor with urine collection device and handheld potentiostat hardware.
d) Package the sensor
The printed sensor was packaged in a lateral flow cassette with lateral flow materials. The lateral flow cassette was cut to allow the electrical contact pads of the electrochemical sensor to extend outside of the lateral flow device. An EmSTAT Pico Development Kit was used as the potentiostat to drive and read the sensor. The electrical contact pads of the packaged sensor were interfaced with the EmSTAT Pico by a screen printed electrode (SPE) adapter/connector for simple and reproducible measurement setup. Lastly, the lateral flow design of the packaged sensor was chosen to easily interface with the urine collection vessel. The urine collection vessel has a spigot at the bottom, used to evacuate the vessel. The lateral flow sensor can be placed in direct contact with the spigot of the urine collection vessel to deliver 1 drop of urine to the inlet port of the lateral flow sensor.


RESULTS:
The NTx printed sensor strip was successfully prototyped using an In-Space Manufacturing approach. A combination of CNT and AuNP inks were used to improve the sensors electrochemical response and provide a simple method of manufacturing the telopeptide selective ink. Sensor manufacturing proved to be very reproducible with sensor devices achieving a suitable variance for real testing applications. The lateral flow fluid delivery provided a simple method of delivering liquid specimens to the sensor surface without the need for more complex microfluidics and/or crew provided laboratory operations. The packaged sensor design provided a reliable interface between the urine collection device and handheld potentiostat reader. Lastly, detection of NTx was accomplished in low concentrations, down to 0.1 nM NTx, for a sensitive measurement.

investigators: Principal Investigator: LeBlanc, Adrian
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In microgravity, bones and muscles are not used as they are on Earth. As many studies have shown, this altered use results in calcium loss, degeneration of the skeleton, lengthening of the spine by expansion of the intervertebral discs, change in spinal bone marrow composition and muscle atrophy. Bedrest patients on earth show this same musculo-skeletal response with the exception of bone marrow alterations.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is one method that can be used to measure the resulting muscular and skeletal changes. MRI is a safe, non-invasive scanning technique that uses a large magnet and low frequency radio waves to form an image by reading the amount of hydrogen in an area of the body. These images can be used to examine soft tissues in the body, as well as determine muscle volume, spinal bone marrow mass and cross-sectional area of intervertebral discs. This investigation examined the muscle, intervertebral disc, and bone marrow changes in several crewmembers of varying ages and compared the results to data from previous studies.

APPROACH:
Imaging was performed pre- and postflight using a 1.5 Tesla Siemens Magnetom MRI system (1.5 Tesla denotes the strength of the magnet used for the test) with various coils, including spine, Helmholz neck and whole body coils. These coils are the antenna of the MRI system that broadcast the radio frequency signal to the patient and/or receive the return signal to form an image. Specific coils are used to image different parts of the body1 for example, Helmholz coils are used to image the cervical spine and muscles in the neck.

MRI testing consisted of the following:

• Bone marrow spectroscopy (L3)
• Muscle volume of the back, calf and thigh
• Muscle T2 (spin-spin relaxation time) of the calf and thigh
• Intervertebral disc area, spine length and T2 (lumbar vertebrae (L)1-5)

The crew also filled out questionnaires during flight and postflight to document the frequency, severity and location of back pain or discomfort.

RESULTS:
During the mission, all muscle regions except the hamstrings significantly decreased 3-10% compared with baseline. During the shuttle/Mir missions, there were significant decreases in muscle volume (5-17%) in all muscle groups except the neck. These changes, which reached a new steady state by 4 months of flight or less, were reversed within 30-60 days after landing. Postflight swelling and elevation of calf muscle transverse relaxation time persisted for several weeks after flight, which suggests possible muscle damage. In contrast to the 17-day flight, in which loss in fat, but not lean body mass, was found, losses in bone mineral content and lean body mass, but not fat, were seen after the longer shuttle/Mir missions. The percent losses in total body lean body mass and bone mineral content were similar at approximately 3.4-3.5%, whereas the pelvis demonstrated the largest regional bone loss at 13%.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Postflight orthostatic hypotension has been noted since the Mercury flights and can be expected after exposures to weightlessness. Orthostatic hypotension arises from fluid shifts, fluid loss, decreased peak physical loads, and from neurological adaptation. Due to concerns related to hypotension during Space Shuttle reentry, crewmembers were provided with antigravity suits (AGSs).
Concerns were expressed over orthostatic problems directly affecting the astronauts during and immediately following reentry.

APPROACH:
Blood pressure and heart rate were the standards by which orthostatic status was determined. A commercial blood pressure-heart rate recorder was used in space motion sickness (SMS) studies on several missions, and by one crewmember during reentry with AGS activation and deactivation. After several near-syncopal (fainting) episodes on Shuttle missions following seat egress, presumed to be orthostatic hypotension, this experiment was designed to make a series of blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) records during entry and egress.
The BP-HR recorder was an extensively tested and used, commercially available, ambulatory unit. More information is provided in the hardware description below.
For preflight tests, the subject had a 30 minute briefing session on the recorder use and then made two recordings during simulations. For in-flight and postflight tests, 30 minutes was required for installation of the recorder; it was a one person effort, except for the wrapping of the arm cuff, which involved a second crewmember for less than one minute. The recorder was installed and started at least 30 minutes prior to strapping in for reentry. The recorder was carried on an elastic waist belt and did not interfere with other hardware. The recorder was worn through reentry without any restrictions on the crewmember. Inflation of the AGS was done as desired.

RESULTS:
Ambulatory blood pressures (BP) and heart rates (HR) were recorded on a series of early Shuttle flights during preflight and pre-entry, entry, landing and egress. There were no significant differences between flight and preflight values during routine activity. Systolic blood pressure was slightly elevated in the deorbit period and systolic and diastolic blood pressure and heart rates were all elevated with onset of gravitoinertial loads and remained so through egress. Two of seven subjects had orthostatic problems in egress but their data did not show significant differences from others, except in heart rate. Comparison of this data to data from recent studies show even larger increase in HR/BP values during current deorbit and entry phases, which is consistent with increased heat and weight loads imposed by added survival gear. Both value and limitations of ambulatory heart rate/blood pressure data in this situation are demonstrated.

investigators: Principal Investigator: O'Banion, Kerry
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study examines inflammatory responses following exposure to space radiation. In particular, investigators sought to explore the effects of protons and mixed particle radiation, at doses and fluences expected during space travel, in the brain and lung as well as the systemic circulation of mice. Dose and time dependent alteration in inflammatory indices will be correlated with brain and lung degenerative changes, including failure of hippocampal neurogenesis and alterations in hippocampal dependent learning. Investigators also explored whether space radiation influences Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis using a unique transgenic mouse model and lung inflammation following challenge with inhaled lipopolysaccharide. Together these studies address specific gaps in the current knowledge about the acute and late effects of space radiation on vulnerable tissues.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Based on the studies conducted in this grant, the following conclusions can be made:
• Acute 1000 MeV/n proton exposure and simulated solar flare exposures at doses up to 200 cGy showed no demonstrable effects on hippocampal-dependent memory as assessed by contextual fear conditioning at times ranging from 3 to 12 months post irradiation in both male and female C57BL/6 mice irradiated at 10-12 weeks of age.
• These same exposures reduced acute (within first 12 h) proliferation of adult hippocampal neural precursor cells with dose effects as low at 50 cGy for male mice and 10 cGy for female mice, but had modest or no effects on long term hippocampal neurogenesis assessed by doublecortin staining.
• Neuroinflammatory changes assessed by markers of glial or endothelial activation were essentially absent in brains from mice irradiated under the conditions described above.
• Addition of 10 cGy HZE irradiation (1000 MeV/n iron particles) further reduced acute neural precursor proliferation, but otherwise showed no effect in other measured indices.
• There was no evidence of radiation induced late effects in lung tissue or exacerbation of inhaled LPS exposure.
• APPswe/PS-1dE9 transgenic mice showed behavioral deficits and increased amyloid plaque burden following exposure to 1000 MeV/n iron particles; the later effect was observed in male mice at 9.5 months of age, 6 months post 100 cGy irradiation.

One caveat of this work was the choice of contextual fear conditioning for the behavioral assay. The adoption of this approach was based on previous experience exploring cognitive changes following neuroinflammation localized to the hippocampus and discussions with other NASA investigators, who had also adopted this approach for their work. More recent work suggests that other tasks may be more sensitive to radiation, including novel object recognition, which investigators did incorporate into some of their later studies. Selection of the proper tests for behavioral effects remains a major challenge, particularly with mice.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Azzam, EdouardCo-Investigator: de Toledo, SoniaCo-Investigator: Harris, AndrewCo-Investigator: Howell, RogerCo-Investigator: Pain, Debkumar
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this project is to investigate biochemical and molecular aspects of two inter-related fundamental biological processes, namely gap-junction intercellular communication and oxidative metabolism, in determining human cellular responses to exposures of very low to moderate fluences of protons (of energies such as found in the space environment) or high charge (Z) and high energy (E) particles (1 GeV/nucleon 56Fe ions). Gap junctions are found between most cells in the body, and the molecular signaling they mediate is crucial for normal development, physiology and response to disease. By allowing direct intercellular transfer of cytoplasmic molecules, they provide a powerful pathway for direct molecular signaling between cells. On the other hand, oxidative metabolism is primarily regulated by mitochondria, which mediate respiration and ATP synthesis in eukaryotic cells. They also participate in numerous indispensable metabolic pathways. It is hypothesized that exposure of human cells to high or low fluences of protons and/or HZE particles results in distinct molecular and biochemical changes not only in irradiated but also neighboring bystander cells. These events are modulated by oxidative metabolism and gap-junction coupling, which together induce persistent changes in mitochondria and in nuclear DNA in progeny of irradiated and affected bystander cells.

In Aim 1, it is proposed to define the aspect(s) of junctional communication leading to proton- and high charge/high energy (HZE) particle-induced toxic effects. Specifically, to examine the role of different connexin proteins in propagating death-inducing (growth delay, apoptosis) or pro-survival effects (proliferative capacity) among irradiated cells and also between irradiated and non-irradiated cells.

Aim 2 is to identify specific connexin channel permeabilities that correlate with intercellular propagation of toxic or protective effects in cultures exposed to HZE particles or protons. An emphasis will be to determine the nature of molecules communicated among irradiated cells and between irradiated and non-irradiated cells.

In Aim 3, mitochondrial function will be evaluated in cells exposed to low fluences of high energy charged particles. Specifically, mitochondrial protein import will be examined, mitochondrial protein synthesis, assembly of large protein complexes including respiratory complexes, and oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins and DNA. The persistence of oxidative effects in the progeny of exposed cells and correlate the observed results with the overall cellular redox environment will be evaulated.

APPROACH:
Eight-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to 0 or 50 cGy from 1100 MeV/nucleon titanium ions at the NASA’s Space Radiation Laboratory located at the Brookhaven National Laboratory in Upton, NY. During the irradiation, the rats were placed in well-ventilated plastic restraining tubes that restricted the movement of the animal. The plastic tube was placed perpendicular to the beam and positioned so that the head of the rats was in the center of the beam. As such, the rat’s shoulders may have also received some radiation dose.

RESULTS:
The role of in vivo investigation of intercellular communication and oxidative metabolism in the biological responses to high charge (Z) and high energy (E) HZE particles has been extended. Twelve-week-old and 9-months-old male mice have been exposed to low (5 cGy) or moderate (50 cGy) mean absorbed doses of 1000 MeV/amu iron ions or 500 MeV/amu titanium ions delivered to the whole body. In young mice, the regulation of the MAF1 protein has been identified, a downstream effector of the TOR (target of rapamycin) pathway that regulates various cellular functions in response to environmental cues, is highly sensitive to space particulate radiations. Maf1 has been implicated in processes related to protein biosynthesis and RNA maturation. It is essential for the activity of the enzyme RNA polymerase III that regulates cell growth and cell cycle progression. Global analyses of post-translational modification of proteins in organs of control and irradiated young mice has been performed. Specifically, S-nitrosylation of proteins from mice exposed to 5 or 50 cGy of energetic titanium ions has been analyzed. S-nitrosylation is emerging as a fundamental mechanism that modulates the function of several proteins engaged in many signaling pathways. Our results showed that S-nitrosylation of proteins in space irradiated rodents is organ and radiation dose dependent. The S-nitrosylation level of brain proteins was significantly increased after whole body exposure to a mean absorbed dose of 5 cGy. Compared to control, 151 proteins were identified as newly S-nitrosylated 12 days after irradiation. A large fraction of the proteins (56%) were classified as enzymes. Pathway analysis showed that they are related to free radical scavenging, cellular assembly and organization.

In vitro studies in progeny of non-targeted bystander cells that were co-cultured with HZE-particle irradiated cells have been extended. Several biological endpoints, including chromosomal damage, gene expression and cellular senescence have been analyzed. It has been confirmed that stressful effects propagated from irradiated to bystander cells persist in their progeny. It has been shown that functional gap junction coupling between parental bystander and irradiated donor cells is a critical mediator of the observed stressful effects.
