experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During future long duration missions, international crews will be engaged in complicated activities over long periods of time. A number of interpersonal issues likely to impact these missions must be addressed to ensure healthy crewmember interactions and optimal performance. The objectives of this study were to measure and characterize changes over time in a number of important interpersonal factors, such as tension, cohesion, leadership role, and the relationship between space crews and ground support personnel during the NASA/Mir missions.

The formal hypotheses addressed a number of aspects related to crew and ground control tension, cohesion, and leadership role. Over the course of long-term space missions, tension in the crew environment and crew cohesiveness were expected to change. Researchers expected an association between the level of tension in the crewmembers and their relationship with people on the ground, and between tension in mission control personnel and their relationship with management. Also, it was hypothesized that the perception of both the leadership role and outside monitoring support would change over time.

Although specific stressors that occur during the mission, there is evidence, can influence these issues, that time alone may be a factor. One approach, the biphasic model, proposes that significant psychological and interpersonal difficulties may occur after the halfway point of a mission. Hence, a sense of relief that half of the mission is over is outweighed by the realization that another half is yet to come, and this results in decrements in mood and interpersonal functioning of the crew. The triphasic model describes three phases of reaction for people working in isolating and confined conditions for long periods. The initial anxiety in the first few weeks are mainly due to the novelty of the situation; depression during the long middle period of the mission are mainly due to monotony and homesickness; and euphoria and adolescent behavior during the last few weeks due to anticipation of returning home.

When crews are composed of people from different countries or different ethnic backgrounds, language and cultural differences are important since they may lead to intra-crew tensions and disruptions in cohesion, and this in turn may negatively affect morale and interfere with the performance of mission tasks. Issues related to language and cultural differences have been reported in both simulation and space environments. Language and cultural issues also may adversely affect the interactions of mission control personnel on the ground, although these individuals have not been studied previously.

The relationship between the crewmembers and their mission control support personnel is important, since miscommunication or insensitivity between these two groups may lead to misaligned work schedules or inappropriate responses during times of danger. A phenomenon that may negatively influence crew ground communication is displacement, which occurs when tension and distressful dysphoric emotions (e.g., anger, depression) that arise within the crewmembers during the mission cannot be expressed openly and are instead transferred outside to ground personnel, who are perceived as unsupportive and negative. Interactions suggestive of displacement have been reported during space missions and during space simulation studies on Earth. In simulations, crewmember anger directed to outside monitors has been especially observed when overt anger and tension were not seen between the confined subjects, and vice versa.

Earlier work explored several of the above psychosocial issues in confined groups and included a questionnaire study of 54 astronauts and cosmonauts who had flown in space and a study of three male Russian subjects who were secluded in the Mir space station simulator in Moscow for 135 days. The study described in this paper involved a series of space missions in which two Russian cosmonauts and one American astronaut worked together on board the Mir space station for periods of four to seven months. The objectives of the study were to determine how tension, cohesion, and leader support affected the space crewmembers and mission control personnel on the ground and to determine how these factors changed over time.

Several of the hypotheses predicted decreases in crew behavior during the second half of the missions in accordance with the biphasic model. The value of the triphasic model was also explored and other time effects that might be present while the crewmembers were on orbit. As stated in the hypothesis, displacement of tension and dysphoria would occur from crewmembers to mission control personnel and from mission control personnel to management; differences in response between Russians and Americans and between crewmembers and mission control personnel, were explored. We made no predictions concerning these differences since little empirical evidence existed that would allow us to form hypotheses related to these socio-cultural factors.

APPROACH:
American astronauts, Russian cosmonauts, and American and Russian mission control personnel who were involved with the Shuttle/Mir space program were asked to participate in our study. The number of subjects who volunteered, gave informed consent, and participated in the study during the on orbit periods included 5 astronauts (in 5 U.S. missions), 8 cosmonauts (in 4 Russian missions), and 42 American and 16 Russian mission control personnel, who included flight surgeons, operations leads, engineers, mission scientists, spacecraft communicators, and psychological support staff.

To measure mood state and group interpersonal climate, standardized measures were used which have been shown to be valid and reliable in a number of studies on Earth. To assess emotions, we utilized the Profile of Mood States, or POMS, which consisted of 65 adjectives describing various affective states, such as "tense" and "cheerful", and were rated on a weekly basis by the subjects on 5 point Likert scales:

  • 0 = Not at all
  • 1 = A little
  • 2 = Moderately
  • 3 = Quite a bit
  • 4 = Extremely

    • To assess the interpersonal climate in the crew and mission control groups, subscales from two well-known instruments: the Group Environment Scale, or GES, and the Work Environment Scale, or WES. Both of these instruments measured dimensions of a group's interpersonal environment through subject endorsements of statements as being either "true" or "false" of their particular group during the previous week. An example of a question is: "There is a feeling of unity and cohesion in this group".

    Subscale scores were determined by summing the scores from related POMS, GES, or WES items. Examples of subscales were Tension-Anxiety (from the POMS), Cohesion (from the GES), and Supervisor Support (from the WES). Changes in subscale scores over time were regarded as alterations in the subjects' perception of mood and group climate. Descriptive analyses of the data suggested that the subjects considered the full range of responses when completing the measures. For example, on 63 of the 65 items from the Profile of Mood States, subjects gave all possible responses from 0-4 with exceptions for: "spiteful" and "forgetful", and on all 126 items from the GES and WES, subjects answered both true and false responses. For most items, however, the distributions were skewed in the direction of adaptive functioning (i.e., low values on negative subscales and high values on positive subscales).

    The above measures comprised our study questionnaire, which was available in both English and Russian computerized and hard copy formats. The questions took 15-20 minutes to complete. Both crew and ground subjects completed the questionnaire with reference to the preceding seven days Overall, 82% of the expected questionnaires were received from subjects participating during the on-orbit periods (70% from crewmembers and 85% from mission control personnel). This totaled 212 from crew subjects and 1,088 from ground subjects.

    Data analysis strategies

    One analyses examined the data for differences between U.S. and Russian subjects and between crewmembers and personnel in mission control personnel. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales. Subsequently, the number of observations that contributed to it weighted each mean, and a two-way repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed. The model included main effects for country (American, Russian), group (crewmember, mission control personnel), and their interactions.

    A second set of previous analyses dealt with hypotheses related to the displacement of negative emotions for both crew and ground subjects. Displacement was operationalized as the negative association between measures of tension and dysphoria with WES Supervisor Support over the course of a mission. For the crewmembers, supervisors were defined as members of the outside monitoring staff in mission control, and for the mission control subjects, supervisors were defined as members of the American or Russian space agency management staff. A mixed model analysis was used to test the effects for each measure of tension or dysphoria. During weeks that there was high tension and dysphoria in the "in-group" (i.e., the crew or ground), we hypothesized that there would be a tendency to displace these feelings outwardly to the respective mission control or management "out-group" and to perceive these supervisors as not being supportive.

    A third set of analyses examined hypotheses related to the biphasic model, which predicted decrements in crewmember emotional state and interactions during the second half of the missions. Before analysis, the distribution of the raw data was examined for normality. Several subscales (dependent variables) had scores that were normally distributed. Others were successfully normalized using a logarithmic transformation. Still others had greatly skewed distributions and needed to be dichotomized. Cutoffs were made as close as possible to include 50% of the scores in the "high" category and 50% in the "low" category. These dichotomous variables were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) fixed effect models with logit link functions and binomial variance. All other variables were analyzed using a mixed model approach that modeled random intercepts and slopes and assumed a decreasing correlation as the lag interval increased. Both the GEE and the mixed model approaches accounted for the effects of autocorrelation and were not handicapped by missing values in our longitudinal data caused by random events that prevented the subjects from completing the measures during a given week.

    The bi-phasic analysis used a piecewise linear regression approach. The weekly subscale scores for each subject for each mission were arrayed around the midpoint of the mission (counted as week = 0) because the launches and mission periods of Americans and Russians were staggered in calendar time and were of differing lengths. The missions varied from 16 weeks (an American astronaut) to 28 weeks (two Russian cosmonauts). From the actual weekly subscale scores, overall estimates of the average slope in the first half and in the second half of the missions were calculated, with these slopes intercepting at the midpoint.

    Another analyses also tested for the effects of time during the on-orbit period but modeled the effects of triphasic rather than biphasic changes. A regression approach with a quadratic function was selected to test for a pattern indicative of the presence of three phases in all crewmembers and in the Americans and Russians taken separately. For example, the literatures have suggested that crew tension levels would be high initially, and then drop during the middle phase of the mission. Tension would then rise again at the end as the termination approaches. Since quadratic functions describe curves with one bend, this analytic procedure was a reasonable way for us to test for U-shaped patterns among the variables in the data. However, since other curvilinear patterns may give a significant quadratic result as well, we had to visually inspect the data to see if a U-shape or some other curve best defined it.

    Since the regression models with a quadratic function included tests for linear functions in the analysis, a comparison of the quadratic pattern with a linear pattern was explored for the subscales throughout the course of the mission. If both of these tests for a given subscale are significant, then it is appropriate to present only the quadratic results. It is important to realize that the pattern of change in the actual data for a given subscale variable may not in itself be linear. For example, for variables that were dichotomized and subject to a GEE analysis, what was being evaluated was the presence of a linear pattern in the logit transformed values, not in the actual data. The most one could infer from such a case was that there was an overall tendency for a variable to increase or decrease versus showing no change over time (e.g., the tension level rose or fell during the course of the total mission versus staying pretty much the same). Therefore, one needs to visually examine the plot to deduce what kind of pattern is evident.

T-tests were used to compare mission means with normative scores from other groups on Earth, both in terms of all subjects pooled and in terms of American and Russian subjects taken separately.

Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales for the mission itself and for the pre- and post-mission periods. Subsequently, each mean was weighted by the number of observations that contributed to it, and a one-way repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed that compared crewmember subscale mean scores during the missions with pre- and post-mission means. Again, we looked at all crewmembers pooled and at Americans and Russians taken separately.

The t-tests were conducted using the SAS t-test procedure, and the ANOVAs were conducted using the SAS GLM procedure. To control for a possible inflated Type I error rate associated with multiple significance tests, the false discovery rate procedure was utilized to determine an adjusted significance threshold. This procedure controls the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses (i.e., the false discovery rate). For each effect being evaluated, the actual p-values from each of the total number of N subscales being tested were rank ordered from smallest to largest. Multiplying .05 by the rank number of each subscale result and then dividing by N calculated a cutoff significance threshold. The p-value from each subscale result then was compared against the threshold p-value until a comparison was found that did not exceed the threshold. This p-value became the significance level threshold for that particular effect. The results reported below have been interpreted with reference to the appropriate calculated Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold.

    RESULTS:
    Interpersonal and cultural results

    To examine the potential impact of interpersonal and cultural factors, we used an analysis of variance to explore differences between Americans and Russians and between crew and ground subjects. Seven of the total of 21 subscale comparisons gave p-values lower than the adjusted significance threshold for the country main effect: Americans scored higher than Russians on POMS Vigor-Activity and WES Work Pressure, and lower on WES Managerial Control, GES Task Orientation, GES Self Discovery, WES Physical Comfort, and GES Leader Support. For the group main effect, four comparisons were significant, with mission control subjects scoring higher than crewmembers on four POMS measures of dysphoria (Tension-Anxiety, Fatigue-Inertia, Confusion-Bewilderment, and Total Mood Disturbance). There were significant country by group interactions for three GES subscales: Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Independence. American crewmembers scored lower than any other group on all three measures. Taken together, these findings suggested that Americans (especially U.S. crewmembers) experienced more emotional and work related problems than Russians, and that mission control personnel were more dysphoric than crewmembers.

    Displacement results

    Strong support was found in favor that displacement would occur for both crewmembers and mission control personnel using a mixed model analysis. Six subscales were picked to evaluate displacement (POMS: Tension-Anxiety, Depression-Dejection, Anger-Hostility, Total Mood Disturbance; GES Anger & Aggression; WES Work Pressure), and the phenomenon was indicated operationally when there was a significant negative association of each of these subscales with a measure of outside support (WES Supervisor Support). All six predicted associations were significant for the crewmembers, and five of the six were significant for the mission control subjects with the exception of WES Work Pressure. These results strongly suggested that crewmembers displaced tension and negative emotions to mission control personnel and that mission control personnel displaced tension and negative emotions to management.

    Biphasic model results

    According to the biphasic model, as hypothesized, there would be a significant rise in measures of crew tension, a drop in measures of crew cohesion and leader support, and a drop in measures of mission control leader support during the second half of the missions. The cohesion hypothesis was tested by examining six subscale variables: GES Cohesion, GES Task Orientation, GES Order and Organization, POMS Depression-Dejection, POMS Fatigue-Inertia, and POMS Vigor-Activity. We tested our tension hypothesis in terms of four variables: POMS Tension-Anxiety, POMS Anger-Hostility, GES Anger & Aggression, and WES Work Pressure. Finally, leader support was examined for both the crewmembers and the mission control personnel by exploring two variables: GES Leader Support and WES Supervisor Support. Using a piecewise linear regression approach with the appropriate mixed model or GEE analyses, only one of the, variables was significant when the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold was applied: there was a significant drop in GES Leader Support for crewmembers in the second half. Overall, the results did not indicate the presence of a moderate to strong biphasic time effect.

    The findings reported below deal with triphasic and linear time effects and with emotional and group climate responses reported by the crewmembers during their time on-orbit (the mission period). Unlike mission control personnel, the crewmembers were confined in space during the missions in an environment quite different from that on Earth. This isolation made them especially vulnerable to group and time pressures. Consequently, the results will have special relevance for the crew subjects.

    The triphasic model was evaluated in terms of a regression approach with a quadratic function, since this gives a reasonable test of the U-shaped pattern one would expect to see in the subscales over the course of the missions if this pattern was in operation. Since all three of these variables had a skewed distribution and were dichotomized, they ~ere analyzed using a GEE model.

    Crewmember subjects were asked to complete the POMS, GES, and WES questions each week during the time they were on the Mir. They also were asked to complete these measures for four consecutive weeks pre-mission, ending at one month before launch (i.e., baseline data collection period), and for two consecutive weeks after they returned to Earth. Taken together, the results from these three subscales suggested that the American crewmembers might have been impacted by the novelty of the situation during the first few weeks of their missions.     The above results were found only for American astronauts. Thus, the cosmonauts were much more likely to endorse higher scores throughout the mission than their American counterparts. This difference may have reflected actual cultural differences or differences based on interpretations of the English and Russian versions of our measures. But it also might have reflected the specific interpersonal characteristics of the Shuttle/Mir missions, where there usually were two Russians and one American on-board, where the leader was always a Russian, where the Mir and its operation was in Russian control, and where the predominate language being spoken was Russian. Thus, an American astronaut was psychosocially isolated during these missions, and the U.S./Russian differences may have been more a reflection of the crew composition and operational situation than of characteristic cultural differences.

    First, although the estimated curves were significant, an inspection of the figures suggests that the estimates are not idea fits of the actual proportion data. The smooth estimated probability curves contradict the variation that is occurring in the mean weekly responses. Only biphasic, quadratic, and linear functions were tested, and perhaps some other function would give a better fit to the data. Second, for GES Order & Organization, GES Task Orientation, and GES Cohesion, the high/low splits were at 9/8. This means that about half of the total responses were the highest possible value of nine, and about half were eight and below. Therefore, in many cases, the indicated drop in scores was from a high of nine to a low of eight or seven, still in the upper part of the subscale range. In contrast, the high/low split for GES Self Discovery was 5/4, which gave more room at the top and bottom of the subscale range for the subjects to score. Little support was found for the presence of moderate to strong time effects in the crewmembers during the Shuttle/Mir missions.

    In comparison with other work and task groups on Earth, the crewmembers were significantly less dysphoric and perceived more cohesion and direction from their leaders and managers. They also felt that their group environment allowed them less opportunity to express themselves and to be independent and innovative, and they reported lower levels of group anger and aggression. American and Russian subjects taken separately generally echoed these overall findings. In addition, unlike many work environments on Earth, the Shuttle/Mir missions were busy and highly structured, with many timelines, procedures, and directions from the ground that needed to be followed. One interesting difference between Russian and American crewmembers pertained to GES Self Discovery, with the former scoring significantly higher than the normative sample and the latter Scoring significantly lower. Although the Russian crewmembers perceived their interpersonal environment as conducive to such discussion (compared with the normative group on Earth), the American crewmembers had an opposite perspective. Perhaps language differences and a sense of psychosocial isolation handicapped the latter and prevented them from learning about themselves through such informal group interactions. No significant differences were establish in crew response before, during, or after the missions in terms of all crewmembers or Americans and Russians taken separately.

    Significant pre/post seclusion differences using the same measures were found in our 135-day Mir simulator study, and we expected to replicate some of the findings. For example, POMS Tension-Anxiety levels were significantly lower, and GES Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Self Discovery levels were significantly higher during the Mir simulation seclusion period than before. However, the psychological meaning of this simulation was much different from the Shuttle/Mir missions in terms of anxiety and perceived danger, and one must be cautious in extrapolating the findings from earth-bound psychosocial simulation research into space.

    Crewmembers may be more comfortable with their work environment in space than mission control personnel are with their work environment on Earth, and it is possible that for astronauts and cosmonauts, the excitement of being in space offsets any negatives from living and working on earth. Thus, crewmembers perceived their work environment differently form people on Earth, and they demonstrated equanimity in mood and group perceptions, both in space and on the ground.

OBJECTIVES:
During future long duration missions, international crews will be engaged in complicated activities over long periods of time. A number of interpersonal issues likely to impact these missions must be addressed to ensure healthy crewmember interactions and optimal performance. The objectives of this study were to measure and characterize changes over time in a number of important interpersonal factors, such as tension, cohesion, leadership role, and the relationship between space crews and ground support personnel during the NASA/Mir missions.

The formal hypotheses addressed a number of aspects related to crew and ground control tension, cohesion, and leadership role. Over the course of long-term space missions, tension in the crew environment and crew cohesiveness were expected to change. Researchers expected an association between the level of tension in the crewmembers and their relationship with people on the ground, and between tension in mission control personnel and their relationship with management. Also, it was hypothesized that the perception of both the leadership role and outside monitoring support would change over time.

Although specific stressors that occur during the mission, there is evidence, can influence these issues, that time alone may be a factor. One approach, the biphasic model, proposes that significant psychological and interpersonal difficulties may occur after the halfway point of a mission. Hence, a sense of relief that half of the mission is over is outweighed by the realization that another half is yet to come, and this results in decrements in mood and interpersonal functioning of the crew. The triphasic model describes three phases of reaction for people working in isolating and confined conditions for long periods. The initial anxiety in the first few weeks are mainly due to the novelty of the situation; depression during the long middle period of the mission are mainly due to monotony and homesickness; and euphoria and adolescent behavior during the last few weeks due to anticipation of returning home.

When crews are composed of people from different countries or different ethnic backgrounds, language and cultural differences are important since they may lead to intra-crew tensions and disruptions in cohesion, and this in turn may negatively affect morale and interfere with the performance of mission tasks. Issues related to language and cultural differences have been reported in both simulation and space environments. Language and cultural issues also may adversely affect the interactions of mission control personnel on the ground, although these individuals have not been studied previously.

The relationship between the crewmembers and their mission control support personnel is important, since miscommunication or insensitivity between these two groups may lead to misaligned work schedules or inappropriate responses during times of danger. A phenomenon that may negatively influence crew ground communication is displacement, which occurs when tension and distressful dysphoric emotions (e.g., anger, depression) that arise within the crewmembers during the mission cannot be expressed openly and are instead transferred outside to ground personnel, who are perceived as unsupportive and negative. Interactions suggestive of displacement have been reported during space missions and during space simulation studies on Earth. In simulations, crewmember anger directed to outside monitors has been especially observed when overt anger and tension were not seen between the confined subjects, and vice versa.

Earlier work explored several of the above psychosocial issues in confined groups and included a questionnaire study of 54 astronauts and cosmonauts who had flown in space and a study of three male Russian subjects who were secluded in the Mir space station simulator in Moscow for 135 days. The objectives of the study were to determine how tension, cohesion, and leader support affected the space crewmembers and mission control personnel on the ground and to determine how these factors changed over time.

Several of the hypotheses predicted decreases in crew behavior during the second half of the missions in accordance with the biphasic model. The value of the triphasic model was also explored and other time effects that might be present while the crewmembers were on orbit. As stated in the hypothesis, displacement of tension and dysphoria would occur from crewmembers to mission control personnel and from mission control personnel to management; differences in response between Russians and Americans and between crewmembers and mission control personnel, were explored. We made no predictions concerning these differences since little empirical evidence existed that would allow us to form hypotheses related to these socio-cultural factors.

Subsequently, each mean was weighted by the number of observations that contributed to it, and a one-way repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed that compared crewmember subscale mean scores during the missions with pre- and post-mission means. Again, we looked at all crewmembers pooled and at Americans and Russians taken separately.

    All of the previously conducted and new regression analyses were performed using a SAS macro based to execute the GEE analysis and the SAS MIXED procedure for the mixed models. The t-tests were conducted using the SAS t-test procedure, and the ANOVAs were conducted using the SAS GLM procedure. To control for a possible inflated Type I error rate associated with multiple significance tests, the false discovery rate procedure was utilized to determine an adjusted significance threshold. This procedure controls the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses (i.e., the false discovery rate). For each effect being evaluated, the actual p-values from each of the total number of N subscales being tested were rank ordered from smallest to largest. Multiplying .05 by the rank number of each subscale result and then dividing by N calculated a cutoff significance threshold. The p-value from each subscale result then was compared against the threshold p-value until a comparison was found that did not exceed the threshold. This p-value became the significance level threshold for that particular effect. The results reported below have been interpreted with reference to the appropriate calculated Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold.

    RESULTS:
    Interpersonal and cultural results

    To examine the potential impact of interpersonal and cultural factors, we used an analysis of variance to explore differences between Americans and Russians and between crew and ground subjects. Seven of the total of 21 subscale comparisons gave p-values lower than the adjusted significance threshold for the country main effect: Americans scored higher than Russians on POMS Vigor-Activity and WES Work Pressure, and lower on WES Managerial Control, GES Task Orientation, GES Self Discovery, WES Physical Comfort, and GES Leader Support. For the group main effect, four comparisons were significant, with mission control subjects scoring higher than crewmembers on four POMS measures of dysphoria (Tension-Anxiety, Fatigue-Inertia, Confusion-Bewilderment, and Total Mood Disturbance). There were significant country by group interactions for three GES subscales: Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Independence. American crewmembers scored lower than any other group on all three measures. Taken together, these findings suggested that Americans (especially U.S. crewmembers) experienced more emotional and work related problems than Russians, and that mission control personnel were more dysphoric than crewmembers.

    Displacement results

    Strong support was found in favor that displacement would occur for both crewmembers and mission control personnel using a mixed model analysis. Six subscales were picked to evaluate displacement (POMS: Tension-Anxiety, Depression-Dejection, Anger-Hostility, Total Mood Disturbance; GES Anger & Aggression; WES Work Pressure), and the phenomenon was indicated operationally when there was a significant negative association of each of these subscales with a measure of outside support (WES Supervisor Support). All six predicted associations were significant for the crewmembers, and five of the six were significant for the mission control subjects with the exception of WES Work Pressure. These results strongly suggested that crewmembers displaced tension and negative emotions to mission control personnel and that mission control personnel displaced tension and negative emotions to management.

    Biphasic model results

    According to the biphasic model, as hypothesized, there would be a significant rise in measures of crew tension, a drop in measures of crew cohesion and leader support, and a drop in measures of mission control leader support during the second half of the missions. The cohesion hypothesis was tested by examining six subscale variables: GES Cohesion, GES Task Orientation, GES Order and Organization, POMS Depression-Dejection, POMS Fatigue-Inertia, and POMS Vigor-Activity. We tested our tension hypothesis in terms of four variables: POMS Tension-Anxiety, POMS Anger-Hostility, GES Anger & Aggression, and WES Work Pressure. Finally, leader support was examined for both the crewmembers and the mission control personnel by exploring two variables: GES Leader Support and WES Supervisor Support. Using a piecewise linear regression approach with the appropriate mixed model or GEE analyses, only one of the, variables was significant when the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold was applied: there was a significant drop in GES Leader Support for crewmembers in the second half. Overall, the results did not indicate the presence of a moderate to strong biphasic time effect.

    The findings reported below deal with triphasic and linear time effects and with emotional and group climate responses reported by the crewmembers during their time on-orbit (the mission period). Unlike mission control personnel, the crewmembers were confined in space during the missions in an environment quite different from that on Earth. This isolation made them especially vulnerable to group and time pressures. Consequently, the results will have special relevance for the crew subjects.

    Quadratic (triphasic) model results

    The triphasic model was evaluated in terms of a regression approach with a quadratic function, since this gives a reasonable test of the U-shaped pattern one would expect to see in the subscales over the course of the missions if this pattern was in operation. However, since quadratic functions also describe non U-shaped curves, it is important to inspect the data visually to see just what kind of curve is depicted. A significant quadratic component in the model indicates that the quadratic function is a better representation of the data than a linear function.

    For the crewmembers, all of the 21 subscale variables from the POMS, GES, and WES were tested. After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, the results indicated that none of tests for the quadratic function in these subscales met the adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024). Additional evaluations were made of the quadratic function in the 21 subscales for Russian and American crewmembers taken separately. For the Russians, none of the tests resulted in significant findings. For the American crewmembers, three of the subscales were significant for quadratic functions, with the p-value being less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold of p =.0024. These were: GES Order & Organization (beta = .007, p = .000); GES Task Orientation (beta = -.007, p = .000); and GES Self Discovery (beta = -.099, p = .000). Since all three of these variables had a skewed distribution and were dichotomized, they ~ere analyzed using a GEE model.

    Linear model results

    For all the crewmembers and for the Russians taken separately, regression analyses for the linear model were made on all 21 subscales. In both cases, none of the subscales resulted in p-values that were less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024).

    For the American crewmembers taken separately, only one subscale variable (other than GES Self Discovery) had a p-value that was less than the Benjamini and Hochberg threshold of p = .0048: GES Cohesion. A GEE analysis had been performed on GES Cohesion since the data were skewed and needed to be dichotomized, and this resulted in findings of beta = -.144 and p = .003. The negative beta meant that the probability of achieving a high score decreased in some manner from the beginning to the end of the mission. Although the shape of the logit curve was better described by a linear than a quadratic function, this did not imply that the actual data necessarily would plot as a straight line.

    Crewmember results versus scores from normative samples on Earth

    For nearly every subscale, the crewmember means were in the positive half of the subscale range. That is, where a high score defined a negative outcome (e.g., POMS Tension-Anxiety), the crew mean was below the scale midpoint (18 for this subscale), whereas where a high score defined a positive outcome (e.g., GES Cohesion), the crew mean was above the scale midpoint (4.5 for this subscale). This suggested that the crewmembers generally endorsed positive adaptive responses, especially for the POMS emotion variables.

    The normative means and standard deviations were determined from several thousand people participating in non-patient work and task groups. The POMS sample consisted of 1,130 adult males who participated in a smoking cessation program; the GES sample consisted of individuals who participated in 101 task-oriented groups in health care, correctional, and educational settings [41]; and the WES sample consisted of 8,146 individuals who participated in 116 general and health care work groups [42]. Using t-tests and the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, a total of 13 subscales resulted in p-values that were below the adjusted significance threshold of p = .033. For all six significant POMS variables, the crewmembers endorsed significantly less dysphoria than the POMS normative sample. They also scored lower on GES and WES measures of group expressiveness, independence, anger & aggression, and innovation; and higher on measures of cohesion, leader control, and managerial control.

    The subscale means and standard deviations for Russian and American crewmembers were taken separately, along with their respective comparisons with the normative samples; a given difference did not always reach significance (probably due to the smaller sample sizes). One notable new finding is GES Self Discovery, where the Russian mean is significantly greater than the norm, and the American mean is significantly smaller.

    Mission versus pre-and post-mission results

    Crewmember subjects were asked to complete the POMS, GES, and WES questions each week during the time they were on the Mir. They also were asked to complete these measures for four consecutive weeks pre-mission, ending at one month before launch (i.e., baseline data collection period), and for two consecutive weeks after they returned to Earth. However, it was discovered that during the post-mission period the American and Russian subjects were separated from each other, so there was no group environment to evaluate using the GES and WES items. Consequently, only POMS data were collected. To look for differences in subscale scores before, during, and after the missions, mean scores were calculated and compared using a repeated measures ANOVA (pre-mission versus on-orbit versus post-mission for the POMS subscales, and pre-mission versus on-orbit for the GES and WES subscales). After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, none of these comparisons were significant in terms of all crewmembers, Russians alone, or Americans alone.

    CONCLUSION

    There was no support for the triphasic or linear models for all crewmembers or for Russian cosmonauts alone when the Benjamini and Hochberg criteria were applied to contol for Type I errors. Although there were three significant quadratic findings for American astronauts, only one variable, GES Order & Organization, showed a U-shaped pattern consistent with the triphasic model. This finding suggested that Americans in space felt that their interpersonal environment was comparatively more organized at the beginning and end of the on-orbit period than during the middle. This makes some sense because the new astronauts were formally oriented to the Mir shortly after arriving by the departing astronauts and by the continuing cosmonauts, and because the preparation for the return to Earth required the astronauts to undergo a number of specific procedures during the end of their on-orbit period.

    The other two significant quadratic functions for the Americans, GES Task Orientation and GES Self Discovery, gave a different pattern, with the probability of a high score being greater during the beginning weeks of the missions, then declining as time progressed. This pattem also was evident for the significant linear function finding for GES Cohesion. Taken together, the results from these three subscales suggested that the American crewmembers might have been impacted by the novelty of the situation during the first few weeks of their missions. They perceived the crew environment to be one where orientation to tasks was high, where they could grow individually, and where there was a strong bond among the crewmembers. Over time, there was a significant decrease in these areas. Perhaps the novelty of the situation simply disappeared. Alternatively, the decreases may have reflected an emotional change in the Americans due to homesickness or asthenia, although one would have expected to find some POMS changes as well if this explanation was valid.

    The above results were found only for American astronauts. The Russian estimated probabilities for high scores were in the .4 to .8 ranges for all four of the subscales shown in the figures, and they did not vary significantly over time. Thus, the cosmonauts were much more likely to endorse higher scores throughout the mission than their American counterparts. This difference may have reflected actual cultural differences or differences based on interpretations of the English and Russian versions of our measures. But it also might have reflected the specific interpersonal characteristics of the Shuttle/Mir missions, where there usually were two Russians and one American on-board, where the leader was always a Russian, where the Mir and its operation was in Russian control, and where the predominate language being spoken was Russian. Thus, an American astronaut was psychosocially isolated during these missions, and the U.S./Russian differences may have been more a reflection of the crew composition and operational situation than of characteristic cultural differences.

    First, although the estimated curves were significant, an inspection of the figures suggests that the estimates are not idea fits of the actual proportion data. The smooth estimated probability curves contradict the variation that is occurring in the mean weekly responses. Only biphasic, quadratic, and linear functions were tested, and perhaps some other function would give a better fit to the data. Second, for GES Order & Organization, GES Task Orientation, and GES Cohesion, the high/low splits were at 9/8. This means that about half of the total responses were the highest possible value of nine, and about half were eight and below. Therefore, in many cases, the indicated drop in scores was from a high of nine to a low of eight or seven, still in the upper part of the subscale range. In contrast, the high/low split for GES Self Discovery was 5/4, which gave more room at the top and bottom of the subscale range for the subjects to score. Little support was found for the presence of moderate to strong time effects in the crewmembers during the Shuttle/Mir missions.

    In comparison with other work and task groups on Earth, the crewmembers were significantly less dysphoric and perceived more cohesion and direction from their leaders and managers. They also felt that their group environment allowed them less opportunity to express themselves and to be independent and innovative, and they reported lower levels of group anger and aggression. American and Russian subjects taken separately generally echoed these overall findings. In addition, unlike many work environments on Earth, the Shuttle/Mir missions were busy and highly structured, with many timelines, procedures, and directions from the ground that needed to be followed. One interesting difference between Russian and American crewmembers pertained to GES Self Discovery, with the former scoring significantly higher than the normative sample and the latter Scoring significantly lower. Although the Russian crewmembers perceived their interpersonal environment as conducive to such discussion (compared with the normative group on Earth), the American crewmembers had an opposite perspective. Perhaps language differences and a sense of psychosocial isolation handicapped the latter and prevented them from learning about themselves through such informal group interactions. No significant differences were establish in crew response before, during, or after the missions in terms of all crewmembers or Americans and Russians taken separately.

    Significant pre/post seclusion differences using the same measures were found in our 135-day Mir simulator study, and we expected to replicate some of the findings. For example, POMS Tension-Anxiety levels were significantly lower, and GES Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Self Discovery levels were significantly higher during the Mir simulation seclusion period than before. However, the psychological meaning of this simulation was much different from the Shuttle/Mir missions in terms of anxiety and perceived danger, and one must be cautious in extrapolating the findings from earth-bound psychosocial simulation research into space.

    Crewmembers may be more comfortable with their work environment in space than mission control personnel are with their work environment on Earth, and it is possible that for astronauts and cosmonauts, the excitement of being in space offsets any negatives from living and working on earth. Thus, crewmembers perceived their work environment differently form people on Earth, and they demonstrated equanimity in mood and group perceptions, both in space and on the ground.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Resistive exercise has been recommended as a means to ease musculoskeletal de-conditioning due to spaceflight. Currently, the interim Resistive Exercise Device (iRED) is used on-board the International Space Station (ISS) as a method of providing resistive exercise. The iRED may not provide an adequate stimulus to bring about changes in muscle strength and mass and bone mineral density (BMD) compared with free weights (FW). During a 16-week training study, conducted by the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Exercise Physiology laboratory, the rate of increase in muscle strength using iRED was slower compared to FW. In addition, iRED training resulted in no change in BMD, while FW training lead to an increase in lumbar BMD.

Differences in strength gains between iRED and FW training may be due to greater eccentric loads produced during FW training. Despite performing resistive exercise with the iRED, International Space Station (ISS) astronauts still experience losses in muscle strength and endurance and BMD following long-duration space missions (>4 months). The peak iRED load level may be inadequate to ease musculoskeletal losses in microgravity where the subject is not required to lift their body weight.

The aRED was developed to address the limitations of iRED. This new device was intended to mimic the force loading characteristics of FW exercise. In addition, aRED was designed to provide a more constant force throughout the range of motion with resistance generated by vacuum cylinders. The vacuum cylinders provide a concentric load up to 600 pounds with an eccentric load up to 90% of the concentric force. In addition, aRED is equipped with an inertial flywheel to mimic the inertial force characteristics of FW.

The purpose of this study was to compare the musculoskeletal adaptations to 16 weeks of resistive exercise training utilizing either aRED or FW in healthy, untrained men and women. Because the aRED was designed to be similar to FW, the investigators hypothesized increases in skeletal muscle strength, leg muscle volume, lean body mass, and BMD after 16 weeks of training with no differences between the groups.

APPROACH:
Twenty-four volunteers were recruited by the Human Test Subject Facility at NASA Johnson Space Center to participate in this study. All subjects were required to pass a modified Air Force Class III physical examination. Testing protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. Subjects were instructed to maintain their pre-study exercise habits (intensity, frequency, and duration) and to not initiate any new exercise programs during the study. Additionally, subjects only performed the prescribed resistive exercise protocol, which did not include any upper body resistive exercise. Although diet was not controlled, subjects were instructed to maintain dietary habits for the duration of the study. Subjects were instructed not to take any nutritional supplements or similar products that may affect muscle performance, lean tissue mass, or bone metabolism.

Subjects participated in a 24-week study, comprised of six weeks of pre-training, sixteen weeks of training and two weeks of post-training testing. The volunteers were placed into one of two groups; one group worked with the aRED exercise device and the other with FW. The following tests were conducted during the pre- training, training, and/or post training:

Muscle Strength (1RM) - a one-repetition maximum (1RM) strength test was used as the criterion measure of muscle strength and was performed for each exercise, using both aRED and FW. Vertical Jump (VJ) test – is a measure of muscle power. Three counter-movement jumps were performed, and the VJ height determined was defined as the maximum height achieved over the three repetitions. This was performed on the same day but prior to 1RM testing to minimize the affect of fatigue on VJ performance.

Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) scans – whole body and regional DXA scans were performed to determine area bone mineral density (aBMD) and volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) of the spine and hip.

Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) - used to measure whole body and leg lean tissue mass and thigh and lower leg muscle volume, respectively.

Blood and urine – collected for determination of markers of bone and muscle metabolism. All blood samples were collected fasting in the morning prior to performing any exercise. Following completion of the blood draw the 24-hour urine collection began, with the completion with the first void of the following day.

During the pre-training period, each subject had two DXA scans, one QCT scan, and one MRI scan. Urine and blood were collected at the end of pre-training. During this six week period subjects from both the aRED group and the FW group underwent weekly Muscle Strength (1RM) for each exercise and VJ training.

In the 16 weeks of training, each volunteer group (either aRED or FW) performed a set of lower body exercises prescribed during spaceflight (parallel squat, heel raise and dead lift). The training loads for the first half of this period was based on a percentage of the pre-training 1RM. Halfway through training, the muscle strength (1RM) for each exercise was re-measured. The training loads for the remainder of the training period were based on this 1RM value. Both group of subjects followed a periodized training protocol in which the resistance varied in a predetermined fashion within each week and incrementally increased every subsequent week. VJ, DXA, blood, and urine measurements were also determined.

Post-training, the VJ and 1RM on each exercise for both the aRED and FW groups were determined. QCT, MRI and DXA scans were conducted. Blood and urine samples were also taken.

RESULTS:
Total lumbar spine BMD significantly increased (p <0.05) after training in both the FW (Pre: 1.073 ± 0.140; Post: 1.091 ± 0.139 g·cm-2; + 2.6%) and ARED (Pre: 1.026 ± 0.071; Post: 1.053 ± 0.0732 g·cm-2; + 1.8%) groups with no difference between groups. Similarly, there was a main effect of training (p <0.05) on femoral neck BMD (FW, Pre: 0.870 ± 0.036, Post: 0.883 ± 0.057, + 1.6%; ARED, Pre: 0.846 ± 0.172, Post: 0.850 ± 0.176 g·cm-2, + 0.4%) with no between group differences. ARED exercise is not different than FW exercise with regard to stimulating increased BMD in the lumbar spine and femoral neck during 16 weeks of training in ambulatory subjects. The efficacy of ARED exercise to prevent space flight-induced BMD losses remains to be validated.

During Session 2, the SQ and DL 1RM (SQ: 90.2 ± 4.3, DL: 75.9 ± 3.3 kg) were less than Session 3 (SQ: 95.3 ± 4.1, DL: 81.5 ± 3.5 kg) and Session 4 (SQ: 96.6 ± 4.0, DL: 82.4 ± 3.9 kg), but there were no differences between Session 3 and Session 4. HR 1RM measured during Session 2 (150.1 ± 3.7 kg) and Session 3 (152.5 ± 3.9 kg) were not different from one another, but both were less than Session 4 (157.5 ± 3.8 kg). The reliability (ICC) of 1RM measures for Sessions 2-4 were 0.88, 0.83, and 0.87, for SQ, HR, and DL, respectively. When considering only Sessions 3 and 4, the reliability was 0.93, 0.91, and 0.86 for SQ, HR, and DL, respectively. One familiarization session and two test sessions (for SQ and DL) were required to obtain excellent reliability (ICC = 0.90) in 1RM values with novice subjects. The investigators were unable to attain this level of reliability following three HR testing sessions; additional sessions are required to obtain an ICC of =0.90. Resistive exercise training studies should consider the reliability of specific measures to ensure that reported strength changes are attributable to training and not to learning effects associated with 1RM testing.

SQ, HR, and DL 1RM increased in both FW (mean ± SE; SQ: 49 ± 6%, HR: 12 ±2 %, DL: 23 ±4 %) and ARED (SQ: 31 ± 4%, HR: 18 ± 2%, DL: 23 ± 3%) groups. Both groups increased muscle volume in the V (FW: 13 ± 2%, ARED: 10 ± 2%), H (FW: 3 ± 1%, ARED: 3 ± 1%), ADD (FW: 15 ± 2%, ARED: 10 ± 1%), LG (FW: 7 ± 2%, ARED: 4 ± 1%), MG (FW: 7 ± 2%, ARED: 5 ± 2%), and DP (FW: 2 ± 1%; ARED: 2 ± 1%) after training. There were no between-group differences in muscle strength or volume. The increase in muscle volume and strength following ARED training is not different than FW training. These findings indicate that ARED will likely protect against space flight-induced muscle atrophy and strength loss.

Resistive exercise training studies should consider the reliability of specific measures to ensure that reported strength changes are attributable to training and not to learning effects associated with 1RM testing.

SQ, HR, and DL 1RM increased in both FW (mean ± SE; SQ: 49 ± 6%, HR: 12 ±2 %, DL: 23 ±4 %) and ARED (SQ: 31 ± 4%, HR: 18 ± 2%, DL: 23 ± 3%) groups. Both groups increased muscle volume in the V (FW: 13 ± 2%, ARED: 10 ± 2%), H (FW: 3 ± 1%, ARED: 3 ± 1%), ADD (FW: 15 ± 2%, ARED: 10 ± 1%), LG (FW: 7 ± 2%, ARED: 4 ± 1%), MG (FW: 7 ± 2%, ARED: 5 ± 2%), and DP (FW: 2 ± 1%; ARED: 2 ± 1%) after training. There were no between-group differences in muscle strength or volume. The increase in muscle volume and strength following ARED training is not different than FW training. These findings indicate that ARED will likely protect against space flight-induced muscle atrophy and strength loss.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The purpose of this demonstration project was to assess the compliance of crewmembers to perform exercise countermeasures similar to those planned for use during stays aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and to assess the outcome of performing these countermeasures.

The objectives of the Exercise Countermeasures Demonstration Projects were:

  • to assist in the development and evaluation of exercise testing and prescription methods being considered for ISS

  • to provide realistic perturbations of carbon dioxide production and oxygen utilization as anticipated during ISS to challenge the environmental control systems.

    Four crewmembers participated in each of two chamber tests. Phase IIa was a 60-day chamber test while the Phase III test had a duration of 91 days. Previous chamber studies were conducted in which exercise was performed, but these two projects were the first in which specific exercise prescriptions were developed for the crewmembers and the outcomes of the exercise protocols were measured. These two chamber studies served as ground-based test beds for exercise countermeasure procedure development in support of future activities for the crews of the International Space Station (ISS).

    APPROACH:

    In each project, eight crewmembers were selected for participation, four as prime and four as back-up. Crewmembers were screened for health status by means of a modified Air Force Class III Physical and a graded treadmill exercise test to volitional fatigue with 12-lead electrocardiogram. Subjects received written and verbal explanation of the procedures specific to the exercise countermeasures demonstration project and signed informed consent documents confirming their understanding and acceptance. All testing procedures and protocols were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Institutional Review Board. All pre and postchamber testing, as well as prechamber training, were performed in the NASA Johnson Space Center Exercise Physiology Laboratory. Eventually, four crewmembers entered the chamber in each study and remained there for the duration of the test project. In Phase IIa, the crew consisted of three men and one woman. In Phase III, the crew consisted of two men and two women. Data presented here are from the four prime crewmembers only from each of the two chamber tests.

    For the 60-day Phase IIa test, the characteristics of the prime crewmembers, three males and one female, were: age - 31 ± 4 years; height - 175 ± 5 cm; and body mass - 70.4 ± 10.9 kg. Prior to entry into the chamber, crewmembers completed both a graded maximal cycle exercise test to volitional fatigue and a submaximal cycle ergometer exercise protocol. Crewmembers also received training on the aerobic and resistance exercise countermeasures prior to chamber entry. At the conclusion of the chamber test, the four crewmembers repeated the maximal cycle exercise test.

    The 91-day Phase III test provided an opportunity to evaluate potential exercise countermeasure and testing procedures during an even longer, 91-day chamber stay. In Phase III, two men and two women served as crewmembers with a mean (± standard deviation (SD)) age of 34 ± 6 years, height of 173.5 ± 11.9 cm, and body mass of 68.3 ± 10.4 kg.

    The testing and monitoring procedures were similar to those used in Phase IIa, except that isokinetic tests of muscle strength and endurance were added to the testing regime. Prechamber testing included maximal cycle and treadmill tests to volitional fatigue, two submaximal cycle ergometer exercise tests, training sessions for the cycle and treadmill aerobic exercise countermeasures, and two isokinetic muscular strength and endurance tests. Subjects also received two training sessions on the CES, the same resistance exercise training device used in Phase IIa. During the chamber stay, crewmembers performed the submaximal cycle exercise test biweekly on the seventh day of the week. After chamber stay, crewmembers returned to the laboratory for the maximal cycle and isokinetic strength and endurance tests.

    During the chamber test, on alternate days the crewmembers completed the aerobic and the resistive countermeasures three times per week. In several instances, exercise was delayed or cancelled due to malfunction of the environmental control systems. Three times during the 60-day period, on days 15, 30, and 58, crewmembers completed the submaximal exercise test in place of the aerobic exercise training to assess their training status.

    The aerobic exercise testing protocols chosen for this project are similar to those proposed for use in the Space Medicine Project (SMP) on the ISS as a means to monitor crew health. Similarly, the exercise countermeasures, both aerobic and resistive, were similar to those suggested for use on the ISS to maintain crew health. However, no pre to postchamber resistance exercise testing was performed during the Phase IIa test.

    During the 60-day Phase IIa project, crewmembers exercised for six consecutive days alternating between aerobic and resistive exercise, and rested on the seventh day. On the aerobic exercise days, subjects exercised for 30 minutes on an electronically braked cycle ergometer using an interval protocol. On the resistive exercise days, crewmembers performed five major multijoint resistive exercises (bench press, seated press, lat pull, squats, and heel raises) in a concentric-only mode, targeting those muscle groups and bones that are believed to be most severely affected by space flight.

    During the 91-day Phase III project, the frequency of the exercise countermeasures was increased to include both aerobic and resistive exercises each day for six days, with rest on the seventh day. For aerobic exercise, the cycle protocol was performed three days/week similar to the Phase IIa project. However a steady-state treadmill protocol was added on the remaining three exercise days. The same resistance exercise protocol was performed as in Phase IIa, except that the upper- and lower-body exercises were divided and performed on separate days.

    More information about these tests

    RESULTS:

    60-day Phase IIa project: subjects performed maximal efforts with each repetition. Both exercise protocols were well tolerated by the subjects, demonstrated by 98% compliance with the aerobic exercise prescription and 91% adherence to the resistive exercise prescription. After 60 days, the crewmembers improved their peak aerobic capacity by an average of 7%. Strength gains during all exercises were noted.

    91-day Phase III project: three of the four subjects tolerated the aerobic exercise training well. One crewmember developed knee pain in the final third of the chamber test and did not perform further cycle or lower-body resistive exercises for the remainder of the study. The three crewmembers who participated in all countermeasures and postchamber testing had an average increase in aerobic capacity of 14%. Of these remaining three crewmembers, one consistently refrained from resistive exercise one day per week. Strength gains were not consistently obtained during this study. These results, showing little or no change in muscle strength while demonstrating some improvement in aerobic capacity, may be consistent with an overtraining syndrome.

    Taken together, the results from these two studies suggest that the prescribed aerobic and resistive exercises generally were well tolerated. However, combining both resistive and aerobic exercises with only one day of rest each week may result in a decreased benefit of strength training. Periodization of exercise protocols and/or reduction of exercise intensity or frequency may be desired to obtain optimum increases in both aerobic and resistive exercise capacities.

    These LMLSTP studies have allowed preliminary evaluation of potential exercise testing and countermeasure procedures. Lessons learned from these projects may be applied to space flight with the important consideration that training responses in a 1-g environment may not be exactly representative of space flight; exercise in the chamber projects were intended to increase exercise capacity, while exercise countermeasures in a microgravity environment are intended to maintain overall conditioning. Additionally, exercise performed within the constraints imposed by microgravity (e.g., subject loading during treadmill exercise) or with the actual flight hardware may provide a different training stimulus. Further, thresholds for training and over training may differ between the two conditions and vary among the target organ systems. Data collected during actual space flights will be required to provide the final confirmation of our countermeasure programs.

    The data collected during these chamber studies also must be considered extremely preliminary due to the small number of subjects. In many cases, appropriate statistical analyses could not be performed due to the limited sample size.

    With these considerations, preliminary observations from these studies are:

    • The aerobic and resistive countermeasures tested in these projects provided a training stimulus when performed on separate days (Phase IIa). Further work is needed to explore a possible negative effect on strength training when aerobic exercise was performed on the same day as resistive training (Phase III).
    • Most crewmembers preferred treadmill exercise over cycle exercise. This has been reported also by long-duration space flight crews. However, due to effects of microgravity on treadmill exercise loading, exercise prescriptions and testing protocols can be more accurately applied on a cycle.
    • Compliance to our exercise prescriptions was very good, but some discontent was evident from the postchamber debriefs. Increasing the variety of exercise protocols, exercise devices and addition of virtual reality head gear or other forms of entertainment during exercise may improve exercise compliance. Almost all subjects reported a desire for more variety of exercise prescriptions.
    • The lack of strength increase may suggest that the rest periods between sets that were too long or that there was an overtraining response in the Phase III crew with the increased aerobic exercise volume. In future studies and during space flight, crew exercise time should be protected to optimize the effect of training. Also, the addition of muscle damage markers to future training studies may help to elucidate this issue.
    • The exercise logging materials used in this study and the feedback from these subjects has been used in developing the computer-based flight logs currently planned for the ISS.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment used the Solid Sorbent Air Sampler (SSAS) to continuously sample the Shuttle orbiter atmosphere throughout flight. This SSAS was used to verify that volatile organic contaminant levels in the Shuttle internal atmosphere were within established safety levels. The SSAS was flown on first flights of a new vehicle, first flights of a vehicle after extensive nonmetallic materials refurbishment in the orbiter cabin, and on all Spacelab manned module flights. Examples of refurbishment are interior repainting, extensive addition or replacement of wiring, and equipment, or other similar modifications which would make a significant change in the off-gassing products to the orbiter atmospheres.

APPROACH:
The SSAS was placed in a designated sampling location either in the middeck or in the Spacelab. A crewmember activated the switch on the SSAS and recorded mission elapse time (MET). After 24 hours of sampling, the valve was placed in the next sampling position and the MET was recorded. This procedure continued for the duration of the mission. Five minutes was required for a crewmember to destow, place, and activate the SSAS during flight. An additional five minutes was required to deactivate and stow the samples prior to landing.

RESULTS:
STS-37:
A total of 31 contaminants were desorbed from one or more of the five SSAS tubes exposed during the mission. The collective toxicity potential of the chemicals found in the cabin air was estimated by adding each ratio of compound concentration to a 7-day spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC). Based on the analysis of the atmospheric samples collected on STS-37, the air was deemed toxicologically safe for crewmembers to breathe throughout the mission.

STS-40:
A total of 108 chemical contaminants were desorbed from one or more of the six SSAS tubes exposed during the mission. Analysis of orbiter and Spacelab atmospheric samples collected throughout the mission showed the air was generally safe to breathe. The only exception was the air quality degradation caused by the Orbiter Refrigerator/Freezer (OR/F) malfunction. Odors and symptoms reported by the crewmembers during the malfunction, as well as postflight failure analysis of the OR/F, indicated that while the SSAS was in the middeck area early in the mission, crewmembers were temporarily exposed to harmful concentrations of thermodegradation products.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this investigation was to study the effect of 0-G on lymphocyte proliferation in order to establish possible alterations in natural defense mechanisms against infective diseases during prolonged space missions.

Lymphocytes from cosmonauts of spaceflights Soyuz 6, 7 and 8 and from astronauts of the Apollo-Soyuz mission showed a depression of their reactivity toward mitogens after flight. On the other hand, no effect was observed on lymphocytes from crewmembers on other Apollo missions. It is not clear whether the observed effect is due to the stress of spaceflight on the organism with consequent changes in the concentration of certain components of body fluids (e.g., calcium), or to an effect of weightlessness per se. Consequently, only the exposure of lymphocytes to mitogens in vitro during a spaceflight would give a clear answer to the question.

The investigator hypothesized that the absence of gravity affects lymphocyte proliferation. This was tested using three major lines of investigation:

  • the effect of stress and the effect of weightlessness per se on lymphocyte activation.
  • the kinetics of lymphocyte proliferation in space.
  • the effects of a gravitational environment between 0 and 2G.

    APPROACH:
    Culture preparation: The activation by concanavalin A (ConA) of human peripheral blood lymphocytes in the presence of monocytes (as accessory cells) was investigated in cultures exposed to microgravity conditions in Spacelab. Lymphocytes were drawn from the peripheral blood of one healthy male donor 24 hours before launch; they were purified by gradient centrifugation on Ficoll-Hypaque. Differential counting showed that the preparation contained 84% small lymphocytes, with the remainder of the cells being 13% macrophages and polymorphonuclear cells. Cell viability was 90%. The cells were resuspended in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 40 mmol/L HEPES, 5 mmol/L sodium carbonate, 50 microg/L gentamycin, 20% heat activated fetal calf serum, and 4 mmol/L L-glutamine. A 10 ml sample was sealed in each of 8 flasks; eight other flasks were preincubated for 4 hours at 37 degrees Celsius with MC beads, Cytodex 1 at a ratio of 100 cells/bead. Therefore, 4 sets of 4 cultures were prepared 15 hours before launch and stored at room temperature in the Shuttle. Two cultures in each set had MC beads and two did not. Two sets were used as ground controls, one set was put in the flight incubator, and another set was put into the Low-G Centrifuge to serve as a flight control.

    Flight operations: Six hours after launch, the two flight sets of cultures were transferred to the incubator and centrifuge and were exposed to ConA. One of the two ground sets was not treated with ConA. Two cultures from each of the 4 sets (one with and one without MC beads) were treated with a 2-h pulse of 74 kBq/ml of tritiated thymidine 46 and 65 hours after injection of ConA. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at a final concentration of 10% was injected into the cultures before storage in the freezer.

    Biochemical analyses: Cell proliferation was determined by measuring:

  • the rate of tritiated thymidine incorporated into DNA. Triplicates (1 ml each) of each culture were used.
  • secretion of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and gamma interferon
  • expression of IL-2 receptors

    Electron microscopy: Postflight electron microscopy was performed on cells fixed inflight with DMSO. After careful thawing postflight, the samples were fixed with glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide

    RESULTS:
    Activation of resuspended T cells is strongly inhibited in space, a result also seen in earlier investigations. However, activation of cells attached to microcarrier beads is more than doubled in microgravity. The results suggest that the depression of the activation in resuspended cells may be attributed to a malfunction of monocytes acting as accessory cells. In fact, although the ultrastructure of resuspended monocytes is not altered in microgravity, the secretion of IL-1 is strongly inhibited. The data suggest:

  • IL-2 is produced independently of IL-1
  • IL-1 production is triggered only when monocytes adhere to microcarriers
  • the expression of IL-2 receptors depends on IL-1
  • provided sufficient IL-1 is available, activation is enhanced in microgravity.

    Finally, cultures of resuspended peripheral blood lymphocytes and monocytes in microgravity constitute a complete and natural system in which monocytes are not operational. This may be useful for studies of the role of accessory cells and cell-cell interactions in T lymphocyte activation.

Differential counting showed that the preparation contained 84% small lymphocytes, with the remainder of the cells being 13% macrophages and polymorphonuclear cells. Cell viability was 90%. The cells were resuspended in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 40 mmol/L HEPES, 5 mmol/L sodium carbonate, 50 microg/L gentamycin, 20% heat activated fetal calf serum, and 4 mmol/L L-glutamine. A 10 ml sample was sealed in each of 8 flasks; eight other flasks were preincubated for 4 hours at 37 degrees Celsius with MC beads, Cytodex 1 at a ratio of 100 cells/bead. Therefore, 4 sets of 4 cultures were prepared 15 hours before launch and stored at room temperature in the Shuttle. Two cultures in each set had MC beads and two did not. Two sets were used as ground controls, one set was put in the flight incubator, and another set was put into the Low-G Centrifuge to serve as a flight control.

    Flight operations: Six hours after launch, the two flight sets of cultures were transferred to the incubator and centrifuge and were exposed to ConA. One of the two ground sets was not treated with ConA. Two cultures from each of the 4 sets (one with and one without MC beads) were treated with a 2-h pulse of 74 kBq/ml of tritiated thymidine 46 and 65 hours after injection of ConA. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at a final concentration of 10% was injected into the cultures before storage in the freezer.

    Biochemical analyses: Cell proliferation was determined by measuring:

  • the rate of tritiated thymidine incorporated into DNA. Triplicates (1 ml each) of each culture were used.
  • secretion of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and gamma interferon
  • expression of IL-2 receptors

    Electron microscopy: Postflight electron microscopy was performed on cells fixed inflight with DMSO. After careful thawing postflight, the samples were fixed with glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide

    RESULTS:
    Activation of resuspended T cells is strongly inhibited in space, a result also seen in earlier investigations. However, activation of cells attached to microcarrier beads is more than doubled in microgravity. The results suggest that the depression of the activation in resuspended cells may be attributed to a malfunction of monocytes acting as accessory cells. In fact, although the ultrastructure of resuspended monocytes is not altered in microgravity, the secretion of IL-1 is strongly inhibited. The data suggest:

  • IL-2 is produced independently of IL-1
  • IL-1 production is triggered only when monocytes adhere to microcarriers
  • the expression of IL-2 receptors depends on IL-1
  • provided sufficient IL-1 is available, activation is enhanced in microgravity.

    Finally, cultures of resuspended peripheral blood lymphocytes and monocytes in microgravity constitute a complete and natural system in which monocytes are not operational. This may be useful for studies of the role of accessory cells and cell-cell interactions in T lymphocyte activation.
