experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts are routinely exposed to atmospheric decompressions that incur significant risks of decompression sickness (DCS). This study will refine and apply methods that allow DCS risks to be quantitatively estimated throughout the time courses of pressure/respired gas/time profiles of varying complexity. Integrated system software for running optimized models on personal computers will be packaged and delivered at the conclusion of the study for evaluation and use by NASA personnel.

APPROACH:

  • Acquire and code information about individual exposure profiles and their outcomes from human altitude decompression trials
  • Implement and establish the feasibility of a linearization scheme to hasten the process of model fitting to DCS data
  • Fit different model versions to the expanded training data and evaluate the statistical significance of new model features
  • Assess cross-correlations between simulated gas bubble dynamics that underlie model-estimated DCS risks and observed venous gas emboli data
  • Package and deliver system software for use during training and space flight operations

    RESULTS:
    Training data augmentation
    The compilation of data from the NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) historical database of altitude tests is complete. The data are from eleven (11) chamber tests conducted at NASA-JSC between 1980 and 1995. They are tabulated in Excel spreadsheets, each sheet containing data from a single test protocol. The number of protocols per test varies from 1 to 6, with a total of 31 across the 11 tests. The data are from 237 subjects; 176 males and 61 females. The total number of altitude exposures is 549, of which 82 culminated in diagnosed cases of DCS and 467 were completed with no DCS. Thus, the overall DCS incidence in these exposures is 82/549 or 14.9%. The spreadsheet data include information such as subject’s age, height, weight, body surface area, cholesterol level, and so on, as well as descriptions of the pressure, breathing gas, and exercise profiles for each exposure.

    Data items specifically needed for present model development and testing were extracted from the spreadsheets into 31 Augmented NMRI (Navy Medical Research Institute) text format data files. Comments were inserted in each line of data for easy identification. From a modeling perspective, the investigators have accurately detailed machine-readable descriptions of the NASA-JSC exposure profiles; including oxygen pre-breathe time, exercise times and levels, and either the DCS onset time or the right-censored time (no symptoms by end of test) for each exposure. The data also include observations on grade (0 – IV Spencer scale) and onset time of venous gas emboli detected using a Doppler ultrasound instrument.

    Data from more than 3322 hyperbaric man-exposures have also been augmented with appropriate information about exercise performed during the exposures. In most cases, the added information was obtained by review of original reports and Navy Experimental Diving Unit laboratory logbooks. These hyperbaric data have been combined with the altitude exposure data to develop a model that will be applicable to the full range of altitude, diving, and flying after diving exposures encountered by NASA personnel. Limited success of such models to date has long been suspected due to the different temporal distributions of exercise in typical altitude and diving exposures. Exercise tends to be performed after decompression in altitude exposures and before decompression in diving exposures. Without proper accommodation of this difference in a model or the data to which the model is fit, different exercise effects are averaged over the entire training data set with adverse impact on overall model fit and applicability.

    Linearization schemes and parameter optimization
    A new variable tissue volume model (VTVM) of tissue gas bubble dynamics has been developed that takes advantage of a linear scalability property of our gas and bubble dynamics equations. A scaled VTVM with arbitrary values of all model parameters except tissue volume produces a model equivalent to any unscaled VTVM model. A model of DCS incidence and time of occurrence based on the scaled VTVM is consequently fit to DCS data with linear optimization schemes that are much simpler than the nonlinear schemes required to fit unscaled models. The simplicity affords substantial reductions in the times required to optimize the model about any given training data set and in the times required to solve the optimized model to estimate DCS risks of new decompression exposures. As a result, the model promises great utility in application to real-time prescriptions of decompression schedules for exposures of arbitrary complexity.

    Linear optimization procedures have been developed that provide fits of the scaled VTVM to collections of widely heterogeneous diving exposure profiles with goodness-of-fit measures comparable to those obtained for unscaled models optimized about the same data. However, the reliability of DCS risk estimates yielded by the fitted scaled models for profiles not within the training data has been poor compared with the reliability of estimates yielded for the same profiles by fitted unscaled models. Analytical modifications to the fitting and risk estimation procedures have been implemented to address this lack of reliability, but need further testing. At any rate, it is clear that any scaled VTVM model will require validation with an unscaled version optimized about the same training data

    Evaluation of newly parameterized model features
    1. Exercise versus VGE. Nonlinear optimizations of models based on the unscaled version of the fully elaborated VTVM have been attempted about expanded training data including both diving and altitude exposures. The focus of this effort has been on models that accommodate the influences of multiple inert gases and oxygen on bubble dynamics, with tissue O2 contents determined in accord with physiological Hb-O2 dissociation in the compartmental perfusate. Behavior of resultant models on the majority of profiles in the training data was consistent, but the solutions for select profiles, particularly those involving diving saturation exposures with long slow decompressions, was erratic. The erratic behavior was traced to numerical instabilities in the solutions for the coupled nonlinear differential equations that are required to deal with gas bubble dynamics (dr/dt), compartmental dissolved gas tensions (dpt/dt), Hb-O2 dissociation, bubble nucleation, and exercise effects on compartmental perfusion and oxygen content.

    2. A new and efficient numerical procedure for solving the gas and bubble dynamics equations has recently been developed that promises to minimize or eliminate numerical instability. The procedure is semi-analytic in that it allows model state variables at the end of each successive small time interval to be computed directly from their values at the beginning of the interval. The procedure is readily applicable to bubble dynamics governed by exchanges of multiple diffusible gases between bubble and surrounding tissue.

    System Software
    A prototype Planner for altitude, flying after diving, and diving exposures has been developed based on the graphical user interface of the U.S. Navy Thalmann Algorithm Dive Planner. The latter has been extensively tested and approved for operational use under waiver by select users in the U.S. Navy diving community. Unlike the Thalmann Algorithm Dive Planner, which is based on the deterministic neo-Haldanian Thalmann Algorithm, the new prototype Planner incorporates the much more complex and compute-intensive probabilistic gas and bubble dynamics models that are being developed in this and related work. The software structure of the prototype will allow ready incorporation of new models as they become available.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Kozlovskaya, InessaPrincipal Investigator: Bloomberg, JacobCo-Investigator: Lange, GregCo-Investigator: Layne, CharlesCo-Investigator: McDonald, VernonCo-Investigator: Melton, ShannonCo-Investigator: Mulavara, AjitkumarCo-Investigator: Voronov, Andrei
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Significant locomotor and postural equilibrium disturbances frequently occur following space flight and have been reported by both the U.S. and Russian space programs. The general overriding objective of this investigation was to understand the underlying sensorimotor adaptive alterations that contribute to these postflight locomotor disturbances. Previous investigations typically assessed how specific sensorimotor subsystems, such as vestibulo-ocular and otolith-spinal reflexes, function during the process of adaptation to weightlessness and readaptation to 1-G. However, little documentation exists of changes in the strategies used for coordination among these subsystems.

This experiment was designed to determine if extended exposure to the microgravity environment encountered during long-duration space flight adaptively modified eye and head control mechanisms required to maintain gaze stability during terrestrial locomotion; and determine if head-trunk coordination strategies that occur during terrestrial locomotion were modified following extended duration space flight and to determine if these changes were associated with disturbances in lower limb kinematics and muscle activity patterns of the leg during locomotion.

APPROACH:
To evaluate the vestibular changes, participating subjects performed several tasks both before and after flight. The data collected before flight was used as a baseline, and data gathered postflight was compared to preflight values to evaluate the changes or differences. All data collection sessions were performed three times before launch at L-120, L-45 and L-20 (days before launch), and three times after return to Earth on R+1, R+3 and R+8 (days after landing).

Treadmill locomotion:
Subjects walked and ran on a motorized treadmill while fixating their gaze on a centrally placed target under four conditions (20 seconds per condition), slow walk (4 km/hr), fast walk (6.4 km/hr), and running (6.9 km/hr). During both the slow walk and running conditions, subjects visually fixated on a far target 2 meters away. While fast walking, the subjects visually fixated on a far target 2 meters away; while visually fixating on the target, subjects were asked to point and perform number recognition tasks. The number recognition task measures dynamic visual acuity (DVA). Also during the fast walk condition, subjects visually fixated on a near target located 30 cm from the subject.

To measure head and trunk movements, passive retro-reflective markers (with negligible mass), which served as tracking landmarks, were affixed to the vertex, occipital, right temporal positions of the head, on the seventh cervical vertebrae (C7), two markers to the right and left of the midline at approximately the tenth thoracic vertebrae (T10) and on the sacrum. Leg motion was measured by placing markers on the foot, ankle, knee and hip. The movements of these markers were simultaneously recorded with video cameras that sampled concurrent video images at 60 Hz. The position of each marker in space was uniquely determined with the aid of a video-based motion analysis system. Subjects were outfitted with shorts, sleeveless shirts, athletic socks and running shoes with electronic pressure switches attached to the heels and toes so that times of heel strike and toe off could be determined. After the skin was cleaned with alcohol wipes, preamplifier surface EMG electrodes were placed on the subjects over the bellies of the splenius capitis (SC), sternocleidomastoid (SCM), erector spinae (ES), rectus femoris (RF), biceps femoris (BF), tibialis anterior (TA), and gastrocnemius (GA) in parallel to the muscle fibers. The electrodes were attached with hypoallergenic tape and then those on the legs were covered with elastic wraps to prevent the electrodes from moving on the skin. The analog EMG data were bandpassed at 30-300 Hz before being digitized at 500 Hz. An accelerometer was affixed to the shin using a mounting plate strapped to the leg with a neoprene strap with a Velcro closure. Another accelerometer was attached to the helmet that was worn on the subject's head during walking. The accelerometer and foot-switch information was sampled at 500 Hz. Horizontal and vertical eye positions relative to the head were recorded using standard DC-electrooculographic (EOG) methods.

Before initiating each trial, the subject straddled the treadmill belt while the treadmill speed was increased to the required speed. With the treadmill belts at speed the subject was free to begin walking. A few strides were permitted to allow the subject to become comfortable with the treadmill speed and to attain a steady gait. After a verbal "ready" indication from the subject, data collection was initiated with the subject continuing to walk/run while visually fixating the target for 20 seconds. The subject was instructed to maintain fixation of the target for the full duration of the trial. To prevent potential injury through falling, each subject wore a torso harness that was attached to an overhead frame. During nominal treadmill performance, this harness provided no support and did not act to interfere with the natural movement of the head or limbs.

Overground locomotion:
Subjects walked on a 6.1-meter walkway with one embedded force plate at three selected speeds (normal, slow, fast). The subject was instructed to visually fixate on a wall-mounted target during walking. Four trials at each pace comprised the complete data set. An accelerometer was affixed to the shin using a mounting plate strapped to the leg with a neoprene strap with a Velcro closure. Another accelerometer was attached to a bite-bar that was held in the subject's teeth during walking. The subject performed the overground protocol in bare feet.

RESULTS:
Several conclusions were made after a review of the data collected during the NASA-Mir program: 1) Exposure to space flight induces adaptive changes in head-trunk coordination along with alterations in lower limb kinematics during treadmill locomotion; 2) Following space flight, crewmembers experienced decrement in dynamic visual acuity (DVA) during treadmill locomotion; 3) Postflight changes in head movement control were also present during overground locomotion; and 4) Changes in head-trunk movement strategy coupled with alterations in lower limb kinematics may have contributed to the decrement in DVA observed during postflight locomotion.

After space flight all subjects showed altered head-trunk coordination strategies, modified lower limb kinematics, and reduced DVA during locomotion. Full recovery of function was not complete within the 9-day post landing testing period. The outcome of all these changes is a loss of integration of the multiple full-body cascade of sensorimotor events responsible for efficient control of terrestrial locomotion.

From these data, scientists have begun to better understand the vestibular system and its re-adaptation process. The information obtained and techniques developed during the NASA-Mir program were used to formulate a clinical test of dynamic visual acuity while walking. This test is currently being used to assess the recovery rate of crewmembers returning from space flight as part of the Space Medicine and Countermeasure Program at NASA and to assess the recovery rate of patients following vestibular surgery at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, Texas.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Human adaptation to space flight is accompanied by a loss of red blood cell mass (RBCM), a loss of plasma volume (PV), and a decrease in total blood volume. This leads to a decrease in gravity-dependent space below the heart. In this study, rats were examined to determine whether similar hemodynamic changes occur, making them a suitable subject for study. SLS-1 marked the first time PV and RBCM were measured before and after flight. SLS-2 allowed for repeat determinations and the first opportunity for inflight assessment of erythropoiesis. An additional inflight experiment tested the ability of the rat bone marrow to respond to a bolus of erythropoietin, the major hormone controlling erythropoiesis in animals and humans.

Approach:

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The D-2 experiment, Cardiovascular Regulation in Microgravity, flown on Spacelab, was designed to test the general hypothesis that human cardiovascular adaptation to microgravity is rapid and effective but associated with significant dysfunction on return to Earth. The principal specific objectives were to (1) contribute to better understanding of the control of body fluid volumes at microgravity by characterizing the responses to rapid expansion of intravascular volume before, during, and after space flight, and (2) to define the mechanisms underlying post-flight orthostatic hypotension.

APPROACH:
Responses to rapid intravenous fluid loading
Preflight measurements were obtained, supine and sitting, in the four D-2 payload crewmembers at six and nine months before flight and in-flight on mission day 5. A system for warming saline to 37 degrees Celsius and an air-free intravenous infusion system was developed through a collaborative effort involving the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and NASA Johnson Space Center. The isotonic saline solution, 22 ml/kg, was delivered over 20 minutes by air pressure from two inflatable bladders compressing a plastic saline bag. The driving pressure was generated by a hand-held inflation bulb and displayed by an aneroid manometer. Mean delivery in microgravity was 95.9% of the intended volume which ranged from 1595 to 1919 ml. Finger arterial pressure was monitored. Cardiac output was measured by the foreign gas rebreathing technique.

Mechanisms of post-flight orthostatic intolerance
The stand test had a scheduled duration of 10 minutes with detailed cardiovascular measurements at rest supine, after five minutes standing, and during the last minute of the test. An electrocardiogram and Finapres arterial pressure were recorded continuously. Cardiac output was measured with the acetylene rebreathing technique. Leg volume was measured at rest and during standing using a stocking plethysmograph.

RESULTS:
Studies of the four D-2 payload crewmembers before and immediately after flight were an essential part of a detailed study of orthostatic intolerance that also involved crewmembers from the flights of the Spacelab life sciences missions SLS-1 and SLS-2, in 1991 and 1993 respectively. Combined, 14 crewmembers, 11 men and 3 women, were examined preflight and within four hours of landing after flights of 9 to 14 days.

Preflight, all crewmembers were able to complete the ten-minute stand test. Post-flight, nine of the fourteen (64%) were unable to finish. Pre- and post-flight supine haemodynamics were similar in both groups except slightly (p < 0.05) higher systolic and mean arterial pressures in the finishers. Post-flight, finishers and non-finishers had equally large postural decreases in stroke volume during standing, and also similar degrees of leg pooling. Non-finishers had a greater (but not significantly so) heart rate increase. Cardiac outputs during standing were also similar. The salient difference between finishers and non-finishers was a greater vasoconstrictor response among the finishers with a mean total peripheral resistance during standing (p <0.01).

The cardiovascular effects of fluid load on-orbit were significantly different from the preflight supine data and closely approached, but did not consistently reach, the preflight sitting response levels. The stroke volume data from microgravity were virtually identical to preflight measurements in the sitting position.

At the time of this experiment, the exact mechanism(s) underlying the inadequate vasoconstrictor response early after return to 1-G were yet to be defined. Maximal oxygen uptake was reduced post-flight but maintained at preflight levels after five to eight days in space, which was consistent with grossly intact cardiovascular regulatory mechanisms at microgravity.

Responses to a graded intravenous infusion of the alpha-adrenergic agonist phenylephrine were measured as changes in leg and total peripheral resistance; responses noted two days after return to 1-G were not different from preflight. However, a series of stand tests performed early after return from space demonstrated lower plasma norepinephrine levels in non-finishers than in finishers.

The results from D-2, SLS-1, and SLS-2 provided the base for a new series of detailed and specific studies of cardiovascular control mechanisms planned for Neurolab, a Spacelab flight, flown in 1998, and for a series of long duration flights in the Russian space station Mir.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Schreckenghost, DebraCo-Investigator: Billman, Dorrit
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As crewed missions move deeper into space and communication latency increases, strategies for carrying out tasks must shift. Astronauts will be unable to depend on real-time support from flight controllers; controllers will not be able to perform procedures in the same way they do for the International Space Station (ISS), nor to advise on changed applicability of procedures in real-time. This change threatens to increase astronaut workload, decrease efficiency, and increase the risk of suboptimal task execution.

Automation is an important resource for adapting to this altered environment. To help rather than harm, however, automation must be effectively integrated with the humans it supports. This research aimed to: 1) identify and refine candidate strategies for allocating tasks to automation and the factors when guidelines apply, 2) define effectiveness measures for these task allocation strategies, 3) conduct empirical assessment of the effectiveness of human-automation integration(HAI) based on the proposed allocation strategies, and 4) integrate findings as proposed task allocation strategies with automation. The approach to automation investigates the use of procedures as the basis of automation. By using a human-oriented procedure to organize automation, automation is designed to be more comprehensible to operators. For procedure automation, the actions in a procedure are enabled for automatic execution when instrumentation is available to perform the action. The degree of automation can be varied by changing which actions are designated for automatic execution. Strategies for determining which steps should be automated range from pre-defined allocations to flexible adjustment while the procedure is being executed.

APPROACH:
Ground
TRACLabs and its partners from NASA and San Jose State University evaluated human performance for different task allocation strategies for procedure automation and used the results to articulate a set of allocation strategies. In addition, they defined operational scenarios for the evaluation, including a set of multi-step procedures and simulation that works with these procedures, provided procedure automation software for executing these procedures on the simulation, and performed ground-based human subject testing where subjects used the procedure automation to perform the tasks. The investigators selected the task allocation strategies for evaluation that included both predefined and flexible allocation of tasks and measured and analyzed human and automation performance for each of these strategies under both nominal and off-nominal circumstances.

NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA)
A study was completed in the HERA facility during Campaign 2 evaluating PRIDE electronic procedure software. Sixteen subjects participated, four per mission. Each subject was trained for two hours prior to the two-week mission, then performed seven 1-hour sessions during the mission. Investigators embedded two study-designs within the larger seven-session activities. The Step-List Study tested the hypothesis that performance using procedures with actions grouped into functional units of work called steps (Step Format) would be better than using procedures without this grouping (List Format). The Problem-Solving Study investigated 1) the effects of repetition on problem solving, 2) the effects of a secondary manual task done in conjunction with the primary habitat task where problem occurs, and 3) the effects of encouragement to plan in advance on subsequent execution. Several exploratory tasks were distributed over the mission as well, including the Automation-Manual Investigation comparing human performance with an electronic procedure to the same procedure done using as much automation as possible.

RESULTS:
Ground
Investigators analyzed data comparing manual execution of the new procedure system (PRIDE Interface) to a system analogous to procedures for ISS (Legacy Interface). They assessed whether manual performance with PRIDE would be as good as or better than with the legacy system. This lays the foundation for integrating automated execution into the flow of procedures designed for humans. They found speed and accuracy of manual procedure execution was better using the PRIDE interface over Legacy interface. When using the PRIDE interface, less than three percent of procedures had errors. For Legacy Interface, 33 percent of procedures had errors. Using PRIDE interface took less time than Legacy interface for all trials. Using the original PRIDE interface it was hard to predict what can be automated, what should be automated, and the consequences of attempting to automate elements that cannot or should not be automated. Methods to identify what cannot or should not be automated were an important direction for development. Support for constructing and checking an advance automation plan also was identified as valuable. Automation plans may be more complex than was easily supported by the original approach of automating between the focus bar and a breakpoint. Users may find it useful to specify spans of procedure lines to automate. Since steps are a central unit of work in procedures, supporting step-level automation control may be valuable.

HERA
HERA Step-List Study: Investigators found significant effects of format on both markup errors and mode-execution errors given a correct markup. This suggests the Step Format made it somewhat easier to assign execution mode (Manual or Automated) and execute from those assignments; there was no influence of Format on time measures. These results suggest that the Step format reduces errors in setting function allocation relative to List format and they merit further investigation.

HERA Problem Solving Study: Behavior across users and days for the HERA experiment is both less successful in accomplishing the task-specified goals and more variable in the strategies adopted, than in the earlier study of problem-solving behavior. The most striking result is the degree of variation in strategy and outcome across this user group. Some users were successful in using electronic procedure software to recover from an unexpected situation where the procedure could not be executed directly and normally. Other users were not, and their difficulties included an assumption that automation would prevent any harmful action, reluctance to do anything not directly specified in their daily tasks, and uncertainty about what might be causing the specific value or its importance. There are many possible contributors to the reduced likelihood of accomplishing the task goal in HERA over that in the ground study. The task was structurally more complexly in HERA, because the user needed to identify and execute the recovery procedures for two habitat systems instead of one. Additionally, the absence of experimenter available for the ground study, and differences in training may have increased the difficulty of the problem-solving tasks in HERA.

HERA Automation-Manual Investigation: Error analyses suggest that the mode differences (manual versus automated), between two low error rates, would be expected again in similar conditions. Thus executing with maximal automation may reduce errors relative to manual execution. Executing procedures with maximal automation may also reduce execution timing relative to executing the same procedures by manual alone. Small reductions in execution timing with automation were observed. Faster execution time with automation versus manual only modes should be investigated further.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Clear mechanistic understanding of the biological processes elicited by high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation increased cancer risk will reduce the uncertainties in assessing the risk of space flight. Classic targeted radiation effects such as cell kill and mutation are proportional to dose and their LET dependence is described by relative biological effectiveness (RBE). However recent data suggests that high LET radiation affects multicellular processes that promote cancer. The investigators propose that radiation carcinogenesis results from two classes of ionizing radiation effect: targeted effects that alter genomic sequence and non-targeted effects (NTE) that alter phenotype and multicellular interactions. Since NTE are not proportional to dose, new approaches are required to assess the impact of NTE, which alter gene expression, cell signaling, genomic stability, and cell phenotypes, on carcinogenesis. It is unknown to what extent NTE contribute to the significantly greater carcinogenic effect of high LET radiation. Investigators hypothesize that NTE promotes epithelial cancer.

APPROACH:
This project used experimental studies and modeling to define the efficiency and physiological context in which high LET radiation exposure increases epithelial cancer risk. Investigators hypothesized that NTEs both contribute to radiation carcinogenesis. Targeted effects includes DNA damage responses and changes in genomic sequence that is the result of interaction between ionizing irradiation and DNA. NTE alter the phenotype and multicellular interactions that can contribute to cancer. The hypothesis proposed that the greater carcinogenic risk from high LET irradiation is due to NTE promotion of targeted radiation effects. The NSCOR was composed of three projects at New York University (NYU), University of California San Francisco (UCSF), and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL).

RESULTS:
The goal of Project 1 was to determine the contribution of NTE as a function of radiation quality on breast cancer. Investigators used a radiation chimera mammary model to discern the effects of radiation-induced microenvironment from DNA damage and potential mutation. In this model they first surgically cleared the mammary gland of endogenous epithelium. Then the mouse was irradiated and the fat-pad subsequently orthotopically transplanted with un-irradiated, non-malignant epithelial cells primed for malignant transformation by Trp53 deletion that were evaluated for tumors for 600 days.

To compare the contribution of targeted and NTE, investigators irradiated mice after Trp53 null outgrowth was established (i.e., epithelium was exposed, i.e., targeted and NTE) and the other group was irradiated before transplantation (i.e., NTE only, epithelium was not exposed). Tumors in mice irradiated with densely ionizing 600 MeV/amu Fe charged particles or sparsely ionizing gamma-ray radiation were compared to those in contemporaneous sham-irradiated controls. Irradiation of the in situ mammary outgrowth with either radiation quality decreased Trp53 null tumor latency and increased tumor frequency a year after. Mammary tumor latency arising from non-irradiated Trp53 null outgrowths in irradiated hosts was also decreased indicating that this effect was mediated by the microenvironment. Tumors arising from densely ionizing irradiated outgrowths gave rise to aggressive tumors with increased growth rate compared to sham-irradiated mice. Importantly, increased tumor aggressiveness was also observed in tumors arising from irradiated hosts, suggesting that this effect was mediated by NTE. Only densely ionizing radiation affected tumor markers of differentiation in both models. The data from these studies supports the conclusion that tumor aggressiveness is indirectly promoted by NTE and that NTE elicited by HZE particles results in more aggressive tumors. The RNA of these tumors has been sequenced. Notably, preliminary analysis using unsupervised clustering separated tumors arising from irradiated epithelium in irradiated hosts (i.e., targeted) from those that arose in irradiated mice.

Investigators also evaluated the effect of age in the radiation chimera-experiment; mice were irradiated at 10 months, simulating the average age for astronauts. Notably high LET exposure of aged mice is much more efficient inducing tumorigenesis than low LET. Cancer incidence in humans increases exponentially with age, with 75% of newly diagnosed cases occurring in susceptible populations aged 55 years or older. The aging process has been shown to be associated with increased levels of chronic inflammation, which are thought to contribute to many age-associated diseases, including cancer, and increased serum levels of IL-6 have been reported in older individuals. Interestingly, A-bomb survivors have significant increases in serum IL-6 levels that are still detectable five decades after exposure. These findings suggested the possibility that radiation carcinogenesis, at least in part, is mediated by induction of a pro-inflammatory environment similar to the aging process.

To test this, mice were irradiated at 10 months of age, comparable to the middle age of astronauts during space flight missions to test the hypothesis that NTE overlap with the biology that increases cancer incidence in aged versus young people. The inguinal mammary glands of 200 mice were cleared at three weeks of age and the mice housed under standard conditions. Hosts were irradiated at 10 months of age with 10, 50, or 100 cGy gamma-radiation or 350 MeV/amu Ar or Si, or 600 MeV/amu Fe at a fluence of 1 particle per 102 mm, and transplanted three days later with Trp53 null epithelium. Tumorigenesis was monitored for 600 days. As expected due to decreased ovarian hormones in aged mice, fewer mammary outgrowths were obtained in aged mice; outgrowth efficiency is greater than 90% in young mice mammary but approximately 50% in aged mice. This limited the ability to compare dose or particles individually. However, investigators were able to compare tumors arising in sham-irradiated mice to gamma-irradiated hosts or HZE-irradiated hosts. Age and radiation NTE were not epistatic as both low- and high-LET irradiation of aged hosts significantly increased tumor incidence and tumor growth rate. Moreover, this experiment revealed a strong radiation quality effect in which HZE NTE was considerably more effective than gamma-radiation.

Expression profiling of these tumors indicate that the top ranked (p> 0.00001) processes that distinguish tumors from aged mice irradiated with HZE particles from age-matched, sham-irradiated tumors were inflammation (70 genes), immune cell trafficking (79 genes), and cancer (271 genes). Among the 20 most significant upstream regulators ranked by z-score (p <0.05), the majority are pro-inflammatory factors such as IL-1ß, TNFalpha, and IL6. Consistent with previous findings, TGFß1 is predicted by IPA to also be a significant regulator in cancers from both HZE and gamma-irradiated host. Investigators speculate that gamma- and HZE-irradiated microenvironments might evoke common mediators, but their magnitude or persistence might be different. Among the top-ranked upregulated molecules are COX2 and granzyme H. They validated this signature using relative COX2 transcript abundance and protein expression, which support high levels of COX-2 in tumors arising in HZE-irradiated mice.

Together these data lead investigators to postulate that a high degree of immunosuppressive inflammation promotes these aggressive tumors. To test this idea, investigators used immunostaining to evaluate lymphoid and myeloid cellular subsets within tumors. Most strikingly, tumors arising in HZE-irradiated aged hosts have significantly (p <0.05) more myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSC) and Treg cells compared to tumors arising in age-matched, sham-irradiated hosts. Treg frequency inversely correlates with tumor growth rate and MDSC is positively correlated with Cox2 staining, leading to the new hypothesis that HZE radiation exposure in mid-life is strongly immunosuppressive.

Project 2, directed by Dr. Allan Balmain at UCSF, had the ultimate goal of identifying the genetics associated with susceptibility to cancer risk from high LET radiation. The strategies employed were based on systems genetics approaches to identify germ line polymorphisms and somatic genetic changes associated with tumor development. This project focuses heavily on genetic analysis of radiation-induced tumors.

Interestingly the irradiated tumor spectrum of both Trp53 deltaP and Trp53+/- mice in the FVB/N background falls into three main tumor types: thymic lymphomas, mammary tumors, and skin carcinomas. It should be noted that lymphomas are often observed post-radiation in mice of compromised Trp53 function, particularly after exposure to high radiation doses (4 Gy). After exposure to a low dose (50cGy) of either low or high LET radiation, investigators observed increased frequency of mammary tumors and skin carcinomas in both genotypes. Although the tumor spectrum is similar between mice exposed to high or low LET radiation, there was an increased incidence of mammary tumors following high LET radiation.

A small number of mammary tumors developed following high LET radiation (n=3), whilst none were observed in the gamma-irradiated group. These data demonstrate that FVB/N mice are particularly susceptible to radiation-induced mammary tumor development. High LET radiation was also more potent at inducing a higher incidence of mammary tumors with a shorter latency compared to gamma-radiation (p= 0.0004 CoxPH).

Little is known about the mechanisms by which high LET induces carcinogenesis. Exposing mice of abrogated Trp53 function to either high or low LET radiation provided investigators with a unique opportunity to compare and contrast the genetic aberrations and potential radiation-quality specific signatures in tumors. Next generation sequencing offers a powerful tool to gain a deeper understanding of the complex mutational processes driving radiation-induced tumorigenesis.

Project 3, led by Dr. S. V. Costes and Dr. Mao, undertook to use computational modeling of experimental data. Linear-quadratic models have been used for decades to interpret cell survival after exposure to ionizing radiation. However, parameters for these models change with LET, forcing investigators to measure experimentally cell survival for any LET of interest. In contrast to the current paradigm, investigators hypothesize that double strand breaks (DSBs) are moved into repair domains and consequently merge into clusters. Overall, this work suggests that microdosimetric properties of ion tracks at the sub-micron level are sufficient to explain both RIF data and survival curves for any LET, similarly to the Local Effect Model assumption.

experiment_title: Gene Expression Profile Analysis as a Prognostic Indicator of Normal Tissue Response to Simulated Space Radiations

investigators: Principal Investigator: Story, MichaelCo-Investigator: Stivers, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project was funded as a pilot project to determine the feasibility of using gene expression profiles to characterize the response of human cells to exposure to particulate radiations such as those encountered in the space flight environment. The investigators proposed to use microarray technology to examine the gene expression patterns of a bank of well-characterized human fibroblast cell cultures. These fibroblast cultures were derived from breast or head and neck cancer patients who exhibited normal, minimal, or severe normal tissue reactions following low LET radiation exposure via radiotherapy. Furthermore, determination of SF2 values from fibroblasts cultured from these individuals was predictive of risk for severe late reactions. The investigators hypothesized that by determining the expression of thousands of genes they could identify gene expression patterns that reflect how normal tissues respond to high Z and energy (HZE) particles, that is, that there are molecular signatures for HZE exposures. They also hypothesized that individuals who are intrinsically radiosensitive may elicit a unique response.

The objectives of this study were to 1) determine molecular profiles (gene expression patterns} for normal human skin fibroblasts that have been exposed to heavy particles of increasing LET; 2) determine if there are unique, or signature, expression patterns that define exposure to a particular HZE particle

APPROACH:
In the last decade we have collected fibroblasts from head and neck and breast cancer patients. We have developed fibroblast lines from 100 patients. A significant number of the patients have had adverse reactions to radiotherapy with documented late normal tissue reactions scored according to the RTOG/EORTC scoring system. Late effects documented include skin fibrosis, subcutaneous fibrosis, skin retraction, and soft tissue and bone necrosis. For all of these primary cultures, fibroblast SF2 values were obtained. Interestingly, SF2 ranking appears as a continuous variation which is best approximated by a normal distribution of phenotype, which can be explained by multiple interacting Mendelian factors, that is, a genetic basis for differences in SF2. Because this was a pilot project the investigators limited themselves to 5 cell lines, all having a normal response to radiation exposure.

RESULTS:
Statistical analysis revealed 45 genes that met the investigators cutoff criteria of 1.5X fold, false discovery rate of 0.05. Two major signaling pathways were identified by gene ontology analysis, and they include genes associated with DNA repair, replication, recombination, and cell growth and death. BAD and BID, and CIOE are unregulated, while BCl-2 is comparatively down-regulated. This opens the door for predicting radioresponse without having to irradiate. More data are needed on other radiosensitive cells lines to validate this supposition.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Paloski, WilliamCo-Investigator: Bloomberg, JacobCo-Investigator: Reschke, Millard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Neurological adaptation to microgravity is driven by the stimulus rearrangement associated with loss of gravitational loading of the vestibular otolith organs, the proprioceptive organs (muscle spindle, golgi tendon and joint pressure) and the exteroceptive organs (pacinian corpuscles, etc.). It is also driven by altered biomechanical constraints on body stabilization in space and locomotion through space. The neurological adaptive response to microgravity is characterized by alterations in CNS integration of sensory information, perceptions of spatial orientation, and motor coordination strategies. Upon return to gravity following extended stay in microgravity, the lost sensory stimuli and biomechanical contraints return, and a period of readaptation occurs. During readaptation, crews cannot perform duties and activities requiring keen sensorimotor control or spatial orientation skills on a par with their preflight abilities. The amplitudes and time constants associated with recovery of preflight performance capabilities are much greater for a long duration flight (>60 days) than for a short duration flight (<20 days).

APPROACH:
Evaluation of fitness to return to affected duties was assessed quantitatively using performance measures obtained from the following standardized test batteries:
Balance Control (Posture): this test battery provided a quantitative assessment of the ability of crewmembers to fully utilize vestibular, proprioceptive and visual information to estimate spatial orientation (balance status) and to maintain stable control of upright stance. At each test session, the subject completed a standard clinical battery of sensory organization tests (SOT) on the Equitest dynamic posturography system. Each test lasted for 20 seconds, during which the subject maintained a quiet, upright posture with normal, absent, and or mechanically altered visual add proprioceptive sensory inputs. Test conditions were: standard eyes open Romberg test with support surface fixed; standard eyes open Romberg test with visual surround and support surface fixed; sway-referenced visual surround with fixed support surface; sway-referenced support surface with fixed visual surround; sway-referenced support surface with eyes closed; sway-referenced support surface with sway-referenced visual surround. Performance assessment was based on the peak body sway during each condition.

Locomotor Control (Locomotion): tests of dynamic visual acuity (DVA) and impaired modulation of shock wave transmission during locomotion served as global indicators of sensorimotor dysfunction. This test was a two-part test in which subjects first walked along a short overground track and then on a treadmill. During overground locomotion, the subject gripped a bitebar in the teeth while walking 6-8 meters at a freely chosen pace across a walkway with a built in force plate. The task was repeated 4-6 times to ensure clean right foot contact with the force plate. Performance assessment was based on the relative amplitude of the shock wave transmitted from the heel to the head. During the treadmill locomotion, the subject walked t 6.4 km/hr and focused gaze on a laptop computer screen placed 2 meters in front of the treadmill at eye level. While walking, the subject read aloud a series of numbers of varying sizes that flashed across the screen. Performance assessment was based on the number of correct responses to the dynamic visual acuity task.

Eccentric Gaze-Holding: this task provided a quantitative assessment of stability (state) of the brainstem neural integrator function, and indirectly, of the eye movement control system following space flight. This test was only performed on NASA 7.

The study was conducted preflight and postflight. Preflight baseline data collection was performed at 60, 30 and 10 days before flight, and postflight collection occurred on landing day (2-3 hours after landing) and on days 1, 2, 4, 8, 12 after landing. Sessions at 16, 32 and 64 days after landing were conducted if the investigator did not see a return to preflight responses in the preceding sessions.

RESULTS:
Results of this experiment are not available.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Wang, YaCo-Investigator: Guida, Peter
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study aimed to determine whether the major reason for high-linear energy transfer (LET) ionizing radiation (IR) to induce excess relative risk (ERR) as compared with low-LET IR on carcinogenesis is because of inefficient Ku-dependent non-homologous end-joining repair. Investigators sought to answer the question whether inefficient Ku-dependent repair is the major reason for high-LET IR to induce ERR on carcinogenesis.

High-LET ionizing radiation (IR), when compared with low-LET IR, induces more death both in vitro as well as in vivo, induces more mutations in vitro and induces more cancers in vivo. IR-induced DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) are the severest threat for IR-induced killing as well as are the initial and the essential event for IR-induced genomic integrity. Two kinds of major DSB repair exist in eukaryotic cells, homologous recombination repair (HRR) and non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). HRR is the major pathway for repairing DSBs in yeast, but both the NHEJ and HRR pathways are required for DSB repair in mammalian cells. NHEJ repair includes a Ku-dependent main pathway and a PARP-1 dependent complementary pathway. High-LET IR induces more cell killing when compared with low LET IR and is described as relative biologic effectiveness (RBE), which is believed to be caused by ineffective rejoining of DNA DSBs involved in the Ku-dependent NHEJ pathway. However, it remains unclear whether high-LET IR also affects the pathways of HRR and PARP-1-dependent complementary NHEJ. Recent data suggest that high-LET IR affects only the Ku-dependent main NHEJ but not other repairs, including HRR and PARP-1-dependent complementary NHEJ. Based on the data, investigators hypothesized that the major reason for high LET IR to induce excess relative risk on carcinogenesis is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair. The purpose of this experiment was to test the following three specific aims:


  1. Determine whether the major reason for high-LET IR inducing excess deaths in cells and in mice is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair.
  2. Determine whether the major reason for high-LET IR inducing ERR on carcinogenesis in mice is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair.
  3. Determine whether the major reason for high-LET IR inducing ERR on genomic instability is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair.

APPROACH:
To test their hypothesis that the major reason for high-LET IR inducing excess death in mammals is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair, investigators compared high-LET IR and low-LET IR-induced death of different repair deficient mice at one month following whole body radiation exposure after a single dose. They also compared high-LET IR and low-LET IR-induced carcinogenesis frequencies in different repair deficient mice at six months to a year following whole body exposure to single or fractionation dose of high-LET or low-LET IR. In addition, investigators compared the effects of the repair pathways (NHEJ or HRR) on the low dose-induced cell protective response and the protective role of checkpoint activation in protecting cells from high-LET or low-LET radiation induced killing by using different repair deficient cell lines.

RESULTS:
Cell work: Investigators carried out the experiments by using different types of cells and obtained the following results:

  1. They elucidated why S-phase cells are more sensitive to heavy ion, the high LET radiation, although they are more resistant to x or gamma rays. After further studying the mechanism, investigators believe that the phenotype of S-phase sensitive to high-LET radiation is due to the fact that high-LET radiation could generate much smaller fragments that result in inefficient Ku binding in S-phase, which further supports their hypothesis that high-LET killing more cells when compared with low-LET radiation is because of the inhibition of Ku-dependent NHEJ.
  2. They demonstrated that the checkpoint response plays a more protective role in HZE particle-irradiated cells than in X ray-irradiated cells. Investigators previously reported that the DNA double strand break (DSB)-activated checkpoint mainly facilitates HRR and has little effect on NHEJ.
  3. They indicated that low dose radiation-induced adaptive responses are through promoting NHEJ and explain that low dose radiation could not induce any protective role in high-LET irradiated cells. It has been known for more than two decades that low dose radiation (< 0.1 Gy) could induce adaptive responses. The adaptive responses could protect cells and animals from high-challenge dose-induced killing and carcinogenesis. Because DNA DSBs induced by radiation are the severest threat for cell survival and genetic integrity, the low dose adaptive responses are believed to promote DNA repair. However, it remains unclear which DNA DSB repair pathway, NHEJ or HRR, is promoted by the low dose radiation. Investigators found that low dose radiation could not induce any protective role in high-LET irradiated cells.
  4. They show for the first time that microRNA-21 (miR-21) plays an important role in HZE particle-induced carcinogenesis. By obtaining the paraffin-embedded liver tissues from irradiated mice, investigators found that miR-21 was much higher expressed in liver tumors than in normal liver tissues and further found that ionizing radiation, especially high LET radiation could stimulate miR-21 expression. Investigators further demonstrated that after the non-irradiated, low-LET or high-LET irradiated human hepatocytes were over-expressed with miR-21, these cells became tumorigenesis in nude mice. The tumors derived from high-LET-irradiated-cells were largest, and accompanied by more significant changes in the miR-21-targets: PTEN and RECK. In addition, investigators found that IR-induced up-regulation of miR-21 depended on the up-regulation/activation of AP-1 and the ErbB/Stat3 pathway, which was also IR dose dependent. OBJECTIVES:
This study aimed to determine whether the major reason for high-linear energy transfer (LET) ionizing radiation (IR) to induce excess relative risk (ERR) as compared with low-LET IR on carcinogenesis is because of inefficient Ku-dependent non-homologous end-joining repair. Investigators sought to answer the question whether inefficient Ku-dependent repair is the major reason for high-LET IR to induce ERR on carcinogenesis.

High-LET ionizing radiation (IR), when compared with low-LET IR, induces more death both in vitro as well as in vivo, induces more mutations in vitro and induces more cancers in vivo. IR-induced DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) are the severest threat for IR-induced killing as well as are the initial and the essential event for IR-induced genomic integrity. Two kinds of major DSB repair exist in eukaryotic cells, homologous recombination repair (HRR) and non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). HRR is the major pathway for repairing DSBs in yeast, but both the NHEJ and HRR pathways are required for DSB repair in mammalian cells. NHEJ repair includes a Ku-dependent main pathway and a PARP-1 dependent complementary pathway. High-LET IR induces more cell killing when compared with low LET IR and is described as relative biologic effectiveness (RBE), which is believed to be caused by ineffective rejoining of DNA DSBs involved in the Ku-dependent NHEJ pathway. However, it remains unclear whether high-LET IR also affects the pathways of HRR and PARP-1-dependent complementary NHEJ. Recent data suggest that high-LET IR affects only the Ku-dependent main NHEJ but not other repairs, including HRR and PARP-1-dependent complementary NHEJ. Based on the data, investigators hypothesized that the major reason for high LET IR to induce excess relative risk on carcinogenesis is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair. The purpose of this experiment was to test the following three specific aims:


  1. Determine whether the major reason for high-LET IR inducing excess deaths in cells and in mice is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair.
  2. Determine whether the major reason for high-LET IR inducing ERR on carcinogenesis in mice is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair.
  3. Determine whether the major reason for high-LET IR inducing ERR on genomic instability is because of inefficient Ku-dependent NHEJ repair.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective for this activity was to use the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Haughton Mars Project (HMP), a ground based model for planetary surface exploration, to validate immune system monitoring assays designed to support a proposed immunology Supplemental Medical Objective (SMO). Immune system abnormal regulation has been demonstrated to occur during space flight and has the potential to cause serious health risks to crewmembers participating in exploration class missions. This may be caused by mission-associated factors, other than the direct influences of microgravity or radiation, such as stress, confinement or an altered microbial environment. These mission-associated factors may be simulated to reasonable accuracy in ground-based spaceflight analogs such as the HMP. Data from other ground-based models for space flight (extended bed rest, closed chamber confinement, etc.) have confirmed their value for human physiology studies.

The HMP consists of simulated Mars exploration missions performed at the Haughton meteorite impact crater. The Haughton crater is located on Devon Island, in the province of Nunavut, in the high Canadian Arctic. The remote location, harsh polar desert environment, local impact-related and other Mars-like geological features make the Haughton crater one of the closest analogs on Earth to the true Mars environment. While there are significant differences between Devon Island and Mars, many aspects of field exploration activities conducted at Haughton present challenges that are relevant to human planetary exploration. At Haughton crater, a full-size prototype Mars habitat was recently constructed by the Mars Society under the auspices of the NASA Haughton-Mars Project and based on the NASA reference-mission projections for the possible size and capabilities of a Mars habitat capable of supporting human life. HMP participants conduct field exploration while adhering to specific sets of 'true Mars' conditions to ensure the quality of the spaceflight analog situation:

  • Relatively long travel to and from Devon Island.
  • Disruption of circadian rhythms (24 hour daylight).
  • Harsh polar desert conditions.
  • Removal from familiar surroundings.
  • Possible mission-simulation confined to the prototype habitat.
  • Performance of Mars-relevant surface exploration and field activities.
  • Performance of simulated spacesuited Extra-Vehicular Activities (EVA's) (including timed pre-breathe activities, etc.)
  • Performance of Mars-relevant Intra-Vehicular Activities (IVA's) (data analysis, reporting, EVA planning, repairs, etc.)
  • Reliance on remote telemedicine and communications equipment (including artificially-inserted 4 to 20-minute communication delays).

These conditions and factors combined make the HMP a well suited opportunity for simulated Mars exploration and research. In addition, the conditions to which the crewmembers were subjected made the HMP an excellent opportunity to evaluate monitoring strategies and potential countermeasures for spaceflight human factor concerns. The data generated from this activity directly addressed (in a ground-based spaceflight analog) the following questions identified by the NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) Critical Path Roadmap as a research priority for space flight:

7.01 Are there assays of immune function that reliably predict immune compromise?

7.03 Do factors associated with flight (stress, environment, microgravity, nutritional status, radiation) affect humoral or cell-mediated immune function, non-specific immunity, mucosal immunity, or immune surveillance capabilities of crewmembers in a manner that exposes them to unacceptable medical risk (disease, allergy, delayed wound healing)?

7.29 Are there surrogate marker assays that can be adapted to space travel that will quantitate the degree of immunodeficiency for antibody, T-cell, phagocyte, and complement function?

In addition, the data derived from this study identified the most relevant assays for routine monitoring of the immune system and provided a system to monitor the effectiveness of immune countermeasures development. There are currently no standardized immune monitoring assays. This data was a necessary and critical prerequisite for initiating studies designed assess immune countermeasures and to answer the following Critical Path questions:

7.22 Are there countermeasures for space flight-associated defects in antibody, T-cell, phagocyte, and complement systems?

7.23 Are there countermeasures for infections developed in space travel, especially latent virus infections?

APPROACH:
The Haughton Mars Immune Assessment (HMIA) was designed to assess the immune function, cellular distribution, and viral reactivation status of HMP crewmembers in a fashion mirroring a space flight experiment (pre, mid, and post-mission assessments). A unique obstacle for this study was the multinational distribution of the subjects over North America with respect to both pre and post-mission sample collection. All mid-mission sample collection and processing occurred on location at Devon Island during the 2002 field season. For pre- and post-mission sampling, arrangements were made with individual local clinics that possessed both phlebotomy capabilities and the availability of the appropriate sample collection tubes. The protocol was designed to tolerate 24 hour shipping delays of specimens with minimal loss of data, despite the requirement for live cells. When possible, immediate testing is preferred for live cell assays.

ASSAY LIST
The assays selected for the HMIA were designed to comprehensively assess both the functional capabilities and the activation status of the immune system and correlate that data with latent viral Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reactivation. EBV reactivation is a demonstrable adverse clinical outcome that can be quantitatively measured. The assays were designed so that samples may be processed remotely and transported without cold storage, making these assays compatible with current spaceflight experiment requirements. The following is a list of the assays used to monitor immune status:

Immune System
Peripheral blood immune cell subsets
Cell-specific activation status
Th1/Th2 cell cytokine production profiles
Plasma cytokine levels

Viral reactivation
EBV-specific humoral responses
EBV-direct plasma viral DNA via PCR

FIELD SAMPLE PROCESSING ACTIVITIES
The field activities required to be performed on Devon Island consisted of cell culture and sample processing to render all sample types stable for storage and transport to JSC for subsequent analysis. The individual field requirements per assay are as follows:

Blood collection: On Devon Island, a phlebotomy station was set up in the main laboratory tent. Samples were collected from each subject by venipuncture using sterile techniques and butterfly type collection equipment.

Leukocyte subset analysis: Whole blood was treated with a newly developed preservative that maintains the antigenic structure of the cell surface molecules. Samples may be stored at room temperature for up to two weeks. There are several markers that are incompatible with this preservative. For those markers, actual fluorescent antibody staining for flow cytometry analysis was performed on Devon Island and samples were preserved for later analysis.

Plasma cytokine levels/ plasma EBV humoral responses/ EBV Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR): A micro-centrifuge was transported to Devon Island and used to purify plasma from Ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) whole blood samples.

Cytokine production profile cultures: Heparinized whole blood was mixed with media and the appropriate mixture of mitogens and a reagent to halt extracellular transport of proteins. The cultures were then incubated for 5 hours (T cell) or 24 hours (Monocyte) to allow full activation. A portable lightweight field incubator developed by the Cell and Molecular Research (CMR) laboratory was used for these activities. Following culture the supernatant was removed and the activated cells were preserved using a leukocyte preservative.

RESULTS:
The protocol developed for immune sample processing in remote field locations functioned properly. Samples were processed on Devon Island, and stabilized for subsequent analysis at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. The data indicated that some phenotype, immune function and stress hormone changes occurred in the HMP field participants that were largely distinct from pre-mission baseline and post-mission recovery data. These immune changes appear similar to those observed in astronauts following space flight.

The immune system changes described during the HMP field deployment validate the use of the HMP as a ground-based space flight/planetary exploration analog for some aspects of human physiology. The sample processing protocol developed for this study may have applications for immune studies in remote terrestrial field locations. Elements of this protocol could possibly be adapted for future in-flight immunology studies conducted during space missions.

Ten subjects participated during the HMP 2002 field season. One pre, mid, and post-mission sample was collected for each subject. Pre-mission samples collection ranged from 36 days prior to launch of the mission (L-36) to L-4. In-mission samples were collected between Mission Day 4 (MD 4) to MD 18. Post-mission samples were collected from 47 days after the end of the mission (Recovery (R)+47) to R+110. One subject did not provide a post-mission sample.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ocular counterrolling is a principal measurement of otolith function in humans, and is consequently of great interest in the study of space motion sickness and adaptation to weightlessness. There has been success with ocular torsion analysis of video and photographs of eyes to which soft contact lenses with visible markings have been attached. Contact lenses have been frequently used to measure, by optical or mechanical means, the motions of the eye relative to an external frame of reference. Prior to this investigation, only rigid (hard) contact lenses had been used for this purpose. Hard lenses are usually poorly tolerated by the subjects unless a topical anesthetic is used, and the investigator must also maintain a large trial kit of lenses to fit all subjects.

The objective of this experiment was to determine the effectiveness of a method of application and fixation of specially marked hydrogel (soft) contact lenses to the eyes during orbital flight. If distilled water is introduced into the eye, the lens becomes adherent to the corneal surface for a five to ten minute time interval. Investigators aimed to quantitatively document the dependency of lens adhesion on factors such as lens diameter, thickness, construction type, extent of subject blinking, tearing, etc. so that the lenses might be used in torsion measurement.

This was done in 1g by "dehydrating" the lens-eye interface with sterile water. In zero-g KC-135 flights, there had been difficulties in achieving fixation, therefore a simple inflight demonstration was requested.

APPROACH:
The placement method called for mounting the lens in the eye, application of distilled water droplets and wicking away the excess. Two methods of irrigating the lenses, verified in KC-135 flights, were used. Method 1 called for holding the squeeze bottle in front of the eye and squirting water on the lens; the water forms a blob that covers the lens and sometimes the upper lids. Method 2 involved producing a blob of water on the end of the squeeze bottle and then bringing the blob up to the eye; the water rapidly transfers to the eye once it contacts the eye. Once the distilled water was in the eye it needed to be wicked away so that the contact lens could adhere to the cornea. A lint free paper towel (e.g. Kim Wipe) was held to the corner of the eye and put in contact with the water bolus. The surface of the contact lens may also have been dabbed to assure all the water had left the eye. Investigators wanted to test the best methods of irrigation and removal, as there was not sufficient sustained time on the KC-135 to do so. Both irrigation then removal of water, as well as simultaneous irrigation and removal were tested.

Once the lens was in the eye, investigators needed to know how long and how well the lens stuck to the eyeball. After waiting about 15 seconds, the crewmember attempted to move the lens once again, first by vigorous eye movements, then by pressing on the lens with his finger, to determine if it shifts position. When the lens was properly adhered, pressing on it rotated the entire eye and contact lens together, and the effect could be felt and seen in the mirror. The crewmember was asked to do this every 45 seconds to determine whether the lens slips freely, sticks slightly, or adheres rigidly to the eye. The lens was not expected to adhere any longer than 10 minutes under the best of conditions. To repeat the test, the lens was bathed in physiological saline solution and the process could be repeated without requiring reinsertion of the lens on the eye. The crewmember was asked to repeat the test using different amounts of water and different times of wicking away the excess water to achieve the best lens adhesion to the eye. After all tests were complete, the eye was irrigated with saline to loosen the lens, which was then removed.

RESULTS:
Inflight, the installation was extremely simple, but in spite of a wide range of maneuvers lasting several hours, the lens would not adhere using the prescribed procedures. After extraordinary difficulty, the subject managed to get a lens in place, confirming the results from KC-135 flights. The same was experienced postflight. Because of this, the concept was redesigned for use on subsequent flights; it was only after procedures were modified that reliable adherence would occur. It was hoped that the use of multiple small applications of water would improve performance in future flights.

Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

Method 1 called for holding the squeeze bottle in front of the eye and squirting water on the lens; the water forms a blob that covers the lens and sometimes the upper lids. Method 2 involved producing a blob of water on the end of the squeeze bottle and then bringing the blob up to the eye; the water rapidly transfers to the eye once it contacts the eye. Once the distilled water was in the eye it needed to be wicked away so that the contact lens could adhere to the cornea. A lint free paper towel (e.g. Kim Wipe) was held to the corner of the eye and put in contact with the water bolus. The surface of the contact lens may also have been dabbed to assure all the water had left the eye. Investigators wanted to test the best methods of irrigation and removal, as there was not sufficient sustained time on the KC-135 to do so. Both irrigation then removal of water, as well as simultaneous irrigation and removal were tested.

Once the lens was in the eye, investigators needed to know how long and how well the lens stuck to the eyeball. After waiting about 15 seconds, the crewmember attempted to move the lens once again, first by vigorous eye movements, then by pressing on the lens with his finger, to determine if it shifts position. When the lens was properly adhered, pressing on it rotated the entire eye and contact lens together, and the effect could be felt and seen in the mirror. The crewmember was asked to do this every 45 seconds to determine whether the lens slips freely, sticks slightly, or adheres rigidly to the eye. The lens was not expected to adhere any longer than 10 minutes under the best of conditions. To repeat the test, the lens was bathed in physiological saline solution and the process could be repeated without requiring reinsertion of the lens on the eye. The crewmember was asked to repeat the test using different amounts of water and different times of wicking away the excess water to achieve the best lens adhesion to the eye. After all tests were complete, the eye was irrigated with saline to loosen the lens, which was then removed.

RESULTS:
Inflight, the installation was extremely simple, but in spite of a wide range of maneuvers lasting several hours, the lens would not adhere using the prescribed procedures. After extraordinary difficulty, the subject managed to get a lens in place, confirming the results from KC-135 flights. The same was experienced postflight. Because of this, the concept was redesigned for use on subsequent flights; it was only after procedures were modified that reliable adherence would occur. It was hoped that the use of multiple small applications of water would improve performance in future flights.

Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

experiment_title: Assessment of the State of Communication Delay Research in Preparation for Missions Beyond Low Earth Orbit
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE
NASA’s mission-operations paradigm originated with Project Mercury and endured through the Apollo Program, Space Shuttle Program, and ISS missions. This ground team has served as the safety net for crewed for spaceflight missions over the past 60 years.
This operational paradigm will be significantly challenged by long-duration exploration missions beyond low Earth orbit; deep-space crewed missions will be confronted with infrequent resupply, inability to evacuate or be rescued, and high-latency communications that prohibit real-time operational and medical support.
The Human Systems Risk Board has identified the risk of adverse mission outcomes due to Earth Independent Human-Systems Operations (EIHSO), a risk associated with reduced ground support and a shift towards Earth independent operations. In order to fully understand the magnitude of this risk, it is crucial to understand the effects of communication delays on executing complex operations and solving problems. Real-time communication ensures that the crew has access to a large and extensively resourced ground team at any time to oversee and direct operations and diagnose and resolve issues. Behavioral health and performance of the individuals and crews operating across the multi-team space-to-ground system is also negatively affected by communication delays. Previous research shows increased stress, frustration, and adverse behavioral symptoms, and reduced performance at the individual level with the increased isolation and difficulty of delayed comm. It also showed a decline in family connectedness and interpersonal relationship satisfaction. Team cohesion and performance declines under communication delay at the team and multi-team levels.
This study was proposed to examine the evidence generated through decades of communication delay research. The specific aims of this study included:
1.Examine and compare study parameters, including operational regimens and measures of simulation fidelity, outcomes, and situational or task complexity.
2.Review results and implications for mission plans.
3.Assess limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of repeatability, and controls.
4.Capture lessons learned.
5.Map specific aims 1 through 4 against the comm delay problem domain to illuminate remaining gaps in knowledge.


APPROACH

Over the course of 12 months, the investigator team conducted a literature review to summarize the state of the research to characterize what has been studied and the methods employed. This served to identify gaps in the evidence base that threaten upcoming mission priorities. The gap in studies of short communication delays (i.e., 3 to 14 seconds one-way) possible on lunar missions and long delays (up to 20 minutes one-way) anticipated for Mars missions were of particular interest.
In addition to the literature review, interviews with program points of contact were also held internally. These interviews sought to capture program perspectives on communication delay and what was being worked on to mitigate those issues.

RESULTS

This work reviewed, characterized, and synthesized the past 20+ years of research concerning the effects and mitigation of communication latencies during spaceflight missions. Fifty-two spaceflight-relevant, published studies on a variety of aspects were examined first; the review was then focused to a subset of studies (15) that evaluated the effects of communication delay on an outcome measure. Reviewing the published literature contributed to a coherent understanding of what has been studied, how it has been approached, and the outcomes measured. Additional perspectives were gained from interviews with the researchers, research participants, and operations experts. Analyses were integrated across BMed, Team, and EIHSO Risks.
 
Findings from this review highlight the lack of research for lunar length latencies—only two lab studies have been performed and documented for one-way delays < 10 sec, revealing that risks associated lunar missions remain largely uncharacterized. More research (17 studies) has been conducted on longer communication latencies (30 to >60 sec). The majority of these were conducted in Earth-based analogs, simulations that can be hindered by overly simplified tasks, unrealistic habitat system mock-ups, and mild operational consequences.

Overall, the studies reviewed indicate the following effects of communication delays:
• Even short communication delays can disrupt interactions between MCC and the crew.
• As transmission delays increase, space-ground communications degrade significantly.
• Degraded communications adversely affect team performance.
• Individuals experience increased stress and reduced effectiveness of countermeasures, including PPCs and PFCs.
• Over time, space-to-ground cohesion diminishes, including reduced connectedness with family and friends.
• Countermeasures for asynchronous communication require more study.

 A number of limitations were noted from these studies, including the:
• Lack of experimental controls for variables
• Limited range of team structures tested
• Inability to separate effects of experimental covariates
• Lack of simulation fidelity (e.g., physical fidelity including implementation of communication delays, task and functional fidelity)
• Lack of situational or task complexity
• Insufficient measures of outcomes
• Insufficient sample sizes, repeatability
 
This work found that additional research is needed to characterize risks and mitigate the effects of communication latencies. In addition to analogs, research should be pursued in diverse simulation settings, such as isolated habitats, extreme environments, and analogous aviation or other time- and safety-critical domains as well as in lab studies and aboard the ISS. Crew autonomy, in particular, requires much more study across a range of conditions, tasks, and countermeasures. Training and preparation for managing communication delays is also an understudied area.
