experiment_title: A Novel Membrane Microbial Fuel Cell for Energy and Resource Recovery from Solid Organic Wastes
parameter_html:
Water contaminants
Contaminants, air
investigators: Principal Investigator: Rittmann, Bruce
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Membrane Microbial Fuel Cell (MMFC) is an innovative approach that could produce modest amounts of electricity while removing contaminants from the water and breaking down organic waste into water and other harmless compounds. The MMFC marries membrane technology with biotechnology. Bacteria catalytically oxidize the organic material in the MMFC to produce electrons that flow in an external circuit. Unlike a standard fuel cell, which operates at high temperature, the microbially catalyzed reactions in an MMFC occur at room temperature. Thus, the MMFC processes organic waste and wastewater in a way that helps produce pure water, generates electricity, and avoids extreme conditions in the spacecraft.

Although the MMFC is a very new approach, the potential advantages are enormous: processing organic waste to produce pure water and electricity with small size and no extreme conditions. Thus, the MMFC addresses several aspects of wastewater and solid waste in the AHST Critical Path Roadmap. To determine if and how this technology can be brought into practice, the investigators established the following objectives for the proposed study: a. Develop a bench-scale MMFC for laboratory testing b. Testing the MMFC with simple substrates to begin assessing its performance c. Establish the ecology and electrochemistry principles underlying the performance of an MMFC

APPROACH:
As a simple prototype MMFC, investigators constructed an HFMC in two steps. First, they sputter-coated 20 hollow-fiber membranes with metal to create a conductive layer on the membrane surface. The conductive layer was 60-nm-thick 60/40 Au/Pd and was applied using a Denton Vacuum Desk III. The membranes were fixed in place with cardboard to avoid fiber twisting, and, after coating one side, they rotated the cardboard to coat the other side. The resistance of the individual hollow-fiber membranes after sputter-coating was only 9 ohms/cm. Since each fiber was 7 cm long, the resistance of the individual fibers was approximately 60 ohms.

Second, they assembled sputter-coated membranes into a bundle wrapped inside a graphite foam, which serves as the porous graphite electrode. They attached the Au/Pd-coated fibers to plastic tubing with polyurethane adhesive. While they left one end of the fibers open to allow pressurized oxygen to flow into the fibers, they completely sealed the other end with polyurethane adhesive. They wrapped the bundle of 20 fibers with conductive graphite foam and sealed the two ends of the conductive graphite foam using polyurethane adhesive.

RESULTS:
During Phase I Pilot Study, the investigators accomplished the following tasks:
1. Created a simple MMFC by using a hollow-fiber membrane cathode (HFMC), in which the MFC cathode is attached directly onto a hollow-fiber membrane that supplied O2 for the cathode reaction.
2. Preformed kinetic characterization in single- and double-compartment MFC.
3. Compared the rate of degradation of common fermentation byproducts (acetate, butyrate, propionate, ethanol, and H2) in a dual-compartment MFC.

Investigators made an experimental MMFC in which the cathode and anode are immersed in the liquid media without separating them with a membrane. This MMFC generated electricity successfully (188 mA) and maintained the current for weeks. The design is unique and potential advantageous, because the MMFC design allows MFC electrodes to be placed directly into wastewater without the need of specialized compartments, simplifying the overall design. The simple MMFC design also demonstrates the concept investigators proposed for integrating the membrane and electrode in an MFC.

Investigators tested the MFC with acetate, which is one of the simplest organic contaminants in ALS wastewater and a simple substrate that MFC bacteria can use. Their fundamental studies make it possible for them to identify critical operational parameters. Although initial startup of an MFC took about 60 days with anaerobic digester sludge as inoculum, once suitable bacteria accumulated, starting up a new electrode was a rapid process that occurred over only about a week.

Investigators assessed the dual-substrate limitation effects on the bacterial kinetics. The current output of MFC depended strongly on the working electrode potential, especially at potentials lower than -0.1 mV against the Ag/AgCl electrode. When the current output was plotted against the potential, the current showed the classic Monod like saturation response. Substrate concentration and the electrode potential controlled the output current. A high substrate concentration produces more current; however, one goal of MFC is to remove the substrate. Thus, the result illustrate one of the tradeoffs in MFC. The Monod-Tessier model appears to capture overall behavior of the current generation better than the Monod-Monod model. Investigators plan to conduct more comprehensive studies on how the substrate concentration, biofilm density and structure, and the electrode potential together limit the current output response, because these are the factors that can be controlled via MFC design and operator.

Investigators tested the ability of MFC to remove typical fermentation byproducts acetate, propionate, butyrate, and H2. The fraction of electron of the substrates consumed (i.e. Coulombic efficiency) increased with the acclimation of bacteria. While acetate and ethanol were consumed fairly rapidly, butyrate and H2 consumption was slow. The presence of butyrate and H2 increased the current production in respect to the decay; however, their contribution to the overall current was small. The current production of propionate was much more favorable compared to butyrate, and further improvement in the current production was observed for ethanol and acetate. While the saturation type response was observed for propionate, saturation was not observed for acetate, indicating that the bacteria for the acetate biofilm were limited more by the anode potential than by the donor. The results indicate that fermentation, which converts complex mixtures of organic materials to simpler byproducts, such as ethanol and acetate, is essential for good MFC performance.

MFC can generate electricity from many of simple alcohols, acids, and amino acid. More complex organic materials such as glucuronate can be fermented to ethanol, acetate, and lactic acids. A next crucial step will be to identify conditions required to directly utilize or ferment other major ALS wastewater constituents, such as Igepon and creatine, in an MFC.

The pH of the reactor was crucial operational variable for system performance. In general higher pH improved the system performance, and the pH dependencies were different for types of substrate utilized. While acetate had a most stringent pH requirement for maximum performance (pH > 7.3), propionate and ethanol was able to tolerate pH below 7 without significant loss in the current density. Wastewater that has a high pH value, such as those in Early Planetary Base Wastewater Ersatz, should be favorable for MFC performance.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts are often required to work (exercise) at moderate to high intensities for extended periods while performing extra-vehicular activities (EVA). Although the physiologic responses associated with prolonged exercise have been documented, the mechanisms involved in blood pressure regulation under these conditions have not been fully elucidated. An understanding of this issue is pertinent to the ability of humans to perform work in microgravity and complies with the emphasis of NASA's Space and Physiology and Countermeasures Program.

Prolonged exercise and a constant workload is known to result in a progressive decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) concomitant with a decrease in stroke volume and a compensatory increase in heart rate (HR). The continuous decrease in MAP during exercise, which is related to the thermoregulatory redistribution of circulating blood volume to the cutaneous circulation, raises the question as to whether there is a loss of baroreflex regulation of arterial blood pressure. The researchers proposed that with prolongation of the exercise to 60 minutes, progressive increases in central command reflect a progressive upward resetting of the carotid baroreflex (CBR) such that the operating point of the CBR is shifted to a pressure below the threshold of the reflex rendering it ineffectual in correcting the downward drift in MAP. In order to test this hypothesis, several experiments were designed to uncouple the global hemodynamic response to prolonged exercise from the central command mediated response via continuous maintenance of cardiac filling volume by intravenous infusion of a dextran solution and whole body surface cooling to counteract thermoregulatory cutaneous vasodilation.

As the type of work (exercise) performed by the astronauts is inherently arm and upper-body dependent, the researchers also examined the physiologic responses to prolonged leg cycling and arm ergometry exercise in the supine positions with and without lower body negative pressure (-10 torr) to mimic spaceflight-related decreases in cardiac filling volumes.

APPROACH:

Experiment 1
Subjects performed two 1-hour bouts of leg cycling exercise with 1) no intervention and 2) continuous infusion of a dextran solution to maintain central venous pressure constant at the 10-min pressure.

Experiment 2
Carotid baroreflex (CBR) stimulus-response relationships were compared in seven subjects using the neck pressure-neck suction technique during dynamic exercise that ranged in intensity from 50 to 100% of maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). Leg (L) exercise alone was performed at 50 and 75% VO2max, and L exercise combined with arm (A) exercise (L + A) was performed at 75 and 100% VO2max.

Ancillary Investigations to Experiments 1 and 2

Ancillary Study 1
Subjects performed four bouts of exercise: exercise with no intervention (CON); exercise with bilateral thigh cuffs inflated to 90 mm Hg (CUFF); exercise with application of lower-body positive pressure (LBPP) to 45 torr (PP); and exercise with 90 mm Hg thigh cuff inflation and 45 torr LBPP (CUFF+PP). Ventilatory responses and pulmonary gas exchange variables were collected breath-by-breath with concomitant measurement of leg intramuscular pressure.

Ancillary Study 2
Subjects performed 3.5 min of static one-legged exercise (20 % maximal voluntary contraction) and 7 min dynamic cycling (20 % maximal oxygen uptake) under two conditions: control (no intervention) and with the application of medical anti-shock (MAS) trousers inflated to 100 mmHg (to activate the exercise pressor reflex). Carotid baroreflex function was determined at rest and during exercise using a rapid neck pressure/neck suction technique.

Ancillary Study 3
Carotid baroreflex (CBR) function was evaluated at rest and during 20 min of arm cycling at 50% peak oxygen uptake using 5-s periods of neck pressure and neck suction.

Experiment 3: Part 1
Arterial (aortic + carotid) baroreflex control of HR was quantified using ramped changes in MAP induced by bolus injection of phenylephrine (PE) and sodium nitroprusside (SN). To assess aortic-cardiac responses, neck pressure (NP) and suction (NS) were applied during PE and SN administration, respectively, to counter alterations in CSP thereby isolating the aortic baroreflex. Graded levels of NP and NS were delivered to the carotid sinus using a customized neck collar device to assess the carotid-cardiac baroreflex, independent of drug infusion. The operating characteristics of each reflex were determined from the logistic function of the elicited HR response to the induced change in MAP.

Experiment 3: Part 2
Arterial and aortic baroreflex (ABR) functions were assessed utilizing hypo- and hyper-tensive challenges induced by graded bolus injections of sodium nitroprusside (SN) and phenylephrine (PE), respectively. Carotid baroreflex (CBR) sensitivity was determined using ramped 5-s pulses of both pressure and suction delivered to the carotid sinus via a neck chamber collar, independent of drug administration.

Experiment 3: Part 3
Acute hypotension was induced nonpharmacologically in subjects, half of which were of high fitness (HF) and the other half were of average fitness (AF), by releasing a unilateral arterial thigh cuff after 9 min of resting ischemia under two conditions: control, which used aortic and carotid baroreflex (ABR and CBR, respectively) deactivation; and suction, which used ABR deactivation alone.

RESULTS:
Experiment 1
Volume infusion resulted in a significant reduction in the decrement in mean arterial pressure seen in the control exercise bout (6.7+/-1.8 vs. 11.6+/-1.3 mmHg, respectively). However, indexes of central command such as heart rate and ratings of perceived exertion rose to a similar extent during both exercise conditions. In addition, the carotid-cardiac baroreflex stimulus-response relationship, as measured by using the neck pressure-neck suction technique, was reset from rest to 10 min of exercise and was further reset from 10 to 50 min of exercise in both exercise conditions, with the operating point being shifted toward the reflex threshold. It was concluded that the progressive resetting of the carotid baroreflex and the shift of the reflex operating point render the carotid-cardiac reflex ineffectual in counteracting the continued decrement in mean arterial pressure that occurs during the prolonged exercise.

Experiment 2
Oxygen consumption and heart rate (HR) increased in direct relation with the increases in exercise intensity. The threshold and saturation pressures of the carotid-cardiac reflex at 100% VO2max were >75% VO2max, which were in turn >50% VO2max (P < 0.05), without a change in the maximal reflex gain (Gmax). In addition, the HR response value at threshold and saturation at 75% VO2max was >50% VO2max (P < 0.05) and 100% VO2max was >75% VO2max (P < 0.07). Similar changes were observed for the carotid-vasomotor reflex. In addition, as exercise intensity increased, the operating point (the prestimulus blood pressure) of the CBR was significantly relocated further from the centering point (Gmax) of the stimulus-response curve and was at threshold during 100% VO2max. These findings identify the continuous classic rightward and upward resetting of the CBR, without a change in Gmax, during increases in dynamic exercise intensity to maximal effort.

Ancillary Study 1

During exercise, the application of MAS trousers (MAS condition) increased mean arterial pressure (MAP), plasma noradrenaline concentration (dynamic exercise only) and perceived exertion (dynamic exercise only) when compared to control (P < 0.05). Activation of the exercise pressor reflex by MAS trousers further reset carotid baroreflex control of MAP, as indicated by the upward and rightward relocation of the curve. However, carotid baroreflex control of HR was only shifted rightward to higher operating pressures by MAS trousers. Furthermore, estimated baroreflex sensitivity for the control of MSNA at rest was the same as during exercise (P = 0.74) across the range of neck chamber pressures. Thus CBR control of sympathetic nerve activity appears to be preserved during moderate-intensity dynamic exercise.

The arterial pressures at which the threshold was located on the stimulus-response curves determined for the arterial, aortic and carotid baroreflexes were not significantly different (72+/-4, 67+/-3, and 72+/-4 mm Hg, respectively, P > 0.05). These data suggest that the baroreceptor populations studied operate over the same range of arterial pressures. Experiment 3: Part 2
During vasoactive drug injection, mean arterial pressure (MAP) was similarly altered in average fit (AF) and high fit (HF) groups. However, the heart rate (HR) response range of the arterial baroreflex was significantly attenuated (P < 0.05) in HF (31+/-4 beats x min(-1)) compared with AF individuals (46+/-4 beats x min(-1)). The application of neck suction to counteract changes in carotid sinus transmural pressure during cuff release significantly attenuated the MSNA response (which increased 134 +/- 32 U/14 s) compared with control (which increased 195 +/- 43 U/14 s) and caused a greater decrease in MAP (19 +/- 2 vs. 15 +/- 2 mmHg; P < 0.05). OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts are often required to work (exercise) at moderate to high intensities for extended periods while performing extra-vehicular activities (EVA). Although the physiologic responses associated with prolonged exercise have been documented, the mechanisms involved in blood pressure regulation under these conditions have not been fully elucidated. An understanding of this issue is pertinent to the ability of humans to perform work in microgravity and complies with the emphasis of NASA's Space and Physiology and Countermeasures Program.

Prolonged exercise and a constant workload is known to result in a progressive decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) concomitant with a decrease in stroke volume and a compensatory increase in heart rate (HR). The continuous decrease in MAP during exercise, which is related to the thermoregulatory redistribution of circulating blood volume to the cutaneous circulation, raises the question as to whether there is a loss of baroreflex regulation of arterial blood pressure. The researchers proposed that with prolongation of the exercise to 60 minutes, progressive increases in central command reflect a progressive upward resetting of the carotid baroreflex (CBR) such that the operating point of the CBR is shifted to a pressure below the threshold of the reflex rendering it ineffectual in correcting the downward drift in MAP. In order to test this hypothesis, several experiments were designed to uncouple the global hemodynamic response to prolonged exercise from the central command mediated response via continuous maintenance of cardiac filling volume by intravenous infusion of a dextran solution and whole body surface cooling to counteract thermoregulatory cutaneous vasodilation.

As the type of work (exercise) performed by the astronauts is inherently arm and upper-body dependent, the researchers also examined the physiologic responses to prolonged leg cycling and arm ergometry exercise in the supine positions with and without lower body negative pressure (-10 torr) to mimic spaceflight-related decreases in cardiac filling volumes.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Microgravity Vestibular Investigations (MVI) studied the underlying perceptual and physiological mechanisms associated with sensori-motor adaptations to space flight. Human perception of orientation in space depends on the interaction of virtually every sensory system. Changes in the environment and the interaction with the new stimuli result in a different interpretation by the central nervous system (CNS) of the incoming sensory information. Because the human orientation system is adaptable and complex, it is difficult to trace a change in behavior to any one sensori-motor unit in the synergistic orientation system. In this investigation, the effects of different stimuli on the human sense of orientation was determined; thereby an interactive model for orientation was used.

APPROACH:
The MVI experiment used a rotator chair, which provided angular rotation stimuli about a single axis (subject’s yaw, pitch or roll). The drive rotators were computer controlled and provided three types of velocity profiles: pseudorandom, step, and sinusoid. The rotator axis was oriented for earth-vertical rotation for the ground tests, and perpendicular to the Spacelab floor for inflight testing. The chair utilized straps and padding to stabilize the subject and minimize pressure points. A helmet with inflatable bladders was used to fix the head in respect to the chair. The helmet also blocked any external light sources and integrated earphones masked any noises from other ongoing Spacelab activities. The helmet-mounted optokinetic stimulus (OKS) module provided visual stimuli, including targets for eye calibrations. The OKS module was mounted over the subjects right eye and a camera module was mounted over the left eye. The visual scene, visible for the subject when wearing the helmet was a black-red checkerboard pattern and illuminated by red Light Emission Diodes (LEDs). The speed, direction and pattern of the LED display were computer controlled.

Eye measurements were recorded with both electro-oculographic (EOG) and video techniques. For EOG recordings, surface electrodes were placed at the outer canthi of both eyes to record horizontal eye movements, and above and below the right eye to record vertical eye movements. Video was used to analyze roll rotation of the eyeball. To record nystagmus, the subject wore a contact lens with reference markings in the left eye.

The MVI experiments were integrated into eight different functional objectives to address: (1) semicircular canal dynamics, (2) vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression, (3) visual-vestibular interaction, (4) VOR responses to velocity steps, (5) optokinetic nystagmus, (6) sensory perception and motion sickness reports, (7) positional and spontaneous nystagmus and (8) changes in dynamic posture. The objectives (1) through (6) were performed pre-, post- and inflight, while objectives (7) and (8) were only tested pre- and postflight.

(1) Semicircular canal dynamics. The vestibular system provides information of angular acceleration (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration (otoliths) to the central nervous system (CNS). There is evidence that under some circumstances one set of receptors can modulate the input of the other system. It was hypothesized that in the microgravity environment, which is defined by the absence of the gravity vector, the semicircular canals would continue to supply input about the direction and magnitude of any rotation, while the otoliths would not provide the expected information regarding linear acceleration. Thus, this sensory conflict would cause a change in the VOR.

Sinusoidal and pseudorandom rotational stimuli, provided by the rotator chair, were used to study the dynamic response characteristics of the VOR. The selected frequencies covered a broad range to observe any changes in the interactions between the VOR and other visual tracking reflexes caused by different frequencies. Four single frequencies were tested during pitch rotation, including 0.05 Hertz (Hz) (for 100 seconds), 0.2 Hz (for 25 seconds), 0.8 Hz (for 20 seconds) and 1.25 Hz (for 20 seconds). The peak angular velocities of these profiles were maintained constant at 60 degrees per second (except for 1.25 Hz which was limited to 40 degrees per second). The test subjects had their vision occluded and were asked to fixate an imaginary wall target approximately 1 meter (1.1 yards) away. To evaluate the horizontal VOR, a pseudorandom (sum-of-sine) stimulus was used, and corresponding single sine measurements were obtained during 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz yaw rotations. The pseudorandom stimulus was comprised of seven frequencies ranging from 0.02 to 1.39 Hz.

(2) Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression. Turning the head produces a vestibular stimulus which activates the VOR and generates a compensatory eye movement in the opposite direction to hold the gaze stationary. When humans use head and eye movement to track a (moving) target the VOR is suppressed at low frequencies and diminishes slowly with increasing frequencies. During the MVI experiment, the vertical VOR was tested during pitch sinusoidal chair rotations at frequencies of 0.05 Hz (low frequency) and 1.25 Hz (high frequency). During the tests, the subjects were asked to fixate on the stationary checkerboard pattern displayed inside the OKS module. Yaw VOR suppression was tested by pseudorandom stimulus profiles utilizing the rotator chair.

(3) Visual-vestibular interaction. The vestibular motion sensors detect transient head rotation, but during sustained rotation their signal becomes progressively less accurate. During head rotation in light, the optokinetic system compensates for the fading vestibular response, which leads to the conclusion that during light both systems are stimulated and the eye movement response, called the visual-vestibular nystagmic response (VVR), is the result of the combined response of both systems. The objective of this part of the experiment was to evaluate the relative role the vestibular and optokinetic systems encounter during adaptation to microgravity.

The subjects were sinusoidally oscillated at 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz with the rotator chair while viewing a constant velocity optokinetic stimulation at + 35 degrees per second inside the OKS module. This procedure caused a nystagmic response of different quality when both stimuli were of same or opposite directions. The visual-vestibular interactions were tested both in the horizontal plane (rotation of subject in yaw combined with horizontal optokinetic stimulation), and in the vertical plane (rotation in pitch combined with vertical optokinetic stimulation).

(4) VOR responses to velocity steps. When a human subject is rotated in the earth vertical axis and in darkness for an extended period of time, the nystagmus decays and after several minutes of rotation the nystagmus disappears and the subject is no longer aware of the rotation. If the rotation is suddenly stopped, the subject indicates rotation in the opposite direction. This phenomenon is called post-rotatory nystagmus. Previous experiments demonstrated that the duration and magnitude of post-rotary nystagmus is gravity dependent. During the MVI investigation, post-rotatory VOR was studied after chair rotations of one minute at a speed of 120 degrees/second clockwise with fast accelerations and an abrupt stop. During the test, the subject was instructed to gaze straight ahead. The eye movements were recorded for 1 minute after the chair was stopped. After a brief pause, the procedure was repeated with counter-clockwise rotation.

(5) Optokinetic nystagmus. The objective of this experiment was to detect any changes in optokinetic nystagmus, which was induced by a rotating image inside the binocular OKS module. Horizontal and vertical optokinetic responses were recorded while the subjects were restrained into the rotator chair, positioned in yaw and pitch chair orientations, respectively. For each optokinetic stimulus run, three speeds of OKS-rotation were presented in succession (20, 60 and 40 degrees per second) in one direction for 15 seconds each. Immediately after the last image, the optokinetic nystagmus was recorded in darkness for 15 seconds. The same stimulus sequence was then presented with OKS-rotations in the opposite direction. Later during the IML-1 mission, the protocol was repeated while the test subjects were free-floating inside the Spacelab module.

(6) Sensory perception and motion sickness reports. The IML-1 crewmembers were asked to report their perceptions of particular motions while in microgravity and define if those motions were (1) different than on earth and (2) more or less confusing (or disturbing) than on Earth. The subjects were also asked to describe, quantify, and record any changes in space motion sickness symptoms during the space flight. The occurrence of motion sickness and the nature and degree of symptoms were important to the interpretation of the collected data, as was the intake of anti-motion sickness medication. Motion sickness symptoms were reported using a special score (0=no symptoms to 20=vomiting) during other MVI experiments. To do so, the astronauts used a voice recorder during the experiments and a checklist for evaluations performed at the end of each test and at the end of their work shift.

(7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Positional or spontaneous nystagmus occurs when the vestibular receptors indicate that the head is accelerating. In microgravity, the presence of spontaneous nystagmus (positional nystagmus has no meaning in 0-g) suggests that the CNS is receiving a head acceleration signal and is forwarding motor signals to the eye muscles. During baseline data collection, eye movements to detect spontaneous nystagmus were recorded during the following tests: (1) gaze nystagmus test (at + 10 and 20 degrees), (2) sinusoidal pursuit tracking test, using a swinging pendulum over + 30 degrees, (3) Benign Paroxysmal nystagmus test (test for positional nystagmus), and (4) positional nystagmus testing with eyes open and occluded vision and with eyes closed using the following sequence: sitting, supine with head hanging, supine with head straight up, supine with head turned to the right, and then to the left, and finally with the right ear to the floor and repeated with the left ear to the floor. The subject was returned to an upright (sitting) position between each test position. Eye movements were recorded with electro-oculography (EOG). During the space flight, eye movements were recorded during all test sessions to enable observations of transient spontaneous nystagmus before and after each rotational test.

(8) Changes in dynamic posture. Many astronauts returning from space exhibit some degree of postural dysfunction. To quantify these dysfunctions, a posture platform system (used for clinical diagnosis of disorders in balance control) was modified for postflight testing of movement coordination and sensory organization. For movement coordination tests, the foot plate was rapidly translated (maximum translation + 7 cm) or rotated (maximum tilt + 10 degrees) to provide stimuli to the subject’s posture control system. The postural responses to the sudden perturbations were monitored and recorded for a period of 2.5 seconds each. Sensory organization tests required the subjects to attempt a stable upright stance under different sensory input conditions. The conditions could be altered by a tilting foot-plate and a skipping visual surround which could be changed individually or both at the same time. The postural reaction to each sensory input was recorded for 20 seconds after each input.

Preflight, the MVI testing was completed in six single test sessions which were conducted on L-130 (130 days prior to launch), L-68, L-30 and L-15. The inflight test schedule included tests on seven flight days of the 8-day IML-1 mission for the MVI. Each of the four test subjects followed an individual test schedule. Postflight sessions were conducted on landing day, and 1, 2, 5, 8, and 30 days after landing.

RESULTS:
(2) Vestibulo-ocular reflexes. There was a consistent increase in the VOR gain observed at the mid-to-high frequencies (0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz) of chair rotation towards the end of the space flight. And the observed changes were greater in pitch than in yaw position of the chair.

(5) Optokinetic nystagmus. Although not statistically different, there was a trend for the gain of the optokinetic nystagmus to be increased during the space flight and during early postflight testing.

(6) Motion Sickness and perceptual reports. All four subjects reported some form of motion sickness symptoms. One subject reported severe malaise through most of the flight; the other three crewmembers reported significantly subsided symptoms by the third flight day prior to the majority of most MVI measurements. Three of the four crewmembers reported an increase in motion sickness symptoms while performing the MVI experiments. Reports from two subjects indicated that sensations of rotation, induced by both oscillatory and ramp stimuli, were somewhat more intense in orbit than on Earth. Also, during the pitch ramp stimuli, three of the four subjects tested inflight indicated that they felt they were tumbling “head-over-heals” rather than rotating in pitch (laying on their side).

(7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Before the flight, positional nystagmus was observed in all four subjects. During the inflight performance of the MVI experiments, transient spontaneous nystagmus was observed: all four subjects displayed some form of nystagmus, and one subject displayed vertical downbeat nystagmus, a form of nystagmus which exhibits all the characteristics of vestibular origin.

(8) Changes in dynamic posture. Two subjects participated in postural equilibrium tests on landing day and several times during the recovery period. The other two subjects were tested for the first time at R+1 and several times during the slower, secondary phase of recovery. The two subjects tested for the first time on R+1 displayed signs of disturbed postural equilibrium control 24 and 27 hours after landing, recovered to preflight levels by 47 and 48.5 hours after landing, and overshot preflight levels by 120 and 122.5 hours post landing. The two subjects tested on landing day (R+0) showed little or no improvement in recovery on R+1 and R+2. At about 120 hours after landing, both subjects had recovered to preflight levels and by 190 hours after landing one subjects displayed hyperstability. This led to the conclusion, that some postflight tests (most likely the pitch axis rotation test) interfered with the readaptation process.

The chair utilized straps and padding to stabilize the subject and minimize pressure points. A helmet with inflatable bladders was used to fix the head in respect to the chair. The helmet also blocked any external light sources and integrated earphones masked any noises from other ongoing Spacelab activities. The helmet-mounted optokinetic stimulus (OKS) module provided visual stimuli, including targets for eye calibrations. The OKS module was mounted over the subjects right eye and a camera module was mounted over the left eye. The visual scene, visible for the subject when wearing the helmet was a black-red checkerboard pattern and illuminated by red Light Emission Diodes (LEDs). The speed, direction and pattern of the LED display were computer controlled.

Eye measurements were recorded with both electro-oculographic (EOG) and video techniques. For EOG recordings, surface electrodes were placed at the outer canthi of both eyes to record horizontal eye movements, and above and below the right eye to record vertical eye movements. Video was used to analyze roll rotation of the eyeball. To record nystagmus, the subject wore a contact lens with reference markings in the left eye.

The MVI experiments were integrated into eight different functional objectives to address: (1) semicircular canal dynamics, (2) vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression, (3) visual-vestibular interaction, (4) VOR responses to velocity steps, (5) optokinetic nystagmus, (6) sensory perception and motion sickness reports, (7) positional and spontaneous nystagmus and (8) changes in dynamic posture. The objectives (1) through (6) were performed pre-, post- and inflight, while objectives (7) and (8) were only tested pre- and postflight.

(1) Semicircular canal dynamics. The vestibular system provides information of angular acceleration (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration (otoliths) to the central nervous system (CNS). There is evidence that under some circumstances one set of receptors can modulate the input of the other system. It was hypothesized that in the microgravity environment, which is defined by the absence of the gravity vector, the semicircular canals would continue to supply input about the direction and magnitude of any rotation, while the otoliths would not provide the expected information regarding linear acceleration. Thus, this sensory conflict would cause a change in the VOR.

Sinusoidal and pseudorandom rotational stimuli, provided by the rotator chair, were used to study the dynamic response characteristics of the VOR. The selected frequencies covered a broad range to observe any changes in the interactions between the VOR and other visual tracking reflexes caused by different frequencies. Four single frequencies were tested during pitch rotation, including 0.05 Hertz (Hz) (for 100 seconds), 0.2 Hz (for 25 seconds), 0.8 Hz (for 20 seconds) and 1.25 Hz (for 20 seconds). The peak angular velocities of these profiles were maintained constant at 60 degrees per second (except for 1.25 Hz which was limited to 40 degrees per second). The test subjects had their vision occluded and were asked to fixate an imaginary wall target approximately 1 meter (1.1 yards) away. To evaluate the horizontal VOR, a pseudorandom (sum-of-sine) stimulus was used, and corresponding single sine measurements were obtained during 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz yaw rotations. The pseudorandom stimulus was comprised of seven frequencies ranging from 0.02 to 1.39 Hz.

(2) Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression. Turning the head produces a vestibular stimulus which activates the VOR and generates a compensatory eye movement in the opposite direction to hold the gaze stationary. When humans use head and eye movement to track a (moving) target the VOR is suppressed at low frequencies and diminishes slowly with increasing frequencies. During the MVI experiment, the vertical VOR was tested during pitch sinusoidal chair rotations at frequencies of 0.05 Hz (low frequency) and 1.25 Hz (high frequency). During the tests, the subjects were asked to fixate on the stationary checkerboard pattern displayed inside the OKS module. Yaw VOR suppression was tested by pseudorandom stimulus profiles utilizing the rotator chair.

(3) Visual-vestibular interaction. The vestibular motion sensors detect transient head rotation, but during sustained rotation their signal becomes progressively less accurate. During head rotation in light, the optokinetic system compensates for the fading vestibular response, which leads to the conclusion that during light both systems are stimulated and the eye movement response, called the visual-vestibular nystagmic response (VVR), is the result of the combined response of both systems. The objective of this part of the experiment was to evaluate the relative role the vestibular and optokinetic systems encounter during adaptation to microgravity.

The subjects were sinusoidally oscillated at 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz with the rotator chair while viewing a constant velocity optokinetic stimulation at + 35 degrees per second inside the OKS module. This procedure caused a nystagmic response of different quality when both stimuli were of same or opposite directions. The visual-vestibular interactions were tested both in the horizontal plane (rotation of subject in yaw combined with horizontal optokinetic stimulation), and in the vertical plane (rotation in pitch combined with vertical optokinetic stimulation).

(4) VOR responses to velocity steps. When a human subject is rotated in the earth vertical axis and in darkness for an extended period of time, the nystagmus decays and after several minutes of rotation the nystagmus disappears and the subject is no longer aware of the rotation. If the rotation is suddenly stopped, the subject indicates rotation in the opposite direction. This phenomenon is called post-rotatory nystagmus. Previous experiments demonstrated that the duration and magnitude of post-rotary nystagmus is gravity dependent. During the MVI investigation, post-rotatory VOR was studied after chair rotations of one minute at a speed of 120 degrees/second clockwise with fast accelerations and an abrupt stop. During the test, the subject was instructed to gaze straight ahead. The eye movements were recorded for 1 minute after the chair was stopped. After a brief pause, the procedure was repeated with counter-clockwise rotation.

(5) Optokinetic nystagmus. The objective of this experiment was to detect any changes in optokinetic nystagmus, which was induced by a rotating image inside the binocular OKS module. Horizontal and vertical optokinetic responses were recorded while the subjects were restrained into the rotator chair, positioned in yaw and pitch chair orientations, respectively. For each optokinetic stimulus run, three speeds of OKS-rotation were presented in succession (20, 60 and 40 degrees per second) in one direction for 15 seconds each. Immediately after the last image, the optokinetic nystagmus was recorded in darkness for 15 seconds. The same stimulus sequence was then presented with OKS-rotations in the opposite direction. Later during the IML-1 mission, the protocol was repeated while the test subjects were free-floating inside the Spacelab module.

(6) Sensory perception and motion sickness reports. The IML-1 crewmembers were asked to report their perceptions of particular motions while in microgravity and define if those motions were (1) different than on earth and (2) more or less confusing (or disturbing) than on Earth. The subjects were also asked to describe, quantify, and record any changes in space motion sickness symptoms during the space flight. The occurrence of motion sickness and the nature and degree of symptoms were important to the interpretation of the collected data, as was the intake of anti-motion sickness medication. Motion sickness symptoms were reported using a special score (0=no symptoms to 20=vomiting) during other MVI experiments. To do so, the astronauts used a voice recorder during the experiments and a checklist for evaluations performed at the end of each test and at the end of their work shift.

(7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Positional or spontaneous nystagmus occurs when the vestibular receptors indicate that the head is accelerating. In microgravity, the presence of spontaneous nystagmus (positional nystagmus has no meaning in 0-g) suggests that the CNS is receiving a head acceleration signal and is forwarding motor signals to the eye muscles. During baseline data collection, eye movements to detect spontaneous nystagmus were recorded during the following tests: (1) gaze nystagmus test (at + 10 and 20 degrees), (2) sinusoidal pursuit tracking test, using a swinging pendulum over + 30 degrees, (3) Benign Paroxysmal nystagmus test (test for positional nystagmus), and (4) positional nystagmus testing with eyes open and occluded vision and with eyes closed using the following sequence: sitting, supine with head hanging, supine with head straight up, supine with head turned to the right, and then to the left, and finally with the right ear to the floor and repeated with the left ear to the floor. The subject was returned to an upright (sitting) position between each test position. Eye movements were recorded with electro-oculography (EOG). During the space flight, eye movements were recorded during all test sessions to enable observations of transient spontaneous nystagmus before and after each rotational test.

(8) Changes in dynamic posture. Many astronauts returning from space exhibit some degree of postural dysfunction. To quantify these dysfunctions, a posture platform system (used for clinical diagnosis of disorders in balance control) was modified for postflight testing of movement coordination and sensory organization. For movement coordination tests, the foot plate was rapidly translated (maximum translation + 7 cm) or rotated (maximum tilt + 10 degrees) to provide stimuli to the subject’s posture control system. The postural responses to the sudden perturbations were monitored and recorded for a period of 2.5 seconds each. Sensory organization tests required the subjects to attempt a stable upright stance under different sensory input conditions. The conditions could be altered by a tilting foot-plate and a skipping visual surround which could be changed individually or both at the same time. The postural reaction to each sensory input was recorded for 20 seconds after each input.

Preflight, the MVI testing was completed in six single test sessions which were conducted on L-130 (130 days prior to launch), L-68, L-30 and L-15. The inflight test schedule included tests on seven flight days of the 8-day IML-1 mission for the MVI. Each of the four test subjects followed an individual test schedule. Postflight sessions were conducted on landing day, and 1, 2, 5, 8, and 30 days after landing.

RESULTS:
(2) Vestibulo-ocular reflexes. There was a consistent increase in the VOR gain observed at the mid-to-high frequencies (0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz) of chair rotation towards the end of the space flight. And the observed changes were greater in pitch than in yaw position of the chair.

(5) Optokinetic nystagmus. Although not statistically different, there was a trend for the gain of the optokinetic nystagmus to be increased during the space flight and during early postflight testing.

(6) Motion Sickness and perceptual reports. All four subjects reported some form of motion sickness symptoms. One subject reported severe malaise through most of the flight; the other three crewmembers reported significantly subsided symptoms by the third flight day prior to the majority of most MVI measurements. Three of the four crewmembers reported an increase in motion sickness symptoms while performing the MVI experiments. Reports from two subjects indicated that sensations of rotation, induced by both oscillatory and ramp stimuli, were somewhat more intense in orbit than on Earth. Also, during the pitch ramp stimuli, three of the four subjects tested inflight indicated that they felt they were tumbling “head-over-heals” rather than rotating in pitch (laying on their side).

(7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Before the flight, positional nystagmus was observed in all four subjects. During the inflight performance of the MVI experiments, transient spontaneous nystagmus was observed: all four subjects displayed some form of nystagmus, and one subject displayed vertical downbeat nystagmus, a form of nystagmus which exhibits all the characteristics of vestibular origin.

(8) Changes in dynamic posture. Two subjects participated in postural equilibrium tests on landing day and several times during the recovery period. The other two subjects were tested for the first time at R+1 and several times during the slower, secondary phase of recovery. The two subjects tested for the first time on R+1 displayed signs of disturbed postural equilibrium control 24 and 27 hours after landing, recovered to preflight levels by 47 and 48.5 hours after landing, and overshot preflight levels by 120 and 122.5 hours post landing. The two subjects tested on landing day (R+0) showed little or no improvement in recovery on R+1 and R+2. At about 120 hours after landing, both subjects had recovered to preflight levels and by 190 hours after landing one subjects displayed hyperstability. This led to the conclusion, that some postflight tests (most likely the pitch axis rotation test) interfered with the readaptation process.

experiment_title: Advanced Diamond Electrodes for Electrochemical Based Monitoring of Spacecraft Water
parameter_html: Total inorganic arsenic
investigators: Principal Investigator: Swain, Greg
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This research was focused on developing advanced water quality monitoring methods for the potable and technical water supplies onboard the International Space Station (ISS). The methods being developed could also have broad application on other long-duration space flight and habitation projects. Electrochemical methods were developed for water quality monitoring with two contaminant types targeted: (i) heavy metal ions including Ag(I), Cu(II), Cd(II), Pb(II) and Zn(II) and (ii) iodine and iodide as well as phenol and iodinated phenols. The key enabling material is the boron-doped diamond electrode, which provides a sensitive, reproducible and stable response for these analytes.

APPROACH:
Investigators completed studies of the electrode and method for a series of laboratory-prepared standard solutions. They also redesigned a small flow cell that could be used in microgravity environments for water quality assessment. They devised and tested a multiple step analysis protocol that involved sampling the water from the galley, mixing with a prepackaged supporting electrolyte (in a sealed syringe), adding the solution to the cell, making the anodic stripping voltammetric measurements of the metal ion content and analyzing the data. The focus was on Ag(I).

RESULTS:
Investigators demonstrated that a Au-coated, boron-doped, diamond thin-film electrode provides a sensitive, reproducible, and stable response for total inorganic arsenic (As(III) and As(V)) using differential pulse anodic stripping voltammetry (DPASV). As is pre-concentrated with Au on the diamond surface during the deposition step and detected oxidatively during the stripping step. Au deposition was uniform over the electrode surface with a nominal particle size of 23 +/- 5 nm and a particle density of 109 cm-2.

experiment_title: Spinal Elongation and its Effects on Seated Height in a Microgravity Environment
parameter_html:
Height, seated
Height, standing
investigators: Principal Investigator: Rajulu, SudhakarCo-Investigator: Young, Karen
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Spinal elongation due to microgravity is an important consideration for the seated height dimension. Previous research has demonstrated that crewmembers tend to increase in stature by up to three percent, which has driven current requirements to allow for such growth in dimensions such as stature and seated height. However, no spinal elongation induced seated height growth data has been collected from crewmembers so far. The Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV), Orion, designers requested relevant anthropometric data in order to ensure that the vehicle accommodates a full range of crewmembers as a result of being exposed to microgravity environment.. Seated height measurements are of particular interest due to the nature of seat layout within the vehicle. The criticality of this measurement is such that changes in seated height on the order of magnitude of inches have significant impacts on the level of crew accommodation available.

This data will also be valuable in the design of lunar vehicles, habitat modules, and suit hardware sizing components. Without adequate information, the impact of spinal elongation on seat positioning and fit may pose risks to crew accommodation and comfort during seated operations along with being able to ingress and egress the seats. The effectiveness of the crew may be reduced due to impaired access to displays and controls, and the selected crewmembers may not fit into seats following exposure to microgravity. Because of the criticality of the seated height dimension with respect to Orion seat layout design, the selection of crews may therefore be impacted in order to ensure fit. Through systematic measurements and analysis, it is possible to provide relevant seated height data. The proposed procedure involves measurement of crew subjects seated in the Shuttle cockpit by use of traditional anthropometry tools as well as photographic scaling. Results of the evaluation will feed into design requirements for MPCV and future vehicles as well as provide valuable insight for future human space flight programs.

APPROACH:
Baseline Data Collection
Upon arrival to the Crew Compartment Trainer, the subject received a description of the Spinal in-orbit activity and the objectives of the data collection. The subject entered and positioned himself/herself into the commander seat on the flight deck. The investigator team member recorded the Anthropometer value. An orthogonal photograph was taken. The subject exited the seat, and then re-entered for the second set of data points. Two rotations into the seat constituted a full data collection session. The data collected during the overview session comprised the preflight baseline data.

Inflight Data Collection
The operator unstowed the Anthropometer assembly from the International Space Station (ISS) stowage and set it up on the commander seat in the Shuttle flight deck. Next, the operator set up the camera and mounted it in position that allowed for an orthogonal photograph of a subject in this seat. The operator took a test photograph and downlinked to the ground for the investigator team to verify correct placement before the first subject’s data collection. Upon the first subject’s arrival to the Shuttle Flight deck, the subject entered and positioned himself/herself into the commander seat. The Spinal operator made adjustments with the subject to ensure good positioning and recorded the Anthropometer value. An orthogonal photograph was taken. The subject exited the seat, and then re-entered for the second set of data points. Two rotations into the seat constituted a full session. The operator repeated the data collection with each subsequent subject participating in the study. If the operator was also a subject, the backup operator switched positions with the prime operator to collect the data on the prime operator. After the data collection was complete, the hardware was detached from the seat on the Shuttle flight deck and stowed back in ISS stowage.

RESULTS:
Spinal elongation is the growth that occurs potentially due to the straightening of the spinal curve and with the probable expansion of the inter-vertebral discs in microgravity. The safety of the crew, the design of seats, seat layout, and suit fit are all affected by spinal elongation due to the resulting increase in height (seated as well as standing); which could lead to inadequate clearances that would have implications for the ability of crewmembers to perform their task(s) and return safely to earth. The design of the Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle, Orion, has a different seat configuration and layout, stacked, than the Orbiter Space Shuttle. The stacked seat layout of the Orion causes seated height to be much more critical than it was in the Shuttle, where overhead space was more plentiful due to the different seat configuration. In Orion, the crew seats are in a stacked configuration with the inner mold lining already fixed. Therefore, it is essential that all seats provide adequate growth clearance adjustments so as to ensure that the crew can safely egress and ingress their seat for a safe return to Earth. This is the same with the suit. The suit also needs to be designed to accommodate spinal growth. Fit and comfort level should also be taken into consideration.

Results from this investigation show that crewmembers experienced up to 6% seated height growth. In stature, the maximum consistent growth observed was 3%, which correlates well with the historical findings on stature height increase.

The data obtained from this experiment and the interpretation of the data analysis will be used to provide designers information regarding how microgravity affects anthropometric measurements and to update all related documents that have a reference to spinal elongation growth.

experiment_title: New Automated System for Real-Time Bio-Imaging of a Vascular Cell Function in Microgravity
parameter_html:
Cell adhesion
Cells extracted
Leukocytes
Monocytes
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kucik, Dennis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is critical to NASA's mission for human exploration and development of space to understand the influence of the space environment, specifically microgravity, on human physiology. Previous work has shown that microgravity can modify host cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, and thereby exert potentially deleterious effects on human vascular and immune functions and regeneration processes. For simulated microgravity, such as in a rotating wall vessel (RWV), adhesion assays as currently conducted have important limitations. First, to remove a cell sample from the RWV, rotation must be stopped, interrupting the simulated microgravity, not just for the sample, but for all cells in the chamber. Second, adhesion assays can take over an hour to perform when one considers cell preparation, transfer of cells from the microgravity chamber to the assay, and incubation periods. While these delays may be acceptable for general adhesion research, it is important to minimize elapsed time when studying gravitational effects, so that the cells won’t have time to recover from microgravity. In this project, investigators developed a novel human tissue bio-imaging technology applicable to microgravity research to overcome these shortcomings. Lessons learned from development of this Earth-based system can form the basis for a future space-flight culture and assay system to allow NASA to monitor microgravity-inducible physiological events during space flights.

The purpose of this project was to develop a novel human tissue bioimaging technology applicable to microgravity research. This system was to integrate automated bioreactor sampling and real-time bioimaging. This will enable researchers to monitor, for the first time, effects of simulated microgravity on an important vascular function--adhesion between white blood cells and the blood vessel wall, without interruption of the culture conditions and with essentially no delay between sample extraction and cell-function assay. Technology developed in this project ultimately has potential applications for monitoring astronaut immune system function on long-term space flights. Task Objective: To develop a new, automated system for real-time bio-imaging of effects of microgravity on cell-cell adhesion through completion of the following objectives:

1. Design and develop a system to automatically extract and deliver cell samples from a rotating wall vessel to an assay system at predetermined intervals.
2.Design and develop a small, integrated, real-time digital bio-imaging system to produce digital images of cell samples.
3.Integrate into the bio-imaging system an assay of vascular cell function that utilizes the unique Amgel matrix system and sensitive real-time computer tracking of adhesive cell interactions.
The system developed for this purpose can be adapted to assay other effects of simulated microgravity on cultured cells. It can also be useful as a compact, portable flow-cell based adhesion assay to measure adhesion of leukocytes or other cells under shear-stress conditions similar to those found in the blood stream.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Objective 1: Development of the cell extraction and delivery system
Even though extraction of fluid from a rotating RWV was a relatively straightforward engineering project, extraction of the cells from a rotating system is not trivial. Beyond the technical issue of a leak-free rotating interface between the chamber and external tubing, there is the issue that cells are often not uniformly distributed within the chamber. Although various models have been proposed to describe the location of cells in such a system, models do not always agree. Investigators determined the best sample points empirically. Their current system reliably delivers cells at a uniform concentration from two separate locations (after an initial mixing period of approx. 10 minutes.) without interrupting rotation.

In the first year, feasibility was confirmed with a largely manual system of valves and a syringe pump system that used a command line interface for each action of the pump. However, entering of individual commands made experimentation cumbersome and time consuming. The control process was improved by transitioning to a graphical control program where embedded script files are created and programmed into the syringe pump. These pre-programmed script files are executed directly from the laptop graphical control program. This software configuration for control of the syringe pump streamlines the control process and also increases the reliability of the commands. In addition, a system of several manual valves in various locations has been replaced by one central multivalve that controls the entire system. These advances represent major improvements in efficient extraction of cells, optimization of valves and control points, miniaturization, and automation of the system.

Objective 2: Development of the real-time bio-imaging system
One of the problems with previous adhesion assay systems for cells undergoing shear stress is that a research microscope is required for imaging of the process. This necessarily requires relatively long tubing between the RWV and the assay chamber, which increases the time between rotation and assay. The research microscope also costs more than all of the other components of the system the system combined. Therefore, a completely new, low cost, custom-designed optical system was developed to reliably image cell adhesion under flow conditions in our adhesion assay system. The mini-microscope was tested extensively in real experiments, and has provided video image data of sufficient quality for the high-speed motion analysis necessary for flow-chamber cell adhesion data. In addition, the investigators have converted from a tape-storage system to direct digitization, streamlining data analysis and improving fidelity of motion tracking.

Objective 3: Integration of the bio-imaging system and the cell adhesion assay
In preparation for biological experiments, a new flow chamber was developed, with an improved sealing mechanism, to provide a more portable and robust flow chamber. Although beyond the scope of the current project, these modifications are an important step in development of a space flight system. In order to accommodate budget cuts and shortened time frame, however, it was necessary to focus on developing a basic flow-chamber-based adhesion assay, setting aside the work on the Amgel matrix system and the real-time computer tracking. This has resulted in a complete system for assay of the microgravity effect on leukocyte adhesion that, although lacking the real-time computer analysis system originally planned, will permit state-of-the-art analysis as good as current systems in use for conventional adhesion studies.

In this project, investigators developed a novel human tissue bio-imaging technology applicable to microgravity research to overcome these shortcomings. Lessons learned from development of this Earth-based system can form the basis for a future space-flight culture and assay system to allow NASA to monitor microgravity-inducible physiological events during space flights.

The purpose of this project was to develop a novel human tissue bioimaging technology applicable to microgravity research. This system was to integrate automated bioreactor sampling and real-time bioimaging. This will enable researchers to monitor, for the first time, effects of simulated microgravity on an important vascular function--adhesion between white blood cells and the blood vessel wall, without interruption of the culture conditions and with essentially no delay between sample extraction and cell-function assay. Technology developed in this project ultimately has potential applications for monitoring astronaut immune system function on long-term space flights. Task Objective: To develop a new, automated system for real-time bio-imaging of effects of microgravity on cell-cell adhesion through completion of the following objectives:

1. Design and develop a system to automatically extract and deliver cell samples from a rotating wall vessel to an assay system at predetermined intervals.
2.Design and develop a small, integrated, real-time digital bio-imaging system to produce digital images of cell samples.
3.Integrate into the bio-imaging system an assay of vascular cell function that utilizes the unique Amgel matrix system and sensitive real-time computer tracking of adhesive cell interactions.
The system developed for this purpose can be adapted to assay other effects of simulated microgravity on cultured cells. It can also be useful as a compact, portable flow-cell based adhesion assay to measure adhesion of leukocytes or other cells under shear-stress conditions similar to those found in the blood stream.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Objective 1: Development of the cell extraction and delivery system
Even though extraction of fluid from a rotating RWV was a relatively straightforward engineering project, extraction of the cells from a rotating system is not trivial. Beyond the technical issue of a leak-free rotating interface between the chamber and external tubing, there is the issue that cells are often not uniformly distributed within the chamber. Although various models have been proposed to describe the location of cells in such a system, models do not always agree. Investigators determined the best sample points empirically. Their current system reliably delivers cells at a uniform concentration from two separate locations (after an initial mixing period of approx. 10 minutes.) without interrupting rotation.

In the first year, feasibility was confirmed with a largely manual system of valves and a syringe pump system that used a command line interface for each action of the pump. However, entering of individual commands made experimentation cumbersome and time consuming. The control process was improved by transitioning to a graphical control program where embedded script files are created and programmed into the syringe pump. These pre-programmed script files are executed directly from the laptop graphical control program. This software configuration for control of the syringe pump streamlines the control process and also increases the reliability of the commands. In addition, a system of several manual valves in various locations has been replaced by one central multivalve that controls the entire system. These advances represent major improvements in efficient extraction of cells, optimization of valves and control points, miniaturization, and automation of the system.

Objective 2: Development of the real-time bio-imaging system
One of the problems with previous adhesion assay systems for cells undergoing shear stress is that a research microscope is required for imaging of the process. This necessarily requires relatively long tubing between the RWV and the assay chamber, which increases the time between rotation and assay. The research microscope also costs more than all of the other components of the system the system combined. Therefore, a completely new, low cost, custom-designed optical system was developed to reliably image cell adhesion under flow conditions in our adhesion assay system. The mini-microscope was tested extensively in real experiments, and has provided video image data of sufficient quality for the high-speed motion analysis necessary for flow-chamber cell adhesion data. In addition, the investigators have converted from a tape-storage system to direct digitization, streamlining data analysis and improving fidelity of motion tracking.

Objective 3: Integration of the bio-imaging system and the cell adhesion assay
In preparation for biological experiments, a new flow chamber was developed, with an improved sealing mechanism, to provide a more portable and robust flow chamber. Although beyond the scope of the current project, these modifications are an important step in development of a space flight system. In order to accommodate budget cuts and shortened time frame, however, it was necessary to focus on developing a basic flow-chamber-based adhesion assay, setting aside the work on the Amgel matrix system and the real-time computer tracking. This has resulted in a complete system for assay of the microgravity effect on leukocyte adhesion that, although lacking the real-time computer analysis system originally planned, will permit state-of-the-art analysis as good as current systems in use for conventional adhesion studies.

experiment_title: Early Markers of Space-Radiation Induced Human Cataractogenesis

Cataractous lesions
CD44 protein
Extracellular matrix genes
Lens cell differentiation
Lens epithelial cell growth
Posterior subcapsular cataractous dots
investigators: Principal Investigator: Blakely, EleanorCo-Investigator: Chang, Polly
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The study is an emphasis focused on reducing the risk of radiation-induced cataract in human space travel. A clear understanding of the underlying mechanisms for cataractogenesis is necessary for early diagnosis and mitigation of cataract risks. The hypothesis driving this research is that particle radiation induces early molecular signaling alterations in the lens epithelial cells, which disrupt normal differentiation mechanisms necessary for the maintenance of lens clarity.

APPROACH:
In order to assess the time course of the expression and the natural history of the developing lesion, two experimental models of the lens were proposed. Differentiating human lens cells in vitro were used to extend the investigation of molecular mechanisms of action that follow particle radiation induced changes in key marker proteins using beams defined by NASA's operational parameters, eg. low doses and dose-rates of protons or heavy ions. Mice were irradiated and early lenticular changes associated with molecular aggregation were followed using an exquisitely sensitive dynamic light scattering method to map the unique signatures of particle radiation-induced lens opacification. Information gathered from these measurements were used to determine when the lenses were harvested for protein identification.

RESULTS:
The long-term objectives of this project are to elucidate the underlying molecular basis for heavy-ion-induced radiation cataractogenesis, and to obtain a more complete understanding of the normal process of lens cell differentiation. The weight of experimental evidence indicates that the germinative epithelium is the primary target for radiation damage leading to cataract. However, there are potentially three hypotheses for the mechanism of radiation-induced cataractogenesis: 1) the increased genotoxic load of radiation damage leads to cataract through a number of intermediate steps involving altered expression, 2) gene expression is altered without genomic changes (the effect here may be at the level of signaling), or 3) the effect is on protein expression directly. There is of course the possibility that these three hypotheses are not mutually exclusive, and that some combination of these hypotheses is involved. Investigators postulate that cytokines play a role in driving the cell-cycle regulation in lens epithelial cells. The cascades of signals trigger multiple membrane-based events, including alterations in actin cytoskeletal dynamics, integrin extracellular matrix expression, adhesion complex remodeling, intra- and inter-cellular communication, and cell movement. For homeostasis, these interactions are tightly coupled. Using a high throughput quantitative approach to query selected genes known to be important for extracellular communication, they show dynamic changes in gene expression profile including characteristic differences in both the number and distribution of genes in our in vitro differentiating human lens epithelial cells system (HLE) after a low- or high-dose of either low- or high-LET, in a short time course up to 8 hours after exposure. They noted that the profile of expression of Extracellular Matrix (ECM) genes was dependent not only on the dose of radiation and sampling times, but also on the radiation quality of the beams. The expression of more than 20 ECM genes, dominated by ECM proteases, cell matrix adhesion and transmembrane molecules, were upregulated within 4 hours after exposure to low doses of protons. However, these changes were transient and did not persist for more than 8 hours post irradiation. On the other hand, more ECM genes were impacted after 100 cGy of protons and the expression persisted beyond 8 hours post irradiation. In sharp contrast with the ECM expression profile after protons, fewer genes had altered gene expression patterns after exposure to titanium ions when compared to the controls. In particular, genes that were affected were primarily down regulated in the 1, 4 and 8 hour time points studied.

Investigators examined the expression profile of a similar set of extraceullar matrix and adhesion molecules in whole lenses from Sprague-Dawley rats collected nine months after exposure to 10 or 100 cGy of 600 MeV/u iron ions. The results were compared to a set of control sham-treated lenses that were confirmed to be non-cataractous. Detailed visual inspection of iron-ion irradiated lenses at harvest confirms that the cataractous lesions are multifocal and polymorphic, with anterior cortical opacification, and anterior cortical involvements. Opacities appear to aggregate in the equatorial periphery. In addition, posterior subcapsular cataractous (PSC) dots are clearly visible in 50% of the lenses that were examined ex vivo. Results from focused microarray analysis revealed that lenses from 10 cGy-iron-ion-irradiated rat lenses showed significant 3- to 4-fold increases in genes in CAM & ECM functional groups in lenses. On the other hand, 100 cGy-iron-ion-irradiated rat lenses show a completely different gene response. Only 2 genes in the ECM & CAM series were increased 2- to 3-fold in the high-dose irradiated cataractous lenses, and two CAM series genes were significantly down-regulated 2- to 3-fold nine months after exposure. The high responsiveness of ECM gene families after a single low radiation dose to the lens in vivo contrasts with the decreased gene expression seen after a 10-fold higher radiation dose. The fact that such changes were persistent nine months after the exposures is unexpected. Clearly, different genes are affected at each dose level. It is not yet known how this gene profile correlates with the status of the opacifications observed at each dose at the same time post-exposure.

CD44, a cell-surface glycoprotein and a member of the cell adhesion molecule was shown to be a candidate that was upregulated at 8 hours after 100 cGy protons. Misregulation of this gene was also found in rat lenses >9 months after 10 cGy iron ions. CD44 in rat lenses have previously been reported and surgical removal of lens fiber cells from adult mice often results in a robust upregulation of CD44 protein, which preceded the upregulation of alpha-smooth muscle actin expression typically used as a marker of epithelial-mesenchyma transition in this model of lens epithelial cell fibrosis. CD44 protein has also been shown to increase in the lens epithelium after injury and is rodent-strain dependent. The CD44 family of receptors includes multiple variant isoforms due to post-translational modification and alternative splicing. Several isoforms have been linked to malignant properties, including migration, invasion and metastasis. The Western results with isoform specific antibodies to probe for translation of CD44 variant gene product suggest that although CD44 protein levels were reduced 1 hour after a small 10 cGy of protons, the v6 variant levels remained similar to the control levels. On the other hand, while the CD44 levels were elevated at 1.5 hours after 100 cGy Titanium, the v6 variant also remained similar to the control levels. C57Bl6 male mice were sham-treated or exposed to 10, 50, 100 and 200 cGy of 600 MeV/u iron or 1 GeV/u protons in two separate large scale studies during NSRL08C and 09C. The animals were maintained for a period of 12 – 18 months post irradiation to measure (1) body weight changes, (2) changes in lens clarity using (a) slit lamp, and (b) quasi-elastic light scattering (QLS) technique. Lens tissues were also ex vivo imaged using stereo microscopy to document lens pathology and preserved for molecular analysis. The time constant for tau is an indicator of the size of the protein aggregation and light scatting centers in the lens. To date, comparisons have been made to show if the early in vitro human lens cell responses within hours after exposure correlate with the persistent in vivo whole rat lens response profile nine months after low doses.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Glass, JohnCo-Investigator: Douglas, Grace
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In a contingency cabin depressurization event, it is expected that crewmembers would be in a pressurized suit for up to 144 hours, requiring nutrition to be safely delivered against a pressure differential of 4 psi. The Advanced Food Technology (AFT) group sought to develop both a prototype fluid delivery system that would overcome the pressure differential and guidelines for a nutritional beverage compatible with the delivery system. Two prototypes were developed and analyzed. The bag-in-bag (BiB) prototype, designed to equalize the suit pressure with the beverage pouch and enable a crewmember to drink normally, was operated successfully in both vacuum chamber and suited subject tests. The Boa restrainer pouch, designed to provide mechanical leverage to overcome the pressure differential, was not successful, and recommendations for improved performance have been offered. Guidelines for developing contingency beverage prototypes, including viscosity and rehydration properties, were compiled based on their compatibility with the delivery hardware. Contingency beverage shelf life predictions were calculated based on generated vapor sorption isotherm curves. Evaluation results and food product parameters have the potential to be used to improve future prototype designs and develop complete nutritional beverages for contingency events and extended EVAs.

The objectives of this experiment are to develop food product parameters to meet nutritional, acceptability, stability, and suit interface criteria, and to test several concepts for dispensing liquid through a feed port into a pressurized suit.

AFT will receive energy requirements and nutritional requirements from HHC (Nutritional Biochemistry Laboratory). The food parameters that enable compatibility with the in-suit feeding system will be defined by interfacing with Crew Survival Systems (CSS).

APPROACH:
An approach for this experiment is currently not available.

RESULTS:
The BiB prototype was successful to allow the crewmember to drink nominally. Additional work will be done to improve this protoype. The Boa was not successful, and a decision was made not to continue work on this prototype.
