experiment_title: Performance and Sleep Consequences of Slam Shifts in Schedule
parameter_html:
Alertness
Light levels
Performance
Sleep
Circadian rhythm
investigators: Principal Investigator: Monk, Timothy
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The experiment seeks to answer several questions about coping with slam shifts (i.e., abrupt shifts in work/rest schedule of six hours), including the following: 1) In the light levels and comparative social isolation typical of the International Space Station (ISS), how long does the human Endogenous Circadian Pacemaker (ECP) take (i.e. how many days) to entrain completely (at the correct phase angle) to: a) a six hour phase advance (slam shift out)? and b) a six hour phase delay (slam shift back)? 2) To what degree, and for how many nights, is objectively and subjectively recorded sleep disrupted by: a) a six hour phase advance (slam shift out)? and b) a six hour phase delay (slam shift back)? 3) To what degree, and for how many days, is objectively measured performance and subjectively reported alertness and mood disrupted by a) a six hour phase advance (slam shift out)? and b) a six hour phase delay (slam shift back)? 4) To what extent (if any) are the disruptions noted in #2 and #3 ameliorated by a 90-minute daytime nap scheduled for the workday following each of the two slam shifts? 5) To what extent (if any) are the total disruptions in circadian rhythms, sleep, alertness, and performance occasioned by slam shifts better or worse than those occasioned by the repeated gradual phase shifts studied in the previous grant (NAG 9-1234)? 6) How will the disruptions noted in #3 vary by the particular task used?

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The investigators accommodated the unexpected movement of the termination date of this grant by NASA from 6/1/2009 to 9/30/2006 (with associated cuts in funds) by running fewer subjects through the protocol, rather than by reducing the length or complexity of the protocol. In order to save money they also did not assay the urine samples they had already collected. Fortunately they had not yet run any subjects through the “nap" condition of the protocol, so they did not run any subjects through the “nap” protocol and were thus not able to test any hypotheses regarding naps as a countermeasure. The hypotheses regarding circadian rhythms will thus be tested using only the circadian rhythms in core body temperature and urine volume. Hypotheses regarding sleep, mood, alertness and performance will be tested using the measures outlined in the grant application. Investigators ran eight subjects through this protocol by 9/30/2006, simultaneously performing quality control on the data, archiving the data, and performing summary statistics on the data. Data analysis has not yet been completed.

The final sample data set will be compared (with the obvious limitation in sample size resulting from the untimely truncation) to the other two data sets in this series of experiments (supported by NAG9-12334) which involved repeated two hour phase delays and repeated 0.5 hour phase advances. This may allow some limited conclusions to be made regarding the important question as to whether slam shifts or repeated gradual phase shifts are a better means of phase shifting the work/rest schedule of astronauts.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies have shown that chronic elimination of weight-bearing activity induces both fiber atrophy and changes in isomyosin expression. This study was measure isomyosin expression in different muscles involved with locomotor and antigravity functions. A second objective was to determine the oxidative capacity in muscles homogenates, and assess any alterations in mitochondrial and glycogenolyc enzymes.

Approach:

The relative and total content of isomyosin protein expression was determined by gel electrophoresis for type I, type IIa-IIx and type IIb isoforms. Total RNA was isolated from muscles for slot-blot analysis, and mRNA was determined for type I, type II and type IIb isoforms. Oxidative rates of palminate and pyruvate were determined from measurements of 14CO2 production. Oxidative enzymes were measured and mitochondrial and cytoplasmic isoforms were identified by alcohol inactivation.

Results:

Findings demonstrate a reduced expression of the two slow myosin heavy chain and an increased expression of the two fastest myosin heavy chain isoforms. Coupled with muscle atrophy, this tends to reduce the effective muscle mass to support antigravity function and locomotor activity. There also appeared to be a selective reduction in the capacity of the muscle to produce long-chain fatty acids, which may impair endurance during spaceflight. A decrease in palminate oxidizing capacity was observed in the flight animals, but no decrease was found in pyruvate oxidizing capacity in fast twitch muscles.

__description:
Objectives:

Previous studies have shown that chronic elimination of weight-bearing activity induces both fiber atrophy and changes in isomyosin expression. This study was measure isomyosin expression in different muscles involved with locomotor and antigravity functions. A second objective was to determine the oxidative capacity in muscles homogenates, and assess any alterations in mitochondrial and glycogenolyc enzymes.

Approach:

The relative and total content of isomyosin protein expression was determined by gel electrophoresis for type I, type IIa-IIx and type IIb isoforms. Total RNA was isolated from muscles for slot-blot analysis, and mRNA was determined for type I, type II and type IIb isoforms. Oxidative rates of palminate and pyruvate were determined from measurements of 14CO2 production. Oxidative enzymes were measured and mitochondrial and cytoplasmic isoforms were identified by alcohol inactivation.

Results:

Findings demonstrate a reduced expression of the two slow myosin heavy chain and an increased expression of the two fastest myosin heavy chain isoforms. Coupled with muscle atrophy, this tends to reduce the effective muscle mass to support antigravity function and locomotor activity. There also appeared to be a selective reduction in the capacity of the muscle to produce long-chain fatty acids, which may impair endurance during spaceflight. A decrease in palminate oxidizing capacity was observed in the flight animals, but no decrease was found in pyruvate oxidizing capacity in fast twitch muscles.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA’s future deep space missions to the lunar environment, lunar surface, and to Mars involve both a long-duration and long communication delays. These factors drive a requirement for durable training, specifically training that can survive long delays between time of training and actual use of the learned knowledge and skills. In addition, the training needs to be flexible to allow for transfer to new and unexpected situations beyond those included in a standard training regimen, as it will not be possible to accurately anticipate all possible situations in which crewmembers might encounter. Furthermore, onboard just-in-time (JIT) training and performance support tools will be required.

On such long-duration space missions with communication delays, the crew will need to be semi-autonomous at minimum. Current crew training practices are based on the assumption that ground support is available continuously and in real-time, which will not be the case in future long-duration space missions. With no direct experience with long-duration space missions, serious gaps exist in current data upon which new crew training must be based. This experiment aims to test the retention and transfer of specific motor, perceptual and cognitive processes learned pre-launch to assess the need for onboard refresher and JIT training.

APPROACH:
Two experimental tasks were conducted with crew and crew-like subjects tested at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, and with university undergraduate students tested at the University of Colorado, performing the same tasks under the exact same experimental paradigm. Six experimental sessions were conducted over a period of 480 days, in the following order:

Session 1: Pretest. Subjects performed 50 trials of the standard data entry task (typing 4-digit numbers, e.g., 2154, using right hand), 50 trials of a word task (typing 4-digit numbers presented as words, e.g., two one five four, using right hand), 50 trials a left-hand task (typing 4-digit numbers, e.g., 2154, using left hand), 50 trials of a 3-digit task (typing 3-digit numbers, e.g., 215, using right hand), and 50 trials of a code task (typing positions of letters within the alphabet, e.g., baed, using right hand).

Session 2: Training Session 1. Subjects competed three blocks of trials of the standard data entry task. Each block consisted of 100 trials, and the same 100 numbers were repeated in each of the three blocks.

Session 3: Training Session 2. Identical to Training Session 1; subjects competed three blocks of trials of the standard data entry task. Each block consisted of 100 trials, and the same 100 numbers were used as during the first training session.

Session 4: Onboard Session 1. Subjects completed 100 trials of the standard task followed by 100 trials of the left-hand task. For both the standard task and the left-hand task, fifty trials were on old numbers (numbers that had been practiced during training), and fifty trials were on new numbers.

Session 5: Onboard Session 2. Subjects completed 100 trials of the standard task followed by 100 trials of the code task. For both the standard task and the code task, fifty trials were on old numbers (numbers that had been practiced during training), and fifty trials were on new numbers. To create old numbers for the code task, digits for each old 4-digit number were replaced with letters (a = 1, b = 2, etc.).

Session 6: Post-test. The post-test was identical to the pre-test.

RESULTS:
Training: Averaging across training sessions and blocks, there were differences in accuracy between subject types; crew and crew-like subjects demonstrated higher accuracy than did undergraduate subjects. Average total response time (TRT) decreased from the first training session to the second training session, as well as across blocks within each training block. There was a marginally significant difference in TRT between subject types, with faster TRT for crew than for crew-like and undergraduate subjects. A post-hoc test revealed that the difference between NASA subjects (combining crew and crew-like) and undergraduate subjects was significant.

Test 1 (Standard, Left Hand): For the standard task, accuracy was higher for old numbers than for new numbers for crew and crew-like subjects; the opposite pattern was observed for undergraduate subjects. For the left-hand task the opposite pattern was observed: accuracy was higher for new numbers than for old numbers for crew and crew-like subjects, but accuracy was higher for old numbers than for new numbers for undergraduate subjects. Subjects were faster to perform the standard task than the left-hand task. Averaging across task, old numbers were entered more quickly than new numbers. However, the repetition priming effect was larger for the left-hand task than for the standard task. The repetition priming effect was marginally significant for the standard task but significant for the left-hand task.

Test 2 (Standard, Code): Overall accuracy was higher for the standard data entry task than for the code task. There were also differences in accuracy between subject types; on average, accuracy was higher for crew and crew-like subjects than for undergraduate subjects. However, the increase in accuracy for crew and crew-like subjects was restricted to the code task; accuracy was similar for the three subject types on the standard task. Subjects were also faster to perform the standard task than the code task, with a significant repetition priming effect. Averaging across tasks, old numbers were entered more quickly than new numbers. The repetition priming effect was larger for the code task than for standard task, although it was significant for both the standard task and the code task.

Overall, similar results were obtained for the crew and crew-like subjects as found for university students, although the crew and crew-like subjects consistently performed at a higher level than the university students. Importantly on both tasks, the crew and crew-like subjects showed different patterns of response under cognitive load (i.e., by the extra requirements of the code task in the first task and by the secondary counting task in the second task) than the patterns shown by the university students. Thus, crew members’ performance under cognitive load on the ground cannot be predicted from the performance of university undergraduate students. Given the criticality of cognitive performance during space missions and given the significant cognitive loads space missions impose on the astronaut crew, this finding has important implications for research assumptions that are driven by university-based research.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Impaired thermoregulation may have significant impact during space flight operations such as extravehicular activities (EVA), entry, landing and egress. Impaired thermoregulation, as represented by an increase in core (intestinal) temperature in response to a given thermal load, has been consistently observed in subjects confined to bed rest or immersed in water (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Further, these changes were observed during exercise following these simulated microgravity exposures (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Similar changes were expected to occur during space flight.

This impairment of temperature regulation may be manifested as decreased exercise capacity and increased orthostatic intolerance; it may also be manifested as higher levels of core body temperature for a given level of work (oxygen consumption, Vo2) both during and after space flight. The higher core temperatures may be due to altered cutaneous vasodilatory reflex (delayed onset of vasodilatation and decreased skin perfusion for a given level of core temperature), increased sweating threshold, and decreased sweating sensitivity, while heat production might not be altered. The purpose of this preliminary experiment was to assess human core (intestinal) temperature and thermoregulatory responses to exercise after adaptation to long-duration spaceflight. Specific objectives of this experiment were to:

1) Determine whether overall thermoregulation is impaired during space flight by comparing core temperature (Tin) during two submaximal levels of aerobic exercise preflight, inflight, and postflight;

2) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by altered heat production, as calculated by indirect calorimetry;

3) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by impaired heat loss, as assessed by the skin blood flow/core temperature relationship (where changes in skin blood flow are measured pre- and postflight by laser Doppler flowmetry, and estimated during all tests by calculations of tissue conductance) and by the sweating response. Local sweat response/core temperature relationship was measured pre- and postflight using a dew point hygrometer, and total body sweat loss is estimated during all tests by measuring body weight loss.

It was anticipated that, for a given absolute level of work, body temperatures would increase to a greater degree due to (1) a smaller production and/or decreased efficiency of evaporation of sweat, and (2) decreased convective heat loss from the surface of the skin.

APPROACH:
This investigation examined body temperatures (skin and core), heat production (indirect calorimetry), and evaporative heat loss during 2 standard levels of exercise (40% and 65% of preflight VO2peak).

Submaximal Cycle Exercise Test (before and after flight) - Graded maximal cycle exercise testing was first conducted to volitional fatigue on 2 crewmembers in the supine position. These sessions occurred 2-3 days before the preflight submaximal exercise tests, repeated during the last 5 days of the mission, and 6 days after landing (R+6). The graded maximal cycle exercise test protocol consisted of:

  • 5 minutes of supine rest on the ergometer
  • 2 minutes of warm-up at 50 Watts (W)
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 100 W
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 125 W
  • 5 minutes of pedaling at 150 W

    After the 150-W segment of the protocol, exercise intensity was increased by 25 W-per-minute until the subject could no longer maintain the 75-rpm pedaling frequency. Cool down was conducted at 50 W for 3-5 minutes after maximal exercise. During each maximal test, oxygen (O2) uptake and carbon dioxide (CO2) production were measured and averaged over 30-s intervals using a gas analysis system. Heart rate was continuously monitored with a standard electrocardiogram (ECG). Blood pressure was measured during the last 30 seconds of each exercise level using manual sphygmomanometry. The highest level of O2 uptake, averaged over a 60-s period, was designated peak oxygen consumption (VO2peak). Exercise intensities requiring 40% and 65% of the preflight peak value were used during the submaximal tests.

    The supine submaximal cycle tests were conducted 145-146 days before flight (L-145) and on R+5. All testing was performed at room temperature (22.6-23.3°C; 56-64% humidity) and at the same time of day to mitigate circadian effects. Postflight sessions occurred during the summer (July, 1995), but the crewmembers were almost exclusively confined to air-conditioned buildings. The submaximal exercise tests consisted of a continuous protocol of the following:

  • 20 minutes of quiet rest
  • 20 minutes of exercise at 40% preflight VO2peak (50 or 60 W)
  • 20 minutes of exercise at 65% preflight VO2peak (100 or 110 W)
  • 10 minutes of quiet resting recovery

    Heart rates during submaximal exercise were monitored with a heart watch. Blood pressure was measured twice before exercise and every 10 minutes during exercise with a manual sphygmomanometer. Skin temperatures were measured continuously with four external skin thermistors (forearm, calf, thigh, chest) and recorded with a data logger. Core temperature was measured using a small ingestible telemetry thermal sensor pill that was ingested 6 hours before exercise. Temperature data was sampled every 30 seconds and stored in a receiver.

    Skin blood flow velocity was measured continuously with a laser Doppler skin blood flow monitor using an integrated probe attached to the forearm with a local skin-heating (38°C) collar. Local sweating rate at the upper quadrant of the chest was measured continuously with a dew point hygrometer sweat system. The dew point sensor was ventilated (500-800 ml· min-1) with ambient air from the room. Subjects towel dried after each exercise session and were weighed in the same dry gym shorts before and after exercise. All measurement devices were calibrated before each exercise session.

    Submaximal Exercise Test (during flight): No submaximal data was collected during flight due to the late arrival of the Spektr module and scheduling problems after the module arrived.

    RESULTS:
    These results should be viewed as preliminary results only, since the low number of subjects did not allow for statistical analysis of the data. However, the results do suggest that thermoregulation was impaired following long-duration space flight.

    Maximal Exercise: The preflight maximal exercise supine cycle VO2peak values for the subjects were 32.6 and 29.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. Due to the limited active muscle mass with this form of exercise, these supine cycle values were each approximately 20% lower than the measured upright treadmill VO2peak values. During flight, Subject 1 was reported to have performed approximately 70% of the standard prescribed Russian countermeasure program (which consists of approximately 2 hours each day of aerobic and resistive exercises), while Subject 2 was reported to have performed less than 70% of the prescribed countermeasures. Near the end of the mission, on flight day 112, Subject 1 had a cycle VO2peak of 27.2 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 17% from preflight); for Subject 2, the value was 20.8 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 29%). After flight, neither crewmember could complete the exercise protocol, stopping after 28-29 minutes. Postflight, cycle VO2peak on R+6 was further reduced to 23.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subject 1 (reduced 28% from preflight). For Subject 2, no value was obtained because the medical monitor would not allow the postflight maximal exercise test to be performed because of the subject's delayed recovery from the mission.

    Submaximal Exercise: Both crewmembers were able to complete the preflight submaximal exercise protocol; final exercise heart rates were only 137 and 123 bpm for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. On R+5, Subjects 1 and 2 could not complete 11 and 12 minutes of the 65% VO2peak level, respectively. In both cases, the medical monitor terminated the test shortly after the exercise heart rate exceeded the preflight response. In each case, the subject appeared fatigued and was having difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency.

    Blood pressure responses to exercise were similar before and after flight. Oxygen uptake on R+5 was similar to preflight values, except at the last sampling time for Subject 1, where the lower value was most likely due to his difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency. The Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) value was higher at most sampling times on R+5.

    A consistent difference was not seen between pre- and postflight supine resting skin temperatures at any measurement site. Resting intestinal temperature was similar preflight and at R+5. During postflight exercise, the core temperature, (Tin, ingestible telemetry pill) at test termination was similar (37.8 degrees C for both subjects despite a 29% shorter exercise time and a 40% reduction in the total cumulative work (W• min-1).

    The sweating and skin blood flow responses for the two subjects were altered postflight. The slope of the sweating/Tin relationship (mg• min-1• cm-2• °C-1) was reduced from 4.5 preflight to 2.1 postflight for Subject 1 and from 11 to 3.6 for Subject 2. The slope of the skin blood flow/Tin relationship (percent change Perfusion Unit• °C-1) was also reduced from 346 preflight to 214 postflight for Subject 1 and from 214 to 143 for Subject 2. Tin thresholds for the onset of sweating and vasodilation were not altered in a consistent manner after flight. For sweating, Tin thresholds (°C) were 37.4 preflight and 37.6 postflight for Subject 1 and 36.6 and 36.6 for Subject 2. For skin blood flow, Tin thresholds were 37.3 preflight and 37.5 postflight for Subject 1 and 37.6 preflight and 37.7 postflight for Subject 2. Total body sweat (weight) loss during preflight exercise was 636 g vs. 272 g postflight for Subject 1 and 455 g vs. 45 g postflight for Subject 2. Subject 2 had just reached the sweating threshold postflight when the session was terminated. Body weight on R+5 was reduced in both crewmembers from the preflight value--for Subject 1 by 0.8 kg and for Subject 2 by 2.3 kg.

    In conclusion, these preliminary findings suggest alteration of heat loss responses in two crewmembers following a 115-day space flight. The sensitivity of the heat loss responses was reduced after long-duration space flight, resulting in a faster rate of increase in core temperature.

Near the end of the mission, on flight day 112, Subject 1 had a cycle VO2peak of 27.2 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 17% from preflight); for Subject 2, the value was 20.8 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 29%). After flight, neither crewmember could complete the exercise protocol, stopping after 28-29 minutes. Postflight, cycle VO2peak on R+6 was further reduced to 23.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subject 1 (reduced 28% from preflight). For Subject 2, no value was obtained because the medical monitor would not allow the postflight maximal exercise test to be performed because of the subject's delayed recovery from the mission.

    Submaximal Exercise: Both crewmembers were able to complete the preflight submaximal exercise protocol; final exercise heart rates were only 137 and 123 bpm for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. On R+5, Subjects 1 and 2 could not complete 11 and 12 minutes of the 65% VO2peak level, respectively. In both cases, the medical monitor terminated the test shortly after the exercise heart rate exceeded the preflight response. In each case, the subject appeared fatigued and was having difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency.

    Blood pressure responses to exercise were similar before and after flight. Oxygen uptake on R+5 was similar to preflight values, except at the last sampling time for Subject 1, where the lower value was most likely due to his difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency. The Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) value was higher at most sampling times on R+5.

    A consistent difference was not seen between pre- and postflight supine resting skin temperatures at any measurement site. Resting intestinal temperature was similar preflight and at R+5. During postflight exercise, the core temperature, (Tin, ingestible telemetry pill) at test termination was similar (37.8 degrees C for both subjects despite a 29% shorter exercise time and a 40% reduction in the total cumulative work (W• min-1).

    The sweating and skin blood flow responses for the two subjects were altered postflight. The slope of the sweating/Tin relationship (mg• min-1• cm-2• °C-1) was reduced from 4.5 preflight to 2.1 postflight for Subject 1 and from 11 to 3.6 for Subject 2. The slope of the skin blood flow/Tin relationship (percent change Perfusion Unit• °C-1) was also reduced from 346 preflight to 214 postflight for Subject 1 and from 214 to 143 for Subject 2. Tin thresholds for the onset of sweating and vasodilation were not altered in a consistent manner after flight. For sweating, Tin thresholds (°C) were 37.4 preflight and 37.6 postflight for Subject 1 and 36.6 and 36.6 for Subject 2. For skin blood flow, Tin thresholds were 37.3 preflight and 37.5 postflight for Subject 1 and 37.6 preflight and 37.7 postflight for Subject 2. Total body sweat (weight) loss during preflight exercise was 636 g vs. 272 g postflight for Subject 1 and 455 g vs. 45 g postflight for Subject 2. Subject 2 had just reached the sweating threshold postflight when the session was terminated. Body weight on R+5 was reduced in both crewmembers from the preflight value--for Subject 1 by 0.8 kg and for Subject 2 by 2.3 kg.

    In conclusion, these preliminary findings suggest alteration of heat loss responses in two crewmembers following a 115-day space flight. The sensitivity of the heat loss responses was reduced after long-duration space flight, resulting in a faster rate of increase in core temperature.

experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study was conducted during NASA's Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO). It provided an opportunity to compare team performance across varying amounts of communication delays, using tasks that differ in criticality and novelty. This study examined how teams interact and perform tasks with and without communication delays. The tasks performed by the crew varied along two dimensions: 1) tasks that were either critical or not critical (criticality) and 2) tasks that were either novel or familiar (novelty). Tasks varied by criticality and novelty as it is assumed that highly novel and highly critical tasks are similar to tasks that a crew may encounter during a long-duration mission in which they have no prior training but must address. This feasibility study provided a preliminary understanding of what impact communication delay has on individual and team performance as well as insight into how teams perform and interact in high-fidelity, autonomous environments. Findings from this study were used for the second phase of this project, which took place on the International Space Station (ISS).

APPROACH:
Crewmembers in the Aquarius habitat and mission control personnel participated in performing tasks identified as highly novel and critical under three different scenarios: 1) response to smoke in the habitat involving no delay in communications; 2) response to a crewmember who had been stung by a lionfish involving a five minute one-way delay; and 3) response to a crack in the habitat window involving a 10 minute one-way delay. Participants included the four Aquarius crewmembers and three mission control personnel. Six of the seven participants provided complete data for each scenario, and the three mission control personnel participants provided assessments of individual and team performance.

RESULTS:
Levels of perceived autonomy in task performance appear to be associated with increased delays in communication. Reported quality of communication between crew and mission control declined significantly under conditions of the five minute one-way delay, but then appeared to increase during the ten minute delay scenario. Objective and subjective measures indicated a decline in task performance associated with difficulty in communications between the crew and mission control during the five minute one-way delay. Crewmembers that had become used to communicating under conditions of a 50 second one-way delay reported that a five-minute delay was equivalent to having no contact with mission control. However, performance appeared to improve during the ten minute one-way delay scenario, perhaps due to the debriefing conducted after the five minute delay scenario and team adaptation to the challenges of delayed communications.

This experiment was transitioned to the International Space Station (ISS). Please see experiment ID Comm_Delay for the inflight aspects of this study.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In this investigation, the water on the Mir space station was analyzed in detail to study the effectiveness of the Mir purification system. Potable water, water used to maintain hygiene, and water that accumulates from humidity condensate were analyzed to confirm that any potentially harmful contaminants were maintained at acceptably safe levels. The information gathered by this research supported the development and evaluation of water purification units, water quality standards, and in-flight water sampling hardware for the International Space Station. The experiment objectives were to:

  • Characterize the chemical composition of Mir recycled water, Russian ground-supplied water prior to launch and on orbit, and the Mir humidity condensate to support development and testing of the water recycling and monitoring systems for the ISS.
  • Determine and compare the chemical composition of Mir and Space Shuttle condensate.
  • Determine whether the potable water on board Mir meets the Joint U.S./Russian water quality specifications for ISS.

    This experiment has flown under the NASA Human Life Sciences Discipline during the Mir 18/NASA 1, Mir 19, Mir 20/STS-74, and Mir 21/NASA 2/STS-79 missions. In addition, this activity was performed under the Space Medicine Program during the Mir 22/NASA 3/STS-81, Mir 23/NASA 4/STS-84, Mir 23/NASA 5/STS-86, Mir 24/NASA 6/STS-89 and the Mir 25/NASA 7/STS-91 missions. Shuttle flights were used to return items and resupply the experiment.

    APPROACH:
    Recycled and stored water samples were collected periodically during each mission using U.S. developed water sampling hardware. In addition, raw unprocessed humidity condensate was collected using Russian-supplied hardware, while partially processed condensate was collected using U.S. supplied hardware. The partially processed condensate samples were collected as a result of ethylene glycol leaks on board the Mir, to assess the ability of the water processor system to remove this contaminant.

    RESULTS:
    In general, the recycled and stored water supplied to the Mir Space Station met NASA, Russian Space Agency (RSA), and/or U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) standards. Exceptions were found to include total organic carbon (TOC) and turbidity in the recycled water which routinely exceeded NASA standards. The TOC in some cases, exceeded Russian standards as well. Other parameters such as ethylene glycol, barium, nickel, chloroform, phenol, and dioctyl phthatate occasionally exceeded NASA, RSA or EPA standards. All but the TOC violations were transient.

    The humidity condensate exhibited steadily increasing levels of ethylene glycol throughout the missions. This is believed to reflect the increased levels of ethylene glycol in the Mir atmosphere following coolant loop leaks and maintenance activities. In one case, the presence of ethylene glycol in a condensate sample alerted the ground and crew to the presence of a previously undetected coolant loop leak.

    The chemical quality of the recycled and stored water, as determined through post-flight analysis met performance and potability requirements. The analysis of samples has provided important data for assessing the potability of recycled water. In addition, these data will be instrumental in developing appropriate water quality monitoring standards for ISS.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Data from previous studies of the influence of space flight on hematologic functions have consistently shown that exposure to microgravity significantly reduces the circulating red blood cell mass (RCM). These results have been noted in numerous American astronauts and Russian cosmonauts. The RCM is a measure of the number of erythrocytes (red blood cells) circulating in the blood stream. The objective of this experiment was to measure factors involved in the control of erythrocyte turnover that might be altered during weightlessness. Many of these biochemical and hematological parameters had not been previously measured during space flight.

APPROACH:
The mission specialists (MS1 and MS2) and payload specialists (PS1 and PS2) who flew on the Spacelab 1 mission served as the subjects for the experiment. As a control for the blood draw protocol and a comparison of inflight results to bed rest results, the mission was simulated on the ground with a group of five subjects selected from a human test-subject pool. In order to simulate the inflight period, control subjects were placed at -6 degrees head-down bed rest for 10 days (mission duration). Blood samples were obtained from each crewmember and bed-rest subject three or four times (depending on the subject) during the preflight (pre-bed rest) period, two or three times inflight (during bed rest) and four times during the postflight (post-bed rest) period. Inflight samples were taken on flight days (FD) 1 and 7. Radionucleotide measurements of red cell mass and plasma volume were made 65 days before flight (L-65), on landing day (R+0), and 8 days postflight (R+8). Preflight and postflight blood samples and all samples from the bed-rest subjects were collected by venipuncture with the use of standard clinical materials and procedures.

Inflight blood samples were collected with the Inflight Blood Collection System (IBCS). Samples were collected in plain tubes for serum and in heparin / EDTA tubes for plasma. The samples were immediately separated by centrifugation into fluid and cellular phases. The centrifuged samples were then stored in an on-board cryogenic freezer (-195 degrees C). After landing, the samples were stored frozen in the laboratory until analysis was performed. Slides for reticulocyte count, white cell differential, and reticulocyte age classification were prepared inflight. Hematocrit was also determined during the inflight period. Postflight hematology analyses were performed on whole blood that had been stored at the spacecraft ambient temperature during the flight. The effect of space flight on erythrocyte survival time was measured by injecting 51Cr-labeled red blood cells immediately after landing and determining the percentage of labeled cells that remained after 8 days. Reticulocytes were counted by the standard manual method and by flow cytometry using stained cells. Erythropoietin was measured with fetal mouse liver cell cultures; when a radioimmunoassay became available later, it was used to assay frozen samples. Histogram contouring of stained blood cells was used to measure the amount of RNA in reticulocyte cytoplasm. Data were analyzed using a multi-way analysis of variance with repeated measures and the Student-Newman-Keuls multiple comparison test.

The pre- and postflight diet of the crewmembers was not controlled or monitored. Bed rest subjects consumed the standard hospital diet. Two weeks before launch, the sleep-wake cycle of MS1 and PS1 was shifted by 12 hours to prepare them for a sleep-wake cycle that would permit a continuous 24-hour operation cycle of the Spacelab. To attempt to monitor any shift in metabolic functions, urine specimens were collected from MS1 and PS1 throughout several 24-hour periods 6 months before the flight, when they were on their normal daytime work schedule, and during the preflight period, when they were adapting to their new work-rest schedule. These samples were analyzed for calcium, potassium, and cortisol and compared to samples taken immediately postflight to determine if the individuals had adapted to the imposed time change. Two hours before landing, MS1 and MS2 consumed salt tablets with water as a countermeasure to postflight gravity stress on the cardiovascular system. During the first three days of the mission, all crewmembers ingested anti-motion sickness medication.

RESULTS:
Circadian Rhythms: Cortisol, calcium, and potassium had statistically significant circadian rhythms 6 months before flight, and the peak time of these rhythms did not change while crewmembers were on a shifted schedule.

Preflight Period: Changes in some variables occurred during the preflight period, most of them between L-7 and L-1. For this reason, the mean of the values for the first two preflight days was compared with the other days on which samples were taken. No consistent preflight changes occurred in bed-rest subjects.

Erythrocyte Production and Destruction: Red cell mass (ml/kg) was decreased on landing in all four crewmen, with a significant mean decrease of 9.3 percent from preflight. By R+8, only 3.3 percent had been replaced and the decrease was still significant. Neither hyperoxia nor an increase in blood phosphate, nor a lack of iron, was a cause of the decrease in RCM, and a decrease in erythrocyte production could not be the sole cause of such a large, rapid change. Although the number of erythrocytes with abnormal shapes was elevated on R+8, erythrocyte survival time on R+8 had not changed significantly from preflight survival time. Erythropoietin decreases found with the fetal mouse liver assay were not significant, but radioimmunoassay results showed significant decreases on FD1 and FD7. Since serum haptoglobin did not decrease, intravascular hemolysis was not thought to contribute substantially to the RCM decrease.

Leukocytes and Platelets: The total white blood cell (WBC) count and the percentage and number of segmented neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils and basophils remained unchanged during and after flight. The percentage and number of band neutrophils were significantly increased on the first inflight sampling day, and the percentage and number of monocytes were significantly increased on the last postflight sampling day. The number of platelets did not change significantly during or after the flight. Data from the bed-rest experiment showed that on R+0, the number of neutrophils was significantly higher than during the preflight period.

Plasma and Blood Volume: A 6 percent decrease in plasma volume (ml/kg) at landing was not significant compared to preflight, and recovery was complete by R+8, at least a week before RCM recovered. Blood volume (ml/kg) was significantly decreased (10.5 percent) on landing, but was close to its preflight level a week later.

Serum Chemistry: Sodium was significantly decreased during flight, on R+1, and on R+12/13. Osmolality was significantly lower than its preflight level on R+8 and R+12/13 .

Proteins: Total serum protein was decreased from the preflight value by 3.8 percent on FD7. The decrease in serum protein was significant (7.6 percent) on R+8, when albumin, alpha-2 globulin, beta globulin, and gamma globulin were decreased. On R+12/13 alpha-l and alpha-2 globulin were significantly increased. From the second inflight measurement (FD7) through at least 12 hours after landing, ferritin in crewmembers increased significantly over its preflight level.

Simulation: Red cell mass decreased significantly in all bed-rest subjects, with a greater decrease (8.4 percent) on R+8 than on R+0 (4.6 percent). Ferritin was significantly decreased on R+8 and R+12/13. Potassium was significantly increased in simulation subjects on FD1. Red cell shape classification was not performed for this part of the experiment.

Conclusions: The most likely causes of RCM decrease resulting from space flight are a premature loss of erythrocytes and a failure of erythropoiesis to make up for the loss. The number of subjects in this study was small and they were not a homogeneous group in several respects. Moreover, changes in some of the measured variables occurred during the preflight period. These results must be considered preliminary until more experiments can be done.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Smilenov, LubomirCo-Investigator: Young, Erik
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The effects of space flight on human physiology are complex and represent a sum of many factors, the main two of which are microgravity and radiation. The effect of exposure to the space environment is illustrated in studies that show altered immune response of T lymphocytes following spaceflight dating back to Apollo and Skylab missions. Although this is reversed once the astronauts are back to the Earth, these effects are persistent in space and were more recently documented in astronauts during their six month mission to the International Space Station. While difficult to estimate which one of the stress factors is dominant in low Earth orbit flights, a flight to Mars for example will lead to radiation exposure that is above NASA's current standards and its effect has to be studied in advance. The human hematopoietic system is one of the most radiosensitive tissues in the human body given that it is comprised of a large number of continuously and rapidly proliferating cells. It is well known that an insult to the hematopoietic system will generate effects that are not limited in scope to hematologic endpoints. There is an interrelationship between the correct function of the hematopoietic system and other organ systems. All of this knowledge taken together has sparked much scientific effort on studies of the effects of radiation on human hematopoietic system in the last decades using in vitro and in vivo studies in model organisms. A noticeable gap in these studies is the lack of in vivo studies of radiation effects on the human hematopoietic system. The recent development of immunodeficient mouse models allows for first time such studies. These mouse models allow the engraftment of human hematopoietic stem cells in the mouse bone marrow, leading to reconstitution of functioning human hematopoietic system in the mouse bone marrow, spleen, thymus, and blood. Importantly, the side effect for the mice is minimal. This permits long term human cell engraftment and gives excellent opportunity for radiation studies.

The main hypothesis was that studies of the effects of high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation on a human hematopoietic system, reconstituted in immunodeficient mice, will provide meaningful information on not only post-radiation depletion and repopulation kinetics but also tumor formation. Such information can then be applied to space radiation risk assessment. The importance of this work is clear given the lack of in vivo data on the effects of high LET radiation on human organ and tissue systems. The study had two key objectives: The first was to characterize the early and late response of a human immune system reconstituted in mice to high LET radiation and gamma-rays. The goal was to build a detailed picture of the series of changes that the reconstituted human hematopoietic system undergoes after a high LET radiation exposure. The second objective was to characterize the human tumors that may arise in the irradiated and non-irradiated mice.

APPROACH:
To accomplish these objectives investigators produced and irradiated mice engrafted with a human hematopoietic system. The mice were exposed to either HZE (high energy) ions or x-rays and subsequently monitored along with non-irradiated control mice. The early effects of the radiation on the human cells were assessed by periodic peripheral blood tests. The obtained differential counts were compared with differentials acquired before the irradiation. Monitoring the peripheral blood cell counts for extended periods of time may show the depletion and recovery kinetics of peripheral blood cells which was a measure of the degree and duration of the radiation induced damage and also the ability of the human hematopoietic system to recover after radiation induced insults. In addition, the mice were monitored for tumor development. The tumor characterization was done by a team of pathologists from the Columbia University Department of Pathology and Cell Biology using established clinical laboratory methods for human tumor characterization with corrections based on the specificity of the mouse model.

RESULTS:
Assessment of the early and late effects of high LET 28Si irradiation and X-ray irradiation on the depletion and recovery kinetics of human peripheral blood cells in humanized mice: Clinical and physiologic assessment of any radiation exposure entails a survey of circulating lymphocyte counts. This is no different with high LET radiation and so the investigators assessed the response of engrafted human cells by examining these blood cell counts. Two very important endpoints can be measured by determining the blood cell counts at different periods after the irradiation. These are cell killing and depletion-recovery kinetics. Any detectable loss of cells as a result of radiation was a measure of the radiation damage to the hematopoietic system. Monitoring the peripheral blood cell counts for extended periods of time may show the depletion and recovery kinetics of peripheral blood cells which measured the degree and duration of the radiation induced damage. Depletion-recovery kinetics also report the ability of the human hematopoietic system and the whole organism to recover after radiation induced blood cell losses. To obtain data on these endpoints, investigators used irradiated and control mice irradiated at NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL). Blood samples were obtained at 3 weeks before the irradiation and at 7 days, and 30 days and 75 days after the irradiation. A dose of 0.4 Gy of 350 MeV/n 28Si-ions were used for these irradiations. The depletion-recovery findings show the overall changes of the blood cell counts for each mouse. The investigators observed a statistically significant decrease of the white blood cell (WBC) counts at day 7 after the irradiation. This is specifically due to the reduction in the B cells counts which are the most sensitive human blood cells and comprise the majority of circulating lymphocytes in the humanized mouse. Remarkably, there is no statistically significant difference between the WBC and the B cells and T cells pre-irradiation and day 30 or day 75 after the irradiation. Two important results can be derived from this data. Firstly, irradiation of a human hematopoietic system, reconstituted in mice, is affected by 0.4 Gy of 350 MeV/n 28Si-ions. Secondly, the engrafted hematopoietic system does recover after some period of time.

Additional data was obtained by the analysis of 28Si irradiated mice done at 5-7 months after the irradiation. The data analysis shows that there is no statistically significant difference between mice irradiated with 28Si ions versus control mice when assessed for human CD45 blood cell counts in the BM, spleen, and blood. Further, there is no statistically significant difference in the weight of the mice also analyzed at this point. All these results indicate that Si irradiation does not have long-term effect on the human blood cell counts in the hematopoietic compartments and most probably on the overall physiology of the mice.

Depletion-recovery kinetics after Si irradiation has never been measured in neither human blood cells or humanized mice. As such there was a requirement for a reference irradiation to provide context for the physiological significance of the Si irradiation. For this, the investigators studied a parallel cohort of humanized mice subject to 1Gy of 250kVp x-rays. This dose, at the selected energy, is considered a standard reference radiation having relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of 1. The results show, surprisingly, a pronounced effect of the x-ray irradiation in blood cell counts. This effect was specifically significant at day 7 after the irradiation where the WBC cell numbers were reduced 5.5 fold. Again, this effect was primarily B cell losses. The number of B cells recovered slightly at day 30 after the irradiation but decreased again at day 60. All surveyed populations (WBC, T, and B cells) exhibited statistically significant changes relative to pre-irradiated baseline for these time points. As expected, the effect of the x-rays was less pronounced on the T cells. A separate cohort of x-ray irradiated humanized mice and controls was investigated for blood cell counts between six and eight months after irradiation with 1Gy of x-rays. Not surprisingly, the percent human cells in the spleen of the irradiated mice was an average of 14% while the percent of the human cells in the spleen of the control mice was an average of 47%. Interestingly, the T cell/B cell ratio was two times higher in the irradiated mice in comparison with the non-irradiated. These results show that mice can recover from X-ray irradiation, but the human cell population decreases significantly.

Assessment of early and late effects of high LET 28Si ion irradiation on the depletion and recovery kinetics of human hematopoietic stem cells in humanized mice: The array of cell types and relative population proportions of the human hematopoietic system are a function of the activity of the hematopoietic stem cells (HSC). Obviously the effect of radiation on these cells is most significant. To test the effect high-LET radiation on the HSC, investigators obtained HSC counts and their relative abundance as a fraction of the lineage negative population in the BM. The cells they focused on were characterized by the following surface markers: hCD45+, Lin-, CD34+, and CD 38-. The cells that are defined by these markers included the HSC, multipotent progenitors (MPP), and multilymphoid progenitor (MLP) cells. These cell types give rise to the lineage negative progenitors that from their side give rise of the different blood cell lineages. Investigators determined the HSC in the BM of mice irradiated with 0.4 Gy of 350 MeV/n 28Si-ions and control mice at day 7, day 30, day 60 after Si irradiation. They found statistically significant reduction of the HSC between the irradiated and control mice at all the indicated time points. An important question was when (if ever) the difference between irradiated and control mice is reduced to non-significant. To answer to this question, they accessed the HSC population in the BM of Si irradiated and control mice at 5 and 7 months after the irradiations. At this later time, no statistically significant difference between the irradiated and control mice is observed for either endpoint. In addition, there was no statistically significant reduction of human CD45 cells (WBC) in the BM of irradiated and control mice. Overall, these results show that large proportion of the BM HSC are killed by the Si ion irradiation and recover at lower pace. However, the results from the blood depletion and recovery kinetics show that the peripheral blood cells are back to the pre-irradiation counts at day 30 after the irradiation. This means that the HSC in the BM are capable of maintaining the peripheral blood cell counts even if a their counts are reduced. Taken together, these results indicate that the human hematopoietic system is capable of recovery after high-LET radiation, as already shown for low-LET radiation during HSC transplantation of tumor patients. While resilient and capable of regenerating various populations of human blood cells in the host mouse, we do observe depletion of human HSC numbers in vivo in response to high-LET radiation.

The central finding of this study is there were no detectable differences between the Si-irradiated mice and the controls. The human cell counts were statistically similar in the BM, the spleen, and the blood of the irradiated and control mice. The differentiation of both lymphocyte and myeloid lineages was normal. Importantly, no aberrant marker expression was detected. These results in combination with the result from the blood and the HSC cell depletion and recovery kinetics build a very detailed picture of the effect of high LET radiation on developing human HS that investigators believe is first of its kind for a radiation study. They monitored the entire process of hematopoietic cell development from BM to the spleen and blood in the greatest resolution currently achievable. Combined, these results give a basis for the conclusion that the effects of high LET radiation at the studied dose and energy is not detrimental to the human hematopoietic system at least on developmental level. The damage induced initially by the irradiation did not persist in the system of study. Also the lack of tumor development shows that at this energy and dose and time point, high LET radiation is unable to transform human cells in vivo.

No datasets exist for this study, A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Middleware for Exploration Medical System
parameter_html: Medical technologies
investigators: Principal Investigator: Rubin, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The middleware is an intelligent data management and communications software that facilitates the acquisition, integration, management, and distribution of data from on-orbit vehicle medical and environmental devices, sensors, and systems. The software reduces crew time and ensure the accuracy of data collection and timeliness of data delivery.

The objectives of the Middleware were to:

  1. Reduce or eliminate the time required of an on-orbit crew and ground personnel [which include Surgeon, Biomedical Engineer (BME), and Medical Operations Data Specialist] to access, transfer, and manipulate medical data.
  2. Support the integrated demonstration that the on-orbit crew has the ability to access medical data/information via an intuitive and crew-friendly solution to assist/aid in the treatment of a medical condition.
  3. Develop a common data management framework and architecture that can be ubiquitously used to automate repetitive data collection, management, and communications tasks for all crew health and life sciences activities.
  4. Ensure crew access to medical data during periods of reduced or unavailable ground communication.
  5. Develop a common data management framework and architecture that allows for scalability, extensibility, and interoperability of data sources and data users.
  6. Lower total cost of ownership for development and sustainment of peripheral hardware and software that utilize the Middleware for data management.
  7. Provide better crew health via reduction in crew errors, crew time, and ground time.

APPROACH:
The Exploration Medical System was designed to demonstrate the integration of complimentary and disparate pieces of medical informatics software. The Middleware software, as part of the larger Exploration Medical System, has potential training and simulation opportunities for future astronauts and ground personnel. In addition, the Exploration Medical System can serve as software infrastructure for future development and integration of medical devices and software.

RESULTS:
The development, integration, and testing of all EMSD components - electronic medical record, assisted medical procedures software, Middleware infrastructure, and associated Middleware "adapters" were completed.

experiment_title: Etiology and Countermeasure for Back Pain Associated with Microgravity

investigators: Principal Investigator: Hargens, Alan
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this investigation was to compare the effect of spine compression with a harness to the physiologic condition of an upright position on the lumbar spine.

APPROACH:
Twelve men and three women (aged 24.4 ±4.8 yrs, mean±SD) with no prior history of back pain volunteered for the 2-day study. On day 1, the baseline scan of the lumbar spine in a supine subject was obtained followed by a scan after 30 minutes exposure to a compression load of 50% of body weight applied by a harness. On the second day, supine subjects were scanned followed by a scan after 30 minutes in an upright position (kneeling in lieu of standing).

RESULTS:
Both spinal compression with a harness and upright posture increased the anterior disk height and decreased the posterior disk heights. This resulted in a curvature of the spine that was similar after 30 minutes in both loading conditions (14.1±5.3o after harness and 11.5±6.0o after upright posture). Spinal compression with a specially designed harness has the same effect as the physiologic loading of the spine in the kneeling upright position within the first hour after loading when 80% of the changes occur. Further studies will be required to evaluate the effect of the harness in space flight.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

In spaceflights as short as seven days, an 8 to 15 percent reduction in red blood cell mass (RBCM) has been measured in astronauts upon landing. Current theories regarding the regulation of erythropoiesis would require an increased rate of RBC destruction to produce such changes in RBCM. However, data from humans has indicated that RBC survival time is unchanged during space flight. The objectives of this experiment were to evaluate whether the rat is a suitable animal model for researching the mechanism responsible for the RBCM loss observed in humans.

Approach:

Radioactive tracers were administered to animals pre- and post flight. Plasma volume (PV) was measured using 125I-labeled albumin, and 51Cr-labeled donor RBCs were used to measure RBCM and RBC survival. RBCM and PV were measured eight days before launch (L-8), at recovery (R+0) and eight days post flight (R+8). 51Cr RBC survival studies were from L-7 to R+0, and R+1 to R+8. Blood samples fixed with 0.5% glutaraldehyde were coded and the proportion of cells that had echinocytic morphology were determined in a blinded fashion. To study iron kinetics, 59Fe was injected on R+0 and incorporation into RBCs was followed over the next eight days. Serum ferritin levels and 51Cr spleen to liver ratios were determined on R+0 and R+9.

Results:

Since no statistical difference could be attributed to housing conditions, measurements from single- and group-housed animals were combined. No flight related changes were found in hematocrit values number of echinocytes or 51CR spleen to liver ratios. Upon landing, mean RBCM of flight rats was significantly less than controls, both when expressed as absolute volume or volume normalized for body mass. __description:
Objectives:

In spaceflights as short as seven days, an 8 to 15 percent reduction in red blood cell mass (RBCM) has been measured in astronauts upon landing. Current theories regarding the regulation of erythropoiesis would require an increased rate of RBC destruction to produce such changes in RBCM. However, data from humans has indicated that RBC survival time is unchanged during space flight. The objectives of this experiment were to evaluate whether the rat is a suitable animal model for researching the mechanism responsible for the RBCM loss observed in humans.

Approach:

Radioactive tracers were administered to animals pre- and post flight. Plasma volume (PV) was measured using 125I-labeled albumin, and 51Cr-labeled donor RBCs were used to measure RBCM and RBC survival. RBCM and PV were measured eight days before launch (L-8), at recovery (R+0) and eight days post flight (R+8). 51Cr RBC survival studies were from L-7 to R+0, and R+1 to R+8. Blood samples fixed with 0.5% glutaraldehyde were coded and the proportion of cells that had echinocytic morphology were determined in a blinded fashion. To study iron kinetics, 59Fe was injected on R+0 and incorporation into RBCs was followed over the next eight days. Serum ferritin levels and 51Cr spleen to liver ratios were determined on R+0 and R+9.

Results:

Since no statistical difference could be attributed to housing conditions, measurements from single- and group-housed animals were combined. No flight related changes were found in hematocrit values number of echinocytes or 51CR spleen to liver ratios. Upon landing, mean RBCM of flight rats was significantly less than controls, both when expressed as absolute volume or volume normalized for body mass. PV, normalized for body mass, was also significantly decreased at R+0. The 51Cr survival data did not suggest an increased RBC destruction rate as the cause of the decreased RBCM. Instead post-flight decreases in 59Fe incorporation could indicate a decrease in RBC production in response to spaceflight or to decreased food intake and weight gain post flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Crewmembers on the International Space Station (ISS), similar to operators from other industries, complain about using current checklist-like procedures to complete tasks. Issues include procedures having too much or too little detail and poor usability. Due to obstacles, mistakes still occur and time to accomplish procedures is misestimated. NASA crew presently use static paper or electronic “cue cards” and procedures that provide guidance on both nominal and off-nominal tasks. Existing tools may not account for the lack of recent training, be optimized for the task, or the number of users, and/or be resilient to resumption after interruption. A more interactive cognitive aid can overcome the limitations of these cue cards and procedures by matching task, individual, team structure, and environment.

Investigators designed a prototype of a hybrid aid for medical equipment maintenance tasks, while at the same time building a library of tools to create similar aids for other procedures. Second, they developed a taxonomy of cognitive aid design that considers the most important variables affecting performance with aids: user knowledge and experience, time pressure on performance, task criticality, and the number of operators expected to interact with the aid.

APPROACH:
Through a literature review, two controlled experiments, and a validation study, investigators examined the potential attributes of cognitive aids as they interact with task demands, time pressure, and number of team members. All studies were performed using a dual-task/interruption paradigm to better approximate the environments where cognitive aids are likely to be used. The investigators hypothesized that a taxonomy of cognitive aids for non-experts will need to contain a variety of information on aid design for number of operators, highly spatial versus highly verbal sub-tasks, highly visual versus highly auditory sub-tasks, and combinations thereof. A second product to come from these studies was a software program that supports the development of hybrid cognitive aids, the Hybrid Aid Toolkit (HAT). The HAT was developed in iterative design cycles, with portions of it being used to create testable aids in the experiments as features were implemented. Wizard-of-Oz techniques were used to fill in features not yet implemented. HAT development was complete before the validation study and usability data from that study allowed a last iteration before a software release at the end of the project.

RESULTS:
Experiment 1 examined the effects of sensory resource conflict by manipulating which resources were demanded by the task (visual, auditory) and which were demanded by the aid (visual, auditory). The amount of resource conflict did not have as much of an effect as the sensory modality of the aid: the visual cognitive aid outperformed the auditory aid no matter what the modality of the task. A follow-up experiment allowed operators to interact with the aid by speaking, to make interaction with the auditory aid more natural. The results replicated the first experiment with the visual aid supporting the highest performance from operators.

In the second experiment, operators were randomly assigned to use the aid alone or in a team of two. For part of the task, participants performed under time pressure and for part they experienced no time pressure (task sections were counterbalanced). Time pressure adversely affected the accuracy of single operators but not teams. Time to complete the task varied greatly. Dependence on the cognitive aid was high, but did not significantly vary according to the conditions. Participants who scored highly on conscientiousness ratings also scored their team more highly on teamwork ratings. Workload is increased by time pressured environments, even when operators can rely on others and even when a cognitive aid is in place. When designing an emergency aid, minimalistic design should be applied to not overload an already high cognitive load. Aid design should incorporate elements that promote elements of conscientiousness, which will require further research to ascertain.

In the third experiment, an extreme age groups design was utilized to understand the best way to design an aid when spatial resources are low or reduced. Analysis showed age differences in performance, with younger adults making fewer initial errors, fewer changes, and completing the task faster than older adults. Spatial ability was analyzed separately and found to be related to performance measures: those who score better on spatial ability measures were more likely to make fewer errors and complete the task faster.

In each of these experiments, the design of the HAT was iterated resulting in a final prototype used for the validation study with participants from Johnson Space Center. In the validation study, the type of task and aid was manipulated, where the HAT-created cognitive aid was compared to a traditional static aid. Operators performed better when given the HAT-created cognitive aid compared to the static aid on all tasks, however they rated it as less usable. Usability data showed that this was likely because participants perceived the static procedure to be more simple to interact with but that when using it, they were unaware the were committing errors. The results of this validation study established the effectiveness of the interactive cognitive aid and suggested design changes that were later iterated into the software.

The literature review focused on cognitive aid research published in the last twenty years. General findings were that the literature on cognitive aids is vast and split across many domains, with mixed findings regarding aid effectiveness, proper design, and even nomenclature. In this review, we bring together these disparate findings and organize them at their most basic level: which cognitive processes do the aid need to support? Which processes do they support? Such processes included cognitive, perceptual, communication, and higher-order processes. Support of these processes could serve two goals: directly affecting the outcome of the task or indirectly affecting the outcome by making the cognitive aid more effective. This divided research studies on cognitive aids into those which introduced a direct support and those which introduced a usability change to the aid itself, which then affected the outcome of the task. Emergent themes for these articles are discussed, the empirical articles listed for future potential meta-analysis, and gaps in the literature summarized.

Last, the review presented the design-related variables for cognitive aids in a design taxonomy, based on the empirical literature and provide a process for using the taxonomy in planning/designing new cognitive aids. These variables included task criticality, operator experience level, number of operators, and presence or absence of time pressure.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Lackner, James
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
How the neuromotor system controls the reactive forces that arise between moving segments of the arm has been studied for years, because several patient populations, including stroke patients and Parkinson’s patients have been shown to suffer from specific deficits in control of interaction forces among limb segments. Previous studies in a rotating artificial gravity environment opened a new perspective on the issue which was relevant for both astronauts and terrestrial patients. The new finding was that Coriolis forces generated between the arm and torso during every day turning and reaching movements are much larger than interaction forces between arm segments, yet we can adapt to them rapidly and completely.

Investigators developed a turn and reach paradigm to assess post-flight disturbances of arm-trunk coordination. Their recent ground-based work has shown that simultaneous turn and reach movements involve high rotational velocities of the trunk that generate large, potentially disrupting Coriolis forces on the reaching arm and on balance. Nevertheless, reaching accuracy is preserved because the central nervous system programs compensation for the self-generated Coriolis forces. Failure to predict accurately Coriolis force magnitude produces disruption of coordination and potentially loss of balance.

Specific Aims:
1. Parametrically evaluate Coriolis force influences on kinematics and dynamics of voluntary turning and reaching to targets under conditions of normal and increased body weight.
2. Measure reaching movements and postural control after motor adaptation to rearrangement of the relationship between voluntary torso rotation relative to the feet and inertial torso rotation in space.
3. Assess whether motor adaptation to Coriolis force perturbed reaching acquired in a rotating room transfers to turn and reach movements in a natural environment. These experiments will be of value in pinpointing factors contributing to post-flight postural and arm-trunk coordination deficits. They will also have significance for understanding potentially contributing factors in populations at risk for falling.

The overall goal of this project was to study reaching movements made during simultaneous voluntary torso rotations, which investigators call turn and reach movements (T&R). These movements generate Coriolis forces which are large enough to cause substantial reaching errors, but such errors do not occur. Understanding the process of compensation for T&R is tantamount to understanding motor learning in novel force environments.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
The first experiment was motivated to understand the process by which we compensate for Coriolis forces generated on the moving arm by simultaneous voluntary torso rotation. Investigators wanted to distinguish between two alternative mechanisms: either a predictive feed forward muscle activation profile is generated on the basis of an internal estimate of the forthcoming combination of torso angular velocity relative to space or arm linear velocity relative to the torso, or reactive feedback compensation is produced due to spinal stretch reflexes and vestibulospinal reflexes. The experimental rationale was to distort motor control of torso rotary movements and then measure whether arm movements would consequently be distorted. If arm movements were normal then accurate feedback about the abnormal torso rotation would have to be considered responsible for correcting it, but if the arm movements showed directional then an improper feed forward compensation based on planned but erroneously executed torso rotation would be the most likely mechanism. The investigators altered motor control of torso rotation movements by having subjects swivel their torso while standing on a platform programmed to swivel at a proportion of the angular speed of their torso (relative to their feet). If the floor turned in the same direction as their torso, it created a situation where the motion of the torso relative to space was larger than the angular rotation of the torso relative to the feet. Inertial motion governs the torque required to move, so in this situation subjects had to learn to increase their foot-to-torso rotary torques in order to achieve a constant rotary excursion of their torso relative to the feet. This was done in darkness, and subjects did not detect that their inertial motion had changed. After many leftward torso movements (without moving the arms) during progressively larger leftward floor rotations, investigators stopped the floor and had subjects make either additional torso movements without arm movements, arm movements without torso movements, or T&R movements. The post-adaptation spatial extent and speed of torso movements were amplified relative to baseline movements. After adaptive potentiation of leftward torso rotation the finger velocity relative to the torso was the same as pre-adaptation, so the rightward Coriolis force was increased. During post-adaptive T&R movements, there was a radial deviation of the arm final position and peak velocity relative to the torso, rightward of the pre-adaptation baseline. Arm movements made without torso rotation did not differ before and after adaptive recalibration of torso movements. The arm deviations seen in the T&R movements indicate subjects had pre-programmed their reaches to compensate for the rightward Coriolis force that would be present if they physically turned leftward the amount they intended rather than the actual larger amount.

The second set of experiments investigators completed evaluated the effects of the background force environment and of hefted loads on compensation for Coriolis forces in T&R movements. One experiment examined T&R movements under conditions of normal, decreased and increased body weight, in parabolic flight. The experimental results demonstrate that under 1g conditions subjects when turning and reaching for a target are very accurate, regardless whether they reach slow or fast, or without visual feedback. Normal subjects show temporally overlapping arm and torso velocities, with the peak velocities occurring virtually simultaneously. As a consequence, very large Coriolis forces are generated on the reaching arm; nevertheless these forces do not disrupt movement accuracy. By contrast, reaching movements during passive body rotation have large trajectory deviations and endpoint errors. These results confirm that in natural turn and reach movements there is an anticipatory feed forward compensation for the impending Coriolis force which maintains straight and accurate reaches in external space coordinates. Subjects exposed to 0 g (feet anchored to the floor) and 1.8g force levels in parabolic flight initially exhibit disruptions of movement paths and endpoints. Within 40-50 turn and reach movements they achieve a great deal of compensation. This indicates that the T&R paradigm is useful for evaluating whole body performance in non-1g environments and for pre-adapting subjects who are about to undergo force transitions (e.g., re-entry to Earth gravity, transition from weightlessness to artificial gravity).

Another experiment explored the effects of hefted loads on T&R movements. Subjects made T&R movements while grasping objects weighing 500g or 1000g. In addition to providing a static vertical load, the objects increased the dynamic Coriolis force which needed to be compensated during the T&R movements. Investigators found the compensation was optimal under both loads conditions as well as in unloaded conditions. This was true when subjects used their preferred or non-preferred hand. The results indicate the humans can generate automatic compensations for impending Coriolis forces based on estimates of their own body dynamics and the dynamics of a hefted object.
