experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study is to develop an inflight treadmill training protocol that enhances adaptive generalization of locomotor function to facilitate rapid and robust recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight. Specifically, the investigator hopes to determine whether subjects exposed to a special inflight treadmill protocol will have greater proficiency in reassembling an appropriate, full-body postflight locomotor response. Will they recover locomotor function sooner than subjects not exposed to the inflight treadmill protocol? Data from this experiment are planned to be used to develop a countermeasure system.

APPROACH:
Locomotor function were assessed before and after space flight using two tests of gait function.

Test 1: The Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test characterizes alterations in the integrated function of multiple sensorimotor subsystems. This test required subjects to walk on a motorized treadmill while researchers assessed changes in dynamic postural stability, head-trunk coordination, visual acuity and lower limb coordination strategies.

Subjects walked at 6.4 km/h on a motorized treadmill while performing a visual task consisting of identifying the position of the gap in the letter "C" that is presented centrally on a laptop computer positioned 4 meters in front at eye level. Each trial lasted approximately 30 seconds and was repeated four times. Subjects also walked at 6.4 km/h on the treadmill while performing the same visual task described above, but in this case, with the letter "C" presented centrally on a micro-display positioned 50 centimeters in front at eye level. Each of these trials lasted approximately 30 seconds and were repeated four times. While subjects were walking on the treadmill and performing the visual task, 3-dimensional full-body motion data were acquired using a video-based motion analysis system; gait cycle timing was measured using foot switches placed in the shoes and dynamic visual acuity was assessed by the visual task described above.

Test 2: The Functional Mobility Test provides a corresponding assessment of the functional and operational changes in locomotor function by testing a subject's ability to negotiate an obstacle course placed over a medium-density foam floor. Subjects walked at a preferred pace through an obstacle course set up on a base of 10 cm thick medium density foam. The foam provided an unstable surface that increases the challenge of the test. The 6.0 m x 4.0 m course consists of several pylons and obstacles made of foam. Subjects were instructed to walk through the course as fast as possible without touching any of the objects on the course. experiment_title: Evaluation of the Space Therapeutics Assessment Recorder (STARx) and the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) on the Palm PDA Platform:  A Device for Real-Time Monitoring of Drug Effectiveness
parameter_html:
Drug effectiveness
Medication consumption
investigators: Principal Investigator: Putcha, Lakshmi
image_name: Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES)
Clayton Anderson Performs ARES Test for STARx Experiment
experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the STARx study performed during the NEEMO missions was three-fold. First, the relative efficacies of medications taken by each NEEMO 4 and 5 crewmember were evaluated. Second, the effect of medications on NEEMO 5 crewmembers' neuro-cognitive performance was evaluated. The third objective was to evaluate the functionality of the device used to collect drug effectiveness and neuro-cognitive data during both NEEMO 4 and 5 missions.

APPROACH:
A hand-held Palm Personal Data Assistant (PDA) preloaded with both the Space Therapeutics Assessment Recorder (STARx) application and the ANAM (Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) was provided to each crewmember.

The STARx software application allowed crewmembers to record drug effectiveness data in real time using a severity of symptoms scale specific for each class of medications, as well as information about the clinical status. Each time a crewmember took a medication, they entered that information into the Palm PDA. The crewmember then decided when to be notified by the PDA to enter in data regarding the drug’s effectiveness. At the specified time, an alarm sounded on the PDA, and the crewmember entered in the requested data. In addition to the effectiveness data, crewmembers completed a sleepiness score loaded as part of the STARx application, which recorded the ability of medications to induce drowsiness. Any additional information was entered as notes using the "Memo Pad" application also loaded on the Palm PDA.

The ARES software application consisted of two short-term memory tests known as the Match to Sample (MTS) and Continuous Processing Task (CPT) for neuro-cognitive analysis. The crew completed the ARES test two times a day, once in the morning and once before retiring to bed.

RESULTS:
The STARx software application was not used during the mission due to the fact that no medications were taken during the 14-day NEEMO 5 mission.

All four NEEMO 5 aquanauts completed the pre-mission training sessions and daily ARES data collection during the 14-day mission. A total of 26 sessions were completed in the Aquarius habitat. However, changes in cognitive performance could not be correlated with medication use, because no medications were taken.

A comparison between early morning and late evening ARES scores was performed with the following results:

  1. Evening MTS response times were 10 to 22% less than morning response times. The decrease in two of the four aquanauts was statistically significant (p<0.01).
  2. Evening CPT response times were 2 to 8% less than morning response times. The decrease in one of the four aquanauts was statistically significant (p<0.05).
  3. Aquanaut accuracy scores during all test sessions for the MTS and CPT tests were very high regardless of morning or evening conditions, i.e., greater than 80% and 88%, respectively.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The addition of automation has greatly extended humans’ capability to accomplish tasks, including difficult, complex and safety critical tasks. The majority of Human - Automation Interaction (HAI) results in more efficient and safe operations; however, certain unexpected automation behaviours, or “automation surprises” can be frustrating and, in certain safety critical operations (e.g. transportation, spaceflight, medicine), may result in injuries or the loss of life.

The next generation of space exploration systems will place an increased reliance on automation. Traditional techniques for the design and evaluation of automation interfaces rely on subject-matter-experts, human-in-the-loop testing (i.e. usability testing), guidelines, heuristics and rules-of-thumb. Given the volume and time-line for the development of new automation required for space exploration, the time and cost required to perform these evaluations by human factor experts will be prohibitive. Further, guidelines, heuristics, and rule-of-thumb have previously yielded sub-optimum designs (as they are focused on the interface, not on the process of interaction between human and automation interface. State of the art cognitive science and Human-Automation Interaction (HAI) approaches may provide the type of analysis needed, but are not currently usable by designers without extensive cognitive science expertise.

The automation design community needs methods that are usable by designers early in the design process to meet the demands for the development and testing of automation required for space exploration. The objective of this research project is to develop a set of methodologies and tools to support the design and evaluation efficient, and robust interaction with automation. The research plan is to integrate existing foundational research results into HAI methods and tools usable by designers.

APPROACH:
This work is divided into three areas, with the ultimate goal of developing a suite of tools to support each area. It is important to note that the idea of the project is to develop and evaluate the tools in actual design processes, and the level and type of support and evaluation will be dependent upon the scope and maturity of each design domain. The three areas are organized around an abstraction of the primary focii of the design process.

Analyze: The first set of methods and tools are intended to help designers to identify, describe and evaluate the different parts of the job. Depending on the stage of the design process, these methods are referred to as work domain analyses, task decompositions, task analyses, knowledge elicitation, and in the later stages, validation.

Formulate: The second set of methods and tools is intended to bridge the gap from the analysis of the work domain. Specifically, once the structure of the work domain and tasks has been determined, methods and tools are needed to link the task structures to corresponding interface structures that can later be refined and evaluated. We will be drawing upon research from a number of different communities for this effort including ecological interface design and design patterns.

Build: This set of methods and tools are intended to enable rapid development and evaluation of automation, including the user-interface and the underlying automation behavior. The specific focus of this effort is to develop methods and tools that are usable by designers who are expert in the design domain, but aren’t necessarily formally trained in computer programming, or human performance analysis. We will primarily be using research in formal methods to help support the Build effort.

RESULTS:
The outcomes of this research will be methods and tools for the automation of the design and evaluation of the automation interfaces. These tools will provide the means to: (i)meet the demand for analysis required for space exploration development time-line, (ii)enable increased iterative human factors testing of automation prototypes early in the design process (ii) reduce the cost of development by design and testing of proposed systems early in the development life-cycle (iii) reduce the cost of training and the maintenance of proficiency (iv)improve safety (and reduce the costs of inefficiency and unsafe operations) through significant reduction in failure to complete task metrics.

This research makes contributions at two levels. At one level, the problems of interaction between humans and computers/automation in a particular application domain was addressed. The domain of application was the planning work done by Attitude Determination and Control Officers (ADCO), part of Mission Control for the International Space Station (ISS). At a second, higher level, it was abstracted from this case to suggest a more general method for needs analysis and this was the primary motivation for this research. A brief summary on the ADCO domain follows, before describing the methods and tools that emerged from working on this case.

A core aspect of this research was a detailed study of the planning work done by ADCO and identification of the work needs that should be supported by software. As the analysis was carried out of the ADCO planning domain, the characterization of the problem was changed. It was realized that rather than focusing on the current tasks and practices, as in Task Analysis, the needs future software should meet were identified. One result of this work was support for ADCO by providing an analysis of ADCO needs. An illustrative prototype designed to better fit these needs was developed. An experimental study of this prototype, comparing performance to that with the legacy system was conducted. These products are of value to ADCO operators seeking the design of software that is more effective than their current legacy systems. The second, more general result was development of methods and tools for carrying out such analyses. The ADCO domain was used to develop Structure Identification, our approach to needs analysis. Structure Identification was developed to be particularly appropriate for rapid identification of needs for safety critical, technical, information work. Needs analysis based on Structure Identification finds the high-level structure in the work domain and uses this to design the structure of the interaction between the human and computer or automation. A combination of eliciting function information from expert users, identifying candidate structure from documents and functional descriptions, and vetting the developing characterization with experts was relied on.

Structure Identification contrasts with conducting needs analysis based on Task Analysis; task analysis identifies current tasks, yet a change in the work applications naturally brings with it change in the tasks so that matching the old tasks is not a reliable design guide. Task Analysis can be a helpful approach to identifying structure, but we prioritize identifying the domain structure not the activities. This approach is related to both Work Domain Analysis (WDA) and Contextual Inquiry (CI), in that these also seek to identify stable aspects of work in order to guide design. WDA focuses on identifying constraints, particularly constraints in how a physical system, such as a chemical plant, operates; it is directly applicable to control tasks, but much less applicable to work consisting of finding, transforming, building, and distributing information products. CI methods focus on observing users, typically carrying out office work; this approach is less adequate in highly technical domains where critical aspects of work cannot be understood from watching users.

The goal was to make needs analysis more efficient and effective. To this end the methods that were developed focused on gathering important information quickly. We consolidated what we learned to make the methods easier to reuse and to apply to another case, by building simple tools as we carried out the needs analysis for the ADCO planning domain and developed the SI approach. These include templates for gathering high-level function information from experts, templates for presenting the identified structure to experts for verification, and templates for comparing the contents of multiple product documents.

An additional contribution of the research was a preliminary assessment of Structure Identification. Broadly, whether Structure Identification, followed by Structure Matching from the domain to an application structure, contributes to better design of the application was investigated. An illustrative study using the ADCO planning domain was conducted. The domain structure was used to guide the design of an experimental prototype for ADCO planning. An experiment was conducted comparing the experimental prototype, which closely matched the domain structure, versus the legacy system, which matched much more poorly. A variety of measures were included, from speed of performance to conceptual understanding and retention of periods of disuse. Differences in performance on a variety of planning tasks that are detailed analogs of simple ADCO planning tasks were predicted: overall faster performance by users of the new, well-matched system compared to that by users of the legacy, poorly-matching system; and particular performance advantage for the new system at points where the legacy system most mismatched domain structure. It was found that performance times were cut in half for the new prototype vs legacy system on some tasks, accompanied by much lower error rates as well. Further, it was also found the predicted pattern of poor performance at legacy points of mismatch.

The whole design cycle was run through, from needs analysis through evaluation, in the ADCO domain. This process provided an illustrative case showing the feasibility of this approach. The results from this experiment suggest that capturing and matching domain structure may be an efficient, productive way to guide design of interaction between humans and computers/automation for technical information work.

experiment_title: Photographic Documentation of Body Fluid Shift
parameter_html: Fluid shifts
investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The known large shifts of fluid from lower to upper body assumed a fresh importance through the possibility that the central nervous system (CNS) or inner ear pressures might be altered and contribute to or even cause space motion sickness (SMS). There is currently no satisfactory way to measure shifts to the head and there is always a need for simpler procedures for other areas. The objective of this experiment was to gather data on the course and amount of fluid lost from the legs and gained by the head region to assess the role of fluid shift in SMS.

APPROACH:
A background grid with a standard STS 35mm Nikon camera, interior film, and flash were set up at known distances and angles and the subject placed his heel in a fixture at a known position. experiment_title: Dose-Rate Effects and Components of Systems Governing Variations in Susceptibility for Carcinogenic and Acute Radiation Risks following Gamma-Ray, Proton, or HZE Irradiation
parameter_html:

Chromosome aberrations
Radiation dose
Radiation dose rate

investigators: Principal Investigator: Bedford, JoelCo-Investigator: Nagasawa, HatsumiCo-Investigator: Peng, YuanlinCo-Investigator: Weil, Michael
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The central hypothesis is that dose-rate effects in the 1 to 0.005 Gy/min range will be the same for protons vs. gamma-rays for chromosomal aberration induction. Second, levels of chromosomal radiosensitivity, and their dose-rate dependence will be similar for cells from individuals with genetic differences in radiosensitivity. Such a biomarker may help identify differences among individuals in a component contributing to their susceptibility to these effects.

APPROACH:
The approach for this investigation is unavailable.

RESULTS:
For low passage normal human fibroblasts and for MCF10A human mammary epithelial cells, the dose rate effect for induction of chromosomal aberrations seen for gamma-rays in the range of 70cGy/min (HDR) to 0.005cGy/min (LDR) was virtually identical for protons with energies of 1000MeV or 50MeV and corresponded to a dose rate reduction factor(DREF) of about 2.0 for all these radiations. There was a smaller, but still a significant dose rate effect for 1GeV/n Fe ions corresponding to a DREF of about 1.3 despite the fact that the LET for the Fe ions was approximately 150 keV/micrometer. For the MCF10A cells, the responses (aberration induction, cell killing and gamma H2AX formation at low dose rates) in 2D or 3D culture were identical. Indistinguishable dose rate effects were also seen for ATM +/- cells compared to ATM +/+ cells with the two cell strains that were derived from individuals who were siblings from the same family.

experiment_title: Long-Term Effect of Space Radiation on Cardiomyocyte Turnover
parameter_html:
Cardiomyocytes
DNA damage response
Radiation exposure
DNA double strand breaks (DSBs)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Sadek, HeshamCo-Investigator: Asaithamby, Aroumougame
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The risks to astronauts from exposure to space radiation have long been of great concern to NASA. These risks are now more important with the advent of long-duration space missions, which raise the risk of exposure to space radiation. While the effect of space radiation on the incidence of cancer and coronary artery disease has been studied, little is known about the effect of space radiation on the heart muscle, in particular on the ability of the heart muscle to replenish itself. The adult heart is incapable of regenerating itself after injury because the vast majority of heart muscle cells cannot divide. Nevertheless, the adult human heart slowly replenishes one to two percent of its muscle every year, and it is estimated that in a human heart close to 50 percent of the heart muscle is renewed during its lifespan. Therefore, preventing the formation of new heart muscle cells could result in a loss of up to 50 percent of heart muscle leading to heart failure.

Investigators recently discovered that after birth, the increase in oxygen in the atmosphere results in formation of harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS), which in turn damage the DNA of heart muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) and cause them to stop dividing. However, a small population of dividing heart muscle cells is protected from DNA damage by maintaining themselves in a low oxygen environment within the heart. If prolonged exposure to space radiation damages the DNA of these cells, then the heart will lose any ability to replenish itself. The long-term goal of this study was to develop countermeasures to reduce heart failure risk in astronauts due to space radiation exposure.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Characterize the effect of space radiation on oxidative DNA damage in cardiomyocytes.
  2. Determine the effect of space radiation on cardiomyocyte turnover in the adult heart.

APPROACH:
Using echocardiography to verify the effect of space radiation on cardiac function, investigators exposed a group of 9-12 middle aged (6 months old) mice to both acute (1 Gy) and fractionated (0.2 Gy per day for five consecutive days) doses of 600 MeV/n iron particles. Afterwards, left ventricular systolic function was determined via echocardiography on conscious mice. Ejection fraction and fractional shortening was calculated based on end diastolic and end systolic dimensions obtained from M-mode ultrasound. Echocardiography was performed at multiple time points after each type of radiation exposure - three months and one year after exposure.

RESULTS:
Investigators found that iron particles-induced complex double-strand breaks (DSBs) are irreparable in cardiomyocytes and that iron particles trigger cardiac hypertrophy in mice. In addition, both fractionated (20 cGy X 5) and acute (100 cGy) doses of 600 MeV/n iron particles significantly increase the ejection fraction of mouse heart approximately one year after the iron particle irradiation.

No datasets are available. A final report was archived.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Gernhardt, MichaelCo-Investigator: Acock, KeenaCo-Investigator: Conkin, JohnnyCo-Investigator: Hamilton, Douglas
experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this project was to perform an operational evaluation of an in-suit Doppler (ISD). The effectiveness of the written procedures, hardware, and human interface of the in-suit Doppler device were assessed. This study was important because it addressed a risk and critical question involving the prevention and treatment of decompression sickness.

APPROACH:
Crewmembers received two 1-hour training sessions prior to the mission. These sessions focused on the Doppler hardware: donning the device, obtaining a good signal, and recording the data. A separate 2-hour training session was held for the subjects outlining the use of the software for data transfer.

While on Aquarius, subjects took Doppler readings after each dive to monitor nitrogen bubbles in the blood stream. These recordings began as soon as possible upon returning from a dive (within 30 minutes). Placement of the Doppler and initiation of data recording took approximately 15 minutes. The device was then worn for 2-4 hours, as time and activities allowed. The data was stored in an attached solid-state memory device, which left the subjects free to move about the habitat and engage in other activities. At the end of the designated interval, the subject removed the hardware and downloaded the data. After the data were transferred, the subject selected several sample (.wav) files to e-mail to the surface for analysis.

The data collected included Doppler recordings taken during an increment of every minute. In addition to the Doppler data, recordings of the subject's activity (collected as part of a separate objective) via an Actiwatch® were also used.

Doppler readings were also taken after decompression from saturation upon arrival at the shore base, 20-24 hours after decompression, and 44-48 hours after decompression in four-hour increments.

RESULTS:

Evaluation of Doppler Data:

Approximately 150 digital wave files were recorded as part of each post dive Doppler record. Each wave file represents 24 sec of recording in a total 73 sec period; therefore, 49 sec are when the ISD is off. Each wave file was assigned a Doppler Quality Score (DQS) and evaluated for unusual Doppler Events (DEs). Doppler Events are sounds that could be attributed to the presence of a moving gas phase (bubbles) within the sampling envelope of the Doppler sensor.

The Doppler Quality Score (DQS) reflects the recorded quality of the pulmonary artery (venous blood) blood flow, termed the right ventricular outflow tract. A quality blood flow signal is about the potential to hear bubbles, so is based only on the quality of the venous blood flow sound through the pulmonary artery. The blood flow "swish-swish" sounds are good sounds in which to hear bubbles followed by the pulmonary valve "whip" sounds. The heartbeat is not a good sound in which to hear bubbles.

The design of the hands-off Doppler sensor means that all of the sounds described above will likely appear on the recordings. The score is developed based on a perfect ideal flow sound given a perfect Doppler and a perfect placement by a trained technician. It is more important in our space application to have high confidence that we are not hearing bubbles since the negative predictive value is about 98% while the positive predictive value given Grade IV venous gas emboli (VGE) is only about 50%. If a superior recording to determine if bubbles are present is available, then one can guarantee that no bubbles are present, and have the confidence to grade the bubbles.

Four categories and definitions were used to assess the quality of the Doppler ultrasound bubble detectors, both within one subject over multiple monitoring periods and between multiple subjects over multiple monitoring periods. See datasets for this information.

The standard operating procedure was to dive in buddy pairs and conduct two dives per day. The buddy pairs were not always the same, and all four divers would normally dive at once, and dive twice a day. There were 62 dives conducted over the 12-day mission, but no diving was done on Mission Day 7. Thirty-nine of the dives were the first dive of the day with 23 dives as the second dive of the day. The mean maximum depth in meters below the surface was 23 msw + 3.8 msw SD, n = 62, with a range from 18.3 msw to 28.9 msw. The mean dive time was 169.6 min + 66.8 min SD, n = 62, with a range from 48 min to 333 min. Only 32 of the 62 dives had post-dive Doppler measurements collected.

The post-mission monitoring was performed with a Techno Scientific Model DBM9008 Ultrasound Bubble Detector to verify that no VGE were present after the decompression from saturation conditions. No VGE were detected.

Doppler Quality Scores:

DQS varied between data recording sessions and between subjects. DQS also varied throughout a single data session (not shown) possibly due to the subject's body position or the subject being less active during portions of the data session. The subjects received equal amounts of training and were trained together. It is reasonable to conclude that the within and between-subject variability is not attributable to training.

Two divers were better able to find and maintain a quality Doppler flow signal (DQS 3 or 4) compared to the other two divers. Our observation in training was that these two groups of subjects had significantly different chest anatomies. The group with the high percentage of poor quality signal had chests with more muscle mass, requiring considerable pressure to obtain a quality signal. It is difficult to apply the necessary pressure with the current ISD adhesive design. Thus, a conclusion that explains the data is that the quality of the Doppler flow signal is greatly influenced by the chest anatomy. Matching the current ISD with the person that can provide a quality flow signal is a better approach than simply assigning an ISD to anyone willing to use it during an EVA.

Doppler Events:

Only 50 of 4,893 total useful wave files (1%) contained DEs. The majority of DEs were detected in the two subjects with more quality DQS (DQS 3 and 4). However, most DEs (22 of 50) were detected in wave files with the poorest DQS (DQS 1). There were 11 DEs with a DQS 2, 16 DEs with DQS 3, and 1 DE with DQS 4. It is interesting that even the poorest quality signal is capable of detecting DEs, and more frequent in those subjects that clearly had a better signal overall. This may be due to a better transducer placement and/or a more accommodating chest anatomy, as confirmed in an adjunct study described later in this report.

Doppler Events versus Venous Gas Emboli:

The time distribution of DE after an excursion dive and through the multi-day mission was not inconsistent with what would have been expected for VGE. The sound and onset characteristics of the DEs were very different than observed in previous decompression tests. Transient showers of gas phase were observed intermittently during the monitoring periods, and there was no pattern of sustained VGE with time or increase in VGE quantity.

The signal has the same character in all 50 examples, and just varies in intensity in a few cases. We would expect the signal from VGE to be rich in high and low frequencies indicating different size bubbles traveling at different rates as they are propelled toward the lungs in synchrony with the heart rate.

These atypical results drove a closer review of the data to other possible sources of the DEs. An adjunct study was conducted on two subjects (1 male, 1 female), collecting data with the ISD while drinking and eating varying quantities of liquid and food at varying intervals. Optimum and non-optimum Doppler signals were evaluated for liquid detection. Liquid intake (presumably with entrained air) produced sounds identical to the DEs in both of the subjects, using an optimum signal. DE were occasionally detected with the transducer in a non-optimum position, but were not detected most of the time. DEs were not detected with food intake in either subject.

Correlation of DE with Liquid Intake: During the NEEMO mission the aquanauts also participated in a nutritional assessment study, which involved bar code inputs of all food and liquids at the time of consumption. These records were reviewed and correlated with the DEs. Twelve of the 32 data sessions were missing blocks of wave files and/or some log on/off times were not consistent with the number of wave files, making it impossible to calculate the time with any measure of certainty. The times for the DEs that occurred during the other 20 data sessions could be calculated using the wave file number, Mission Elapsed Time, and the logs giving on/off times for the ISD. The results from data showing the % DE correlated with liquid intake combined with the qualitatively identical sounds produced in the adjunct study using the ISD, suggested that the DEs were air entrainment associated with liquid intake. This observation had not been made in previous studies because continuous Doppler monitoring was not performed over a multi-hour period. The normal Doppler monitoring period was generally less than five minutes, with the subjects neither drinking nor eating since they were at altitude and wearing an oxygen mask.

In-Suit Doppler (ISD) Questionnaire

The subjects were asked to complete a questionnaire after the mission. Questions were asked on operational and human factors such as the acceptability of set up time, transducer placement procedures, transducer adhesive design, ISD software, and download operations. All subjects wrote that the training, procedures, and set up time were adequate.

Most recommendations concerned the transducer adhesive and the downloading process. One subject experienced severe skin irritation and the other subjects had minor problems. We believe shaving prior to the application precipitated the severe reaction, made worse by repeated applications of adhesive tape. The NEEMO mission required daily applications of the adhesive, while a Shuttle or ISS mission would not. One subject recommended a transducer that would disconnect from the rest of the Doppler modules, thereby requiring only one application of the adhesive tapes.

There were multiple comments about the downloading operations. The ISD software is not compatible with the more recent operating systems, and requires Windows 95. This was an inconvenience. The time and battery power required for downloading caused significant problems. This issue requires extensive evaluation before use in a space flight scenario.

experiment_title: Novel Microstructures for Vascular Tissue Engineering
parameter_html:
Endothelial cell response
Vascular smooth muscle
investigators: Principal Investigator: Wong, Joyce
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this research project was to tissue-engineer small diameter blood vessel substitutes. Such tissue-engineered blood vessels can also serve as tissue models for studying the effects of microgravity environmental changes on tissue adaptation and to assess potential therapeutic strategies. Requirements for a blood vessel substitute include sufficient burst pressure, viscoelastic mechanical properties, vasoactivity, and nonthrombogenicity. Native blood vessels have evolved a sophisticated structure and hierarchical organization of cell types and matrix molecules in order to satisfy these requirements.

The central hypothesis is that the physiological spatial arrangement of cells and extracellular matrix in an engineered blood vessel will affect the viscoelastic mechanical properties, which in turn, will affect vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cell response. This hypothesis will be tested by answering questions directly posed in Specific Aims 1 and 2 in which the effects of two main biomaterial scaffold properties on tissue function will be explored: (1) microstructure and (2) mechanics.

APPROACH:
The strategy of fabricating novel scaffolds with defined microstructure and mechanical properties will help to reveal the effects of specific ultrastructural and mechanical factors on cell response and tissue development. Investigators used this approach to develop a new generation of biomaterials for vascular tissue engineering that will provide an in vitro model tissue in which parameters can be varied systematically to investigate cell mechanics, tissue development, cell-substrate and cell-cell interactions in controlled microgravity environments in order to attain a better understanding of effects of microgravity on human physiology. Furthermore, the investigators recognize that these tissues may also be used as potential blood vessel replacements that are in high demand and are an integral part of more complex organs and tissues.

RESULTS:
Investigators have made significant progress in investigating the role of microstructure on vascular smooth muscle cells, specifically studying the role of substrate microtopography combined with mechanical cyclic strain on cell orientation. They also developed novel methodologies to self-assemble biomacromolecules such as collagen that are critical components of blood vessels. __description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this research project was to tissue-engineer small diameter blood vessel substitutes. Such tissue-engineered blood vessels can also serve as tissue models for studying the effects of microgravity environmental changes on tissue adaptation and to assess potential therapeutic strategies. Requirements for a blood vessel substitute include sufficient burst pressure, viscoelastic mechanical properties, vasoactivity, and nonthrombogenicity. Native blood vessels have evolved a sophisticated structure and hierarchical organization of cell types and matrix molecules in order to satisfy these requirements.

The central hypothesis is that the physiological spatial arrangement of cells and extracellular matrix in an engineered blood vessel will affect the viscoelastic mechanical properties, which in turn, will affect vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cell response. This hypothesis will be tested by answering questions directly posed in Specific Aims 1 and 2 in which the effects of two main biomaterial scaffold properties on tissue function will be explored: (1) microstructure and (2) mechanics.

APPROACH:
The strategy of fabricating novel scaffolds with defined microstructure and mechanical properties will help to reveal the effects of specific ultrastructural and mechanical factors on cell response and tissue development. Investigators used this approach to develop a new generation of biomaterials for vascular tissue engineering that will provide an in vitro model tissue in which parameters can be varied systematically to investigate cell mechanics, tissue development, cell-substrate and cell-cell interactions in controlled microgravity environments in order to attain a better understanding of effects of microgravity on human physiology. Furthermore, the investigators recognize that these tissues may also be used as potential blood vessel replacements that are in high demand and are an integral part of more complex organs and tissues.

RESULTS:
Investigators have made significant progress in investigating the role of microstructure on vascular smooth muscle cells, specifically studying the role of substrate microtopography combined with mechanical cyclic strain on cell orientation. They also developed novel methodologies to self-assemble biomacromolecules such as collagen that are critical components of blood vessels. They also showed that they could stack several layers of microtopographically patterned thin scaffold films and keep the cells viable in this configuration, a critical step in forming the blood vessels.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The success of a human space flight critically depends on the interaction between the crewmembers and the mission controllers. The ability of both the crew and the controllers to be alert and to maintain high levels of cognitive function while operating and/or monitoring complex, technical equipment is essential. Optimal human health, performance and safety during space flight operations requires sufficient sleep and synchrony between the circadian pacemaker—which regulates the timing of sleep, endocrine function, alertness and performance—and the timing of the imposed sleep-wake schedule.

Flight mission controllers often work extended duration shifts, rotating shifts, including night shifts. Such schedules instigate significant acute and chronic sleep deprivation and consequently fatigue. Although the effects are often unrecognized, both the acute and chronic lack of sleep substantially degrades a federal air marshal’s ability to react and think quickly, to make good decisions, and to recognize when fatigue is impairing his or her own performance and safety. Further, both acute and chronic sleep deprivation adversely affects personal health, increasing the risk of gastrointestinal and heart disease, impairing glucose metabolism and immune function, and substantially increasing the risk of injury due to motor vehicle crashes. In addition, it is likely that a significant proportion of mission controllers suffer from undiagnosed sleep disorders which will further impair their sleep and exacerbate fatigue. The deleterious effects of fatigue are readily observed in a wide range of safety-sensitive professions, including law enforcement officers, and include increased risk of self-injury, higher rates of fatigue-related motor vehicle accidents, and greater incidence of serious errors.

The investigators implemented a Fatigue Risk Management Program (FRMP) for the flight controllers. The goals of this program were to reduce the adverse consequences of fatigue on the flight controllers’ alertness, performance, health, and safety. The objectives of the program were to: 1) Evaluate the current flight controller schedules; 2) Develop an online education training program; 3) Offer an efficient online screening for common sleep disorders; and 4) Evaluate the acceptability, feasibility and efficacy of a combined fatigue countermeasure including shorter-wavelength light exposure during operational night shifts.

APPROACH:
Investigators enrolled 17 flight controllers and three flight directors selected from the seven International Space Station (ISS) mission control consoles regularly staffed for Orbit 1 operations (Flight, OPS Planning, ADCO, SPARTAN, ETHOS, CRONUS, Ground Control). Data were collected during one off-console week and each controller was scheduled to work two blocks (4-7 days each) of Orbit 1 shifts during the study. They randomized each block to either the control or experimental condition. During the experimental condition, controllers were encouraged to visit the Experimental Break Room (EBR) once before the shift, twice during the shift, as operations allowed, and following the Orbit 1 shift. The EBR provided subjects with passive exposure to blue-enriched fluorescent lamps installed in existing ceiling fixtures. In addition, subjects were encouraged to exercise on treadmills or stationary bikes located in the room (10 minute bouts, not to exceed more than 65% maximum heart rate). The controllers were instructed to continue their normal routines during the control block.

The controllers completed Visual Analog Scales and a 5-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Task before, twice during, and following each Orbit1 shift. They also wore actigraphs to monitor sleep and completed daily work/sleep logs. All subjects completed drive diaries following each commute and a subset of the subjects wore Optalert drowsiness monitoring glasses on commutes to and from work to objectively monitor fatigue. A mixed model with repeated measures was used to compare data between the control and experimental Orbit 1 shifts.

RESULTS:
The fatigue countermeasure proved feasible and acceptable as controllers reported taking 2.9 breaks per experimental shift and 90% of prescribed exercise sessions were completed. Flight controllers reported being significantly more alert and happy and had faster response times during Orbit 1 shifts with access to the EBR as compared to control Orbit 1 shifts.

experiment_title: Individual Genetic Susceptibility
parameter_html:
Rad9 gene
ATM gene
BRCA1 gene
BRCA2 gene
investigators: Principal Investigator: Hall, EricCo-Investigator: Brenner, DavidCo-Investigator: Smilenov, Lubomir
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The hypothesis upon which this study is based is that the human population is not homogeneous in radiosensitivity, but that radiosensitive sub-groups exist which would suffer an increased incidence of detrimental radiation effects, and distort the shape of the dose response relationship. The radiosensitivity of these groups depends on the expression levels of specific proteins. In a previous proposal funded by NASA the investigators used knock-out mice to show unequivocally that haploinsufficiency for the ATM gene resulted in increased sensitivity to gamma-rays for both ocular cataracts (a deterministic effect) and oncogenic transformation in embryo fibroblasts (a stochastic effect).

It would be extraordinarily difficult and expensive to conduct similar experiments with the high energy Fe-59 ions of principal interest to NASA, because of the need to breed a large number of animals, all of the appropriate age, to be available on the few occasions each year when Fe-59 ions are available at the Brookhaven Laboratory. It would be even more difficult and expensive to expand the study to include a number of other genes that are suspected of being involved with radiosensitivity, and to investigate the possible interaction of these various genes.

The investigators instead chose to screen cells heterozygous for a number of genes; ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2 and Rad9, as well as double heterozygotes for pairs of these genes. Wild type animals as well as heterozygotes and double heterozygotes were exposed to graded doses of x-rays at Columbia or Fe-56 heavy ions at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and thymocytes assayed for early apoptotic death. By this means they planned to discover which genes or combinations of genes, are important in conferring radiosensitivity. For genes, or combinations of genes that look promising for this apoptotic endpoint, more extensive studies would be carried out with the more relevant endpoint oncogenic transformation using the embryo fibroblasts. This strategy was based on preliminary studies with gamma-rays and cell lines with a mutated gene (namely ATM) which show that a reduction in radiation-induced apoptosis is mirrored by an increase in oncogenic transformation.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Radiation exposures in Space are relatively difficult to reduce, and impossible to eliminate entirely. At the same time, other risks to humans in the hostile environment in space may be more acute than those of radiation. For this reason, larger annual dose limits have been tolerated for astronauts than recommended by NCRP for radiation workers on the ground, though career limits of risk have been roughly equalized.

There are now two clear instances from human epidemiological studies which suggest that the human population is not homogeneous in its response to radiation, but rather that radiosensitive sub-groups exist. One involves the clustering of meningiomas in certain North African families where children were epilated with x-rays in the course of the treatment of Tinea Capitis. The other involves a study of breast cancer in young people monitored by frequent diagnostic x-rays in the management of scoliosis. In this case, the dose-response was significantly greater for women who reported a family history of breast cancer in first or second degree relatives. While in each of these instances there is a clear indication of a radiosensitive sub-group, the gene(s) involved were not identified though there were obvious suspects, ATM in the case of the North African children and BRCA1 in the case of the young people with scoliosis.

Against this background, the investigators chose to study the effect on the biological response to heavy particles, similar to those found in space of cells heterozygous for three low frequency, high penetrance genes, namely ATM, BRCA1 and Rad9. This study was possible because knock-out mice, heterozygous for each of these genes, were available. Furthermore, by cross-breeding these animals the investigators were able to obtain animals heterozygous for pairs of these genes.

Fibroblasts from mid-term embryos were harvested from all of these animal types, irradiated with heavy ions at Brookhaven, and the incidence of oncogenic transformat ion assessed (this is an in vitro surrogate for carcinogenesis). At the same time, thymocyes were harvested from each animal type, irradiated at Brookhaven, and the incidence of early cell death by apoptosis assayed.. For all three genes, the incidence of radiation induced transformation was greater in heterozygous than in wild type cells, and conversely the incidence of radiation-induced apoptosis was lower in heterozygous cells. The reduced apoptotic levels associated with heterozygous genotypes shows that more cells with unrepaired DNA survive, leading to increased transformation.

Mutations and/or polymorphisms are present in the homologues of these genes in the human population, suggesting an explanation for the presence of a radiosensitive sub-population of approximately five percent. The study of the double heterozygotes also raises an interesting point. The cells heterozygous for both the ATM and Rad9 genes were more radiosensitive than cells heterozygous for ATM or Rad9 alone, suggesting an additive effect of the two genes. By contrast, cells heterozygous for both ATM and BRCA1 were no more radiosensitive than cells heterozygous for ATM alone. A possible explanation for this difference is that the ATM and BRCA1 genes operate in the same pathway, whereas ATM and Rad9 do not.

experiment_title: Women Astronaut Health
parameter_html:
Pulse

investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
In October 1997, the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) reported on some variables concerning astronauts and their first flights. These data, valid through 1996, detailed various laboratory measurements including the mean differences in blood pressure and pulse values for pre- and postflight examinations.

In 1996, there were 135 active astronauts: 30 women and 105 men. There were only 6 inactive women and 129 inactive men. The average age for active women astronauts is 39.9 years while the same average for active men is 41.9 years. For inactive corps members, men have a mean age of 50.9 years while women have a mean age of 46.5 years. At first flight, women average 39 years of age. Approximately 59 percent of men and 29 percent of women received a Master's degree as their highest degree earned. Fifty-one percent of women astronauts received a doctoral degree (M.D. or Ph.D.) while 28 percent of the men hold a doctoral degree in medicine, philosophy, or veterinary medicine. Racial makeup for the astronaut corps includes five groups: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American. Eighty-eight percent (30) of female astronauts and 89.2 percent (141) of male astronauts are White. The next largest racial group is Blacks with 9 percent (8) of men and 5 percent (3) of women.

From 1978 through 1996, women have been eligible to participate in 82 different missions. Of all flights:

  • Women were crewmembers on 42 of those missions (51%)
  • A woman was a pilot on 1 mission (1.2%)
  • There were at least 2 women on 13 of those missions (15.9%)

    The purpose of this study was to examine the differences between male and female astronaut physiological parameters.

    APPROACH:
    Blood Pressure: The preflight (L-10) and postflight (R+0) examinations were used to calculate the differences in blood pressures for all astronauts.

    Pulse: Again, these values were obtained from L-10 and R+0 examinations, with the subjects in the sitting position.

    RESULTS:
    Blood pressure: In particular, women had a mean difference in sitting diastolic BP:

  • 10 mmHg for flights of six days or less (N=5)
  • 8.2 mmHg for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=11)
  • 0 mmHg for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=3)

    The mean differences in sitting systolic BP are:

  • 14 mmHg for flights of six days or less (N=5)
  • 12.7 mmHg for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=11)
  • 14 mmHg for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=3)

    The mean differences for men were less than the mean differences for women on all flights except those 11 to 17 days in length. For those flights, men had a mean difference of 11.9 and 16.8 mmHg for diastolic and systolic BP, respectively.

    Sitting Pulse Values for Women:
    The average mean differences in sitting pulses for women are:

  • 17 beats per minute (bpm) for flights of six days or less (N=4)
  • 11.2 bpm for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=6)
  • 1.3 bpm for flights of 11 though 17 days (N=3)

    The average mean differences in sitting pulses for men are:

  • 7.7 bpm for flights of six days or less (N=22)
  • 16.2 bpm for flights of 7 through 10 days in length (N=23)
  • 8.0 bpm for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=17)

    Physiological differences between men and women will continue to be investigated.

experiment_title: Vitamin D Metabolites and Bone Demineralization
parameter_html:
Albumin
Calcium
Phosphorus
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D), plasma
24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (24,25(OH)2D), plasma

Parathyroid hormone (PTH), plasma
investigators: Principal Investigator: Schnoes, HeinrichCo-Investigator: de Luca, Hector
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Research data from previous calcium imbalance studies have shown that exposure to microgravity during space flight may cause bone mineral loss, increased plasma calcium, increased urinary calcium excretion, and an overall negative calcium balance. The objective of this experiment was to determine whether plasma levels of vitamin D metabolites, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) were altered in the crew of the 8 day Spacelab 2 mission. Significant changes in these hormones during space flight may indicate that the calcium homeostatic mechanism is adversely affected by exposure to microgravity.

The calcium homeostatic mechanism operates through the integration of intestinal calcium absorption, calcium deposition and resorption from bone, and calcium excretion. The mechanism is regulated by the interaction of several hormonal factors, including PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Vitamin D plays a key role because one of its metabolites, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D), regulates intestinal calcium absorption and, in conjunction with PTH, induces bone mineral resorption to maintain normal blood calcium levels. An increase in circulating levels of these two hormones could be responsible for initiating changes in the calcium homeostatic mechanism by activating bone remodeling sites and by regulating calcium transport in the intestine, kidneys, and in bone. Long term space flight may cause hormonal imbalances in this mechanism which can lead to detrimental effects such as bone demineralization and kidney stone formation.

APPROACH:
During the preflight testing phase, investigators studied hormone levels in blood samples from both humans and animals to devise new and better methods for metabolite analysis. The results of the tests helped investigators choose the best methods for analysis of the in flight samples and provided them with a broad range of data to use for comparative analysis.

Four crewmembers participated in the study and were divided equally into two teams, the red team and the blue team. The protocol called for samples to be collected at 24, 18, and 3 days prelaunch, immediately after landing, and at days 3 and 10 postlanding. The in flight protocol required each subject to collect two blood samples during the mission. One sample was collected early in the mission while the other was collected toward the end of the mission. The blue team collected their early samples at 18 hours into the mission while the red team collected samples at 31 hours. The late samples were collected at 6 days, 19 hours and 7 days, 7 hours for the blue and red teams, respectively. Two tubes of blood were taken during each sample session; one tube was used for the vitamin D metabolite analysis while the other tube was used for measurements of PTH, albumin, calcium, and phosphorus. All samples were collected in glass tubes, centrifuged to separate the plasma from the blood cells, and frozen until the analysis was performed. The volume collected for all samples was 25 ml and each sample yielded 4 to 5 ml of plasma. The vitamin D metabolite analysis included measurements for 24,25(OH)2D, 25 OHD, and 1,25(OH)2D.

RESULTS:
The results of the plasma analyses showed no significant difference between preflight and postflight mean values for any parameter measured. However, the early in flight samples indicated that levels of 25 OHD did increase significantly when compared to preflight means but the in flight value was within the normal range. The level of 24,25(OH)2D increased markedly in one crewmember late in the mission, however, this increase was within the normal range and not significant when compared to preflight values. Essentially, the levels of two biologically active vitamin D metabolites, 25OHD and 24,25(OH)2D, remained unchanged at all time points. In contrast, levels of the key biologically active vitamin D metabolite, 1,25(OH)2D, did change. The first inflight measurement of this hormone showed an increase of 57 percent when compared to preflight means. This increase was significant at the (p < 0.05) level. The second in flight value was 22 percent lower than the preflight mean but was not significantly different. Thus, levels of this key vitamin D metabolite were elevated early in flight but returned to normal by the end of the seventh day. Measurements of parathyroid hormone from the early and late in flight samples showed decreases of 47 and 34 percent, respectively, when compared to preflight means. These decreases were not statistically significant due to the small number of subjects. Plasma levels of calcium, phosphorus, and albumin were essentially normal throughout the mission.

OBJECTIVES:
Research data from previous calcium imbalance studies have shown that exposure to microgravity during space flight may cause bone mineral loss, increased plasma calcium, increased urinary calcium excretion, and an overall negative calcium balance. The objective of this experiment was to determine whether plasma levels of vitamin D metabolites, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) were altered in the crew of the 8 day Spacelab 2 mission. Significant changes in these hormones during space flight may indicate that the calcium homeostatic mechanism is adversely affected by exposure to microgravity.

The calcium homeostatic mechanism operates through the integration of intestinal calcium absorption, calcium deposition and resorption from bone, and calcium excretion. The mechanism is regulated by the interaction of several hormonal factors, including PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Vitamin D plays a key role because one of its metabolites, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D), regulates intestinal calcium absorption and, in conjunction with PTH, induces bone mineral resorption to maintain normal blood calcium levels. An increase in circulating levels of these two hormones could be responsible for initiating changes in the calcium homeostatic mechanism by activating bone remodeling sites and by regulating calcium transport in the intestine, kidneys, and in bone. Long term space flight may cause hormonal imbalances in this mechanism which can lead to detrimental effects such as bone demineralization and kidney stone formation.

APPROACH:
During the preflight testing phase, investigators studied hormone levels in blood samples from both humans and animals to devise new and better methods for metabolite analysis. The results of the tests helped investigators choose the best methods for analysis of the in flight samples and provided them with a broad range of data to use for comparative analysis.

Four crewmembers participated in the study and were divided equally into two teams, the red team and the blue team. The protocol called for samples to be collected at 24, 18, and 3 days prelaunch, immediately after landing, and at days 3 and 10 postlanding. The in flight protocol required each subject to collect two blood samples during the mission. One sample was collected early in the mission while the other was collected toward the end of the mission. The blue team collected their early samples at 18 hours into the mission while the red team collected samples at 31 hours. The late samples were collected at 6 days, 19 hours and 7 days, 7 hours for the blue and red teams, respectively. Two tubes of blood were taken during each sample session; one tube was used for the vitamin D metabolite analysis while the other tube was used for measurements of PTH, albumin, calcium, and phosphorus. All samples were collected in glass tubes, centrifuged to separate the plasma from the blood cells, and frozen until the analysis was performed. The volume collected for all samples was 25 ml and each sample yielded 4 to 5 ml of plasma. The vitamin D metabolite analysis included measurements for 24,25(OH)2D, 25 OHD, and 1,25(OH)2D.

RESULTS:
The results of the plasma analyses showed no significant difference between preflight and postflight mean values for any parameter measured. However, the early in flight samples indicated that levels of 25 OHD did increase significantly when compared to preflight means but the in flight value was within the normal range. The level of 24,25(OH)2D increased markedly in one crewmember late in the mission, however, this increase was within the normal range and not significant when compared to preflight values. Essentially, the levels of two biologically active vitamin D metabolites, 25OHD and 24,25(OH)2D, remained unchanged at all time points. In contrast, levels of the key biologically active vitamin D metabolite, 1,25(OH)2D, did change. The first inflight measurement of this hormone showed an increase of 57 percent when compared to preflight means. This increase was significant at the (p < 0.05) level. The second in flight value was 22 percent lower than the preflight mean but was not significantly different. Thus, levels of this key vitamin D metabolite were elevated early in flight but returned to normal by the end of the seventh day. Measurements of parathyroid hormone from the early and late in flight samples showed decreases of 47 and 34 percent, respectively, when compared to preflight means. These decreases were not statistically significant due to the small number of subjects. Plasma levels of calcium, phosphorus, and albumin were essentially normal throughout the mission.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex, unique radiation environment including energetic protons and charged particles from galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events. Although these radiations can result in significant cumulative doses to astronauts during long-duration space flights, most exposures occur at low fluences, so that particle traversals through an astronaut's body are well separated in tissue location and time. Under such conditions, bystander effects, where unirradiated cells express biological changes in response to signals from irradiated cells, have increased significance. The overall hypothesis of this investigation is that increased oxidative stress caused by charged particle-stimulated intercellular signaling-- bystander effects-- in cells and tissues creates a microenvironment conducive to altered carcinogenic processes; responses can be triggered at very low doses, with the lowest effective dose depending on radiation type, but the magnitude of the response being radiation quality-independent. Previous studies showed that bystander responses can be induced in unirradiated cells in a 3D skin model, including after low fluences of protons or iron ions, and that in 3D both irradiated and bystander cells are more resistant to induction of DNA damage than cells in monolayer. Different epithelial tissues can differ in their 3D architecture and, therefore, might be expected to have different radiation and bystander responses. This project proposes to compare bystander signaling in 3D models of colon with previous data for the skin epithelial model. The specific aims for this study are:
  1. Develop a 3D model of colonic epithelium for testing effects of low fluences of charged particles in comparison with the responses in our previously developed 3D skin model.
  2. Quantify DNA damage, apoptosis, differentiation and proliferation in the 3D model of colonic epithelium exposed to low fluences of charged-particles
  3. Determine whether the bystander response in the colon model has the same radiation dose and LET dependence as the skin model, and whether reactive oxygen species (ROS) play a role in the intercellular signaling. <\li>

APPROACH:
The Caco2 colon cancer cell line was chosen for initial studies since this line has been used as a model for colon epithelium in published literature, including one radiation study. The 3D colon model was established with the CaCo2 cells as the epithelium and AG01522 normal human fibroblasts as the stromal cells embedded in collagen. Cells were irradiated with X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With the cells in monolayer, a transwell insert co-culture system was used to assess DNA damage in both irradiated cells and unirradiated bystander cells sharing medium with the irradiated cells.

RESULTS:
Data show induction of micronuclei (MN; surrogate for chromosome aberrations) in Caco2 cells 72 h after irradiation with X-rays, 1 GeV protons or 1 GeV/n silicon or iron ions. In all cases, there is a large, radiation dose-dependent increase in MN in irradiated cells, but importantly, there is up to a 3-fold increase in the fraction of unirradiated bystander cells having MN after co-culture with irradiated cells. Additional studies using induction of foci of the DNA repair-related protein 53BP1, a surrogate for DNA double-strand breaks, as an endpoint have been done in irradiated and bystander Caco2 cells after exposure to X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With all radiation types, in the irradiated population, the fraction of cells with foci is substantially increased at 1 h, is maximum 5 h after irradiation, then decreases substantially by 24 h. In the bystander cell population, the increase in fraction of cells with foci is slower, not being maximal until 12 h after irradiation and the start of co-culture, and still being elevated at 24 h. The maximum fraction of bystander cells with increased level of foci is about 3-fold higher than in untreated cells, similar to the magnitude of bystander effect seen using MN as endpoint. This delayed development and removal of damage in bystander cells compared to irradiated cells is similar to the responses seen in the 3D skin model.

Comparing the 2D and 3D data in the CaCo2 cells suggests several findings: First, in 3D there are fewer foci per cell, including in untreated samples, so a cut-off of only 1 focus per cell for analysis was used in 3D compared to 5 foci per cell minimum for scoring in 2D. If the 5 foci per cell cut-off had been used in the 3D samples, the fraction of cells with damage would be much lower in 3D, consistent with the finding with the skin model. Second, the time courses for development and disappearance of foci in 3D are similar to those in 2D, with cells in both architectures showing the delay in bystander responses compared to responses in irradiated cells. The model has been extended to use normal human colon epithelial cells (FHC cells) in both 2D and 3D studies. The early data had some scatter, but the trends show that in monolayer, 53BP1 foci appear to be maximal at 5 h after irradiation in both irradiated and bystander FHC cells, but replicate experiments are needed to confirm this finding. Furthermore, although these cells grow very slowly, 3D constructs in which the FHC cells form a single epithelial layer on the basement material containing fibroblasts, consistent with the single-layered colon epithelium have been successfully produced.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Skeletal muscle is made up of many "motor units." Each unit consists of a group of muscle fibers and a motor neuron that innervates them. For each nerve impulse, the muscle fibers perform a single twitch contraction (contract and immediately relax). This single twitch of a single motor unit could be considered the quantal unit of exercise. Prolonged weightlessness results in a loss of muscle strength and volume and decreased bone density, particularly in the legs. At this time, the only effective treatment for these problems appears to be in-flight exercise. No form of physical activity can be maximally efficient or effective, however, if motor neuron recruitment is compromised. This may be the case, as previous observations have suggested that Achilles' tendon tap responses and Hoffmann Reflexes in the soleus muscle are abnormal after several days in space. However, most of these data were obtained days after landing or were incidental observations during experiments designed for other purposes. The effect of weightlessness on spinal cord excitability has not been fully studied. The objective of this experiment was to determine if spinal cord excitability gradually decreases during prolonged spaceflight, and if so, to measure the extent of the change, and how long it continues after return to the ground.

APPROACH:
During experiment operations, the test subject was fitted with five electrodes. Electromyography (EMG) activity was recorded differentially from two recording electrodes applied to the soleus muscle. The locations of these electrodes on the posterior surface of the leg were critical. A single reference electrode was applied to the anterior surface of the same leg. The electrical stimulus to the posterior tibial nerve was applied through an adjustable, spring-loaded electrode located behind the knee. A knee brace provided a rigid and stable structure on which to mount the stimulating electrode. The stimulus circuit was completed through a stimulus return path electrode positioned just above the knee cap. Following application of the electrodes, the subject was restrained in a sitting position. The feet were strapped to a foot brace that established fixed and consistent knee (120 degrees) and ankle (90 degrees) angles that varied somewhat between subjects. During the “Locate Phase” of the experiment, the subject received electrical shocks (600 microseconds in duration, 40-90 volts amplitude) at the rate of one shock every three seconds. The purpose of this phase was to allow the operator to locate the posterior tibial nerve (the stimulating electrode could be adjusted for optimum data collection), and determine the shock strength (the electrical shock was varied to find the minimum and maximum values required for the experiment). No data was stored during the Locate Phase.

During the “Data Collection Phase” of the experiment, sixty test shocks were delivered at the rate of one every five seconds. The stimulus was incrementally increased and then slowly decreased within the determined maximum range. The resulting EMG response from each shock was recorded from the soleus muscle.

After the last shock was applied, a computer analyzed and displayed the recorded data, allowing the crew member to determine if the test was successfully completed. At the end of the session, the computer analyzed the data and determined the minimum and maximum of spinal cord excitability for each session. Subsequently, the ratio of H-max to M-max (the measure of spinal cord excitability) was determined. Data was saved on the hard drive and down-linked to ground operations as soon as possible.

During flight, H-Reflex recruitment curves were recorded four times during each subjects stay onboard the Station: three times early in flight (pre-docked and docked) and once late in the mission. The principal investigator added an additional early session during Expedition 3, after results received during Expedition 2 indicated that an additional session would better define the rate of change in this reflex. For comparison, the experiment was also run three times preflight and four times post-flight.

RESULTS:
This study of spinal cord excitability using the Hoffman reflex was completed by a total of eight subjects over ISS Expeditions 2-4. H-Reflex measured how excitable the nerve cells were by applying small electrical shocks behind the knee. Each shock produced a reflex response in the calf muscles (the H-Reflex response); the data collected indicated that this response decreased significantly while in microgravity. The study found that spinal cord excitability decreased by about 35% in weightlessness, and stayed at this new level for the duration of the mission. Although there was notable improvement in the H-Reflex response the day after landing, it took about ten days back on Earth for astronauts to fully recover their muscle strength and spinal cord excitability.

This difference in excitability means that only a portion of muscle fiber units are contracting in response to signals from the nervous system and explains functionally why muscle mass declines in weightlessness, even with exercise. Reduced excitability means that there might be limits on the degree to which heart muscle strength, leg muscle tone, and bone density (for which muscle contraction is an important regulating factor) can be maintained through exercise on long-duration missions. Because this decrease in excitability is only observed on orbit and not during bed rest, an analogue for weightless space travel, the results highlight the possibility that reduced excitability with corresponding loss of muscle and bone might be partly a nervous system response and not simply due to disuse of the legs.

Based on the results of this study, decreased spinal cord excitability could be an issue for long-duration stays in partial-gravity environments such as are found on the moon and Mars. Future designs of exercise equipment that provide feedback on work actually performed would help crewmembers compensate for decreases in exercise efficiency.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Determining the position of our bodies, relative to the environment, is a complex function requiring the brain to integrate information from virtually every sensory system, including the eyes and inner ear, as well as receptors in our muscles and joints. The absence of gravity causes adaptive changes in the sensorimotor and perceptual systems, and some of these changes are fundamental.

The adaptive mechanisms of the sensorimotor and perceptual systems rely on adjustments in control strategies. Thus, the first aim of the Canal and Otolith Integration Studies (COIS) was a better understanding of the changes in the strategies of oculomotor performance (eye movement), particularly those that rely on spatial orientation. This was tested by systematically evaluating changes in the different classes of eye movements, including the vestibulo-ocular reflex, smooth pursuit and saccades. Changes in eye movements reflect disruptions in the coordination process.

The second aim of the study was to test the hypothesis that the absence of an orientational extrinsic gravity vector would result in a change in oculomotor and perceptual responses such that the subjects would begin to use intrinsic coordinates to orient themselves. This hypothesis was tested by evaluating changes in cross-coupling of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) response axes and by evaluating changes in spatial reorientation performance.

APPROACH:
The COIS experiment was composed of three different protocols: Voluntary Head Shakes (VHS), Smooth Pursuit Tracking and Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN). The VHS and Smooth Pursuit Tracking protocols were always performed at the same time (first VHS, then Smooth Pursuit Tracking), while the OKN protocol was not necessarily performed on the same day.

During the VHS and Smooth Pursuit Tracking protocols, the subjects were seated and the lower body and trunk restrained. The subject wore a vest called the Instrumented Vest Assembly (IVA), which contained amplifiers and data recorders (called the Superpocket Assembly) and provided the connections to the peripheral hardware. The peripheral hardware included an electrooculograph (EOG) to monitor eye movements, a triaxial rate sensor to record head movements, the Luminous Target Display (LTD) and the Electronic Light Occlusion Goggles (ELOG). The LTD provided a cruciform array of Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and was used as a visual target. The ELOG goggles occluded vision under normal conditions and were translucent when a 30-volt DC electrical current was applied.

The VHS protocol included two test conditions, both featuring voluntary head shakes at two different frequencies, 0.33 and 1.0 Hertz (Hz), in both the horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) planes. Instructions were given to the subjects via a prerecorded audio tape that played a modulated tone. The subject was asked to move the head so that during the lowest tone the head was at the far right and at the highest tone it was at the far left. During the first test condition, the subjects performed the head shakes using the central light of the LTD as their visual target. During the second test condition, the subject's vision was occluded using the ELOG goggles. The subject was asked to move their head according to the auditory cues and use an imaginary target to fixate gaze.

Smooth Pursuit Tracking required the subjects to track a moving target in two ways. In the first type of tracking, the head was held stationary, and the target was pursued with eyes only. In the second type of tracking, both the eyes and head were allowed to move. Two frequencies, 0.33 and 1.0 Hz, were used for both the horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) planes. The diodes of the LTD functioned as targets, providing a peak amplitude of 25 degrees.

During the Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) protocol, the subjects wore the Optokinetic Stimulus (OKS) goggles. The head-mounted OKS goggles provided the stimuli to provoke optokinetic nystagmus by means of a pattern of red and black 4-degree-wide stripes viewed through a Fresnel lens. The stripe pattern could be moved at a constant velocity of a maximum of 40 degrees per second in the horizontal, vertical or 45 degrees oblique direction.

The optokinetic stimulus was maintained in one direction for 20 seconds, followed by 10 seconds in darkness, during which optokinetic after-nystagmus was observed. This was followed by 5 seconds with a stationary display to visually suppress any remaining after-nystagmus before providing 20 seconds of OKS in the opposite direction, followed again by 10 seconds of darkness. During the initial darkness period, eye movements (EOG) were recorded with the subject looking straight ahead to quantify any spontaneous and/or positional nystagmus that might be present.

In space, the subjects were free-floating during the OKN trials to avoid external orientation cues. For pre- and postflight testing, the gravitational effects on the OKN were inferred by evaluating the horizontal-to-vertical cross-coupling effects with either visual stimulus by tilting the subject's head by 30 degrees with respect to the spatial vertical.

Crewmembers participated as test subjects and operators for COIS, obtaining measurements before, during and after flight. Three preflight data collection sessions were used as a baseline with which to compare inflight and postflight data. Space flight data collection occurred four times for each subject -- two times early and two times late during the mission. Postflight data collection occurred on landing day (R+0), and continued on R+1, R+2, R+4 and R+8.

RESULTS:
The responses to self-induced, sinusoidal head rotations further indicates that VOR gain and phase are modified as is gaze.
