experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a safe and non-invasive scanning technique that uses low frequency radio waves to form an image by reading the amount of hydrogen in an area. This method provides outstanding anatomical images for volume measurements and quantification of chemical and physical changes induced in tissues. Using MRI, the objectives of this study were 1) to determine the specific loss and recovery of muscle volume in the calf, thigh and lumbar region of the back, 2) to determine whether residual effects resulting from intervertebral disc expansion during weightlessness are evident upon return to Earth's gravity and 3) to determine changes in bone marrow composition as reflected by changes in the marrow transverse relaxation time.

APPROACH:
MRI was performed on L-90 (90 days preflight), L-60 and L-30, R+1 (one day after landing) and R+15 using two Siemens 1.5 Tesla magnets. A whole body coil was used to image the subject's calf and thigh. An aluminum shield covered the lower torso during calf imaging and was moved to cover the lower legs during thigh imaging. A single acquisition of 32 contiguous 1 cm slices was obtained for both calf and thigh using a Te=22 msec, Tr=1500 msec and a 256 x 256 matrix. Following these images, a standard spine coil obtained three separate sequences. A sagittal scout image centered the coil through L3, and a coronal scout image positioned a 1 cm region of interest through the center of the spinal column. A Carl-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) sequence with a Tr=1 sec, spin echoes at 20, 45, 72 and 106 msec and 4 aquisitions was used. The CPMG sequence was followed by a multislice sagittal, gradient echo sequence using a Te=7 msec, Tr=88 msec and 24 contiguous 3 mm slices. A transverse spin echo sequence was obtained consisting of twenty, 0.5 cm transverse slices centered on L3 with Te=20 msec, Tr=1 sec and 2 acquisitions.

Extremity slice matching from one imaging session to the next was accomplished by comparing marrow areas. Back muscle image slices were matched by positioning the center slice on the third lumbar vertebra (L3) and acquiring slices above and below this region. Muscles were grouped as follows: gastrocnemius, soleus, anterior calf (all calf muscles excluding the gastrocnemius and soleus), quadriceps, hamstrings, intrinsic lower back (rotatores, multifidus, spinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis), and psoas. For each muscle region, the outlined area (in pixels) was plotted against position (in millimeters). After comparing identical regions as described above, muscle volume was obtained by adding the number of pixels under each curve. Volumes were expressed as a percent of preflight or pre-bedrest averages.

Using a spine coil, the spinal imaging area was centered within the L3 vertebra, determined from a sagittal scout view. A coronal scout image positioned a 1 cm region through the center of the spinal column. A CPMG sequence obtained images with a Tr=1500 sec and spin echoes at 20, 45, 72, 106 msec (n=5) or 30, 60, 90, 126 msec (n=2). A phantom was imaged during each MRI session to correct for changes in pixel size.

Disc areas for T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4 and L4-5 were obtained by calculating the number of pixels in each image in the following manner. Using the echo 1 image, a large region was drawn around the disc to determine the average pixel intensity. All pixels having intensity values greater than one half the mean value were displayed and again the mean and one half the mean were determined. The resultant pixel number was used as the disc area after corrections for pixel size changes. The same procedure was used for the other three echoes using the starting template as echo 1. Echo 1 was selected to represent the entire disc, and echo 3 represented the nucleus.

To examine changes in mobile proton concentrations, the spin-spin relaxation constant (denoted as T2) of discs was measured using the four spin echoes. Each pixel was fit by the weighted least squares method to calculate a T2 value, assuming a single exponential. Signal intensity was used to compute relative weights. T2 was determined by taking an average T2 of all pixels within L2-3 and L3-4. These discs were selected because the field of view was centered on L3 where a high signal to noise ratio would result. T2 was also measured in the lumbar vertebral bodies to determine changes in the fat to water content ratio.

Changes in disc height were determined by calculating the distance from the center of L1 to the center of L5, assuming that spine curvature does not change between measurements.

The statistical analysis was limited to discs L2-3 and L3-4 to reduce the number of comparisons. Preflight measurements were averaged to obtain three time points: preflight, immediate postflight and late postflight (15 days). Data were tested using repeated measures ANOVA and a Greenhouse-Geisser adjustment factor with significance set at p<0.05.

RESULTS:
Significant muscle-specific atrophy was seen after only 8 days in weightlessness. Muscle volume changes found in the four SL-J crewmembers were: -3.9% from the anterior calf, -6.3% from the soleus and gastrocnemius, -6.0% from the quadriceps, -8.0% from the hamstrings, -10.3% from the intrinsic lower back and -3.1% from the psoas. Statistical analysis of R+1 data demonstrated that the soleus, gastrocnemius, anterior calf, hamstrings and intrinsic back muscle volumes were significantly decreased compared to preflight values. The quadriceps (p=0.06) and the psoas (p=0.13), while lower immediately following recovery, were not significantly decreased. All muscle regions increased in volume by R+15 relative to R+1. However, the hamstrings and intrinsic lower back muscles were still significantly lower in volume than preflight. These changes explain in part the large losses in muscle strength reported after Shuttle missions. The muscle volume changes observed after flight are similar to those observed after bed rest of similar duration.

Results indicate that the disc area of bed rest patients expanded, reaching an equilibrium value of 22%. Disc area of SL-J crewmembers had returned to preflight values within the first 24 hours after landing. As expected from the disc area results, no changes were observed in the lumbar spine lengths (L1-L5), intervertebral discs, lumbar vertebral bodies, or marrow transverse relaxation times. This work has demonstrated that significant adaptive changes in intervertebral discs can be expected during weightlessness. Knowledge of these changes is important in understanding spine mechanics and in selection of exercise countermeasures employed during flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss is a critical concern for crewmembers in space. Free radicals have been shown to affect bone in vivo and in vitro by stimulating osteoclasts and increasing the rate of bone resorption. In space, increased exposure to radiation increases the possibility of oxidative damage to bone, and antioxidant nutrients may protect the skeletal tissue.

Rodent hindlimb unloading (HLU) is an alternative method to space flight for investigating microgravity-induced physiological changes. HLU produces a deficit in bone formation, lowers the number of osteoblasts, and has been used as a model for examining bone changes in simulated weightlessness.

This ground-based study evaluated the potential of vitamin E for preventing bone loss associated with weightlessness in the HLU rat model. The long-term goal was to identify an optimal dose of vitamin E to reduce the risk of bone loss and fractures under conditions of weightlessness. The hypothesis was that the dietary antioxidant vitamin E would reduce deterioration of bone in a dose-dependent manner when the bone loss was due to weightlessness and, possibly, oxidative stress. There were two specific aims. One was to investigate whether vitamin E prevents the loss of bone mineral density and deterioration of biomechanical properties in the HLU rat model in a dose-dependent manner. The other specific aim was to examine some of the underlying mechanisms by which vitamin E exerts bone-protective effects using histomorphometric, biomechanical and biochemical analyses.

APPROACH:
Eight and one-half-month-old rats were assigned to one of three diets containing 15, 75 or 500 International Units (IU) of dl-alpha tocopherol, a form of vitamin E. These amounts were low, recommended or high for this vitamin intake. The rats were assigned to either ambulatory (AMB) or HLU conditions. Diets began nine weeks prior to the start of the hindlimb unloading period and the rats were either HLU or AMB for four weeks. At eight days and at one day prior to necropsy, rats were injected with calcein for dynamic bone histomorphometric analysis. They were scanned using a small animal software package prior to unloading and at the end of the treatment period. Rats were anesthetized for scanning and blood was drained by cardiac puncture. Serum was then analyzed for various markers. Age at necropsy was approximately eleven months.

Mechanical strength of the femur was assessed with three-point bending. The femur was placed on two rods spaced 20 mm apart and force was delivered to the mid-shaft. The fourth lumbar vertebral body (L4) was prepared with parallel flat ends and placed on a fixed lower pressure plate while an upper plate moved downwards at a rate of three mm/min to cause compression in the front to rear direction in order to conduct compression analysis. Load displacement plots were analyzed to determine material properties. The average cross section for each vertebral body was used to calculate its ultimate stresses and Young's modulus, which is a number representing the ratio of stress divided by strain. Histomorphometric analysis of the femur produced multiple measurements.

Bone mineral area, bone mineral content, and bone mineral density (BMD) of the excised fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and of the left femur were estimated. Femurs and the third lumbar vertebra were ashed, and the mineral residue was dissolved in concentrated nitric acid and diluted for analysis of calcium, magnesium, iron, copper and zinc.

RESULTS:
Results were divided into two parts. HLU and AMB conditions were compared and dose-dependent effects of vitamin E on bone parameters of interest under both conditions were evaluated. Significant effects of near weightlessness were seen in 11-month old rats. Both the L5 and femur BMD were significantly lowered in HLU animals compared to AMB controls. Lower BMDs in the HLU group were accompanied by reduced structural properties. The material properties of L4, ultimate stress, yield stress, and Young's modulus of elasticity were significantly decreased by HLU. Histomorphometric data indicated that HLU decreased the rate of bone formation and increased the rate of bone resorption. Serum markers indicated an increase in tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase activity, a marker of bone resorption, but no change in either marker of bone formation (alkaline phosphatase activity or osteocalcin). The findings confirmed that deleterious effects on bone of older animals due to HLU were similar to the deleterious effects on younger, growing animals. However, alterations in bone metabolism that result in bone loss of mature animals appeared to more closely mimic the metabolic bone changes occurring in crewmembers in space.

Dietary treatments were effective in creating differences in serum vitamin E concentrations even though diet was not begun until the rats were eight and one-half months old. The diet produced significant differences in ferric reducing ability of serum and strong trends for decreased malondialdehyde, a product of lipid peroxidation, in the liver. Both ferric reducing ability of serum and liver malondialdehyde are indicators of antioxidant status. In HLU animals, high intakes of vitamin E had a positive effect on material properties of vertebrae measured by increased yield stress and by Young's modulus of elasticity. The positive effects of the high vitamin E intake were not observed in AMB controls. Histomorphometry data indicated that higher doses of vitamin E produced positive effects on bone volume parameters in HLU rats. Contrary to expectations, the same doses of vitamin E had negative effects on these histomorphometric parameters in AMB controls. Serum alkaline phosphatase, a marker of bone formation, increased with increased vitamin E in the diet.

Data indicated that higher doses of vitamin E improved skeletal health. Higher bone volume and biomechanical properties in HLU animals were observed with the increased dietary vitamin E. Contrary to expectations, vitamin E at higher doses was found to be deleterious to bone in AMB control animals. Research previous to this study showed that higher doses of vitamin E were beneficial in aged mice but had no beneficial effects on the bone of younger mice. It is possible that the bone of older animals or of those in HLU conditions benefit from more vitamin E, particularly if the HLU resulted in greater oxidative damage.

Research of the mechanisms of vitamin E in mature bone is critical to understanding its role in bone health. There is the potential for vitamin E to protect against oxygen derived from free radicals. In the mature, 11-month old rats of this study, dietary vitamin E did not produce significant effects on bone mineral area, bone mineral content or BMD. Since dietary changes are cumulative over time and subtler than the bone response was to HLU, the bone mineral area, bone mineral content and BMD might not be apparent during the relatively brief time course of this experiment. Nutrition studies may require extended depletion or supplementation periods before HLU to enable differences to be observed during the relatively short HLU period. Additional data may be obtained through studies that analyze markers over time. Time series studies examining markers of bone resorption and also changes in gene expression due to HLU and nutritional or pharmacological interventions could provide insight into alterations in bone metabolism.

Time series studies examining markers of bone resorption and also changes in gene expression due to HLU and nutritional or pharmacological interventions could provide insight into alterations in bone metabolism.

experiment_title: In-flight Pharmacokinetics of Acetaminophen in Saliva
parameter_html: Acetaminophen, maximum concentration, saliva
investigators: Principal Investigator: Putcha, LakshmiCo-Investigator: Cintron, NitzaCo-Investigator: Parise, Cecilia
experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Evidence exists that the therapeutic effectiveness of some drugs may change in space. The objective of this study was to determine whether acetaminophen, a drug used frequently for pain relief by astronauts in space, actually reaches its site of action at concentrations sufficient to elicit a therapeutic response. The absorption and distribution of acetaminophen were examined to monitor potential changes in drug pharmacokinetics during spaceflight.

APPROACH:
A noninvasive saliva sampling technique was used. Tablets of acetaminophen were administered orally to 1 or 2 crew members on each of 7 missions (total of 13 subjects) twice before and at least once during space flight (ideally on flight day 3 or 4). Using the Saliva Collection Kit, saliva samples were collected 10 times, from 0 to 8 hours, after each drug administration. The concentration of acetaminophen in the samples, determined by high-performance liquid chromatography, was used to calculate parameters for pharmacokinetic evaluation.

RESULTS:
Salivary acetaminophen concentration profiles during space flight were different from those obtained on the ground. Changes were more pronounced in the absorption phase than in the elimination phase. The time needed to reach maximum concentration of acetaminophen increased during flight, indicating that absorption time was prolonged. Changes in the maximum acetaminophen concentration depended on mission length. Results of this study supported predictions that drug dynamics change during flight and suggested that these changes depend upon mission length and individual physiologic responses to space flight. The limited in-flight data accumulated for this study were insufficient to characterize the degree and magnitude of pharmacokinetic changes and the mechanisms underlying them.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Majeska, Robert
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this experiment was to investigate: 1) whether microgravity induces changes in osteoblastic cells similar to those caused by bone resorption-stimulating agents like parathyroid hormone (PTH), and 2) whether those phenotypic changes are associated with alterations in cell shape and/or adhesive interactions with the extracellular matrix.

Approach:

A permanent cell line derived from a rat osteosarcoma and stably exhibiting an osteoblast-like phenotype (ROS 17/2.8) was cultured on microcarrier beads and inoculated into 24 STL cartridges. At times ranging from 6 hrs to 10 days post-launch, samples of conditioned medium were collected from pairs of cartridges from the 12 flight and 12 ground control groups, and the cartridges were perfused with fixative. Upon recovery after landing, the medium was assayed for lactate (an indicator of metabolic activity and cell viability), alkaline phosphatase (an osteoblast marker enzyme), cyclic AMP (produced by osteoblastic cells in response to PTH) and prostaglandin E2 (a locally produced mediator of bone turnover). The cells were examined by phase contrast and fluorescence microscopy to assess shape changes, cytoskeletal organization and interactions with their substrata.

Results:

Measurements of lactate, alkaline phosphatase, cAMP and PGE2 indicated the presence of viable cells expressing an osteoblastic phenotype; however, no differences were found in any of these parameters between the flight and ground samples. Microscopic examination of the beads indicated that a loss of cells occurred early after inoculation into cartridges in flight and ground samples alike, followed apparently by slow recovery and growth. No gross differences were found in cell shape between flight and ground samples.

experiment_title: Impact of Space Radiation on Cognition, Synapses and Biomarkers in Aging and Alzheimer's Disease

Brain inflammation
Brain synaptic changes

investigators: Principal Investigator: Lemere, CynthiaCo-Investigator: O'Banion, Kerry
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this work was to identify early and late effects of space radiation on the connections between nerve cells in the brain (i.e., synapses), inflammation, and cognition so that one can assess the central nervous system (CNS) risk to future astronauts involved in long-duration lunar missions and/or a mission to Mars. These early changes, along with changes in brain inflammation that may relay signals between cells in the brain and blood flow, may help define those individuals at risk for developing long-term learning and memory problems.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the gender-specific early and late effects of space radiation on cognition, synaptic changes, Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathogenesis, cerebral blood flow (CBF) and neuroinflammation (GE180 PET) in a well-characterized Alzheimer’s Tg mouse model bearing 2 familial mutations (APPswe and PS1dE9) associated with early-onset AD, and strain-, age- and gender-matched C57BL/6 WT mice.
  2. Compare the effects of a single dose versus fractionated irradiation with 1000 MeV/µ 56Fe ions on cognition and locomotion, as well as changes in cerebral blood flow, brain volume, neuroinflammation, synapses, AD pathogenesis, and neuron loss.

APPROACH:
This study utilized normal, wildtype mice and a genetic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Female and male four month-old mice were irradiated once with varying doses of heavy ions or protons and examined two or ten months later. Chronic dosing was compared with a single dose for long-term effects as well. PET imaging was performed to assess brain inflammation and blood flow, and behavioral testing before being sacrificed. Investigators performed a close-up inspection of synapses, Alzheimer’s amyloid plaques, neuron loss, and inflammation in the brain.

RESULTS:
Results suggest that female mice are somewhat resistant to iron irradiation while male mice appear to be more vulnerable, especially to the long-term central nervous system effects. One caveat is that survival was reduced in female Alzheimer’s mice exposed to the higher single dose of iron irradiation; however, those female Alzheimer’s mice that survived until the end of the study showed fewer radiation effects on cognition, amyloid pathology, and inflammation compared to their male irradiated counterparts. Iron-irradiated male but not female Alzheimer’s mice showed short- and long-term cognitive deficits and long-term increases in brain amyloid and neuroinflammation. Similar to iron irradiation, a single exposure to proton irradiation caused sex- and dose-specific effects that varied according to the mouse model (wildtype or Alzheimer’s). For example, motor coordination was worsened by low-dose (but not high dose) proton irradiation in wildtype mice but not Alzheimer’s mice, and improved by iron irradiation in Alzheimer’s mice. Both proton and iron irradiation induced spatial memory impairment in male but female Alzheimer’s mice. And, while iron irradiation increased brain amyloid, proton irradiation decreased brain amyloid in male Alzheimer’s mice. Lastly, a comparison of single dose versus six smaller, fractionated doses of the equivalent amount of total iron irradiation in male Alzheimer’s mice, using a new genetic knockin mouse model, revealed that fractionated dosing induced fewer detrimental effects than a single larger dose. For example, spatial memory deficits were observed following a single but not fractionated dose of iron irradiation. Neither single nor fractionated iron dosing altered brain amyloid levels in this new mouse model.

There are no data sets for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Intraocular Pressure
parameter_html: Intraocular pressure (IOP)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Mader, ThomasCo-Investigator: Bagian, JamesCo-Investigator: Charles, JohnCo-Investigator: Meehan, RichardCo-Investigator: Taylor, Gerald
image_name: STS-44 Crewmember Using a Tono Pen
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been shown to be an objective and quantitative measure of fluid shifts toward the head in the 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest model of microgravity. However, insufficient numbers of measurements have been made in microgravity to correlate bed rest changes with changes that occur in weightlessness.

A study by Mader and Meehan (Mader et al., 1990) has quantified IOP changes that occurred with a 10-degree whole body head-down tilt over 48 hours. An immediate rise in IOP was documented upon assuming the head-down position. For the next 48 hours, variations in IOP were observed. Upon resuming the sitting position, there was a significant drop in IOP below the initial sitting values. The results of this study support the theory that distension of the retinal veins is a mechanism for the sudden changes in IOP that occur with changes in position. Assuming that head-down tilt is a valid model for fluid shifts in microgravity, the results from this study predict a similar sustained IOP increase in microgravity and a corresponding temporary drop in IOP (to below preflight values) upon return to Earth. Significant increases in IOP could result in visual impairment affecting crew performance and operations.

This study was designed to test the following hypothesis: Intraocular pressures will rise immediately upon entering microgravity due to fluid shifts toward the head, and will drop to below preflight levels upon return to 1-G. The objectives of this study were:

1. To establish a database of changes in intraocular pressures that can be used to evaluate crew health,
2. To validate 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest as a model for fluid shifts toward the head in microgravity,
3. To facilitate the interpretation of data by providing a quantitative measure of microgravity induced fluid shifts toward the head,
4. To validate the hand-held tonometer as an effective tool for diagnostic and scientific data collection that can be used in on orbit investigations.

APPROACH:
A series of measurements were taken (on one eye only) preflight at Launch-6 (L-6) weeks, L-4 weeks, and L-10 days (dates are approximate) using the Tono-Pen (a clinical instrument commonly used by non-physicians in an ophthalmologist's office for measuring IOP). All preflight measurements were taken with the subject in the seated position. During flight, measurements were taken as soon as possible on orbit, post-sleep on flight day (FD) 2 and on the final flight day post sleep. Additional measurements were desired on orbit (pre- and post sleep), but were optional. Postflight measurements were taken at return (R)+0 and during the postflight physical on R+3.

One drop of the short-activity topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5 percent) was instilled into the left eye and the subject instructed to look straight ahead. During flight, the drop of proparacaine was brought into contact with the lower conjunctival fornice to be absorbed onto the cornea by capillary action.

The operator performed the following steps:

1. Replaced the tonometer tip cover.
2. Instilled one drop of proparacaine into left eye.
3. Gently tapped the cornea 3-6 times until a beep is heard.
4. Recorded the data displayed on the Tono-Pen LCD screen.
5. Repeated the procedure 5 times.

Measurements were taken in the subject's left eye at each data collection point (in prior studies, there have been no significant differences between the measurements taken in 2 healthy eyes of an individual). The data collection sessions were approximately 5 minutes per subject; however, 15 minutes was scheduled to allow for the effects of the proparacaine to abate (the anesthetic deadens the eye for approximately 15 minutes). Neither the anesthetic nor the pressure measurement with the Tono-Pen caused discomfort to the eye when used properly.

RESULTS:
Acceptable data was acquired from 9 subjects on missions STS-31, 32, 34, 41, 52 and 53. Sufficient data was not collected on STS-33, 44, and 50. There was a mean increase in intraocular pressure during the first two days of space flight. This increase of approximately 20 percent above baseline values decreased during the remainder of the flight but was elevated above baselines on landing day.

experiment_title: Phoenix Scout Lander: Countermeasures Testbed for Spaceflight Ground Controllers
parameter_html:
Fatigue
Light exposure
Performance
Sleep
Work hours
Circadian rhythm
investigators: Principal Investigator: Barger, LauraCo-Investigator: Andrea, VincentCo-Investigator: Brainard, GeorgeCo-Investigator: Gilliland, KirbyCo-Investigator: Lockley, StevenCo-Investigator: Sipes, Walter
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A multi-institutional team of investigators provided fatigue management education to the scientists and engineers working on the Mars Phoenix Lander project. This project was funded by NASA/JSC Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) research program element and provided an operational opportunity, in a Mars Time Analog, to evaluate countermeasures in a real-time, field setting. Investigators sought to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of a photic countermeasure used to treat fatigue, circadian misalignment, and sleep loss associated with the Phoenix Mars Lander mission.

The proposed research could have significant implications for both sleep disorders medicine and space life sciences. The results of the proposed research could lead to the development of a new treatment regimen for sleep disturbances of various etiologies during space flight missions, where crewmembers, mission controllers, and support personnel are scheduled to live on non-24 hour days, which could enable these individuals to avoid the decrements in alertness and performance associated with sleep deprivation.

APPROACH:
The Phoenix spacecraft landed on Mars on May 25, 2008 and the scientists and engineers supporting the Phoenix Mars Lander worked on a Mars sol schedule until August 11, 2008 when the official schedule reverted to an Earth schedule. A multi-institutional team of investigators provided fatigue management education to the scientists and engineers working on the Mars Phoenix Lander project. The investigators also recruited 19 subjects to participate in a research study to investigate the work hours, sleep, circadian rhythmicity, and performance of individuals living on a Mars sol schedule in an operational environment. Investigators sought to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of countermeasures used to treat fatigue, circadian misalignment, and sleep loss associated with the Phoenix Mars Lander mission.

Investigators provided three educational sessions to the scientists, engineers, and support personnel working on the Phoenix Mars Lander project in the week prior to the mission. During those 1-hour sessions, the scientific team provided information on sleep, circadian rhythms, and appropriate countermeasures to facilitate entrainment to a Mars sol schedule and to maximize alertness and performance during work hours.

Investigators provided a blue light box to research subjects as well as instructions for when to seek and avoid light to facilitate entrainment to the Mars sol schedule. Ocular light exposure of a specific narrowband wavelength (±30 nm half-peak bandwidths) was encouraged using a light delivery system developed by Apollo Light Systems Inc., (American Fork, UT).

Research subjects continuously wore actigraphs on their wrists to monitor sleep and light exposure. They completed daily logs indicating work times and the fatigue countermeasures they used, and provided subjective evaluations of sleep and alertness. Subjects also accomplished daily performance testing and completed 48-hour urine collections about every two weeks to permit analysis of a melatonin conjugate to estimate circadian timing.

Subjects wore a Motionlogger on their wrists throughout the study period to provide sleep/wake activity and light exposure information. Each subject was given a personal digital assistant that contained two programs: a sleep-work log that was completed each day and a 5-minute version of the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) that was completed twice per day. Subjects were requested to complete the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM4) at the beginning and end of each work shift. The ANAM battery also included a mood scale.

RESULTS:
Nineteen subjects completed the study, although data collection was abbreviated in some subjects who traveled throughout the data collection period. The Mars Phoenix Lander project provided an operational opportunity, in a Mars Time Analog, to evaluate countermeasures in a real-time, field setting.

Ocular light exposure of a specific narrowband wavelength (±30 nm half-peak bandwidths) was encouraged using a light delivery system developed by Apollo Light Systems Inc., (American Fork, UT).

Research subjects continuously wore actigraphs on their wrists to monitor sleep and light exposure. They completed daily logs indicating work times and the fatigue countermeasures they used, and provided subjective evaluations of sleep and alertness. Subjects also accomplished daily performance testing and completed 48-hour urine collections about every two weeks to permit analysis of a melatonin conjugate to estimate circadian timing.

Subjects wore a Motionlogger on their wrists throughout the study period to provide sleep/wake activity and light exposure information. Each subject was given a personal digital assistant that contained two programs: a sleep-work log that was completed each day and a 5-minute version of the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) that was completed twice per day. Subjects were requested to complete the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM4) at the beginning and end of each work shift. The ANAM battery also included a mood scale.

RESULTS:
Nineteen subjects completed the study, although data collection was abbreviated in some subjects who traveled throughout the data collection period. The Mars Phoenix Lander project provided an operational opportunity, in a Mars Time Analog, to evaluate countermeasures in a real-time, field setting.

image_name: Leg Volume Measurements on Skylab and ASTP
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this investigation was to determine the response of the cardiovascular system to weightlessness. However, during reentry, the crew was exposed to toxic gases (mostly nitrogen tetroxide). Because of this episode during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP), most planned postflight evaluations were curtailed, altered or deleted.

APPROACH:
Cardiovascular evaluations were performed on each of the crewmen 45, 30, and 15 days prior to launch (L-45, 30, and 15). The following parameters were measured:

1. Orthostatic intolerance by lower body negative pressure (LBNP) including heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, percentage change in calf volume, systolic time intervals, and vectorcardiograms (VCGs)
2. Heart size by posterior-anterior chest x-rays (L-15 only)
3. Resting (supine) leg volume
4. Echocardiogram

The postflight protocol consisted of:
1. LBNP test performed on recovery day (R+0) on one subject.
2. Chest x-rays
3. Leg volume measurements.

The test protocol for LBNP consisted of following six evaluation periods:
1. Supine resting in the LBNP for five minutes
2. Up to 25 mm Hg negative pressure for two minutes
3. 30 to 35 mm Hg negative pressure for three minutes
4. 40 mm Hg negative pressure for five minutes
5. 50 mm Hg negative pressure for five minutes
6. Recovery supine in LBNP device for five minutes

LBNP level, heart rate, ECG or VCG, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure were monitored continuously. Age, body weight, body temperature, duration of sleep, time since sleep, time since last meal, amount of fluid intake, time of day, ambient temperature, and environmental test conditions were also noted.

RESULTS:
During LBNP, time of day, ambient and LBNP temperature, time since last meal, and amount of sleep were all nominal and within desired limits of experimental control. No results were considered beyond acceptable limits. Preflight, one subject experienced one episode of presyncope during the later portion of the 40 mm Hg protocol at L-15. Postflight, only one subject was evaluated by LBNP, this occurring approximately 2 hours 20 minutes after recovery. Two minutes into the 50 mm Hg level of LBNP, the protocol was terminated due to progressively declining blood pressure. The crewmen vehemently denied any associated symptomology. This postflight measurement was made prior to the decision to cease all nondiagnostic and nonclinical testing. This decision was made in response to the medical complications arising from the crew exposure to the toxic gases during reentry.

Because LBNP recordings scheduled immediately after flight were deleted, no useful information was obtained from systolic time intervals, echocardiograms, or VCGs. Strictly resting VCGs were taken on recovery day in conjunction with clinical ECGs. All tracings were considered to within normal limits. One crewmember experienced occasional premature supraventricular beats similar to those observed before flight.

Chest x-rays provided heart size determinations by cardiothoracic (C/T) ratios. No notable or consistent findings developed, but this data must be considered in the light of significant postflight pulmonary involvement.

Apart from the noxious gas event with the recovery of the ASTP crewmen and their ensuing pulmonary consequences, no findings would lead to conclusions different from that reached with all previous US manned space missions: a modest postflight orthostatic intolerance without operational significance was demonstrated.

experiment_title: Model-based Support for Crew Activity Planning

Eye fixations
Gaze duration
Performance
Time to complete
investigators: Principal Investigator: Remington, RogerCo-Investigator: Matessa, Michael
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigators proposed to leverage previous research to provide a tool that will allow mission planners to easily construct a CPM-GOMS model of crew activities. The resulting model will enable predictions of the time required to complete common, routine tasks using parameters determined from the existing literature on human performance. The reduction in time to model will now make it feasible to model and simulate performance on several candidate task designs with varying interfaces. The reduction in time to model will now make it feasible to model and simulate performance on several candidate task designs with varying interfaces.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
Experiment 1- Multifunction Electronic Display System (MEDS ) : An experiment was run by the Intelligent Spacecraft Interface Systems (ISIS) lab at NASA Ames Research Center using the Space Shuttle Cockpit Simulator to examine the performance of novice and expert shuttle operators in handling single and multiple malfunctions. The experiment was used to test the hypothesis that reusable templates could predict performance of different participant populations in different workload conditions (low workload for single malfunction trials and high workload for multiple malfunction trials). Five former airlines captains with an average of 15,000 flight hours experience participated in the novice condition. Five current astronauts with a minimum of two years of training participated in the expert condition.

Each trial simulated the ascent phase of shuttle operations, starting from launch to Main Engine Cut-Off (MECO) and lasting 8 minutes and 30 seconds of simulated mission elapsed time. In the single malfunction condition, a main engine malfunction was inserted. In the multiple malfunction condition, a combination of helium system regulator failure, General Purpose Computer failure, and coolant system failure malfunctions were inserted. The Flight Data File procedure checklist, which lists all the steps required to recover from the malfunctions, was provided to the subjects during the simulation. Eye fixations were analyzed on regions of interest relevant to solving malfunctions.

Conclusions: The experiment tested the hypothesis that reusable templates could successfully predict performance of different participant populations in different experimental conditions. The phrase-reading template made generally good predictions of gaze durations for pilots and astronauts in the single malfunction condition, but there are some noticeable differences. The template represents the process of identifying visual information, but does not include the time to search for the information. The increased gaze time on the switch panel for the pilots relative to the model may represent some search, as the switch panel contains many similar-looking switches. The template also assumes that all information at a location is processed only once. The decreased gaze time on procedures for the astronauts relative to the template may represent the astronaut reading only a relevant subset of the procedure. Likewise, the increased gaze time on procedures for the pilots relative to the template may be due to the pilots reading parts of the procedure more than once. The phrase-reading template made very good predictions of astronaut gaze duration in the multiple malfunction condition, showing that the template generalizes across workload conditions.

For the screen touch template, there were not enough data points to evaluate generality across population or workload conditions. When creating the screen touch template, it was assumed that eye fixations were made before touching the screen. Close examination of the data suggests this may be incorrect and that some screen touches may be made without fixations.

Experiment 2 – new Cockpit Avionics Upgrade (CAU) : The phrase-reading and screen-touching templates were used to make predictions for an experiment comparing original CAU displays to new CAU in sessions with single or multiple malfunctions. The time for initial finding a malfunction page in the flight data file (FDF ) procedures was calculated as gazes at 3.5 (out of 7 possible) tabs plus a gaze to read the malfunction heading for a total of (3.5+1) x 470 = 2115 msec. The time for subsequently finding the correct place on the FDF page after looking at the screen was calculated as an orienting gaze to the FDF and a gaze to a finger keeping place on the page for a total of 2 x 470 = 940 msec. The time for reading information on the screen after looking at the FDF include an extra orienting gaze to the screen.

Conclusions: The model assumes the pilots are well-practiced in the procedures. The increased times of the pilots for the first switch throw of procedures may indicate task orientation that is not represented in the model. From analysis of pilot speech, the last switch throw of the single malfunction procedure is sometimes forgotten in the original CAU condition until a later time, and this forgetting is not part of the model. These initial and final increased times are not seen in performance with single malfunction procedures with newCAU, which may assist in task orienting and remembering. In multiple-malfunction procedures, newCAU appears to lessen the increase of initial time due to task orientation.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As evidenced by Skylab and Mir missions, bone loss, which can increase the risk of fracture by weakening the skeleton, is an established medical risk in long-duration spaceflight. Moreover, there is little information about the extent to which the lost bone is recovered after spaceflight. Almost all of the measurements of bone loss and recovery have utilized an imaging technique called Dual X-Ray Absorptimetry (DXA). DXA systems are specially calibrated x-ray devices which measure the mass of an entire bone (e.g., a hip or a vertebrae). This approach has two limitations. First, it computes the summed mass of a given bone and cannot look separately at the porous inner core of the bone (trabecular bone) and the outer sheath which surrounds the core (cortical bone). Studies of osteoporosis and other bone diseases show that cortical and trabecular bone mass may underestimate the change in one of the components. A second limitation is that DXA computes the bone mass over a large volume of bone. If the loss of bone is localized in a small sub-region, the DXA image will detect a smaller change averaged over a large volume.

With the addition of Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) and Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) techniques, this study will provide the first information on spaceflight-related compartmental bone loss (magnitude and distribution) in the axial skeleton and on the extent to which lost bone is recovered in the year following return. Furthermore, this study will have implications for the frequency of assignment to long duration missions and for the health of the astronauts in older age. The results may also be of use in the design of exercise or pharmacological countermeasures to prevent bone loss.

Comparison of QCT bone mineral density (hip and spine) between astronauts and healthy normal subjects will help to improve understanding of the prevalence of osteoporosis between different race and gender sub-groups.

The objective of the experiment is to determine the compartmental and sub-regional distribution of bone loss in the spine and hip in long-duration spaceflight and to assess how bone is recovered after return. The extent to which the spaceflight-induced changes in bone distribution compare to the spread of bone mineral density (BMD) measures in healthy men and women and the validity of calcaneal Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) will also be determined.

APPROACH:
In an earlier study, areal BMD (aBMD) measurements by DXA showed that cosmonauts making flights of 4- to 12-month duration on the Soviet/Russian MIR spacecraft lost bone at an average rate of 1% per month from the spine and 1.5% per month from the hip. However, because DXA measurements represent the sum of the cortical and trabecular compartments, there is no direct information on how these bone envelopes are affected by spaceflight. To address this, the investigators performed a study of 16 crewmembers (male and female, age range 40–55 years) on long-duration missions (4–6 months) on the International Space Station (ISS). DXA was used to obtain aBMD of the hip and spine and volumetric QCT (vQCT) to assess integral, cortical, and trabecular volumetric BMD (vBMD) in the hip and spine. In the heel, DXA was used to measure aBMD, and quantitative ultrasound (QUS)was used to measure speed of sound (SOS) and broadband ultrasound attenuation (BUA).

These techniques can examine the trabecular and cortical bone separately and can determine whether the loss is localized in a small sub-region of the bone. Bone loss in the spine and hip was determined by comparing preflight and postflight QCT measurements. Bone recovery was assessed by comparing QCT data taken immediately postflight and one year after return. The QCT results were compared with Dual X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) measurements taken at these time points. These measurements include DXA of the spine, hip, and heel and QUS of the heel. Finally, to determine how the bone loss in space compares to the range of bone density values in a normal adult population, astronaut QCT measurements in the spine and hip were compared to measurements of 120 healthy normal control subjects consisting of healthy black and white males and females between ages of 35-45.

For the DXA measurements, the lumbar spine, hip and heel were scanned. Following completion of the DXA scan, the subject underwent hip and spine QCT scans, followed by a QUS scan of the heel. DXA, QCT, and QUS scans were performed once preflight in the year before launch and two times postflight. There were no inflight measurements taken.

RESULTS:
There was no compartment-specific loss of bone in the spine. Cortical bone mineral loss in the hip occurred primarily by endocortical thinning. aBMD was lost at rates of 0.9% per month at the spine (p<0.001) and 1.4–1.5% per month at the hip (p<0.001). Spinal integral vBMD was lost at a rate of 0.9% per month (p<0.001), and trabecular vBMD was lost at 0.7% per month (p<0.05). In contrast to earlier reports, these changes were generalized across the vertebrae and not focused in the posterior elements. In the hip, integral, cortical, and trabecular vBMD was lost at rates of 1.2–1.5% per month (p<0.0001), 0.4–0.5% per month (p<0.01), and 2.2–2.7% per month (p<0.001), respectively. The cortical bone loss in the hip occurred primarily by cortical thinning. Calcaneal aBMD measurements by DXA showed smaller mean losses (0.4% per month) than hip or spine measurements, with SOS and BUA showing no change. In summary, the results show that ISS crewmembers, on average, experience substantial loss of both trabecular and cortical bone in the hip and somewhat smaller losses in the spine. These results do not support the use of calcaneal aBMD or QUS measurements as surrogate measures to estimate changes in the central skeleton.

Proximal femoral bone mass was substantially recovered in the year after spaceflight, but measures of vBMD and estimated bone strength showed only partial recovery. The recovery of BMC, in the absence of a comparable increase in vBMD, was explained by increases in bone volume and CSA during the year after spaceflight. The investigator concludes that adaptation of the proximal femur to reloading entailed an increase in bone size and an incomplete recovery of vBMD. The data indicate that recovery of skeletal density after long-duration space missions may exceed 1 year and supports the evidence in the aging literature for periosteal apposition as a compensatory response for bone loss. The extent to which this compensatory effect protects against fracture remains to be seen.

OBJECTIVES:
As evidenced by Skylab and Mir missions, bone loss, which can increase the risk of fracture by weakening the skeleton, is an established medical risk in long-duration spaceflight. Moreover, there is little information about the extent to which the lost bone is recovered after spaceflight. Almost all of the measurements of bone loss and recovery have utilized an imaging technique called Dual X-Ray Absorptimetry (DXA). DXA systems are specially calibrated x-ray devices which measure the mass of an entire bone (e.g., a hip or a vertebrae). This approach has two limitations. First, it computes the summed mass of a given bone and cannot look separately at the porous inner core of the bone (trabecular bone) and the outer sheath which surrounds the core (cortical bone). Studies of osteoporosis and other bone diseases show that cortical and trabecular bone mass may underestimate the change in one of the components. A second limitation is that DXA computes the bone mass over a large volume of bone. If the loss of bone is localized in a small sub-region, the DXA image will detect a smaller change averaged over a large volume.

With the addition of Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) and Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) techniques, this study will provide the first information on spaceflight-related compartmental bone loss (magnitude and distribution) in the axial skeleton and on the extent to which lost bone is recovered in the year following return. Furthermore, this study will have implications for the frequency of assignment to long duration missions and for the health of the astronauts in older age. The results may also be of use in the design of exercise or pharmacological countermeasures to prevent bone loss.

Comparison of QCT bone mineral density (hip and spine) between astronauts and healthy normal subjects will help to improve understanding of the prevalence of osteoporosis between different race and gender sub-groups.

The objective of the experiment is to determine the compartmental and sub-regional distribution of bone loss in the spine and hip in long-duration spaceflight and to assess how bone is recovered after return. The extent to which the spaceflight-induced changes in bone distribution compare to the spread of bone mineral density (BMD) measures in healthy men and women and the validity of calcaneal Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) will also be determined.

APPROACH:
In an earlier study, areal BMD (aBMD) measurements by DXA showed that cosmonauts making flights of 4- to 12-month duration on the Soviet/Russian MIR spacecraft lost bone at an average rate of 1% per month from the spine and 1.5% per month from the hip. However, because DXA measurements represent the sum of the cortical and trabecular compartments, there is no direct information on how these bone envelopes are affected by spaceflight. To address this, the investigators performed a study of 16 crewmembers (male and female, age range 40–55 years) on long-duration missions (4–6 months) on the International Space Station (ISS). DXA was used to obtain aBMD of the hip and spine and volumetric QCT (vQCT) to assess integral, cortical, and trabecular volumetric BMD (vBMD) in the hip and spine. In the heel, DXA was used to measure aBMD, and quantitative ultrasound (QUS)was used to measure speed of sound (SOS) and broadband ultrasound attenuation (BUA).

These techniques can examine the trabecular and cortical bone separately and can determine whether the loss is localized in a small sub-region of the bone. Bone loss in the spine and hip was determined by comparing preflight and postflight QCT measurements. Bone recovery was assessed by comparing QCT data taken immediately postflight and one year after return. The QCT results were compared with Dual X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) measurements taken at these time points. These measurements include DXA of the spine, hip, and heel and QUS of the heel. Finally, to determine how the bone loss in space compares to the range of bone density values in a normal adult population, astronaut QCT measurements in the spine and hip were compared to measurements of 120 healthy normal control subjects consisting of healthy black and white males and females between ages of 35-45.

For the DXA measurements, the lumbar spine, hip and heel were scanned. Following completion of the DXA scan, the subject underwent hip and spine QCT scans, followed by a QUS scan of the heel. DXA, QCT, and QUS scans were performed once preflight in the year before launch and two times postflight. There were no inflight measurements taken.

There was no compartment-specific loss of bone in the spine. Cortical bone mineral loss in the hip occurred primarily by endocortical thinning. aBMD was lost at rates of 0.9% per month at the spine (p<0.001) and 1.4–1.5% per month at the hip (p<0.001). Spinal integral vBMD was lost at a rate of 0.9% per month (p<0.001), and trabecular vBMD was lost at 0.7% per month (p<0.05). In contrast to earlier reports, these changes were generalized across the vertebrae and not focused in the posterior elements. In the hip, integral, cortical, and trabecular vBMD was lost at rates of 1.2–1.5% per month (p<0.0001), 0.4–0.5% per month (p<0.01), and 2.2–2.7% per month (p<0.001), respectively. The cortical bone loss in the hip occurred primarily by cortical thinning. Calcaneal aBMD measurements by DXA showed smaller mean losses (0.4% per month) than hip or spine measurements, with SOS and BUA showing no change. In summary, the results show that ISS crewmembers, on average, experience substantial loss of both trabecular and cortical bone in the hip and somewhat smaller losses in the spine. These results do not support the use of calcaneal aBMD or QUS measurements as surrogate measures to estimate changes in the central skeleton.

Proximal femoral bone mass was substantially recovered in the year after spaceflight, but measures of vBMD and estimated bone strength showed only partial recovery. The recovery of BMC, in the absence of a comparable increase in vBMD, was explained by increases in bone volume and CSA during the year after spaceflight. The investigator concludes that adaptation of the proximal femur to reloading entailed an increase in bone size and an incomplete recovery of vBMD. The data indicate that recovery of skeletal density after long-duration space missions may exceed 1 year and supports the evidence in the aging literature for periosteal apposition as a compensatory response for bone loss. The extent to which this compensatory effect protects against fracture remains to be seen.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Study 1: The purpose of the first study is to investigate the effect of paralysis on bone density and structural parameters of the tibia. Study 2: The purpose of the second study was to investigate bone mass and structure in the tibia after resection of the fibula.

APPROACH:
Study 1: were two male and two female adults aged 17-32 years who had sustained a spinal cord injury at least 4 years prior to the study. Cross-sectional structural parameters including area (A), principal area moments of inertia (Imax, Imin), polar area moments of inertia (J), and major principal axis orientation of the tibia and fibula were computed every millimeter along the scan length for the three scans of the leg using the lower energy for its larger dynamic range. Study 2: Subjects who had undergone a fibular resection at least 2 years earlier were recruited (n=3). Fibular resection was carried out in all 3 men to remedy avascular necrosis in the hip. In addition to anthropomorphic data (BW, Ht, tibial length) a set of 3 scans of the tibia on right and left sides as above was done as well as a DXA scan of the right and left calcaneus to measure areal bone density, an indication of loading symmetry. Structural parameters of the tibia and fibula as enumerated above were performed on one leg and on the tibia of the other leg.

RESULTS:
Study 1: Body weights in paraplegics were greater than in controls. Two male subjects had lower values for cross-sectional areas and density as well as lower structural parameters in the midshaft, distal tibia and femoral midshaft. Data supporting bone loss in the two female paraplegics was not convincing except at the tibial midshaft where the data was not scaled to body size. In one male subject, cross sectional areas and principal moments of inertia of the tibia were not symmetrical. Conclusions of study 1: The large variation in results of just a few subjects point to the need for longitudinal studies and more subjects to definitively measure changes in structural parameters due to paralysis and unloading. Study 2: Subject 1. The cross-sectional area of the tibia on the side of the fibular resection (rt) was increased 2% at the midshaft and 33% at the distal third compared to the unaffected tibia. The principal and polar moments of inertia on the right tibia were increased 51% and 89% at the midshaft and distal third, respectively. The midshaft was also more symmetric, but not the distal section. Subject 2: The tibia on the resected side (left) showed an increase in cross-sectional area (8% at midshaft and 10% at distal third) and an increased minimum moment of inertia of 22 % in the mid and 47% in the distal third. Imax increased by 9% in both sites. Subject 3: The increases in the cross-sectional area were 32% at the mid and 27% at the distal third, compared to the unaffected left side. Imin increased by 74% and 95% at the distal third and Imax increased 15 and 24 % in the same respective regions, an indication the tibia is more symmetric. Calcaneal density was not consistent in the 3 subjects and showed R and L differences outside the 0.6% observed in normal men. Calcaneal density was less (by 5.7 and 8 %) in the affected than the unaffected limb in two subjects who also had functional problems in gait. The lower heel density may be an indication of less load on the affected limb and was not present in the subject who reported normal gait and skiing activity post surgery. Conclusions: All three subjects with fibular resection showed an increase in cross-sectional area as well as structural parameters related to stiffness and strength, an indication of increased loading of the tibia from the ipsilateral side of the fibular resection resulting in increased bone deposition. This points to a role of the fibula in driving the shape of the tibia cross-section and in load bearing.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microgravity may have a deconditioning effect on the capacity to perform aerobic exercise. Regular aerobic exercise during space flight might help to maintain aerobic capacity. Changes in the body's protein, mineral, and water content might occur during space flight and could contribute to a decline in aerobic performance.

The objectives of this study were:
(1) to measure aerobic exercise capacity before and after space flight
(2) to investigate the use of aerobic exercise during flight to reduce the severity of postflight aerobic deconditioning
(3) to test a new method for monitoring changes in the protein, mineral, and water content of the body before and after space flight
(4) to determine how decreases in aerobic capacity are related to changes in body composition.

APPROACH:
The exercise tests were performed on a treadmill by four astronauts, on a rower by three astronauts, and on a cycle ergometer by 10 astronauts. The astronauts were instructed to exercise to the point of fatigue. Heart rate, heart rhythm, and blood pressure were monitored during the tests. Aerobic capacity was defined as the peak oxygen consumption during the tests and was measured with a Q-Plex system. The Q-Plex system is a computer driven device for cardiac, respiratory, and rehabilitation stress test (similar to an EKG stress monitor). The composition of exhaled air was analyzed either with a mass spectrometer preflight or with zirconium oxide and infrared sensors postflight.

Twenty astronauts on missions of 5 to 17 days' duration completed one or two exercise tests before space flight and another test on landing day. Seventeen of the astronauts exercised during the flight, using a rower (three astronauts), a cycle ergometer (10) or a treadmill (four) that had a harness and tether to simulate gravity. They followed continuous (one) or interval (16) exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 65 to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. Some subjects had difficulty achieving these heart rates on the treadmill. A monitor displayed and recorded the heart rate. The total exercise performed during flight was quantified by multiplying the percentage of the maximal heart rate by the number of minutes per exercise session and by the number of sessions per week.

The body composition of 10 of the astronauts was analyzed preflight and on R+2 after flights lasting seven to 16 days. Extracellular water, intracellular water, total body fat, percent fat, and fat-free mass were derived from body weight, body density, and body water. Body density was determined by weighing the astronauts under water and correcting for residual lung volume. Body water was determined from a previously validated bioelectrical response spectroscopy model to avoid taking the multiple blood samples and using the radioactive tracers or other tracers that are usual for this purpose. Total body protein and mineral contents were derived from total body water and body density by using a mathematical model that assumes the body is made up of three compartments (fat, water, and dry lean mass).

The effects of changes in body composition on aerobic capacity were studied in eight astronauts from 7- to 16-day missions. Preflight and R+0 or R+2, their body composition was analyzed by the methods described above, and their aerobic capacity was determined in treadmill exercise tests on the same day, after the body composition measurements.

RESULTS:
Postflight peak oxygen consumption during the exercise tests was 13% lower than that of the astronauts who did not exercise preflight. The exercise test results from this DSO were analyzed together with those from DSO 476, and the combined results indicated that the capacity to perform aerobic exercise was reduced after space flight, but that aerobic exercise during flight attenuated this effect. The results did not indicate the optimal exercise device or protocol for maintaining aerobic capacity.

Results of the analysis of body composition showed that the astronauts lost about two percent of their fat-free mass, about three percent of their intracellular water and about four percent of their total body protein and minerals from preflight to postflight. Little change occurred in extracellular water or in fat. The decrease in intracellular water may have been largely due to the loss of proteins and minerals, because differences in the concentrations of dissolved proteins and minerals cause water to move by osmosis. These losses could affect the performance or health of the astronauts during or after space flight.

The eight astronauts who underwent both body composition analysis and exercise testing lost 12% of their aerobic capacity from preflight to postflight. Statistical analysis of covariance, which was performed to separate the effects of the various body composition variables, showed that the decreases in aerobic capacity were due at least in part to decreases in total body protein. The protein loss most likely represented a loss of muscle mass.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to assess the renal stone-forming potential of humans as a function of mission duration and to determine how long after space flight the increased risk exists. In addition to the analyses of mineral components, this study was designed to determine levels of the naturally occurring urinary protein inhibitors of calcium crystallization. This investigation provides a direct understanding of and overcoming human limitations in space that may affect crew health and potentially mission success. If a crewmember were to develop a kidney stone, only supportive action is possible at this time. Medical support would involve pain relief through on-board medication with the hope that the crewmember would pass the stone over time. The afflicted crewmember may not be able to perform his/her duties or, more significant, cause the mission to be aborted and return to Earth.

Previous data have demonstrated that human exposure to the microgravity environment of space increases the risk of renal stone development during and immediately after space flight. In-flight assessment has shown a greater risk of calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate and sodium urate stones. Postflight changes to the urinary chemical composition increase the risk of uric acid and calcium oxalate stone formation.

Astronauts in the U.S. program have experienced multiple postflight stone events (2 crewmembers had 2 postflight stones). The length of time for appearance of symptomatic stone formation ranged from 9-120 months. Six of these postflight stones have occurred since 1994 and have taken place concurrently with the beginning of the extended shuttle missions of greater than 12 days in space. Discussions with Russian medical science investigators have noted multiple stone events among cosmonauts, with one in-flight renal stone episode nearly causing the crewmember to abort the mission. These epidemiologic data may suggest that that risk of stone formation may extend beyond the testing period implemented during this investigation in some crewmembers.

APPROACH:
Potassium citrate (K-cit), a proven Earth-based therapy to minimize calcium-containing renal stone development, was tested during space flight as a countermeasure to reduce the risk of renal stone formation. Preflight baseline data collection sessions were performed at approximately L-180, L-60 and L-45 days. Two 10 mEq potassium citrate tablets (total dose 20 mEq) or placebo were ingested daily with the evening meal beginning three days before launch, all days during flight, and following landing through R+14. Urine was collected before, during, and after flight. Food, fluid, exercise, and medications were monitored before and during the urine collection period in order to assess environmental influences other than microgravity. During ISS operations, 24 hour urine collections and 48 hour dietary monitoring were performed early (< FD 30), mid-mission (FD30-FD100), and late (within 30 days of landing). Postflight urine and dietary monitoring were performed at approximately R+0-2, R+7 and R+14 days.

Subjects were active astronauts and cosmonauts who were certified for space flight. There were no gender specific requirements, therefore both male and female crewmembers participated in this study. This investigation was designed as a double blind study with neither the investigators nor the subjects knowing whether the subjects were ingesting potassium citrate or placebo.

RESULTS:
This investigation was successfully completed by 19 crewmembers. The majority of renal stones are composed of calcium containing salts. The risk of calcium oxalate stone formation as determined by the urinary supersaturation of calcium oxalate was observed to be lower in the potassium citrate treated group. The decreased risk was evident during the in-flight and immediate postflight assessment sessions. The risk of calcium phosphate (brushite) risk followed the same trend observed with the risk of calcium oxalate stone formation.

This study also evaluated the effect of fluid intake and urinary output on the supersaturation of the urine and the potential risk of stone formation. Regarding the correlation between 24-hr urinary volume and the risk of calcium oxalate stone development, data indicate an inverse relationship between urine volume and risk of calcium oxalate stone formation.

Approval for elimination of the double blind requirement was received from NASA in December, 2005. As a result, the participating crewmembers ingested only potassium citrate as a countermeasure to the risk of renal stone formation. Data from all the ISS missions were combined for a detailed analysis involving statistical analysis and evaluation of the pharmacologic countermeasure to reduce the risk of stone formation.

Potassium citrate-treated crew members had decreased urinary calcium excretion and maintained the calcium oxalate supersaturation risk at preflight levels compared to that in controls. Increased urinary pH in the treatment group decreased the risk of uric acid stones. Results from this investigation suggest that supplementation with potassium citrate may decrease the risk of renal stone formation during and immediately after spaceflight.

As a result, the participating crewmembers ingested only potassium citrate as a countermeasure to the risk of renal stone formation. Data from all the ISS missions were combined for a detailed analysis involving statistical analysis and evaluation of the pharmacologic countermeasure to reduce the risk of stone formation.

Potassium citrate-treated crew members had decreased urinary calcium excretion and maintained the calcium oxalate supersaturation risk at preflight levels compared to that in controls. Increased urinary pH in the treatment group decreased the risk of uric acid stones. Results from this investigation suggest that supplementation with potassium citrate may decrease the risk of renal stone formation during and immediately after spaceflight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Maintaining crew health during extended periods in space can be complicated by contamination of the general living environment. High standards for air, water, and radiation shielding quality have been established to ensure the continued health and safety of long duration crews. Water provided for crew consumption has either been launched from the ground or produced in flight by the recycling of humidity condensate. Water delivered from Earth can be tested for microbial contaminants before leaving the ground, but the water produced on orbit must be analyzed to determine its potability. The water must therefore be tested for the presence of microbial contamination, such as bacteria and fungi. In the past, this analysis has been done in Earth-based laboratories after returning to Earth. This investigation allowed water testing in-flight by the crew. The Water Microbiological Monitor (WMM) was one of several technology demonstrations planned for the NASA-Mir missions that were aimed at developing and testing in-flight, the sampling kits needed to support quality assurance for future space platforms. Having the capability to conduct the analysis during the mission gives both the crew and researchers feedback about the quality of the water in a timely manner.

The experiment objectives were to quantify bacteria in potable and hygiene water in a space environment, characterize the microbial population of a reclaimed water system, and have a water microbiology analysis system ready for the International Space Station (ISS). Findings from this investigation will help in redesigning water-sampling hardware and microbial procedures for future routine application on the ISS. Successful completion of the proposed investigation was expected to validate technology for in-flight detection, quantitation and limited identification of waterborne bacteria. Lessons learned from this technology demonstration will be applied toward the development of the ISS Crew Health Care System (CheCS), which will ensure the maintenance of high water quality standards.

APPROACH:
Water samples were scheduled for collection and processed on flight days 15, 55, 85, 115, and 135 during the NASA 3, 4 and 5 missions. Samples were collected in Teflon bags, and known volumes were processed through a microbial capture device (MCD) contained in the Water Experiment Kit (WEK) using a syringe pump assembly. Each sample was processed through three MCDs, one with 10 ml of water, a second with 50 ml, and the third with 100 ml. A modified R3A nutrient broth growth medium was added to the MCD by syringe to cultivate microorganisms trapped on the filter. Mir sampling locations included the galley hot and cold water ports (reclaimed water) and the SVO-ZV port (ground-supplied water). MCDs were incubated at 25-35 degrees Celsius in an area of the spacecraft chosen by the crewmember to promote bacterial growth.

Cultures were examined after 2 and 5 days of incubation for bacterial growth. Growth on the filters was matched to a bacterial colony density chart, and results were recorded in the flight data file and on the MCD using a "Sharpie" marker. Video and photographic documentation of the bacterial colonies were also performed. After examination on the second day, MCDs were returned to the incubator. After incubation was complete (at 5 days), samples were stowed at ambient temperature in a return kit and returned to Earth for complete analysis. Aerobic bacteria and fungi were identified using a Vitek Automated Identification System, Biolog Automated Identification System, or by classical means. Species not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification.

RESULTS:
This investigation verified the ability of the WMM to provide the means to detect and quantify bacteria in potable and hygiene water supplies during spaceflight. A modified formulation of growth medium, designed specifically for this investigation, allowed visualization of microbes trapped on the filter membrane of the MCD. Colony density results were converted to bacterial concentrations per unit of water. The results from the three sample volumes (10 ml, 50 ml, 100 ml) were inconclusive. Theoretically, the microbial count would be correspondingly higher in larger volumes of water. The results recorded by crewmembers did not hold to this pattern; in some cases, the MCDs processed with 10 ml of water had higher counts than the corresponding MCDs processed with 50 or 100 ml volumes. However, approximately half of the MCDs processed during the NASA 3 mission were processed incorrectly, as indicated by the presence of residual water in the MCDs. Proper processing required that all water be evacuated from the MCD before the growth medium was added. Failure to remove all of the water produced an aqueous suspension of organisms, which made accurate quantitation with this device impossible. Improved procedures and training techniques for subsequent missions seem to have corrected the incorrect processing of samples. None of the MCDs processed during the NASA 4 mission contained residual water. Human factors were another probable influence on the accuracy of results. The NASA 4 crewmember reported difficulty in interpreting what was or was not bacterial growth. Samples were not collected during the NASA 5 mission as scheduled, because the water experiment kit was lost when the Spektr module depressurized and was sealed off after Mir collided with a Progress resupply vehicle.

This experiment also provided insight into the microbial characterization of a reclaimed water system. Analyses of the hot water samples indicated that the treatment train and final heating step of the Mir system was able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below the proposed US level of 100 colony forming units (CFU)/100 ml set for the International Space Station. The bacterial content of the cold reclaimed water supply did not exceed 125 CFU/100 ml; this count was within the Russian acceptability limit. The SVO-ZV ground-water supply contained the highest bacterial levels, but did not exceed 300 CFU/100 ml. Both the cold and SVO-ZV counts were slightly above the proposed US acceptability limit for the International Space Station, 100 CFU/100ml. The types of organisms recovered were consistent with those seen in previous analyses of Shuttle water and those seen in typical ground-water supplies. All water supplies were judged safe to drink.

Although the full configuration of hardware needed to process the samples was somewhat awkward to handle, the goal of limited in-flight water analysis was achieved. Only minor problems were encountered with a small number of MCDs. The method of attaching Luer-lok fittings proved to be inadequate. These fittings occasionally became detached from the MCD during sample processing. A modification of this attachment method has been initiated.
