experiment_title: Gene Expression Patterns Predictive of Radiation-Enhanced Colon Tumorigenesis: Diet as a Countermeasure
parameter_html:
PolyA, feces
PolyA mRNA
investigators: Principal Investigator: Turner, NancyPrincipal Investigator: Lupton, JoanneCo-Investigator: Braby, LeslieCo-Investigator: Carroll, RaymondCo-Investigator: Chapkin, RobertCo-Investigator: Ford, John
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is currently no reliable, non-invasive method to determine the response to radiation exposure and development of colon cancer throughout the disease process. One potential method to monitor changes in colonocyte gene expression that occur during the various stages of the disease is through global transcriptional profiling using exfoliated colonocyte mRNA. This proof of principle project has as its main goal the modification of existing protocols in order to improve the effectiveness of polyA isolation from feces in preparation for analysis of gene expression using microarray techniques.

Specific Aims
1. The first aim was to optimize polyA isolation and sample handling steps prior to array hybridization in order to develop a protocol that could reliably be used to measure gene expression from exfoliated colonocytes.
2. The second aim was to establish normalization procedures capable of handling the problem of sample degradation that occurs in fecal samples.

APPROACH:
Weanling Sprague-Dawley rats (n = 60) were provided one of two diets that contained either the combination of fish oil and pectin, or the combination of corn oil and cellulose. Half of the rats were exposed to 1 Gy of 1 GeV/nucleon Fe ions at Brookhaven National Laboratory 3 weeks after starting the experimental diets. All rats received injections of a colon-specific carcinogen (azoxymethane, AOM) on days corresponding to 10 and 17 after irradiation. Fecal samples were collected 7, 14 and 28 weeks after the last AOM injection. Fecal pellets were collected soon after defecation, stored in RNA protection buffer and frozen (-80 Celsius) until processed.

RESULTS:
Modifications to the isolation and processing procedures for fecal polyA samples has resulted in highly improved quality and quantity of polyA that can be used for micorarray analysis of gene expression. We have developed a two-stage normalization procedure to process the data generated from the partially degraded RNA that is capable of handling this type of data, yet can be computed in a reasonable amount of time. Analysis of the data indicates there are strong effects of radiation on gene expression documented throughout this model of colon carcinogenesis, and that the effects can be tracked using a non-invasive procedure.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Palinkas, Lawrence
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space crews of exploration missions in the future will need to be more autonomous from mission control and act and operate independently, in part, due to the expectation that communication quality between the ground and exploration crews will be more limited by communication delays and other quality factors than on any mission to date. Communication delays and the impact these delays have on the quality of communications to the crew will create performance decrements if crews are not given adequate training and tools to support more autonomous operations. This study examined the impact of implementing a communication delay on the International Space Station (ISS) on individual and team factors and outcomes, including performance and related perceptions of autonomy.

Specifically, this study examined how interdependent teams interacted and performed tasks with and without delays in communications between the team elements. The tasks performed by the teams varied along two dimensions: 1) those that were either critical or not critical (“criticality”) and 2) those that were either novel or familiar (“novelty”). Tasks included variations in both dimensions as it is assumed that highly novel and highly critical tasks are similar to those that a team may encounter during a long-duration mission in which they have no prior training but must address. This study provided a preliminary understanding of the impact of communication delays on individual and team performance as well as insight into how teams perform and interact under autonomous conditions in the analog environment most comparable to deep space.

The overall aim of the study was to determine whether the communications delays (as an indicator of communication quality) likely to be experienced on a long-duration mission to an asteroid or to Mars will result in clinically or operationally significant decrements in crew performance and well-being on the ISS. Specifically, the investigators aimed to accomplish the following:

  1. Determine the feasibility and acceptability of conducting a study of communication delays on the ISS.
  2. Determine if there is an association between delays in communication (like those expected to be experienced during a Mars mission), individual and crew performance, and well-being.
  3. Determine whether this association is affected by task complexity (criticality and novelty), social support, perceived stress, and task autonomy.

APPROACH:
The study included three astronauts on the ISS. Participants also included 18 mission control support personnel. Participants performed 16 tasks, 8 under conditions of no delay in communications, and 8 under conditions of a 10 minute one-way delay. Tasks were designated by subject matter experts (SMEs) in collaboration with the Mission Operations Directorate (MOD) for monitoring based on their level of novelty (high/low) and criticality (high/low).

Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the astronaut participants approximately four months prior to mission launch. Participants were asked open-ended questions as to prior experience in working on a team. After each task, participating ISS crewmembers and mission support personnel were asked to complete post-task questionnaires that included questions about individual and team behavior, performance and mood. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the astronaut participants less than 21 days post-mission to obtain their opinions about feasibility of data collection, importance of delays in communications, and communication delay factors that influenced their well-being.

RESULTS:
The quantitative results suggest crew morale and the quality of communications were significantly reduced in communication delay tasks compared to control tasks. In addition, both quantitative and qualitative data suggest communication delays increased stress and frustration. However, no significant differences in individual, crew or team performance or autonomy were observed across control and delay tasks. The qualitative data expanded on these findings. The astronauts reported the quality of support from the ground support team was good regardless of whether or not there were communication delays. Furthermore, the performance-related challenges that were reported under situations of communication delays were not explicitly linked to individual or team failures, but rather involved operational outcomes and teamwork processes, such as reduced task efficiency and decreased situational awareness. Given these findings, future studies should consider including post-task questions that assess efficiency and team/task coordination issues.

Qualitative data from post-mission interviews also identified factors that contributed to performance and mood-related challenges of communication delays, including task-specific factors such as high task-related communication demands (either due to low crew autonomy or poor communication strategies), complex tasks, and time-critical tasks. The astronauts reported communication delays interfered with the crewmembers ability to receive the support they needed in a timely fashion, which in turn made it difficult to move forward with the task procedures, and importantly these challenges were amplified in tasks that involved high levels of back-and-forth communications. Given these findings, and the limited availability of crewmember time on the ISS, future studies should prioritize research time on the ISS to include tasks that are most likely to negatively impact individual and team outcomes.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment was designed to study the effects of space flight on both sensorimotor (especially vestibular) and cognitive functions (especially orientation.) Optimal human performance depends upon integrated sensorimotor and cognitive functions both of which are known to be exquisitely sensitive to loss of sleep. The main objective of this study was to investigate variations in sleep and dreaming over an extended period of space flight, with special attention to changes in sleep and dreaming associated with the vestibular adaptation that occurs with adaptation to microgravity, and readaptation to 1-G conditions. To achieve this, a sleep monitoring system was tested that could accurately identify periods of wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on-board the Mir space station.

APPROACH:
Five crewmembers completed measurements relating to the protocol before, during and after space flight. During each phase, the experiment was divided into approximately three 12-day segments called measurement blocks. The inflight measurement blocks were scheduled early in the mission (mission day 37-49), in the middle (MD 79-91) and at the end (MD 110-122) of the mission. This investigation was conducted for the first time as part of the NASA 4 and Russian Mir 23 missions with three crewmembers participating. The experiment protocols were repeated on the Mir 24 mission with two additional crewmembers.

In each of the 12-day blocks, test subjects monitored sleep by wearing an apparatus called a Night Headband. It consisted of a simple athletic headband into which a head movement sensor had been sewn, along with a self-adhesive eyelid movement sensor that attached to the surface of the upper eyelid. The sensors were connected by two cables to a wallet-sized recording unit called the Night Headband Monitor (NHM). Subjects wore the NHM in a supplied arm band or attached the unit to a nearby wall with Velcro. The NHM analyzed data from the sensors and could store up to 30 nights before transfer to a computer. Usually, data from the NHM was uploaded to a laptop computer daily and subsequently stored on disk. Data was stored as one-minute counts of the number of 250 ms epochs during which eye or head movement was detected.

Because the head movement sensor originally designed for the Night Headband utilized a gravity-dependent mercury switch, the sensor was redesigned as an inertial switch. The inertial switch had appropriate sensitivity in microgravity; no head movements were detected during quiet rest, but gentle rotations of the head were adequate to produce clear head movement signals. Inflight Night Headbands all had these inertial switches built into them; baseline data collection Night Headbands continued to use the mercury switch version.

Data was used to determine both the percent of sleep spent in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (REM %) and the absolute amount of time spent in REM sleep (REM time). The allowed testing of the hypotheses that REM % and REM time would increase during the period of adaptation to microgravity and then return to preflight baseline levels. It was also hypothesized that the REM % and REM time would again increase during the period of readaptation to normal gravity.

In addition to the objective sleep data described above, subjects were also asked to dictate dream reports into a pocket voice recorder at each awakening. Researchers hoped to observe a shift in the fictive vestibular and motor activity of the subject's dreams as he went through adaptation first to microgravity and then, on return, to normal gravity.

RESULTS:
Subjects recorded an average of 26 nights of sleep during the preflight period, 24 nights inflight, and 14 nights postflight during the postflight recovery period. All told, 317 nights of sleep data were recorded, of which 120 were collected inflight, between the 24th and 171st day in orbit. Sixty of the 120 nights were recorded more than three months into the flight. Analysis of data was made using repeated measures ANOVA's.

For all five subjects, REM sleep was severely diminished during flight. Both REM time and REM % were significantly diminished (REM time, F=20.5, p<0.001; REM %, F=16.5, p<0.002). On average, REM time was reduced by 53% and REM % was reduced by 35% inflight compared to preflight. All subjects showed at least a 40% reduction in REM time. In contrast, postflight rates were essentially the same as preflight, showing on average a 4% increase in both REM time and REM % compared to the preflight period. There was also decrease in total sleep time inflight (F=7.1, p<0.02). Inflight values were reduced by 27% on average, while postflight values were 0.3% higher. All subjects showed at least a 13% decrease in average nightly total sleep time inflight. This did not result from a decrease in time in bed (F=0.2, p=0.84); subjects spent on average 4% longer in bed while inflight. Rather it resulted from decreased sleep efficiency (F=24.1, p<0.005). Sleep efficiency dropped from a mean of 89% in the preflight period to 63% inflight.

The Night Headband Kit sleep system permitted more extensive sleep recording during space flight than had previously been possible. Data collected over 6 months of flight indicated that extended space flight leads to a consistent and pronounced decrease in sleep efficiency, time spent in REM sleep, and the percent of total sleep time spent in REM sleep as measured by the Nightcap.

__description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment was designed to study the effects of space flight on both sensorimotor (especially vestibular) and cognitive functions (especially orientation.) Optimal human performance depends upon integrated sensorimotor and cognitive functions both of which are known to be exquisitely sensitive to loss of sleep. The main objective of this study was to investigate variations in sleep and dreaming over an extended period of space flight, with special attention to changes in sleep and dreaming associated with the vestibular adaptation that occurs with adaptation to microgravity, and readaptation to 1-G conditions. To achieve this, a sleep monitoring system was tested that could accurately identify periods of wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on-board the Mir space station.

APPROACH:
Five crewmembers completed measurements relating to the protocol before, during and after space flight. During each phase, the experiment was divided into approximately three 12-day segments called measurement blocks. The inflight measurement blocks were scheduled early in the mission (mission day 37-49), in the middle (MD 79-91) and at the end (MD 110-122) of the mission. This investigation was conducted for the first time as part of the NASA 4 and Russian Mir 23 missions with three crewmembers participating. The experiment protocols were repeated on the Mir 24 mission with two additional crewmembers.

In each of the 12-day blocks, test subjects monitored sleep by wearing an apparatus called a Night Headband. It consisted of a simple athletic headband into which a head movement sensor had been sewn, along with a self-adhesive eyelid movement sensor that attached to the surface of the upper eyelid. The sensors were connected by two cables to a wallet-sized recording unit called the Night Headband Monitor (NHM). Subjects wore the NHM in a supplied arm band or attached the unit to a nearby wall with Velcro. The NHM analyzed data from the sensors and could store up to 30 nights before transfer to a computer. Usually, data from the NHM was uploaded to a laptop computer daily and subsequently stored on disk. Data was stored as one-minute counts of the number of 250 ms epochs during which eye or head movement was detected.

Because the head movement sensor originally designed for the Night Headband utilized a gravity-dependent mercury switch, the sensor was redesigned as an inertial switch. The inertial switch had appropriate sensitivity in microgravity; no head movements were detected during quiet rest, but gentle rotations of the head were adequate to produce clear head movement signals. Inflight Night Headbands all had these inertial switches built into them; baseline data collection Night Headbands continued to use the mercury switch version.

Data was used to determine both the percent of sleep spent in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (REM %) and the absolute amount of time spent in REM sleep (REM time). The allowed testing of the hypotheses that REM % and REM time would increase during the period of adaptation to microgravity and then return to preflight baseline levels. It was also hypothesized that the REM % and REM time would again increase during the period of readaptation to normal gravity.

In addition to the objective sleep data described above, subjects were also asked to dictate dream reports into a pocket voice recorder at each awakening. Researchers hoped to observe a shift in the fictive vestibular and motor activity of the subject's dreams as he went through adaptation first to microgravity and then, on return, to normal gravity.

RESULTS:
Subjects recorded an average of 26 nights of sleep during the preflight period, 24 nights inflight, and 14 nights postflight during the postflight recovery period. All told, 317 nights of sleep data were recorded, of which 120 were collected inflight, between the 24th and 171st day in orbit. Sixty of the 120 nights were recorded more than three months into the flight. Analysis of data was made using repeated measures ANOVA's.

For all five subjects, REM sleep was severely diminished during flight. Both REM time and REM % were significantly diminished (REM time, F=20.5, p<0.001; REM %, F=16.5, p<0.002). On average, REM time was reduced by 53% and REM % was reduced by 35% inflight compared to preflight. All subjects showed at least a 40% reduction in REM time. In contrast, postflight rates were essentially the same as preflight, showing on average a 4% increase in both REM time and REM % compared to the preflight period. There was also decrease in total sleep time inflight (F=7.1, p<0.02). Inflight values were reduced by 27% on average, while postflight values were 0.3% higher. All subjects showed at least a 13% decrease in average nightly total sleep time inflight. This did not result from a decrease in time in bed (F=0.2, p=0.84); subjects spent on average 4% longer in bed while inflight. Rather it resulted from decreased sleep efficiency (F=24.1, p<0.005). Sleep efficiency dropped from a mean of 89% in the preflight period to 63% inflight.

The Night Headband Kit sleep system permitted more extensive sleep recording during space flight than had previously been possible. Data collected over 6 months of flight indicated that extended space flight leads to a consistent and pronounced decrease in sleep efficiency, time spent in REM sleep, and the percent of total sleep time spent in REM sleep as measured by the Nightcap.

Neither the causes nor the consequences of these alterations were clear as the result of this experiment. It was hypothesized that a continued reduction in the above values might well lead to diminished performance of crewmembers in space.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Radiation constitutes one of the most important hazards for humans in long-duration space missions. Leaving the earth's surface, humans are exposed to a wide spectrum of particles and energies of galactic and solar origin. The intensity, energy, and elemental composition of the radiation field changes considerably with orbital parameters, shielding thickness and solar activity. Results from numerous space probes demonstrate heightened radiation levels compared to the earth's surface and a change in the nature of the radiation field, particularly the heavy ion component.

Although considerable data has been accumulated from several spaceflights, it is not yet possible to provide a quantitative description of the radiation field, especially at the edge of the radiation belt, because of its highly complex composition regarding the particles present and their energy spectra. Data comparison is hampered by uncertain angular distribution of the single radiation components, by missing knowledge on the angular response of instruments and missing information about shielding distributions at the instrument locations. Current models either under- or overestimate the contribution of different radiation components.

Due to the variety of particles and energies present in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), no single detector system is capable of providing sufficient information. Therefore, the DOSMAP (Dosimetric Mapping) dosimetry package consisted of several types of detectors to allow for measurement of different particle types and energies. The DOSMAP dosimetry package was further supplemented with instruments contributed by NASA (Phantom Torso) and NASDA (Bonner Ball). The different systems allowed for the first time inflight cross-calibration of measurements at the same shielding configurations. This is absolute necessary when recognizing that the comparison of currently available data is often not possible due to not well known angular response of the detector systems combined with unknown angular incidence of radiations and only approximate knowledge of shielding distributions.

APPROACH:
Several components of the DOSMAP dosimetry package (dosimetry telescopes [DOSTELS], computer interface unit [CIU], and the thermoluminescent dosimeter [TLD] reader and bulbs) were brought to the International Space Station (ISS) aboard A Shuttle flight. These components were unstowed and set-up in the Retention Net of the Human Research Facility (HRF). Another shuttle brought the remaining DOSMAP hardware (mobile dosimetry units [MDUs] and nuclear track detector packages [NTDP] to the ISS. The MDUs were charged, and an initial read-out was performed for the MDUs and the TLD bulbs prior to their installation throughout the U.S. Lab and Node 1. The NTDPs were also placed at the required locations. All placements were photo documented.

Data collected from the TLD bulbs by the TLD Reader were downloaded to the HRF PC every 7-10 days, and data collected from the MDUs were downloaded through the CIU to the HRF PC every 5 days. During the same time intervals the MDUs were recharged. The DOSTELs were activated and data downloads to the HRF PC were performed every 10 days. All data of the active instruments were downlinked during the mission. All of the dosimetry hardware was returned to Earth on A shuttle flight.

RESULTS:
All data received by the investigators was of good quality. Several hardware issues resulted in small amounts of data loss. Due to the retirement of Prof. W. Heinrich the evaluation of the CR39 NTDP detectors by the group of the University of Siegen could not be completed. The science return may be roughly quoted at about 95%.

TLD Results:

Based on the characterization of the different detector systems, the following can be concluded. The data for all the different applied TLD systems agree very well taking into account the different Linear Energy Transfer (LET) efficiency of the detector types used as well as the different neutron sensitivity of 6Li doped and 7Li doped TLD materials. The higher dose values for TLD600 and TLD700 dosimeters are due to the higher LET efficiency of these dosimeter materials compared to Cu, P doped LiF crystals.

Neutron Dose Results:

The determination of neutron dose equivalent using chiefly recoil protons can give too high of a dose value depending on the amount of primary protons contributing to the signal. For this reason, two methods of neutron dose equivalent determination were used. However, both methods still have their limitations and uncertainties. On the other hand, the neutron dose values determined by the two different methods are almost comparable within the standard deviations determined by uncertainty propagation, which indicates that the assumptions made are not too wrong.

Measurements with converters with even higher sensitivity to thermal neutrons may improve the standard deviation and better spectral knowledge of the neutron spectra in space may improve the uncertainty of the calibration factor for Albedo dosimeters.

Passive Dosimetry System (PDS) Results:

The use of the Pille reader in automatic mode permitted dose to be measured as a function of orbit number by TLD A0101. Orbits that passed through the SAA received doses of 30 to >50 µGy/orbit. During these particular orbits, the spacecraft received a substantially larger exposure to trapped protons than during orbits that did not pass through the SAA. For orbits that did not traverse the SAA, the absorbed dose was ~10 µGy/orbit. All orbits that passed through the SAA do not receive the same dose because each orbit passed through only a fraction of the SAA and the size of this fraction changed as the ISS orbit precessed around the Earth. Generally, the ISS passed through the SAA twice during each twenty-four hour period.

Following exposure and return to the laboratory, each PDS detector was disassembled and the individual CR-39 PNTD layers were selected for chemical processing (etching). The combined LET spectrum for the x-, y- and z-oriented short-etch CR-39 PNTDs was generated following readout of the 3 detectors. Similarly, the combined LET spectrum was generated for the x-, y- and z-oriented long-etch detectors. There is fairly close agreement between the three mutually orthogonal spectra measured in the long-etch detectors. Similarly, for LET <100 keV/µm, there is fairly close agreement between the 3 mutually orthogonal detectors measured in the short-etch detectors. Only above 100 keV/µm is there a difference in the 3 spectra, where the curve measured in the short-etch x-oriented detector lies significantly above those measured in the short-etch y and z detectors. This is likely due to greater shielding in the x direction relative to the other two directions.

The relative contribution to the LET spectrum from neutron- and proton-induced target fragments tend to increase with increasing LET. The reduced efficiency with which tracks are detected in the short-etch detectors below ~30 keV/µm is apparent, as is the increased signal due to target fragmentation in the LET region above 100 keV/µm in the short-etch detectors. There is fairly close agreement between the detectors for the 2 etch regimes in the LET interval between 30 and 100 keV/µm. The crossover point of the short-etch and long-etch spectra, 35 keV/µm for PDS A0103, was located in the plot differential LET fluence spectra and used in combining the short-etch and long-etch curves into one total LET spectrum.

During the DOSMAP experiment, mean total dose rate measured in the PDS dosimeters ranged from 6.88 ± 0.42 µGy/hr in Node 1, above the forward hatch leading to the FGB module, to 10.36 ± 0.54 µGy/hr above the aft hatch of Node 1. The mean total dose equivalent rate varied from 14.06 ± 0.93 µSv/hr to 18.81 ± 1.11 µSv/hr at these same respective locations. The average quality factor varied from 1.82 ± 0.13 above the aft hatch of Node 1 to 2.11 ± 0.16 on the starboard side of the US Lab near the aft hatch.

DOSTEL Results:

By chance a significant solar particle event occurred during the active phase of DOSTEL on April 15, 2001. Thanks to the action of the crew, DOSTEL 1 was switched into a special mode while DOSTEL 2 remained in the mode for article and dose rate measurement. In the special mode, the 2 detector signals of DOSTEL 1 were stored for each individual particle. Stopping protons impinging from the top and bottom of the telescope were clearly seen, along with some stopping He-particles that were also identified. A plot of dose rates during the mission clearly shows the dependence of dose rates from the altitude, which ranged from 404 km to 386 km. Based on the mean quality factor derived from the LET spectra by applying the LET dependence of the quality factor as defined in ICRP Report No. 60 equivalent doses can be calculated.

Mobile Dosimetry Unit (MDU) Results:

Approximately 4.5 MB of rough compressed information was received by each MDU. After decompression, the volume of data increases by an approximate factor of 30. The values of the mean doses per day was 180.7, 189.9, 166.1, 126.3 µGy/day in MDU#1 to MDU#4, respectively. When graphed these doses lie on the AP8MAX prediction line.

Comparison of fluxes by 4 different MDUs shows that large differences are produced by the differences in the position of MDU and shielding distributions for them. In the time span 27 June-4 July 2001 four MDUs were placed at fixed locations: one unit (MDU#4) in the ISS "Unity" Node-1 and three (MDU #1-3) units were located at different locations in the US Laboratory module.

MDU #2 results showed that the spectra inside the ISS has a maximum energy of 300 MeV and that the place of the maximum of the spectra moves from about 100 MeV at low L values toward 50-60 MeV at higher L values. The agreement of the data received by active and passive detectors is in the range of ±10%. Comparisons of the passive devices yield even a smaller range, when corrected by the efficiency function of the different materials. Dose equivalents were calculated from the measurements using the quality factor (Q) as defined in ICRP Report No. 60.

Conclusion:

In comparison to other spaceflight missions, the lower dose equivalents seen for ISS are due to less solar activity during the measurement period and due to higher shielding of the ISS. The dose equivalents received by the combination of nuclear track detectors with TLDs show values close to the DOSTEL dose equivalents. The error in the determination of the dose equivalent from passive detectors is about 6%. The combined CR39 NTDP/TLD dose equivalent appears too low compared to the DOSTEL dose equivalents. Since the low let measurements of the TLDs are in good agreement with DOSTEL and the CR39 NTDP LET spectra as well, further investigations are needed to close this gap of knowledge. Adding the neutron dose from the personal dosimeter would increase the dose equivalent measurements by about 33 µSv/day.

The DOSMAP experiment was the first effort to map dose and dose equivalent as function of the location in the US lab and in Node 1 of the ISS. Having a fully developed 3-D ray tracing model the obtained data can be used to validate the Model. A quite impressive set of data has been produced by the "Dosimetric Mapping" experiment from which only a part could be presented in this summary. Since the radiation field is both complex and dynamic, measurements across the ISS need to be continued in future missions to study the radiation field and its modification by mass shielding, leading to attenuation, build up and/or activation. There is a continuous need for information on absorbed dose, particle and linear energy transfer spectra in real time.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Past studies show that disuse-induced bone loss in the canine skeleton evolves through a loss of trabecular bone structural elements, involving both thinning and subsequent perforation and loss events. Moreover, during the bone loss process with disuse, there is a discrete, temporal separation of thinning of trabeculae from the later perforation and complete loss of trabecular elements. In these experiments, we took advantage of this sequence of bone changes in the development of disuse-induced bone loss to establish different architectural baseline points from which recovery of structure and mechanical function with reloading were be examined.

The objectives were to characterize the microarchitectural and structural-mechanical correlates of recovery from osteoporosis secondary to decreased mechanical usage. Specifically, the experiment examined recovery from disuse osteoporosis in a canine model so that the bone processes could be studied in all bone envelopes, in a skeletal system that has a physiology similar to that in adult humans. While recovery in trabecular bone was the principal focus of these studies, recovery and function in diaphyseal compact bone was also studied.

Specific Aims:
1. Determine whether bone architecture can recover from the changes resulting from long-term disuse osteoporosis, to test the hypothesis that with recovery after long-term disuse, bone will be apposed only to existing surfaces, resulting in restoration of bone mass but not microarchitecture.
2. Determine whether bone mechanical properties can recover from long-term disuse osteoporosis, to test the hypothesis that there are negative functional-mechanical consequences to having fewer thick trabeculae versus smaller more interconnected trabecular elements after recovery from existent osteoporosis.

APPROACH:
The investigators built on an existing data set for evolution of disuse-induced bone loss (osteoporosis) in Beagle dogs originally performed in collaboration with the Department of Energy Radiobiology Laboratory at the University of Utah; specifically, 5-7 year old bred for purpose retired breeder Beagle dogs (12-15 kg body weight) were used. Use of a consistent breed minimized phenotypic variation among experimental animals, and only female animals were examined to control for possible hormonal differences. Dogs were housed singly, in 8.5 ft x 4.75 ft kennel runs in the Animal Resources Facility at Henry Ford Hospital. Dogs were fed a standard diet with water available ad libitum. Body weights were determined weekly.

Use of an adult canine model allowed the study of this physiology on all bone envelopes (both cortical and trabecular bone), in a well characterized skeletal system, which has been demonstrated to possess a remodeling physiology similar to adult humans and other primates in each skeletal envelope. In addition, canine metaphyses are sufficiently large to make direct mechanical assessments of the functional mechanical integrity of the recovered bone architecture.

Immobilization and Remobilization Procedures: Non-traumatic immobilization was used to establish two distinct architectural baseline points for initiating studies of the recovery from disuse osteoporosis. Immobilization Procedure: Right forelimbs of adult Beagle dogs (females, N=28, 5-7 years old) were non-traumatically immobilized using a modified body jacket-splint. The splint was custom-formed for each animal using thermoplastic resin (Aquaplast, Smith and Nephew, IN). Right forelimbs were splinted with the elbow flexed at 90 degrees and the carpal joint volar-flexed slightly. The splint devices were removed 3 times per week and the animals placed in a canvas hammock with the forelimbs placed freely hanging through the hammock opening so as to be non-weight-bearing . Fifteen minutes of passive flexion-extension motion was then applied manually to reduce the effects of immobilization on the development of joint contractures. Dogs were conditioned to handling so that no sedation was needed during splint removal and treatment. Immobilization lasted either 3 or 6 months. Remobilization: Time periods to start remobilization were chosen (based on preliminary data) to correspond to microarchitectural events. At 3 months (acute disuse), there is loss of bone volume corresponding to thinning of trabeculae, but there is no loss of trabecular elements. After 6 months of immobilization (chronic disuse), there is a significant reduction in the number of trabecular elements. Groups of animals were sacrificed after 3 and 6 months of immobilization to provide baseline values for the disuse osteoporosis. For the remaining acute and chronic disuse groups, splints were removed and the animals allowed to resume quadrupedal gait as tolerated. Normal weight-bearing function was achieved by 4-6 weeks after splint removal, assessed from ground reaction force determined using a strain gauge force-plate. Remobilized animals were euthanized after 12 months of remobilization. This long time period for remobilization was chosen based on several criteria. First, it encompassed the completion of at least 2 remodeling periods in dogs* to provide a steady state for long-term recovery period (*the remodeling period, sigma, in dogs is reported to be from 3 - 5 months; mean and standard deviation for the remodeling period in our control Beagles from previous studies is 111+47 days). Second, it assures that newly formed bone during the recovery process is completely mineralized, so that mechanical property measurements are not confounded by the latency of normal secondary mineralization processes. Comparisons of final architecture and mechanical function were based principally on the basal, immobilized and long-term remobilized groups.

Mechanical function of long bones was evaluated from metacarpal-3 from the immobilization studies described above. Four-point bending tests were performed to assess structural-mechanical properties. Prior to mechanical testing, pQCT scans were performed to determine the axial moments of inertia at mid-diaphysis. Testing was performed using a servohydraulic materials test system. Intact long bones were positioned in the test apparatus with the dorsal side in compression and volar side in tension. The mid-diaphysis was centered over two supports positioned 21mm apart with upper loads spaced 7 mm apart. Bones were loaded to failure at a displacement rate of 0.1mm/sec. Structural properties (stiffness, ultimate load, work to failure) were determined from the load-displacement curves. Tissue level properties of cortical bone (bending modulus) were derived using pQCT-determined moments of inertia. Differences among groups were tested using the ANOVA with post-hoc testing using the Mann-Whitney U test; significance values reported p< 0.05.

Changes in trabecular bone architecture were studied from distal metacarpal epiphyseo-metaphyseal regions. Distal metacarpals were scanned using a micro-computed tomography system. Images were acquired at a voxel resolution of 22 µm. Computer-based stereological techniques were used to determine the bone fraction (Tb.V/TV) and mean intercept lengths in each of the principal orthogonal (anatomical) planes (IS-MIL, AP-MIL, ML-MIL) and the degree of anisotropy for the full 3-D cancellous bone data set for each bone.

Metacarpal diaphyses from dogs forelimbs immobilized for up to 1.5 months were studied, as this time period corresponds to the onset of significant increases in intracortical resorption in unloaded dog forelimbs. Diaphyses were stained in basic fuchsin, which stains osteocyte nuclei and the proteoglycans that line the lacunar and canalicular walls in vital bone. Loss of basic fuchsin staining of osteocytes and canaliculi under fluorescence confocal microscopy corresponds to loss of osteocyte viability in regions of bones. Sections were examined using confocal microscopy with long wavelength (568 nm) to excite basic fuchsin fluorescence. Osteocyte integrity was assessed in bone surrounding osteoclastic resorption spaces in immobilized tissue and compared to non-immobilized control bone.

RESULTS:
Immobilization: Consistent with previous studies, immobilization resulted in a profound loss of bone, with bone area reduced nearly 15 percent from control levels by 3 months of disuse and by approximately 35 percent from control levels after 6 months. Bone loss occurred principally from endocortical surfaces, resulting in an almost 250 percent increase in marrow cavity size by 6 months of immobilization. Periosteal surfaces did not contribute significantly to bone loss; hence total cross-sectional area remained unchanged.

Bones at 3 months of immobilization showed significant reductions in stiffness (-23%), strength (-34%) and work to fracture (-29%). A 17% loss of bone tissue modulus was also observed. After 6 months of immobilization, whole bone stiffness, strength and work to fracture were reduced to about half that of control bones. Tissue modulus was more than 60% lower than control, suggesting an impairment of bone matrix properties beyond that expected from the osteoporosis alone.

Remobilization: Structural properties of bones remobilized after either 3 or 6 months were not significantly different from the control group (p>0.22). In contrast, remobilized bone tissue modulus remained approximately 13% less than normal tissue. Moments of inertia of remobilized bone were approximately 10-15% larger than those in the control group.

Recovery of bone mass: Animals immobilized for 3 months recovered approximately 95 percent of their bone mass with remobilization (p=n.s. vs. control). In contrast, with remobilization after 6 months of immobilization bone mass, remained approximately 15 percent below control levels. In both remobilization groups, histomorphometric indices of periosteal and endocortical bone formation and resorption were similar to control levels, indicating that the diaphyses had achieved a steady state in their adaptation.

Mechanism of bone recovery: The architectural bases for recovery of diaphyseal bone mass were different from those associated with bone loss. Recovery of some bone occurred by apposition along the endocortical surface; however, in both remobilization groups, marrow cavity size remained at least 60 percent larger than that in controls. However, with recovery, there was marked periosteal expansion of the bones, such that remobilized bones were 10-18% larger than control bones.

Accordingly, consistent with the uniform increase in MIL for all orthogonal planes, long-term disuse osteoporosis did not result in any changes in the degree of anisotropy of trabecular bone.

Osteocyte integrity in unloaded bone was found to be dramatically impaired in regions surrounding osteoclastic resorption spaces. There was loss of normal osteocyte staining, pyknotic nuclei and the canalicular system was no longer evident. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Oral health is important to effective work in space, and is also crucial because the oral region serves as an entry point for pathogenic agents, acts as a reservoir for infectious microorganisms, and plays a role in cross contamination and disease transmission. Oral health studies were performed during all Skylab missions. Three general areas were studied: clinical dentistry, provisions for in-flight care, and research dedicated to the identification of potential oral problems in long-duration missions.

The emphasis of clinical dentistry was on the prevention of dental disease and included pre- and postflight restorative procedures, measurements of oral health indices, and in-flight provisions for emergency dental care.

Inflight care dealt with the risks of an unanticipated problem, which could impair effective work. This risk was computed at 0.92 % for a 3-man 28-day mission, was based on studies of dental experiences in other isolated environments and on a 3-year study of the astronaut population. The two most likely problems were a painful tooth due to pulpitis or severe, localized gingival inflammation. Dental caries was not considered a problem in missions up to 3-month duration, because of the high level of oral health of all crewmen and the frequent dental evaluations they received.

Oral research was conducted on Skylab by monitoring the crew to assess the effects of the space flight on the population dynamics of oral microflora, the secretion of specific salivary components, and clinical changes in oral health. Laboratory intraoral changes can precede clinical manifestations of acute and chronic infectious disease. Clinically detectable alterations of oral tissue can identify changes caused by local and/or systemic disorders of microbial and nonmicrobial origin. Changes in saliva composition and volume may also reflect local and systemic disorders.

One objective of the Skylab oral health studies concerned metabolic profiles that were established to discern microorganisms associated with oral disease conditions. In addition, effects of space flight on salivary electrolyte levels were determined. A practical and reproducible method was needed to definitively identify closely related strains of oral microorganisms associated with dental disease. High resolution gas liquid chromatographic (GLC) techniques provided a means of effectively establishing metabolic profiles between physiologically and serologically closely related, potentially pathogenic oral microbes. Emphasis was placed on the definitive characterization of Streptococcus mutans since this microorganism has been directly implicated in the etiology of dental caries and indirectly associated with periodontal disease. A high prevalence of S. mutans in the Skylab crew provided the interest for discerning the different strains of this organism.

Salivary electrolytes were also examined in this study. Changes in the concentration of such electrolytes may be due to emotional stress, drugs, drug toxicity, metabolic changes, and systemic disease. If the mineral imbalance revealed by the urinary and fecal elevations in specific electrolytes during the Skylab missions is also evidenced by electrolyte changes in saliva, prolonged spaceflight might have an impact on the buffer systems in saliva and upset a basic homeostatic mechanism in the oral cavity. Thus, this study had two specific aims:
1. Adapt and/or develop analytical chemical procedures to establish metabolic profiles for fingerprinting microorganisms associated with oral disease conditions.
2. Assess the effects of the 28, 59, and 84-day Skylab missions on the salivary electrolytes.

APPROACH:
All Skylab crewmembers took utmost oral care during the preflight timeframe. Oral hygiene procedures consisted of brushing the teeth two minutes twice a day and flossing once a day. Regular topical applications of stannous fluoride were provided to all crewmen up to six months before launch; oral exams and evaluation were performed every six months. Because of the risks of inflammation to the dental pulp, no dental restorations were provided during the last 90 days prior to flight. Complete oral Panorex radiographs were made of each crewman prior to his mission.

All crewmen were placed on a space food diet about 21 days before flight. The backup crewmen continued on the space diet until launch and prime crewmen until 18 days after recovery.

Prime and backup crews of all Skylab missions received two days of training in pertinent dental procedures to be able to treat the most likely dental problems that might arise. Training included lectures, demonstrations, and supervised clinical procedures, which were as complex as tooth removal, and were performed on volunteer patients. Instruments and medications were part of the In-flight Medical Support System-Dental, which also included a manual with line drawings of complete intraoral radiographs of each crewman and integrated, illustrated diagnostic, and treatment procedures. The crew also had air-to-ground communication access with a dentist and/or surgeon.

The eighteen prime and backup crewmembers of the three Skylab missions were monitored for quantitative changes in oral microorganisms, saliva partitions considered potentially important to oral health, and alterations in clinical indices of oral health and preexisting dental disease. Over 100 saliva samples were analyzed. All samples were collected before oral hygiene and breakfast. To produce stimulated saliva, crewmembers chewed sterile paraffin and spat into a sterile cup, measuring and recording the time each took to produce a 5-ml volume. This time was used to calculate the saliva flow rate. The samples were grouped into three categories, which were preflight/conventional diet, preflight/space diet and postflight/space diet.

High resolution GLC and pyrolysis-GLC procedures were used to obtain distinctive metabolic profiles of closely related genera, species and strains of oral microbes associated with dental caries and periodontal disease, with emphasis on serologically unique strains of S. mutans. Uninoculated culture media and pure cultures of known strains of the same and different serotypes of cariogenic and noncariogenic S. mutans, Streptococcus sanguis, and Lactobacillus fermenti, along with uncharacterized strains of S. mutans isolated from the crew were analyzed.

Microbiological Assessments: Oral specimens were collected from the crewmembers weekly or semiweekly from three intraoral sites from 31 days preflight to 18 days postflight for Skylab 2, from 51 days preflight to 20 days postflight for Skylab 3, and from 57 days preflight to 17 days postflight for Skylab 4. All collections took place between 7 and 8 am, before oral hygiene procedures or breakfast. The specimens included dental plaque, crevicular fluid (exudates absorbed from the gingival sulcus area), and stimulated saliva (all sites associated with the development of dental caries, periodontal disease, and alveolar bone loss).

Serial 10-fold dilutions of each specimen were plated onto a variety of bacteriologic media for the enumeration of up to 17 microbial categories including mycoplasma and yeast. Duplicate platings were incubated at 37ºC either aerobically or anaerobically.

In addition to microbial assessments, stimulated saliva was used to determine total protein, secretory Immunoglobulin A, and lysozyme.

RESULTS:
All preflight dental conditions were resolved before launch. The radiographs revealed two asymptomatic, previously unrecognized areas of disease conditions about the apex of the teeth of two crewmen, which were successfully resolved. During the last nine months prior to the Skylab missions, six crewmen required treatment for dental problems, which were other than routine replacement of restorations and dental prophylaxes. All dental problems were resolved successfully with no recurrence. No in-flight dental problems requiring the use of the Inflight Medical Support System-Dental occurred during the Skylab 2, 3, and 4 missions. Laboratory and clinical parameters related to dental injury were evaluated in order to monitor mission-related effects on oral health. The most distinctive changes observed concerned microbial and IgA concentrations, and analysis of calculus and gingival inflammation. Increased counts of specific anaerobic and streptococcal components, primarily of the saliva and dental plaque microflora were observed, and were more diet related than flight related. An elevation in secretory IgA occurred with a reduction of salivary lysozyme. Also observed was an incidence of increased increments of dental calculus and gingival inflammation, especially on Skylab 2. There was less increase in the scores of plaque, calculus, and inflammation in the Skylab 3 mission despite this mission being 59 days in length rather than 28 days. The lower scores are believed to be due to better oral health status of the prime crew of the Skylab 3 mission. Thus, the preexisting state of dental health was believed to be responsible for the clinical changes rather than any adverse space-flight effect. These studies show that the better the preflight oral health status, the lesser the flight-related changes on oral health.

The high resolution GLC techniques on oral microbes disclosed pronounced metabolic distinctions between two physiologically related genera of the same bacterial family (Streptococcus and Lactobacillus of the family Lactobacillaceae), and between two closely related oral species of the same genus (S. mutans and S. sanguis). Differences between and within serologically unique strains of the same species of S. mutans were detected, but were less striking than between inter-species profiles. Overall, the GLC procedures provided a practical and reproducible means of obtaining metabolic markers for identifying closely related strains of pathogenic oral microbes unattainable by conventional techniques.

The major pathogenic microorganisms present in crew specimens the morning of launch of Skylab 2 included Klebsiella pneumoniae from the gargle of one crewmember, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus from the gargle of another crewmember. None of these species created any problems during and after flight, although the S. aureus did spread to the mouth and scalp of the crewmember during the mission. From the gingival fluid, counts of bacteroides, veillonella, fusobacteria and leptotrichia increased significantly in all crewmembers after the initiation of the space diet at 18 days before launch. Similar increases were noted for species similar to S. mutans and Neisseria sp. Counts of S. mutans, which were relatively high in the prime crew at the onset of the study, appeared to increase during the recovery period, but this was not statistically significant. In stimulated saliva, significant increases occurred in mycoplasma, streptococci and bacteroides. Enteric bacilli, which were unusually numerous in saliva at the onset, declined during the investigative period. These enterics included isolations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae, and Achromobacter lwoffi. Changes in microorganisms in the dental plaque were within the expected range. However, bacteroides, veillonella and lactobacilli increased significantly after the initiation of the space diet. The conclusion drawn from Skylab 2 was that extensive microbial sampling of the crew before and after the mission revealed no changes of medical significance. The most distinctive changes noted from Skylab 3 assessments of gingival fluid, dental plaque and saliva include elevations in counts of specific anaerobic components of the gingival fluid microflora, increased counts of streptococci, enteric bacilli, and specific anaerobic components of saliva, and increased numbers of streptococci, lactobacilli, and leptotrichia in dental plaque. Except for the post-flight increases of enteric bacilli, the diet was believed responsible for the oral microbial changes. Preflight regular diet, versus preflight space diet data were compared, along with postflight space diet data. Specifically, increases were noted in Fusobacteria, Bacteroides melaninogenicus, and leptotrichia in gingival fluid. Streptococcus salivarius, enterics, fusobacteria, veillonella, and leptotrichia were elevated in stimulated saliva, and S. mutans, lactobacilli, and leptotrichia were elevated in dental plaque. The microbial changes observed in Skylab 3, with few exceptions, were similar to those noted previously in the ground-based trial and the Skylab 2 mission. As in the prior studies, the changes occurred during the preflight period after the incorporation of the space diet.

The changes detected in Skylab 4 were very similar to those observed in the ground-based study and the two previous Skylab missions. Most of the microbial changes were diet-related rather than flight-related. This was shown by statistical comparisons of cumulative counts from the 18 crewmembers before and after the incorporation of space diets during preflight samplings. The most distinctive changes noted in Skylab 4 included increased counts of specific anaerobic and streptococcal components, primarily of the saliva and dental plaque microflora. The most significant finding from Skylab 4 and previous Skylab missions was the decrease of intraoral changes.

Most of the chemical composition changes in saliva were minimal. There was an increase in saliva flow rate that was observed with the space diet. Investigators hypothesized that this increase could have been caused by flight-associated anxiety since stress can affect salivary flow rate. The total salivary protein decreased in combined missions, although this finding was downplayed since it was significant in only one mission, the 59-day mission, and that corresponded with the increase in salivary flow rate. The changes in the saliva electrolytes were a decrease in sodium along with an increase in magnesium concentrations. The increase in magnesium was significant, but since its concentration was extremely low, it was probably not clinically meaningful. Investigators suggested that the sodium decrease might have stemmed from higher production of adrenocortical steroids, especially aldosterone, which was elevated in urine over each mission. The increase in IgA was the most prominent compositional change. This finding was explained as a possible response to a subclinical infection that could have spread among the crew during preflight activity. This result is similar to the 56-day land-based, simulated Skylab mission. No clinical problems were detected despite the rise in IgA. Lysozyme, which is 0.5% to 1% of the total protein, decreased in the middle of the preflight stage, and continued to decrease throughout the study. This result was unexpected, and investigators were not able to explain the cause. No changes were noted throughout the missions in saliva calcium, potassium, chloride, phosphate, albumen or IgG concentrations. The salivary electrolyte changes did not parallel the increased urinary electrolyte excretion observed during each mission. Thus, the indication here is that saliva does not play a decisive role in regulating the water and electrolyte balance of the body.

The Skylab oral health studies results showed that the better the preflight oral health status, the lesser the flight-related changes on general oral health, such as occurrence of cavities, plaque and gingivitis. Most of the microbial changes were due to switching from conventional diets to space diets, and all Skylab mission data showed only a small effect of microbial intraoral changes. Chemical changes in saliva, such as protein and electrolyte levels were also minimal. Thus, the most significant aspect of the investigations was the relative nonexistence of health hazardous intraoral changes during Skylab missions.

The two most likely problems were a painful tooth due to pulpitis or severe, localized gingival inflammation. Dental caries was not considered a problem in missions up to 3-month duration, because of the high level of oral health of all crewmen and the frequent dental evaluations they received.

Oral research was conducted on Skylab by monitoring the crew to assess the effects of the space flight on the population dynamics of oral microflora, the secretion of specific salivary components, and clinical changes in oral health. Laboratory intraoral changes can precede clinical manifestations of acute and chronic infectious disease. Clinically detectable alterations of oral tissue can identify changes caused by local and/or systemic disorders of microbial and nonmicrobial origin. Changes in saliva composition and volume may also reflect local and systemic disorders.

One objective of the Skylab oral health studies concerned metabolic profiles that were established to discern microorganisms associated with oral disease conditions. In addition, effects of space flight on salivary electrolyte levels were determined. A practical and reproducible method was needed to definitively identify closely related strains of oral microorganisms associated with dental disease. High resolution gas liquid chromatographic (GLC) techniques provided a means of effectively establishing metabolic profiles between physiologically and serologically closely related, potentially pathogenic oral microbes. Emphasis was placed on the definitive characterization of Streptococcus mutans since this microorganism has been directly implicated in the etiology of dental caries and indirectly associated with periodontal disease. A high prevalence of S. mutans in the Skylab crew provided the interest for discerning the different strains of this organism.

Salivary electrolytes were also examined in this study. Changes in the concentration of such electrolytes may be due to emotional stress, drugs, drug toxicity, metabolic changes, and systemic disease. If the mineral imbalance revealed by the urinary and fecal elevations in specific electrolytes during the Skylab missions is also evidenced by electrolyte changes in saliva, prolonged spaceflight might have an impact on the buffer systems in saliva and upset a basic homeostatic mechanism in the oral cavity. Thus, this study had two specific aims:
1. Adapt and/or develop analytical chemical procedures to establish metabolic profiles for fingerprinting microorganisms associated with oral disease conditions.
2. Assess the effects of the 28, 59, and 84-day Skylab missions on the salivary electrolytes.

APPROACH:
All Skylab crewmembers took utmost oral care during the preflight timeframe. Oral hygiene procedures consisted of brushing the teeth two minutes twice a day and flossing once a day. Regular topical applications of stannous fluoride were provided to all crewmen up to six months before launch; oral exams and evaluation were performed every six months. Because of the risks of inflammation to the dental pulp, no dental restorations were provided during the last 90 days prior to flight. Complete oral Panorex radiographs were made of each crewman prior to his mission.

All crewmen were placed on a space food diet about 21 days before flight. The backup crewmen continued on the space diet until launch and prime crewmen until 18 days after recovery.

Prime and backup crews of all Skylab missions received two days of training in pertinent dental procedures to be able to treat the most likely dental problems that might arise. Training included lectures, demonstrations, and supervised clinical procedures, which were as complex as tooth removal, and were performed on volunteer patients. Instruments and medications were part of the In-flight Medical Support System-Dental, which also included a manual with line drawings of complete intraoral radiographs of each crewman and integrated, illustrated diagnostic, and treatment procedures. The crew also had air-to-ground communication access with a dentist and/or surgeon.

The eighteen prime and backup crewmembers of the three Skylab missions were monitored for quantitative changes in oral microorganisms, saliva partitions considered potentially important to oral health, and alterations in clinical indices of oral health and preexisting dental disease. Over 100 saliva samples were analyzed. All samples were collected before oral hygiene and breakfast. To produce stimulated saliva, crewmembers chewed sterile paraffin and spat into a sterile cup, measuring and recording the time each took to produce a 5-ml volume. This time was used to calculate the saliva flow rate. The samples were grouped into three categories, which were preflight/conventional diet, preflight/space diet and postflight/space diet.

High resolution GLC and pyrolysis-GLC procedures were used to obtain distinctive metabolic profiles of closely related genera, species and strains of oral microbes associated with dental caries and periodontal disease, with emphasis on serologically unique strains of S. mutans. Uninoculated culture media and pure cultures of known strains of the same and different serotypes of cariogenic and noncariogenic S. mutans, Streptococcus sanguis, and Lactobacillus fermenti, along with uncharacterized strains of S. mutans isolated from the crew were analyzed.

Microbiological Assessments: Oral specimens were collected from the crewmembers weekly or semiweekly from three intraoral sites from 31 days preflight to 18 days postflight for Skylab 2, from 51 days preflight to 20 days postflight for Skylab 3, and from 57 days preflight to 17 days postflight for Skylab 4. All collections took place between 7 and 8 am, before oral hygiene procedures or breakfast. The specimens included dental plaque, crevicular fluid (exudates absorbed from the gingival sulcus area), and stimulated saliva (all sites associated with the development of dental caries, periodontal disease, and alveolar bone loss).

Serial 10-fold dilutions of each specimen were plated onto a variety of bacteriologic media for the enumeration of up to 17 microbial categories including mycoplasma and yeast. Duplicate platings were incubated at 37ºC either aerobically or anaerobically.

In addition to microbial assessments, stimulated saliva was used to determine total protein, secretory Immunoglobulin A, and lysozyme.

RESULTS:
All preflight dental conditions were resolved before launch. The radiographs revealed two asymptomatic, previously unrecognized areas of disease conditions about the apex of the teeth of two crewmen, which were successfully resolved. During the last nine months prior to the Skylab missions, six crewmen required treatment for dental problems, which were other than routine replacement of restorations and dental prophylaxes. All dental problems were resolved successfully with no recurrence. No in-flight dental problems requiring the use of the Inflight Medical Support System-Dental occurred during the Skylab 2, 3, and 4 missions. Laboratory and clinical parameters related to dental injury were evaluated in order to monitor mission-related effects on oral health. The most distinctive changes observed concerned microbial and IgA concentrations, and analysis of calculus and gingival inflammation. Increased counts of specific anaerobic and streptococcal components, primarily of the saliva and dental plaque microflora were observed, and were more diet related than flight related. An elevation in secretory IgA occurred with a reduction of salivary lysozyme. Also observed was an incidence of increased increments of dental calculus and gingival inflammation, especially on Skylab 2. There was less increase in the scores of plaque, calculus, and inflammation in the Skylab 3 mission despite this mission being 59 days in length rather than 28 days. The lower scores are believed to be due to better oral health status of the prime crew of the Skylab 3 mission. Thus, the preexisting state of dental health was believed to be responsible for the clinical changes rather than any adverse space-flight effect. These studies show that the better the preflight oral health status, the lesser the flight-related changes on oral health.

The high resolution GLC techniques on oral microbes disclosed pronounced metabolic distinctions between two physiologically related genera of the same bacterial family (Streptococcus and Lactobacillus of the family Lactobacillaceae), and between two closely related oral species of the same genus (S. mutans and S. sanguis). Differences between and within serologically unique strains of the same species of S. mutans were detected, but were less striking than between inter-species profiles. Overall, the GLC procedures provided a practical and reproducible means of obtaining metabolic markers for identifying closely related strains of pathogenic oral microbes unattainable by conventional techniques.

The major pathogenic microorganisms present in crew specimens the morning of launch of Skylab 2 included Klebsiella pneumoniae from the gargle of one crewmember, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus from the gargle of another crewmember. None of these species created any problems during and after flight, although the S. aureus did spread to the mouth and scalp of the crewmember during the mission. From the gingival fluid, counts of bacteroides, veillonella, fusobacteria and leptotrichia increased significantly in all crewmembers after the initiation of the space diet at 18 days before launch. Similar increases were noted for species similar to S. mutans and Neisseria sp. Counts of S. mutans, which were relatively high in the prime crew at the onset of the study, appeared to increase during the recovery period, but this was not statistically significant. In stimulated saliva, significant increases occurred in mycoplasma, streptococci and bacteroides. Enteric bacilli, which were unusually numerous in saliva at the onset, declined during the investigative period. These enterics included isolations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae, and Achromobacter lwoffi. Changes in microorganisms in the dental plaque were within the expected range. However, bacteroides, veillonella and lactobacilli increased significantly after the initiation of the space diet. The conclusion drawn from Skylab 2 was that extensive microbial sampling of the crew before and after the mission revealed no changes of medical significance. The most distinctive changes noted from Skylab 3 assessments of gingival fluid, dental plaque and saliva include elevations in counts of specific anaerobic components of the gingival fluid microflora, increased counts of streptococci, enteric bacilli, and specific anaerobic components of saliva, and increased numbers of streptococci, lactobacilli, and leptotrichia in dental plaque. Except for the post-flight increases of enteric bacilli, the diet was believed responsible for the oral microbial changes. Preflight regular diet, versus preflight space diet data were compared, along with postflight space diet data. Specifically, increases were noted in Fusobacteria, Bacteroides melaninogenicus, and leptotrichia in gingival fluid. Streptococcus salivarius, enterics, fusobacteria, veillonella, and leptotrichia were elevated in stimulated saliva, and S. mutans, lactobacilli, and leptotrichia were elevated in dental plaque. The microbial changes observed in Skylab 3, with few exceptions, were similar to those noted previously in the ground-based trial and the Skylab 2 mission. As in the prior studies, the changes occurred during the preflight period after the incorporation of the space diet.

The changes detected in Skylab 4 were very similar to those observed in the ground-based study and the two previous Skylab missions. Most of the microbial changes were diet-related rather than flight-related. This was shown by statistical comparisons of cumulative counts from the 18 crewmembers before and after the incorporation of space diets during preflight samplings. The most distinctive changes noted in Skylab 4 included increased counts of specific anaerobic and streptococcal components, primarily of the saliva and dental plaque microflora. The most significant finding from Skylab 4 and previous Skylab missions was the decrease of intraoral changes.

Most of the chemical composition changes in saliva were minimal. There was an increase in saliva flow rate that was observed with the space diet. Investigators hypothesized that this increase could have been caused by flight-associated anxiety since stress can affect salivary flow rate. The total salivary protein decreased in combined missions, although this finding was downplayed since it was significant in only one mission, the 59-day mission, and that corresponded with the increase in salivary flow rate. The changes in the saliva electrolytes were a decrease in sodium along with an increase in magnesium concentrations. The increase in magnesium was significant, but since its concentration was extremely low, it was probably not clinically meaningful. Investigators suggested that the sodium decrease might have stemmed from higher production of adrenocortical steroids, especially aldosterone, which was elevated in urine over each mission. The increase in IgA was the most prominent compositional change. This finding was explained as a possible response to a subclinical infection that could have spread among the crew during preflight activity. This result is similar to the 56-day land-based, simulated Skylab mission. No clinical problems were detected despite the rise in IgA. Lysozyme, which is 0.5% to 1% of the total protein, decreased in the middle of the preflight stage, and continued to decrease throughout the study. This result was unexpected, and investigators were not able to explain the cause. No changes were noted throughout the missions in saliva calcium, potassium, chloride, phosphate, albumen or IgG concentrations. The salivary electrolyte changes did not parallel the increased urinary electrolyte excretion observed during each mission. Thus, the indication here is that saliva does not play a decisive role in regulating the water and electrolyte balance of the body.

The Skylab oral health studies results showed that the better the preflight oral health status, the lesser the flight-related changes on general oral health, such as occurrence of cavities, plaque and gingivitis. Most of the microbial changes were due to switching from conventional diets to space diets, and all Skylab mission data showed only a small effect of microbial intraoral changes. Chemical changes in saliva, such as protein and electrolyte levels were also minimal. Thus, the most significant aspect of the investigations was the relative nonexistence of health hazardous intraoral changes during Skylab missions.

experiment_title: Hyperpolarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance Imaging
parameter_html:
Brain function
Hyperpolarized noble gas
Pulmonary function
investigators: Principal Investigator: Albert, Mitchell
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A novel biomedical imaging technique, hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is capable of generating high-resolution images of the lung, heart, and brain by using the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe. The HP gases, created via spin-exchange optical pumping, have greatly enhanced MR detectability. Unlike conventional proton MRI, HP gas MRI does not require a large magnetic field and, therefore, can be performed in very low magnetic fields (~ 0.01 Tesla). Thus, a small, portable, low-power MRI system, practical for space flight, may be designed to implement very low field HP gas MRI. The imaging capacity of HP gas MRI itself is also relevant to space flight research. Under prior NASA funding, the investigators have obtained (i) cerebral blood flow measurements and (ii) lung gas transfer measurements using HP 129Xe MRI in rats. Additionally, in humans they have (i) obtained high-resolution images of the distal airways in lungs up to the 7th generation, (ii) created models of the three-dimensional lung airway tree, and (iii) obtained very low field (0.015 Tesla) images of the lungs, using HP 3He MRI. They now propose to apply this novel technique to investigations of the physiological and functional states of the lungs, heart, and brain. Studies will focus on regional ventilation and perfusion inhomogeneities of the lungs, patent foramen ovale and pulmonary embolism of the heart, and cerebral function and blood flow of the brain. Their proposed ground-based investigations with HP gas MRI will impact space flight research in three important ways: (i) by facilitating the acquisition of novel information about the physiological structure and function of organs and systems most affected by changes in microgravity; (ii) by developing a new technology that may have clinical applications for the diagnosis of pathologies endemic to microgravity environments; and (iii) by developing treatment strategies that address the continuum of a space-induced illness.

APPROACH:
Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project.

RESULTS:
Hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas MRI using 3He or 129Xe provides highly detailed images of the lungs and brain, and offers the immense advantage of providing information on physiological function, including lung ventilation (3He or 129Xe), lung perfusion (129Xe), and cerebral blood flow (129Xe). For example, HP gas MRI allows investigators to pinpoint precise sections of the lungs where gas is reaching, and where gas is not reaching (ventilation defects), something other measurements of lung function cannot do. Because of its greater sensitivity, HP gas MRI can detect pulmonary or cerebral dysfunction at earlier stages, allowing treatment or counteracting measures to be provided earlier and with greater effectiveness. In addition, HP gas MRI provides imaging of physiological function without exposing subjects to ionizing radiation or chemical contrast agents. This increases safety, and also allows investigators and/or care providers to non-invasively image subjects repeatedly over time.

HP gas MRI has countless applications to evaluating vascular and pulmonary problems that could arise in human space flight. Such applications include investigating the effects of microgravity and pressure changes on the physiological functioning of the lungs, and studying the effects of microgravity and pressure changes associated with space flight on vascular functioning. In addition, HP gas MRI is ideal for evaluating aerosol drug administration, a delivery method of particular interest for space flight because it avoids the need for injections of medicines in space.

In this study, investigators further developed hyperpolarized noble gas MRI for use in examining pulmonary and brain function in animal models and in humans, building upon previous work by the PI funded by NASA. HP gas MRI has immense potential for applications to the study of the physiology of the lungs and brain, and for helping diagnose and inform treatment for adverse reactions to microgravity and low pressure environments. Low-magnetic-field MRI, which is made possible by HP gas MRI, is particularly advantageous in this regard because it provides extraordinarily detailed images of lung and brain function with lightweight, low-cost, easy-to-operate equipment that could be used in space environments. With the assistance of generous funding from NASA, the investigating team was able to make significant advances in many areas of HP gas MRI, including pulmonary ventilation analysis and low-magnetic-field MRI.
