experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
One of the most important physiological changes that negatively impact flight operations and crew safety is postflight orthostatic intolerance. Orthostatic intolerance is commonly experienced by astronauts when they return to Earth and can lead to hypotension and syncope (temporary loss of consciousness, fainting, or dizziness). This problem affects about 30% of crewmembers who fly short-duration missions (4-18 days), and 83% of astronauts who fly long-duration missions. This condition creates a potential hazard for the returning crew by impairing their ability to exit the vehicle after landing. A major driver for orthostatic intolerance is plasma volume loss. Despite the use of a mandatory fluid load before re-entry, astronauts return from space with plasma volume deficits ranging from 7-20%.

To provide additional protection against space flight induced orthostatic intolerance during re-entry and landing, both NASA and the Russian Federal Space Agency use compression garments, or antigravity suits. NASA astronauts use an inflatable antigravity suit (AGS) that is worn under the Advanced Crew Escape Suit. It has five interconnected air bladders that cover the abdomen, thighs, and calves. The AGS can be inflated to pressures ranging from 0.5 per square inch (psi), which is equivalent to 25.9 mmHg, to 2.5 psi (129.3 mmHg) in increments of 0.5 psi. When inflated, the AGS provides mechanical protection that reduces venous pooling and maintains arterial pressure.

Russian cosmonauts wear a non-inflatable compression garment, called the Kentavr, which is made of an elastic fabric. It is composed of shorts that extend from the waist to the knee and a pair of gaiters that cover the calves. Each component of the Kentavr has lacings to allow for an individualized fit. The nominal pressure provided by the Kentavr is 0.6 ± 0.1 psi (30 ± 5 mmHg).

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of NASA’s AGS and the Russian Kentavr garment, to prevent hypovolemia-related orthostatic intolerance.

APPROACH:
Prior to participation, 19 healthy volunteers, ages 32 – 54 years, passed a modified Air Force Class III physical. Subjects were randomly assigned to one of two groups: AGS (six men and three women) or Kentavr (six men and four women). A separate group of 16 subjects (11 men and 5 women) from a related study participated in the same protocols and served as controls (no countermeasure group).

Data collection was completed in two visits to the cardiovascular laboratory. For the first session, subjects reported to the laboratory following voluntary reduction of their dietary salt intake for 24 hours. Subjects provided a urine sample to confirm that urinary sodium was less than 100 mEq/gm-1 creatinine. Those meeting the selection criteria participated in a carbon monoxide re-breathing protocol to measure plasma volume. Subjects then received a single dose of furosemide (a loop diuretic commonly marketed under the brand name Lasix) and consumed a low salt diet provided by the investigators.

Subjects returned to the laboratory 36 hours later, when the plasma volume measurement was repeated and subjects underwent a tilt test protocol to assess orthostatic tolerance with (AGS inflated to 1.5 per square inch or Kentavr) or without a compression garment (separate study). Subjects did not consume any caffeine, nicotine, or alcohol for 12 hours and did not participate in maximal exercise or take any medications for 24 hours prior to testing.

RESULTS:
Hypovolemia
Control subjects experienced a mean loss of plasma volume of 17.1 ± 1.7%. AGS and Kentavr groups had a plasma volume loss of 16.9 ± 4.0% and 18.4 ± 2.6%, respectively. There were no statistically significant differences in plasma volume loss between groups.

Incidence of Orthostatic Hypotension/Presyncope
The ability to complete the tilt test was significantly greater in both the AGS and Kentavr subjects compared to the controls. All subjects wearing a compression garment (either AGS or Kentavr) during the tilt test completed the test without symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or presyncope (0% incidence). In contrast, only nine control subjects (56%) were able to complete the tilt test without signs or symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or presyncope.

Hemodynamic Responses
Both compression garments prevented the decrease in systolic blood pressure at test termination which was observed in control subjects. The change in systolic blood pressure of control subjects was significantly greater than in the AGS and Kentavr subjects, but no differences were found between countermeasure groups. There were no differences in diastolic blood pressure between the groups.

The change in heart rate was greater in the control subjects than in the AGS and Kentavr subjects. The elevation of heart rate in AGS and Kentavr subjects due to tilt was not significantly different between treatment groups. The drop in stroke volume at the end of tilt was significantly less in the AGS compared to the control subjects but not different between the Kentavr and controls. However, the standing stroke volumes for the AGS and Kentavr subjects were significantly higher than the controls at the end of tilt, and there was not a significant difference between AGS and Kentavr subjects. Neither the change from supine to tilt nor the final cardiac output and total peripheral resistance at tilt termination were different between groups.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During space flight, astronauts lose muscle mass, muscle strength, and muscle power. The decrease in muscle performance is concerning because it might impair the astronauts’ ability to perform various tasks that are critical to mission success and safety. There are currently exercise devices used on the International Space Station (ISS) to counteract the effects of zero gravity, but those are too large (weight and size) for use on the upcoming crew exploration vehicle, Orion. With this in mind, new more compact exercise devices are being designed and prototyped to evaluate their capabilities. The Exercise Physiology and Countermeasures (ExPC) Project was tasked with performing evaluations of these prototype devices in order to assess their potential for being included in an exploration vehicle. This evaluation was performed as an engineering checkout of two proposed exercise devices: an Inertia Wheel prototype exercise device and an Air Spring prototype exercise device. During the functional evaluation, a rowing exercise (aerobic and anaerobic) and a series of resistance exercises were performed at sub-maximal effort to ensure the devices were operating properly and to evaluate the performance of each device.

APPROACH:
Seven exercise subjects participated in this evaluation. All subjects were approved by the Human Test Subject Facility and provided informed consent. The evaluation was approved by the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. Subjects were in general good health with no recent sickness or injury, had no history of cardiovascular or musculoskeletal disease, and were free of significant muscle, joint, or bone injury for the last six months. Subjects were briefed on the protocol they performed and signed the consent form before proceeding with any testing.

Prior to any test sessions, subjects participated in a familiarization session during which they had the opportunity to practice exercising on each device, and received instruction on how to properly perform the resistance training exercises in the evaluation on each device. For each resistance exercise, subjects had the opportunity to perform at various loading levels. The resistance in the Inertial Wheel is created by a spinning flywheel, and was dependent upon how fast or slow the subject moved. The resistance in the Air Spring is created by air pressure inside a resistance cylinder, and can be lowered or raised by the user, just like a typical weight lifting machine. Because it was important that subjects lift approximately the same level of resistance with each device, they completed their practices on the Inertial Wheel first, and the loads that they developed during practice were measured and recorded. When subjects completed their practice on the Air Spring, the loads they developed with the Inertial Wheel were used to determine the Air Spring loads. Those loads were used on the Air Spring during the later data collection. After the familiarization session, subjects were scheduled for two exercise tests during which data was collected. There was at least 48 hours between scheduled sessions to ensure that subjects were fully recovered and free from fatigue.

During the exercise tests subjects participated in the following protocol:

Subjects reported to the specified test location in comfortable exercise shoes. They were provided with a spandex shirt and shorts to wear during the testing. They were given a chance to practice with the equipment and perform some simple muscle stretches. They then began the rowing exercise. They were instructed to row slowly and with a steady motion, and not to strain themselves or pull hard. While rowing, the test operators recorded force and speed data from the device. Subjects rowed for up to five minutes at a pace that they selected. Subjects were encouraged to row at a pace that made them feel like they’re moderately exercising, but that they could continue at for the entire five minutes. When the five minute session was complete, subjects were given a questionnaire asking about their experience exercising on the device. After they were rested, subjects completed a second rowing exercise trial. During this trial, subjects were asked to complete one minute of exercise, and to exercise at a pace they could sustain for one minute, but would have trouble continuing after a minute had passed. During space flight, the astronauts will need to perform high intensity exercise to stay healthy, and the investigators needed to understand if the devices are capable of allowing high intensity exercise to occur. After one minute, subjects stopped exercising, and were once again asked to complete a questionnaire detailing their experience with the device.

After completing the rowing exercise, subjects completed resistance exercises on the other device. Subjects had another opportunity to try the squat, dead lift, diagonal dead lift, heel raise, bench press, shoulder press, full body press, upright row, bicep curls, bent over rows, and triceps press. For each movement, subjects were asked to perform a light lift, medium lift, and a heavy lift at their self-selected intensity level. If a device was not capable of allowing a certain exercise, it was not attempted. Subjects completed a questionnaire during the rest periods. They rested from 30-90 seconds between each set. Subjects could request longer rest periods between tests if necessary. Load and speed data from the device were collected during each set.

During each exercise session, the motions of the subject’s arms, legs, and upper body were measured using a motion capture system with 12 cameras. Reflective markers were placed on the subjects with double-sided adhesive tape. The markers were attached to their clothing. If markers need to be attached to a body location that is not covered with clothing (knees), the marker was attached to fabric prewrap. A digital video camera recorded the subjects’ movements. They wore a chest strap heart rate monitor that was used to measure heart rate during all exercise.

RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded. Data will be used only to characterize capabilities of each device. No data will be published; this is an engineering evaluation only.

Subjects were briefed on the protocol they performed and signed the consent form before proceeding with any testing.

Prior to any test sessions, subjects participated in a familiarization session during which they had the opportunity to practice exercising on each device, and received instruction on how to properly perform the resistance training exercises in the evaluation on each device. For each resistance exercise, subjects had the opportunity to perform at various loading levels. The resistance in the Inertial Wheel is created by a spinning flywheel, and was dependent upon how fast or slow the subject moved. The resistance in the Air Spring is created by air pressure inside a resistance cylinder, and can be lowered or raised by the user, just like a typical weight lifting machine. Because it was important that subjects lift approximately the same level of resistance with each device, they completed their practices on the Inertial Wheel first, and the loads that they developed during practice were measured and recorded. When subjects completed their practice on the Air Spring, the loads they developed with the Inertial Wheel were used to determine the Air Spring loads. Those loads were used on the Air Spring during the later data collection. After the familiarization session, subjects were scheduled for two exercise tests during which data was collected. There was at least 48 hours between scheduled sessions to ensure that subjects were fully recovered and free from fatigue.

During the exercise tests subjects participated in the following protocol:

Subjects reported to the specified test location in comfortable exercise shoes. They were provided with a spandex shirt and shorts to wear during the testing. They were given a chance to practice with the equipment and perform some simple muscle stretches. They then began the rowing exercise. They were instructed to row slowly and with a steady motion, and not to strain themselves or pull hard. While rowing, the test operators recorded force and speed data from the device. Subjects rowed for up to five minutes at a pace that they selected. Subjects were encouraged to row at a pace that made them feel like they’re moderately exercising, but that they could continue at for the entire five minutes. When the five minute session was complete, subjects were given a questionnaire asking about their experience exercising on the device. After they were rested, subjects completed a second rowing exercise trial. During this trial, subjects were asked to complete one minute of exercise, and to exercise at a pace they could sustain for one minute, but would have trouble continuing after a minute had passed. During space flight, the astronauts will need to perform high intensity exercise to stay healthy, and the investigators needed to understand if the devices are capable of allowing high intensity exercise to occur. After one minute, subjects stopped exercising, and were once again asked to complete a questionnaire detailing their experience with the device.

After completing the rowing exercise, subjects completed resistance exercises on the other device. Subjects had another opportunity to try the squat, dead lift, diagonal dead lift, heel raise, bench press, shoulder press, full body press, upright row, bicep curls, bent over rows, and triceps press. For each movement, subjects were asked to perform a light lift, medium lift, and a heavy lift at their self-selected intensity level. If a device was not capable of allowing a certain exercise, it was not attempted. Subjects completed a questionnaire during the rest periods. They rested from 30-90 seconds between each set. Subjects could request longer rest periods between tests if necessary. Load and speed data from the device were collected during each set.

During each exercise session, the motions of the subject’s arms, legs, and upper body were measured using a motion capture system with 12 cameras. Reflective markers were placed on the subjects with double-sided adhesive tape. The markers were attached to their clothing. If markers need to be attached to a body location that is not covered with clothing (knees), the marker was attached to fabric prewrap. A digital video camera recorded the subjects’ movements. They wore a chest strap heart rate monitor that was used to measure heart rate during all exercise.

RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded. Data will be used only to characterize capabilities of each device. No data will be published; this is an engineering evaluation only.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During space flight, space motion sickness (SMS) and perceptual disturbances have led to reductions in performance efficiency and sense of well-being. During entry and immediately after landing, such disturbances could have a serious impact on the ability of the commander to land the Orbiter, as well as on the abilities of all crewmembers to egress from the Orbiter, particularly in a non-nominal condition or following extended stays in microgravity. An understanding of spatial orientation and motion perception is essential for developing countermeasures for SMS and perceptual disturbances during space flight and upon return to Earth. Countermeasures for optimal performance in-flight and a successful return to Earth require the development of preflight and in-flight training to help astronauts acquire and maintain a dual adaptive state.

This study was intended to enhance the understanding of adaptation to space flight and readaptation after flight on various aspects of human spatial orientation, neurosensory, sensory-motor, physiological, and perceptual functions and on autonomic gastric functions associated with space motion sickness (SMS). This experiment correlated the postflight recovery of postural equilibrium control, head and gaze stability, readaptation changes in vestibular function, and examined the relationship between voluntary oculomotor performance and passive vestibulo-ocular responses following space flight. Changes in stomach nerve response to food consumption over the first few days of flight were to be observed and analyzed, and evaluated when SMS symptoms occurred. The investigators were also interested in how nerve activity correlated with the symptoms before, during, and after their occurrence.

APPROACH:
Protocol A
Voluntary Head Movement (VHM)
Standard electro-oculography (EOG) techniques recorded horizontal and vertical eye position. A head mounted tri-axial rate sensor measured head velocity in the pitch, yaw and roll planes. The BOG and rate sensor signals were collected with the Superpocket physiological monitoring system and recorded on a TEAC cassette recorder. A goggle assembly controlled visual conditions via an electronic shutter, changing instantly from a clear state to an opaque state according to the experiment protocol. A cruciform target and four additional visual targets were mounted on the middeck locker for on-orbit data collection and on a screen during baseline data collection. A microcassette recorder delivered a sinusoidally-modulated audio tone during one portion of the VHM protocol. Tasks performed in-flight were tested pre- and postflight as well. Subjects were asked to report perceptual sensations associated with each stimulus.

VHM Inflight - Four of the six inflight experiments were designed to investigate voluntary oculomotor function. Two additional experiments were performed pre- and postflight only investigated this function. The protocols involved a combination of eye and/or head movements to acquire targets along a visual display. Calibrations of eye and head signals were performed. Each task was repeated three times in both the horizontal and vertical planes. The tasks are described below:

  • Head Calibration - the subject directed a head-mounted laser spot to the central target and moved their head to pre-selected targets in both the horizontal and vertical planes.
  • Eye Calibration - with head fixed, subject acquired a successive sequence of target positions in the horizontal and vertical planes, visually fixating on each target for two seconds.
  • Target Acquisition - a cruciform target arrangement, located 34 inches from the subject's eyes was used to display a series of targets in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Subjects acquired each target with both a head and eye movement.
  • Gaze Stabilization - the subject first visually fixated on a wall-fixed target with the head in a central position. When the goggles became opaque and vision was occluded the subject rotated the head while maintaining ocular fixation on the just-seen wall-fixed target. When the goggles became clear the subject refixated the target with the eyes only. The subject then rotated the head back to center, keeping eyes on the target.
  • Spontaneous/Gaze Nystagmus - was measured with the crewmember fixating on a wall target, and then imagining the same wall-fixed target with vision occluded, and then with the eyes closed. Gaze nystagmus, or the effect of a change in eye position was evaluated by having the crewmember fixate on imaginary 40 degree targets (vision occluded) in both the vertical and horizontal planes for 20 seconds per imaginary target. Measurement of eye movements continued for an additional 20 seconds when the eye position was returned to straight ahead gaze.
  • Sinusoidal Head Oscillations -
    With Vision: Subjects attempted to maintain visual fixation on a wall-fixed target while smoothly oscillating his/her head in yaw or pitch in cadence with an audio tone that is sinusoidally modulated to sweep over the bandwidth of interest (chirp).
    Without Vision: Subject repeated the chirp with vision occluded while attempting to maintain ocular fixation on the remembered location of the target. The subject repeated this entire procedure in each plane for each condition.

    VHM Pre/Postflight

  • Non-Predictable Target Tracking - for these trials, the target was initially stationary in the center of the field of view. At an unpredictable time, the target began to move at constant velocity, either rightward, leftward, upward, or downward. The onset time of target motion, direction of motion, target velocity, and final target displacement was randomized.
    Predictable Target Tracking - the target oscillated at 0.3 Hz. For each trial, tracking was performed for at least six cycles.
  • Positional Nystagmus - spontaneous eye movements were collected with the crewmember in seven different static positions:
    1. Seated upright
    2. Supine
    3. Supine with head turned to the right
    4. Supine with head turned to the left
    5. Supine with head and neck extended over the edge of the examination table (head and neck will be supported by test operator)
    6. Body and head turned to the right side
    7. Body and head turned to the left side

    Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN)
    A binocular Optokinetic Stimulator provided a full visual field optokinetic stimulus during the OKN protocol. Standard electro-oculography (EOG) techniques recorded horizontal and vertical eye position. The EOG signals were collected with the Superpocket physiological monitoring system and recorded on a TEAC cassette recorder. Tasks performed inflight were tested pre and postflight as well. Subjects were asked to report perceptual sensations associated with each stimulus.

    Postural Equilibrium (pre/postflight)
    Measurements pertaining to postural equilibrium were collected using standard electromyography (EMG) techniques on the upper thigh and lower calf segments of the subject's left leg, sway-bars situated at the shoulders and hips, and force transducers situated in the foot plate of the posture platform. In addition, overhead and full field video was recorded through the entire test session. The subject's primary task was to maintain a normal upright stance.

    Head and Gaze Stability During Locomotion (pre/postflight)
    Whole body movement during locomotion on a treadmill and during a jump task was videotaped and the locations of retroreflective markers placed on specific locations on the body were analyzed with the aid of a computerized motion analysis system. In addition, eye movement and leg muscle activity during these tasks were recorded using standard electro-oculography (EOG) and electromyography (EMG), respectively.

    Path Integration ((pre/postflight)
    To examine the cognitive processing of spatial orientation information, whole body movement during locomotion along a previously memorized path (parallelogram or square) were videotaped and the locations of retroreflective markers placed on specific locations on the body were analyzed with the aid of a computerized motion analysis system.

    Protocol B
    This experiment marked the first attempt to obtain measurements of the stomach muscle activity in humans during space flight. In this study, myoelectric activity of the stomach was examined following a meal. Gastric activity associated with space motion sickness was measured using EGG in which electrical impulses associated with stomach secretion and movements were recorded. To perform this EGG, three electrodes were situated on the abdomen.

    Each subject participated in two preflight training sessions which occurred at 12 months prior to launch (L-12) and at 10 months prior to launch (L-10). To compare subject inflight EGG data that were associated with eating to eating under normal ground conditions, there were two baseline data collection sessions. These sessions occurred after both preflight training sessions. During one baseline data collection session, subjects were given fluids and during the other session, they were given a small meal. Subjects fasted for 6.5 hours before a data collection session. When the small meal was consumed, data collection began 20 minutes before the 5 to 10-minute meal and continued for three hours following the meal. To ensure proper and consistent placement of EGG electrodes on the abdomen inflight, a permanent marker was used to mark the correct locations after a meal had been consumed within eight days prior to flight.

    The EGG data were collected using a portable recording instrument designed for space flight. The electrodes amplified the signal at its source and the main part of the recording instrument amplified it further. A one Mb RAM card held twenty-four hours of data. The hardware was lightweight and worn on a belt. It was capable of registering input from the crewmember regarding food or water consumption and SMS symptoms. There were five events that were coded by number: eating, drinking, stomach awareness/discomfort, nausea and vomiting. When a crewmember experienced one of these events, he pressed the event marker with the correct code number and the event with its corresponding Mission Elapsed Time (MET) was recorded. Insertion of event markers did not disrupt data collection or logging.

    The EGG equipment was donned as early as possible in the flight. Continuous data collection occurred for at least the first three flight days. The electrodes, RAM card and battery were replaced every 24 hours.

    RESULTS:
    Protocol A
    Results for this portion of the experiment aren’t available at this time.

    Protocol B
    Crewmembers responded normally to ingestion of a meal preflight, showing an increase in the amplitude and power of the normal three gastric cycles per minute. An abnormal decrease in the dominant power occurred on Flight Day (FD) 1 for all subjects but the response returned to normal on FD3. Individual differences were observed and one crewmember actually showed a slight abnormal preflight response to the meal. All three crewmembers experienced moderate to severe loss of appetite on FD1 and two of them showed mild loss of appetite on FD3. When appetite returned and SMS symptoms resolved, the gastric responses after a meal returned to normal.

    Two nausea events were recorded by one crewmember and one vomiting event was recorded by another crewmember. Percent spectral power was assessed to determine the regularity of normal gastric slow waves. The percent of time that normal waves are recorded by the EGG and the percent of time that abnormal (faster or slower) waves are recorded is the percent spectral power. EGG data showed that in the first episode of nausea 60% of spectral power was associated with deviations in normal contraction cycles before nausea was reported. Forty percent of the power was associated with fewer contractions per minute and 20% was associated with higher contractions per minute. The percent of spectral power associated with these alterations of rhythmic contractions increased to approximately 75% for 15 minutes following the report of nausea, then decreased to about 45%, which was noted at 45 minutes following the nausea report.

    In the second report of nausea, the percent spectral power associated with altered stomach contractions was high (75-80%) throughout the entire period of EGG recording. The researchers speculated that the data indicated that this second report of nausea lasted longer than the first. Also of note was that the first nausea report data corresponded to slower gastric contractions two to three times more than faster ones throughout the entire recording period. In the second episode, data was associated with faster frequency contractions during the time following the nausea report. Other studies have shown that faster frequency contractions are associated with motion sickness as compared to slower frequency contractions.

    Similar to the nausea, the EGG data showed altered stomach contraction rhythms before and up to 30 minutes following the vomiting episode. For this entire time, 75 to 80% of the spectral power was associated with abnormal rhythms. Forty-five minutes after the report the gastric activity was normal. One interesting point is that this crewmember specifically stated that he had no symptoms prior to vomiting, which is a fairly common characteristic of SMS. For both nausea and the vomiting episodes, crewmembers had altered rhythmic gastric contractions at least 30 minutes prior to reporting the symptom.

    The abnormally fast neural myoelectric waves that are detected by EGG have been associated in other studies with decreased spontaneous movement of the stomach and the absence of stomach contractions. Findings in this study indicate that spontaneous stomach movement may be decreased during both mild and severe symptoms of SMS, which occur during the first few days of space flight. The perturbations of this movement may affect absorption of nutrients and oral medications for both astronauts and motion sickness victims on Earth. Since astronauts must treat several physiologic abnormalities that occur in space, it is important that drug absorption and bioavailability be preserved for pharmaceutical effectiveness. Also, crewmembers must maintain adequate nutrition for physically and mentally demanding work, much of which is critical to safety of the crew or the vehicle.

    This investigation utilized a noninvasive technique to successfully record human stomach myoelectric activity in space over a long period. Future work should involve confirmation of these findings and further characterization of the altered stomach rhythms in relation to the presence of nausea and vomiting, especially in regards to the precise timing of the EGG data and the subjective reports of the SMS symptoms. This technique could potentially be utilized for monitoring stomach muscle and nerve conditions as an early warning before SMS symptoms appear. It could also potentially assist flight surgeons in making decisions regarding medication administration and timing. However, in order to function in such a manner, the data would have to be available real-time or near real-time.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Muscle atrophy during space flight is known to result in postflight decrements, even after short duration missions (LeBlanc et al. 1995). The objective of this study was to use Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to determine leg muscle volumes in all subjects at the start and end of bed rest.

APPROACH:
Prior to the MRI session, subjects were positioned supine for at least 30 minutes. Proton magnetic resonance images were then collected (Adams et al 1993), using a 1.5 T G.E. imaging system. Ten mm-thick image "slices" were collected at 5 mm intervals along the entire length of the right and left lower limbs. To ensure that the images cover the same range of the limb, an invariant anatomical feature, the greater trochanter of the femur, was palpated and used to set the electronic land marking of the first image slice. Images were ported to a computer workstation, and the cross sectional area (CSA) of the individual thigh and leg muscles were determined using image analysis software. These data was used to calculate the volume of each muscle and also determined the degree of muscle atrophy elicited by the bed rest and Artificial Gravity (AG) protocols.

To accurately register the images from one session to the next, the marrow area (of either the tibia or femur) was measured for each slice. High contrast between the marrow and the surrounding bone was facilitated by semi-automatic analysis. In one of the central images, a region inside the marrow was selected, and a mask was created. A program was then used to expand this mask to cover the whole marrow region. The program was iteratively expanded and contracted the mask until a stable region was selected. A file containing all the marrow size values for a particular subject was then imported into a spreadsheet from which the position offset for each session was determined by plotting the position versus number of pixels for two sessions and visually determining the offset required for the two curves to coincide. The images were corrected for non-uniformity resulting from the coil sensitivity. The normalized images were windowed to select only muscle excluding the fat pixels. The windowing script also included procedures for excluding a ring around the marrow and around the outer edge of the leg.

Individual muscles were outlined. Prior to the MRI session, subjects were positioned supine for at least 30 minutes. Proton magnetic resonance images were then collected (Adams et al 1993), using a 1.5 T G.E. imaging system. investigators: Principal Investigator: Dulchavsky, ScottCo-Investigator: Hamilton, DouglasCo-Investigator: Melton, ShannonCo-Investigator: Sargsyan, Ashot
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Advanced Diagnostic Ultrasound in Microgravity (ADUM) experiment used ground-based studies and on-orbit sessions to demonstrate the accuracy of ultrasound in potential aerospace medical contingencies (pneumothorax, sinusitis, dental infection, abdominal disorders, orthopedic injury, urologic disorders, and cardiovascular compromise). The experiment also determined optimal training methodologies for advanced ultrasound techniques using both CD-ROM based instruction and remote guidance.

APPROACH:
A pre- and postflight scan of each subject was performed to obtain a baseline prior to flight and recovery data postflight. In addition, an in-depth debrief was performed postflight as a tool to evaluate the inflight comprehensive study and obtain lessons learned and improvements for future studies.

This experiment required two International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers, one as a subject and one as an operator. Each scan was performed by the operator on the subject. Prior to a scan, the operator reviewed the On-board Proficiency Enhancer (OPE), a software refresher tool. After completing the OPE, the operator scanned the subject via real-time remote guidance from an expert sonographer located in the Telescience Support Center (TSC) in the Mission Control Center-Houston (MCC-H). Video and still images from all scans were stored on the ultrasound and downlinked for the investigator's analysis prior to that scan's session analysis. Restricted access real-time data downlinking was required for the ultrasound images (which are medically sensitive; therefore, private information) and voice communications between the ISS and the TSC. Video from cabin cameras was downlinked non real-time (also restricted/private data) to evaluate the real-time operations and for post-activity human factors-like analysis. Analysis of sessions were conducted within three days following the exams to obtain human factors information and feedback from the crewmember who functioned as the operator for the scan.

RESULTS:
Results of the CD-ROM-based On-board Proficiency Enhancer (OPE) sessions were used to modify the instructions during a complete 35 minute real-time thoracic, cardiac, and carotid/jugular ultrasound study. Following commands from the ground-based expert, the crewmember acquired all target views and images without difficulty. The anatomical content and fidelity of ultrasound video were adequate for clinical decision making.

Complex ultrasound experiments with expert guidance were performed with high accuracy following limited preflight training and multimedia based inflight review, despite a two-second communication delay. Inflight application of multimedia proficiency enhancement software, coupled with real-time remote expert guidance, facilitates the successful performance of ultrasound examinations in orbit and may have additional terrestrial and space applications.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Meck, Janice
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Following exposure to space flight, upright posture can result in an inability to maintain adequate arterial pressure and cerebral perfusion (orthostatic or postural hypotension). This may result in presyncope (lightheadedness) or syncope (loss of consciousness) during reentry or egress. A significant number of astronauts experience orthostatic hypotension and presyncope during upright posture. The severity of this problem increases with the length of the space flight mission, as seen in approximately 20% of short-duration and 83% of long-duration crewmembers. It is expected that orthostatic hypotension will be severe on exploration class missions.

To date, available countermeasures (LBNP, fluid loading, Florinef) have not eliminated postflight orthostatic hypotension. This study was designed to evaluate a new pharmacologic countermeasure for protection from postflight orthostatic hypotension. Investigators were studying the ability of the drug Midodrine to reduce the incidence and/or severity of orthostatic hypotension in astronauts returning to Earth. The subject pool included subjects who experienced presyncope as well as those who did not.

APPROACH:
Preflight:
A familiarization session and drug tolerance test was performed before flight. The familiarization session provided subjects with details of the drug tolerance test and the experimental protocol for preflight (L-10) and postflight (R+0) testing. Prior to the start of the drug tolerance test, an electrocardiogram (ECG) was obtained to determine if there was abnormal electrical activity of the heart. If no abnormal activity was detected, the drug tolerance test began. First, the baseline blood pressure was measured, followed by an ingestion of 10 mg of Midodrine. The subject’s blood pressure was monitored at regular intervals for four hours, to ensure that Midodrine did not cause a significant increase in the subject’s blood pressure. During this monitoring period, a record was kept of any subjective effects Midodrine may have caused.

Postflight:
Shortly after return to Earth, the subject ingested the Midodrine pill. Then, an Operational Tilt Test (MR001L) was performed in the Crew Transport Vehicle (CTV) to determine the crewmember’s orthostatic tolerance. The subject was instrumented with an electrocardiogram, a beat-to-beat finger blood pressure device, and an automatic blood pressure cuff. ECG measurements were made to determine aortic cross-sectional diameter and aortic flow while lying on a tilt table. Following this, the subject was brought upright by the tilt table to approximately 80 degrees for 10 minutes while the measurements continued. The tilt test was used to assess the effects of prolonged weightlessness on orthostatic tolerance during upright posture, as measured by supine and standing heart rate, blood pressure, stroke volume, cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance. After completion of the Tilt Test, blood pressure was monitored at regular intervals for an additional period of time. During this time the crewmember also completed a questionnaire.

It is critical that the postflight Operational Tilt Test was performed within 2.5 hours of pill ingestion. Arrangements were made to perform the postflight data collection on the CTV to accommodate this time interval.

RESULTS:
It was successfully shown that of the seven astronauts that participated, two had been presyncopal after previous missions and five had not. After taking Midodrine, the two previously presyncopal astronauts finished the tilt test and the five astronauts, who had not previously suffered from presyncopal symptoms after space flight, finished the tilt test and importantly, did not show signs of hypertension when supine or vertical.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Bloomberg, Jacob
experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Newly returned astronauts have shown instability in walking and in making jump landings and have experienced oscillopsia (apparent bouncing of viewed objects). The mechanisms of these abnormalities are not known, although changes in muscle tone, muscle activation patterns and vestibular function could contribute. Instability of gaze could result from changes in the coordination of head and body movements. The objectives of this study were to investigate space flight-induced changes in locomotor control, including changes in the coordination of movements of the head, trunk and legs during walking, and the relation of those changes to the ability to maintain a stable gaze; changes in the ability to maintain spatial orientation while walking; and changes in motor strategies for absorbing impact during jump landings.

APPROACH:
Locomotor control was studied in 5 protocols. For 4 of the protocols, reflective markers affixed to appropriate places on the astronaut's head, spine, and limb joints were tracked by 4 video cameras. The position of each marker in space was determined with the aid of a video-based motion analysis system. In some of the studies, some subjects also wore shoes with foot switches beneath the heel and great toe.

In 3 of the protocols, the astronauts walked on a motorized treadmill at 6.4 km/h (4 mph) while wearing a safety harness attached to an overhead frame. (The protocol using the treadmill was denoted as DSO 614A and was performed on the following missions: STS-43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 53, 57, 58, 63, and 65). The treadmill tests were performed under 3 conditions: with the astronauts fixating on a visual target either 30 cm or 2 m in front of them, or alternating open eyes and closed eyes for 5 seconds at a time while trying to keep the eyes directed at the target. Eye closures were confirmed by electro-oculography. Data from about 10 days before flight and from 2 to 4 hours after landing were used for comparisons. Head-trunk coordination was studied in 23 astronauts (19 male, 4 female) who flew on 8- to 15-day missions. Fifteen were veterans of previous space flights. Recordings were made of the vertical movements of the trunk and the pitch movements of the head. Lower limb movements were studied in 7 astronauts (6 male, 1 female) on 8- or 9-day missions. Five were veterans of previous space flights. The angular displacement and angular velocity of the hip, knee and ankle in the front-to-back and vertical directions were determined from the video recordings, and the times of heel strike and toe off were determined from foot switch data or from toe velocity. Plots of angular velocity versus angular displacement were used to represent the periodic motion of each joint. Neuromuscular activation patterns were studied in 10 astronauts (7 male, 3 female) who flew on 8- to 15-day missions. Six were veterans of previous space flights. This protocol did not make use of the reflective markers and cameras; instead, electromyographic (EMG) recordings were made from electrodes placed on the skin over selected muscles of the lower limb. Foot switch data were also collected. The EMG recordings were normalized with regard to the level of activation and the temporal relation to heel strike, yielding reduced waveforms that represented the activity of each muscle throughout the gait cycle.

Spatial orientation while walking a path was studied in 7 astronauts (5 male, 2 female) who flew on 8- to 14-day missions (STS-64, 66, 67, 68); this protocol was referred to as DSO 614B. The astronauts walked clockwise and counterclockwise around a triangular path, either with their eyes open or with their vision blocked after they had looked at the path. The astronauts wore a helmet equipped with blackened goggles to block vision and headphones that played white noise to mask auditory spatial cues. Three reflective markers extended above the helmet, and their positions were used to compute the astronauts' walking direction and velocity. Data from 15 days before flight and from 2 hours after landing were used for comparisons.

Movements of the lower limb and the center of mass during jump landings were studied in 9 astronauts (8 male, 1 female) who flew on 7- to 14-day missions. The tests were performed 2 to 6 months and 9 to 15 days before launch and within 4 hours of landing. While wearing a safety harness and reflective markers, an astronaut jumped from a platform 30 cm (1 ft) high and landed on both feet. Jumps made with eyes open and fixated on a target were alternated with jumps made with eyes closed and directed toward the remembered target. The angles and angular velocities of the ankle, knee and hip joints were computed from the positions of the markers. The time of impact was determined from foot switch data or from toe velocity. The position of the astronaut's center of mass was estimated from the marker positions, and the velocity of the center of mass was calculated. A simple mathematical model for the vertical motion of the center of mass, in which a spring and a parallel damping mechanism represented the legs, was used to evaluate the stiffness and damping functions of the legs.

RESULTS:
In the preflight treadmill tests of head-trunk coordination, pitch head movements were smoothly coordinated to oppose the vertical movements of the trunk, thereby helping to maintain a stable gaze. The coherence between these wavelike movements decreased significantly after space flight, and the decrement in coherence was greater with the far visual target than with the near target. Both before and after space flight, the amplitude of the pitch head movements was greater with the near visual target, which would have larger apparent motion and would provide stronger feedback. After space flight, with near (or far) visual targets, the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced in 6 (8) astronauts, unchanged in 13 (11), and increased in 4 (4) astronauts. The reductions occurred in novice astronauts, but not in veterans. Both before and after flight, when the eyes were closed the head was tilted forward and the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced. The amplitude was restored almost immediately when the eyes were again opened.

In the treadmill studies of lower limb movement, variability in the gait cycle increased after space flight. Variability increased for the knee at the time of heel strike, for the ankle during the swing phase and for the hip at the moment of toe off. However, the increased variability in the motion of individual joints did not interfere with the basic pattern of lower limb coordination, and the stability of the system as a whole was retained. The basic temporal characteristics of the gait cycle were also retained: the stride time and the proportion of time spent standing during each step varied less than the variability of the treadmill speed. It was surprising that so little change was detected in the overall gait pattern, considering the wide-based, cautious, shuffling gait of several astronauts when they entered the testing room after flight. Use of the treadmill may have limited the gait abnormalities that could be detected by requiring a subject to keep the pace and restricting the width of the gait. Also, some astronauts chose not to walk on the treadmill after landing, perhaps feeling that their coordination was not yet sufficient for the task. Perhaps greater changes would have been detected in these astronauts' gait.

In the treadmill studies of neuromuscular activation, the symmetry of activation of the muscles of the 2 lower limbs was not affected by space flight. Few preflight-to-postflight differences occurred in the all-subject average of reduced waveforms for each muscle. However, significant functional increases and decreases were observed after space flight in the normalized mean amplitudes for various muscles around the times of toe off and heel strike. Also, between the preflight and postflight tests, co-contraction of the opposing muscles of the lower leg increased before toe off and decreased before heel strike, while co-contraction of the opposing thigh muscles increased before heel strike. In addition, many statistically significant preflight-to-postflight differences were found in the timing and duration of activation of specific muscles for individual subjects. The temporal relationship between the offset of the gastrocnemius and the onset of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was altered after space flight in 8 of the 10 subjects. In half of the subjects, the order of activation of these muscles was actually reversed. Also, the relative amplitude of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was reduced after flight. In the normal toe-off process, activity of the gastrocnemius with corresponding inhibition of the tibialis anterior pushes the toes back against the ground. Then, activity of the gastrocnemius ceases and the tibialis anterior is activated to lift the foot so that the toes will clear the ground as the foot swings forward. The changes that were found after space flight might explain the excessive scraping of the feet on the treadmill that was observed in postflight tests.

In the studies of spatial orientation while walking the triangular path, distance error was not significantly increased after flight. Astronauts tended to underestimate turns when walking with eyes closed, and the resulting directional error was larger after space flight than before. The astronauts walked the path more slowly after spaceflight, both with eyes open and eyes closed.

In the studies of jump landings, closing the eyes did not affect the astronauts' performance, perhaps because they had already judged the height. Some astronauts showed a preflight-to-postflight increase in lower limb compliance, with greater joint flexion and flexion rates. Some showed a decrease in compliance, and some showed no change. In the preflight jumps, after reaching its lowest point, the center of mass moved up and overshot the final rest position. After space flight, astronauts whose compliance had increased had much slower upward responses with little overshoot, while those whose compliance had decreased had faster upward responses with greater overshoot. The simple spring-and-damper model was able to predict the postflight alterations in the motion of the center of gravity by changing leg stiffness only; changes in damping did not appear to play a significant role.

These results are important for understanding how astronauts' abilities to manage an emergency egress, or even to walk on another planet, could be impaired after space flight The results show that space flight alters the coordination between vertical trunk movements and compensatory pitch head movements during walking. This alteration may partly account for the oscillopsia that was reported during the postflight treadmill tests. The postflight changes that were observed in the neuromuscular control of heel strike might affect the transmission of the jolt from the heel strike to the head, possibly exacerbating the postflight oscillopsia. Various head movement strategies were observed after flight. Astronauts who reduced the amplitude of their pitch head movements may have been trying to reduce confusing signals from the vestibular organs. It is also possible that the various strategies were not subject-specific but were part of an ongoing process of relearning motor strategies that are appropriate to Earth's gravity. The results indicate that veteran astronauts adapt more quickly upon returning to gravity, suggesting that preflight exposure to conflicting visual and vestibular inputs during locomotion could be used to train astronauts to rapidly reorder their motor control strategies to reduce postflight motor disturbances.

In the preflight treadmill tests of head-trunk coordination, pitch head movements were smoothly coordinated to oppose the vertical movements of the trunk, thereby helping to maintain a stable gaze. The coherence between these wavelike movements decreased significantly after space flight, and the decrement in coherence was greater with the far visual target than with the near target. Both before and after space flight, the amplitude of the pitch head movements was greater with the near visual target, which would have larger apparent motion and would provide stronger feedback. After space flight, with near (or far) visual targets, the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced in 6 (8) astronauts, unchanged in 13 (11), and increased in 4 (4) astronauts. The reductions occurred in novice astronauts, but not in veterans. Both before and after flight, when the eyes were closed the head was tilted forward and the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced. The amplitude was restored almost immediately when the eyes were again opened.

In the treadmill studies of lower limb movement, variability in the gait cycle increased after space flight. Variability increased for the knee at the time of heel strike, for the ankle during the swing phase and for the hip at the moment of toe off. However, the increased variability in the motion of individual joints did not interfere with the basic pattern of lower limb coordination, and the stability of the system as a whole was retained. The basic temporal characteristics of the gait cycle were also retained: the stride time and the proportion of time spent standing during each step varied less than the variability of the treadmill speed. It was surprising that so little change was detected in the overall gait pattern, considering the wide-based, cautious, shuffling gait of several astronauts when they entered the testing room after flight. Use of the treadmill may have limited the gait abnormalities that could be detected by requiring a subject to keep the pace and restricting the width of the gait. Also, some astronauts chose not to walk on the treadmill after landing, perhaps feeling that their coordination was not yet sufficient for the task. In addition, many statistically significant preflight-to-postflight differences were found in the timing and duration of activation of specific muscles for individual subjects. The temporal relationship between the offset of the gastrocnemius and the onset of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was altered after space flight in 8 of the 10 subjects. In half of the subjects, the order of activation of these muscles was actually reversed. Also, the relative amplitude of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was reduced after flight. Then, activity of the gastrocnemius ceases and the tibialis anterior is activated to lift the foot so that the toes will clear the ground as the foot swings forward. The changes that were found after space flight might explain the excessive scraping of the feet on the treadmill that was observed in postflight tests.

In the studies of spatial orientation while walking the triangular path, distance error was not significantly increased after flight. Astronauts tended to underestimate turns when walking with eyes closed, and the resulting directional error was larger after space flight than before. The astronauts walked the path more slowly after spaceflight, both with eyes open and eyes closed.

In the studies of jump landings, closing the eyes did not affect the astronauts' performance, perhaps because they had already judged the height. Some astronauts showed a preflight-to-postflight increase in lower limb compliance, with greater joint flexion and flexion rates. Some showed a decrease in compliance, and some showed no change. In the preflight jumps, after reaching its lowest point, the center of mass moved up and overshot the final rest position. After space flight, astronauts whose compliance had increased had much slower upward responses with little overshoot, while those whose compliance had decreased had faster upward responses with greater overshoot. The simple spring-and-damper model was able to predict the postflight alterations in the motion of the center of gravity by changing leg stiffness only; changes in damping did not appear to play a significant role.

These results are important for understanding how astronauts' abilities to manage an emergency egress, or even to walk on another planet, could be impaired after space flight The results show that space flight alters the coordination between vertical trunk movements and compensatory pitch head movements during walking. This alteration may partly account for the oscillopsia that was reported during the postflight treadmill tests. The postflight changes that were observed in the neuromuscular control of heel strike might affect the transmission of the jolt from the heel strike to the head, possibly exacerbating the postflight oscillopsia. Various head movement strategies were observed after flight. Astronauts who reduced the amplitude of their pitch head movements may have been trying to reduce confusing signals from the vestibular organs. It is also possible that the various strategies were not subject-specific but were part of an ongoing process of relearning motor strategies that are appropriate to Earth's gravity. The results indicate that veteran astronauts adapt more quickly upon returning to gravity, suggesting that preflight exposure to conflicting visual and vestibular inputs during locomotion could be used to train astronauts to rapidly reorder their motor control strategies to reduce postflight motor disturbances.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Shuttle astronauts are typically exposed to "sleep cycle shifting" due to mission-dependent orbital mechanics and mission requirements. This is equivalent to imposition of a non-24 hour 'day' and is likely to result in misalignment of the endogenous circadian timing system with respect to the desired sleep-wake cycle, even among crewmembers who begin the mission with their sleep-wake cycle well synchronized to mission elapsed time (MET) on the day of launch. Such misalignment is known to produce sleep disturbances, daytime sleepiness, reduced attention, negative mood, slower reaction times, gastrointestinal disorders and impaired daytime alertness. Although appropriately scheduled exposure to bright light has been shown to be capable of resetting the phase of the human circadian pacemaker, existing Shuttle technology precludes use of such bright light delivery systems aboard the Shuttle. Several lines of evidence, including the discovery of melatonin receptors on the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the human hypothalamus and the results of animal and human studies, indicate that melatonin administration may be effective in generating phase shifts of the circadian pacemaker. The current study evaluated the ability of melatonin to entrain the human circadian pacemaker in sighted humans to a shorter-than-24-hour day length.

The current research was designed to test the following hypotheses:

  1. the human circadian pacemaker will be unable to maintain synchronization with a sleep-wake cycle of 23.5 hours, typical of that required on Shuttle missions;
  2. that such loss of synchronization will result in sleep-onset insomnia, decreased sleep efficiency, and decreased daytime alertness and performance resulting from imposition of the 23.5-hour day; and
  3. that a daily dose of melatonin (5 mg), administered one hour before bedtime, will be sufficient to entrain the circadian pacemaker to a 23.5-hour scheduled sleep-wake cycle.

To test the hypotheses, researchers conducted long-term (50-day) inpatient trials utilizing methodologies that allowed direct measurement of endogenous circadian phase and amplitude before, during and after extended duration exposure to a shorter-than-24-hour day length (i.e., similar to that occurring on many space shuttle flights). Each trial took place in an environment with low light intensities similar to that measured aboard the space shuttle on STS-90. It was anticipated that when subjects were scheduled to a 23.5-hour day and room lighting conditions were maintained to 8 lux maximum, that the endogenous circadian pacemaker would oscillate with a period that was different (24.1 to 24.2 hours) from the period of the imposed sleep-wake/work cycle. Failure to entrain the human circadian pacemaker to the 23.5-hour day was expected to be associated with disturbed sleep, and impaired waking alertness and performance. It was also expected that a daily dose of 5 mg of melatonin, one hour prior to scheduled sleep, would entrain the human circadian pacemaker to the 23.5-hour day. The melatonin countermeasure was expected to maintain normal sleep and circadian patterns, and normal waking alertness and performance.

APPROACH:
Five healthy male subjects (age: mean ± SD, 34 ± 7.25; range, 26-44) were studied. All subjects were required to pass a rigorous health screening including medical history, physical and psychological exams, blood and urine chemistries and an electrocardiogram. Toxicology screens for drug use, including alcohol and caffeine verified that participants were drug-free upon admission to the laboratory.

Blood was sampled for melatonin and cortisol during circadian phase estimations (constant routines) and 28-hour sampling windows throughout the intervening study days between constant routines. (In general, during a constant routine protocol, subjects remain under constant conditions, awake, engaged in light, mainly sedentary activity, and consume identical food and fluid every hour.) Core body temperature, waking electroencephalogram (EEG) and polysomnography were recorded throughout most of the protocol. Subject's performance, alertness and mood were assessed every 2 hours during wakefulness using valid, reliable standardized measures, which are sensitive to circadian misalignment and homeostatic sleep drive.

Ceiling-mounted fluorescent lamps with a 4100 K color temperature produced a spectrum of white light. Clear polycarbonate lenses filtered 99.9% of the light in the UV range. Light-dark cycles during the 23.5-hour day were of very dim light (< 8 lux maximum at ~183 cm with the sensor aimed toward the light fixtures) during scheduled wakefulness and darkness during scheduled sleep. Light intensity was measured with a photometer. The < 8 lux maximum light intensity was very similar to the light intensity measured on the middeck of the Space Shuttle during research on the Neurolab STS-90 mission.

Subjects were assigned to one of two cells: A or B. The protocol was divided into 9 segments:

CELL A

Segment A1 (Ambulatory Baseline) consisted of a minimum of 7 days, during which wrist activity and light levels were recorded using ambulatory-recording devices while the subjects were at home on a normal routine maintaining a sleep log.

Segment A2 (Adaptation) began with admission to the Intensive Physiologic Monitoring (IPM) Unit of the Brigham & Women's Hospital on Experimental Day 1 and ended on the morning of Experimental Day 4. Physiologic and neurobehavioral monitoring commenced upon admission on Experimental Day 1 and continued throughout the duration of the study. Subjects continued to sleep and wake at their regularly scheduled times for three normal scheduled nights. A placebo, was administered (single blind) one hour prior to lights out on nights 2-3 to determine if .

Segment A3 (Endogenous Circadian Phase Assessment-ECPA) began on the morning of Experimental Day 4 and ended on the evening of Experimental Day 5. Upon waking on Experimental Day 4, the subjects were placed on a constant routine protocol for 40 hours after which time subjects underwent an 8-hour recovery sleep. The constant routine protocol, as is true with the rest of the protocol from this point forward, was conducted in dim room light. Blood was sampled for melatonin and cortisol until the morning of Experimental Day 5. The constant routine was used to assess the phase and amplitude of the endogenous circadian pacemaker under strictly controlled conditions.

Segment A4 consisted of eighteen successive 23.5-hour days, which began on the morning of Experimental Day 6 and ended on the evening of Experimental Day 23. Each day consisted of 15.67 hours of scheduled wakefulness and 7.83 hours of scheduled sleep. Melatonin (5.0 mg) was administered orally, double blind, one hour prior to lights out each night. Light exposure was maintained at < 8 lux maximum during scheduled wakefulness. In addition to the blood sampled during the constant routines, one 28-hour window of blood sampling took place during Experimental Days 14-15. During this window, blood was sampled for melatonin and for cortisol.

Segment A5 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A3.

Segment A6 (Adaptation) consisted of a repetition of the adaptation that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A2.

Segment A7 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segments A3 and A5. In addition, this segment was used to reestablish a normal phase relationship between sleep and the phase of the endogenous circadian pacemaker.

Segment A8 consisted of a repetition of the eighteen 23.5-hour-day segment that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A4. Placebo was administered, double blind, one hour prior to lights out each night.

Segment A9 (ECPA Reassessment) consisted of a repetition of the constant routine and recovery sleep that was used in the protocol for subjects in Segment A3, A5 and A7.

CELL B

The procedures for this cell were identical to that of Cell A except that in Segment B4 subjects received placebo instead of melatonin one hour prior to each sleep episode and in Segment B8 subjects received melatonin instead of a placebo one hour prior to each sleep episode.

In order to determine whether assessment of endogenous melatonin levels provided a method to assess the status of circadian phase and period, researchers assessed the potential impact of the sleep-wake cycle and associated light-dark cycle on the endogenous circadian rhythm of plasma melatonin. Researchers performed a detailed analysis of the melatonin phase during a 20-hour forced desynchrony protocol.

In this protocol, twelve young healthy subjects (5F, 7M) aged 24.1 ± 3.70 years (mean ± SD) were studied in an environment free of time cues for 18-27 days. Following three 24-hour baseline days (16 hour wake / 8 hour sleep), the subjects were scheduled to 24 cycles of a 20-hour flight day (FD) protocol (13.33 hour wake/6.67 hour sleep). Ambient light intensities were <15 lux during all scheduled wake times and <0.03 lux during all scheduled sleep episodes. Melatonin data were fitted with a non-orthogonal spectral analysis (NOSA) program, which simultaneously fit the imposed (20-hour, 2 harmonics) and endogenous (near 24-hour, 6 harmonics) components (and their interactions) of melatonin in order to calculate the subjects' intrinsic circadian periods t (tau). Each subject's melatonin data were then folded by their fitted t. For each circadian day researchers calculated: 1) duration of melatonin peak (DMP, time between upward and downward crossings of the mean); 2) circadian phase of melatonin peak (MIDPT, midpoint of upward and downward crossings of the mean); and 3) area under melatonin curve (AUC, estimated using the trapezoidal rule, z-scored for each subject). Linear regressions were fitted to the AUC and DMP data from the entire FD protocol to assess any overall change in the mean levels of melatonin secretion during the experiment. To determine whether the timing of the 20-hour sleep/wake schedule systematically modulated the phase or amount of melatonin secretion, each subject's AUC, DMP and MIDPT data were folded by the beat period (mean ± SD = 117.27 ± 0.13 hour) of their &964; (mean ± SD = 24.12 ± 3.10 hour) and the 20-hour FD protocol. For each variable, sine curves were then fitted to the data from all 10 subjects, and a Student's t-test was used to determine whether the fitted amplitude of the sinusoid was significantly different from 0.0.

RESULTS:
Hypothesis 1: Entrainment Studies of the Human Circadian Pacemaker to a 23.5 hour day.
Most subjects who received the placebo treatment failed to entrain to the scheduled 23.5-hour day, whereas most subjects given 5.0 mg of melatonin one hour prior to each bedtime maintained normal phase relationships between the timing of their core body temperature rhythms and the timing of the scheduled sleep-wake cycle. Two of three subjects in the melatonin condition maintained phase angles in the normal range with low levels during sleep suggesting that they entrained to the 23.5-hour day.

Hypothesis 2: Impaired Neurobehavioral Performance During Circadian Misalignment.
The neurobehavioral function during the entrainment studies to the 23.5-hour day with and without melatonin (n=3) was also examined. Daily performance averages were computed for subjects who completed both melatonin and placebo conditions. Researchers assessed vigilance performance every two hours during wakefulness using the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). The primary outcome measures analyzed were median reaction time and lapses (response times > 500 ms). Results of these analyses showed that reaction time performance and lapses in attention were similar in the melatonin and placebo conditions. Researchers also assessed working memory, cognitive speed and accuracy trade-offs using the Addition Performance Task and the Digit Symbol Substitution Test. Both tasks showed significant interaction effects (P < 0.05) between Drug Condition and Day such that performance continued to improve (i.e., learning occurred) in the melatonin but not the placebo condition. Subjective Sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale was significantly lower (less sleepiness) near the end of the protocol for the melatonin compared to the placebo condition (P < 0.05).

Hypothesis 3: Progress on the relationship between melatonin and circadian entrainment.
The AUC (p<0.20) and the DMP (p<0.15) did not show any significant changes in their mean levels over the course of the FD protocol. The DMP also showed no systematic alteration in relation to the 20-hour FD regimen. However, the AUC (p<0.0001) and the MIDPT (p<0.0001) manifested systematic modulations in relation to the 20-hour FD protocol. When sleep episodes were scheduled near circadian phase 240°, MIDPTs occurred approximately one hour later in the circadian day than when sleep was scheduled to occur near circadian phase 60°. When sleep episodes were scheduled near circadian phase 180°, the AUC was approximately 1.5 standard deviation larger than when sleep was scheduled to occur near circadian phase 0°.

These data demonstrated that the quantity of melatonin secreted and the phase of the midpoint of the melatonin curve are significantly affected by the timing of the sleep/wake, light/dark, upright/supine conditions during a 20-hour FD protocol. The data also demonstrated that the endogenous melatonin rhythm was robust and provided an accurate estimate of the period of the pacemaker under the current space-flight conditions of dim light.

The current results suggest that:

  1. additional research is necessary to evaluate the impact of non-24-hour sleep-wake/work schedules on circadian entrainment, sleep and performance during ground-based simulations and space-flight conditions;
  2. a dose of 5.0 mg of melatonin taken daily one hour prior to bedtime appears to be well tolerated and may be able to entrain the human circadian pacemaker to a shorter-than-24-hour day in some but not all individuals. Thus, additional research is needed to determine the effective dose necessary to entrain all individuals to non-24-hour day lengths. A flight-based test of daily administration of a larger dose of melatonin (=5.0 mg per day) as a countermeasure to circadian misalignment during space flight is warranted since melatonin appears to hold promise as an entraining agent at this higher dose;
  3. individual differences, likely due to differences in the intrinsic circadian period, make some individuals more vulnerable to circadian misalignment. These individual differences in vulnerability to circadian misalignment suggest that robust countermeasures need to be developed to ensure entrainment of all astronauts to a variety of imposed sleep-wake schedules during space flight.
  4. some sleep disturbances in space are likely related to a failure to maintain entrainment of the human circadian pacemaker to the imposed schedule, especially for missions with schedules that deviate from the 24-hour day; and
  5. measurement of the endogenous melatonin rhythm can be used to assess the status of the circadian time keeping system in humans under the current dim lighting conditions of space flight.

A flight-based test of daily administration of a larger dose of melatonin (=5.0 mg per day) as a countermeasure to circadian misalignment during space flight is warranted since melatonin appears to hold promise as an entraining agent at this higher dose;

These individual differences in vulnerability to circadian misalignment suggest that robust countermeasures need to be developed to ensure entrainment of all astronauts to a variety of imposed sleep-wake schedules during space flight.
  4. some sleep disturbances in space are likely related to a failure to maintain entrainment of the human circadian pacemaker to the imposed schedule, especially for missions with schedules that deviate from the 24-hour day; and
