experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this experiment was to determine the influence of Subject Loading Device (SLD) external load (EL) magnitudes on the ground reaction force (GRF) and kinematics during locomotion in microgravity. The SLD is currently used by crewmembers while they are exercising on the Treadmill with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization (TVIS) onboard the International Space Station (ISS). The TVIS with integrated SLD is intended as a countermeasure to bone loss and neuromuscular deconditioning. A crewmember exercising on the treadmill receives an external load by means of an upper-body harness that attaches to the SLD via extender straps or bungees. GRF is imparted as the SLD pulls the crew member toward the treadmill surface during locomotion. The SLD utilizes a mechanical spring-loaded cable and pulley system to transfer specific loads to the crew member via an upper-body harness. It is not known how this type of loading affects the gait, GRF, and kinematics during locomotion on the ISS.

The primary objective of this investigation was to determine if gait kinematics and GRF during locomotion at 0-G, using a simulated ISS treadmill and SLD, were significantly different from those found during locomotion at 1-G. The secondary objective of this investigation was to quantify the load magnitude, variability, and stiffness of the external load (EL) applied.

APPROACH:
Four subjects (3 men, 1 woman, 28.0 ± 5.6 years, 170.8 ± 9.1 cm, 75.1 ± 11.2 kg) walked at 3 mph (4.8 km/h) and ran at 5, and 7 mph (8.0 and 11.2 km/h) during microgravity (0-G) on the KC-135 aircraft and on the ground (1-G). The KC-135 creates microgravitational conditions by flying a "roller-coaster" parabolic-shaped path. Before the study began, all subjects passed a modified Air Force Class III physical exam and signed an informed consent document. This study was approved by the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS).

A treadmill instrumented with force plates (Kistler Gaitway, Amherst, NY) was used to measure vertical ground reaction forces. A ¼-inch-thick aluminum plate with a cutout equal in size to the TVIS running surface was placed over the treadmill running surface. The two bilateral SLD units were mounted on either side of the treadmill in a configuration similar to that used during actual space flight. Two harnesses were used: a Russian-designed harness and the U.S.-designed harness currently in use on the ISS. Both harnesses were tested because it was anticipated that either will be used with the ISS treadmill. Each harness was attached to the SLD in two manners: relatively non-compliant extender straps and compliant bungees.

RESULTS:
The mean EL provided to subjects during dynamic locomotion was smaller than that predicted from static measurements. When extender straps were used, the EL decreased by 4 to 10% as locomotion speed increased from 3 to 7 mph. Furthermore, as the EL setting was increased from low (70% BW) to full (100% BW) loading, EL decreased approximately 2-3% at each speed. When bungees were used in series with the SLD, the dynamic EL decreased 14% for walking and 4-8% for running. The mean EL stiffness with extender straps was 3.55 kg/cm, and 0.71 kg/cm with bungees. Thus, the bungees decreased load stiffness by a factor of approximately 5. This greatly reduced the variation in EL during locomotion. Bungees also reduced asymmetries in EL. Both the reduced stiffness and reduced asymmetry should improve crewmember comfort.

The similarity of kinematic parameters obtained at 0-G and 1-G suggests that locomotion patterns in microgravity are similar to that occurring in 1-G, especially when EL levels approach full body weight loading. However, a more extensive kinematic analysis is required to further support this conclusion.

The ability of the SLD to reproduce 1-G-like GRFs was more limited. The SLD was able to reproduce 1-G-like peak impact force, and at higher load levels also reproduced 1-G-like impulse magnitudes. However, even at EL levels close to full body weight, locomotion with the SLD device does not reproduce the peak active force or loading rate experienced at 1-G.

A limitation of this study was that the treadmill used was not the actual TVIS. Although the tread area replicated the TVIS, the test treadmill was bolted to the floor of the aircraft. The TVIS on the ISS floats in a pit in the service module and is connected to the structure only by soft springs, which provide vibration isolation from the ISS structure. TVIS is equipped with gyroscopes to maintain stability of the device during exercise. It is possible that the vibration isolation system associated with the TVIS may result in decreased resistance of the treadmill surface to any applied forces, thereby dampening ground reaction forces. Therefore gait timing patterns, kinematics, and ground reaction force parameters may be different on the TVIS. For these findings to be confidently applied to the TVIS, an experiment needs to be conducted in microgravity on a device that reproduces the vibration isolation system used for TVIS.

Because peak active force and loading rate are considered to be important factors for maintenance of bone mineral density, the development of next-generation subject loading devices should strive to replicate 1-G levels of these parameters. In addition, more research should be conducted; possibly including long-term training and bed rest studies, to determine how the alterations in GRF that would be expected to occur at 0-G might affect neuromuscular conditioning and bone mineral density.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment was designed to study changes in the immune system coincident with sleep physiology during extended space flight and relate any found changes to preflight and postflight conditions. In particular, researchers wanted to determine if there are any long-term adverse effects of microgravity on the immune system that can be related to the sleep-wake cycle. Such disturbances in neuroendocrine system and immune system functions might have an impact on the risk for ill health, especially infectious disease. The study would contribute to our understanding of the role of the immune system in the sleeping-waking brain especially during and following spaceflight microgravity conditions.

In addition to the theoretical and space flight importance, there are important clinical implications to psychiatric and medical disorders. The associations of stress and depression with altered immune functions have been reported in medical literature. Stress, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep deregulation, and reduced slow wave sleep are related to major depressive disorders. Specifically, natural killer cell (NK cell) activity is reduced in sleep disturbed depressed patients. Furthermore, altered non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep physiology and immune function changes have been described in fibrositis/fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome that shares features of unrefreshing or non-restorative sleep, diffuse myalgia, multiple tender points, fatigue and depression. The outcome of the research would have important implications on the contributions of disordered sleep and immune functions for the pathogenesis of these illnesses.

APPROACH:
This investigation was conducted for the first time as part of the NASA-Mir Increment 4 mission. Three crewmembers completed measurements preflight, inflight and postflight. For each phase of the flight, the experiment was divided into segments called measurement "blocks". The inflight measurement blocks were scheduled early in the mission (mission day 37-49), in the middle (MD 79-91) and at the end (MD 110-122) of the mission. Preflight baseline data collection was performed once. Readaptation data was collected during two sessions postflight. The experiment protocols were repeated on the NASA 5/Mir 24 mission with two additional crewmembers.

During the preflight and postflight phases of the experiment, subjects answered questions before and after sleep periods on sleepiness, fatigue, pain and mood as well as performance. These questions were the main focus of a separate sleep study performed simultaneously with this investigation (see: "Human Circadian Rhythms and Sleep in Space" by Timothy H. Monk, Ph.D.)

In addition to the questionnaires, preflight baseline blood collection (BDC) involved 25 blood samples collected over a 24-hour wake/sleep cycle. Five daytime samples of 4-ml of blood were taken at 0800, 1000, 1200, 1400 and 1600 hours. A catheter was inserted before 2200 hours to allow for frequent blood sampling during sleep. Starting again at 2200 until 0700 half-hourly and again at 0800 hours, twenty 3-ml blood samples were taken in sterile, heparinized, pyrogen-free tubes connected to a 4-meter line and manifold located outside the bedroom. Samples were transported immediately to the laboratory for analysis. A total of 80 ml for each subject was collected.

The following immunologic assays were carried out: natural killer cells and T-cell subsets were stained and sorted using the two-color immunofluorescence technique with flow cytometry; plasma cortisol and human growth hormone (hGH) were determined by radioimmunoassay (RIA); plasma IL-1ß, IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1ra) and IL-2 and IL-2r concentrations were determined using enzyme-linked-immunosorbent-assay (ELISA). Cytokine biological activities were determined by reactions with D10 and CTLL cell lines; natural killer cell activity was tested by Chronium-51 release assay; IL-1ß mRNA from peripheral blood monocyte cells was studied by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (Rt-PCR). Plasma obtained from subjects was stored at -70 degrees C until use.

During flight, pre- and post sleep questionnaires were also completed. Blood samples were drawn on days 4 and 5 of the second and third blocks. Samples were drawn in the early afternoon (approximately 1400 hours) and prior to sleep. For each blood sample collection, two 3-milliliter (ml) blood samples were taken. One 3 ml sample was taken in a 5 ml plasma separator tube for centrifugation and storage at -20° C. One milliliter of the second 3 ml sample was injected into each of three 7 ml tubes prefilled with a cryopreservative. The procedure was repeated on the second day. Eight samples each of 6 mls for a total of 48 ml blood was collected from each subject in flight. Blood samples obtained during the mission were used to examine natural killer cells and plasma for lymphokines and endocrine substances. Immunologic and endocrine assays were carried out on samples returned to principal investigator.

Also on days 4 and 5 of the second and third blocks, subjects attached electroencephalography (EEG) electrodes and donned a Medilog Sleep Research Recorder (MSRR) skull cap prior to sleep. This piece of hardware was used to make standard sleep-wake physiologic assessments. The Medilog recorder was donned within two hours of sleep and removed within two hours after awakening. Data were recorded on magnetic tape and stored for return to Earth.

After flight, sleep tape recordings were scored without subject identification by a trained observer using standard criteria on a Medilog replay unit located at the principal investigator’s laboratory. Brain wave frequencies recorded on the MSRR tapes were analyzed to assess the relationship of brain waves delta (slow wave) sleep activity to immune functions. The method allowed for an objective, quantifiable, and reliable method for analyzing sleep EEG frequencies during sleep. Blood analyses and MSRR data were compared to test that changes in sleep, particularly between wakefulness and slow wave sleep, are indices of causal mechanisms that produce changes in the immune system.

RESULTS:
Immunologic and endocrine assays were carried out on blood samples collected preflight, inflight, and postflight to examine the relationship between sleep activity to immune functions. Preflight baseline data collection from all crewmembers were compared to a group of healthy male volunteers to determine if sleep/wake age-related immune and endocrine functions were present in the middle-aged male crewmembers during baseline conditions before flight on Mir versus young healthy males. Middle-aged crewmembers in preflight baseline conditions differed from young healthy males in the timing of the diurnal pattern of natural killer cell cytotoxicity, hGH and cortisol. They also secreted less hGH and more cortisol over a 24-hour period. These hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis endocrine differences in healthy middle-aged men were similar to those seen in healthy older men. While the dynamic structure of natural killer cell cytotoxicity differed, there was no overall mean difference from young males.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

A key design challenge for future long-duration exploration missions is determining the appropriate volume of a spacecraft/habitat to accommodate habitability functions and ensure optimal crew health, performance, and safety. Because spacecraft/habitat volume directly drives mass and cost, this information is needed early in the design process. The objective of this study was to develop a constraint-driven, optimization-based model that can be used to estimate and evaluate spacecraft/habitat volume.

To accomplish this, the team was structured to leverage expertise from diverse fields, including architecture and habitation design, human factors engineering, industrial engineering, optimization-based modeling, and simulation. A computational model for spacecraft/habitat volume is an invaluable tool for designers, mission planners, integrators, and evaluators who are shaping space habitats and working toward a truly habitable environment for future long-duration exploration missions.

The computational model development was completed through four specific aims:

  1. Estimate spacecraft/habitat volume based on mission parameters and constraints.
  2. Provide layout assumptions for a given volume.
  3. Assess volumes based on a set of performance metrics.
  4. Inform risk characteristics associated with a volume.

APPROACH:

Investigators developed a model that can be used to measure spacecraft and habitat volumes. This involved selecting a software platform; developing model requirements; defining model inputs, outputs, and constraints; developing strategies for optimization approaches; and working on verification and validation plans.

RESULTS:

The SOLV project successfully conducted the Final Design Review (FDR) on 3/7/2018. SOLV achieved this project milestone on schedule, meeting all its objectives. A compliance assessment performed by the SOLV team indicated that the prototype model meets the established goals in credibility factors such as verification, validation, data pedigree, uncertainty characterization, and results robustness, as defined by NASA-STD-7009A. The team also provided an out brief and a model demonstration to the Human Research Program (HRP) and Human Factors and Behavioral Performance (HFBP) teams and HHP/SF management at the conclusion of the FDR. Investigators delivered the SOLV model and associated software files, and seven project documents capturing the project’s technical approach, verification and validation plans, test results, software specification, and development plans to the HFBP team.

No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Douglas, GracePrincipal Investigator: Cooper, Maya
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is planning for long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit. In order to ensure sustainment of crew health and performance, adequate nutrition must be delivered by the food system and efficiently absorbed by crewmembers to prevent micronutrient deficiency. No collective source of literature on nutrient bioavailability in processed foods is available. The purpose of this task is to conduct a literature review of nutrient bioavailability taking into account the form of food ingredient interactions and processing conditions. The review will identify where information is inadequate and be used to propose formulation and processing suggestions for the development of food products with improved bioavailability.

The Specific Aims were:

  1. Review current scientific literature on bioavailability of nutrients and how it is affected by form, ingredient interactions and processing conditions.
  2. Characterize the conditions that reduce or improve bioavailability of nutrients for future food development.
APPROACH:
The methodology isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Supplemental forms of vitamins and minerals generally are better absorbed by the body than the natural forms of the micronutrient though this phenomena is not always the case. The bioavailability of vitamin E and riboflavin is higher from natural sources as compared to their synthetic counterparts. Additionally, natural forms of vitamin C, biotin, calcium, magnesium, potassium, and zinc were shown to achieve equal serum concentrations as the supplements after consumption of like amounts in controlled test scenarios. Hence, as necessary, food fortification can occur with many of the micronutrients without adverse consequence to the physiological delivery provided that adequate stability of supplemental micronutrients can be achieved.

Many ingredient interactions and matrix effects occur with micronutrients that impact nutrient absorption. One ingredient interaction which occurs during the absorption phase is the competitive absorption of similar compounds in the body. For example, beta-carotene competes with other carotenoids for intestinal absorption. Likewise, zinc limits iron absorption when the two are consumed simultaneously. Another interaction affecting bioavailability is the inhibitory nature of phytate and phytic acid, naturally occurring compounds in plants, with the mineral absorption of calcium, chromium, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and zinc. Some vitamins, such as vitamins A and E, have increased bioavailability if some fat is consumed simultaneously. Vitamin A, riboflavin, and vitamin C show increased absorption if more dietary fiber is present at consumption so that the vitamins have a longer gastrointestinal residence time for absorption. Processing impacts to the bioavailability of micronutrients were very limited. Vitamin concentrations in foods are commonly affected by heat, water leaching, or oxidation. However only two vitamins actually had documentation of bioavailability differences that was dependent on the processing method. Vitamin A provitamins, because of their placement in the microstructure of plants, often become more bioavailable after cooking or pureeing. The niacin in grains must be released by acid or alkali extraction to allow significant absorption.

Future work with regards to nutrient bioavailability in the space food system should focus on ensuring that micronutrients are provided in an optimal matrix within many food items. Both vitamin and mineral absorption in many instances was dose-dependent, meaning that percent absorption was higher at lower doses, up to a physiological nutrient saturation level, but overconsumption of micronutrients did not result in absorption at the same rate above saturation. Hence, micronutrients should be spread across many food items to ensure continued nutrient delivery at each meal occasion. Competing nutrients should be staggered in their consumption. Additionally, fortification efforts must take into account the data here in terms of surrounding food matrix and form of the supplemental micronutrient used.

experiment_title: In-flight Holter Monitoring
parameter_html:
Heart rate
Premature atrial contraction (PAC)
Premature ventricular contraction (PVC)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Charles, JohnCo-Investigator: Bungo, MichaelCo-Investigator: Mulvagh, Sharon
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The incidence of cardiac rhythm abnormalities during Space Shuttle Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) is about 40% in individuals who do not exhibit such abnormalities during equivalent preflight stresses. It was hypothesized that some aspect of the space flight EVA environment was the instigating factor. Potential candidates included: a physiological response to microgravity (including fluid volume loss and/or uncorrected electrolyte imbalance due to diuresis, which is detected only during EVAs due to the lack of Electrocardiogram (ECG) information during other flight phases; a response to the EVA workload; a response to the EVA environment of pure oxygen at 4.3 per square inch-; and a response to other environmental factors, such as low humidity. Strenuous activities during previous U.S. manned space flights did not produce equivalent frequencies of arrhythmias, for reasons that are unknown. Therefore, efforts to document the current phenomenon are considered of operational importance.

APPROACH:
During the last 24 hours inflight, the crewmembers instrumented themselves with ECG electrodes, attached and activated the Holter recorder, and went about their normal activities. During this period, they donned the Operational Bioinstrumentation System (OBS) harness, mounted the treadmill, donned the bungee restraint cords, and stood quietly on the treadmill for five minutes. They then exercised at 70-85% of their maximum heart rate for a period of 20 minutes.

Following the exercise period, the crewmembers removed the OBS harness, stowed the treadmill, replaced any ECG electrodes loosened by sweat, and resumed their normal daily activities. The crewmembers continued wearing the Holter recorder through de-orbit preparations, landing, seat egress, and arrival at the medical facility for postflight testing.

RESULTS:
There wasn’t an increase in ectopic activity (relating to a heartbeat that has its origin other than in the sinoatrial node) during space flight and/or exercise in contrast to increased dysrhythmias seen during previous Shuttle EVA activities. This may be due to the natural variability between subjects or may relate more specifically to the particular environmental conditions unique to EVAs.

experiment_title: Crew Height Measurement
parameter_html:
Eye-level height
Height, seated
Height
investigators: Principal Investigator: Brown, Jeri
image_name: Internal Arrangement of the Apollo and Soyuz Spacecraft
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Gross effects of zero-g on man's anthropometry were observed during and after extended orbital flights of the Skylab missions. In weightlessness, crewmen "grew taller" and the one-g erect posture was altered at several skeletal joints, namely the neck, shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle.

Quantification of these effects was important for optimizing the physical interfaces between the crewman and his workstation and flight clothing, particularly the space suit. The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) provided an opportunity to quantify the effects of zero-g on crewman height and to determine the change as a function of time over mission length.

APPROACH:
Data on ASTP crewmen were obtained during routine physical examinations conducted on L-45 (45 days before flight), L-30, L-15 and R+0 (day of recovery). Data requirements for all height measurements consisted of maximum stature, seated height, and eye-level height. Inflight data requirements were completed during three mission phases:

1. In the Command Module (CM), before docking module (DM) transfer, seated height and eye-level height were measured immediately after weightlessness was attained.
2. In the DM, stature and eye-level heights were measured periodically.
3. In the CM after DM jettison, seated height and eye-level height were measured immediately prior to reentry.

Measurements in the CM were made with the crewman on the center couch. Seated height was measured with the seat in the 90-degree seat-to-backpan position. Eye-level height was measured with the seat in the 180-degree (flat) position. The crewman relaxed to the neutral, zero-g posture, his back parallel to the couch back and his feet touching the lower equipment bay (LEB) bulkhead. Measurements were made from the top of the couch support frame, parallel to the back of the couch, down to the top of the head and then to eye-level height. The measuring tape from the Leg Volume Measuring Kit was used for these measurements.

Stature measurements were made as the crewman assumed a fully extended posture on the control and display (C&D) panel with his feet touching the DM hatch (Soyuz end). For eye-level height, the crewman assumed the neutral, zero-g posture, with his back to the C&D panel and feet touching the hatch. Measurements were read from a measuring tape decal affixed to the C&D panel.

RESULTS:
Because of scheduling problems and the limited number of data points completed, only the stature measurements were quantified. In addition, only R+0 measurements were obtained due to crew health concerns.

An increase in stature was noted for each ASTP crewman. This increase was attributed to the absence of g-loading on the spine, which resulted in loss of normal spinal curvature and an expansion of the intervertebral discs. A slight increase (less than 1.3 cm (0.5 in)) occurred between launch and mission day 6, which was the first measurement opportunity in the DM. The next larger increase, as much as 6.6 cm (2.6 in), occurred between mission days 6 and 9. This data, in conjunction with Skylab height data, indicated a two-step height increase.

The smaller initial change may result from removing g-loads on the body and thus permitting loss of thoracolumbar curvature. A similar expansion is observed on Earth when stature is compared between standing and supine body positions. The second larger change may be accounted for from the expansion of the now unloaded intervertebral discs. When the muscles relax in weightlessness, the vertebral discs are unloaded and absorb water from the vertebral bodies. This expansion may be further affected by the headward fluid shifts in zero-g. Application of this data was used to develop workstation interface designs for future missions.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of the ocular tests was to monitor subjects’ ocular health during the study. Recent evidence from astronauts returning from long-duration missions on the International Space Station (ISS) indicated vision disturbances linked to intracranial pressure affecting the optic disk and optic nerve. A Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) was constituted to monitor ocular health of the bed rest subjects.

APPROACH:
A battery of ten tests was used to assess and monitor subjects’ ocular health during the bed rest study. The tests were designed to gather data on visual acuity, retinal health and structures, strabismus, ocular muscle function, peripheral vision, pupillary reflex, intra-ocular pressure, and eye refractive error.

  1. Review of Systems Questionnaire – This questionnaire was used to ask subjects if they experienced any physical symptoms in the past week. Questions regarding eye health were included. This questionnaire was administered weekly in all phases of the bed rest study.
  2. Best Corrected Visual Acuity (near and far) – Visual acuity is a measure of the spatial resolution of the visual processing system. Corrective lenses were used if needed by the subject to achieve their best performance.
  3. Cycloplegic Refraction – Refraction is the procedure by which the natural optical error is characterized and quantified. This procedure helps to distinguish between blurred vision caused by refractive error and medical abnormalities of the visual system. Cycloplegic refraction refers to refraction done with a cycloplegic agent to dilate the pupil. The cycloplegic agent was used to overcome accommodation by paralyzing the ciliary muscle so that the absolute refractive error can be measured.
  4. Modified Amsler grid testing – The Amsler grid is a grid of horizontal and vertical lines used to evaluate the central visual field for damage to the macula or optic nerve. In this test, the person looks with each eye separately at a small dot in the center of the grid composed by black lines on a white background. Wavy, blurred, distorted lines, or missing areas of the grid may be indicative of retinal disturbances.
  5. Red Dot test – The Red Dot test is used to evaluate visual fields. The person focuses their vision on a black dot centered within a circle of red dots located 14” (33cm) away. The person looks at the center black dot and indicates whether or not all the red dots can be seen. Each eye was examined separately by covering the opposite eye. Corrective lenses were worn if needed. Inability to see the black dot or any of the red dots suggested a visual field deficit.
  6. Confrontational Visual Field testing – This test is used to assess peripheral vision. The subject covers one eye while the other fixates a point straight ahead. A target is moved from the far periphery to the near periphery in each of the visual quadrants. Subjects were asked to indicate when the target appears in their field of view.
  7. Color Vision testing – For color vision testing, subjects identify shapes that vary in color and intensity and lie within a background of dots. The type and degree of color vision deficiency is then assessed based upon subject’s responses. Hardy-Rand-Rittler plates were used for this purpose.
  8. Tonometry – Applanation tonometry was used to assess Intracular Pressure (IOP). Using this method, IOP was determined by the amount of force required to flatten the cornea by a specified standard amount. Because the instrument is placed on the eye, a topical anesthetic was used to numb the eye prior to taking the measure.
  9. Non-mydriatic Fundus Photography - This test allows the examination of the posterior segment of the eye, mainly the retina and optic disc. The subject was directed to look straight ahead at a distant object. The ophthalmoscope illuminates the retina through the pupil. Structures that are observed lie in the innermost aspect of the globe: retina, retinal blood vessels, optic nerve head (disc), and to a limited degree, subjacent choroid.
  10. Optical coherence tomography - OCT is a noninvasive, noncontact, transpupillary imaging technology that can image retinal structures in vivo with a resolution of 10 - 17 microns. Cross-sectional images of the retina are produced using the optical backscattering of light. The anatomic layers within the retina can be differentiated and retinal thickness can be measured.

RESULTS:
Subjects completed the 14- and 70-day head-down-tilt (HDT) bed rest studies. The magnitude of HDT bed rest–induced changes was not significantly different between the two studies for all outcomes, except the superior, nasal, and inferior peripapillary retinal thickness. IOP increase from baseline occurred during 14- and 70-day HDT bed rest.

On November 20, 2012, the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) concluded after review of the subjects from the 14 day (C17) and subjets from the 70 day (C11) head-down tilt bed rest studies, that there were no significant safety issues based on the review of accumulated data. The members, therefore, have reached a consensus decision to conclude safety monitoring by the DSMB and to officially close-out the DSMB monitoring.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Following exposure to space flight, upright posture can result in an inability to maintain adequate arterial pressure and cerebral perfusion (orthostatic or postural hypotension). This may result in presyncope (lightheadedness) or syncope (loss of consciousness) during reentry or egress. A significant number of astronauts experience orthostatic hypotension and presyncope during upright posture. The severity of this problem increases with the length of the space flight mission, as seen in approximately 20% of short-duration and 83% of long-duration crewmembers. It is expected that orthostatic hypotension will be severe on exploration class missions.

This study was designed to evaluate a new pharmacologic countermeasure for protection from postflight orthostatic hypotension. Investigators were studying the ability of the drug Midodrine to reduce the incidence and/or severity of orthostatic hypotension in astronauts returning to Earth. The subject pool included subjects who experience presyncope as well as those who do not. Midodrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that is used clinically to treat orthostatic hypotension. It is almost completely absorbed after oral administration and is hydrolyzed enzymatically to its active metabolite, desglymidodrine, which has a bioavailability of 93%. Midodrine acts by increasing vaso- and venoconstriction, thereby decreasing peripheral venous capacity and blood pooling, but does not pass the blood-brain barrier and therefore has no central stimulant effects. Preflight: A familiarization session and drug tolerance test was performed before flight. If no abnormal activity was detected, the drug tolerance test began. First, the baseline blood pressure was measured, followed by an ingestion of 10 mg of Midodrine. The subject’s blood pressure was monitored at regular intervals for four hours, to ensure that Midodrine did not cause a significant increase in the subject’s blood pressure. Echocardiographic measurements (measurements of blood vessels by non-invasive ultrasound) were made to determine aortic cross-sectional diameter and aortic flow while lying on a tilt table. Using a tilt table, the subject was brought upright and supported by the tilt table at 80? for 10 minutes while the measurements continued.

After the decision for deorbit burn was confirmed on the scheduled landing day, crewmembers donned the Advanced Crew Escape Suit (ACES) and ingested 10 mg of midodrine approximately one 1 hour before the scheduled landing time. The midodrine pill and a cue card with medication instructions had been stowed in the subjects’ ACES for their convenience. All crewmembers participated in the standard oral fluid-loading protocol and inflated their antigravity suits during reentry and landing.

The subject was instrumented with an electrocardiogram, a beat-to-beat finger blood pressure device, and an automatic blood pressure cuff. ECG measurements were made to determine aortic cross-sectional diameter and aortic flow while lying on a tilt table. Following this, the subject was brought upright by the tilt table to approximately 80 degrees for 10 minutes while the measurements continued. The tilt test was used to assess the effects of prolonged weightlessness on orthostatic tolerance during upright posture, as measured by supine and standing heart rate, blood pressure, stroke volume, cardiac output and total peripheral resistance. After completion of the Tilt Test, blood pressure was monitored at regular intervals for an additional period of time. During this time the crewmember also completed a questionnaire.

It is critical that the postflight Operational Tilt Test was performed within 2.5 hours of pill ingestion. Arrangements were made to perform the postflight data collection on the CTV to accommodate this time interval.

Midodrine appears to prevent orthostatic intolerance in test subjects after bed rest and in astronauts after space flight when testing is conducted in a controlled laboratory setting within 2 to 4 hours after landing. It is unclear at this time whether similar effects can be expected during reentry and immediately after landing, particularly in warmer environments and/or when the crewmembers are still wearing the ACES. Accurate interpretation of the current data requires that similar data be collected in control subjects (without midodrine) on the CTV. However, concerns about drug interactions with commonly used anti-emetics and prolonged QTc intervals observed in astronauts returning from long-duration missions make the routine use of midodrine unlikely and reliance on lower-body compression garments preferable.

experiment_title: Radiation-Induced Early Changes in Gene and Protein Expression, Lipid Oxidative States, and Vascular Function Related to Atherosclerosis

Aortic dimensions

investigators: Principal Investigator: Kucik, DennisCo-Investigator: Kabarowski, JanuszCo-Investigator: White, C.
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Epidemiological studies have established that radiation from a number of terrestrial sources increases the risk of atherosclerosis (a cause of heart attack and stroke), even at relatively low doses. The effect of galatic cosmic radiation (GCR), such as encountered on deep space missions, is not clear; however, because this kind of radiation interacts with tissues very differently than does most terrestrial radiation. Previously it has been shown that heavy ions, an important component of GCR, indeed accelerate the development of atherosclerosis-related plaques in the mouse, but only at relatively high doses. Mouse models, however, are known, from comparison of animal experiments to human epidemiological data, to require much higher radiation doses for plaque formation than humans, so while this type of experiment yields valuable information about the effect of radiation, it is not very useful in predicting risk at a given dose. This is likely due to species differences in lipid metabolism and the immune system. Plaque formation is a very late endpoint, however. Very early steps in atherosclerosis, such as changes in gene expression, protein expression, and lipid oxidation, should be much more similar in humans and mice. Analysis of these early changes in response to doses of simulated GCR that astronauts are likely to encounter on a Mars mission will enable a better prediction for the risk of cardiovascular consequences from space radiation while it increases an understanding of the mechanisms involved. The hypothesis of this study was that irradiation of blood vessels leads to early, species-independent changes in endothelial cell genes, proteins, and lipids that cause vascular dysfunction and are therefore likely to be predictive of cardiovascular disease. An understanding of these changes can be used to help predict risk and propose countermeasures.

This experiment had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine, as a function of radiation dose, acute, radiation-induced atherosclerosisassociated changes in gene and protein expression in aortic endothelial cells of irradiated mice.
  2. Determine, as a function of radiation dose, changes in oxidation states of aortic endothelial cell lipids.
  3. Determine the dose dependence of functional consequences of 56Fe, and protons with respect to perturbations in endothelial reactivity and aortic adhesivity.
  4. Develop a systems biology model of response of aortic endothelial cells to radiation damage to determine molecular mechanisms.

APPROACH:
Following irradiation (x-, proton-, and iron-irradiation) tissue and fluid samples were collected and analyzed for indicators of the development of atherosclerosis. Proteomic methods were also used to investigate changes in the levels of certain proteins in blood. These changes have important implications for the mechanism of radiation-induced atherosclerosis. These analyses should help determine how space-related forms of radiation affect the protein composition of circulating blood in ways that have implications for the risk of cardiovascular consequences of interplanetary travel.

RESULTS:
Using an ex vivo experimental system for aortic monocyte adhesion that the investigators developed, they determined last year that increased vascular adhesion is a major early event following exposure to space relevant doses of 56Fe radiation. Investigators also determined by pertussis toxin incubation of monocytes prior to addition to ex vivo aortic preparations from control and 56Fe irradiated C57Bl/6J mice that this adhesive effect requires signaling from Gi class of G proteins to which chemokine receptors typically signal to mediate firm adhesion of leukocytes to activated endothelium. Using a cytokine/chemokine array, they were also able to identify chemokines that are elevated in the blood of mice after exposure to 56Fe. These may prove to be useful biomarkers for cardiovascular risk prediction.

The investigators completed analysis of potential effects of protons on atherosclerosis in the hyperlipidemic Apolipoprotein E knockout (ApoE-/-) mouse model and subsequently analyzed possible effects of the same dose of protons on aortic adhesivity in normal mice. Unlike exposure to 56Fe, which they have previously shown to accelerate atherosclerosis in ApoE-/- mice and promote adhesivity of aortae from C57BL/6J mice, protons had no such effect; atherosclerosis in ApoE-/- mice was not accelerated even by doses of 2, 5, or 10 Gy protons and aortae from C57BL6/J mice exposed to the same proton dose showed no sign of increased adhesivity. These results not only support the notion that protons may not be as damaging for the cardiovascular system compared to heavy ions like 56Fe.

To understand how early vascular adhesive effects of 56Fe radiation are mediated in the vascular tissue and to identify biomarkers for better risk prediction and countermeasure development, the investigators completed analyses of lipids in the aorta of mice six weeks after exposure to space relevant doses of 56Fe (a time-point at which aortic adhesion is maximal). The numbers of lipids changed in the aortae by 56Fe exposure of the mice depended on the dose of radiation and several important lipid classes already linked to vascular inflammation and/or atherosclerosis were elevated, including sphingomyelins that are known to have inflammatory effects on smooth muscle cells and/or other vascular cell types, and ceramides that may be associated with vascular cell death. Most interestingly in terms of possible countermeasures to protect against oxidation related injury caused by space radiation exposure, ether-linked phosphatidylcholines were elevated within six weeks of 56Fe exposure; these lipids are thought to have antioxidant properties and are thus excellent candidates for countermeasure development in the future. Analysis of the plasma lipidome revealed that only 10 lipid species changed following exposure to the same 56Fe doses and time-points employed in the aortic lipidomic analyses. All changes were reductions in abundance. These lipids included N-acylphosphoethanolamines (NAPEs), which are members of the endocannabinoid system, as well as SMs. Most interestingly, ether-linked phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs), structurally related to the ether-linked PCs increased in aortae at the same time-point and similarly having potential anti-oxidant function, were among the lipids decreased in the plasma. This suggests that these potentially antioxidant ether-linked PEs may be consumed following total body exposure to 56Fe and may thus serve as a possible biomarker for atherosclerosis risk assessment. The investigators also completed a genomics analysis of gene expression changes in endothelium enriched aortic tissue from 56Fe exposed C57Bl/6J mice in which the adhesive effects of the same 56Fe radiation doses were observed at the six weeks’ time-point.

No datasets are available for this experiment. A final report is in the archive.

experiment_title: Human Cerebral Cortex Plasticity in Response to Long-term Bedrest as an Analog to Microgravity
parameter_html:
Corticospinal plasticity
Motor cortex excitability
Motor-evoked potentials
investigators: Principal Investigator: Roberts, DonnaCo-Investigator: Ramsey, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This investigation assesses the effects of weightlessness on the central nervous system and specifically the sensorimotor system by inducing cortical reorganization through altered cortical excitability. The measures of cortical excitability will be evaluated for correlation with measures of lower limb functional recovery.

APPROACH:
Transcranial magnetic stimulation was used to evaluate motor cortex plasticity through the acquisition of recruitment curves. The location for application of the magnetic stimulation was determined by functional and structural brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Data collected from these control subjects included resting motor threshold, paired pulse sequences and cortical silent periods, The compound motor action potential and Hoffman reflex (H-reflex) response were collected as measures of peripheral stimulation.

RESULTS:
Significant leg RC slope decreases were observed on post-bed rest day 1 (P1) (t(2805) = -4.14, P < 0.0001), P2 (t(2805) = -6.59, P < 0.0001), P3 (t(2805) = -6.15, P < 0.0001), P5 (t(2805) = -7.93, P <0.0001), P8 (t(2805) = -3.30, P = 0.001), and P12 (t(2805)= -3.33, P = 0.0009), suggesting a group decrease in corticospinal excitability in the immediate post-bed rest period with recovery approaching baseline over the following 2 wk. Significant effects were observed for hand RC slopes only for P2 (t(2916) = 1.97, P = 0.049), P3 (t(2916) = -2.12, P = 0.034), and P12 (t(2916) = -2.19, P = 0.029); no significant effects were observed for days P0 (t(2916) = -1.32, ns), P1 (t(2916) = 1.00, ns), P5 (t(2916) = -0.21, ns), or P8 (t(2916) = -0.27, ns). fMRI showed no change in activation for the hand but an increase in activation post-bed rest for the leg. On an individual basis, a more heterogeneous response was found which showed a potential association with performance on FMT.

Results of this research include a better understanding of the cortical plasticity associated with leg disuse and may lead to applications in patient and astronaut rehabilitation.

experiment_title: Are Medications Involved in Vision and Intracranial Pressure Changes Seen in Spaceflight?
parameter_html:
Dexamethasone usage
Gender

Ibuprofen usage
Optic neuritis
Optic neuropathy
Visual acuity

Vitreous floaters
Intracranial pressure (ICP)

investigators: Principal Investigator: Wotring, Virginia
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It has recently been reported that intracranial pressure (ICP) and/or vision changes, have occurred in a number of long-duration astronauts. Some crewmembers have experienced changes in their vision after long-duration space flight on the International Space Station (ISS). These impairments include visual performance decrements, development of cotton-wool spots or choroidal folds, optic-disc edema, optic nerve sheath distention, and/or posterior globe flattening with varying degrees of severity and permanence. These changes are now used to define the visual impairment/intracranial pressure (VIIP) syndrome.

The reasons for these potentially debilitating medical issues are currently unknown. The potential role of administered medications has not yet been examined, but it is known that many medications can have side effects that are similar to VIIP symptoms. Some medications raise blood pressure, which can affect intracranial pressure. Many medications that act in the central nervous system can affect intracranial pressures and/or vision. About 40% of the medications in the ISS kit are known to cause side effects involving changes in blood pressure, intracranial pressure and/or vision. For this reason, investigators aimed to study the potential relationship between ISS medications and their risk of causing or exacerbating VIIP-like symptoms.

APPROACH:
This study employed a two-fold strategy to evaluate the role of medications in crewmembers' visual problems. First, the NASA Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) and Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) data repositories were queried for crew health information regarding in-flight use of medications by all crewmembers who received sufficient testing to be assigned a Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG) severity score. Use of medications was correlated in affected crew compared to the control group (CPG = 0) to assess the role of these medications in vision and ICP changes seen in space flight. Secondly, the FDA Adverse Event Reports were used a terrestrial source of data. These are publicly available and represent hundreds of thousands of cases in each quarterly data set. The quarterly reports were compiled into a database format and queried for data of interest. This resource represents a huge database; incorporating it into the study was an attempt to compensate for the extremely small sample number in the NASA data archive. For this data mining study, data associated with adverse events involving vision changes and intracranial pressure changes was examined.

RESULTS:
Medication use during space flight missions was similar to that during the Space Shuttle flights and in adult medicine, with the exception that usage of sleep aids was about 10 times higher during space flight missions.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Early in human space exploration, there were concerns that exposure to microgravity would lead to hypoxemia since cardiopulmonary physiology was disrupted. Any potential disruptions did not impact performance or operational success in short-duration flights, so detailed investigation into pulmonary gas exchange were devised when longer duration flights were possible.

Research continued on Skylab with a normoxic atmosphere of 70% oxygen (O2) at 5 psia and an inspired O2 partial pressure (PIO2) of 148 mmHg. The study found no indication that pulmonary gas exchange in microgravity was impeded. Studies on the Shuttle resulted in the implementation of the shuttle staged denitrogenation protocol in 1984. This protocol allowed for the safe and effective extravehicular activity (EVA) by reducing the risk of decompression sickness (DCS) to an acceptable level in the spacesuit without lengthy in-suit denitrogenation (prebreathe) time.

This experiment furthered the investigations from Skylab and Shuttle and provided additional data on the effects of microgravity and extra vehicular activity (EVA) on impairment of oxygen exchange in the lung.

APPROACH:

Four male astronauts on STS-69 (1995) and four on STS-72 (1996) were exposed on Earth (baseline, taken between 5 and 45 days before launch) to a 20-minute seated acute sequential hypoxic challenge by breathing for 4 minutes at 18.0%, 14.9%, 13.5%, 12.9%, and 12.2% oxygen–balance nitrogen. A Novametrix CO2SMO Model 7100 recorded hemoglobin (Hb) oxygen saturation through finger pulse oximetry (SpO2, %). Measurements were taken at baseline, in-flight, the day of (R+0) and 2 d after (R+2) return to Earth. The same baseline process was followed postflight for R+0 and R+2, with astronauts resting and seated at the KSC in Titusville, FL. In-flight measurements were taken between 17 to 95 hours into the flight. The astronauts breathed the Shuttle atmosphere at 10.2 psia 26.5% O2, which was an equivalent partial pressure of oxygen (PIO2) of 128 mmHg as the 18.0% O2 mixture at sea level for 10 minutes. The Novametrix device was also used for in-flight measurements.

RESULTS:

The persistent increase in pulmonary diffusion capacity (DLCO) and membrane diffusing capacity (Dm) is evidence that pulmonary edema did not occur in microgravity. In addition, gravity imposed a degree of matching between ventilation and perfusion. These increases in pulmonary diffusing capacity and pulmonary capillary blood volume, rapidly revert to preflight levels on return to 1G This results in more uniform filling of the pulmonary capillary bed and an attendant increase in the surface area available for gas exchange. So an otherwise normal lung with no change in the apparent range of ventilation-perfusion (VA/Q ) in microgravity has no impediment to gas transfer. The study shows that exposure to and recovery from microgravity did not significantly alter the gas exchange process that dictates the oxygen saturation (SpO2) response to mild hypoxia in astronauts.

In summary, the findings of the study determined:


  1. There was no difference in astronaut oxygen saturation (SpO2) (about 97%) after breathing 18% O2 for 4 minutes at 760 mmHg before and after spaceflight and breathing 26.5% O2 at 527 mmHg for 10 minutes after days in microgravity both at a partial pressure of oxygen (PIO2) of about 128 mmHg.

  2. There was no difference in astronaut oxygen saturation (SO2) between baseline, R+0, or R+2 during the acute, sequential hypoxic challenge.

  3. There was no acclimatization to mild hypoxia during spaceflight that alters oxygen saturation (SpO2) levels upon return to 1 G.

In conclusion, the multitude of physiological changes associated with microgravity and during recovery from microgravity did not affect astronaut oxygen saturation (SpO2) under hypoxic conditions.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is hypothesized that changes in the baroreceptor reflex play a major role in the development of conditions responsible for the fall of blood pressure (orthostatic hypotension) after space flight. This is especially pronounced in many astronauts when they try to stand up shortly after their return to Earth; they may feel faint and some are unable to remain standing. Although this and other effects associated with cardiovascular deconditioning disappear within a relatively short time period (days), all efforts must be made to understand the causes of this condition which affects the health, safety, and productivity of the astronauts.

Changes in arterial pressure are detected by pressure sensors called baroreceptors, located in two areas of the arterial tree: the bifurcation of the carotid arteries in the neck and the arch of the aorta, located in the chest. Since carotid baroreceptors are more accessible, this protocol focuses on them.

Previous experiments showed that changes of the intra-carotid pressure can cause changes of the heart period. The relationship was identified as a sigmoidal curve, consisting of a threshold region, a linear portion, and a saturation range. In the threshold range, pressure within the carotid sinus must rise to a certain level before heart period prolongation occurs. In the linear range, heart period increases more or less linearly as intra-carotid pressure rises. In the saturation range, additional increments of intra-carotid pressure do not increase heart period. With the intervals between each heart beat rising, the diastolic blood pressure decreases.

APPROACH:
The investigation used the technique of neck suction. A neck chamber made of silicone rubber, which is molded to fit the contour of the anterior three fourths of the neck, is the centerpiece of the system. It has a silastic rubber diaphragm inside the chamber which seals against the neck during positive pressure and a gel edge which seals when suction is applied. The system was programmed to deliver a complex baroreceptor stimulus for use in space. First, the pressure inside the diaphragm was increased to about 40 mmHg. The positive pressure reduced carotid sinus diameter, and in most subjects, reduced the level of afferent (toward the brain) carotid baroreceptor activity to levels below the threshold necessary to provoke cardiographic changes. After about 5 seconds a series of ECG triggered pressure reductions was delivered which lowered the neck chamber pressure in a stepwise fashion to 25, 10, -5, -20, -35, -50, and -65 mmHg. The external application of negative pressure stretched the wall of the carotid artery and the carotid sinuses were stimulated and responded. After the last pressure reduction, neck chamber pressure returned to ambient levels. For each subject the stimulus train was applied seven times and the results were averaged.

Once the ECG electrodes and the neck chamber were properly attached, the pressure reduction sequence was initiated. Each subject was required to complete two normal respiratory cycles, holding his breath (approximately 15 seconds) after the second expiration. The complex baroreceptor stimulus then was applied. In addition, plasma catecholamine levels were measured from blood samples obtained during other D-2 experiments.

Experiment sessions were completed preflight, inflight and postflight. During data collection on Earth, all subjects assumed a recumbent positon (the experiment operations were done by other personnel). During the flight the astronauts performed the procedures by themselves. For each astronaut, four inflight sessions were planned.

RESULTS:
On landing day, baseline R-R intervals and their standard deviations were significantly below pre-launch values. Both maximum slopes and R-R interval ranges were significantly reduced 2 and 10 days post flight. The data document transient reductions of baseline vagal-cardiac neural outflow, and protracted impairment of vagal responses to baroreceptor stimulation after space missions.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Eckberg, DwainCo-Investigator: Baisch, FriedhelmCo-Investigator: Cooke, WilliamCo-Investigator: Cox, JamesCo-Investigator: Kuusela, TomCo-Investigator: Mano, TadaakiCo-Investigator: Tahvanainen, Kari
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The microgravity environment present during low-earth orbit (LEO) spaceflight may contribute to changes in autonomic cardiovascular regulation experienced by long-duration spaceflight crewmembers when they return to Earth's gravity. Theses changes manifest themselves as increased heart rates when standing, decline in arterial blood pressure, and even frank syncope. Several factors likely contribute to these changes, blood volume reductions, impaired baroreceptor-cardiac reflex responses, and inadequate increases in total peripheral resistance during standing.

This experiment explored the probability that the disordered arterial baroreflex malfunction, documented during weightlessness or after simulated or actual weightlessness, is part of and a contributor to a broad range of autonomic abnormalities. The researchers developed this experiment using the following hypotheses as a guide:

  1. Vagal baroreflex impairment progresses during long-duration space missions, and plateaus to reach some asymptotic limit.
  2. Weightlessness impairs aortic as well as carotid baroreceptor reflexes, and that therefore, the baroreflex malfunction that develops in space may be due to central nervous system factors, rather than local changes in the wall of carotid arteries.
  3. Progressive impairment of integrated vagal baroreflexes in astronauts is expressed in reduced levels of vagal-cardiac nerve traffic, as reflected in fluctuations of R-R intervals during rigorously-controlled breathing.
  4. The progressive reduction of minimum R-R interval during baroreflex testing observed in previous space flight missions reflected increased sympathetic-cardiac neural activity.
  5. Diminished vagal-cardiac nerve traffic is associated with a reduced prevalence of atrial, and an increased prevalence of ventricular dysrhythmias in space.
  6. Low-frequency diastolic pressure power reflects quantitatively, levels of efferent human muscle sympathetic nerve activity.
  7. Reductions of baroreflex gain are related directly and significantly to impairment of vasoconstrictor responses to lower body negative pressure in space.
  8. Hypocapnia leads to a greater reduction of R-R interval power at respiratory frequencies, and carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex gain in space than on Earth.

The researchers used the data obtained from this experiment to determine the adaptive changes that occurred in the autonomic nervous system of the flight subjects and to obtain insight into the various mechanisms that caused the observed integrated autonomic output.

APPROACH:
The design of this experiment was built around a battery of tests that activated different afferent nerve fibers, evoking different patterns of neural and cardiovascular responses through both separate and common mechanisms. These tests included:

  1. Controlled frequency breathing - a predetermined breathing protocol carried out using the Medikro Laptop Computer as an instructional guide.
  2. Valsalva’s Maneuver - performed by attempting to forcibly exhale with the nose closed and the mouth blowing into a pressurized breathing apparatus in order to increase blood pressure.
  3. Isometric Handgrip Exercise> - required the subject to sustain a muscular contraction, using a handgrip balloon assembly, to raise arterial blood pressure.
  4. Cold Pressor Test - involved rapid, sustained, severe cooling of a crewmember’s hand using the Cold Glove Assembly in order to elicit an increase in the subject's blood pressure and heart rate.
  5. Graded Lower Body Negative Pressure - provided a controlled, measured orthostatic stress to the cardiovascular system using the Chibis Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) Device.

RESULTS:
The data obtained from this experiment showed a decrease in RR-interval standard deviations for all subjects and a decrease in respiratory frequency RR-interval spectral power for two subjects while in microgravity. RR-interval spectral power was decreased and systolic pressure spectral power was increased in all subjects two weeks after returning to Earth. The data also showed that while in microgravity the transfer function between systolic blood pressures and RR-intervals was reduced. The transfer function showed a further reduction the day after the subjects returned to Earth, and had not returned to preflight levels by 14 days after landing.

These results suggested that long-duration spaceflight decreased vagal-cardiac control (reduced R-R interval oscillations at a given respiratory frequency) and baroreflex gain (reduced systolic to R-R interval transfer function magnitude), and that after returning to Earth, the effects of weightlessness may persist for at least 2 weeks. This experiment did not come to any conclusions about the cause of the decreased vagal-cardiac nerve traffic; however, the well documented reduction of blood volume that occurs while in microgravity is a probable explanation.

The researchers attempted to document the time-course of in-flight adaptations, however, they were unable to adequately record directional trends. It is not yet clear whether changes in autonomic cardiovascular regulation progress or stabilize as a function of the duration of exposure to microgravity. Although the data obtained from this experiment was limited, the researchers hope the information obtained from this experiment can help to guide future research onboard the International Space Station.

image_name: Diagram of Rectilinear Bone Mineral Scanner
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone is a living organ that is continuously remodeling itself. When mechanical forces applied to the skeleton during normal activity in a 1-G environment are removed, bone mineral is lost because bone resorption is greater than bone formation. Bone resorption represents a danger not only because of the risk of fracture in demineralized bones, but also because the concomitant increased urinary calcium excretion might increase the risk for the formation of kidney stones.

The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effect of microgravity on the skeletal system during space flight. Studies conducted during the Gemini 4, 5, and 7, and Apollo 7 and 8 missions used x-ray densitometry to measure the amount of bone mineral present in the os calcis, radius, ulna, and phalanges. The studies revealed significant bone mineral losses in all areas measured. The degree of loss appeared excessive for such short periods in microgravity. Further evaluation of the data determined that bone mineral loses were lower than what was first measured. The overestimates were primarily due to problems inherent in the measurement techniques used. Scientists concluded that x-ray densitometry was unreliable for calculating bone mineral losses. It was not until a much more stable method of measuring bone mineral content, called photon absorptiometry, was developed that bone mineral studies continued during Apollo 14, 15, and 16.

Early reports of significant bone mineral losses in the 5- to 14-day Gemini and Apollo missions emphasized the need for correlating mineral losses observed in ground-based studies with those observed during microgravity. Ground-based studies designed to mimic the microgravity condition were used to estimate when changes were likely to occur during a mission. Bed rest served as an experimental model since the loss of bone mineral in bed rested and immobilized patients had been observed during periods of up to 36 weeks.

It was determined during these studies that the amount of initial mineral content in the os calcis could influence the rate of mineral loss. Bed rested subjects who exhibited a high mineral content at the beginning of bed rest showed the least mineral loss both in percentage and in quantity. Conversely, subjects who exhibited a low mineral content at the onset of bed rest showed a greater rate of mineral loss. The bed rest model was also used to determine what remedial measures might be used to both reduce bone mineral loss and predict bone mineral losses in the astronauts.

Thus, another goal of this study was to establish time courses for both the bed rest and flight situations so that better estimates could be obtained on the risk of prolonged space flight as translated from the ground-based bed rest studies.

APPROACH:
Bone scans using the photon absorptiometry technique were made on the crewmembers of Apollo 14 (10-day mission), Apollo 15 (12-day), and Apollo 16 (11-day) approximately one month, two weeks, and one week before flight. Each data collection session consisted of one x-ray and three bone scans of the left central os calcis, the right radius and the right ulna. Four postflight measurement sessions were conducted for each crewmember at various times. A series of control subject measurements was made in parallel with the crewmembers. Three subjects each were studied during Apollo 14 and Apollo 15, and four subjects were studied during Apollo 16.

A photon scanning device, called a rectilinear bone mineral scanner, was used during the experiment. The extremity to be measured was placed in tissue equivalent material (TEM) to compensate for the irregular thickness of tissue cover that surrounded the bone. The extremity, encased in the TEM, was placed between the photon source, Iodine-125 (125I), and a photon detector. The photon source and detector were aligned in direct opposition to each other so that a 3-millimeter source beam was directed into a 3-millimeter entrance on the detector. The absorptiometer scanned the section of bone in a series of sixteen straight, parallel lines covering the entire area. The scanner could be configured to accommodate either the upper or lower extremity. As the transmitted beam passed through the segment of bone, the detector on the opposite side measured the intensity of the radiation after it had passed through the TEM and the bone. Researchers were then able to calculate the amount of mineral content in the bone segment. The entire system was calibrated before and after each scan by making four passes over a Witt-Cameron standard.

Because of space restrictions in the quarantine facility and isolation restrictions, only a single scanner device could be used during the postflight period of Apollo 14. For this reason, arm and heel scans were performed separately using the same scanner in each of the two configurations. On the two subsequent missions, arm and heel studies were performed simultaneously both preflight and postflight, because quarantine was no longer required.

RESULTS:
Mineral losses were not observed in the os calcis, radius, or ulna in the Apollo 14 or Apollo 16 crewmembers. Only two Apollo 15 crewmembers lost mineral from the os calcis. Both crewmembers regained the bone mineral losses and were near baseline values by the end of two weeks. The magnitude of loss, when compared to the control subjects, was 5 to 6 percent. Mineral losses were not observed in radius or ulna mineral during the Apollo 15 flight.

A significant increase in fatty tissue was observed on the plantar side of the os calcis in one subject of Apollo 14 immediately postflight. This subject showed a 34 percent increase in fat equivalence when compared to immediate preflight measurements. This increase would have resulted in a 4.3 percent overestimation of bone mineral if the soft tissue contribution had not been measured. In contrast, the other two crewmembers showed between a 8.1 and 8.4 percent increase in fat equivalence with a potential 2.5 and 2.2 percent overestimation in bone mineral. No significant changes in the soft tissue composition were observed in the Apollo 15 or 16 crewmembers.

Researchers established a predictive model for bone mineral loss for the bed rested subjects. In this model, the ratio of initial bone mineral content to the initial 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was compared to observed losses. The greater the ratio, the slower and smaller the mineral losses and, conversely, the smaller the ratio, the faster and greater the mineral losses. The accurate measurement of baseline 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was therefore an essential requirement for these predictions. Unfortunately, no time course could be established for the microgravity state because of limited data. Researchers hoped that additional data collected during the Skylab missions would determine a time course of bone mineral losses that could be compared with the bed rest data. Therefore, bed rest studies could be established as a good model for the effects of weight unloading. Secondly, bed rest studies could serve as a predictive measure for longer space missions.

__description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone is a living organ that is continuously remodeling itself. When mechanical forces applied to the skeleton during normal activity in a 1-G environment are removed, bone mineral is lost because bone resorption is greater than bone formation. Bone resorption represents a danger not only because of the risk of fracture in demineralized bones, but also because the concomitant increased urinary calcium excretion might increase the risk for the formation of kidney stones.

The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effect of microgravity on the skeletal system during space flight. Studies conducted during the Gemini 4, 5, and 7, and Apollo 7 and 8 missions used x-ray densitometry to measure the amount of bone mineral present in the os calcis, radius, ulna, and phalanges. The studies revealed significant bone mineral losses in all areas measured. The degree of loss appeared excessive for such short periods in microgravity. Further evaluation of the data determined that bone mineral loses were lower than what was first measured. The overestimates were primarily due to problems inherent in the measurement techniques used. Scientists concluded that x-ray densitometry was unreliable for calculating bone mineral losses. It was not until a much more stable method of measuring bone mineral content, called photon absorptiometry, was developed that bone mineral studies continued during Apollo 14, 15, and 16.

Early reports of significant bone mineral losses in the 5- to 14-day Gemini and Apollo missions emphasized the need for correlating mineral losses observed in ground-based studies with those observed during microgravity. Ground-based studies designed to mimic the microgravity condition were used to estimate when changes were likely to occur during a mission. Bed rest served as an experimental model since the loss of bone mineral in bed rested and immobilized patients had been observed during periods of up to 36 weeks.

It was determined during these studies that the amount of initial mineral content in the os calcis could influence the rate of mineral loss. Bed rested subjects who exhibited a high mineral content at the beginning of bed rest showed the least mineral loss both in percentage and in quantity. Conversely, subjects who exhibited a low mineral content at the onset of bed rest showed a greater rate of mineral loss. The bed rest model was also used to determine what remedial measures might be used to both reduce bone mineral loss and predict bone mineral losses in the astronauts.

Thus, another goal of this study was to establish time courses for both the bed rest and flight situations so that better estimates could be obtained on the risk of prolonged space flight as translated from the ground-based bed rest studies.

APPROACH:
Bone scans using the photon absorptiometry technique were made on the crewmembers of Apollo 14 (10-day mission), Apollo 15 (12-day), and Apollo 16 (11-day) approximately one month, two weeks, and one week before flight. Each data collection session consisted of one x-ray and three bone scans of the left central os calcis, the right radius and the right ulna. Four postflight measurement sessions were conducted for each crewmember at various times. A series of control subject measurements was made in parallel with the crewmembers. Three subjects each were studied during Apollo 14 and Apollo 15, and four subjects were studied during Apollo 16.

A photon scanning device, called a rectilinear bone mineral scanner, was used during the experiment. The extremity to be measured was placed in tissue equivalent material (TEM) to compensate for the irregular thickness of tissue cover that surrounded the bone. The extremity, encased in the TEM, was placed between the photon source, Iodine-125 (125I), and a photon detector. The photon source and detector were aligned in direct opposition to each other so that a 3-millimeter source beam was directed into a 3-millimeter entrance on the detector. The absorptiometer scanned the section of bone in a series of sixteen straight, parallel lines covering the entire area. The scanner could be configured to accommodate either the upper or lower extremity. As the transmitted beam passed through the segment of bone, the detector on the opposite side measured the intensity of the radiation after it had passed through the TEM and the bone. Researchers were then able to calculate the amount of mineral content in the bone segment. The entire system was calibrated before and after each scan by making four passes over a Witt-Cameron standard.

Because of space restrictions in the quarantine facility and isolation restrictions, only a single scanner device could be used during the postflight period of Apollo 14. For this reason, arm and heel scans were performed separately using the same scanner in each of the two configurations. On the two subsequent missions, arm and heel studies were performed simultaneously both preflight and postflight, because quarantine was no longer required.

RESULTS:
Mineral losses were not observed in the os calcis, radius, or ulna in the Apollo 14 or Apollo 16 crewmembers. Only two Apollo 15 crewmembers lost mineral from the os calcis. Both crewmembers regained the bone mineral losses and were near baseline values by the end of two weeks. The magnitude of loss, when compared to the control subjects, was 5 to 6 percent. Mineral losses were not observed in radius or ulna mineral during the Apollo 15 flight.

A significant increase in fatty tissue was observed on the plantar side of the os calcis in one subject of Apollo 14 immediately postflight. This subject showed a 34 percent increase in fat equivalence when compared to immediate preflight measurements. This increase would have resulted in a 4.3 percent overestimation of bone mineral if the soft tissue contribution had not been measured. In contrast, the other two crewmembers showed between a 8.1 and 8.4 percent increase in fat equivalence with a potential 2.5 and 2.2 percent overestimation in bone mineral. No significant changes in the soft tissue composition were observed in the Apollo 15 or 16 crewmembers.

Researchers established a predictive model for bone mineral loss for the bed rested subjects. In this model, the ratio of initial bone mineral content to the initial 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was compared to observed losses. The greater the ratio, the slower and smaller the mineral losses and, conversely, the smaller the ratio, the faster and greater the mineral losses. The accurate measurement of baseline 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was therefore an essential requirement for these predictions.
