investigators: Principal Investigator: Taylor, Gerald
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) was a unique space flight in which spacecrafts from America and the Soviet Union docked together in space. This presented an opportunity to study cross-contamination of one crew with the medically important microorganisms carried by the other crew. Accordingly, the objectives of this study were to identify and trace all microorganisms of potential medical importance. Medical microbiological analysis of U.S. crewmembers was performed as a part of a larger study, the Microbial Exchange Experiment (AR-002), conducted during the historic ASTP space flight.

APPROACH:
Microbial samples were collected from the three Apollo crewmembers and two Soyuz crewmembers on L-45 days, L-30, L-15, L-7, L-0 (launch day), once during flight, and on recovery days R+0, R+15 and R+30. Backup crewmembers served as experimental controls. Sample collection sites included:

1) A 20 square centimeters area of hair (and scalp) on the top of the head
2) Right and left external auditory canals
3) 20 square centimeters area below hairline at base of neck
4) Internal area of both nostrils
5) The tonsils and posterior pharyngeal vault
6) 20 square centimeters area on right and left palms
7) 20 square centimeters area below the hairline of each axilla
8) 5 centimeter strip from rear to front on right and left inguinal area between legs
9) Area between the two smallest toes of each foot
10) The throat and mouth

Preflight and post flight, microbial specimens were collected from each crewmember using calcium alginate swabs wet with 0.3 millimolar phosphate buffer. Dry calcium alginate swabs were used to sample the tonsils and pharyngeal vault prior to the collection of the gargle specimen.

In-flight samples, consisting of the first six areas outlined above, were obtained from all five flight crewmembers on flight day 3. A specially developed microbial sample collection device was used to collect in-flight samples. This device consisted of a cotton-tipped Teflon swab on a capillary tube containing a conservative fluid, which kept the microorganisms alive. Each swab was housed within an airtight case to prevent desiccation.

Each sample was serially diluted under aseptic conditions and inoculated onto nutrient media. The variety of media, number of plates inoculated and dilution range were selected on the basis of what was required to isolate and quantitate the autoflora present in each sample area. Sabauraud's Dextrose Agar (SAB) plates were incubated at 30 degrees Celsius for five days. Cornmeal, malt-extract, yeast extract (CMMY) agar plates were incubated at 25 degrees Celsius for 7 days and all others were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 48 hours. Following incubation, the resulting aerobic bacterial colonies were categorized and counted with one sample of each morphologically different colony type transferred to nutrient media and stained with Gram's stain. Apollo sample analysis was conducted at the NASA Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, Texas.

RESULTS:
Gram-negative Rods:
Escherichia coli, Enterobacter aerogenes and Proteus mirabilis, members of the enteric bacilli group, were found on the ASTP crewmembers at sites other than the lower intestinal tract. Bacilli species are generally considered of potential medical importance when they are recovered repeatedly, or in large numbers, from sites other than the lower digestive tract.

Escherichia coli is generally accepted as the most reliable evidence of fecal contamination. Outside the intestinal tract it can cause urinary tract infections, peritonitis, gall bladder infections, wound infections, septicemia and enteritis. E. coli was repeatedly recovered from the groin of ASTP subject B and occasionally from the upper respiratory tract of the other two prime crewmembers. In all cases, no medical significance was indicated by the occurrence or quantities of E. coli.

Enterobacter aerogenes is found in the large intestine of man. Its pathogenic significance is similar to that of E. coli. This species was always carried in the nasal and buccal cavities of ASTP subjects B and C and was frequently isolated from two backup crewmembers. E. aerogenes was not spread to ASTP subject A or to other sites on the carrier subject during the flight. In addition, E. aerogenes quantities were not increased postflight.

Proteus mirabilis can cause urinary tract infections, abscesses and gastroenteritis. More often, they cause secondary infections of the middle ear, mastoid process, meninges and urinary tract, as well as in existing wounds. P. mirabilis was carried in low numbers in the nasal passage of ASTP subject A. This species and E. aerogenes provided a good model system for analyzing the response of Gram negative rods to space flight conditions. It has previously been reported that the Gram-negative rod component of the autoflora could change during or following confinement in a closed environment and that this change could result in "dysobacteriosis," such as flooding of an area with a particular species. The ASTP mission had no such effect on the qualitative or quantitative presence of these microorganisms.

Moraxella species are parasites found in the mucous membranes of man that can cause diseases such as conjunctivitis. Although carried in the mouth of ASTP subject C for 45 days preflight, no discernible microbial alteration was demonstrated following the mission.

Acinetobacter calcoaceticus, of minor medical importance, was isolated from multiple sites on ASTP subject B. It did not contribute significantly to the microbial load of Gram-negative rods recovered from ASTP crewmembers.

Four species of Haemophilus were isolated from the oral cavity of each ASTP astronaut. These were H. influenzae, H. haemolyticus, H. parahaemolyticus and H. parainfluenzae. Although each of these species is a common inhabitant of the human mouth, each is a strict parasite, requiring certain growth factors present in blood. H. influenzae is found in lesions and in the upper respiratory tract of carriers. It may be either a primary or a secondary invader. This microorganism is responsible for meningitis, septicemia, conjunctivitis and upper respiratory tract infections, and as a secondary invader in influenza and pertussis cases. H. influenzae was isolated from each crewmember preflight in quantities from 10,000 to 600,000 viable cells/ml of gargle. The post flight loss from two crewmembers and quantitative reduction in contamination of ASTP subject A was contraindicative of a space flight mediated increase in infective potential.

H. haemolyticus and H. parahaemolyticus are often associated with acute pharyngitis when present in high numbers. As with the H. influenzae, the overall incidence and quantitation of H. haemolyticus and H. parahaemolyticus decreased following the ASTP flight. H. parainfluenzae is the least harmful of the four species recovered and is used largely as a marker organism due to its universal appearance.

Candida albicans
Candida albicans has been recovered from astronauts throughout the Apollo and Skylab missions. Because this species can cause serious oral cavity diseases, its presence was carefully monitored. C. albicans was isolated from ASTP subjects B and C at all sampling periods. Data analysis indicates the inflight transfer of C. albicans to ASTP subject A. No such transfer occurred in the backup crew, although C. albicans was carried by one crewman. All of these events demonstrate the importance of this species in space flight. The importance could increase during the in-flight use of antibiotics, because this could cause a loss of competing bacterial species and eventual overgrowth of C. albicans.

Staphylococcus aureus
Although Staphylococcus aureus is a common skin and nasal contaminant, all strains are potential pathogens. S. aureus can cause boils, abscesses, meningitis, furunculosis, pyemia, osteomyelitis, suppuration of wounds and food poisoning. Several studies have indicated increases in the toxigenic activity, virulence and pathogenicity of this species with stressful confinement of the human host. Lesions caused by S. aureus in space flight were important because of their interference with close contact surfaces, such as the tight fitting and abrasive pressure suits. Accordingly, the presence and activity of this species was monitored before and after each space flight. Data from Apollo 13, 14 and 15 missions, and from the Skylab missions confirm in-flight cross contamination with S. aureus.

Data show that each crewmember (flight and backup) carried a different strain of S. aureus. Different strains are expressed as bacteriophage types. One type (52,52A,80,81), carried by ASTP subject C, was transferred to ASTP subject A during flight. Apparently colonization did not ensue, as this strain was not recovered from subject A post flight.

During the ASTP mission, a post flight increase of S. aureus did not occur among the astronaut population, as reported during previous missions, and disease events did not result from its presence.

Total Load of Potential Pathogens
One idea that resulted from previous space flight microbial studies was that crewmembers could suffer "microbial shock" upon return to Earth, and therefore, respond negatively to renewed contact with the potentially pathogenic microorganisms absent in the space flight environment. This was based on the assumption that contact with potential pathogens during space flight would be very limited, resulting in a reduction of immunocompetence. However, there was no demonstrable decrease in the incidence of medically important microorganisms recovered from the astronauts on R+0, a finding which supports earlier results. Therefore, if a reduction in total immunocompetence occurred during the ASTP mission, it was not in response to decreased contact with medically important components of the resident microflora.

Although several potential pathogens were recovered from each of the flight and backup crewmembers before and after flight, no disease events were reported. C. albicans and S. aureus were transferred from one crewmember to another in-flight, but no other medically significant changes in the microbial population were observed.

experiment_title: Heavy Isotope Enrichment of Shuttle Galley Water
parameter_html:
2H enrichment
Oxygen-18 (18O) enrichment
investigators: Principal Investigator: Leach- Huntoon, CarolynCo-Investigator: Charles, JohnCo-Investigator: Inners, Lamar Daniel
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The main objective of this experiment was to provide science verification for inflight total body water (TBW) methodology. Because the potable water provided by the Space Shuttle is enriched in both 2H (deuterium) and 18O (oxygen-18), possible interference with total body water determination was investigated.

APPROACH:
The investigation required the preflight and in-flight collection of samples of Shuttle galley water. Samples were collected on days when total body water was determined, and at least once a day on a mission that did not include TBW determination. Each sample consisted of approximately 100 mL of water collected in beverage container assemblies. The technique of sample collection was essentially the same as filling a beverage package for a drink of water. One preflight sample was collected three days before launch (L-3). In-flight sampling was completed twice during each 24-hour cycle, and 16 in-flight samples were actually collected during the nine-day STS-35 mission. Each consisted of approximately 100 mL of water collected in beverage container assemblies which were included as part of the Shuttle food system. The technique of sample collection was essentially the same as filling a beverage package for a drink of water. The containers were double-bagged in polyethylene re-sealable bags for stowage in an empty food locker at ambient temperature. Postflight gasisotope-ratio mass spectrometric analyses for 18O and 2H enrichment were performed in ground-based facilities.

RESULTS:
Space Shuttle galley water was found to be enriched in both 18O and 2H; however, the observed level of heavy isotope enrichment of the crew's drinking water is not regarded as a source of error in the measurement of TBW.

experiment_title: Microgravity and Development of Vestibular Circuits
parameter_html:
Content, Biochemicals, central nervous system, rat, Poly- and monoclonal antibodies, immunofluorescent microscopy
Content, Biochemicals, peripheral nervous system, rat, Poly- and monoclonal antibodies, immunofluorescent microscopy
Central nervous system (CNS), structure
Peripheral nervous system, structure
investigators: Principal Investigator: Raymond, Jacqueline
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Exposure of the vertebrate inner ear to microgravity has been shown to result in an alteration of the gravity receptors of the vestibular system as well as vestibular sensory-motor rearrangement. If this exposure is experienced as an adult, the effect is temporary and reverses upon return to 1 G. In contrast, it is hypothesized that if such structural modifications occur during the developmental period, they may induce permanent changes in the vestibular sensorineuronal circuits. This experiment investigated the vestibular system at the level of the gravity receptors (sensory hair cells) and the primary neurons relaying the sensory signals (the vestibular neurons) and their potential plasticity at the structural and biochemical levels. Structures not involved in gravity detection (the cochlea and cochlear nuclei) were used as a control.

Approach:

Inflight tissue samples were collected as part of the integrated neonate perfusions and dissections on FD 8 and FD 15. Postflight samples were collected eight hours after landing. Vestibular receptors were dissected out in cold phosphate buffer solution (PBS). For Vibratome sectioning, the ampullar cristae and utricular and saccular maculae were separately embedded in 4% agarose in PBS and cut into 50 mm sections with a Vibratome. For cryostat sectioning, the receptors were incubated overnight at 4 °C in 30% sucrose in PBS and cut into 14 mm sections. Vibratome sections were prepared for immunofluorescent microscopy by incubation with varied primary and secondary antibodies. Some samples were double-stained using different combinations of poly- and monoclonal antibodies applied simultaneously. Brainstems were sectioned and prepared for immunofluorescent microscopy with similar procedures. Immunostained sections were analyzed with a BioRad-MRC 1024 laser scanning confocal microscope.

Results:

Preliminary observations did not indicate a significant reorganization of the macular sensory organs, or their afferent and efferent connections. Expression of parvalbumin, calretinin, and calbindin were unaffected. Sensory cells and their afferent fiber distribution, as well as the distribution of synaptic proteins, remained unchanged in flight animals. This lack of effect on the organization of the maculae and ganglion may indicate that the peripheral otolithic organs and their afferent networks are less sensitive to environmental changes than the integrative structures of the brain. Another possible explanation is that the critical periods of development for these peripheral organs occur at an earlier age than post-natal day 8. __description:
Objectives:

Exposure of the vertebrate inner ear to microgravity has been shown to result in an alteration of the gravity receptors of the vestibular system as well as vestibular sensory-motor rearrangement. If this exposure is experienced as an adult, the effect is temporary and reverses upon return to 1 G. In contrast, it is hypothesized that if such structural modifications occur during the developmental period, they may induce permanent changes in the vestibular sensorineuronal circuits. This experiment investigated the vestibular system at the level of the gravity receptors (sensory hair cells) and the primary neurons relaying the sensory signals (the vestibular neurons) and their potential plasticity at the structural and biochemical levels. Structures not involved in gravity detection (the cochlea and cochlear nuclei) were used as a control.

Approach:

Inflight tissue samples were collected as part of the integrated neonate perfusions and dissections on FD 8 and FD 15. Postflight samples were collected eight hours after landing. Vestibular receptors were dissected out in cold phosphate buffer solution (PBS). For Vibratome sectioning, the ampullar cristae and utricular and saccular maculae were separately embedded in 4% agarose in PBS and cut into 50 mm sections with a Vibratome. For cryostat sectioning, the receptors were incubated overnight at 4 °C in 30% sucrose in PBS and cut into 14 mm sections. Vibratome sections were prepared for immunofluorescent microscopy by incubation with varied primary and secondary antibodies. Some samples were double-stained using different combinations of poly- and monoclonal antibodies applied simultaneously. Brainstems were sectioned and prepared for immunofluorescent microscopy with similar procedures. Immunostained sections were analyzed with a BioRad-MRC 1024 laser scanning confocal microscope.

Results:

Preliminary observations did not indicate a significant reorganization of the macular sensory organs, or their afferent and efferent connections. Expression of parvalbumin, calretinin, and calbindin were unaffected. Sensory cells and their afferent fiber distribution, as well as the distribution of synaptic proteins, remained unchanged in flight animals. However, it is not clear if this implies delayed development or a definitive failure resulting from microgravity exposure during a critical period of development.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This Detailed Supplementary Objective (DSO) consisted of studies of the electro-oculogram (EOG) during a voluntary head motion protocol on Space Shuttle missions. There were eight variations to this study, which occurred during STS-5, STS-6, STS-7, STS-8, and STS-51D.

The general objectives across all of these missions were to:
1. Document any abnormalities of horizontal and vertical extra ocular motion (EOM), including pathological nystagmus and oscillopsia, or image slip, preflight, on orbit, postflight, and during and after space motion sickness (SMS).
2. Measure visual/vestibular-ocular (VVOR), vestibulo-ocular gain (VOR), and visual and vestibular suppression during flight and after space motion sickness.
3. Demonstrate the technique and hardware in space flight for the first time.

APPROACH:
Standard clinical techniques and protocol were used with voluntary head oscillation and fixed targets, with eyes closed and with head-synchronized targets. Electro-oculography (EOG) recorded extra ocular eye motion (EOM) and a precision potentiometer recorded head motion. EOG was calibrated by pseudo-random light position. In-flight data were transmitted via a Shuttle data channel and graphically recorded. Analysis included a search for anomalies and standard analysis for reflex gains. EOG were routinely recorded. Analog data were recorded with magnetic tape and transcribed to charts postflight for analysis.

Orbit/entry on STS-6: a model-airplane gyroscope with battery supply was mounted on the subject's flight helmet and replaced the flexible cable potentiometer. On orbit on STS-8: a miniature 2-axis rate designed for missile use was repackaged and placed on a head harness such that rotational velocities around the Z (vertical) and Y (pitch) axes could be recorded. A minimal support structure for a kneeling subject in weightlessness allowed subject rotation around the Z (vertical) axis. Low friction bearings were connected to a spiral spring whose rate could be varied. A subject could thus be passively rotated at various rates in damped angular oscillation.

RESULTS:
STS-5: Two subjects were studied in flight and EOGs were routinely recorded. A flexible shaft on the head position potentiometer induced errors. No EOM abnormalities were found, and the practicality of the technique was demonstrated. One record had EOG artifacts. There wasn't any evidence of abnormal EOM during space flight, with or without SMS. Investigators found that a flexible shaft coupling for a head potentiometer is unsuitable for use.

STS-6: Except for loss of the data channel for head motion during the initial in-flight study, two subjects were routinely studied, and data were received and analyzed. No abnormalities were found and reflex gains were essentially unchanged. EOM was unchanged during space flight and there wasn't any evidence of SMS in these subjects. A slight increase in horizontal VVOR and VOR gain was observed in some subjects. The single-axis gyro was flown successfully on ascent and entry by one subject on STS-6; however, an improved pantograph mounting for the potentiometer proved superior and was used in subsequent flights.

STS-7: Recording of EOG was routine in 3 subjects. An error was detected in on-orbit head position and was found to be caused by the head position potentiometer being mounted out of limits. No abnormalities were noted. Optokinetic motion was unchanged. No abnormalities were noted during space flight, or during or after SMS. No significant changes were seen in saccadic EOM or in EOM reflexes. There were significant increases in saccade velocity in flight, with and without SMS, but no significant differences in accuracy.

STS-8: Data were routinely recorded in 5 subjects without evidence of abnormality. EOM was unchanged during space flight and SMS in these subjects. There were significant increases in saccade velocity in flight, with and without SMS, but no significant differences in accuracy. A slight increase in horizontal VVOR and VOR gain was observed in some subjects. The 2-axis rate gyro was used to record horizontal motion from two subjects on the rotating device on STS-8 and horizontal and vertical head motion on EOG studies during entry on one subject. The data were routinely reproduced on analog strip charts and a preliminary analysis done; however, resources were not available to complete the analysis and report the results. Both the 2-axis rate gyro and passive subject rotators demonstrated ample capacity for on orbit studies at a fraction of the weight, size, and cost of conventional hardware.

STS-51D: The subject was severely affected by SMS for the initial 48 hours in flight and did not perform any studies during this time. All studies done following this period, including postflight, were unremarkable. EOM was normal after severe SMS.
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.

experiment_title: Visual Light Flash Phenomena
parameter_html: Light flash count, total
investigators: Principal Investigator: Hoffman, RudolfCo-Investigator: Bailey, VernonCo-Investigator: Osborne, W.Co-Investigator: Pinsky, Lawrence
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The first reporting of flashes of light, visible primarily when the eyes were closed, was from Apollo 11 astronauts and occurred during transearth-coast (TEC) travel. Subsequent light flashes were reported by astronauts on the remaining Apollo missions, during both translunar-coast (TLC) and transearth-coast (TEC) travel. Although it had been generally accepted that the observed light flashes were caused by cosmic ray particles passing through the eye, the exact mechanism of particle interaction was still unknown. Some investigations supported the premise that the visual flashes were caused by direct cosmic ray particle and retina interaction, while others tended to favor Cerenkov radiation from relativistic particles as the etiology. While both mechanisms probably contributed, the consensus was that most of the flashes resulted from direct ionization energy loss as the particle traversed retinal cells. In either case, if cosmic particles were the cause, a strong latitude effect of the light flash rate would exist for an observer in Earth orbit, due to the Van Allen Radiation Belts. Near the equator, only cosmic particles with very high energy can reach orbital altitudes, while near the magnetic poles, particles of much lower energy can reach comparable altitudes.

The primary objective of the study was to investigate the frequency and character of visual light flashes in low-Earth orbit as the Skylab trajectory passed from northern to southern latitudes. Because the trajectory periodically passed through the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), another objective was to investigate possible visual flashes during passage through this region.

APPROACH:
Two periods of observation by one observer were planned for the Skylab 4 mission. These observation sessions were accomplished on orbits selected to provide the best data on both latitude and SAA effects. The first observation session occurred on mission day 74 and was 70 minutes in duration. The second occurred on mission day 81 and was 15 minutes shorter because of very critical time limitations during the last few days of the mission.

At the start of each session, the observer got into his sleep restraint, set a timer for the prescribed period (either 70 or 55 minutes), donned a blindfold, and began observing for light flashes. The subject allocated the first 10 minutes of each session for dark adaptation. During the first session, no particular position in the sleep restraint was specified. The spacecraft was in Solar Inertial Mode during both periods and local noon occurred very close to the equator in both cases. For the second session, directions were given for head positioning that placed the anterior-posterior axis of the head parallel to the Earth’s magnetic field lines in the SAA.

The astronaut described each light flash event on a voice tape recorder and a transcript was obtained after flight for analysis.

RESULTS:
Unfortunately, no single orbit possessed ideal geomagnetic latitude and SAA conditions. The first session provided the best latitude conditions, but Skylab passed through the edge of the SAA region. The second session passed through the center of the SAA but did not achieve geomagnetic latitudes as high as in the first session.

A total of 168 flashes were reported. During the second session, there were 144 reported flashes while the spacecraft was in the center of the SAA, greatly outnumbering the 24 flashes observed when Skylab passed through the edge of the SAA in the first session. The relationship between flash occurrence and geomagnetic latitude of High Mass Energy (HZE) particle flux was difficult to determine because of the few flashes observed and the varying lengths of time spent at different latitudes. It was known, however, that the time from equator passage was directly related to latitude. When the cosmic ray flux was plotted against time from equator passing, and the number of light flashes observed inside and outside the SAA was added, a correlation of flash occurrence with cosmic ray flux (or geomagnetic latitude) appeared. Dosimeter data from the Van Allen radiation belts indicated increased radiation levels in the SAA, and the flash rate coincided well with the increased radiation levels.

Although light flashes were reported as casual observations by the crews of Skylab 2 and Skylab 3, the events reported during Skylab 4 represented the first dedicated observations made in Earth orbit. No flashes were observed during the Mercury and Gemini flights or during Apollo missions prior to Apollo 11. One explanation as to why no flashes were observed prior to Apollo 11 was that the eye must be dark-adapted. Furthermore, it was thought that the observer must be reasonably relaxed and free from most distracting activities to observe light flashes. This was not the case on earlier flights. Also, without a precedent for their observation, there would probably be the tendency to discount minor flashes as nothing unusual and simply a harmless event in an environment where there were more important observations to be made. Once the phenomenon was known to occur, astronauts could observe and record these events.

The following conclusions were drawn from the data:

  1. Dark-Dark adaptation of at least 10 minutes was required to begin observing the flashes.
  2. There was a strong correlation of very high flash rates with passage through the SAA. From physical arguments and event descriptions, it appeared certain that these flashes were due to radiation trapped inside the Van Allen Radiation Belts.
  3. There was evidence for the predicted latitude effect, although existing data were insufficient for a thorough statistical evaluation.
  4. A greater particle flux in the trajectory through the SAA during the second observation period probably explained the increased number of flashes observed at that time. However, there were also more flashes observed outside the anomaly during the second period where the cosmic particle environment should have been comparable. Researchers were unable to explain the phenomena.

It was suggested from the event rates and description of flashes during the SAA passes that particles heavier than protons may have been in the inner belt of trapped radiation. Existing knowledge of the inner belt included an upper limit of approximately one heavy nucleus per 1000 protons. The Skylab 4 light flash data were compatible with this limit, but suggested the existence of a significant flux of energy particles with atomic number (Z)>2. This provided strong motivation for making detailed and accurate measurements of the SAA (inner belt) heavy component during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project mission.

experiment_title: Acute and Long Term Outcomes of Simulated Deep Space Radiation Exposure on Latent Viral CNS Infection and CNS Pathology

Inflammation markers

Trigeminal ganglia

Herpes simplex virus (HSV)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Sawtell, NancyCo-Investigator: Thompson, RichardCo-Investigator: Williams, Richard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The successful diaspora of humans into deep space requires an understanding of the risk of deep space radiation exposure on short- and long-term health outcomes, including risks to the central nervous system (CNS). Assessing CNS risk must consider the impact of deep space radiation on the behavior of latent neurotropic infectious agents that reside within the human CNS. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is among the most widespread agent in this category, permanently infecting the nervous systems of more than 80% of the global population. Latent HSV cannot be eliminated from the nervous system and there is no vaccine to prevent infection. Thus for the foreseeable future, humans traveling into deep space will harbor this and other alpha-herpesviruses. While uncontrolled HSV replication in the CNS results in often fatal encephalitis, this virus also has the capacity to promote chronic inflammation and neurodegeneration. Indeed there is substantial evidence that in combination with genetic risk factors, HSV infection in the CNS further increases the probability of developing Alzheimer’s disease. During this study, the effects of simulated deep space radiation on the development of CNS pathology (reactive lesions) and the impact of latent and induced in vivo reactivation of HSV infection on the development of CNS pathology was determined together with the role that human ApoE alleles play in these processes.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the combined effect of latent HSV infection and mission relevant doses of 56Fe and Protons in acute and long term CNS health.
  2. Determine the combined effect of latent HSV infection and mission relevant doses of 56Fe and Protons on long term CNS health in the background of huApoE allelic variation.

APPROACH:
Investigators employed their well characterized mouse model of HSV latency and in vivo reactivation in combination with quantitative measures of reactive lesions in the CNS to determine the effect of simulated deep space radiation on HSV mediated CNS damage. The acute stage of infection was monitored using their standard approaches including quantitative evaluation of infectious virus titers. Latent infection in the trigeminal ganglia and brain were quantified at 30-40 days post-infection using their quantitative real time PCR assay for the viral genome. Spontaneous and induced exit from latency was quantified at the single neuron level using their whole TG immunohistochemical assay. This approach permitted investigators to identify even a single positive neuron in groups of ganglia. Viral reactivation (production of infectious virus) was evaluated using their standard assay. Reactivation was induced using their well-established hyperthermic stress procedure (temperature of the mice is raised to 42.5 C for 10 minutes). Investigators have shown and published that this procedure reliably induces viral reactivation and can be repeatedly employed two times per week for periods of up to at least one year post-infection. Investigators have determined the repeated reactivation stress of C57Bl/6 mice results in reactive astrocytic lesions in the CNS of HSV infected but not in uninfected mice. Interestingly this damage is much more extensive in mice that express the human ApoE4 allele or in IL10 knock out mice. This suggests important relevance to human biology since both IL10 polymorphisms and the ApoE4 allele have been shown to be associated with increased risk of acquiring Alzheimer’s disease. The investigators collaborated with radiation biologists at NASA to determine appropriate conditions to simulate deep space radiation and to quantify the effects of such radiation on CNS damage induced by reactivation of HSV latent infections.

The goal of this project was to assess the risk of combined simulated galactic cosmic radiation (sGCR) exposure and the presence of latent HSV in the nervous system. Using a well-characterized model of acute and latent HSV infection in the mouse as the working platform, risk associated with sGCR exposure in the context of the full complexity of host responses in the presence and absence of viral latency was evaluated. Two time frames were investigated: (i) acute effects, i.e., does sGCR cause viral reactivation in the latently infected nervous system, and if so, what is the outcome, and (ii) long term effects, i.e., are long term outcomes of latent virus in the nervous system altered by sGCR exposure.

RESULTS:
sGCR exposure of HSV latently infected mice resulted in no widespread lytic activation of latent viral genomes in the nervous system but did result in the highly restricted and temporally limited reactivation associated with terrestrial stimuli (i.e., occurring in 1-3 neurons and resolving in the nervous system within 48 hours). In addition, studies modelling moderate immune suppression (a known space mission risk) combined with HSV reactivation (space mission risk) revealed that moderate immune suppression does not alter the control of HSV spread following a reactivation event. In contrast, this same immune suppression resulted in severe disease outcomes in newly HSV infected hosts. Thus HSV latent infection and commensurate immunity to HSV, even considering the potential for reactivation from latency, may be an advantage to crew unless all crew are uninfected or a vaccine becomes available.

Despite reduced spleen weight in sGCR exposed group, immunity to HSV was fully maintained. Thus reduced spleen weight did not correlate with a detectable defect in long term maintenance of immunologic memory or the downstream ability to mount a protective immune response. Furthermore, long-term HSV latency results in cognitive impairment, a finding observed in three independent groups in both sGCR exposed and unexposed groups. However, these behavioral effects were not significantly exacerbated by radiation exposure. The cognitive impairment was associated with AD like changes in the brain and especially prominent in the huApoE4 targeted replacement mice. This model, combining two known AD risk factors, aging and the ApoE4 allele with a latent viral infection is an important advance. Radiation exposure had some effect independent of infection, but with rare exceptions, did not significantly exacerbate the effects of infection alone.

No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

Indeed there is substantial evidence that in combination with genetic risk factors, HSV infection in the CNS further increases the probability of developing Alzheimer’s disease. During this study, the effects of simulated deep space radiation on the development of CNS pathology (reactive lesions) and the impact of latent and induced in vivo reactivation of HSV infection on the development of CNS pathology was determined together with the role that human ApoE alleles play in these processes.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the combined effect of latent HSV infection and mission relevant doses of 56Fe and Protons in acute and long term CNS health.
  2. Determine the combined effect of latent HSV infection and mission relevant doses of 56Fe and Protons on long term CNS health in the background of huApoE allelic variation.

APPROACH:
Investigators employed their well characterized mouse model of HSV latency and in vivo reactivation in combination with quantitative measures of reactive lesions in the CNS to determine the effect of simulated deep space radiation on HSV mediated CNS damage. The acute stage of infection was monitored using their standard approaches including quantitative evaluation of infectious virus titers. Latent infection in the trigeminal ganglia and brain were quantified at 30-40 days post-infection using their quantitative real time PCR assay for the viral genome. Spontaneous and induced exit from latency was quantified at the single neuron level using their whole TG immunohistochemical assay. This approach permitted investigators to identify even a single positive neuron in groups of ganglia. Viral reactivation (production of infectious virus) was evaluated using their standard assay. Reactivation was induced using their well-established hyperthermic stress procedure (temperature of the mice is raised to 42.5 C for 10 minutes). Investigators have shown and published that this procedure reliably induces viral reactivation and can be repeatedly employed two times per week for periods of up to at least one year post-infection. Investigators have determined the repeated reactivation stress of C57Bl/6 mice results in reactive astrocytic lesions in the CNS of HSV infected but not in uninfected mice. Interestingly this damage is much more extensive in mice that express the human ApoE4 allele or in IL10 knock out mice. This suggests important relevance to human biology since both IL10 polymorphisms and the ApoE4 allele have been shown to be associated with increased risk of acquiring Alzheimer’s disease. The investigators collaborated with radiation biologists at NASA to determine appropriate conditions to simulate deep space radiation and to quantify the effects of such radiation on CNS damage induced by reactivation of HSV latent infections.

The goal of this project was to assess the risk of combined simulated galactic cosmic radiation (sGCR) exposure and the presence of latent HSV in the nervous system. Using a well-characterized model of acute and latent HSV infection in the mouse as the working platform, risk associated with sGCR exposure in the context of the full complexity of host responses in the presence and absence of viral latency was evaluated. Two time frames were investigated: (i) acute effects, i.e., does sGCR cause viral reactivation in the latently infected nervous system, and if so, what is the outcome, and (ii) long term effects, i.e., are long term outcomes of latent virus in the nervous system altered by sGCR exposure.

RESULTS:
sGCR exposure of HSV latently infected mice resulted in no widespread lytic activation of latent viral genomes in the nervous system but did result in the highly restricted and temporally limited reactivation associated with terrestrial stimuli (i.e., occurring in 1-3 neurons and resolving in the nervous system within 48 hours). In addition, studies modelling moderate immune suppression (a known space mission risk) combined with HSV reactivation (space mission risk) revealed that moderate immune suppression does not alter the control of HSV spread following a reactivation event. In contrast, this same immune suppression resulted in severe disease outcomes in newly HSV infected hosts. Thus HSV latent infection and commensurate immunity to HSV, even considering the potential for reactivation from latency, may be an advantage to crew unless all crew are uninfected or a vaccine becomes available.

Despite reduced spleen weight in sGCR exposed group, immunity to HSV was fully maintained. Thus reduced spleen weight did not correlate with a detectable defect in long term maintenance of immunologic memory or the downstream ability to mount a protective immune response. Furthermore, long-term HSV latency results in cognitive impairment, a finding observed in three independent groups in both sGCR exposed and unexposed groups. However, these behavioral effects were not significantly exacerbated by radiation exposure. The cognitive impairment was associated with AD like changes in the brain and especially prominent in the huApoE4 targeted replacement mice. This model, combining two known AD risk factors, aging and the ApoE4 allele with a latent viral infection is an important advance. Radiation exposure had some effect independent of infection, but with rare exceptions, did not significantly exacerbate the effects of infection alone.

No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This experiment examined the effect of long-term exposure to microgravity (µG) and the effects of Extra Vehicular Activity (EVA) on pulmonary function. A longitudinal study was performed of four crews of the International Space Station (ISS), measuring aspects of pulmonary function that may be affected by long-term exposure to µG per se, and by exposure to noxious gases, or particulate matter present in the atmosphere of the ISS. The investigators proposed to evaluate the effect of EVA on the lung by studying those crewmembers who perform EVAs before and after single and repeated EVAs. Crewmembers who did not perform EVAs served as a flying control group for this aspect of the study. Because EVA poses a significant risk of decompression sickness including bubble events within the pulmonary circulation, non-invasive tests of pulmonary function that are altered by changes in the pulmonary vasculature presented an ideal way to follow a subject over the course of multiple EVAs.

To test the hypotheses researchers used the following: the standard respiratory function measurement of forced spirometry, the measurement of intra-breath respiratory exchange ratio (intrabreath R), a hyperventilation-breathhold measurement of the distribution of pulmonary perfusion, slow spirometry for lung volume subdivision, and the measurement of maximum inspiratory and expiratory pressures to test the hypotheses.

APPROACH:
Each in-flight test session consisted of five non-invasive tests of lung function: (1) intra-breath respiratory exchange ratio, (2) distribution of pulmonary perfusion, (3) maximum inspiratory and expiratory pressures, (4) slow spirometry, and (5) maximum expiratory flow-volume. Each of these tests involved breathing only cabin air.

On the day of testing, the experiment system was set up and calibrated. After the initial calibration, each subject performed a standard sequence of breathing tests. After all subjects completed testing, a final calibration was performed and the data archived. The system was then deconfigured and stowed.

The first in-flight data collection was scheduled to occur two weeks into the mission, providing a data point comparable to the data already collected previously during several Spacelab flights. Thereafter, data collection sessions occurred at approximately monthly intervals for the duration of each flight. EVA-related in-flight data collection was performed as an experiment of opportunity. All subjects performed a test session within one week prior to the EVA. Following an EVA, the same session was repeated by those crewmembers who performed EVA, preferably on the same day that EVA was completed or, if necessary because of crew scheduling, on the day immediately following. An abbreviated sequence (two breathing tests) could be implemented if time was limited on the day of EVA. For subjects performing repeat EVAs (i.e., EVAs on successive days, or close to successive days), the abbreviated sequence was performed following every EVA in order to document the effect of repeated decompressions on the lung in µG.

Testing was also conducted four times preflight and four times postflight. Each of these sessions included the in-flight protocol and additional tests (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, single and multiple breath nitrogen washout, and cardiac output), measurements not possible in flight due to hardware limitations. Hemoglobin level was also required once preflight and four times postflight.

RESULTS:
Excellent quality data were collected from four Expeditions, comprising eight crewmembers who performed EVAs. The investigators reported no significant changes in pulmonary gas exchange one day after an EVA was performed. A small increase in metabolic rates in the astronauts was observed on the day following the EVA. The investigators reported that testing was not ideal because acute effects resulting from EVAs could not be measured immediately after performing the spacewalk due to EVA protocols and logistics, but remain confident in their primary conclusion. The small effect observed on the day following an EVA suggested that current protocols prevent the decompression stress associated with EVA from causing any major lasting disruption to gas exchange in the lung. The results clearly showed that vital capacity in prolonged periods of µG is essentially unchanged compared to that measured standing and that respiratory muscle strength is maintained throughout approximately six months in µG.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Berkowitz, Dan
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An appropriate examination of the health risks associated with manned space flight necessitates an understanding of the molecular consequences of exposure to the radiations encountered in space. Human radio-epidemiologic data and animal studies indicate that irradiation of the heart can cause a spectrum of cardiovascular complications. The mechanisms suggested for these alterations are chronic inflammation induced by oxidative stress. It is well known that ionizing radiation (IR) produces biological damage by direct effect on DNA and indirectly by generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the cellular milieu. The xanthine oxidoreductase (XOD) system is one of the major sources of free radicals in biologic systems. Since the XOD system is present primarily in the reduced XDH form in normal tissue, the production of free radicals is negligible. However, emerging data demonstrates that IR irreversibly converts the xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH) to xanthine oxidase (XO) leading to amplification and persistence of IR induced, ROS dependent cell damage. It is well known that ROS interferes with cellular signaling (nitrosylation and phosphorylation) and is pro-apoptotic (releases mitochondrial cytochrome-C and activates apoptotic pathways). One of the postulated mechanisms of radiation related tissue injury is endothelial cell damage. However little is known regarding other cellular and molecular targets in the pathophysiology of radiation-induced cardiovascular system dysfunction. Furthermore, little is known regarding the response of endothelial cells and cardiac myocytes to high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation. In this study, the investigators used established in vivo and in vitro bioassays to characterize the radiation response to charged particle exposure. Furthermore, mechanistically they focused on the interaction between ROS and nitric oxide (NO) pathways in the regulation of myocardial and vascular structure and function following oxidative stress (OS) induced by high LET radiation. This study had the following specific aims:
  1. Time- and dose-responses for multiple indices of endothelial and myocardial function will be established in adult Wistar rats exposed to 600 MeV/n Fe (iron) beams at the NASA's Space Radiation Laboratory, Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL).
  2. To determine whether low-fluences of iron ions alter the balance in NO signaling as a function of increased ROS production thereby impairing endothelial and myocardial function.
  3. Rats were exposed to 600 MeV/n iron ions to determine the specific roles of XO, NOS, and arginase in modulating cellular and tissue response to charge particle-induced oxidative stress.
  4. To determine if enzyme inhibitors and ROS scavengers can modulate the cardiovascular effects of iron ions, Wistar rats and/or tissue preparations were treated with enzyme inhibitors or ROS scavengers prior to and following 600 MeV/n Fe beam irradiation.

APPROACH:
The investigators developed an animal model incorporating four groups of mice: one group exposed to a hyperoxic environment, one exposed to radiation alone, and one group exposed to hyperoxia in addition to radiation. A group without exposure to hyperoxia or radiation served as controls. Hyperoxia treatment was performed by exposing mice to more than 95 percent oxygen for eight hours three times during one week in special chambers. Radiation treatment was performed by exposing mice to 1 Gy gamma radiation at rate of 100 rad/minute. Mice were exposed for a period of two weeks. At the end of the two week period, terminal endpoints were determined: 1) In vivo integrated cardiovascular function was measured using non-invasive Doppler to measure pulse wave velocity (PWV) and 2) Ex-vivo endothelial function by measuring endothelial dependent vasodilation in aortic rings.

RESULTS:
Compared to unexposed animals PWV was increased both following exposure to hyperoxia and to radiation alone. Combined exposure to both hyperoxia and radiation resulted in additive effect and resulted in worse cardiovascular function as evidenced by a maximum increase in PWV. In the ex-vivo experiments of endothelial function the investigators did not find any difference between control and exposed to radiation and hyperoxia groups. The data confirm that both hyperoxia and radiation adversely affect cardiovascular function and provides evidence that their negative effects are additive in nature.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Microbial Monitoring (DSO 437) was an experiment specifically designed for the Spacelab 3 Shuttle mission. This Spacelab mission was the first to use an animal facility for biomedical investigations. The mission also served as the Flight Verification Test of the Research Animal Holding Facility (RAHF). This DSO was developed and implemented to evaluate the impact of the animals in the Spacelab environment and to determine the ability of the RAHF to contain microorganisms.

Microbiological testing conducted on previous Space Shuttle flights has shown that some microbial buildup occurs in the closed crew environment during the course of the mission. The inclusion of animals in the crew environment represents a potential source of microbial contamination that may result in cross-contamination between the animals and crewmembers.

The first flight utilizing the RAHF required a more extensive microbial sampling protocol to monitor the microbial flora of the spacecraft and the crewmembers and to assess the containment capabilities of the RAHF. The microbiology effort for this mission was comprehensive and involved the Ames Research Center, Kennedy Space Center and the Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
CREWMEMBER

Samples from the crewmembers' ears, nose, throat, and hands were collected by the Culturette system during all sampling periods. With the exception of the throat cultures, all other samples were obtained after moistening the Culturette swab with 0.8 mM sterile phosphate buffer. After sampling, the Culturettes were stored at ambient temperature until processing.

Sputum and fecal specimens were collected in appropriate sterile containers and stored at 5°C until processing. A 10 ml blood sample was collected from each crewmember for the determination of antibody titers to specific viral agents such as Hepatitis A and B, Epstein-Barr, and Herpesvirus saimiri, etc. A throat swab was collected from each crewmember for isolation of any viral agents that may have been present. The throat swab was placed in Veal Infusion Broth for stabilization and maintained at 5°C until processing.

SURFACE SAMPLES

Preflight and postflight surface samples from the Orbiter, Spacelab, and RAHF were collected using two sterile calcium alginate swabs moistened with 0.8 mM sterile phosphate buffer for each site. One swab was placed in trypticase soy broth for bacterial analysis; the other swab was placed in yeast malt broth for fungal analysis. All swabs were stabilized at 5°C until processing.

In-flight surface samples of the RAHF and crewmembers' gloves were collected using the Culturette system. One Culturette per site was used. The Culturette was moistened with 0.8 mM sterile phosphate buffer before sampling. The samples were stored at ambient temperature until processing.

AIR SAMPLES

Air samples were collected in the Orbiter, Spacelab, Life Sciences Support Facilities (LSSF), and the JSC and KSC Crew Quarters using a Reuter Centrifugal Air Sampler. Two strips were taken at each site. One strip contained trypticase soy agar for bacterial analysis and the other contained rose bengal agar for fungal analysis. Additionally, particulate samples were taken in flight using the same air sampler with a modified Biotest sampling strip. All samples were maintained at ambient temperature until processing. Particulates were enumerated by light microscopy and further analyzed by scanning electron microscopy.

ANIMAL FECAL SAMPLES

Fecal samples were collected at the LSSF from the rats and squirrel monkeys. Samples were stabilized at 5°C and delivered to JSC for processing.

RESULTS:
Crewmembers

PREFLIGHT

As part of the routine L-l0 preflight physical exam, samples were collected from the ears, nose, and throat of each crewmember. In addition to the routine samples, fecal and serum samples were collected from each crewmember. The fecal samples were analyzed for the presence of ova and parasites and pathogenic bacteria and fungi. The serum sample was assayed for antibody titers to specific viral agents. A sputum sample was received from one crewmember. Additional throat cultures were taken at L-0 on all crewmembers.

Air samples were taken preflight at L-30 (KSC) and L-10 (JSC) to assess the microbial load in the Crew Quarters prior to crew occupancy of these facilities. Overall, the microbial levels obtained at KSC and JSC were consistent with those observed from preflight sampling for previous missions. Three types of potentially pathogenic fungi were isolated from the Crew Quarters (Aspergillus, Aspergillus flavus, Drechslera hawaiiensis). These organisms are common fungal atmospheric contaminants, and no action was taken.

INFLIGHT

Throat and hand cultures were collected from selected crewmembers on MDl, MD2, MD4, and MD6. With the exception of the Bacillus sp. and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, all other microorganisms were isolated from the crewmembers' preflight throat samples. Neither of these microbial species are considered to be fecal contaminants or of probable animal origin.

POSTFLIGHT

Microflora recovered from the ear, nose, throat, and sputum samples was similar to preflight findings. Postflight samples do not indicate any cross-contamination between the animals and the crewmembers. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Penicillium sp. were isolated at R+3 and are not considered to be of flight origin.

Spacecraft

PREFLIGHT

Orbiter

Analysis of surface swab samples did not demonstrate any unusual microbial levels. However, a small number of samples collected from the Waste Management System (WMS) at R+0 showed very high levels of non-pathogens. This was attributed to improper temperature control of the samples prior to processing at JSC.

Spacelab

No bacteria were isolated from the six locations in the Spacelab module after wipe down. Only 10 fungal colonies were recovered from the workbench handrail and were not of medical or epidemiological interest. Analysis of the samples collected from the interior and exterior surfaces of the primate and rodent RAHFs showed low to moderate levels of microbial contamination. Only two species of potentially pathogenic fungi were isolated from the primate RAHF. Both are common environmental fungal species and represented no significant problem.

INFLIGHT

Orbiter

No surface samples were collected from the Orbiter inflight. Bacterial levels were markedly elevated on the Middeck on MD1 and decreased steadily throughout the mission. Conversely, bacteria on the Flight Deck increased tenfold during the course of the flight. No significant changes were observed in fungal levels during the flight. The majority of potential pathogens were fungi of the Aspergillus genus. Staphylococcus aureus was the only pathogenic bacterial species isolated. No microorganisms of probable animal origin were isolated from the Orbiter in-flight samples. Particulates on the Middeck decreased during the flight in much the same manner as the bacterial levels. However, Flight Deck particulate values were high throughout the mission. The elevated values for bacteria and particulates on the Flight Deck may be a result of the directional airflow from the Spacelab to the Flight Deck.

Spacelab

No samples from the Spacelab surfaces were collected in flight. Air samples were collected daily in conjunction with the waste tray change out procedure. Bacterial, fungal, and particulate levels remained nearly constant throughout the flight. An increase in particulate counts was noted during and following the waste tray change out on MD4. Aspergillus sp. was the only potentially pathogenic microorganism isolated during the in-flight sampling period.

POSTFLIGHT

An approximate ten-fold increase from the preflight counts was seen in the number of bacteria in 11 of the 22 orbiter collection sites. The number of fungal organisms did not increase significantly during the mission. Only two microbial species of interest, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumonia, were detected. E. coli, a fecal contaminant, was recovered from the air inlet ring and the slide valve which are two interior components of the Orbiter Waste Management System. This microbial species has been routinely recovered from these sites on previous flights. K. pneumonia was isolated from the air return of the Aft Flight Deck. The origin of this contaminant is uncertain; K. pneumonia was isolated immediately preflight from a flight squirrel monkey. Postflight data correlates with the bacterial and fungal levels observed preflight.

Spacelab

Increases in bacterial growth were observed on five of the six surface locations. No fungal growth was detected. Staphylococcus aureus was the only potential pathogen isolated.

Bacterial and fungal levels were similar to preflight values in the Spacelab module. The postflight particulate strip could not be enumerated due to the presence of numerous fine particles, presumably dust, which contaminated the Spacelab module during the ventilation procedure.

Postflight sampling of the RAHFs followed the preflight sampling protocol. These samples were taken immediately after animal cage removal. A slight overall increase in bacterial growth was observed in samples from R+0.

Animal Monitoring

Air samples were collected from the KSC LSSF at R+30. The microbial air sample levels were low and consistent with previous sampling data. Only common fungal environmental contaminants were isolated.

The mission also served as the Flight Verification Test of the Research Animal Holding Facility (RAHF). This DSO was developed and implemented to evaluate the impact of the animals in the Spacelab environment and to determine the ability of the RAHF to contain microorganisms.

Microbiological testing conducted on previous Space Shuttle flights has shown that some microbial buildup occurs in the closed crew environment during the course of the mission. The inclusion of animals in the crew environment represents a potential source of microbial contamination that may result in cross-contamination between the animals and crewmembers.

The first flight utilizing the RAHF required a more extensive microbial sampling protocol to monitor the microbial flora of the spacecraft and the crewmembers and to assess the containment capabilities of the RAHF. The microbiology effort for this mission was comprehensive and involved the Ames Research Center, Kennedy Space Center and the Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
CREWMEMBER

Samples from the crewmembers' ears, nose, throat, and hands were collected by the Culturette system during all sampling periods. With the exception of the throat cultures, all other samples were obtained after moistening the Culturette swab with 0.8 mM sterile phosphate buffer. After sampling, the Culturettes were stored at ambient temperature until processing.

Sputum and fecal specimens were collected in appropriate sterile containers and stored at 5°C until processing. A 10 ml blood sample was collected from each crewmember for the determination of antibody titers to specific viral agents such as Hepatitis A and B, Epstein-Barr, and Herpesvirus saimiri, etc. A throat swab was collected from each crewmember for isolation of any viral agents that may have been present. The throat swab was placed in Veal Infusion Broth for stabilization and maintained at 5°C until processing.

SURFACE SAMPLES

Preflight and postflight surface samples from the Orbiter, Spacelab, and RAHF were collected using two sterile calcium alginate swabs moistened with 0.8 mM sterile phosphate buffer for each site. One swab was placed in trypticase soy broth for bacterial analysis; the other swab was placed in yeast malt broth for fungal analysis. All swabs were stabilized at 5°C until processing.

In-flight surface samples of the RAHF and crewmembers' gloves were collected using the Culturette system. One Culturette per site was used. The Culturette was moistened with 0.8 mM sterile phosphate buffer before sampling. The samples were stored at ambient temperature until processing.

AIR SAMPLES

Air samples were collected in the Orbiter, Spacelab, Life Sciences Support Facilities (LSSF), and the JSC and KSC Crew Quarters using a Reuter Centrifugal Air Sampler. Two strips were taken at each site. One strip contained trypticase soy agar for bacterial analysis and the other contained rose bengal agar for fungal analysis. Additionally, particulate samples were taken in flight using the same air sampler with a modified Biotest sampling strip. All samples were maintained at ambient temperature until processing. Particulates were enumerated by light microscopy and further analyzed by scanning electron microscopy.

ANIMAL FECAL SAMPLES

Fecal samples were collected at the LSSF from the rats and squirrel monkeys. Samples were stabilized at 5°C and delivered to JSC for processing.

RESULTS:
Crewmembers

PREFLIGHT

As part of the routine L-l0 preflight physical exam, samples were collected from the ears, nose, and throat of each crewmember. In addition to the routine samples, fecal and serum samples were collected from each crewmember. The fecal samples were analyzed for the presence of ova and parasites and pathogenic bacteria and fungi. The serum sample was assayed for antibody titers to specific viral agents. A sputum sample was received from one crewmember. Additional throat cultures were taken at L-0 on all crewmembers.

Air samples were taken preflight at L-30 (KSC) and L-10 (JSC) to assess the microbial load in the Crew Quarters prior to crew occupancy of these facilities. Overall, the microbial levels obtained at KSC and JSC were consistent with those observed from preflight sampling for previous missions. Three types of potentially pathogenic fungi were isolated from the Crew Quarters (Aspergillus, Aspergillus flavus, Drechslera hawaiiensis). These organisms are common fungal atmospheric contaminants, and no action was taken.

INFLIGHT

Throat and hand cultures were collected from selected crewmembers on MDl, MD2, MD4, and MD6. With the exception of the Bacillus sp. and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, all other microorganisms were isolated from the crewmembers' preflight throat samples. Neither of these microbial species are considered to be fecal contaminants or of probable animal origin.

POSTFLIGHT

Microflora recovered from the ear, nose, throat, and sputum samples was similar to preflight findings. Postflight samples do not indicate any cross-contamination between the animals and the crewmembers. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Penicillium sp. were isolated at R+3 and are not considered to be of flight origin.

Spacecraft

PREFLIGHT

Orbiter

Analysis of surface swab samples did not demonstrate any unusual microbial levels. However, a small number of samples collected from the Waste Management System (WMS) at R+0 showed very high levels of non-pathogens. This was attributed to improper temperature control of the samples prior to processing at JSC.

Spacelab

No bacteria were isolated from the six locations in the Spacelab module after wipe down. Only 10 fungal colonies were recovered from the workbench handrail and were not of medical or epidemiological interest. Analysis of the samples collected from the interior and exterior surfaces of the primate and rodent RAHFs showed low to moderate levels of microbial contamination. Only two species of potentially pathogenic fungi were isolated from the primate RAHF. Both are common environmental fungal species and represented no significant problem.

INFLIGHT

Orbiter

No surface samples were collected from the Orbiter inflight. Bacterial levels were markedly elevated on the Middeck on MD1 and decreased steadily throughout the mission. Conversely, bacteria on the Flight Deck increased tenfold during the course of the flight. No significant changes were observed in fungal levels during the flight. The majority of potential pathogens were fungi of the Aspergillus genus. Staphylococcus aureus was the only pathogenic bacterial species isolated. No microorganisms of probable animal origin were isolated from the Orbiter in-flight samples. Particulates on the Middeck decreased during the flight in much the same manner as the bacterial levels. However, Flight Deck particulate values were high throughout the mission. The elevated values for bacteria and particulates on the Flight Deck may be a result of the directional airflow from the Spacelab to the Flight Deck.

Spacelab

No samples from the Spacelab surfaces were collected in flight. Air samples were collected daily in conjunction with the waste tray change out procedure. Bacterial, fungal, and particulate levels remained nearly constant throughout the flight. An increase in particulate counts was noted during and following the waste tray change out on MD4. Aspergillus sp. was the only potentially pathogenic microorganism isolated during the in-flight sampling period.

POSTFLIGHT

An approximate ten-fold increase from the preflight counts was seen in the number of bacteria in 11 of the 22 orbiter collection sites. The number of fungal organisms did not increase significantly during the mission. Only two microbial species of interest, Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumonia, were detected. E. coli, a fecal contaminant, was recovered from the air inlet ring and the slide valve which are two interior components of the Orbiter Waste Management System. This microbial species has been routinely recovered from these sites on previous flights. K. pneumonia was isolated from the air return of the Aft Flight Deck. The origin of this contaminant is uncertain; K. pneumonia was isolated immediately preflight from a flight squirrel monkey. Postflight data correlates with the bacterial and fungal levels observed preflight.

Spacelab

Increases in bacterial growth were observed on five of the six surface locations. No fungal growth was detected. Staphylococcus aureus was the only potential pathogen isolated.

Bacterial and fungal levels were similar to preflight values in the Spacelab module. The postflight particulate strip could not be enumerated due to the presence of numerous fine particles, presumably dust, which contaminated the Spacelab module during the ventilation procedure.

Postflight sampling of the RAHFs followed the preflight sampling protocol. These samples were taken immediately after animal cage removal. A slight overall increase in bacterial growth was observed in samples from R+0.

Animal Monitoring

Air samples were collected from the KSC LSSF at R+30. The microbial air sample levels were low and consistent with previous sampling data. Only common fungal environmental contaminants were isolated.

Kotov during the PFE-OUM Experiment in the US Lab during Expedition 15
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Periodic Fitness Evaluation with Oxygen Uptake Measurement (PFE-OUM) was performed to demonstrate the capability of crewmembers to perform periodic fitness evaluations (PFE) with continuous oxygen consumption measurements within 14 days after arrival on ISS, and once monthly during routine PFEs. Once the capability of the pulmonary function system (PFS) is verified to then perform PFEs, crewmembers will be able to integrate their monthly PFE with oxygen consumption measurements to fulfill the requirement for cardiovascular fitness evaluations during long-duration space flight.

This experiment was a collaborative effort between the European Space Agency (ESA) and NASA. A medical requirement performed on the International Space Station Medical Operations called for the performance of a Periodic Fitness Evaluation (PFE) on board the International Space Station (ISS) with oxygen consumption measurements, referred to as OUM.

A measurement of aerobic capacity (VO2max) reflected the maximum rate that oxygen can be taken up and utilized by the body during exercise. The magnitude of VO2max depends on the capacity of the lungs to exchange oxygen between the air and blood in lung capillaries, the capacity of the cardiovascular system to transport oxygen to the muscles, and the muscles' capacity to use oxygen. The highest rate of oxygen uptake and use reflects the upper limit in the ability of the body to supply energy via aerobic metabolism to the active muscles during strenuous exercise and the ability to carry out weight-bearing tasks. Currently, the crew aerobic capacity on-board is only estimated using heart rate and work load while the crew goes through a set exercise protocol. It was assumed that the oxygen consumption per given work load was equivalent to the pre-flight measurements. The validity of this assumption has not been verified with in-flight data. This investigation provided the necessary hardware to measure oxygen uptake with the crewmember breathing through a mouthpiece in the performance of the routine PFE evaluations.

APPROACH:
Crewmembers routinely performed a ground-based exercise test using metabolic gas analysis before and after space flight. During these tests, OUMs were made and used to estimate the crewmember's aerobic capacity. Measurements of aerobic capacity allowed exercise physiologists and flight doctors to assess crew health and fitness and accurately prescribe exercise countermeasures for use on-board the ISS.

While performing this test, the crewmember's heart rate and blood pressure were recorded using the Blood Pressure/Electrocardiograph (BP/ECG). Heart rate data along with the prescribed cycle ergometer workloads, allowed ground personnel to estimate changes in crewmember aerobic capacity by comparing the heart rate response to increases in workload performed during pre-flight evaluations. There were several limitations to this approach. First, a method does not currently exist to verify that the cycle ergometer was correctly calibrated or maintaining calibration over time on orbit. Second, due to the fact that the cycle ergometer aboard the ISS is vibration isolated, which lead to instability between the exercising subject and the cycle, the metabolic cost associated with exercising on the cycle may differ than that measured during cycle ergometer tests performed on the ground. These factors may lead to misinterpretation of the crewmember's changes in aerobic fitness during long-duration space flight.

At the time of this experiment, OUMs had not been possible during the PFE because hardware capable of measuring oxygen uptake had not been available aboard the ISS. Now, the NASA/ESA Pulmonary Function System (PFS) provided the ability to perform the required OUMs. This evaluation was performed in two phases. The first phase was used to assess the feasibility of making OUMs during the PFE. The data provided investigators the necessary information to determine if the PFS was able to accurately perform OUMs aboard the ISS within the current crew timelines designated for the PFE.

The second phase of this evaluation was used to compare the current methods of estimating ISS crewmember's aerobic fitness with the more direct method of performing OUMs. The data collected during this phase along with data collected during phase one was analyzed using the current method of estimating changes in aerobic fitness (i.e., workload and heart rate observations alone) and direct analysis of the heart rate data in association with OUMs.

Preflight, crewmembers performed their required medical testing, Cycle Ergometry (MR080L), using nominal metabolic gas analysis hardware. The testing included a maximum cycle ergometry test at approximately 270 days prior to flight and (L-270 days) and a submaximal cycle test at approximately 30-45 days before flight.

Post-flight, the crewmember performed the nominal submaximal cycle test 5-7 days following landing and again at 30 days post-flight as part of the medical testing using the nominal metabolic gas analysis hardware. Crewmembers performed the same submaximal cycle exercise test post-flight as performed pre-flight.

The PFS hardware measured the O2 and CO2 concentrations using the Photoacoustic Analyzer Module (PAM) and the ambient humidity, temperature and pressure. During the exercise test, the subject inhaled cabin air and expired through a mouthpiece, and the nostrils were occluded with a nose clip. The fractions of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the expired air was measured by the PFS and used to calculate oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production and metabolic rate. Blood pressure was measured at designated time intervals throughout the protocol, while ECG was recorded continuously via the BP/ECG.

The initial in-flight PFE-OUM session was performed at mission day 14 and then every 30 days after throughout the mission.

The NASA/ESA Pulmonary Function System (PFS) was one of the major components of the HRF Rack 2 and was launched to International Space Station (ISS) aboard STS-114 in July 2005. The PFS was a facility class research hardware consisting of:

  • The Photoacoustic Analyzer Module (PAM) developed by ESA.
  • The Pulmonary Function Module (PFM) developed by ESA.
  • The Gas Analyzer System for Metabolic Analysis Physiology (GASMAP) developed by NASA.
  • The Gas Delivery System (GDS) developed by NASA

All hardware pertaining to the OUM activity was stored in the HRF Rack 2 and was checked out during Increment 12. Initial use of the system on-board the ISS was performed by an ESA augmentation crewmember in July 2006 during Increment 13. The PAM determined the concentration of seven respired gas components that also contained significant concentrations of nitrogen and water vapor utilizing two photoacoustic analyzers and the oxygen analyzer mixture.

The PFM, when operated together with either the Gas Analyzer System for Metabolic Analysis Physiology (GASMAP) or PAM plus the GDS, formed a respiratory facility capable of a wide range of respiratory and cardiovascular measurements including, breath-by-breath measurements, diffusing capacity of the lung, expiratory reserve volume, forced expired spirometry, functional residual capacity, cardiac output, alveolar ventilation, volume of pulmonary capillary blood, and numerous other specialized tests of pulmonary function. It consisted of the Respiratory Valve Unit with associated flow-meters, a re-breathing bag and an electronics unit. The GDS provided special gas mixtures needed for the calibration of the GASMAP and PAM and for the performance of such physiological tests as re-breathing and washout measurements. The GDS supported five canisters of gas mixtures which were permanently presented on-orbit and supported re-supply of these gases.

RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded on the ISS as a collaborative effort between the ESA and NASA agency. Eight subjects completed two peak cycle ergometer tests and exercise stage through 250 Watts (W). Therefore, the planned comparisons of the dependent variables were conducted at 100, 150, 200 and 250 W. The oxygen consumption (VO2) did not differ between devices at 100, 200 and 250 W; however, a statistically significant difference between the devices was observed at the 150 W stage. At this stage, the percent difference in VO2 between the two devices was 5.4%.

In addition, the peak VO2 of the subjects demonstrated a non-significant difference of 3.8% between the two devices, also within the ranges reported in the literature of day-to-day variation in VO2PK. No differences were seen in expired pulmonary ventilation (VE), even though the systems compute pulmonary ventilation using differing methods. Both the PFS and ParvoMedics use a differential pressure pneumotach to measure flow; however, the PFS measures flow on the inspiratory side, while the ParvoMedics measures flow on the expiratory side. Additional information can be found in the NASA Technical Report NASA/TP-2007-214756.
