The amino acids were dissolved in 250ml of a non-caloric, non-caffeinated soft-drink and consumed as a bolus at 1100.

RESULTS:
Plasma cortisol levels were significantly elevated in the C+AA group (p<0.05). 24hr urinary cortisol levels were 67±15 and 773±136 mg.24hr-1 for the AA and C+AA groups respectively (P<0.05).

Following ingestion of 15g EAA, arterial and venous phenylalanine concentrations in the AA and C+AA groups increased significantly (P<0.05). However, the magnitude of the arterial and venous concentration change was significantly blunted by cortisol infusion {arterial peak values: 272.4±12.1 (AA) vs. 208.1±17.8 nmol Phe.ml-1 (C+AA)}(P<0.05). Further, hypercortisolemia resulted in arterial phenylalanine concentrations remaining elevated for a longer period of time post-EAA drink.

During the post-absorptive period, hypercortisolemia increased muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations. EAA ingestion further increased muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations, with the greatest increase occurring in the C+AA group.

During the postabsorptive period, phenylalanine rate of appearance (Ra), a reflection of leg muscle protein breakdown, was not significantly increased by acute hypercortisolemia. Hypercortisolemia did not alter phenylalanine rate of disappearance (Rd), a reflection of muscle protein synthesis, during the postabsorptive period. However, following EAA ingestion, Rd was blunted by hypercortisolemia, yet remained above postabsorptive levels for a greater period of time (P<0.05).

No differences in net phenylalanine balance (NB) were identified while subjects remained in the post-absorptive state. Both groups experienced a significant increase in net phenylalanine balance following ingestion of 15g EAA; however the response in the C+AA group was blunted but remained positive for a greater period of time.

Calculation of net phenylalanine uptake (NB area under the curve: above baseline NB=0) by the leg for the immediate 1hr and 3hr post-drink periods also reflect the blunted, yet prolonged period of positive net balance associated with hypercortisolemia.

Both groups experienced an increase in mixed muscle FSR in response to ingestion of 15g EAA (P<0.05). However, no between group differences were evident during the pre- or post-drink periods, or in absolute changes in FSR following EAA ingestion.

Postabsorptive plasma insulin concentrations were elevated in response to hypercortisolemia. Following EAA ingestion, insulin levels increased in both groups (P<0.05), but remained significantly higher in the C+AA group (P<0.05). Hypercortisolemia also increased plasma glucose concentrations (p<0.05).

The researchers found that while muscle phenylalanine kinetics was altered by acute hypercortisolemia, ingested EAA were still able to stimulate muscle protein synthesis and acutely reverse negative net phenylalanine balance. The present study was the first to investigate the time course and progression of the interaction between acute hypercortisolemia and protein metabolism in response to a bolus oral ingestion of an essential amino acid solution.

These data may reflect the very early stages of the catabolic process. Indeed, the increased circulating and muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations noted during the post-absorptive period raises the possibility that acute exposure to elevated cortisol levels primes the system by raising energy expenditure, increasing amino acid turnover and increasing amino acid movement between pools. The net loss of nitrogen from muscle may not actually occur unless hypercortisolemia is prolonged, combined with inactivity and/or combined with other mediators of the injury/trauma response.

Ingestion or infusion of essential amino acids provides a strong anabolic stimulus. Consistent with these previous data, a significant increase in mixed muscle FSR in both experimental conditions during the 4hr period following EAA ingestion was observed. Using the net balance approach to estimate the relationship between protein synthesis and breakdown, it is clear that hypercortisolemia acutely and transiently altered muscle phenylalanine kinetics immediately following EAA ingestion.

The mechanisms resulting in the altered phenylalanine concentrations and kinetics during hypercortisolemia are not entirely clear. Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid and is not synthesized or metabolized in the body, consequently changes in the rate of appearance or disappearance of plasma phenylalanine in the plasma reflects protein synthesis and breakdown. The fact there was an increase in arterial and venous phenylalanine concentration, yet only a trend towards an increase in muscle protein breakdown (Ra) during hypercortisolemia suggests that increased protein breakdown in non-muscle tissues may have contributed to the elevated plasma amino acid levels during the pre- and post-EAA drink periods. Certainly, the liver represents a large potential source of amino acids that could be rapidly released into the circulation given an appropriate signal. There are some data suggesting that the gut may provide a source of amino acids during periods of exercise-induced stress. Certainly, given the high protein turnover rate in the gut, even a slight imbalance between synthesis and breakdown could produce relatively large changes in plasma amino acid concentrations.

The infusion of cortisol to produce hypercortisolemia in healthy human subjects has broad ranging effects and ultimately influences a range of hormonal responses including the regulation of glucose metabolism. Consequently, it is possible that the altered phenylalanine kinetics observed during hypercortisolemia may have also been influenced by the concomitantly elevated plasma insulin levels both before and following ingestion of 15g EAA.

Results from the current study indicated that hypercortisolemia increased plasma glucose concentrations despite an accompanying increase in insulin levels. This elevation in plasma glucose levels was most likely due to a reduction in the rate of glucose disposal and not an increase in production. The suggestion that there was no increased requirement for glucose is congruent with the theory that acute exposure to hypercortisolemia primes the muscle for the subsequent use of glucose and amino acids for energy production if an additional stimulus presents (i.e., prolonged hypercortisolemia, inactivity, physical trauma).

In conclusion, the pattern of the anabolic response to amino acid ingestion is altered by hypercortisolemia. Nevertheless, dietary amino acids are still able to effectively stimulate muscle protein synthesis and reverse the negative net phenylalanine balance associated with hypercortisolemia and may provide an effective means of minimizing muscle loss during the first few days following debilitating injury.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Wronski, ThomasCo-Investigator: Miller, Scott
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies have shown that stress-induced corticosteroid hormones increase during spaceflight. Negative effects on bone, such as decreased bone formation, are also associated with these hormones. The objective of this study was to determine whether corticosteroid excesses contribute to the bone loss that occur during spaceflight.

Approach:

Prior to the flight, male Sprague Dawley rats were anesthetized and subjected to bilateral adrenalectomy. Pellets made of cholesterol with dissolved corticosterone and aldosterone were implanted in each adrenalectomized rat. All rats had been injected with a label to mark the bone forming surfaces. After the flight, serum samples of corticosterone and aldosterone concentrations were measured by radioimmunoassay techniques. The left tibia was frozen and subsequently used to measure dry and ash bone weights. Bone samples were sectioned, stained, and counterstained for measurements of cancellous bone volume (%), osteoclast surface (%), an index of cancellous bone resorption, and osteoblast surface (%), an index of cancellous bone formation. The right tibia underwent a polymerization process and was cut into cross-sections. From the cross-sections, cortical bone area, cortical width, and marrow area were measured.

Results:

From the data in this study, it was found that rats in both the experiment and control populations had increased in body weight. This result indicated that the rats went through the flight well and were healthy. The flight group that did not undergo adrenalectomy showed significant increased adrenal gland weights. Thus, it suggests that the rats had corticosteroid excess during spaceflight. It was determined that the intact flight rats had normal bone mass, thus the objective of this experiment was not met.

experiment_title: Metric Development to Quantify Change in Mission Risk Due to a Physician-Trained Crew Medical Officer
parameter_html: Medical models
investigators: Principal Investigator: Myers, Jerry
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA currently requires a physician-trained Crew Medical Officer (CMO) for missions exceeding 210 days in length. This is based on the nominal 180-day length of an International Space Station (ISS) mission, which affords relatively quick and easy return to Earth for treating complicated cases. As NASA considers various Design Reference Missions (DRMs) for exploration, there are DRMs of only a few weeks duration that could not quickly return to Earth. Accordingly, they may well carry a medical risk level high enough to warrant the judgment of a physician-trained CMO. In contrast, the current assumption that missions to Mars would be less medically risky with a physician-trained CMO may be invalid. Due to rigorous preflight screening, which lessens the likelihood of a disease state, and the limited nature of the envisioned medical kits, perhaps NASA's treatment options are limited enough that the judgment of a physician-trained CMO would not appreciably reduce medical mission risk. This study had the following specific aims:
  1. To develop a Medical Judgment Pathway Metric (MJPM) for assessing clinical judgment based on evidenced-based practice for treating two common conditions from the Exploration Medical Condition List (EMCL).
  2. To validate the MJPM by a multi-disciplinary expert medical team to confirm principal components of the MJPM.
  3. To test the MJPM in an analog population using populations that mirror those of the astronaut corps in terms of both age and training.

APPROACH:
This investigation was completed by Summa Health Systems with advice from the Integrated Medical Model (IMM) team about the suitability of the metric for modeling. This study achieved two aims: 1. Develop a MJPM assessing clinical judgment; and 2. Demonstrate evidence of validity and reliability of MJPM scores. The individual MJPM items, domains, and sections of the MJPM were built based on existing standardized frameworks. Content validity was determined by a convenient sample of eight experts. The MJPM instrument was pilot tested in four medical simulations with a team of three medical raters assessing 40 participants with four levels of medical experience and skill.

RESULTS:
Raters were highly consistent in their MJPM scores in each scenario as well as their evaluation of the expected patient outcome. For each simulation scenario, average rater score cut-scores significantly predicted expected loss of life or stabilization.

experiment_title: Comparison of Bone Bending Stiffness in Elite Female Synchronized Swimmers and Judo Athletes
parameter_html:
Size, length; Bone
Bone mineral density, tibia
Bone mineral density, ulna
Body mass index (BMI)
Body mass
Height
Bending, stiffness
investigators: Principal Investigator: Arnaud, Sara
experiment_description:
Objectives:
There is a great deal of information on the bone densities of athletes with different loading histories, but limited information on the effect of sports activities on the structure and mechanical properties of bone. It is known that gymnasts have high density bone because of their exposure to high-impact loads. It is also known that swimmers have lower density bone because of their exposure to a buoyant environment. We asked the question: Are the bones of synchronized swimmers, stimulated primarily by non-impact loads and muscular contractions, weaker than those of gymnasts?

Approach:
Thirty seven young (20-22 years) women were recruited from Olympic level synchronized swimming (n=13) and gymnastic (n=8) clubs as well as from an untrained population (n=16) of college students. All gave informed consent for the study. Historical information was acquired before the tests for muscle in the athletes and the non-invasive test of length and bone strength in the ulnas and tibias of all subjects. The MRTA delivers a "buzz" and then detects the response of the bone on which the probe is centered on the skin surface. The response curve to the vibratory stimulus is analyzed by software that generates a measurement for E (the modulus of elasticity) and for I (the moment of inertia) for the ulna and the tibia. The instrument had been previously validated in the bones of monkeys (correlation of non-invasive measurement with a three-point bending test in the same bone extracted at necropsy was found to be 0.95, highly significant).

Results:
The synchronized swimmers (SYN) were taller than the gymnasts (GYM) and the untrained women (UNT), partly due to a longer tibia in SYN. The SYN also had higher body weights and lower BMI measurements then GYM or UNT groups. Years of training in GYM exceeded those in SYN by 3.5 years. The BMD in the wrist was highest in GYM, lowest in SYN and intermediate in UNT. In contrast, the ulnar EI was similar in GYM and SYN and 50% higher than in UNT. Ulnar EI was related to Ulnar width, but not to wrist density. EI in the tibia was similar in both athletic groups, and twice the value of the UNT. The knee flexor strength correlated with tibial EI.

We concluded that in spite of different loading histories that could be related to bone mineral density in the wrist, the bending stiffness of synchronized swimmers and gymnasts was similar and in the athletes, much higher than in the untrained women. EI (bending stiffness) in the ulna could be related to the width of the bone and in the tibia, to muscle strength. It seems clear that vigorous physical training of the type used in synchronized swimming can increase bone strength without necessarily increasing bone density.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Sirmons, TakiyahCo-Investigator: Arias, DianaCo-Investigator: Barrett, AnnCo-Investigator: Baskin, PamelaCo-Investigator: Cooper, MayaCo-Investigator: Douglas, GraceCo-Investigator: Ploutz- Snyder, RobertCo-Investigator: Richardson, MichelleCo-Investigator: Schneiderman, JasonCo-Investigator: Williams, Thomas
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Meal replacement bars have been postulated as a means to decrease mass and volume of the food system. Bars have previously been used to supplement a meal every three days in the Skylab food system, indicating that regular consumption of bars will be acceptable, but commercially available products do not meet the requirements for a meal replacement in the space flight food system. The bar and instant beverage prototypes produced in a preceding validation study demonstrated that a full meal may be replaced and mass may be conserved with the strategy of implementing palatable, nutrient dense, nutritionally balanced, single meal items. However, the frequency with which meals can be replaced by these items, and the resulting amount of mass that may be conserved, is dependent on acceptability to crew and associated physical and psychosocial impacts.

The purpose of this study was to complete the development of a limited variety of true meal replacement options that meet space flight and nutritional requirements and to assess the frequency with which actual meal replacements may be implemented based on impact to satiety and psychosocial subjective ratings of hunger, cravings, mood, and stress pre-meal, post-meal, and pre-sleep daily throughout NASA's Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) mission for all meals, including the standard International Space Station (ISS) diet and the meal replacement bars. The microbiological, nutritional, and acceptable sensory shelf life stability of these meal replacement options stored at ambient temperature over two years will be analyzed.

APPROACH:
Data was collected from four HERA 30 day campaigns, each with four subjects participating in this experiment, totaling n=16 subjects. All subjects filled out various questionnaires. Future exploration missions are mass constrained and as a result the mass of the food system must be reduced by 10%, at the same time maintaining safety, nutrition, and acceptability.

RESULTS:
The purpose of this task was to develop a variety of nutritionally balanced breakfast replacement bars, which meet space flight nutritional, microbiological, sensorial, and shelf-life requirements, while enabling a 10% food mass savings. Seven nutrient-dense meal replacement bars containing approximately 700 kcal per serving have been developed. Bars were evaluated in the HERA to assess the frequency with which actual meal replacement options may be implemented. Feedback from HERA crews show that the bars are generally acceptable but additional flavor development is required to combat the effects of food monotony and aversion. The data suggest that meal replacement on an interrupted schedule (every three days) may be acceptable on a mission up to 30 days, but meal replacement every day may result in reduced food intake, greater body mass loss, and increasingly negative changes in mood, affect, and somatic complaints in some individuals.

experiment_title: Physiological Variables of EVA Participants--An Update
parameter_html:
Body fat
Body mass index (BMI)
Heart rate, maximum
Maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max)
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The physiological variables of extravehicular activity (EVA) participants were first explored in the October 1998 issue of the LSAH Newsletter. This initial article investigated EVA participants within the Shuttle program, up to January 1998. Between then and December 2001, 26 additional EVAs within 12 missions have been performed. All but three of these EVAs were performed in support of assembly and maintenance of the International Space Station. As this assembly and maintenance process is a continual one, many more EVAs will have to be performed in the future.

APPROACH:
The following is an updated look at EVA astronauts, to see if the increased number of participants leads to observations different than previously noted. As before, this analysis compares physiological variables between astronauts who have flown in space (i.e., crewmembers) and those who have performed EVAs. Currently, 312 individuals have been selected into the NASA astronaut corps. Of these, 197 have flown in the Shuttle program through the launch of STS-108 on December 5, 2001. Within the same time period, approximately 109 EVAs have been performed. In analyzing the data, each mission is counted as an individual even for both Shuttle astronauts who have flown and EVA participants. Therefore, one astronaut may count for more than one crewmember, and be in more than one age group. Through December 2001 there have been 536 NASA crewmembers, with 79 EVA participants.

Of the Shuttle crewmembers, 519 had available data from the annual examination closest to, and before, their missions. Their gender distribution shows that 86.4% are males. Almost half of these crewmembers were between 38 and 43 years of age, making this age group the largest subset. About 70% of the entire group was younger than 44 years of age. Means of the following variables were measured for the Shuttle crewmembers: age (at time of examination), body mass index (BMI), percentage of body fat, mean VO2max, and maximum heart rate (MHR). BMI and percentage of body fat provide measures of fatness for the group. BMI, which is more accurate for a group of people than for an individual, is calculated by dividing the weight (in kilograms) by the squared height (in meters). A BMI between 22-26 for both men and women is about standard. Percentage of body fat is an estimation of fatness based on the sum of three skin-fold measurements and age at last birthday. Values of 10%-15% for men, and 20%-25% for women, are considered to be the norm for the general population. VO2max and MHR are estimations of cardiovascular fitness that are measured during an Exercise Tolerance Test. VO2max is measured by the volume of oxygen, in milliliters per kilogram of body weight, expired per minute, and is an indicator of an individual's max aerobic capacity. A higher number indicates a higher aerobic capacity. The normative values of VO2max for men and women in good aerobic condition in the 30-49 years age group are 41 ml/kg/min and 37 ml/kg/min respectively. The MHR is measured in beats per minute, and lower values are more desirable. For individuals in the 38-49 years of age group, the expected MHR is 179.7 beats per minute.

Each EVA per mission is accounted for, so that an astronaut is counted for every EVA mission and the age group s/he has achieved. All 79 EVA participants had data available from examinations closest to and before their missions. The majority (70.9%) of the EVA participants were under the age of 44, and 91.1% of them were male. The small number of female participants precludes data analysis of this subset.

RESULTS:
As expected, the crewmembers, those in the 30-43 year age group, had higher VO2max and lower MHR values than the previously mentioned norms.

All of the parameters varied only slightly between EVA participants and Shuttle crewmembers. The largest age group representation for both EVA participants and crewmembers is in the 38-43 year age group (48.1% and 47.2%, respectively). In comparing the majority of each group's subjects (38-43 year age group), there is very little difference in the BMI, average percentage of body fat, or mean MHR between the two age groups. When these values are compared in terms of aging trend, EVA participants, unlike Shuttle crewmembers, did not show the expected trend of increasing BMI, increasing percentage of body fat, and decreasing VO2max in progressing from the younger to older age groups. This may mean that EVA participants maintain better overall fitness within the older age group than crewmembers as a whole. However, the small age group subsets of this sample may also affect their mean values.

There is little difference in the age makeup between the Shuttle crewmembers and EVA participants. The majority of crewmembers and EVA participants also have very similar fitness levels, as shown in the small difference in the physiological variables values between the two age groups. The difference in aging trend between the two groups may indicate that EVA training facilities maintenance of aerobic fitness for the crewmembers. As the entire astronaut corps ages, and more EVA data accumulate from the maintenance and assembly of the ISS, a more comprehensive analysis can be performed to substantiate this observation.

The following is an updated look at EVA astronauts, to see if the increased number of participants leads to observations different than previously noted. Currently, 312 individuals have been selected into the NASA astronaut corps. Of these, 197 have flown in the Shuttle program through the launch of STS-108 on December 5, 2001. Within the same time period, approximately 109 EVAs have been performed. In analyzing the data, each mission is counted as an individual even for both Shuttle astronauts who have flown and EVA participants. Therefore, one astronaut may count for more than one crewmember, and be in more than one age group. Through December 2001 there have been 536 NASA crewmembers, with 79 EVA participants.

Of the Shuttle crewmembers, 519 had available data from the annual examination closest to, and before, their missions. Their gender distribution shows that 86.4% are males. Almost half of these crewmembers were between 38 and 43 years of age, making this age group the largest subset. About 70% of the entire group was younger than 44 years of age. Means of the following variables were measured for the Shuttle crewmembers: age (at time of examination), body mass index (BMI), percentage of body fat, mean VO2max, and maximum heart rate (MHR). BMI and percentage of body fat provide measures of fatness for the group. BMI, which is more accurate for a group of people than for an individual, is calculated by dividing the weight (in kilograms) by the squared height (in meters). A BMI between 22-26 for both men and women is about standard. Percentage of body fat is an estimation of fatness based on the sum of three skin-fold measurements and age at last birthday. Values of 10%-15% for men, and 20%-25% for women, are considered to be the norm for the general population. VO2max and MHR are estimations of cardiovascular fitness that are measured during an Exercise Tolerance Test. VO2max is measured by the volume of oxygen, in milliliters per kilogram of body weight, expired per minute, and is an indicator of an individual's max aerobic capacity. A higher number indicates a higher aerobic capacity. The normative values of VO2max for men and women in good aerobic condition in the 30-49 years age group are 41 ml/kg/min and 37 ml/kg/min respectively. The MHR is measured in beats per minute, and lower values are more desirable. For individuals in the 38-49 years of age group, the expected MHR is 179.7 beats per minute.

Each EVA per mission is accounted for, so that an astronaut is counted for every EVA mission and the age group s/he has achieved. All 79 EVA participants had data available from examinations closest to and before their missions. The majority (70.9%) of the EVA participants were under the age of 44, and 91.1% of them were male. The small number of female participants precludes data analysis of this subset.

RESULTS:
As expected, the crewmembers, those in the 30-43 year age group, had higher VO2max and lower MHR values than the previously mentioned norms.

All of the parameters varied only slightly between EVA participants and Shuttle crewmembers. The largest age group representation for both EVA participants and crewmembers is in the 38-43 year age group (48.1% and 47.2%, respectively). In comparing the majority of each group's subjects (38-43 year age group), there is very little difference in the BMI, average percentage of body fat, or mean MHR between the two age groups. When these values are compared in terms of aging trend, EVA participants, unlike Shuttle crewmembers, did not show the expected trend of increasing BMI, increasing percentage of body fat, and decreasing VO2max in progressing from the younger to older age groups. This may mean that EVA participants maintain better overall fitness within the older age group than crewmembers as a whole. However, the small age group subsets of this sample may also affect their mean values.

There is little difference in the age makeup between the Shuttle crewmembers and EVA participants. The majority of crewmembers and EVA participants also have very similar fitness levels, as shown in the small difference in the physiological variables values between the two age groups. The difference in aging trend between the two groups may indicate that EVA training facilities maintenance of aerobic fitness for the crewmembers. As the entire astronaut corps ages, and more EVA data accumulate from the maintenance and assembly of the ISS, a more comprehensive analysis can be performed to substantiate this observation.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness (SMS) is experienced by about 50% of crewmembers during the first several days of exposure to the microgravity space flight environment. Predominant symptoms of the syndrome are headache, depressed appetite, general malaise, lethargy, gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea, and vomiting. As in other forms of motion sickness, the syndrome may reduce self motivation and result in decreased ability to perform demanding tasks. The syndrome is self limiting. Complete recovery from major symptomatology, in other words adaptation to the space flight environment, occurs within two to four days. After complete adaptation occurs, crewmembers appear to be immune to the development of further symptomatology.

Available data regarding overall incidence to date of SMS in the U.S. and Soviet manned space programs indicates that the frequency of occurrence of this syndrome has been approximately equal in both countries. An important feature of these data is that with the advent of larger spacecraft in the U.S. program (i.e., Apollo, Skylab and Shuttle) that permit greater mobility of crewmembers, the incidence of SMS has increased. In an effort to resolve the SMS or at least minimize the operational impact of the syndrome, NASA has significantly expanded its research efforts in this area. As part of this expanded effort, a systematic program of operationally oriented motion sickness data collection was implemented on most individuals assigned to Shuttle flights from April 1981 to April 1985. The primary objective of this program was to collect preflight, inflight and postflight data on the crewmembers in an effort to begin validating ground based tests which may be predictive of susceptibility to the syndrome. The development of reliable predictors is operationally important because they would permit the a priori identification of individual crewmembers for whom special preventative measures should be taken. A secondary objective of the program was to acquire data which could be used to validate countermeasures for the syndrome.

APPROACH:
Preflight data collection involved several different procedures. Approximately three to six months prior to flight, each crewmember completed a questionnaire designed to elicit information regarding past experiences with various types of motion environments and responses to those environments. Also during the three to six months before flight each crewmember was tested at least one time for susceptibility to experimentally induced motion sickness. Three different laboratory test procedures were used to provide a ground-based data point against which inflight susceptibility could be compared.

For the first nine Shuttle missions, which involved 29 different crewmembers, a standard Coriolis Sickness Susceptibility Index test (CSSI), originally developed by Miller and Graybiel was used. This procedure, which stimulates primarily the semi-circular canals, requires the performance of head movements while rotating. Prior to the start of the test the crewmember was instructed on how to report his or her symptoms of motion sickness to an observer who was skilled in the recognition of signs and symptoms of motion sickness. The signs and symptoms were recorded and scored according to diagnostic categorization. The test was terminated when the blindfolded crewmember reached the Malaise III level of motion sickness or performed 150 head movements, whichever occurred first. The higher the score, the longer the subject continued the test, indicating a greater resistance to motion sickness. A majority of the crewmembers on the first nine Shuttle missions were tested at least one additional time with the CSSI procedure in order to evaluate the efficacy of an anti-motion sickness medication. The medication most frequently evaluated was oral scopolamine (.4 rag) plus dexedrine (5 mg).

The second motion sickness susceptibility procedure used was a modified version of an off-vertical rotation or OVR test originally developed by Graybiel and Miller. The OVR produces a rotating linear acceleration and is essentially an otolith stimulus. During this procedure crewmembers were blindfolded and restrained in the rotating chair with lap, shoulder and leg straps. The head was also restrained. While in the vertical position the chair was accelerated to a velocity of 20 rpm and rotated for 5 minutes. Following stabilization of 0 degrees tilt the angle of tilt of the chair was increased in 5 degree increments at 5 minute intervals until the crewmember reached the Malaise III maintained at 30 degree tilt for 5 minutes. The OVR test was performed on 29 individual astronauts most of whom flew subsequent to the ninth Shuttle flight.

The third procedure used was a modified version of an eyes open sudden-stop test developed by Graybiel and Lackner. This test assessed susceptibility to a vestibulo-visual interaction stimulus. Visual stimulation was provided by a stationary optokinetic field which surrounded the chair in which the crewmember was restrained. The chair was accelerated to a velocity of 50 rpm and held at that velocity for 30 seconds. The chair was then decelerated at 150 deg/sec to a complete stop and maintained at zero velocity for 30 seconds, after which the sequence was repeated for a total of 20 clockwise and 20 counterclockwise stops or until the Malaise III level of symptoms was reached, whichever occurred first. Data were collected on only six crewmembers with this procedure.

Inflight data collection was limited to the use of a microcassette tape recorder and a motion sickness symptom checklist. The checklist was similar in content to the diagnostic scale and allowed comparisons between the pattern of symptoms that occurred during the preflight pro vocative tests and those that occurred inflight. The checklist also required crewmembers to report on preventative measures used such as anti-motion sickness drugs and voluntary restriction of head and body movements. Each crewmember was required to use the recorder and checklist each mission day to report any symptoms or sensations that had been experienced during that day. Operational definitions for SMS were categorized as:

  • None (0): No signs or symptoms reported with the exception of mild transient headache or mild decreased appetite

  • Mild (1): One to several symptoms of a mild nature; may be transient and only brought on as the result of head movements; no operational impact; may include single episode of retching or vomiting; all symptoms resolved in 36-48 hours

  • Moderate (2): Several symptoms of a relatively perisistent nature which may wax and wane; loss of appetite, general malaise, lethargy and epigastric discomfort may be most dominant symptoms; includes no more than 2 episodes of vomiting; minimal operational impact; all symptoms resolved in 72 hours

  • Severe (3): Several symptoms of a relatively perisistent nature which may wax and wane, in addition to loos of appetitie and stomach discomfort; malaise, and/or lethargy are pronounced; strong desire not to move head; includes more than 2 episodes of vomiting; significant performance decrement may be apparent; symptoms may persist beyond 72 hours

    Questions pertaining to SMS, vestibular sensations, and performance were also asked of each crewmember on the day of landing and during postflight medical debriefings. Both the inflight and postflight crew debriefing data were used to categorize crewmembers as susceptible or non-susceptible to SMS. Those who were defined as being susceptible were further classified into mild, moderate and severe subgroups for subsequent data analysis.

    RESULTS:
    Results include preflight and inflight symptomatology data, antimotion sickness drug data and preflight versus inflight motion sickness susceptibility data. There was a striking difference in the pattern of symptomatology generated inflight versus during the ground-based tests. Subjective warmth, sweating, and pallor, which were dominant ground-based test symptoms, were almost nonexistent inflight. In contrast, vomiting, anorexia, headache, malaise and lethargy were dominant inflight symptoms. The vomiting episodes often occurred abruptly with little or no prodromal nausea, although a sensation of stomach fullness or discomfort was often present prior to vomiting. In most cases, vomiting resulted in relief from the uncomfortable stomach sensations, although for some crewmembers the discomfort would gradually return.

    The specific nature and time course of inflight symptomatology tends to be highly variable. Some crewmembers reported that symptoms appeared within the first one to two hours of the mission. Others did not become aware of symptoms until the second day of flight. In general, however, symptoms began during the first day of flight, plateaued between 24-48 hours and gradually diminished between approximately 48-96 hours. During this time the symptoms usually waxed and waned in severity. Unquestionably, head and body movements exacerbated the symptomatology. Accelerometric data obtained by Oman during the Spacelab 1 mission (STS-9), and subsequently confirmed by verbal reports from a number of crewmembers, indicate that in microgravity head movements in the pitch and roll planes are the most provocative. Anti-motion sickness and/or anti-emetic medication was used by 40 of the 65 crewmembers included in this study. The oral scopolamine plus dexedrine combination was the most frequently used with 25 crewmembers taking one or more doses during the first few days of flight. Oral metoclopramide was used by 18 crewmembers in an effort to restore gastric motility and alleviate nausea and vomiting. Of the 31 crewmembers who experienced symptoms, 29 used medication during the course of their symptomatology.

    Results related to a comparison of preflight motion sickness data with SMS are by no means unequivocal. The motion experience questionnaire indicated that all of the crewmembers had a minimal history of susceptibility to terrestrial forms of motion sickness. The questionnaire revealed that a few had experienced some motion sickness during past exposures to aerobatic flight, parabolic flight, and heavy sea conditions. The questionnaire results, however, did not correlate with the actual incidence of SMS reported.

    The subgroups of astronauts who experienced SMS were slightly more susceptible to the preflight motion sickness tests than were the non-SMS susceptible astronauts. However, the test score ranges for all subgroups are large and the difference between the means of the subgroups for each test are not statistically significant. In a further attempt to establish a relationship between the ground-based tests and SMS, correlation coefficients between the ground-based test scores and the scores assigned for the inflight level of severity of SMS symptoms were computed. The correlation coefficients were non-significant for all three ground-based tests.

    As an alternative approach to determining whether or not the preflight susceptibility tests might have some predictive value for SMS, the astronaut data for each test was compared to a frequency distribution of non-astronaut normative data. The normative data were collected over the past several years by the Johnson Space Center Neurophysiology Laboratory. Figure 2 summarizes the CSSl test data. The hatched bars are the normative data and the closed circles are the astronaut data. The "star" symbol indicates astronauts who reported SMS. The astronaut mean CSSI score is 28.7 while the normative population mean CSSI score is 14.0. Of potentially greater significance is the finding that 67% of the astronauts whose CSSI score was below the population mean experienced SMS, while only 40% whose scores were above the population mean experienced SMS.

    Data from the OVR test show virtually no difference between the astronaut and normative population data. The mean OVR test scores are almost identical and there were as many crewmembers above the normative population mean who reported SMS as there were below the mean. For the sudden-stop test data, the number of astronaut data points were too few to permit drawing any meaningful conclusions. However, it is of interest to note that two astronauts who were very susceptible to the preflight sudden stop test experienced SMS.

    All of the data summarized thus far in this report have compared SMS susceptibility to a single preflight test. The weighted score is the algebraic sum of the differences between the astronaut's test scores and the normative population means for each test. It would be predicted that a positive weighted score (i.e., greater than average resistance to experimentally induced motion sickness) should relate to a lack of SMS and a negative weighted score should be related to the presence of SMS. A correct match was obtained in 64% of the cases.

    In conclusion, on the basis of data collected during this study, it can be generally concluded that the prediction of SMS susceptibility on an individual crewmember basis remains a difficult and challenging task. Certainly the use of a single ground-based parameter or test procedure is inadequate. The use of a composite index or weighted score which takes into account several response parameters appears to have greater predictive potential. A larger sample size of composite scores based on the collection of preflight CSSI, OVR and sudden-stop data on Shuttle crewmembers would be desirable. The data needed to derive these composite scores do not exist, nor do plans currently exist to collect these data.

    Despite inability to identify preflight, ground-based predictors of SMS susceptibility, there does appear to be one reasonably accurate predictor and that is space flight itself. Out of 16 individuals who have flown two or more space missions only 3 changed their response pattern from one flight to the next. Out of the remaining 13, 7 individuals were symptom free on all of their flights, while the other 6 experienced symptoms on each of their flights. Obviously, the routine use of space flight as the method of identifying SMS susceptible individuals is impractical. Thus the need to identify and validate ground-based methods remains an important issue. It is important to emphasize that efforts in this area have not been abandoned. The collection of inflight and postflight symptom reporting data is continuing as a standard operating procedure. Improved methods for characterizing the exact nature and time course of SMS are being evaluated. Also, various pre-, in- and postflight measurements of vestibular function are being conducted, the data from which may be useful in our attempts to develop predictors of SMS susceptibility.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

The major stimulus for secretion of atrial natriuretic factor is increased pressure in the cardiac atria. Since weightlessness induces a fluid shift from the lower to upper parts of the body the secretion of ANF may be enhanced. The objective of the experiment to determine possible alterations of ANF regulation in weightlessness.

Approach:

The responsiveness of the ANF-sensitive, guanylyl cyclase system was studied. Guanylyl cyclase activity was measured in the liver, and enzymatic activity was determined in response to various ANF analogs. Formed cyclic GMP was measured by radioimmunoassay.

Results:

The activity of ANF-sensitive guanylyl cyclase was unaltered. Stimulation with various ANF analogs showed the same pattern response for all three groups: twofold increase with ANF as well as with urodilatin, slight increases with C-type natriuretic peptide and ANF-AP 1. These patterns indicate that there is no apparent altered receptor subtype distribution during weightlessness.

Since weightlessness induces a fluid shift from the lower to upper parts of the body the secretion of ANF may be enhanced. The objective of the experiment to determine possible alterations of ANF regulation in weightlessness.

Approach:

The responsiveness of the ANF-sensitive, guanylyl cyclase system was studied. Guanylyl cyclase activity was measured in the liver, and enzymatic activity was determined in response to various ANF analogs. Formed cyclic GMP was measured by radioimmunoassay.

Results:

The activity of ANF-sensitive guanylyl cyclase was unaltered. experiment_title: Defining the Role of miR-182 in HZE-Induced Tumorignesis
parameter_html:
Lung tumorigenesis
Linear energy transfer
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kirsch, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Important opportunities for space travel in the decades ahead include a proposed mission to Mars. However, an important deterrent to such interplanetary travel is the risk of radiation-induced carcinogenesis. There are many uncertainties in predicting the risk of space travel because the mechanisms of carcinogenesis from space radiation, which is dominated by high-energy protons and high (H) charge (Z) and energy (E) (HZE) particles, are poorly understood. Investigators will test the hypothesis that microRNAs that regulate the expression of proteins that are known to regulate radiation-induced cancer, will function as non-protein encoding genetic factors that mediate radiation carcinogenesis from HZE particles.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Investigate radiation carcinogenesis in mice lacking microRNA-182.
  2. Investigate radiation carcinogenesis in mice overexpressing microRNA-182.

APPROACH:
The investigators bred, infected, and irradiated various strains of genetically engineered mice to assess the effect of miR-182 loss or overexpression on tumorigenesis. These mice were treated with multiple doses and fractionations of x-rays at Duke University and 56Fe and 28Si particles at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). Investigators tested the hypothesis that microRNAs that control the expression of proteins known to regulate radiation-induced cancer will function as genetic factors in radiation carcinogenesis. In order to study the role of microRNA-182 (miR-182) in radiation-induced lymphomagenesis and lung tumorigenesis following exposure to x-ray or space irradiation, they developed a mouse model that lacks miR-182 expression or expresses an elevated level of miR-182.

RESULTS:
Investigators did not observe a significant impact of miR-182 expression level on the latency or the incidence of radiation-induced lymphomas. In the absence or presence of radiation, they found that loss of miR-182 reduced overall survival when compared to littermates that retained wild type expression of miR-182. From these data, the investigators conclude that miR-182 functions to regulate the survival of lung-tumor bearing mice. However, they have not seen evidence that there is a significant interaction between miR-182 expression and radiation exposure on survival. Consistent with their hypothesis that miR-182 promotes radiation-induced tumorigenesis, mice overexpressing miR-182 developed lymphomas at an accelerated rate post radiation exposure.

No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Cowings, PatriciaCo-Investigator: Toscano, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Susceptibility of healthy astronauts to orthostatic hypotension and presyncope is exacerbated upon return from space flight. Up to 64% of astronauts experience post-flight orthostatic intolerance. A promising countermeasure for post-flight orthostatic intolerance is fluid loading by giving crew salt tablets and water prior to re-entry. The primary goal of the current study was to determine the optimal time window prior to re-entry when individual crewpersons would initiate fluid loading.

APPROACH:
Sixteen participants were given two, 6-hour exposures, with and without fluid loading (condition), to Head-Down Tilt (HDT) to simulate the effects of microgravity. Pre- and post-HDT stand tests of orthostatic tolerance were given. Physiological responses recorded included measures of heart rate, blood pressure, peripheral blood volume, total peripheral resistance, and impedance cardiography. Echocardiography measures of stroke volume and cardiac output were also recorded.

RESULTS:
Physiological data (30-minute means) from HDT tests were analyzed with repeated measures 3-way ANOVA: gender x condition x time (HDT hours 1 to 6). Gender was not significant for any of the measures. Condition was significant for finger pulse volume and mean arterial pressure, and the time was significant for all measures. The condition x time interaction was significant for mean arterial pressure, skin conductance, thoracic fluid volume, and total peripheral resistance. Tukey-Kramer tests revealed significantly higher mean arterial pressures at 60, 90, 120, and 150 minutes following fluid loading HDT when compared to no-fluid HDT. None of the other variables showed significant differences at these time-points. Echocardiography measures (30-second means) for gender and condition were not significant for either stroke volume or cardiac output, while the time was significant only for cardiac output. However, there were no significant two or three-way interactions for either measure. Only one participant experienced syncope and another subject was pre-syncopal during stand tests following no-fluid loading HDT. Analyses of physiological data from stand tests (pre versus post HDT) showed no significant gender or condition effects for any of the measures, while the main effect of stand tests was significant for all measures except skin temperature, skin conductance, and stroke volume. The gender x condition interaction was significant for mean arterial pressure, cardiac output measured with impedance cardiography, and total peripheral resistance with men generally higher although not significantly, than women after fluid loading. The condition x stand interaction was only significant for mean arterial pressure. Tukey-Kramer tests for mean arterial pressure of all subjects revealed significant increases from pre- to post- stand tests for both two conditions; however, there was no difference between the post-test following fluid loading and no fluid loading.

Conclusion: These findings indicate that the optimal time for crew to begin fluid loading is within 1 to 3 hours prior to re-entry. Non-significant trends of multiple cardiovascular responses showed similar time profiles. The large amount of individual variability suggests that fluid loading alone may be an inadequate countermeasure for all crewmembers. Further research is needed on possible adjunct methods of tailoring countermeasures for individuals.

experiment_title: Hypobaric Hypoxia in Space Data Mining
parameter_html:
Hypoxia levels
Shuttle cabin pressure
Carbon dioxide levels
Oxygen levels
investigators: Principal Investigator: Norcross, JasonCo-Investigator: Wessel, James
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Extravehicular activity (EVA) is a vital component of human space exploration. The pressure differential between the internal cabin of a spacecraft and a space suit pressurized to 4.3 psia introduces the risk of decompression sickness (DCS). The risk of DCS is currently reduced with lengthy denitrogenation protocols. To reduce both the denitrogenation time and the risk of DCS during EVA, the option of an intermediate habitat pressure of 8.2 psia with 34% oxygen (herein referred to as 8.2/34) has been proposed for NASA’s exploration missions. However, the proposed atmosphere creates partial pressure of inspired oxygen inspired oxygen (PIO2) of 128 mm Hg, which is equivalent to breathing air at approximately 4,000 feet altitude. Coincidentally, one of the denitrogenation protocols used during the Shuttle Program was a staged protocol that exposed astronauts to 10.2 psia and 26.5% oxygen (10.2/26.5). The Shuttle-staged protocol resulted in a mildly hypoxic PIO2 of 127 mm Hg, almost identical to that of the proposed 8.2/34 environment. Terrestrial data suggests that this hypoxic dose is acceptable for unimpeded mission operations; however, the interaction between adaptation to microgravity, the space flight environment, and mild hypobaric hypoxia is uncertain.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine accurate environmental exposure doses and durations for crewmembers during the shuttle program including hypoxia and elevated carbon dioxide (CO2).
  2. Identify and evaluate any available flight data from the Shuttle program that may aid in clarifying the physiologic and health effects of exposure to mild hypobaric hypoxia in microgravity.
  3. Review terrestrial hypoxia literature with respect to very mild hypoxia at altitudes of 6000 feet or less.

APPROACH:
Retrospective environmental data were examined to determine shuttle mission time at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) and partial pressure of oxygen (ppO2) and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (ppCO2) values for missions that performed a Staged pre-breathe protocol. Private medical conferences and post-flight debriefs were examined and data related to 14 possible hypoxia symptoms were compared with equivalent data collected during normoxic Space Shuttle operations at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) using logistic regression.

RESULTS:
Over the Space Shuttle program, there were 134.1 days (788.8 person-days adjusted for crew size) under the 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) Staged condition (average 3.17 ± 2.2 days per mission, maximum 8.1 days) and 258.81 days at 101.3kPa (14.7 psia) and 2192.95 total person-days of normoxic operations. An average of 4.31 potentially hypoxia-related symptoms per mission day was documented under Staged conditions compared with 4.08 per mission day during normoxic operations. Logistic regression analysis found none of the hypoxia signs and symptoms to be significantly associated with the 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) condition versus the 14.7 psia condition.

Terrestrial experience indicates that chronic exposure to a PIO2 of 876 kPa (137 mmHg) is well-tolerated by healthy humans. Shuttle experience indicates that similar levels of hypoxia in space at a pressure of 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) resulted in no increased reporting of possible hypoxia related symptoms, and no obvious crewmember performance issues related to completion of mission objectives. However, these results may not be representative of how chronic mild hypoxia interacts with physiologic changes due to microgravity over long duration missions.

experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Oxidative damage in our bodies is the result of oxidation, which is the reaction of products of oxygen with other molecules. Oxidative damage is known to occur during and after space flight. Astronauts, particularly those performing extravehicular activities (EVAs), are exposed to multiple oxidative insults, including increased oxygen exposure, radiation, and exercise. Risks from oxidative damage include increased muscle fatigue and risk of cataracts, cardiovascular disease, and many forms of cancer. Currently, no effective countermeasure exists to mitigate oxidative damage during space flight. As we contemplate lunar missions, with greatly increased EVA frequency and durations (two or three times per week, 8–10 hours each time), minimizing oxygen-related health risks is critical.

In an underwater-based analogue of space flight, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) project, crewmembers live in an underwater laboratory for days to weeks. NEEMO missions are saturation dives, meaning that the diver’s tissue gases reach equilibrium with the pressure environment and therefore divers are allowed to live and work underwater for long periods. Aquarius, the unique laboratory in which the divers stay, provides a remote, confined environment similar to that found aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The habitat is located 19 meters below the ocean surface, 4.8 kilometers off the coast of Key Largo, Florida. The 2.5-atm (253 kPa) pressure and 21% oxygen inside the habitat provide increased oxygen availability, similar to that on ISS EVAs, during which spacewalkers breathe 100% oxygen at reduced pressure (0.3 atm). Because of the increased air pressure in the Aquarius habitat, crewmembers are exposed to higher oxygen pressures, which increase their risk for oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids in tissues and blood.

APPROACH:
The NEEMO XII and XIII missions took place in April and August of 2007. The NEEMO XII and XIII missions were 12-day and 10-day saturation dives, respectively. Each mission involved six divers living in an underwater habitat for the duration of the mission. Subjects were required to undergo a 17-hour decompression before resurfacing at the end of the dive. The NEEMO XIV mission was a 13-day saturation dive that took place in May 2010. Four male divers from NASA and 2 male habitat technicians participated in the study.

All subjects were required to pass a modified Air Force Class III physical examination and were required to have logged a minimum of 25 dives before they were selected to participate in the mission. The combined crew consisted of one female and eleven males, all of whom were subjects in the study. The female was on the NEEMO XII mission. Subjects were trained in all procedures required for successful completion of the in-dive sample and data collections. Their mean body weight before the dive was 85 ± 14 kg.

Sample collection days before the dive were designated as Dive–X days (D-X days), during the mission as Mission Day X (MDX), and after the dive as Return + X days (R+X days). Blood was collected before (D-7 and D-2), during (MD6 or 7 and MD9 or 11), and after the dive (R+10 and R+16 or 7). During the dive, NEEMO XII blood samples were collected one or two days later in the mission than NEEMO XIII blood samples because of the length of the mission. Blood collections (14.2 mL at each session) were performed at the same time each day after an eight hour fast. Pre- and post-dive (D-6, D-2, R+10, and R+16/7) blood samples were collected near the Aquarius habitat (on shore) and centrifuged for processing within 45 minutes of phlebotomy. Aliquots of whole blood were made before centrifugation. Serum aliquots were frozen at -20°C until they were transported to Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. Whole blood was transported to JSC and analyzed for hemoglobin and hematocrit within 48 hours of blood collection. Aliquots used for other tests remained frozen at –20°C until they were transported on dry ice to JSC.

RESULTS:
Hemoglobin and hematocrit both decreased during the dive but not consistently in the two NEEMO missions. Immediately after the dive, hemoglobin and hematocrit were lower in NEEMO XII than in NEEMO XIII crewmembers. Body iron stores increased during the dive, as indicated by increased ferritin and decreased transferrin and transferring receptors. Total body iron, estimated from ferritin and transferrin receptors, increased up to 29% during and after the dive. Total body iron was negatively correlated with superoxide dismutase (SOD). Total plasma heme increased 48% during the dive and was generally higher in NEEMO XII crewmembers than in the NEEMO XIII crew. Statistical analyses were not conducted for non-transferrin–bound iron and labile plasma iron, because they were not detectable in most samples; however, when these pro-oxidant forms of iron were detectable, it was always during or immediately after the dive and never before the dive. One-fourth of the subjects had detectable levels of nontransferrin–bound iron at the end of the dive period (MD 9/11) and five of the 12 crewmembers had detectable levels of labile plasma iron during or immediately after the dive. These data indicate that the NEEMO environment increases body iron stores and labile forms of iron, which may contribute to oxidative damage.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Somers, JefferyCo-Investigator: Jones, DerekCo-Investigator: Newby, NathanielCo-Investigator: Putnam, JacobCo-Investigator: Weaver, Ashley
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Currently, injury assessment reference values (IARV) are based on volunteer and post-mortem human subjects tested in non-space flight setups specific to the environment of interest. In automotive research, the occupant is put in the "super-slouched" position and is subjected to either frontal or side impacts at specific velocities with a three-point restraint and airbags. In military research, test configurations are commonly based on ejection seats. These tests employ seating geometries, restraint, and loading directions that are not consistent with space flight configurations. Acute seat pan angles, non-extended legs (fetal position), combined axis loading, as well as other seat, restraint, and loading conditions may induce unforeseen changes in injury risk. Because the current data available do not account for these variations, a sensitivity and extensibility study was needed.

This study had the following specific aims:

1. Validate the response of each finite element model against matched physical Anthropomorphic Test Dummy (ATD) tests in the baseline seat from existing datasets.

2. Quantify ATD and human numerical model response variance and sensitivity to a limited set of small perturbations in seat, and restraint initial conditions.

3. Quantify the effects of spacecraft-specific seating and restraint configurations on ATD and human numerical model responses.

APPROACH:

In Phase I, 35 Hybrid III, 26 THOR, and 212 human volunteer tests were chosen to validate the Humanetics 50th percentile Hybrid III, NASA version of the 50th percentile THOR-K, and the Global Human Body Models Consortium (GHBMC) simplified 50th percentile male (GHBMC M50-OS) finite element (FE) models, respectively. experiment_title: Hyperpolarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance Imaging
parameter_html:
Cardiac perfusion

Xenon

investigators: Principal Investigator: Albert, Mitchell
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems that provide three-dimensional internal imaging of the body have been off-limits for use in spacecraft due to their large size and power requirements. A new technology utilizes hyperpolarized (HP) noble gases, such as xenon and helium to perform similar, but superior, non-invasive imaging of the body. The HP noble gas MRI does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional medical MRI machine, so it offers a potential for a more practical device that is both small in size, low on power demands and easy to use. HP noble gas MRI may be the ideal imaging tool for use in space. This three-year ground-based study evaluated HP noble gas MRI as a means to: 1) help acquire new information about the physiological structure and function of organs and systems of the body while they are affected by microgravity; 2) diagnose disease in microgravity environments; and 3) develop real-time treatments for space-related illnesses.

APPROACH:
From previous research, a very low-field MRI system using a signal generated from HP helium-3 and xenon-129 was built. This investigation began the phase of feasibility testing on this prototype unit as a diagnostic tool capable of imaging the function and structure of the lungs, heart and brain. The detailed protocol for testing was developed using a conventional commercial MRI scanner operating at 1.5 and 0.2 Tesla, a reliable and proven platform. The procedures were transferred for use on the prototype HP gas MRI and compared to those developed initially on a conventional MRI.

The HP noble gas imaging studies were conducted on the ground using both animal and human subjects. Imaging was aimed at determining lung structure, gas diffusion in the lung, cardiac perfusion, lipid membrane structure, blood flow, and general organ structure. Other specific goals were to: 1) develop small, distal lung airway imaging at resolutions below 1 mm; 2) measure regional ventilation and perfusion irregularities of the lung; 3) detect right to left shunt in subjects with foramen ovale, a condition that needs to be detected prior to EVA (space walks); and 4) test the imaging of lung ventilation and perfusion at very low magnetic fields (0.015 Tesla).

RESULTS:
In addition to the investigators’ lung studies, advances have been made in their effort to develop hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI for the assessment of brain structure and function. The three most significant advances in this area include: 1. The method of chemical shift imaging was validated in the laboratory, 2. Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI CSI was carried out in rat brain. 3. In vivo Functional Brain Imaging Using Hyperpolarized 129 Xe was demonstrated.

Previously, the investigators reported that the rigorous airway diameter quantification algorithm they developed has been tested on an anthropomorphic lung phantom, and presented the results. Five subjects who have had their airways scanned using HP 3He MRI have also been imaged with CT.

The algorithm computing the local ventilation coefficient of variation from HP 3He MRI images previously developed was applied to all ventilation data sets available. The resulting heterogeneity maps, viewed in the context of the ventilation maps, clearly demonstrate the capture of the ventilation heterogeneity characteristics.

The algorithms for mapping ventilation have been applied to four non-asthmatics and 13 asthmatic subjects. Statistical significant differences were observed in the heterogeneity scores as well as ventilation distribution standard deviation for various cases of comparison.

The results of this study support the idea that HP 3He MRI can serve as a diagnostic tool that can be regularly used to evaluate astronaut physiology, how that differs from their earth status, how it progresses with continued space flight, and how it alters in the presence of disease or impairment.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Baulch, JanetCo-Investigator: Morgan, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Among NASA's concerns for astronaut health risk is space radiation-induced carcinogenesis. At present, there is no practical way for astronauts to avoid radiation exposure, so it is important that the best possible risk estimates be made. Recent studies have demonstrated that epigenetic mechanisms play a key role in the radiation response and carcinogenesis. Epigenetic mechanisms regulate gene expression by DNA methylation, chromatin modifications and microRNA. This project tests the hypothesis that in vitro irradiation of cells alters epigenetic profiles and that these epigenetic profiles are affected radiation quality. Using proton and iron ion radiations the delayed effects of radiation exposure will be investigated in the progeny of irradiated cells multiple cell generations after the initial exposure. Global, repeat element and specific locus DNA methylation will be measured. Further this project explores the possibility that DNA methylation or miRNA mediated gene silencing is involved in initiating or perpetuating radiation-induced genomic instability.

APPROACH:
To determine whether epigenetic aberrations affect genomic instability investigators measured DNA methylation, mRNA and microRNA (miR) levels in well characterized chromosomally stable and unstable clonally expanded single cell survivors of irradiation.

RESULTS:
Results for this experiment are found in several publications cited below.

1. The study of the DNA methylation and miRNA profiles of the GM10115 CHO cell line ~16-20 population doublings following Fe ion or x-ray exposures was completed and has been published: Aypar, U., Morgan, W.F., Baulch, J.E. (2011) Radiation-induced epigenetic alterations after low and high LET irradiations. Mutation Research, 707:24-33. This study develops the initial picture of the effect of high and low LET radiations on DNA methylation and also begins to delve into the potential role for miR in the delayed radiation response.

2. The manuscript submitted in 7/2010 to Radiation Research was accepted and has been published. Goetz, W., Morgan, M.N.M., Baulch, J.E. (2011) The effect of radiation quality on genomic DNA methylation profiles in irradiated human cell lines. Radiation Research, 175:575-587. To date, studies of radiation-induced changes in DNA methylation have focused on the low LET radiation response, using gamma- and x-rays. This study presents data demonstrating that radiation induced changes in DNA methylation are affected in a radiation quality dependent manner. This was accomplished using protons, x-rays and iron (Fe) ions. X-rays and protons are similarly low LET radiations (2 KeV/µm and 0.55 keV/µm, respectively) that differ in other ways such as energy deposition patterns or ionization density and d-ray contribution. Fe ions are a high LET particle radiation (150 keV/µm). Low LET proton and high LET Fe ions were selected for comparison to x-rays because they are the most prevalent species in space radiation. This project also tested the hypothesis for differences in the epigenetic radiation response between normal and cancer cell lines using normal human fibroblasts and colon carcinoma cells. The results demonstrate differences in basal DNA methylation profiles between normal and cancer cell lines, but similar epigenetic radiation responses that seem to be based on radiation quality.

3. Completed the epigenetic profile (DNA methylation, miR expression and mRNA levels) of cell lines that exhibit radiation induced genomic instability, as well as validation RT-PCR for the miR and mRNA data. The manuscript for these experiments is in preparation and should be submitted by the end of 2011.

experiment_title: Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI of the Brain, Lungs and Plants Augmented with MRI Pulse Sequence Development--NNX07AP80G
parameter_html:
Hyperpolarized noble gas
Nervous system damage
Pulmonary system damage
investigators: Principal Investigator: Albert, Mitchell
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Investigators are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe. An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow investigators to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. This ground-based investigation with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.

An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in a medical MRI. As a result, at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system). The recent progress made lays the foundation for the continued development of hyperpolarized xenon MRI for brain imaging. Specifically, imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis) and angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system), are now viable research goals. Because HP 129Xe is an MR signal source with properties very different from those generated from water-protons, it may yield structural and functional information not detectable by proton-based MRI methods. Thus brain imaging with hyperpolarized xenon should be of great benefit to the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of a number of neurological diseases.

APPROACH:
Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project.

RESULTS:
The overall goal of this proposal was to develop hyperpolarized noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (HP MRI) for the assessment of pulmonary and nervous system damage that may be incurred during human space flight. Hyperpolarized noble gas MRI is showing dramatic results for diagnostic imaging of the lungs, brain, and other parts of the body, some of which have been resistant to conventional proton MRI. Most notably, investigators have achieved high resolution dynamic images of the lungs and airways using hyperpolarized 3He, and have measured cerebral perfusion and functional activity in the brain using hyperpolarized 129Xe (HP 129Xe). The number of space flight-related pathologies which may benefit from this technique are vast and range from pulmonary dysfunction caused by microgravity to cognitive and neurobehavioral problems resulting from the stress and isolation of extended term space travel. This novel technology should also offer a rapid, sensitive method to detect treatment effects and thus may expedite the development of therapeutic strategies for treating space flight related injury, such as aerosol administration of drugs via the lungs, which may obviate the need for medicinal injections during space flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In order to select candidate astronauts for high stress resilience, it is first necessary to identify traits that prognosticate resilience in high-achieving (astronaut-like) adults. Together, a combination of such traits would be compiled into a valid assessment tool to maximize accuracy. This study tested whether objective markers derived from innovative personality assessment and event-related potentials (ERPs; e.g., electroencephalography recorded during reaction time tasks) prognosticated stress resilience in high-achieving adults recruited from a naturally high-stress environment (e.g., Science, Technology, Engineering, and Medicine (STEM) graduate training programs).

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Test personality facets as predictors of resilience after accounting for cognitive ability, over-claiming response bias, and Big 5 traits.
  2. Evaluate contributions of neurophysiological markers for predicting resilience.

APPROACH:
207 high-achieving adults were recruited from graduate and post-graduate training programs to participate in a longitudinal stress study. The baseline assessment was approximately two hours and included several domains. 26 personality facets were assessed using a modified version of the Facet Inventory of the Five Factor Model, an empirically-designed self-report instrument. EEG was recorded while participants completed two speeded reaction time tasks designed to yield event-related potential (ERP) indices of error monitoring. Stimuli were presented briefly in order to increase likelihood of behavioral mistakes. Response locked (for error and correct response trials, respectively) and stimulus locked (N200 and P300 amplitudes) ERPs were created by averaging trials in the usual way. Cognitive ability, a standard marker of resiliency, was assessed using a standardized computer battery. Response bias was assessed using the Over-claiming Questionnaire (OCQ), which was designed to capture the tendency to report oneself as especially competent and knowledgeable. The baseline assessment also included stress (perceived stress scale, a Work-Life inventory) and behavioral health outcomes (mood, anxiety, and psychosocial functioning).

After the baseline assessment, participants were invited to repeat online assessments of stress and behavioral health outcomes monthly for five months. This allowed investigators to carefully monitor fluctuations in stress and link them to corresponding fluctuations in behavioral health outcomes. In this way, stress-related declines in each outcome could be modeled as a linear slope and resilience could be defined by baseline predictors associated with less decline in behavioral health during periods of high stress.

RESULTS:
As expected, level of ten behavioral health outcomes over five months could be predicted by personality facets assessed at baseline. Also as expected, increases in stress were associated with worsening behavioral health across five months. Importantly, certain baseline personality facets prognosticated the rate of stress-induced decline, especially for three key behavioral health outcomes. This prognostic validity of facets largely held when controlling for cognitive ability, response bias, and standard superordinate Big 5 traits. Neural traits recorded during repeated trials of speeded reaction time tasks (e.g., ERPs) did not prognosticate level of behavioral health outcomes, but prognosticated worsening behavioral health outcomes at high levels of stress for some traits. In other words, some personality facets and some ERPs appear to represent promising prognostic tools to identify resilient individuals for high stress situations, at least for some relevant behavioral health outcomes. On the other hand, stress resilience for other relevant behavioral health outcomes were poorly prognosticated by the candidate predicators included in this study.
