Moreover, as astronauts have dysfunctional immune systems during spaceflight, the susceptibility of an immunocomprised C. elegans mutant to infection with these same microbes will also be evaluated. Results from this work hold potential to provide deeper insight into the likelihood, consequence and respective uncertainties of this HRP risk.

The design of this study was such that only the bacteria were cultured in the RWV, while the C. elegans hosts (wild type and an immunocompromised mutant) were grown prior to infection on standard nematode growth media (NGM) agar plates on their normal laboratory diet of Escherichia coli OP50. The infections then took place in liquid medium using a variety of exposure times (1-18 hours) in order to minimize any reversion of the low-shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG)-associated phenotypes (i.e., changes in virulence and pathogenesis-related stress resistance) during the infection.

RESULTS:
Under the conditions of this study, we found that transient exposure of the RWV-cultured microbes to C. elegans in a static dish was not sufficient for establishing a lethal infection in the nematode relative to the uninfected control nematodes fed on OP50. The outcomes of the infection process in liquid were quite different from what was previously reported for these pathogens using a solid agar medium. This indicates the need for further study design optimization. Persistence studies with S. Typhimurium did however indicate an early difference in the bacterial colonization numbers within the nematode intestine infected with LSMMG versus control cultures. We also observed an interesting phenotype following S. aureus infection, in which the bacterium appeared to form a biofilm-like structure around the anterior of the worm in liquid. Studies are ongoing to further investigate these findings.

experiment_title: Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI of the Brain, Lungs and Plants Augmented with MRI Pulse Sequence Development
parameter_html:
Nervous system damage
Pulmonary system damage
investigators: Principal Investigator: Albert, Mitchell
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow investigators to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. This ground-based investigation with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology.

An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in a medical MRI. As a result, at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system). The recent progress made lays the foundation for the continued development of hyperpolarized xenon MRI for brain imaging. Specifically, imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis) and angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system), are now viable research goals. Because HP 129Xe is an MR signal source with properties very different from those generated from water-protons, it may yield structural and functional information not detectable by proton-based MRI methods. Thus brain imaging with hyperpolarized xenon should be of great benefit to the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of a number of neurological diseases.

APPROACH:
Investigators are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe.

RESULTS:
The overall goal of this proposal was to develop hyperpolarized noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (HP MRI) for the assessment of pulmonary and nervous system damage that may be incurred during human space flight. Hyperpolarized noble gas MRI is showing dramatic results for diagnostic imaging of the lungs, brain, and other parts of the body, some of which have been resistant to conventional proton MRI. Most notably, investigators have achieved high resolution dynamic images of the lungs and airways using hyperpolarized 3He, and have measured cerebral perfusion and functional activity in the brain using hyperpolarized 129Xe (HP 129Xe). The number of space flight-related pathologies which may benefit from this technique are vast and range from pulmonary dysfunction caused by microgravity to cognitive and neurobehavioral problems resulting from the stress and isolation of extended term space travel. This novel technology should also offer a rapid, sensitive method to detect treatment effects and thus may expedite the development of therapeutic strategies for treating space flight related injury, such as aerosol administration of drugs via the lungs, which may obviate the need for medicinal injections during space flight.

experiment_title: Documentation of the Action of Metoclopramide
parameter_html:
Bowel sounds
Space motion sickness (SMS)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness (SMS) differs in many of its signs and symptoms from 1g motion sickness, so much so that the traditional signs of SMS cannot be used to evaluate the presence, severity, or treatment of SMS. On STS-7 and 8 it was found that bowel sounds were strikingly absent during SMS and that GI symptoms were consistent with ileus (temporary paralysis of the bowel). A method of recording bowel sounds had been devised and demonstrated on STS-8. A ground-based study of subjects with acute MS was also done.

This study had three objectives:
1. To demonstrate that presence or absence of bowel sound was related to SMS and especially GI symptoms.
2. To document any changes in motility, as evidenced by bowel sounds, produced by a drug known to effect GI motility in many situations.
3. To document any effects of weightlessness on bowel sounds of individuals not affected by SMS.

APPROACH:
Crewmembers with SMS were requested to make a recording on the day of recovery from the symptoms with a non-affected crewmember making a control recording if possible. Anyone electing to use the motility stimulating medication metoclopramide was requested to make a 45 minute recording during the initial drug dosage. The hardware consisted of four miniature professional two channel tape recorders and two small microphones and miniature battery supply mounted on an elastic Velcro coupled belt. Operations consisted of turning on the recorder, checking preset contro1s and connecting the microphone belt and placing it around the waist. A recording time of 45 minutes per cassette side was available and requested. The crewmember was free to perform his usual tasks during the recording.

The recordings were analyzed by replaying and: 1) recording through a filter on a high frequency two channel graphics recorder; 2) having a skilled observer listen through stereo headphones and electrically mark the graphic record whenever a sound was heard. The marks were then counted, averaged over five minute epochs, and plotted or otherwise analyzed.

RESULTS:
During investigation of space motion sickness on STS-4 through STS-8, it was discovered that the upper gastrointestinal system's normal action is stopped or greatly reduced. This explains the vomiting without nausea and other stomach complaints. On these flights, the drug metaclopramide, which restores GI activity in certain conditions, was effective in restoring bowel sounds and reversing symptoms in two individuals. It was ineffective in two others who were taking scopolamine, a known antagonist of the drug.

Three subjects made a total of four in-flight and three postflight recordings during STS-41D. Two of these were during the periods of SMS and one subject without SMS took the metoclopramide drug in-flight. Since this was the first opportunity to use this methodology after STS-8, a number of points are of interest including: with a trained observer it is possible to reliably record and quantify bowel sounds in all but the most active or the noisiest conditions in-flight. Secondly, the scheme works with a minimum of training and crewmember interference. With SMS there is barely detectable bowel activity and after recovery (MD-7) bowel sounds were essentially normal. Bowel sounds were also normal during the period of SMS in a third subject who had been affected on a previous mission. The differences are orders of magnitude.

On STS-41G, four subjects made preflight records, and all except 1 recording (microphones were apparently not actuated) were nominal and reproduced without difficulty. Inflight, a total of 8 recordings were made. Only one channel was recorded on three of the recordings; three other recordings seem as if the microphones were partially elevated from the body. The recordings were reproduced and analyzed with the exception of the latter three. No crewmember made recordings during SMS or medication.

That any recordings were made is a success in view of the few that have been obtained. New data were added to help understand the problem. Unfortunately, there was not a recording of the drug's action nor a complete series from any subject with SMS (pre or post, during sickness, during recovery or late in the flight). These records add support to the concept of bowel sounds as an unequivocal marker of SMS, and further suggest a rebound in GI activity on recovery from SMS (and possibly hyperactivity in weightlessness in some subjects--a new finding).

Regarding hardware anomalies inflight, the loss of 1 channel on the three STS-41G records was due to the record gain knob being mis-set. On disassembly, the circuit board supporting the gain control was found to be cracked, thus interrupting the signal to the channel.

This experiment was later included as part of DSO 456.

Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Badler, Norman
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ambitious space missions presented new challenges for space human factors as crews interact with and maintain complex equipment and automation. This demands that procedures for task design, rehearsal, and procedure refreshing be based on on-ground validated procedure instructions. This experiment investigated requirements for formulating, interpreting, and validating procedure instructions. Crew instructions should express clearly and unambiguously complex actions and their expected results. As NASA moves toward a "what to do" rather than a "how-to-do" approach, it is essential that textual instructions convey what is meant and correlate with equipment function and construction. Natural language instructions must coordinate with graphical simulations to provide both textual and visual guidance and context-sensitivity for procedures, especially when the equipment functions and features are accessible to the simulation. Current manuals and procedures need all alternatives to be made explicit, leading to documentation which must be laboriously prepared in advance. Any documentation for a complex procedure should "understand" the equipment and the human factors of the crew. One important aspect of "what-to-do" procedure documentation is that purposes and termination conditions of continuous processes are very frequently cited. These need to be generated from or interpreted by simulated actions. Although the focus in this project has been on ground-based procedure execution and validation, it is envisioned that future applications for spaceflight crews will use natural language to communicate with each other, the on-board automation, and to training and refresher simulations. The specific research goals were to use various user interfaces -- such as natural language instructions or virtual reality -- to control virtual crewmembers for procedure formulation, validation, inflight training, crew task allocation, and unusual procedure simulation. This project had its genesis in the confluence of prior research efforts for NASA, the Air Force, and the National Science Foundation (NSF). Having investigated computer graphics digital human models for quite some time, and having been familiar with their use for ergonomics and human factors applications, it is understood that some of the compelling problems today still add constrains to effective and widespread utilization of those models.

From prior NASA research spaceflight applications for human models, and the difficulties in modeling in-flight biomechanics, micro-gravity actions, and complex maintenance task manual manipulations were understood. This project was begun with the belief and expectation that digital human models could simulate spaceflight procedures to insure human competency to perform similar tasks in reality. Such simulations would insure good preflight designs, but required significant software investment and proper utilization by craft contractors. Indeed, some ergonomics human modeling tools do exist and are used in the design stages of a major project, but most of these are interactive systems and are not structured for flexible simulation: they are not particularly capable of taking instructions and executing them in a variety of design alternatives, and considerable operator expertise is required to set-up and run an analysis.

From prior Air Force research, extensive studies of instruction manuals were done for both aircraft maintenance and other mechanical applications. From this work an understanding was gained of the existing state-of-the-art in automated (electronic) instructions, and a priority ordering of problems that need to be addressed in order to produce better electronic instruction validation. The roles of validation and simulation are intertwined: a simulation may or may not succeed, and if not, the causes of failure must be established and understood. Failures may stem from or involve accommodation problems due to anthropometric variations, equipment design flaws, unforeseen procedure steps, impossible equipment access, misunderstanding or ignorance of equipment function, or inadequate or ambiguous instructions. Validation requires an integration of human modeling with equipment functional simulation, and a more automated analysis framework in which to probe the space of success and failure modes.

From prior NSF research the interrelationships between natural language and human animation was studied, and developed a Parameterized Action Representation (PAR) and an Actionary of digital definitions suitable for an action database. This work focused on how manual procedure instructions might be set on a computational basis appropriate to both natural language processing and computer animation on virtual human models. PAR describes actions with parameters such as agent, object, motion qualities, paths, preparatory specifications, termination conditions, and sub-actions so they can be re-used in a wide variety of spatial contexts, by various virtual actors, and with action modifiers.

APPROACH:
The approach for this experiment is not available.

RESULTS:
This NASA project sought to combine these observations, knowledge, and methodologies to serve the objective of designing better instruction delivery, simulation, and validation tools. This project has led to several specific accomplishments, which are summarized below.

Automated constrained human arm reach

This portion researched a novel way of computing real-time human arm reach actions for maintenance, operation, or scientific tasks in constrained physical environments. Such movements are essential for computer software that must automatically synthesize complex arm motions in confined spaces, such as glove box. Rather than rely on a human operator to guide the synthetic reach, the program can do the analysis itself, and do so in a fashion that:

1. Uses a simple spatial partition and spatial search algorithm to move the hand through space toward the goal,

2. Avoids arm and body contacts with the environment using the graphics hardware board to do fast collision detection,

3. Does not use the traditional configuration-space planning approach common in robotics, and

4. Uses arm strength data to favor more natural (less awkward) shoulder, elbow, and wrist postures during solution search.

This work is being extended to incorporate better empirical data (reported by others) to extend the reach chain beyond the shoulder joint to the whole upper body.

Shape Preserving object simplification

This addressed the very general question of converting geometric models from complex mega-polygon meshes into more compact representations that automatically preserved shape features such as pointed parts or sharp edges. The motivation for this arises from placing a simulated human (maintainer) in a complex modeling 3D environment. The numerous surfaces needed in a polygon model mostly arise from visual needs and local details that are possibly not very relevant to the accomplishment of a maintenance task. But some features, such as points and sharp edges, are important for safety. Semantically careless polygon decimation can eliminate some of these features and affect task accomplishment methods or viability. Although we have not been able to apply these results directly, the issues are nonetheless important for both equipment design and automatic human task simulation. In the former, the design features at the human manipulation level of detail are important, but make be overwhelmed by essential engineering detail. In the latter, fewer polygons means faster computation of reach and positioning tasks, since collision detection costs are highly dependent on the mesh size of the 3D model.

Interactive vibrotactile experience for confined arm reach

For maintenance and operational training, a virtual environment can provide visual feedback, but a human operator will not have the tactile benefit of feeling the mechanical constraints in a confined space such as an equipment bay or a glove box. Here, the question of whether a physical stimulus in a virtual reality experience could effectively substitute for a physical obstacle was explored. The physical component that is missing is the collision detection and response, so an array of vibrotactile devices (tactors) on the arm were used to simulate the "feel" of touching a real object though none is physically present. These small, inexpensive computer-controlled tactors deliver vibration to a small area of skin. Up to twenty-four of these were positioned on the arm and hand of a subject. In experiments, users were able to perform reaches to occluded targets in confined volumes faster with the vibrotactile display on their arm. Such a haptic array may help motor learning of complex tasks and provide valuable physical feedback (though not physical constraint) during initial task learning or later rehearsal. This could translate to reduced training time for complex assembly or disassembly tasks, with the added benefit that the human subject must actually perform the task without having the cost or expense of a physical model.

Deformable arm model with biomechanical tissue properties

A human arm model was created with biomechanical deformation parameters. Using a novel device to measure a local pressure/displacement function, the indentation of the arm tissue can be simulated when an external blunt (spherical) obstacle is applied. The purpose of such a model is to see whether the deformation of soft tissues can affect the reachable space of the arm, since all existing ergonomic digital human models have rigid surfaces. Reach analyses performed with rigid body collision detection are apt to be conservative (underestimating reachable space) with respect to what a real (deformable) arm model can reach. In informal experiments it was found that reach could be extended up to about 15% if deformation over small obstacles was considered. Results for larger obstacles (such as flat areas) will be closer to the predictions from rigid geometry models since volume-preserving tissue displacements limit the travel of the obstacle into the arm space. Accordingly, this research showed a local effect but not enough to continue with more detailed deformable arm models at this time. It is possible than these ideas can be profitable if applied to lower torso for whole body maintenance access problems or buttocks deformations for optimizing seat design, but to date it has not specifically addressed data acquisition methods for these body regions nor these particular applications.

The personality factor

As possibilities for crew simulation were investigated, it became clear that very important factors to consider in task accomplishment and success were an individual's personality and psychological state. This might even be the most important subjective issue for long duration flights: actually having the crew do what they need to do and not do what they should not do. Understanding how to include these considerations in task, workload, and mission simulations would presumably lead to better working conditions and overall mission success. This difficult aspect of human behavioral modeling was to look at a classification of plotlines from narrative stories. These plotlines could provide a "backbone" of human actions and reactions to support the selection of individual tasks. Plot action choices are highly dependent on an individual's personality, culture, and motivators. Work plans could then seek to include countermeasures to mitigate plotlines that might lead to negative crew consequences.

Parameterized Actions and the Actionary

This involved developing a parameterized action representation (PAR) and simulation system that creates a system in which domain experts, not simulation experts, can build a simulation to test maintenance procedures, habitability, or work schedules. Previous versions of the PAR system were based on Python and C++ under the IRIX operating system. In order to optimize the code and make it more accessible to a larger community, a Windows based operating system was used with a commonly-used free database called MySQL to store the database of available actions, the Actionary. PAR data is entered into MySQL through a graphical user interface (GUI) consisting of various windows. Through the main windows, the Object Edit and Action Edit windows, the user can create new objects, agents, and actions, as well as edit, and search through those already defined in the database. The programming of flexible base dialogs for repeated functionality among objects and actions (e.g., coordinate entry, object/action search dialogs) allows the user to quickly become accustomed to the interface, while the size of the program stays minimal. The object, agent, and action data are stored in a relational MySQL database in a normalized structure such as to speed up the retrieval of objects, agents, and actions. Also, because of the possibility of integrating this data into a mobile environment, the database model has been tuned to efficiently occupy a minimal storage space. This work has influenced future instruction delivery models for NASA, since the PAR allows re-use of stored instructional components and detail level-dependent delivery of instructional materials.

From this work an understanding was gained of the existing state-of-the-art in automated (electronic) instructions, and a priority ordering of problems that need to be addressed in order to produce better electronic instruction validation. The roles of validation and simulation are intertwined: a simulation may or may not succeed, and if not, the causes of failure must be established and understood. Failures may stem from or involve accommodation problems due to anthropometric variations, equipment design flaws, unforeseen procedure steps, impossible equipment access, misunderstanding or ignorance of equipment function, or inadequate or ambiguous instructions. Validation requires an integration of human modeling with equipment functional simulation, and a more automated analysis framework in which to probe the space of success and failure modes.

From prior NSF research the interrelationships between natural language and human animation was studied, and developed a Parameterized Action Representation (PAR) and an Actionary of digital definitions suitable for an action database. This work focused on how manual procedure instructions might be set on a computational basis appropriate to both natural language processing and computer animation on virtual human models. PAR describes actions with parameters such as agent, object, motion qualities, paths, preparatory specifications, termination conditions, and sub-actions so they can be re-used in a wide variety of spatial contexts, by various virtual actors, and with action modifiers.

APPROACH:
The approach for this experiment is not available.

RESULTS:
This NASA project sought to combine these observations, knowledge, and methodologies to serve the objective of designing better instruction delivery, simulation, and validation tools. This project has led to several specific accomplishments, which are summarized below.

Automated constrained human arm reach

This portion researched a novel way of computing real-time human arm reach actions for maintenance, operation, or scientific tasks in constrained physical environments. Such movements are essential for computer software that must automatically synthesize complex arm motions in confined spaces, such as glove box. Rather than rely on a human operator to guide the synthetic reach, the program can do the analysis itself, and do so in a fashion that:

1. Uses a simple spatial partition and spatial search algorithm to move the hand through space toward the goal,

2. Avoids arm and body contacts with the environment using the graphics hardware board to do fast collision detection,

3. Does not use the traditional configuration-space planning approach common in robotics, and

4. Uses arm strength data to favor more natural (less awkward) shoulder, elbow, and wrist postures during solution search.

This work is being extended to incorporate better empirical data (reported by others) to extend the reach chain beyond the shoulder joint to the whole upper body.

Shape Preserving object simplification

This addressed the very general question of converting geometric models from complex mega-polygon meshes into more compact representations that automatically preserved shape features such as pointed parts or sharp edges. The motivation for this arises from placing a simulated human (maintainer) in a complex modeling 3D environment. The numerous surfaces needed in a polygon model mostly arise from visual needs and local details that are possibly not very relevant to the accomplishment of a maintenance task. But some features, such as points and sharp edges, are important for safety. Semantically careless polygon decimation can eliminate some of these features and affect task accomplishment methods or viability. Although we have not been able to apply these results directly, the issues are nonetheless important for both equipment design and automatic human task simulation. In the former, the design features at the human manipulation level of detail are important, but make be overwhelmed by essential engineering detail. In the latter, fewer polygons means faster computation of reach and positioning tasks, since collision detection costs are highly dependent on the mesh size of the 3D model.

Interactive vibrotactile experience for confined arm reach

For maintenance and operational training, a virtual environment can provide visual feedback, but a human operator will not have the tactile benefit of feeling the mechanical constraints in a confined space such as an equipment bay or a glove box. Here, the question of whether a physical stimulus in a virtual reality experience could effectively substitute for a physical obstacle was explored. The physical component that is missing is the collision detection and response, so an array of vibrotactile devices (tactors) on the arm were used to simulate the "feel" of touching a real object though none is physically present. These small, inexpensive computer-controlled tactors deliver vibration to a small area of skin. Up to twenty-four of these were positioned on the arm and hand of a subject. In experiments, users were able to perform reaches to occluded targets in confined volumes faster with the vibrotactile display on their arm. Such a haptic array may help motor learning of complex tasks and provide valuable physical feedback (though not physical constraint) during initial task learning or later rehearsal. This could translate to reduced training time for complex assembly or disassembly tasks, with the added benefit that the human subject must actually perform the task without having the cost or expense of a physical model.

Deformable arm model with biomechanical tissue properties

A human arm model was created with biomechanical deformation parameters. Using a novel device to measure a local pressure/displacement function, the indentation of the arm tissue can be simulated when an external blunt (spherical) obstacle is applied. The purpose of such a model is to see whether the deformation of soft tissues can affect the reachable space of the arm, since all existing ergonomic digital human models have rigid surfaces. Reach analyses performed with rigid body collision detection are apt to be conservative (underestimating reachable space) with respect to what a real (deformable) arm model can reach. In informal experiments it was found that reach could be extended up to about 15% if deformation over small obstacles was considered. Results for larger obstacles (such as flat areas) will be closer to the predictions from rigid geometry models since volume-preserving tissue displacements limit the travel of the obstacle into the arm space. Accordingly, this research showed a local effect but not enough to continue with more detailed deformable arm models at this time. It is possible than these ideas can be profitable if applied to lower torso for whole body maintenance access problems or buttocks deformations for optimizing seat design, but to date it has not specifically addressed data acquisition methods for these body regions nor these particular applications.

The personality factor

As possibilities for crew simulation were investigated, it became clear that very important factors to consider in task accomplishment and success were an individual's personality and psychological state. This might even be the most important subjective issue for long duration flights: actually having the crew do what they need to do and not do what they should not do. Understanding how to include these considerations in task, workload, and mission simulations would presumably lead to better working conditions and overall mission success. This difficult aspect of human behavioral modeling was to look at a classification of plotlines from narrative stories. These plotlines could provide a "backbone" of human actions and reactions to support the selection of individual tasks. Plot action choices are highly dependent on an individual's personality, culture, and motivators. Work plans could then seek to include countermeasures to mitigate plotlines that might lead to negative crew consequences.

Parameterized Actions and the Actionary

This involved developing a parameterized action representation (PAR) and simulation system that creates a system in which domain experts, not simulation experts, can build a simulation to test maintenance procedures, habitability, or work schedules. Previous versions of the PAR system were based on Python and C++ under the IRIX operating system. In order to optimize the code and make it more accessible to a larger community, a Windows based operating system was used with a commonly-used free database called MySQL to store the database of available actions, the Actionary. PAR data is entered into MySQL through a graphical user interface (GUI) consisting of various windows. Through the main windows, the Object Edit and Action Edit windows, the user can create new objects, agents, and actions, as well as edit, and search through those already defined in the database. The programming of flexible base dialogs for repeated functionality among objects and actions (e.g., coordinate entry, object/action search dialogs) allows the user to quickly become accustomed to the interface, while the size of the program stays minimal. The object, agent, and action data are stored in a relational MySQL database in a normalized structure such as to speed up the retrieval of objects, agents, and actions. Also, because of the possibility of integrating this data into a mobile environment, the database model has been tuned to efficiently occupy a minimal storage space. This work has influenced future instruction delivery models for NASA, since the PAR allows re-use of stored instructional components and detail level-dependent delivery of instructional materials.

experiment_title: Development of Spaceflight Foods with High Microbial Concentrations
parameter_html:
Microbial monitoring, food
Probiotics, food
investigators: Principal Investigator: Cooper, MayaCo-Investigator: Catauro, PatriciaCo-Investigator: Elliott, ToddCo-Investigator: Oubre, Cherie
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Strict microbiological standards have been established for the thermostabilized, freeze dried, low moisture, and intermediate moisture foods that make up the current space flight food system. However, for long-duration missions, it may be prudent to consider space food items with higher microbial counts. The feasibility of including shelf-stable probiotics and establishing appropriate handling procedures for extraterrestrially grown and processed foods needs to be determined in order to re-evaluate microbiological guidelines for the space flight food system.

A space habitat food system that involves growing and processing fresh produce in situ (bioregenerative foods) and launching payloads of unprocessed grain, legumes, and seeds (bulk foods) is being explored as an avenue to longer shelf life. However, these foods could contain a high concentration of microorganisms with respect to current microbiological standards for microbial load of space flight foods. With mounting evidence of a link between the consumption of probiotic microorganisms and health benefits, including increased immune function and cancer prevention, the inclusion of probiotics in the space flight food system is also being considered. The potential to impact crew member health through functional foods is yet unexplored but highly relevant to risks associated with space travel. As with extraterrestrial food processing, probiotic foods and supplements fall outside of the current microbiological standards for space flight.

The purpose of this study was to perform a review of relevant information to assess the feasibility of developing a microbially-safe, space flight food system that includes extraterrestrial processing and/or probiotics. If deemed feasible, guidance for standards of microbial acceptability and appropriate testing methods for foods/supplements will be recommended. The study proceeded as follows:
1. Determine the potential of microbial load from bioregenerative produce.
2. Determine the current microbial strains and uses of live cultures in shelf stable foods.
3. Compare levels of microbial load in these foods/supplements to current requirements and assess the level of additional risk.
4. Investigate current literature and commercial operations to provide guidance in establishing microbiological requirements and testing methods for foods with high and diversified microbial concentrations.

APPROACH:
Current space flight food requirements are inadequate for microbial monitoring associated with crop production, the use of bulk foods, and subsequent processing and handling, as well as foods with inherently high microbial concentrations, such as probiotics, which may be beneficial for crew health. This review provided an initial investigation into (a) the potential of microbial load from bioregenerative produce, (b) the current microbial strains and uses of live cultures in shelf stable foods, (c) a comparison of levels of microbial load in these foods/supplements to current requirements and an assessment of additional risk, and (d) an investigation of current literature and commercial operations to provide guidance in establishing microbiological requirements and testing methods for foods with high and diversified microbial concentrations.

RESULTS:
The evidence from this review indicates a need for further research to determine the procedures necessary for growing and processing regenerative produce and development of specific cleaning methods to mitigate microbiological risks. In addition, data mining performed during this review identified potential benefits for the use of food products with high microbial concentrations. Specifically, this review has performed an extensive market survey to generate a comprehensive list of potential probiotic products, which should be evaluated in future research to determine preferred probiotic formulations for space flight. Future research would also determine the specific microbial testing procedures for those formulations and assess the risk of adding the formulation to the food system.

experiment_title: Physical Activity Profiles of LSAH Participants
parameter_html:
Exercise frequency
Exercise type
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The physical activity profile of LSAH participants can be gleaned from their responses in the Lifestyle Questionnaire (LSQ).

APPROACH:
The questionnaire has been used to collect lifestyle data from each class of astronauts and comparison participants since 1993, with an update in 1997.

RESULTS:
Of 223 astronaut and 820 comparison participant respondents, the most recent data show that 58.8% of the former and 72.4% of the latter report 2 or fewer types of exercise (as defined in the LSQ) performed in their usual routine.

When broken down into exercise types, the data show that 69.8% of astronauts and 58.7% of comparison participants report running or jogging as their usual form of exercise (exercise types are not mutually exclusive). More astronauts report weight lifting as an activity than comparison participants, while fewer astronauts report walking as an activity than comparison participants (56.5% to 28.5%, and 29.2% to 48.9%, respectively). Note that the LSQ question on exercise type does not specify any flexibility exercise in its list of possible answers.

In terms of frequency, a higher percentage of astronauts reported more frequent exercise per week than comparison participants. Almost 29% of the astronauts reported exercising from five to seven days a week compared to 18% of comparison participants. Conversely, a higher percentage of comparison participants reported rarely exercising (occasionally to not at all) as compared to astronauts (31.8% to 11.2%, respectively).

These data suggest that both astronauts and comparison participants may benefit from incorporating additional modes of exercise into their usual routine, as well as varying activities. A well-rounded fitness program has three main components: cardiovascular exercise (e.g., running, walking, swimming), strength training (e.g., weight training, plyometrics), and flexibility (e.g., yoga, Pilates).

experiment_title: Cytogenetic Effects of Space Radiation in Human Lymphocytes
parameter_html:
Chromosomal aberration, frequency
Chromosomal aberrations, lymphocytes
Radiation dose
investigators: Principal Investigator: Yang, Tracy
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space radiation can be a major health risk to crews of long-term missions, e.g., International Space Station and Mars flights. The measurement of physical dose received during a mission, as well as the LETs, energies and charges of particles is important for assessing health risk. It is also important to obtain quantitative information regarding the effectiveness of space radiation in causing damage to critical biological targets, e.g., chromosomes. At present the estimated uncertainty of biological effects of space radiation is more than a factor of two. Such large uncertainty makes accurate health risk assessment very difficult, if not impossible.

The primary goal of this study with the Mir 18 crew was to determine the effectiveness of space radiation in inducing chromosomal aberrations, especially translocations in lymphocytes. Chromosomal translocations remain stable in the human body for many years and can be important in the initiation of cancer. Specific reciprocal translocations, for example, are the cytogenetic hallmarks of leukemia and lymphomas in humans. Consistent chromosome aberrations are observed not only in rare tumor types but also in the relatively common lung, colon, and breast cancers. The specific objectives of this study were to measure chromosomal aberrations in human lymphocytes preflight and postflight, to correlate postflight chromosomal aberration results with inflight radiation dosage, and to determine relative biological effectiveness (RBE) by comparing the chromosomal aberration frequencies between flight results and ground studies.

APPROACH:
Blood samples were collected in tubes containing sodium heparin and were incubated in medium containing Phytoaemagglutinin (PHA). 0.2 ug/ml colcemid was added after 48 hours. After swelling the cells in 0.075M potassium chloride they were fixed in methanol/acetic acid. Chromosome spreads were prepared by dropping cells onto clean slides.

Chromosome spreads were hybridized with DNA probes specific for human chromosome 2 and 4 and the "painted" chromosomes were detected using a fluorescence microscope. For dicentric analysis, chromosomes were stained with Giemsa dye and examined using a light microscope.

Preflight samples were irradiated with gamma rays and a dose response curve for induction of translocations was generated. Postflight samples were analyzed and dose absorbed in space was extrapolated from the preflight calibration curves.

RESULTS:
No major preflight or postflight anomalies were observed. Data obtained to date show that space radiation can induce chromosomal aberrations in human cells and can be many times more effective than gamma rays in causing cytogenetic damages. Furthermore, these results suggest that, complementary to physical dosimetry, the chromosome painting technique can be useful as a noninvasive biodosimetry to determine radiation exposure in crewmembers.

experiment_title: Sleep-Wake Actigraphy and Light Exposure During Spaceflight
parameter_html:
Alertness
Caffeine consumption
Luminance
Nap
Sleep disturbance
Sleep latency
Sleep quality
Sleep time
Wake after final awakening
Medication consumption
Awakenings, number
investigators: Principal Investigator: Czeisler, CharlesCo-Investigator: Barger, LauraCo-Investigator: Ronda, JosephCo-Investigator: Wright, Kenneth
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The success and effectiveness of manned space flight depends on the ability of crewmembers to maintain a high level of cognitive performance and vigilance while operating and monitoring sophisticated instrumentation. Astronauts, however, commonly experience sleep disruption and may experience misalignment of circadian phase during space flight. Both of these conditions are associated with insomnia and impairment of alertness and cognitive performance. Relatively little is known of the prevalence or cause of space flight-induced insomnia in short-duration missions, and less is known about the effect of long-duration space flight on sleep and circadian rhythm organization.

This experiment used state-of-the-art ambulatory technology to monitor sleep-wake activity patterns and light exposure in crewmembers aboard the Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS). In this investigation, test subjects wore a small light-weight activity and light recording device (Actiwatch) for the entire duration of their mission. The sleep-wake activity and light exposure patterns obtained during flight are compared with data collected before and after space flight. The study also evaluated the effects of space flight on crewmembers' subjective evaluation of the amount and quality of their sleep.

APPROACH:
Baseline Data Collection: Baseline Data Collection (BDC) occurred twice before launch. The first session was two weeks in duration and occured in the window between 120 days before launch (L-120) and L-75. Crewmembers either wore the Actiwatch continuously for two weeks or they wore the watch for two one-week periods. Along with wearing the watch, crewmembers also completed a short paper sleep log every morning. The log consisted of questions relevant to the quantity and quality of the crewmembers’ sleep for the previous night. This allowed the investigator to compare watch data with written data and analyze the crewmember's sleep patterns and any disruptions they experienced.

The second BDC session was from L-11 to L-0. The Actiwatch was again worn continuously for the eleven days before launch and paper sleep logs were again completed in the mornings. The two sessions were designed to document the differences in sleep quality and quantity of crewmembers in their regular routines right before a launch.

After the mission is over, recovery from space flight was assessed from the day of landing (R+0) through R+7. The watches were worn continuously for the eight days upon arriving back on Earth. The paper sleep logs were again completed in the mornings.

Inflight Operations: Each crewmember participating in the experiment donned the Actiwatch as soon as possible upon entry into orbit on flight day 1 (FD1) and wore the watch continuously throughout the flight. Sleep logs were completed each day within 15 minutes of awakening. On the last day of the mission, the crewmember removed and stowed the Actiwatch.

RESULTS:
Investigators collected data from astronauts on space shuttle missions and ISS missions with ground-based data from all astronauts. Crewmembers attempted and obtained significantly less sleep per night as estimated by actigraphy during space shuttle missions, 11 days before space flight, and about 3 months before space flight compared with the first week post-mission. Crewmembers on ISS missions obtained significantly less sleep during space flight, in the 11 days before space flight, and during the 2-week interval scheduled about 3 months before space flight compared with in the first week post-mission. 61 of 78 shuttle-mission crewmembers reported taking a dose of sleep-promoting drug on 500 of 963 nights while 12 of 16 ISS crewmembers reported using sleep-promoting drugs.

OBJECTIVES:
Experimental results from SLS-1 showed a decrease in the number of Epo-responsive total bone marrow progenitors in flight rats compared to the ground controls. APPROACH:
Flight animals were divided into four groups: group A (n=5) was used to collect blood, group B (n=5) was injected with recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEpo), group C (n=5) received saline as a control, and group D (n=5) was sacrificed in flight. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The response of the cardiovascular system to a quantified workload is a frequently used index of the general physical condition of an individual. The objective of the Inflight Exerciser and Work Tolerance (M003) experiment was to evaluate the day-to-day general physical condition of the Gemini 4 , Gemini 5, and Gemini 7 astronauts during space flight by evaluating the cardiovascular system. In this examination, variation in heart rate, blood pressure, and respiration rate to a calibrated workload was studied preflight and inflight, as the basis for measuring the response of the cardiovascular system.

APPROACH:
The exercise device used for the experiment consisted of a pair of rubber cords. The cords were attached to a nylon handle at one end and to a nylon foot strap at the other. A stainless steel cable limited the stretch length of the rubber bungee cords and limited the isotonic workload of each pull. The device exercised the arms by holding the feet stationary while the astronaut pulled the handle. In flight, a bioinstrumentation system was used to collect the cardiovascular data. These data were simultaneously recorded by the onboard biomedical magnetic tape recorder (for real-time evaluation) and telemetered to the ground-based monitoring stations.

Exercise periods lasted for 30 seconds, during which time the astronaut stretched the bungee cords through a full extension one time per second. Ten exercise periods were performed by subject A of the Gemini 4 mission, while seven exercise periods were performed by subject B. Exercise periods were performed three times daily by the Gemini 5 astronauts. During the Gemini 7 mission, the exercise was scheduled twice daily. Additional isometric and isotonic exercises were performed by the Gemini 7 astronauts approximately three times daily.

Heart rate was determined by counting beats during 15-second intervals for 2 minutes before and after exercise, as well as during the first and last 15-second intervals during each exercise. Blood pressure measurements were obtained before and after each exercise period.

RESULTS:
Comparison of data from preflight exercise periods with data obtained during flight revealed little difference in heart rate response for all astronauts. In addition, comparison of data collected from the inflight exercise periods from the first to the last day of Gemini 5 revealed little difference in heart rate response. Gemini 4 astronauts exhibited a moderate rise in heart rate during exercise, with a rapid return to near pre-exercise levels within 1 minute following exercise. The astronauts' heart rates returned more rapidly to pre-exercise values than did the Mercury 9 astronaut tested (a 34-hour mission). The heart rate of the Gemini 4 astronauts returned to pre-exercise values 45 to 60 seconds after cessation of exercise. The one astronaut of the Mercury 9 mission had a mean post-exercise heart rate during flight that was slightly increased for approximately 2 minutes after exercising. However, the environmental control system of the Gemini spacecraft was superior to that of the Mercury spacecraft; therefore, the data were not strictly comparable. Evaluation of the heart rate data revealed no significant difference between the heart rate responses (of both Gemini 4 astronauts) to exercise during the mission and the responses obtained before the mission. Thus, using the rate of return of the heart rate to pre-exercise values as an index of physical condition, there was no evidence of cardiovascular deconditioning at any time during the Gemini 4 mission. Results were similar for Gemini 5 and 7 astronauts.

During Gemini 4, blood pressure changes were minimal. Generally, blood pressure measurements, before and after exercise periods on Gemini 5 were not remarkable. Post-exercise systolic pressures of both astronauts tended to be higher than pre-exercise values. Generally, post-exercise diastolic pressures were slightly higher than, or were identical to, pre-exercise values. After the fourth day of flight, both astronauts used the exerciser frequently between scheduled medical data passes. Both Gemini 5 astronauts remarked that exercise was essential and beneficial on long-duration space flights. The results were similar for Gemini 7 astronauts.

On the basis of the data obtained during the missions, investigators concluded the following:
1) The response of the cardiovascular system to a calibrated workload was relatively constant for a given individual during space flights lasting up to 14 days.

2) Crewmembers were able to perform mild-to-moderate amounts of work under the conditions of space flight and within the confines of the Gemini spacecraft. This ability continued essentially unchanged for up to 14 days in flight.

3) Using a variant of the Harvard Step Test as a cardiovascular deconditioning index, no decrement in the physical condition of the crewmembers was apparent during space flights of up to 14 days. No decrement was observed under the stress of the relatively mild workloads imposed in this experiment.

experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study represents the first systematic evaluation of dysrhythmias during extravehicular activity (EVA). Twenty-four-hour electrocardiograph (ECG) tracings of Shuttle crew members (n=7) were recorded before, during and after spaceflight including EVA. A comparison of the incidence and severity of dysrhythmias across subjects and time was performed.

APPROACH:
Participating crewmembers were required to wear either a Holter ECG recorder or the standard operational bio-instrumentation system (OBS) ECG monitors. The protocol involved 3 specific phases: Phase 1, before flight - acquisition of 3 separate 24-hour Holter recordings; Phase 2, during flight - 24 hours of data collection during and after each EVA (including one 24-hour period within 2 days of landing). Phase 3, after flight - 24 hours of Holter monitoring on postflight days R+0, R+7, and R+30.

RESULTS:
Although limited by sample size, the data suggested that the incidence of dysrhythmias is no greater during EVA than in any other phase of a mission. The cardiac response during EVA was statistically no different from the response during the preflight and postflight phases. With the advent of Space Station and the necessity for increased EVA, knowledge of both electrophysiologic and cardiovascular changes will be needed. The data from this study suggested that EVA does not precipitate deleterious cardiac events during space flight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Crewmembers on space flight missions use medications to treat space flight-associated conditions like space adaptation syndrome as well as common ordinary complaints. They do so under the remote guidance of their flight surgeons, who base prescriptions on their knowledge and experience in terrestrial medicine. However, even after decades of space flight missions, it is unknown if medications act the same in the space flight environment as they do on Earth. Aspects of the space flight environment (low gravity, radiation exposure, closed environment, stress) have been shown to alter human physiology. Some of these physiological changes could be expected to alter either pharmacokinetics (PK), how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolizes and excretes administered medications or pharmacodynamics (PD), receptors or signaling systems that are the targets of medication action. Anecdotal data has suggested that, at least for certain medications or indications, inflight medication efficacy is poor, and space flight crew use high doses, repeated doses, or even experience apparent treatment failures. Fortunately none of these episodes has been serious enough to cause injury or evacuation from low-Earth orbit (LEO). However, in order to prepare for exploration missions where speedy evacuation to Earth may not be a possibility, the likelihood of unexpected medication action must be determined. This study aimed to determine if the LEO environment of the International Space Station (ISS) alters the actions of two common medications, a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic and an antibiotic.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine PK for medication frequently used by crewmembers in two different environments: on Earth and during a space flight mission.
  2. Determine space flight versus ground differences in medication-associated effects on sleep, wakefulness, and several measures of cognitive function as measures of pharmacodynamics.

APPROACH:
Investigators aimed to measure PK for two medications used by crewmembers in two different environments: on Earth and during a space flight mission. Circulating concentrations in the bloodstream were going to be measured over time after medication administration, permitting modeled estimation of absorption rates and metabolism/excretion rates. Same-subject comparisons using pre-flight and post-flight test sessions will permit measurement of same-subject variability that will provide a baseline for determination of clinically relevant changes during space flight. Space flight versus ground differences in medication-associated effects on sleep, wakefulness, and several measures of cognitive function was going to be used as measures of pharmcodynamics.

RESULTS:
This study ended before data was collected from crewmembers. A final report containing EEG evaluations was archived. No datasets are available.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The carotid baroreceptors, which are located in the neck, monitor the blood pressure and alter the activity in the autonomic nervous system to adjust the heart rate (by means of the vagus nerve) and peripheral resistance (by means of the sympathetic nervous system), so that a normal blood pressure is maintained. Disruption of this autonomic control may be responsible, at least in part, for the orthostatic intolerance that astronauts frequently experience after space flight. This study was designed to investigate both the vagal and sympathetic aspects of the carotid baroreceptor reflex response. Its specific objectives were to evaluate the function of the carotid baroreceptor reflex before and after space flight, to measure resting plasma levels of catecholamines (neurotransmitters of the sympathetic nervous system), and to perform power spectral analyses of variability in the interval between R waves on the electrocardiogram (the R-R interval).

APPROACH:
This was a follow-on study to DSO 467, which addressed effects of short-duration flights only. The degree of change in baroreceptor function was unexpected, causing concern about further decrements with longer missions. For DOS 601, therefore, carotid baroreceptor stimulation tests and assessments of orthostatic function were performed on 16 astronauts after space flights of 8 to 14 days. While the astronauts held their breath after exhaling (Valsalva's maneuver), a motorized bellows increased the pressure in a neck chamber to 40 mm Hg and then decreased it in steps down to -65 mm Hg. Blood samples were taken for analysis of catecholamine levels before the baroreceptor stimulation tests. The R-R interval (the inverse of the heart rate) was plotted against the carotid distending pressure (the systolic blood pressure minus the pressure in the neck chamber). These plots illustrated the stimulus-response relationship of the carotid baroreceptor cardiac reflex. In another test of baroreceptor stimulation, the heart rate and blood pressure were recorded as the astronauts performed Valsalva's maneuvers. In addition, five-minute electrocardiograms were recorded for a power spectral analysis of R-R variability. In this analysis fluctuations in the R-R interval were resolved into component waves, and the power at each frequency was displayed.

RESULTS:
When results from landing day were compared with preflight results, heart rate had increased, body weight and orthostatic tolerance had decreased, the range of R-R intervals had decreased, the maximum slope and the operational point (the R-R interval at zero neck pressure) of the carotid baroreceptor cardiac reflex response had decreased and resting plasma levels of norepinephrine and epinephrine had increased. The lower operational point indicated that the hypotensive buffering capacity was reduced. The blood pressure and heart rate responses to Valsalva's maneuver had altered, with wider swings of blood pressure and changes in the shape of the curve of arterial pressure versus time. In the power spectral analysis, power had increased in the frequency band of 0.05 to 0.15 Hz, thereby increasing the low-frequency to high-frequency power ratio. This ratio reflects the relative control of the sympathetic nerves and the vagus nerve over the heart rate. These results showed that autonomic regulation of blood pressure and heart rate was disturbed after space flights of 8 to 14 days. Vagal control of the heart rate in response to blood pressure changes was significantly reduced.

When results from landing day were compared with preflight results, heart rate had increased, body weight and orthostatic tolerance had decreased, the range of R-R intervals had decreased, the maximum slope and the operational point (the R-R interval at zero neck pressure) of the carotid baroreceptor cardiac reflex response had decreased and resting plasma levels of norepinephrine and epinephrine had increased. The lower operational point indicated that the hypotensive buffering capacity was reduced. The blood pressure and heart rate responses to Valsalva's maneuver had altered, with wider swings of blood pressure and changes in the shape of the curve of arterial pressure versus time. In the power spectral analysis, power had increased in the frequency band of 0.05 to 0.15 Hz, thereby increasing the low-frequency to high-frequency power ratio. This ratio reflects the relative control of the sympathetic nerves and the vagus nerve over the heart rate. These results showed that autonomic regulation of blood pressure and heart rate was disturbed after space flights of 8 to 14 days. Vagal control of the heart rate in response to blood pressure changes was significantly reduced.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

The objectives of this experiment were; 1) to determine if exposure to microgravity causes a significant decrease in bone mineralization at the outer surface of limb bones within the first week of flight and to assess those bone parameters causing, or affected by, this decrease, 2) to measure activity of osteoblast immediately postflight, 3) to determine if bone mineralization is restored following two weeks of recovery from spaceflight, 4) to determine total skeletal and site-specific bone mineralization rates mineralization and resorption, as well as calcium absorption and excretion, 5) to relate effects of microgravity on bone to changes in calcium metabolism and 6) to determine gut and renal responses during postflight recovery period.

Approach:

Preflight, rats were subcutaneously injected with flourescent bone marker in order to determine the rate of bone development. During flight, rats were fed food bars containing 40Ca to help determine relative rates of bone formation/resorption. Postflight, some rats were treated with tritiated proline to measure the rate of new bone formation. Body mass, blood pH, urine volume were also measured. Upon sacrifice, the vertebrae, maxillae, tibias, femurs, humeri, calvaria were removed and processed. Bone samples were analyzed for bone mineralization rates, alkaline phosphatase activity, bone dimensions, osteoblast populations, matrix and mineral content, and biomechanics. Ca and crosslink content was determine for the urine as well as bone samples. Bone samples were also analyzed under electron micrscopy and 3-D x-ray topographic microscopic images.

Results:

Ionic calcium and pH were similar in all groups at the end of the flight period suggesting that any changes induced by flight had returned to normal prior to the time that the animals were sacrificed. All groups had similar bone length in both front and hindlimbs as well as in the jaw. Bone mineralization on the periosteal surface at the tibiofibular junction was suppressed in the flight rats during the flight period and did not return to normal until the second week of the recovery period. Alkaline phosphatase activity, a marker of bone matrix maturation, was suppressed in the endosteal osteoblast immediately postflight and at two weeks postrecovery. This data suggest that bone response to unloading and reloading may be different at different bone sites. Urinary collagen crosslinks were slightly decreased following flight suggesting that resorption was not dramatically effected during the recovery period. Surprisingly, very few significant changes in bone were noted in these very young, rapidly growing rats (38 days old at launch).

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The effect of space flight on the skeletal system is one of the most critical issues that needs to be resolved to assure crew well-being during extended duration missions. Due to the absence of weight bearing loads and other factors, bone mineral is lost during space flight. There is significant evidence of the negative impact of microgravity on bone homeostasis. Negative calcium balance has been noted previously in extended duration space flights (84-day Skylab) as well as following bed rest (simulated microgravity). The negative balance has been corroborated with increased excretion of calcium in the urine and feces, as well as decreased calcium absorption.

In addition, the hydroxylated metabolites of vitamin D (e.g., calcidiol, 25(0H)D3 and calcitriol, 1,25(0H)2D3) have been shown to play an important role in calcium homeostasis, primarily at the level of intestinal absorption of dietary calcium. Vitamin D intake is particularly important during extended duration space flights due to the decreased in vivo production of vitamin D through skin exposure to ultraviolet light.

This study was designed to assess changes in several indices of bone and calcium homeostasis during extended-duration space flight and after return to earth. Specific objectives were to: a) determine the effects of microgravity and diet on calcium absorption/kinetics; b) determine the effect of microgravity on total and ionized serum calcium; c) evaluate bone/calcium homeostasis during space flight by measuring regulatory hormones such as parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcitonin, vitamin D metabolites, osteocalcin, and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase; d) determine changes in bone density following flight in order to assess the impact and recovery from flight; and e) determine the accretion of bone mass following extended duration space flight.

APPROACH:
Three astronaut subjects participated in this experiment. Calcium absorption and kinetics were determined before, during, and after the mission. Other related measurements included the monitoring of bone density, bone and calcium regulating hormones, and urinary markers of bone metabolism. Postflight studies were designed to examine the recovery of bone mineral loss during the mission, as well as re-adaptation of bone regulating hormones and calcium metabolism after space flight.

Baseline specimen collection was performed over three five-day periods before and after flight on all three subjects. Blood, urine, feces and saliva were collected from 150 to 145 days before launch (L-150 to L-145), L-60 to L-55, and L-35 to L-33. Postflight samples were collected in two sessions beginning immediately after landing until six days postflight (R+0-6) and R+9-15. Additional data were also collected on R+75 and R+115. Samples were analyzed for 43 Ca and 46 Ca calcium isotopes, vitamin D metabolites, and indices of bone metabolism, e.g., pyridinoline, hydroxyproline:creatinine ratio.

Inflight blood, urine and saliva collections were performed two times in flight on Mir 18 (mission day 12 (MD 12)) and MD 93, and on flight day 5 (FD 5) on STS-71. A fourth inflight session, planned for MD 70 was not performed. A total of 32 blood samples was collected aboard Mir and 25 samples on board the Shuttle. All blood samples were aliquoted and frozen at -20 degrees Celsius for postflight analysis except for blood ionized calcium and osmolality (pH), which were determined in "real time" with a portable clinical blood analyzer (PCBA.) Inflight urine samples were collected using void-by-void techniques. Urine collection devices (UCD) were configured such that: a) a known volume of lithium chloride was included as a volume marker, and b) syringe aliquots could be withdrawn and stored appropriately. Inflight urine samples were either frozen at -20 degrees Celsius or preserved with thimerosal or thymol. Overall, 51 urine samples were collected aboard Mir and 22 samples aboard STS-71. Prior to each calcium absorption and kinetics study, urine samples were collected as soon as possible postsleep. Crewmembers were instructed to avoid food and fluids at least 8 hours prior to urine collection and at least 15 minutes before saliva collection.

Calcium absorption and kinetics were examined using a double stable isotope method. After baseline blood, urine, saliva and stool (pre/post sessions only) collection, subjects ingested 125 mg calcium carbonate (43Ca) as soon after sleep as possible. This was followed 1 hour +/- 15 minutes later by an 8 mg intravenous injection of labeled calcium chloride (46Ca). Crewmembers were to be fasting and unexercised for at least 10 hours prior to testing. Blood was collected 24 hours +/- 1 hour after the 46Ca injection. The blood was allowed to clot at +4 degrees Celsius for a minimum of 1 hour to a maximum of 3 hours prior to centrifugation. The separated plasma was stored for calcium and bone regulatory hormone determinations (PTH, calcitonin, vitamin D metabolites, and osteocalcin) following return to earth. Calcium isotopic enrichments in biological samples were determined using thermal ionization mass spectrometry. Absorption data were determined using the ratio of the two isotopes.

All foods, fluids and medications consumed were recorded in flight using a Bar Code Reader and/or recorded in a log book. The intake of certain dietary elements, especially calcium and Vitamin D, was evaluated postflight as part of the calcium absorption and kinetics determinations. This enabled investigators to understand the impact of dietary calcium on bone loss. The type and duration of exercise were also logged using the Bar Code Reader.

Bone density measurements were made preflight and postflight using Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). Whole body DEXA scans were used to calculate total body and regional bone mass. Any associated loss of bone mass during the study was observed by this same technique. Three sessions were scheduled preflight for baseline data. Postflight, bone density determinations were to be made during the first week after landing and at 3 months, 6 months, and once every 6 months until recovery (but no longer than three years). Calcium absorption/kinetics were determined at landing and monthly thereafter (concurrent with bone density determinations).

RESULTS:
Analysis of hormone levels in blood serum revealed that concentrations of intact PTH were reduced almost 30% during flight compared to preflight. Calcidiol (25-0H Vitamin D) decreased during winter training in Russia (compared to autumn in Houston), and decreased further during flight. Calcitriol ((1,25(0H)2 Vitamin D) concentrations were also reduced almost 30% during flight. Osteocalcin tended to decrease during winter, and was increased or unchanged during flight. Bone-specific alkaline phosphatase concentrations were an average of 39% lower on flight day 14 and 11% lower on flight day 110 than preflight values. Serum total calcium was unchanged, the ionized fraction increased slightly. Venous whole blood pH did not change.

Despite incomplete urine collections inflight and postflight, investigators concluded that urinary calcium excretion was higher during flight than before. Urinary collagen metabolite excretion (n-telopeptide and pyridinium crosslinks) was almost 40% greater than the preflight level. Calcium absorption decreased during (38+/-18% below preflight values on flight day 110) and after flight (56+/-9% below preflight on landing day, n=2; and 29+/-28% below preflight on return +6 days). Three months postflight calcium absorption had returned to 4+/-20% below preflight values. These data showed that inflight bone loss was associated with increased resorption and decreased formation. Calcium balance was further altered by decreased PTH activation of calcidiol, with subsequent decreased calcium absorption.
