experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Under this NSCOR grant, investigators made a number of findings that help provide a mechanistic framework for biologically-based risk models. Investigators requested and received a cost extension to finish off experimental characterization of proton and iron irradiation studies to address angiogenesis processes that are important in radiation carcinogenesis and can be viewed as bottlenecks to carcinogenesis advancement. The significance of this in the carcinogenesis risk context lies in the challenge it presents to the standard radiogenic cancer paradigm. This paradigm holds that cancer may be understood as an autonomous expansion of an initiated cell clone, followed by the chance genetic creation of a cancer cell in that clone that then inevitably expands to become a diagnosed cancer. At the basis of these events is thought to be the DNA lesion. Investigators argue that essential population-level and tumor-environmental dynamics can alter this picture dramatically, either promoting cancer development or slowing the course of existing cancers. Their basis extends beyond DNA damage to include the familiar “hallmarks” of cancer that constitute “bottlenecks” to tumor advancement – population-level logistic growth effects, acquisition of angiogenic potential, and competency for invasion, to name three. Investigators have shown that radiation can progress or limit cancers by modifying these bottlenecks. Because these bottlenecks may be significant enough to increase the likelihood of transforming an initiated cell, or to change the likelihood an existing cancer advances to clinical detection over a lifetime, they must be included in the overall assessment of radiogenic cancer risk. It follows that existing models that fail to include such bottleneck effects are inherently flawed in that they do not include all radiation actions bearing on the development of manifest cancer disease.

APPROACH:
Proton-induced gene regulation was investigated in a number of human cell types that actively contribute to carcinogenesis progression, including not only cancer cells but also primary non- transformed stromal and microvascular endothelial cells. A baseline was obtained by analysis of the proton-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0Gy and 2Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated six hours after proton exposure.

RESULTS:
Investigations to this end show that cancer-progression-modifying tumor-host interactions indeed occur at a number of levels, including: 1) reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma); 2) reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures; in contrast with 3) augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions; 4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation; effects opposite to 5) the stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma). In addition, 6) mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression. Lastly, investigating the potential influence of intercellular interactions within the tumor on radiation modulation of cancer progression, investigators found that 7) cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course.

1) Reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma):
Using pan-genomic arrays, expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found generally to be downregulated by protons (1GeV). RT-PCR reconfirmed this down-regulatory trend for a number of specific angiogenesis-regulating genes, including VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, and IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1, in human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC), normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHCF), and A549 lung carcinoma 6 hours after receiving doses of sizes 0.5, 1 and 2Gy. In contrast, when the fibroblast, endothelial and tumor cells were gamma-irradiated at the same doses, the expressions of VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A and IL-6, were upregulated in a dose-dependent manner relative to control (0Gy) 6hr post-irradiation.

Having established the proton-induced downregulation of these angiogenic genes (6 hours post-irradiation), regulation of the corresponding proteins was examined. ELISA assays specific for VEGF and IL-8 were performed after irradiation of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cultures. At 24h hours post-irradiation, levels of secreted IL-8 in the culture supernatants were reduced by 31% and 50% in endothelium and tumor cells respectively. Secreted VEGF was also significantly reduced in proton-irradiated fibroblast (17%) and tumor cells (34%) versus sham-irradiated controls (although results with endothelial cells were indeterminate). These findings indicate a dose-dependent downregulation of important angiogenic genes and, for the most part, a significant reduction in protein levels following proton irradiation.

For comparison, 56Fe-induced gene regulation was investigated in the same cell types as for protons. Again, a baseline was obtained by analysis of the iron ion-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0, 0.2, 0.4, and 1Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated 6 hours after radiation (or sham) exposure. Expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including, VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found to be upregulated. The expression patterns of a number of the angiogenesis-regulating genes, including: VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1 were again investigated using quantitative RT-PCR. Results from the quantitative assessment of a number of these genes are shown. Significant upregulation of expression was observed for these genes in both the irradiated HLMVEC and NHDF cells, compared to sham-irradiated controls (p<0.05). To further investigate the ability of 56Fe ion irradiation to upregulate specific pro-angiogenic genes, expression levels were also investigated in human lung adenocarcinoma (A549). Just as for primary human fibroblast and endothelial cells, these cancer cells also showed upregulation of VEGF, IL-8, IL-6 and HIF-1A, at 6hr post-irradiation.

2) Reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures:
Beyond the suppression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that proton irradiation could also suppress the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. The invasion of the proton-irradiated endothelial, fibroblast, and tumor cells was investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, proton-irradiated cells (2Gy) showed significantly reduced invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix. Quantification of the results demonstrated that following proton irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549, NHDF and HLMVEC cells was reduced, by 46, 15 and 14% respectively.

Next, the invasion/migration of endothelial (HLMVEC) in response to soluble factors produced by either proton-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) or proton-irradiated tumor cells (A549) was analyzed. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk that occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and microvascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor or fibroblast cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated endothelial cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that chemoattract endothelial cells, investigators studied how proton irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. Compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 2-Gy proton-irradiated fibroblasts and tumor cells were less effective (19% and 16% respectively) at inducing endothelial cells to invade and traverse to the underside of the membrane. They propose that the reduced invasion of endothelial cells was, in part, a direct consequence of the demonstrated reduced secretion of angiogenic factors from the proton-irradiated cells. Indeed, addition of either recombinant VEGF or IL-8 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the anti-migratory effect of proton irradiation.

3) Augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions:
Extending the finding of increased expression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that iron ion irradiation could also augment the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. Thus far, the invasion of the iron ion-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cells has been investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, iron ion-irradiated cells (0.2Gy) showed significantly increased invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix; even more so than 1Gy. Quantification of the results demonstrated that, following 0.2Gy iron ion irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549 and NHDF cells was increased by 47% and 18% respectively.

Investigators next analyzed the invasion/migration of HLMVEC in response to soluble factors produced by either iron ion-irradiated A549 or iron ion-irradiated NHDF cells. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk which occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and micro-vascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 or NHDF cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated HLMVEC cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that are chemoattractant to endothelial cells, investigators studied how iron-ion irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. They found that, compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 0.2-Gy iron-irradiated fibroblast and tumor cells were more effective at inducing endothelial cells to traverse to the underside of the membrane.

Investigators hypothesized in this case that increased secretion of angiogenic factors from the iron ion-irradiated cells was responsible for the increased invasion of endothelial cells. Addition of small molecule inhibitor of VEGF, SU11248 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the pro-migratory effect of iron ion irradiation.

Invasion of tumor (A549), fibroblast (NHDF) and human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLVMEC) towards conditioned media from 56Fe-exposed cells was also analyzed. A dose-dependent upregulation in invasion was observed. Interestingly, breaking this trend was a dramatic upregulation of invasion of fibroblast cells towards CM from tumor cells irradiated at 0.2Gy, and a downregulation of tumor cells towards CM from LMEC cells irradiated at 0.2Gy. As a matter deserving further investigation, an upward deviation in the vicinity of 0.2Gy from linearity has been consistently noted for the pro-progression effect of 56Fe radiation.

4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation:
To investigate the modulation of additional aspects of tumor progression by proton radiation, the ability of endothelial (HLMVEC) cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with proton-irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor (A549) or fibroblast (NHDF) cells. Cancer cells are already known to secrete pro-angiogenic factors e.g. VEGF and IL-8 that can recruit endothelial cells and stimulate their proliferation. Decreased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with proton-irradiated fibroblasts or proton-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls. In contrast, when this same assay was conducted using photon-irradiated fibroblast or tumor cells, an increased, rather than a decreased, proliferation of endothelial cells was observed.

Next examined was the degree to which proton-irradiated cells (cancer, fibroblast, or endothelial), plated in the upper chambers of transwell plates modulates the proliferation of fibroblast or endothelial cells in the lower chambers. A measurable reduction in proliferation of both fibroblasts and endothelial cells associated with proton-irradiated cancer cells was detected compared to that of controls. Investigators further investigated whether addition of the angiogenic factors VEGF or IL-8 could restore the original proliferation capacity. The proton radiation-induced reduction in responding cell proliferation was partially ameliorated by the addition of VEGF (20ng/ml) or IL-8 (20ng/ml) to the irradiated cell compartment (normalized to sham-irradiated controls). The data suggests that proton-induced suppression of these specific angiogenic factors may well play a direct role in inhibiting adjacent cell proliferation. Such proton-induced suppression of cell proliferation could well have ramifications for treatment optimization. The reduction in proliferation/survival was most pronounced for the NHDF stromal fibroblasts that shared media with 2Gy-irradiated tumor cells. Proliferation levels of the fibroblast cells that shared media through transwells with proton-irradiated tumor cells were less than 50% of their matched fibroblast controls that shared media with sham-irradiated tumor cells. In line with other growth factor rescue experiments, addition of recombinant VEGF or IL-8 partially restored the proliferation levels to 71% and 90% respectively. Similar results were observed for the other cell combinations.

To ascertain the dose dependence of survival of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF), or tumor (A549) cells, and whether proton-irradiation induced inhibition of IL-8 might actually contribute to the radiation sensitivity of these cells, clonogenic assays were performed with or without the addition of recombinant human IL-8 (20ng/ml). Cells were irradiated at 1, 2 and 4Gy of protons. It was found that treatment of cells with recombinant IL-8 significantly spared the 2-Gy proton irradiated cells from clonogenic inhibition. The SF2 (survival fraction after 2Gy) of proton and photon/gamma (results not shown) was found to be 0.68 and 0.78 respectively, with the cell killing effect of proton being slightly higher than that of photon radiation.

5) Stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma):
The ability of the HLMVEC cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with iron ion irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 tumor (or NHDF fibroblast) cells. Contrary to protons, increased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with iron ion-irradiated fibroblasts or iron ion-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls.

6) Mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, and was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression:
Tumor progression dynamics for young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice, with or without iron irradiation at 1GeV/u, were studied for LLC implanted in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice with and without 5x0.2Gy of iron irradiation. Progression was gauged in terms of two quantities: tumor growth rates after approximately exponential growth starts, and “effective” initial tumor volumes, which is proposed to account for differential tumor/stromal “reorganization” times following injection and before growth of the tumor mass.

To do this, the two quantitative aspects of tumor development just mentioned were taken to be the growth rate c and the “effective initial tumor volume” b, obtained by extrapolating the fitted exponential curve backwards to time zero and interpreted as mainly a measure of either stromal incorporation into the tumor, or how supportive the microenvironment was prior to the near exponential growth phase. Growth data were fitted to V = b*exp(ct), with b the geometric mean of the b’s for individual mouse fits, and c the arithmetic mean of the c’s for individual mouse fits.

The data show generally that tumor growth rates are dependent on host age, and that there was a statistically significant decrease in average growth rates c for the unirradiated middle age (MA) as compared to the unirradiated young (Y) hosts, with only a modest increase in the effective initial volume. As regards perturbation by irradiation, the following results were found: i) the effective initial volume b was very significantly decreased by irradiation in both young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice; ii) the overall progression decrease by irradiation in the young (Y) mice was due exclusively to a dramatic decrease in effective initial volume; while iii) the more modest decrease in progression by irradiation in middle-aged (MA) mice was due to a slight increase in growth rate compensating for a substantial decrease in effective initial volume; and iv) modest decreases in both average growth rates and effective initial volumes were noted for irradiated middle-aged (MA) mice compared to irradiated young (Y) mice.

To gain some molecular-level understanding, protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed from the gene array data. Demonstrated were highly regulated protein interactions for tumors of the young (Y) iron-irradiated mice compared with those of the unirradiated groups and of the middle-aged (MA) iron-irradiated compared with those of the unirradiated groups. Overall, the network based on data from tumors growing in irradiated versus unirradiated young (Y) mice demonstrated more regulation of activity than did the network based on data from tumors growing in the irradiated versus unirradiated middle-aged (MA) mice. The general directions of the significantly regulated proteins due to irradiation also coincided with the direction of regulations of genes; mostly down in young (Y) hosts, and a slight bias upward in the middle-aged (MA) hosts. As was also true for the gene regulations, iron irradiation induced a greater genetic response overall in young (Y) compared to middle-aged (MA) hosts.

Interestingly, two central network hubs, FASN (fatty acid synthase) and AKT1 genes, were found to be downregulated within the tumors of young (Y) mice in response to iron-irradiation. FASN is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for lipogenesis and it plays a central role in energy homeostasis. It has been shown that FASN can be highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic tumors. AKT1 is one of three homologous isoforms of the AKT (PKB) protein kinase family that control a wide variety of cellular functions including proliferation, survival, and metabolism. Given the wide range of pro-growth cellular functions AKT1 modulates, it is not surprising it is also implicated in tumor progression and metastases.

Using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) software, specific pathways were constructed around FASN and AKT1 that included those genes directly or indirectly up or down regulated for tumor samples from young (Y) or middle-age (MA) mice with and without iron irradiation. Comparisons between groups were done by calculating the log2-fold change, with increasing levels of up- (red) or down- (green) regulation indicated by the darker shades of the respective color and with grey indicating genes present in the network without a 2-fold change under the perturbation studied. In the case of young (Y) unirradiated versus irradiated mice, FASN is seen to be downregulated. By contrast, no FASN regulation was detected between the tumors from the middle-aged (MA) irradiated and unirradiated groups, consistent with the reduced degree of suppression of progression by irradiation noted for these hosts.

7) Cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course:
In recent years cancer stem cells (CSCs) have been hypothesized to comprise only a minor subpopulation in solid tumors that drives tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; the so-called "cancer stem cell hypothesis." While a seemingly trivial statement about numbers, much is put at stake. If true, the conclusions of many studies of cancer cell populations could be challenged, as the bulk assay methods upon which they depend have, by, and large, taken for granted the notion that a "typical" cell of the population possesses the attributes of a cell capable of perpetuating the cancer, i.e., a CSC. In support of the CSC hypothesis, populations enriched for so-called "tumor-initiating" cells have demonstrated a corresponding increase in tumorigenicity as measured by dilution assay, although estimates have varied widely as to what the fractional contribution of tumor-initiating cells is in any given population. Some have taken this variability to suggest the CSC fraction may be nearly 100% after all, countering the CSC hypothesis, and that there are simply assay-dependent error rates in the ability to "reconfirm" CSC status at the cell level. To explore this controversy more quantitatively, investigators developed a simple cellular automaton model of CSC-driven tumor growth dynamics. Assuming CSC and non-stem cancer cells (CC) subpopulations coexist to some degree, we evaluated the impact of an environmentally dependent CSC symmetric division probability and a CC proliferation capacity on tumor progression and morphology. Their model predicts, as expected, that the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric highly influences the frequency of CSCs in the population, but goes on to predict the two frequencies can be widely divergent, and that spatial constraints will tend to increase the CSC fraction over time. Further, tumor progression times show a marked dependence on both the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric and on the proliferation capacities of CC. Together, these findings can explain, within the CSC hypothesis, the widely varying measures of stem cell fractions observed. In particular, although the CSC fraction is influenced by the (environmentally modifiable) CSC symmetric division probability, with the former converging to unity as the latter nears 100%, the CSC fraction becomes quite small even for symmetric division probabilities modestly lower than 100%. In the latter case, the tumor exhibits a clustered morphology and the CSC fraction steadily increases with time; more so on both counts when the death rate of CCs is higher. Such variations in CSC fraction and morphology are not only consistent with the CSC hypothesis, but lend support to it as one expected byproduct of the dynamical interactions that are predicted to take place among a relatively small CSC population, its CC counterpart, and the host compartment over time.

Overall conclusions:
Cell-cell interactions between the tumor and host, and between tumor cell subcompartments, affect radiation-induced cancer progression, and thus cancer risk, in a highly radiation-quality-dependent fashion. Investigators focused on two radiation types, 56Fe and protons, and found them to generally encourage and discourage, respectively, a number of molecular and functional indicators of progression. This fact must be considered alongside the risks of cancer cell creation when making conclusions as to astronaut safety during long-term space flight. Closer to home, the favorable tumor-host dynamical effects noted for proton radiation in space may work to supplement its well-established physical attributes as a therapeutic modality.

The expression patterns of a number of the angiogenesis-regulating genes, including: VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1 were again investigated using quantitative RT-PCR. Results from the quantitative assessment of a number of these genes are shown. Significant upregulation of expression was observed for these genes in both the irradiated HLMVEC and NHDF cells, compared to sham-irradiated controls (p<0.05). To further investigate the ability of 56Fe ion irradiation to upregulate specific pro-angiogenic genes, expression levels were also investigated in human lung adenocarcinoma (A549). Just as for primary human fibroblast and endothelial cells, these cancer cells also showed upregulation of VEGF, IL-8, IL-6 and HIF-1A, at 6hr post-irradiation.

2) Reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures:
Beyond the suppression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that proton irradiation could also suppress the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. The invasion of the proton-irradiated endothelial, fibroblast, and tumor cells was investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, proton-irradiated cells (2Gy) showed significantly reduced invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix. Quantification of the results demonstrated that following proton irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549, NHDF and HLMVEC cells was reduced, by 46, 15 and 14% respectively.

Next, the invasion/migration of endothelial (HLMVEC) in response to soluble factors produced by either proton-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) or proton-irradiated tumor cells (A549) was analyzed. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk that occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and microvascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor or fibroblast cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated endothelial cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that chemoattract endothelial cells, investigators studied how proton irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. Compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 2-Gy proton-irradiated fibroblasts and tumor cells were less effective (19% and 16% respectively) at inducing endothelial cells to invade and traverse to the underside of the membrane. They propose that the reduced invasion of endothelial cells was, in part, a direct consequence of the demonstrated reduced secretion of angiogenic factors from the proton-irradiated cells. Indeed, addition of either recombinant VEGF or IL-8 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the anti-migratory effect of proton irradiation.

3) Augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions:
Extending the finding of increased expression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that iron ion irradiation could also augment the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. Thus far, the invasion of the iron ion-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cells has been investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, iron ion-irradiated cells (0.2Gy) showed significantly increased invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix; even more so than 1Gy. Quantification of the results demonstrated that, following 0.2Gy iron ion irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549 and NHDF cells was increased by 47% and 18% respectively.

Investigators next analyzed the invasion/migration of HLMVEC in response to soluble factors produced by either iron ion-irradiated A549 or iron ion-irradiated NHDF cells. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk which occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and micro-vascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 or NHDF cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated HLMVEC cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that are chemoattractant to endothelial cells, investigators studied how iron-ion irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. They found that, compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 0.2-Gy iron-irradiated fibroblast and tumor cells were more effective at inducing endothelial cells to traverse to the underside of the membrane.

Investigators hypothesized in this case that increased secretion of angiogenic factors from the iron ion-irradiated cells was responsible for the increased invasion of endothelial cells. Addition of small molecule inhibitor of VEGF, SU11248 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the pro-migratory effect of iron ion irradiation.

Invasion of tumor (A549), fibroblast (NHDF) and human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLVMEC) towards conditioned media from 56Fe-exposed cells was also analyzed. A dose-dependent upregulation in invasion was observed. Interestingly, breaking this trend was a dramatic upregulation of invasion of fibroblast cells towards CM from tumor cells irradiated at 0.2Gy, and a downregulation of tumor cells towards CM from LMEC cells irradiated at 0.2Gy. As a matter deserving further investigation, an upward deviation in the vicinity of 0.2Gy from linearity has been consistently noted for the pro-progression effect of 56Fe radiation.

4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation:
To investigate the modulation of additional aspects of tumor progression by proton radiation, the ability of endothelial (HLMVEC) cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with proton-irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor (A549) or fibroblast (NHDF) cells. Cancer cells are already known to secrete pro-angiogenic factors e.g. VEGF and IL-8 that can recruit endothelial cells and stimulate their proliferation. Decreased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with proton-irradiated fibroblasts or proton-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls. In contrast, when this same assay was conducted using photon-irradiated fibroblast or tumor cells, an increased, rather than a decreased, proliferation of endothelial cells was observed.

Next examined was the degree to which proton-irradiated cells (cancer, fibroblast, or endothelial), plated in the upper chambers of transwell plates modulates the proliferation of fibroblast or endothelial cells in the lower chambers. A measurable reduction in proliferation of both fibroblasts and endothelial cells associated with proton-irradiated cancer cells was detected compared to that of controls. Investigators further investigated whether addition of the angiogenic factors VEGF or IL-8 could restore the original proliferation capacity. The proton radiation-induced reduction in responding cell proliferation was partially ameliorated by the addition of VEGF (20ng/ml) or IL-8 (20ng/ml) to the irradiated cell compartment (normalized to sham-irradiated controls). The data suggests that proton-induced suppression of these specific angiogenic factors may well play a direct role in inhibiting adjacent cell proliferation. Such proton-induced suppression of cell proliferation could well have ramifications for treatment optimization. The reduction in proliferation/survival was most pronounced for the NHDF stromal fibroblasts that shared media with 2Gy-irradiated tumor cells. Proliferation levels of the fibroblast cells that shared media through transwells with proton-irradiated tumor cells were less than 50% of their matched fibroblast controls that shared media with sham-irradiated tumor cells. In line with other growth factor rescue experiments, addition of recombinant VEGF or IL-8 partially restored the proliferation levels to 71% and 90% respectively. Similar results were observed for the other cell combinations.

To ascertain the dose dependence of survival of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF), or tumor (A549) cells, and whether proton-irradiation induced inhibition of IL-8 might actually contribute to the radiation sensitivity of these cells, clonogenic assays were performed with or without the addition of recombinant human IL-8 (20ng/ml). Cells were irradiated at 1, 2 and 4Gy of protons. It was found that treatment of cells with recombinant IL-8 significantly spared the 2-Gy proton irradiated cells from clonogenic inhibition. The SF2 (survival fraction after 2Gy) of proton and photon/gamma (results not shown) was found to be 0.68 and 0.78 respectively, with the cell killing effect of proton being slightly higher than that of photon radiation.

5) Stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma):
The ability of the HLMVEC cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with iron ion irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 tumor (or NHDF fibroblast) cells. Contrary to protons, increased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with iron ion-irradiated fibroblasts or iron ion-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls.

6) Mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, and was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression:
Tumor progression dynamics for young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice, with or without iron irradiation at 1GeV/u, were studied for LLC implanted in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice with and without 5x0.2Gy of iron irradiation. Progression was gauged in terms of two quantities: tumor growth rates after approximately exponential growth starts, and “effective” initial tumor volumes, which is proposed to account for differential tumor/stromal “reorganization” times following injection and before growth of the tumor mass.

To do this, the two quantitative aspects of tumor development just mentioned were taken to be the growth rate c and the “effective initial tumor volume” b, obtained by extrapolating the fitted exponential curve backwards to time zero and interpreted as mainly a measure of either stromal incorporation into the tumor, or how supportive the microenvironment was prior to the near exponential growth phase. Growth data were fitted to V = b*exp(ct), with b the geometric mean of the b’s for individual mouse fits, and c the arithmetic mean of the c’s for individual mouse fits.

The data show generally that tumor growth rates are dependent on host age, and that there was a statistically significant decrease in average growth rates c for the unirradiated middle age (MA) as compared to the unirradiated young (Y) hosts, with only a modest increase in the effective initial volume. As regards perturbation by irradiation, the following results were found: i) the effective initial volume b was very significantly decreased by irradiation in both young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice; ii) the overall progression decrease by irradiation in the young (Y) mice was due exclusively to a dramatic decrease in effective initial volume; while iii) the more modest decrease in progression by irradiation in middle-aged (MA) mice was due to a slight increase in growth rate compensating for a substantial decrease in effective initial volume; and iv) modest decreases in both average growth rates and effective initial volumes were noted for irradiated middle-aged (MA) mice compared to irradiated young (Y) mice.

To gain some molecular-level understanding, protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed from the gene array data. Demonstrated were highly regulated protein interactions for tumors of the young (Y) iron-irradiated mice compared with those of the unirradiated groups and of the middle-aged (MA) iron-irradiated compared with those of the unirradiated groups. Overall, the network based on data from tumors growing in irradiated versus unirradiated young (Y) mice demonstrated more regulation of activity than did the network based on data from tumors growing in the irradiated versus unirradiated middle-aged (MA) mice. The general directions of the significantly regulated proteins due to irradiation also coincided with the direction of regulations of genes; mostly down in young (Y) hosts, and a slight bias upward in the middle-aged (MA) hosts. As was also true for the gene regulations, iron irradiation induced a greater genetic response overall in young (Y) compared to middle-aged (MA) hosts.

Interestingly, two central network hubs, FASN (fatty acid synthase) and AKT1 genes, were found to be downregulated within the tumors of young (Y) mice in response to iron-irradiation. FASN is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for lipogenesis and it plays a central role in energy homeostasis. It has been shown that FASN can be highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic tumors. AKT1 is one of three homologous isoforms of the AKT (PKB) protein kinase family that control a wide variety of cellular functions including proliferation, survival, and metabolism. Given the wide range of pro-growth cellular functions AKT1 modulates, it is not surprising it is also implicated in tumor progression and metastases.

Using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) software, specific pathways were constructed around FASN and AKT1 that included those genes directly or indirectly up or down regulated for tumor samples from young (Y) or middle-age (MA) mice with and without iron irradiation. Comparisons between groups were done by calculating the log2-fold change, with increasing levels of up- (red) or down- (green) regulation indicated by the darker shades of the respective color and with grey indicating genes present in the network without a 2-fold change under the perturbation studied. In the case of young (Y) unirradiated versus irradiated mice, FASN is seen to be downregulated. By contrast, no FASN regulation was detected between the tumors from the middle-aged (MA) irradiated and unirradiated groups, consistent with the reduced degree of suppression of progression by irradiation noted for these hosts.

7) Cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course:
In recent years cancer stem cells (CSCs) have been hypothesized to comprise only a minor subpopulation in solid tumors that drives tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; the so-called "cancer stem cell hypothesis." While a seemingly trivial statement about numbers, much is put at stake. If true, the conclusions of many studies of cancer cell populations could be challenged, as the bulk assay methods upon which they depend have, by, and large, taken for granted the notion that a "typical" cell of the population possesses the attributes of a cell capable of perpetuating the cancer, i.e., a CSC. In support of the CSC hypothesis, populations enriched for so-called "tumor-initiating" cells have demonstrated a corresponding increase in tumorigenicity as measured by dilution assay, although estimates have varied widely as to what the fractional contribution of tumor-initiating cells is in any given population. Some have taken this variability to suggest the CSC fraction may be nearly 100% after all, countering the CSC hypothesis, and that there are simply assay-dependent error rates in the ability to "reconfirm" CSC status at the cell level. To explore this controversy more quantitatively, investigators developed a simple cellular automaton model of CSC-driven tumor growth dynamics. Assuming CSC and non-stem cancer cells (CC) subpopulations coexist to some degree, we evaluated the impact of an environmentally dependent CSC symmetric division probability and a CC proliferation capacity on tumor progression and morphology. Their model predicts, as expected, that the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric highly influences the frequency of CSCs in the population, but goes on to predict the two frequencies can be widely divergent, and that spatial constraints will tend to increase the CSC fraction over time. Further, tumor progression times show a marked dependence on both the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric and on the proliferation capacities of CC. Together, these findings can explain, within the CSC hypothesis, the widely varying measures of stem cell fractions observed. In particular, although the CSC fraction is influenced by the (environmentally modifiable) CSC symmetric division probability, with the former converging to unity as the latter nears 100%, the CSC fraction becomes quite small even for symmetric division probabilities modestly lower than 100%. In the latter case, the tumor exhibits a clustered morphology and the CSC fraction steadily increases with time; more so on both counts when the death rate of CCs is higher. Such variations in CSC fraction and morphology are not only consistent with the CSC hypothesis, but lend support to it as one expected byproduct of the dynamical interactions that are predicted to take place among a relatively small CSC population, its CC counterpart, and the host compartment over time.

Overall conclusions:
Cell-cell interactions between the tumor and host, and between tumor cell subcompartments, affect radiation-induced cancer progression, and thus cancer risk, in a highly radiation-quality-dependent fashion. Investigators focused on two radiation types, 56Fe and protons, and found them to generally encourage and discourage, respectively, a number of molecular and functional indicators of progression. This fact must be considered alongside the risks of cancer cell creation when making conclusions as to astronaut safety during long-term space flight. Closer to home, the favorable tumor-host dynamical effects noted for proton radiation in space may work to supplement its well-established physical attributes as a therapeutic modality.

experiment_title: Sleep Monitoring
parameter_html:
Sleep duration
Sleep monitoring
Sleep quality
investigators: Principal Investigator: Frost, JamesCo-Investigator: Shumate, William
image_name: Astronaut Joseph Kerwin Strapped into Sleep Restraint in Crew Quarters
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Prior to Skylab, very little objective information had been obtained concerning the ability of man to sleep in space. Only by continuous EEG (electroencephalographic) monitoring can such information be obtained, and the technical problems associated with acquisition and analysis in space are significant. Before the advent of manned spaceflight, there was some concern about the possible adverse effects of this weightless environment upon sleep characteristics. During the Gemini program, however, it became apparent that fairly long duration space flight was not associated with drastic alterations of sleeping behavior. Astronauts could sleep in space and, on at least some occasions, did so fairly well. In the Gemini and Apollo programs, though, it became clear that in many instances insomnia was a problem. Sleep loss, while not absolute, was sufficient in some instances to result in performance decrements. In some instances, sleeping difficulties resulted in the use of hypnotic drugs to promote sleep and amphetamine-type medication to increase alertness following sleep loss

APPROACH:
A complete system for analyzing sleep during space flight was designed for this 'experiment and included data-acquisition hardware, onboard-analysis components, and a capability for real-time telemetry. Automatic analysis of the electroencephalogram (EEG), electro-oculogram (EOG), and head-motion signals was accomplished by onboard equipment. The system's output, consisting of sleep-stage information, was telemetered in near 'real time to Mission Control, where a profile of sleep stage versus time was accumulated. The analog signals (EEG, EOG, and head motion) were also preserved by onboard magnetic-tape recorders, thus allowing a more detailed postflight analysis.

The recording cap was worn during the 59-day mission (Skylab 3). The electrodes, attached inside the elastic cap, were joined by wires to a miniature connector at the vertex, which permitted rapid linkage with the preamplifier assembly. The cap contained seven electrodes; four electrodes (left and right central positions, C l and C 2 , and left and right occipital positions, 0 1 and 0 2) provided a composite EEG channel (Cl and C2 paired and referenced to 0 1 and 0 2 paired); two (one lateral to and one above the left eye) provided one EOG channel; and one served as a ground. Following the sleep period, the preamplifier was disconnected, and the used cap was discarded; i. e., a new cap was used for each recording session.

RESULTS:
During a sleep monitoring session, true real-time data was available only during the few minutes when the spacecraft passed over a ground tracking station. Throughout the frequent periods when the spacecraft was out of communication range, the sleep-stage data was accumulated by the spacecraft telemetry recorder and transmitted to ground at a high rate during a subsequent tracking-station pass. The tracking stations, in turn, relayed the telemetered sleep-stage information to Mission Control. Consequently, the data ultimately received during a sleep period was somewhat sporadic, ranging from actual real time to delays of up to several hours. Data-processing equipment in Mission Control collated the incoming data so that the time relationships were preserved, and eventually a complete tabulation of sleep stage versus elapsed time evolved.

archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.

experiment_title: Assisted Medical Procedures
parameter_html:
Medical procedures
Medical technologies
investigators: Principal Investigator: Hurst, VictorCo-Investigator: Chin, DuaneCo-Investigator: Rubin, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Exploration Medical System Demonstration (EMSD) project acted as a test bed to demonstrate to crew and ground personnel that an end-to-end medical system can assist clinician and non-clinician crewmembers in optimizing medical care delivery and data management during a mission. This system was designed to assist crewmembers in nominal, non-emergent situations and in emergent situations when they may be suffering from performance decrements due to environmental, physiological, or other factors.

Any exploration class mission will have medical care challenges, such as resource and resupply constraints limiting the extent to which medical conditions can be treated, inability for crewmembers to evacuate to Earth during many mission phases, and rendering of medical care by a non-clinician. The system demonstrated the integration of medical technologies and medical informatics tools for managing evidence and decision making.

The objectives of the EMSD were to:

  1. Reduce time required of on-orbit crew and ground personnel to access, transfer, and manipulate medical data.
  2. Demonstrate the on-orbit crew’s ability to access medical information via an intuitive and crew-friendly solution to aid in the treatment of a medical condition.
  3. Develop a common data management framework and architecture that can be ubiquitously used to automate repetitive data collection, management, and communications tasks for all activities pertaining to crew health and life sciences.
  4. Ensure crew access to medical data during periods of restricted ground communication.
  5. Develop a common data management framework and architecture that allows for scalability, extensibility, and interoperability of data sources and data users.
  6. Lower total cost of ownership for development and sustainment of peripheral hardware and software that use EMSD for data management.
  7. Provide a better standard of healthcare for crewmembers by reducing the time required by crew and ground personnel to provide medical treatment and the number of crew errors experienced during treatment.

APPROACH:
The functionality of the EMSD was verified through a series of ground-based demonstrations. An electronic medical procedure system called the Assisted Medical Procedures (AMP) is an electronic system that helped crewmembers select the appropriate medical procedure for a particular medical encounter, as well as guide them through that procedure.

The AMP was designed to present an initial screen that requires users to enter their unique user identification and password credentials before granting access to any EMSD data and system functions. This allows the AMP to meet the various security requirements for the privacy and confidentiality of medical information captured by the EMSD, as well as allows user interface elements and screens to be tailored to the specific needs of each user.

The AMP was designed to present a secondary screen that requires the user to select a patient on which to perform an exam. All patients displayed are pulled directly from the Open Electronic Medical Record (EMR) database, which contains each crewmember’s identify and role. The AMP allows for the user and the patient to be the same crewmember, as some exams may be self-administered.

In addition to handling simple alphanumeric information, the AMP was designed to accommodate rich media content such as images, audio/video files, real time video input, and other proprietary device data and document files. A rich media area was incorporated into the AMP user interface which captures and displays rich media content. This rich media area can also be hidden and resized dynamically by the user, per user preference.

RESULTS:
The development, integration, and testing of all EMSD components - electronic medical record, assisted medical procedures software, middleware infrastructure, and associated middleware "adapters" has been completed.
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.

experiment_title: Serum CPK Reported in LSAH Participants
parameter_html: Creatinine phosphokinase (CPK)
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) is an enzyme found in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and the brain. All of these areas have elevated serum levels of CPK when stressed, therefore, monitoring the serum level of CPK is important because elevated levels may indicate a serious health disorder, such as heart attack, stroke, or brain tumor.

However, other factors such as age, sex, and exercise also affect CPK levels. In fact, elevated CPK is common in adults who exercise regularly. Normal levels of serum CPK vary from 0 to approximately 188 micrograms per liter. Different laboratories may report slightly different upper limits as within the normal range because of differences in test procedures and population differences.

During exercise, especially of the highintensity burst type, considerable amounts of CPK leak into the extracellular fluid and plasma as a result of changes in membrane activity. The type of exercise and the duration affect the elevation of serum CPK. Non-weight-bearing activities such as rowing and swimming cause less pronounced CPK elevations than comparable weightbearing events. CPK elevations have been found to be linear with the duration of exercise up to 5.5 hours. Longer durations of exercise are associated with an accelerated increase in CPK.

Exercise-induced increases in the level of serum CPK are temporary. Resting levels of CPK changes generally become elevated during exercise days and then return to normal levels during rest days. Peaks in serum CPK have been reported to occur at 5 minutes, 11 hours, 24 hours, 25 hours, and even 4-6 days following exercise. With continued physical activity, CPK levels remained elevated. Resting levels of serum CPK are higher in exercised trained individuals than in untrained ones.

CPK elevations vary with age and sex. Older individuals are less likely to have elevations after exercise than are middle-aged or young adults. Women are more likely to have exercise induced elevations than are men.

Some researchers suggest that muscle cell permeability increases during exercise and others think that muscle degeneration and necrosis occurs. Muscular soreness has been reported to accompany elevated CPK levels. While increases in serum CPK are common in adults who exercise, there are also pathological states, such as myocardial infarction or heart attack, which may be accompanied by an increase in serum levels of CPK.

APPROACH:
Serum CPK is used as an indicator of muscle integrity with the level of specific isoenzymes aiding in the diagnoses regarding which type of muscle (cardiac, skeletal, or brain) has been stressed.

There are two isoenzymes, i.e., chemically different but functionally identical forms of CPK. The isoenzyme produced in the brain is identified as CPK B and the isoenzyme produced in muscle is identified as CPK M. As a rule of thumb, cardiac muscle stress produces CPK MB, and skeletal muscle stress produces CPK MM. CPK BB is an indicator of stress of brain tissue and is not usually examined in routine physical examinations unless there is a suspicion of stroke, tumor, etc.

There are divergent opinions about the proportion of CPK MB in skeletal muscle as well as about the proportion of total CPK in association with acute myocardial infarction. Studies have shown large elevations in CPK MB in some women after step exercise and in highly trained female endurance runners. In the absence of symptoms and other positive physical examination information, elevated CPK MB is not usually considered sufficient evidence of a heart attack.

Identification of these isoenzymes requires laboratory testing procedures not routinely completed for LSAH.

RESULTS:
Approximately 16 percent of the 211 CPK tests completed for the LSAH participants during 1992-94 reported elevated serum levels. __description:
OBJECTIVES:
Creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) is an enzyme found in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and the brain. All of these areas have elevated serum levels of CPK when stressed, therefore, monitoring the serum level of CPK is important because elevated levels may indicate a serious health disorder, such as heart attack, stroke, or brain tumor.

However, other factors such as age, sex, and exercise also affect CPK levels. In fact, elevated CPK is common in adults who exercise regularly. Normal levels of serum CPK vary from 0 to approximately 188 micrograms per liter. Different laboratories may report slightly different upper limits as within the normal range because of differences in test procedures and population differences.

During exercise, especially of the highintensity burst type, considerable amounts of CPK leak into the extracellular fluid and plasma as a result of changes in membrane activity. The type of exercise and the duration affect the elevation of serum CPK. Non-weight-bearing activities such as rowing and swimming cause less pronounced CPK elevations than comparable weightbearing events. CPK elevations have been found to be linear with the duration of exercise up to 5.5 hours. Longer durations of exercise are associated with an accelerated increase in CPK.

Exercise-induced increases in the level of serum CPK are temporary. Resting levels of CPK changes generally become elevated during exercise days and then return to normal levels during rest days. Peaks in serum CPK have been reported to occur at 5 minutes, 11 hours, 24 hours, 25 hours, and even 4-6 days following exercise. With continued physical activity, CPK levels remained elevated. Resting levels of serum CPK are higher in exercised trained individuals than in untrained ones.

CPK elevations vary with age and sex. Older individuals are less likely to have elevations after exercise than are middle-aged or young adults. Women are more likely to have exercise induced elevations than are men.

Some researchers suggest that muscle cell permeability increases during exercise and others think that muscle degeneration and necrosis occurs. Muscular soreness has been reported to accompany elevated CPK levels. While increases in serum CPK are common in adults who exercise, there are also pathological states, such as myocardial infarction or heart attack, which may be accompanied by an increase in serum levels of CPK.

APPROACH:
Serum CPK is used as an indicator of muscle integrity with the level of specific isoenzymes aiding in the diagnoses regarding which type of muscle (cardiac, skeletal, or brain) has been stressed.

There are two isoenzymes, i.e., chemically different but functionally identical forms of CPK. The isoenzyme produced in the brain is identified as CPK B and the isoenzyme produced in muscle is identified as CPK M. As a rule of thumb, cardiac muscle stress produces CPK MB, and skeletal muscle stress produces CPK MM. CPK BB is an indicator of stress of brain tissue and is not usually examined in routine physical examinations unless there is a suspicion of stroke, tumor, etc.

There are divergent opinions about the proportion of CPK MB in skeletal muscle as well as about the proportion of total CPK in association with acute myocardial infarction. Studies have shown large elevations in CPK MB in some women after step exercise and in highly trained female endurance runners. In the absence of symptoms and other positive physical examination information, elevated CPK MB is not usually considered sufficient evidence of a heart attack.

Identification of these isoenzymes requires laboratory testing procedures not routinely completed for LSAH.

RESULTS:
Approximately 16 percent of the 211 CPK tests completed for the LSAH participants during 1992-94 reported elevated serum levels. investigators: Principal Investigator: Walton, Kerry
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The force of gravity is one of the few constant factors during the evolution of the nervous system and is deeply embedded in its functionality. An animalï¿½s posture is dependent on the appropriate force being maintained at every joint of the skeleton in order to counteract the force of gravity. This experiment examines the adaptability of the motor nervous system to environmental demands. Since young animals are particularly susceptible to changes in their environment, they offer a sensitive model for nervous system plasticity. The hypothesis tested in this experiment is: 1) a normal gravitational field is essential for the normal postnatal development of the motor system; 2) elimination of weight-bearing will lead to profound changes in motor system organization; 3) changes in motor function will be most marked when animals are exposed to microgravity during sensitive periods of development; and 4) functional changes will persist into adulthood when animals are exposed during critical periods of motor development.

Approach:

Rat pup ages at flight allowed exposure to microgravity during both the sensitive period (P8-P24) and critical period (P14-P30) of neuromotor development. Inflight experiments evaluated locomotion, complex motor skills, and vestibular reflexes with the use of an Animal Walking Apparatus (AWA). Animals were videotaped inflight using two cameras simultaneously while they progressed along rods of varying diameters, along a 1/2-inch mesh surface, on a foam surface, and during tests of surface (or contact) righting. Postflight, animals underwent numerous non-invasive behavioral tests to test their motor skills including, swimming, walking, startle reflex and surface righting.

Results:

Three general observations were made over the course of the experiment: (1) The exact set of movements used to achieve a goal, i.e., motor tactics, is influenced by the physical environment during development. This was found in both swimming and walking. Other aspects of movement, such as how fast the movement is made, are not as sensitive. (2) The age of the animals influenced the magnitude and duration of the effect. For example, locomotion was more affected in the older than in the younger animals. However, the immaturity of surface righting tactics were more marked in the younger animals. (3) The length of time an animal spends in an altered environment determines if the effects will be transient or long lasting. Locomotion in the microgravity environment was dominated by the forelimbs; when the hind limbs were used, overstepping was observed. In addition, poor interlimb coordination was observed in these animals. Anatomical studies found that the arborization of the dendritic tree of cervial motorneurons is less rich in flight animals on the day of landing. Studies in the cerebral cortex have found differences on the day of landing that persist for at least three months post-flight.

A preliminary analysis indicates that an Earth-normal gravitational field is needed for the normal postnatal development of motor function. The tactics an animal used to achieve its motor goal, such as turning over, walking, or swimming are influenced by the environment. Thus, animals spending 16-days in microgravity use a different set of tactics to achieve their goal than ground-based control animals. In the case of surface righting, which did not occur in microgravity, the tactics for turning over were identical at launch and landing. This indicates that the postnatal development of motor skills requires activity in an environment context. Thus, postnatal development of motor skills represents a ï¿½tuningï¿½ of the nervous system to the environment. Further, the anatomical substrates for this tuning are at the level of the spinal cord and cerebral cortex.

experiment_title: Commercial Biomedical Testing Module (CBTM)
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Bateman, Ted
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Commercial Biomedical Testing Module: Effects of Osteoprotegerin on Bone Maintenance in Microgravity (CBTM) provides the capability to use the microgravity environment for evaluation of new pharmaceutical candidates in small mammals. Results may expedite the review of new pharmaceuticals for allowing immediate access to new disease treatments.

Osteoporosis is a debilitating disease that afflicts millions of people worldwide. One of the physiological changes experienced by astronauts during spaceflight is the accelerated loss of bone mass due to the lack of gravitational loading on the skeleton. This bone loss experienced by astronauts is similar to osteoporosis in the elderly population. Osteoprotegerin (OPG), a bone metabolism regulator, is being considered by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a new treatment for osteoporosis.

APPROACH

Laboratory mice were treated with either OPG or a placebo before launch. The mice were housed in an Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) designed specifically for spaceflight. This experiment provided a preclinical trial model to determine the effectiveness of OPG in treating bone loss.

RESULTS:

Mice exposed to microgravity exhibited a 15 - 20 percent decline in femur elastic strength and a 40 - 60 percent decrease in bone formation when compared to the controls. The femur elastic strength decline was caused by three mechanisms: reduced bone formation, increased bone resorption, and inhibition of mineralization. OPG treatment in mice exposed to microgravity nearly reversed the decline in strength and the increase in bone resorption found in untreated mice.

Gene expression data is available in the NASA GeneLab Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/ (accession number GLDS-21, Effects of spaceflight on murine skeletal muscle gene expression).

experiment_title: Risk of Cancer Mortality Among LSAH Participants
parameter_html: Cancer mortality rate
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A significant health concern associated with space travel is the potential exposure to radiation. NASA has addressed this concern with medical projects that monitor exposures and maintain lifelong exposure records. Early detection of precancerous conditions is a primary effort of the occupational physical examinations provided to astronauts and to the LSAH comparison population. A task of LSAH is to monitor the incidence of medical events and to provide data to NASA Medical Operations management to aid program decision-making.

APPROACH:
Recently, reviews have been implemented on cancer mortality rates and the news is promising for the LSAH population as a whole. The cancer mortality rates among LSAH participants have been compared with the cancer mortality rates for the general population of the Texas Gulf Coast area residing in Public Health Region 6. Public Region 6 includes Harris County and the surrounding counties of Austin, Colorado, Montgomery, Wharton, Brazoria, Fort Bend, Liberty, Walker, Chambers, Galveston, Matagorda, and Waller. The age-specific average annual cancer mortality rates for the years of 1987 through 1993 were obtained for this area from the Texas Cancer Data Center.

The rate of the astronauts has also been compared with the rate of the LSAH comparison participants.

All cancer deaths among the LSAH population have been among males; therefore only males were included in these analyses. This is a conservative analysis approach since the denominator used in the rate calculation is based on the total population being examined. Given a consistent numerator (the number of cancer cases) the smaller denominator obtained by including only males results in a higher rate. All males selected as astronauts between 1959 and 1995 (210) and male comparisons for the same time period selected from the JSC employee population (618), as participants in LSAH were included in this cancer mortality investigation. Person years of follow-up time for each of the two study groups were calculated for the same age-specific groupings identified in the reference population of Public Health Region 6. The expected rates of cancer mortality are obtained by applying the age-specific rates of the reference population to the study population. The results are those rates that would be expected if the study population had experienced the same cancer mortality as the reference population. The observed rates of cancer mortality in each of the two LSAH study groups were compared with the expected rates.

The ratio of the observed rate to the expected rate is known as the Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR). An SMR of 100 indicates that identical rates exist for two groups. Confidence intervals (CI) around the SMRs (CI, 95%) were calculated.

RESULTS:
Both the astronauts and the comparison group currently have lower age-specific rates of total cancer mortality than that seen in the general population residing in the Texas Gulf Coast area. The rate among the astronauts is somewhat higher than the comparison participants but not significantly higher. The difference may be from chance alone.

There have been three cancer deaths among the astronaut population. The SMR of 47 indicates that the observed cancer deaths among the astronaut population are 53 percent less than the 6.25 expected deaths. The confidence intervals indicate that, even though the observed rate of cancer mortality is noticeably lower than expected, it is not statistically different from the general population.

There have also been three cancer mortalities among the LSAH comparison population versus an expected 17.3 cases. The resulting SMR of 17 (CI = 3.5, 37.9) is significantly lower than expected.

The particular types of cancers experienced among the LSAH population are relatively rare among the general population. Conversely, the more common cancers among the general population (lung, colorectal, prostate) have not been identified as causes of mortality among the LSAH population.

Comparisons made between astronaut health data and general population health data should be viewed with some skepticism because of the differences between the astronauts and the general public. Risk factors associated with many cancers are also associated with life-styles and education. The astronauts are highly educated and receive routine preventive medical care. They are, in general, physically fit and nonsmokers. Because of the difficulties associated with making comparisons between the astronauts and the general population, the comparison population was selected from the JSC employees. Age, sex, and body mass index were used as matching criteria, and all JSC employees have access to preventive medical care through the Occupational Medicine Clinic. A comparison of cancer rates between these two groups is much more statistically sound than comparisons made with the general public.

If the astronauts experienced the same age-specific rates of cancer as the comparison participants, 0.87 deaths would have been expected compared with the three observed deaths. This results in an SMR of 345 (CI = 69.5 to 756.2). The rate of total cancer mortality among the astronauts is elevated when compared with the LSAH comparison participants, but not significantly different.

experiment_title: The Effect of Daily Activity and Age on Bone Density
parameter_html:
Activity, exercise; Weight load, whole body
Bone mineral density
Body mass
Age
Height
investigators: Principal Investigator: Whalen, Robert
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to 1) develop a new method of quantifying daily activity level in terms of the daily history of ground reaction forces and 2) to clarify the relationship between musculoskeletal tissue stress (strain) histories and the material and structural properties of bone during normal daily activity and 3) to establish equivalent loading histories in space compared to baseline activity levels on Earth.

APPROACH:
Male subjects, aged 30-55 years of average weight and similar shoe size were selected. An insole sensor (1/8th inch thick) was fitted to a foot of each subject. Pressure between the foot and shoe sole caused the sensor to deform and output a voltage (2.5 Volts maximum) proportional to the applied force. A shielding wire threaded through the pant leg connects the insole sensor with a microprocessor unit that is attached to the waist for data acquisition. The sensor is calibrated to zero and one body weight by lifting the foot off the ground for 2.5 seconds and then a second reading is taken after placing the foot on the ground for 2.5 seconds. These static data points are stored to obtain a linear force voltage output calibration and compared with a set of dynamic points from a swaying subject to ensure no difference in readings greater than 5% that would indicate a defective sensor.

RESULTS:
Peak cyclic ground reaction forces (GRFz), normalized to subject body weight were recorded for three consecutive weekdays. Average daily histograms of the number of loading cycles vs cycle-magnitudes (loading histories) were obtained by averaging 24 hour periods. The total number of cycles for men were 4526 ±1187 and for women, 4744 ±1383. The total number of cycles greater than 0.8 BW were 3649 ±1139 for men and 3909 ±1259 for women. Mean cycle magnitude for all cycles greater than 0.8 BW were 1.11 ±0.07 BW for men and 1.13 ±0.09 for women. The number of cycles at the higher >0.2 BW for men were 7.3±12.5 and for women 5.4±9.5. A trend toward reduced high load activity was observed with age. These results demonstrate for the first time objective force measurements of human activity in men and women. The range in frequency and magnitude of daily loading may be an important contributor to variation in bone density in lower limb skeletal sites loaded down by internal forces supporting the ground reaction force.

experiment_title: Effects of Prolonged Weightlessness on the Humoral Immune Response of Humans

investigators: Principal Investigator: Voss, Edward
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The human internal defense mechanisms are divided into two main categories based upon the specificity of their actions. Nonspecific defense includes mechanisms that provide protection from a variety of pathogens by preventing their entrance into the body or, if the invader gains entrance, quickly destroying it. Specific defense includes mechanisms which react selectively to destroy specific pathogens or toxins. The humoral immune response is categorized as a specific defense mechanism and functions mainly to produce immunoglobulins (Ig) in response to specific antigens. Serious immune system deficiencies can result if Ig production is compromised. This experiment was designed to analyze and measure the effect of microgravity on the humoral immune response during the 10 day Spacelab 1 mission.

APPROACH:
Preflight, inflight, and postflight serum samples obtained from crewmen aboard STS-9 were analyzed for immunoglobulin content. Control studies for circadian rhythm were conducted to further validate the analyses.

Two separate preflight studies were conducted to validate the immunoglobulin (Ig) measurements. The first study was designed to provide information regarding alterations in Ig measurements which might be due to changes in circadian rhythms.
