investigators: Principal Investigator: Wheeler, RaymondCo-Investigator: Massa, GioiaCo-Investigator: Stutte, Gary
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is planning for long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit. To sustain crew health and performance and prevent micro-nutritional deficiencies, adequate nutrition must be provided through the food system. The current food system is processed and shelf stable to meet space flight requirements, resulting in insufficiencies of several nutrients. One approach to address this is to grow fresh foods in situ, focusing on dietary variety and nutrients that are deficient in packaged food, or that diminish over time with storage. Dwarf tree fruits have never before been studied for use in space flight, but fresh fruits are rich sources of vitamins and bioactive compounds and could enhance crew diet by expanding nutritional diversity, and by augmenting flavors, aromas, and overall dietary acceptability. Kennedy Space Center (KSC) solely possesses dwarf cultivars of plums (Prunus domestica) that are expected to be compatible with the volume constrained plant growth hardware on the International Space Station (ISS), such as Veggie. Previous studies have shown that plums have the potential to reduce loss of bone density and to increase the intake of potassium and vitamin K, which are both deficient in the packaged food system. This experiment aimed to study the growth and productivity of the dwarf plums in controlled environments under the same environmental conditions found on the ISS (light, temperature, relative humidity and CO2).

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Establish dwarf plum trees in controlled environment growth chambers and monitor a range of growth and horticultural parameters using flight constraints (growing volumes, environmental conditions, watering techniques, CO2 levels, and electrical lighting).
  2. Establish feasibility of growth protocols and cultivar selection for space flight, and make recommendations to guide future research solicitations.

APPROACH:
Plum trees that were genetically modified by USDA researchers to overexpress the FT flowering gene were studied as a candidate crop for space food systems. The FT transformation eliminated dormancy requirements and allowed the plants to flower and develop fruit at a very early age (<1 yr), essentially on dwarf plants. Prior horticultural testing at KSC compared the performance of several GM plum genotypes in controlled environment chambers, and four of the better performing lines, NASA-5, -6, -10, and -11, were used for most of the testing reported here. Tests showed that regular irrigations with Peters Excel 13 N – 2 P - 13 K soluble fertilizer produced good growth using commercial potting mixes. But many plants appeared sensitive to having soils too wet or too dry (based on visual assessments). Tests were conducted to improve cloning techniques using branch cuttings dipped in rooting hormone powder (Indole-3-butyric acid —IBA). Studies were also conducted to monitor leaf transpiration and stomatal conductance rates of several genotypes grown at two CO2 concentrations, since CO2 is known to affect stomatal opening and transpiration.

RESULTS:
Fruit development from these GM plants required cross pollination using wild type pollen to get reliable fruit set. Time from pollination to first sighting of fruit was approximately 7 days, with time from pollination to mature fruit showing purple color taking about 68 days. Genotypes NASA-5 and NASA-11 were the most reliable for pollination and fruit set. The fruit flesh at maturity was light green, smooth, and juicy. Fruits saved from these and prior tests were analyzed for elemental composition, carotenoids (lutein and zeaxanthin), ORAC antioxidant values, total phenolics, and Vitamin K. Lutein averaged 0.1-0.2 mg / g dry weight, while zeaxanthin was below detection; Vitamin K ranged from 55-75 µg / 100 g dry weight; ORAC from 122 to 257 TE / g dry weight; and total phenolics from 15-23 mg / g dry weight. Plums and prunes are known to slow or reverse bone loss, which could be linked to their high phenolic content and high ORAC values (Smith et al., 2014).

Based on some horticultural challenges and need for cross pollination, the investigators recommend that the ptFT plums undergo further testing before consideration for space flight. Among the challenges will be testing the potential for launching vegetative cuttings, refining branch pruning techniques to maintain short stature, further breeding to get self-compatible pollination, and further understanding plant water and nutritional requirements, particularly for environments like the ISS, which have CO2 levels of ~2500 ppm or higher. But the effects of the FT genetic transformation of plums are dramatic and should be explored with other fruit trees to bring them into the discussions for future space food crops.

No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Risk uncertainties related to radiation exposure during space exploration are unacceptably large. These include the effects of sporadic solar particle events (SPEs) which can produce relatively high levels of radiation, principally from protons. The notion that dose rate effects from protons will be the same as for x- and gamma rays is widely held. However, not much direct experimental evidence to support this contention exists. In fact, the resultant dose to personnel from an SPE can be high enough to warrant concerns of cancer induction. Because human epidemiological data in this area are not available, reduction in risk uncertainties will require data from meaningful surrogate endpoints. For this investigation, structural damage to chromosomes of human cells in culture has been chosen as a surrogate endpoint for cell death and cancer.

An SPE will be simulated using proton emissions from the National Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). Owing to differences in ionization density that may translate to differences in biological effect, proton energies of 50 MeV and 250 MeV will be studied. These will be delivered at both high and low dose rates. Results will then be compared to those obtained for gamma rays from a 137-Cesium source.

Objective 1 Construct quantitative dose responses for the induction of chromosome aberrations found in cells when they arrive at the first mitosis following exposure. For this and other objectives, multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) will be used, which effectively paints each of the 23 pairs of human chromosomes a unique color. This allows even very complicated rearrangements among all chromosomes to be visualized simultaneously.

Objective 2 Complete an analysis of chromosome damage in clonal descendants of single cells that survive exposure to radiation. Several such clones will be expanded in culture and examined by mFISH for transmissible chromosome aberrations. A subset of these clones will be further examined for structural aberrations that are too small to be seen under the microscope, by employing comparative genomic hybridization applied to DNA microarrays (aCGH). Genetic damage in cells surviving radiation may be diagnostic of the type of radiation encountered, and that such damage has more direct relevance to carcinogenesis.

APPROACH:
Energies and dose rates that were compatible with the investigation’s scientific objectives were determined on the basis of biophysical modeling, and constraints of NSRL facilities. Two runs were made at NSRL. For the first run, 150 MeV protons and 1 GeV protons were used. Both were delivered at high (30 cGy/min) and low (30 cGy/h) dose rates to telomerase-immortalized human fibroblasts to total absorbed doses of (not including the sham-irradiated zero-dose control) 100, 200, and 300 cGy. For the second run, 50 MeV protons became available, and this energy was used instead of the previous 150 MeV treatment group. As in the first run, 1 GeV protons were used again, serving as a repeat. For both NSRL runs, density-inhibited telomerase-positive BJ-1 human fibroblasts were re-fed with conditioned medium prior to shipment to NRSL. The morning following exposure, flasks were shipped back to UTMB (University of Texas Medical Branch) for immediate subculture.

RESULTS:
The expected diminution of chromosome damage per unit dose following reduction in dose rate was confirmed, as was the predicted attenuation in upward curvature. These results are consistent with the assumption that protons and photons elicit a qualitatively similar biological response. Curvature in the dose response following 150 MeV protons was effectively eliminated at the LDR of 0.05 cGy/min. This is evidence that the limiting low dose rate (LLDR) was reached, and is consistent with expectations based on gamma ray studies. Irrespective of energy, the preponderance of curvature in all responses derives from complex exchanges, which is also similar to the situation for photons.

The above conclusions regarding similarity of effect between high energy protons and gamma rays need to be tempered by the following observations:

The unexpected observation that higher energy protons were more effective at producing chromosome damage per unit dose. More data for the 50 MeV protons would be needed to establish whether this is a trend. The fact that curvature in the response was not altogether eliminated for the higher energy 1 GeV protons following LDR. It is unknown whether the LLDR hadn’t yet been reached for this radiation, or whether single track action is capable of producing such curvature. Additional work may eventually be needed to put hard numbers on quantitative differences regarding gamma photons versus protons in order to estimate meaningful RBEs. In particular this would include more dose points over the lower dose range.

Regarding clones recovered from exposed cell populations, roughly 25% following 3 Gy of protons harbored transmissible chromosome rearrangements, most of which were simple reciprocal translocations; a significant number contained complex exchanges as well that involve simultaneously three or more chromosomes. These results are consistent with those observed following exposure to 4 Gy 137Cs gamma-rays. Because they are homogeneous for the particular rearrangements they carry, these clonal derivatives serve as ideal material for molecular analysis, as for example, analysis by array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH)

High-density CGH arrays (aCGH) were used to examine the distribution of large (megabase-sized) and small (tens of kilobase size) deletions in several of the surviving clones described above. The size-frequency distribution of such deletions, on both the megabase and kilobase scales suggest that the formation of smaller deletions are favored over larger ones, but that the distributions are characterized as having “long asymmetrical tails.” In at least one case, a clone had suffered a deletion in near proximity to an apparently simple reciprocal translocation, suggesting the rearrangements was “complex,” i.e., a co-deletion, as part of the translocation/exchange process.

experiment_title: Asthma in the LSAH Population
parameter_html: Asthma
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by the inability to breathe properly. Asthma affects 5% to 10% of the world's population, and more than 17 million Americans have asthma. The elderly and urban poor are at the highest risk for severe asthma and death. Highly trained athletes such as long-distance runners and swimmers are more susceptible to asthma. For example, 10% of U.S. athletes in the 1996 Olympics had asthma. Occupational exposures to a wide range of chemicals and other substances may increase the risk of asthma. Obesity and asthma have been associated, but it is not clear if one causes the other. The objective of this experiment was to compare asthma occurrence in LSAH participants with the general population.

RESULTS:
In a 2000 survey of the U.S. general population, 7.2% of the respondents reported having asthma. In comparison, the prevalence rate among LSAH participants as documented in their medical records is lower: less than 4% of comparison participants were diagnosed with asthma. For the astronauts, the diagnosis rate was even lower, with less than one percent diagnosed with asthma.

experiment_title: Effect of Radiation on Human Peripheral Blood Dendritic Cells
parameter_html:
Heavy ions
Human dendritic cells
Protons
Radiation
investigators: Principal Investigator: Reuben, James
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to investigate the effect of proton, heavy ion, and gamma radiation on human dendritic cells (DCs) and their ability to process antigens and, thus, impact the immune system. Increased exposure of the body to ionizing radiation suppresses the formation of bone marrow tissue, which, in turn, suppresses development of blood cells within bone marrow. This affects the differentiation, maturation, and function of dendritic cells, which are believed to be the link between innate and cell-mediated immunity. Thus, it is suspected that the increased exposure to ionizing radiation during long-term space flight may severely impair the immune system unless appropriate countermeasures are taken.

APPROACH:
Cultured human monocyte-derived dendritic cells were exposed to proton-, heavy ion- and gamma-radiation. The life cycle and formation of DCs were studied by determining the effects of the radiation on the differentiation of non-lymphocyte white blood cell precursor cells into immature dendritic cells. Then, the ability of these immature DCs stimulate cellular immunity were determined. In addition, this study determined the ability of activated mature DCs to present antigen to T-lymphocytes (T-cells). Countermeasures to prevent the harmful effects of proton-, heavy ion- and gamma-radiation on myelosuppression and the subsequent immune suppression were also identified.

RESULTS:
The investigators have accomplished the following based on the data obtained from 12 healthy normal subjects: 1. Compared with un-irradiated PDC or MDC, there were no significant differences in the percentage of cytokine-producing PDC or MDC subject to low-dose g-radiation. 2. There is an irradiation dose dependent reduction of the mean channel fluorescence intensity (MFI) of intracellular IFN-a (P = 0.004) and TNF-a (P = 0.000) of the plasmacytoid DC upon stimulation with 5 uM of CL097. 3. The amount of IL-12 (p = 0.007) and TNF-a (p = 0.028) produced by individual MDC was significantly reduced upon the activation through TLR-8 with CL097 in an irradiation dose-dependent manner. In summary, the suppression of PDC to synthesize IFN-a and TNF-a by low-dose g-irradiation is unprecedented and suggests the possible attenuation of innate immune surveillance, whereas the reduced production of IL-12 and TNF-a by low-dose g-irradiated MDC might negatively impact the ability of MDC to mediate adaptive immunity and effector T-cell function. As DC are essential for the development of an immune response and clearance of microbial infection, low-dose g-radiation might pose a serious threat to long-term health in space.

As DC are essential for the development of an immune response and clearance of microbial infection, low-dose g-radiation might pose a serious threat to long-term health in space.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Considerable development of the hippocampus occurs in rats after birth. Therefore, the hippocampus, which is required for spatial learning, is more likely to be affected by microgravity exposure at a young age. This experiment examined the hypothesis that exposure of rat neonates to microgravity will result in altered activity that will lead to altered development. This study evaluated the cognitive mapping abilities of rats that spent part of their early development in a microgravity environment. Another objective of this experiment was to analyze neuronal morphology and determine the synaptic functional plasticity in the developing nervous system of rat neonates raised in microgravity. Finally an analysis of the distribution of specific protein components of the nervous system was conducted, with particular emphasis on the cytoskeletal synaptic proteins, in rat neonates raised in microgravity.

Approach:

Litters of male and female Sprague-Dawley rat pups were launched into space aboard the NASA Space Shuttle Columbia on either post-natal day 8 (P8) or 14 (P14), and remained in space for 16 days. These animals were designated as flight (FLT) groups. Two age-matched control groups remained on Earth: those in standard vivarium housing (VIV) and those in identical housing to that aboard the Shuttle (SIM, Simulated Caged Control). Upon return to Earth, all animals were tested in three different tasks, the Morris water maze (MWM), a modified version of the radial arm maze (RAM), and an open field apparatus (OFA), to measure general activity and exploratory activity. Performance and search strategies were evaluated in each of these tasks using an automated tracking system (Poly-Track, San Diego Instruments). The analysis of the hippocampus included a determination of dendritic extents, a quantitative analysis of the synaptic structure and spinal architecture, an analysis of isoform expression of specific cytoskeletal and synaptic proteins, and a determination of the onset of long-term potentiation.

Results:

There were remarkably few differences between the FLT groups and their earth-bound controls in these tasks. FLT animals learned the MWM and RAM as quickly as controls. Evaluation of search patterns suggested subtle differences in patterns of exploration and in the strategies used to solve the tasks, but these differences normalized rapidly. Together, these data suggest that development in an environment without gravity has minimal long-term impact on cognitive mapping. Any differences due to development in microgravity quickly reversed after return to Earth normal gravity.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Pandya, AbhilashCo-Investigator: Baker, KennethCo-Investigator: Cao, AlexCo-Investigator: Chien, Chiun-HongCo-Investigator: Chintamani, KeshavCo-Investigator: Ellis, DarinCo-Investigator: Maida, James
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this Rapid Technology Development grant was to provide the operator of the Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator (SPDM) with simple, intuitive cues for control of the manipulator during grasping, removing, stowing and inserting orbital replacement units (ORUs) as opposed to just looking at multiple video views which requires extensive training and can be error prone. The science of presenting and displaying complex 3D images in an augmented and operationally meaningful way is the basis of this Space Human Factors Engineering research proposal. The technical development was validated and proven with the appropriate Human Factors testing. Efficient methods of remote image data display were implemented and tested against more traditional methods.

The proposal’s objective was to improve the human-robot interface to reduce operator work load, task time and to simplify operator training to make skill-based training practical as opposed to task-based training with particular focus on the SPDM and its training facility the DMT.

Because of the risky environment of space, teleoperations are commonplace for NASA. Visualization of the remote data and its human performance impact are important to successful teleoperations. During space missions, astronaut robotic operators primarily depend on visual feedback that is provided by strategically placed video cameras. Operating a robotic arm from indirect visual information poses many technical and human performance challenges for the operator. Astronauts performing remote functions like operating the SPDM or the RMS need to maintain mental 3D real-time environment maps for successful operations.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
(1) Physically based Augmented Reality for Remote Robot Teleoperation Applications in Training and Simulation
Space station service telerobots have been extremely useful to the space program and the astronaut. However, the high cost of using these robots in pre-mission astronaut training calls for low cost and efficient training platforms. In addition, local gravitational fields (i.e. microgravity) cannot be accurately simulated in robot tele-operation training platforms on Earth. Investigators have developed a robot tele-operation interface that allows remote camera views to contain dynamic simulations using Augmented Reality (AR). In these views, virtual and physical robot arms co-operate in the remote worksite and can be manually (end-effector) controlled. In the current system, a virtual payload is placed in the remote worksite views and operators can control the virtual robot’s end-effector to grasp and transport this payload in any user defined gravity condition. The physical effects arising from these interactions and the resulting motion of the payload when a collision with the robot occurs is simulated. There are practical implications of such simulations, particularly in pre-mission training of astronauts.

(2) Improved Tele-manipulator Navigation with Augmented Coordinate Frames
The application of simple Augmented Reality (AR) cues for remote robot tele-operation has been implemented and tested with human participants. Space robot arms, for example, are manipulated by orienting and translating the body fixed coordinates at the end-effector (EE) using hand controllers with cameras providing visual feedback. The pose of the end-effector seen on 2-dimensional images however, challenges operator performance due to misalignments between the displayed EE axes and the hand controller (HC) axes. In this study, the coordinate system of the EE is graphically overlaid in 3-dimensions on the live video with unique colored axes using AR. The same color scheme is used to label the appropriate axis on the HCs. Operators can use these color cues to map each axis on the HCs to the corresponding colored axis on augmented coordinates at the EE to obtain EE motion in the desired direction. A within-participant experiment comparing the EE trajectory distance, deviation from path and navigation errors was used to determine the effectiveness of augmented coordinates over conventional tele-operation without augmented coordinates. Significant reductions in EE trajectory distance, deviation from path and navigation errors were observed when participants manipulated the remote robot with augmented coordinates. Observations and inferences demonstrate that the use of AR in remote robot arm tele-operation is beneficial to the operator.

(3) Operator Performance in Robotic Tele-operation Using End-effector vs. Disjointed Wrist Kinematics Control
Tele-operated robot arms in space are controlled by manipulating points of resolution (POR) at the end-effector, wrist and other joints using joystick like hand controllers. Depending on motion constraints at the POR, the POR’s motion perceived by the operator can vary. Typical tele-operation is performed by rotation and translation of the end-effector (EE-POR). Incongruence between the EE-POR axes and joystick axes due to misaligned exocentric camera views along with prolonged closed loop operation can lead to high levels of mental workload and longer task times. Control at the wrist POR (WR-POR) is proposed as a means to ease the workload levels and improve operator performance. Twelve participants performed payload insertion tasks using a remote robot arm equipped with the EE-POR and WR-POR modes. Subjective mental workload scales (NASA-TLX) were obtained along with task time, distance and reversal error data. Time and subjective workload were found to be lower with WR-POR, although average path distances were longer with reversal errors indistinguishable for both modes. Findings confirm that it is possible to ease the inherent difficulties in remote tele-operation by introducing an alternative POR control scheme like WR-POR. Although this POR control may not be dexterous enough for precise tasks, its use in conjunction with EE-POR control can ease operator workload. This work can be applicable to any tele-operated robotic system (space, medical and military) where the user has to control multiple degrees of freedom at the POR.

experiment_title: Development of Vestibular Organs in Microgravity
parameter_html:
Behavior, crawling
Volume, Otolith, Xiphophorus helleri (swordtail), fish, Electron microscopy
Volume, Statoconia, snail, Biomphalaria glabrata (pond snail,), Electron microscopy
Volume, Statocyst, snail, Microscopy
investigators: Principal Investigator: Wiederhold, Michael
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Many species sense gravity, and therefore linear acceleration, by way of otoliths (dense calcium carbonate crystals attached to hair cells and associated nerve fibers). As the mass moves with acceleration, a signal is sent through each hair cell to the central nervous system. The knowledge of the factors that control development of these otoliths (and their analogs in some species) is limited. Previous studies suggest that altered gravity does not substantially affect the volume of the otoliths or their analogs in adult animals. This study was designed to test the hypothesis that during development the mass of the otolith is regulated to achieve a desired weight; as such, one would expect to reference larger-than-normal otoliths in animals reared in microgravity.

Approach:

The statoconia (analogous to otoliths) of the pond snail, Biomphalaria glabrata, and the otoliths of the swordtail fish, Xiphophorus helleri, were the focus of this study. Thirty-five adult snails, four pre-mated adult female swordtail fish, and 50 to 200 juvenile swordtail fish were flown in the Closed Equilibrated Biological Aquatic System (CEBAS), which contained seven liters of water and 50 grams of the hornweed, Ceratophylum. The specimen container was videotaped for later analysis. Many of the snails mated in flight, and produced the juvenile snails used in the experimental analysis. The pregnant adult swordtail fish were selected at a stage that they would produce developing fry but not have any hatch by the end of the mission. On landing day, approximately half the juvenile snails were fixed; the other half were fixed five days postflight. Adult fish ovaries and juvenile fish were fixed in alcohol on landing day. Fixed snails were removed from their shell and sectioned at 1-2 micrometer; serial sections were examined by transmission electron microscopy.

Results:

Results were obtained from both the Neurolab flight (16-day) and a similar experiment of nine days duration, using the same organisms, flown on STS-89. Total statoconia volume in the snails varied considerably within both the flight and ground control groups. However, the difference in mean values for the two groups was significant at p < 0.05, with the average total volume greater in the flight group. In most of the groups of flight snails (divided into groups by shell diameter), the increase in statoconia volume increased as the animals developed another five days on Earth. Overall, the flight-reared snails had approximately 50 percent more statoconia than the ground controls. This indicated that rearing in microgravity causes the supporting cells to produce more statoconia, of approximately the same size as in ground-reared animals.

Otoliths of the embryonic fish from STS-90 (Neurolab) exhibited a greater growth, with increased body length in the flight-reared animals, compared to ground controls. Although there was a trend for larger otoliths in the flight-reared juvenile swordtails, this difference did not reach statistical significance. The embryos from STS-89 were much smaller that those retrieved after STS-90, since this was a shorter mission. In this case, the growth of otoliths of the ground-reared fish embryos was actually larger than that of the flight-reared animals. These results suggest a critical period, in the late embryonic stages, where rearing in microgravity produces larger otoliths.

experiment_title: Vision and Aging in the Astronaut Population
parameter_html:
Cataracts
Diabetic retinopathy
Glaucoma
Macular degeneration
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Aging causes changes that may weaken your eyes, and affect your vision. Probably the most common aging effect of the eye is presbyopia, which affects more than 60 million Americans. This condition is caused by the loss of lens elasticity, resulting in the loss of the ability to focus on near objects or small print. Other aging-related conditions are less benign and can lead to irreversible blindness when left untreated. These diseases tend to begin painlessly and without symptoms in their earliest stages. Risk factors for these diseases include being over the age of 60, having a family history of the disease, or having the predisposing condition (e.g., diabetes). These eye diseases are described below.

Cataracts are cloudy areas or opacities in the lens, which may be caused by aging, or trauma. Cataracts, which form slowly and painlessly, may stay small and not interfere with vision. Fortunately, surgical treatment for advanced cataracts has a higher than 90% success rate. Cataracts affect almost 20.5 million people in the U.S. age 40 and older. The corresponding figures for the astronaut and comparison participants are 29 and 37, respectively.

Glaucoma is a buildup of pressure in the eye caused by an imbalance in fluid production and drainage. This increased pressure can damage the optic nerve, retina, or other parts of the eye. In some cases, elevated intraocular pressure is a clue to the condition, but in most instances glaucoma is only detected through a dilated eye examination. Glaucoma is controlled by medication, and surgery if necessary. More than 2.2 million people in the U.S. age 40 and older have glaucoma. Three astronauts and ten comparison participants age 40 and older have been diagnosed with glaucoma.

Retinal disorders: the two most relevant retinal disorders are age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic retinopathy. In AMD, vision deteriorates when the macular cells in the retina break down for reasons that are yet unknown. AMD rarely leads to complete blindness; however, it will lead to loss of central vision function, thereby potentially effecting one's ability to perform discriminating tasks such as reading, driving or watching television. Its effects can range from mild to profound. AMD cannot be cured, but it may be slowed by laser treatment, or medication and nutritional supplementation with antioxidants. Vision loss can be improved by low-vision aids. More than 1.6 million people in the U.S. age 50 and older have AMD. This condition affects one astronaut and five comparison participants age 50 and older.

In diabetic retinopathy, chronic high glucose levels lead to damage in retinal blood vessels. This condition is the most common vision complication that diabetics suffer, and is the leading cause of new blindness. Controlling the underlying disease, diabetes, is the best prevention. Diabetic retinopathy may be slowed or stopped through surgery, when it is diagnosed in its early stages. This disease affects more than 5.3 million people in the U.S. age 18 and older. No Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participant has reported being diagnosed with diabetic retinopathy.

APPROACH:
The data represents the prevalence of these diseases in the LSAH participants as compared to that of the general U.S. population, as estimated by the National Eye Institute.

RESULTS:
In general, both astronauts and comparison participants show lower prevalence of these eye conditions than the U.S. population, which may be a result of the healthy worker effect. For all of the diseases except cataracts, astronauts also have a lower prevalence than comparison participants.

Cataracts, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy have silent onset, and when left untreated can lead to irreversible blindness. Therefore, regular and thorough eye examinations, including dilated pupil examination, every one to two years are essential for early detection and prevention of these diseases.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment aimed to determine microgravity effects on connectivity of afferent neurons, inner ear hair cells, and vestibular nuclei neurons, as well as characterize changes in innervation patterns of inner ear afferent and efferent neurons.

Approach:

Tissues were examined, microdissected, postfixed with 10% formalin, embedded in paraffin and cut at 10 mm thick. Sections with comparable inner ear structures from embryonic days 3, 7, and 10 were placed on the same slide and stained together for anti-S100b or anti-NF68/200. All incubations were done at room temperature in a humidity chamber. Two negative controls were used: 1) omission or replacement of the primary antibody with an unrelated antiserum, and 2) pre-absorption of antibody when the substrate was available. The hues, saturation, and intensity (HSI) of reaction products was used to calculate the relative concentration of the antibody in the tissue sections.

Results:

Due to improper fixation, E3 (embryonic day 3) and E7 embryos did not stain with the neurofilament antibody. In E10 embryos, 77% of vestibular ganglion cells stained positive with anti-neurofilament in synchronous controls, whereas 90% of those counted from selected sections of the flight group were positive. This difference could be due to fixation artifact. The surface area of the vestibular neurons of the synchronous embryos was 202 square micra, whereas the surface area of the flight was 169 square micra. The anti-neurofilament reacted with its antigenic sites of the sensory inner ear structures at E10, but failed to recognize similar sites in E3 and E7 specimens. Positive staining in the E7 embryos was expected. The staining patterns of the neurofilament antibody was not always the same in all three groups when stained together, suggesting that there were marked differences in the mode of fixation and/or initial preparatory conditions for specimens in each group.

experiment_title: Human Lymphocyte Locomotion in Microgravity
parameter_html:
Collagen
Immunocompetence
Lymphocytes
investigators: Principal Investigator: Spaulding, GlennPrincipal Investigator: Goodwin, ThomasCo-Investigator: Goodwin, ThomasCo-Investigator: Spaulding, Glenn
image_name: Schematic Drawing of the Rotating Wall Vessel
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Understanding the movement of white blood cells (leukocytes) is a vital step for cancer researchers to determine how to help lemphocytes penetrate tissue to kill tumors. This is important because the lymphocytes fight cancers and all types of infection by moving into the diseased area. In the case of cancer, however; researchers have discovered that the closer a lymphocyte gets to a tumor, the more impaired its movement is.

The impact of long-term weightlessness on immunity has been revealed in extended manned space flights. This investigation (a) provided data which illuminates microgravity effects on locomotion and migration of human lymphocytes through an intercellular matrix, a function that is crucial to immunocompetence, (b) tested the adequacy of the Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV), a laboratory-based microgravity simulation environment developed by NASA, and (c) verified the Specimen Temperature Controller which is necessary to control the thermal environment of the living cells inflight. Analysis of in-flight data was performed in the Biotechnology Laboratory at Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
In single-phase microcarrier experiments, microcarriers were transferred to RWVs at a concentration of 200 microcarriers per 107 PBLs/100 ml c-RPMI culture volume. Controls were incubated at the same density in 24-well culture trays in stationary mode. In dual-phase microcarrier experiments, microcarriers were placed in RWVs at a concentration of 200 microcarriers/100 ml culture volume. Control cultures contained the same microcarrier-to-media density as their RWV counterparts. In a humidified, seven percent C02 incubator at 37° C, RWV cultures were rotated at 14 rpm, whereas control cultures were incubated in 24-well culture trays in stationary mode. At 24-hour intervals, four to six microcarriers were removed from the RWV and from control cultures and transferred to tubes containing one percent paraformaldehyde fixative, and the locomotion distance was measured.

Cell locomotion was defined as the distance between the microcarrier surface (single-phase microcarrier) or cell/collagen interface (dual-phase microcarrier) and the three leading-edge cells. This measurement was determined by fine focus microscopy using an inverted microscope with phase contrast (Nikon Diaphot, Japan). Using a predetermined calibration factor, this measurement was converted from fine focus units to locomotory distance in micrometers (gin).

RESULTS:
In the randomized gravity of the rotating-wall vessel culture system, peripheral blood lymphocytes did not locomote through Type I collagen, whereas static cultures supported normal movement. Although cells remained viable during the entire culture period, peripheral blood lymphocytes transferred to unit gravity (static culture) after 6 hours in the rotating-wall vessel culture system were slow to recover and locomote into collagen matrix. After 72 hours in the rotating-wall vessel culture system and an additional 72 hours in static culture, peripheral blood lymphocytes did not recover their ability to locomote. Loss of locomotory activity in rotating-wall vessel cultures appears to be related to changes in the activation state of the lymphocytes and the expression of adhesion molecules. Culture in the rotating-wall vessel system blunted the ability of peripheral blood lymphocytes to respond to polyclonal activation with phytohemagglutinin. Locomotory response remained intact when peripheral blood lymphocytes were activated by anti-CD3 antibody and interleukin-2 prior to introduction into the rotating-wall vessel culture system. Thus, in addition to the systemic stress factors that may affect immunity, isolated lymphocytes respond to gravitational changes by ceasing locomotion through model interstitium. These in vitro investigations suggest that microgravity induces non-stress-related changes in cell function that may be critical to immunity. Preliminary analysis of locomotion in true microgravity revealed a substantial inhibition of cellular movement in Type I collagen. Thus, the rotating-wall vessel culture system provides a model for analyzing the microgravity-induced inhibition of lymphocyte locomotion and the investigation of the mechanisms related to lymphocyte movement.

experiment_title: Assessing and Mitigating the Impact of Transmission Delays on Teleoperations
parameter_html:
Communication delays
Movement time
Peak magnitude
Task precision
investigators: Principal Investigator: Adelstein, BernardCo-Investigator: Ellis, StephenCo-Investigator: Kaiser, Mary
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to examine coupled human-system performance in the presence of temporally varying communication delays between the human controller(s) and remotely operated robot(s), and to propose countermeasures for delay-induced performance decrements. This DRP will be conducted in support of the NASA Enabling Technology Development and Demonstration (ETDD) Program’s Human Exploration Telerobotics (HET) Project, in which ground-station operators will control robotic assets on board the International Space Station (ISS). Specifically, the DRP will concentrate on the element led by NASA ARC that is focused on ground-to-orbit control of the “Synchronized Position, Hold, Engage, and Reorient Experimental Satellites” (SPHERES) free-flying robots on the International Space Station (ISS).

The DRP will focus on the range of time delays encountered in the ground-based control of the robotic assets on the ISS, ranging from 20-50 ms (effectively for line-of-sight communication) up to 2-10 s for multiple satellite ground-station relayed (Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System, or TDRSS, and associated ground network) communication, and, in particular, as delay instantaneously varies because of real-time changes in communication paths and data buffering.

The aims of the proposed work were: 1) to employ human-in-the-loop (HITL) testing to empirically investigate the impact of variable communication delays, with latencies spanning from tens of milliseconds up to approximately five seconds, on coupled human-system performance for telerobotic systems; 2) to evaluate empirically the efficacy of existing time delay compensation schemes for this range of latencies for telerobotic tasks and control modes that have different required movement precision levels; and 3) to use the data resulting from these studies to identify the trade points between latency compensation schemes as a function of time delay and required task precision and then design and test strategies for gracefully switching between mitigation techniques as telerobot system time delays vary.

The guidelines, tools, mitigation techniques and performance metrics developed from this research will help provide a rational basis for the design of teleoperation tasks to be carried out in the presence of communication delays. These products will in turn assist subsequent task, technology design, and validation experiment decisions regarding acceptable or desirable delay compensation techniques and define at what point to engage more autonomous operational modes.

APPROACH:
Investigators conducted human-in-the-loop (HITL) performance experiments using visual display of a dynamic simulation representative of a variety of SPHERES operations requiring different movement precision under this range of time-delay conditions. Next, they examined HITL performance under these conditions employing mitigation techniques for short time delays such as prediction algorithms that generated compensatory in command signal lead and, for longer delays, predictive “feed-forward” graphical overlays that “look ahead” and provided a virtual view showing the future pose and location of the robot. The goal of the second of the studies was to understand the performance trades between these techniques in a wider variety of environmental and latency conditions than is usually achievable during in situ experimentation. Based on these empirical HITL results, investigators designed and tested a strategy for combining and gracefully switching between mitigation techniques as telerobot system time delays vary across the millisecond to second range.

To conduct the DRP studies, investigators built their experiment testbed derived from elements of the HET ground-to-orbit SPHERES task, encompassing ground operator user interfaces as well as computer-based simulations of the SPHERES robots and ground-ISS communication links. This strategy allowed them to run HITL tests that will reduce the operating environment to offer sufficient flexibility and control for human performance experiments, yet still maintain salient features of the HET tasks key for face-validity and applicability of the results. The results from the experimental studies will help define more focused and scientifically revealing experiments that could subsequently be conducted on the ISS.

RESULTS:
Movement time and trajectory data from all twenty participants, pooled across all experiment conditions, were significantly positively correlated, indicative of a speed-accuracy tradeoff in their performance. Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) conducted separately on path length and movement time (transformed to correct for data skew) produced identical results. These ANOVAs showed a significant effect of rotation angle and an interaction between rotation angle and axis, but did not reveal a significant effect of the sequence of rotation axis. General features of the data indicate that the MDF, whether expressed in terms of movement time or path length, reaches a peak at or near 120 degrees for all axes and that the peak’s magnitude was significantly greater for rotation about the roll axis.

The results from this study indicate that the MDF, i.e., the effect of the control-display rotation, is not isotropic with respect to axis of rotation: roll produces a distinctly larger nonlinearity and peak magnitude. Investigators conjecture this is due to the displacement arising from the roll misalignment being projecting into the participant’s two key body reference axes, i.e., the lateral (left-right) axis and the vertical axis (usually aligned with gravity), which contrasts with pitch and yaw disturbances being projected into only one of these axes in the frontal plane.

experiment_title: Bone Health and Physical Activity in LSAH Participants
parameter_html:
Exercise, running
Exercise, walking
Exercise, weightlifting
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Physical activity, primarily weight bearing exercise, is an important factor in the development and maintenance of bone health. Weight bearing exercise is defined as any physical activity in which someone supports their weight (e.g., running, walking) or moves weights using their muscles (e.g., weightlifting, resistance training). For this study, weight bearing exercise was represented by the specific physical activities of walking, running, and weightlifting. This study compared the amount of participation in these activities between the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants, a group of comparisons, and the U.S. general population.

APPROACH:
The data were obtained through the Lifestyle Questionnaire, where respondents were asked to select the types of exercises they usually performed. A total of 1080 participants responded to the questionnaire (238 astronauts and 842 comparisons). Results of a national survey, the 1998 National Health Interview Survey, were used to compare the LSAH participants to the U.S. general population (N=32,440). The survey had values for the U.S. general adult population’s participation in walking, running, and weightlifting.

RESULTS:
Astronauts reported the highest participation in running and weightlifting as compared to comparison participants and the general population. The most striking difference between the astronauts and the other two groups was in running, where about two thirds of the astronauts reported participating, whereas more than one third of the comparison participants and only about a tenth of the general population did. Astronauts reported higher participation in the more vigorous activities of running and weightlifting than the comparison participants or the general population. The comparison participants appeared to have a similar pattern with the general population in the types of exercise they participated in, albeit with higher participation percentages.

Female astronauts (N=31) participated more in running and weightlifting than in walking. The female comparison participants (N=117) and the female general population (N=18,238) respondents showed a clear preference for walking over the other two activities.

Overall, LSAH participants reported higher participation in weight bearing exercises as compared to the general population, with astronauts having the highest rates. The difference between astronauts and comparison participants is to be expected as astronauts by definition need to maintain their health for mission readiness. Both astronauts and comparison participants therefore have a better chance of maintaining their bone density as they age as compared to the general population.

experiment_title: GASMAP Facility Operations
parameter_html:
Expired respiratory gas
Inspired respiratory gas
investigators: Principal Investigator: Booker, Floyd
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Gas Analyzer System for Metabolic Analysis Physiology (GASMAP) is an instrument that analyzes the inspired and expired breath of subjects and performs metabolic calculations to aid in the health assessment of astronauts in microgravity. GASMAP can be used in conjunction with a bicycle ergometer, treadmill, EKG, blood pressure monitor, and a rebreathing apparatus.

The GASMAP system consisted of: 1) a volumetric flow transducer to quantify the volume of inspired and expired gas, 2) a mass spectrometer with two internal processors, to measure the quantity and identify the species of the inspired and expired respiratory gases, 3) a laptop computer to control mass spectrometer operation, process and communicate data/diagnostics, display real time data, provide limited floppy disk data storage, and perform metabolic calculations, and 4) a calibration assembly to enable mass spectrometer accuracy verification.

The objectives of this study were: 1) Assure the greatest possible analyzer accuracy and response time, 2) Exceed 2.5 year operational life with a goal of 5 years, and 3) Deliver a GASMAP with minimal logistical overhead.

APPROACH:
Pre and Inflight Procedures:
In a long-term facility the ability to recalibrate the GASMAP analyzer is critical. The mass spectrometer designer considered several procedures under the heading of GASMAP calibration. These included hardware and software adjustments. They were: 1) Hardware Potential and Magnet Adjustment, 2) Mass Tuning Alignment, 3) Offset and Minor Interaction Adjustment, and 4) User Calibration.

The first procedure occurred immediately after assembly. The mass spectrometer was first calibrated by adjusting hardware potentiometers and by placing magnets. The goal in this calibration procedure was to achieve good sensitivity and good peak shapes. This is generally only performed once after assembly or after filament replacement. The second calibration procedure was performed to adjust a look-up table for each mass and to set the resolution for each mass that was measured. This was a software setup procedure and was called "Mass Tuning Alignment." The third calibration procedure adjusts the offsets or analyzer background that exists for certain masses, and several minor interactions that occur between gasses. Last, the User Calibration, the major interactions and gain adjustments for each gas were corrected. Except for Potential and Magnet Adjustment, all of the above mentioned procedures can be performed in-flight with the appropriate software and calibration gases. However; the User Calibration is the only calibration that the crew were trained to routinely perform. The Offset and or Mass tuning calibration would only be performed by crew members as a malfunction procedure.

RESULTS:
The first generation GASMAP analyzer onboard Mir exhibited exceptional stability. Investigators think the He and CO2 measurements can be corrected by changing the analyzer warm-up period to include filament run time.

__description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Gas Analyzer System for Metabolic Analysis Physiology (GASMAP) is an instrument that analyzes the inspired and expired breath of subjects and performs metabolic calculations to aid in the health assessment of astronauts in microgravity. GASMAP can be used in conjunction with a bicycle ergometer, treadmill, EKG, blood pressure monitor, and a rebreathing apparatus.

The GASMAP system consisted of: 1) a volumetric flow transducer to quantify the volume of inspired and expired gas, 2) a mass spectrometer with two internal processors, to measure the quantity and identify the species of the inspired and expired respiratory gases, 3) a laptop computer to control mass spectrometer operation, process and communicate data/diagnostics, display real time data, provide limited floppy disk data storage, and perform metabolic calculations, and 4) a calibration assembly to enable mass spectrometer accuracy verification.

The objectives of this study were: 1) Assure the greatest possible analyzer accuracy and response time, 2) Exceed 2.5 year operational life with a goal of 5 years, and 3) Deliver a GASMAP with minimal logistical overhead.

APPROACH:
Pre and Inflight Procedures:
In a long-term facility the ability to recalibrate the GASMAP analyzer is critical. The mass spectrometer designer considered several procedures under the heading of GASMAP calibration. These included hardware and software adjustments. They were: 1) Hardware Potential and Magnet Adjustment, 2) Mass Tuning Alignment, 3) Offset and Minor Interaction Adjustment, and 4) User Calibration.

The first procedure occurred immediately after assembly. The mass spectrometer was first calibrated by adjusting hardware potentiometers and by placing magnets. The goal in this calibration procedure was to achieve good sensitivity and good peak shapes. This is generally only performed once after assembly or after filament replacement. The second calibration procedure was performed to adjust a look-up table for each mass and to set the resolution for each mass that was measured. This was a software setup procedure and was called "Mass Tuning Alignment." The third calibration procedure adjusts the offsets or analyzer background that exists for certain masses, and several minor interactions that occur between gasses. Last, the User Calibration, the major interactions and gain adjustments for each gas were corrected. Except for Potential and Magnet Adjustment, all of the above mentioned procedures can be performed in-flight with the appropriate software and calibration gases. However; the User Calibration is the only calibration that the crew were trained to routinely perform. The Offset and or Mass tuning calibration would only be performed by crew members as a malfunction procedure.

RESULTS:
The first generation GASMAP analyzer onboard Mir exhibited exceptional stability. Investigators think the He and CO2 measurements can be corrected by changing the analyzer warm-up period to include filament run time.

experiment_title: Vestibular Influences on Autonomic Cardiovascular Control
parameter_html:
Autonomic reflexes
Orthostatic intolerance
Vestibular afferents
Vestibular reflexes
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kaufmann, Horacio
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Although there is substantial evidence that the vestibular and autonomic systems interact, the functional importance of the vestibular input in cardiovascular control is unknown. The goal of this proposal was to determine if activation of vestibular afferents triggers reflexes that engage autonomic pathways involved in cardiovascular regulation, particularly those that were studied in the Neurolab Project. The hypothesis is that linear acceleration along the long axis of the body (Z axis), or along the naso-occipital axis (X axis), signaling changes in body orientation with regard to gravity, causes vestibular-induced alterations in autonomic outflow to stabilize blood pressure. Novel scientific approaches include the use of paradigms that will allow investigators to distinguish between stimulation of semicircular canals and otolith organs.

Specific Aims:
1. Investigators used "radial" centrifugation to produce acceleration along the Z axis, and rotation about axes tilted from the vertical (off-vertical axis rotation, OVAR) to produce sinusoidally varying naso-occipital acceleration while monitoring autonomic function. On-center rotation about a vertical axis and "tangential" centrifugation were provided to control conditions in which the semicircular canals and otolith organs were activated.
2. Microneurography was used to determine the effect of vestibular stimulation on sympathetic outflow in normal subjects and in patients with baroreflex failure.
3. Investigators assessed the impact of vestibular reflexes on orthostatic tolerance.
4. Investigators explored the effect of promethazine on vestibular and autonomic reflexes and reflex interactions.

In summary, this proposal used state-of-the-art techniques to determine in a definitive way whether vestibular reflexes have an important cardiovascular autonomic component and contribute to orthostatic tolerance. Because space-induced vestibular dysfunction may contribute to the orthostatic intolerance experienced by astronauts returning to Earth, understanding vestibular/autonomic interactions can help develop more effective countermeasures to alleviate space motion sickness and post-flight orthostatic intolerance.

APPROACH:
Investigators studied subjects during on- and off-vertical axis rotation (VAR and OVAR). In previous ancillary experiments they found 15° tilt to be a good neurovestibular stimulus. During off-vertical axis rotation (OVAR), this projects 0.26 g onto all axes in the horizontal plane of the head. The original testing protocol consisted of four consecutive experimental conditions, each lasting six minutes:
1. Vertical axis, stationary.
2. Vertical axis rotation (VAR) clockwise at 60°/s.
3. Off-vertical axis (tilted 15°, right ear down), stationary.
4. Off-vertical axis rotation (OVAR) (tilted 15°), clockwise at 60°/s.

RESULTS:
Investigators have solved technical problems related to blood pressure and respiratory monitoring during OVAR. Specifically, the OVAR chair has been fitted with the portapres device (a new small device for beat to beat blood pressure measurements) and the slip rings modified to transmit its signals. Software has been modified to accept signals from both the ISCAN device and the portapres. Pilot trials of rotation during tilt have been successfully carried out, confirming the ability to carry out these studies.

experiment_title: Analysis of a Clinical Database as a Means to Validate Non-invasive Assessment of Intracranial Pressure Using the Cerebral and Cochlear Fluid Pressure (CCFP) Analyzer
parameter_html:
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Intracranial pressure (ICP)
Lumbar puncture (LP)
Tympanic membrane displacement (TMD)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Ebert, DouglasCo-Investigator: Danielson, DickCo-Investigator: Gianoli, GerardCo-Investigator: Hart, StephenCo-Investigator: Ploutz- Snyder, RobertCo-Investigator: Soileau, James
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Visual impairment intracranial pressure (VIIP) is a top risk for human space flight, yet there are no reliable means to monitor intracranial pressure (ICP) non-invasively, particularly in flight. A lumbar puncture (LP) is invasive and isn’t a viable option for in flight monitoring, and are only used on crewmembers exhibiting significant VIIP symptoms. Development and validation of a noninvasive means of monitoring ICP would result in collection of data that could define the involvement of elevated ICP in the VIIP syndrome. The Cochlear and Cerebral Fluid Pressure (CCFP) analyzer measures tympanic membrane displacement (TMD) in both evoked and passive modes. These TMD waveforms change in response to ICP alterations, allowing a noninvasive means to monitor ICP changes. Additional clinical validation of the CCFP analyzer is necessary to better understand the device’s utility. The Ear and Balance Institute has over 1,000 patient records of CCFP tests, many with accompanying LP measures. Analysis of the results of these tests has helped validate the use of the CCFP technology as a surrogate measure of ICP. The purpose of this retrospective clinical study was to examine this unique CCFP and LP data set, in order to identify characteristics that could contribute to follow-on studies employing the CCFP analyzer.

APPROACH:
This study was a retrospective chart review of Ear and Balance Institute patients. Personnel at the Ear and Balance Institute reviewed physical and electronic charts and compiled data into coded, de-identified spreadsheets and file structures. This data was transmitted to the investigative team in Houston, who performed the analysis. The analysis had several components that addressed the specific aims of this study: 1) evaluate both evoked and passive TMD waveforms as measured by CCFP and compare with LP data; and 2) determine the age-dependent distribution of cochlear aqueduct patency.

RESULTS:
Because the CCFP had been used as a clinical screening tool, many patients had begun medical intervention between administration of the CCFP test (Vm) and the LP, or had been undergoing treatment prior to any test being administered. Another caveat associated with this analysis is that CCFP measures had not been collected at the same time as LP. To address these issues, analysis focused on patients whose LP was performed in close temporal proximity to CCFP (within an average of approximately five days), and those who had no interventions between measures. These factors have reduced the number of charts available for analysis (approximately 70 out of 1000 available with CCFP and LP measures). Nearly all patients in this database had ear-related pathology, with the largest contributors being superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD), and perilymph fistula that likely affect CCFP response. Despite these factors, a negative correlation between tympanic membrane displacement in an evoked CCFP test and LP opening pressure was found in the non-SSCD patient population in the seated position, and expectation-maximization estimates suggested that Vm in the supine position trends negatively with LP. These results are encouraging as to the potential utility of the CCFP as an ICP screening tool in a non-clinical population, and deserve further investigation in an experimental setting.

experiment_title: Habitability Assessment:  Habitat Utilization Analysis from Human Factors Perspective
parameter_html:
Environment acceptability
Habitability
investigators: Principal Investigator: Whitmore, MihribanPrincipal Investigator: Blume, Jennifer
experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the habitability assessment project is to evaluate the Aquarius from the human factors and habitability perspective as an isolated, confined analog for the International Space Station (ISS), determine the human factors and habitability requirements for such an isolated and confined analog, and identify potential enhancement for the next generation habitat via use of naturalistic data capture, habitability questionnaire, and Space Operations Issues Reporting Tool (SOIRT).

By identifying how participants use the Aquarius habitat, conclusions can be drawn about which habitability attributes cause specific interactions and behaviors facilitating a systematic design to achieve desired human performance. In addition, the inclusion of objective data may provide inputs to other analysis of work/rest schedules.

Finally, naturalistic data collection has been under investigation as a means to opportunistically gather data during NASA training and actual International Space Station (ISS) missions. Inclusion of this method of data collection served as a test case to identify pros and cons and associated technological challenges.

APPROACH:
Crewmembers filled out a habitability survey, including questions regarding acceptability of the Aquarius habitat such as its interior layout, physical environment (e.g., noise, humidity), tasks, and individual experience/comments. This survey was required to be completed only once for the duration of each mission.

Crewmembers also filled out an issue reporting form, called SOIRT, to note any design or activity based issues and/or enhancements. This form was filled out on an as-needed basis throughout each mission.

The NEEMO 5 project also involved taping live feed from cameras, positioned with a view to the central common areas in the Aquarius. Taping took place during pre-defined periods of the 14-day mission. A heads-up signal was given at bedtime the night prior to taping, to remind the crewmember of the taped monitoring the following day. A second heads-up was given upon wake-up the following day, and a third at the end of the taping. The videos, which showed how crewmembers chose to use common spaces in Aquarius during the course of the day, were analyzed by computer to extract objective data. Once the data was extracted and analyzed, the videotapes were destroyed.

After the mission, the videotapes were reviewed and the amount of time each area was used by the crew at various times during the length of the mission was calculated. In addition, qualitative and descriptive analysis of the types of behaviors in each area was performed with the purpose of identifying any behaviors not typical of a certain area. If a participant used an area in a way different than expected, a subsequent analysis of the features of that area may result in conclusions of certain features that cause certain behaviors.

Finally, questionnaire data was analyzed to look for common pros and cons of the habitat across NEEMO/Aquarius crews, as well as consistency across different analogs used for space missions. This will help identify the functional needs and human factors requirements for living and working in an isolated, confined environment.

RESULTS:
From analysis of the video, several habitability issues related to the Aquarius habitat became apparent:

  • Workstations were poorly placed and interfered with the flow of traffic in and out of the Main Lock. Particularly, the two workstations located near the entrances were problematic both for people trying to pass through, as well as for people working at them who were interrupted in their work. When more than one person was at either of the two workstations, sitting on the step ladder or standing and looking over the shoulder of the other person, traffic flow was obstructed even more. In at least one instance, the stepladder was left behind after two crewmembers were working together, and another crewmember passing through had to step over it.

  • Another habitability issue revealed by the video analysis was the inappropriate size of the table. Used for eating, working, meetings, and group teleconferences with ground, the table sometimes needed to accommodate up to six people at once. Even for four people, as was more often the case, the table was far too small and it was obvious from the video that the crewmembers were uncomfortable. Often during group meetings some of them would have to sit on the step ladder or stand. Given its frequency of use, the table should be larger to comfortably seat all members of the crew to improve comfort, work, and social interaction. From the videos it also became evident that the food storage was poorly sited. Multiple instances were recorded where crewmembers were seen reaching across the small galley, blocking traffic or standing precariously on the stepladder to reach the storage areas. This also occurred frequently near and during meal times when most of the crewmembers were in and moving about the Main Lock.

  • Also noted during these periods was the fact that the refrigerator and microwave/storage areas were located too far from each other, as lots of back and forth traffic occurred between them. Given the narrow passage, it was readily apparent that traffic within the Main Lock could be much ameliorated simply by moving these two areas closer together.

    In conclusion, video analysis provided useful ideas as to how an enclosed habitat might be improved. As with the common human factors method of link analysis (e.g. Thelwell, 2004), simply noting which areas are accessed frequently together can provided insight into how to rearrange the habitat to improve efficiency and even reduce risk of injury. While web cast video had its technological problems, such as erratic skips, lags, graininess, blocked views, and lighting inconsistencies, it did provide useful overall information for practical recommendations. Systematic research, however, would require a higher standard of data collection. Perhaps in the future, notes regarding crew activity could be added by those recording the video to aid those tasked to analyze it later. This feature was sometimes present in the NEEMO 5 video; however, it was not present often enough to prove useful to the researchers. Also, video size and quality should be closely monitored to ensure that a larger percent of the captured video is analyzable.

    Naturalistic data capture by webcast video was found to be effective for getting the broad picture of habitat use by the NEEMO 5 crew. While there is obviously room for improvement, predominantly with the technology, there are some major benefits to be taken from this type of effort, as Adams (2002) reported previously. This type of work is crucial for designing and optimizing a habitat to support crew behavior as it will occur, especially since many of the findings were not captured in crew debriefings. This may be due to the unconscious influence of environmental performance shaping factors; however, more research is needed to support this claim. The inclusion of automation, such as sensors and location tracking, in future studies would make recording and analyzing certain metrics far easier and improve accuracy (e.g., entries and exits, frequency of use). The significant input that this type of research provides for generating optimal habitat designs and guidelines should not be neglected in any future long duration spaceflight effort.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Foegeding, EdwardCo-Investigator: Lila, Mary Ann
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Consuming the necessary amount of protein to reach dietary needs can be challenging, particularly for individuals who are recovering from strenuous exercise, dieting, or experiencing space flight. Therefore, diverse, convenient protein-dense and calorie-rich food sources are needed to supplement nutrition. Protein bars can be formulated with fruits, nuts, grains, and vegetables to address nutritional and health requirements, but may fail to meet shelf life needs, due to a phenomenon known as “bar hardening”. Over time, soft, chewy bars transform into hard, brittle solids with an undesirable texture. This hardening reaction is associated with various transformations of ingredients in the bars.

The proposed research was a ground-based investigation which evaluated high protein-polyphenol bar formulations for prevention of inadequate nutrition which may compromise the health of crewmembers during space flight. Typically, high protein bars have a short shelf-life due to hardening of bars over time. Therefore, the use of protein-polyphenol particles, which will not participate in the bar hardening reaction, was proposed. The bars delivered whey proteins, a high quality protein source that maintains muscle strength and function, and immune-protective polyphenols from berries that can improve cognitive function and prevent oxidative stress. Complexation of polyphenols to proteins will stabilize food quality and bioactivity for extended periods of space travel. The objective of the study was to produce a bar that contains optimal levels of whey proteins and plant polyphenols and that will maintain nutrient bioavailability and desirable sensory properties over the shelf life needed for space travel.

Mitigation of bar hardening with the use of protein-polyphenol ingredients is of interest to a wide range of individuals who need nutrients in a shelf stable for extended periods of time and those looking for the added health benefits of plant polyphenols.

APPROACH:
The approach used to support the above objectives comprise several phases. In the first phase, the bars were formulated. In the second phase the bars were evaluated for texture, sensory and rheological properties. In the third phase the shelf-life of the bars, at various temperatures, was determined. At specific times of shelf-life, the bars were tested for total phenolics, protein digestibility, and bar hardness.

RESULTS:
The goal of the project was to produce a protein-polysaccharide ingredient that was dense in nutrients and increase the quality of high-protein bars for use in space flight. It was hypothesized that using a functionally “inert” protein ingredient would resist changes that cause the undesirable textural property known as “bar hardening,” which shortens the shelf life of protein bars. Particles were formed where aggregation was driven by mixing whey protein isolate (WPI) with cranberry juice to form particles, separating the particles from the fluid phase, and spray drying. This provided an additional benefit of adding healthy plant polyphenols to a bar already containing high quality protein.

Methods were evaluated to produce protein-polyphenol particles designed for reducing bar hardness and explored potential mechanisms for reduced bar hardening. It was determined that particle formation based on co-aggregation of whey proteins with cranberry juice polyphenols (WP-CP particles) produced the most ideal particles. When used in a bar formation, WP-CP particles reduced the initial bar hardness and showed less hardening over time. The effect was thought to be the result of the particles not participating in reactions that produce bar hardening.

A critical step in forming WP-CP particles was the production of protein-polyphenol aggregates that were insoluble in the pH range of 4 to 6. While there is no agreed upon mechanism for bar hardening, the proposed mechanisms are related to phase equilibration, phase separation, or network formation over time. All of these require a protein-water phase with the ability for proteins to move about and form new interactions. Just mixing protein and juice polyphenols under conditions where proteins remain water soluble – at amounts similar to the WP-CP particles – showed increased bar hardness. experiment_title: Temporal Transcriptomics Analysis of Archived Spaceflight Biological Samples from ALSDA from 1991 to 2016
parameter_html: RNA integrity number (RIN)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Delgadillo-Talburt, Elizabeth
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
The purpose of this study is to assess the quality of spaceflight tissues stored in Ames Life Science Data Archive (ALSDA) freezers. Garnering information – for downstream functional analysis such as generation of omics datasets – from tissues is, in part, dependent on the state of sample preservation. To assess the viability of a select group of tissues, RNA integrity number (RIN) values were calculated for RNA extracted from rodent livers. Rat livers from Space Launch System 1 (SLS-1) and mouse livers from Commercial Biomedical Test Module 3 (CBTM-3), Rodent Research 1 (RR1), and Rodent Research 3 (RR3) were tested. It was found that mean RIN values from CBTM-3, RR1, and RR3 were suitable for downstream functional analysis (RIN > 5) while the mean RIN value for SLS-1 was not (RIN = 2.5 ± 0.1). Information from this study could lay the foundation for future efforts in determining the types of assays that are most appropriate for different tissues in ALSDA freezers, which would maximize the scientific return on rare spaceflight samples.

APPROACH:
RNA integrity numbers will be determined for rat and mouse liver specimens stored at -70ºC to -80ºC. We hypothesize that the RNA of specimens stored in the ALSDA freezers may vary across all specimens and that RIN analyses will confirm sample viability for downstream functional omics analyses.

The study will be conducted on rat liver specimens from SLS-1 (1991) and SLS-2 (1993) and mouse specimens from RR1 (2014) and RR3 (2016). It will be ensured that aliquots from a single animal will not be depleted.

RIN values will be calculated using GeneLab’s bioanalyzer. These values will be plotted against time to assess if there is a temporal trend. A positive control, which was determined when the STS-135 mouse liver samples were processed, will also be included.

Although the species varies, this is not a concern. The focus of the study is to examine the ability to garner information from spaceflight specimens stored at -70ºC to -80ºC regardless of the model organism.

RESULTS:
RIN values differ between biospecimens held in ALSDA freezers. These difference in RIN values could be attributed to the age, storage method, and fixative used on these tissues. Additional work should be done to expand this study to other organ types and animal models. Assessing the RIN value provided a glimpse into the current state of the biospecimens stored by the ALSDA. This knowledge is a foundation for future studies that can aid Principal Investigators in their assay and biospecimen selection.

experiment_title: Combined Blood Investigations
parameter_html:
Aldosterone
Angiotensin I
Glutamate decarboxylase (GAD)

investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, WilliamPrincipal Investigator: Leach- Huntoon, CarolynCo-Investigator: Cintron, NitzaCo-Investigator: Landry, RudolphCo-Investigator: Schneider, Howard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The primary objective of this investigation was to measure selected hormone and electrolyte components of the blood early in space flight. The blood components selected reflect the status of fluid and electrolyte metabolism. Measurement of these variables may help investigators determine whether responses predicted by the fluid redistribution hypothesis occur. According to this hypothesis, losses of body fluid and electrolytes result from the headward shift of fluid brought about by exposure of the human body to weightlessness. Estimation of early changes previously was not possible because of inflight scheduling priorities and constraints. The most dramatic changes in the adaptive response to weightlessness are believed to occur in the first hours of a mission.

APPROACH:
The Inflight Blood Collection System was used to collect samples by venipuncture from 6 subjects on 2 missions 1 or 3 times before flight; on mission days 2, 4, and 6 during flight; and within 2 hours (R+0) and 3 days (R+3) after landing. The concentrations of electrolytes and other blood components were determined using established clinical laboratory procedures such as spectrophotometry and radioimmunoassay.

RESULTS:
The earliest inflight blood collection time of 31 hours may not have been early enough. High levels of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may have been related to space motion sickness. Angiotensin I levels increased while aldosterone was suppressed at the inflight times measured. Cortisol secretion appeared to have been stimulated by high levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone. Most hormones increased at landing. Serum sodium decreased slightly during flight, and potassium decreased in the first 4 days but increased on flight days 6 and 7. The results, especially those for hormone levels, indicated that the fluid redistribution hypothesis does not explain changes in the regulation of body fluid and electrolytes during weightlessness. Renal function and other factors involved in fluid and electrolyte regulation, such as atrial natriuretic factor and prostaglandin E, need to be measured during flight.
