experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space motion sickness, a disorder which produces symptoms similar to those on Earth, has affected half of the astronauts and cosmonauts exposed to microgravity. Symptoms can be severely debilitating and a solution to this biomedical problem is a high priority for the safety end effectiveness of spaceflight. The objective of this study was to develop a method of training people to control their own motion sickness symptoms. The method of treatment is Autogenic Feedback Training (AFT). It is a combination of biofeedback and Autogenic Therapy which involves training physiological self-regulation as an alternative to pharmacological treatment. By studying the physiological and behavioral responses to microgravity, it may be possible to facilitate adaptation to the spaceflight environment.

APPROACH:
Preflight baseline data were collected including: 2 resting baselines, 1 KC-135 flight, 1 reclining baseline in 1g mockup, 2 mission simulations, 12 formal AFT sessions, 3 rotating chair tests, 8 follow up AFT practice sessions and 1 baseline session at L-10 days. Inflight data collection included: continuous daytime monitoring on mission days 0 through 2, timelined and symptom- contingent diagnostic sessions, and timelined and symptom-contingent AFT sessions. Post flight data collections consisted of 10 minute debriefing with each crewmember on the day of landing, and a 2 hour debriefing 14 days post flight.

RESULTS:
Results were collected across several different missions, however flight data were collected for only 6 crewmembers (3 treatment and 3 controls). The experiment was cancelled before validation could be completed on N=16 (8 treatment and 8 controls) as originally proposed. The flight results showed 2 of the 3 AFTE subjects were symptom free, the third had moderate symptoms on the first mission day. None of the AFTE subjects took medication during the flight. Two of the Control subjects experienced multiple vomiting episodes on the first 3 mission days, despite having taken medication. The third experienced only mild symptoms. It was concluded that that AFT is effective for controlling space motion sickness in some crewmembers, and that inflight effectiveness is related to demonstrated learning ability preflight. Autonomic measures and self-assessment scales are an effective method for assessing effects of microgravity on individual crewmembers functional state.

experiment_title: NEXGEN Approaches to Chromatid Painting
parameter_html:
Chromosomal inversions
Inversion frequency
Radiation dose
investigators: Principal Investigator: Ray, F.
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is every reason to believe that large and small scale chromosomal intra-changes (inversions) are just as important as inter-changes between chromosomes, e.g., translocations, the latter of which are well known to cause cancer. And yet, inversions, especially small ones, have been historically difficult, if not impossible to detect. Recently, KromaTiD Inc., using SBIR funding from NASA, successfully demonstrated a new platform technology to detect small chromosomal inversions using directional oligonucleotide probes called chromatid painting. In this study, the investigators propose to develop the next generation of whole chromatid paints using a much faster, more cost effective approach. If successful, this will facilitate the rapid development of additional chromatid paints, with the goal of ultimately covering the entire genome. These next generation chromatid paints will be of even higher resolution than currently possible, so they will greatly expand potential biodosimetric applications.

APPROACH:
The approach for this study is not available.

RESULTS:
KromaTiD Inc. previously completed a prototype of the methodology, i.e. a fluorescent chromatid paint to human chromosome three, and then demonstrated the predicted capability to detect inversions after exposure to ionizing radiation. Inversions were evidenced as fluorescent signal switches that appeared on the opposite chromatid of chromosome 3, opposite to their original position, allowing relative ease of scoring and suggesting that scoring might be automated completely in the future. The assay was then used to count the increased frequency of inversions that were produced after gamma radiation exposure, a proof of concept that the technology could be used for biodosimetry.

Subsequently, in collaboration with NASA space radiation investigators, the production of chromosome inversions caused by high linear energy transfer (LET), high energy ions (HZE) particles was described. Results showed a dramatic dose-dependent increase in the yields of inversions that were induced by high LET charged particles, similar to those encountered in deep space as compared to low LET gamma rays.

New directional genomic hybridization (dGH) chromatid paints to human chromosomes 1 and 2 were developed, and the previously created dGH chromosome 3 chromatid paint was recreated using a more efficient and less costly method. These paints have improved the performance of KromaTiD’s biodosimetry assays while reducing the cost per assay. This will allow the rapid development of increasingly sensitive biodosimetry inversion assays to be used in the analysis of radiation risk for astronauts.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Allen, Josephine
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The negative effects of space flight on cardiovascular health has been demonstrated and documented over many years. One of the body’s normal vascular repair mechanisms is the recruitment of adult stem cells from bone marrow to integrate into the vasculature. These recruited cells are involved in blood vessel wall repair and the formation of new blood vessels. This proposal seeks to study the effect of microgravity on adult stem cells. Of specific interest is how well these cells can differentiate into vascular cells under altered environmental conditions such as microgravity, and how well these cells function as healthy vascular cells once differentiated. Differentiation studies using a bioreactor will be conducted to expose the cells to microgravity conditions. Once differentiated, the cells will be exposed to several stimulatory environments that will demonstrate their functional ability. Molecular biology techniques, such as gene expression studies, will elucidate the effect of microgravity on these cells.

Studying adult stem cells is a means towards the goal to develop countermeasures for the negative effects of space flight on vascular health. This proposal addresses one of NASA's research interest, specifically, studies of the effect of gravity and the space environment on cellular and molecular processes. In this proposal, the cellular and molecular processes under investigation are stem cell differentiation and the corresponding molecular changes the stem cells undergo.

APPROACH:
To achieve our goal, we have established 2 specific aims, briefly, 1) Differentiate circulating stem cells into vascular endothelial (EC) and smooth muscle cells (SMC) under conditions of microgravity and normal gravity; 2) Assess the functional potential of the microgravity exposed differentiated cells. Our approach to achieving these goals involves first isolating blood derived stem cells, then culture under microgravity conditions in a rotating wall vessel bioreactor or static (normal gravity) in tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS) plates. Following dynamic and static culture, the cells are assessed for differentiation. Our assessments include both protein and gene expression changes, using western blot analysis and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (rt-PCR), respectively. We are interested in the loss of stem cell protein and gene expression and upregulation of endothelial and smooth muscle cell protein and gene expression. For our second aim, our goal is to assess the changes in functional capacity of the differentiated cells, particularly the changes in function as a results of microgravity. To assess SMC function, we proposed to evaluate the ability of the differentiated cells to respond to contractile stimulation, migration, secrete extracellular matrix proteins, and modulate between synthetic and proliferative phenotypes. Our approach involves culture under stimulatory conditions where appropriate and assessments of SMC functions can be made. For endothelial cell functional analysis, we are interested in assessing the production and secretion of antithrombogenic factors, nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2) by the differentiated endothelial cells. In addition, our approach involves assessing the hemocompatibility of the cells in terms of clotting and platelet activation when exposed to whole blood from human subjects.

RESULTS:

1. Goal: Optimizing bioreactor and experimental set-up and methodology with Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs)

The experimental set-up we proposed using a commercially available rotary cell culture system (RCCS) bioreactor (Synthecon) was optimized using HUVEC cells. Our goal was to optimize various bioreactor/experimental parameters such as microcarrier bead handling and protein coating, cell seeding density and culture parameters, bioreactor rotational speed, culture maintenance and sample extraction from bioreactor chambers, as well as overall training within the experimental system. Early project challenges such as low cell adhesion on microcarrier beads and cell detachment under dynamic conditions in the rotating wall vessel (RWV) were eventually overcome by changing our experimental design. Our results show successful cell attachment and faster proliferation of HUVECs under microgravity than under static conditions.

2. Goal: Isolation and culture of human endothelial progenitor cells and differentiation into endothelial cells

Once our bioreactor and experimental setup was optimized, we extended our work to the target cell population that is the focus of this work, human endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) derived from circulating blood. The human EPCs are a rare population of stem/progenitor cells that are isolated from the peripheral mononuclear cell (PBMNC) fraction of whole blood. PBMNCs were isolated from human blood obtained from donors as per Institutional Review Board (IRB) guidelines. Circulating progenitor cells contained within the PBMNC fraction of whole blood were differentiated into endothelial-like cells, as confirmed by the formation of colonies (within 2-6 weeks) with EC specific ‘cobble-stone’ morphology, and positive expression of EC specific proteins.

3. Goal: Study the effect of microgravity on the differentiated endothelial cells in culture

We assessed the ability of these cells to adapt to simulated microgravity conditions after short term culture and expansion. More specifically, the functionality of the differentiated ECs following exposure to simulated microgravity assessed conditions such as proliferation, release of soluble factors, changes in gene expression, and anti-thrombogenic potential was investigated. The results of the present study demonstrated that the populations of human blood EPC derived ECs when exposed to simulated microgravity proliferate faster, release higher amounts of soluble NO and lower amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, when compared to their normal gravity cultured controls. This can be possibly attributed to the ability of the cells to sense simulated microgravity as a “stressful” condition and adapt by upregulating gene expression of hsp70. However these secretory as well as proliferative functions had no effect on the anti-thrombogenic functions of these cells. Their anti-coagulative and anti-thrombogenic ability as assessed by both upregulation of tPA as well their ability to delay plasma clotting, were impaired upon exposure to simulated microgravity. This study is the first step towards understanding the ability of these repair cells to regulate clotting mechanisms and cardiovascular health in space. Further studies to assess alternate and synergistic mechanisms involved in regulation of cardiovascular health as well as inflammatory dysfunction under microgravity are required to develop possible cell based countermeasures to prevent cardiovascular deconditioning due to space travel.

4. Goal: Expand to include porcine EPCs to further study the effect of microgravity on differentiation of the blood derived EPCs.

Due to the initial challenges we had faced with differentiating as well exposing human blood derived progenitor cells during the pre- differentation stage under simulated microgravity, our goal was to extend our work to an alternative cell source, porcine EPCs. Our lab has previously obtained porcine PBMNCs (under University of Florida IACUC approval) and differentiated these into cells with endothelial cell phenotype (PE-like cells). Circulating progenitor cells contained within the PBMNC fraction of porcine whole blood were exposed to simulated microgravity, using a RWV bioreactor. After exposing the circulating progenitor cells to 6, 12, and 18h of simulated microgravity, the cells were then cultured on fibronectin coated TCP under static conditions and their ability to differentiate into endothelial cells was assessed by the formation of colonies with EC specific ‘cobble-stone’ morphology and confirmed by immunohistocytochemical staining for CD31 as well as eNOS. Our results showed that longer exposure to simulated microgravity delayed the onset of differentiation of EPCs to PE-like cells.

Clotting behavior assessment showed that following the clotting rate for 6h-µg exposed cells are the clotting times for the 12h and 18h-µg exposed cells. Normal gravity cultured cells clotted the next while the last to clot was the plasma exposed to the EC control cells. Similarly, the whole blood clotting kinetics showed that the kinetic profile of whole blood when incubated with PE-like cells differentiated after exposure to simulated microgravity, showed faster clot formation than normal gravity controls. However, longer exposure times showed greater inhibition of clotting.

Collectively, the data shows that within the 3 time points of µg exposure, the longer exposure times showed greater inhibition of clotting, which may be attributed to the increased ability to release soluble anti-thrombogenic factors, NO and PGE2. While both the migration and proliferation of cells were inhibited by microgravity exposure, prolonged exposure of EPCs to microgravity resulted in decrease in the migration abilities of EPC derived EC and the proliferative capacity of the ECs seemed to recover on longer time of exposure. The initial decrease and subsequent increase in release of soluble factors such as NO and PGE2 reaffirmed the possibility of recovery mechanisms being involved on prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Finally the assessment of whole blood and plasma clotting, indicated that microgravity pre exposure at the progenitor stage caused inhibition, in the ability of PE-like cells to delay blood or plasma clotting while this effect was again nulled with increase in time of exposure of EPCs to microgravity. This data collectively provides some insight into the role of short term exposure to low shear stress environment due to simulated microgravity, on cardiovascular deconditioning during space travel.

experiment_title: Investigation of Neural Strategies of Visual Search

Saccadic eye movements
Superior colliculus

investigators: Principal Investigator: Krauzlis, Richard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Human performance is easily impaired in a variety of aerospace tasks - such as remotely docking a spacecraft, or flying an aircraft in poor visibility, or finding and tracking a particular target airplane on a crowded air-traffic control display. These impairments occur because aerospace environments can degrade or remove the sensory cues used to drive and coordinate voluntary actions, and display systems may not be optimally matched to the human user. Fortunately, much progress has been made recently in the field of neuroscience toward understanding the physiological mechanisms responsible for voluntary motor behaviors. Visual search is the process that allows us to quickly respond to important items in our surroundings, even in the presence of other irrelevant stimuli. Understanding how individual neurons participate in this process is critical for identifying the factors that limit the speed and accuracy of visual search. Knowledge of these neural factors could be used to design visual displays that conform to the temporal and spatial constraints imposed by human neurobiology, thereby directly improving human performance in man-machine interfaces and virtual environments.

Arguably the most important class of movements made by primates during visual search are eye movements, because control of the position of the eyes determines which visual information is sampled and for how long. Decades of anatomical and physiological research have provided a detailed outline of the brain pathways that are responsible for the control of eye movements in primates. These pathways involve a network of areas including visual areas of the cerebral cortex (which provide information about the content of the visual scene), motor regions of the cerebellum and brainstem (which form the final motor commands), and several regions that lie in-between (and which possess a mixture of sensory and motor properties). They recorded from saccade-related neurons (n=85) in the SC of two subjects during a luminance discrimination task. After a random interval, two Gaussian-blurred discs were added, with a luminance increment (SNR = 0 to 4) added to one disk. The subject was rewarded for making a saccade to the brighter disc. The former explanation is the traditional interpretation, whereas the latter explanation is a more recent interpretation based on signal detection theory and applications of Bayesian inference.

The results of the analysis favor the weighted evidence interpretation. The subjects’ performance in the task showed a clear cue validity effect: higher percent correct when the cue correctly indicated the target location. Neurons in the superior colliculus showed a neural correlate of this cueing effect: higher activity on validly cued trials compared to invalidly cued trials. However, ROC analysis indicated that this effect was almost entirely due to a bias in activity caused by the presence or absence of the cue in the neuron’s response field. The ability of the neuron to visually discriminate between target and distracter was largely unaltered by the presence or absence of a cue.

These findings are consistent with the idea that saccadic choice behavior is guided by a weighted integration of sensory evidence, and that the activity recorded in the superior colliculus lies after the point at which those weights are applied. Eye movements generated during visual search have two components: saccades that rapidly redirects the line of sight to new objects, and smooth pursuit that smoothly changes the line of sight to follow moving objects. On the other hand, they also identified two specific differences between pursuit and saccades in how the putative decision signal is read-out to determine the eye movement choices. First, the pursuit system employs a lower response threshold than saccades; this difference accounts for approximately seventy percent of the time-shift as well as the occurrence of trials in which the two motor choices disagree. Second, the saccadic system is subject to an additional motor delay that is not present in the pathways for pursuit; this difference accounts for the remainder of the time-shift observed between the two responses.

The investigators have also developed a novel task to examine how knowledge of target probability affects visual search. In these new studies, they have compared the ability of humans to learn a Markov process. Markov chains (stochastic processes where probabilities are assigned based on the previous outcome) are commonly used to examine the transitions between behavioral states, such as those that occur during foraging or social interactions. However, relatively little is known about how well primates can incorporate knowledge about Markov chains into their behavior. Saccadic eye movements are an example of a simple behavior influenced by information about probability, and thus are good candidates for testing whether subjects can learn Markov chains. In addition, when investigating the influence of probability on saccade target selection, the use of Markov chains could provide an alternative method that avoids confounds present in other task designs. To investigate these possibilities, investigators evaluated human behavior on a task in which stimulus reward probabilities were assigned using a Markov chain. On each trial, the subject selected one of four identical stimuli by saccade; after selection, feedback indicated the rewarded stimulus. On sessions where reward magnitude varied across stimuli, subjects (n = 6) demonstrated preferences for both greater reward probability and greater reward magnitude, resulting in a preference for greater expected value (the product of reward probability and magnitude). These results demonstrate that Markov chains can be used to dynamically assign probabilities that are rapidly exploited by human subjects during saccade target selection

Deciding where to look next demands the integration of bottom-up intrinsic image salience with top-down information of goals, motivation, and past experience of reward. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight, by impairing the differentiation program of stem cells residing within bone marrow results in bone loss, increased bone marrow adiposity, anemia, and impaired immune function. Because these disturbances may potentially compromise the success of long-duration flights, there exists an urgent need to identify the underlying mechanisms and implement effective countermeasures. This experiment will test the novel hypothesis that negative energy balance during space flight results in 1) bone marrow dysfunction and increased marrow adiposity and 2) altered signaling by peripheral adipokines (cytokines produced by adipocytes) all of which, in turn, contribute to negative bone turnover balance and bone loss. The proposed research will focus on the precise role of adipose tissue and the important adipokine leptin in mediating the detrimental effects of simulated spaceflight (hindlimb unloading) on bone marrow cells in mice by accomplishing the following 2 specific aims: Specific Aim 1 will test the hypothesis that increased bone marrow adiposity plays a causal role in mediating simulated space flight-induced changes in bone metabolism. This will be accomplished by comparing the skeletal response to hindlimb unloading of wild type (WT) mice with mice incapable of generating bone marrow adipocytes (kit-receptor-deficient KitW/W-v mice). Specific Aim 2 will test the hypothesis that the adipokine leptin, by targeting the differentiation of bone marrow stem cells, plays a key role in mediating energy sensitive changes in bone metabolism during simulated spaceflight. This will be accomplished by examining whether transplantation of mesenchymal or hematopoietic stem cells from leptin receptor-deficient db/db mice into WT mice alters bone loss during simulated space flight. Completion of the proposed project is expected to increase our understanding of the role of energy metabolism in mediating bone loss during simulated space flight and suggest specific non-pharmacological and pharmacological interventions to mitigate the detrimental effects of space flight on bone marrow.

APPROACH:
Aim 1
Experiment 1 was designed to evaluate differences in skeletal response of WT and adipocyte-deficient kitw/w-v mice to simulated spaceflight. 1) Duel energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) measurements were performed to measure body composition; 2) femur, tibia, and lumbar vertebra were scanned ex vivo by microcomputed tomography (microCT) and the 3D reconstructions analyzed for determination of bone microarchitecture; 3) serum glucose levels were measured at necropsy; and 4) femurs were embedded in plastic for sectioning and quantitative histomorphometry. Experiment 2 was designed to evaluate differences in skeletal response of WT mice to simulated spaceflight following transplantation of bone marrow from WT or kitw/w-v mice. We performed a pilot study to verify feasibility of transplanting hematopoietic stem cells into kitw/w-v and WT mice. Although found to be more radiosensitive, we developed a successful protocol for stem cell transplantation into the mutant mice.

Aim 2
Experiment 1 was designed to determine whether a high level of fat within bone marrow is associated with accelerated bone loss during simulated spaceflight. Weanling (1-month-old) WT and leptin-deficient ob/ob mice were maintained for 3 months under thermoneutral (32ºC) housing conditions to equalize resting energy expenditure between WT and ob/ob mice. The ob/ob mice were pair-fed to the WT mice to prevent development of morbid obesity in the ob/ob mice. Additionally: serum glucose, P1NP (bone formation marker), osteocalcin (bone turnover marker), and corticosterone (stress hormone) levels were measured at necropsy.

RESULTS:
Aim 1 Results: We evaluated the impact of a 14d spaceflight (in slowly growing ovariectomized rats) and a 14d simulated spaceflight (hindlimb unloading (HU) in adult male mice) on bone marrow adiposity. As described in detail in Keune et al., 2016, bone marrow adipose tissue (MAT) increased in the distal femur metaphysis during spaceflight. During the same interval there was a reduction in cancellous bone volume fraction. The observed bone loss was due to increased bone resorption; osteoblast number, osteoblast activity and osteoblast turnover were normal. In agreement, HU resulted in bone loss in male mice and the bone loss was due to increased bone resorption. However, we were surprised to find that HU did not result in an increase in MAT (publication under review) in WBB6F1/J mice. It should be noted that this unexpected finding was replicated in HU C57BL6 mice (publication in preparation). We conclude from these results that increased MAT is not a prerequisite for bone loss in HU mice.

We originally hypothesized that mice incapable of producing MAT would be protected from HU-induced cancellous bone loss whereas mice with excessive MAT would exhibit increased bone loss. We tested these hypotheses using kitw/w-v (MAT-deficient) mice and ob/ob (excessive MAT) mice. As expected, decreased MAT was associated with increased bone formation and increased MAT was associated with decreased bone formation. However, HU-induced cancellous bone loss was exaggerated in MAT- mice and not impacted by excessive MAT (publication in preparation).

Taken together, our studies demonstrate that spaceflight-induced cancellous bone loss in ovariectomized rats and HU-induced cancellous bone loss in male mice each occur as a result of increased bone turnover, where the increase in resorption is inadequately compensated for by bone formation. While lineage decision (mesenchymal stem cells to osteoblasts or adipocytes) was shown to influence bone formation and MAT levels, our findings do not support a causal relationship between MAT infiltration and bone loss during spaceflight. Indeed, our studies in MAT-deficient mice suggest that MAT may have a protective role in limiting bone loss. Further research will be required to verify these findings and determine the underlying mechanisms.

Aim 2 Results:
We performed a series of studies to test this hypothesis. Initial studies were focused on establishing the effects of leptin on MAT and bone turnover in normal rats and leptin-deficient ob/ob mice (Turner et al., 2014; Turner et al., 2015; Philbrick KA et al., 2015; Lindenmaier et al., 2016). We also addressed the controversy as to whether the physiological actions of leptin on bone are mediated through peripheral or central nervous system (CNS)-mediated signaling (publication under review). This question is important because leptin regulates energy metabolism through CNS signaling. Subsequent studies focused on how leptin impacts bone and energy metabolism during HU (publication in preparation).

Taken together, our studies provide strong evidence that leptin administered subcutaneously and hypothalamic leptin gene therapy have surprisingly similar effects on bone metabolism in ob/ob mice; specifically, leptin decreased MAT, increased osteoblast number and activity, and increased osteoclast activity. Dose response studies revealed that the skeletal effects of leptin occur at very low circulating levels of the hormone (levels having minimal effects on food intake or body weight), suggesting that previously published reports demonstrating skeletal effects of leptin delivered into the hypothalamus were due to transport of leptin into peripheral circulation and not due to CNS mediated actions. If confirmed, our finding that the actions of peripheral leptin on bone and central actions of leptin on energy metabolism are dissociable from one another would represent a paradigm shift.

It is well established that there is a close association between the magnitude of mechanical loading of the skeleton and bone mass, and that bone loss often accompanies weight loss induced by dieting (Iwaniec and Turner, 2016). Potentially, this is due to combined decreases in peripheral and CNS leptin levels. In support, we have shown that increasing hypothalamic levels in adult rats can reduce body weight but, in contrast to caloric restriction, promote weight loss without bone loss (Turner et al., 2015). It is well established that weight loss due to reduced food intake contributes to bone loss during HU and for this reason, weight bearing controls are normally pair-fed to HU rodents. However, as shown for weight bearing rodents (Turner et al., 2015), leptin treatment of HU ob/ob mice, although inducing weight loss, did not result in further bone loss (publication in preparation).

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In microgravity, bones and muscles are not used as they are on Earth. As many studies have shown, this altered use results in calcium loss, degeneration of the skeleton, lengthening of the spine by expansion of the intervertebral discs, change in spinal bone marrow composition and muscle atrophy. Bedrest patients on earth show this same musculo-skeletal response with the exception of bone marrow alterations.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is one method that can be used to measure the resulting muscular and skeletal changes. MRI is a safe, non-invasive scanning technique that uses a large magnet and low frequency radio waves to form an image by reading the amount of hydrogen in an area of the body. These images can be used to examine soft tissues in the body, as well as determine muscle volume, spinal bone marrow mass and cross-sectional area of intervertebral discs.

The objectives of this investigation were to use MRI procedures (1) to measure the muscle volumes of the calf, thigh, back and neck of the Mir astronauts and cosmonauts before and after flight; (2) to determine and compare muscle volume changes on the day of landing and four days after landing; (3) to determine the change in intervertebral disc size in the lumbar spine after flight, and determine the rate of recovery after return to gravity; and (4) to determine the bone marrow cellularity of the third lumbar vertebra (L3) before and after flight.

Findings from this investigation will lead to improved therapies that will facilitate the recovery of patients on Earth who have been bedridden for extended periods and will aid in the development of countermeasures allowing longer duration space flights.

APPROACH:
All crewmembers of the NASA 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 missions, as well as the Mir 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25 missions participated as subjects in this study. MRI scans were performed 30 and 60 days before launch, on the day of landing (U.S. crewmembers only), and 4, 14 and 30 days after landing on all crewmembers.

Imaging was performed using a 1.5 Tesla Siemens Magnetom MRI system (1.5 Tesla denotes the strength of the magnet used for the test) with various coils, including spine, Helmholz neck and whole body coils. These coils are the antenna of the MRI system that broadcast the radio frequency signal to the patient and/or receive the return signal to form an image. Specific coils are used to image different parts of the body; for example, Helmholz coils are used to image the cervical spine and muscles in the neck.

To begin the test, crewmembers were to lie down on a padded table, which would enter the magnet. Crewmembers were recumbent for approximately 10-15 minutes before beginning the test to minimize the effects of fluid shifts caused by lying down after standing. The order in which the measurements were made was kept the same for each crewmember from one imaging session to the next. The normal order was L3 spectroscopy, and then imaging of the intervertebral discs, then differential muscle volume measurements of the back muscles, neck muscles, thigh muscles and calf muscles.

A number of variables are used to acquire MRI images, including echo time, echo sequence, repetition time and matrix size. The echo time is the amount of time between magnetic pulses. Echo sequences are the number of magnetic pulses used to create an image. The repetition time is the amount of time between repetitions of the echo sequence, and the matrix size determines the resolution quality, or clearness, of the image.

Muscle volume of calf, thigh, lower back and neck:
For imaging of the calf and thigh muscles, the feet of the subject were positioned in a holder during the test to minimize movement and insure repositioning. The portion of the leg being imaged was suspended, while the non-imaged portion was supported with foam supports. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portion of the leg to remove artifacts in the image, which arise from parts of the body outside the imaging region but near the edge of the gradient coils.

For the thigh and calf muscles of NASA 2, 3, 4 and 7 and Mir 21, 22, and 23 crewmembers, 32, 1 centimeter slices (0.8 centimeter slices for NASA 5, NASA 6, Mir 24, and Mir 25) with a 0.2 millimeter gap between slices were obtained using an echo time equal to 10 milliseconds (msec), a repetition time of 800 msec and a 256 x 512 matrix.

Every tissue in the human body has its own spin-spin relaxation time (T2) value. Therefore, it can be used to differentiate between different tissue types (e.g. fat and muscle) and changes due to tissue changes (e.g. edema in sore muscles). Calf muscle spin-spin relaxation time (T2) was measured by rescanning the calf region using the same receiver gain at an echo time of 50 msec. Spin-spin relaxation times for each muscle pixel were calculated by comparing the image intensity between the echo times of 10 msec and 50 msec. T2 for a particular muscle was obtained by averaging the T2 for all pixels within that muscle.

For the back muscles, 20, 0.5 centimeter slices centered on the third lumbar vertebra were obtained using a spine coil and a 10 msec echo time, an 800 msec repetition time and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the neck muscles, a similar protocol was used with 32, 3 millimeter thick slices, and a Helmholtz neck coil in place of the spine coil.

Lumbar spine disc size and lumbar spine length:
To measure lumbar spine intervertebral disc size and lumbar spine length, subjects were positioned within the MRI machine so that the imaging area was centered within the third lumbar vertebra, determined from a sagittal scout view. A coronal scout image was used to position a 1 centimeter slice of interest down the center of the spinal column.

Imaging sequences of the lumbar spine varied between missions. During NASA 2 and 3 and Mir 21 and 22, two acquisitions of a four echo, spin echo sequence were obtained using echo times of 20, 45, 72 and 106 msec and a repetition time of 1 second.

For NASA 4, 5, 6 and 7 and Mir 23, 24 and 25, two different sequences were performed. First, one gradient echo sequence was obtained with an echo time of 7 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. Second, two single echo, spin echo sequences were obtained using echo times of 10 and 25 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. The matrix size for spinal images of all NASA-Mir crewmembers was 256 x 256.

Disc area was obtained for intervertebral discs in the lower back (T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4 and L4-5) from the number of pixels in each image. A phantom was also imaged during each imaging session to correct for any changes in pixel size.

To measure spine length, templates (small sub-images) were taken from the first preflight images, each containing a spinal disc. Each of these was registered (a mathematical best fit of position) for each subsequent measurement. The change in separation from the preflight positions to postflight positions was the change in spine length.

Bone marrow content (L3 spectroscopy):
To measure the fat to water ratio in vertebral bone marrow, volume selective proton spectroscopy was performed on a 15mm x 15mm cubic volume of interest in the third lumbar vertebra (L3) using a surface receive coil. Spectroscopy uses absorption, emission or scattering of electromagnetic radiation by atoms or molecules to qualitatively or quantitatively study the atoms or molecules. The Gradient Inversion Spectroscopy (GIS) technique was used to acquire spectra at echo times equal to 12, 18, 24 and 30 msec with a repetition time of 2 sec. Images were corrected for T2 weighting by exponential extrapolation of the spectra obtained at various echo times. Non-linear peak fitting was performed on the final spectrum to separate the water peak and different fat peaks from the background and to calculate their relative intensities. Bone marrow cellularity was determined from the fat to water ratio. T2 of the fat and water component was determined by fitting the decay of fat and water peaks with an exponential function.

Back pain questionnaire:
The crew also filled out questionnaires to document the frequency, severity and location of back pain or discomfort during the first 10 days of flight and the first 10 days after flight.

RESULTS:
Muscle volume:
The muscle volume changes as a percentage of the mean baseline volume in 16 crewmembers after long-duration flight were determined. To calculate percent change from baseline, the first postflight measurement at 0 to 4 days after landing was used. These flights ranged from 115 to197 days in duration. Paired t-tests of the average preflight volume to the first postflight measurement showed significant decreases for all regions except the neck muscles. The values, expressed as a percent of baseline (%±SD), for the 16 subjects were: anterior leg, 85.5±2.9%; gastrocnemius, 83.1±4.4%; soleus, 83.2±4.4%; quadriceps, 89.9±4.4%; hamstrings, 87.3±3.4%; intrinsic back, 84.1±5.8%; psoas, 95.6±6.1%; neck, 100.9±8.3%. A linear regression of the percent loss against flight duration showed no significant slope for any of the regions suggesting that the volume changes reached a new steady state by or before about four months of flight.

After landing, each of the flight crew were measured at multiple time points. Results indicate that muscle volume recovers at variable rates depending on the region, but generally have returned to baseline by 30-60 days postflight.

A comparison of percent change in muscle volume versus the size of the muscle before flight showed poor or no correlation for any of the muscle groups except the hamstrings, r=0.71. This was also true for when change in muscle volume was correlated with total weight or total body lean mass. This indicates that the suggestion that the percentage loss might be greater in those individuals with greatest mass before flight is not supported by the results in this study.

There was no significant correlation between the percentage loss in spinal bone mineral content and intrinsic back muscle volume during flight (n=12). However, when 12 bed rest subjects, half who performed an exercise countermeasure and the remaining who served as controls, were added to the flight data, the correlation was significant (r=0.61, p<0.0009). This may indicate that muscle atrophy might provide an early indicator for the extent of bone loss.

Comparison of flight results with bed rest data shows that the changes in the leg muscles during flight were generally less than bed rest. This is likely a consequence of the exercise countermeasure employed during flight since the bed rest data did not include exercise. The back muscles, however, showed greater loss during flight compared to bed rest, which may be reasonable, considering that the back muscles are active to a substantial degree in bed rest.

Muscle T2:
No muscle T2 measurements were possible on landing day. Therefore, the initial postflight measurements were obtained several days after landing which would obviously include significant ambulation prior to the first T2 measurement. The general pattern, however, is that T2 tends to be increased relative to baseline at the first postflight measurement and was almost always elevated at R+14 compared to the initial postflight measurement or baseline. By 30-70 days postflight the T2 decreased toward baseline in all cases where these measurements were available. The general response pattern is consistent with postflight muscle swelling associated with muscle damage.

Muscle Swelling:
Results show that muscle swelling can occur during the early reambulation period after landing. A similar pattern is seen following reambulation after bed rest. The largest changes were in the calf, particularly the gastrocnemius. The explanation for this swelling could represent rehydration of the muscle following dehydration of the muscle in microgravity. However, the muscle T2 postflight were invariably elevated above baseline, increased further for several weeks after flight and then returned toward the original baseline. These changes along with the reported sore muscles postflight would suggest muscle damage. The large change in the intrinsic back muscles of one crewmember has not been seen previously and may represent postflight swelling.

Intervertebral Disc:
Data indicate only minor spine lengthening and disc expansion by the time measurements were obtained on landing day. Measurements were made within 2-4 hours after landing with some walking and sitting up on a stretcher by the crewmember before testing. By 2-4 days postflight, slight residual expansion remained which by 2 weeks was back to baseline. Importantly, no long-term residual changes in disc size were found following these flights.

Proton Spectroscopy:
Comparison of NASA-Mir data to the LMS 17-day mission suggests that although the postflight T2 tends to increase as in the shorter LMS flight followed by a gradual return to baseline levels, there appears to be some differences. The first postflight T2 values were significantly reduced relative to preflight values; this was not detected after the shorter LMS flight. There is some evidence that the degree of decrease in the cellular bone marrow T2 is correlated with the percent change in spinal bone mineral density. Two distinct patterns exist. Postflight, some individuals begin below baseline and simply return to values close to baseline, while others like the LMS crew increase above baseline and gradually return to baseline over a period of several months.

Back Pain:
Out of 17 crewmembers (including one German guest cosmonaut on the Mir 97 mission), 9 (53%) indicated that they experienced back pain or discomfort during the flight. Generally, this occurred in the lower lumbar region during the first week or two of flight. The pain was typically described as "can be ignored," lasted a few hours to several days in duration and was most noticeable during or after resting. In one crewmember, it was most noticeable during exercise or applying bungies. Some crewmembers indicated that bending or application of massage seemed to relieve the pain. Postflight 8 of 17 (47%) crewmembers reported significant discomfort for some or all 10 days that monitoring was reported following flight. There were a number of cases where written reports were not available or were not filled out. Whenever possible, the crew were asked about their experience during and after flight. When no information was available these were treated as being negative reports and therefore, the incidence rates above may underestimate actual rates.

Conclusion:
There are measurable decreases in muscle volume during flight, which presumably represents muscle atrophy. These changes appear to be maximized within the first 4 months of flight. This degree of atrophy may indicate that bone loss may also reach a maximum probably at or around this same point, i.e., the rates of loss are different, but it seems reasonable that the degree of loss may be similar at the equilibrium point. If this turns out to be the case, muscle atrophy might be used as an early indicator of bone loss. Compared to bed rest without exercise, the inflight muscle changes are less, except in the back muscles. Recovery in all muscle groups is complete within the first 30-60 days after return to Earth, similar to recovery after bed rest. There are muscle volume and T2 changes during the first days and weeks after return from space flight compatible with muscle damage. We did observe small, but no long-term changes in disc size following these flights. There was a significant decrease in the T2 of the cellular component of the bone marrow of L3 which either increases to baseline during the first few weeks after landing or increases above baseline and subsequently returns to baseline over several months. No significant changes in the T2 of the lipid fraction of the same bone marrow or in the cellular to lipid fraction was seen. About 50% of the crewmembers reported some back pain during flight, however, the duration and magnitude of this problem seems not to be of major concern for long-duration flight. A more important consideration may be the potential for significant injury/pain after flight since about 47% reported significant postflight discomfort lasting for a number of days to weeks. This may be an important consideration after lengthy flights in microgravity followed by a visit to a planet that has significant gravity.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Dietlein, Lawrence
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
With each passing year, radioisotope techniques become more important in biological research and clinical medicine. With the flight of Gemini IV, medical radioisotope investigations were extended, for the first time, into the realm of near space. The radioisotope studies that started with Gemini IV have subsequently proven to be an efficacious means of studying various aspects of man's response to this new environment. To date, the human radioisotope studies performed for the Gemini program have included plasma volumes, red cell masses, and red cell survivals.

The objective of this experiment was to study various clinical aspects of astronauts in space, such as plasma volume, heart rate, workload, blood pressure, hematology, and orthostatic intolerance.

APPROACH:
All determinations of plasma volume and red cell mass were preceded by a 15-minute recumbent interval. Background blood samples were obtained prior to each radioisotope series to correct for any previously injected radioactivity. All plasma volume measurements were accomplished with iodinated human serum albumin.

The erythrocyte survival half-times were measured from the disappearance of chromium-tagged red cells and were corrected for changes in red cell mass. A sample obtained 24 hours after the injection of the radioactive cells was used as the zero time for each survival determination. This prolonged mixing time was used to allow removal of cells inadvertently injured during the tagging procedure.

RESULTS:
Plasma volume, red blood cell mass, and erythrocyte survival determinations were performed for the Gemini astronauts before and after Gemini orbital flights IV, V, and VII. Plasma volume decreases similar to those seen after bed rest and water immersion were found in Gemini IV and V. While each of these flights was affected by different stresses and the data accumulated are not as complete or extensive as desired, the results suggest that the plasma volume changes associated with the shorter flights may have been compensated for in the longer Gemini VII flight.

The objective of this experiment was to study various clinical aspects of astronauts in space, such as plasma volume, heart rate, workload, blood pressure, hematology, and orthostatic intolerance.

APPROACH:
All determinations of plasma volume and red cell mass were preceded by a 15-minute recumbent interval. Background blood samples were obtained prior to each radioisotope series to correct for any previously injected radioactivity. All plasma volume measurements were accomplished with iodinated human serum albumin.

The erythrocyte survival half-times were measured from the disappearance of chromium-tagged red cells and were corrected for changes in red cell mass. A sample obtained 24 hours after the injection of the radioactive cells was used as the zero time for each survival determination. This prolonged mixing time was used to allow removal of cells inadvertently injured during the tagging procedure.

RESULTS:
Plasma volume, red blood cell mass, and erythrocyte survival determinations were performed for the Gemini astronauts before and after Gemini orbital flights IV, V, and VII. Plasma volume decreases similar to those seen after bed rest and water immersion were found in Gemini IV and V. While each of these flights was affected by different stresses and the data accumulated are not as complete or extensive as desired, the results suggest that the plasma volume changes associated with the shorter flights may have been compensated for in the longer Gemini VII flight.

experiment_title: Functional Fitness Assessment (Flight Analog)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Physical fitness was assessed pre- and post- bed rest to guide individual physical training and to determine individual responses to training countermeasures. Functional Fitness pre- and post- bed rest testing captured a subject’s flexibility, endurance, and strength in absolute numbers.
APPROACH:
Functional fitness evaluations were performed by each subject before and after bed rest. Lower back and hamstring flexibility were tested by a sit and reach exercise immediately following a brief warm up and stretching exercises. Upper body strength was measured using a Smith Bench Press and lower body strength was measured using a leg press. Both measures used the 1 repetition maximum (RM) protocol. The 1 RM is typically achieved within 3 to 5 trials. The 1-RM value was recorded as the maximum weight lifted for the last successful trial.
Endurance of the latissimus dorsi, elbow flexors, and pectorals was assessed by the number of pull-ups the subject was able to complete. Endurance of the pectoral and shoulder muscles was assessed by the number of push-ups the subject was able to complete in 2 minutes, and abdominal muscle endurance was assessed by the number of sliding crunches the subject was able to complete in 2 minutes.
RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASAs) Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during Bed Rest Campaigns 1 and 3, 5, Artificial Gravity (AG), and Head Down Tilt - 30 day (HDT30).
There was no significant change in flexibility when comparing pre- bed rest day 2 to post- bed rest day 1. This may be due to the fact that subjects followed a daily stretching routine during the bed rest. Both genders had reduced endurance after bed rest. Both male and female subjects showed a significant reduction in strength between pre- and post- bed rest scores. The biceps and muscles of the back are used very little during bed rest, which leads to a reduction in muscular endurance. The tests of the leg press show a significant change from the pre- and post. During bed rest the subjects are not permitted to use their lower bodies; this provides the best representation to space flight that the investigators could record with Functional Fitness testing. Subjects lost substantial percentages of lower body strength from pre- bed rest day 2 to post- bed rest day 1. Strength returned to nearly the original pre- bed rest score on the final day of post-testing.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this experiment was to delineate the early changes that occur in both weight bearing and non-weight bearing bone tissues in growing animals in different cage configurations during space flight, and to relate these changes to alterations in cell proliferation and mineralization, bone subcellular characteristics, and bone biomechanics. Other objectives were to delineate the early changes that occur in both weight bearing and non-weight bearing bone tissues in growing animals, in different cage configurations during space flight, and to relate these changes to alterations in calcium metabolism.

Approach:

Bone markers for measuring mineralization rates were injected intraperitoneally into all animals before and after launch. Bone mass and length were measured. Bone tissues were processed for bone progenitor populations and matrix synthesis using histomorphometric and autoradiographic techniques. Alkaline phosphatase and Golgi activity of the osteoblasts and perivascular cells was investigated in humoral heads. Femur, L1 vertebra and calvaria were processed for mineralization. Nuclear volume of osteoblast cells was investigated in the maxilla. Humerus, tibia and L4 vertebra were processed for density, calcium, collagen parameters, and mechanical properties.

Results:

Group housed rats (AEM) had fewer bone changes and a faster recovery than singly housed animals. Bone mineralization rates showed significant suppression at the periosteal, but not corticoendosteal, surface during flight, and singly-housed flight rats showed a greater suppression. Structural properties indicated that the flight had little effect on the humerus of either singly or group-housed rats. Also, not all regions of the bones, or all bones were affected by flight; in the long bones, the periosteal surface showed suppression of formation while the endosteal surface showed little change, and no changes were noted in the ribs, calvaria, vertebra or maxilla suggesting that the response to space flight is not uniform throughout the skeleton.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
While a large body of research has documented the effects of microgravity on the cardiovascular system, body fluids, skeletal muscle, and bone metabolism, there is a renewed interest in the understanding how long-term space flight affects cognitive functioning and in particular neuroplasticity. In spite of increasing knowledge on behavioral adaptations during space flight, these studies remain controversial and are not necessarily reliable predictors of changes in brain structure and function. Data from the investigators’ ground-based analog experiments (i.e. bed rest and isolation studies in Antarctica) indicate that the hippocampus will be particularly vulnerable to detrimental effects associated with the various stressors during long-duration space flight. The hippocampus is part of the limbic system and plays important roles in learning and memory formation, and specifically spatial learning and episodic memory. Any malfunction and/or structural changes of the hippocampus could have substantial consequences on learning and memory consolidation as well as general cognitive performance.

In spite of ongoing research projects employing state-of-the-art imaging techniques, none of these experiments focused on the hippocampus. The primary objective of this project was to identify the changes in hippocampal subfield volume. Investigators hypothesize that hippocampal subfield volume will be reduced after 30 days of isolation and confinement in NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility. Moreover, investigators expect that these changes correlate with decrements in visuo-spatial navigation and memory. They also expect that these changes can be explained by changes in important neurotrophic key factors. This study aimed to assess the impact of human isolation and confinement on:


  1. The neuroplasticity of the brain.
  2. Cognitive performance and mood.
  3. Biomarkers of neuroplasticity.
  4. The proliferation and differentiation into hippocampal neurons and their underlying gene expression patterns of an immortalized multipotent, human hippocampal progenitor cell line.

APPROACH:
The study compared 16 participants living in the HERA facility for 30 days to 16 control subjects, matched for gender, age, and educational level, who continued their normal living conditions. Subjects completed the Cognition Test on their iPads. Cognition is a test battery that consists of 10 different cognitive tests that are administered with the Cognition software. The battery started with a brief questionnaire, followed by administration of the 10 cognitive tests. Subjects were asked to perform the Cognition battery (all 10 tests) three times pre-mission, once weekly in-mission, and three times post-mission. To assess visuo-spatial performance, working memory, and executive function visuospatial ability testing (10 computer-based tasks) were performed four times pre-mission, once weekly in-mission, and twice post-mission. Subjects also completed Visual Analog Scales (VAS) on their iPad. It is a standardized questionnaire of perceived mental and physical exhaustion, fatigue, stress, workload, conflict, depression, anxiety, personality, social desirability, and sleep quality. They performed this three times pre-mission, once weekly in-mission and up to three times post-mission.

The investigators used an innovative, state-of-the art technique for high-resolution hippocampal neuroimaging as well as a unique human 3-D water maze task, which was used as a human analog model for the classical spatial learning task typically employed for laboratory rodents to assess spatial orientation. In addition, biomarkers were obtained from blood and plasma samples to determine key neurotrophic and inflammatory factors related to neuroplasticity. To further elucidate the effects of isolation on neuronal growth investigators assessed hippocampal plasticity in-vitro using an immortalized multipotent, hippocampal progenitor cell line.

RESULTS:
NASA does not currently have an agreement to archive the hippocampal plasticity and biomarker data from this International investigation. However, the Co-Investigator, Dr. Mathias Basner, submitted the cognitive and behavioral data from all subjects.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ultrasound forms medical images with a probe called a transducer that sends high-frequency sound waves and then receives their echoes. This transducer can be moved and angled to gain different views. An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to create a moving picture of the heart. Ultrasound is ideal for medical imaging in space because it is compact, risk-free, and inexpensive. However, operator skill is required to acquire quality images. Errors can occur because there are few landmarks to let the sonographer identify the exact location of the probe relative to the organ it is analyzing.

A visual anatomic guidance system was developed in this ground-based study to help crewmembers: (1) acquire correctly positioned medical ultrasound images and (2) display the location of the current image plane relative to the anatomy of the target organ. The line of intersection, the planes of intersection, and the numeric angle of intersection can be displayed relative to a previous image. The sonographer can monitor a real-time graphic display in addition to the ultrasound screen while performing the procedure. This system can improve the diagnostic accuracy of the ultrasound when performed in space. The hypothesis stated that persons untrained as sonographers can acquire more accurately positioned images with real-time guidance than without it, and guidance will improve accuracy and reproducibility in quantitative analysis of ultrasound images.

There were three specific aims. The first specific aim was to develop three methods for visual anatomic guidance and compare performance. The second was to test a prototype system for tracking the location and orientation of the ultrasound transducer that offers immunity to ambient ferromagnetic interference. Finally, the third specific aim was to widen the applicability of the technology on Earth by applying guidance in imaging the right ventricle of the heart.

APPROACH:
Computer software was developed to implement three methods of visual anatomic guidance. The left ventricle of the heart was used for evaluation, but other organs could also be used. The first method, the line of intersection method, displays the current image plane location as a line drawn on short and long axis scout images recorded at the beginning of the study. The disadvantage is that it does not indicate whether the current image plane is tilted inappropriately in the third out-of-plane dimension unless two scout images are monitored. The second method, the intersecting planes method, displays scout images in three dimensions with the current image overlaid semi-transparently. It shows position and orientation of the current image relative to the heart as revealed in the selected scout images.

The third method of visual anatomic guidance involved visualizing the image plane's intersection with the three-dimensional target surface. This method assists in understanding where the current image plane is located and where it should be to cut a short axis or long axis view, making the current image position and orientation visible relative to the heart. Because of the need to prepare a three-dimensional surface reconstruction of the heart to serve as the anatomic guide, a method called SmartFit was created. Prior information about heart shape variations was used to estimate the heart's three-dimensional surface. The shape variations stemmed from a catalog of three-dimensional reconstructions of the surface from patients with diverse diagnoses. Input data was fitted to a weighted average of shapes in the catalog to generate the estimated surface. This SmartFit method consistently produced a ventricle-like shape.

The impact of visual guidance on the accuracy and reproducibility of quantitative analysis was tested. Left ventricular volume values acquired with and without anatomic guidance in patients and normal subjects were compared. The effect of guidance on measuring right ventricular volume was also tested.

The second specific aim tested a commercial prototype magnetic field tracking system. The tracking system's receiver was mounted on a stylus with a ball tip that was used to locate two sockets ten centimeters apart on a Plexiglas box. The stylus mimicked a transducer. The precision in locating each socket at baseline without ferromagnetic interference and on top of a hospital stretcher, such as that used for echocardiography, was measured repeatedly.

The third specific aim was to widen the applicability of visual guidance technology in clinical practice. The accuracy of a piece-wise smooth subdivision surface reconstruction method for determining the shape and volume of the right ventricle was validated, and guidance was applied for its imaging. Three-dimensional echo imaging of animal hearts in a water bath was performed. The volume and mass obtained from the image analysis was compared with the true values measured from the hearts. To validate the ability of the reconstruction of accurately representing the shape of an organ, plaster casts were prepared of the right ventricular endocardium and laser scanned. The three-dimensional surface reconstructed from the dense accurate laser scan data was compared to that reconstructed from the echo images.

RESULTS:
The left ventricle catalog for the SmartFit method was adequate for reconstructing a variety of patient ventricles. It consisted of fifty-two normal subjects and fifty-two patients with diverse diagnoses. However, the catalog for the right ventricle contained only twelve studies.

All three methods of visual guidance were implemented. Thirty subjects were evaluated, but, because the protocol was long, the subject often moved, and data were unable to be utilized. Data from only thirteen subjects could be analyzed in the left ventricular volume study and five subjects in the right ventricular volume study.

The quantitative analysis of the left ventricle did not show benefit from visual guidance. Accuracy and reproducibility of the left ventricular volume measurement from two-dimensional images was the same with and without guidance. The result is likely because the left ventricle had such a regular shape that deviations in image plane position did not introduce much error in volume measurement. Scanning the right ventricle produced a different result. The visual anatomic guidance system's SmartFit surface, the three-dimensional surface estimation used for guidance, provided an untrained physician with measurements of right ventricular volume that varied from true by a mean error of only 14.2%, comparable to the error of the best published two-dimensional echo method, which was 16.3% by biplane pyramidal approximation. Calculations using a modification from this study of the biplane pyramidal method showed that the guidance gave the inexperienced physician an error of only 5.0%, which is smaller than previous studies and comparable to an experienced sonographer.

The guidance system accelerated the rate at which an untrained resident learned to perform scanning by assisting in relating the image to the anatomy. It also helped a trained sonographer perform cardiac sonograms more efficiently. Thus, the guidance system was a teaching tool for the novice and was valuable in assisting a trained sonographer to improve performance in the technique.

The results of the second specific aim demonstrated that the prototype magnetic field tracking system allowed the ultrasound transducer to be tracked accurately even in the vicinity of ferromagnetic interference, such as over a hospital stretcher. Distance between two points could be measured with high accuracy.

The result of the third specific aim showed that the piece-wise smooth subdivision method was capable of reconstructing the endocardial surface of the complexly shaped right ventricle. There was a close correlation between the three-dimensional echocardiogram measurements and the true right ventricular volume. The method was able to reconstruct the right ventricle with shape accuracy in three dimensions. Results suggested that visual anatomic guidance using the third method of the first specific aim, intersection with three-dimensional surface, was feasible for organ systems besides the heart.

The visual anatomic guidance was shown to be feasible for assisting crewmembers with space-obtained images of optimal diagnostic quality. It could also facilitate preflight training in ultrasound procedures. It could be upgraded to give ground control the ability to provide the crewmember feedback on operating the transducer.

Benefits to healthcare include the ability of the visual guidance system to assist sonographers in positioning images. Variability in organ dimension measurements could be reduced, enabling the measurements to reliably indicate patient status and allow serial measurements to detect changes in the patient condition more efficiently. Three-dimensional anatomic guidance could teach sonographers how to manipulate the transducer and reduce training time because trainees are shown in real time how the image plane changes position and orientation as the ultrasound transducer is manipulated. Guidance to the trained sonographer of the correct views could reduce the time needed to conduct the ultrasound and increase the clinical laboratory efficiency. The ability to document accuracy in image plane positioning may reduce duplication of the ultrasound studies by consultants. An expert in a remote location could utilize the guidance system to assist the person doing the imaging.

Left ventricular volume values acquired with and without anatomic guidance in patients and normal subjects were compared. The effect of guidance on measuring right ventricular volume was also tested.

The second specific aim tested a commercial prototype magnetic field tracking system. The tracking system's receiver was mounted on a stylus with a ball tip that was used to locate two sockets ten centimeters apart on a Plexiglas box. The stylus mimicked a transducer. The precision in locating each socket at baseline without ferromagnetic interference and on top of a hospital stretcher, such as that used for echocardiography, was measured repeatedly.

The third specific aim was to widen the applicability of visual guidance technology in clinical practice. The accuracy of a piece-wise smooth subdivision surface reconstruction method for determining the shape and volume of the right ventricle was validated, and guidance was applied for its imaging. Three-dimensional echo imaging of animal hearts in a water bath was performed. The volume and mass obtained from the image analysis was compared with the true values measured from the hearts. To validate the ability of the reconstruction of accurately representing the shape of an organ, plaster casts were prepared of the right ventricular endocardium and laser scanned. The three-dimensional surface reconstructed from the dense accurate laser scan data was compared to that reconstructed from the echo images.

RESULTS:
The left ventricle catalog for the SmartFit method was adequate for reconstructing a variety of patient ventricles. It consisted of fifty-two normal subjects and fifty-two patients with diverse diagnoses. However, the catalog for the right ventricle contained only twelve studies.

All three methods of visual guidance were implemented. Thirty subjects were evaluated, but, because the protocol was long, the subject often moved, and data were unable to be utilized. Data from only thirteen subjects could be analyzed in the left ventricular volume study and five subjects in the right ventricular volume study.

The quantitative analysis of the left ventricle did not show benefit from visual guidance. Accuracy and reproducibility of the left ventricular volume measurement from two-dimensional images was the same with and without guidance. The result is likely because the left ventricle had such a regular shape that deviations in image plane position did not introduce much error in volume measurement. Scanning the right ventricle produced a different result. The visual anatomic guidance system's SmartFit surface, the three-dimensional surface estimation used for guidance, provided an untrained physician with measurements of right ventricular volume that varied from true by a mean error of only 14.2%, comparable to the error of the best published two-dimensional echo method, which was 16.3% by biplane pyramidal approximation. Calculations using a modification from this study of the biplane pyramidal method showed that the guidance gave the inexperienced physician an error of only 5.0%, which is smaller than previous studies and comparable to an experienced sonographer.

The guidance system accelerated the rate at which an untrained resident learned to perform scanning by assisting in relating the image to the anatomy. It also helped a trained sonographer perform cardiac sonograms more efficiently. Thus, the guidance system was a teaching tool for the novice and was valuable in assisting a trained sonographer to improve performance in the technique.

The results of the second specific aim demonstrated that the prototype magnetic field tracking system allowed the ultrasound transducer to be tracked accurately even in the vicinity of ferromagnetic interference, such as over a hospital stretcher. Distance between two points could be measured with high accuracy.

The result of the third specific aim showed that the piece-wise smooth subdivision method was capable of reconstructing the endocardial surface of the complexly shaped right ventricle. There was a close correlation between the three-dimensional echocardiogram measurements and the true right ventricular volume. The method was able to reconstruct the right ventricle with shape accuracy in three dimensions. Results suggested that visual anatomic guidance using the third method of the first specific aim, intersection with three-dimensional surface, was feasible for organ systems besides the heart.

The visual anatomic guidance was shown to be feasible for assisting crewmembers with space-obtained images of optimal diagnostic quality. It could also facilitate preflight training in ultrasound procedures. It could be upgraded to give ground control the ability to provide the crewmember feedback on operating the transducer.

Benefits to healthcare include the ability of the visual guidance system to assist sonographers in positioning images. Variability in organ dimension measurements could be reduced, enabling the measurements to reliably indicate patient status and allow serial measurements to detect changes in the patient condition more efficiently. Three-dimensional anatomic guidance could teach sonographers how to manipulate the transducer and reduce training time because trainees are shown in real time how the image plane changes position and orientation as the ultrasound transducer is manipulated. Guidance to the trained sonographer of the correct views could reduce the time needed to conduct the ultrasound and increase the clinical laboratory efficiency. The ability to document accuracy in image plane positioning may reduce duplication of the ultrasound studies by consultants. An expert in a remote location could utilize the guidance system to assist the person doing the imaging.

experiment_title: Peripheral Quantitative Computed Tomography (pQCT)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study is to obtain more precise measures of bone mass and structure to be used in estimating bone strength particularly with regard to prolonged disuse, experienced by subjects participating in long duration bed rest studies.
Peripheral Quantitative Computerized Tomography or pQCT, is a relatively new bone measurement technology that provides information beyond that obtained by traditional DXA. This additional information includes area and bone mineral density of trabecular vs. cortical bone as well as estimates of bone strength (strength-strain index). pQCT scans can be obtained on peripheral sites including the tibia. Because pQCT can distinguish between cortical and trabecular bone (the latter of which loses bone preferentially with disuse), pQCT may prove to be a more sensitive measure than DXA for detecting disuse bone changes. If this is so, pQCT measurements might in the future allow for earlier acceptance or rejection of bone-related countermeasures than would be provided by DXA alone. JSC's long duration bed rest studies provide an important opportunity to validate the utility of pQCT measurements for monitoring disuse bone loss, with minimal associated time requirements or radiation exposure. In addition, pQCT provides important information regarding bone strength by measuring a strength-strain index for the scanned bone region. This information is not available with DXA.
APPROACH:
pQCT scans will be performed using an XCT 3000 manufactured by Stratec, Medizintechnik. Three scans will be performed on each subject's tibia (distal tibia, mid shaft tibia, and 1-3 regions of the proximal tibia) where positions will be measured from the endplate of the tibia. Scan analyses will be performed using the analysis software provided by the manufacturer. The following parameters will be measured from each scan: trabecular area (TrA) and density (TrD) (except at mid shaft), cortical area and density, bone mineral content (BMC), and a strength-strain index (SSI), which is a density weighted section modulus. It is expected that pQCT results will provide baseline data for long duration studies and evaluation of bone countermeasure studies
RESULTS:
This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during Bed Rest Campaigns 3A-3F and Campaign 5A - 5C and the Artificial Gravity Study.
