experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Twenty percent of astronauts experience orthostatic hypotension, a decrease in blood pressure upon standing, when they return to Earth from space. The reasons for this orthostatic hypotension are considered to be related to either hypovolemia or low sympathetic nerve activity. Although some astronauts have been treated with fludrocortisone to increase plasma volume, this countermeasure was not accepted since fludrocortisone caused either a spaceflight headache or reduction of sympathetic nerve activity on landing day. Midodrine, an a1-adrenergic agonist, has been shown to prevent orthostatic hypotension in patients, in subjects during head-down bed rest simulating the space environment, and in astronauts after spaceflight. Midodrine constricts both arteries and veins to increase blood pressure and venous blood return, but does not increase sodium and water re-absorption.

Some astronauts experience not only upright low blood pressure but also nausea and vomiting during reentry. Promethazine, a histamine H1-receptor antagonist, has been used to combat motion sickness and vertigo in astronauts. There are instances when an astronaut might need to use both midodrine and promethazine at the same time. Cardiovascular effects of promethazine have been found to include increased or decreased blood pressure, tachycardia or bradycardia, and dizziness. The interactions of midodrine and promethazine have not yet been studied.

The primary objective of this study was to evaluate potential interactions between midodrine and promethazine on hemodynamic responses to upright tilt testing.

APPROACH:
A total of eight healthy subjects (5 males and 3 females) with normal blood pressure were used in this study. Their average age, body weight, and height were 42.0 ± 1.6 yr, 73.1 ± 5.4 kg, and 175.6 ± 4.0 cm (mean ± SE), respectively. The subjects had no history of cardiovascular disease, hypercholesterolemia, diabetes mellitus, liver disease, or renal disease. Midodrine (10 mg) or placebo midodrine (blank capsule without midodrine) was given orally. Promethazine (25 mg) or placebo promethazine (0.9% sodium chloride) was administrated intravenously. There were four test session days and the subject received one of the following medications on each day: 1) placebo midodrine + placebo promethazine (control group); 2) midodrine + placebo promethazine (midodrine group); 3) placebo midodrine + promethazine (promethazine group); and 4) midodrine + promethazine (combination group). The order of the test medication combination was randomized. The test personnel and subjects did not know what combination subjects received. Subjects abstained from caffeine, alcohol, and any medications for 24 hours prior to any testing. Subjects had been requested to eat a light breakfast composed of complex carbohydrates and adhere to this regimen for each test day.

For each test session, a baseline pulse and arterial pressure were measured and blood samples were collected after a 20-min supine rest period. Arterial pressure was measured at five-minute intervals for 40 minutes after administering 10 mg of midodrine or placebo midodrine and blood sample was taken 60 minutes post midodrine administration. Heart rate and arterial pressure were measured at one-minute intervals during promethazine infusion or placebo promethazine and once again a supine blood sample was collected at 20 minutes post-promethazine. After a six-minute supine rest, an 80º head-up tilt test was carried out for 20 minutes. Hemodynamic measurements were taken at one-minute intervals. A final blood sample (post-tilt) was drawn at the end of the tilt-up period. If a subject experienced orthostatic hypotension, he/she was returned to a supine position, and the blood sample was drawn immediately. All data were recorded on digital and video tapes for later analyses. All analog signals were also recorded on paper.

Only four points of systolic pressure, diastolic pressure, heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance were reported: a supine baseline before given any medications; last supine measurement after given midodrine or placebo midodrine; last supine measurement after promethazine or placebo promethazine administration; and last measurement of upright tilt test.

Urine samples were also collected prior to the test, at various points following the administration of the medications and after the test. Containers of urine samples were used to assay nitric oxide (NO) concentrations.

RESULTS:
Three of eight (38%) subjects in the control group, none of eight (0%) in the midodrine group, all eight (100%) in the promethazine group, and five of eight (63%) in the combination group experienced orthostatic hypotension during upright tilt test. Promethazine significantly increased the incidence of orthostatic hypotension. Compared to the midodrine group, the combination group even increased orthostatic hypotension.

The combination of 25 mg of promethazine given intravenously one hour after 10 mg of oral midodrine caused profound akathisia in 8 of 8 ground-based subjects. The symptoms of akathisia in these subjects involved uncontrolled foot movements, rocking, facial tick, anxiety, plus a panic attack in one individual and physical aggression in another. This result was reported to the flight surgeons who suggested that 12.5 mg promethazine was probably a more realistic dose. Five of the 8 subjects returned to be tested with 12.5 mg promethazine with midodrine. The combination of 12.5 mg of promethazine given intravenously one hour after 10 mg of oral midodrine again caused noticeable akathisia in 4 of 5 subjects.

The results showed that supine systolic and diastolic pressures increased significantly only in the combination group. Upright tilt systolic pressure decreased significantly only in the promethazine group. Upright tilt diastolic pressure did not change in all groups. In the supine position, heart rate did not change before and after given midodrine, promethazine, or both, in all groups. However, upright tilt heart rate increased significantly in all groups.

Supine plasma NO showed no change before and after given medications in the four groups. There is no difference in plasma NO between supine and upright positions in all groups.

The results clearly show that midodrine helps to overcome orthostatic hypotension while promethazine enhances orthostatic hypotension. The combination still shows a slight increase in orthostatic hypotension. Of further interest, promethazine caused akathisia, sometimes severe, both alone and in combination with midodrine. These results were reported to the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS) with the following recommendations: If midodrine is administered at Time of Ignition (TIG), promethazine cannot be administered within 4 hours (T1/2 of midodrine); midodrine cannot be taken at TIG if promethazine has been administered within 70 hours (5 half-times). The CPHS instituted a policy that midodrine and promethazine will not be given to astronauts simultaneously. This information was subsequently sent to the FDA Med Watch as an adverse event from a midodrine/promethazine interaction.

experiment_title: Acceleration Detection Sensitivity

investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A fundamental question in understanding the evolution of Space Motion Sickness (SMS) is whether the gain of the otolith organs, detectors of linear acceleration, is changed by weightlessness and in what direction. The objective of this experiment was to measure the threshold level at which the body will detect linear and angular acceleration and determine if this threshold changed during flight.

APPROACH:
Five electrooculograph (EOG) electrodes were attached to the face of the test subject. The electrodes recorded the electrical activity of the muscles surrounding the eye. Surface electrodes were placed at the outer canthi of each eye aligned with a straight-ahead gaze to record horizontal eye movements, and above and below the eye to record vertical eye movements. The derived EOG signals were routed through the control box to the Operational Instrumentation System.

The test subject was placed in his rescue harness and suspended by four linear extension springs. The eye shield and ear plugs were attached. The assisting crewmember then initiated a horizontal (head to foot) and a rotary oscillation of the test subject, slowly increasing the amplitude of the oscillation until it was perceptible to the test subject. The amplitude, frequency, and phase of the oscillation were recorded by the position sensors and the EOG signals were routed through the control box to the Operational Instrumentation System.

RESULTS:
Launch and entry monitoring was done on 7 subjects, all of whom exhibited no changes, except for VCOR gains. For the on-orbit studies, 9 subjects were normal while 4 had SMS. No significant changes were seen, except VCOR gains. Oscillopsia during head oscillation was seen in two isolated instances: (a) in a subject with SMS and (b) in a subject with post-SMS.

Regarding hardware, attempts were made inflight to use the harness with 2 subjects while oscillations could be initiated and sustained as planned. Small angular oscillations developed since the springs could not be attached at precise fore-aft locations of the center of mass. The great sensitivity to angular motion made the detection of associated linear motion questionable. The conclusion was that this system must have better subject/spring interface, possibly through a light rigid frame. In addition, some form of lateral restraint may be required.

Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A spider is not an insect, although it is commonly mistaken to be an insect. Spiders, along with ticks, mites, and scorpions, belong to the class arachnida. A spider has eight legs with no visible antennae and a two-piece body. A spider has silk-spinning organs, called spinnerets, at the back end of its abdomen, and usually eight eyes of various sizes and shapes. In addition, a spider's mouth parts are different from an insect's. Instead of mandibles capable of chewing, spiders have fang-tipped jaws called chelicerae used to inject digestive enzymes into it’s prey.

Araneus diadematus, the garden spider, is a very common resident of homes and gardens. It has a distinctive white "cross" mark on the abdomen which has given rise to the alternative aliases “cross spider” and “diadem spider.” It produces the traditional orb web, characterized by a pattern of concentric circles of silk threads that are small in the center of the web and get larger towards the outer area of the web. Since the spider senses its own weight when constructing the web to determine the required amount of silk to make the web, gravity plays an important role in the construction of the web. Therefore, the objectives of this experiment were to observe how microgravity affects the weight sensing mechanism for web construction in the common cross spider.

A bag with two "brackish water" minnows known as "Mummichog Minnows" was added to the flight at the request of Scientist-Astronaut Dr. Owen K. Garriott. The objective of this experiment was to show what disorientation the fish experienced when exposed to weightlessness. The fish were flown to obtain a better understanding of the vestibular or otolith organ, which enables an animal to maintain its balance or normal orientation to the gravity force of its natural environment.

In addition, crewmembers took photographs and video of the spiders during the course of the mission.

Also, they had to respond quickly and consistently with regard to their vestibular function. The obvious candidate was a small fish, the common mummichog minnow, found along the United States Atlantic coast. Two fingerlings and 50 fertile eggs were flown. The Skylab aquarium (bag) simulated a natural environment for the fish, except for gravity, by providing a dark background (bottom of pond) and a lighted surface (sky).

Spider: One day following the deployment of Arabella, a rudimentary web was constructed in the corners of the cage which was thought to be the web frame. A day later, a complete web was observed. These results prompted crewmembers to extend the original protocol by feeding the spiders rare filet mignon, providing an additional water supply, and deploying Anita at mid mission. On August 13, the Science Pilot removed half of Arabella’s existing web to initiate the construction of a new web. Arabella ingested the remaining half and refused to rebuild another web. Subsequently, water was provided where upon she proceeded to build a new web. The new web was better than the previous web indicating that Arabella had started to adapt to the microgravity environment. Arabella was returned to her launch vial and Anita was established in the cage. Anita’s reaction to the openness of the cage was recorded on video and described as being similar to Arabella's reaction, characterized as an erratic swimming motion. Both spiders died during the mission and both showed signs of dehydration which was thought to have caused their death. Examination of the returned web samples indicated that the thread spun in flight was significantly finer than that spun preflight, giving evidence that the spider utilized a weight sensing mechanism to size the thread.

Visual orientation was immediate upon hatching; the young fish kept their backs toward the light as their Earth-hatched cousins also did. However they also exhibited the abnormal swimming in tight circles only when the bag aquarium was shaken.

It appears that the Skylab fish utilized visual orientation, turning their backs to the light, as a substitute for gravity. Earth studies on a centrifuge have indicated that the orientation of fish is influenced both by the direction from which the light comes and the direction of the pull of gravity. In Skylab's zero gravity, the fish kept their backs to the light with no measurable deviation. The phototropic (orientation toward light) orientation and the relatively flat aquarium probably explain why they swam in loops. The fish were probably responding to signals from extremely fine hairs in their otolith which straighten out in the absence of gravity. They reacted by swimming in a forward loop which was distorted into a sideways loop by the tendency to keep their backs to the light.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Risk Assessment Project at Johnson Space Center is responsible for the integration of results from NASA space radiobiology research into computational models used for astronaut radiation risk assessments. The purpose of the Project was fourfold: (1) evaluate the extent to which ongoing research leads to reduction in the uncertainty of risk assessments and provide, as a metric of program progress, the number of days in space during which the radiation exposure of astronauts remains below NASA limits within a 95% confidence interval (“safe days in space”); (2) perform mission planning studies to predict the number of safe days for any mission; (3) assess the radiation risk to astronauts for ongoing missions in real time; and, (4) provide recommendations for research directions most likely to reduce risk or improve the accuracy of risk predictions.

The four categories of risks from radiation in space are defined by the NASA Bioastronautics Roadmap (BR). They are: 1) Carcinogenesis, 2) Acute and late effects to the Central Nervous System (CNS), 3) Degenerative Tissue Effects such as heart disease and cataracts, and 4) Acute Radiation risks. The number of safe days currently predicted for an astronaut’s career is less than required by mission planning, due to the large uncertainties in risk prediction. In particular, a projection uncertainty below + or - 50% is the goal for the 1000-day Mars mission because the high level of risk will require high precision risk evaluations. The current approach used to project risk is based on epidemiology data and on phenomenological models used to derive risk prediction from them. This approach cannot lead to improvements in the accuracy of risk prediction beyond a factor of approximately 2. New approaches using molecular biology and genetics are the only viable ones for achieving the level of accuracy required by space exploration and a robust program to obtain the required data is supported by the Space Radiation Program. However, how to incorporate these data into risk prediction and assessment models is not well understood.

APPROACH:
This Project Plan describes the approaches that will be used to develop models of risk assessment based on mechanistic space radiobiology research funded by the Space Radiation Program, leading to incremental uncertainty reduction based on new experimental data, and to the development of application software to be used in the NASA operational radiation protection program. To accomplish these goals, investigators established new molecular based models of risk. The molecular pathways that are the hallmarks of genomic instability and cancer, and the perturbation of these pathways by radiation will be described using systems biology approaches and Monte-Carlo simulation. Investigators developed descriptive models of such pathways utilizing track structure models of biomolecular damage, and deterministic and stochastic kinetic models of dominant molecular pathways causative of BR radiation risks. These simulations will make maximum use of results from mechanistic space radiobiology, and will replace traditional hazard functions and their inherent uncertainties due to reliance on epidemiological or phenomenological approaches.

RESULTS:
Project A: Integration and Review: Several Graphical Users Interface’s (GUI) of risk assessment models and computational tools were developed and published including: a) ARRBOD (Acute Radiation Risk and BRYTNRN Organ Dose); b) NSCR (NASA Space Cancer Risk) c) GERMCode (GCR Event-based Risk Model); d) RITracks (Relativistic Ion Track Structure). The GERMcode was developed to accurately describe fragmentation in the NSRL beam-line and biological samples, and basic radiobiology experiments.

Project B: Cancer Risk Projection Model and Uncertainties: New findings and knowledge from NSRL and other sources were used to revise the NASA’s risk model for space radiation cancer risks:
1) Revised values for low LET risk coefficients for tissue specific cancer incidence.
2) An analysis of lung cancer and other smoking attributable cancer risks for never-smokers show significantly reduced lung cancer risks as well as overall cancer risks for astronauts as compared to the risk estimated for the average U.S. population.
3) Derivation of track structure based radiation quality functions that depend on charge number, Z and kinetic energy, E in place of a dependence on LET alone. The assignment of a smaller maximum in the quality function for leukemia than for solid cancers.
4) Revised uncertainty assessments for all model coefficients in the risk model (physics, low LET risk coefficients, DDREF, and quality factors), and an alternative uncertainty assessment that considers deviation from linear responses due to non-targeted effects (NTE).

Results of calculations for the average U.S. population show more restrictive dose limits for astronauts above age 40 years as compared to NCRP Report 132, and a modest narrowing of uncertainties if NTEs are not included and much broader uncertainties with NTEs. Risks for never-smokers compared to the average U.S. population are estimated in a mixture model to be reduced by more than 20% and 30% for males and females, respectively. A larger reduction is possible if purely multiplicative risk transfer is assumed.

Project C: Biochemical Kinetics Models of Molecular Pathways: A system biology model of the NHEJ pathway was developed and used to make quantitative descriptions of the gamma H2AX foci and DSB rejoining experiments. The model is extended to consider the radiation quality dependence of the relative fraction of simple and complex DSB, rejoining and associated repair defects, and the kinetics of various radiation induced foci (RIF). In further work, the addition of ATM and the MRN complex to the model was achieved and the role of processing damaged ends by the Artemis proteins is being modeled. The interaction of several growth factors with NHEJ components was studied, including the interaction of the growth factors EGFR, IGF1, and TGFbeta-Smad with ATM and DNA-PK. New approaches to Green’s functions for stochastic treatment of molecular diffusion processes were developed. Flow cytometry or immune-staining considers signals in individual cells and thus provide several unique capabilities to support computation modeling using stochastic approaches. In contrast, methods that average the values of many cells such as Western blots, gene arrays, etc. are limited in elucidating events at low dose where fluctuations are expected to be important. To improve the understanding of DNA repair complexes numerical approaches to simulate immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry experiments were developed. These models embed a basic understanding of track structure with statistical approaches of flow cytometry data sorted by cell cycle phase, and fluorescence intensity taking into account background levels. Following flow cytometry analysis, investigators were able to distinguish the kinetics of these phospho-proteins in relationship to the cell cycle and to each other in an individual cell. Results revealed a unique pattern of kinetics for high versus low LET radiation, with a failure to initiate full activation of the ATM pathway being evident following High LET exposure. In the process of these studies investigators have noted that different populations of cells making up normal human tissues can be sorted based on intrinsic qualities of the cells and differences in their radiation sensitivity have been noted. In addition, an increase in proliferation of a specific mammary cell population was observed with low doses of radiation.

Project D: DNA Damage in Cancer Initiation and Genomic Instability: Foci size and clustering including strings of foci along HZE tracks were modeled for the first time and provide a useful analysis tool of NSRL experiments on DNA damage foci. These models have been extended to predict chromosomal aberration formation including the distribution of small rings normally below detection levels with fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) (<5 Mbp), and to describe complex aberrations. Stochastic track structure models were combined with a human genome model that considers random walk polymer models of each chromosomes pair built from 2 kbp monomers and constrained to nuclear territories in interphase.

Project E: Acute Radiation Risk Models: Investigators extended the granulopoietic model for rodents for the prediction of solar particle effects in canines, non-human primates and humans. An important feature of this approach is that the dynamics of cell populations are described by non-linear differential equations. Validation of the model was achieved by comparison to comprehensive data sets for animals exposed to acute and chronic radiation and to the Chernobyl and other radiation accident victims.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The space radiation environment poses unique hazards that include solar particle events and galactic cosmic rays. These types of radiations have been shown to cause acute and long-lasting chemical changes referred to as oxidative stress that can alter the normal physiology of the central nervous system (CNS). The chemical species produced can cause a wide range of effects in cells within the CNS that largely depend on the types of pathways they activate and the types of damage they produce. Proper functioning of the CNS depends on many factors, but is known to require subpopulations of neural stem and precursor cells that participate in the repair of CNS injury resulting from irradiation. This proposal focused on analyzing the effects of space radiation on these critical populations of multipotent neural stem and precursor cells. Investigators have developed the technology to isolate and grow these cells in culture and will use a variety of techniques to analyze how cells exposed to space radiation change. They planned to monitor the time course of oxidative stress in these cells and how that depends on the dose, the dose rate and type of radiation applied. They will determine how radiation-induced oxidative stress impacts cellular proliferation, signaling between cells, cell fate and survival. Collectively their studies using both rodent and human neural stem and precursor cells will help NASA understand the acute and longer-lasting sequelae associated with the exposure of the CNS to the space radiation environment. These studies will facilitate efforts to more appropriately establish estimates of risk for radiation exposure to the CNS in space.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Past data collected by the investigators has demonstrated that the radiation response of multipotent neural precursor cells to x-rays, protons, and HZE nuclei involves an acute and persistent oxidative stress that can last for months. The importance of neural precursor cells to the repair and remodeling of the irradiated CNS is underscored by the data showing that the radiation-induced depletion of these cells is linked to the inhibition of neurogenesis and the onset of cognitive impairment. Investigators believe oxidative injury is critical in this context, and plays a contributory if not causal role in determining neural precursor cell function, survival and fate. A summary of the study findings are listed below.
1. Mice genetically manipulated to overexpress human catalase in the mitochondria were found to exhibit higher basal levels of neurogenesis and after low dose exposure to 150 MeV protons. These data suggest that interventions targeted to reduce oxidative stress in the mitochondria are neuroprotective.
2. A great deal of work characterizing the response of cultured neural stem cells from both rodents and humans were performed. These data reveal a marked predisposition of neural stem cells to exhibit radiation-induced oxidative stress. The functional importance of radiation-induced oxidative stress in regulating adaptive responses was also shown, as treatment of cells with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine eliminated the protective effect of prior exposure on cell survival following exposure to a subsequent higher dose of protons. Collectively, these data provide further evidence in support of the ides that space relevant fluences of charged particles elicit significant levels of oxidative stress that impact survival and proliferation.
3. Work characterizing the effect of HZE particle irradiation on cultured neural stem cells and the irradiated rodent brain was performed. There was a marked and persistent increases in oxidative stress found months after exposure to very low fluences of 600 MeV iron ions. Oxidative stress measurement made in vivo found that low dose exposure caused marked changes in the level and activity of several key antioxidant enzymes two weeks after exposure that returned to background one month after irradiation. Importantly, exposure to 5 or 30 cGy of 600 MeV oxygen or titanium ions was found to elicit significant deficits in novel object recognition 12 weeks after exposure. These data link key changes in redox metabolism to functional changes in cognition, changes that have important implications for astronauts exposed to the space radiation environment.
4. Investigators were able to assess the metabolic activity of neural stem cells after low dose irradiation using non-invasive 2-photon spectroscopy.
5. This is a comprehensive study that has defined the radiobiological response and consequences of human neural stem cells exposed to low LET radiation.
6. A review of the redox stress biology of irradiated neural stem cells and stem cells from other organ systems.

In summary, investigators have obtained significant data over the course of their funding period demonstrating that low dose charged particle irradiation can elicit oxidative stress in multipotent neural stem and precursor cells, derived from both rodents and humans. Their data shows conclusively that prior exposure elicits adaptive responses that are capable of attenuating oxidative stress and survival. Collectively their data suggest that radiation-induced oxidative stress constitutes a biochemical mechanism of functional significance to neural stem cell biology and cognition.

The importance of neural precursor cells to the repair and remodeling of the irradiated CNS is underscored by the data showing that the radiation-induced depletion of these cells is linked to the inhibition of neurogenesis and the onset of cognitive impairment. Investigators believe oxidative injury is critical in this context, and plays a contributory if not causal role in determining neural precursor cell function, survival and fate. A summary of the study findings are listed below.
1. Mice genetically manipulated to overexpress human catalase in the mitochondria were found to exhibit higher basal levels of neurogenesis and after low dose exposure to 150 MeV protons. These data suggest that interventions targeted to reduce oxidative stress in the mitochondria are neuroprotective.
2. A great deal of work characterizing the response of cultured neural stem cells from both rodents and humans were performed. These data reveal a marked predisposition of neural stem cells to exhibit radiation-induced oxidative stress. The functional importance of radiation-induced oxidative stress in regulating adaptive responses was also shown, as treatment of cells with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine eliminated the protective effect of prior exposure on cell survival following exposure to a subsequent higher dose of protons. Collectively, these data provide further evidence in support of the ides that space relevant fluences of charged particles elicit significant levels of oxidative stress that impact survival and proliferation.
3. Work characterizing the effect of HZE particle irradiation on cultured neural stem cells and the irradiated rodent brain was performed. There was a marked and persistent increases in oxidative stress found months after exposure to very low fluences of 600 MeV iron ions. Oxidative stress measurement made in vivo found that low dose exposure caused marked changes in the level and activity of several key antioxidant enzymes two weeks after exposure that returned to background one month after irradiation. Importantly, exposure to 5 or 30 cGy of 600 MeV oxygen or titanium ions was found to elicit significant deficits in novel object recognition 12 weeks after exposure. These data link key changes in redox metabolism to functional changes in cognition, changes that have important implications for astronauts exposed to the space radiation environment.
4. Investigators were able to assess the metabolic activity of neural stem cells after low dose irradiation using non-invasive 2-photon spectroscopy.
5. This is a comprehensive study that has defined the radiobiological response and consequences of human neural stem cells exposed to low LET radiation.
6. A review of the redox stress biology of irradiated neural stem cells and stem cells from other organ systems.

In summary, investigators have obtained significant data over the course of their funding period demonstrating that low dose charged particle irradiation can elicit oxidative stress in multipotent neural stem and precursor cells, derived from both rodents and humans. experiment_title: Actigraphy:  A Tool for Monitoring Sleep and Activity in an Isolated Environment (Aquarius)
parameter_html:
Illumination level
Movement
Sleep duration
Sleep efficiency
Sleep latency
investigators: Principal Investigator: Putcha, Lakshmi
experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Sleep quality may be disturbed in crowded, isolated environments such as the International Space Station (ISS) and the Aquarius habitat. Potential disturbances in the sleep/wake cycles of astronauts and aquanauts compared to ground-based sleep/wake cycles need to be defined in order to understand its consequences on human performance and well-being. The purpose of this study is to quantitate objective measures of sleep quality such as sleep duration, sleep latency and sleep efficiency with a non-intrusive wrist-worn sleep/wake activity monitor known as the Actiwatch®. Crewmembers wore the Actiwatch® on the non-dominant hand at all times while inside the habitat. A record of activities and sleep was kept, including in-suit Doppler use. The collection of actigraphy data with an Actiwatch® allowed an objective measure of crewmember activity and sleep quality. Altered activity and sleep quality data were correlated with data obtained in the in-suit Doppler and STARx/ARES studies.

APPROACH:
Baseline sleep/wake measurements were recorded for five days approximately three weeks prior to the mission. During the NEEMO 5 mission, Actiwatches® were worn on the non-dominant hand at all times while inside the habitat. The watches were removed for dives. The Actiwatch® Activity Log reflects don/doff of the Actiwatch® along with sleep/wake and dive times, as well as in-suit Doppler use.

RESULTS:
The average illumination during the mission decreased significantly (p<0.05). All four aquanauts completed six days/five nights of actigraphy data collection approximately two-weeks prior to the mission. Three of four aquanauts were able to complete 14 days/13 nights of actigraphy data collection during the two-week mission in the Aquarius habitat. An increase of 9 minutes was observed in sleep latency during the mission, however this difference is not statistically significant.

One aquanaut failed to collect data on days three and 11 to 14 because the original and spare Actiwatches® were submersed in saltwater (Actiwatches® are advertised to not be water proof). This same aquanaut also failed to wear the Actiwatch® during the sleep period of day nine.

The crew reported that Actiwatches® are water-resistant as the two splashed watches continued collecting data after being momentarily submerged during the mission. Remembering to record the doff and don times was the only inconvenience. Crewmembers recommended that all bands should be Velcro for easy doff and don and having a time display incorporated into the watch to make logging times easier.

experiment_title: Synaptogenesis in Microgravity
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Keshishian, Haig
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The effects of spaceflight on nervous system development and neuromuscular synapse formation were tested in a model genetic organism, Drosophila melanogaster. Specific objectives were: 1) To utilize the organism's genetic expression of a highly fluorescent mutant form of Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) to visualize singly identified motoneurons and muscle targets as well as all aspects of the nervous system development; and 2) To examine the critical developmental times of Drosophila embryos and larvae for the effects of microgravity during spaceflight.

APPROACH:

Both embryos and larvae at different stages in development were prepared, examined with fluorescent microscopy, and stored at 11 degrees C in order to arrest development. Specimens were housed on petri plates containing a culture medium in the incubator containment module (ICM) and launched on the STS-93 mission. The petri dishes were housed in seven Group Activation Packages (GAPs) within the ICM. At specific time points inflight, each GAP was heated to 25 degrees C to restart development for a set duration. Prior to landing and recovery, the GAPs were be cooled to 11 degrees C to halt development. Cell-specific Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) expression methodologies were used to analyze the data. This allows targeting errors and subtle defects to be detected in a large sample set.

RESULTS:

Preliminary results indicated that although the CGBA hardware operated successfully, there were unexpected temperature drifts above the planned temperature in two of the seven containers. While ground tests were completed for comparison to the in-flight samples, final data analysis has not been released.

experiment_title: The Genetic Basis of the Loss of Musculo-Skeletal Tissue during Weightlessness: Towards the Identification of Individuals that are at Greatest Risk
parameter_html: Bone loss
investigators: Principal Investigator: Judex, StefanCo-Investigator: Donahue, Leah- RaeCo-Investigator: Rubin, Clinton
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
One of the main physiologic hurdles to human presence in space on long-duration missions is the loss of bone and muscle mass that accompanies microgravity. Although bone and muscle have been proven to be lost at considerable rates during extended stays in microgravity, there appears to be considerable variation in loss among individuals. Some astronauts lose large amounts of tissue, while others are nearly unaffected. This finding has also been observed in ground-based bed rest studies on humans, as well as ground-based research on mice. Individual variability in bone and muscle loss may be due to genetic variations that cause differences in the mechanical sensitivity of the muscles and skeleton.

The objective of this study was to better understand the genetic basis of the sensitivity of the muscle and skeleton to the loss of one-G mechanical stimuli by identifying the location of genetic traits responsible for the difference in sensitivity to loading. The results of this research may be used to help identify astronauts that have the greatest need for pharmacologic or biomechanical countermeasures, as well as to discover new drugs that work to curtail bone and muscle loss caused by disuse.

APPROACH:
A genetically heterogeneous mouse population was created by double crossing two inbred strains of mice with very distinct skeletal responses to the loss of functional weightbearing. More than 400 of these mice were subjected to hindlimb unloading and reambulation. Longitudinal changes in the morphology and mechanical properties of these mice were determined by in vivo microCT and finite element modeling.

RESULTS:
Similar to data from astronauts and bed rest patients, changes in bone morphology during disuse and re-ambulation were associated with large variations in this genetically heterogeneous mouse population. The loss of bone quantity and quality during disuse was particularly dramatic in trabecular bone. Even though most mice were able to recover at least some of the tissue mass that was lost during disuse, this recovery occurred by re-thickening of individual trabeculae while the connectedness of the structure further deteriorated. The amount of tissue recovery was neither associated with any baseline bone morphology parameter nor with the rates of tissue loss induced by disuse. These data indicate the strong influence of genetic variations on the changes in bone morphology and strength induced by rapid changes in its mechanical milieu, emphasize that is critical to preserve bone’s micro-architecture before individual trabecular connections are lost, and suggest that the genes modulating changes in morphology during disuse are, at least in part, distinct from those regulating tissue recovery. The weak correlations between bone and muscle loss and recovery further suggest that there is little overlap between the mechanosensory elements of muscle and bone.

experiment_title: Prevalence of Hypertension in LSAH Participants
parameter_html:
Blood pressure
Hypertension
Pulse pressure
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Blood pressure is the force of the blood pushing against the walls of arteries. It is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg), and given in two numbers. The higher number indicates systolic pressure, which is the amount of force exerted on the walls of arteries within and leading from the heart when it contracts (i.e., during systole). The lower number is the diastolic pressure, which is the force existing between contractions (i.e., during diastole).

Normal blood pressure is usually considered to be 120/80 mmHg; measurements above 140/90 mmHg are considered to be hypertensive. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, simply refers to the increased tension or pressure in the arteries. Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney failure. Most hypertensive people have no symptoms.

For most people, there is no single known cause of high blood pressure. This type of high blood pressure is called primary or essential hypertension. Essential hypertension can't be cured, although in most cases it can be controlled. In some cases, high blood pressure can be traced to a known cause like tumors of the adrenal gland, chronic kidney disease, hormone abnormalities, use of birth control pills, or pregnancy. This is called secondary hypertension, and is usually cured if the underlying cause passes or is corrected.

The goal of this study was to examine hypertension among the astronaut and comparison populations.

APPROACH:
According to data from the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey conducted from 1988-1991 (NHANES III), 20.4% of the US adult population is hypertensive (defined as systolic pressure of at least 140 mmHg or diastolic pressure of at least 90 mmHg).

RESULTS:
Annual examination data for active and inactive NASA astronauts between 1959-1999 show 5.5% of them (21 of 291) have been diagnosed with hypertension. In comparison, data from the annual examinations of comparison participants over a similar time period show 13.9% (121 of 870) had corresponding hypertension diagnoses. As physical fitness is a requirement for astronauts, they are expected to show a lower rate of hypertension as compared to the general population. The comparison participants had more than double the hypertension rate of the astronauts, but still had a lower rate than the general population. This lower rate of hypertension may be an effect of being a healthy working population.

Cross-sectional data of LSAH participants by age group show that most of them have average systolic pressure around or below 120 mmHg. Up to age 49, male comparisons show the same trend of systolic pressure measurements, although with slightly higher values, with that of the male astronauts. Male comparison participants aged 50 and older showed a higher increase of their systolic pressure as compared to male astronauts aged 50 and older. The diastolic pressure measurements for the male comparisons do not show a corresponding upward trend. Although the highest average measurement from the oldest age group of male comparisons is still below the hypertensive value of 140 mm Hg, this trend follows one observed in the general population. Data from NHANES III show that the highest increase in hypertension prevalence occurs between the 40-49 and 50-59 years age group for men. The small sample size of female participants does not allow for age group comparisons beyond the 40-44 age group.

experiment_title: Simulated Microgravity and Radiation-Induced Bone Degeneration: Oxidative Stress- and p53-Dependent Mechanisms
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Globus, Ruth
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To determine the risks and mechanisms of tissue degeneration in the space flight environment, investigators examined the combined effects of radiation and simulated weightlessness on bone. They focused their studies on two important pathways, p53 and oxidative and nitrative stress-related species, in bone marrow progenitor populations because there is abundant evidence that the biological effects of weightlessness and those of radiation share these mechanism. Experiments were conducted using the rodent hindlimb unloading model, the best validated animal model for simulating weightlessness, followed by irradiation. In Aim 1, they tested the hypothesis that simulated weightlessness of mice modulates the response of bone and bone marrow to radiation, both acutely and during tissue regeneration. In Aim 2 they sought to identify the target marrow-derived stem, progenitor and differentiated cell populations sensitive to the combined stimuli of simulated weightlessness and radiation. In Aim 3, they explored the relevance of specific ROS/RNS and p53-dependent mechanisms for mediating cellular responses to combined simulated weightlessness and radiation. The results of these studies are expected to provide important information for the development of countermeasures both to help prevent degeneration of connective tissues such as bone during spaceflight and to improve subsequent tissue regeneration.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
Key questions are whether or not low doses and unique types of radiation that astronauts are exposed to in space are detrimental to mineralized tissue, and if space radiation worsens the bone loss that occurs due to unloading of muscles and bones in the reduced gravity environment of space. First, investigators conducted relatively extensive dose-response and time course experiments using radiation such as high energy Fe-56 (iron), which is encountered in space. Results show that total body irradiation of adult male mice with doses of iron as low as 0.10 Gy and doses of photons (Cesium-137) as low as 1.0 Gy can cause significant loss of mineralized tissue within the spongy areas of bone. This bone loss is very rapid (within 3 to 7 days), and appears to be caused by an increase in the activity of bone resorbing osteoclasts. The importance of the osteoclasts for radiation-induced bone loss is further supported by our findings that radiation can increase the number of osteoclasts in cultured cells.

When unloading to simulate weightlessness and radiation are combined, changes emerge over time, which are greater than each treatment alone can exert. Mechanical tests are arguably the gold standard for assessing the main function of bone, which is to support the body at rest and in motion. Unloading and radiation each alone have modest effects to lower the yield force in the lumbar spine, defined as the force applied that causes failure, here in compression. However, when unloading and radiation are combined, there is a significant reduction in yield force. This combined effect was accompanied by compromised structural integrity of cancellous tissue in the long bones (tibiae) as well as in the spine. One of our surprising findings is that radiation-induced bone loss is restricted to high turnover rate cancellous tissue, in contrast to unloading-induced bone loss, which manifests in both cortical bone tissue (outer shell) as well as cancellous tissue. As a consequence, the mechanical properties of the spine are largely preserved after low dose, total body irradiation alone and are likely to be preserved for most bones, at least in the short term.

Investigators also obtained several lines of evidence in support of the hypothesis that cells responsible for bone formation, osteoblasts and their stem cells and progenitors that reside in bone marrow, may contribute to bone loss caused by radiation. Irradiation can reduce the activity of osteoblasts in cancellous bone. In the short term, the combination of unloading and iron has a greater acute effect (-60%) to reduce the number of stem/progenitors in the marrow for osteoblasts than either treatment alone (-20%, -25% respectively). These results suggest bone marrow stem and progenitor cells for the bone-forming osteoblasts may be more sensitive to adverse effects of radiation under conditions of disuse in space, than occurs under normal conditions on Earth.

These findings raise the possibility that radiation may damage stem cells or progenitors for osteoblasts so that recovery of skeletal tissue from the space environment also is impaired. In the short term (1 mo), investigators found that recovery of the spine from disuse in irradiated mice (0.5Gy iron) was similar to controls. Reasoning that if low dose radiation damages stem and osteoprogenitor cells, adverse effects may manifest much later in life as the mice age. To test this possibility, mice were unloaded then exposed to iron, then released to ambulate normally for six months. Investigators found that bone structural changes in mice that had been unloaded (but not irradiated) were consistent with the adaptive changes that occur in astronauts one year after prolonged space flight. In contrast, irradiation of unloaded mice with a low dose of iron (0.5Gy) impaired adaptive recovery. These results support these hypothesis that low dose, iron radiation impairs adaptive remodeling of bone due to the damage inflicted upon stem and osteoprogenitor cells that reside within the marrow.

The question of whether or not weightlessness and/or radiation exert chronic, system-wide effects is an important one. The results show exposure to space radiation causes persistent oxidative damage to bone marrow proteins in unloaded mice at lower doses of radiation than in normally loaded controls. Investigators propose weightlessness interferes with the ability of cells in bone and marrow to protect from oxidative damage, which leads to persistent oxidative stress, osteoclast-mediated resorption, damage to stem and osteoprogenitors and impaired adaptive remodeling. Although other explanations are possible for their findings, given the well-established effect of radiation to cause oxidative and DNA damage to stem cells and inflammation, we will test this hypothesis in future efforts to improve understanding of space flight.

The importance of these findings is that simulated weightlessness at the time of radiation exposure appears to impair skeletal remodeling even during a prolonged period of recovery. Furthermore, relatively low doses of space radiation can exert system-wide and persistent change. All of the experiments have been conducted using adult, male mice of a single strain (C57Bl/6J). Differences in biological responses to treatments can occur simply due to age, gender, strain, as well as species, and therefore further studies are needed to help assess human risk. Nonetheless, the findings suggest space radiation, alone and combined with musculoskeletal disuse, may pose a long-term risk to the skeletal health of astronauts.

In the short term, the combination of unloading and iron has a greater acute effect (-60%) to reduce the number of stem/progenitors in the marrow for osteoblasts than either treatment alone (-20%, -25% respectively). These results suggest bone marrow stem and progenitor cells for the bone-forming osteoblasts may be more sensitive to adverse effects of radiation under conditions of disuse in space, than occurs under normal conditions on Earth.

These findings raise the possibility that radiation may damage stem cells or progenitors for osteoblasts so that recovery of skeletal tissue from the space environment also is impaired. In the short term (1 mo), investigators found that recovery of the spine from disuse in irradiated mice (0.5Gy iron) was similar to controls. Reasoning that if low dose radiation damages stem and osteoprogenitor cells, adverse effects may manifest much later in life as the mice age. To test this possibility, mice were unloaded then exposed to iron, then released to ambulate normally for six months. Investigators found that bone structural changes in mice that had been unloaded (but not irradiated) were consistent with the adaptive changes that occur in astronauts one year after prolonged space flight. In contrast, irradiation of unloaded mice with a low dose of iron (0.5Gy) impaired adaptive recovery. These results support these hypothesis that low dose, iron radiation impairs adaptive remodeling of bone due to the damage inflicted upon stem and osteoprogenitor cells that reside within the marrow.

The question of whether or not weightlessness and/or radiation exert chronic, system-wide effects is an important one. The results show exposure to space radiation causes persistent oxidative damage to bone marrow proteins in unloaded mice at lower doses of radiation than in normally loaded controls. Investigators propose weightlessness interferes with the ability of cells in bone and marrow to protect from oxidative damage, which leads to persistent oxidative stress, osteoclast-mediated resorption, damage to stem and osteoprogenitors and impaired adaptive remodeling. Although other explanations are possible for their findings, given the well-established effect of radiation to cause oxidative and DNA damage to stem cells and inflammation, we will test this hypothesis in future efforts to improve understanding of space flight.

The importance of these findings is that simulated weightlessness at the time of radiation exposure appears to impair skeletal remodeling even during a prolonged period of recovery. Furthermore, relatively low doses of space radiation can exert system-wide and persistent change. All of the experiments have been conducted using adult, male mice of a single strain (C57Bl/6J). Differences in biological responses to treatments can occur simply due to age, gender, strain, as well as species, and therefore further studies are needed to help assess human risk. Nonetheless, the findings suggest space radiation, alone and combined with musculoskeletal disuse, may pose a long-term risk to the skeletal health of astronauts.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Anthropomorphic test devices (ATDs) – the Hybrid III and THOR – used to test the Occupant Protection requirements are not well correlated to low injury risk, as these devices were designed for automotive use. Automotive research is directed at preventing severe injuries in very low probability events. NASA vehicles, such as the Orion, require a lower risk of injury during dynamic phases of flight because the occupants will experience dynamic loading during every flight. The objective of this study is to develop injury risk functions for the Hybrid III and THOR ATDs.

This study is focused on five areas of the body, each evaluating a unique injury response mechanism lower neck injury in rearward loading, vertical neck loading, upper and lower neck under lateral loading, thorax in lateral loading and pelvis in lateral loading.
The biomechanics and potential injuries of each location were investigated using the following specific aims:

  1. Identify appropriate datasets for THOR comparison
  2. Test THOR in same conditions as historical testing
  3. Use historical human data to establish tolerance and injury risk focusing on lateral responses and sex differences
  4. Use Bayesian analysis combined with survival analysis along with human tolerance to estimate injury risk.
  5. Use results of prior data mining and existing literature as prior distribution
  6. Develop new Injury Assessment Reference Values based on the new statistical analysis


APPROACH:

Historical human data will be selected from the Wright-Patterson Collaborative Biodynamics Network (CBDN) and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) databases. The data will be selected based on loading dynamics and subject demographics. Once these data are selected, the THOR ATD will be tested in identical conditions. A Bayesian analysis along with survival analysis will be used to relate the resulting THOR responses to improve injury risk predictions. The results of the Occupant Protection Data Mining and Modeling Task will be used as prior distributions.

Matched- pair tests between postmortem human surrogates (PMHS) and each ATD are used to determine ATD- specific injury criteria. The merit of the matched-pair design is the one-to-one correlation of the results from external loads to both surrogates.

To achieve specific aim 1, historical PMHS test cases for the five areas of the body focused on in this experiment were selected from the Medical College of Wisconsin (MCW) database for matched-pair testing. Selection of these cases were made based on their similarity to spaceflight loading dynamics and astronaut demographics.

The first area of the body that was tested to evaluate a unique injury response mechanism was lower neck . Lower neck injury in rearward loading was tested when two different PMHS historical data sets were used for this study. A group of five intact PMHS were seated and belted in a custom metal seat on an accelerator sled and were subjected to low or high velocities. A group of 13 PMHS were isolated at the T2 level. The PMHS in the second group were exposed to 4 different severities.

A matched-pair test for each PMHS was conducted for both the THOR and Hybrid-III 50th percentile male ATDs. For the intact PMHS test conditions, the full ATD was placed in the same custom chair and subjected to the same input conditions. For the head-neck complex PMHS tests, the head and neck were removed from the rest of the ATD and tested on the same sled-pendulum test rig. Internal accelerometers and neck load cells were used to capture dynamic data.

Vertical neck loading was tested by using PMHS from multiple studies. They were organized into 2 groups: upright and inverted; denoted by groups A and B respectively. In total, there were 42 subjects (26 males and 16 females). The upright subjects were isolated at T2-T3 and the applied loading rates ranged from 0.05 to 8.9 m/s. The specimens for the inverted subjects were raised approximately 0.53 m and dropped to the platform of a drop apparatus with velocities of 2.3 to 3.3 m/s. Matched pair tests could not be completed because the necks of both the Hybrid III and THOR are much less compliant than the human neck, and therefore could not match the posture and alignment of PMHS.

Upper and Lower neck were tested under lateral loading. Biomechanical data were gathered for 11 subjects and organized into 3 groups: : (1) fully restrained torso with belts securing both the torso and extremities, (2) torso secured with a three-point center-mounted buckle, and (3) a different design of the three-point belt in which the specimens were positioned on a custom-designed seat rigidly fixed to the platform of a sled. The subjects were seated facing forward and upright. Tension force and extension bending moment data at the upper and lower neck were analyzed in this report to develop neck IRCs. Matched-pair tests were conducted for Groups A and B. Both the THOR and Hybrid-III were placed in the same seat and belt setup as each PMHS group and given the same sled dynamics.

Thorax was tested in lateral loading conditions. Seventeen PMHS were used in this part of the study, each instrumented with 3 chest band strain gauge suites wrapped around the circumference of the thorax at the level of rib 4, xiphoid process, and rib 10. The PMHS was seated on a custom seat which was fixed to an accelerator sled, and each test was conducted at 6.7 m/s. The Hybrid-III lacks instrumentation on the ribs to calculate chest deflection and therefore could not be used for matched-pair testing. The THOR was also not used for matched- pair testing for this injury metric because its internal rib sensors demonstrated very little deflection in side impacts.

Pelvis was tested in lateral loading when biomechanical data was gathered from 2 different data sets. A total of 63 tests were performed, split between two groups. The first data set included 10 PMHS, with thirty -seven tests performed, seated in a driving posture and unbelted without lateral support. The second group had 12 subjects tested in a similar manner. The Hybrid III-ATD does not have acetabulum/ hip internal load cells and hence is incapable for matched-pair tests in this study.


RESULTS:

Injury risk correlations derived from PMHS and ATD comparisons were used to improve upon the injury metrics previously developed under the Occupant Protection (OP) Data Mining and Modeling Task. For upper and lower neck assessments, forces and interaction criteria had differences of risk levels between the magnitudes of metrics. Forces curves were noted to be similar to the upper and lower necks, while the moment curves were amplifies at the lower neck due to the kinematics of the cervical column during lateral acceleration.

The inverted drop test series indicated that age of the specimen is a significant covariate. It was noted to be negatively associated with the risk of injury. A comparison between the forces at all risk levels indicated a greater magnitude of force with the upright than the inverted model, reflecting the differences between the bony in the former versus soft tissue and distractive nature of injuries sustained in the latter set up.

All injury risk methods had an additional calculation at 35-45 years of age, since age was found to be a significant covariate. The results from the upright experimental model indicated that age is a significant variable and increasing age was associated with higher risk of injury.

These results suggest that for compression- related injuries, specimen age should be used as a covariate or individual specimen data may be scaled to derive risk curves. Results for distraction or extension-related injuries showed that specimen age does not need to be used as a covariate in the statistical analysis. The findings from these tests and survival analysis indicate that age factor modulates human cervical spine tolerance to impact injury.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Pierson, DuaneCo-Investigator: Mehta, Satish
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Reactivation of latent viruses may pose an important health risk for people living and working in extreme environments, such as space and Antarctica. Risks associated with many infectious agents are reduced by the preventative measures of the health stabilization program before each mission. However, reactivation of latent viruses is unaffected by such actions. A variety of stess factors may cause reactivation of these viruses, such as psychosocial stress, trauma, sunlight, resiratory infection, and fever. Stress-induced changes in immune function under such conditions may also increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a DNA virus that infects more than 90% of the adult population worldwide and is the etiologic agent of infectious mononucleosis, is highly infectious. Normally, primary infection is a self-limiting disease leading to a lifelong persistence of EBV in the B-lymphocytes or epithelial cells of the oropharynx of infected individuals. EBV can be found in saliva after reactivation, which can be triggered by a variety of factors, perhaps including space flight. The physical and psychological stresses associated with the launch and landing of spacecraft, and living and working in the crowded, closed environment in microgravity, may result in viral reactivation and shedding.

The limited access to space requires the use of ground-based analogs of space flight. Environmental chambers have been used since the Skylab program (1973-1974) to simulate specific aspects of space flight. In the present study, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was used to identify EBV DNA in saliva and CMV DNA in urine as a measure of viral shedding in response to 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center.

APPROACH:
Viral shedding and reactivation patterns were studied for eight subjects (five male and three female) participating in the 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center. Saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects before, during, and after chamber isolation. Blood and urine samples were collected once before entry and once after exit.

Samples from 11 healthy age-matched adults were collected as controls (ten males and one female). Saliva, urine, and blood samples (one of each) were collected from each of these subjects on day 1, day 7, and day 22 of the tests. This collection schedule closely approximates the pre- and postflight collection schedule of a 12-day Shuttle flight. One-time urine samples were also collected from 30 additional healthy age-matched subjects for CMV analysis.

Saliva samples were collected with Salivette kits, which consist of a cotton roll in a polypropylene vial. Subjects placed the roll in their mouth until it became saturated, and then returned the roll to the vial. Saliva samples were centrifuged immediately after collection and stored frozen at -70ºC. All samples collected from a given subject were analyzed simultaneously. Using a polymerase chain reaction assay, saliva samples were processed for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA and urine samples were analyzed for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA detection. Saliva (2 to 3 ml) and urine (3 ml) specimens were concentrated with a 100-KD filtration unit. DNA was extracted by a nonorganic extraction method, and EBV DNA was detected as described here briefly. The PCR primers were directed at the EBV polymerase accessory protein gene (BMRF1): P1, 5-GTC CAA GAG CCACCACAC CTG and P2, 5-biotin CCC AGA AGT ATA CGT GGT GAC GTA GA. These primers were used at a concentrationof 200 µM with 10 µM deoxynucleic acid triphosphates. PCR was optimized using buffer II with 2.5 mM MgCl2. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was added to a final concentration of 5%. AmpliGold (2.5 units per 100 µl reaction mixture) was added, and 5 µl of the purified DNA was added to 20 µl of the reaction mixture. The cycle parameters were 95ºC for 9 min, followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 15 sec, 61ºC for 15 sec, and 72ºC for 15 sec, with a final extension step at 72ºC for 5 min.

CMV DNA was detected using primers that target the major immediate early gene (P1, 5-TGT CCT CCC GCT CCT C and P2, biotin 5-ATG AAG GTC TTT GCC CAG TA). All reactions were carried out using a Perkin-Elmer GenAmp system 9600. An initial denaturation step of 94ºC for 9 min was followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 30 sec, 69ºC for 15 sec, 72ºC for 30 sec, 72ºC for 7 min, and a 4ºC hold. The amplified product was analyzed for the presence of EBV or CMV using the Digene Sharp Signal System according to the manufacturer's instructions.

EBV and CMV antibody titers from blood samples were determined by indirect immunofluorescence assay. Commercially prepared substrate slides and control sera were used for determining antibody (IgG) titers for viral capsid antigen (VCA) and early antigen (EA) of EBV, CMV, and measles (Bion Enterprises, Park Ridge, IL). Four-fold dilutions of plasma were prepared with phosphate-buffered saline. The endpoint titer was determined as the highest dilution of serum in which immunofluorescent-positive cells could be detected. All specimens were batch analyzed and read blind-coded.

The frequency of viral shedding in saliva and viral antibody titers in plasma from chamber study subjects and controls were tested for normality. One-way analysis of variance was performed to study significant differences across different times during the study.

The method of generalized estimating equations with a logit link was used to find significant difference between the phases (pre-, in-, and postchamber). The differences between sampling periods were considered significant if P < 0.05.

RESULTS:
A total of 418 saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects participating in the two chamber studies. Overall, EBV DNA was detected in 35% of the 418 total saliva samples collected from these subjects. The subjects in the 60-day chamber study had EBV DNA in 13% (range 0 to 31%) of their samples, and the subjects in the 91-day study had EBV DNA in 51% (range 33 to 81%) of their samples. During both studies, all but one subject (in the 60-day chamber study) shed EBV.

Sixteen urine samples collected from the subjects of both chamber studies before and after the in-chamber phase were analyzed for CMV DNA. Interestingly, not a single sample showed evidence of CMV DNA. The presence of CMV DNA in urine from the control group was also rare (1/81 samples).

Viral antibody titers for EBV and CMV measured in samples from all 8 subjects before and after the study were not significantly different. Therefore, the data were pooled for further analysis. No significant differences in EBV VCA, EBV EA, or CMV IgG antibody titers were observed before and after either of the studies. Interestingly, EBV antibody titers did not differ significantly from the controls. However, CMV antibody titers of subjects were greater than those of the control group before and after the study.

Our current finding of increased viral reactivation in closed chamber study subjects agrees with our previous Space Shuttle and Antarctic data. These results support and extend our previous observations that latent viral reactivation increases during space flight, which is consistent with a stress-induced decrease in immune function.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Little is currently known about the effects of microgravity on tissue repair. In the era of a long-term human presence in space, the probability of minor injury requiring on orbit treatment will increase. This experiment aims to evaluate the effects of spaceflight on the histological and tensiometric properties of full-thickness abdominal incisional skin wounds in the rat. A second objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (bb-homodimer, PDGF) in promoting granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition.

Approach:

Before flight, both flight and control rats received abdominal implants of polyvinyl acetal sponge disks containing either recombinant human bFGF, recombinant PDGF-BB, or a placebo. After flight, animals received an injection of hypothalamic-releasing hormones. After sacrifice, the sponges were removed and prepared for biochemical and histological analysis of DNA, protein, and collagen content. Histological organization, amount of visible collagen, and the resolution of hemorrhage at the infiltrating interface were also examined.

Results:

Histological analysis showed that both bFGF and PDGF showed positive effects in the ground control rats, but only immediate-release bFGF and delayed-release PDGF had significant, positive effects in the flight rats. This may be due to the 2-day launch delay of the shuttle mission, which caused the growth factor to be released earlier during flight than planned. Although cellular influx into the tissue space of placebo-treated sponges was unaffected by spaceflight, there was a significantly blunted response to either bFGF or PDGF-BB in flight animals. Microgravity significantly reduced wound collagen concentration regardless of the treatment group. The collagen concentration of granulation tissue in flight animals treated with bFGF was significantly less than in those treated with PDGF, but not significantly less than in the placebo treated group. These results show that a highly standardized wound repair process in young rats is significantly altered by spaceflight.

experiment_title: Spatial Organization within Prostate Cancer Spheroids
parameter_html:
DU 145 cells
E-cadherin
LNCaP cells
Prostate cells
investigators: Principal Investigator: O'Connor, Kim
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Multicellular spheroids have a remarkable capacity to mimic solid tumors to a greater extent than cell monolayers. Spatial organization within spheroids is seminal to their in vivo-like behavior and is instrumental in the acquisition of drug resistance and expression of antigens that can serve as biomarkers for carcinogenesis. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the spatial profile and assembly of multicellular spheroids, using prostate cancer cells as a model system. Spheroid differentiation and viability will be determined as a function of radial position. This analysis was performed on spheroids produced using conventional methods and in a rotating-wall vessel (RWV). The knowledge gained from this research will ultimately improve the fidelity of multicellular spheroids in the extent to which they resemble micrometastases and avascular regions of larger tumors.

The objective of the proposed research was to improve the understanding of how culture conditions affect the spatial profile and assembly of multicellular cancer spheroids, using prostate cancer cells as a model system. During the study, the investigators fulfilled the following specific aims:
1) Developed mathematical models of spheroid formation with population balances and Monte Carlo technique.
2) Elucidated the biological and physical mechanisms underlying spheroid formation of prostate cancer cells with the mathematical models.
3) Assessed the ability of the mathematical models to predict spheroid self-assembly of prostate cancer cells.
4) Characterized the spatial composition of prostate cancer spheroids with respected to viability, differentiation and multidrug resistance.

APPROACH:
The methodology for the study is embedded in the results section below.

RESULTS:
Aggregation of attachment-dependent animal cells represents a series of motility, collision, and adhesion events applicable to such diverse fields as tissue engineering, bioseparations, and drug testing. Aggregation of human prostate cancer cells in liquid-overlay culture was modeled using Smoluchowski's collision theory. Using well (LNCaP) and poorly differentiated (DU 145 and PC 3) cell lines, the biological relevance of the model was assessed by comparing aggregation rates with diffusive and adhesive properties. Diffusion coefficients ranged from 5 to 90 microm(2)/min for single LNCaP and PC 3 cells, respectively. Similar diffusivities were predicted by the persistent random walk model and Einstein relation, indicating random motion. LNCaP cells were the most adhesive in the study with reduced cell shedding, 100% adhesion probability, and enhanced expression of E-cadherin. There was an increase in DU 145 cells staining positive for E-cadherin from nearly 20% of single cells to uniform staining across the surface of all aggregates; fewer than 30% of PC 3 aggregates stained positive. Aggregation rates were more consistent with adhesive properties than with motilities, suggesting that aggregation in the study was reaction-controlled. Relative to other assays employed here, aggregation rates were more sensitive to phenotypic differences in cell lines and described size-dependent changes in aggregation at a finer resolution. In particular, model results suggest similar aggregation rates for two-dimensional DU 145 and PC 3 aggregates and upwards of 4-fold higher rates for larger three-dimensional DU 145 spheroids, consistent with expression of E-cadherin. The kinetic model has application to spheroid production, to cell flocculation and as an adhesion assay.

Neoplastic multicellular spheroids are in vitro models of solid tumors employed in drug testing and basic research. This study compares differentiation in static and mixed prostate cancer spheroids. Staining intensity of prostate specific antigen (PSA) was down-regulated upon mixing, from 0.21 +/- 0.03 to 0.13 +/- 0.03 in LNCaP multicellular spheroids, and from 0.13 +/- 0.04 to 0.03 +/- 0.02 in DU 145 multicellular spheroids. This was accompanied by 65% increase in the expression of cytokeratins 8 and 18 in DU 145 spheroids. PSA expression extended 60 micro m within static spheroids and was disrupted in mixed culture. Diminished PSA expression and spatial organization suggests a more aggressive cancer. Higher cytokeratin expression could result from either differentiation towards a luminal phenotype or activation of the Ras pathway during dedifferentiation. Thus, the existing paradigm of differentiation established for normal tissue does not apply for our neoplastic spheroids. Cell dedifferentiation is attributed to improved interstitial transport and synthesis of extracellular matrix.

experiment_title: Lightweight, Wearable Metal Rubber-Textile Sensor for In Situ Lunar Autonomous Health Monitoring
parameter_html:
Health monitor
Physiological sensors
Smart clothing
investigators: Principal Investigator: Hill, Andrea
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This NASA Phase II SBIR program would develop comfortable garments with multiple integrated sensor functions for the monitoring of astronauts during long-duration space missions. During Phase I, NanoSonic demonstrated the feasibility of using its patented Metal RubberTM sheet and fabric materials as both sensor elements and highly flexible electrodes integrated into prototype instrumented garments. Heart rate and EKG data taken using the Metal RubberTM sensors are essentially identical to those obtained using standard biomedical instrumentation. The combined high electrical conductivity, low mechanical modulus, and environmental robustness of the Metal RubberTM materials make them a lightweight, stretchy and comfortable alternative to conventional metal wiring and cabling. During the proposed Phase II program, NanoSonic would work with a large-volume U.S. textile manufacturer, the sensor and electronics design group of a major aerospace company, and a biomedical sensor and devices laboratory of Food and Drug Administration. NanoSonic would improve the Metal RubberTM materials and methods for their integration as sensor and interconnect materials into instrumented garments, design, fabricate and evaluate the performance of sensor jerseys based on the results of Phase I tests, develop data acquisition electronics needed to interface to standard storage and communication modules, and investigate requirements for scaled-up manufacturing.
