experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
HZE particles are part of the Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) which exist in deep space and cannot be shielded completely inside spacecraft. However, little is known about the interaction of HZE particles with the human body. This study will focus on leukemia, i.e., on the bone/bone-marrow interface from realistic mouse or human dimensions down to single cells. The latency time of leukemia is 2-3 years which coincides more or less with the mission time for the planned expedition to Mars.

The interpretation of data from mechanistic studies on radiation biology requires detailed descriptions of the local patterns of energy deposition in the appropriate cellular or sub-cellular sites to explore the effects of radiation quality on biological response.

The objective of this project is to provide Monte Carlo (MC) simulations on the local patterns of energy deposition by HZE particles in the appropriate cellular environment including effects of micro-, and macro-geometrical considerations. More specifically, this investigation aims to:

1. Determine the frequency of energy deposition in the target regions of importance to the initiation of leukemia in laboratory animals. Volumes appropriate to chromosomal damage in cell nuclei (micrometer dimensions) and local damage to DNA (nanometer dimensions) will be explored for HZE ions, including iron, silicon, and protons. Calculations will be made for similar volumes for low-LET radiation such as 250 kVp x-rays and 60Co gamma rays for comparison of RBE effects.

2. Determine the relative probability of damage cluster formation in volumes comparable to DNA strand break formation. Determination of the relative probability of event size clusters from a few to many events per nanometer can provide the quantitative information necessary to correlate radiation quality with reparability of lesion damage

3. Determine the effects of bone and bone marrow geometry on the frequency of energy deposition events in hematopoietic tissue structures, such as the cell nuclei and DNA. This information is particularly important in efforts to scale biological response from animals to human bone structures.

4. Determine the effects of experimental structures on the dose to blood forming organs. The supporting experimental structures required to position animals, tissues, and cells for irradiation in the HZE beam line can influence the local patterns of energy deposition in the targets of interest. Because of the energetic secondary particles that can be produced when HZE particles interact with tissue and support structures, effects of charged particle equilibrium, or the lack thereof, might have profound effects on local energy deposition

APPROACH:
Calculations focused on interpretation of microscopic “event” or “dose” distributions appropriate to studies of HZE radiation induced leukemia in animal and cellular models [NSCOR Program, Colorado State University, R. Ulrich, PI] and those encountered in the production of clustered damage in DNA [e.g., Brookhaven National Laboratory, B Sutherland, PI].

Progenitor cells for leukemia are haematopoietic stem cells that are located in clusters within marrow cavities having dimensions on the order of a few hundred microns. These cavities are surrounded by trabecular bone matrix, which forms a wall of several hundred microns thickness around the marrow. The dimensions and geometry of the bone marrow are too irregular for direct dosimetry measurements and dose-averaging methods are inappropriate for chronic low dose-rate (single particle) exposures.

Detailed Monte Carlo charged particle track structure simulation provided quantitative information on spatial patterns of energy deposition in cellular targets of dimensions as small as a few nanometers on a particle-by-particle basis; these distributions were the starting point to characterize the detailed nature of radiation-induced damage produced by high-LET radiation.

The modeling approach combined the capabilities of full event-by-event Monte Carlo track simulation codes with codes employing condensed history capabilities; the latter was more appropriate for the description of high-energy secondary electrons. The event-by-event ion code PROTRAC (which is part of the biophysical simulation tool PARTRAC) developed at GSF Neuherberg for protons and alpha particles will be extended for heavy charged particle (HZE) interactions using appropriate relativistic theory. Generated secondary electrons that traverse specific regions of interest, e.g., bone marrow cells or their nuclei, were followed also event-by-event using ETRAC (the electron transport code of PARTRAC) whereas electron transport in adjoining tissues and the surrounding structural material will be followed by the more computer efficient condensed history general purpose MC transport code PENELOPE developed at the University of Barcelona. Appropriate interaction cross sections for a wide range of target materials will be added to the ETRAC and PROTRAC codes, specifically to explore the effects of bone-tissue interfaces on energy deposition in bone marrow cells. Comparison of the spatial pattern of energy deposited in volumes of interest obtained from models of the HZE particles with that obtained from low-LET radiation will provide a firm basis to interpret radiation quality effects on biological response and the mathematical structure developed is amenable to scaling to volumes appropriate to human dimensions for considerations of risk assessment.

RESULTS:
A simple, non-bone-site-specific, non-species specific, and computationally-efficient geometrical model for trabecular spongiosa was developed using the general purpose Monte Carlo code PENELOPE.

Internal dimensions for human models were obtained from path-length distributions as measured in different human bones. The murine model, referred to as the scaled mouse model, consists of the human model scaled by a factor of 0.1. Internal dimensions of murine bones published in the literature strongly suggest that simple scaling of the human model suffice.

The track structure transport code PARTRAC has been extended to transport HZE particles (bare heavy ions) through liquid water to energies up to 1 GeV/u.

The optical constants of metallic calcium were determined and the dielectric response function was modeled in a suitable way to use it for cross section calculations at relativistic energies. Total and energy differential interaction cross sections were calculated as well as stopping powers, straggling parameter and mean free paths for calcium. The cross sections and a transport model for calcium remain to be implemented into PARTRAC.

In combining the geometry with electron and HZE transport in a simple, but not too efficient, way, a hybrid transport code was created. Simulations of an external pencil beam of heavy ions (4He, 16O, 28Si, and 56Fe) in the energy range from 10 to 300 MeV/u were performed.

Microdosimetric concepts were used to characterize the energy deposition within the bone/bone-marrow geometry. In particular, the spongiosa deposition factor (SDF) was used as the dosimetric quantity for interspecies comparisons. The SDF is defined as the ratio of energy deposited in the marrow to the energy deposited in the spongiosa. It also serves for comparisons between different ions used in irradiation of a single species. There is a substantial difference in SDF values between human and mice models for incident energies below 50 MeV/u. This can be attributed to the attenuation of the incident particles, charge particle equilibrium (or the lack of), and the Bragg-peak location. However, for incident energies above 50 MeV/u the same SDF values (except for alpha particles) were seen for both the human and murine models. This strongly suggests that scaling or extrapolating from mouse model findings to human risks should be possible, at least for sufficient fast HZE particles.

experiment_title: Characterization of Microbial Transfer Among Crewmembers During Space Flight
parameter_html:
Microbial transmission
Staphylococcus aureus
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pierson, Duane
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Increased risk of infections among crewmembers during space flight results from working and living in a crowded, closed environment with limited capabilities for air revitalization and disinfection. Alterations in the immune response during space flight as well as stress, aerosols, and altered fluid distribution within the body could increase the incidence of infectious disease during long-duration space missions. Staphyloccus aureus has been the target of many epidemiological studies because of its known virulence potential and as a prominent cause of nosocomial infections. This bacterium has also been of interest to NASA's human space flight program. Staphyloccus aureus was chosen as the subject for this study because it is frequently isolated from both crewmembers and the spacecraft environment and has been examined in previous space flight programs, providing a benchmark for the current missions as well as the technology employed.

Studies initially conducted during the Apollo Program and Apollo-Soyuz Test Project using bacteriophage typing patterns reported that the transfer of Staphyloccus aureus among crewmembers was a common occurrence. A phage typing experiment was also conducted during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project to study microbial exchange among the U.S. and Russian crewmembers. Further phage typing studies were conducted during the Skylab program, which also included data regarding dissemination of the organism through the spacecraft environment. Data from the Skylab 3 mission suggested two incidences of intercrew transfer.

APPROACH:
Isolates of Staphyloccus aureus were collected over a two-year period from nasal, throat, urine, and feces specimens of Space Shuttle flight crewmembers and from surfaces inside the spacecraft. Clinical specimens were collected from crewmembers 10 and 2 days prior to flight, and immediately after landing. The internal surfaces and air of the spacecraft were sampled 30 days and I day before flight, and at landing.

RESULTS:
Staphyloccus aureus was chosen as the target bacterium to study the spread of microbes in the spacecraft because it is frequently isolated from crewmembers and from the Space Shuttle environment. This 2-year study included 10 Space Shuttle missions ranging from 5 to 16 days in duration, with 5-7 crewmembers per mission. A total of 57 astronauts (45 male and 12 female) participated in the study, and 33 (58%) were culture-positive during one or more sampling periods for Staphyloccus aureus.

The 139 isolates collected during the study included 96 Staphyloccus aureus strains isolated from culture-positive subjects, and 43 strains isolated from surfaces inside the Shuttle crewmember compartment. In 37% of the subjects, Staphyloccus aureus was isolated at all three sample collection periods while 21% of the subjects were intermittent carriers, from which the bacteria was isolated during one or two of the three sampling periods. Staphyloccus aureus was not isolated during the pre- or postflight sample collections from 42% of the subjects. Of those harboring the target bacteria, the most common site for isolation was the nose. Isolates were also obtained from throat and urine specimens, however, these comprised only about 25% of the Staphyloccus aureus isolates.

Objectives:

The objective of this experiment was to test the hypothesis that a growth-hormone (GH) deficiency occurs during space flight and that this deficiency contributes to the bone loss and decreased tissue function observed following microgravity exposure. It was expected that replacement with recombinant GH inflight, in combination with adequate nutrition and exercise, would halt the process of bone and tissue degeneration. As the first commercially sponsored life science payload, the experiment was to investigate whether biological changes caused by microgravity were similar enough to Earth-based medical conditions to facilitate pharmacological evaluation of potential new therapies. Other objectives included evaluation of muscle and immune function, which are known to be affected/regulated by GH.

Approach:

Static measurements were made of long bone length, diaphyseal cross-sectional surface area, medullary areas, and cortical sectional areas in femora and humeri. Dynamic measurements were made of the periosteal surface of femora and humeri. The soleus muscles were weighed, and cross sectional surface area was determined. Surface area of the myotendinous junctions (MTJ) was also measured. Immunocompetence of T-lymphocytes from the lymph nodes and spleen was determined.

Results:

Neither short-term spaceflight nor rhGH treatment altered long bone length, diaphyseal cross-sectional surface area, medullary areas, and cortical sectional areas in femora and humeri. In both flight and ground control animals, rhGH treatment significantly increased bone formation and mineral apposition rates at the periosteal surface of femora and humeri. However, because 4 days of spaceflight was not enough to inhibit periosteal bone formation, the effect of rhGH treatment on spaceflight-induced osteopenia could not be determined. Muscle weight, muscle fiber cross-sectional area, and MTJ surface area were significantly reduced by 4 days in space, comparable to reductions seen after 7-14 days of spaceflight. Administration of rhGH did not reduce the muscle atrophy observed. This is consistent with the hypothesis that another hormone is mediating the response to muscle unloading. T-lymphocyte responsiveness in the lymph nodes was significantly depressed compared to ground controls. There appeared to be a tissue-specific immune response to microgravity exposure.

experiment_title: Effects of High Versus Low Autonomy on Space Crewmember Performance (Autonomy)
parameter_html:
Autonomy
Cohesiveness
Fatigue
Innovation
Mental clarity
Mood
Work pressure
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kanas, NickCo-Investigator: Marmar, CharlesCo-Investigator: Neylan, ThomasCo-Investigator: Ritsher, JenniferCo-Investigator: Weiss, Daniel
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In future space missions to an asteroid or Mars, crewmembers will be given more autonomy to plan and carry out their activities due to the long distances involved and the tasks that will be needed to explore a planetary surface. The impact of increased autonomy on crew performance has not been evaluated formally. In addition, while the evidence is largely anecdotal, strict adherence to timelines sent from mission control has been reported to be fatiguing and stressful for astronauts. Furthermore, such stressors can affect interpersonal interactions, resulting in increased team conflict and reduced morale and productivity.

The long-term goal of this experiment was to conduct a scientific hypotheses-testing study involving a series of on-orbit missions to the International Space Station (ISS) in which the investigators measured the effects on crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction of “high” autonomy conditions (where crewmembers plan much of their work schedule and perhaps experience a “Mars-like” communication delay with family members and mission control personnel back on Earth). This was contrasted with “low” autonomy conditions (where mission control personnel communicate in real-time with the crew and develop the work schedule, much as happens now). The impact of high versus low crew autonomy on mission control personnel was also be studied.

Before engaging in the flight experiment, the investigators were asked by NASA/JSC management to test the feasibility and safety of their methods during pilot studies involving a series of ground-based space analog missions (e.g., NEEMO, Houghton-Mars Project, Mars-500 105-day Simulation), where key elements of the flight experiment can be evaluated. Thus, the short-term goal was to conduct such feasibility pilot studies involving such missions. This is the purpose of the current “Autonomy” pilot project, which deals with NEEMO and HMP simulations. Under separate funding from NASA and the NSBRI, the investigators also studied the Mars-500 105-day Simulation, but this will not be reported here.

APPROACH:
The investigators conducted a series of pilot studies in this project: NEEMO 12 and 13, and the Haughton-Mars Project in 2008 (HMP 2008). In the series of pilot studies reported below, crewmember and mission control subjects filled out a weekly Study Questionnaire, which included mood and interpersonal interactions questions from the Profile of Mood States, the Group Environment Scale, and the Work Environment Scale, as well as a critical incident log. Additionally, new measures were developed and tested in the Mars 500 105-day Simulation but not on any of the simulations described in this report. The investigators had planned to test these in the NEEMO 14 mission, but this mission was postponed due to operational reasons unrelated to the research done on this experiment.

The independent variable was low versus high autonomy, and the dependent variables were scores on the measures of crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction. It was not expected that autonomy would adversely affect mood, group interactions, and performance. In fact, it was expected that mood, group interactions, and performance would be the same or better during high autonomy periods.

RESULTS:
NEEMO
One study involved the NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) program. The purpose of this program is to study human survival in the Aquarium underwater laboratory in preparation for future space missions. The Aquarius is located near Key Largo, Florida. Missions typically last 10 to 14 days and involve research and other activities conducted by 4 or more “aquanauts”, who are usually astronauts or other NASA personnel. These activities are conducted within the habitat or during simulated EVAs in the ocean. “Mission control” personnel located topside monitor crewmember progress and timeline the schedule.

The investigators studied two NEEMO missions: 12 and 13. NEEMO 12 consisted of two weeks of low autonomy, where the crewmember work schedules were timelined by the topside mission control. Subjects included three NASA crewmembers and 6 topside personnel. NEEMO 13 consisted of one week of low autonomy and one week of high autonomy (where the crew had more flexibility to plan their own work schedule). Subjects included four NASA crewmembers and eight topside personnel. At the end of each week, subjects completed a measure of mood [Profile of Mood States (PMS)], items from two measures of social climate [Group Environment Scale (GES), Work Environment Scale (WES)], and a critical incident log.

Due to the small number of data points, investigators could only analyze the data descriptively by examining change scores of the subscales of their measures from the first to the second week, separately for the two missions. Preliminary analyses suggested that the autonomy condition was successfully employed in NEEMO 13 with no adverse results. There seemed to be clear differences between the low and high autonomy weeks by the results, the crewmembers reported more direction from the mission commander (reflected by an increase in “Leader Control”) as well as a decrease in fatigue from the low to the high autonomy weeks during NEEMO 13 as compared to NEEMO 12, which only had low autonomy conditions. For the topside personnel, work pressure was stable in NEEMO 13, whereas it rose in the second week during NEEMO 12. However, confusion increased during the high autonomy second week of NEEMO 13 as compared to the second week of NEEMO 12 (where it declined), suggesting that the topside personnel were not as clear in their roles when the crew took over more of the schedule.

HMP 2008
A second pilot study involved some of the summer 2008 crewmembers working on the Haughton-Mars Project (HMP) on Devon Island in Canada. The location was an old, large impact crater which had similarities to the Martian surface in appearance and geological characteristics. People participating in this program dress up in space suits, travel in a Mars rover, and conduct tasks similar to those anticipated during an actual expedition to Mars. There is no formal “mission control” and the participants have great freedom to plan their activities each day. Hence, there is great autonomy in the work schedule.

Investigators studied the last three weeks of the 2008 mission. Eight non-NASA scientists and graduate students served as subjects. As in their previous work, they completed weekly POMS, GES, WES and critical incident log measures. Since they had no contrasting low autonomy period with which to compare their results, investigators decided to compare the subscale scores of the HMP subjects with those from published adult norms in the POMS, GES, and WES manuals, and with subscale scores from mission control subjects who participated in their previous on-orbit studies.

The HMP group reported greater levels of in-group leader direction and innovation and less need for outside direction as compared with other work groups on Earth, which presumably had more managerial control. These findings suggest that they were working under fairly high autonomous conditions. In addition, they reported being more cohesive than as compared with other work groups as well. They also reported being more tired than mission control groups, but this might have been an artifact of their working in the Canadian north in the summertime, when there is constant daylight and the work if more physically taxing than sitting in front of a mission control console. Taken together, these results suggest that people working under relatively high autonomous conditions are not adversely affected and may even bond together more cohesively than other work groups.

The results of these pilot studies suggest that in isolated and confined conditions that are meant to simulate those encountered during space missions, high autonomy is safe, well-received by crewmembers, and offers some potential advantages over low autonomy conditions. The crews have reported that they enjoy the high autonomy condition, and there have been no untoward effects to date. There have been some suggestions that high autonomy improves mood and cohesion, with more innovation and reliance on the crew leader. Outside mission monitors reported less work pressure but some confusion concerning their role. Clearly, these results are suggestive based on limited pilot data, but they point to the safety and possible advantages of high autonomy on crew functioning during actual space missions.

experiment_title: Integrated Medical Model - Chest Injury Model
parameter_html:
Probability of injury
Probability of occurrence
investigators: Principal Investigator: Lewandowski, Beth
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is important to know the likelihood of medical events that can happen during a space flight mission so that the resources needed to treat the event are available. Since there is limited volume, mass, and power on a spacecraft, the medical resources must be optimally chosen so that the resources are there when needed and so that space is not wasted on excess supplies. The NASA Integrated Medical Model (IMM) project is systematically working towards developing an optimal medical kit, using probabilistic risk assessment. The IMM project has identified all of the credible medical conditions that could occur during a space flight, and they are working to assign a likelihood of occurrence and a severity of impact for each condition. Decisions on the proper resources to include in the medical kit are made by comparing the risk of each medical event against all of the others. The purpose of this study was to estimate the probability of traumatic chest injury during an International Space Station (ISS) mission.

APPROACH:
Traumatic chest injury is a medical event that has a low probability of occurrence but could have a significant impact if it were to happen. Since there has not been an occurrence of traumatic chest injury to date in space, deterministic modeling combined with Monte Carlo simulations were used to estimate the probability of it occurring. The key components of the model were a profile of masses and velocities of equipment that could impact an astronaut. A biomechanical model of the thorax was used to calculate an impact response to the input profile. Normalized compression of the chest was the output response of the biomechanical model and it was correlated to severity of injury. The correlation was used in a logistic regression to determine the probability of injury. The probability of injury was combined with the probability of occurrence of an impact to the chest during one year on the ISS, to determine the overall probability of traumatic chest injury during one year on the ISS.

RESULTS:
The model parameters were modeled as distributions, so that the variability and uncertainty of each parameter was captured within the probability estimate. Monte Carlo simulations were performed and the probability of traumatic chest injury during one year on ISS was determined to be: 5.32 x 10-4 ± 5.95 x 10-4 (4.16 x 10-5 - 1.39 x 10-3), presented as the most likely probability ± the standard deviation (90th percentile confidence interval). In addition to the probability estimate, results of a sensitivity analysis and a verification and validation analysis of the biomechanical model of the thorax are given. The most sensitive parameters of the model are, in order of sensitivity: 1) velocity of the impactor; 2) rate of occurrence of an impact; 3) The intercept coefficient in the probability of injury equation; and 4) mass of the impactor. The output of the biomechanical thorax model matches the output obtained by the original authors of the biomechanical thorax model, which verifies that the biomechanical thorax model was implemented correctly. Additionally, the output response of the biomechanical thorax model falls within the response corridor derived from the results of another cadaver impact study.

experiment_title: Characterization of Respirable Airborne Particulate Matter in Shuttle Atmosphere
parameter_html:
Dichloromethane
Particle masses
Shuttle atmosphere
Spacecraft Allowable Maximum Concentrations (SMACs)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Russo, DaneCo-Investigator: Kotz, T.Co-Investigator: Liu, BenjaminCo-Investigator: McMurry, P.Co-Investigator: Rubow, K.
image_name: Shuttle Particle Sampler (SPS) and Shuttle Particle Monitor (SPM)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Shuttle crewmembers have reported eye and respiratory irritation they attributed to visible debris in the air. Some cases of equipment failure can be attributed to airborne debris. Large amounts of particulate matter have been found in microbial air samplers and on filters and vacuum bags after flights. However, airborne particulate matter in the Shuttle had never been systematically collected. The objectives of this study were to assess the concentration, size distribution, composition, and potential sources of airborne particles on the Shuttle flight deck and middeck.

APPROACH:
Two Shuttle Particle Samplers (SPSs) and one Shuttle Particle Monitor (SPM) were carried on each of two Shuttle missions. One particle sampler was activated early in the flight, and another, late in the flight. The particle sampler trapped particles during a 24 hour period and separated them according to their aerodynamic size into four fractions: < 2.5 micrometers µm, 2.5 to 10 µm, 10 to 100 µm, or >100 µm. Particles larger than 100 µm were trapped on a screen with 100 µm openings, in the inlet cap. The other particles were collected on Teflon filters. The particle sampler had two virtual impactor stages, each with six nozzles. After a flight, the SPSs were returned to the laboratory, where the largest particles were vacuumed from the filter onto another filter and weighed, and the other particles were weighed on the filters that had trapped them. The filters had been weighed when empty. The elemental composition was determined by X-ray fluorescence for the smaller particles and by energy-dispersive spectroscopy for the larger particles. Some larger particles were also examined by scanning electron microscopy.

The SPM measured particle concentrations by photometric detection of light scatter. It automatically recorded the minimum, maximum, and average particle concentrations over 15-minute intervals throughout the flight. It was set to zero by running it in clean air and was calibrated by running it alongside the particle sampler. The particle monitor was useful for following changes in particle concentration over time; however, it recorded only particles that were smaller than 100 µm.

RESULTS:
The particle concentration averaged 56 µg/m3 on one flight and 35 µg/m3 on the other. The particle concentration did not increase over time. Judging by the elemental composition, most of the particles were probably of organic origin. These results should be useful for evaluating the effectiveness of modifications to cabin air filtration systems.

experiment_title: Avian Blood Vessel Formation in Space
parameter_html:
Density, Blood vessel, chorioallantoic membrane, quail, Autofluorescent bright light microscopy (counts, descriptive)
Size, diameter, Blood vessel, chorioallantoic membrane, quail embryo, Autofluorescent microscopy (counts, descriptive)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Lelkes, Peter
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To determine whether prolonged space flight causes a change in the pattern of vascularization during the development and maturation of the chorioallantoic membrane (CAM).

Approach:

This experiment was performed twice, once during Mir 18 (returning on STS-71) and once during Mir 19 (returning on STS-74). Fertilized eggs were carried to the Mir space station aboard a Russian Progress (227) supply vessel, and placed in an incubator supplied by the Institute for Biomedical Problems. experiment_title: Medical Consumables Tracking -GRC
parameter_html:
Medical consumables tracking
Medication tracking
investigators: Principal Investigator: Zoldak, John
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study sought to identify current practices and develop controls, processes, and technical solutions to accurately track the inventory of medical consumables. When International Space Station (ISS) medical kits are returned to Earth, fewer medical consumables remain in the medical kits than would be expected based on reported use by the astronauts. This is significant because the possibility exists that exploration missions could be undersupplied and run the risk of not being able to treat an ill or injured crewmember, particularly given the small volume available for the medical kits. This study identified current practices and develop controls, processes, and technical solutions to accurately track the inventory of medical consumables.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Track medical consumables and medications accessed with an accuracy of 95% or better.
  2. No additional scheduled crew time to access a medication or medical consumable.
  3. Work in a microgravity environment.
  4. Work in space vehicles that have electronically noisy environments.
  5. Encrypted data transfer.
  6. Know how much of a particular medication is available.
  7. Read the electronic ID tagged items inside of Convenience Medications Pack.
  8. Have the ability to scale; to track small quantities or large quantities of medicines and medical consumables.

    APPROACH:
    The Medical Consumables Tracking (MCT) project was a demonstration of hardware capable of tracking medical consumables within the Crew Health Care System (CHeCS), allowing for autonomous CHeCS inventory. The MCT System is a battery-powered system that utilizes a Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) system comprised of a reader/scanner/interrogator, antennas, a transponder and a single board computer. The system was designed to perform an automated inventory cycle every 720 hours and provided the capability to manually initiate an inventory cycle via a switch located on the exterior of the CHeCS locker door. When a cycle was completed an inventory report of RFID tagged items detected within the locker was transmitted wirelessly to the Joint Station Local Area Network.

    RESULTS:
    With the exception of an anomalous tag read and missing scan, all inventory (resultant tag file) downlinks were received as designed. In addition, all health and status data from the MCT system, controls (manual reads, door open sensor, etc.), communication links and configuration file uploads operated and were received as designed. The MCT system successfully demonstrated the ability to perform an autonomous inventory of CheCS medical consumables.

experiment_title: Vortex Dehumidification System
parameter_html:
Air streams
Cabin air dehumidification
Liquid vortex
Mass
Temperature
Volume
investigators: Principal Investigator: Best, Fredrick
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Dehumidification in air handling systems aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and future space vehicles is problematic and not efficient. The proposed project was to demonstrate that utilizing the Texas A&M Vortex Separator (part of the Immobilized Microbe Microgravity Wastewater Processing System (IMMWPS) Flight Unit) as part of a dehumidification system for future spacecraft or as an ISS replacement unit is feasible. The ITP planned to accomplish the following main objectives:
1. Demonstrate, through microgravity experimentation, the capability of the separator to provide a passive solution to cabin air dehumidification that is simpler, more adaptive, and less prone to failure than current mechanically driven technology.
2. Thoroughly test and optimize a modified separator design and flow loop for this application.

Currently, dehumidification systems utilize mechanically driven separators. Due to the nature of these separators, moving parts, maintenance, and therefore additional modes of failure are introduced into these systems. While these statements are true for any mechanical system, the current systems have proven them true through failure. In January 2003, the primary rotary separator on the Spacehab module failed due to design limitations. The secondary separator was brought on-line, but failed due to mechanical problems, resulting in complete failure of the dehumidification system. This failure delayed experiments and produced uncomfortable living conditions for the crew of Spacehab.

Mechanical failure can be avoided by replacing the rotary separator with a passive separator. Using the intrinsic momentum of the fluids, whether two-phase, all gas, or all liquid, the ITP separator drives the buoyancy process with no moving parts, thereby significantly reducing the opportunity for failure. This is an important and attractive advantage of passive separators.

Secondly, the design of current rotary separators is sensitive to large variations in flow conditions. The primary rotary separator of the Spacehab system failed because the design could not accommodate the flow conditions, resulting in flooding of the cabin air conditioning system. One of the aspects of the ITP design is the unique ability to accommodate significant flow variations. In effect, this separator acts as an accumulator for the system, handling system volume variations and eliminating the need for a separate component to do so. While the possibility of flooding or dry-out does exist, the hydrodynamic limits resulting in such failure have been studied extensively by the ITP and are well known. For this reason, the separator can be designed to handle any flow variations required by the system. This reduces the sensitivity of the system to flow changes and further reduces modes of failure.

Moreover, the ITP has recently completed development of a dynamic volume sensing technique that allows control software to monitor and adjust microgravity flow conditions without operator interaction. This technique increases both the reliability and efficiency of the accumulation function associated with the ITP separator.

Aside from significantly reducing the probability of failure, the simplicity of a passive separator also reduces required system space, mass, and power. The ITP has achieved successful separation with driving flows of 4 cfm using a 4.5 inch diameter, 4.5 inch tall separator. It is important to note that the maximum air flow rate for this size has not been tested, but the tested flow is comparable to the 6.3 cfm currently processed by the Common Cabin Air Assembly (CCAA) of the ISS. Furthermore, the separator size can be optimized to accommodate air flow ranges required by cabin air conditioning systems.

In conclusion, the passive vortex separator developed by the ITP has the potential to significantly reduce failure modes, required space, system mass, and power requirements for cabin air conditioning systems. The simplified designed relates to less crew time spent on maintenance, while failure reduction minimizes crew time spent in undesirable living conditions. All of these factors indicate the passive approach to cabin air dehumidification provide positive answers to the questions posed by the AHST program, as well as a method to better optimize current cabin air conditioning systems.

APPROACH:
The vortex separator was chilled to low temperature and ambient air was injected through the device. Air leaving the device would be saturated at the chilled temperature and then heated to ambient conditions reducing the relative humidity. A further feature of the system is that it could potentially be used in other gas/liquid separation such as microgravity showers or other high gas volume flows to reduce the entrained liquid. It is expected that the vortex system will reduce power requirements and relative mass/volume while increasing reliability.

RESULTS:
The Vortex Dehumidification System (VDS) developed at Texas A&M University (TAMU) was successfully tested aboard reduced gravity aircraft. These tests showed the Vortex Separator (VS) to be more than capable of dehumidifying and cooling prototypic ISS inlet air streams by maintaining the liquid vortex at a temperature below the dew point of the incoming humid air. Furthermore, the research demonstrated the ability to control the outlet air conditions through the temperature of the liquid within the separation volume. Regardless of inlet air conditions, the air stream reached equilibrium with the liquid before exiting the VS. The VS demonstrated humidity removal rates in excess of 16 grams of water per cubic meter of air (16g/m3).

The TAMU vortex separator dehumidification system can replace the current CCAA system on the ISS or be considered for future spacecraft due to two primary advantages:
1. Mass and Volume are reduced and performance is improved. Based on the preliminary trade study, the TAMU vortex separator dehumidification system requires only a third of the mass and half the volume of the existing system without a loss in performance. The power required is significantly decreased due to the removal of a powered rotary separator.
2. Maintenance is simplified and the need for consumables is reduced. Compared with other separators, there are no high precision or high speed moving parts which can cause vibration or require frequent maintenance and there are no capillary pores to be plugged. Since the separator catches dust in a liquid layer, no separate filters are required.

The condensation rate is a result of the difference in the inlet air stream properties and the equilibrium condition maintained by the liquid temperature. For air of consistent inlet temperature and humidity, condensation rates can be increased by lowering liquid temperature or increasing the inlet flow rate. As inlet temperature, humidity, and flow rate levels fluctuate, the condensation rate will change to maintain a stable outlet temperature and humidity level. The outlet flow rate will be equivalent to the inlet flow rate less the condensation rate.

Furthermore, the separation rate always matches the condensation rate as these two processes are essentially one. In other words, since condensation occurs at the bubble interface, any condensate that forms is simultaneously separated to the liquid vortex. This is the major advantage of direct contact heat exchange over plate type heat exchangers. For the latter type, condensate accumulates on the heat transfer surface. With current technologies, this condensate is either removed from the surface through capillary forces to a low pressure sump, such as with a porous heat exchanger, or sheared by the air flow through a slurper type separator and directed to a rotary separator for final separation. If the condensation rate overcomes the separation or removal rate, condensate builds up on the heat exchanger surface and increases the thermal resistance between the air flow and low temperature plate, reducing thermal energy transfer. Hydrophobic and hydrophilic coatings have been developed to combat this issue but cannot completely overcome this effect. In addition, these treated surfaces are subject to microbial growth and fouling of the special coatings, resulting in degraded performance over time. By using direct contact heat exchange, the VDS does not encounter these problems.

The ability of the VDS to maintain a stable outlet condition despite varying inlet conditions is due to the large heat transfer area of the device. This area is large due to the direct contact heat exchange method and the unique operating characteristics of the VS. Inlet gas is quickly broken up into bubbles on the order of a millimeter in diameter by the high velocities present in the liquid vortex near the injection point. The surface area of these bubbles provides the direct contact heat exchange area. As the TAMU VS is capable of handling large inlet volumetric flow rates, this heat exchange area is considerably large compared with the overall volume of the system. For example, a 4.5 inch diameter, 4.5 inch tall separator can have heat transfer areas of several square meters. Furthermore, testing showed that, for higher than normal cabin air conditions approaching 120 degrees Fahrenheit, at most 30% of the available heat transfer area was required to reach thermal equilibrium between the inlet air stream and liquid vortex. For typical cabin air conditions, less than 10% of the available area is required. This indicates that the VDS is far from maximum capacity and could handle considerably larger flow rates than the maximum tested, 120 SLPM.

Another unique aspect of the VDS is that the heat transfer area is linearly proportional to the inlet flow rate. As a result, as demand increases and cabin air flow rates increase, the available heat transfer area increases passively. This feature allows the VDS to handle large and sudden changes in inlet volumetric flow rate with flow rate being the only change in outlet air conditions. This is a considerable performance advantage over the current rotary systems, which have shown to fail during sudden or large inlet flow rate transients.

The research conducted by TAMU and presented in this document successfully demonstrated that the VDS is more than capable of providing cabin air dehumidification in reduced gravity environments. Unlike current approaches, this system does not require a separate condensing heat exchanger and separation device but combines phase separation and dehumidification into a single unit. Furthermore, the VDS is not sensitive to inlet flow rate, temperature, or humidity variations and, during these transients, passively adjusts to produce a constant air quality at the outlet. As shown through experiment, a VDS operating with a liquid temperature of 40 degrees Fahrenheit will produce a stable outlet air stream with a vapor content 8.4 grams of water per cubic meter of air. Upon remixing with cabin air at 72 degrees Fahrenheit, this equates to a relative humidity of 33 percent.

experiment_title: Electronic Medical Records for Exploration Medical System
parameter_html: Medical technologies
investigators: Principal Investigator: Rubin, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Electronic Medical Record (EMR) is an electronic system that provides a repository for medical data, images, videos, and reports and makes the information accessible to the crew in flight via a graphical user interface to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic medical conditions.

The system is used to access medical data for all medical encounters, especially during periods of exploration missions when contact with ground resources (e.g., flight surgeon) will either be minimal or absent. During these periods of autonomous medical care, the crew will need such a system for urgent and non-urgent medical events.

The objectives of the EMR were to:

  1. Reduce or eliminate the time required of an on-orbit crew (i.e., clinician and non-clinician) to store, access, and process medical data, images, and reports.
  2. Reduce the time required of the ground crew to access medical data, images, or reports.
  3. Ensure Crew Medical Office (CMO) access to all relevant crewmember medical data, images, or reports for improved quality of care.
  4. Ensure crew access to personal medical data, images, or reports during periods of restricted ground communication.
  5. Ensure crew ability to capture onboard medical data regardless of the state of the communication link to the ground.
  6. Ensure privacy protection of onboard crewmember medical data.

APPROACH:
Development of the OpenEMR application programming interfaces (APIs), required for integration into the Exploration Medical System, can be made available to the OpenEMR open source community for potential inclusion into future releases of the EMR software. These APIs enhance the ability to import and export data into/out of the EMR database.

RESULTS:
All required development of the EMR for integration into the greater Exploration Medical System Demonstration (EMSD) project has been completed. This includes the development of APIs, data forms, and associated intermediate software "adapters" and databases.

experiment_title: Epidemiologic Analyses of Risk Factors for Bone Loss and Recovery Related to Long Duration Space Flight
parameter_html: Bone density
investigators: Principal Investigator: Amin, Shreyasee
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss is estimated to occur at a rate of one percent per month in space, particularly in weight-bearing bones in the legs and spine. This rate of loss is equivalent to what a human might lose in a year with advancing age on Earth. It remains unknown what this loss signifies for future fracture risk in crewmembers. While unloading of the skeleton in the weightless environment of space is considered the key factor contributing to bone loss, there are likely other factors that also play a role. Current prevention strategies have not been effective at preventing this bone loss. Improved understanding on the risk for fracture following long-duration space flight, as well as the factors contributing to bone loss in microgravity, and its recovery, are needed in order to develop better prevention strategies for the benefit of crew health, both during and after long-duration space exploration, and mission success.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Investigate the risk of microgravity exposure on long-term changes in bone health and fracture risk.
  2. Provide a summary of the current evidence available on potential risk factors for bone loss, recovery and fracture following long-duration space exploration.

APPROACH:
Data assembly at NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) on risk factors known to be related to bone loss and fracture risk was completed in early 2012. The investigators performed analyses on these available data to help better understand the variability in hip bone mineral density (BMD) loss and recovery, postflight. Risk factor data included, medication use, bone turnover markers, and surrogates of exercise status inflight, such as changes in strength measures, and lean muscle mass. Data assembly and data cleaning were completed. The investigators noted that there were limited data on risk factors available beyond the initial return post long-duration flights, so analyses were restricted to the immediate post-flight period.

RESULTS:
Following review of all the different measures available for analyses, the investigators identified several different risk factors which may help identify those at greatest risk for bone loss during long-duration missions. These included pre-flight measures of elevated bone resorption, as well as surrogate markers of better muscle strength and greater aerobic capacity preflight. OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss is estimated to occur at a rate of one percent per month in space, particularly in weight-bearing bones in the legs and spine. Improved understanding on the risk for fracture following long-duration space flight, as well as the factors contributing to bone loss in microgravity, and its recovery, are needed in order to develop better prevention strategies for the benefit of crew health, both during and after long-duration space exploration, and mission success.

This study had the following specific aims:

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this experiment was to evaluate digital still camera procedures written for the Photodocumentation of Skin Injuries and Allergic Reactions medical requirement for International Space Station (ISS) crews. Photodocumentation of injuries and illnesses provides visual images to support diagnosis and documentation of cutaneous injuries and illnesses.

APPROACH:
Test subjects reported all minor and major injuries, infections, allergies, and hypersensitivities incurred during the mission to the crew surgeon, including the time when the injury occurred or illness began. Using the onboard digital still camera, the area(s) of concern were photographed to document the injury/illness. A small ruler was positioned within the field of view to provide scale.

Photos were taken both at a distance of 3-5 feet to include some anatomic landmarks for orientation and as a close-up view with an oblique light source positioned at a 45 degree angle to the area. Images were downloaded to the laptop computer and downlinked to the crew surgeon, so the image quality could be evaluated and procedures revised if necessary. Photographs were taken at 24-hour intervals until the injury/illness healed.

RESULTS:
Results for this investigation are not available.

experiment_title: Impact of Microgravity on the Cell-CelInteractions between a Mutualistic Bacterium and Its Animal Host
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Foster, Jamie
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
Beneficial microbes play a significant role in the normal development of animal tissues. Through the formation of healthy stable associations between host and symbiont, particularly during post-embryonic development, carefully regulated developmental pathways can be induced.

This experimental research plan will examine the impact of microgravity on the normal molecular interactions between host and symbiont. To examine these effects, the model system between the squid Euprymna scolopes and the luminescent bacterium Vibrio fischeri will be used. For over two decades this squid-vibrio model has served as an ideal ecosystem to examine the influences of mutualistic bacteria on animal development. To simulate microgravity, rotating bioreactors called high-aspect-ratio rotating wall vessel bioreactors (HARVs) will be used to provide a low-shear environment for both the host and symbiont, thereby simulating microgravity.

The proposed work has several implications for the field of space biology. First, by examining how normal healthy symbioses are initiated and maintained under microgravity conditions, we can begin to determine the sensitivity of these ecosystems to perturbations in the space environment. Secondly, genetic and metabolic responses to gravity in the presence and absence of symbiosis will be assessed, potentially identifying previously unknown triggers or cues associated with post-embryonic animal development.

APPROACH:
Specifically, the following is proposed: 1) Examine the mechanism(s) associated with the delay of bacteria-induced immune cell trafficking that occurs in simulated microgravity; 2) Characterize the changes in the transcriptome of the host squid in the presence and absence of symbiotic bacteria exposure under microgravity conditions; 3) Develop a flight-ready microtiter plate for future flight experiments and optimize the conditions needed to initiate and maintain the symbiosis in this new hardware.

RESULTS:
1. The symbiotic V. fischeri appear to modulate the host innate immune and oxidative stress response of the host light organ during modeled microgravity conditions. Using RNA-seq we analyzed the transcriptome of the host light organ (i.e., the site of symbiosis) of the squid in the presence (symbiotic) and absence (aposymbiotic) of beneficial V. fischeri under simulated microgravity conditions. At 12 h post inoculation both the symbiotic and aposymbiotic animals exhibited an upregulation of genes associated with hemocyanin, oxidative stress, and the innate immune system. However, by 24 h post inoculation only the aposymbiotic animals exhibited an upregulated stress response, whereas those animals exposed to V. fischeri no longer showed the stress response suggesting that V. fischeri is helping to modulate the host response. Results were published in Casaburi et al., 2017 – See cumulative bibliography for citation; reported in FY2018 report.

2. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) shedding by V. fischeri is increased under simulated microgravity conditions. Under modeled microgravity conditions V. fischeri releases a statistically higher amount of the virulence factor LPS, known to cause apoptosis and inflammation in both mutualistic and pathogenic microbes. The LPS production is primarily associated with flagellar movement and by knocking out flagellar production and motion the amount of LPS produced under both microgravity and gravity conditions was reduced. However, even with the removal of the flagella, the LPS shedding was still statistically higher in modeled microgravity conditions compared to gravity conditions. We have ascertained that under modeled microgravity the V. fischeri membrane integrity is compromised and is more susceptible to antibiotic treatment. We are examining whether we can further inhibit the differential shedding of LPS under modeled microgravity conditions.

3. Sequencing and closure of the Euprymna scolopes genome revealed two evolutionary mechanisms for symbiotic organ evolution. Using the RNA-seq data generated during this project we generated a reference transcriptome for the host animal and use that as a scaffold to close the genome of E. scolopes. Although this task was not originally part of our project goals the data was invaluable in providing a closed genome for the squid-vibrio research community. Analysis of the genome and reference transcriptome revealed that there are two distinctive evolutionary processes associated with the origin of symbiotic organs in animals. A manuscript is currently in press at PNAS.

4. Modeled microgravity alters the innate immune pathway of host squid. Using the new technique NanoString, we complemented the previously generated transcriptomes by analyzing the differential gene expression along additional time points (0, 2, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 24 h) and have generated a new model of the receptor and signal cascade of the innate immune system. We have also determined that modeled microgravity impacts the expression of the innate immune genes and we have identified key parts of the pathway that are being disrupted.

5. Modeled microgravity does not significantly alter the transcriptome of the symbiont V. fischeri; however, the global regulatory gene hfq is critical to regulate the bacterial stress responses in low shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG). The transcriptome of the bacterial symbiont was examined during both exponential and stationary phase growth and results indicated that modeled microgravity had no significant impact on gene expression at 12 and 24 h. However, when the global regulator gene hfq was deleted from the bacteria, there was a pronounced change in gene expression under LSMMG conditions. There was a dramatic increase in the number of transcripts associated with TCA cycling and stress responses suggesting that the Hfq protein serves as a critical regulator for the bacteria under modeled microgravity conditions.

Additional data is available from GeneLab's Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/genelab/accession/GLDS-119/

investigators: Principal Investigator: Anderson, Page
experiment_description:
Objectives:

To determine the effects of microgravity on developmentally programmed expression of Troponin T and I isoforms known to regulate cardiac and skeletal muscle contraction.

Approach:

This experiment was performed twice, once during Mir 18 (returning on STS-71) and once during Mir 19 (returning on STS-74). Fertilized eggs were carried to the Mir space station aboard a Russian Progress (227) supply vessel, and placed in an incubator supplied by the Institute for Biomedical Problems. On days 7, 10, 14 and 16, eight eggs were fixed and stored for return to Earth.

Results:

During both runs of the experiment, internal incubator temperature was higher than nominal throughout the experiment, and most of the quail embryos failed to develop as expected, resulting in low science return. During Mir 19, ten embryos developed past 7 days and four embryos developed to an appropriate age. Analysis of the effects of microgravity on isoform expression are still underway.

Coriolis forces

Mean power frequency
Reaching movements
Sway amplitude

investigators: Principal Investigator: Lackner, JamesCo-Investigator: DiZio, Paul
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this study was to provide a technical base for evaluating the feasibility of a rotating "artificial gravity" environment for long-duration space missions. The investigators previously demonstrated that Coriolis forces generated during rotation at 10 rpm disrupt head and arm movements but adaptation is possible. Specific goals were to study 1) the rotation rates up to which adaptation is possible, 2) whether measurements of disruptions caused by rotation and subsequent adaptation in 1-G underestimate or overestimate the effects to be expected during rotation in environments with a background force level less than 1-G, and 3) how the magnitude and orientation of the background force affect retention and transfer of adaptation to rotation.

APPROACH:
Twelve subjects stood in a heel-to-toe stance in the rotating room. Each test session involved three phases: 1) pre-rotation, 2) per-rotation, and 3) post-rotation. In each phase, subjects were tested in both eyes open and eyes closed conditions. Four measures were used to characterize center of mass movement and head movement: mean sway amplitude, total power, mean power frequency, and frequency of maximum power. Each measure was computed for anterior-posterior and medial-lateral sway.

RESULTS:
Both anterior-posterior and medial-lateral head and center of mass sway during rotation had significantly greater mean sway amplitude and total power compared with pre- and post-rotation values. Mean power frequency and frequency of maximum power were little affected. Eyes open conditions were significantly more stable in all test phases than eyes-closed, but vision did not completely suppress the effects of rotation. The greatest effect of rotation was in the eyes-closed condition with mean sway amplitude and total power increasing more than twofold. Inverted pendulum sway was maintained in all phases of both test conditions. No aftereffects of rotation were present after the four 25-s exposures each subject received.

experiment_title: Body Mass Changes in NASA/Mir Astronauts
parameter_html: Body weight
investigators: Principal Investigator: No Principal Investigator,
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
International Space Station (ISS) Phase I, more commonly known as Phase I, served as a precursor to the ISS experience. In this program, the existing resources of the US Shuttle orbiters and the Russian Space Station Mir were used to test the challenges facing the international partners in the areas of cooperation, data gathering, and logistics. As part of Phase I, seven NASA astronauts served as Mir crewmembers between March 1995 and June 1998. Physiological data gathered on these NASA astronauts can give insight on the effects of long-term weightlessness on individuals, which in turn is important for future ISS considerations.

APPROACH:
Changes in body weight during periods of prolonged weightlessness were examined for six of the seven US astronauts who have flown on Mir. The data present mean body weight and standard deviations (SD) at four intervals: the annual examination in the year prior to flight (Preflight Annual), inflight on approximately Flight Day 90 (FD 90), the third day after return to Earth (R+3), and the annual examination in the year after flight (Postflight Annual).

RESULTS:
Mean weight was 77.2 kg at the preflight annual examination, 73.8 kg at FD 90, 77.3 kg at R+3, and 78.1 kg at the postflight annual examination. There was a downward shift in mean weight inflight, with return to preflight mean weight occurring by R+3. However, inflight mean weight was not statistically significantly different from the preflight and postflight mean weights.

Another way to look at this type of data is to calculate and examine the percent change between preflight and inflight values. Data are inflight data, comparing weight on FD 30, FD 60, and FD 90 to weight at preflight annual examination. Percent of change is calculated by the difference between the preflight annual examination weight and the inflight weight divided by the preflight weight multiplied by 100. The resulting negative value indicates that weight decreased early in the mission (-3.5% by FD 30) and then remained relatively constant at the next two inflight intervals (-4.0% by FD 60 and -4.25% by FD 90).

The method of measurement is different for inflight and on ground, which may contribute to the differences in weight reported here. These results suggest that during periods of prolonged weightlessness, astronauts may experience weight loss early in the mission. Inflight weight appears to stabilize at the new level, and return to preflight levels after return to Earth. Further research into nutritional status during long duration spaceflight may reveal the causes and consequences of this temporal weight loss.

experiment_title: Effect of Microgravity on the Peripheral  Subcutaneous Veno-Arteriolar Reflex in Humans
parameter_html:
Blood flow
Blood pressure
Heart rate
investigators: Principal Investigator: Gabrielsen, AndersCo-Investigator: Norsk, Peter
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

When a person stands after an extended period of inactivity, there is a pooling of blood in the lower part of the body and legs. This leads to a reduced filling of the heart resulting in a decrease in blood pressure and syncope (brief loss of consciousness), if reflex regulation of the circulation is impeded. An important mechanism which is activated to protect the circulation is a local reflex in muscle and skin (local veno-arteriolar reflex). This reflex is elicited by the pooling of blood in the legs during orthostatic intolerance. Activation of these local reflexes results in constriction of the small blood vessels in skin and muscle tissue which increase the resistance to blood flow and assists in maintenance of blood pressure during upright posture. After space flight the ability to regulate blood pressure while upright is attenuated, which can severely inhibit the functional cerebral capacity of crewmembers during re-entry and landing. At present there is no effective treatment to prevent spaceflight-induced orthostatic intolerance. The effect of weightlessness on the function of this subcutaneous local vasoconstrictor reflex was investigated by the use of local 133Xenon washout technique that monitors local blood flow. This experiment was performed to investigate whether the local veno-arteriolar reflex is active, attenuated, or absent following exposure to weightlessness.

APPROACH:

During this study, the local veno-arteriolar reflex are activated by lowering the lower leg relative to the heart. Subcutaneous blood flow in the lower leg (133Xenon washout) and arterial blood pressure were measured in the relaxed supine position and during lowering of the leg relative to the heart. The local vascular resistance was calculated by mean arterial pressure divided by the local blood flow.

There were no inflight operations for this experiment. Before and after flight, a small amount of a radioactive isotope, 133Xenon, dissolved in sterile saline solution was injected into the subcutaneous tissue of the outer lower leg (approximately 10 cm above the ankle) of participating crewmembers. The crewmember was instrumented with an Arterial Blood Pressure Measurement Device, and arterial blood pressure was recorded continuously throughout the experiment. This measurement was used to calculate subcutaneous vascular resistance, which helps to regulate arterial blood pressure and prevent orthostatic hypotension (dizziness when standing after an extended period of inactivity). The Xenon Detector Unit was circled slowly over the injection area, while the Xenon Memory Box displayed the counting rate. The position of maximal counting rate was marked with a pen, and the Xenon Detector Unit was secured in place over the marked position. OBJECTIVES:

experiment_title: Human Factors and Habitability Assessment Tool
parameter_html:
Habitability
Performance
investigators: Principal Investigator: Thaxton, SherryCo-Investigator: Litaker, HarryCo-Investigator: Morency, RichardCo-Investigator: Pace, JohnCo-Investigator: Schuh, Susan
experiment_type_lk: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Multiple tools play a role in assessing habitability based on human performance data. Software-based tools provide crewmembers with the opportunity to self-report habitability and human factors observations near real-time. In addition to this capability, software-based tools have the capability to administer a targeted set of questions related to habitability and human factors concerns deemed specifically to be of interest. The targeted use of video provided crewmembers with the opportunity to provide insight into human factors and habitability observations within a habitat or vehicle, with associated training, scheduling, and flow of information to maximize the impact of these videos.

Another major component of this study was the evaluation of space utilization assessment methods. This effort resulted in tools to aid in the design of the next generation of vehicles and habitats. In order to most effectively design layouts of interiors, it is important for designers to understand how space is utilized. This includes details such as the time crewmembers spend at workstations and traffic patterns between workstations. This study examined potential benefits of using automated methods to collect such data. APPROACH:
During NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) 16, four crewmembers used the iPad-based Space Habitability Observation Reporting Tool (iSHORT) daily throughout the 12-day mission, reporting observations ranging from glitches in scheduling software and communications difficulties to concerns about bathroom operations. The iSHORT is an application that allows users to use text, photographs, video, and audio recordings to document positive or negative observations about their environment near real-time. Reports are immediately emailed to the test director and saved locally on the iPad.In addition to providing a database of observations to analyze, there was an opportunity to elicit subjective feedback from the crewmembers. Crewmembers documented their impressions of iSHORT using end-of-mission electronic questionnaires, during post-mission one-on-one debrief, and in some cases elected to use iSHORT itself to document their praises and criticisms during the mission.

RESULTS:
The major accomplishment of this study was successful testing of the iSHORT during NEEMO 16. Testing began during NEEMO 15 but was cut short when inclement weather caused an early termination of the mission. In the interim months, updates to iSHORT were made and test plans were modified based on lessons learned. Overall, iSHORT was highly accepted, and the resulting observations were considered to demonstrate high potential for the tool in an operational setting. The success of iSHORT during the mission led to a plan to assess the feasibility of transitioning iSHORT to operations for the International Space Station (ISS).

In addition to iSHORT, NEEMO 16 crewmembers also provided video clips targeting human factors and habitability issues using a head-worn camera and a standard iPad camera, which enabled the assessment of these strategies for future use. These methods will require further development prior to implementation in an operational environment, but the lessons learned will feed into this process and may also shed light on alternate approaches to collecting this type of data.

experiment_title: A Multipurpose Fruit and Vegetable Processing System for Advanced Life Support
parameter_html:
Electrolyzed oxidizing water
Electrolyzed reducing water
investigators: Principal Investigator: Singh, R.
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The research data on concentrating tomato juice using new generation membranes is valuable for the food industry. Only one Japanese company is currently employing this technique in a food plant located in California. Data s study from this should prove useful for those food processors who are seeking optimization of the process.

APPROACH:
The following tasks were identified in the proposal:
1) Year 1 (January 1, 2003-December 31, 2003): a. Select varieties of tomatoes and other vegetables suitable for processing b. Develop conceptual design for the MFVP c. Develop computer-aided simulations of each operation to assist in design d. Build bench-scale components of the MFVP and conduct preliminary trials for technical feasibility e. Select optimum design parameters f. Select membranes for water cleaning and product recovery.

2) Year 2 (January 1, 2004 – December 31, 2004) a. Construct MFVP from components b. Select membrane systems for concentration of tomato juice c. Conduct trials with MFVP to determine operational feasibility d. Determine ESM and other operational variables e. Conduct optimization trials.
3) Year 3 (January 1, 2005 – December 31, 2005) a. Conduct experimental trials to determine safety, quality and acceptability of foods processed in MFVP b. Develop final modifications as indicated from the experimental data c. Write final project report.

The development of the fruit and vegetable processor represents the first attempt to miniaturize and integrate the array of unit operations required for preparation and processing of fruits and vegetables such as tomato. Additionally, the developers integrate the ESM metric evaluation throughout the development process as the primary project management tool.

RESULTS:
During the one-year no-cost extension, investigators completed the fabrication of the multipurpose fruit and vegetable food processor (MFVP) and the remaining trials with its components. In addition, they conducted a comprehensive study to obtain data on using electrolyzed water for cleaning-in-place (CIP) of the MFVP. CIP with electrolyzed water is an attractive option for cleaning as it does not require detergents (caustic solution) or disinfectants (chlorine). Therefore it could be more suitable for application in a controlled environment system. Electrolyzed water is generated from salt mixed in water. Investigators conducted trials with a stainless steel test-bed containing various components used in the MFVP. The cleaning and disinfection of the components after inoculation was validated with microbial testing. Specifically, the effectiveness of electrolyzed oxidizing water (EOW) and electrolyzed reducing water (ERW) used in clean-in-place (CIP) applications for MFVP were studied using 38 mm (1.5 in) diameter stainless steel (SS316L) pipes fouled with apple juice. Data were compared with industrial CIP cleaner (chlorinated NaOH) and antimicrobial solution (mixture of peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide). Cleanliness of stainless steel (SS) pipe surfaces was quantified by a hygiene monitoring test and aerobic plate count. Data were obtained to determine the removal of organic debris and microorganisms at 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes of washing using electrolyzed water and industrial cleaning chemicals. Electrolyzed water showed potential use in CIP applications, it is easy to use and less hazardous compared to the industrial cleaning chemicals. Microbiological evaluation showed 5 minutes of cleaning with EOW followed by 5 minutes of cleaning with ERW was sufficient to drop cell levels from 5.2±0.3 log CFU (colony forming units)/stainless steel chip to below the limit of detection (<0.69 log CFU/cm2). In contrast, in case of bioluminescence tests, there were detectable ATP even after 15 minutes of cleaning, even though the system was microbiologically at below detection. Furthermore, bioluminescence tests revealed that industrial cleaning chemicals were faster in cleaning compared to electrolyzed water. Electrolyzed water needs to be circulated more than 20 min at 0.6 m/s (2 ft/s) flow velocity to achieve acceptable cleaning. Whereas industrial cleaning takes only 5 minutes of circulation for acceptable cleaning based on the bioluminescence readings.

experiment_type_lk: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Loss of muscle strength and endurance after long exposure to microgravity can interfere with the safe completion of critical tasks during space flight, emergency or routine landing, or during egress. Decreases in leg strength have been documented after Skylab missions as well as after Russian space flights. The objectives of this study were to assess pre flight-to-postflight changes in muscle strength and endurance and to evaluate the effect of in flight exercise on these changes. Changes in muscle performance after missions of shorter or longer duration were compared.

APPROACH:
Muscle performance was tested before and after space flight in 19 astronauts (3 women, 16 men), 10 from 5-day missions and 9 from missions lasting 9 to 11 days. LIDO isokinetic dynamometers were used to measure muscle performance in the back and abdomen and at the knee, ankle, shoulder, and elbow. These dynamometers provide variable resistance so that movements will continue at the same speed (i.e., they are isokinetic) regardless of the force applied. Both concentric and eccentric strength were measured. Concentric strength is the strength of a muscle as it contracts to move a body part, while eccentric strength is the strength of the muscle as it is gradually lengthened while resisting the motion of a body part. Endurance was tested during 25 repetitions of concentric knee flexion and extension.

The eccentric torque maximum was 400 foot pounds. Subjects abstained from food for 2 hours before testing, from caffeine 4 hours before, and from exercise 12 hours before. The dynamometers were calibrated externally and internally (electronically) before each test session. Joint configurations and ranges of motion were recorded for each subject and reproduced for each test session. Testing of the limbs was unilateral with the dominant limb, unless contraindicated. Verbal instructions were consistent and given before each joint test. No verbal encouragement was given during the tests.

Mean results from tests conducted approximately 1, 2, and 3 weeks before launch were compared to results from landing day and from 7 days after landing. Only 17 subjects were tested on landing day. Losses greater than about 9% were considered to be operationally relevant.

Four of the astronauts also performed in flight exercise as part of DSO 476, using a treadmill with a tether system to simulate gravity. They followed continuous or interval exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 60% to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. The percentages of change in their strength and endurance test results were compared with those of 5 astronauts who did not exercise during the flight.

RESULTS:
From before the flight to landing day, large decreases in the strength of the back and abdomen occurred. Strength had decreased by 23% in the concentric tests of the back, 14% in the eccentric tests of the back, and 10% in the concentric tests of the abdomen. The loss in back strength was greater after flights of 9 to 11 days (concentric, 28%; eccentric, 17%) than after flights of 5 days (concentric, 18%; eccentric, 11%). Eccentric abdominal and concentric back strength had recovered significantly 7 days after landing. A significant (12%) decrease in concentric strength of the quadriceps muscle of the thigh was also seen on landing day. No significant loss of strength was seen in the hamstring muscles or in the tests at the ankle, shoulder or elbow, except for a few minor losses that were not considered operationally relevant.

The four astronauts who exercised during flight actually gained eccentric strength of the gastrocnemius muscle of the calf. Although the exercising astronauts lost concentric strength in the quadriceps, the percent change was significantly less than for the four nonexercising astronauts. For the other results of the knee and ankle tests, decreases in strength were generally smaller in those who exercised; although, the differences between exercisers and nonexercisers were not statistically significant. Treadmill exercise did not prevent losses of strength in the back or abdomen. Decrements exhibited by muscles of the five astronauts who did not exercise during flight indicated that muscles are less able to maintain endurance and resist fatigue after space flight. The astronauts who exercised had no loss of endurance.

There was no change in endurance after 5-day flights, but the endurance of the quadriceps decreased after flights of 9 to 11 days. Endurance recovered within 7 days of landing.

These results showed that space flight results in losses of skeletal muscle strength and endurance, and that the losses are greater after flights of longer duration. Strength was lost primarily in the antigravity muscles of the legs and torso. Exercise may prevent losses of muscle strength and endurance.
