OBJECTIVES:
Extravehicular activity (EVA) glove-related injuries are a known problem that some crewmembers experience and others do not. There have been various efforts to evaluate a specific EVA glove, document injuries over a limited time window, or look into a possible mechanism of glove related injury. To date, there is no comprehensive documentation of all EVA glove related injuries and possible injury mechanisms.

APPROACH:
The specific aims of this task were twofold: First, to develop the best current understanding of what glove-related injuries have occurred to date, and when possible, identify the specific mechanisms that caused those injuries. Second, to create a standardized method for comparison of glove injury potential from one glove to another. The type and format of the standard were largely a function of the results of the injury incident analysis and determination of leading factors causing said injury. The specific intent of this standard was to assess the injury potential of gloves delivered as part of the larger High Performance EVA Glove project. This facilitated direct comparison of these and future gloves against each other and against the current Phase VI glove.

RESULTS:
This literature review and data mining study was conducted between 2012 and 2014. The study was bound by events occurring between 1981 and 2010, crossing both the Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) eras. Only US NASA crew were investigated regarding 4000 Series and Phase VI glove models utilized during Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) spacesuit EVA training and flight.

Utilizing both literature and anecdotal causation comments recorded in crewmember injury data, investigators were able to identify several types of risks associated to the 23 types of injuries indicated in the study. These risks can be generalized to force based, task based, environment based, and individually based. A large majority of the risks identified point to force against the body (such as axial or shear loading, sustained and/or constricting forces). Task related risks include those that require exposure to repetitive motions and/or overexertion. Environmental variables also could be causational factors, such as fluid shifting due to microgravity or inverted work, moisture accumulation, or extreme temperatures. Lastly, individual factors such as allergic reactions to chemicals or material can act as an injury factor. As force related and task related variables were not assessed by this study, further future work assessing and quantifying these risks will need to be performed. With that, there were many significant findings as a result of this study. These key findings were divided into three primary categories:

1. Glove Injury Descriptive Statistics
2. Glove Injury Reporting Methods
3. Glove Injury Risk Causation Analysis

Glove Injury Descriptive Statistics
1. EVAs were performed by 96 crewmembers during the 322 EVAs that occurred through the investigation period of 1981 to 2010. There was a report of at least one injury during 96 (29.8%) of these 322 EVAs. Further, 50 of the 96 crewmembers (52.1%) who participated in an EVA reported at least one injury.

2. Most reported injuries were from only 1-2 individual incidents. This may indicate that most reported injuries were not chronic or cumulative problems with frequent recurrence, but due to injury data recording inconsistencies over time; there is not enough evidence available to support that chronic/cumulative injury is or is not a considerable risk. Future follow-up correlation studies will need to be performed to confirm this.

3. Injury types reported differed between training and flight exposures. This could be due to actual differences between the exposure events, but more likely indicates a need for standard injury type nomenclature and reporting timeframes.

4. Training injury locations were most commonly reported at the fingernail, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, or finger crotch with pain, erythema (redness), and onycholysis the most common reported injuries.

5. EVA flight injury locations were most commonly reported at the hand, MCP joint, or finger with fatigue, abrasion, and paresthesia the most commonly reported injuries.

Glove Injury Reporting Methods
1. Injuries were tracked with different methods over time. Moving forward, there needs to be one standard approach to reporting all suit related injuries regardless of exposure type (EVA flight or training) or suit/glove model.

2. Terms used to describe the injury types were not standardized. Investigators had to group injuries into one large category, and other than onycholysis, no other injury type was investigated separately. Future work should look to investigate other specific injury types.

3. Body part locations were inconsistently labeled, and oftentimes reports were too general citing only the hand or finger as the injury location. Standardized locations including specific finger, joint, or crotch should be used for glove related injuries.

4. There was no use of an injury severity scale for recorded injuries. Without severity information, all injuries had to be treated with equal severity. Also, there was limited information on the duration or persistence of an injury, therefore, investigators could not estimate a severity scale.

5. Suit sizing information was not available consistently per exposure. If engineering design solutions are to be used to mitigate glove related injury, then a record of relevant suit and glove sizing metrics needs to be included with every EVA training or flight event.

6. Injury data were stored in multiple databases and had to be consolidated. If it is to be studied as an occupational exposure, suit related injury data should be clearly identified from other medical data in a crewmember's medical record. In addition to currently implemented countermeasures, suit related injuries should be mitigated using engineering and operational controls wherever possible.

Glove Injury Risk Causation Analysis
1. Likelihood of reporting an injury during training was related to handedness, glove model, duration of the training event, and whether the training occurred in the years 2002-2004. Ergonomic task analysis including an evaluation of handedness bias in EVA training classes should be considered. Also, since many of the training event durations were estimated, this should be rectified with an exact recording of suited exposure duration. While this is specific to training, EVA flight recording should also be treated the same.

2. Likelihood of reporting an injury during inflight EVA was related only to the Anthropometric Principal Component 1 (hand size). This indicates that crew with smaller hand anthropometry were at higher risk for reporting an injury. While there are no clear recommendations from this finding, it supports general recommendations for optimizing fit and possibly controlling for and reducing hand intensive tasks and EVA durations for crew with smaller hand anthropometry.

3. Likelihood of reporting an injury earlier in career during training increased with Anthropometric Principal Component 1 (hand size), duration of the training event, and the delta between glove size and anthropometry for middle finger length and decreased with higher age and total number of prior events. Of all of these factors, the most striking finding was how the delta between glove size and middle finger length increased the risk early in a career. This indicates the need to optimize glove sizing as soon as possible in a crewmember's career and to not substitute a poorly fitted glove.

4. Likelihood of reporting an injury earlier in career during inflight EVA increased with exposure event duration and the delta between glove size and middle finger length. Again, this points towards shorter exposures decreasing risk and the need to optimize glove sizing early in a crewmember's career.

5. Likelihood of reporting an onycholysis (fingernail delamination) injury increased with age, duration of the training or EVA event, delta between glove size and middle finger length, and being female. This again points to the need for shorter exposures and optimal glove sizing.

6. Likelihood of reporting a onycholysis injury earlier in one’s career increased with Anthropometric Principal Component 1 (hand size), duration of training or EVA event, and the delta between glove size and middle finger length. In this case, it was the larger handed crewmembers who reported injury earlier, but it still points to shorter exposure and optimal glove fit as important controls.

7. Another interesting find was specific to glove model, indicating that Phase VI gloves could possibly influence the likelihood of developing onycholysis specific injuries versus wearing the 4000 Series glove. To note, there were changes made to the design of the EMU vent tube length where the vent tube was reduced from the wrist to the upper arm around the same time period as the Phase VI implementation. This may contribute in some way to glove related environmental changes in the EVA glove. Additionally, a separate unpublished NASA 2014 Glove Sensor Feasibility study noted that there may be a possible difference between the glove models in how much force is transmitted to the fingertips and fingernails (with the 4000 Series showing lower levels). Further investigation is needed to confirm these results though.

8. A previous study by Opperman et al. (2010) found an increased risk of onycholysis injury with greater hand circumference. Substituting hand circumference for Anthropometric Principal Component 1 in any of the statistical analyses found hand circumference to be a non-significant factor.

Future Work
1. NASA should implement a suited injury data collection standard across all EVA training and flight to allow for future causation analysis studies. This data collection standard should clearly define injury, assess severity, and elucidate recurrence/chronicity. A prospective pilot phase of this project would allow for validation of the findings of this current research. Specific follow-up studies can refine the risk quantities to allow for more specific risk thresholds for glove size, age, event exposure time, and event exposure frequency. Additionally, this will also allow for investigators to better assess the acute versus cumulative risk towards these injuries.

2. Additional quantification of the cause-effect risk factors outside of this data mining study, such as those specific to the environment in the glove (forces on the body, moisture, temperature, etc.), should be examined to determine how they contribute to injury. These studies will help understand the glove environment as it relates to injury; this understanding could help provide better operational controls and lead to improved designs for the EVA glove.

3. Approximately 3,000 pages of suit fit and glove fit comments were received. Due to the enormity of the data received, the team was unable to assess these thoroughly in the timeframe allowed by the project. Potentially, additional risk factor data and injury information may be derived from these comments. As these records were mainly provided in a non-queriable format, these comments should be digitized and assessed towards injury risk in a follow-up study.

experiment_title: High Performance TiO2 Photocatalytic Coatings and Membranes for the Purification, Disinfection and Recycle of Water and Air in Space Applications
parameter_html:
Air purification system
Water purification system
investigators: Principal Investigator: Dionysiou, Dionysios
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study deals with the application of novel methods for the fabrication of robust nanostructured TiO2 photocatalytic films for the development of efficient water and air purification systems for advanced life support in space missions and terrestrial applications. The catalytic films immobilized on a variety of ceramic, metallic, and composite substrates was used to fabricate reactors and membrane systems that posed unique pore orchestration for the effective capture of incident radiation, enhanced photocatalytic activity, excellent adhesive properties, good mechanical stability, controlled hydrophilicity, and anti-biological fouling capability. These immobilized films were the crucial component for the fabrication of integrated photocatalytic-disinfection-antifoulant reactors and membranes for the room-temperature production of clean potable and hygienic water in space missions as well as for the purification of water in terrestrial applications. Alternatively, these methods were used for the fabrication of immobilized TiO2 films aiming at the preparation of surfaces possessing self-cleaning, disinfecting, and anti-biofouling properties for air purification. These purification systems can be used as stand-alone technologies or as supplementary and complementary to existing treatment technologies. In addition, they can serve as back-up processes or as a means of emergency-respond technologies to chemical and biological terrorism.

This research is considered as an important task within the scope to develop high performance photocatalytic coatings for water purification. The completion of the tasks and objectives is crucial for the fabrication of highly efficient robust integrated advanced oxidation reactors for the purification, disinfection, and recycle of water in space missions.

APPROACH:
The investigators applied a novel fabrication procedure for the preparation of high performance TiO2 films immobilized on non-porous stainless steel substrates. The procedure concerns a novel combination of the alkoxide sol-gel and the colloidal suspension (Degussa P-25) preparation routes for the synthesis of the catalyst. They optimized the P-25 concentration and calcination temperature for enhanced photocatalytic activity and good mechanical stability. The purpose of this research is to better understand the relationship of surface microstructure and film composition and their effect on the photocatalytic activity of the films. After the optimization of the modified sol-gel procedure, they evaluated the photocatalytic activity of these films for the degradation of target contaminants. Their goal is to optimize the conditions for the destruction and mineralization of these compounds with prepared TiO2 photocatalyst and to identify any inhibition factors. Another goal is the design of a new reactor with higher surface area per unit liquid volume treated, increased photocatalytic activity, and better optimization for efficient utilization of UV radiation. In addition, they applied novel nanofabrication and self-assembling procedures to prepare highly porous nanostructured photocatalytic TiO2 particles, films immobilized on nonporous glass substrates, and membranes incorporated onto porous alumina membrane supports. The objective for this task is to use self-assembling modified sol-gel methods for the fabrication of TiO2 thin films of controlled intraparticle (framework) and interparticle (textural) porosity to be used on top of non-porous or porous supports. In the latter case (i.e., porous supports), the method is used for the fabrication of nanocomposite TiO2-ceramic membranes with tailor-designed pore size (mesoporous, 1-50 nm), improved photocatalytic properties, and enhanced mechanical stability.

RESULTS:
The results obtained in this work are promising and are expected to be of high interest to NASA, the scientific community, and many relevant industries for the development of sustainable photocatalytic reactors as well as for the development of coatings with task-specific applications. The good structural properties and enhanced catalytic activities of the prepared TiO2 materials are important requirements for the fabrication of sustainable photocatalytic reactors for water and air purification. The tunable hydrophilic properties of these coatings are also of interest to other industries dealing with special glass fabrication, automotive industry (i.e., completely wetable surfaces), indoor air disinfection and purification.

In addition to physical research activities, the project provided valuable opportunities to graduate, undergraduate, and high school students. The students had an opportunity to learn novel procedures for the fabrication of nanostructured TiO2 films and membranes and exchange valuable experience and knowledge in the area of materials synthesis and their environmental applications. The students involved in this project also had an opportunity to develop their analytical skills for the detection of primary compounds and their secondary metabolites. In addition, they enhanced their understanding for the reactivity of hydroxyl radicals and the degradation routes that these active species follow. Students in the Environmental Science and Engineering program at the University of Cincinnati also had the opportunity to learn current issues in the field of nanotechnology and became familiar with the synthesis, characterization, and environmental applications and implications of nanomaterials. Dr. Dionysiou and his group also promoted awareness on the health threat of environmental pollution in water and wastewater as well as the importance of environmental preservation to people, including public and environmental affairs around the Cincinnati regional area. In order to disseminate the importance of nanotechnology in the area of environmental remediation to colleagues, public, and communities, Dr. Dionysiou and his students presented their research findings on the degradation of hazardous organic contaminants using TiO2 photocatalytic films and membranes at several regional, national, and international conferences and meetings and they were acknowledged with several awards, fellowships, and scholarships. Finally, Dr. Dionysiou’s collaboration with other national and international universities, and the US Environmental Protection Agency expanded the opportunities for advanced and international level research.

image_name: D-1 Astronaut Wearing the Accelerometer Recording Unit (ARU)
D-1 Crewmembers with the Vestibular Sled Equipment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Human spatial orientation normally relies upon signals from the inner ear to indicate the vertical position. During the exposure to microgravity this process undergoes adaptive changes. The D-1 investigation extended a previous experiment flown on Spacelab-1 (STS-9) by use of linear acceleration stimuli using the ESA Vestibular Sled, and visual stimuli provided by the Rotating Dome apparatus.

APPROACH:
The Sled is a rail-mounted linear acceleration sled, used to accelerate subjects along a track in the lateral upright (Y-axis) and longitudinal supine (Z-axis) orientations. The sled consists of a chair with an attached head restraint. The chair is mounted on a cart which is guided along two rails and pulled by a cable. The total travel distance is 3.2 meters. Different sinusoidal and constant acceleration motion profiles, ranging from 0.001-G to 0.2-G, can be chosen. The head restraint is equipped with a visor-helmet to blind the test subject to avoid visual cues.

The test protocol included measurements of the ability to detect small linear acceleration steps, perceive motion path, and the performance of the closed loop otolith assessment test (CLOAT). During the D-1 mission the first two protocols were performed preflight, inflight on the first and sixth day of the seven day mission, and postflight 1, 2, and 10 days after landing. The CLOAT task was performed pre- and postflight only.

The ability to detect near-threshold acceleration steps was measured by the time delay between the motion-stimulus and the subjective response. Thirteen different acceleration profiles, ranging from 0.001-G to 0.08-G were presented in a random order, one for each acceleration level. The subject was instructed to indicate the direction of subjective acceleration using a hand-held joystick. The time delay between actual and indicated change in acceleration was measured as the time-to-detect. Tests were valued as incorrect responses when the subject indicated acceleration in the opposite direction than the actual movement, or when the subject did not respond at all. Electrooculography (EOG) was used to measure lateral and vertical eye movements in response to both lateral (Y-axis) and longitudinal (Z-axis) sinusoidal accelerations. Ocular torsion (rotations about the visual axis) was measured during sinusoidal accelerations (rotation between 0.2 and 0.8 Hertz, 0.2-G) using a photographic technique.

The CLOAT task was performed only pre- and postflight using the U.S. Laboratory Sled, which was conceptually and functionally similar to the ESA sled, but performed under 1-G conditions. It allowed controlled acceleration up to 0.7-G with a useable track length of 4.7 meters. During the CLOAT test the subject was in control of the sled velocity using a joystick. A disturbance motion was generated and the subject was asked to try to nullify the disturbance motion and hold the cart still. The CLOAT test was performed once with open eyes and three times with eyes closed for each test session. The results of the sled velocity profiles of the three darkened runs were averaged for analysis.

experiment_title: Factors Modulating Radiation-Induced G2 Delays
parameter_html: Radiation dose
investigators: Principal Investigator: Iliakis, George
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The progression of cells through the cell cycle is maintained by control mechanisms that operate through the activation of checkpoints at defined positions. Feedback controls detect any failure to complete DNA replication, DNA repair, or spindle assembly, and arrest further progression of cells through the cell cycle until proper completion of the event occurs. Delays in the cycle often occur following exposure to ionizing radiation and correspond to activation of specific checkpoints in the phases of G1, S, and G2. The delays may reduce adverse effects of radiation by allowing repairs to occur. Since delays in G1 and G2 are longer than those of S, G1 and G2 are suitable targets in development of strategies to modulate cell sensitivity to radiation.

Compounds such as caffeine can reduce radiation-induced delay in G2, but, to date, no compounds can increase the duration of the G2 delay. Increasing this delay may protect against radiation by allowing cells to repair. Since hypothetical compounds that increase delay may act by enhancing repair, they could be useful when administered after radiation exposure, because repair requires hours for completion.

Biological cells produce many compounds that affect their own function and the function of surrounding cells. Some of these compounds are secreted into the extracellular environment, and when cells are grown in culture, the compounds are secreted into the growth medium creating conditioned medium. Some mammalian cells have been found to produce factors with G2-Arrest Modulating Activity (GAMA). The goal of this study was to characterize and define the effects of these factors. The hypothesis was that GAMA acts as a radioprotector by promoting repair in irradiated cells and could be applied as radiation protection for humans in space. The aims of the study were to demonstrate the production and excretion of GAMA by mammalian cells, standardize production conditions, and characterize the biological properties of GAMA.

The method by which cells produce GAMA, and the characterization of its genes and receptors are worthy of study. The effects of GAMA on cell survival and mutation induction are also of interest. GAMA and other substances with similar action could be developed for use against not only the early and late effects of radiation, but also cancer development and damage to the central nervous system.

APPROACH:
Two main cell lines were used to demonstrate the production of GAMA and its properties. The A1-5 cell line consisted of rat embryo fibroblasts containing a mouse p53 mutant and activated ras oncogene. The p53 protein was temperature sensitive and had an altered shape at 39.5°C. An antibody that could bind normal p53 was able to bind the mutant at 32.5°C but not at 39.5°C. The cells containing the p53 mutant grew at 37°C but stopped replication and arrested at the G1 checkpoint in the cell cycle when subjected to 32.5°C. The cells were subcloned to obtain a cell line displaying a single G1 peak in flow cytometry.

The T101-4 cell line was made from primary rat embryo fibroblasts with a different mutation of mouse p53 and the same ras oncogene. This mutation of p53 did not bind to the same antibody used to bind the temperature-sensitive p53.

Cells were grown under standard conditions in large volumes to prepare material for testing the presence and effects of GAMA. One million cells were grown for four days in twenty milliliters of complete growth medium. The distribution of cells in the various phases of the cell cycle was monitored by flow cytometry. Other cell lines, in addition to A1-5 and T101-4, were also used to test the effects of GAMA and their ability to produce GAMA.

A Siemens therapeutic X-ray machine operated at 250 kV, 15 mA with a 2mm Al filter was used for irradiations. The dose rate at a 50 cm irradiation distance was 2 Gray per minute and the effective photon energy about 70 keV. Dosimetry was performed with a Victoreen dosimeter.

Three different filters with pores that retained molecules larger than 10 kilodaltons (kD), 5 kD, and 1 kD were used to investigate the size of GAMA. To test whether GAMA was a peptide, proteases were incubated with aliquots of the 10kD ultrafiltrate containing GAMA. This medium was incubated with 0.25% trypsin for two hours at 37°C, then neutralized with serum. The medium was also incubated overnight at 37°C with Proteinase K, a protease with less specificity than trypsin. The first attempts for the purification of GAMA used a Biocad station. Western blotting was used for further protein analysis.

Induction and rejoining of radiation-induced DNA double strand breaks were measured using asymmetric field inversion gel electrophoresis. Such double strand breaks are thought to be severe lesions that, if unrepaired or misrepaired, would lead to cell death.

To show that a G2 delay was not a result of a lethal accumulation of cells in G2, the effect of caffeine was observed. Caffeine sensitizes cells to radiation and reduces the duration of G2. If an accumulation of cells in G2 was due to a genuine G2 arrest, caffeine should reduce the duration. If the accumulation of cells was due to non-specific, cell-line-related artifacts, caffeine should only have a minimal effect. Staurosporine, also known to affect cell radiosensitivity and G2 arrest, was used to bolster findings obtained from the caffeine test.

Experiments with heavy ions as the radiation source were conducted because high Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation effects are important to NASA. Exponentially growing A1-5 and T101-4 cells were exposed to various doses of 1 GeV/A Fe ions and growth was followed for 36 hours by cell counting. Cells were collected and fixed in ethanol to study progression through the cell cycle by flow cytometry. The role of caffeine and staurosporine was also investigated.

RESULTS:
A1-5 cells were more radioresistant than the control T101-4 cells. The difference was among the largest observed with cell lines generated after transfection of primary rat embryo fibroblasts with oncogenes or anti-oncogenes of different families. Both cell lines demonstrated similar yields of radiation-induced DNA double strand breaks, severe damage that could lead to cell death. Rejoining was also similar in the two cell lines suggesting a similar capacity in repairing this type of damage. The incidence of misrepair was not a factor in the discrepancy since progression from G1 into S after radiation was similar between both cell lines.

A moderate increase of radiation-induced inhibition of DNA replication in A1-5 cells compared to T101-4 cells was observed. However, dramatic differences in radiation-induced delay in G2 between the two cell lines were observed. T101-4 cells showed a modest accumulation of cells in G2 that increased with increased radiation dose. However, A1-5 cells were found to give a much longer delay in G2 with more than 70% of cells accumulated in G2 after exposure to 6 Gray. Cell division did not occur for up to thirty hours after irradiation. A two millimolar solution of caffeine caused a substantial reduction in the accumulation of A1-5 cells in G2, suggesting a genuine G2 arrest and not a lethal accumulation of cells in G2. A reduction was also observed in the duration of G2 arrest in T101-4 cells but was modest when compared to that of A1-5 cells. Staurosporine confirmed the findings observed from caffeine. There is strong indication that A1-5 cells undergo a genuine long, radiation-induced G2 arrest.

Observations from varied experiments indicated that G2 arrest was modulated in A1-5 cells by a factor produced by the cells and excreted into the growth medium. Duration of the G2 arrest was shorter when cells were at a lower density before radiation and a growth medium change a few hours before irradiation significantly reduced the duration of the delay. A change of medium after irradiaton also reduced the duration of the G2 arrest. Radiation caused the accumulation of cells in G2 that persisted for over forty hours but cells that underwent a medium change at the peak of the G2 accumulation started dividing a few hours later. Thus, GAMA was present in the conditioned medium of non-irradiated cells. The G2 arrest could be reverted by transferring the cells to fresh medium, thus removing GAMA. GAMA was present in the conditioned medium of cultures grown for four days starting at a concentration of one million cells per dish. The concentration of GAMA in cultures of A1-5 cells grown for thirty hours starting from 100,000 cells per dish was not high enough to modulate G2 arrest, unlike what was observed with cells grown for 30 hours starting from 250,000 cells per dish.

GAMA was estimated to have a molecular weight of 1 kD after conditioned medium was filtered through 10 kD, 3 kD and 1 kD filters. Cells that were incubated in fresh medium supplemented with the material left in the 10 kD and 3 kD filters displayed G2 accumulation kinetics similar to that with only fresh medium. Cells transferred to the filtrate displayed a G2 arrest similar to that of cells kept in conditioned medium. GAMA passed through the 10 kD and 3 kD filters and was present in the ultrafiltrate and, thus, was smaller than 3 kD. A reduced effect was observed with the 1 kD molecular weight cutoff suggesting that GAMA is partially retained by this filter. Dialysis experiments produced similar results and confirmed that GAMA is of a low molecular weight.

Further testing indicated that GAMA is stable in heat. When the conditioned medium was exposed to 56°C for an hour, its ability to arrest cells in G2 was not altered. GAMA was proven to be a peptide when exposure to the protease trypsin resulted in a shorter G2 delay. Researchers expected that a less specific protease would have a more dramatic effect on GAMA activity, and, indeed, the Proteinase K experiment showed a dramatically reduced ability to arrest cells in G2.

GAMA was produced in a variety of cell lines other than A1-5. Conditioned medium from these other cells showed a significant ability to retain the irradiated A1-5 cells in G2. Not all cell lines can utilize GAMA to arrest in G2 after irradiation. Conditioned medium from cell lines that produce GAMA was unable to arrest irradiated T101-4 and other cells in G2. An intermediate response was found from cells containing a defect in a protein that causes a defect in the rejoining of DNA double strand breaks. Thus, GAMA must act via a receptor that must also be present for GAMA to exert its G2 arrest modulating activity.

Some conclusions stemmed from the experiments with irradiated cells. Several cell lines produced low molecular weight stable peptides, which had the potential of modulating radiation-induced cell cycle checkpoints. Response to the factors likely required the presence of appropriate receptors in the cells; more cells produced the factors than responded to them. The factors were likely to be active after exposure to low as well as to high LET radiation. Characterization of a compound that prolonged G2-arrest and possibly protected cells from radiation defined a new class of radioprotectors with direct application in radiation protection. Since the compound was made by cells, it was expected to be of limited toxicity in the normal range of concentrations. There may be application in radiation protection during space exploration. Because the compound was expected to act by modulating repair, it could be taken shortly after radiation exposure, as soon as radiation monitors in space register increased cosmic ray activity.

Results from this study indicate the possibility of developing countermeasures to unwanted exposures of radiation by promoting repair processes. Compounds like GAMA may mitigate early or acute radiation exposure and mitigate the carcinogenic effects of radiation. They may also help mitigate damage to the central nervous system from radiation.

Thus, GAMA must act via a receptor that must also be present for GAMA to exert its G2 arrest modulating activity.

Some conclusions stemmed from the experiments with irradiated cells. Several cell lines produced low molecular weight stable peptides, which had the potential of modulating radiation-induced cell cycle checkpoints. Response to the factors likely required the presence of appropriate receptors in the cells; more cells produced the factors than responded to them. The factors were likely to be active after exposure to low as well as to high LET radiation. Characterization of a compound that prolonged G2-arrest and possibly protected cells from radiation defined a new class of radioprotectors with direct application in radiation protection. Since the compound was made by cells, it was expected to be of limited toxicity in the normal range of concentrations. There may be application in radiation protection during space exploration. Because the compound was expected to act by modulating repair, it could be taken shortly after radiation exposure, as soon as radiation monitors in space register increased cosmic ray activity.

Results from this study indicate the possibility of developing countermeasures to unwanted exposures of radiation by promoting repair processes. Compounds like GAMA may mitigate early or acute radiation exposure and mitigate the carcinogenic effects of radiation. They may also help mitigate damage to the central nervous system from radiation.

experiment_title: Dark Focus In-house Study
parameter_html:
Acuity
Diopters
investigators: Principal Investigator: Harm, DeborahCo-Investigator: Kennedy, Robert
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVE:
The definition of dark focus is the resting state of visual accommodation is that refractive state to which the eye tends to return in the absence of any visual stimulus, as in complete darkness. Seven healthy in-house subjects (4 males; 3 females), ranging in age from 27 - 55 years old, participated in this study.

Neurobiological research indicates that changes in visual accommodation are associated with stresses that may occur during space mission. Measures of accommodation may be used to index onset and extent of space motion sickness and other stress of spacelfith. An accurate measure of accommodation may be used to signal that visual performances may be degraded.

APPROACH:
To participate in the study, the subjects were not asked to alter their normal daily routine. Prior to each test session, the subjects completed a short questionnaire that documented their recent pre-test activities. All subjects reported that they were in their usual state of fitness, and that they had a sufficient amount of sleep within the last 24 hours. Although caffeine consumption was not specifically controlled, subjects reported having three of fewer cups of coffee throughout an entire 24 hour period on test days. Six of the seven subjects were nonsmokers, and the 1 subject who was a smoker routinely smoked 2-3 cigars each morning. On average, each subject had sat in front of a video display terminal 1-2 hours prior to each test session. Only 1 subject required glasses for corrected vision, and did wear corrective lenses when performing the test.

Measurements of dark focus were made twice daily, in the morning and afternoon, on four consecutive days. The test sessions were scheduled for approximately the same time of day for each subject across the four days. During each test session, three measurements of dark focus were made in a dark room. The subject was instructed to look in to he Dark-focus Measuring Device (DFMC) using his/her dominant eye while keeping the other eye closed. Sliding the focus adjustment rod back and forth, the subject adjusted the focus of the fiberoptic light until a sharply focused light image appeared. The subjects was instructed to close his/her eyes while the operator recorded the measurement of the dark focus then offset the focus of the fiberoptic light by sliding the focus adjustment rod prior to repeating the test procedure two times for a total of 3 measurements.

RESULTS:
Results are not available for this study.

experiment_title: Methods for the Assessment of Gastrointestinal Physiology and Function in a Lunar Analog Environment
parameter_html:
Antrum pressure contraction patterns
Body temperature
Duodenum pressure contraction patterns
GI transit time
Large-bowel transit time
pH
Small-bowel transit time
Total transit time
investigators: Principal Investigator: Putcha, Lakshmi
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The overall goal of this research is to examine the effects of microgravity analog environments on gastrointestinal (GI) physiology. The specific objective of this modified protocol was to conduct a feasibility study to examine and validate new technology, SmartPill® as a tool to assess the effect of head-down tilt (HDT), the lunar bed rest analog on GI physiology. This test was conducted to investigate the usefulness of this technology for estimating GI motility decrements in a reduced-gravity simulation environment.

This study was conducted at the Flight Analogs Research Unit (FARU) located at The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) in Galveston, Texas. Subjects were recruited, screened, and, if approved, placed in a bed rest facility for testing and data collection during 13 days of ambulatory acclimation, 30 days of 6-degree HDT bed rest, and 14 days of ambulatory recovery.

APPROACH:
SmartPill® is an ingestible wireless capsule that measures pressure, pH, and temperature as it transits the GI tract. This information was used to provide gastric emptying time, combined small and large-bowel transit time, total transit time, pressure contraction patterns from the antrum and duodenum, and motility indices.

Four male and four female subjects completed the experimental protocol once before, twice during, and once after HDT bed rest. Before administration of the capsule, subjects wore a belt with a battery operated SmartPill® data receiver. The data receiver remained on the subject until the capsule stopped transmitting either due to its excretion from the body or termination of battery power, whichever occurred first. After ingestion, the capsule traveled through the intestines by peristalsis and transmitted data continuously for up to 96 hours. All pertinent data transmitted by the SmartPill® was stored on the data receiver and downloaded to a laptop computer after each data collection session was completed. The data from each session was compiled and analyzed using standard statistical programs (e.g. ANOVA) of analysis.

RESULTS:
Results of this technology feasibility study will aid in the validation of a noninvasive diagnostic test for GI physio-pathology associated with space flight environmental conditions. The anticipated outcome will facilitate the identification of prospective changes in GI function leading to a reduction in drug absorption associated with microgravity.

This experiment has concluded. Results will be available once the investigator publishes her findings.

experiment_title: Effects of Chronic and Single-Dose Charged Particle Exposure on Cardiac Function and Structure in Multiple Animal Models
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Boerma, Marjan
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Recent evidence suggests that exposure to high-linear energy transfer (LET) radiation encountered during deep space travel may be associated with short- or long-term risks of cardiovascular disease. However, these risks are not well defined, and potential gender differences are unknown. We have shown that exposure of male mice to low-dose oxygen ions causes small but significant changes in cardiac function and that both protons and oxygen ions cause dose-dependent increases in the markers of inflammatory cells in the heart. While these studies have started to characterize the effects of low-dose charged particles on cardiac function and structure in the male mouse, the dose rates in these studies were relatively high compared to chronic low-dose rate exposures in space. Therefore, additional work needs to be done in animals chronically exposed to low-dose rate charged particle irradiation. Moreover, the inclusion of additional animal species will greatly enhance the potential for translation of the results into humans compared to research in mouse models alone. Here, we aim to provide insight into the effects of chronic low-dose rate high-LET radiation exposures on the heart and identify how animal species differ in their response to high-LET radiation, addressing the Risk of Cardiovascular Disease and Other Degenerative Tissue Effects from Radiation Exposure and assisting in closure of the Gaps Degen – 1, Degen – 2, and Degen – 3.

We pursue three experiments: 1) In collaboration with the Colorado State University Specialized Center of Research on Carcinogenesis, we make use of its long-term studies in male and female mouse models exposed to chronic low-dose rate neutrons to assess cardiac function with echocardiography, and we collect and analyze cardiac tissues obtained from these mice; 2) We perform echocardiography and tissue analysis in rats that are exposed to low-dose rate neutrons in the neutron facility that is part of the Specialized Center of Research on Carcinogenesis; and 3) We assess markers of inflammatory infiltration and mitochondrial morphology and function in cardiac tissue samples of rats and rabbits that had received acute exposures to protons and oxygen ions as part of the Center for Space Radiation Research. These experiments make use of existing animals and tissue samples to aid in defining the risk of cardiovascular disease from space radiation exposure.

APPROACH:
These studies aim to characterize the risk of degenerative cardiovascular disease of space radiation, by comparing the effects of exposure to low-dose protons, oxygen ions, and low-dose rate neutrons in mouse, rat, and rabbit models. Experiment 1 makes of female BALB/c mice and male C3H mice. As part of the Colorado State University (CSU) Specialized Center of Research on Carcinogenesis large cohorts of mice are exposed to low-dose rate or high-dose neutrons, starting at the age of 100-120 days, to a total dose of 0.1 Gy, 0.2 Gy, and 0.4 Gy. Subgroups of mice receive aspirin in the drinking water as a potential countermeasure against adverse radiation effects. At the age of 500 days, 10 mice of each experimental group are anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation, and an ultrasound scan of the heart is obtained. At the age of 800 days, this procedure is performed once more. All animals are euthanized at the age of 800 days, and heart tissue collected for histology and western-blot analysis of markers of inflammatory infiltration and mitochondrial function.

For experiment 2, a total of 10 male Long Evans rats are exposed to low-dose rate neutrons in the same chronic neutron facility, starting at the age of 100-120 days, to a total dose of 0.4 Gy. A total of 10 rats receive sham-irradiation. At the age of 500 days, the rats are anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation, and an ultrasound scan of the heart is obtained. At the age of 800 days, this procedure is performed once more. All animals are euthanized at the age of 800 days, and heart tissue collected for histology and western-blot analysis of markers of inflammatory infiltration and mitochondrial function.

For experiment 3, tissues have been obtained from male Long Evans rats and male New Zealand White rabbits that were exposed to oxygen ions (600 MeV/n, 0.08-0.11 Gy/min tot a total dose of 0.5 Gy), protons (250 MeV, 0.10-0.12 Gy/min to a total dose of 0.5 Gy), or sham treatment at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (9-11 animals per group) and were followed to 12 months after irradiation. Specimens of left ventricle are used for western-blots to quantify protein markers of leukocytes, T-cells, monocytes/macrophages, extracellular matrix, mitochondrial fission/fusion, and mitochondrial enzyme levels.

RESULTS:
Upon re-evaluation of neutron doses delivered to the mice, it was determined that the lowest radiation dose was 0.12 Gy (instead of the scheduled 0.1 Gy). The other neutron radiation doses were delivered as originally indicated. Progress of analysis of animals and tissue samples was excellent, as outlined below for each Specific Aim.
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.

experiment_title: Preflight and Postflight Parallel Swing Tests
parameter_html:
Eye movements
Horizontal nystagmus
Linear translation
Otolith receptors
Otolith signals
Roll translation
investigators: Principal Investigator: Reschke, MillardPrincipal Investigator: Parker, Donald
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An otolith is a structure in the inner ear, specifically in the vestibular labyrinth. They are sensitive to gravity and linear acceleration. The vestibular otolith receptors respond to linear motion and gravity. If motion cues from visual and skin receptors were reduced or eliminated, responses to roll and linear translation attributable primarily to the otolith receptors could be examined. The Miami University Parallel Swing and its associated restraint system made this examination possible. This investigation examined two types of responses associated with roll and linear translation stimulation: perceived self-motion path and eye movements. These responses were examined before and after orbital flight. Because the otoliths are gravity receptors, it was hypothesized that adaptation to the loss of stimulation due to gravity during flight would alter responses to which the otoliths contribute.

This investigation assessed changes in responses associated with otolith receptor activity following prolonged space flight. The results led to the development of an otolith tilt translation reinterpretation hypothesis which, in conjunction with the sensory conflict hypothesis, provides a conceptual framework for comprehending space motion sickness.

APPROACH:
On STS-8, a subject performed head tilts (roll and pitch) and followed a self-motion reporting procedure. On STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11), two subjects repeated the STS-8 protocol, and examined the hypothesis that the brain's reinterpretation of otolith information would affect eye movement reflexes. The STS-41B subjects were exposed to the same motion stimuli as on STS-8 and reported their self-motion in the same manner. In addition, their eye movements were recorded in the dark using an infrared-sensitive video camera.

A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. Ocular counterrolling during static head tilt was recorded preflight and immediately postflight.

RESULTS:
STS-8: This investigation obtained data from one subject. The results indicated that prolonged exposure to weightlessness resulted in reinterpretation by the brain of signals from the otolith organs. The subject was exposed to roll around the head (X axis) and linear translation along the head (Y axis). The subject reported self-motion perception following exposure to the two types of motion. Preflight, the subject's self-motion reports corresponded with the actual motion; roll was perceived as roll and translation as translation. Immediately postflight, the self-motion sensation associated with roll differed dramatically from that reported preflight. At R+2.5 hours, roll motion was perceived primarily as linear translation along the Y axis. At R+36 hours, self-motion sensations were approximately the same as those observed preflight.

The STS-8 observations led to the following hypothesis: During prolonged weightlessness, the adaptive brain learns to interpret all signals from the otolith linear accelerometer as linear translation. In weightlessness, the otoliths do not produce a signal indicating head tilt (roll or pitch) because linear acceleration due to gravity is absent. Following return to earth, and before the brain re-adapts, the interpretation that all otolith signals indicate is that linear motion persists. However, the otoliths produce a signal during head tilt (roll) because gravity is present. Consequently, the observer reports that roll motion is perceived as linear translation plus a roll component due to the semicircular canals. Following re-adaptation to normal gravity, true perception of roll motion returns.

STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11): Preflight and postflight self-motion reports following roll and linear translation were nearly the same as those reported on STS-8. Eye movements recorded preflight indicated that the linear translation stimulus produced nearly pure horizontal translation of the eyeball, and that roll stimuli produced nearly pure ocular counterrolling (eye torsion). Immediately postflight, the eye movements differed dramatically from those seen preflight. For one subject, who was seen at R+70 minutes, both roll and linear motion stimulation produced horizontal translation of the eyeball. For the second subject, seen at R+2 hours, roll stimulation produced horizontal eye movements in combination with a small amount of torsion. Self-motion reports indicated that roll was perceived as a combination of linear translation and roll. The roll component of the perceptual report was probably due to semicircular canal stimulation. At R+2 days, both subjects' self-motion reports had returned to the preflight state. However, some horizontal eye movement was still present. By R+3 days, both perceptual reports and eye movement were approximately the same as preflight.

In conclusion, the otolith reinterpretation hypothesis derived from STS-8 was supported by the results from STS-41B. The eye movement results were consistent with a hypothesis that the reinterpretation of the otolith signals occurs in the brain stem in the nuclei associated with vestibular-ocular reflexes (VOR). The results suggested ways in which an astronaut's performance might be disturbed during the immediate postflight period. The results imply that performance of tasks that require accurate perception of complex self-motion should be avoided. It was also suggested that SAS symptoms and orientation disturbances are related to the period in which the brain is learning to reinterpret the otolith signals in weightlessness. This suggestion is consistent with the reports indicating that head tilts, particularly in the pitch plane, are provocative. This suggestion can be evaluated by performing appropriate inflight observations and employing appropriate preflight countermeasures during future missions.

A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. The large threshold elevation reported for STS-8 was not seen with the STS-41B subjects. Results for ocular counterrolling during static head tilt are not available.

DSO 433 was renamed to DSO 449 prior to the STS-51D flight, and additional subjects' data were obtained on DSO 449.

Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) Dual Energy X-ray Absorptometry (DXA) system

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project addressed NASA's need for a relatively compact and portable x-ray system to perform bone mineral density studies on the International Space Station. The use of a 60 ns x-ray pulse to image biological specimens has been successfully demonstrated.

With the dual-energy flash source, there is no need to change the anode-cathode (AK) voltage since the applied voltage across the AK gap is effectively swept during operation. The x-ray energy is high early in the pulse and lower later in the pulse. Utilizing the dual energy properties of the x-ray source to perform x-ray absorptometry without changing the applied voltage across the AK gap or changing filters simplifies the implementation of the source. A computer simulation model was developed for the x-ray source, which permitted the distribution of radiated energy in a plane normal to the symmetry axis of the x-ray anode to be determined as well as its spectrum. The use of two amorphous silicon (aSi) imaging panels stacked in tandem with a metal x-ray filter yielded both hard and soft x-ray images. X-ray assays of bone mineral density (BMD) to accuracies of 2% percent are possible when the attenuation of the soft tissue is removed by means of a subtraction algorithm and by using a calibration phantom. The dual-energy x-ray absorptometry (DEXA) project implemented a complete system that integrates the dual energy pulsed x-ray source with the aSi digital imaging panels. Experiments were performed to determine the distribution of radiation over the image plane and the sensitivity or modulation transfer function of the imaging panels. Based on the imaging experiments and the ability of the software to generate computed tomographic (CT) images, a decision was made to add CT capability to DEXA imaging so that a 3-D map of the site bone mineral density could be obtained. The addition of the CT capability increases the patient radiation dose; so image-based reconstruction was planned for the purpose of reducing the dose. In this process a limited number (3 to 5) images of a target site are processed using a priori knowledge of the site architecture to construct a CT image. The following questions were examined and answered during this project. Is the fluence, forward distribution, repeatability, and energy spectrum of the pulsed x-ray source sufficient? Will the sensitivity of the aSi digital imaging panels and the choice of conversion phosphor produce an image suitable for DEXA analysis? Will the DEXA software operate correctly, and is it capable of generating a 3D map of bone mineral density?

APPROACH:
System tests were run to evaluate the CT image capability of the software. The DEXA system was configured to examine a Lamb femur. The specimen was frozen to prevent motion during the periods between image collection. The images were recorded on two stacked aSi digital panels and processed. The front panel was designed to be sensitive to 25-45 keV photons. Each image was processed using pixels located within a slice equivalent to a fan-beam. The set of all slices was processed to generate a volume view of the object capable of full 360 degree rotation about the x,y,z axis. Since hard and soft x-ray CT image data were available, the DEXA could be used to extract both the density and composition of the scanned object. Specifically, the DEXA software used a plastic-aluminum calibration phantom to create a raster of all possible values scanned, then correlated this data to the correct attenuation value, generated a surface polynomial to approximate the surface, and used the surface to correct a complete dataset by simulating a monochromatic source. When the corrected dataset was passed through a CT 3D reconstruction, the resulting reconstruction contained calibrated data that could be used to determine the volumetric density.

To further evaluate the DEXA's imaging capabilities, the denser bone-mineral was extracted from the surrounding tissue by applying a cubic volume opacity filter followed by an isosurface reconstruction of the digitized x-ray image. By using both soft (25-45 keV) and hard (67-150 keV) images, the bone mineral density in the CT volume reconstruction could be determined.

RESULTS:
Understanding the process of charge flow in Marx-driven x-ray tubes was one of the goals of this research. The SCL flow in x-ray tubes with conical anodes and coaxial cathodes was successfully modeled using Langmuir's analytic solution for charge flow between coaxial cylinders, provided that the width of the plasma cathode was treated as a free parameter and that magnetic field effects were neglected.

The use of simulated cathode current and AK voltage in a calculation of the x-ray emission spectrum confirmed that the x-ray tube was operating as a SCL diode and that the model could accurately simulate the emission spectrum and total radiated energy in the x-ray pulse. Moreover it was shown that when the filtered hard x-ray pulse was subtracted from the unfiltered x-ray pulse, the residual pulse was the expected soft x-ray pulse with the correct temporal shape. This work experimentally verified the dual energy nature of the x-ray pulse.

The second research goal was to develop a digital imaging system with radiography and computed tomography (CT) capabilities. The ability of the present system to deliver detailed CT volume reconstructions was dependent on the number of views in the sampling set. The excellent resolution in individual images was due to the small diameter, <3 mm, of the x-ray emission spot. The digital images obtained to date, and used to generate 3D volume reconstructions of biologic specimens, were not constrained by hardware or software limitations but by the number of views in the sample. The present system has the necessary software to determine the bone mineral density of specific volumetric sites within a chosen specimen.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Brainard, GeorgeCo-Investigator: Byrne, BrendaCo-Investigator: Gerner, EdwardCo-Investigator: Goel, NamniCo-Investigator: Hanifin, JohnCo-Investigator: Lockley, StevenCo-Investigator: Mollicone, DanielCo-Investigator: Pineda, Carissa
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Currently, the International Space Station (ISS) uses General Luminaire Assemblies (GLAs) that house fluorescent lamps for illuminating the astronauts’ working and living environments. Solid-state light in the form of Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) is an attractive candidate for replacing the GLAs on the ISS as well as all future manned space vehicles and habitats. With respect to space flight, the advantages of LEDs over conventional incandescent and fluorescent lighting systems include lower upmass, power consumption, and heat generation, as well as fewer toxic materials. In addition, LEDs have greater resistance to damage and longer lamp life expectancy. Engineers at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) have developed a prototype Solid-State Lighting Assembly (SSLA) that has been installed on board the ISS. In a consensus document between the KSC engineers, lighting experts from Johnson Space Center (JSC), research management from JSC and NASA’s biomedical research partner, the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI), it was recommended that the SSLAs could provide reasonably equivalent light compared to the GLAs currently onboard ISS. Two crewmembers onboard the ISS have assessed the recently installed SSLA prototype to be acceptable for supporting vision. With regard to the efficacy of the SSLAs for astronaut circadian regulation, there was less certainty. It was suggested that further research was needed to determine the biological and behavioral efficacy of the SSLAs.

This project was a feasibility, pilot study. The goal was to develop and run a multiday study with a small cohort of healthy, male, astronaut-aged volunteers. The primary study objective was to determine the best way to test the acute effects of the prototype LED light designed for use on the ISS. Specific measures were taken on visual performance, color discrimination, alertness and cognitive performance through neurobehavioral testing, measures of plasma melatonin levels, as well as total sleep time, sleep latency and sleep efficiency using electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), and electrocardiography (EKG).

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
This project successfully completed each of the proposed specific aims. Collaborators from four institutions developed and refined controlled, ground-based protocols that assessed the visual, neuroendocrine, alerting, and sleep effects relative to different Correlated Color Temperature (CCT) outputs of the Solid State Lighting Assembly (SSLA). Both the Thomas Jefferson University Institutional Review Board and the NASA Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects approved the study protocols. During the time those activities were completed, two high fidelity simulations of the ISS Crew Sleeping Quarters (CQs) with internal illumination provided by an SSLA were constructed with engineering support from JSC, KSC, and the Lighting Sciences Group. Over 200 astronaut-aged, male volunteers were screened to assure they were physically healthy, psychologically sound, drug-free, and had stable sleep-wake rhythms. Ten subjects were selected from that pool of volunteers to enter the multiday study. Nine of the subjects completed the full multiday study providing data on melatonin secretion, subjective alertness, objective alertness, neurobehavioral responses, and sleep parameters. Eight of those subjects also participated in independent experiments on visual performance and color discrimination inside the CQs. Collateral support from the National Space Biomedical Research Institute made it possible to extend the number of subjects studied, enhance the testing of visual performance and color discrimination as well as augment analysis of polysomnography for both sleep and alertness measures.

As hypothesized, the results of the visual performance and color discrimination testing showed that CCT of 2,300 K and 6,500 K SSLA light supported visual performance as well as indirect midday daylight and common 3,500 K CCT fluorescent light. Also as hypothesized, color vision was significantly compromised under dim 2,300 K SSLA light versus brighter indirect daylight, 3,500 K fluorescent light, and 6,500 K SSLA light. Currently a dim 2,700 K SSLA pre-sleep lighting countermeasure is being considered for use on the ISS. If this setting is operationally used, the astronauts should be made aware of the potential color discrimination difficulties and be advised to save any tasks requiring color discrimination for the other lighting conditions. Going forward additional visual testing should be done in high fidelity mock ups of other spaces onboard ISS as they have very different lighting configurations and reflectant surfaces.

From the outset, the multiday study was intended as a pilot study to determine the feasibility of using a variety of physiological and behavioral measures within the very confined spaces of the replica ISS CQs. Despite the overall study being insufficiently powered, some statistically significant effects were observed. These included: 1) evening plasma melatonin sample; 2) one evening neurobehavioral test; and 3) one morning neurobehavioral test. The evening melatonin and neurobehavioral results support the hypothesis that evening exposure to dim, long wavelength-shifted SSLA light better prepares an astronaut-aged male subjects for sleep. Further, the morning neurobehavioral results support the hypothesis that bright, short wavelength-shifted SSLA light is more alerting than dimmer, long wavelength-shifted SSLA light. These observations are tempered, however, by the fact that the results may have been due to an order effect not the lighting. A fully powered, crossover study is needed to confirm these observations from the multiday pilot study. As intended, the multiday study provided the ability to determine which dependent variables studied could yield statistically significant results through power analyses. The results of the power analyses varied depending of the study measure being assessed. The number of subjects needed for statistically significant results in future studies will be determined by the dependent variables selected for study.

To prepare for manned space missions, NASA utilizes Earth-based research in specific environments with elements that are similar or analogous to some of the conditions of space flight. Analog research environments can be in extreme locations such as Antarctica, rugged deserts, the ocean floor, or inside of a volcano. The work reported here represents a middle ground between research done in highly controlled laboratory conditions and NASA’s experimental field environments.

Finally, the issue of gender needs to be addressed in planning a multiday protocol of seven days or longer. In discussions between the collaborative scientific team and NASA management, it was determined that this feasibility study should include only male subjects to reduce variability across the small sample size. Future studies should include both genders to more accurately reflect the sex distribution in the astronaut corps and future space flight crews.

The sleep deficits experienced by astronauts during space flight can be considered a threat to the success of space missions. The resulting physiological and behavioral changes caused by sleep and circadian disruption can lead to diminished alertness, cognitive ability, and psychomotor performance. A significant portion of the global population suffers from chronic sleep loss and/or circadian-related disorders. Development of an in-flight lighting countermeasure that helps resolves circadian and sleep disruption in astronauts is likely to help optimize use of light therapy for patient populations with affective, circadian, and sleep disorders.

experiment_title: Bone Minerals and Morphological and Functional Changes
parameter_html: Activity, motor, Rat, Microgravity, SLS-2 (counts)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Oganov, VictorCo-Investigator: Kabitskaya, OlgaCo-Investigator: Rodionova, N.
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Observations made on humans during manned flights on spacecraft and orbital stations, as well as on animals flown on biological satellites, have not yet provided an adequate knowledge of mechanisms underlying musculoskeletal changes in space. However, recent data about bone response to microgravity point to several typical changes, such as inhibited bone formation and enhanced osteoporosis, reduced mineral density, and lowered mechanical strength. The purpose of this present study was to investigate the effects of a 14-day exposure of rats to microgravity on spongy bone cells and bone properties as a composition material and to discriminate between the changes caused by gravity from the changes associated with short-term readaptation after return to Earth.

Approach:

Tibia fragments were obtained from rats. Fragments were then massed. Bone density was evaluated on the basis of mass measurements in air and distilled water. Some fragments were placed in a muffle furnace for analysis of ash content. Fragments were then analyzed histologically and under electron microscopy. Morphometric measurements were made using a computer-aided test-point counting method.

Results:

The bone density of the tibial distal epiphyses shows a decrease in animals recovered immediately after flight (R+0) and those recovered 14 days later (R+14) when compared to the appropriate controls. The density of the tibial proximal segment of animals sacrificed inflight (1F) did not differ from the controls. The bone porosity of distal epiphyses of R+0 and 1F rats was significantly higher than their respective controls. After flight, ash content of the tibial fragments decreased significantly. After 14 days of readaptation (R+14), bone porosity and ash content were not significantly different from the controls. Histological studies showing shorter bone trabecules and decrease in the number of osteoblasts in spongy bone reveal osteoporosis type changes in R+0 animals when compared to controls. Flight rats had a more homogeneous osteoblast population, indicating non-optimal osteogenesis. Additionally, osteoclastic density was increased in flight rats.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Successful plant reproduction during spaceflight has always been difficult. The environment within a spacecraft has many factors that make plant growth problematic. Experiments are limited to specific constraints on both available energy and space. Recent studies have shown that near identical gaseous environments can have drastically different effects on plant growth and reproduction. There appears to be a strong correlation between the degree of ventilation that a plant receives and how successfully it grows. This study focuses on the effects of microgravity upon plant reproduction. Specifically, the study looks at whether microgravity reduces the storage reserves available for reproduction.

Approach:

The experiment began with the planting of Brassica rapa seeds in the Russian greenhouse's (Svet) two root zone modules. The crew photographed plant development, made observations and physical measurements in the log book, and took video images. Plant samples were collected and fixed twice during the vegetative stages of the growth cycle, on days 13 and 18. To encourage the plants to stop growing vertically, the tops were pinched off on Flight Day 18. The parts removed were fixed with the plants sampled and returned to Earth. During the flowering phase of growth, pollination was performed once daily for 7 days. The plants were harvested 48 days after sowing, then dried and/or fixed. A portion of the seeds were placed on seed strips for subsequent planting, and the remainder were stowed for postflight analysis.

Results:

During the three growth cycles, seeds formed on Earth had comparable growth and reproductive output. The two growth cycles composed of first generation seeds formed in space produced fewer flower buds and were smaller than reference plants from Earth seeds grown at the same time in the same environment.

There appears to be a strong correlation between the degree of ventilation that a plant receives and how successfully it grows. This study focuses on the effects of microgravity upon plant reproduction. Specifically, the study looks at whether microgravity reduces the storage reserves available for reproduction.

Approach:

The experiment began with the planting of Brassica rapa seeds in the Russian greenhouse's (Svet) two root zone modules. The crew photographed plant development, made observations and physical measurements in the log book, and took video images. Plant samples were collected and fixed twice during the vegetative stages of the growth cycle, on days 13 and 18. To encourage the plants to stop growing vertically, the tops were pinched off on Flight Day 18. The parts removed were fixed with the plants sampled and returned to Earth. During the flowering phase of growth, pollination was performed once daily for 7 days. The plants were harvested 48 days after sowing, then dried and/or fixed. A portion of the seeds were placed on seed strips for subsequent planting, and the remainder were stowed for postflight analysis.

Results:

During the three growth cycles, seeds formed on Earth had comparable growth and reproductive output. The two growth cycles composed of first generation seeds formed in space produced fewer flower buds and were smaller than reference plants from Earth seeds grown at the same time in the same environment.

image_name: Schematic Drawing of ASTP Passive Personnel Dosimeter
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Observation of light flashes in the eyes of Apollo astronauts, which were determined to be caused by radioactive cosmic rays, renewed concern about potential radiobiological effects of high linear energy transfer (LET) particles in space flight. The documentation of high-LET particles in a variety of space flight conditions is an important factor in assessing potential hazards to humans in space.

APPROACH:
The 9-day ASTP mission was flown between July 15 and July 25, 1975, at an altitude of 220 km and an inclination of 51.6 degrees. High-LET particle radiation was recorded in passive dosimeters worn by the three U.S. Apollo-Soyuz Test Project astronauts. The dosimeters consisted of thin films of plastic nuclear track detectors and a silver chloride (Gal) crystal. The radiation is measured by counting the tracks made as the radioactive particles impact the crystal and scar its surface.

After each dosimeter was returned to Earth, the plastics were removed and processed in temperature controlled, mechanically stirred etching tanks. Scanning and measurement of the tracks made in the plastics was done with an optical microscope at 430x magnification. The AgCl crystals were removed, in a darkroom, from each dosimeter and immediately stabilized with yellow light for 30 seconds and placed in a light-tight box for storage. Tracks were developed by decorating each crystal with ultraviolet (UV) light for 17.5 minutes. The crystals were then scanned in red light at 650x magnification in a darkroom. Only tracks which intersected both surfaces (i.e. spanning tracks) of a crystal were counted.

RESULTS:
Generally, near-Earth missions with high inclination orbits (versus low inclination orbits) receive a higher flux of high-LET particles because of the decreased absorption of particles in the atmosphere at higher inclinations. Lunar missions normally receive higher radiation exposures than near-Earth missions due to the absence of shielding of radioactive particles by the Earth's atmosphere.

A total of 48 events were located in a 0.192 square centimeter area of the crystal, giving the fluence value of 250 tracks/cm2. The flux recorded in the plastics and AgCl crystal was, respectively, 1.15 and 27.5 particles/cm2 per day. Thus, there was higher particle registration sensitivity in the AgCl than in the plastics. Comparison of results showed that the high-LET particle flux incident on Skylab astronauts was a factor 2.9 larger than ASTP, due to both the lower altitude orbit of ASTP (220 km compared with 435 km for Skylab) and the greater spacecraft shielding that ASTP had.

The main feature of the ASTP measurements was a sharp decrease in particle flux toward large LET values. Radiobiological damage expected from particles with long range and large LET values can be expected to be quite severe.

experiment_title: Leg Plethysmography
parameter_html: Leg volume
investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, William
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space flight, due to the loss at hydrostatic pressure gradient, results in significant fluid shifts. These shifts are characterized by the movement of fluid from the lower extremities toward the thorax and upper portions of the body. The body recognizes this as a fluid overload and consequently loses some of it in the form of increased urine output and/or decreased intake. Then on re-entry, the reverse occurs. This is exacerbated by the increased gravitational forces of reentry. Another factor that could contribute to the increase in vascular pooling in the lower extremities on landing could be the loss or decrease of venous motor tone in the legs resulting in an increased compliance of the lower extremities. This can also affect the proper functioning of the cardiovascular system through pooling of blood with a decrease in cardiac output, possibly followed by orthostasis syncope.

The main objective of the experiment was to measure, quantify, and establish the time course of leg volume changes related to fluid shifts during space flight, reentry, and landing (especially upon change from horizontal to vertical posture). A leg plethysmography stocking was used to measure leg volume changes.

APPROACH:

Preflight:
Each participating crewmember was requested to make six leg volume change recordings. Each recording consisted of a standing and supine measurement. Training was integrated into the first preflight measurement and plethysmograph stocking fitting session.

In flight:
Each plethysmograph measurement required two persons: one as a subject and one to mark the leg volumes. If both crewmembers did the plethysmographs concurrently, then a total of 15 minutes was used to obtain data on both crewmembers. Otherwise, it was a two person operation with each measurement taking 15 minutes. On Mission Day 1, measurements on each subject at 3, 6, 12 and 24 hours Mission Elapsed Time (MET) were acquired. One measurement per subject near mid-mission and one near the end of the mission were also acquired.

Postflight:
Postflight data collection was performed as part of the R+0 physical exam. The crewmember was given the stocking to take home to make six additional measurements during the first week postflight, to be done at their convenience.

RESULTS:
Please refer to results from DSO 461.
