experiment_title: Food Processing vs. Packaged Food System Trade Study
parameter_html:
Food growth
Food menus
Food system
investigators: Principal Investigator: Cooper, Maya
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Food Processing vs. Packaged Food System Trade Study addresses the efficiencies and adequacies of growing produce and processing baseline crops into edible ingredients as compared to the efficiencies and adequacies of the utilizing the existing prepackaged food system. Specifically, the research was parceled into four specific aims:
1. To determine the requirements on vegetable, fruit, and baseline crops growth and bulk ingredient supply in terms of the estimated pounds required.
2. To determine requirements for food preparation and/or processing equipment at the extraterrestrial habitat.
3. To provide a quantitative assessment of mass penalties and human factors impacts of each proposed menu option.
4. To provide an assessment of feasibility of implementing the proposed systems and identify associated technology gaps.

Recent AFT work to prepare for deep space surface missions identified the shortcomings of using the current prepackaged food system in long exploratory mission application. The degradation of the quality of thermostabilized products and degradation of nutritional content indicates the inadequacy of the current food system for a five-year mission.

This trade study is central to the decision process on whether to continue work on bioregenerative crop development for future space flight missions. Additionally, the trade study supports the decision process on whether to develop food preparation and food processing technologies and, if so, to what extent the development should occur. Because the food system has huge implications to the upmass considerations of the mission as well as measurable impact to the psyche of the crew members, the appropriate decision on the food system will directly relate to the adequacy of the food system for the mission.

APPROACH:
Two 10-day menus were developed in preparation for a Mars habitat mission. The first was built on the assumption, as in previous menu development efforts for closed ecological systems, that the food system would be vegetarian, whereas the second menu introduced shelf-stable, prepackaged meat and entrée items from the current International Space Station (ISS) food system.

RESULTS:
The trade study answered the key question to which it was targeted – is it better to take the food to Mars or grow the food on the surface? – with the ambiguous “yes.” While the advantages of growing the food at the surface involve a tremendous upmass savings, higher acceptability, and higher potential menu variety, it cannot be discounted that even a small addition of prepackaged food prompted a significant decrease in crew time utilization and decreased the likelihood of food scarcity. The results indicate the food system design should focus on a solution that is mixed with food sources, leveraging the advantages of both farming crops and stowing the food supply.

Five food systems were postulated based on three menu designs of equal caloric contribution. The first food system was based on meals derived from crops grown at the Martian habitat with minor dry ingredient additions. The second food system used the same meals as the first but was based on meals derived from a smaller number of crops grown at the Martian habitat, stable bulk commodities (rice, beans, wheat) shipped from Earth, and minor dry ingredient additions. The third and fourth food systems mirror the first and second system food sources, respectively, except both the third and fourth systems are supplemented with prepackaged meat products. The final food system was based solely on existing space food. Many recipes were reproduced to ascertain the amount of raw material, the necessary cookware, and time that was required to complete a meal. The equivalent system mass (ESM) and the food metric value (FMV) for each of the five food systems were then compared to determine which food system is preferable based upon resource utilization and other food system metrics.

For a crew of 6 on a 600-day habitat mission, Food System 3 had the lowest equivalent system mass at 8566 kilograms and the lowest food metric value at 176 kilograms. This food system had both the second lowest mass shipped and second lowest volume shipped but was third in active crew time hours. The ESM for food system 3 was driven primarily by the low mass of stowed ingredients and a crew time utilization that was less than food system 1 or 2. The modified food quality index was not very different between food systems 1-4, and therefore, the value impacted the final results very little.

The combination of the food processing data with the ESM calculations of other linked subsystems (e.g. biomass production, water) will present the most accurate view of the food processing cost to mission planners.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Thornton, WilliamPrincipal Investigator: Schneider, VictorCo-Investigator: Johnson, PhillipCo-Investigator: LeBlanc, Adrian
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Disuse of the musculoskeletal system produces atrophy of bone and muscle causing decreased muscle strength as well as negative calcium, phosphorus and nitrogen balance. Muscle atrophy is seen after a short period of time. If disuse is continued for long periods, a measurable reduction in bone density will be evident. Both the losses in bone and muscle appear to be greater in the human postural and locomotor system (lower trunk and legs, often referred to as weight bearing). Such losses are regularly seen in bed rest and in space flight.

This study was an attempt to demonstrate that bone atrophy can be prevented by an individualized exercise program which adequately mimics the required forces associated with exercise here on Earth. An associated operational problem for NASA is the amount of time required for an astronaut to exercise during space flight. Therefore, reducing the time necessary for an individualized exercise prescription was also evaluated. This study used current knowledge of biomechanics to appropriately bioinstrument individuals to measure their physical activity as well as selected exercise parameters so that an individualized countermeasure could be developed.

The specific aims of the study were:

  1. Muscle and bone atrophy of the locomotor system during bed rest and weightlessness can be prevented by exercise equivalent to the individuals' usual locomotor activity.
  2. A program can be developed reducing exercise time (and repetitions) for space flight which is equivalent to the individual's usual locomotor activity.

APPROACH:
Subjects were studied during one week of equilibration, three weeks of monitored activity ambulation, three weeks of baseline control ambulation, three weeks of bed rest during which the subject performed a tailored exercise program, three weeks of untreated bed rest, and two weeks of re-ambulation. Three weeks was the maximum duration of each phase. Progress was monitored by: (a) calcium, phosphorus, and nitrogen balance studies and urinary hydroxyproline and creatinine; (b) gamma ray transmission scanning of the calcaneus and lower lumbar vertebrae; (c) magnetic resonance imaging of the leg muscles; and (f) Cybex (TM) muscle strength testing.

The subjects were males between the ages of 19-53, who responded to a request for research subjects from the general population. The volunteers were screened by the investigators and members of the General Clinical Research Centers (GCRC) staff. Each subject participating in the study provided the investigator with signed informed consent. Subjects were housed on the GCRC Metabolic Wards at Methodist and Hermann Hospitals in Houston, Texas in private or semi-private rooms.

The 15-week study was divided into six parts and initially was to involve a total of 18 normal test subjects (i.e. three subjects at a time). Each part of the study was divided into six phases:
a. Phase I (week 1-3): Determination of usual force environment and subject capacity. This phase consisted of orientation. The subjects received a complete physical examination, explanation of the study, and were required to give informed consent. The subjects’ normal activity in their usual living situation was monitored, i.e. work, recreation, exercise, etc. while wearing specified devices. An activity diary was also maintained.
b. Phase II (week 4-6): This was the ambulatory monitored period during which the subjects started the metabolic diet. The subjects also received polyethylene glycol 4000, and underwent metabolic equilibration. Baseline balance and urinary measurements were determined. Baseline measurements of muscle strength and volume, bone densitometry, lean body measurements, and normal and maximal muscle and cardiovascular activity were also determined.
All subject activity, determined from Phase I, was controlled, i.e. walking, jogging and running was done on a monitored treadmill (except for toilet needs). Thus, subjects maintained their "standard" activity level as measured during Phase I while baseline data collections were made. Time spent in various postures was controlled and recorded.
c. Phase III (week 7-9): This was the ambulatory control period during which an exercise "prescription" from the previously gathered data was determined.
d. Phase IV (week 10-12): This was the bed rest plus exercise period. During this phase the subjects were at strict bed rest except for an individualized tailored exercise program. The physical activity and length of exercise was chosen to best mimic effective normal activity found during Phase II. Metabolic studies continued. Success or failure of the prescription was based on results of calcium balance, strength testing, and anthropometric measurements. If strength and calcium balance were maintained, the next phase was started to document the atrophy expected to occur without counter measures.
e. Phase V (week 13-15): This was the strict bed rest phase during which no additional exercise was allowed. Metabolic balance testing continued.
f. Phase VI (week 16): This was the re-ambulation period. Metabolic balance testing continued and both densitometry and muscle testing were performed.

All subjects received a Hexavitamin tablet once daily which, with the diet, provided approximately 14,000 I.U. of vitamin A, 630 I.U. of vitamin D, 3mg thiamin, 5mg riboflavin, 42mg niacin, and 192mg ascorbic acid. Docusate sodium (Colace) was given orally in a dose up to 100mg twice daily to prevent constipation. Polyethylene glycol 4000 was used as a fecal marker and was given in an oral dose of 500mg three times daily.

Testing Procedures
a. Activity monitoring
Gravitational Loading - Two gravity sensitive switches were worn by the research subject, one on the trunk and one on the thigh. Changes of position and the time of change were recorded to document the time spent upright, sitting, and lying down.
Locomotor Activity - Recall history of the type of work, diet, sports and recreational activity of the research subject (walking, jogging, and running) was obtained by the investigator. A pedometer counted the subjects’ walking strides daily. The distance and time during jogging or running was recorded. Speed and number of strides was obtained by manual measurement over a known course.
b. Bone densitometry
Bone mineral of the os calcis and the lumbar spine were measured before and after bed rest. Rectilinear 125 iodine scanning was done for the os calcis and rectilinear 153 Gadolinium scanning of the lumbar spine was completed.
c. MRI muscle volume determination
The lower limbs of the research subjects were imaged at the beginning of the first phase and then at the end of each phase of the study. The scan consisted of five slices, 2 cm apart, starting at the lower calf. Before the start of the first scan, the desired start point was determined as the distance in centimeters from the bottom of the heel to a position on the calf where the gastrocnemius muscle mass is negligible.
d. Cybex muscle testing
Cybex muscle testing was performed at the beginning of the study and then at the end of each phase. Peak muscle strength and time to muscle fatigue were determined.
e. Metabolic balance
Sweat was collected through its absorption to cotton clothes furnished to do the research subjects. The subjects were required to wear the same clothes for seven continuous days, wiped themselves with a single towel after exercising, and had an acetic acid "wipe" down once each week. Bed coverings, clothes and towels were "washed" for collection of sweat.
f. Maximal exercise testing
The Bruce Protocol was followed. Bruce Protocol is a diagnostic test used in the evaluation of cardiac function. Additionally, a test for jogging endurance was performed by following the Bruce Protocol except for changing the grade of the treadmill.

RESULTS:
Summarized results aren’t available for this study.

Speed and number of strides was obtained by manual measurement over a known course.
b. Bone densitometry
Bone mineral of the os calcis and the lumbar spine were measured before and after bed rest. Rectilinear 125 iodine scanning was done for the os calcis and rectilinear 153 Gadolinium scanning of the lumbar spine was completed.
c. MRI muscle volume determination
The lower limbs of the research subjects were imaged at the beginning of the first phase and then at the end of each phase of the study. The scan consisted of five slices, 2 cm apart, starting at the lower calf. Before the start of the first scan, the desired start point was determined as the distance in centimeters from the bottom of the heel to a position on the calf where the gastrocnemius muscle mass is negligible.
d. Cybex muscle testing
Cybex muscle testing was performed at the beginning of the study and then at the end of each phase. Peak muscle strength and time to muscle fatigue were determined.
e. Metabolic balance
Sweat was collected through its absorption to cotton clothes furnished to do the research subjects. The subjects were required to wear the same clothes for seven continuous days, wiped themselves with a single towel after exercising, and had an acetic acid "wipe" down once each week. Bed coverings, clothes and towels were "washed" for collection of sweat.
f. Maximal exercise testing
The Bruce Protocol was followed. Bruce Protocol is a diagnostic test used in the evaluation of cardiac function. Additionally, a test for jogging endurance was performed by following the Bruce Protocol except for changing the grade of the treadmill.

Summarized results aren’t available for this study.

experiment_title: Evaluation of the Validity, Acceptability and Usability of Biomathematical Models to Predict Fatigue in an Operational Environment

investigators: Principal Investigator: Flynn-Evans, ErinCo-Investigator: Hillenius, StevenCo-Investigator: Marquez, JessicaCo-Investigator: Pecena, Yvonne
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Biomathematical models hold promise as tools that can be used to manage fatigue risks in an operational setting. There are numerous models available to predict fatigue-related performance impairment arising from sleep loss, circadian misalignment, and sleep inertia. It is imperative that any model considered for use during space flight missions be validated in an operational setting in order to ensure that predictions are reliable and consistent. Given the complexity of the underlying causes of fatigue, there are wide individual differences in response to mission stressors. However, the majority of candidate models provide predictions based on average human responses, making it difficult to use the models to make operational decisions for individuals. In addition, there are no published reports on the acceptability, usability, and feasibility of any of the current models. Effective incorporation in a space flight environment requires model-based software systems that are easy to use by a wide-range of operators and are integrated with other scheduling constraints that are relevant in space flight operations.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Validate model predictions in a space flight analog.
  2. Evaluate acceptability, usability, and feasibility of the selected sleep-wake model software user interface.
  3. Incorporate model predictions into Playbook and assess usability and acceptability of model in the context of scheduling and planning.

APPROACH:
Investigators aimed to identify which models are the best candidates for inclusion in four Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) missions. Crewmembers were trained on how to use the modeling software for the selected models and evaluated the usability of the current model software. Investigators asked crewmembers to collect measures of cognitive impairment and simulated operational data throughout the mission using actigraphy, sleep logs, the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ), Samn-Perelli fatigue Scale (SPS), and the Robotic On-Board Trainer (ROBoT). Investigators used this objective data to validate the predictions generated by the selected models. In an effort to identify whether the utility of the models might be enhanced by integration with crew scheduling tools, they evaluated the selected models after integrating the models into Playbook, the scheduling tool that is currently being evaluated on the International Space Station (ISS) in preparation for deep space missions.

RESULTS:
Investigators studied crews of four individuals during 4.5 missions in the HERA (n = 20). Crewmembers were allowed five hours of sleep during the week and eight hours of sleep on weekends. Crewmembers completed a reaction time test and fatigue ratings five times a day approximately every three days over 45 days. The investigators compared objective performance on the reaction time test to the predictions of biomathematical models designed to predict fatigue. They found that performance deteriorated over the course of the mission on average, however, there were wide individual differences in performance trajectories between crewmembers. Self-reported fatigue did not change over the mission. Biomathematical models were able to predict average performance, but not performance at the individual level.

This evaluation provided operational personnel, including flight surgeons, mission directors, mission operations planners, and flight controllers, with an understanding of 1) the validity of the model predictions in an operational setting, including how model predictions may vary by individual characteristics; 2) the acceptability, usability, and feasibility of the incorporation of the models as is into an operational setting, and; 3) a preliminary, qualitative assessment of the utility of integrating the model predictions into existing scheduling tools.

experiment_title: NASA Food Technology Commercial Space Center
parameter_html:
Food preservation
Food-processing technologies
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pometto, Anthony
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The mission of the Food Technology Commercial Space Center (FTCSC) was to lead a national effort to develop foods and food-processing technologies that enhance space missions and advance commercial food products through cooperative efforts with NASA scientists and technologists, commercial companies, and academic researchers.

The objectives of this study were:
1. Development of foods for NASA 30- to 120-day space missions in support of International Space Station (ISS) missions (minimum of one-year shelf life) .
2. Development of food and food-processing technologies to support NASA human exploration and the development of long-duration space missions (up to five years) . This included stored food systems for transit vehicles as well as food-processing systems for site-grown crops .
3. Development by the commercial partners of terrestrial commercial production and marketing plans for products and processes developed for NASA’s space program.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
NASA FTCSC affiliate faculty and commercial partners worked to develop foods and food-processing technologies that benefit NASA and the public. The Center’s commercial partners developed products for space and terrestrial applications. Following is a summary of the commercial partner activities in the final year of the study:
Ajinomoto Co., Inc., after numerous tests and consultations with NASA, terminated the precooked rice product research and turned their attention to developing food products with a calcium absorption promoter. Following positive initial results from the calcium absorption promoter research, the company plans further studies of calcium solubility, intestinal absorption, and potential benefits for bone health. Furthermore, the company funded Paul Flakoll’s research project at Iowa State University which examines the metabolic interactions of glutamine supplementation with exercise and insulin resistance in humans.

American Specialty Packaging, Alcoa Flexible Packaging, LLC and KSP (Korean Special Packaging) representatives met in Ames with FTCSC Director Anthony Pometto to discuss NASA’s future plans and goals in terms of space food packaging. Since that meeting, the companies have joined FTCSC as a commercial partner and are working on improving space food packaging.

Analytik Jena AG research has resulted in the measurement of changes in antioxidant potential in stored soybeans. Additionally, Analytik Jena has measured the influence of pasteurization and sterilization doses and low pasteurization doses of irradiation on the functional, sensory, and microbial quality of soybeans for soymilk and tofu manufacture. Research also focused on measuring the influence of radiation that soybeans would be exposed to on Mars missions and determining the influence of toasting and storage of full-fat soyflakes on shelf life. In order to conduct this research, the Photochem equipment was used and it was successful in aiding the research.

Arla Foods amba received product approval from NASA for the chocolate milk powder and the thermally-stabilized yogurt and launched the yogurt on Progress 17. Since the launch, Arla has been working to implement a space yogurt production line and to build a special packaging machine.

Biosteam Technologies, Inc. and Selective Micro conducted polymer research and compatibility testing on Selectrocide® for NASA, and completed all EPA testing and approvals for use of the compound as a complete antimicrobial for food, as well as food and non-food surfaces. Also, the company continues to develop a packet towel designed to remove mold and mildew while cleaning surfaces in space vehicles.

Biotecgen s.r.l. continues to work with plant proteinases inhibitors and has determined that they are a significant component of a defense response to plant pathogens and have various technological applications. In addition to that research, the company continues to develop products including liophilised foods for enhanced long-term storage and use in space diets.

California Dried Plum Board researchers are studying the glycemic index values of dried plums, prune juice, and plum juice, and found that dried plum extract can be used as a sweetener in confectionary items. The Board is also sponsoring research that will investigate the effect of dried plums on the acidogenicity of human dental plaque.

Pharmachem Laboratories is performing accelerated stability tests on FruitCare™ chews fortified with ten vitamins. The company is also working to improve their calcium-fortified fruit chews which were found to be less than acceptable during testing at NASA.

The Iowa Soybean Promotion Board and Soyfoods Council sponsored research that was conducted to determine the effects of special soy products, natural antioxidants, wheat proteins, and leavening ingredients to improve the functionality and acceptability of shelf-stable flour tortillas. The research also included evaluating the combined effects of soy products, natural antioxidants, and known anti-staling ingredients in processing, quality, and acceptability of shelf-stable corn tortillas. The ISPB also sponsored Astronaut Clayton Anderson’s visit to the Iowa State Fair in 2005.

Kraft Foods Inc. is developing food packaging with reseal technology using advanced materials; light weight packaging of foods; packaging with no loss of strength via nanocomposite technology; and research on nutrient-bone health technology.

MCC, s.a. researched fortification of foods for astronauts during long space flights. The company determined that synthesis of vitamins and minerals will largely depend on the constituents by the food intake. Shelf life considerations impose processing conditions largely incompatible with the preservation of nutritional value as available in the unprocessed form.

Microbial-Vac Systems™, Inc., is working to commercialize their new wet-vacuum, food-prep surface sampling, and separate sample concentration technologies throughout the U.S. and some NATO-member countries. The company also plans to expand research and development efforts for combining sampling and concentration technology with rapid detection systems.

Microcide® has been researching a water-soluble PRO-SAN® sanitizer package and found that the water-soluble pouch product and original powder pouch product resulted in identical microbicidal activities. After additional positive tests, Microcide® is now working with the EPA to obtain approval for the product. For their research in developing food grade sanitizer and disinfecting wipes for long- duration space flights, Microcide® was awarded an SBIR Phase I grant.

Monsanto is working with NASA to research biotech soybeans for their ability to grow under controlled conditions aboard the space station or as appropriate. The company has developed a Space Act Agreement with Kennedy Space Center to provide the Center with unique soybean cultivars for potential benefit to space exploration and in situ food production for habitats on Moon and Mars. Tests will include growing the soybeans in plant growth chambers to assess their potential for space life support applications.

MTI BioTech, Inc., has continued formulation work on products designed to maintain and restore muscle mass as well as improve healing. The company finished testing of primary products containing HMB combined with amino acids and continues its studies involving cancer and trauma patients.

ORBITEC received a SBIR Phase II award in January 2004 for the “Deployable Vegetable Production System (VEGGIE)”, a system for growing salad type crops on the International Space Station and other space platforms. The company is currently working with Aubrey Mendonca to develop a HACCP program for VEGGIE.

Pactech has been focusing on selecting and developing flexible packaging to extend shelf-life from less than 12 months to over two years. The company has set a goal of producing packaging that would extend shelf life to up to 15 years. Another avenue Pactech is researching is the production of Thermal Pouches and will send those to Cape Canaveral for consideration for use in transport of food and pharmaceuticals.

ScentSational Technologies has been researching the different applications for their Encapsulated Aroma Release technology and how it could potentially benefit space foods and beverages by making them more aromatic. Current work is focused on scenting the straw spout used for drinking from flexible pouches.

Triple “F”, Inc. is focusing their research work on the development and formulation of a textured soy protein-based, meatless Sloppy Joe product, specifically on product preservation through thermal processing. The company was awarded a SBIR in January 2005 to develop a versatile, compact, lightweight, energy efficient, and easily maintained extruder for seed processing in low gravity environments.

experiment_title: Electromyographic Analysis of Skeletal Muscle
parameter_html:
Fatigue index
Maximal voluntary contraction (MVC)
Muscle efficiency
Spectral power
investigators: Principal Investigator: LaFevers, EarlCo-Investigator: Hursta, WilliamCo-Investigator: Nicogossian, Arnauld
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The first opportunity to study the effects of long-duration weightlessness on human skeletal muscle function occurred during the Skylab missions. The results of the Skylab experiments provided ample evidence that normal muscle function is altered by periods of weightlessness of 59 days or more. This conclusion was supported by the occurrence of certain physiological and biochemical changes during the Skylab missions. The results of ground-based studies showed that these changes were related to abnormal muscle function.

The purpose of this study on the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) mission was to investigate changes in skeletal muscle electrical activity that occur after exposure to short-term weightlessness (less than 10 days). The following changes were hypothesized:

  1. Increased muscle fatigability when the muscles are subjected to a moderate fatigue-inducing stress.
  2. Reduced muscle electrical efficiency.
  3. Heightened excitability.

APPROACH:
A skeletal muscle stress apparatus was designed and built to enable controlled isometric muscle testing and measurements. A two-channel electromyogram (EMG) detector was built to record the EMG.

Data were obtained on 3 preflight days: 45, 30 and 15 days before launch. Surface electrodes were placed on the lower leg muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) and on the arm muscles (biceps brachii and brachioradialis). Seated in the muscle stress apparatus, the crewman was instructed to exert a series of graded muscle contractions as follows:

  1. 10 seconds at 10% maximum voluntary contraction (MVC), followed by 20 seconds rest.
  2. 10 seconds at 20% MVC, followed by 20 seconds rest.
  3. 10 seconds at 30% MVC, followed by 20 seconds rest.
  4. 60 seconds at 50% MVC (leg) and 40-percent MVC (arm).

Leg measurements and arm measurements were collected sequentially. On the day of landing, data was collected on only one astronaut because of toxic gas infiltration into the Apollo command module crew cabin during descent to Earth and the resulting concern for the health of the crewmen.

RESULTS:
After 9 days of weightlessness, the skeletal muscles investigated in this study showed an increased excitability. The brachioradialis muscle showed the least excitability effect from weightlessness. Both upper- and lower-extremity muscles showed changes in excitability which suggests that skeletal muscles are susceptible to functional changes associated with the reduced muscle activity in weightlessness. Since all changes showed increased sensitivity, the probable site for this effect is the muscle fibers, for the following reason: previous clinical studies have shown that random loss or reduced activity in muscle fibers, as in myopathy, result in higher firing frequencies of the muscle, whereas dysfunctions of neural loci result in lower firing frequencies.

The results of this study demonstrated that short-term exposure to weightlessness heightened fatigability in skeletal muscle (shown in the antigravity muscles). The results suggested that the disuse associated with whole-body weightlessness temporarily rendered muscles supersensitive, which led to more rapid fatigue.

experiment_title: Ensemble Neural Coding of Place and Direction in Zero-G
parameter_html:
Behavior, Body position, pitch axis, rat, Position-image-locator cameras, data acquisition system
Behavior, Body position, roll axis, rat, Position-image-locator cameras, data acquisition system
Behavior, Spatial orientation, head-direction (H) cells, thalamus and limbic cortex, brain, rat, Implanted probes, neuronal spikes
Behavior, Spatial orientation, place cells, hippocampus, brain, rat, Implanted probes, neuronal spikes
Neural firing rate, rat position
Neural spike data, rat position data
investigators: Principal Investigator: McNaughton, Bruce
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Brain cells in the hippocampus play an important role in the ability of animals to orient themselves within their environment. Called place cells, they encode a mental map of the environment, which is then used to remember locations and determine routes between them. Another class of neurons associated with spatial orientation, called head direction (HD) cells, are located in the thalamus and limbic cortex. Firing properties of the place cells in the hippocampus and HD cells are tightly coupled; one function of the HD cells may be to orient the acquired cognitive map in the hippocampus. The fact that this orientation system is based on information with respect to gravity suggests that problems may develop in low gravity conditions leading to an inability of the hippocampus to develop stable place codes. The purpose of this experiment was to study how the hippocampal neural representations of place and direction are affected by zero-gravity conditions in rats performing tasks requiring navigation in three dimensions.

Approach:

The first part of the experiment addressed the question of whether the hippocampal place system can maintain stable representations of the environment under zero-G. Three rats were singly tracked with two position-image-locator cameras synchronized with a data acquisition system as they navigated a special walking apparatus. The walking apparatus consisted of three orthogonal planes in which a track permits the animal to walk in a continuous loop, having three 90 degree turns in its yaw axis interspersed with three 90 degree backward pitches. When the animal returns to the origin, it has completed only 270 degrees of yaw. Animals were implanted with probes that monitored neuronal spikes simultaneously from about 20 or more hippocampal neurons, to determine whether they fired in a stable fashion with respect to the rat's location in three-dimensional space. In the second part of the experiment, rats were trained to visit each of four arms on a two dimensional cross-shaped track. The rat was then rotated 180 degrees in the pitch axis followed by a 180-degree rotation in the roll axis; as a result, the rat faced 180 degrees opposite its original position without experiencing rotation in the yaw axis. The animals were tracked as above to determine whether place cells fire in synchronization with the ratï¿½s spatial location relative to the track or relative to the reference frame of the work volume of the General Purpose Work Station.

Results:

During the first zero-G recording session on FD 4, rat 2 did not show strong spatial tuning in any of the cells that fired while on the track. In contrast, this animal had normal, highly specific place fields in cells that fired when tested on a very similar track four days before launch. Objectives:

Brain cells in the hippocampus play an important role in the ability of animals to orient themselves within their environment. Called place cells, they encode a mental map of the environment, which is then used to remember locations and determine routes between them. Another class of neurons associated with spatial orientation, called head direction (HD) cells, are located in the thalamus and limbic cortex. Firing properties of the place cells in the hippocampus and HD cells are tightly coupled; one function of the HD cells may be to orient the acquired cognitive map in the hippocampus. The fact that this orientation system is based on information with respect to gravity suggests that problems may develop in low gravity conditions leading to an inability of the hippocampus to develop stable place codes. The purpose of this experiment was to study how the hippocampal neural representations of place and direction are affected by zero-gravity conditions in rats performing tasks requiring navigation in three dimensions.

Approach:

The first part of the experiment addressed the question of whether the hippocampal place system can maintain stable representations of the environment under zero-G. Three rats were singly tracked with two position-image-locator cameras synchronized with a data acquisition system as they navigated a special walking apparatus. The walking apparatus consisted of three orthogonal planes in which a track permits the animal to walk in a continuous loop, having three 90 degree turns in its yaw axis interspersed with three 90 degree backward pitches. When the animal returns to the origin, it has completed only 270 degrees of yaw. Animals were implanted with probes that monitored neuronal spikes simultaneously from about 20 or more hippocampal neurons, to determine whether they fired in a stable fashion with respect to the rat's location in three-dimensional space. In the second part of the experiment, rats were trained to visit each of four arms on a two dimensional cross-shaped track. The rat was then rotated 180 degrees in the pitch axis followed by a 180-degree rotation in the roll axis; as a result, the rat faced 180 degrees opposite its original position without experiencing rotation in the yaw axis. The animals were tracked as above to determine whether place cells fire in synchronization with the ratï¿½s spatial location relative to the track or relative to the reference frame of the work volume of the General Purpose Work Station.

Results:

During the first zero-G recording session on FD 4, rat 2 did not show strong spatial tuning in any of the cells that fired while on the track. experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Over four hundred medical conditions have been identified that may present and require treatment during long-duration space exploration. Of the conditions, approximately 25 percent may require medical fluids during the course of treatment. Some of the conditions that may require IV fluid treatment include major bone fracture, burns, and acute anemia. NASA is currently developing hardware that can produce IV solution using spacecraft cabin water (also called the feedstock.)

The IntraVenous Fluid GENeration for Exploration Missions (IVGEN) experiment was designed to demonstrate a water purification and pharmaceutical mixing system that can make intravenous (IV) fluid in microgravity. IVGEN utilized a deionizing resin bed to remove contaminants from cabin water to a purity level that meets the standards of the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), which is chartered by the United States Food and Drug Administration to function as the governing body for pharmaceuticals in the United States. The water was then introduced into an IV bag where the fluid was mixed with USP grade crystalline salt to produce USP normal saline. Inline conductivity sensors quantified the feedstock water quality, output water purity, and normal saline mixing uniformity.

APPROACH:
The resin bed was made from 0.5 mm diameter beads packed into a cylinder including bubble-trapping hardware upstream from the filter to insure that no failures occurred from trapping bubbles within the filter to insure optimal performance. The hardware quantified system performance using flow and pressure transducers. If the hardware were to experience performance degradation, these transducers would allow the fluid physicists to identify and fix the problem.

IVGEN operated inside the Microgravity Sciences Glovebox (MSG) laboratory and utilized cameras and video recording devices to observe system performance. IVGEN required MSG resources such as electrical power, video capability, and data collection/transmission. IVGEN also required access to pressurized nitrogen to pressurize the accumulator. The experiment protocol required that one 1.5 liter bag of IV fluid be returned in refrigerated stowage for ground-based analysis. IVGEN also required the return of a second 1.5 liter bag of IV fluid, but it remained ambient. Each IVGEN run took approximately 1.5 hours, but did not require crew interaction for the duration of the session.

Astronauts installed IVGEN inside the MSG per procedures. The astronaut transferred ISS potable water from the Water Processing Assembly (WPA) to the IVGEN accumulator. When that was completed, the astronaut pressurized the IVGEN accumulator with nitrogen. The pressure forced water through the IVGEN system, beginning with a bubble trap to eliminate unwanted air, and a conductivity sensor to quantify the quality of the incoming water. Following the conductivity sensor, the water passed through the packed resin bed, through another bubble trap to remove any air that may have been present in the filter, and then into the mixing bag. The mixing bag contained the salt required to make a saline solution, as well as a sterile magnetic stir bar. After the bag had been filled with 1.5 liters of water, the stir bar mixed the solution. Following mixing, the fluid passed out of the mixing bag, through a conductivity sensor to measure uniformity, and into a final collection bag. After all of the solution was in the collection bag, it was disconnected from the system, sealed, and appropriately stowed.

RESULTS:
On-orbit results indicated that all of the experimental success criteria were met with the exception of the salt concentration. Problems with a large air bubble in the first bag of purified water resulted in a slightly concentrated saline solution of 117 percent of the target value of 0.9 g/L. The second bag had an inadequate amount of salt premeasured into the mixing bag resulting in a slightly deficient salt concentration of 93.8 percent of the target value. The USP permits a range from 95 to 105 percent of the target value.

experiment_title: Microorganisms in the Spacecraft Environment
parameter_html:
16S rRNA
Cytosine
Uracil
investigators: Principal Investigator: Fox, George
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The mass spectrometric approach to bacterial identification that was developed is extremely fast and utilizes instrumentation that can be used for a variety of other tasks. Thus, for some applications in areas such as environmental microbiology, medical diagnosis, and biodefense it may offer advantages over sequencing approaches.

The low shear modeled microgravity results point out that different organisms can respond quite differently to these conditions. Similar low shear conditions are found in the human body and hence the results of studies done using the rotating bioreactor (HARV) may be more representative of how a pathogenic organism will respond to factors such as antibiotics than traditional culture studies.

The original project had two long-term objectives: (1) To develop general and specific microbial monitoring systems that utilize technologies that can be readily implemented in spacecraft. (2) To better understand the long-term effects of the space environment on representative bacteria.

Three project tasks were to address these objectives. The primary task was to develop microbial monitoring technology that can be used on long term space missions. 16S ribosomal RNA, (16S rRNA), is the single most useful molecule for bacterial identification and therefore it was the target of choice in the monitoring work. In order to develop a general sentinel system for pathogens and other problematic organisms without prior knowledge of what organism might be encountered, we sought to take advantage of our earlier discovery that there are a large number of informative subsequences in 16S rRNA (“signature sequences”) whose presence in a unknown sample provide information that can be used to provide information on phylogenetic position (genetic affinity) or specific identity. For routine monitoring we proposed to look for the presence of specific genera and species as expected indicators of anticipated problems such as contaminated water or air. In a more sophisticated mode, we would seek to determine the genetic affinity of any problematic organism without prior knowledge of what it would be.

APPROACH:
Three approaches were investigated for this purposes; (A) microarrays of 16S rRNA targeted probes; (B) mass spectrometry and (C) solution hybridization with detection by fluorescence using molecular beacons. The essence of the second task was to conduct experiments with the objective of understanding how a low gravity/high background radiation environment affects bacteria over extended time periods. The third project task which was abandoned due to the early project termination was extension of the core monitoring technology to detection of microbial escape from an advanced life support system.

RESULTS:
The key advantage of mass spectrometry is that the core instrumentation is compatible with space flight and potentially has many uses. The investigators initially made a detailed investigation of the feasibility of using the information obtained by digesting 16S rRNA from an unknown organism with a base specific nuclease such as ribonuclease T1 and identifying the mass of all the resulting fragments. Their analysis of this scenario identified two key issues. The first was loss of information due to the inability of mass spectrometry to distinguish fragments with the same composition but different sequence (e.g. CACAAAG vs. AAAACCG). It was found that fragments of length six and larger contained useful information and that enough of such fragments would be available to allow identifications to be made. The second difficulty is that the mass of cytosine and uracil are so close together that the relatively low resolution instruments that likely would be available during a space flight would not be able to distinguish them. The investigators therefore implemented an alternative experimental protocol in which the rRNA is first converted to DNA and then regenerated as RNA with a mass labeled analog of uracil. Using this protocol they successfully identified five out of five bacteria in test runs. A subtraction algorithm was devised to deconvolute the spectra. This approach was applied to the analysis of the spectra obtained from a complex human cheek sample. They were able to identify the same dominant organisms that were found by a more traditional cloning and sequencing approach.

In the array area, the investigators developed an evolutionary programming approach to the design of a universal array of less than 1000 15mer signature sequence probes. No organism is uniquely identified by a single probe. Instead, the design is such that any organism will test positive with at least 40 probes. The pattern obtained then serves to determine the genetic affinity of the unknown organism. With less than a thousand probes, this "signature chip" can in principle determine the genetic affinity of any bacterium. The investigators have completed extensive computational validation of the concept, and developed an optimized set of signature sequences. These have been tested in small scale for methods development and optimization of spacer offset sequences, rRNA fragmentation methods, and labeling and analysis methods. Based on these results, a custom microarray was obtained from Combimatrix. Tests of this chip with E. coli resulted in a positive identification. However, many probes either failed to hybridize or gave false positive signals. This was expected because the behavior of individual hybridization probes is notoriously unpredictable from sequence information alone. These bad probes will need to be eliminated from the chip and replaced with alternatives that work. It therefore was necessary to revise the software so that it could start a new optimization using a partially specified set of probes, e.g. those that work. This is now complete and further testing of the arrays is continuing.

The third approach to microbial monitoring that the investigators expected would be useful for routine monitoring was molecular beacons. Beacons carry a fluor that is initially quenched. When reaching their target in the 16S rRNA, the beacon probe hybridizes to the 16S rRNA resulting in exposure of the fluor and generation of a strong fluorescent signal. This solution hybridization approach would be advantageous because it would require minimal sample preparation and could be conducted with easily prepackaged reagents. The key problem is that the signal produced is insufficient for identification of small numbers of bacteria. The proposed solution to this problem was to use a “beacon swarm” in which multiple probes would target the 16S rRNA molecule in multiple signature sites but emit fluorescence at a single wavelength. With ten targets a single molecule of target would produce an order of magnitude more fluorescence than is normally produced. To date, the investigators have not been able to successfully demonstrate feasibility of the approach; possibly because of unintended interactions between the individual beacon probes.

Since molecular beacons are unlikely to resolve the routine monitoring need, the investigators have revised efforts began during a prior NSBRI award to develop small arrays that target a modest number of informative organisms. Thus, an array is envision that would test for E. coli, enterics in general, gram positives and gram negatives in general, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, etc. Probes were previously designed for many of these targets and tested but not in an array format. The investigators have constructed small arrays with these probes and begun testing them. Most of them work. The primary problem is false positives. The offending probes were removed and replaced with alternatives.

A second major project goal was to better understand the response of bacteria to the space environment. In order to do this, the investigators examined the growth of representative bacteria under simulated microgravity conditions using the NASA developed rotating wall bioreactor (HARV). An initial comparison of aerobic and anaerobic results revealed that there was no gene uniquely responding to these two growth conditions as would occur if the response was actually to gravity and that its response is quite different from that of its close relative Salmonella.

experiment_title: Particulate Containment Demonstration Test (PCDT)
parameter_html: Activity, Water release, GPWS containment, Video, audio tape
investigators: Principal Investigator: Dalton, Bonnie
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The Particulate Containment Demonstration Test (PCDT) was performed to ensure particulates from animals and inflight operations were contained and did not contaminate the crews living or working environment. The three main objectives were; 1) to determine that the RAHF and GPWS can contain solid particles of 150 microns and larger, 2) to determine that the GPWS can operationally contain fluids in nominal airflow mode, and 3) to determine that the GPTU can provide adequate secondary containment during cage transfer and servicing operations.

Approach:

Packages of particulates consisting of food bar crumbs, rodent hair and black eyed peas were placed in RAHF cage positions 2 and 9 (rats were not in these cages). These particulate loads were released into the cages upon activation of a pull knob which unsheathed the particulate bag. Following release of the particulates, the Biotest Reuter Centrifugal Sampler (RCS) was held in front of the RAHF to collect escaped particulates on a screen. The screens were capped and stowed for postflight analysis. Fluid containment was examined in the GPWS by pricking a fluid filled balloon in both an empty cabinet and cabinet with laboratory equipment. Voice recordings and eight millimeter video photography were used to document the test.

Results:

Postflight microscopic examination of the centrifugal sampler screens revealed particulate accumulation on only one screen and this was due to inadequate cleaning of the GPWS prior to the test. Particulates on this screen were less than 50 microns and did not exceed 20 particles per square inch. The PCDT proved particulated containment in the RAHF and GPWS to be highly successful and live rat transfer was approved by the Administration.

experiment_title: Novel Explorations Into the Interactions Between Light and Gravity Sensing in Plants - Seedling Growth-1
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Medina, F.Principal Investigator: Kiss, JohnCo-Investigator: Edelmann, Richard
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

The major goals of this project are to determine how gravity and light responses influence each other in plants and to better understand the cellular signaling mechanisms involved in plant tropisms. This proposed project builds on our previous spaceflight experiments on the ISS (TROPI-1, 2006; TROPI-2, 2010) with the EMCS using the model plant Arabidopsis. In this new proposed project, we plan to confirm and extend our discovery during the recent TROPI-2 ISS experiment of a novel red-light-based positive phototropic response in plant shoots.

Thus, the specific objectives of this proposed research are: (1) To confirm and characterize the novel red light-dependent phototropic response in flowering plants. (2) To investigate the relationship between light and gravity by measuring thresholds in fractional gravity. (3) To determine whether the red light effect on blue-light-based phototropism is a direct or indirect effect.

APPROACH:

The Seedling Growth series of experiments (1, 2, 3 and possibly 4) is supported collaboratively by NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA). The experiment will be conducted in the European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS) on the International Space Station (ISS). The EMCS is operated by ESA and is located in the Columbus Module of the ISS.

These experiments can be accomplished with telemetric science and therefore fit with the extremely limited down mass capabilities of current spaceflight opportunities. The EMCS is an automated facility and can be operated largely with telemetry. Experimental containers will be launched via Space-X, and during an experimental run, images of seedling growth responses can be downlinked to Earth. Seedlings will be returned to Earth in the GLACIER freezer.

RESULTS:

Project 1: Phototropic curvature

Utilizing the European Modular Cultivation System (EMCS) on board the International Space Station (ISS), we investigated the interaction between phototropic and gravitropic responses in three Arabidopsis thaliana genotypes, Landsberg wild type, as well as mutants of phytochrome A and phytochrome B. Onboard centrifuges were used to create a fractional gravity gradient ranging from reduced gravity up to 1 g. A novel positive blue-light phototropic response of roots was observed during conditions of microgravity, and this response was attenuated at 0.1 g. In addition, a red-light pretreatment of plants enhanced the magnitude of positive phototropic curvature of roots in response to blue illumination. OBJECTIVES:

The major goals of this project are to determine how gravity and light responses influence each other in plants and to better understand the cellular signaling mechanisms involved in plant tropisms. This proposed project builds on our previous spaceflight experiments on the ISS (TROPI-1, 2006; TROPI-2, 2010) with the EMCS using the model plant Arabidopsis. experiment_description:
Objectives:

The development of sensory systems has been shown to be affected by stimulation. It is hypothesized that exposure to microgravity reduces the stimulation of the developing fetal vestibular system and alters early vestibular functions in fetal rats. The purpose of this experiment is to explore that hypothesis as well as to study the effects of spaceflight on the behavior and physiology of pregnancy, labor, delivery and the onset of postnatal care, especially with respect to lactation.

Approach:

Vestibular development was studied prenatally and postnatally. During flight, a kinematic analysis of dams' was conducted using daily videorecordings of their activity. Postflight, prenatal fetuses were externalized from the uterus while keeping umbilical and placental connections to the dam intact. EKG electrodes were implanted in the embryos and EKG was monitored during vestibular perturbations of a 10s, 70° degree tilt. Postnatally, pups were placed supine in and out of water and videorecorded in order to evaluate their standard righting response and water immersion righting response. Pups were also subjected to rotary stimulation to evaluate their responses to horizontal rotation. Rat pregnancy and parturition were also studied. Animals were recorded inflight to observe the behavior of the dams. Immediately postflight, dams were placed in a glass chamber and videotaped before and after parturition.

Results:

Results from the vestibular portion of the study are as follows: Flight fetuses responded more dramatically than the controls to vestibular perturbations. Pups had no difference in the success or latency of the righting response indicating the flight groups retained the ability to orientate themselves with respect to gravity. Flight pups tested on recovery day 3, had a diminished water righting response, but flight pups tested on recovery day 5 could not be distinguished from control animals. Flight pups showed the same response as controls during the rotary stimulus, but were less-likely to perform the post-rotary righting response. Results from the pregnancy and parturition portion of this study are as follows: The flight dams displayed seven more times rolling movement than controls, probably due to the increased number of surfaces available in microgravity. Immediately postflight, flight dams in general moved less. Flight dams had uncomplicated, and successful vaginal deliveries, and had similar size litters. However, flight dams had significantly more lordosis contractions probably related to spaceflight muscle atrophy.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Krasnov, IgorCo-Investigator: Grindeland, RichardCo-Investigator: Sawchenko, PaulCo-Investigator: Vale, Wylie
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Morphological and physiological investigations of animals have demonstrated that the cerebellar vermis receives proprioceptive signals from hindlimbs and produces a regulatory effect on antigravitational muscles. Morphological examinations of the nervous system of Cosmos and SLS-1 rats have revealed structural changes in spinal ganglia, somatosensory cortex and spinal cord, which pointed to a reduced number of extero- and proprioceptive signals entering the brain and reduced activity of spinal motoneurons. Another change is decreased tone of antigravitational muscles. In this context, it is important to study the anterior vermis, one of the structures regulating antigravitational muscles, of animals flown in space with the purpose of better understanding the mechanism of adaptation of antigravitational muscles to microgravity. In this study quantitative histochemical and morphometric examinations of the upper central lobe of the vermis were performed.

Approach:

The upper central lobe of the vermis of rats was examined. Cytochrome oxidase activity was determined histochemically. In parallel sections the neuronal soma and nucleolus were stained according to the modified method of Howell and Black. The dorsal central lobe was identified using a rat brain atlas. Cytochrome oxidase activity in the Purkinje cell cytoplasm, molecular layer, neuropile and granular layer glomerules of the dorsal central lobe was measured densitometrically at 450 mm. Optical density of the cytoplasm was measured in 3-5 sites of 50 Purkinje cells of each animal. 50 optical density measurements were taken in the molecular layer, neuropile and granular layer glomerules. The nucleolar and neuronal cross-sections were measured in 40 stained Purkinje cell sections by means of an image analyzer. The resulting data were processed according to the Student-Fisher statistical test.

Results:

The results of quantitative histochemistry of flight rats sacrificed 4-5 hours after spaceflight showed a trend toward a higher cytochrome oxidase activity in Purkinje cells, molecular layer and granular layer glomerules. This trend was most significant in the molecular layer with an increase of 10 percent. Cytochrome oxidase activity measured histochemically indicates dorsal central lobe function during flight. No changes were observed in the size of the Purkinje cell nucleolus and cell body taken from the dorsal central lobe of flight rats. This suggests there were no changes in the synthesis rate of Purkinje cells, and their activity was equal to that of vivarium controls. Therefore, these Purkinje cells maintained their capability to inhibit neurons of the dorsal caudal compartment of the lateral vestibular compartment during spaceflight. Observations give evidence that the number of afferent signals reaching the dorsal central lobe in microgravity is adequate to maintain its activity at a level comparable to that on the ground.

experiment_title: The Role of Oxidative Stress and Inflammation on Synaptic Functions after Exposure to Space Radiation
parameter_html:
Cognitive function
Dendritic complexity
Memory
Spine density
investigators: Principal Investigator: Rosi, SusannaCo-Investigator: Huang, Ting-TingCo-Investigator: Nelson, Gregory
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This work focused on studying changes in synaptic functions associated with the development of cognitive dysfunction after low doses of space irradiation and the relative role of oxidative stress and inflammation. Irradiation of the central nervous system (CNS) can significantly affect the hippocampus, a structure critical for cognitive function. Activity-dependent modification of synapses underlies memory formation and involves changes in the dendritic arbors. The maintenance of the dendritic system, including spine density, dendritic arbors, BDNF and plasticity-related protein expression are essential to maintain proper synaptic functions. The dendritic system connects the neuronal network, mediates functional integration of newborn neurons, and controls synaptic functions; yet it is sensitive to increased oxidative stress and inflammation.

The purpose of this study was to determine how space-relevant doses of radiation affect dendritic maintenance as it pertains to synaptic functions and memory. Investigators hypothesized that space radiation, even at low doses, impairs synaptic functions with negative consequences for cognition and that these effects are mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Quantitatively determine the short and long term effects of irradiation with protons (150 MeV/n; 0.15, 0.5, 0.9 Gy), 56Fe (600 MeV/n; 0.15, 0.4 Gy), and 16O (600 MeV/n; 0.15, 0.4 Gy) on synaptic functions and the role of oxidative stress and inflammation.
  2. Determine if altered levels of extracellularly generated oxygen free radicals play a prominent role in synaptic function following low doses irradiation with protons, 56Fe and 16O.

APPROACH:
Investigators used novel mouse models with neuronal-specific overexpression of an antioxidant enzyme to address the role of oxidative stress. The mice were exposed to space-relevant doses of proton, 56Fe, or 16O and analyzed for acute and late effects. Experimental endpoints included cognitive functions, dendritic structures and synaptic functions, molecules that control the dendritic system, inflammatory responses, and indices of oxidative stress. This systematic approach allowed them to connect the functional output of cognition to the molecular pathway that controls synaptic plasticity and memory; and to determine the role of oxidative stress and inflammation in space radiation-mediated changes.

RESULTS:
Despite the late start during the first 10 months investigators were able to make significant progress in their proposed studies addressing both short and long-term consequences of proton irradiation on CNS function. Sixty four animals were trained in the contextual fear conditioning paradigm and two weeks later animals were irradiated with 0, 0.15, 0.5, 1Gy doses of protons. The animal previously trained in the CFC were tested for memory recall two weeks after irradiation. Significant reduction in contextual and cued freezing following proton irradiation across all experimental groups was observed. Because sham-irradiated mice also showed significant reduction in contextual and cued freezing, the reduction was likely affected by the intensive animal shipping and handling during the experimental period. Although baseline freezing before irradiation, both before training and the baseline before cued test, in the 0.5 Gy group was not significantly lower than that of other experimental groups, the Post-IR baseline freezing in this group was significantly lower than that in 0, and 0.15 Gy experimental group, suggesting reduced anxiety in a novel environment in mice receiving 0.5 Gy proton irradiation. To account for differences in baseline freezing before tone/light was turned on; the ratio of Post-IR cued freezing to Post-IR baseline freezing was calculated and compared among experimental groups. A trend of increased cued freezing post-IR was suggested in mice received 0.5 Gy proton irradiation. The data suggested a subtle change in the fear memory at 0.5 Gy, but not at lower (0.15 Gy) or higher (1 Gy) doses. Notably, in these animals there was about a significant reduction in spine density in hippocampal granule cells. Examination of dendritic structures in other brain regions and the extent of oxidative stress in hippocampal formation is currently underway and will be terminated in the next few months. Hippocampal gene array analysis demonstrate that exposure to low doses of space radiation alters the expression of molecules known to be involved in the recruitment of various types of monocytic cells. The up regulations of these genes were most pronounced at the lowest dose and were abolished at the highest dose (1Gy).

Sixty four animals were used for the long-term studies: Novel object recognition test was used to measure hippocampal-dependent episodic memory three months after proton irradiation. Results suggest that 0.15Gy proton irradiation affect the hippocampal dependent novel object recognition test measured. Object in Place was used to measure associative recognition memory and requires a subject to make an association between an object and place in which it was previously encountered and depends on the interactions between the hippocampus, perirhinal, and prefrontal cortices. Results demonstrate that associative recognition memory was impaired in animals irradiated with 0.5 and 1Gy. Examination of dendritic structures and the extent of oxidative stress in hippocampal formation and the prefrontal cortex is currently underway.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Spaceflight Effects on Regeneration in Lower Vertebrates: Molecular-Biology and Cytochemistry Examinations
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Almeida, EduardoCo-Investigator: Domoratskaya, ElenaCo-Investigator: Grigorian, EleonoraCo-Investigator: Mitashov, VictorCo-Investigator: Vercoutere, Wenonah
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

To identify molecular-biological mechanisms of spaceflight stimulating effects on cell proliferation and tissue regeneration in newts Pleurodeles waltl.

APPROACH:

Our experimental procedure involves the administration of the immunodetectable nucleotide analog bromedeoxyuridine (BrdU) in the water available in the triton habitat, followed by recovery of available tissue samples for measurement of nucleotide incorporation in specific cell types. Delivery of BrdU will be performed using a miniature osmotic pump that will be programmed to start delivery after the animals reach orbit. Programming is achieved by layering the BrdU containing solution with a layer of inert oil that will delay drug delivery for as long as necessary for preflight animal loading into the launch vehicle. We will measure overall proliferation, morphology and gene expression in flight tissues compared to 1g controls as well as in cells that express stem cell markers specific to tissues of interest.

RESULTS:

Cells in spaceflight tail regenerates proliferated at a slightly slower rate and were more undifferentiated than those in ground synchronous controls. In addition, the size of regenerating tails from spaceflight was smaller than synchronous controls. However, onboard temperature recordings show that the temperature in the spaceflight was about 2°C lower than ground synchronous controls, possibly txplaining the observed differences. (See results for Foton-M3).

investigators: Principal Investigator: De Witt, JohnCo-Investigator: Everett-Downs, MeghanCo-Investigator: Guilliams, MarkCo-Investigator: Newby, NathanielCo-Investigator: Ploutz- Snyder, LoriCo-Investigator: Scott- Pandorf, Melissa
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the Kinematics T2 experiment is to collect quantitative data from which to assess current exercise prescriptions for participating crewmembers on the International Space Station (ISS). Detailed biomechanical analyses of locomotion are needed to determine if biomechanics differ between normal and microgravity environments and to determine how combinations of external loads and exercise speed influence joint loading during in-flight treadmill exercise. Biomechanical analyses will aid in understanding potential differences in gait motion and allow for model-based determination of joint and muscle forces during exercise. The data will be used to characterize differences in specific bone and muscle loading during locomotion in the two gravitational conditions. By understanding these mechanisms, appropriate exercise prescriptions can be developed that address deficiencies.

Specific Aim 1: To quantify joint kinematics during treadmill locomotion on the ISS, and to compare those to treadmill locomotion on Earth. The goal of this aim is to measure joint kinematics during treadmill exercise using motion capture data collection. Exercise prescriptions have been developed under the assumption that walking and running in microgravity have the same training effects as during normal gravity. However, if locomotion kinematics differ between microgravity and normal gravity, it is reasonable to hypothesize that training effects may also differ. Furthermore, treadmill locomotion in microgravity occurs on a vibration isolation and stabilization (VIS) treadmill, which may increase the potential for training differences. Similarities and differences in joint kinematics during treadmill locomotion between normal gravity and microgravity on the ISS will be quantified.

Specific Aim 2: To develop a computer model that will assess locomotion speed and external loading condition influences upon joint torque. The overall goal of the advanced exercise prescription being provided to the crewmembers is to increase loading at the joints in order to provide a greater stimulus for bone and muscle health. The computer modeling approach requires inputs of anthropometric measurements, motion kinematics, and external forces applied to the body. External forces applied to the body will be measured with instrumentation built into the treadmill. A subject-specific computer model will be developed and will provide joint kinetic approximations. These approximations will be used to assess the effectiveness of the exercise prescription and will allow for an iterative approach in exercise prescription modification based on evidence. Furthermore, these data will provide better understanding of how exercise speed and external load affects the forces experienced by the joints and muscles. Providing subject loading information for exercise prescriptions will increase the effectiveness of exercise prescription.

APPROACH:
The ground-based portion of this study consisted of a single preflight data collection session to be conducted in the Exercise Physiology Countermeasure (ExPC) Project Biomechanics Laboratory, at Johnson Space Center. This Baseline Data Collection (BDC) session included crew instruction for placing Kinematics T2 markers and positioning of the calibration card in view of the video camera. A Kistler Gaitway instrumented treadmill housed in the laboratory was used for data collection, and the entire session lasted approximately 75 minutes. Prior to exercise, subjects donned a chest-band heart rate (HR) monitor and resting HR was recorded. Detailed biomechanical analyses of locomotion are needed to determine if biomechanics differ between normal and microgravity environments and to determine how combinations of external loads and exercise speed influence joint loading during in-flight treadmill exercise. Biomechanical analyses will aid in understanding potential differences in gait motion and allow for model-based determination of joint and muscle forces during exercise. The data will be used to characterize differences in specific bone and muscle loading during locomotion in the two gravitational conditions. By understanding these mechanisms, appropriate exercise prescriptions can be developed that address deficiencies.

Specific Aim 1: To quantify joint kinematics during treadmill locomotion on the ISS, and to compare those to treadmill locomotion on Earth. The goal of this aim is to measure joint kinematics during treadmill exercise using motion capture data collection. Exercise prescriptions have been developed under the assumption that walking and running in microgravity have the same training effects as during normal gravity. However, if locomotion kinematics differ between microgravity and normal gravity, it is reasonable to hypothesize that training effects may also differ. Furthermore, treadmill locomotion in microgravity occurs on a vibration isolation and stabilization (VIS) treadmill, which may increase the potential for training differences.
