experiment_description:
Objectives:

It is possible that the mechanical behavior of the baroreceptor region of the aortic arch may be changed, or a resetting of the baroreceptor response may occur, when mammals are exposed to chronic microgravity. The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of microgravity on the structural and functional development of the aortic baroreflex, a neural control system for blood pressure. The experiment objectives were to observe and analyze the effect of microgravity on the baroreflex responses and on the fine structure of the aortic nerves, which are the afferent pathways of the aortic baroreflex, in growing rats raised in space.

Approach:

Six 9-day-old rat neonates raised for 16 days in space were selected for physiological and histological examinations on the day of landing (Recovery + 0 days = R+0), and another six neonates were reserved for experiments on 30 days postflight (R+30). Following administration of anesthesia, blood pressure, heart rate and aortic nerve activity were recorded, and baroreflex tests were pharmacologically performed. The animal body was perfused with a fixative and tissues were prepared for electron and light microscopy analysis. Rheological properties of the aorta extirpated on R+0 were also observed.

Results:

Flight pups (FLT) had significantly lower body weights than the Simulated Caged Control (SIM) and Vivarium (VIV) ground controls, but there were no significant correlations between body weight and other parameters examined. The FLT group initially had difficulty walking, and the tip of the tail in most was slightly necrotic. Two FLT pups could not be used for baroreflex tests because of very low blood pressure observed on R+0.

Differences in blood pressure and heart rate seen at R+0 between the FLT and control groups dissipated by R+30. Each parameter of blood pressure, including mean blood pressure (MBP), systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure (DBP), was lower in the FLT group than either the SIM and VIV groups at R+0, though there was no significant difference between FLT and control groups at R+30. Blood pressure in the R+30 FLT group was significantly higher than that measured on R+0. Similarly, basal heart rate (HR) at R+0 was higher in the FLT group than in the control groups, though there was no significant difference between FLT and SIM. On R+30 all three groups showed lower HR than at R+0 with no significant differences between both VIV groups.

Baroreceptor reflexes behaved similarly. On R+0 the index of baroreceptor reflex sensitivity (delta HR%/ delta MBP%) showed significant differences between the FLT and SIM group, with the FLT pups having the lowest value. At R+30 there was no significant index differences between the three groups. Afferent sensitivity in the aortic baroreceptor reflex was also decreased in the FLT group on R+0, and again differences were not seen between any groups at R+30.

Structural changes in the aortic nerves and wall appeared more fixed. Due to structural and technical problems, samples of aortic nerve available for electron microscopic analysis were extremely limited. On R+0, the numbers of unmyelinated fibers and the ratio of unmyelinated to all other fibers were significantly less in the FLT group than in the controls, and these differences were still observed at R+30. Aortic wall tension produced by strain was significantly smaller in FLT than in both control groups on R+0. The thickness of the aortic walls in FLT pups was about 70% of those in the other groups; the amount of smooth muscle cells and fine elastin fibers were markedly reduced.

In conclusion, the space environment, probably its microgravity component, affects development of the aortic baroreflex system and autonomic regulation of the blood circulation. However, the function of the baroreflex system can develop normally and adapt to the earth environment of 1 G if the animal returns during its developing stage; although, there is a possibility that the structural differences of the afferent pathway may be permanent.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Cytokines, proteins that serve as messengers to activate immune responses in lymphocytes and macrophages, appear to be altered during spaceflight. Because of this suppression of the immune system in otherwise healthy subjects, spaceflight offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of biological substances without the complications of illnesses normally present in immunosuppressed subjects. Polyethylene Glycol-Interleukin 2 (PEG-IL-2) is an immunological mediator and enhancer developed and manufactured by Chiron Corporation. The purpose of this experiment in conjunction with the Immune 2 experiment was to confirm and define the ability of Polyethylene Glycol-Interleukin 2 (PEG-IL2) to prevent or ameliorate the detrimental effects of space flight on immune responses of rats.

Approach:

Half of the animals in each group were injected intravenously with PEG-IL-2 two to three hours before transfer to the Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs). Upon recovery of flight subjects, the following tissues and organs were removed and weighed: brain, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, trachea, spleen, and thymus. Blood samples were collected and analyzed for blood cell counts and differentials. They were also analyzed for corticosterone concentration with radioimmunoassay. Macrophage (M-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage stimulating factor (GM-CSF) dependent macrophage colony formation from bone marrow cells was assayed. Lymphocytes were obtained from the spleen and lymph nodes and assayed to determine cell proliferation rates and the secretion of cytokines, M-CSF, IL-6, IFN-g, and TGF-§. Peritoneal macrophages were assayed for secretion of TNFa and IL-6. The femur and tibia were collected and underwent biomechanical testing to calculate strength (N), deflection (mm), and energy (mJ). Bones were then dried and ashed in order to assess mineral content.

Results:

The results of this experiment are joined with the Immune 2 experiment. There was no significant pattern observed for body weight and organ weight parameters. Additionally, few immunological parameters were consistent across the Immune 1 and Immune 2 experiments, making conclusive observations difficult. Significant changes in bone parameters were observed in Immune 2, but not Immune 1. The inconsistencies between the two experiments prevented any conclusive evidence concerning the effectiveness of the PEG-IL-2 treatment. Several factors may have played a role in these discrepancies. Some of the animals flown were found to have damage to their tails upon recovery (necrosis, loss, and gangrenous tissues). However, compared to the animals in the same group, these changes did not correlate with any of the parameters measured. While there were the expected trends in the Immune 1 experiments, the control animals did not exhibit as many of the flight-related changes as were anticipated. In contrast, the control group in the Immune 2 study did have more dramatic changes associated with spaceflight. These differences in the control groups may have been due to the fact that flight animals in the Immune 2 experiment were exposed to significantly higher ambient temperatures than animals in Immune 1.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are responsible for tissue development, help maintain homeostasis in mature tissues, and are being considered for therapeutic treatments of a variety of cellular lineages including bone, skeletal muscles, and fatty tissues. Chemical and mechanical factors modulate lineage commitment; however, spaceflight can drastically change these cues and hence, influence physiologic processes, such as bone formation. We hypothesize that such changes arise from altered cell-cell interactions and chemotactic behaviors brought about by cell morphologies and cytoarchitectures adopted during microgravity.

The effects of microgravity on MSC morphology, migration and osteogenic differentiation using a newly developed clinorotation time-lapse microscopy (CTM) system and lab-on-chip devices to generate chemical gradients were investigated. While the underlying principles of CTM are identical to conventional clinostats, CTM is amenable to live-cell imaging, without prohibitively large experimental setups or disruption of culture environments. Importantly, CTM represents a significant step forward in space biology research, because it enables ground-based microgravity studies of not only traditional end-point outcomes, but also dynamic cellular processes.

Specific aims include: (1) investigate the long-term, dynamic behaviors of MSCs in simulated microgravity by analyzing the time-dependent alterations to morphology, motility, and cell density and (2) quantify changes in distributions of focal adhesions and osteogenic phenotype indicators by using CTM to monitor a live-cell alkaline phosphatase (AP) stain and end-point vinculin, lipids, and AP stains. This investigation provides novel insight into how dynamic MSC events are affected by microgravity. We believe that our hypothesis may partially explain a mechanism responsible for reduced bone mass and impaired fracture healing in space.

APPROACH:
The experiments will be conducted using commercially available cultured human mesenchymal stem cells in custom lab-on-chip (clinochip) devices. To investigate the long-term effects of microgravity on cellular behavior, we constructed a stand-alone incubation chamber that houses our clinorotation apparatus to maintain controlled 37 ºC, 50% humidity, and 5% CO2 culture conditions while under constant clinorotation. Each day, clinochips will be transferred from the incubator to our clinorotation time-lapse microscopy (CTM) system for imaging in an environmental enclosure with identical 37 ºC, 50% humidity, and 5% CO2 conditions. The environmental chamber is housed on the stage of an inverted epi-fluorescence microscope programmed for multi-position, time-lapse microscopy. Both fluorescence and brightfield (DIC or phase contrast) microscopy will be used to capture images during the course of clinorotation for morphology and motility studies. After clinorotation, cells are chemically-fixed for immunostaining.

Images will be analyzed with custom algorithms in Matlab (Mathworks) to create time-varying cell density maps and to calculate motility parameters including persistence times, random motility coefficients, and migration speeds. Cell-cell interactions are investigated by correlating density maps with local morphology, actin characteristics, and motility data.

RESULTS:
In our first set of experiments using the clinochip system, we demonstrated that MSC spreading events are profoundly affected by the angular frequency of clinorotation. In contrast to our expectations, MSC motility appeared to be influenced more by cell shape than by clinorotation directly. Regardless of rotation speed, circular MSCs exhibited little migration, whereas elongated MSCs migrated similarly to those in standard gravity. Because cell shape was the most sensitive to clinorotation, we expanded the scope of Aim 1 to include the development of a technique to study cell-substrate interactions. This led to our first ever characterization of cell traction forces during clinorotation.

Toward the completion of Aim 2, we worked in parallel to build and validate a new system for long-term clinorotation of cells in clinochips for up to 28 days. Our findings of cell rounding in clinorotated cells suggested that simulated microgravity might have an adverse effect on osteogenesis, as others have shown using soft or micropatterned islands to limit cell attachment. Consistent with these previous reports, our MSCs did not exhibit any osteogenesis when subjected to clinorotation over 14 days, while cells in standard gravity were robustly osteogenic and producing calcified matrix by day 14. Overall, our work under this NASA grant has laid the foundation toward future studies in the characterization of molecular mechanisms in gravisensing and in the discovery of therapeutic countermeasures against adverse health changes during space exploration.

experiment_title: Effects of Microgravity on Ocular Vascular Hydrodynamics
parameter_html: None
investigators: Principal Investigator: Zawieja, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is reported to affect ~40% of astronauts completing long-duration spaceflights (as of May 2017) and has been characterized as the development of one or more findings: optic disc edema, hyperopic shifts, globe flattening, cotton-wool spots, or choroidal folds. The leading hypothesis for the development of ocular changes is that prolonged exposure to the headward fluid shift that occurs in weightlessness is the primary instigating factor, and additional factors such as genetic disposition, ambient CO2 on the International Space Station, or on-orbit exercise countermeasures may augment or diminish the development of ocular symptoms. However, the pathophysiology of SANS remains unclear. Evidence for the contribution of intracranial pressure alone in SANS is controversial. Therefore, studies of ocular vascular hydrodynamics are required to clarify if chronic mild elevations of ocular pressure variables compromise ocular structure and function. Since all blood and lymph vessels are compliant, fluid-filled structures whose pressures are strongly influenced by gravity, we propose to focus our studies on the potential changes directly to the ocular vasculature caused by microgravity. Perfusion of the optic nerve and inner retina for sufficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients is dependent on retinal blood flow. The pressure gradient for driving blood flow through the inner retina begins with the arterial pressure in the feed artery, which is the central retinal artery in humans. Changes in retinal blood flow or pressure may contribute to the formation of cotton wool spots and optic disc edema. Optic disc edema, choroidal folds, and optic nerve thickening may also result from ocular venous congestion and/or elevated venous compliance, disruption of the blood-retinal barrier, and/or reduction in ocular lymph flow. There has been no systematic analysis of the ocular vascular changes in microgravity. We have assembled a team of experts in SANS and all 3 main vascular types (arteries, veins, and lymphatics) to address this information gap. Thus, the objective of this application is to determine whether microgravity alters the structure and function of the ocular vasculature at the level of feed arteries, venous exchange and capacitance vessels, and lymph vessels. This provides a novel comprehensive evaluation of the ocular vascular elements. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that microgravity/spaceflight-induced changes in the structure/function of the ocular vasculature lead to alterations in ocular hydrodynamics and promote symptoms of SANS. We will accomplish this objective using in vivo measures of vascular function (retinal artery blood flow, retinal arteriole and venular diameter measurements, and retinal venular permeability measures) and in vitro studies of freshly isolated vascular structure and function (vessel/tissue histology, arterial vasomotor regulation, venous compliance measures, and lymphatic transport characteristics). These studies will be conducted in mice flown in space and the corresponding ground controls to address the following specific aims:1: Evaluate the effects of microgravity on ocular artery structure/function.2: Evaluate the effects of microgravity on ocular vein structure/function.3: Evaluate the effects of microgravity on ocular lymphatic structure/function.

APPROACH:
To examine the Specific Aims 1-3 outlined in the research proposal, Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) will be used. The in vivo assessments of blood flow velocity (Doppler ultrasound) and permeability (intravital microscopy) between eyes (left and right) from flight and ground animals will be analyzed using two-way ANOVA without repeated measures. For in vitro assessment of vascular reactivity to pharmacological agonists at different concentrations between eyes (left and right) from flight and ground animals, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures will be used. All statistical tests will be two-sided and a test resulting in a p-value of less than or equal to 0.05 will be considered statistically significant. The post hoc unpaired least significant difference tests will be performed and interpreted with the Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons. All the p values will be based on two-sided tests.

RESULTS:
This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

experiment_title: Effects of Age and Activity Level on Tibia Mass and Distribution
parameter_html:
Activity, exercise; Weight load, whole body
Bone density index (BDI)
Body mass
Age
Height

investigators: Principal Investigator: Whalen, Robert
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study is to gain a better understanding of the relationship between age, activity level (runners vs non-runners) and site specific bone mass and long bone structure.

APPROACH:
Three studies were performed because nonbone soft issue in the path of the x-ray beam bone is comprised of materials that have different attenuation properties than mineralized bone. The first accuracy study involved the construction of a large plexiglass tube with a bladder filled with saline to emulate soft tissues for the leg. An aluminum phantom was used to estimate in vivo setup accuracy at 3 different angles and two energies by two sets of three scans. The second study determined the in vivo precision of cross-sectional structural parameters in the long bones of 15 female human non-runners on the same day repeated measures for 60o and 90o. The third study compared the parameters in the legs of 14 25-35 year old women with the same in 12 women >age 60 and at two activity levels (recreational runners and non-runners). Scans were taken of the middle third of the lower right leg; structural parameters for the tibia and fibula were determined on each scan line, averaged over the section and adjusted by factors accounting for body size variations.

RESULTS:
Study one: Parameters for the eight rectangular sections of the aluminum phantom were averaged over four lines per section and errors computed as differences from expected values. Principal moments were estimated within 2.3% and principal angles were estimated within 2.3o. Study two: Low energy yielded slightly better precision than high with the area measurement the highest precision (CV <1%). Principal and polar moment CV were 2-6% and the precision of the principal angle was 3-6o. Study three: Low loaders had higher body weights than high loaders, emphasizing the need to account for body size in estimates of bone structure. All differences in the tibia were related to load level, not age. Imax was higher by 46%, Imin by 30%, J by 41% and A by 27% and along the midshaft, the principle angle for runners was consistently aligned closer to the AP direction than in nonrunners. Fibula results did not show the same pattern of results as in the tibia. There was no dependence on age or load group in any parameter for the fibula. Conclusions: A three-scan densitometric method for measuring cross-sectional structural parameters in long bones in vivo was validated; accuracy and precision measurements established confidence limits. Structural parameters related to bone stiffness and strength are increased in female recreational runners compared with nonrunners and these increases are maintained with age. These measures that incorporate bone mass distribution all had larger percent differences than area (A) and were therefore more sensitive measures in detecting differences between runners and nonrunners than simple bone mass measurements (A) alone or I in a single, nonprincipal plane. From the activity study results, it is postulated that higher loads associated with running lead to increased cross-sectional parameters to support axial loads, bending and torsion in the tibia.

experiment_title: Targeting Protein Cross Talk Signaling as a Biological Predictor for Space Radiation Cancer Risk
parameter_html:
Bystander cells
DNA damage
Free radicals
Human aortic endothelial cells
Luciferase activity
Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kB)
Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Natarajan, MohanCo-Investigator: Blakely, EleanorCo-Investigator: Mohan, SumathyCo-Investigator: Prihoda, Tom
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
One of the important concerns of 'late effects' after space radiation exposure is the onset of cancers. The onset of cancer could be initiated by radiation-induced molecular changes that are persistently maintained through a positive feedback cycle and amplified over time. Investigators proposed that two key proteins, nuclear factor kappa Beta (NF-kB) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-a), sequentially co-ordinate and control this cascade of events. A novel role of these proteins in radiation-induced tumor development is identified through recent in vitro and in vivo studies after low linear energy transfer (LET) radiation exposure. In this project investigators addressed: (i) how low doses of high LET radiation trigger initial damage signals that remain persistent and are maintained in the memory of the cell/tissue, (ii) how these signals are amplified, (iii) how these amplified signals are transmitted to result in a sustained radial expansion of initial damage, and finally (iv) how radial communication of these signals activates factors that are responsible for predisposing the susceptible cells to carcinogenesis. Investigators aim to examine these objectives using both in vitro (parallel plate flow model) and ex-vivo (mouse-artery organ culture) approaches, in which irradiated normal vascular endothelial cells in an intact tissue setup or organ culture will be allowed to communicate with the co-existing non-targeted normal or pro-tumorigenic cells from lung, skin, and breast tissue.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Study the significance of low doses (0, 0.2, 0.4, or 0.8 Gy) of high-LET radiation exposure on an altered autocrine signaling mechanism that initiates, amplifies, and sustains a positive feedback cycle, i.e., triggering NF-kB -->TNF-a --> NF-kB signaling in the targeted cells.
  2. Study and compare the significance of the intercellular communication that is responsible for amplification of the signals by replicating the activation of NF-kB - TNF-a positive feedback loop in the non-targeted bystander cells.
  3. Study, in targeted versus non-targeted bystander cells, the influence of sustained amplification of NF-kB - TNF-a positive feedback loop on (a) stimulating predisposing factors for carcinogenesis and (b) potentiating in vitro and in vivo tumorigenesis.

APPROACH:
Experiments were conducted with pro-tumorigenic cells (BEP2D, and MCF-10A) that were either irradiated with 56Fe or 28Si (600 MeV/amu) to a dose of 0.2 Gy x 3 or mock irradiated. The cells were repeatedly cultured to 30 to 40 passages after radiation exposure and injected into nude mice to determine the tumorigenic potentials. Similarly, the cells pre-incubated with NF-kB inhibitor, isohelanin, for 30 minutes prior to exposure were also, in parallel, cultured to subsequent passages. Cells at a density of 10 x 10(6) cells in 0.2 ml saline were injected into nude mice. In a second set of experiments, the pro-tumorigenic cells were irradiated and co-cultured with non-irradiated pro-tumorigenic cells. Non-targeted pro-tumorigenic cells that are co-cultured with the irradiated tumor cells were continuously passaged to 30-40 passages. The later experiments were conducted in order to identify whether the TNF-a secreted out from the irradiated cells are responsible for initiating a similar TNF-a-NF-kB feedback cycle in the bystander cells and those cells are capable of transforming into tumorigenic cells. A total of 5 nude mice (Foxn1nu/Foxn1nu) at a 6-8 weeks of age per group was used in this study.

RESULTS:
The first set of results indicated that the pro-tumorigenic cells co-cultured with irradiated cells were capable of transforming into tumorigenic cells. Both group of mice, i.e., mice either receiving cells that were directly irradiated or mice that were injected with bystander cells that were co-cultured with irradiated cells, showed palpable tumors on day 5.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Radiation and Gliomagenesis: A Sensitive Model System to Evaluate the Tumorigenic Potential of HZE Particles
parameter_html:
INK4a-ARF
MET amplification
MET signaling
Ink4a gene
Ink4b gene
Pten gene
investigators: Principal Investigator: Burma, SandeepCo-Investigator: Bachoo, RobertCo-Investigator: Boothman, David
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is a paucity of systematic studies carried out with well-defined model systems to evaluate the tumorigenic potential of HZE particles that are presumed to pose a significant cancer risk to astronauts. The investigators have shown that these particles induce DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that are repaired slowly and incompletely and trigger persistent DNA damage signaling events. In order to evaluate the carcinogenic consequences of such unrepaired DNA lesions, they utilized genetically engineered astrocytes and neural stem cells (NSCs) as well as transgenic mouse models representing progressive steps in the development of Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM). These lethal brain tumors are the third leading cause of cancer-related death among adults aged 30 to 50 years that are known to be induced by ionizing radiation. The past years have seen unprecedented advances in the genomic analyses of adult GBM tumors by the Cancer Genome Atlas Network, which reveal that these tumors have radically altered genomes with five key genetic changes dominating: loss of Ink4a, Arf, p53, or PTEN and amplification of estimated glomerular filtration rate (EGFR) (especially the constitutively active EGFRvIII). The investigators developed astrocyte and NSC lines as well as mouse models with targeted deletions of these genes in logical combinations representing the progression of primary or secondary GBMs. This genetic progression model, though reductionist in approach, provides a realistic framework for evaluating and understanding how known genetic mutations may cooperate with charged particle radiation and contribute to the initiation and progression of high-grade gliomas. The investigators hypothesized that poorly repaired DNA damage produced by charged particles will result in malignant progression towards brain cancer, and that this progression can be accelerated by predisposing oncogenic activations/tumor suppressor losses. More importantly, these "pre-initiated" murine astrocytes/NSCs will allowed investigators to rapidly quantify the transforming potential of charged particles relative to gamma rays both in vitro and in vivo.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Evaluation of DNA damage responses to charged particles in neural stem cells (NSCs) and astrocytes in vitro and in vivo.
  2. Evaluation of the tumorigenic potential of charged particles relative to gamma rays in vitro and in vivo.
  3. Identification of the genetic and gene expression changes underlying particle-induced tumorigenesis.

APPROACH:
This study consisted of two components: 1) An ‘in vitro’ component where primary murine astrocytes and NSCs with glioma relevant genetic alterations are assayed for transformation after particle radiation; and 2) For the ‘in vivo’ component, investigators used genetically engineered mice in which deletions of the most critical, glioma-relevant tumor suppressor genes (Ink4a, Ink4b, Arf, p53, and/or PTEN) can be targeted to the mouse brain. The Ink/Arf and p53 deletions are generally mutually exclusive in GBM, hence two distinct cohorts of mice were used. These models, in a reductionist manner, represent progressive steps in gliomagenesis, and based on published in vitro work, investigators hypothesized that they may have heightened sensitivity to transformation by particle radiation. Furthermore, investigators compared brain tumor development in these models after irradiation with 1Gy or 0.5Gy of 600 MeV/n Fe ions, in comparison with 1Gy or 4 Gy of x-rays.

RESULTS:
The investigators discovered that Fe ions are more tumorigenic than gamma rays and that loss of the Ink4a/4b/Arf tumor suppressor locus is a critical event in HZE-induced transformation. Brain tumor incidence observed at nine months with loss of Ink4a and Arf alone was low after exposure to X-rays (4Gy) or Fe ions (1Gy). Importantly, the incidence of brain tumors increased significantly with additional loss of Ink4b, corroborating in vitro studies which showed that Ink4b is an important barrier to radiation-induced transformation. The tumor incidence was the same (25%) with 1Gy of Fe ions and a 4-fold higher dose of X-rays, suggesting a RBE of 4 for transformation by Fe ions. Genomic analyses indicate that MET amplification is a critical event in HZE-induced gliomagenesis in this model and that MET signaling supports a GBM cancer stem cell phenotype. Similar tumor incidence (~30%) was observed in the second mouse cohort which carries heterozygous deletions of the p53 and Pten genes. Deletion of a single allele of either gene, in combination with 0.5 Gy of 600 MeV/n Fe ions, is sufficient to trigger gliomagenesis with low frequency. Heterozygous deletions of both p53 and Pten (p53+/-;Pten+/-) increase the frequency of tumor formation to 30 percent.

OBJECTIVES:
For extended missions in space, astronauts will be exposed to a radiation environment unlike any on the earth's surface. Galactic cosmic rays include a particularly worrisome component of energetic iron nuclei which are high atomic number, high energy (HZE) charged particles with linear energy transfer (LET) similar to alpha particles but with very different track structures. While the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of a particular radiation roughly depends on the LET, the very different track structures for these two radiations may well modulate this RBE even if they have identical average LETs. Further, this "radiation quality" for the exposures actually relevant for astronauts will be modified by interactions with materials in the spacecraft, including their own bodies.

Basic to virtually all relevant biological effects of ionizing radiation is the underlying damage produced in DNA, and the subsequent cellular processing of such damage. The damage can be qualitatively different for different kinds of radiations, and the genetics of the biological systems exposed can greatly affect damage processing and ultimate outcome the biological effect of concern. The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosome rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. It is important, therefore, to understand cellular responses to DNA damage and to elucidate the mechanisms and phenotypic consequences of DSB misrepair.

APPROACH:
The general aim in this proposal is to examine connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis, namely chromosome aberration formation, mutagenesis and telomere fusions, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining system, using RNA interference to systematically knockdown gene products known to be involved, either singly or in combination.

RESULTS:
This project utilized the powerful technique of RNA interference (RNAi) to deplete levels of various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) double-strand break (DSB) repair system, then to study the effects on HZE radiation-induced chromosomal rearrangements, gene mutation and telomere dysfunction.

The accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is critical for the maintenance of genomic integrity and function. Incorrect repair of such lesions results in chromosomal rearrangements and mutations that can lead to cancer and heritable defects in the progeny of irradiated parents. Focus was on the consequent phenotypic effects of faulty repair by examining connections between cellular radiosensitivity phenotypes relevant for carcinogenesis after exposure to IR, and deficiencies in various components of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) system. In the past year, the deficiency of a protein, called Apollo, was produced using RNAi in a human lymphoblastoid cell line. Exposure of cells exhibiting reduced protein expression to either gamma-rays or 1GeV/nu Fe particles demonstrated differential effects on telomere dysfunction and mutation frequency, as well as differential effects between radiation qualities.

Apollo is a nuclease required for DNA interstrand cross-link repair, and in fact it appears to interact with FANCD2, also involved in that repair pathway. In addition, Apollo may be involved in a more generalized response to DNA damage, in that it may stimulate the activation of ATM, and it seems to interact with the MRN complex, which is a focal point for several modes of repair.

The Apollo nuclease is also implicated in the protection of telomeres; it interacts with TRF2 in S-phase, and actually is an attractive candidate for the processing of telomere ends to generate 3’ single strand overhangs, a critical event and integral part of proper telomere formation. Knockdown of Apollo produced an increase in radiation mutagenesis, both for gamma-ray exposures and for 1 GeV/n Fe particles. The increases were of the same order as those caused by inhibition of DNA-PKcs, and furthermore there were no interactions, synergistic or antagonistic, of Apollo knockdown and DNA-PKcs inhibition. These results suggest that Apollo may be involved in the same pathway as DNA-PKcs, namely repair of DSB by NHEJ.

Telomere instability was also examine following siRNA knockdown of Apollo. Telomere uncapping was found with knockdown of Apollo that was similar to that seen with inhibition of DNA-PKcs and similar between radiation types. These results suggest possible Apollo involvement in repair of IR-induced damage, as well as support a telomeric role for Apollo.

Most recently, a collaborative effort with Dr. Sandy Chang at M.D. Anderson, TX in which SNMIB/Apollo knockout mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) were generated, resulted in data implicating SNMIB/Apollo as a key 5’-3’ exonuclease required for generation of 3’ single-stranded overhangs at newly replicated leading-strand telomeres to protect them from engaging the non-homologous end joining pathway. Results and informtion on this can be found in the EMBO Journal citation listed below.

These experiments have resulted in valuable information regarding CPR question 10.12, “What are the effects of inter-individual diversity?” It was hypothesized that NHEJ repair components are major genetic determinants controlling individual susceptibility to radiation-induced cancer, as well as heritable effects of exposure. Therefore, naturally occurring deficiencies of these proteins within the population will put these individuals at increased risk. Our RNAi approach of experimentally mimicking highly relevant human deficiencies has shed light of this important issue. Our results support the relevance of deficiencies/hypomorphic mutations in NHEJ factors in that they can deregulate rejoining reactions sufficiently to increase incidence of oncogenic rearrangements (misrepair).

This work supports the concept that inherited or acquired mutations in NHEJ factors represent important risk factors for developing cancer, an especially relevant consideration following exposure to ionizing radiations (increased complexity the damage and its repair), and so also impact on CPR question 10.07, “What are the cancer risks in humans from spaceflight?” Our characterizations of telomere dysfunction, chromosome aberration formation and gene mutation serve as important and informative surrogate endpoints for predicting cancer risks.

experiment_title: Workload Tools and Guidelines
parameter_html:
Workload
Task performance
investigators: Principal Investigator: Gore, BrianCo-Investigator: Ahumada, Albert
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Short-duration mission operations are designed to maintain workload levels that are neither too high nor too low. Long-duration mission tasks duplicate those of short-duration missions; however, the possible effects of the extended mission duration are poorly understood. In addition, the cumulative impact that workload-inducing tasks might have on the operator’s performance is ignored if one simply extends short-duration workload planning techniques to long-duration operations. When durations extend to days, weeks, months, and years, social factors such as loneliness and isolation may increasingly influence performance, occasionally to the detriment of the system’s operation. This discrepancy between short and long-duration perspectives contributes to the complexity of evaluating workload’s impact on operator performance and on mission success in space operations.

This Directed Research Project (DRP) delivered simple-to-use techniques to measure and evaluate human workload in space flight applications. A first deliverable was to generate specific guidance on which workload measurement techniques are most useful for particular kinds of human tasks and activities. A second deliverable was to provide guidance on how human workload can be best managed across a mission. This guidance considered the negative effects of high and low workload but also recognized the need for human operators to vigorously exercise important skills in a balanced regime of work and rest. The techniques and guidance proposed were tested in a practical space flight application by the Information Presentation DRP. The research conducted in this first year was conducted to address the needs of space flight application designers to unobtrusively measure workload, and to create appropriate levels of human workload through the allocation of work between human space flight crew and automated systems. At the end of the first year, a gap on workload measurement and management was revealed, namely the need to identify research on workload during long-duration operations and ways to measure it unobtrusively.

The second and third years of the DRP applied the findings from the Year 1 study to specific system-level concerns regarding workload’s impact on the system performance. For example, an understanding of the effects of workload on error rates, on repeated multitask performance, over extended operations, with additional crewmembers was required in order to develop conceptual models of acceptable system levels of workload. The ultimate goal of this phase of the research was to provide answers to the following human-system related workload questions: (1) how to measure workload from a system perspective; (2) how to manage workload to appropriate levels that ensure robust human performance throughout the mission or timeline; and (3) how can the human-system related workload guidance be used in future space flight operations.

APPROACH:
The challenge in predicting workload’s impact on operator performance stem from the difficulty in correctly identifying precursors to task failure, the impact that pending tasks have on operator performance, the impact of workload on vigilance levels/boredom, queue length, taskload, and task complexity on successful task scheduling and task performance. Some of these previously listed variables are driven from the system (e.g. taskload), while others emerge from the astronaut’s performance (e.g. in situ task scheduling ability). The challenge outlined is exacerbated when applying workload’s impact at the system-level because of the increased number of free parameters within a system that are not considered at the individual level. The outcome of this research produced guidance on the variables that impact human-system workload within the context of an end-to-end system (i.e. from beginning of a mission to the end of the mission), and culminated suggesting potential methods to develop a boundary of performance from the workload perspective that is neither too high nor too low to maximize individual and system performance, particularly for repetitive workload intensive operations.

RESULTS:
The Workload DRP provided an overview of system, system operations, system engineering processes, and presented a conceptual model, termed the Unified Theory of Cognition, that served as a framework for an initial conceptual representation of the manner that workload variables impact performance for long-duration mission operations. A formal review of three crew debriefs was used to identify the likely long-duration, workload-inducing variables that need to be considered when designing and using interfaces, procedures, and schedules in an integrated system perspective such that acceptable workload is maintained throughout a mission. A workshop that brought together a series of academics, government, and industry experts to discuss workload variables was used to support the crew debrief variables that were integrated into a conceptual model of long-duration mission operations. The final chapter culminated in the development of two conceptual models rooted in Newell’s Unified Theory of Cognition as it might pertain to long-duration mission operations. It is anticipated that future research use these potential models as a starting point to further recommend considerations for unobtrusively measuring workload over a long-duration mission through analogous environments, and to flesh out the primary, secondary, and tertiary variables that need to be considered for unobtrusively measuring workload over long duration missions.

Technologies have also been highlighted in various developmental stages that may provide unobtrusive ways to measure workload, while providing feedback to astronauts who can use the information to manage their tasks with the ultimate goal of insuring safety of the entire system in order to achieve mission success. In terms of the technology-based option, a prototype mobile screening system that unobtrusively detects behavioral patterns and characteristics of individuals who perform specific actions will be required. Such a prototype system will track the homeostasis of an individual’s pupil, skin/pore dilation, or other characteristic behavioral patterns and compare the baseline data to conditions when the operator experiences excessive workload. Sensor technology will be used to measure and monitor physiological, behavioral and auditory markers characteristic of individuals that experience performance decrements due to workload over a long duration mission. Research is needed to specify the markers and the thresholds that are characteristic of such performance changes. Data collection of physiological information (ocular measures, temperature, heart and breathing rates, perspiration, pore dilation, vocal measures), of behavioral information (physical movements/patterns, facial recognition measures), and of auditory information (pitch of voice) will be required so that baseline profiles can be created. These baseline profiles can then be compared against profiles of situations that are associated with performance decrements. These physiological, behavioral, and auditory markers will serve as the requirements specifications for systems developed for use in long-duration missions. Research is required to identify the critical thresholds for the physiological, behavioral, and auditory markers over a longer duration space mission.

Percutaneous Electrical Muscle Stimulator (PEMS) -- sketch drawing
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Data on animals exposed to space flight (Spacelab-3, Cosmos 1887) seem to indicate that skeletal muscle atrophy particularly affects those muscles comprised predominantly of slow-twitch fibers. However, recent human biopsy data collected after space flight (STS-32, -33, -34) showed a greater atrophy of fast-twitch fibers. The functional implications of muscle atrophy may be evaluated by studying changes in skeletal muscle contractile features. By stimulating the muscle directly, it is possible to measure force beyond the volitional control of the subject and to assess fine contractile characteristics typical of muscle mechanics, which cannot possibly be determined from voluntary contractions. The contractile parameters studied by muscle percutaneous stimulation have shown to be fiber type-specific, resulting in changes of twitch characteristics, loss of force at specific frequencies of stimulation and changes in fatigability.

The specific objectives of the experiment were:
1. To determine the relationship between the twitch-torque of the calf muscle triceps surea (TS) and the joint position of the angle.
2. To determine the maximum voluntary strength of the TS as well as the ability to voluntarily activate all TS motor units.
3. To determine the relationship between the frequency of stimulation and torque.
4. To determine the resistance to fatigue during repeated electrically evoked contractions.
5. To determine the force per unit of cross-sectional area of the TS muscle group (evaluated in collaboration with experiment 284054).

APPROACH:
The contractile characteristics of the triceps surea (TS) were investigated during both voluntary and electrically-evoked isometric contractions using the Percutaneous Electrical Muscle Stimulator (PEMS) and by recording the torque generated with the Torque-Velocity Dynamometer (TVD). For the test, four PEMS electrodes were positioned on the subject's leg: the cathode was placed over the two heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and the anode over the soleus muscle. Two safety electrodes were positioned on the head of the femur on the lateral side of the thigh. The lower limb was fixed to the TVD with a knee angle of 90 degrees. The ankle joint angled from 20 degrees dorsiflexion to 30 degrees plantar flexion, while resting on the TVD-footplate. During each test session, five different protocols of muscle stimulation were performed with the PEMS:
1. Supramaximal Current Intensity (SMCI) determination: The TS was stimulated with 50-microsecond pulses at an ankle angle of 15 degrees dorsiflexion, increasing the stimulation intensity from an initial 100 milliamperes (mA) up to a maximum of 800 mA (in 50 mA steps), and monitoring the twitch torque developed with the TVD, until no further increase in torque was observed.
2. Angle-force relationship: Twitches were measured at 7 different angles of the ankle joint (30, 25, 15, and 5 degrees plantar flexion, and 5,15, and 20 degrees dorsiflexion; degrees relative to the TVD footplate), two twitches per angle, 5 seconds apart.
3. Maximum Voluntary Contraction (MVC) with superimposed twitch. Three isometric MVCs (at 20 degrees dorsiflexion), each lasting 4 seconds and interspaced by 20 seconds were performed. During each contraction, the degree of muscle activation was assessed using the twitch superimposition technique. This technique consists of two single stimuli at SMCI, in response to which an increase in force on top of the voluntary contraction is obtained if the contraction is submaximal.
4. Frequency-force relationship: This was obtained by stimulating the muscle at varying frequencies. Three twitches (5 seconds between each two twitches) were given followed by consecutive trains of pulses, each 1 second in duration at 10, 20, 30, and 50 Hertz. This was performed with a current intensity of 60% SMCI. This lower SMCI was used to minimize the subject's discomfort at the higher frequencies and represented a good compromise between subjects' tolerance to the test and scientific outcome.
5. Fatigue test. During this protocol the fatigability of the triceps surea (TS) was tested during 120 seconds stimulation at 60% SMCI using trains of stimuli at 20 Hertz lasting 350 milliseconds, repeated once per second.

Preflight, the protocols were performed at L-90 (days before launch), L-60, L-30, and L-15. During the flight, they were repeated by the astronauts on Flight Day (FD) 3/4, FD 8/9, FD 13/14 and FD 16. After the flight, the protocol was carried out on R+2 (days after landing), R+4, R+8, R+15, and R+30. Also, the cross-section of the calf muscle plus bone was determined anthropometrically from calf circumference and skinfold measurements in the sessions which took place before and after the flight. In addition to the measurements taken with the PEMS, this investigation compares those results with the MRI measurements of the muscle volume taken pre- and postflight for experiment E920 (The Effects of Weightlessness on Human Single Muscle Fiber Function).

RESULTS:
The present results on electrically evoked human gastrocnemius muscle function assessed during the NASA-LMS mission (Shuttle flight STS-78), show a significant impairment in contractile parameters during recovery, but not during spaceflight. The observed decrease in muscle tetanic torque (24%) was greater than the decrease in calf CSAm+b (7%) as shown by a significant decrease in tetanic torque/CSA.

1. Supramaximal Current Intensity (SMCI) determination: The TS was stimulated with 50-microsecond pulses at an ankle angle of 15 degrees dorsiflexion, increasing the stimulation intensity from an initial 100 milliamperes (mA) up to a maximum of 800 mA (in 50 mA steps), and monitoring the twitch torque developed with the TVD, until no further increase in torque was observed.
2. Angle-force relationship: Twitches were measured at 7 different angles of the ankle joint (30, 25, 15, and 5 degrees plantar flexion, and 5,15, and 20 degrees dorsiflexion; degrees relative to the TVD footplate), two twitches per angle, 5 seconds apart.
3. Maximum Voluntary Contraction (MVC) with superimposed twitch. Three isometric MVCs (at 20 degrees dorsiflexion), each lasting 4 seconds and interspaced by 20 seconds were performed. During each contraction, the degree of muscle activation was assessed using the twitch superimposition technique. This technique consists of two single stimuli at SMCI, in response to which an increase in force on top of the voluntary contraction is obtained if the contraction is submaximal.
4. Frequency-force relationship: This was obtained by stimulating the muscle at varying frequencies. Three twitches (5 seconds between each two twitches) were given followed by consecutive trains of pulses, each 1 second in duration at 10, 20, 30, and 50 Hertz. This was performed with a current intensity of 60% SMCI. This lower SMCI was used to minimize the subject's discomfort at the higher frequencies and represented a good compromise between subjects' tolerance to the test and scientific outcome.

In addition to the measurements taken with the PEMS, this investigation compares those results with the MRI measurements of the muscle volume taken pre- and postflight for experiment E920 (The Effects of Weightlessness on Human Single Muscle Fiber Function).

RESULTS:
The present results on electrically evoked human gastrocnemius muscle function assessed during the NASA-LMS mission (Shuttle flight STS-78), show a significant impairment in contractile parameters during recovery, but not during spaceflight. The observed decrease in muscle tetanic torque (24%) was greater than the decrease in calf CSAm+b (7%) as shown by a significant decrease in tetanic torque/CSA.

experiment_title: Cancer Induction by Repeated Doses of High-LET Radiation
parameter_html:
Vitamin A
Nine Gray radiation
Eighteen Gray radiation
investigators: Principal Investigator: Burns, FredricCo-Investigator: Roy, Nirmal
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Past research has shown that radiation is a strong carcinogen. Vitamin A, a retinoid, can reduce the cancers caused by radiation in rat skin. This ground-based study focused on identifying genes whose expression is either induced or blocked by radiation and on the counteraction of retinyl acetate on those changes in gene expression.

Although retinoids, which are chemical derivatives of vitamin A, have been shown to counteract carcinogenic effects in several animal models, the molecular mechanisms behind the retinoid inhibition of radiation-induced cancer are not established. To better understand the mechanisms, this project focused on how a non-toxic naturally occurring retinoid in the diet called retinyl acetate, or vitamin A acetate, alters gene expression upon exposure of rat skin to radiation. This study may apply to the identification of genes involved in the broad mechanism of the retinoid role in skin cancer, such as its influence on cell proliferation, cell differentiation and apoptosis, which is also known as programmed cell death. Although these and other cellular responses to ionizing radiation are protective, if the responses are insufficient or overwhelmed, genetic errors may accumulate in cells. Those cells then divide, and cancer could eventually occur.

Preliminary findings with low Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation showed that dietary retinyl acetate counteracts radiation-induced expression in hundreds of genes. The most prominently affected genes were markers of cell proliferation in keratinocytes suggesting that the retinoid prevented radiation-induced increases of cell proliferation genes. No information is available on the effect of high LET radiation such as ƒ56/ƒFe on gene expression in skin keratinocytes. It is of interest to obtain information on gene expression patterns following skin exposure to the ƒ56/ƒFe beam in rats on normal diet and diet with retinyl acetate supplement. Similarities and differences between high and low LET radiation could then be analyzed. Earlier results suggested that the vitamin A retinoid is almost as effective against induction of skin tumors induced by ƒ56/ƒFe as by those induced by low LET electron radiation, thus gene expression studies are of interest.

One approach to study genes of interest is to find the genes that are altered by radiation and vitamin A in opposite ways. The expression of such genes may change in response to radiation exposure. These same genes may be expressed in the opposite manner upon vitamin A exposure without the radiation. In addition, some genes may not be affected by the vitamin A treatment without the radiation, but, if radiation is given and it causes changes, the vitamin A may be able to reverse those changes even though an effect of vitamin A alone is not observed. Organization of the genes into groups with similar functions in the cell can enable researchers to glean insight on whether certain functions of the cell are affected by radiation and, possibly, the counteraction of vitamin A.

APPROACH:
Eight rats that were 23 days old were divided into two dietary groups of four rats each. One dietary group was fed the regular food while the second group received the same food mixed with 250 ppm vitamin A acetate supplement. After one week, all of the rats received nine Gray and eighteen Gray of low LET electron radiation on two different dorsal skin patches about the size of 1.5 cm by 2 cm. A separate dorsal patch that was not exposed to the radiation was analyzed as a control. Each rat then had three patches of skin that were evaluated. One patch received zero radiation, one received nine Gray and the other received eighteen Gray. Twenty-four hours or seven days after the irradiation, the rats were euthanized, and the irradiated skin and non-irradiated skin sections were excised and pooled according to the radiation dose and vitamin A condition.

Total ribonucleic acid (RNA) was extracted from the skin samples and reverse transcribed to synthesize a special type of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). This particular DNA, called cDNA, was comprised only of the genes that were expressed at the time of analysis. The reverse transcription utilized a primer, a short segment of nucleic acid, which hybridized adjacent to the RNA polymerase promoter region. Double stranded cDNAs were then transcribed into a cRNA probe that was labeled with biotin through in vitro transcription as suggested by the gene chip manufacturer.

The cRNAs were differentially displayed using a rat genome gene chip. Each chip contained 8740 specific probes for rat genes. They represented every known functional category of genes. With this chip, expression all 8740 genes and gene groups were examined in one hybridization. The function of the chip was to recognize the genes that were expressed under the radiation and retinyl acid conditions. The gene chip identified by name those genes that were expressed and recognized. Northern blotting and reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) confirmed the genes that were differentially displayed, those that were identified when the probe bound to the specific genes on the rat genome gene chip. Finally, the patterns of the gene expression alterations from the radiation and vitamin A were categorized. Affected genes were grouped by their cellular functions to focus on pathways that are involved in the process of carcinogenesis by radiation and its reversal by retinyl acetate.

The gene chip analysis was not used for the eighteen Gray plus vitamin A treatment. Thus, five skin samples were analyzed for gene expression under low LET radiation. The five samples were from rats with normal diet and zero Gray radiation, normal diet with nine Gray radiation, normal diet with eighteen Gray radiation, vitamin A diet with zero Gray radiation and vitamin A diet with nine Gray radiation exposure.

For a study of carcinogenesis, the skin of approximately 200 rats was exposed to high LET radiation, a ƒ56/ƒFe beam. The rats were observed weekly for four weeks, then at six-week intervals thereafter. All skin abnormalities were noted, photographed and identified for histological diagnosis. The effects of multiple doses of high-LET ƒ56/ƒFe radiation in comparison to single doses of argon ion radiation were examined.

A different experiment utilizing the high LET radiation was to obtain information on gene expression patterns in a manner similar to that of the low LET electron radiation experiment. Rats were grouped into groups of three, with only twelve rats irradiated. One group of rats, the control group, received no treatment. Another group received vitamin A dietary retinoid and no radiation. Of the twelve irradiated rats, one group received vitamin A and three Gray of ƒ56/ƒFe high LET radiation. Another group received vitamin A plus 1.5 Gy ƒ56/ƒFe. Two groups of irradiated rats had no vitamin A supplement; one of these received three Gray of ƒ56/ƒFe and the other 1.5 Gy. At 24 hours or seven days after radiation exposure, the rats were euthanized, and the irradiated tissue was excised and frozen in liquid nitrogen for future analysis of RNA expression patterns with the gene chip technology.

RESULTS:
Retinol concentration in the skin was measured in rats with both diets. By seven days after the retinyl acid diet was begun, the retinol had accumulated in the skin but not in the blood of the rats that were given the supplement. The skin concentration of retinol in rats on that diet was 4.5-fold higher than in the rats that did not consume the retinyl acid diet. Plasma retinol levels were steady with or without the retinyl acid diet.

Gene expression signals ranged from zero to 278,710, with an average of 4217. Signal strength above 1000 was considered significant. For the five experimental groups, normal diet at zero, nine and eighteen Gray and vitamin A diet at zero and nine Gray, 50.4% of the genes were considered positive in at least one of the groups and the remaining 49.6% were considered as not significantly expressed in any of the five gene chips. Thus, 4402 of the 8740 genes were altered in expression for at least one of the five conditions, and 4338 of the genes did not show an alteration in expression in any of the five conditions.

Genes with induction or inhibition were compared among experimental conditions. Normal diet with nine Gray radiation versus normal diet with no radiation showed 188 altered genes. Eighteen Gray radiation versus normal diet with no radiation gave 92 altered genes, with 54 of those genes also altered under the nine Gray of radiation versus zero Gray, showing a radiation response dependent on dose. Eighteen Gray versus nine Gray of radiation with a normal diet showed 77 altered genes. For vitamin A supplemented diet, the vitamin A with no radiation compared to normal diet with no radiation showed 231 altered genes. Nine Gray of radiation on normal diet versus nine Gray of radiation with the vitamin A diet showed 58 altered genes.

There were 56 genes that showed at least 2.5 fold change between nine Gray and nine Gray with the vitamin A diet gene chips, and also had consistency in the other chips. In one group, genes were repressed by vitamin A alone and were induced by radiation, and the radiation induction was reduced by the vitamin A retinoid. In a different group, vitamin A alone did not change the expression in comparison to control but the combination of vitamin A and radiation reverted the radiation back to control levels. Other genes were inhibited by radiation, but were reversed to control level by vitamin A. The genes that showed the greatest reversal of radiation effects by vitamin A were a keratin gene, ornithine decarboxylase, an intracellular calcium-binding protein and a gene that is similar to an intracellular calcium-binding protein.

Genes that share similar functions were grouped together to learn if any groups were more susceptible to the radiation or the mitigating effects of vitamin A. The genes were checked to see if a significant change of greater than two-fold in expression levels were observed. Several functional groups did not show any genes with significant changes after radiation with or without vitamin A treatments. Tumor suppressor genes and genes related to apoptosis were two of the functional gene groups of interest that showed no changes in expression. The gene chips contained 16 cytokines and only one, Cyclin G, showed a greater than two-fold change between nine Gray with normal diet and nine Gray with vitamin A supplement.

The top one hundred genes with the greatest alteration in expression between nine Gray versus zero Gray normal diet and between vitamin A with no radiation versus zero Gray normal diet were grouped into one category. As a control, one hundred random genes from the expressed control sample were assigned into different functional categories. The genes affected most by the radiation or the vitamin A belonged to the categories of differentiation, stress response, inflammation or immune related and nucleic acid metabolism.

Northern blots, which analyzed RNA, showed a similar trend of expression as the gene chip for the keratin gene, a putative marker of proliferating basal cells. Although the Northern blot supports the gene chip results, the expression ratios differed between the two techniques for expression analysis. On the gene chip, the keratin gene showed 11.7-fold increase in expression with radiation versus the zero radiation. The vitamin A treatment (vitamin A with radiation) reversed the expression back to the control level. On the Northern blot, the increase in the radiation over control was only 4.9-fold rather than 11.7-fold, and the vitamin A reduced the expression to 2.2-fold above the control level rather than control level. The increase in gene expression from radiation that was reversible by vitamin A suggested that the vitamin A may have inhibited the dedifferentiating effects of radiation, and restored the normal differentiation status of the rat skin. Another laboratory technique, PCR, was also used to confirm gene chip results, and the gene chip expression pattern of the involucrin gene was confirmed by RT-PCR.

For the carcinogenesis study in which rat skin was exposed to radiation and the rats observed for tumors, a strong tendency was observed for the tumors to be inhibited by the presence of 250 ppm retinyl acetate in the food. Multiple doses of high LET ƒ56/ƒFe ion radiation in comparison to single doses of argon ion radiation were examined and indications were that multiple exposures produced more carcinomas than expected from the summation of single dose responses. Cancer induced by high LET radiation was indicated to be possibly as preventable by retinyl acetate in the diet as low LET radiation was in previous experiments.

Most tumors found in rats that had been irradiated with the ƒ56/ƒFe beam appeared to be fibromas. Single doses of ƒ56/ƒFe ions were somewhat more effective than argon in producing tumors at 4.5 Gy but not at three Gray or nine Gray. The 250 ppm of dietary retinyl acetate reduced the incidence of tumors to approximately 30% of the incidence found in groups that did not have the supplement in the diet.

Beneficial effects of vitamin A have been observed upon exposure to both high LET radiation and low LET electron radiation. Vitamin A reduced tumor incidence in rats exposed to high LET radiation. Under low LET radiation exposure, vitamin A blocked the expression of genes associated with increased proliferation and inflammation, and accelerated the expression of genes associated with epidermal differentiation. Some fibroblast or macrophage migration or invasion responses may have been inhibited as well. Vitamin A promoted epidermal differentiation on top of the abnormal differentiation from the radiation. Thus, it possibly protected the skin from cancer by preventing damaged cells from producing more cells and by promoting their death. Inhibition of epidermal cell proliferation and stimulation of differentiation limited the number of irradiated cells that could pass the genetic damage to future cells.

experiment_title: Duke NSCOR: Lung Cancer Risk from HZE Ions
parameter_html:
Lung progenitor cells
Tumor suppressor p53
High energy (HZE) space radiation
investigators: Principal Investigator: Kirsch, DavidCo-Investigator: Bloom, RochelleCo-Investigator: Onaitis, MarkCo-Investigator: Stripp, BarryCo-Investigator: Yoshizumi, Terry
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The goal of this study was to understand mechanisms of high charge and energy (HZE) ion-induced lung cancer. To accomplish this goal, the Duke NSCOR brought together experts in radiation biology, lung cancer development, lung injury and repair, radiation dosimetry, and education. They combined sophisticated mouse genetics, in vivo lineage tracing, ex vivo isolation of lung epithelial progenitor cells, and analyses of lung cancers induced by HZE nuclei to dissect mechanisms of HZE ion-induced lung cancer. Investigators integrated three separate projects to understand how the cell of origin influences lung cancer development after HZE ion exposure, identify mechanisms of cellular response to HZE ions in different progenitor populations in the lung, and define how and when the p53 tumor suppressor, which is the most commonly mutated gene in human lung cancer, regulates HZE ion-induced carcinogenesis in the lung. Investigators anticipate that their hypothesis-based research will ultimately lead to the development of better models for HZE ion carcinogenic risk assessment for individual astronauts and novel approaches to prevent HZE ion-induced lung cancer through biological countermeasures.

In addition to studying lung cancer development, the Duke NSCOR also studied lung progenitor cell injury and repair after exposure to either terrestrial or space radiation. Injury and inflammation of the lung are key components of many diseases in people including emphysema, asthma, and lung fibrosis. Furthermore, patients receiving radiotherapy for either primary lung cancer or other neoplasms of the thoracic region (e.g. breast cancer) undergo lung tissue remodeling and declining lung function that is directly related to the dose and location of radiation exposure. By exploring which lung cells are injured by space radiation and how these injured lung cells are repaired, investigators anticipate that this knowledge may also lead to a better understanding of how lung diseases besides cancer develop and strategies that may be employed to moderate the effects of radiotherapy on lung tissue remodeling. This information may ultimately be used to develop novel approaches for the prevention and treatment of these lung diseases, and the improvement of public health.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Study the role and timing of the tumor suppressor p53 in radiation-induced lung cancer using mice with an extra copy of p53.
  2. study the role and timing of the tumor suppressor p53 in radiation-induced lung cancer using mice with an extra copy of p53 and reversible knockdown of p53.
  3. Develop a model of radiation-induced small cell lung cancer.

APPROACH:
Investigators proposed to study the role and timing of the tumor suppressor p53 in radiation-induced lung cancer using mice with an extra copy of p53 and reversible knockdown of p53. In addition, they proposed to develop a model of radiation-induced small cell lung cancer.

RESULTS:
For Aim 1, investigators analyzed lung tumor development in the lung cancer prone KrasLA1 mice, bearing normal levels of p53 or an extra copy of p53. They observed that an extra copy of p53 suppressed lung tumor initiation in the absence of radiation, without affecting tumor grade or proliferation. Although radiation exposure did not impact lung tumor initiation in mice with wildtype expression of p53, the results suggest that space radiation may increase tumor grade. In contrast, mice with an extra copy of p53 had enhanced lung tumor burden following either terrestrial or space radiation. These results suggest that an extra copy of p53 can promote radiation induced lung tumorigenesis.

For Aim 2, investigators utilized an in vivo knockdown system that enabled temporal regulation of p53 expression in mice. They found that when p53 expression was permanently decreased following irradiation, mice developed soft-tissue sarcomas. Space radiation increased the sarcoma incidence as compared to terrestrial radiation. Furthermore, they showed that temporarily blocking p53 expression during radiation exposure was sufficient to ameliorate acute hematologic toxicity while simultaneously reducing lymphoma development. Results suggest that the p53 response to radiation promotes radiation-induced lymphomagenesis and that inhibiting p53 could be a promising approach to prevent hematopoietic injury following exposure to large doses of radiation.

For Aim 3, investigators developed a mouse model of radiation-induced small cell lung cancer. Using this model, they found that space radiation was more effective than terrestrial radiation at accelerating lung and brain tumor development. Radiation dose and quality also impacted tumor incidence and histological subtype. Consistent with data in humans, results suggest that female mice may have a higher excess relative risk of lung and brain tumor development following irradiation.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

Investigators anticipate that their hypothesis-based research will ultimately lead to the development of better models for HZE ion carcinogenic risk assessment for individual astronauts and novel approaches to prevent HZE ion-induced lung cancer through biological countermeasures.

In addition to studying lung cancer development, the Duke NSCOR also studied lung progenitor cell injury and repair after exposure to either terrestrial or space radiation. Injury and inflammation of the lung are key components of many diseases in people including emphysema, asthma, and lung fibrosis. Furthermore, patients receiving radiotherapy for either primary lung cancer or other neoplasms of the thoracic region (e.g. breast cancer) undergo lung tissue remodeling and declining lung function that is directly related to the dose and location of radiation exposure. By exploring which lung cells are injured by space radiation and how these injured lung cells are repaired, investigators anticipate that this knowledge may also lead to a better understanding of how lung diseases besides cancer develop and strategies that may be employed to moderate the effects of radiotherapy on lung tissue remodeling. This information may ultimately be used to develop novel approaches for the prevention and treatment of these lung diseases, and the improvement of public health.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Study the role and timing of the tumor suppressor p53 in radiation-induced lung cancer using mice with an extra copy of p53.
  2. study the role and timing of the tumor suppressor p53 in radiation-induced lung cancer using mice with an extra copy of p53 and reversible knockdown of p53.
  3. Develop a model of radiation-induced small cell lung cancer.

APPROACH:
Investigators proposed to study the role and timing of the tumor suppressor p53 in radiation-induced lung cancer using mice with an extra copy of p53 and reversible knockdown of p53. In addition, they proposed to develop a model of radiation-induced small cell lung cancer.

RESULTS:
For Aim 1, investigators analyzed lung tumor development in the lung cancer prone KrasLA1 mice, bearing normal levels of p53 or an extra copy of p53. They observed that an extra copy of p53 suppressed lung tumor initiation in the absence of radiation, without affecting tumor grade or proliferation. Although radiation exposure did not impact lung tumor initiation in mice with wildtype expression of p53, the results suggest that space radiation may increase tumor grade. In contrast, mice with an extra copy of p53 had enhanced lung tumor burden following either terrestrial or space radiation. These results suggest that an extra copy of p53 can promote radiation induced lung tumorigenesis.

For Aim 2, investigators utilized an in vivo knockdown system that enabled temporal regulation of p53 expression in mice. They found that when p53 expression was permanently decreased following irradiation, mice developed soft-tissue sarcomas. Space radiation increased the sarcoma incidence as compared to terrestrial radiation. Furthermore, they showed that temporarily blocking p53 expression during radiation exposure was sufficient to ameliorate acute hematologic toxicity while simultaneously reducing lymphoma development. Results suggest that the p53 response to radiation promotes radiation-induced lymphomagenesis and that inhibiting p53 could be a promising approach to prevent hematopoietic injury following exposure to large doses of radiation.

For Aim 3, investigators developed a mouse model of radiation-induced small cell lung cancer. Using this model, they found that space radiation was more effective than terrestrial radiation at accelerating lung and brain tumor development. Radiation dose and quality also impacted tumor incidence and histological subtype. Consistent with data in humans, results suggest that female mice may have a higher excess relative risk of lung and brain tumor development following irradiation.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.
