experiment_title: Protocols for Asynchronous Communication in Space Operations: Communication Analysis
parameter_html:
Communication delays
Team communication
Task performance
investigators: Principal Investigator: Mosier, KathleenPrincipal Investigator: Fischer, Ute
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Effective and efficient communication between Mission Control and space crews is essential for successful task performance and mission safety. The importance of team communication is heightened when unforeseen problems arise, such as system failures that are time-critical and require extensive coordination and collaboration between space and ground crews. During long-duration missions and missions beyond Low Earth Orbit, space-ground communications will involve delays up to 20 minutes one-way, a reality that poses a formidable challenge to team communication and task performance. The overall aim of this study was to develop and validate medium-specific communication protocols that enable flight controllers and space crews to establish and maintain common ground (i.e., mutual task and situation awareness) and coordinate problem solutions in response to different operational tasks during periods of communication delays. This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Determine the impact of communication delays on communication, teamwork, and task performance in relation to varying task demands, i.e., procedural tasks versus tasks requiring analysis and decision making, and different communication media (voice vs. text).
  2. Develop and validate communication protocols to support joint problem solving and decision making by mission controllers and space crews during periods of asynchronous communication. To achieve these objectives several ground-based studies were conducted using a space analog and laboratory setting.

The first set of studies aimed to determine how transmission delays of various lengths impact team communication and performance under different media conditions. Findings then informed the design of medium-specific communication protocols. Their feasibility for space missions was assessed in two analog environments, NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) and NASA’s Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO). A complimentary laboratory study was conducted to examine whether the availability of protocols enhanced remote team members’ communication and task performance during periods of communication delay.

APPROACH:
The first study consisted of an analysis of the communications between astronauts and Mission Control personnel recorded as part of the Advanced Exploration Systems Autonomous Mission Operations Project: Crew Autonomy Experiment - 1 (AMO) study conducted in NASA’s Deep Space Habitat (DSH). Investigators analyzed the crew-mission control communications that occurred during the baseline condition of that study. In a second laboratory study, investigators examined the impact of communication delay in relation to different communication media. Findings from these studies informed the design of medium-specific communication protocols as they highlighted which aspects of the communication process need support to ensure successful communication between remote partners under asynchronous conditions. The effectiveness and feasibility of communication protocols for space operations was subsequently assessed in two studies, resulting in refinements of the protocols and the design of a communication training module.

In a companion laboratory study investigators explored the impact of transmission delay on team communication and task performance in relation to varying task demands and different communication media. Spatially distributed teams of three collaborated in a computer-based task environment and communicated either by voice-over-internet or via a texting tool. The micro-world for the study was AutoCAMS 2.0 which simulates the life support system of a spacecraft and requires team members to monitor and control different subsystems, and to diagnose and repair failures. Each team was required to perform procedural and problem solving tasks during one synchronous and one asynchronous flight segment with a 5-minute one-way delay in communications transmission. Each flight segment lasted for 90 minutes. In order to guarantee the requirement of communication and collaboration on the experimental tasks, task-related expertise concerning diagnostic and repair procedures was differentially distributed among team members. The Flight System Engineer (FSE) received extensive training on AutoCAMS systems, diagnoses, and repairs, and had access to a comprehensive reference manual. The two Pioneer crewmembers were given basic training on AutoCAMS and were instructed to contact the FSE for guidance on diagnosis and repair whenever a failure occurred on their system.

In all NEEMO and HERA missions, communication delay occurred on consecutive mission days. Communication between crew and Mission Control was delayed by 5 minutes or 10 minutes one-way. In some simulations communication medium was limited to voice or text on a given day with transmission delay, or the crewmembers could choose their communication medium. Copies of the communication protocols were given to trained participants at the start of a mission to serve as a reference aid on days with a communication delay. Surveys were administered throughout a mission asking participants to rate the effectiveness of the protocols and their interactions with mission control, and in a final survey to provide feedback on individual elements of the communication protocols.

RESULTS:
AMO
Analysis of the AMO data provided first insights into the effects of transmission delays on team communication. Specifically, investigators observed that transmission delays disrupted the timing and structure of turns such as communications by different team members. Communications by different speakers co-occurred (i.e., step-ons in which team members talked over each other) or were out of sequence (i.e., related turns by partners did not follow each other as one partner inserted a turn before the addressee could respond to the initial contribution). Both types of disruptions likely increased team members’ cognitive workload and jeopardized common ground. Step-ons compromised mutual understanding insofar as parts of a message were inaudible and required additional turns to repair which, given the transmission delay, were likely associated with considerable costs both in terms of time and workload as partners had to wait for critical information and keep track of concurrent tasks.

Laboratory
Analyses of team performance revealed that transmission delay impacted time required to initiate a successful repair and more importantly, that its effect varied by communication medium. When communication was delayed, teams used a comparable amount of time to repair system failures, irrespective of the communication medium used. However, when communication was synchronous, voice teams outperformed text groups. Likewise, teams’ accuracy in performing system repairs was influenced by communication medium. Overall, teams communicating by text undertook more incorrect repairs than teams communicating by voice.

Analysis of FSE/Pioneer communications revealed that communication delay influenced both the rate of turns by team members and the length of their contributions. Team members made fewer but longer contributions when they communicated under time delay than when no time delay was present. Moreover, these effects were more pronounced for teams communicating by voice than those communicating via text. This finding suggests that team members using text may have been more concise than team members in the voice condition. However, subsequent content analyses of Pioneer Crew/FSE interactions during transmission delay revealed that text communication was also associated with an increased potential for misunderstanding. Text teams were more likely than voice teams to split up related information and present it in separate turns. Related communications by distributed team members were also further apart in text- than in voice-based communications. Text communication also included more threats to common ground, in particular missing responses and anaphora (i.e., terms whose meaning could not be established within a turn but depended on information provided in preceding turns).

NEEMO and HERA
Trained crewmembers generally rated protocol elements and conventions as fairly critical to ensuring effective communication during asynchronous conditions. Very high ratings across crews for several items—providing a topic, using a log to track related messages, and announcing complex or critical messages—reflect the value of protocols for keeping track of message threads. Compliance with the protocols was also high as crewmembers generally followed the protocols in their communications on mission days with a transmission delay.

Overall these findings suggest that asynchronous communication may be facilitated by protocols that aid conversational partners in keeping track of conversational threads and the temporal sequence of messages. Results from this study led to the development of a communication training module that can be used to prepare crewmembers and members of Mission Control for the challenges of communication delay. Moreover, the communication protocols not only target how to speak or write during asynchronous conditions but also point to specific technological solutions.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
An astronaut will lose lean body mass if energy balance is not maintained. This is especially true if energy expenditure exceeds energy intake. However, astronauts on Skylab lost lean body mass in spite of the apparent adequate intake of energy and protein. Energy requirements could be affected by microgravity and by the limits on physical activity in the close confines of the spacecraft. Before this study, energy requirements during space flight had only been estimated from metabolic balance studies and food intake records. The objectives of this study were to measure total energy expenditure (TEE) during space flight and to compare the results with calculated energy intake.

APPROACH:
Two five-day test sessions (one before and 1 during flight) were completed by each of 13 astronauts on six Shuttle flights lasting eight to 14 days. The astronauts consumed doubly labeled water (labeled with the heavy isotopes 2H and 18O) and periodically provided urine and saliva samples. It was necessary to account for baseline differences in the isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in the Shuttle's drinking water, which is made by fuel cells from liquid oxygen and hydrogen. Total energy expenditure was determined by indirect calorimetry and was corrected for body weight and fat-free mass. Energy intake was calculated from records of food and fluid intake. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA identified differences in energy intake and expenditure between the preflight and postflight periods. The Student-Newman-Keuls test was used for post-hoc comparisons. Paired t-tests were used to detect any differences between preflight and inflight dietary intake.

RESULTS:
Energy expenditures were similar before and during flight. However, energy and fluid intake were lower during flight (energy intake was 23% less; fluid intake was 19% less.) Weight changes ranged from a gain of 1.0 kilogram (kg) to a loss of 3.9 kg, with a mean weight loss of 1.5 kg. In flight energy expenditures were similar to estimates published by the World Health Organization (WHO) of energy requirements for healthy adults. The results indicated that energy expenditure was not changed during space flight and that the WHO estimates of energy requirements were appropriate for estimating the dietary needs of space crews. However, most of the 13 astronauts were in negative energy balance because they had reduced their caloric intake. This is undesirable because the loss of lean body mass reduces work capacity and promotes the loss of electrolytes that are important to muscle function and cardiovascular function. The astronauts also consumed inadequate fluid. The importance of maintaining adequate food and fluid intake should be emphasized in future flights.

__description:
OBJECTIVES:
An astronaut will lose lean body mass if energy balance is not maintained. This is especially true if energy expenditure exceeds energy intake. However, astronauts on Skylab lost lean body mass in spite of the apparent adequate intake of energy and protein. Energy requirements could be affected by microgravity and by the limits on physical activity in the close confines of the spacecraft. Before this study, energy requirements during space flight had only been estimated from metabolic balance studies and food intake records. The objectives of this study were to measure total energy expenditure (TEE) during space flight and to compare the results with calculated energy intake.

APPROACH:
Two five-day test sessions (one before and 1 during flight) were completed by each of 13 astronauts on six Shuttle flights lasting eight to 14 days. The astronauts consumed doubly labeled water (labeled with the heavy isotopes 2H and 18O) and periodically provided urine and saliva samples. It was necessary to account for baseline differences in the isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in the Shuttle's drinking water, which is made by fuel cells from liquid oxygen and hydrogen. Total energy expenditure was determined by indirect calorimetry and was corrected for body weight and fat-free mass. Energy intake was calculated from records of food and fluid intake. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA identified differences in energy intake and expenditure between the preflight and postflight periods. The Student-Newman-Keuls test was used for post-hoc comparisons. Paired t-tests were used to detect any differences between preflight and inflight dietary intake.

RESULTS:
Energy expenditures were similar before and during flight. However, energy and fluid intake were lower during flight (energy intake was 23% less; fluid intake was 19% less.) Weight changes ranged from a gain of 1.0 kilogram (kg) to a loss of 3.9 kg, with a mean weight loss of 1.5 kg. In flight energy expenditures were similar to estimates published by the World Health Organization (WHO) of energy requirements for healthy adults. The results indicated that energy expenditure was not changed during space flight and that the WHO estimates of energy requirements were appropriate for estimating the dietary needs of space crews. However, most of the 13 astronauts were in negative energy balance because they had reduced their caloric intake. This is undesirable because the loss of lean body mass reduces work capacity and promotes the loss of electrolytes that are important to muscle function and cardiovascular function. The astronauts also consumed inadequate fluid. The importance of maintaining adequate food and fluid intake should be emphasized in future flights.

investigators: Principal Investigator: Xiao, HangCo-Investigator: Decker, EricCo-Investigator: He, LiliCo-Investigator: Liu, AnnaCo-Investigator: McClements, DavidCo-Investigator: Peleg, Micha
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Currently, shelf stable foods that do not require refrigeration or freezing are the sole source of nutrition for the space flight crew. It is therefore crucial that these foods provide adequate nutrition to support the crew throughout the shelf life of the product. However, knowledge is currently lacking on the degradation kinetics of essential vitamins such as vitamins B1 and K during the processing and storage of space flight foods. To address this critical knowledge gap, this study aimed to measure vitamins B1 and K degradation kinetics and use this information to establish robust computational models to predict vitamin stability in space flight foods during processing and years of storage. The main approach was to identify the influence of food processing, food matrix composition, and storage conditions and other factors on the degradation kinetics of vitamins B1 and K, and then to use this knowledge to establish robust models and guiding principles to predict and prevent degradation of these vitamins.

APPROACH:
The investigators measured vitamin content in space flight foods periodically over a two-year period to determine the degradation kinetics of vitamins B1 and C in each product. The foods were produced and stored under various temperature conditions (e.g., -80, -20, 4, 20, and 37°C) for two years, and the degradation kinetics of vitamins B1 and C were systematically determined both in isothermal and non-isothermal conditions. Mathematical models were developed to receive inputs of experimental data sets to allow for the simulation and prediction of vitamins B1 and C degradation in space flight foods at times and temperatures not tested, and their accuracy was assessed. The results were analyzed based on the nature of different space flight foods to develop guiding principles on how to minimize vitamin degradation.

RESULTS:
At the conclusion of the two-year storage lifetime, vitamin B1 was generally most stable in thermally processed brown rice, less so in split pea soup, and drastically less in BBQ beef brisket, based on NASA’s formulation. Although degradation of B1 was slowest and less influenced by temperature in the thermally processed rice, B1 was more abundant in the split pea soup product at the end of the 2-year storage period at any temperature tested, compared to the more stable brown rice product. B1 in BBQ beef brisket was undetectable at the end of the storage period at 37°C storage and approaching an undetectable limit for the two other storage temperatures.

The process of freeze-drying these foods resulted in unique differences of vitamin B1 stability compared to the non-freeze-dried versions. Freeze-dried brown rice demonstrated better resistance to vitamin B1 degradation at higher temperatures, but a diminished protective effect in refrigeration conditions, comparing the final vitamin B1 concentrations between thermally processed and freeze-dried brown rice. This same trend of decreased temperature dependence on degradation rate was observed in the split pea soup, but not in the BBQ beef brisket, where differences in food matrix composition and chemistry are though to play a role on vitamin B1 degradation differentially. Vitamin B1 was also quantified in brown rice, split pea soup, and BBQ beef brisket that were either thermally processed or freeze-dried, and then stored at either -20°C or -80°C for two years as a quality control measure.

For vitamin C, freeze-drying preserved the vitamin better throughout all foods under all temperatures except 37°C. The degradation rate was the most noticeable difference because in many cases freeze-drying caused the food to approach a zero residual concentration quicker than the thermally processed foods. However, the freeze-drying concentration started with a higher vitamin C amount. As long as the vitamin C was detectable or had a nonzero concentration, freeze-drying still had more vitamin C than the thermally processed foods. This finding stressed how the initial concentration and an elevated storage temperature can influence vitamin C degradation. Sugar snap peas had many bewildering findings for the thermally processed and freeze-dried foods. Specifically for thermally processed sugar snap peas, the vitamin concentration considerably declined for all temperatures and was undetectable for all temperatures before the end of the two-year storage study. The stability was better during freeze-drying, but a sharp drop occurred at 12 months for 20°C freeze-dried sugar snap peas, which seemed valid considering the remaining time points stabilize near that concentration. The cause of the dropped has yet to be determined, and the investigators assume there had to be some form of phenomenon that increased vitamin C dissolved oxygen leading to a more rapid degradation.

experiment_title: Staged Decompression with an Argon-Oxygen (ARGOX) Breathing Mixture to 3.5 PSIA
parameter_html:
Pressure, pounds per square inch (psi)
Severe venous gas emboli (SVGE)
Venous gas emboli (VGE)
Decompression sickness
investigators: Principal Investigator: Pilmanis, AndrewCo-Investigator: Balldin, UlfCo-Investigator: Webb, James
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Long-term NASA goals include permanent occupation of the International Space Station (ISS) and missions to both the moon and Mars. One of the critical issues to be addressed for reaching these goals is the definition of an optimum pressure for extravehicular activity (EVA) suits. Currently, a 4.3 psia (pounds per square inch absolute) pressure suit is used for space shuttle EVAs in zero gravity. This suit, in combination with current preoxygenation schedules, is effective for decompression sickness (DCS) prevention. However, at 4.3 psia, the astronauts experience hand and arm fatigue due to the 'stiffness' of the suit. Also, due to the gravitational forces that exist on the moon and Mars, the current suit will be too heavy for planetary EVA. The trade-off for the advantage of a space suit with a lower pressure will be an increase in preoxygenation time. The first objective of this study was to test a decompression schedule for DCS prevention for a 3.5 psia EVA suit. In addition to the need for a lower pressure EVA suit, potential changes in the breathing gas composition needed to be evaluated. The Martian atmosphere has argon as a constituent, which will appear in the breathing mixture unless costly and heavy systems are provided to separate it from the nitrogen. The second objective of this study was to determine the DCS implications of breathing a 38% oxygen and 62% argon mixture (ARGOX) during decompression prior to EVA.

The hypothesis was that breathing the ARGOX during denitrogenation at 7.3 psia for a maximum of 4 hours would not increase the risk of DCS during exposure to 3.5 psia, as compared with an identical exposure with 100% oxygen breathing. No attempt was made to define an operational preoxygenation schedule, nor to determine an operationally acceptable level of DCS risk. The data obtained from this experiment provides a crucial starting point, from which future experiments can be designed to determine an operationally specific preoxygenation schedule for a 3.5 psia pressure suit.

APPROACH:
Forty (40) subjects completed three hypobaric exposures each. Exposure A was a 5-hour preoxygenation routine (including ascent time) for exposure to 3.5 psia. Exposure B was a 5-hour preoxygenation routine (including ascent times) for exposure to 3.5 psia, utilizing a 7.3 psia stage. Finally, Exposure C was a 5-hour preoxygenation routine (including ascent times) for exposure to 3.5 psia, utilizing a 7.3 psia stage with an ARGOX breathing mixture. For exposures B and C the subject was decompressed to 7.3 psia and remained at that level for 4 hours. For this time period, the probability of DCS was expected to be extremely low. After this 4-hour stage, the subject was decompressed to the final pressure of 3.5 psia and remained there for 3 hours. During the 3.5 psia portion of the exposure, the subjects performed simulated EVA exercise. Exercise took place during the first 10 minutes of preoxygenation and consisted of dual-cycle ergometry performed at approximately 75% of each subject's maximal oxygen uptake. The 10 minutes of supine exercise was estimated to be equivalent to 60 minutes of supine resting preoxygenation.

To simulate microgravity, subjects were supine on a gurney for the entire experiment session. All ascents were at 1,000 ft/min. Precordial echo-imaging for venous gas emboli (VGE) was accomplished at approximately 15-min intervals throughout the exposures using a Hewlett Packard SONOS 1000 echo-imaging System. The VGE were graded using a modified 4-grade Spencer Scale, where Grade 1 was infrequent VGE and Grade 4 VGE was of sufficient magnitude to overwhelm heart sounds. Grades 3 and 4 were classified as severe VGE (SVGE). The grading system was used as an indication of relative severity of exposure.

Subjects were continuously monitored for symptoms, including self-reported mild symptoms of joint pain or any other DCS symptoms. The experiments were terminated with the completion of the 3 hour exposure to 3.5 psia or the occurrence of signs or symptoms of DCS. Thus, for any given subject, total exposure to 3.5 psia ranged from 3 hours maximum to a low of 0 hours (if the subject developed DCS during the staged decompression).

RESULTS:
All statistical tests were performed at a confidence level of 95%. McNemar's tests for correlated proportions were used to compare the overall DCS, SVGE, and VGE incidence rates among the three profiles. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, with associated log-rank tests, was used to compare DCS, SVGE, and VGE incidence curves among the three profiles. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to compare the maximum VGE of the three profiles.

Of the 40 subjects, 13 (33%) developed DCS in profile A, 22 (55%) in profile B, and 31 (78%) in profile C. The difference in DCS incidence between profiles A and B was not statistically significant (McNemar's test), but was significantly different between profiles A and C, and B and C. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis tests showed significant differences between all three profiles, when compared to one another. 13 (33%) of the 40 subjects developed VGE in profile A, 18 (45%) in B, and 29 (73%) in C. Overall VGE incidence was significantly different (McNemar's test and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis) between profiles A and C, and B and C. SVGE (grade 3-4) were observed in 8 subjects (20%) in profile A, 13 subjects (33%) in profile B, and 23 subjects (58%) in profile C. Statistical analysis of SVGE showed the same pattern of statistically significant incidence as was shown for VGE. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that profile C had the highest maximal VGE score and profile B had the second highest.

In profile A, the subjects remained at ground-level for preoxygenation before being decompressed to 3.5 psia and, therefore, did not develop any VGE or DCS during that time. In profile B, two subjects developed VGE during preoxygenation at the stage decompression pressure of 7.3 psia. In profile B, two subjects also developed DCS at the stage decompression pressure, before the scheduled 3.5 psia was reached. One subject developed DCS during the 17 min ascent from the stage pressue. In profile C, six subjects developed VGE during ARGOX breathing at the stage decompression pressure of 7.3 psia. Three of these subjects also developed SVGE at the staged decompression pressure. Three subjects developed DCS during the ascent from the stage pressure before the scheduled 3.5 psia pressure was reached. Of the three, one developed VGE at the stage and SVGE during the ascent from the stage.

This study showed that the staged decompression pressure of 7.3 psia during oxygen breathing for 4 hours did not protect against DCS at 3.5 psia compared with similarly long preoxygenation period at ground-level pressure. The overall incidence of DCS and SVGE tended to be higher, the incidence curve of DCS was steeper, and the maximal VGE scores were higher. The fact that 2 subjects developed VGE and three subjects presented with DCS before that final scheduled decompression to 3.5 psia was completed indicates that the staged decompression pressure of 7.3 psia likely allows development of some nitrogen bubbles in the tissues. If the staged decompression pressure had been higher (lower altitude), the increased risk of DCS and higher incidence of VGE may have been reduced. The results of this study suggest that if using 100% oxygen breathing, reduction of risk of DCS can be achieved by either using a higher stage decompression pressure, or by not using a staged decompression at all.

A breathing mixture of ARGOX during the staged decompression has the advantage of using an inert oxygen diluent obtained directly from the Martian atmosphere, and being acceptably fire-safe. However, the results of this study indicate that it also results in a higher incidence of VGE and an increased risk of DCS compared with 100% oxygen breathing during stage decompression.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As astronauts work and live in crowded and confined conditions on board spacecraft for longer periods of time, the risk of infectious disease increases. They experience a unique set of stressors that contribute to a diminishment of many immune responses. Exploration class human space flight missions will require astronauts with robust immune systems. Innate immunity will be an essential element for the healthcare maintenance of astronauts during these lengthy expeditions. This investigation was designed to determine the functional status of important elements of the immune response, and will provide valuable data to help in the assessment of infectious disease risks associated with long-duration space flight.

Astronauts live and work in relatively crowded, confined environments on the Space Shuttle. They experience a unique set of stressors that contribute to a diminishment of many immune responses. Exploration class human space flight missions will require astronauts with robust immune systems. Innate immunity will be an essential element for the healthcare maintenance of astronauts during these lengthy expeditions. The investigators studied the innate arm of immunity. Specifically, the natural-killer (NK)-cells, neutrophils, and monocytes were identified to be studied. The goal was to measure the cellular functions of these three immune cells.

This study will complement ongoing and previous investigations in space immunology. The hypothesis being tested for this experiment is that essential functions of neutrophils, monocytes, and cytotoxic cells (lymphokine-activated (LAK) and natural killer (NK) cells) will be altered during space flight.

The specific aims were 1) Conduct functional analysis of neutrophils and monocytes before and after space flight and 2) Assess cytotoxic cells and cytokine production before and after space flight

APPROACH:
To understand the effects of space flight on innate immunity, a 10 ml blood specimen and a 10 ml urine specimen were collected during the astronaut's physical examination at 10 days prior to launch (L-10), at landing (R+0), R+15, and at the crewmember's annual medical exam (AME). The samples collected at the AME served as a low-stress baseline and were collected either preflight or postflight, whichever was furthest from the participant's mission.

Neutrophils: Changes in leukocyte subpopulations and function after space flight have been observed but the mechanisms underlying these changes are not well defined. This first study of 16 astronauts from three shuttle flights investigated the effects of short-term spaceflight (8 –14 days) on circulating leukocyte subsets, stress hormones, immunoglobulin levels, and neutrophil function.

A second study investigated neutrophil phagocytosis, oxidative burst, and degranulation of 25 astronauts after four space shuttle missions and in nine healthy control subjects. Space flight duration ranged from five to eleven days. Blood specimens were obtained 10 days before launch, immediately after landing, and three days after landing.

Monocytes: The study included four space shuttle missions and 25 astronauts. Nine non-astronauts served as controls. Blood specimens were collected 10 days before launch, within three hours after landing, and again three days after landing.

This study also investigated the ability of the shuttle crewmembers’ monocytes to respond to Gram-negative endotoxin that they could encounter during infections. Blood specimens were collected from 20 crew members and 15 control subjects 10 days before launch, three to four hours after landing, and 15 days after landing and from crewmembers during their annual medical examination (AME) at six to twelve months after landing.

NK-cells: Cytotoxic activity of non-major histocompatibility complex-restricted (CD561) (NMHC) killer cells and cell surface marker expression of peripheral blood mononuclear cells were determined before and after space flight. Ten astronauts (nine males, one female) from two space shuttle missions (nine- and 10-day duration) participated in the study. Blood samples were collected 10 days before launch, within three hours after landing, and three days after landing. All peripheral blood mononuclear cell preparations were cryopreserved and analyzed simultaneously in a four-hour cytotoxicity 51Cr release assay using K562 target cells. NMHC killer cell lytic activity was normalized per 1,000 CD561 cells.

RESULTS:
Neutrophils:

At landing, a 1.5-fold increase in neutrophils was observed compared with preflight values; lymphocytes were slightly decreased, whereas the results were variable for monocytes. The magnitude of increase in neutrophils varied across individual studies, but a significant increase in neutrophils following space flight was a very consistent finding. Even though neutrophil bands were observed in nine of sixteen astronauts, demargination of neutrophils from the vascular was thought to be the major contributor to the very consistent finding of increased circulating neutrophils following space flight.

A second study found the number of neutrophils increased by 85% at landing compared to preflight levels. The mean values for phagocytosis of Escherichia coli and oxidative burst capacity in neutrophils from astronauts on the five-day mission were not significantly different from those observed in neutrophils from the control subjects. Before and after nine- to eleven-day missions, however, phagocytosis and oxidative burst capacities were significantly lower than control mean values. No consistent changes in degranulation or expression of surface markers were observed before or after any of the space missions. This study indicates that neutrophil phagocytic and oxidative functions are affected by factors associated with space flight and this relationship may depend on mission duration.

OBJECTIVES:
As astronauts work and live in crowded and confined conditions on board spacecraft for longer periods of time, the risk of infectious disease increases. They experience a unique set of stressors that contribute to a diminishment of many immune responses. Exploration class human space flight missions will require astronauts with robust immune systems. Innate immunity will be an essential element for the healthcare maintenance of astronauts during these lengthy expeditions. This investigation was designed to determine the functional status of important elements of the immune response, and will provide valuable data to help in the assessment of infectious disease risks associated with long-duration space flight.

Astronauts live and work in relatively crowded, confined environments on the Space Shuttle. They experience a unique set of stressors that contribute to a diminishment of many immune responses. experiment_title: Fecundity of Quail in Spacelab Microgravity
parameter_html:
Damage, Developmental abnormalities, alveolar cells, quail, Microscopy, histology
Embryonic development, gonad, quail, microscopy, histology
Morphology, Embryonic development, embryos, Light microscope (descriptive)
Respiration, Commencement, quail. hatchlings, Observation
investigators: Principal Investigator: Wentworth, Bernard
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In all vertebrates, the germinal cells (future sperm and eggs) must migrate from outside the embryo to the gonads, where they will proliferate and differentiate to form spermatogonia and oogonia. The objectives of this experiment were to assess the effects of microgravity on arrangement, normal development, and primordial germ cell (PGC) migration in the gonads of Japanese Quail embryos, and to determine the effects of microgravity on normal respiratory function. The fundamental question being addressed is whether complete normal embryogenesis of the Japanese quail can be accomplished in microgravity. Basic knowledge of the role that Earth gravity and space microgravity have on cell and tissue migration during embryo development differentiation is vital for long term reproductive studies in space.

Approach:

Quail eggs were fertilized and laid at 1-G on Earth, and held at 16 degrees C until placed into the incubator on Mir. Eggs were incubated for 16 days, starting incubation 6 days post lay. Histological, histochemical, and immunochemical analyses were performed on lung and reproductive tissue.

Results:

Gross morphological development appeared to indicate that between 33% of the E-16 (fixation age in days) and 59% of the E-3 to E16 flight embryos developed at a normal rate in space microgravity. Gross abnormalities were observed in 13% of the flight embryos. None of the laboratory or synchronous controls showed abnormalities. Approximately 33% of the E-16 embryos showed normal male and female sexual development, as well as the ability to initiate breathing. Although it must be tested, the ability to hatch is presumed from these data. One difficulty that may be encountered in the hatching process of embryos developed in space is that some of the flight embryos had their head oriented in the small end of the egg, which may have impeded their hatching ability. A question that still must be answered is whether the initial development of the embryo (which, in this experiment, occurred on Earth) can proceed successfully in microgravity.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of four variables on histological properties of three muscles from the rat body wall. The muscles examined were the rectus abdominis (RA), transversus abdominis (TA), and external oblique (EO). These muscles function in both locomotion and in raising intra-abdominal pressure to expel material, including pups at birth, from the body cavity. The variables examined were: 1) gestation, 2) animal caging, 3) the effect of a midline laparotomy performed early in gestation to determine fetus numbers, 4) exposure to spaceflight.

Approach:

One group of flight rats underwent cesarean section immediately following flight after which muscles were removed and frozen for shipment. Serial cross sections were taken from frozen muscles of the specimens. Fiber size and density were determined by image analysis. Samples were incubated with monoclonal antibodies specific for slow myosin heavy chain (MHC) and fast MHC. Metabolic enzyme markers succinate dehydrogenase and alpha-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase were used to determine fiber oxidative capacity. Changes in enzyme levels were correlated with fiber type.

Results:

All four variables listed in the objectives had effects specific to both individual muscles and to experimental conditions. The TA and RA muscles showed signs of stretching with increased gestation. EO, a rotator of the torso, hypertrophied in rats housed in complex 3 dimensional group cages as compared to control rats housed singly in flat bottom cages. The TA and EO muscles, whose contractions would pull on the suture line, showed signs of atrophy in laparotomized animals. The hypertrophy of EO, an unexpected result, was consistent with the behavior of the rats in orbit. In microgravity, the rats did not float freely, but instead crawled over the cage walls and each other. This behavior requires active rotation of the torso, indicating weightlessness does not necessarily involve muscle inactivity or unloading. Changes in these muscles did not compromise the ability of the rats to give birth.

experiment_title: Development of a Solid-State Compressor for Closed-Loop Air Revitalization Systems
parameter_html:
Carbon dioxide
Temperature
Environmental testing
investigators: Principal Investigator: Mulloth, Lila
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The temperature-swing adsorption compressor (TSAC) is a solid-state compressor that has the capability to remove CO2 from a low-pressure source and subsequently store, compress, and deliver at a higher pressure as required by a processor. The TSAC is an ideal interface device for CO2 removal and reduction units in the air revitalization loop of a spacecraft such for oxygen recovery. The concept of TSAC as a potential interface for the carbon dioxide removal and reduction units in a life support system has already been proven and its operation has been demonstrated

APPROACH:
The ultimate objective of the task was to build an Engineering Development Unit (EDU) of an air-cooled TSAC with flight-like components and configuration and to test it in a relevant environment for certifying the technology readiness level of 6 (TRL 6) for this device. This two-bed prototype of TSAC was configured so that it permitted continuous acquisition of CO2 from a low-pressure source such as CDRA and continuous supply of CO2 to the Sabatier reactor at the specified pressure, and was sized to support a four-person crew load on the International Space Station (ISS). The project involved three phases: 1) Development of the thermal model, mechanical design, and model validation (testing) of the air-cooled TSAC, 2) Fabrication and testing of a full-size prototype to process 4kg CO2 per day, and 3) Develop an engineering development unit (EDU) with a technology readiness level (TRL) 6.

RESULTS:
Phase I targets were met on schedule on December 15, 2003. Test results indicated that efficiency of the compressor exceeded the design specification by about 50% with less than 30% of the estimated power. Under phase II, a full-size (sized to serve the ISS at a full-crew load) prototype was built and tested in 2004. The validation tests on the compressor were completed successfully on December 31, 2004. After the validation tests, the compressor was reassembled in a shipping crate to prepare for a relevant environment testing at the Space Station Simulation Laboratory at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center. The relevant environment tests on the TSAC were completed successfully in February 2006. The tests were performed in two phases. The Phase I tests were completed in December 2005 and phase II tests were completed in January 2006. Phase I tests included the TSAC performance characterization in integration with the flight-like CDRA. Phase II experiments included integration tests of the TSAC with the CDRA and the Sabatier reactor EDU (Engineering Development Unit). The integrated tests of the TSAC with the CDRA and the Sabatier EDU were the precursor for the third phase of the TSAC EDU development process.

experiment_title: Ocular Counter Rolling and Subjective Visual Vertical
parameter_html:
Otolith sensitivity
Perception
Subject visual vertical
Ocular counter-rolling (OCR)
investigators: Principal Investigator: Moore, Steven
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
To assess whether head down bed rest diminishes inner ear (otolith) sensitivity, the ocular counter-rolling response to postural tilting was measured before and after bed rest. Furthermore, to assess whether head down bed rest alters the perception of spatial orientation, the subjective visual vertical (SVV) was assessed before and after bed rest each using settings of a visual line to upright.

APPROACH:
Ocular Counter-Rolling (OCR) refers to the rotation of the eye about the line of sight. Measures of an otolith-mediated reflex was made using a Personnal Computer (PC)laptop-based head and eye tracker, developed by the investigators (MacDougall and Moore). Torsional eye movement (rotation about the line of sight) was calculated using images acquired from a miniature digital camera at a rate of 30 Hertz. Subjects were seated while wearing lightweight goggles with one digital video camera attached. Subjects looked straight ahead for 10 seconds and were then instructed to lie on their right side. After a period of 60 seconds, to allow semicircular canal input to diminish, the subjects looked straight ahead for 10 seconds. This process was repeated with the subject lying on their left side. The gain of OCR was calculated from the actual head roll position (i.e., upright, 90 degrees to the right or left) and the amount of roll eye movement.

Following removal of the video goggles, perception of the spatial upright was assessed using settings of a visual line to the Subjective Visual Vertical (SVV) using hardware and software developed for the Neurolab STS-90 vestibular experiment. Subjects were asked to adjust (using a handheld controller) the orientation of a luminous bar on a laptop display which is visible through a circular cut-out and shroud. The shroud was used to control for orientation cues from the computer itself. Subjects made 10 settings from start positions randomly offset of ±15° either side of the vertical meridian while seated with their head in the upright position. This sequence was repeated with the subject lying on their right side and left side. Subjects completed two pre-bed rest test sessions at approximately 2 sessions before bed rest and up to five post-bed rest test sessions.

It was expected that if bed rest induces deconditioning of otolith-ocular reflexes that this would not be reversed by Artificial Gravity (AG) exposure since the positioning of the subject on the centrifuge only allows for partial gravity stimulation of the otoliths during AG exposure. It is also expected that only a small decrease in OCR gain will be observed post bed rest, due to the partial unloading of the saccule.

RESULTS:

Results indicated that OCR was unaffected by bed rest and bed rest plus artificial gravity. Performance on the subjective visual vertical task was unaffected in the control group, but revealed a significant increase in error for 48 h after bed rest in the treatment (artificial gravity) group. Intermittent application of linear acceleration along the long body axis may have increased the weighting of the idiotropic vector, resulting in an increased of the SVV toward the long body axis during 90 degrees roll tilt.

This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study however, more information can be found through the publication listed.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Although some portions of the musculoskeletal system have been examined as part of other astronaut examinations (doctor’s physical, stress test, X-rays, et cetera) there has been no specific integrated examination for this largest system of the human body. Conversely, the musculoskeletal system plays a primary role in space operations and research. The state of muscles and the subject’s use of them determines, not only their condition and potential performance, but also condition of the cardiovascular and respiratory system on Earth and in space. Defects or limitations of this system can make it impossible for a subject to perform essential functions in operation and thus are disqualifying. A number of such limitations are specified in the physical requirements, but measurement of them requires equipment and techniques not usually available to the flight surgeon. Anthropometric measurements are urgently required by many man-machine designers in the space program. Anthropometric data have also become increasingly important as a research tool for investigation of effects of weightlessness of the body. Such information is particularly important for Shuttle, which is accepting an entirely new space-flight population.

APPROACH:
In 1978, approximately 207 astronaut candidates were examined during a NASA astronaut selection for the first Space Shuttle missions. Of this number, 80% were men and 20% were women. The crew positions to be assigned included male pilots, and both male and female mission specialists.

Basic physical examinations were conducted in addition to numerous specialty exams. The tests included a treadmill stress test and musculoskeletal examinations of each candidate. The treadmill test used the standard Balke-Ware protocol. The musculoskeletal exam consisted of a detailed history and physical examination, a large series of anthropometric measurements, and strength testing of major muscle groups by means of an isokinetic ergometer.

RESULTS:
The results of the examinations were immediately supplied to the medical examination board to use in the selection process. As expected from historical and general experience, the females were significantly weaker than the males, especially in the upper extremities. Also, as in general experience, there were one or two exceptionally strong females well outside the normal range in the entire group of females. This difference was most marked in the upper extremities when absolute comparisons were made. If strength relative to body weight in pilot candidates, male mission specialist candidates, and female mission specialist candidates were compared, the difference was less but marked. Since body fat was so different in males versus females (15 percent versus 25 percent in this case), the question was raised as to what happens if the female singly loses weight. This was indicated by calculating strength per lean body mass. In this case, back and leg differences in strength were much less, but arm and shoulder strength remained significantly different.

Some minor surprises were the differences in shoulder and back strength in pilots and mission specialists. Mission specialists were stronger in both areas even when they were normalized for body weight and lean body mass. As a matter of fact, the females had greater back strength on the basis of lean body mass than the pilots.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA has established the goal of returning human expeditions to the moon and extending exploration to Mars. The length of proposed Mars missions increases the importance of nutritional content in the food system. Proper nutrition is essential to prevent or mitigate physiological effects of long-term space travel as well as maintain astronaut health.

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the nutritional content of the existing International Space Station (ISS) and Shuttle food system for a mission to Mars by determining the effects of thermal processing, freeze drying, irradiation, and subsequent storage time on the nutritional content of the food. In order to ensure the safety of the food system and in order to deactivate metabolic enzymes that may cause the food to spoil, the packaged foods are processed to commercial sterility. This level of processing can reduce the quality of the food including nutritional content and acceptability.

There has been limited measurement of the nutritional content of the flight food items. Some macronutrients and minerals are determined chemically at the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) Water and Food Analytical Laboratory. However nutrients, such as vitamins, are currently only determined through a computer program released by the ESHA Research company, the Food Processor Nutrition Analysis software. While this program calculates the combined nutritional content based on the ingredients used in the food product’s formulation, the program provides only a close approximation of the true nutrient content and does not take into account the loss of nutrients during the thermal, freeze drying, or irradiation processes. While kinetic data have been presented in the literature for the loss of nutrition during processing, the kinetic constants provided are specific to the food and the conditions in each test. Therefore, use of the data and kinetic models in the literature will only provide a rough estimate of remaining nutritional content.

APPROACH:
One hundred and nine processed food items and 25 micronutrients were selected per for this study to determine the nutrient content of prepackaged food over time. A nutritional profile was determined by an off-site laboratory on each of these products at three points of its shelf life – one month after processing, at one year, and at three years. The one year time period was chosen because it is currently the average time after production that these food items are consumed on the ISS and Shuttle missions. Food items were selected for testing based on the importance of assumed nutritional content, frequency in the menus and the type of food. Products were stored at ambient conditions during the three year period to mimic the environmental storage conditions of the flight food. This will help identify the food factors that promote and/or inhibit vitamin sustainment in shelf stable food. The research has implications to the selection and formulation of relief food supplies and military rations that are commonly stored at ambient conditions for long periods before use.

This study does not seek to address the effect of processing on nutrients in detail, but rather aims to place in context the overall nutritional status at the time of consumption. Data showing the effect of processing and subsequent storage will be of value pending the need to develop an “Adequate Food System” or institute countermeasures to provide health promoting foods for long duration manned space exploration.

RESULTS:
The task was completed in September 2015. This study evaluated the nutritional suitability of the existing food items, utilized by current NASA programs, for long duration space exploration. The data indicate that several nutrients are nutritionally inadequate or degrade to inadequate levels in the food system over the shelf life required for a Mars mission, and mitigation strategies or countermeasures will be required.

From 2008 – 2012, a total of 109 space foods were collected directly after processing and packaging and sent to a subcontracted laboratory to determine the post-stabilization content of 23 micronutrients. At the same time, duplicate samples of the food were placed in a 21°C environmental chamber for storage. After one year of storage and three years of storage passed, these duplicate samples were pulled from the chamber and sent to the subcontracted laboratory for repeat nutritional analysis. Initial, one-year, and three-year nutritional analysis was gathered for each food.

Overall, the processing impacts of irradiation, thermostabilization, and freeze-drying on the nutritional quality of space food were aligned with previous researcher findings. Vitamin stability was dependent upon the micronutrient, the food matrix, and the processing method. Although in most foods vitamin C decreased during stabilization processing, there were instances where vitamin C appears to be sustained. Vitamin A, folic acid, thiamin, niacin, and vitamin B6 concentrations are dependent upon the food matrix and the processing method. Only four micronutrients – potassium, calcium, vitamin K, and vitamin D - have inadequate levels in the overall diet initially. The levels are not due to degradation but to low formulated levels in the space food system. Vitamin D is already supplemented but countermeasures for the other micronutrients should be considered. The storage data from the study would suggest that significant degradation occurs with vitamin A, vitamin C, thiamin, and vitamin B6. More data would likely be needed to assess the stability of folic acid and vitamin B12. Degradation also occurs with other vitamins on a more food-specific basis but without substantially shifting the nutritional delivery of the space food system.

Because of the prevalence of the vitamins within many foods and high initial concentrations, only the degradation of thiamin and vitamin C across three years of ambient storage are expected to have significant impact to nutritional delivery within our period of interest if degradation rates hold consistent after year three. Thiamin delivery is projected to be inadequate after the first year of storage. Deficiency in even one nutrient could lead to crewmember illness or death.

To reduce the risk that crewmember food choice impacts the total nutrition delivery, an effort to stabilize the nutrients of the degrading foods should be considered. Nutrition countermeasures could include changing the processing method to protect nutrients initially, fortifying foods with additional nutrient supply, or reformulating with the more stable food matrices. The possibility also exists for cold storage of the fresh space food supply to suspend much of the vitamin degradation that occurs. Validation of nutritional quality and organoleptic acceptability of any of these changes must occur before implementation.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The muscular system and the neural control elements of the neuromuscular system are significantly affected by space flight. Rapid adjustments in motor control are required just after launch and throughout the mission in order to function effectively in microgravity. Degradation in skeletal muscle function associated with space flight may be caused, at least partially, by altered motor functions. This experiment was designed to examine questions related to 1) the control of movement under a variety of conditions, 2) a human's ability to adapt movement skills to perform successfully under rapidly changing gravitational conditions, 3) the physiological adjustments occurring in these different conditions that may be responsible for alterations in movement precision and limitations in physical performance during postflight and recovery procedures, and 4) the physiological mechanisms that trigger neuromuscular adaptations to space flight.

The investigation was designed to determine the relationship between the electromyographic (EMG) activity of the calf and elbow muscles and the level to which their functional integrity can be maintained in prolonged space flight. The selected muscles to be tested were located in the calf of the right leg and the upper right arm: the ankle dorsiflexor (m. tibialis anterior, TA) and plantar flexor (m. gastrocnemius medialis, GM, and m. soleus, SO) of the calf, the elbow flexor (m. biceps brachii, BB) and elbow extensor (m. triceps brachii, TB) in the arm.

The specific objectives of the experiment were:
1. To determine daily activity of the musculus soleus (SO), m. gastrocnemius medialis (GM), m. tibialis anterior (TA), m. biceps brachii (BB), and m. triceps brachii (TB) before, during and after space flight.
2. To determine the EMG-torque relationship for the SO, GM, TA, BB and TB muscles during maximal and submaximal efforts before, during and after flight.
3. To determine the changes in motor control of the ankle, elbow and hand-grip.
4. To determine the fatigability of the ankle plantar flexors (SO and GM) before, during and after flight.
5. To determine the blood plasma levels of immunoreactive growth hormone (IRGH), insulin-like growth factor (IGF1), growth hormone carrier protein, thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3), testosterone, insulin, and cortisol before, during, and after flight.
6. To determine the bioassayable growth hormone (GH) response to exercise before, during and after space flight.
7. To determine the relationship between plasma hormone levels and the decrease in plantar flexor torque associated with muscle fatigue.

APPROACH:
The experiment was composed of the following tests:
1) 24-hour EMG recordings to quantify the subject's daily level of muscle activity.
2) Motor control tests designed to provide information on the strategies of the nervous system to regulate controlled muscle activity, and on how microgravity modifies these neural strategies.
3) A fatigue test protocol and its resulting endocrine response, which indicated the relative importance of neural, as compared to muscular, fatigue.

The functional integrity of the calf muscles, and the elbow and wrist flexors, was assessed during maximal and submaximal efforts, using the Torque-Velocity Dynamometer (TVD) and Hand Grip Dynamometer (HGD). The calf muscles of the right leg were tested in a protocol using the TVD, followed by the 8913020 protocol of Dr. Fitts and a fatigue test. The elbow flexors of the right arm were also tested in a similar protocol on the TVD, followed by the E407 protocol of Dr. diPrampero. The stand-alone Hand Grip test of the wrist flexors was composed of a reference test and a force curve. The protocols on the TVD were composed of six different tests: 1) reference test, 2) estimate position, 3) torque curve, 4) maintain constant torque, 5) dynamic stiffness and 6) position curve. These six tests monitored different aspects of the subject's motor control capabilities, and allowed determination of the torque-velocity/EMG relationship. Motor control capability of the ankle and arm were tested through a variety of tasks requiring precision in force production and displacement. Specific temporal and amplitude characteristics of the EMG signal were correlated with the maximal torque, velocity, and power. EMG of predominately slow and predominately fast ankle plantar flexors and elbow flexor and extensor muscles during the maximal and submaximal efforts were studied to compare the magnitude of the presumed decrease in total EMG throughout repeated 24-hour periods before, during, and after space flight with torque, velocity, and power potentials of these muscle groups. Similarly, the changes in torque, velocity, and power potentials associated with prolonged flight were related to plasma hormonal changes during space flight.

During both the early and late mission right leg TVD-test protocol, small amounts of blood were collected prior to and immediately after the fatigue test, to measure the level of growth hormone (GH), which increases in the bloodstream during exercise. It was hypothesized that the stay in microgravity would affect GH production and result in a lower value. In addition to the described measurements, plasma levels of other hormones that play a major role in regulating muscle protein metabolism were analyzed. Additional samples were taken pre- and postflight.

These data will help define the relative importance of muscle function to muscle maintenance in prolonged space flight. Furthermore, these data will provide insight into the relative impact of neural and muscular components on changes in movement control and maximal performance capacity as might be needed in an emergency egress procedure.

RESULTS:
The 24-hour electromyography (EMG) showed an increase in muscle activation on FD 1 for the soleus (SO), tibialis anterior (TA), biceps brachii (BB) and triceps brachii (TB) muscles. The SO and TA activation was increased during the entire space flight, whereas a slight decrease in the gastrocnemius medialis (MG) daily level of muscular activity was observed. The TB values were increased for the entire space flight, while for BB the daily values measured on FD 7 and FD 13 were similar to the baseline and recovery values.

The measured torque values (for Hand Grip Dynamometer force values) showed no obvious effects caused by space flight. A small but significant (p<0.05) increase in elbow flexor torque was observed across subjects during flight. In addition, a decrease in elbow flexor torque (p<0.01) was seen in 3 of 4 subjects at FD 2-3, although one crewmember showed larger elbow flexor torque during this measurement session. The steep decrease in torque seen in the plantarflexor muscle group on FD 2-3 with a sudden recovery at the next session (FD 6-7) was caused by problems with seating and securing the subject to the TVD during the FD 2-3 session.

For changes in muscle output estimation (subjects were asked to apply a certain force level, expressed in percent of MVC) there was no specific trend observed. However, in a number of instances output estimation was altered inflight relative to preflight (elbow extensors for all subjects, plantarflexors for 3 subjects, dorsiflexors and hand grip for 2 subjects). In all such instances the direction of the change was toward an overestimation of output at lower force levels.

No significant difference between pre- and inflight for the ability to maintain a constant torque output at a faster (1 Hertz) or slower (0.5 Hertz) passive isokinetic movement was observed. Similarly, there was no significant difference in the ability to maintain torque with or without continuous feedback, with the exception of the 50% MVC ankle plantarflexion. All subjects were significantly (p<0.05) more accurate at maintaining a constant torque for ankle plantarflexion at 50% MVC when given continuous feedback, and the torque was underestimated by 10% without feedback. For elbow testing, subjects consistently overestimated 10% MVC and underestimated 50% MVC for elbow extension. In opposition, for elbow flexion, 10% MVC was consistently underestimated while 50% MVC was overestimation.

Torque output for the ankle flexor and elbow flexor muscles were the most affected during space flight. On the second inflight test (FD 4-5) there was a significant decrease in torque levels for ankle dorsiflexion at 50% MVC with feedback. For elbow flexors, on the first day of space flight, the mean difference from requested torque increase significantly for elbow flexion at 10% MVC, such that subjects underestimated to a greater degree. This effect continued throughout the flight and for the first eight days postflight.

The EMG measurements during the experiment sessions revealed no significant changes for agonist or antagonist muscles whether or not subjects were given continuous feedback. However, significant changes were observed for the agonist EMG activity recorded during low level ankle extension or elbow flexion. __description:
OBJECTIVES:
The muscular system and the neural control elements of the neuromuscular system are significantly affected by space flight. Rapid adjustments in motor control are required just after launch and throughout the mission in order to function effectively in microgravity. Degradation in skeletal muscle function associated with space flight may be caused, at least partially, by altered motor functions. This experiment was designed to examine questions related to 1) the control of movement under a variety of conditions, 2) a human's ability to adapt movement skills to perform successfully under rapidly changing gravitational conditions, 3) the physiological adjustments occurring in these different conditions that may be responsible for alterations in movement precision and limitations in physical performance during postflight and recovery procedures, and 4) the physiological mechanisms that trigger neuromuscular adaptations to space flight.

The investigation was designed to determine the relationship between the electromyographic (EMG) activity of the calf and elbow muscles and the level to which their functional integrity can be maintained in prolonged space flight. The selected muscles to be tested were located in the calf of the right leg and the upper right arm: the ankle dorsiflexor (m. tibialis anterior, TA) and plantar flexor (m. gastrocnemius medialis, GM, and m. soleus, SO) of the calf, the elbow flexor (m. biceps brachii, BB) and elbow extensor (m. triceps brachii, TB) in the arm.

The specific objectives of the experiment were:
1. To determine daily activity of the musculus soleus (SO), m. gastrocnemius medialis (GM), m. tibialis anterior (TA), m. biceps brachii (BB), and m. triceps brachii (TB) before, during and after space flight.
2. To determine the EMG-torque relationship for the SO, GM, TA, BB and TB muscles during maximal and submaximal efforts before, during and after flight.
3. To determine the changes in motor control of the ankle, elbow and hand-grip.
4. To determine the fatigability of the ankle plantar flexors (SO and GM) before, during and after flight.
5. To determine the blood plasma levels of immunoreactive growth hormone (IRGH), insulin-like growth factor (IGF1), growth hormone carrier protein, thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3), testosterone, insulin, and cortisol before, during, and after flight.
6. To determine the bioassayable growth hormone (GH) response to exercise before, during and after space flight.
7. To determine the relationship between plasma hormone levels and the decrease in plantar flexor torque associated with muscle fatigue.

APPROACH:
The experiment was composed of the following tests:
1) 24-hour EMG recordings to quantify the subject's daily level of muscle activity.
2) Motor control tests designed to provide information on the strategies of the nervous system to regulate controlled muscle activity, and on how microgravity modifies these neural strategies.
3) A fatigue test protocol and its resulting endocrine response, which indicated the relative importance of neural, as compared to muscular, fatigue.

The functional integrity of the calf muscles, and the elbow and wrist flexors, was assessed during maximal and submaximal efforts, using the Torque-Velocity Dynamometer (TVD) and Hand Grip Dynamometer (HGD). The calf muscles of the right leg were tested in a protocol using the TVD, followed by the 8913020 protocol of Dr. Fitts and a fatigue test. The elbow flexors of the right arm were also tested in a similar protocol on the TVD, followed by the E407 protocol of Dr. diPrampero. The stand-alone Hand Grip test of the wrist flexors was composed of a reference test and a force curve. The protocols on the TVD were composed of six different tests: 1) reference test, 2) estimate position, 3) torque curve, 4) maintain constant torque, 5) dynamic stiffness and 6) position curve. These six tests monitored different aspects of the subject's motor control capabilities, and allowed determination of the torque-velocity/EMG relationship. Motor control capability of the ankle and arm were tested through a variety of tasks requiring precision in force production and displacement. Specific temporal and amplitude characteristics of the EMG signal were correlated with the maximal torque, velocity, and power. EMG of predominately slow and predominately fast ankle plantar flexors and elbow flexor and extensor muscles during the maximal and submaximal efforts were studied to compare the magnitude of the presumed decrease in total EMG throughout repeated 24-hour periods before, during, and after space flight with torque, velocity, and power potentials of these muscle groups. Similarly, the changes in torque, velocity, and power potentials associated with prolonged flight were related to plasma hormonal changes during space flight.

During both the early and late mission right leg TVD-test protocol, small amounts of blood were collected prior to and immediately after the fatigue test, to measure the level of growth hormone (GH), which increases in the bloodstream during exercise. It was hypothesized that the stay in microgravity would affect GH production and result in a lower value. In addition to the described measurements, plasma levels of other hormones that play a major role in regulating muscle protein metabolism were analyzed. Additional samples were taken pre- and postflight.

These data will help define the relative importance of muscle function to muscle maintenance in prolonged space flight. Furthermore, these data will provide insight into the relative impact of neural and muscular components on changes in movement control and maximal performance capacity as might be needed in an emergency egress procedure.

RESULTS:
The 24-hour electromyography (EMG) showed an increase in muscle activation on FD 1 for the soleus (SO), tibialis anterior (TA), biceps brachii (BB) and triceps brachii (TB) muscles. The SO and TA activation was increased during the entire space flight, whereas a slight decrease in the gastrocnemius medialis (MG) daily level of muscular activity was observed. The TB values were increased for the entire space flight, while for BB the daily values measured on FD 7 and FD 13 were similar to the baseline and recovery values.

The measured torque values (for Hand Grip Dynamometer force values) showed no obvious effects caused by space flight. A small but significant (p<0.05) increase in elbow flexor torque was observed across subjects during flight. In addition, a decrease in elbow flexor torque (p<0.01) was seen in 3 of 4 subjects at FD 2-3, although one crewmember showed larger elbow flexor torque during this measurement session. The steep decrease in torque seen in the plantarflexor muscle group on FD 2-3 with a sudden recovery at the next session (FD 6-7) was caused by problems with seating and securing the subject to the TVD during the FD 2-3 session.

For changes in muscle output estimation (subjects were asked to apply a certain force level, expressed in percent of MVC) there was no specific trend observed. However, in a number of instances output estimation was altered inflight relative to preflight (elbow extensors for all subjects, plantarflexors for 3 subjects, dorsiflexors and hand grip for 2 subjects). In all such instances the direction of the change was toward an overestimation of output at lower force levels.

No significant difference between pre- and inflight for the ability to maintain a constant torque output at a faster (1 Hertz) or slower (0.5 Hertz) passive isokinetic movement was observed. Similarly, there was no significant difference in the ability to maintain torque with or without continuous feedback, with the exception of the 50% MVC ankle plantarflexion. All subjects were significantly (p<0.05) more accurate at maintaining a constant torque for ankle plantarflexion at 50% MVC when given continuous feedback, and the torque was underestimated by 10% without feedback. For elbow testing, subjects consistently overestimated 10% MVC and underestimated 50% MVC for elbow extension. In opposition, for elbow flexion, 10% MVC was consistently underestimated while 50% MVC was overestimation.

Torque output for the ankle flexor and elbow flexor muscles were the most affected during space flight. On the second inflight test (FD 4-5) there was a significant decrease in torque levels for ankle dorsiflexion at 50% MVC with feedback. For elbow flexors, on the first day of space flight, the mean difference from requested torque increase significantly for elbow flexion at 10% MVC, such that subjects underestimated to a greater degree. This effect continued throughout the flight and for the first eight days postflight.

The EMG measurements during the experiment sessions revealed no significant changes for agonist or antagonist muscles whether or not subjects were given continuous feedback. However, significant changes were observed for the agonist EMG activity recorded during low level ankle extension or elbow flexion. The EMG signals for both the MG and BB muscles decreased significantly during the 10% MVC early into the flight. SO and TB demonstrated no significant alterations in EMG activity.

The hormone response (BGH response) to exercise was clearly present before space flight (p<0.05), blunted at FD 2-3, and was essentially absent by FD 13-14. Following space flight, the BGH response remained absent at R+2 but had returned by R+4. In conclusion, the exercise induced release of BGH was inhibited during space flight and early recovery, but has returned to normal four days after recovery.

experiment_description:
Objectives:

Cytokines, proteins that serve as messengers to activate immune responses in lymphocytes and macrophages, appear to be altered during spaceflight. Because of this suppression of the immune system in otherwise healthy subjects, spaceflight offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of biological subtances with out the complications of illnesses normally present in immunosuppressed subjects. Polyethylene Glycol-Interleukin 2 (PEG-IL-2) is an immunological mediator and enhancer developed and manufactured by Chiron Corporation. The purpose of this experiment in conjunction with an Immune 1 experiment was to confirm and define the ability of Polyethylene Glycol-Interleukin 2 (PEG-IL2) to prevent or ameliorate the detrimental effects of space flight on immune responses of rats.

Approach:

Half of the animals in each group were injected subcutaneously with PEG-IL-2 two to three hours before transfer to the Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs). Upon recovery of flight subjects, the following tissues and organs were removed and weighed: brain, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, trachea, spleen, and thymus. Blood samples were collected and analyzed for blood cell counts and differentials. They were also analyzed for corticosterone concentration with radioimmunoassay. Macrophage (M-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage stimulating factor (GM-CSF) dependent macrophage colony formation from bone marrow cells were assayed. Lymphocytes were obtained from the spleen and lymph nodes and assayed to determine cell proliferation rates and the secretion of cytokines, M-CSF, IL-6, IFN-g, and TGF-§. Peritoneal macrophages were assayed for secretion of TNFa and IL-6. The humerus, femur and tibia were collected and underwent biomechanical testing to calculate strength (N), deflection (mm), and energy (mJ). Bones were then dried and ashed in order to assess mineral content.

Results:

The results of this experiment are joined with the Immune 1 experiment. There was no significant pattern observed for body weight and organ weight parameters. Additionally, few immunological parameters were consistent across the Immune 1 and Immune 2 experiments, making conclusive observations difficult. Significant changes in bone parameters were observed in Immune 2, but not Immune 1. The inconsistencies between the two experiments prevented any conclusive evidence concerning the effectiveness of the PEG-IL-2 treatment. Several factors may have played a role in these discrepancies. Some of the animals flown as a part of the Immune 1 experiment were discovered to have various degrees of damage to their tails (necrosis, loss, and gangrenous tissues). Additionally, flight animals in the Immune 2 experiment were exposed to significantly higher ambient temperatures than animals in Immune 1. These data illustrate some of the issues that can arise when small numbers of animals are studied under flight conditions that are difficult to reproduce from one flight to the next.
