experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A number of physiological changes have been demonstrated in bone, muscle and blood from exposure of humans and animals to microgravity. It was hypothesized that during space flight, all of the following would increase: atrophy of the muscles, the intervertebral disc space, and percentage of fat in the bone marrow. It was also hypothesized that the changes in bone marrow fat would be accompanied by a decrease in the cellular component. Determining the mechanisms of space-flight-induced physiological changes and the development of effective countermeasures for long duration space missions is an important goal of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans performed on the leg and lower back muscles of the crewmembers of the Spacelab-J (STS-47) mission showed significant muscle atrophy after only eight days in microgravity. The 17-day Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission provided the opportunity to determine whether long duration space flight would result in postflight changes and whether measurements taken early after landing would demonstrate any expansion of intervertebral discs.

The specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To measure the volumes of the calf, thigh, and back muscles using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and to measure whole body lean mass using Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) before and after flight. These data were compared with pre- and postflight muscle performance measurements.
2. To determine the change in intervertebral disc size and spine length in the lumbar spine after flight and determine the rate of recovery after return to 1-G.
3. To determine the changes in the muscle volumes (by MRI) and soft tissue distribution (by DEXA) between landing day and two days after landing, and to determine the calf muscle transverse relaxation time (T2) before and after flight.
4. To determine the bone marrow transverse relaxation time (T2) and cellularity of the Lumbar 3 (L3) vertebra before and after flight using MRI spectroscopy.

APPROACH:
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) was used to measure changes in the volume of individual muscles (soleus, gastrocnemius, quadriceps, hamstrings, adductors, intrinsic low back, and psoas) and to determine the degree and rate of recovery to their preflight states. During all MRI sessions, measurements were made in the same order, starting with the spine and back, and followed by the limb measurements.

For spine imaging, subjects were positioned so that the imaging area was centered within the L3 vertebra. The cross sectional area of the disc space was measured for the T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4, and L4-5 discs. For imaging of the back muscles, twenty (20) 0.5 cm slices, centered on the L3 vertebra, were obtained. For limb measurements, the feet were positioned in a holder to minimize movement during image acquisition and to ensure repositioning. For the thigh and calf muscles, thirty-two (32) 1 cm slices were taken.

The calf muscle transverse relaxation time (T2) was measured by repeating the calf region scan using the same receiver gain with a longer echo time. The T2 values of each pixel were determined by comparing the image intensity at two different echo times, Te=10 and 50 msec. The determined T2 value represents the averages of the individual pixels taken from each muscle.

To measure fat and water percentages in the vertebral bone marrow, volume selective proton spectra were obtained using a surface receive coil. A cubic volume of interest of 15mm x 15mm x 15mm, located at the center of the L3 vertebra, was selected from the scout scan. The spectra were obtained at four echo times (Te = 12,18, 24, 30 msec). Bone marrow cellularity was determined from the fat to water peak areas.

At the end of each MRI session, a whole body Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) scan was performed as well. The DEXA scan required approximately 15 minutes and gave a radiation exposure of less than 1 mrem. The whole body scan was analyzed for bone mineral density (BMD), soft tissue, lean tissue, and fat. In order to examine fluid redistribution between the upper body and the lower limbs, the soft tissue values of the legs were divided by the whole body soft tissue minus the legs. This ratio was used to compare preflight status with postflight status.

MRI and DEXA scans were performed on four crewmembers two times preflight, at 50-51 and 29-31 days before launch. The scans were repeated postflight within 24 hours of Shuttle landing (R+0), and 2, 10, and 30 days after landing (R+2, R+10, R+30).

RESULTS:
Muscle volume: There were no significant changes in the volume of the psoas, anterior calf and gastrocnemius measured immediately after return to Earth (R+0). Significant decreases of 3 to 10% were measured in the volume of soleus, quadriceps, hamstrings and intrinsic back muscles. The data were compared with the measurements obtained on R+1 on Spacelab-J (8-day mission). By comparison, the R+0 muscle volume changes after LMS were somewhat greater, while the R+2 LMS data are somewhat less than the Spacelab-J data obtained on R+1.

The second measurement taken at 10 days after landing of the LMS mission revealed that no differences in muscle volume were apparent when compared to preflight baseline. These results were different than the previous results from Spacelab-J, which showed some muscle deficit remaining two weeks after landing (R+14 days).

Fluid redistribution: The muscle volume data measured at R+0 and R+2 days clearly indicated that fluids moved into the lower limbs after flight. One or two days after landing, most muscles regained a volume in the range of 3 to 6 % (compared to R+0 data). There were two possible explanations for this phenomenon: (1) the muscles were dehydrated during weightlessness and the fluids were redistributed from the upper body because of the gravity vector, or (2) the fluid accumulation was caused by postflight muscle damage and ongoing muscle repair. The first possible explanation was investigated by examining the soft tissue ratio of the legs to upper body from the DEXA scan before and after flight. There was no significant change in the preflight and postflight ratios, indicating that the inflight fluid shift to the upper body from the legs was already reverted back to baseline by the time measurements were taken on R+0. This might indicate that the gravity dependent fluid shift is not responsible for the muscle swelling seen postflight.

To investigate the second theory, the T2 of the calf muscles was measured. The T2 is sensitive to changes in tissue water/protein content. The R+2 and R+10, but not the R+30 data, for the anterior calf and soleus were significantly above baseline. The T2 of the gastrocnemius also appeared elevated, but did not reach significance, p=0.07. These results appear to show an elevated T2 at R+2 and sometimes at both R+2 and R+10 which returns toward baseline by R+30. The T2 is elevated at R+10 when muscle volume differences are not apparent, but performance decrements are still apparent (Narici). This finding suggests that reambulation after flight causes swelling of muscles that lasts several weeks and is probably associated with muscle damage and/or repair.

Intervertebral disc: No evidence of disc expansion was measured on R+0. A slight, but not significant decrease in disc area was observed postflight. Also, the data showed a lengthening of the spine relative to baseline on R+0, which appears to be at variance with the disc area measurements.

Bone marrow: The analysis of the proton spectroscopy data (T2 water, T2 fat, and percent water) from two preflight and seven postflight measurements showed no significant change in the fraction of the water (cellular) component immediately postflight. However, subsequent postflight measurements may have indicated some change. Immediately postflight, a decrease relative to baseline in the T2 of the cellular component was evident. Subsequent measurements showed that the T2 increased. At R+30, an increase in T2 above baseline was clearly evident in all 4 crewmembers. For 3 of the 4 participating crewmembers, T2 remained elevated above baseline for more than 4 months after landing.

Body composition: The bone mineral density (BMD) did not change postflight. Subregional analysis showed no significant change in the lumbar spine or pelvis BMD. There were no significant changes in lean tissue after flight, but there appeared to be loss in total body fat (2.8kg), which paralleled changes in total body weight.

The DEXA scan required approximately 15 minutes and gave a radiation exposure of less than 1 mrem. The whole body scan was analyzed for bone mineral density (BMD), soft tissue, lean tissue, and fat. In order to examine fluid redistribution between the upper body and the lower limbs, the soft tissue values of the legs were divided by the whole body soft tissue minus the legs. This ratio was used to compare preflight status with postflight status.

MRI and DEXA scans were performed on four crewmembers two times preflight, at 50-51 and 29-31 days before launch. The scans were repeated postflight within 24 hours of Shuttle landing (R+0), and 2, 10, and 30 days after landing (R+2, R+10, R+30).

RESULTS:
Muscle volume: There were no significant changes in the volume of the psoas, anterior calf and gastrocnemius measured immediately after return to Earth (R+0). Significant decreases of 3 to 10% were measured in the volume of soleus, quadriceps, hamstrings and intrinsic back muscles. The data were compared with the measurements obtained on R+1 on Spacelab-J (8-day mission). By comparison, the R+0 muscle volume changes after LMS were somewhat greater, while the R+2 LMS data are somewhat less than the Spacelab-J data obtained on R+1.

The second measurement taken at 10 days after landing of the LMS mission revealed that no differences in muscle volume were apparent when compared to preflight baseline. These results were different than the previous results from Spacelab-J, which showed some muscle deficit remaining two weeks after landing (R+14 days).

Fluid redistribution: The muscle volume data measured at R+0 and R+2 days clearly indicated that fluids moved into the lower limbs after flight. One or two days after landing, most muscles regained a volume in the range of 3 to 6 % (compared to R+0 data). There were two possible explanations for this phenomenon: (1) the muscles were dehydrated during weightlessness and the fluids were redistributed from the upper body because of the gravity vector, or (2) the fluid accumulation was caused by postflight muscle damage and ongoing muscle repair. The first possible explanation was investigated by examining the soft tissue ratio of the legs to upper body from the DEXA scan before and after flight. There was no significant change in the preflight and postflight ratios, indicating that the inflight fluid shift to the upper body from the legs was already reverted back to baseline by the time measurements were taken on R+0. This might indicate that the gravity dependent fluid shift is not responsible for the muscle swelling seen postflight.

To investigate the second theory, the T2 of the calf muscles was measured. The T2 is sensitive to changes in tissue water/protein content. The R+2 and R+10, but not the R+30 data, for the anterior calf and soleus were significantly above baseline. The T2 of the gastrocnemius also appeared elevated, but did not reach significance, p=0.07. These results appear to show an elevated T2 at R+2 and sometimes at both R+2 and R+10 which returns toward baseline by R+30. The T2 is elevated at R+10 when muscle volume differences are not apparent, but performance decrements are still apparent (Narici). This finding suggests that reambulation after flight causes swelling of muscles that lasts several weeks and is probably associated with muscle damage and/or repair.

Intervertebral disc: No evidence of disc expansion was measured on R+0. A slight, but not significant decrease in disc area was observed postflight. Also, the data showed a lengthening of the spine relative to baseline on R+0, which appears to be at variance with the disc area measurements.

Bone marrow: The analysis of the proton spectroscopy data (T2 water, T2 fat, and percent water) from two preflight and seven postflight measurements showed no significant change in the fraction of the water (cellular) component immediately postflight. However, subsequent postflight measurements may have indicated some change. Immediately postflight, a decrease relative to baseline in the T2 of the cellular component was evident. Subsequent measurements showed that the T2 increased. At R+30, an increase in T2 above baseline was clearly evident in all 4 crewmembers. For 3 of the 4 participating crewmembers, T2 remained elevated above baseline for more than 4 months after landing.

Body composition: The bone mineral density (BMD) did not change postflight. Subregional analysis showed no significant change in the lumbar spine or pelvis BMD. There were no significant changes in lean tissue after flight, but there appeared to be loss in total body fat (2.8kg), which paralleled changes in total body weight.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As NASA prepares for long-term missions aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and spacecraft destined for Mars, self-contained/closed chambers on Earth have become important test beds for microbiological evaluations. The insight gained from these studies directly benefits NASA as this knowledge is incorporated into the development of monitoring systems and countermeasures against microbiological contamination problems unique to long-duration space missions.

The microbiological study of these chambers and their crew also addresses many Earth-based concerns. Many office buildings are semi-closed systems, which can develop air and surface contamination. Commonly referred to as "sick building syndrome," contamination in these facilities may affect up to 30% of new and remodeled buildings worldwide. The United States Navy has also investigated the problems associated with microbial growth in semi-closed systems to determine the potential health risks during long-term submarine missions. While studies of office buildings and submarines give some insight into changes in the microbial levels and diversity created by an artificial ecosystem, all terrestrial models eventually have access to fresh air and water and can be thoroughly disinfected. The NASA closed-chamber studies provided the unique opportunity to evaluate undisturbed changes in microbial ecology and its relationship to the crew.

During the chamber studies, the primary objective of microbiological evaluations was to ensure crew health by monitoring microbial levels and changes in microbial ecology.

APPROACH:
In every phase of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) studies, the scope of the analyses included the air, potable water, and surfaces that the crew directly contacted. The surfaces that were sampled included not only smooth surfaces, but also carpeting which builds high microbial levels and is difficult to disinfect. In addition, the ability of viral contaminants to survive the water treatment system was evaluated prior to the Phase II test using bacteriophages MS-2 and PDR-1. Monitoring microbial concentrations and diversity provided a way to assess other problems that could affect life support and other systems, such as microbial degradation of materials and the potential fouling of process lines. The use of in-line coupons provided a way to determine both the type of microorganism in the flow systems and the effect of these organisms on in-line materials.

Evaluations of the air, potable water, and surfaces were performed using standard culturing methodologies and biochemical identification. Physical techniques were applied to retrieve microbial samples from carpets, rugs, and biofilm evaluations of water lines from metal coupons that were then assayed for microbial concentration and identity. The viral challenge of the water reclamation system used standard culturing methodologies combined with plaque enumeration to determine phage survival.

To understand the risk of infectious disease among crewmembers during the chamber studies, microbial samples were also collected from the throat, nose, urine, and feces of each crewmember upon entering and exiting. A second throat swab was collected from each crewmember for a viral culture. This data also allowed the identification of microorganisms that may not be considered normal human flora.

RESULTS:
The microbial concentration and diversification in the air and surface samples varied dramatically over time at any given sampling site. Evidence suggested that these changes were directly related to crew activities. These activities range from obvious activities, such as cleaning, to innocuous activities, such as walking through the chamber. Microbial contamination of the air, especially fungal contamination, was maintained at minimal levels, possibly resulting from the complex air revitalization system. In general, the potable water system was successfully disinfected with iodine. The average bacterial concentration was generally kept below the NASA specification throughout the studies. After 60 days during Phase III, the unexpected emergence of various gram-positive Bacillus species as the dominant flora suggested potential long-term contamination problems.

Samples extracted from carpets and rugs indicated high levels of microorganisms; however, the concentration would on occasion drop dramatically, possibly due to housekeeping patterns. The evaluation of metal coupons in a heat exchanger line indicated bacterial biofilm formation. The coupons were coated with a biocide that limited biofilm buildup initially, but inevitably did not prevent bacterial colonization. Lipid analysis of the coupons suggested viable bacteria were not detectable, but did indicate a bacterial presence.

In conclusion, these studies confirm a generally accepted relationship between microorganisms and other living organisms in a closed ecosystem. Disinfection and cleaning patterns changed this equilibrium as displayed by shifts in both microbial concentration and identity. In a small ecosystem, such as the chambers, the relationship is more dramatically affected by the actions of participants and thus more difficult to control. This understanding applies not only to NASA spacecraft, but also other small confined areas such as office buildings. Further complicating the ecosystem is the microbial interrelationship. On surfaces, these studies suggest a competitive inhibition that limits bacterial diversity. This finding could be of great importance in decontamination as a sterile surface may be a more fertile breeding ground than expected for different, possibly pathogenic, microorganisms. The number of potential microorganisms at any given site is large, and thus continued sampling and analysis must continue to gain a better understanding of the diversity of microbial flora, their interrelationship, and the effect of human activities on the consortium.

These studies also showed the ability of advanced water recovery systems to microbially purify water to potable quality, including the removal of viruses. However, the purification process appears to be susceptible to bacterial biofilm formation and potential corrosion problems. The appearance of gram-positive bacteria after 60 days during Phase III suggests a major flora change. Future work should focus on the effect of recycling water on microbial flora after extended periods of time.

Perhaps the most intriguing need for future research may be the changes that occur in the microorganism in a confined environment. Both bacteria and fungi adapt to changes in their environment, and genotypic and phenotypic alterations should be expected. Environmental stresses such as the addition of disinfectants or possibly the proximity of several microbial populations to each other could cause eventual changes in phenotypic characteristics including antimicrobial resistance and virulence. As questions of this nature are answered in closed chambers, the safety and health of the astronauts will be ensured for future long-term missions.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
When crewmembers make the transition from Earth's gravity to the weightlessness of space, they have to adapt to moving around in space and be able to determine their orientation as they move. Normal activities on Earth require the brain to interpret and integrate information coming from all the body's senses. This information is used to give feedback to the body on how the limbs are positioned, how the entire body is oriented, and which muscles need to be moved if reorientation or repositioning is desired.

Loss of muscle mass and strength in the lower extremities was noted as a consequence of exposure to microgravity in reports from Gemini, Apollo, and Skylab programs. Indirect evidence of increased muscle catabolism in humans during space flight has included elevated urinary amino acids, nitrogen, phosphorus and negative potassium balance. At the gross level, decreased circumferential size of the lower extremities has been recorded in American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts.

Preflight and inflight countermeasures have not been completely effective in ameliorating the loss of muscle tissue and development of associated muscle weakness in all crewmembers. While it appears to date that the decrease in muscular function has not compromised the performance of astronauts except possibly during extravehicular activity, longer duration exposure to microgravity including extended (>14 day) Shuttle missions, Space Station habitation, and manned interplanetary flights are anticipated to induce significant muscle atrophy. This will require the development and implementation of appropriate and effective countermeasures to prevent or ameliorate muscle atrophy in order to assure crew health and safety.

Atrophy of skeletal muscle is a response that is considered common to conditions, which result in prolonged periods of markedly decreased muscular activity or physical unloading. Unweighting occurs during periods of chronic bed rest and prolonged exposure to the microgravity environment of space travel or habitation. The loss of skeletal muscle mass and the associated amelioration in function that occurs during space travel represents a multi-factorial conditional adaptation with contributions from peripheral proprioceptive and central nervous system pathways. When microgravity-associated adaptation of skeletal muscle results in functional deficits that are manifested upon return to a unit gravity environment, the muscle is considered to have undergone deconditioning or deadaptation with respect to that environment.

The unloading of skeletal muscles (normally utilized to resist the forces of terrestrial gravity) which accompanies space flight has been documented to result in varying degrees of muscle atrophy. This study examined the development of muscle atrophy in human space flight crewmembers that completed a 115-day space flight. The following measurements were made:

(1) Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of muscle volume in selected muscles and muscle groups
(2) serum markers of muscle damage (creatine phosphokinase and myoglobin)
(3) dry, lean body mass by hydrostatic densitometry

APPROACH:
MRI was performed on a Siemens 1.5 Tesla Magnetom either in Houston, Texas, at the Texas Medical Center/Methodist Hospital or in Moscow, Russia at the Cardiology Research Center. Computer software was used to produce preflight- and postflight-acquired 2-D images that were volume representations of the muscles and intervertebral discs. Phantoms were used judiciously to allow for corrections in pixel sizes between measurement sessions at both locations. In order to minimize fluid shifts caused by assumption of a recumbent position after being upright, the subject was required to lie down for 6-10 minutes before the start of data acquisition, and the order of measurements was consistent during each session. The feet were held static by strapping them to a Lean holder during image acquisition. The portion of the lower limb under analysis was suspended by placing supporting materials on either side of the imaged area. This allows the anatomical area of interest to assume a natural and reproducible shape rather than being distorted by its own weight. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portions of the leg. For the thigh and calf muscles, thirty-two one-millimeter slice images were obtained using a Te=10 milliseconds, Tr=0.8 seconds and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the back muscles, a similar protocol was used, except twenty 0.5-centimeter image slices were obtained. For images of the cervical neck muscles, a Helmholtz neck coil was used in place of the spine coil.

Biochemical assessment of muscle dysfunction and damage were obtained before, during and after flight by venous blood samples taken by standard venipuncture technique or via indwelling venous catheters. Total creatine phosphokinase activity was determined on a Beckman CX5 clinical chemistry instrument using a commercially available assay based upon the conversion of NADP to NADPH. Myoglobin concentrations in venous serum samples were determined with a commercially available system (OPUS) utilizing a 2 site or "sandwich" fluorogenic enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).

Preflight and postflight comparison of dry lean mass was done using a 3-component model of body composition:

1) total body water (TBW)
2) lean body mass (hydrostatic densitometry)
3) fat mass (hydrostatic densitometry)

Hydrostatic weighing was performed in a water tank and weight measurements were made during maximal pulmonary exhalation; lung residual volume was determined by a standard oxygen dilution technique. TBW values determined by the doubly labeled water (DLW) technique were obtained from the Fluid and Electrolyte experiment on Mir 18 and details of the assay can be found in that report.

An exercise log recorded the type and amount of exercise performed 120 days before, during, and 30 days after flight, as well as exercise performance data, and any other countermeasures that were used (required for correlation with morphological and biochemical studies).

RESULTS:
Preflight measurements originally scheduled for the L-60 (60 days before launch) to L-45 timeframe were delayed until L-30. This actually improves the value of the science since the analyses were performed closer to the launch date. Postflight measurements were not performed until R+2 (2 days after landing) or R+3. Although measurements taken as close to R+0 are optimal, this should have little effect on the value of the science. It was not possible to schedule both R+0 and R+14 postflight hydrostatic weighing sessions because of intense postflight science and crew rehabilitation activities. It was elected to schedule one session between the two requested postflight days. Subject 1 declined to participate in the hydrostatic weighing session and the data collection from Subject 2 was suboptimal. Subject 3 did complete the session. Since Subject 1 declined to participate, this portion of the science was extremely compromised and it was elected not to conduct further sessions on other crewmembers. Only a partial data set for Subject 3 was obtained and that was analyzed for comparison to muscle losses demonstrated by MRI. Additionally, Subjects 1 and 2 both declined to participate in the recovery MRI studies at R+56. This was extremely unfortunate as little is known about the recovery rate of muscle loss after long-duration space flight.

With the exception of the above stated preflight and postflight anomalies, all data collection was completed. Inflight blood samples for creatine phosphokinase and myoglobin were originally withdrawn from the protocol because of concern about total inflight blood volumes. It was possible to perform these analyses on serum remaining after all other blood analyses were completed for other experiments. These data compliment the preflight and postflight blood data.

Averages of two preflight measurements were compared to postflight measurements made 2 to 3 days after landing. Significance of comparisons was determined with student's t-test, p<0.05. Summation data for the 3 crewmembers showed that the mean percent change from preflight values for skeletal muscles and muscle groups as calculated from raw data are as follows:

  • Anterolateral compartment -15+3

  • Gastrocnemius -18+1

  • Soleus -18+4

  • Quadriceps -11+3

  • Intrinsic lower back -18+4

  • Psoas -7+4 (not significant)

    Venous blood data did not support the presence of significant ongoing muscle damage in the inflight and immediate postflight period.

    With data from only three subjects, it is perilous to draw more than preliminary conclusions. However, the collective data reasonably supports loss of muscle mass during long-duration space flight even though participation in a highly structured inflight exercise protocol was a crew requirement. In this particular flight, the amount of exercise that was completed by each crewmember evidently was quite variable but the muscle losses in all three crewmembers were similar. Certainly, one of the most important conclusions that can be drawn is that the loss of muscle mass during microgravity exposure does not appear to be purely a linear response with respect to time. Short flights (5-11 days) have resulted in up to a 10% loss in some muscles, while the amount of loss nearly doubled that in this 115-day flight. The precise impact of the exercise program on countering muscle atrophy is not known as no studies of long-duration space missions have been performed on crewmembers that have not exercised during their period of microgravity exposure.

    Venous blood samples collected at various periods during flight and analyzed for creative phosphokinase activity and myoglobin do not support muscle damage during flight as a contributing factor to loss of muscle volume and function.

    Body composition data obtained in one crewmember showed an approximate 20% reduction in dry lean mass. This correlated well with the volume losses measured in the muscles of the back and legs which collectively contribute the bulk of muscle mass and thus dry, lean weight.

    It was suspected that measurements of neck muscle volume would reveal a loss of muscle volume, particularly in the posterior cervical extensors, since head bobbing has been observed in motion analysis studies of crewmembers upon return and weakness of neck muscles has been described and measured. It appears that since the neck muscles are small by comparison to the other measured muscles, the sensitivity of volume measurements for these muscles may not be sufficiently sensitive and the reproducibility of measuring such small volume (50-60 cc) muscles is poor. Thus, although it was not possible to show loss of cervical neck muscle volume, there is still good reason to suspect that atrophy of these muscle groups occurs. Alternative protocols and perhaps methods may be required to make measurements that are sufficiently precise to allow statistically significant comparisons.

In order to minimize fluid shifts caused by assumption of a recumbent position after being upright, the subject was required to lie down for 6-10 minutes before the start of data acquisition, and the order of measurements was consistent during each session. The feet were held static by strapping them to a Lean holder during image acquisition. The portion of the lower limb under analysis was suspended by placing supporting materials on either side of the imaged area. This allows the anatomical area of interest to assume a natural and reproducible shape rather than being distorted by its own weight. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portions of the leg. For the thigh and calf muscles, thirty-two one-millimeter slice images were obtained using a Te=10 milliseconds, Tr=0.8 seconds and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the back muscles, a similar protocol was used, except twenty 0.5-centimeter image slices were obtained. For images of the cervical neck muscles, a Helmholtz neck coil was used in place of the spine coil.

Biochemical assessment of muscle dysfunction and damage were obtained before, during and after flight by venous blood samples taken by standard venipuncture technique or via indwelling venous catheters. Total creatine phosphokinase activity was determined on a Beckman CX5 clinical chemistry instrument using a commercially available assay based upon the conversion of NADP to NADPH. Myoglobin concentrations in venous serum samples were determined with a commercially available system (OPUS) utilizing a 2 site or "sandwich" fluorogenic enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).

Preflight and postflight comparison of dry lean mass was done using a 3-component model of body composition:

1) total body water (TBW)
2) lean body mass (hydrostatic densitometry)
3) fat mass (hydrostatic densitometry)

Hydrostatic weighing was performed in a water tank and weight measurements were made during maximal pulmonary exhalation; lung residual volume was determined by a standard oxygen dilution technique. TBW values determined by the doubly labeled water (DLW) technique were obtained from the Fluid and Electrolyte experiment on Mir 18 and details of the assay can be found in that report.

An exercise log recorded the type and amount of exercise performed 120 days before, during, and 30 days after flight, as well as exercise performance data, and any other countermeasures that were used (required for correlation with morphological and biochemical studies).

RESULTS:
Preflight measurements originally scheduled for the L-60 (60 days before launch) to L-45 timeframe were delayed until L-30. This actually improves the value of the science since the analyses were performed closer to the launch date. Postflight measurements were not performed until R+2 (2 days after landing) or R+3. Although measurements taken as close to R+0 are optimal, this should have little effect on the value of the science. It was not possible to schedule both R+0 and R+14 postflight hydrostatic weighing sessions because of intense postflight science and crew rehabilitation activities. It was elected to schedule one session between the two requested postflight days. Subject 1 declined to participate in the hydrostatic weighing session and the data collection from Subject 2 was suboptimal. Subject 3 did complete the session. Since Subject 1 declined to participate, this portion of the science was extremely compromised and it was elected not to conduct further sessions on other crewmembers. Only a partial data set for Subject 3 was obtained and that was analyzed for comparison to muscle losses demonstrated by MRI. Additionally, Subjects 1 and 2 both declined to participate in the recovery MRI studies at R+56. This was extremely unfortunate as little is known about the recovery rate of muscle loss after long-duration space flight.

With the exception of the above stated preflight and postflight anomalies, all data collection was completed. Inflight blood samples for creatine phosphokinase and myoglobin were originally withdrawn from the protocol because of concern about total inflight blood volumes. It was possible to perform these analyses on serum remaining after all other blood analyses were completed for other experiments. These data compliment the preflight and postflight blood data.

Averages of two preflight measurements were compared to postflight measurements made 2 to 3 days after landing. Significance of comparisons was determined with student's t-test, p<0.05. Summation data for the 3 crewmembers showed that the mean percent change from preflight values for skeletal muscles and muscle groups as calculated from raw data are as follows:

  • Anterolateral compartment -15+3

  • Gastrocnemius -18+1

  • Soleus -18+4

  • Quadriceps -11+3

  • Intrinsic lower back -18+4

  • Psoas -7+4 (not significant)

    Venous blood data did not support the presence of significant ongoing muscle damage in the inflight and immediate postflight period.

    With data from only three subjects, it is perilous to draw more than preliminary conclusions. However, the collective data reasonably supports loss of muscle mass during long-duration space flight even though participation in a highly structured inflight exercise protocol was a crew requirement. In this particular flight, the amount of exercise that was completed by each crewmember evidently was quite variable but the muscle losses in all three crewmembers were similar. Certainly, one of the most important conclusions that can be drawn is that the loss of muscle mass during microgravity exposure does not appear to be purely a linear response with respect to time. Short flights (5-11 days) have resulted in up to a 10% loss in some muscles, while the amount of loss nearly doubled that in this 115-day flight. The precise impact of the exercise program on countering muscle atrophy is not known as no studies of long-duration space missions have been performed on crewmembers that have not exercised during their period of microgravity exposure.

    Venous blood samples collected at various periods during flight and analyzed for creative phosphokinase activity and myoglobin do not support muscle damage during flight as a contributing factor to loss of muscle volume and function.

    Body composition data obtained in one crewmember showed an approximate 20% reduction in dry lean mass. This correlated well with the volume losses measured in the muscles of the back and legs which collectively contribute the bulk of muscle mass and thus dry, lean weight.

    It was suspected that measurements of neck muscle volume would reveal a loss of muscle volume, particularly in the posterior cervical extensors, since head bobbing has been observed in motion analysis studies of crewmembers upon return and weakness of neck muscles has been described and measured. It appears that since the neck muscles are small by comparison to the other measured muscles, the sensitivity of volume measurements for these muscles may not be sufficiently sensitive and the reproducibility of measuring such small volume (50-60 cc) muscles is poor. Thus, although it was not possible to show loss of cervical neck muscle volume, there is still good reason to suspect that atrophy of these muscle groups occurs. Alternative protocols and perhaps methods may be required to make measurements that are sufficiently precise to allow statistically significant comparisons.

experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
In order to enable astronauts to sustain high levels of performance throughout extended duration space missions it will be critical (1) to maintain an appropriate phase relationship of the human circadian pacemaker to the 24-hour sleep-wake/duty schedule aboard the space craft, and (2) to preserve the amplitude of the endogenous circadian timing system. On Earth, the amplitude of the endogenous circadian pacemaker and the phase relationship between the circadian pacemaker and the sleep-wake/duty schedule are preserved by exposure to the 24-hour, robust cycle of light and darkness associated with the Earth's rotation. During extended duration space station and exploration class space missions, astronauts will be exposed to markedly abnormal light/dark cycles in terms of both timing and intensity. Preliminary data suggest that such abnormal light/dark cycles are likely to result in a misalignment between the 24-h sleep-wake/duty schedules and the endogenous circadian timing system. Such circadian misalignment is known to produce sleep disturbances, daytime sleepiness, reduced attention, negative mood, slower reaction times, gastrointestinal disorders, and impaired daytime alertness. To prevent such misalignment, development of effective countermeasures to promote circadian entrainment is needed. Scheduled exposure to 5-h episodes of bright light has been shown previously to induce the necessary phase shifts and amplitude enhancement of the endogenous circadian pacemaker. However, energy and time constraints make such lengthy exposures to bright light impractical aboard the spacecraft.

The purpose of this study was to test three specific hypotheses evaluating the effectiveness of intermittent bright light exposure in resetting the circadian timing system as a countermeasure to circadian misalignment likely to occur during space flight and long-term space missions. Our specific aims were the following:

1) Test the hypothesis that a single 6.5-hour episode of intermittent bright light exposure (six 15 minute bright light pulses / 60 minutes of very dim light) centered 3.5 hours before the nadir of the fitted endogenous circadian temperature rhythm will induce a significant phase delay of the endogenous circadian timing system.

2) Test the hypothesis that the phase-shifting response per minute of intermittent bright light exposure will be greater than that of continuous bright light exposure.

3) Test the hypothesis that the endogenous circadian rhythms of body temperature, plasma melatonin, plasma cortisol, alertness, and performance will phase delay shift by an equivalent amount in response to a single, 6.5 hour episode of intermittent bright light exposure centered 3.5 hours before the nadir of the fitted endogenous circadian temperature rhythm.

APPROACH:
Twenty-one subjects were empanelled in a randomized clinical trial. Upon admission to the Intensive Physiologic Monitoring (IPM) Unit of the Brigham & Women's Hospital on Experimental Day 1, subjects were maintained in an environment free of time cues until the end of the study on experimental day 10. Physiologic and neurobehavioral monitoring occurred throughout the duration of the study. Subjects were adapted to the laboratory with three baseline days (LD 16:8), during which time they continued to sleep and wake at their habitual times. In order to assess their endogenous circadian phase (ECP), subjects underwent a 26.2-h constant routine from day 4 to day 5. On day 5/6, a single 6.5-h light exposure session was scheduled. Subjects were randomly assigned to either continuous bright light exposure, or to intermittent bright light exposure or to continuous very dim light exposure (7 subjects in each group) during their light exposure session. Following the light exposure day, subjects were scheduled to a 64-h constant routine (CR) to reassess their circadian phase and estimate the phase shift from the first ECP estimation. They were then discharged after a ~22-h recovery sleep episode.

Subject Recruitment: Healthy subjects were recruited for participation in this study. Potential subjects were intensively screened including a preliminary phone screening questionnaire and a physical exam. The physical included blood and urine tests, an EKG, and a full physical exam with a physician. A staff psychologist then examined the candidates still under consideration. Every attempt was made to acquaint each prospective subject with all of the procedures involved in this study in order to minimize the possible effect of uncertainty about the experimental procedures on the results.

Ambulatory physiologic monitoring: Subjects were required to maintain a regular sleep-wake schedule for 3 weeks prior to admission to the laboratory. Compliance to this protocol was monitored by evaluating a diary of sleep and wake times kept by the subjects. Furthermore, subjects were also required to call into a date/time-stamped answering machine just prior to going to bed and immediately upon awakening and the times were compared to sleep/wake logs on the day of admission. Finally, wrist activity and light exposure were monitored for 1 week immediately prior to admission to the laboratory with a portable data collection device (Actiwatch-L, Mini Mitter, Sunriver, OR).

Inpatient environment and conditions: Upon admission to the study, subjects were isolated from external time cues, including clocks, radios, television, visitors, and sunlight, but maintained contact with staff members using techniques described elsewhere. All staff members were trained to avoid communicating time of day or the nature of the experimental conditions to the subjects.

Lighting: The experimental suites in the Intensive Physiologic Monitoring Unit of the General Clinical Research Center at the Brigham and Women’s Hospital have ceiling-mounted fluorescent fixtures that are controlled by a computer system. This system automatically turned the lighting on and off at scheduled times to the required pre-set intensity. The light intensity was that of normal indoor room light (~150 lux) during the baseline days, ~1.5 lux during CRs and light exposure day, and <1 lux and/or ~9,500 lux during the 6.5-h light exposure session (depending on experimental condition). Light intensity was <0.03 lux during all sleep episodes. The 6.5 hours of exposure light exposure session was centered 5.8 h before habitual wake time (~3.5 hours before CBTmin). Subjects were exposed either to continuous bright light (~9,500 lux, defined as 100% bright light), or to intermittent bright light (six 15-minute bright light (~9,500 lux,) pulses separated by 60 minutes of very dim light (<1 lux), defined as 23% bright light) or to very dim light (<1 lux, defined as 0% bright light). Light exposure was administered with ceiling-mounted fluorescent lamps mounted in fixtures capable of providing ambient illumination of ~1 to 12,000 lux.

Wake Episodes: During wake episodes, subjects were free to move about the suite as desired, except that they were asked not to lie down or nap during scheduled wake episodes. Subjects were restricted to light, sedentary physical activity; exercise was not allowed. Subjects compliance with the protocol was monitored by means of closed-circuit cameras. Temperature Recording: Environmental temperature was maintained at 74 + 3° Fahrenheit. A real-time, on-line data acquisition system was employed to monitor and collect data. Core body temperature was continuously monitored by means of a rectal thermistor and room temperature by means of a permanent air temperature thermistor; both were stored every minute.

Sleep Recording and Scoring: During scheduled sleep episodes, subjects were instructed not to get out of bed, even if they awakened before the end of the scheduled sleep episode. If requested, a technician brought the subject a urinal or bedpan during the scheduled sleep episode. Sleep was recorded with polysomnography (PSG), including EEG, EOG, EMG, and EKG measures.).

Hormonal Data: Blood samples were collected through an indwelling 18-gauge intravenous catheter every 30-60 minutes during designated portions of the protocol (e.g., the constant routines) using established techniques. A specially designed and manufactured 18-gauge intravenous placement unit with side portholes (Becton-Dickinson Vascular Access, Sandy, Utah) was used to facilitate the collection of blood without disturbance of the subject, even during sleep. This intravenous placement unit was connected to a triple-stopcock manifold (Maxxim Medical, Athens, TX) via an intravenous loop with a 12-foot extension cable (VMR Products, L.C., Fruit Heights, UT). The triple-stopcock manifold was connected to an intravenous microdrip to allow infusion of heparinized saline (0.45% sodium chloride, 10 units of heparin/ml) at a very slow rate (5-10 ml/h) between blood samples. Each subject's hematocrit was measured during the initial selection evaluation, on admission to the IPM, and every morning. No more than 2 pints of blood was taken over the course of each study. We provided participants with Ferrous Gluconate (324 mg) pills to be taken at breakfast and dinner: 1) for a minimum of one week prior to participation in the inpatient research protocol; 2) during the inpatient portion of the protocol; and 3) for three weeks after the ending the protocol. During the study, we tested the subjects’ hemoglobin levels every 1-2 day(s) when there was an indwelling intravenous catheter in place. If the hematocrit or hemoglobin values had fallen below 11.0 for men and 10.3 for women blood sampling would have been stopped, although this did not occur. Blood samples were assayed for melatonin and cortisol using radioimmunoassay techniques.

Constant Routine Procedure: To assess endogenous circadian phase accurately, each subject underwent two constant routines (CR). The initial CR was 26.2 hours (in order to center the 6.5-h light exposure session 5.8 h before habitual wake time (~3.5 h before core body temperature minimum) and the final CR was 64 h in length. The constant routine consisted of a regimen of enforced wakefulness in a semi-recumbent posture in constant very dim illumination (~1.5 lux). Subjects were not permitted to change this posture throughout the constant routine, and avoided standing up, sitting upright, lying on their side, etc. This posture was also maintained for urine samples and bowel movements. Subjects were maintained in an isocaloric diet. Nutritional intake was divided into hourly aliquots. Caloric and fluid intake was calculated for each subject to account for the sedentary nature of the constant routine. A staff member was always with the subject to help maintain wakefulness and to ensure that all protocol requirements were met.

Neurobehavioral Testing: We selected a battery of computer-based tests of performance and mood that are sensitive to the acute effects of misalignment of circadian phase and sleep disruption on performance. Standardized measures of performance and activation were included in the neurobehavioral test battery (NAB) administered every 2 hr all waking periods of every day.

NAB performance tests include the following:
Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT): Sustained attention performance was assessed throughout the protocol, using the psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) approach of Dinges and Powell. The test has been demonstrated to be sensitive to circadian variation and sleep loss. Each PVT involved a 5-minute visual reaction time (RT) performance test in which the subject was required to maintain the fastest possible RT's to a simple visual stimulus.
Calculation Performance Task (ADD): This test, modeled after one described by Klein et al. 12, presented the subject with a series of randomly generated pairs of 2-digit numbers. The subject's task was to sum as many pairs as possible in the allotted 2-min time interval. The test was scored according to the number of calculations completed in the time allowed, irrespective of accuracy.

NAB subjective activation tests include:
Visual Analog Scales (VAS): VAS were used to assess the mood, alertness, and physical well being of the subjects. The scales consisted of a horizontal line drawn on the display with each end of the line labeled with the extremes of a subjective continuum (e.g., words or phrases such as "very alert" and "very sleepy"). The subject's task was to use the trackball to move an arrow to the position on the line between the two defined endpoints that best described how he or she felt at that moment. The subject then pressed a keypad button, transforming the arrow into a hash mark intercepting the line.
Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS): was used as a highly sensitive subjective measurement scale for sleepiness.

Behavioral Event Recording: This system was designed to meet two goals: (1) immediate recording of the time that events occur during the study (e.g., showers, meals); and (2) direct communication between the subject and the technician about requests which might be influenced by the technician's subjective reaction to a verbal interaction. Recording the precise sequence in time of behavioral events, specimen collections and protocol markers was carried out via a centralized event recording system using multiple, inexpensive, hand-held, commercially available terminals (TERMIFLEX/HT20, Nashua, NH).

RESULTS:
Twenty-one subjects completed the study; each was randomly assigned to the bright light exposure condition, the dim light exposure condition or the intermittent bright light exposure condition. These results demonstrate that intermittent bright light exposure is effective in inducing phase shifts of the circadian timing system and that intermittent pulses of bright light have a greater resetting effectiveness on a per minute basis than the continuous bright light exposure. They also suggest that the magnitude of phase shifts is not a linear function of melatonin suppression.

experiment_title: Microbial Analysis of International Space Station (ISS) Air, Surfaces and Water

investigators: Principal Investigator: Ott, C.
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA scientists have continuously performed routine environmental monitoring of the air, surfaces, and water systems of the International Space Station (ISS). Surface sample collection began in 2000 (Expedition 1), air sample collection began in 2001 (Expedition 2) and water monitoring of the U.S. potable water system has occurred since the installation of the potable water dispenser (PWD) in 2009 (Expedition 20). The specific objectives of the air, water, and surface sampling are:

1. To ensure that the air quality is microbiologically safe for crewmembers and to ensure compliance with existing acceptability limits established for microbial air sampling.

2. To ensure a microbiologically safe environment for crewmembers and to ensure compliance with existing acceptability limits established for microbial surface sampling.

3. To check for the presence of microbial contaminants in the potable water provided for crew use on the ISS and verify compliance with established water quality requirements.

APPROACH:
Samples were collected and enumerated during space flight operations. Identification of these isolates occurs on samples returned to the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Microbiology Laboratory. The organisms have been identified as either being collected from air and surfaces or the potable water dispenser. experiment_title: The Response of Single Human Cells to Zero Gravity
parameter_html:
Mitosis
Cell growth rate
Chromosome aberrations
investigators: Principal Investigator: Montgomery, P.
image_name: Woodlawn Wanderer -- schematic of interior configuration
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Studies with centrifuges demonstrated that gravitational acceleration has a significant influence on cell biology systems. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effects of zero-gravity on living human cells during and subsequent to the Skylab 3 mission. A strain of diploid human embryonic lung cells, WI-38, was chosen for this purpose. In general, this experiment was designed to detect the effects of zero-gravity on cell growth rates and on cell structure as observed by light microscopy, transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy, and histochemistry. Studies of the effects of zero-gravity on the cell function and the cell cycle were performed by time lapse motion picture photography and microspectrophotometry. Subsequent study of the returned living cells included karotyping, G- and C- banding, and analyses of the culture media. Some of the living cells returned were stored by deep freeze techniques for possible future experiments.

APPROACH:
The Woodlawn Wanderer 9 was used inflight to support the growth of human embryonic lung cells. Cell cultures were maintained with the proper replacement of media with new fresh media. The cells were kept at a constant temperature of 36 degrees Celsius and at a constant pressure of one atmosphere in a hermetically sealed compartment. Two phase-contrast time-lapse motion pictures of living cells for 28 days was used to collect data on the cell cycle and mitosis. An automated system fixed the cells at predetermined intervals for postflight examination under the light microscope, scanning electron microscope, and transmission electron microscope. Cultures were maintained at approximately 22 degrees Celsius after the first 12 days of the mission for the return of intact cells for subsequent subculture. The cell cultures brought back to ground for subculture were analyzed for chromosomal aberrations, and the cell culture media was analyzed to determine chemical composition.

Cellular growth rates were determined by cell counting procedures accomplished with the aid of a phase-contrast contrast microscope using a grid reticle in a 10X magnification eyepiece. Postflight, cell counting was performed with the 15X eyepiece due to the fact that the high density of the cell population made it difficult to determine single cells. Time lapse films were analyzed with a projector which permitted projection 1-8, 16, and 24 frames/second. Cells were counted every 3 hours. Cell multiplication was determined by adding the number of observed mitoses and mitotic activity, which was calculated from the average cell density. The rate of cell migration was determined by covering the projection screen with paper and tracing the location of the nucleus of individual cells every hour.

Whole coverslips with attached cell monolayers in 4 percent glutaraldehyde fixative with cacodylate buffer were processed for transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and phase contrast microscopy. Scanning microspectrophotometry was performed on selected areas of the nuclei using a scanning microscope photometer having a 1-micron measuring at 1 micron intervals at 540 nanometers. Subcultures were incubated overnight with fresh growth medium, then harvested with standard colchimid arrest and hypotonic treatment procedures. Banding analysis was performed on air dried slides. Five cells from control cultures were analyzed for G-band pattern and 10 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern. At least 10 cells of the flight culture were analyzed for G-band pattern and 20 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern.

RESULTS:
Ten cultures were fixed during the first 12 days of flight. Growth curves, DNA microspectrophometery, phase microscopy, and ultrastructural studies of the fixed cells revealed no effects of a zero-gravity environment on the ten cultures. Two cultures were photographed by means of phase time-lapse cinematography during the first 27 days of the flight. Analysis of the films revealed no differences in mitotic index, cell cycle, and migration between the flight and control cells. No differences between the flight and control cell cultures were observed in the karotype and chromosome banding. Minor unexplained differences have been found in the biochemical constituents of the used flight and control media.

experiment_title: Quantification Of The Dose Response Of The Microvessel Parameters In Retina, Cortex And White Matter Following Iron-56 Irradiation And Proton Irradiation
parameter_html:
Radiation dose response
Endothelial cells, corpus callosum
Endothelial cells, cortex
investigators: Principal Investigator: Archambeau, John Orin
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A main concern of NASA managers is to define the risks of tissue damage of brain and eye for astronauts associated with exposure to galactic cosmic ray particle (GCR) irradiation during a proposed space mission to Mars. Research is needed to specify the tissue effects produced by the high Z, high energy (HZE) particles that are found in space and to define the dose response of these tissues. Current histopathologic methods used to evaluate tissue changes in late-responding, non-proliferative tissues such as the brain and vessel endothelium rely on observations, word descriptions and arbitrary scoring. The approach is considered to be qualitative and lacks rigor. The proposed research introduces a detailed, step-by-step stereology program into radiation biology that will quantify the dose response of tissue population changes in situ following irradiation. These methods are known to anatomists and materials scientists but have been ignored by radiation biologists until this laboratory used them to quantify the dose response of the non-proliferative retinal vasculature following single and split time-dose schedules of protons. The brain and retina microvessel endothelial cell population number, vessel length, and number of microvessel branching will be measured following single and split dose schedules of Iron-56 particles. The results will be compared with the changes produced by protons to define the dose response of the cortex and white matter microvessel endothelial populations and to specify the RBE quality factor of Iron-56 referenced to protons. Three-dimensional reconstructions of the microvessels of the cortex and white matter will be compared.

The objective is to utilize three dimensionsl reconstruction and stereology methods to quantify the microvessel population and vessel cell kinetic parameters in the cortex and white matter regions of the brain in an effort to explain the difference in dose response between the two regions.

The significance of this research for NASA and for radiation biology is that it introduces into radiation biology a valuable quantitative technique that can be applied to quantify population morphologic, kinetic and identifiable functions in-situ following irradiation. It also defines the contribution (role) of the irradiated vasculature in producing radiation changes and the dose response of the brain and retina.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
1. Unbiased stereology was used to determine the population density of the pericytes and endothelial cells of the cortex and corpus callosum as well as the microvessel length density.
2. Using computer assisted 3 dimensional configurations and confocal immunohistochemical microscopy The branching of cortical and corpus callosum microvessels and location of the microvessel population nuclei was demonstrated.
3. The microvessels of the corpus callosum are demonstrated to be nearly straight and less branching than those of the cortex.
4. Using the computer technology of our Czech and Slovak collaborators it was possible to fuse confocal small images into a composite image consisting of 9 adjacent fields of the hippocampus and adjacent corpus.
5. The dose response of the endothelial and pericyte cell density of the cortex and corpus callosum were determined following iron-56 ion and proton irradiation dose schedules. The endothelial cell population of the cortex and corpus and the microvessel length density were proliferative and increased their population. The pericyte population was not proliferative and their population decreased over a period of two years.
6. Using retinal digest techniques we determined the RBE of the iron-56 ion to be 3.45 compared to the proton density change as the standard.

Conclusion:
1. It was documented that the dose response or cell density changes were the same using split dose schedules compared with single dose schedules of protons. This suggeststhat the dose response will not be markedly changed using fractionated irradiation.
2. It was shown that the microvessels of the cortex were more branched, and longer than the vessels of the white matter. The cortical cell density and branchings of the vessels of the cortex were larger than the same measurements for the corpus callosum.
3. The endothelial cells of the cortex and the corpus were proliferative and increased their number over the two year observational period following proton and Iron-56 ion brain irradiation with doses of 5 to 20Gy. Whereas, pericytes showed cell loss, but (surprisingly) there was an increase in vessel length density.
4. The data confirm the concerns of NASA managers that whole brain irradiation will with 5 to 20 Gy of protons or Iron-56 irradiation will produce an increase in cell density of endothelial cells and length density of microvessel, and will produce a significant loss of pericytes.
